These pages make that change explicit for an Emby playback path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Fallback to an embedded audio core Core fallback plays an existing compatible audio component when the full presentation is unavailable. Audio downmixing Audio downmixing combines a presentation with more channels into an output with fewer channels. Audio upmixing Audio upmixing derives a presentation for more output channels from a source with fewer channels. Audio transcoding Audio transcoding decodes a source presentation and encodes a new audio stream for delivery or storage. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.title: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.keywords: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata Preserving immersive audio requires carrying the spatial information needed by a renderer through the supported playback stages. A moving sound needs both its audio and instructions about its position through time. If the goal is letting the receiver render the original immersive scene , the required spatial information must remain available until that receiver's renderer uses it. Preservation depends on where the scene is decoded, transformed, and finally rendered. Make a boundary ledger For an illustrative Atmos source: Boundary or operation Information carried onward Copy compatible encoded source data Audio and relevant spatial information in that bitstream Object-aware decode to a suitable metadata-bearing output Reconstructed audio plus required spatial information Render to a chosen speaker layout The generated speaker-channel presentation Render to binaural headphones The generated ear signals Ordinary channel transcode A new channel presentation, without automatically retaining source objects The first two routes can leave a downstream renderer the scene description. The next two have already completed a render. The final route creates another coded channel result from the signal it was supplied. Rendering can be the intended end of preservation A headphone player can use the original object directions to generate convincing ear cues. Once those cues are delivered to the headphones, there is no need for the headphones to receive and render the original objects again. Likewise, a renderer can generate the supported speaker layout's PCM channels. That presentation can be correct for its target even though the metadata is no longer traveling onward. The distinction is therefore the intended renderer boundary , not whether the word PCM appeared anywhere in the chain. Use an object-aware decoded route when required A conventional PCM decoder/output can supply the compatible channel presentation of an immersive track. Its array of 5.1 or 7.1 values does not by itself encode the original object's position updates. An object-aware decoder can retain the appropriate reconstructed components and metadata. Supported Dolby MAT output can carry such information onward. The downstream system then applies the scene information to its own supported arrangement. The compressed source form still matters: Dolby Digital Plus object carriage and TrueHD delivery require different parsing/reconstruction before reaching that boundary. Identify irreversible combinations A downmix or ordinary channel render combines source components for a chosen output. A later processor cannot uniquely infer the original objects and paths from those sums. A generic E-AC-3 encoder also does not recreate an Atmos scene merely because the input came from Atmos. It needs the relevant scene representation and a supported encoding workflow; ordinary channel PCM is a different input. An existing compatible core can keep a soundtrack audible while leaving the immersive extension unused. That is a particular component-selection result, not proof that the file's spatial information vanished from storage. Verify the route using the active renderer For an Emby session, record the source form, delivered presentation, decoder's output type, and where rendering occurs. If the receiver is intended to render, confirm its detected immersive input instead of only its upmix/listening mode. If the player renders headphones, evaluate that output as the finished ear presentation. A basic channel-count report and height-speaker activity are insufficient evidence because a compatible channel mix and an upmixer can produce those observations. The boundary ledger establishes which spatial instructions actually remained available to the renderer making the final listening presentation. See Also Dolby Atmos DTS:X Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 103 420 V1.2.1: Backwards-compatible object audio carriage using Enhanced AC-3 Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering Dolby: Atmos Renderer guide Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/index.htm.title: Overview: Audio decoding and output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Audio decoding and output The audio playback path connects coded tracks, decoded samples, transport choices and the device producing sound. A track can be delivered for decoding elsewhere or decoded into samples before output. The chosen route affects channel handling, conversion and the spatial information that reaches the receiving system. This branch follows those choices through passthrough, PCM and fallback, then connects them to synchronization and audio-description use. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> The audio playback path The audio playback path connects the selected source track, server delivery, decoding, output transport, and final sound reproduction. Output and transport Audio output and transport determine whether a receiver gets a coded stream, decoded samples or another defined delivery arrangement. Conversion and fallback Audio conversion and fallback adapt a source to the available decoding and listening path. Preserving immersive audio metadata Preserving immersive audio requires carrying the spatial information needed by a renderer through the supported playback stages. Audio/video synchronization Audio/video synchronization aligns sound and picture on a common playback timeline while accounting for their different delays. Audio-description tracks Audio-description tracks add spoken descriptions of important visual information for listeners who cannot see the picture clearly. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Audio Bitstream Passthrough | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Audio Bitstream Passthrough Audio bitstream passthrough sends a supported encoded audio presentation to another device for decoding. A receiver can decode a movie soundtrack only if it receives a compatible encoded presentation . Bitstream passthrough arranges that delivery, leaving audio reconstruction to the downstream decoder rather than producing ordinary PCM in the player. The server's Direct Play decision happens earlier. It can retain a file that the player either decodes locally or passes onward. Encoded audio inside the transport framing The player reads the selected track and its codec configuration. It then supplies the encoded audio using the output API and transport convention required for that format. IEC 61937 defines transport of encoded audio in a digital-audio framework. Transport data includes framing and format identification so the receiver knows that it contains a coded payload to unpack, not ordinary amplitude samples to play directly. A declared carrier rate or channel arrangement can consequently describe the transport , while the encoded content has its own audio rate and presentation. Microsoft's transport documentation explicitly distinguishes those fields. Boundary What must happen File to player Find the correct coded track and configuration Player to output API Request the proper encoded format Driver/link Carry the required framing without treating it as normal mixed PCM Intermediate device Forward a compatible presentation where present Receiver Recognize, unpack, and decode that presentation This is why receiver capability alone cannot fix a player/output route that never supplied the encoded format. Why normal sample processing changes the route A volume multiplier acts on decoded sample amplitudes. Multiplying bytes in a compressed packet would instead alter coding symbols or headers, corrupting their meaning. Likewise, mixing a notification into a soundtrack requires sample-domain combination or a specially supported codec-aware path. An ordinary PCM mixer cannot simply combine arbitrary encoded packets and expect a valid soundtrack. A player may therefore disable some local effects during passthrough, choose PCM when processing is needed, or control downstream volume separately. Those are consequences of where the reconstruction happens, not inherently defects in the source. Confirm the input before interpreting a listening mode If a compatible receiver detects the intended encoded format, its decoder can reconstruct that presentation. It may afterward apply an upmixer, bass management, or other listening mode. The processing-mode name and detected input answer different questions. A height-speaker mode on a conventional input is not the same observation as receiving the original immersive bitstream. For an Emby immersive track, retaining the suitable encoded payload is one way to keep its spatial information available downstream. An object-aware decoded MAT path can perform a different supported route; ordinary channel PCM does not carry original objects just because it has many channels. Use these distinctions to locate a failed boundary: did the player request the format, did the link forward it, and did the decoder accept it? That trace is more informative than changing unrelated codec or speaker settings together. See Also Decoded PCM Output Dolby MAT Audio Transport The Audio Playback Path Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Decoded PCM Output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Decoded PCM Output Decoded PCM output sends reconstructed audio samples to the sound system after decoding occurs in the player or an earlier component. After a decoder reconstructs audio, its output is usually PCM sample values for the next processing stage. A receiver that detects PCM is being given those values rather than the original compressed soundtrack to decode. Follow a lossless music example to see where preservation can change. Trace the samples, not just the output label Consider 24-bit stereo FLAC at 44.1 kHz, a player with a volume setting of one half, and an output fixed at 48 kHz: Stage Audio representation or operation FLAC source Compressed description of the original integer samples Decode Restore those samples into a working representation Volume Multiply their amplitudes by 0.5 Rate conversion Calculate the signal at 48,000 positions per second Output formatting Pack the result for the device's PCM interface Lossless decoding restores the source values. The next steps intentionally make another output representation. The PCM label alone cannot tell you whether those steps occurred. A source sample of +0.6 becomes +0.3 under half gain. If a fractional result cannot fit the final integer grid exactly, rounding/dither becomes another conversion decision. Rate conversion also changes the sequence's positions and count while preserving its intended duration. The properties of the delivered PCM format Output property Why it is needed Sample rate Defines when each frame is presented Channel layout/order Associates values with intended positions Number representation Specifies integer or float interpretation Storage size and valid precision Defines how meaningful bits occupy sample words A 24-bit presentation can occupy 32-bit words. A six-channel output also needs named roles; an array size of six is insufficient to establish where the center belongs. For a block of 480 sample frames at 48 kHz, playback time is 10 ms, regardless of how many channels the frame contains. A device consumes complete frames on that timeline. Lossy decoders produce PCM too MP3 and other lossy codecs reconstruct their encoded approximation as PCM. Sending those samples uncompressed to an amplifier does not restore the missing original data, but it can avoid another lossy encoding. The decoded representation describes the current signal. Its source history must be obtained earlier in the path. Place an immersive render deliberately An object-aware player can render spatial content into speaker-channel PCM or binaural ear signals. Those can be useful finished spatial outputs. They no longer give a later receiver the source's original object instructions to adapt again. A supported metadata-bearing path such as Dolby MAT can instead carry the relevant audio and spatial information onward. It should not be confused with ordinary channel PCM. For an Emby session, record which source was reconstructed and which gain, layout, rate, or spatial operation followed. That explains a PCM result as a sequence of decisions rather than as a verdict that compression quality or immersive content must have been lost. See Also Linear PCM (LPCM) Audio Bitstream Passthrough Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Downmixing References Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Dolby MAT Audio Transport | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Dolby MAT Audio Transport Dolby MAT is a metadata-enhanced audio transport used for TrueHD carriage and supported PCM-based Dolby Atmos delivery. The library file says Dolby Digital Plus with Atmos . The receiver says Dolby MAT . Follow one playback session, and those two labels can fit together: Point in the session What is present Job performed here Library file Dolby Digital Plus with an Atmos presentation Stores the compressed soundtrack Emby Server delivery The selected audio track, supplied without conversion Delivers the source presentation to the app Player processing Decoded audio with the required spatial information retained Decodes the compressed presentation Supported HDMI output A PCM-based Dolby MAT presentation Transports audio and associated Atmos information Receiver The received presentation and the configured speaker layout Renders the audio for those speakers This example assumes a player with the appropriate decoder and a supported PCM-based Atmos output route. Dolby MAT , Metadata-enhanced Audio Transmission, is the transport in the fourth row. The receiver names what arrived there; the file names what was stored in the first row. Decoding, transport, and rendering boundaries 1. Server to player. Supplying the selected compressed track unchanged leaves decoding to the player. A receiver indication farther downstream cannot establish whether the server changed the audio; check the actual server delivery path for that part of the chain. 2. Decoder to output. Decoding reconstructs audio, while rendering determines how a channel or object presentation becomes signals for speakers. An object-aware player can decode a compressed Atmos presentation and retain the information needed for downstream rendering. These are separate jobs, which is what makes a decoded Atmos transport useful. 3. HDMI to receiver. In the PCM-based MAT 2.0 use, the link carries audio together with the associated Atmos metadata. The receiver can use that presentation with its speaker arrangement. It receives more information than an ordinary set of completed 5.1 or 7.1 channel samples. 4. Receiver to speakers. Detected input information and the selected listening mode answer different questions. The former describes what arrived; an upmixer or other listening mode describes processing after receipt. Read the input-format report when tracing the source-to-receiver path. Change one part of the session Keep the same source track and server delivery, but select ordinary channel PCM output in the player. The receiver might now receive a completed 7.1 presentation: eight channels that it can play or further process. Those channels describe that particular rendering. They do not carry the original object presentation simply because the connection has room for multichannel PCM. Select encoded passthrough instead, where the whole path supports it. The downstream device then performs decoding as well as rendering. The placement of the decoder has changed, while the selected source may stay the same. Now change server delivery to an ordinary audio transcode. The app may receive a new channel-based presentation before it makes any output decision. A later MAT-capable output cannot reconstruct spatial information that the earlier conversion omitted. These changes explain why “where was it decoded?” is only part of the investigation. Follow what information survived each boundary , and the audible result becomes easier to account for. The audio playback path describes the surrounding stages. Why TrueHD playback also uses the MAT name MAT originally provided carriage for a variable-rate TrueHD bitstream over the HDMI audio transport arrangement. In that use, the source packs encoded TrueHD data into the transport and the receiving device unpacks and decodes it. PCM-based MAT 2.0 extends the possible route by carrying a decoded Atmos presentation with its metadata. The shared MAT name consequently does not locate the decoder by itself: identify the actual use and the source and output information. A media inspector examines the stored track. It can correctly identify TrueHD in an MKV even though the receiver describes its transport using MAT. There need not be a stored MAT track in the library file. Record the session in terms that can be compared For an Emby playback investigation, collect the selected source track, server delivery mode, player output choice, receiver input report, and speaker/rendering configuration. Together they describe a path. Reading just the file label or just the receiver's listening mode leaves several operations unexplained. Transport also preserves the compression history of the audio it carries. A decoded lossy source already contains the reconstruction from that lossy encode. Sending it onward without another lossy encoding step preserves that result; it does not turn the source into a lossless recording. A lossless TrueHD source can retain its recovered samples through a supported output path that preserves them. The file and receiver labels then have precise roles in the record: one identifies the retained source, and the other identifies the presentation delivered across the audio connection. See Also Dolby TrueHD Audio Dolby Atmos Decoded PCM Output Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Overview: Output and transport | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Overview: Output and transport Audio output and transport determine whether a receiver gets a coded stream, decoded samples or another defined delivery arrangement. Passthrough leaves the relevant decoding work to a compatible receiver. PCM output supplies decoded samples, while Dolby MAT provides its own defined transport arrangement. Comparing those routes helps identify which component interprets the signal and which information must survive the handoff. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Audio bitstream passthrough Audio bitstream passthrough sends a supported encoded audio presentation to another device for decoding. Decoded PCM output Decoded PCM output sends reconstructed audio samples to the sound system after decoding occurs in the player or an earlier component. Dolby MAT Dolby MAT is a metadata-enhanced audio transport used for TrueHD carriage and supported PCM-based Dolby Atmos delivery. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams

articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-DAC..title: Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-DAC..keywords: Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) A DAC converts timed digital samples into an analog signal using conversion circuitry, reconstruction filtering, and an output stage. The loudspeaker ultimately needs an electrical waveform. A digital-to-analog converter , or DAC , turns a timed stream of digital sample values into an analog voltage or current that can feed an output stage. The DAC may be in a phone, television, USB interface, receiver or powered speaker. With an Emby player sending audio to a receiver digitally, the receiver can perform the conversion. A phone's analog headphone connection uses conversion within the phone or its attached adapter. Locating that boundary explains which device's output circuitry is actually being used. Reconstructing a waveform from samples A sample is a value at a time, not a little sound fragment that needs to be audibly held until the next one. The combination of sample rate , sample values and reconstruction defines the continuous signal. A simple hold-type DAC creates a staircase-like intermediate output with additional spectral images around the sampling frequency. Reconstruction filtering retains the intended baseband and attenuates those images. Modern audio converters commonly use digital interpolation and oversampling before the final analog stage, allowing the analog filter's transition to occur farther from the audible band. Different converter architectures realize that process differently. A delta-sigma DAC may use a rapidly changing internal representation rather than directly outputting one physical voltage for each input PCM number. The supplied “24-bit, 48 kHz” format describes the input signal; it does not describe every internal switching step. The output clock also determines when values are converted. The delivery of packets into a buffer and the conversion of samples out of that buffer are separate activities. A USB transfer can be irregular in packet size while a DAC converts at a steady device-clock rate. A gain number becomes a voltage Suppose a hypothetical DAC produces 2 V RMS for a full-scale sine at its line output. An amplitude multiplier of 0.5, equivalent to about −6.02 dB , gives 1 V RMS for the same waveform. A multiplier of 0.25 gives 0.5 V RMS. Digital amplitude multiplier Gain relative to full scale Output in this example 1.00 0 dB 2.0 V RMS 0.50 −6.02 dB 1.0 V RMS 0.25 −12.04 dB 0.5 V RMS These are illustrative line-output values, not a specification for every DAC or headphone port. The amplifier gain and speaker/headphone sensitivity determine the acoustic result. A digital volume control scales the samples before conversion. An analog control attenuates the converted signal later. The location affects the relationship between programme level, converter noise and output-stage noise. Reading the analog specifications Input bit depth is a supported representation. Usable analog performance is described by measurements such as signal-to-noise ratio, distortion, frequency response and output level under stated conditions. Accepting 32-bit data does not imply 32 bits of noise-free analog resolution. The electrical load matters too. A line output designed to feed a high-impedance amplifier input and a headphone output designed to drive a lower impedance have different current and output-stage requirements. A clean digital input can still meet an analog stage that overloads or cannot drive the selected load. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Bit Depth USB Audio S/PDIF digital audio References Analog Devices MT-017: Oversampling interpolating DACs Analog Devices MT-001: Converter SNR and quantization IEC 60958-1:2021: Digital audio interface structure

articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-Excl.title: Exclusive-mode audio output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-Excl.keywords: Exclusive-mode audio output Exclusive audio output grants an application a dedicated endpoint route that bypasses a shared mixer while retaining the device's format and timing requirements. Exclusive output gives an application a dedicated route to an audio endpoint under the platform's access rules. Its common purpose is to bypass a shared mixing stage and negotiate the stream directly with the output device. In an Emby route, this access choice belongs to the app and device performing playback. In Windows WASAPI, this is an explicit sharing mode. A Linux application using a direct ALSA hardware PCM can create a comparable dedicated route, although the APIs and device-ownership rules differ. The general idea should not be mistaken for one identical feature on every operating system. What changes when the mixer is bypassed Question Shared route Dedicated endpoint route Can several ordinary app streams contribute together? Normally supported by the mixer Competing access can be rejected or interrupted under platform policy Which format must be accepted? A format supported by the shared route A format supported by the endpoint for this access mode Who keeps the output supplied? App and shared engine, at their respective boundaries App and driver/device route Does the mode prove that samples are unchanged? No No A source rate of 44.1 kHz can be negotiated directly when the endpoint supports it. If the endpoint only accepts 48 kHz for the selected configuration, the player must choose a supported alternative, convert, or report the failure. Bypassing the shared mixer cannot make unsupported hardware formats valid. Changing format between tracks can also require stopping and reinitializing the output. That can affect gapless playback , even if both formats work individually. Ownership and timing become visible If another application already owns the endpoint, opening an exclusive stream can fail. A device can also be invalidated by unplugging it or changing its resources. A player needs a defined response, such as retrying a suitable endpoint, falling back to an accepted route, or informing the user. Once the stream is running, the application must meet its buffer deadlines. A dedicated route does not protect an audio thread from a delayed decoder or unavailable network data. Reducing buffers increases responsiveness while leaving less queued audio to cover a stall. These mechanics explain why a device that sounds fine in shared mode can fail to start or break up under another mode without any change to the stored soundtrack. The rest of the signal path still exists Player volume, ReplayGain, equalization, resampling and downmixing happen before the endpoint if the player applies them. Driver or device processing can happen afterward. Exclusive access bypasses the defined shared engine; it does not establish that all of those other operations are absent. A bit-perfect claim therefore needs its own sample-domain evidence. Similarly, an encoded bitstream needs the proper supported transport format rather than ordinary PCM simply placed in an exclusive buffer. See Also Windows Audio Session API (WASAPI) ALSA Bit-perfect playback Audio Bitstream Passthrough References Microsoft: Exclusive-mode streams Microsoft: IAudioClient::IsFormatSupported ALSA project: PCM plugins Microsoft: Rendering a stream

articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-SPDI.title: S/PDIF digital audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-SPDI.keywords: S/PDIF digital audio S/PDIF transports a consumer digital audio stream whose framing can carry stereo PCM or supported encoded audio bursts. S/PDIF is a consumer digital audio interface commonly encountered as a coaxial connection or an optical TOSLINK connection. It carries a timed digital stream to another device; the receiver can then convert PCM to analog or decode a supported compressed presentation. The crucial question is what that stream contains . Two-channel PCM and a Dolby Digital surround bitstream can use the same general link framing while requiring different treatment at the receiver. Two subframes make an audio frame In the conventional IEC 60958 structure, each audio frame has two subframes, A and B. For stereo PCM, those carry the left and right samples at one instant. A subframe spans 32 time slots : four for its preamble, up to 24 for the sample field, and four for validity, user, channel-status and parity information. At shorter word lengths, not every position in the sample area holds a valid audio bit. One channel-status bit per subframe accumulates into a 192-frame status block for each channel. This communicates information about the stream, including its consumer-mode interpretation. It is different from compressed-codec metadata inside an encoded payload. At a 48 kHz frame rate, the two 32-slot subframes give: 48,000 frames/s × 2 subframes/frame × 32 slots/subframe = 3,072,000 logical time slots/s This is framing arithmetic, not a claim that the physical biphase-mark waveform has a 3.072 MHz analog bandwidth. Its transitions encode both information and timing. PCM channels and coded surround are different For ordinary stereo PCM, the receiver interprets the sample fields as amplitudes. A PCM volume adjustment can be performed before transmission by scaling those values. IEC 61937 uses the digital audio framework to transport encoded audio bursts . In that case the receiving device recognizes the payload type and decodes it. A supported AC-3 stream can produce 5.1 channels even though the carrier uses the two-subframe framework. That does not mean the same conventional connection carries six independent channels of ordinary LPCM. Nor does it imply support for every newer lossless or immersive codec. The output device, driver, transport convention and receiver must all support the chosen encoded presentation. An Emby player can therefore deliver stereo PCM after a downmix or send a supported encoded track for downstream decoding, depending on its chosen route. The original movie's channel count and the transmitted representation answer different questions. An ordinary sample multiplier cannot change the volume of those encoded bytes as if they were PCM. Volume must be handled through a suitable decoded route or downstream control. Bitstream passthrough develops that distinction. Optical and coaxial carriage The physical implementations differ: one uses light and the other an electrical signal with the appropriate interface and cable. They carry the same kind of logical consumer audio stream; changing between them does not convert a soundtrack codec into another format. The receiver recovers timing from the incoming signal. “Locked” establishes that it has acquired the stream, while a detected codec or PCM indication describes its interpretation. A surround listening mode applied afterward describes additional receiver processing. See Also Audio Bitstream Passthrough Decoded PCM Output Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) USB Audio References IEC 60958-3:2021: Consumer digital audio interface IEC 60958-1:2021: Digital audio interface structure IEC 61937-1:2021: Encoded audio bitstreams over IEC 60958 Texas Instruments DIT4192: Digital audio frame structure

articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-USB..title: USB Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/Audio-USB..keywords: USB Audio USB Audio defines discoverable audio streams and controls, with packet delivery synchronized to the sample clock used by the device. A USB audio device presents audio streams and controls that the host can discover. A player can deliver samples through an operating-system audio API, while a class driver turns those samples into transfers for a DAC, headset or interface. USB Audio Class version and USB bus speed are separate properties. Audio Class 2.0 describes an audio-device protocol and its descriptors; “USB 2.0” describes the bus. A device's actual stream format depends on the capabilities it advertises and the configuration the host selects. The descriptors describe the available stream The device identifies supported channel arrangements, sample representations, endpoints and clock relationships. The host selects a supported streaming setting and supplies audio in that format. A 24-bit sample can occupy three bytes or a larger container, depending on the declared format. Stereo packed into three bytes per sample uses six bytes per PCM sample frame . The packet arithmetic must use that actual container layout. For an illustrative full-speed stream transferring once per 1 ms interval at 48 kHz: 48,000 frames/s × 0.001 s = 48 sample frames 48 frames × 2 channels × 3 bytes = 288 bytes This is a chosen packet schedule. High-speed transfers can use microframe-based intervals, and a device can select another supported interval or layout. USB timing and the audio clock need to agree on average USB transfers occur on the bus schedule. The DAC consumes sample frames according to its audio clock. A buffer bridges the two. An asynchronous audio endpoint uses a sample clock independent of USB timing. Feedback lets the host pace data to match the device's consumption. A synchronous endpoint locks its clock to USB timing; an adaptive endpoint adjusts its clock behavior to the incoming data rate. The word “asynchronous” describes a clock relationship. It does not mean that the stream has no timing, that the host has abandoned flow control, or that audible samples are delivered at arbitrary instants. A clock running 100 parts per million fast Suppose a nominal 48 kHz device actually consumes 48,004.8 frames per second , 100 ppm faster than 48,000. Per 1 ms USB interval, it needs an average of 48.0048 frames . A packet cannot contain a fractional sample frame. The host can therefore send mostly 48-frame packets and occasional 49-frame packets. Over 2,500 intervals, the required total is: 48.0048 × 2,500 = 120,012 frames 48 × 2,500 = 120,000 frames difference = 12 additional frames over 2.5 seconds Those twelve extra frames come from the continuing source stream. They are not twelve invented duplicates. In the six-byte example, a 48-frame packet is 288 bytes and a 49-frame packet is 294 bytes. Pacing complete, consecutive frames into variable packet sizes does not itself perform resampling. If two long-running streams with different physical clocks must remain synchronized, an additional clock-matching strategy may be needed elsewhere in the system. Buffers and the final output The operating system, USB stack and device can each buffer audio. Packet interval alone does not establish the total delay from an app producing a sample to the DAC presenting it. A low-latency configuration must still tolerate scheduling variation and maintain enough queued data. For an Emby device comparison, record the client device, selected USB output, negotiated rate/channel/sample format and any software processing. A media server delivering to a remote client is upstream of that client's USB connection. See Also Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) Audio Sample Rate S/PDIF digital audio The Audio Playback Path References USB-IF Audio Device Class 2.0, September 2026 consolidated specification USB-IF USB 2.0 specification package Analog Devices MT-017: Oversampling interpolating DACs

articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.title: Bluetooth audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.keywords: Bluetooth audio Bluetooth audio uses a negotiated wireless audio profile and codec between a transmitting device and a receiving headset or speaker. A lossless file in an Emby library can reach the app intact and still be encoded into a different format for Bluetooth headphones. The media stream from the server and the wireless audio stream from the client device are separate parts of the route. The client normally decodes the media into PCM, applies any selected audio processing, and feeds the system's Bluetooth output. That output negotiates an audio profile and radio codec with the headphones or speaker. A FLAC label in the library identifies the stored codec. It does not identify the radio codec. Even when the file and radio link both use a codec named AAC, matching names do not prove that the original coded packets were forwarded unchanged. The profile defines the kind of connection Two audio architectures have their own pages: A2DP provides media distribution over Bluetooth Classic, with SBC as its common mandatory codec. LE Audio uses LE isochronous transport and an audio framework supporting unicast and broadcast use cases. A bidirectional communications route can have different format and processing requirements from music playback. Opening a microphone on a Classic headset can cause the operating system to select a communications profile instead of its A2DP media route. The specific behavior depends on the headset and host implementation; a paired device name does not establish the active profile. Media buttons and playback commands are another layer. Successfully pausing a movie from the headset proves that the relevant control path works, not which codec is carrying its sound. What a change during playback can reveal Observation Useful boundary to inspect Sound changes when another app opens the headset microphone Active audio profile, selected format and communications processing Audio is delayed by a roughly constant amount Reported output delay and the player's compensation Audio occasionally breaks up Radio delivery, receiver buffer and local producer timing Sound has different dynamics or tonal balance Player processing, OS output processing and headset DSP Server reports Direct Play but headphones receive lossy audio The client's separate wireless encoding stage These observations are starting points for a trace, not diagnoses based on symptoms alone. A wireless receiver needs time to receive, buffer, decode and present audio. Codec frame duration is one contributor, while transport buffering and device processing contribute others. A fixed delay can be accommodated by scheduling video appropriately; delay that varies or is reported inaccurately creates a different synchronization problem. See Also Bluetooth A2DP Bluetooth LE Audio The Audio Playback Path Audio/Video Synchronization References A2DP 1.4 specification and mandatory erratum Bluetooth SIG LE Audio specifications Bluetooth SIG: LC3 technical overview Bluetooth SIG: A/V Remote Control Profile 1.6.2 Bluetooth SIG: Hands-Free Profile 1.10

articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.title: Bluetooth A2DP | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.keywords: Bluetooth A2DP A2DP defines Bluetooth Classic media-audio distribution with source/sink roles, codec negotiation, and framed audio transport. A2DP , the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile, defines media-audio delivery over Bluetooth Classic. The transmitting device is the source (SRC) ; the receiving headphones, speaker or receiver are the sink (SNK) . A2DP standardizes the supported audio configuration and delivery procedures. It does not mean that every Bluetooth device accepts the same optional codec, nor that an app can assume the codec from the soundtrack's filename. A compatible configuration is selected The source and sink exchange capabilities through the audio/video distribution transport framework, AVDTP, and select an agreed configuration. SBC supplies the mandatory common codec. Optional codecs, including AAC, require compatible support at both ends. Codec support is only the first question. The chosen sampling frequency, channel mode and codec parameters must also be accepted. A device advertising an option does not prove that it was selected for the current stream. In an ordinary Emby route, the app or platform decodes the selected movie or music track before the host's wireless subsystem produces the A2DP stream. This can add another lossy encode after a lossy source decode. A lossless source avoids the source's lossy generation, while the separately negotiated radio coding remains. One SBC frame is not one transport packet SBC divides the signal into subbands and encodes blocks of subband samples. For a selected configuration with 16 blocks and 8 subbands , one SBC frame represents 128 samples per channel . At 48 kHz: 16 × 8 = 128 sample frames 128 / 48,000 = 0.0026667 s ≈ 2.667 ms Quantity Example meaning Sample frame Simultaneous left/right samples at one instant SBC frame 128 sample frames in this configuration Media payload Can contain several complete SBC frames, or specified fragmentation Output delay Includes more than the duration of one coded frame Three of those SBC frames cover 384 sample frames , or 8 ms of audio. Packing several frames together changes transport overhead and delivery grouping; it does not change the waveform's sampling rate. SBC's bitpool contributes to its coded size along with channel mode, block count and subband count. “SBC” therefore does not describe one fixed bitrate. A bitrate number also needs to distinguish codec payload from packet and radio overhead. Controls and conversation use other roles AVRCP supplies remote-control functions such as media commands. A2DP carries the media audio. A headset can support both while their responsibilities remain separate. Likewise, a communications profile for microphone and call audio serves a different use case from A2DP's media distribution. Switching into that use case can change the selected audio format and processing. Successful pairing alone does not establish which route is active. Receiver delay is part of movie playback A sink buffers incoming coded audio before decoding and presenting it. A2DP includes delay-reporting procedures that can help a source account for the receiving side. The resulting end-to-end delay also depends on producer, operating-system and transport buffering. For movie playback, the useful comparison is sound presentation against picture presentation. A 2.667 ms SBC frame does not promise 2.667 ms total latency. If a route changes during playback, the player may need an updated delay estimate and a new output configuration. See Also Bluetooth audio Bluetooth LE Audio Audio Bitrate References Bluetooth SIG Advanced Audio Distribution Profile 1.4 A2DP 1.4 specification and mandatory erratum Bluetooth SIG: A/V Remote Control Profile 1.6.2 Bluetooth SIG: Hands-Free Profile 1.10

articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.title: Bluetooth LE Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.keywords: Bluetooth LE Audio Bluetooth LE Audio combines LC3 coding, isochronous streams, and audio control profiles to coordinate unicast or broadcast sound. Bluetooth LE Audio is an audio architecture built on Bluetooth Low Energy isochronous streams , with LC3 as its baseline codec and profiles for audio discovery, configuration and control. It enables audio to be organized into coordinated streams—for example, a stream for each earbud—and supports both connected unicast audio and broadcast audio. A device's Bluetooth version alone does not establish support for the complete audio architecture. The radio, host software, profiles and receiving device all need the relevant capabilities. Coordinated streams can have separate destinations For unicast, Connected Isochronous Streams ( CIS ) belong to a Connected Isochronous Group ( CIG ). Broadcast uses Broadcast Isochronous Streams ( BIS ) organized in a Broadcast Isochronous Group ( BIG ). The groups provide transport timing relationships. Audio capabilities and controls determine which channels and configurations those streams represent. A stream identifier is not automatically a left/right label; channel allocation and the chosen audio configuration supply that meaning. This arrangement allows a transmitter to supply coordinated devices directly. The device set and selected topology determine the actual delivery; the diagram does not claim that every headset uses this exact route. LC3 frame duration and payload size LC3 encodes a block of audio into a codec frame. At 48 kHz , 10 ms contains 480 sample frames per channel , while 7.5 ms contains 360 . The coded frame's byte count determines its payload bitrate. Two example 48 kHz configurations from the Basic Audio Profile are: Frame interval Samples per channel Encoded bytes per channel per frame Codec payload bitrate per channel 10 ms 480 100 80 kbit/s 7.5 ms 360 75 80 kbit/s For the 10 ms case, 100 bytes × 8 bits / 0.010 s = 80,000 bit/s . Two channels using that configuration total 160 kbit/s of codec payload. That excludes transport headers, retransmissions and other radio overhead. For an Emby route, these byte counts concern the client's wireless encoding stage. The file codec delivered by the media server is upstream of that stage. Holding bitrate constant while shortening the frame reduces the bytes per frame. Holding bytes constant would instead increase bitrate. The negotiated codec and transport configuration must be supported; the frame interval cannot be changed independently of all other parameters. The 48 kHz assumption matters. Some other sample-rate configurations have a different relationship between nominal frame-duration labels and their effective duration, as specified in the profile. A shared presentation time is not zero latency Two earbuds should reproduce corresponding left and right samples at the intended common instant. The audio framework's Presentation_Delay relates presentation to a defined transport synchronization reference and accounts for receiving-side capabilities and processing. Consider an abstract frame with synchronization reference 100 ms . If the chosen presentation delay is 30 ms , its intended presentation starts at 130 ms . Earbud A may finish preparing its audio earlier than earbud B; buffering allows both to wait for that scheduled instant. This is a synchronization example, not a default LE Audio delay. It also does not measure all the time since an Emby app first decoded the samples. Source-side preparation and queues can occur before the transport reference. A small codec frame can help a low-delay design, but frame duration, transport robustness, processing time and presentation delay are separate contributors. Receiver coordination addresses their relative presentation; movie lip sync also needs the overall delay accounted for against video. Unicast and broadcast have different control models A unicast audio configuration establishes connected streams with selected receiving devices and can support bidirectional use cases. Broadcast distributes streams that compatible receivers can discover and join. Auracast refers to the public broadcast audio ecosystem built on this architecture. Broadcast is not simply pairing the same transmitter separately to an unlimited list of headphones. Discovery, stream descriptions, synchronization and any broadcast access requirements form another route. See Also Bluetooth audio Bluetooth A2DP Audio/Video Synchronization References Bluetooth SIG Basic Audio Profile Bluetooth SIG LE Audio specifications Bluetooth SIG: LC3 technical overview

articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.title: Overview: Bluetooth connections | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/bluetooth/.keywords: Overview: Bluetooth connections Bluetooth audio uses particular profiles and transport arrangements to connect an audio source with a wireless listening device. The Bluetooth label alone does not identify the audio route. A2DP and LE Audio belong to different arrangements with their own supported components and capabilities. The fundamentals and profile pages establish what is negotiated before latency or format behavior is attributed to the wireless link. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Bluetooth audio Bluetooth audio uses a negotiated wireless audio profile and codec between a transmitting device and a receiving headset or speaker. Bluetooth A2DP A2DP defines Bluetooth Classic media-audio distribution with source/sink roles, codec negotiation, and framed audio transport. Bluetooth LE Audio Bluetooth LE Audio combines LC3 coding, isochronous streams, and audio control profiles to coordinate unicast or broadcast sound. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References A2DP 1.4 specification and mandatory erratum

articles/audio/devices-output/index.html.title: Overview: Audio devices and operating-system output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/index.html.keywords: Overview: Audio devices and operating-system output Audio devices and operating-system interfaces connect a player's output to its physical or wireless listening path. Decoded samples still have to pass through a device interface, an operating-system audio path and, eventually, a signal converter or receiver. S/PDIF, USB and Bluetooth introduce different transport arrangements. The operating-system and exclusive-mode topics explain how software reaches those arrangements and where format or mixing decisions can occur. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) A DAC converts timed digital samples into an analog signal using conversion circuitry, reconstruction filtering, and an output stage. S/PDIF S/PDIF transports a consumer digital audio stream whose framing can carry stereo PCM or supported encoded audio bursts. USB Audio USB Audio defines discoverable audio streams and controls, with packet delivery synchronized to the sample clock used by the device. Bluetooth connections Bluetooth audio uses particular profiles and transport arrangements to connect an audio source with a wireless listening device. Operating-system audio APIs Operating-system audio APIs define how applications exchange audio with devices and system processing. Exclusive-mode audio output Exclusive audio output grants an application a dedicated endpoint route that bypasses a shared mixer while retaining the device's format and timing requirements. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IEC 60958-1:2021: Digital audio interface structure IEC 60958-3:2021: Consumer digital audio interface

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.title: ALSA | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.keywords: ALSA ALSA supplies Linux audio driver interfaces and a PCM library with configurable device routes, sample formats, and ring-buffer timing. ALSA , the Advanced Linux Sound Architecture, includes the Linux audio driver framework and the commonly used alsa-lib interface. Its PCM interface lets an application or sound server send sample frames to an audio device. A program saying that it uses ALSA has not yet identified the complete route. The name it opens can select direct hardware, conversion plugins, software mixing or a sound-server connection. The PCM name selects a route PCM route or plugin Interpretation hw Communicates with the kernel PCM device without library format conversion plug Can adapt format, rate or channel requirements for its downstream PCM dmix Provides software mixing for suitable PCM routes default A configured name whose meaning depends on the installed configuration For example, hw:0,0 identifies a hardware PCM by card and device number in that system. Card enumeration can change, and the device's supported parameters still need to be established. Opening default does not prove direct hardware access. It may resolve through configuration to a sound server. Nor does the direct hw library route prove that a later driver or device applies no processing. This is why a Linux output comparison needs both the backend name and the resolved PCM route. A ring buffer separates producer and consumer The application writes frames ahead of the hardware position. As playback proceeds, the device consumes them and the application gains writable space. The storage wraps around, while the logical playback position continues forward. Suppose the selected rate is 48 kHz , the period is 240 frames , and the buffer contains 960 frames : period duration = 240 / 48,000 = 5 ms buffer capacity = 960 / 48,000 = 20 ms A period is a unit used in the configured transfer and notification scheme. It is not necessarily the total audible delay. The current amount queued may be less than the buffer capacity, and downstream stages can contribute additional delay. For stereo signed 16-bit PCM, 240 sample frames occupy 960 bytes : 240 × two channels × two bytes. ALSA frame counts do not double just because there are two channels. The interleaved write interface takes successive channel samples together; the noninterleaved interface takes separate channel arrays. Memory-mapped access exposes buffer areas with defined positions and strides. All still require the application to respect the agreed layout and acknowledge transferred frames. What an underrun means Imagine that the buffer contains a full 20 ms of prepared audio, then the producer cannot provide any more for 25 ms . In the idealized timing model, the device exhausts the queue after 20 ms, leaving a 5 ms shortage before the producer returns. ALSA represents a playback underrun as an XRUN , commonly reported by an I/O call as -EPIPE . Recovery can prepare the PCM stream to accept audio again. It cannot retroactively play the missing frames at the time when they should have been heard. A movie player must decide how to restore its timeline after the discontinuity. Blindly resuming old queued content can leave sound late relative to video; skipping content or rebuilding synchronization makes another tradeoff. A larger buffer can tolerate a longer stall but also holds more audio ahead of presentation. A smaller period can provide more frequent opportunities to service the stream while increasing scheduling overhead. Neither value alone explains a failure: the actual producer timing matters. Requested and negotiated parameters ALSA hardware parameters describe the rate, channels, format, access mode, period and buffer. The parameter system narrows available choices until a valid configuration is selected. An API that requests a value “near” a desired rate or size can return another supported value. The application must use the negotiated result in its arithmetic. Interpreting 44.1 kHz frames as if the device were running at 48 kHz would change calculated durations and pacing. The sample container also needs attention. Packed 24-bit PCM and 24 valid bits in a 32-bit container have different byte strides even when they describe the same precision. ALSA on which machine? For remote Emby playback, the server's audio subsystem is generally not the device playing the sound. The server delivers media; the client device's output path drives its speakers or digital connection. On a Linux client, PulseAudio or PipeWire can own the hardware PCM and provide mixing, routing and conversion above ALSA. Changing the server's ALSA default therefore does not automatically change a remote television or browser's audio. Locate the client route first, then record its actual PCM target, negotiated format and XRUN behavior. Those observations identify whether the issue is routing, format selection or keeping the hardware supplied on time. See Also PulseAudio PipeWire PCM Sample Formats Exclusive-mode audio output References ALSA project: PCM interface ALSA project: PCM plugins PipeWire: Configuration and session management

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.title: Apple Core Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.keywords: Apple Core Audio Core Audio is Apple's collection of audio services for formats, conversion, processing, device access, and timed playback. Core Audio is a collection of Apple audio services, rather than one codec or one fixed output mode. It covers reading audio, describing formats, converting data, processing samples, and communicating with output devices. The name therefore does not establish whether a player mixes audio, changes its sample rate, uses spatial processing or preserves PCM values. Those results depend on the services and configuration used by the application. The responsibilities within the framework Part Responsibility Audio file and stream services Interpret stored or incoming audio data Audio Converter services Convert supported representations and sample formats Audio Units Process and route signal blocks, including mixing and output Audio Queue services Manage queued playback or recording buffers Audio hardware abstraction layer, HAL Provide device-oriented access on macOS AVAudioSession on supported Apple platforms Express the app's audio use and preferences, and observe the selected route Higher-level playback facilities can build on these services. An Emby app using a platform player does not have to call every lower-level API itself. The macOS device model and the iOS-family audio-session model also differ. A device access technique on macOS should not be assumed to be an equivalent selectable mode on a phone. A sample frame can span several buffers An AudioStreamBasicDescription , commonly ASBD , describes the stream's rate, format, channels, sample representation and packet/frame dimensions. Buffer organization then determines where the samples are stored. Take 48 kHz stereo with 32-bit floating-point samples : Arrangement Samples in memory Storage for 480 sample frames Interleaved L₀, R₀, L₁, R₁… in one buffer One 3,840-byte buffer Noninterleaved L₀, L₁… and R₀, R₁… in separate buffers Two 1,920-byte buffers Both represent 10 ms of stereo audio . Interleaved frames use eight bytes; each noninterleaved channel plane uses four bytes per frame. The number of buffers has not doubled the duration. A callback receiving 480 frames needs the appropriate amount of storage in each buffer. Treating a per-plane byte count as the total interleaved count can truncate data or overwrite memory. The format flags and buffer list supply the interpretation; a casual “float stereo” label is incomplete. Compressed packets have another relationship to frames. A codec packet can decode to many PCM sample frames. Packet count is not a substitute for the sample clock. A preference is not the actual device format An application can request a preferred sample rate or I/O buffer duration through its audio session. Those values express a preference. The actual route and other active audio requirements can produce another result. After activation or a route change, the application queries the actual sample rate and buffer duration . If a source is 44.1 kHz and the active output route is 48 kHz, some stage must supply suitable 48 kHz samples. A file's original rate remains useful metadata but does not prove the final route's rate. A headphone disconnection, Bluetooth selection or other route event can also change capabilities and timing. The player needs to adapt its stream rather than continuing to interpret buffers using an obsolete configuration. Rendering on the output deadline The output consumes frames at the established clock rate. Callbacks or queues keep it supplied. Data retrieval and expensive preparation need enough advance time so that the render work can meet its deadline. For movie playback, the system's audio timing helps the player align video presentation with the output. The duration of one callback is a processing interval, while the complete route can include additional queued and device delay. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Sample Rate Digital-to-analog conversion (DAC) The Audio Playback Path References Apple: Core Audio Essentials Apple: AudioStreamBasicDescription Apple: AVAudioSession Apple: Preferred sample rate and the actual sample rate Apple Core Audio Format specification: Packet table

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.title: PipeWire | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.keywords: PipeWire PipeWire routes media through a scheduled graph of nodes, ports, and links, with session policy and compatibility interfaces around that graph. PipeWire organizes audio and other media as a processing graph . Applications and devices produce or consume buffers; links carry those buffers between their ports. A separate session manager decides how available devices and streams should be configured and connected. This distinction is useful when a Linux player produces audio but it reaches the wrong output: the processing system may be running correctly while the selected route differs from the intended one. The diagram shows one possible local audio configuration. A remote Emby server delivers media to the client app before this local output graph; it is not automatically a node in that client's graph. Nodes, ports, links and policy A node performs or hosts media processing. A port is one of its inputs or outputs. A link connects an output port to an input port. The graph can represent application streams, processing stages and device-facing nodes. A session manager such as WirePlumber handles policy: selecting device profiles, remembering or choosing targets and creating appropriate connections. The PipeWire daemon coordinates the graph's processing. Consequently, a node can exist without being connected to the intended speakers. A connection can also change when a device appears or disappears. Selecting a default device and observing the links of an already-running stream are related but distinct tasks. Quantum is the amount processed in a graph cycle The graph's rate describes its sample clock. Its quantum describes the number of sample frames processed per cycle. For a chosen quantum of 256 frames at 48 kHz : cycle duration = 256 / 48,000 ≈ 5.333 ms cycles per second = 48,000 / 256 = 187.5 Example quantum at 48 kHz Nominal cycle duration 128 frames 2.667 ms 256 frames 5.333 ms 512 frames 10.667 ms These are examples, not distribution defaults. Reducing the quantum gives the system shorter processing intervals and more frequent scheduling work. It does not change the pitch or duration of correctly delivered audio. The complete audible delay can include client queues, adapters, graph processing, device buffers and a wireless output. A 5.333 ms cycle is therefore not a claim of 5.333 ms total latency. Node latency preferences can influence configuration, while device requirements, active clients or forced settings can determine another result. The observed rate and quantum describe the running graph more accurately than a requested value in one application. A driver starts cycles; another clock can drift A graph driver starts processing cycles and supplies timing information. A device-backed driver can be paced by a physical audio clock, while timestamps are related to the system's monotonic time. Suppose a USB device's nominal 48 kHz clock runs 100 ppm fast. It consumes 4.8 additional frames per second relative to an exact 48,000-frame clock. Buffering absorbs short differences, but a persistent difference accumulates. The graph needs a consistent strategy for relating those clocks. Rate matching and timing compensation at appropriate boundaries keep a queue from growing or emptying indefinitely. A “48 kHz” format label gives the nominal rate; it does not prove that two independent oscillators advance identically. For a movie, the player also relates this output timing to picture presentation. Graph processing that meets every deadline can still require an accurate downstream-delay estimate for lip sync. Existing APIs can enter the same graph A native PipeWire client can create a stream directly. A PulseAudio client can connect through pipewire-pulse . Compatibility support can also expose routes to applications using other audio interfaces. Those interfaces identify how the application communicates, while the running server and graph identify what processes the audio. ALSA remains important as a Linux hardware interface beneath many device nodes. These are layers in a route rather than mutually exclusive labels for the whole machine. Two concrete failures illustrate the distinction. A stream linked to the laptop speakers can play continuously while the listener expects the USB interface: its route is wrong. A stream linked to the correct USB interface can break up when a processing deadline is missed: its timing failed. Changing the default target addresses the first kind of problem only if policy reconnects that stream; changing the quantum addresses the second only if the revised scheduling and buffering meet the deadline. See Also What is a graph? ALSA PulseAudio Audio/Video Synchronization USB Audio References PipeWire: Objects design PipeWire: Configuration and session management PipeWire: Node and scheduling properties PipeWire: Driver architecture and clocks PipeWire: PulseAudio-compatible server

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.title: PulseAudio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.keywords: PulseAudio PulseAudio provides a sound-server interface that routes, mixes, buffers, and converts application streams for selected output sinks. PulseAudio provides a sound-server model in which applications create audio streams and the server routes them to sinks . A sink is a playback destination; an application's playback stream is represented on the server as a sink input . The server can combine streams, adjust levels and convert formats for the output. The physical device may be reached through ALSA, Bluetooth or another supported backend. Term Playback meaning Client Application connected to the server Stream / sink input One application's submitted audio Sink Destination that consumes playback audio Source Capture or monitor destination that supplies audio Sample specification The stream's rate, channels and sample representation A monitor source can expose a sink's mixed audio for capture. That is a server-side signal observation, not necessarily a capture of the final analog output. Buffer requests are expressed in bytes PulseAudio's asynchronous stream interface uses playback buffer attributes. The requested target length , tlength , establishes a buffering goal; maxlength , prebuf and minreq serve other purposes. For 48 kHz stereo float32 , one sample frame contains eight bytes. A target length of 19,200 bytes represents: 19,200 / 8 = 2,400 sample frames 2,400 / 48,000 = 0.050 s = 50 ms That calculation needs the actual sample specification. The same byte count in stereo 16-bit PCM would describe twice as many frames and twice the duration. Attribute Role tlength Target playback buffering amount maxlength Maximum buffer length prebuf Amount required before automatic playback starts or resumes minreq Minimum amount requested from the client at once Without PA_STREAM_ADJUST_LATENCY , the target length concerns the stream's server-side playback buffer. With that flag, the request instead asks the server to configure the combined sink and stream buffering toward that latency. The accepted configuration and measured delay need to be checked; a requested 50 ms is not proof of exactly 50 ms at the speaker. The server can satisfy several clients with different buffering needs. A request also cannot eliminate delay inherent in a separate wireless receiver. Routing and conversion happen after the app's format An application can submit 44.1 kHz audio while the destination uses 48 kHz. The server's output route can perform the necessary conversion. Per-stream gain, sink gain and supported processing can affect what reaches the device. Moving a stream to another sink changes its destination and may change its format or timing requirements. A stored preference, the current default sink and an already-running stream's actual destination are different observations. For an Emby Linux client, inspect the app's stream and the sink it is using. Changing a server setting on the machine hosting the media library does not select the speakers on a separate client. The protocol does not identify the implementation A program using libpulse speaks the PulseAudio client protocol. It can connect to the PulseAudio daemon or to PipeWire's pipewire-pulse compatibility server . The names shown to a PulseAudio client may therefore describe a compatible view of a PipeWire graph. That helps existing applications continue to work; it also means “PulseAudio output” in a player log is not enough to identify the running daemon. See Also ALSA PipeWire The Audio Playback Path Audio/Video Synchronization References PulseAudio: Playback buffer attributes PulseAudio: Client latency control PipeWire: PulseAudio-compatible server PipeWire: Configuration and session management

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.title: Windows Audio Session API (WASAPI) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/Au.keywords: Windows Audio Session API (WASAPI) WASAPI lets Windows applications negotiate and feed endpoint audio streams using shared or exclusive access and explicit buffer accounting. WASAPI is a Windows interface for sending audio to, or capturing audio from, an audio endpoint . For playback, the application opens an endpoint stream, establishes its format and buffering, and supplies data at the pace the output consumes it. It sits after media retrieval and decoding in a typical PCM playback route. An Emby server can deliver an unchanged soundtrack while the Windows client uses WASAPI to send decoded samples to speakers, HDMI or a USB interface. The app's chosen output backend determines whether WASAPI is involved. Shared and exclusive streams In shared mode , streams participate in the Windows audio engine's shared route. This permits multiple applications to contribute audio to one output. The engine's mix format is an important boundary; a player's own decoded format can differ from it. In exclusive mode , the application requests direct use of the endpoint through the driver, bypassing the ordinary shared mixing stage. It must use a format the endpoint supports for that mode. Format support is a property of the endpoint and the sharing mode . A format accepted by the shared engine does not prove that the hardware accepts it in exclusive mode. WASAPI's format-support query and initialization result establish the chosen stream more precisely than the source file's codec label. A complete PCM format includes sample rate, channels and layout, valid precision and container representation. A 24-bit source can be delivered in a 32-bit container; source depth and output container size are not interchangeable. A 44.1 kHz file and a 48 kHz output A source containing 44,100 PCM sample frames for one second cannot simply be submitted as 44,100 frames of a 48 kHz stream and retain its duration. At that output rate, those frames occupy 0.91875 seconds . Correct conversion instead produces the appropriate 48,000-frame representation of the same second. Depending on the player and stream configuration, conversion can occur before submission or in a supported platform route. The format agreed with the API determines how the submitted frames are interpreted. This also distinguishes a shared mix format from an encoded transport format. A passthrough request uses a representation for supported coded audio; its carrier fields do not mean that the ordinary PCM mixer can treat the payload as amplitude samples. A refill cycle in sample frames The application fills an output buffer, while the engine or device consumes queued frames. WASAPI counts a PCM frame as one simultaneous sample for each channel. Suppose a shared-mode stream has an allocated buffer of 960 frames at 48 kHz . Its full capacity represents 20 ms . If a query reports 720 frames of padding —frames queued to play—then: available frames = buffer capacity − queued padding = 960 − 720 = 240 frames = 5 ms For stereo 32-bit float, each frame has eight bytes, so that refill is 1,920 bytes . Writing 960 new frames at this moment would exceed the available space. The player obtains a writable packet, fills it with prepared samples and releases it into the queue. Repeating that operation before the queue empties maintains continuous sound. The allocated capacity can differ from the requested capacity, so the calculation uses the returned value. A buffer's full capacity and its current queued amount also differ. Neither alone necessarily describes the entire delay through later driver, transport and device buffers. Keeping the producer ready An event-driven stream can notify the application when it should service the output. The real-time task is to deliver prepared data promptly. Waiting for a network fetch or a slow decoder operation inside that refill work risks an underrun. A separate producer queue lets retrieval and decoding prepare material ahead of the output deadline. Its depth trades responsiveness against tolerance of stalls. Event notification reduces the need for blind polling; it does not make a blocked thread run sooner. For audio/video synchronization, the player needs the relevant presentation position and timing, not just the number of bytes it has submitted. Data can have been handed to the API while still waiting to become audible. Controls and changes belong to defined boundaries Session volume, endpoint volume, player gain and device controls have different scopes. Shared mixing or supported processing can alter samples. Exclusive access removes one mixing stage, while bit-perfect playback requires the rest of the path to be examined too. Unplugging an output or reconfiguring its resources can invalidate the stream. The application then needs to reopen or select an appropriate endpoint and rebuild the required format and timing state. An HDMI display change, for example, can also change which output capabilities are available. A useful Windows playback trace records the selected endpoint, sharing mode, actual stream format, returned buffer size and any processing. That separates an unsupported format, a producer underrun and a route change—three events that can all appear to a listener as “the audio stopped.” See Also Exclusive-mode audio output Decoded PCM Output Bit-perfect playback Audio/Video Synchronization References Microsoft: WASAPI Microsoft: IAudioClient::IsFormatSupported Microsoft: Rendering a stream Microsoft: Exclusive-mode streams

articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/in.title: Overview: Operating-system audio APIs | Emby Learn
articles/audio/devices-output/os-apis/in.keywords: Overview: Operating-system audio APIs Operating-system audio APIs define how applications exchange audio with devices and system processing. WASAPI, Core Audio and the Linux audio interfaces below expose different routes from an application to playback hardware. A system can include several layers, so the API used by the player may feed another service before reaching a device. These pages explain those roles in the context of format handling, mixing and output access. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Windows Audio Session API (WASAPI) WASAPI lets Windows applications negotiate and feed endpoint audio streams using shared or exclusive access and explicit buffer accounting. Apple Core Audio Core Audio is Apple's collection of audio services for formats, conversion, processing, device access, and timed playback. ALSA ALSA supplies Linux audio driver interfaces and a PCM library with configurable device routes, sample formats, and ring-buffer timing. PulseAudio PulseAudio provides a sound-server interface that routes, mixes, buffers, and converts application streams for selected output sinks. PipeWire PipeWire routes media through a scheduled graph of nodes, ports, and links, with session policy and compatibility interfaces around that graph. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.title: Audio Codecs Explained | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.keywords: Audio Codecs Explained An audio codec defines how sound is encoded and reconstructed for storage or delivery. A player opens a movie, displays the picture, and cannot reproduce its soundtrack. The file reader has located the audio track, but the audio still needs a decoder that understands its coded representation . An audio codec defines that representation and its reconstruction. The same word also commonly names an encoder or decoder implementation. How compressed packets become audio samples For compressed audio, a stream consists of coded information rather than a literal number for every sample. Depending on the codec, it can describe frequency components, predictions, remaining errors, or other signal parameters. The decoder first needs configuration: which coding tools are used, the sample-rate arrangement, channel structure, and other format-specific details. It then interprets successive coded units and produces audio on a sample timeline. Information or component Job Container reader Locates track data and timing Codec configuration Describes how the coded audio should be interpreted Decoder Reconstructs the audio presentation Output processing Maps it to the listening system A container can provide configuration outside the individual audio packets. That is why copying one packet from a file does not necessarily make a complete independently playable recording. The encoder has decisions the decoder does not repeat A standard fixes what valid coded information means. Encoders can nevertheless differ in how they choose that information. They may spend more computation searching for a better prediction or allocate bits differently to minimize audible error. Two encoders can therefore produce different bitstreams from the same recording while one conforming decoder can reconstruct both. Improving an encoder does not necessarily require a new decoder if the encoded format remains within the same supported tools and constraints. With lossless compression , the choices affect storage efficiency and processing while preserving the represented source samples. With lossy compression , they also affect the approximation the decoder reconstructs. Identify the supported presentation precisely Codec families can contain variants requiring different tools. A basic AAC-LC decoder and an xHE-AAC decoder do different reconstruction jobs. Channel count, sample rate, and a supported profile can impose further implementation requirements. The surrounding package is another independent boundary. An M4A file can carry AAC or ALAC. Changing its extension does not change the coded audio, while changing the wrapper can sometimes solve an input-reader problem without making a new audio encoding. Repackaging, transcoding, or channel conversion? For an Emby session: If the audio codec is compatible but the wrapper is unsuitable, repackaging can preserve the coded sound. If the required reconstruction tools are unsupported, a decoder elsewhere in the path can reconstruct and re-encode a compatible presentation. If decoding succeeds but the listening system has fewer channels, layout conversion addresses the output arrangement. These solve different failures. A playback-path trace identifies which boundary changed, and whether the receiver gets coded audio for its own decoder or already reconstructed PCM. See Also Containers and Codecs Audio Bitrate The Audio Playback Path References Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ Xiph.Org: Vorbis I decoder specification and encoder freedom

articles/audio/formats/DSD.html.title: Direct Stream Digital (DSD) | Emby Learn
