The gain belongs to a reproduction stage With bitstream passthrough , the receiver can decode the Dolby stream and use its dialnorm information. When a player delivers decoded PCM , an earlier decoding or reproduction stage can have incorporated that gain. The volume selected by the listener is another factor in the final reproduction level. This is useful when comparing Emby routes that sound different at the same displayed volume. Establish where the Dolby stream was decoded and where metadata gain was applied. Applying the same −4 dB adjustment twice would produce −8 dB; ignoring it would leave the programme at its unadjusted reference. A receiver's codec label or an app's volume number alone does not identify either situation. See Also Dolby Digital (AC-3) Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) Loudness normalization Dynamic range compression References ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 ITU-R BS.1770-5: Programme loudness and true-peak measurement

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Dynamic range compression | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Dynamic range compression Dynamic range compression varies gain according to signal level and time to reduce level contrasts within an audio programme. Dynamic range compression changes the gain during a programme. Louder portions receive more gain reduction than quieter portions, according to the processor's settings. It can make a movie's dialogue and effects fit more comfortably into a limited listening level, or shape the impact of music. This is level processing. The “compression” in a codec such as AAC concerns representing audio with fewer data bits and is a different operation. Dynamic range describes the variation being controlled; loudness normalization often applies one constant gain to an entire programme. Threshold and ratio define the steady-state curve A downward compressor begins reducing gain above a threshold . Its ratio specifies how much a level rise above the threshold is reduced. At 4:1, a 4 dB input rise produces a 1 dB output rise once the signal is in the compressed region. For a hard-knee curve with threshold T and ratio R: below threshold: output level = input level above threshold: output level = T + (input level − T) / R Take T = −24 dBFS and R = 4 . An input level of −12 dBFS is 12 dB above threshold. Its output is −24 + 12/4 = −21 dBFS , a gain reduction of 9 dB . An input level of −30 dBFS remains −30 dBFS. A soft knee rounds the transition between the uncompressed and compressed slopes. The plotted example begins that transition 6 dB below the threshold and completes it 6 dB above. Knee definitions and parameter units vary between processors; the figure uses an explicitly defined 12 dB transition width. The curve shows steady-state detected levels, not an instantaneous rule applied independently to every positive and negative audio sample. Makeup gain moves the processed programme Compression on its own turns the louder portions down. Makeup gain raises the result afterward. In the example above, adding +6 dB gives: Detected input level Compressed level After +6 dB makeup Quiet portion: −30 dBFS −30 dBFS −24 dBFS Loud portion: −12 dBFS −21 dBFS −15 dBFS The original contrast was 18 dB . The new contrast is 9 dB . The quiet portion is now louder than before, while the loud portion is still lower. That combination is the mechanism behind many “night listening” styles of processing. Makeup gain is not automatically safe peak headroom. The static detector calculation does not include every transient, and attack behavior may let an initial peak pass. A limiter or a true-peak check serves another purpose. Attack and release decide how the gain moves The detector estimates a changing signal level. Attack governs the move toward greater reduction when that level rises. Release governs recovery when it falls. These parameters influence the sound as much as the static ratio. This teaching model smooths gain reduction with a 20 ms attack time constant and a 120 ms release time constant. A time constant is not a waiting period followed by an abrupt switch: after one time constant, a first-order response has traveled about 63% of the way toward its new value. Real processors can define their timing differently and can use adaptive behavior. A slower attack can retain the onset of a drum or effect. A very fast attack controls that onset more firmly. A release that is too slow for the material can keep the next quiet phrase suppressed; one that recovers very quickly can make the background audibly swell between louder events. Lookahead can provide advance knowledge of an upcoming peak by adding a delay to the signal being processed. What the detector listens to A peak detector responds to short excursions; an RMS-style detector responds to energy over a window. A sidechain can feed the detector from another signal or from a filtered version of the same signal. These choices determine when the compressor reacts, while the gain stage changes the programme being heard. For stereo or surround content, channels can share a gain decision. Linking helps a sound stay in the same apparent location when it becomes loud in one channel. Independent reduction can change the left/right balance or the relationship between dialogue and other channels. The linked detector's method also matters; a maximum-channel detector and an averaged detector will not react identically. An effect can turn down the dialogue around it Consider a linked soundtrack whose detector reacts strongly to an effect. Its gain reduction can also attenuate dialogue that overlaps that effect. Release may keep the following dialogue reduced for a while after the effect has ended. This is a concrete reason to inspect the detector and timing rather than assuming “more compression” always improves speech. A broadband compressor has no understanding of a speaker's words. Different sidechain weighting, separate processing before a mix, or a designed dialogue-enhancement process can produce different results. The order of fixed gain and compression also matters. Raising the input by 6 dB before a fixed threshold pushes more material into reduction. Raising the output by 6 dB afterward leaves the detector's decision unchanged. Two controls both labeled “gain” can therefore produce different dynamics depending on their position. Where compression enters a playback route A movie can carry recommended dynamic treatment in codec metadata, or a player or receiver can run its own signal processor. The applied result depends on the decoded or passed-through route, selected mode, and device. For Emby, identify the active audio track and where decoding occurs before interpreting a receiver's dynamic setting. A bitstream route can leave decoding and associated metadata treatment to the receiving device. A PCM route may have already applied processing upstream. If the goal is hearing dialogue more easily, compression works on the level contrast. Dialogue normalization instead supplies a programme gain reference. A missing or misrouted centre channel calls for checking channel layout and downmixing , because reducing dynamics does not restore dialogue that never reached the intended output. See Also Audio Dynamic Range Loudness normalization Dialogue normalization (dialnorm) Audio Clipping References FFmpeg compressor source and controls FFmpeg audio filter documentation ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Loudness normalization | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Loudness normalization Loudness normalization chooses gain from a programme measurement while accounting for the peak headroom and the intended playback target. Loudness normalization reduces level jumps between programmes by measuring each programme and choosing a gain that brings it toward a common target. With constant gain , every part of the programme is scaled by the same amount. A quiet verse stays quieter than its chorus. That is different from peak normalization, which aligns the highest peak, and from dynamic range compression , which changes gain as the programme develops. Calculating the adjustment For a programme measured in LUFS , the initial calculation is: gain in dB = target loudness − measured loudness amplitude multiplier = 10^(gain / 20) A measurement of −18 LUFS and a target of −23 LUFS give −5 dB , or an amplitude multiplier of approximately 0.562 . This reduces both the average level and the peaks by 5 dB. The −23 LUFS target is the EBU R 128 broadcast reference used for this example. Playback systems can select another target. The target must be identified along with the measurement method; it is not a universal Emby setting. Constant gain usually shifts the integrated value by the same number of decibels. A material change in which blocks cross the meter's absolute gate can alter that simple relationship, so processed output still merits measurement when an exact result matters. A target and a peak ceiling can disagree Suppose the output has a chosen true-peak ceiling of −1 dBTP , also matching the EBU production example for linear audio. Programme Measured loudness Measured true peak Gain to −23 LUFS Predicted peak A −18 LUFS −1 dBTP −5 dB −6 dBTP B −26 LUFS −2 dBTP +3 dB +1 dBTP A can simply be turned down. B would exceed the ceiling by 2 dB if the full +3 dB were applied. With constant gain alone, B can receive only +1 dB before reaching −1 dBTP. Its resulting loudness is approximately −25 LUFS , short of the target. This is a valid outcome: a programme with prominent transients can remain quieter when the workflow preserves those transients. A limiter could control the peaks and permit more gain. That would be a different processing choice, changing the waveform and potentially its dynamics. Some tools combine loudness targeting with dynamic processing; the label “normalization” by itself does not establish which approach was used. For a playlist, lowering the target can make constant-gain matching possible for more tracks. For a movie, retaining more peak headroom may be preferable to repeatedly constraining effects. The practical choice follows the listening purpose. The gain can live in metadata or in new samples A scanner can store a measurement and recommended gain while leaving the media's samples intact. ReplayGain is one example. A supporting player reads that information and applies the gain during playback. Another player may ignore it or select a different track/album policy. Alternatively, an offline process can multiply decoded samples, then store a new PCM or encoded file. That changes the media. Re-encoding to a lossy format also adds a new codec generation; merely writing a gain tag does not. The distinction makes a useful Emby test concrete. Determine whether the selected app reads a tag, whether a server conversion applies gain, and whether the operating system or receiving device adds another level process. Support for a tag in a library scanner does not automatically imply that every playback route applies it. The analyzed programme must match the delivered one Channel conversion and track selection can change the loudness being reproduced. For example, adding a centre channel into a stereo downmix produces a new combination of signals; the original multichannel measurement does not directly describe that result. A robust processing workflow therefore analyzes the intended programme, chooses the gain and peak policy, applies the processing, and checks the delivered output. In an offline workflow, analysis of the complete programme can inform one constant gain from its first sample. A live process has only the signal seen so far unless measurements arrive in advance. See Also LUFS loudness measurement ReplayGain Dynamic range compression Audio Clipping References EBU R 128-2023: Loudness normalization ITU-R BS.1770-5: Programme loudness and true-peak measurement FFmpeg audio filter documentation Revised ReplayGain specification

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: LUFS loudness measurement | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: LUFS loudness measurement LUFS expresses standardized programme loudness using frequency weighting, channel energy, measurement windows, and level gating. LUFS means Loudness Units relative to Full Scale . It expresses a digital audio programme's loudness using a specified measurement method. LKFS , the term used in ITU-R BS.1770, describes the equivalent scale. A change of 1 LU corresponds to a change of 1 dB in the measured loudness level. For example, −18 LUFS is 5 LU above −23 LUFS. Under ordinary conditions, applying −5 dB of constant gain brings that programme close to −23 LUFS. The number is a programme-level reference, not the sound pressure at the listener's seat. A LUFS meter is doing more than averaging waveform height. Its operations explain why two tools need to agree on measurement mode, channel interpretation and programme boundaries before their results can be compared. Filtering and combining channel energy ITU-R BS.1770 applies K weighting before measuring mean squared signal energy. Its two filter stages alter the contribution of different frequencies: a shelving stage models part of the head's acoustic effect, followed by a high-pass weighting stage. These are measurement filters; measuring a file does not apply their sound to the file being played. For the conventional layout with front left, front right, centre and two surround channels, the channel energies are then summed with defined weights. The three front channels have weight 1; the surrounds have weight 1.41, about +1.5 dB in power. The LFE channel is excluded from this loudness calculation. That exclusion does not remove bass from playback. Larger layouts and object-based material require the corresponding extensions of the recommendation rather than applying this five-channel table indiscriminately. For one block, the basic level calculation is: L = −0.691 + 10 log10(E) E = sum of the weighted mean-square channel energies The calibration constant is part of the specified method. A generic RMS reading without K weighting and channel weighting cannot simply be relabeled LUFS. Channel count changes the summed energy Take a block whose post-filter energy is 0.01 in just the centre channel. With weight 1, E is 0.01 and its level is −20.691 LUFS . Now suppose the same energy is present in both front left and front right. The sum is 0.02, giving −17.681 LUFS , approximately 3.01 LU higher. This follows from doubling power, not from adding two amplitude waveforms into one channel. For one conventional surround channel with energy 0.01, the weight 1.41 gives E = 0.0141 and a level of approximately −19.199 LUFS . These examples concern one measurement block before integrated gating. They show why channel roles and layout must be known rather than inferred from channel count alone. A meter combines measured channel energies; a stereo downmix combines the signals themselves before measuring them. In-phase components can reinforce in a mix and opposite-phase components can cancel. That is another reason a multichannel LUFS reading cannot simply be assigned to its stereo conversion. Integrated loudness uses two gates A whole movie can contain very quiet passages, music, dialogue and long intervals near silence. If every second contributed equally to an ungated average, extending a silent ending could substantially lower the result without making the audible scenes quieter. The integrated measurement evaluates 400 ms blocks , with 75% overlap , so a new block begins every 100 ms. It excludes blocks below an absolute threshold of −70 LKFS . It then calculates an energy mean from the surviving blocks and sets a relative threshold 10 LU below that intermediate level . The final result averages the blocks above both thresholds. The arithmetic averages energies , then converts the mean to a logarithmic level. Averaging decibel numbers would produce a different answer. Four block energies, step by step To make the gates visible, take four illustrative block energies after frequency and channel weighting. This example starts at the energy stage; it is not a simulated PCM recording or a meter compliance test. Block Weighted energy Block loudness Absolute gate Final relative gate A 0.1 −10.691 LUFS Included Included B 0.01 −20.691 LUFS Included Included C 0.001 −30.691 LUFS Included Excluded D 0.00000001 −80.691 LUFS Excluded Excluded The absolute gate leaves A, B and C. Their mean energy is: (0.1 + 0.01 + 0.001) / 3 = 0.037 intermediate level = −0.691 + 10 log10(0.037) ≈ −15.009 LUFS relative threshold = −15.009 − 10 ≈ −25.009 LUFS C is below that relative threshold. A and B remain, with mean energy (0.1 + 0.01)/2 = 0.055 . The final integrated value is therefore approximately −13.287 LUFS . An arithmetic average of A and B's decibel readings would be −15.691 LUFS, which is not the correct energy average. The louder block contributes considerably more energy. The relative gate is based on the absolute-gated intermediate result. It is not an endlessly repeated procedure that keeps recalculating the threshold until no more blocks disappear. Three time views of the programme An EBU Mode meter provides several readings using the same underlying loudness framework: Reading Time basis Useful question Momentary, M 400 ms How strong is this brief phrase or event? Short-term, S 3 s How is a scene or musical passage developing? Integrated, I The selected measurement interval, with level gating What is the overall programme loudness? A whole-file integrated value and an integrated value reset halfway through the file are measurements of different intervals. Momentary and short-term readings do not apply the integrated measurement's two-gate procedure. For an Emby playback investigation, measure the actual stream being compared. A downmix , alternate audio track, or processed transcode may differ from the source's original multichannel programme. A file's recorded analysis value also cannot reveal a later device volume adjustment. True peak measures another property Samples describe a band-limited waveform at discrete instants. The reconstructed waveform can reach a larger value between those instants. A true-peak meter estimates that behavior by interpolation. The figure uses an ideal 12 kHz sine sampled at 48 kHz, with continuous peak amplitude 1.08 and a 45-degree sampling phase. Its stored magnitudes are about 0.764 , or −2.34 dBFS sample peak. Its continuous peak is +0.67 dBTP . This is a mathematical illustration; practical meters have defined interpolation accuracy and practical converters have their own reconstruction behavior. See Also Audio loudness Loudness normalization Audio Dynamic Range References ITU-R BS.1770-5: Programme loudness and true-peak measurement EBU Tech 3341-2023: EBU Mode metering EBU R 128-2023: Loudness normalization

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: ReplayGain | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: ReplayGain ReplayGain stores recommended track and album playback gains so supporting players can match listening levels without rewriting the audio. ReplayGain separates a loudness decision from the stored audio. Analysis supplies recommended gains; metadata stores them; a supporting player decides which gain to apply. The file can retain its original samples while playback becomes more consistent across a collection. The familiar tags come in two pairs: Tag Meaning REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_GAIN Recommended gain for this track considered individually REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_GAIN Recommended common gain for the album REPLAYGAIN_TRACK_PEAK Track sample-peak amplitude, conventionally relative to full scale REPLAYGAIN_ALBUM_PEAK Highest such peak in the album Gain is usually represented in decibels, such as -4.20 dB . A peak value such as 0.98 is an amplitude ratio, not −0.98 dB and not a LUFS measurement. Encoded formats can produce decoded peaks beyond 1.0, so “peak” must be interpreted in the signal domain used by the scanner. Track mode for a mix; album mode for an album Track mode tries to match each song independently. That suits a shuffled collection where the previous song may come from a completely different recording. Album mode applies the same gain to every track in the album. This preserves intentional contrasts between movements, interludes and songs. The album measurement is derived from the combined programme; it is not simply the arithmetic average of the individual gain tags. Imagine an album whose quiet interlude measures −25 LUFS and whose main song measures −17 LUFS. Using an illustrative −18 LUFS reference: Playback policy Interlude gain Main song gain Resulting contrast Individual track matching +7 dB −1 dB Both approach −18 LUFS Common album gain of −2 dB −2 dB −2 dB The original 8 LU difference remains The album gain of −2 dB here is supplied for illustration, not derived by averaging those two readings. Their durations and weighted signal energies affect the album analysis. A player may also limit positive gain to accommodate peaks. The reference convention matters The original ReplayGain proposal uses a perceptual analysis and a calibrated reference based on its original pink-noise model. The revised specification uses a BS.1770-based loudness measurement with a −18 LUFS reference. Existing collections and scanners do not all use the same generation of analysis. A stored gain is already the scanner's recommendation. A player must not treat the decibel tag as the track's measured LUFS value and subtract it from a target again. Scanner version and analysis settings explain why rescanning the same collection can change the tags. The original acoustic calibration is also not a command to set a home system to a particular sound pressure. The listener retains control of the reproduction volume. What happens at playback For a gain of −4 dB, the sample multiplier is 10^(−4/20), approximately 0.631 . A sample amplitude of 0.5 becomes about 0.315 . This is ordinary signal gain, so it changes the PCM values heard by the device even though the file on disk remains unchanged. A player's preamp setting can add to the tag gain. Peak protection can reduce the total gain further. Consequently, inspecting the tag alone does not establish the final level. In an Emby comparison, check the behavior of the specific app and route: whether it reads the tags, selects track or album mode, applies a preamp, and changes policy during shuffle. The tags describe an available playback instruction; the selected implementation determines whether that instruction becomes signal processing. See Also Loudness normalization LUFS loudness measurement Bit-perfect playback References Revised ReplayGain specification Original ReplayGain proposal: Calculation Original ReplayGain proposal: Player scaling

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Overview: Loudness measurement and control | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Overview: Loudness measurement and control Loudness measurement and control use different methods to describe or adjust programme level and dynamic behavior. LUFS measures programme loudness under a defined model. Normalization and ReplayGain use level information for playback decisions, while dynamic-range compression changes the relationship among louder and quieter passages. Dialogue normalization adds another metadata convention. The links below distinguish measurement, metadata and actual signal processing. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> LUFS loudness measurement LUFS expresses standardized programme loudness using frequency weighting, channel energy, measurement windows, and level gating. Loudness normalization Loudness normalization chooses gain from a programme measurement while accounting for the peak headroom and the intended playback target. ReplayGain ReplayGain stores recommended track and album playback gains so supporting players can match listening levels without rewriting the audio. Dynamic range compression Dynamic range compression varies gain according to signal level and time to reduce level contrasts within an audio programme. Dialogue normalization (dialnorm) Dialnorm metadata describes a Dolby programme's dialogue reference level so the reproduction system can choose a corresponding gain. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-R BS.1770-5: Programme loudness and true-peak measurement EBU R 128-2023: Loudness normalization ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Bit-perfect playback | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Bit-perfect playback Bit-perfect playback preserves a defined decoded sample sequence through a specified part of the audio output path. “Bit-perfect” is meaningful when it names a reference sample sequence and an output boundary . For a lossless music file, a useful claim is that the decoded PCM sample values reach a particular digital output unchanged, with the same channel order, sample rate and intended sample count. The compressed file bytes are not the reference PCM. A FLAC file can be decoded to WAV with different file bytes while preserving every audio sample. Comparing the hashes of those two files would answer the wrong question. Identical values can have different packing Digital interfaces need not use the same sample container as the source. A 16-bit value can be represented exactly in a 24-bit signal domain by scaling its integer representation by 256, leaving eight low bits zero. Signed 16-bit integer Corresponding signed 24-bit integer Normalized amplitude −32,768 −8,388,608 −1 −1 −256 −1/32,768 0 0 0 1 256 1/32,768 32,767 8,388,352 32,767/32,768 Dividing the second column by 256 recovers the first exactly. The raw byte streams differ, but the represented amplitudes agree. A comparison therefore has to account for valid-bit alignment, container size, byte order and interleaving. Similarly, converting ordinary signed 24-bit PCM into normalized 32-bit floating point can represent those values exactly. The presence of a floating-point buffer does not by itself prove a loss of precision. Subsequent processing and conversion determine what reaches the output. If a test requires literal byte identity in one specific PCM format, it should say so. That stricter claim differs from preserving the same sample values through reversible repacking. Operations that change the sequence A gain other than unity changes sample amplitudes. ReplayGain , an equalizer, a downmix, spatial rendering or a limiter also changes the sequence. Resampling computes values on a different time grid. Dither intentionally adds noise during a precision reduction. Those processes can serve a useful playback purpose. A result can sound appropriate without satisfying the preservation claim. Conversely, an unchanged sequence can still be delivered late, to the wrong speaker, or into a reproduction system with a problem. For a lossy file, the decoder's PCM output can be the stated reference for an output-path test. That does not mean the codec has recovered the exact pre-encoding samples. The claim begins after that particular decode. Exclusive access narrows the route Exclusive-mode output can bypass an operating system's shared mixing stage. It makes one class of sample modification easier to avoid, but it does not disable every player filter, driver process or device DSP. Shared access can also preserve a particular stream under suitable conditions: matching formats, unity gain, no additional contributing audio and no modifying processing. Whether those conditions hold must be established on the actual route. The mode name alone is insufficient evidence in either direction. An Emby server's Direct Play status concerns media delivery. A client can receive the original FLAC file, decode it accurately, and then apply volume or resampling. Server-side retention and client-side sample preservation are different observations. A useful verification boundary A digital capture at the output boundary can be decoded into a common comparison format, aligned in time, and compared against the reference PCM. Alignment should account for a fixed delay without silently deleting different audio. The check should preserve sample rate, channel identity and count, and report any nonzero differences. An analog recording after a DAC adds the behavior of converters, clocks and noise; it cannot establish literal digital sample identity. A device that receives special encoded data may offer its own recognition test, but that is a test of that supported route rather than a general listening judgment. State the boundary with the result: for example, “decoded 16-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo values preserved to the captured digital output after reversible 24-bit packing.” That description tells a reader exactly what was established. See Also PCM Sample Formats Exclusive-mode audio output Audio Resampling Decoded PCM Output References Microsoft: WASAPI Microsoft: Exclusive-mode streams Apple: Core Audio Essentials Analog Devices MT-001: Converter SNR and quantization

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Audio encoder delay | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Audio encoder delay Encoder delay and end padding are extra decoded frames introduced by codec processing and block alignment that need correct timing and trim information. An audio encoder does not always turn the first input sample into the first sample that a decoder returns. Analysis windows, filter history, lookahead and resampling can introduce priming before the intended programme. A block-based codec may also need to fill its final block, producing padding after the intended end. The file therefore needs enough information to distinguish the decoded representation from the original programme interval. Otherwise, a player can add a pause between tracks or place the start of audio at the wrong time. Stored duration and intended duration For an illustrative codec that returns 1,024 PCM sample frames per block, suppose the intended programme contains 10,000 frames and its signaled leading trim is 1,024 frames . The combined length so far is 11,024. Eleven complete blocks contain 11,264 frames , so the final block needs another 240 frames of padding. decoded total = priming + intended programme + end padding 11,264 = 1,024 + 10,000 + 240 At 48 kHz, the intended programme lasts 208.333 ms . The full decoded representation lasts 234.667 ms . The difference is codec-related framing, not additional music. The actual priming count must come from the codec and file's timing information. A block length of 1,024 does not prove that a real AAC encoder's delay is 1,024; an implementation can introduce a different count, including one that is not a whole number of blocks. Formats describe trimming differently CAF's packet-table information can record valid , priming and remainder frame counts. These explicitly identify the programme interval within the decoded result. Ogg Opus uses a pre-skip value at the beginning of the stream and granule-position rules for the ending. Its time count uses a 48 kHz clock per channel , regardless of the original input rate stored in the header. A pre-skip value of 312, for example, represents 6.5 ms on that clock. It is an example value, not a rule that all Opus streams use 312. The player decodes the required initial material and discards the pre-skip output. It also respects the declared final position. Stereo does not double the time count: 312 simultaneous left/right sample frames still occupy 6.5 ms. Trim information can be carried by a container, codec-specific fields or associated metadata. A decoder's block count alone cannot determine the intended end if the final block is partly padding. Detecting runs of zeros is also unreliable: useful audio can contain silence, and priming output can contain nonzero values. Start trimming, seeking and device latency At a seek point, some codecs need earlier data to rebuild state before producing accurate samples at the requested time. Ogg Opus specifies pre-roll for this purpose. It is distinct from the stream's initial pre-skip. Reapplying the original leading trim at every arbitrary seek would confuse two different positions in the programme. Device latency comes later. Output buffers, a Bluetooth link and a DAC can delay when valid samples become audible. Removing codec priming does not remove those buffers. Conversely, changing an audio/video offset does not tell a player which trailing samples belong to the programme. For a converted Emby stream, timing and duration need to reflect the new encoder's representation. Copying an old delay value into a differently encoded result can trim real audio or expose new padding. In gapless playback , correct trim counts define the boundary; preparation and output scheduling then make that boundary continuous. See Also Gapless playback AAC-LC Audio Opus Audio Audio/Video Synchronization References RFC 7845: Ogg Opus encapsulation Apple Core Audio Format specification: Packet table

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Gapless playback | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Gapless playback Gapless playback joins the intended audio of adjacent tracks without inserting a player-created pause or replaying codec padding. A live concert, a classical movement split into tracks, or an album with continuous transitions should not acquire a little pause at every file boundary. Gapless playback presents the last intended sample frame of one track immediately before the first intended frame of the next. It has two jobs: identify the intended audio accurately, and have the next track ready before the output runs out of data. Solving only one still permits a gap. The boundary in sample frames A PCM sample frame contains one simultaneous sample for each channel. At 48 kHz, each frame occupies 1/48000 second whether the signal is mono or stereo. Consider two tracks encoded with an illustrative block codec: Region in each decoded track Frames at 48 kHz Time Leading priming to discard 1,024 21.333 ms Intended programme to keep 10,000 208.333 ms Trailing padding to discard 240 5.000 ms Each decoded representation contains 11,264 frames , exactly eleven blocks of 1,024. These counts illustrate the arithmetic; they are not universal values for AAC or any other codec. Joining the raw decoded output would place A's 240 padding frames and B's 1,024 priming frames between their intended programmes: 1,264 frames , or about 26.333 ms . Those regions need not be literal zeros to be unwanted at the boundary. Using the signaled trim counts, the player keeps frames 1,024 through 11,023 from each decoded representation. The resulting output is A's 10,000 intended frames followed directly by B's 10,000 intended frames. Encoder delay explains why these extra regions exist and how formats identify them. The next decoder must be ready in time A player often needs to open the next file, obtain its headers, create or prime a decoder, trim its initial output, and prepare the first samples while the current track is still playing. Network retrieval may also need to happen in advance. At the boundary, the output stream can then continue with the next programme instead of stopping, draining, reinitializing and starting again. Equal output sample rate and channel layout make this simpler. A format change may require conversion into a continuing common output format, or a device reconfiguration whose delay must be handled. For an Emby route, the relevant behavior belongs to the selected app and delivered stream. A server can supply valid files while the app still waits until track A has ended before requesting B. Conversely, timely prefetch cannot repair trim information that was lost in a conversion. Intentional silence stays; crossfade overlaps Gapless playback preserves the programme's own timing. If a composer or mastering engineer placed a two-second pause within the intended samples, those two seconds remain. Automatically deleting quiet samples changes the programme and can remove a fade or a deliberate pause. A crossfade is a different operation: the end of A and the start of B are played simultaneously for an overlap interval, usually with changing gains. That can suit shuffled music, but it changes the transition of a continuous album. To test a route, use material with a known continuous boundary and compare the joined intended output. A gap can come from leftover padding, a late next-track request, a stopped output stream or a device format change. Identifying which event occurs makes the result explainable rather than reducing it to a file-extension guess. See Also Audio encoder delay The Audio Playback Path ReplayGain References RFC 7845: Ogg Opus encapsulation Apple Core Audio Format specification: Packet table Apple: Core Audio Essentials

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Playback speed and audio pitch | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Playback speed and audio pitch Playback speed can alter both duration and pitch, while time-scale processing changes duration while largely preserving the original pitch. A 60-second passage played at 1.25× lasts 48 seconds . What happens to its pitch depends on how that speed change is produced. If the original waveform is simply traversed faster, every oscillation also happens faster. A 440 Hz tone becomes 550 Hz . Pitch-preserving time-scale processing instead changes the duration while keeping that tone near 440 Hz. Speed factor Duration of a 60 s passage Tone with ordinary rate change Tone with ideal pitch preservation 0.8× 75 s 352 Hz 440 Hz 1.0× 60 s 440 Hz 440 Hz 1.25× 48 s 550 Hz 440 Hz 2.0× 30 s 880 Hz 440 Hz These are mathematical values. A practical pitch-preserving processor can introduce artifacts whose character depends on the material and algorithm. Compressing the entire time axis changes pitch For ordinary rate change, the output samples a waveform described by y(t) = x(s × t) , where s is the speed factor. At s = 1.25, a second of output covers 1.25 seconds of the source. The waveform's cycles are squeezed into less time. The pitch change in semitones is 12 × log₂(s). At 1.25× it is approximately 3.863 semitones ; at 2× it is one octave. This can be implemented while still sending the device its normal output rate. The player computes a faster traversal into that fixed-rate output stream. Changing a file's declared sample rate without recalculating its samples is another way to change their interpretation in time. Ordinary sample-rate conversion has a different goal: represent the same-duration waveform on another sample grid. Converting 44.1 kHz material correctly to 48 kHz preserves its duration and pitch. Keeping local cycles while changing the sequence One family of time-scale methods divides audio into overlapping windows, selects suitable positions in the input, and blends the windows at different spacing in the output. The waveform inside a window keeps its original local oscillations; the sequence advances through the programme at a new pace. For an illustrative 1.25× process, input window starts can advance 12.5 ms for each 10 ms output advance. Over 48 seconds of output, those advances cover 60 seconds of source. The implementation searches for compatible waveforms near candidate joins, then blends the overlap to avoid abrupt discontinuities. FFmpeg's atempo implementation uses WSOLA, a waveform-similarity overlap method. Other processors use frequency-domain methods such as phase vocoders. Their internal window and alignment choices are not specified by the speed factor alone. Speech, sustained music and sharp attacks present different problems. A long tonal window gives useful periodic information; a short transient benefits from retaining its time shape. Independently choosing joins for left and right channels can disturb stereo relationships, so multichannel processing needs coordinated treatment. The movie uses the same new clock For faster video playback, picture presentation times must advance at the corresponding rate. The audio processor may need an internal lookahead or startup buffer, which the player must incorporate into its synchronization. In an Emby app, a speed control therefore involves more than changing how many audio packets are fetched. The selected player has to produce the required audio, schedule pictures on the new timeline, and keep its buffer/clock accounting consistent. A voice that rises in pitch and a voice that stays natural can both accompany 1.25× playback; they reveal different signal processing. See Also Audio Resampling Audio Sample Rate Audio/Video Synchronization References FFmpeg 8.1 tempo filter source FFmpeg audio filter documentation Apple: Core Audio Essentials

articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.title: Overview: Music playback behavior | Emby Learn
articles/audio/loudness-music-playback/m.keywords: Overview: Music playback behavior Music-playback behavior includes track continuity, codec delay, sample preservation and the relationship between speed and pitch. A brief gap between songs can arise from timing or encoder-delay handling even when both tracks decode correctly. Other questions concern whether samples change before output or how a speed change affects pitch. These pages focus on the boundaries between stored tracks and the continuous signal the listener hears. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Gapless playback Gapless playback joins the intended audio of adjacent tracks without inserting a player-created pause or replaying codec padding. Audio encoder delay Encoder delay and end padding are extra decoded frames introduced by codec processing and block alignment that need correct timing and trim information. Bit-perfect playback Bit-perfect playback preserves a defined decoded sample sequence through a specified part of the audio output path. Playback speed and audio pitch Playback speed can alter both duration and pitch, while time-scale processing changes duration while largely preserving the original pitch. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.title: Understanding Audio in Media | Emby Learn
articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.keywords: Understanding Audio in Media Audio tracks combine encoded sound with timing, channel information, and playback instructions. A movie has three English soundtracks: 7.1 surround, stereo commentary, and audio description. Which one should you select? Start with what the track contains , then consider how it will play on your listening system. The most impressive channel count is irrelevant if you have selected the director discussing the film instead of the film's dialogue. Language, codec, channels, and the selected presentation Each audio track is a separate timed stream in the media file. Its language, title, and accessibility role help identify the intended presentation. Its codec and channel layout describe how that presentation is represented. Part of an example track The question it answers English — Main Is this the language and presentation I want? E-AC-3 Which decoding format is required? 5.1 Which channel roles are in the compatible channel presentation? 48 kHz What sample timeline does decoded audio use? 640 kbit/s How much encoded audio data is carried per second? Those numbers are not different ways of expressing one quality setting. Changing 5.1 to stereo combines spatial channels. Changing 48 kHz to another sample rate changes the time grid. Changing the encoded bitrate gives a compressed-audio encoder a different data budget. Each operation solves a different problem. A container keeps the tracks together with timing and metadata. That is how a viewer can switch language or commentary while the video remains the same. The selected soundtrack must stay aligned with the picture even when its packets and video packets represent different amounts of time. 5.1 audio on a stereo television Suppose you choose the 5.1 film track and listen on a stereo television: Emby selects that track for delivery. If its codec and packaging fit the app, the server may send the stored audio. A decoder reconstructs audio samples for the track's channels. This might happen in the player or during server conversion. A downmix combines those channels into two outputs, including center-channel dialogue that would be lost by simply discarding all but front left and right. The television converts the final signal into sound. On a compatible surround system, the same track can instead keep its separate channel presentation. An object-based soundtrack can additionally supply spatial information that a renderer uses for the connected speaker or headphone arrangement. This is why the source format, Emby's delivery method , and a receiver's input display can have different labels. “PCM” at the receiver can mean that decoding already happened in the player. “Stereo” can describe the final output even though the stored soundtrack has six channels. Use sampling to understand the numbers representing sound, channels to understand its spatial arrangement, or the playback path to locate a conversion between the file and what you hear. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Bitrate Multichannel Audio References ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/automation/api/Automation-API.h.title: Media server APIs and programmable operations | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/Automation-API.h.keywords: Media server APIs and programmable operations A media server API exposes documented operations and data so another program can query or control supported server behavior. A media server API lets software request operations from the server: query a library, inspect sessions or invoke a supported action. The server receives a structured request and returns a result under the operation's documented contract. An Emby app uses such operations to build its interface. An external integration can use documented operations for its own workflow without reproducing the app's entire screen. The contract makes the operation interpretable Contract detail What the caller needs to know Endpoint and method Which operation is requested Parameters and body What inputs the operation accepts Authentication and policy Which identity can request it Response fields and status How the result is represented Version behavior Which documented combination is supported A visible button is a user-interface affordance, not a complete API contract. The operation behind it may need identity, fields or a sequence that is absent from the button's label. Likewise, a JSON response is a public representation. It does not specify which internal database table stores the information. The integration owns the next step A library query returns information for the caller to interpret. If the caller then sends a notification, that notification is another operation in another system. A state-changing API request can also have an uncertain result when its response is lost. The caller needs the documented operation semantics to decide whether checking state or retrying is appropriate. For a small integration, first identify the supported operation and the specific result it needs. Authentication, pagination and delivery behavior then have concrete roles rather than being incidental connection settings. Emby's library-browsing contract is an example of a documented starting point. Plugin architecture describes a different arrangement where extension code participates inside the server process. See Also HTTP API requests and interpretable responses API authentication tokens and request identity Integration permissions and effective operations References Emby server API documentation Emby browsing the library RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/api/Automation-Rate-.title: API rate limits and respectful request scheduling | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/Automation-Rate-.keywords: API rate limits and respectful request scheduling API rate limits bound request activity within a defined scope and interval, so clients need to coordinate polling and retry timing. A rate limit bounds activity such as requests per interval. Its scope might be an identity, endpoint, source address or shared service. Different limit mechanisms can also allow different short bursts. The HTTP standard defines a 429 response for excessive request rate. It does not prescribe one universal numeric limit for every Emby endpoint or deployment. Several small clients add up An original monitoring example has twelve clients, each making one request every five seconds: Per client: 60 / 5 = 12 requests/minute Combined: 12 clients × 12 = 144 requests/minute A single client looks quiet, but the shared service sees the combined demand. Pagination, retries and other background queries add to that total. Design choice Effect on request demand Shorter polling interval More frequent observations and more requests More simultaneous clients More aggregate work Repeating failed requests immediately Can intensify the condition Reusing an applicable result Can avoid duplicate queries Staggering observations Can reduce synchronized bursts Caching must still respect user, query and freshness context. A 429 response provides a particular observation An original response fragment is: HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: 30 The declared value requests a thirty-second wait before another applicable attempt. Retry-After can also use an HTTP-date. Its interpretation needs the response and server contract. The header is optional under the 429 specification. Its absence does not make an immediate unlimited retry loop appropriate. Not every wait is a rate limit A timeout can come from connectivity, a busy database or a slow operation. An HTTP error can have another meaning. Identify the actual status and evidence before choosing a rate-limit response. A client can use bounded backoff with jitter for applicable transient failures, while keeping retry semantics tied to the operation. Repeating a state-changing action needs more than a delay; it needs a safe completion and duplication policy. For an Emby integration, inspect the documented operation and any gateway or deployment rules involved. The rate example explains demand arithmetic rather than asserting a fixed Emby-wide allowance. See Also Polling for updates and observation intervals Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing API pagination and changing result sets References RFC 6585: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/api/Automation-Sessi.title: Playback sessions and current player state | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/Automation-Sessi.keywords: Playback sessions and current player state A playback session describes a current client relationship and player state, distinct from the user, device label and media item involved. A playback session describes a current relationship between a media server and a client, including the player state available through the relevant contract. It is different from the user account and from the media item. One user can be active on more than one client, and the same film can be playing in more than one session. Identify the session before interpreting the state An original normalized integration view is: [ {"session": "S1", "user": "U1", "device": "TV-A", "item": "M1", "paused": false}, {"session": "S2", "user": "U1", "device": "Phone-B", "item": "M1", "paused": true} ] The example uses adapter field names. Emby's session API supplies its documented session objects and player fields. Selecting by user U1 or item M1 alone cannot determine which player the integration intends to control. A session observation has an age Observation What it does not guarantee Session appeared in a query It remains connected at the next operation Last position was reported The player is still at that exact point Device label matches That label alone authenticates the device A control request was accepted The desired physical or player effect has completed The session disappears A complete explanation of why it ended Connection loss, reconnects and lifecycle behavior can change session identity or availability. Use the contract's identifiers rather than assuming a display name is a permanent unique key. Current state and history have different jobs A session helps inspect what a player is doing now. User playback history records application state across completed observations and sessions. A room automation should relate the intended client or session to that room, then decide how playing, paused, stopped and unavailable states affect its policy. Treating every session for one user as the television's state can let phone activity change the wrong room. See Also Playback events and dependable home automation Polling for updates and observation intervals User-specific playback history References Emby session API Emby user authentication

articles/automation/api/credentials/Auto.title: API keys for server integrations | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/credentials/Auto.keywords: API keys for server integrations An API key is a static credential for a documented integration context, allowing access to be tracked and revoked separately from other integrations. Emby's API-key authentication supplies a static token for integrations that are not tied to one user's login context. A named key lets the server administrator associate that credential with a particular external application or service. That name describes intended use. The secret value provides the request evidence. Separate integrations need separate revocation boundaries Integration Original credential relationship Library-report service Key K1 Home-automation adapter Key K2 Another application Key K3 The labels are fictional. If K2 must be revoked, K1 and K3 can retain their own credentials. Sharing one key across all three would make the revocation boundary much broader. This is the reason Emby's documentation recommends a separate API key for each system granted access. The key accompanies applicable requests The documented X-Emby-Token header can carry the key. A query parameter is also documented, but a value placed in a URL can appear in URL logs and other records. An original illustrative fragment is: X-Emby-Token: EXAMPLE_INTEGRATION_KEY It is a placeholder rather than a credential for any server. A key being accepted does not eliminate the endpoint's operation requirements or establish that an integration has a fictional set of narrow scopes. Replacement needs both sides to agree When changing a credential, the server and integration must agree on the accepted value. Installing a new value in one process while another still uses the old one can create intermittent failures. Revocation prevents future applicable access under the server's contract. It does not undo files already changed or notifications already sent. For Emby integrations, record which system uses each credential and distinguish request authentication from the operation it is permitted to perform. Integration permissions develops that effective-access boundary. See Also API authentication tokens and request identity Integration permissions and effective operations References Emby API-key authentication Emby user authentication

articles/automation/api/credentials/Auto.title: API authentication tokens and request identity | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/credentials/Auto.keywords: API authentication tokens and request identity An authentication token supplies request evidence associated with an accepted login or credential, while user labels and device identifiers do not authenticate by themselves. An authentication token is credential evidence that a client supplies with later requests. The server evaluates that evidence under its authentication and session rules. For Emby user authentication, the documented login result includes an AccessToken . Subsequent requests send it in the X-Emby-Token header. A user ID is a claim, not the login proof An app can describe its client, device and user identity in request context. Those labels help the server interpret the request, but naming a user does not establish permission to act as that user. Emby's authentication documentation requires authentication even when the public user's HasPassword field is false. That field affects the login presentation; it does not turn the user ID into credential evidence. An original header fragment uses a placeholder: X-Emby-Token: EXAMPLE_USER_TOKEN The value is not a real credential and no request is made. The token has a lifecycle State What it means for a later request Login succeeds and returns a token The client has the documented credential result Token is supplied The server still evaluates its validity and applicable identity Token is revoked or otherwise no longer accepted Later authentication can fail Client deletes its local copy That client no longer has the stored value; server state is a separate operation Emby's documented logout operation revokes the user token. The documentation also describes preserving a token when an app closes without explicit logout. That is different from inventing a universal short expiration interval. Do not assume every token is a JWT or can be interpreted locally from its characters. Its format and validity belong to the server's contract. A bearer value must stay within its intended use A credential usable by possession should be handled as a secret. HTTPS protects the transport leg, while local storage, logs and request construction affect other exposure paths. A rejected token does not automatically mean the supplied user has been deleted. It can reflect token state or another authentication condition. A valid token also does not grant every possible operation: authorization remains a distinct check. API keys describe Emby's documented static integration arrangement outside a particular user's login context. See Also API keys for server integrations Media server authentication and credential evidence Login sessions, tokens and revocation References Emby user authentication Emby API-key authentication RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/api/credentials/inde.title: Overview: API credentials | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/credentials/inde.keywords: Overview: API credentials API credentials provide request evidence under the server's user-authentication or integration-key contract. A user token and a static API key represent different authentication relationships. Their acceptance and revocation affect later requests without automatically supplying permission for every operation. These topics identify the credential's role before the integration's effective access is evaluated. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> API authentication tokens An authentication token supplies request evidence associated with an accepted login or credential, while user labels and device identifiers do not authenticate by themselves. API keys An API key is a static credential for a documented integration context, allowing access to be tracked and revoked separately from other integrations. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby user authentication RFC 9110: HTTP semantics Emby API-key authentication

articles/automation/api/index.html.title: Overview: Media server APIs | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/index.html.keywords: Overview: Media server APIs Media-server APIs expose supported operations and state through defined request, credential and response contracts. An integration needs to identify the operation it is asking for and the meaning of the returned result. Payloads, pagination, credentials and rate limits shape that exchange, while session data describe current players. This branch supplies those contracts before the result is used in another application. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is a media server API? A media server API exposes documented operations and data so another program can query or control supported server behavior. Requests and responses API requests and responses connect HTTP operations with typed payloads and bounded observations of result sets. API credentials API credentials provide request evidence under the server's user-authentication or integration-key contract. API rate limits API rate limits bound request activity within a defined scope and interval, so clients need to coordinate polling and retry timing. Playback sessions A playback session describes a current client relationship and player state, distinct from the user, device label and media item involved. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby server API documentation RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 6585: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests Emby session API

articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.title: HTTP API requests and interpretable responses | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.keywords: HTTP API requests and interpretable responses An HTTP API request combines a method, target, headers and optional content, while the response status and operation contract define its result. An HTTP request identifies an operation through its method and target. Headers supply additional context, including authentication and content type. Some operations also receive a body. The response contains a status and, when applicable, content describing the result. A successful network connection is only the beginning of that exchange. A request has independently meaningful parts This original HTTP/1.1 fragment illustrates a library query with fictional identifiers: GET /emby/Users/example-user/Items?StartIndex=0&Limit=2 HTTP/1.1 Host: media.example.invalid X-Emby-Token: EXAMPLE_TOKEN Accept: application/json It would be carried over an appropriately authenticated HTTPS connection in the described arrangement. No request is sent by this example. Part Meaning GET Requests a representation under HTTP semantics Target path Identifies the documented server resource Query parameters Supply inputs for this operation X-Emby-Token Emby's documented request credential header Accept States a preferred response media type A GET normally retrieves information rather than requesting a state change. The actual endpoint still defines its parameters and returned representation. The response needs its operation context A 200 response indicates successful handling with the applicable representation. A 202 response means acceptance for processing; it does not assert that all later work is complete. A 401 or 403 points to authentication or refusal under HTTP semantics, but the server's documented behavior supplies the detailed diagnosis. Malformed input, a missing resource and a failed server operation are other outcomes. Parsing JSON successfully is not enough if the response describes an error rather than the expected result. The exact status, relevant headers and body belong together. Response loss creates uncertainty Suppose a state-changing request reaches the server and completes, but the connection closes before the client receives its response. From the client's observation, the outcome can be unknown. Repeating an idempotent operation preserves the intended effect under its contract. Repeating another operation, such as adding another object, can instead duplicate work. A POST method alone does not supply a universal safe-retry rule. Use the documented operation identity, idempotency support or a suitable state query to resolve that uncertainty. Event delivery and retries develops the same distinction between delivery evidence and completed effects. See Also JSON payloads, types and field meaning API authentication tokens and request identity Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics Emby browsing the library Emby API-key authentication

articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.title: JSON payloads, types and field meaning | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.keywords: JSON payloads, types and field meaning JSON represents typed values in a text interchange format, while a schema defines field meanings, units and treatment of missing or null data. JSON represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. A parser can recognize those values without knowing what a particular API field means. The API's schema supplies the next layer: required fields, units, identifiers and relationships. Valid JSON can still be invalid input for a particular operation. Types survive the textual representation An original integration payload is: { "id": "item-A", "positionTicks": 1200000000, "paused": false, "tags": [], "artwork": null } In this declared schema, positionTicks uses ten million ticks per second, so the value represents 120 seconds. The field names are illustrative integration names; use the documented fields of an actual Emby endpoint. The ID is a string. The position is a number. The pause state is a boolean, not the string "false" . A consumer that treats every nonempty string as true would misinterpret that string. Missing, null and empty are different observations Representation What the JSON says Field absent This object did not supply that field "artwork": null An explicit null value was supplied "artwork": "" A string with zero characters was supplied "tags": [] An array containing no elements was supplied The schema determines whether omission means unknown, unchanged, unavailable or invalid. JSON does not provide one global interpretation. Object member names also matter. Id and id are different JSON names even if a particular application applies case-insensitive binding. A number can exceed a consumer's exact range A common JavaScript number uses binary64 representation. The integer 9007199254740993 , one above 2^53, does not round-trip exactly through that representation: ordinary parsing produces 9007199254740992. JSON's number grammar does not automatically solve the consumer's precision limit. A schema can use strings for identifiers or another supported representation for values requiring exact large-integer handling. The producer and consumer must agree. For an Emby integration, retain the documented units and types of positions, IDs and timestamps. Converting a valid payload into a convenient local type can lose meaning even when the syntax remains correct. See Also HTTP API requests and interpretable responses API pagination and changing result sets Resume positions and playback timelines References RFC 8259: JSON Emby browsing the library

articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.title: API pagination and changing result sets | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/requests/Automat.keywords: API pagination and changing result sets Pagination returns bounded portions of a result set, but offsets refer to the list as observed and can shift when its contents change. Pagination divides a large result into bounded responses. Emby's documented item queries include StartIndex and Limit : an index at which to start and a maximum number of records to return. This reduces response size, but a page is an observation of a query result—not automatically a permanent numbered partition of the library. Offsets address the current ordered list An original five-item result with a page size of two is: Ordered result: A B C D E StartIndex 0, Limit 2 -> A B StartIndex 2, Limit 2 -> C D StartIndex 4, Limit 2 -> E The query's filters and ordering must remain meaningful across the traversal. Requesting another page with a different filter is another result set, not the next portion of the first. An insertion can shift the next page After retrieving A and B, suppose X is inserted before A. The current order becomes X A B C D E. The request at offset two now returns B C, repeating B. A deletion before the next offset can instead cause an item to be skipped. Deduplicating IDs can remove repeated entries, but it cannot recover an entry that was never returned. Stable ordering makes the query interpretable. It does not freeze the underlying data. A server-supported snapshot or suitable cursor mechanism can provide a different traversal contract when available; do not infer that guarantee from StartIndex alone. Completion also has a contract Observation Interpretation Returned fewer than the maximum May indicate the current result's end under the endpoint contract Returned no entries No entries observed for that page A total count is supplied Count for its defined observation, potentially affected by later changes An earlier ID repeats The result may have shifted or the query may differ A request fails That page has not been successfully observed A caller should bound its work and handle errors without pretending a failed page is empty. If the purpose is a current inventory, reconciliation can be more appropriate than claiming one mutable offset traversal captured an exact snapshot. For Emby, use the endpoint's documented fields and permissions. An integration's cached list should identify which query and observation it represents. See Also HTTP API requests and interpretable responses JSON payloads, types and field meaning Media item identity References Emby user item queries Emby browsing the library

articles/automation/api/requests/index.h.title: Overview: Requests and responses | Emby Learn
articles/automation/api/requests/index.h.keywords: Overview: Requests and responses API requests and responses connect HTTP operations with typed payloads and bounded observations of result sets. HTTP describes the exchange, JSON represents its data, and pagination limits how much of a query result arrives at once. Each layer has its own meaning and failure conditions. The pages here keep them distinct so a parsed response is interpreted as the intended operation's result. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HTTP API requests An HTTP API request combines a method, target, headers and optional content, while the response status and operation contract define its result. JSON payloads JSON represents typed values in a text interchange format, while a schema defines field meanings, units and treatment of missing or null data. API pagination Pagination returns bounded portions of a result set, but offsets refer to the list as observed and can shift when its contents change. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 8259: JSON Emby user item queries

articles/automation/events/Automation-Ho.title: Playback events and dependable home automation | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/Automation-Ho.keywords: Playback events and dependable home automation Playback-driven home automation maps particular player observations into room policy and physical effects, with multiple sessions and uncertain events requiring explicit state handling. Playback-driven home automation connects media activity to another environment: dimming a room, changing a scene or updating a display. Emby documents webhooks as a way to supply such activity to an integration. The difficult part is deciding which playback observation controls which room, then keeping the desired behavior coherent through duplicates, missed events and independent human actions. A room needs a specific source One user can play media on a television and a phone at the same time. Selecting all events for that user can therefore let a phone change the television room. A mapping can identify the intended device/session relationship, room and applicable event types. Display names alone may not be stable unique keys. An original normalized example maps TV-A to Living Room. Phone-B belongs to another policy even when both sessions have the same user. More than one session needs an aggregation rule Suppose a room can have two relevant sessions. The integration's declared policy is to dim while any relevant session is playing , and to restore its configured scene when none is playing. Session S1 Session S2 Desired room state under this policy Playing Stopped Dim Paused Playing Dim Paused Stopped Restore Stopped Stopped Restore Unknown after an outage Stopped Unknown/reconciliation policy applies This is one teaching policy. A real room may choose to keep dimming during pause or apply another preference. The useful feature is that the decision comes from the relevant combined state, not from whichever single stop event arrived last. If S1 stops while S2 continues, blindly restoring the room would violate the declared policy. Duplicates should not invert the room A command such as “toggle lights” has a different duplication effect from “set brightness to 20%.” Repeating a toggle can undo the intended first effect. An absolute desired state can be repeated under a suitable device contract without intentionally changing direction each time. The destination still needs its own acceptance and completion evidence. An accepted HTTP request to a lighting service does not prove the physical lamps reached the scene. Keep those observations separate if the integration needs to detect and recover a failed effect. Old observations can arrive late An original adapter model supplies a monotonically increasing version within one session : Session S1, version 10: playing Session S1, version 11: stopped Delivery order: version 11 arrives, then version 10 Current stored version 11 rejects the older version 10 as stale. The version rule is explicitly part of this fictional adapter contract. Do not assume every Emby webhook or WebSocket message supplies such a version or identical ordering semantics. A timestamp alone may not supply the same guarantee: clocks, resolution and independent producers can complicate ordering. If the source has no suitable ordering contract, a current-state query and reconciliation rule can establish a newer observation. Event identity detects repeats. Per-entity versioning, where supported, detects stale state. Those are different decisions. Silence and absence are different states If the event channel disconnects, the room does not know that every player stopped. If a session query fails, it did not successfully observe an empty session set. A policy can retain the last known state for a limited interval, enter an explicit unknown state or query again through a supported path. The choice should be visible in the integration's behavior. On restart, an in-memory session map may be empty while playback continues. Querying current state before applying an “all stopped” action prevents that empty local map from being mistaken for the server's current state. Manual actions have their own authority A person can brighten the room during playback. If the integration continually reapplies its scene without an override rule, it can fight that action. A room policy can suspend automation after a manual change, allow an explicit override, or define another supported relationship. Restoring “the previous state” also needs an actual captured baseline; an integration cannot reliably invent it after the fact. The recovered baseline can become stale if other automations change the room. Coordinate the intended ownership rather than assuming the playback integration is the only writer. Recovery returns to observations A dependable workflow identifies the source, reconciles relevant playback state, derives its room policy and verifies the desired effect where the destination permits that observation. It can use webhooks or a continuing message channel for timely changes and polling for recovery. The tools have different observation properties; no single successful event delivery establishes every later stage. The example verifier evaluates the room policy, repeated identities and stale versions on original data. It does not send lighting commands or operate a home-automation system. See Also Playback sessions and current player state Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing Polling for updates and observation intervals Webhooks and pushed event notifications References Emby webhooks Emby session API CloudEvents 1.0.2 event identity and specification

articles/automation/events/Automation-In.title: Integration permissions and effective operations | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/Automation-In.keywords: Integration permissions and effective operations Integration access depends on the accepted identity and permitted operation at each system involved, including server policy and underlying resource access. An integration performs operations under an identity accepted by each system it contacts. On the media server, that can be a user-authenticated context or the documented static API-key arrangement. Those identities have different contracts. Adding a user ID to a path does not by itself authenticate as that user or guarantee permission to act on that user's behalf. Identify the operation and its effective access An original policy model permits playback and denies deletion: Request Identity accepted? Operation permitted? Result under this model Play an allowed title Yes Yes Continue to required media operations Delete that title Yes No Refused Play with an unaccepted credential No Not reached Authentication fails Read a denied library Yes No Refused The model describes separate gates rather than claiming this is every Emby endpoint's exact implementation. Use the current endpoint and account/key contract for the real result. Successful authentication is not a universal authorization grant. Storage introduces another identity A permitted playback request still needs Emby Server to open the source under its operating-system storage identity. A permitted sidecar save needs the relevant write access. Conversely, a server process having filesystem write access does not imply that every viewer or API caller is permitted to request deletion. The chain can be: Integration credential -> accepted server identity Server operation policy -> applicable request permission Server process identity -> source/storage access External action credential -> destination-system permission Each arrow introduces a relationship to establish, not inherited authority that automatically flows from the preceding label. The destination evaluates its own caller If an integration sends a lighting command, the lighting service evaluates the integration's credential there. It does not automatically know or apply an Emby viewer's media permissions. A useful design ties each credential to the needed supported operations and keeps its revocation boundary clear. Emby's API-key documentation recommends distinct keys per integration; it does not supply an invented set of narrowly scoped OAuth permissions. For diagnosing a failure, preserve which system refused which operation. A storage error, media-server policy refusal and rejected downstream credential may all appear during one workflow while having different causes. See Also API authentication tokens and request identity API keys for server integrations Media server authorization and operation-specific access Read-only media access and separate writable data References Emby API-key authentication Emby user authentication RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/events/Automation-No.title: Notification delivery from event to recipient | Emby Learn
