articles/automation/events/Automation-No.keywords: Notification delivery from event to recipient Notification delivery connects a source event to a selected recipient through processing and provider stages, each with its own completion evidence. A notification starts with information worth delivering and ends with some intended recipient outcome. Between those points, an integration selects recipients, formats content and invokes a delivery service. Emby webhooks can supply an event for such a workflow. The webhook's successful delivery is only one stage of the resulting notification. Which stage completed? Observation What it establishes Source event produced The trigger exists Receiver accepted the event Its accepted-processing boundary was reached Notification intent stored Work is recorded for later processing Provider accepted the send The provider accepted that request Device received or displayed it That particular downstream delivery state was observed User read it A separate recipient action, when the channel supplies that evidence A provider's successful API response does not universally mean that a phone displayed an alert. Device connectivity, channel settings and recipient behavior can affect later stages. Repeated input should preserve one intended notification An original design uses event E1 plus recipient R1 to identify notification intent N1. Receiving E1 twice should not automatically create N1 and another independent N2 for the same intended action. A durable intent record and the provider's applicable idempotency contract can help coordinate retries. If the provider offers no duplication guarantee, a response lost after acceptance can leave uncertainty. For multiple recipients, the result can split: R1's send succeeds while R2's fails. One global “event processed” flag is insufficient if the workflow needs separate recovery for each recipient. Preferences and permissions are part of selection Who should receive the message, for which event and with what detail? Those choices depend on the configured integration and recipient preferences. A media-server user ID does not automatically grant permission to send to every address or device in another service. The destination credential and recipient mapping have their own roles. When a notification is missing, inspect the last completed stage rather than repeatedly firing the entire workflow. A rejected destination credential, filtered recipient, provider refusal and offline device call for different handling. See Also Webhooks and pushed event notifications Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing Integration permissions and effective operations References Emby webhooks RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/events/Automation-Re.title: Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/Automation-Re.keywords: Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing Event retries recover from uncertain delivery but can duplicate processing, so event identity, durable recording and effect semantics need separate boundaries. A retry repeats an attempt whose result was unsuccessful or uncertain. For an event, the receiver may already have accepted or processed the first attempt even when the sender did not receive the acknowledgment. That is why reliable event handling needs more than “try again.” It needs an identity for the logical event and a completion rule for the work it causes. Delivery can succeed while acknowledgment is lost An original event E1 reaches a receiver and is recorded. The successful response is lost on the return path. The producer later sends E1 again. Attempt 1: E1 delivered and recorded Response: lost before producer observes it Attempt 2: E1 delivered again Logical events: one Delivery attempts: two Both attempts belong to the same logical event. Treating each delivery as a new event can produce two notifications or two increments. The producer's timeout only establishes that it did not observe completion in time. It does not prove that the receiver performed no work. Deduplication needs an identity and a lifetime CloudEvents defines event identity using source and ID together. Other event systems define their own keys. An integration must use the actual contract rather than assuming every Emby event includes a particular field. A normalized original example uses (server-A, E1) as its deduplication key. The receiver retains the key after accepted processing. A repeated delivery with that key can then be recognized. An in-memory set loses its records on restart. A retention period shorter than the producer's possible retry window can also let a later repeat appear new. Condition Remaining duplication question Key only in process memory What happens after restart? Key expires quickly Can an old delivery arrive after expiry? IDs unique only within a source Is source included in the key? Two workers accept simultaneously Is the claim/record operation coordinated? Same key has different content How does the contract handle an inconsistent replay? The key's identity and the record's durability have to fit the delivery behavior. A crash window remains around an external effect Suppose a receiver sends a phone alert, then records “E1 done.” If it crashes between those actions, a retry can send the alert again. Reverse the order—record “done,” then send—and a crash between them can suppress the alert entirely. Merely choosing one order does not provide exactly-once external effects. A transactional intent or outbox design records the event and intended work under one durable database boundary. A worker then attempts the effect. The downstream service may support an idempotency key so repeating the same intent does not create another effect. If the downstream service has no such contract, uncertainty can remain between applying the effect and recording its result. The receiver should describe that limit rather than claiming a deduplication table automatically solves every failure. The isolated example verifier checks deduplicated durable intent records on toy data and evaluates the distinct external-effect window. It does not send notifications or operate a home system. Arrival order need not be state order An older event can be delayed while a newer event arrives promptly. Different workers can also finish in another order. If an operation applies an absolute desired state, a supported per-entity version can help reject older observations. If the event source supplies no ordering/version guarantee, the integration may need a fresh state query or another reconciliation rule. Deduplicating E1 does not order E1 relative to E2. Identity and ordering solve different problems. Backoff changes load, not completion semantics An original retry policy waits one, two and four seconds between failed attempts, before accounting for operation duration. Its accumulated waiting time is seven seconds. Jitter can spread concurrent clients' attempts so they do not all retry at the same instant. Retry-After, when supplied and applicable, contributes the source's requested timing. Neither delay nor jitter makes an unsafe repeated action idempotent. The operation's effect semantics still govern whether repeating it is appropriate. For Emby webhooks or external integrations, retain the event identity, attempt result and accepted-processing boundary. Recovery can then reconcile uncertain work rather than interpreting every successful HTTP response as proof of a completed downstream effect. See Also Webhooks and pushed event notifications WebSockets and a continuing message connection Playback events and dependable home automation References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics CloudEvents 1.0.2 event identity and specification

articles/automation/events/index.html.title: Overview: Events and integrations | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/index.html.keywords: Overview: Events and integrations Events and integrations connect server observations with accepted work and effects in other application lifecycles. An event can arrive more than once, and a successful receipt can precede a downstream action. Permissions and notification rules add further decisions, while an in-process plugin follows the host's own extension lifecycle. This area gives those boundaries enough context to build a coherent workflow around Emby state. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Receiving events and state Event and state reception uses pushed messages or repeated queries with different timing and recovery properties. Plugins Plugin architecture and compatibility connect an extension's code and persisted state with the host's supported contracts. articles/automation/events/plugins/Autom.title: Plugin compatibility across server and runtime changes | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/plugins/Autom.keywords: Plugin compatibility across server and runtime changes Plugin compatibility requires a supported relationship among host interfaces, runtime dependencies, platform assets and persisted data, not merely a successfully loaded package. A plugin is compatible when its required contracts and behavior match the host environment in which it operates. Successful package installation or assembly loading tests only part of that relationship. The current server release, plugin package and documented extension interfaces establish the actual target. Several layers can disagree Layer Compatibility question Host API Are the required interfaces and members available? Runtime Can this assembly and its dependencies execute here? Native assets Do architecture and operating-system ABI match? Behavior Does the extension handle the operation's current semantics? Persistent state Can it interpret existing configuration and stored data? External services Do its integrations still use a supported contract? A package can load while one later feature fails on a missing native library. Another can load and invoke successfully while misinterpreting a changed result field. The development documentation contains examples for particular runtime targets. Those examples should not be treated as a timeless list of the runtime versions in every installed Emby release. Loading is one checkpoint An original compatibility scenario is: Host H2 loads plugin P1. P1 starts its ordinary configuration path. Later operation requires interface member M2. P1's selected dependency does not provide the required contract. Startup success did not establish that later operation. The labels describe a model rather than real Emby version numbers. Tests should exercise the feature and data path the plugin actually needs. A source-code rebuild can resolve an API mismatch while still leaving behavior or migration work. Conversely, preserving one binary does not prove semantic compatibility after a host update. Stored data have their own version relationship An updated plugin may migrate its configuration. Returning to an older assembly may not reverse that migration or make the resulting state readable by the old code. Backups and supported upgrade/downgrade paths therefore belong to the data lifecycle as well as the software lifecycle. For Emby plugin use or development, record the actual host/package combination and the failed feature. The current plugin-development documentation supplies the extension contracts; a generic “DLL loads” observation does not establish the whole result. See Also Plugin architecture inside a media server Native libraries and runtime dependencies References Emby server plugin development Emby IPlugin interface

articles/automation/events/plugins/Autom.title: Plugin architecture inside a media server | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/plugins/Autom.keywords: Plugin architecture inside a media server A server plugin adds code to the host's extension lifecycle, using supported discovery and interfaces while sharing the host's execution resources. A server plugin adds functionality through the media server's supported extension system. Its code participates in the host's lifecycle and interfaces rather than only sending requests from an external application. Emby's development documentation describes plugin templates, supported interfaces and automatic discovery of particular extension types. Those contracts determine how the host recognizes and uses an extension. Discovery connects code to an extension point An extension point can represent a provider, task, service or another supported role. Implementing an interface is meaningful when the host's discovery and registration rules recognize it. The documented IPlugin interface includes identity and descriptive properties, plus paths for plugin-related data. That is one part of the contract; it does not mean every arbitrary class in every assembly automatically runs at startup. Stage What the host/plugin relationship needs Package selection Compatible software and dependencies Loading Required assemblies and symbols available Discovery/registration Recognized supported extension types Invocation Correct operation and lifecycle behavior Shutdown or replacement Work and resources handled under the host's rules Inside the host is a different resource boundary Plugin work can consume the server's threads, memory and storage resources. A long-running provider or task can therefore affect the same host serving playback. An external API client has its own process lifecycle and reaches the server through request contracts. An in-process extension should not be assumed to have a container-like isolation boundary merely because it is labelled a plugin. That distinction makes cancellation, bounded work and error handling part of a useful extension design. A plugin can own persistent data Configuration and miscellaneous plugin data can have documented storage locations. Their lifetime can differ from cached results or from the plugin assembly itself. Replacing the code does not universally migrate or discard those files. A compatible update needs to interpret the existing state through its supported migration rules. For Emby, use the current plugin-development contract and distinguish package compatibility, discovered behavior and persistent state. The article explains that architecture without prescribing one extension's complete implementation. See Also Plugin compatibility across server and runtime changes Native libraries and runtime dependencies References Emby server plugin development Emby automatic type discovery Emby IPlugin interface

articles/automation/events/plugins/index.title: Overview: Plugins | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/plugins/index.keywords: Overview: Plugins Plugin architecture and compatibility connect an extension's code and persisted state with the host's supported contracts. A plugin participates in the server's discovery, invocation and shutdown relationships. Compatible loading is one checkpoint; feature behavior, dependencies and existing data add others. The two pages explain that lifecycle so replacing an assembly is understood as more than changing a filename. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Plugin architecture A server plugin adds code to the host's extension lifecycle, using supported discovery and interfaces while sharing the host's execution resources. Plugin compatibility Plugin compatibility requires a supported relationship among host interfaces, runtime dependencies, platform assets and persisted data, not merely a successfully loaded package. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby server plugin development

articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.title: Polling for updates and observation intervals | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.keywords: Polling for updates and observation intervals Polling queries current state at intervals, trading observation delay and request volume while potentially missing short-lived intermediate states. Polling repeatedly queries a source for its current state. A playback integration might ask which sessions are active, then compare the returned state with its previous successful observation. The interval controls how quickly a change can be noticed and how often the query runs. One interval, two costs In an ideal ten-second schedule with instantaneous successful queries, a change just before a query is noticed almost immediately. A change just after one waits almost ten seconds. If changes occur uniformly within that interval, the average detection delay is five seconds. One query every 10 seconds -> 6 requests/minute Ideal detection delay -> 0 to almost 10 seconds Uniform-timing average -> 5 seconds Real request duration, scheduling and failures add to those delays. The average is a model assumption, not a response-time guarantee. A current-state sample can miss a transition Suppose a player starts at second two and stops at second eight. Queries at seconds zero and ten can both report stopped. Time Actual state Poll observation 0 Stopped Stopped 2 Playing No query 8 Stopped No query 10 Stopped Stopped The observations can be accurate while the intermediate playback is absent from them. Polling current state is not a complete event history. A failed query is also unknown state, not a successful observation of “no sessions.” Keep the last successful observation and its age separate from the latest failure. Avoid overlapping work unintentionally If a query takes longer than the interval, starting another every interval can create accumulating concurrent requests. A bounded polling design decides whether to wait, skip, cancel or use another supported policy. For Emby integrations, choose observations around the state needed and the endpoint's cost. Rate limits describe shared request demand; event delivery describes a different way to learn about transitions. See Also API rate limits and respectful request scheduling WebSockets and a continuing message connection Playback sessions and current player state References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics Emby session API

articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.title: Webhooks and pushed event notifications | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.keywords: Webhooks and pushed event notifications A webhook pushes event information through an HTTP request to another application's receiver, whose acknowledgment and processing have separate meanings. A webhook sends event information from one application to another through an HTTP request. Instead of the receiver repeatedly asking whether something changed, the producer initiates the event delivery. Emby documents webhooks for integrations such as home automation and notifications, with Emby Premiere requirements. The configured event and destination determine what that integration receives. The producer must reach the receiver A receiver on a private machine is not automatically reachable by an external producer. Conversely, when the producer runs on the local Emby host, its network view can differ from a cloud automation service's view. The destination also needs the expected method, payload and applicable authentication. Knowing a URL is not proof that the intended producer is authorized to use it. Acknowledgment needs a processing boundary An original receiver design stores the event durably in a queue, then returns a successful response. A worker subsequently performs the intended action. Event E1 arrives Receiver stores E1 under its accepted-work rule Receiver acknowledges E1 Worker later applies the downstream action In that design, acknowledgment means accepted durable work, not a completed lamp change or delivered phone alert. If the receiver instead acknowledges before recording anything and crashes, the producer can consider delivery successful while the work is lost. The response code has the meaning chosen by the producer/receiver contract; HTTP alone does not provide a durable event queue. Event data need their own schema Contract detail Why the receiver needs it Event type Selects the appropriate processing Identity or deduplication key Helps recognize a repeated delivery Timestamp or state version, where supplied Helps interpret age and ordering Authentication mechanism Establishes accepted origin under the contract Retry behavior Defines later attempts after an uncertain result CloudEvents is one standard for event context and identity. An integration should not assume that every webhook, including an Emby payload, automatically uses that standard or its exact fields. Use the actual event schema and configured integration's delivery contract. Retries explain why the same logical event can legitimately arrive more than once. See Also Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing Integration permissions and effective operations References Emby webhooks RFC 9110: HTTP semantics CloudEvents 1.0.2 event identity and specification

articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.title: WebSockets and a continuing message connection | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/receiving/Aut.keywords: WebSockets and a continuing message connection WebSocket carries framed messages over a continuing connection, with message boundaries and reconnection state separate from individual network reads. WebSocket provides a continuing, two-way message connection. After the supported connection establishment, either side can send messages without making each message a separate HTTP request. For an Emby-related integration, that can support timely state updates. The transport still needs an application protocol defining which messages mean what. Establishment and messages are different phases The RFC 6455 HTTP/1.1 arrangement uses an opening handshake that upgrades the connection. A successful switching response establishes the negotiated WebSocket connection; it does not by itself authenticate every claimed application identity. A secure WebSocket connection uses wss . A browser's origin and secure-page rules can affect whether it is allowed to establish a particular connection. These are separate from the server's application permissions. A frame encodes a message part An original tiny client-to-server text frame contains “Hi”: 81 82 01 02 03 04 49 6B 81: FIN=1, text opcode=1 82: MASK=1, payload length=2 Mask key: 01 02 03 04 Decoded payload: 49 XOR 01 = 48 ("H") 6B XOR 02 = 69 ("i") The fixed key is for the readable example. RFC 6455 requires a fresh unpredictable masking key for actual client frames. Masking serves the protocol's transport protections; it is not encryption. The simple frame uses one complete message. Larger messages can be fragmented over frames, and control frames have their own rules. A network read is not a message TCP can return part of a frame or several frames in one read. The WebSocket implementation must parse and reassemble according to frame and message boundaries. A caller should therefore use the supported message API rather than assuming each low-level receive corresponds to one JSON event. A text message also has encoding requirements before its content is interpreted by the application. Reconnecting restores a channel, not history If a connection is absent from time T1 to T2, it cannot carry ordinary live messages during that interval. Reconnection creates a new delivery opportunity. Replay, sequence tracking and current-state queries are application capabilities. They are not universal effects of reopening a WebSocket. If an Emby integration needs current playback state after reconnect, its supported recovery path should obtain that state rather than treating silence during the outage as proof that nothing changed. See Also Polling for updates and observation intervals Event delivery, retries and duplicate processing Mixed content and a browser’s secure-page boundary References RFC 6455: WebSocket protocol RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/automation/events/receiving/ind.title: Overview: Receiving events and state | Emby Learn
articles/automation/events/receiving/ind.keywords: Overview: Receiving events and state Event and state reception uses pushed messages or repeated queries with different timing and recovery properties. Webhooks deliver requests to a receiver, WebSockets carry messages during a live connection, and polling observes state at intervals. A gap affects each mechanism differently. These pages explain which observation was actually obtained before silence or a reconnect is interpreted as complete event history. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Webhooks A webhook pushes event information through an HTTP request to another application's receiver, whose acknowledgment and processing have separate meanings. WebSockets WebSocket carries framed messages over a continuing connection, with message boundaries and reconnection state separate from individual network reads. Polling for updates Polling queries current state at intervals, trading observation delay and request volume while potentially missing short-lived intermediate states. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby webhooks RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 6455: WebSocket protocol

articles/automation/index.html.title: Overview: Automation and interoperability | Emby Learn
articles/automation/index.html.keywords: Overview: Automation and interoperability Media-server integrations use supported APIs and event mechanisms to connect server state with operations in other applications. An integration needs to know both what the server observed and what its own action completed. A playback event, an accepted API request and a changed room scene are related results, but they belong to different stages. The API branch covers requests, credentials and current state. Events and integrations cover delivery, retries, permissions and extension lifecycles. These topics help build an Emby-related workflow that remains understandable when messages repeat, a connection drops or another system applies its own access rules. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media server APIs Media-server APIs expose supported operations and state through defined request, credential and response contracts. Events and integrations Events and integrations connect server observations with accepted work and effects in other application lifecycles. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.title: Display color calibration | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.keywords: Display color calibration Display calibration adjusts a defined output state toward a chosen target, while characterization and profiling describe how that state reproduces colors. Calibration starts with a target: the behavior a display should produce in a defined viewing and signal state. Measurement then shows how its current output differs from that target, and suitable controls reduce the difference. An ICC profile serves a related but different purpose. It describes the characterized color behavior so a color-managed route can interpret and transform colors appropriately. Adjustment and description are separate operations The ICC’s display guidance treats calibration and profiling together: first establish a desired display behavior, then communicate the resulting behavior through a profile. A display can be adjusted through internal controls or calibration tables. Some arrangements also apply a correction in the graphics/output path. Profiling measures the resulting state and records its color relationships. If an application uses a profile that describes a different state, its transformation is based on the wrong description. Changing a display preset, white balance or other substantial control after profiling can consequently invalidate that relationship. A profile copied from another unit also describes another measured response. A shared model name does not prove that the units, modes and ages have identical output. A target needs a viewing and signal context Target property What must be defined White appearance Intended chromaticity or white-point reference Luminance Output suitable for the intended viewing condition Tone response How encoded levels become light Color reproduction The source/working space and destination behavior Signal state SDR/HDR interpretation, range and active display mode “Make it look good” does not specify a reproducible target. Conversely, matching a named target numerically does not make every viewing room or every content type use the same presentation. An Emby video route also needs the correct range interpretation . A limited/full mismatch can crush or lift the dark end before a calibration adjustment is even considered. An inverse-response exercise Consider an original one-channel model. Let command u range from zero to one. The uncorrected display produces normalized luminance: Actual display: L = u² Desired response to source value x: Ltarget = x^2.2 To achieve the target, solve the actual response for its required command: u² = x^2.2 u = x^1.1 At source value x = 0.5 : Route Command sent Model luminance No correction 0.5 0.25 Inverse correction 0.466516 0.217638 Desired target — 0.217638 The correction changes the command; the target describes the emitted result. Those are different curves. This exercise assumes an exact, monotonic scalar response, unlimited command precision and a zero black floor. Real calibration has finite code steps, measurement uncertainty, channel interactions and output limits. Real SDR encodings can also have piecewise responses; this power-law model is not an sRGB, BT.1886 or HDR prescription. Finite command levels limit the correction The inverse curve above assumes continuous commands. Suppose an original restricted output can send only 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1. For the midpoint target, the ideal command 0.466516 must be rounded to an available value. Choosing 0.5 produces 0.25 luminance again, rather than the desired 0.217638. Knowing the correct curve did not create an extra output level. A higher-precision implemented path can make finer adjustments, while dithering can change the time/spatial distribution of available levels. Neither case should be described as an exact continuous result without its own assumptions. Measurement tests the combined curve, quantization and display response. Measurement closes the loop A useful sequence is to establish the relevant mode, measure selected patches, calculate or choose adjustments, then remeasure their output. Remeasurement matters because a requested correction and the resulting light are not interchangeable. The display can clip, quantize or apply other processing; the graphics path can change which table is used. Neutral patches test the balance and tone response of gray output. Colored patches test properties that a gray-only adjustment does not establish. A correction that matches one midpoint does not automatically match the whole curve or gamut. Instrument behavior and the display’s spectral output also affect the measurement. The required method depends on the accuracy being sought. A calibrated state has a valid scope An SDR state and an HDR state can use different transfer interpretation and processing. A curve that compensates a toy SDR response is not a universal correction for PQ. HDR output can also depend on patch area, surrounding content and duration. If those conditions change during measurement, the observed variation may belong to a brightness controller rather than to an ordinary fixed tone curve. Peak brightness and automatic brightness limiting explain those conditions. The calibration target should identify which state and patterns were actually characterized. A calibration cannot create colors or luminance outside the display’s usable output range. Transforming an out-of-gamut color into a reproducible one is a mapping decision, not evidence that the panel acquired a larger gamut. The player’s complete path needs validation A photo application using a traditional ICC transform, a video renderer targeting a calibrated output space and an operating system’s Advanced Color route can apply color handling at different stages. For Emby playback, identify the actual client and renderer route before assuming that a desktop profile applies in exactly the same way everywhere. Display color management develops those responsibilities. See Also Display color management ICC color profiles Video Gamma Limited and Full Video Range References ICC: Display calibration and profiling ICC: Profile specifications VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria

articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.title: Display color management | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.keywords: Display color management Display color management relates the source’s defined color meaning to the current output state through transformations implemented by the application, operating system and display path. A color value has meaning only within a defined interpretation. The same triplet of RGB numbers can describe different colors under different primaries, white references and transfer functions. Display color management connects that source meaning to the behavior of the selected output. It requires more than choosing a monitor with a wide gamut. Numbers first need an interpretation A video source may describe its primaries, transfer function, YCbCr matrix and range through its stream/container signaling. A still image may carry an ICC profile. The player needs to interpret those properties before deciding how to present the source. Assigning a different description to unchanged numbers is not the same operation as transforming numbers to preserve their color meaning. For example, marking values as wide-gamut RGB without converting their interpretation does not automatically preserve the original narrow-gamut colors. It changes what the values are said to mean. Video color signaling and ICC profiles describe those source declarations. Assigning a label and converting values differ Use an original scalar tone-encoding exercise, with color primaries omitted. Encoding A means light equals its code squared; Encoding B means light equals its code raised to 2.4. Code 0.5 in A therefore describes light 0.25. Copying code 0.5 unchanged into B describes approximately 0.189465. To preserve light 0.25 in B, calculate its required code: codeB = 0.25^(1/2.4) = 0.561231 codeB^2.4 = 0.25 Relabeling the unchanged code changes its meaning. Converting the code preserves the modeled light relationship. Real color conversion also needs the source/destination primaries, reference state and mapping limits. A transform relates two characterized spaces A traditional ICC route uses a source profile, a profile connection space and a destination profile. The destination describes the display’s characterized state. The transform computes destination values intended to reproduce or map the source colors. The working values may be linearized before color-basis transformations, then encoded for output. Applying a linear-light operation directly to nonlinear encoded values can produce a different result. A calibrated video route can instead target an established reference color space. It need not apply an ordinary per-image ICC transform at every stage if the output is already set up for that reference. These are different implemented arrangements for maintaining intended color relationships. Application and operating system share responsibilities Route Relationship to establish Traditional color-managed application App interprets the source and transforms for its destination profile Calibrated reference video output Renderer produces the intended reference representation for that output state OS-managed Advanced Color App declares a supported surface interpretation; the OS composes/maps it into the current managed output Microsoft documents that Advanced Color changes traditional ICC behavior. Its managed routes distinguish application color conversion from display calibration and output handling. Consequently, an ICC profile being installed does not imply every app applies the same conventional transform. Nor does a managed OS output mean an application can label arbitrary values incorrectly and expect the system to infer their intended meaning. For an Emby client, the renderer, platform and selected presentation mode determine the implemented relationship. A browser player and a native video renderer can enter the output pipeline differently. Why a correction applied twice is different Use an original scalar model from calibration . A display has actual response L = u² , while the target for source value x is x^2.2 . One correction sends u = x^1.1 . At x = 0.5 , one correction gives luminance approximately 0.217638 . If the same command correction is mistakenly applied again, the command becomes: u = (x^1.1)^1.1 = x^1.21 Actual light = u² = x^2.42 At x = 0.5: L ≈ 0.186856 The result no longer matches the intended x^2.2 target. This is an invented calculation illustrating duplicated responsibility, not a report that a particular app or OS performs it. The converse problem is a required transformation being omitted. Correct output depends on establishing which stage owns each operation. HDR adds a luminance interpretation PQ describes a relationship to absolute luminance. A managed desktop can also need to place SDR interface white at an appropriate reference level alongside HDR content. Converting color primaries alone does not solve that luminance relationship. Tone mapping, reference-white handling and the selected output representation remain relevant. Microsoft’s Advanced Color documentation describes surface-format/color-space combinations and their interpretation. Those API choices are factual examples of an implementation contract, not universal configuration instructions for every media app. HDMI HDR signaling covers the later signal sent to a connected display. Correct source metadata, correct surface interpretation and correct output signaling are three connected conditions. Display changes alter the destination Moving a player window to another screen can change the output gamut, luminance, profile and active HDR state. A route that was correct for the first screen may need updated destination information. A desktop screenshot records a representation captured at a particular pipeline stage. Viewing that screenshot later through another application/display is another color route, so it is not automatically a measurement of the first screen’s emitted light. See Also Display color calibration ICC color profiles Video Color Tags and Signaling Limited and Full Video Range HDMI HDR signaling References ICC: Profile specifications Microsoft: Advanced Color display pipeline Microsoft: ICC profile behaviour with Advanced Color

articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.title: Native display resolution | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/Disp.keywords: Native display resolution Native display resolution describes the physical imaging grid, which remains distinct from the accepted input mode and the resolution of the source picture. The resolution of a movie, the output mode of its player and the display’s physical imaging grid can be three different things. Native resolution describes that physical grid. For a conventional fixed-pixel flat panel, it is the number of addressable pixel positions across and down the panel. Resolution being discussed Example Encoded source picture 1920 × 1080 Player’s selected output 3840 × 2160 Panel’s native grid 3840 × 2160 In this example, the source has 2,073,600 pixel positions and the panel has 8,294,400. The larger output does not create four times as much captured detail. Mapping the source onto the grid Scaling 1920 × 1080 to 3840 × 2160 doubles each dimension. An ideal nearest-neighbour exercise could assign each source pixel to a two-by-two group of panel positions. A practical video scaler usually reconstructs a smoother picture using neighbouring samples. Its result depends on the chosen filtering and on the source’s chroma resolution, not just the integer ratio. A 2560 × 1440 source enlarged to the same panel has a 1.5 ratio in each dimension. Source edges no longer all land on integer panel boundaries. The scaler must decide how source samples contribute to the new grid. Video scaling develops those reconstruction choices. Resolution identifies the grids; it does not identify the quality of their mapping. One-to-one requires the complete visible mapping Sending the panel’s native dimensions is one condition for direct pixel mapping. The display must also show the intended full active picture without overscan, zoom or another resampling step. If a 3840-pixel-wide input is cropped to 3600 pixels and then enlarged to the panel width, the horizontal scale is: 3840 / 3600 = 1.066667 It is a roughly 6.67% enlargement despite the input and panel both being described as 4K. A subtitle or test pattern near the edge may reveal the crop more readily than a landscape. Desktop scaling is a separate layer: an application can render its interface at a logical size before the output signal is produced. A small screenshot is consequently not always evidence of the physical output mode. Accepted resolution is an input capability A display can accept a signal larger or smaller than its native grid and convert it internally. An advertised input resolution may therefore describe compatibility rather than the imaging hardware. For an Emby session, a lower-resolution delivered stream can still be presented through the client’s established high-resolution desktop or TV mode. The app’s Direct Play or transcoding decision concerns the media representation, while the output mode concerns its local presentation. The display path helps identify where the mapping occurs. Projectors can create several positions over time Some projectors use optical pixel shifting: an actuator changes the projected position of an imaging device between sub-images. TI documents two-way and four-way mechanisms for relevant DLP arrangements. The physical imager grid, the accepted source dimensions and the positions addressed on the screen during a frame then need separate descriptions. Calling every such product simply “native 4K” or “not 4K” loses the mechanism. Compare the stated imager arrangement, sub-image sequence and delivered picture. The lens, focus and viewing surface also determine whether the resulting detail is visible. Projectors develops that final optical route. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Projectors and the viewing surface HDMI video transport How Video Scaling Works References VESA: Standards and public DSC resources TI: DLP display technology, including optical pixel shifting Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata

articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.title: Automatic brightness limiting | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.keywords: Automatic brightness limiting Automatic brightness limiting reduces permitted display output as picture loading reaches the implementation’s power or drive constraints. A small white highlight and a white screen can request the same local luminance but require very different total light output. Automatic brightness limiting , often abbreviated ABL , describes a display reducing permitted output when the larger picture load reaches an implemented limit. The result can be visible when a white window expands or a movie cuts to a largely bright scene. The picture changes the total load An emissive display drives the light-producing elements themselves. Lighting many elements strongly increases combined electrical loading compared with a small bright region surrounded by dark pixels. Dell documents a picture-pattern loading effect on specified OLED laptop panels: darker regions leave more power available for bright regions. This provides a concrete product example of the mechanism, rather than a universal curve for every OLED. The display’s exact response depends on its implementation, mode, color demands and time. ABL does not define one standard luminance-versus-area function. An original power-budget curve For a deliberately simplified model, assume a white patch covers fraction f of the screen, the background emits no light, and power is proportional to f × L . Let the local luminance ceiling be 600 cd/m² and the allowed full-screen-equivalent light load be 180 cd/m². The model’s permitted patch luminance is: L(f) = min(600, 180 / f), for 0 < f ≤ 1 White area Declared allowed luminance 10% 600 cd/m² 25% 600 cd/m² 50% 360 cd/m² 100% 180 cd/m² Below 30% area, the local ceiling is the binding constraint. Beyond it, the constant total-load condition limits the patch. The model omits real subpixels, color-dependent efficiency, background light, thermal dynamics and control smoothing. It is not a measured panel response or a way to calculate a product’s ABL from its peak specification. Other automatic dimming has different triggers An ambient-light feature responds to the environment. A static-image protection policy can respond to persistent picture structure over time. Local dimming responds to regional demands on an LCD backlight. These processes can coexist, so a brightness change should be described by its trigger. “It dimmed” alone does not identify which one operated. Changing white area while retaining the same local signal values is evidence for a loading relationship. Changing room illumination while the picture is fixed addresses another relationship. A slow change after an unchanged picture has remained visible concerns time as well as area. The encoded source can stay identical In an Emby scene, the decoder can continue producing the same bright pixel values while the display changes the light emitted from them. Subtitles, a menu or a larger bright picture region can alter the combined presentation sent to the display. Consequently, a brightness difference need not imply a different server bitrate or failed decoding. See Also OLED displays Display peak brightness HDR display capabilities Local dimming and backlight zones References Dell: OLED luminance and display-pattern loading VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria

articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.title: HDR display capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.keywords: HDR display capabilities HDR display capability combines accepted signal formats with the display’s usable luminance, contrast, color reproduction and processing behaviour. An HDR movie asks the playback path to preserve and adapt a wider range of light and color than an ordinary SDR presentation. A display’s HDR capability consequently has more than one dimension. The ability to accept a PQ signal is an input capability. The light, black level and colors produced from it are output properties. Both matter to an Emby viewer. Signal support and visible performance Question Evidence needed Can this input accept the chosen HDR representation? Format, transfer-function and metadata support on the actual connection How bright can a highlight become? Luminance under a stated area, duration and mode How dark is a nearby dark area? Black level under a relevant simultaneous picture pattern Which colors are reproducible? Color gamut, luminance and accuracy How is content adapted? The active mapping and processing behaviour A ten-bit input gives more code precision than an eight-bit input under the relevant encoding. It does not supply a particular peak luminance or a wide color gamut by itself. A wide gamut also does not establish how bright every saturated color can become. Color volume develops the connection between color and luminance. VESA’s DisplayHDR criteria assess several performance properties separately. Their published small-patch, full-screen and black-level tests help make the conditions explicit rather than reducing HDR performance to one label. Contrast needs the same measurement context An original simultaneous-picture model has white at 400 cd/m² and dark output at 0.04 cd/m²: 400 / 0.04 = 10,000:1 Now add an original uniform reflected ambient contribution of 0.5 cd/m²: (400 + 0.5) / (0.04 + 0.5) = 741.667:1 This does not predict a product. It shows why the viewing environment changes apparent contrast, especially near black. It also explains why a peak white measured in one pattern and a lowest black measured in another are not automatically the simultaneous contrast experienced during a movie. A local-dimming system can produce different black levels around a bright object than on an entirely dark screen. Local dimming , OLED and projectors develop their light-producing mechanisms separately. Three questions locate the active HDR route What does the source mean? Its transfer function, primaries, range and metadata describe an intended interpretation. File metadata supplies information; it does not prove that the current output is using that interpretation. What does the client send? The player and operating system select a presentation surface and output representation. They can pass HDR through an implemented route, adapt it for another HDR target or produce an SDR presentation. What does the display do? It receives the selected signal and maps that signal into its current mode’s output range. A recognized HDR input can still use substantial internal tone mapping. These stages explain several common situations. Server-side HDR-to-SDR conversion produces an SDR target before the client presents it. A compatible Direct Play route can deliver the original HDR source while the client still performs display preparation. An operating system can also combine SDR interface elements with HDR content in a managed presentation. HDMI HDR signaling describes how input capability and current signal interpretation are communicated. Display color management describes the application/OS handoff. Mapping determines which differences survive Suppose a declared source contains highlights intended for 1000 cd/m², while an original display model has a usable 400-cd/m² highlight ceiling. Values above the ceiling cannot all appear as their original absolute luminance. Clipping would make sufficiently bright values indistinguishable. A mapping can compress their differences into the available range, at the cost of changing their spacing and perhaps the brightness of neighbouring content. The display may also vary its usable output with picture area and duration. A target suitable for a small highlight is not necessarily sustainable over a bright full-screen scene. See Also Display peak brightness Local dimming and backlight zones Automatic brightness limiting HDMI HDR signaling HDR10 References VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria Microsoft: Advanced Color display pipeline CTA: HDR static metadata extensions

articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.title: Local dimming and backlight zones | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.keywords: Local dimming and backlight zones Local dimming adjusts illumination in backlight regions so an LCD can use different light levels across the same picture. Local dimming lets an LCD backlight illuminate different regions at different levels. Darker regions can receive less light while a bright region receives more. The LCD pixels still modulate that illumination. Backlight control and pixel control operate at different spatial scales. A zone covers several picture pixels A dimming zone is a region with a controllable light contribution. It is not generally one independently controlled source for every picture pixel. Consider an original eight-by-four zone grid over a 3840 × 2160 picture. Each ideal rectangular zone covers 480 × 540 pixel positions. A narrow bright subtitle stroke can occupy only part of one zone, but the zone controller must still supply enough light for it. The neighbouring dark pixels then reject the same zone illumination as well as their panel permits. Real zone shapes and optical spread can differ from this rectangular exercise. Light can also reach beyond the nominal control boundary. A simple demand model explains blooming For an invented control rule, let a zone’s drive equal the largest desired normalized light demand among its pixels. A zone containing demands 0, 0, 0.8, 0 gets drive 0.8 . A neighbouring all-dark zone gets drive 0 in this simplified model. If the LCD’s dark-pixel residual transmission is 1% of zone drive, the dark pixels beside the bright object output 0.008 normalized light. They are brighter than the neighbouring unilluminated zone. This is a mathematical illustration of a halo-producing relationship. A real controller can smooth, filter or constrain its response; it does not have to use this maximum-demand rule. Lowering the first zone’s drive reduces its dark leakage but also makes it harder to preserve the bright object. The controller has to choose a compromise across the picture. Spatial detail and time both matter Smaller appropriately placed zones can separate a bright object from more surrounding pixels. Yet the panel’s contrast, optical spread and algorithm still influence the result. A controller also responds over time. If a bright object moves between regions, zone drives can rise and fall. Smoothing those changes may reduce visible pumping, while leaving a moving light footprint. An aggressive instantaneous change can track the object more tightly but create abrupt brightness changes. Extra zone count does not specify which policy the product uses. VESA’s HDR performance criteria include patterns that examine local contrast under simultaneous bright and dark content. Those contexts are more informative than a zone number in isolation. Subtitle composition can change the demand When an Emby client paints a bright subtitle onto a dark movie, that combined picture becomes the display’s input. The subtitle can therefore affect local-dimming behaviour even though the underlying movie frame has not changed. A comparison should preserve the same scene, subtitle appearance and display mode. Changing several of those at once makes it difficult to tell whether the visible difference came from source preparation or backlight control. OLED produces light through emissive elements rather than these LCD backlight zones. Its local emission has a different mechanism, alongside its own whole-screen brightness constraints. See Also LCD and LED-backlit displays OLED displays HDR display capabilities Display peak brightness References VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria LG: OLED emission and LCD backlighting

articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.title: Display peak brightness | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.keywords: Display peak brightness Display peak brightness is a luminance result that needs a defined picture area, duration, mode and measurement context. A display’s peak brightness describes a maximum luminance reached under some conditions. The conditions are part of the number. For a movie highlight, a small bright region may be relevant. For a long bright snow scene, a larger area and sustained output are relevant. Neither measurement automatically replaces the other. Area, duration and mode belong beside the result A useful luminance description identifies: The size and location of the bright region. The rest of the picture’s brightness. How long the region has been displayed. The display’s selected picture, power and signal mode. The measurement method and viewing geometry. A nit is one cd/m². This is a luminance unit, not a video code value, a lumen figure or an electrical power measurement. VESA’s current DisplayHDR criteria distinguish small-patch, full-screen flash and full-screen long-duration tests. The standard’s own pattern definitions should accompany its certification results. Four invented observations The following is an original teaching table, not a measurement of a TV: Bright region Observation time Declared luminance 2% of screen 1 second 900 cd/m² 10% of screen 1 second 800 cd/m² Full screen 1 second 260 cd/m² Full screen 60 seconds 200 cd/m² Calling this model simply a “900-nit display” would hide its full-screen and sustained conditions. Calling it a “200-nit display” would hide its small-highlight capability. Automatic brightness limiting develops one reason those conditions can change the available output. Other display processing and power policies can also participate. The target affects highlight mapping An Emby playback path adapting HDR content needs a useful description of the destination. A source mastering peak is information about the source’s creation context; it is not a measurement of the current display. Likewise, peak-luminance detection estimates or reads content properties. It does not measure the panel’s present physical luminance. Using a small-patch maximum as though it were a full-screen sustainable target can give an incomplete account of a bright scene. A mapping and display controller may then adapt the result further. White is only one output color The maximum white luminance does not specify the maximum luminance of every saturated color. The color-producing arrangement and permitted drive define a broader color-volume relationship. Black level also needs its own simultaneous-picture context. Dividing the highest white from one test by the lowest black from an unrelated test can describe a different condition from the contrast surrounding a movie highlight. See Also HDR display capabilities Automatic brightness limiting Projectors and the viewing surface Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping References VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria SID/ICDM: Information Display Measurements Standard Dell: OLED luminance and display-pattern loading

articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.title: Overview: HDR and brightness | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/hdr/.keywords: Overview: HDR and brightness HDR display behavior relates supported signal interpretation to brightness control across a picture and over time. A peak-brightness figure does not describe every area of every scene. Local dimming and automatic brightness limiting address different spatial or power relationships, while HDR capability includes supported signal handling. These topics make the displayed light behavior more precise than one advertised number. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HDR display capabilities HDR display capability combines accepted signal formats with the display’s usable luminance, contrast, color reproduction and processing behaviour. Local dimming Local dimming adjusts illumination in backlight regions so an LCD can use different light levels across the same picture. Display peak brightness Display peak brightness is a luminance result that needs a defined picture area, duration, mode and measurement context. Automatic brightness limiting Automatic brightness limiting reduces permitted display output as picture loading reaches the implementation’s power or drive constraints. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft: Advanced Color display pipeline

articles/display-av/characteristics/inde.title: Overview: Display characteristics | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/inde.keywords: Overview: Display characteristics Display characteristics describe the screen's picture grid, light production and color interpretation. Native resolution, panel technology and brightness behavior influence different aspects of the visible picture. Calibration and color management add interpretation across the presentation path. This area helps identify which property is being observed before it is attributed to the source file. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Native display resolution Native display resolution describes the physical imaging grid, which remains distinct from the accepted input mode and the resolution of the source picture. Display technologies Display technologies produce light and visible images through different panel or projection mechanisms. HDR and brightness HDR display behavior relates supported signal interpretation to brightness control across a picture and over time. Color calibration Display calibration adjusts a defined output state toward a chosen target, while characterization and profiling describe how that state reproduces colors. Display color management Display color management relates the source’s defined color meaning to the current output state through transformations implemented by the application, operating system and display path. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata Microsoft: Advanced Color display pipeline

articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.title: LCD and LED-backlit displays | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.keywords: LCD and LED-backlit displays An LED-backlit LCD forms pictures by modulating a separate backlight through a liquid-crystal pixel structure. Most televisions described as LED TVs use an LCD panel illuminated by LEDs. The LEDs provide light; the liquid-crystal structure controls how much of it reaches the viewer at each pixel. The names refer to different parts of the same display. The light source and the picture grid An LCD’s backlight passes through optical layers and the pixel structure. Pixel drive changes the liquid crystal’s effect on polarization, allowing different amounts of light through the relevant color channels. Term Part of the arrangement LCD Liquid-crystal modulation of light LED backlight Light source behind or around the panel Mini-LED backlight A backlight using smaller LED elements and an implemented zone arrangement OLED An emissive pixel technology with a different light-producing principle A quantum-dot color-conversion layer can alter the backlight’s spectral/color properties while the display still uses an LCD to form its picture. The number of LEDs is not necessarily the number of independently controlled local-dimming zones . Several emitters can share one zone’s drive. A bright subtitle and a dark background compete Imagine an original zone containing a bright subtitle and nearby dark picture pixels. Raising the zone’s light helps the subtitle reach its intended brightness. The LCD’s dark pixels must then reject that same stronger illumination. If their residual transmission is one-thousandth of the white transmission, a declared 500-cd/m² white gives a simplified 0.5-cd/m² dark result. Reducing the zone’s white-equivalent light to 50 cd/m² lowers the residual to 0.05, but also limits the subtitle’s brightness. These are invented transmission values, with ambient reflections omitted. They explain why a zone controller makes a spatial compromise. They are not measurements of a particular LCD. An Emby subtitle overlay can therefore change the visible local contrast even when the video stream and subtitle timing are correct. Backlight arrangement changes the compromise A uniformly driven backlight sets one light level across the screen. Edge-lit or direct-lit local control divides that responsibility into zones. Smaller appropriately controlled zones can isolate bright objects more closely. Their boundaries, optical light spread and control decisions still matter. A zone can illuminate pixels beyond the object that caused it to brighten. The panel’s own dark-state transmission also matters: adding more zones does not replace that property with perfect rejection. Pixel transitions and light timing affect motion Changing a pixel from one gray level to another takes a finite response. Different transitions can take different amounts of time, and overdrive can alter both speed and overshoot. Separately, the backlight can illuminate continuously or use a timed pattern. A quickly changing LCD pixel under a long light hold can still produce tracking blur. Display response time separates transition speed from persistence. Those properties explain why two LED-backlit LCDs with the same resolution can show a moving edge differently. See Also OLED displays Local dimming and backlight zones Display response time and motion blur HDR display capabilities References LG: OLED emission and LCD backlighting VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria

articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.title: OLED displays | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.keywords: OLED displays An OLED display produces light through independently driven organic emissive elements, with picture behaviour determined by its pixel arrangement, drive and brightness controls. An OLED display generates light in its organic emissive elements instead of passing a shared backlight through a liquid-crystal panel. Its pixel drive controls the local light output. A dark pixel can consequently stop emitting while a neighbouring pixel remains bright. That changes the local-contrast problem encountered with a shared LCD backlight zone. Emission is local; the complete panel has shared limits Property Meaning for the picture Local emission control A small bright object does not require a surrounding backlight zone to brighten Subpixel/color arrangement The panel’s specific arrangement forms the displayed colors Whole-screen electrical loading Many bright elements require more combined drive than a small highlight Pixel response The light output can change rapidly, while presentation timing remains another constraint Different OLED arrangements produce their color channels differently. “OLED” does not specify every subpixel pattern, spectral property or screen-surface treatment. Likewise, a pixel that emits no light does not remove room light reflected by the screen. The apparent black level in a bright room includes that reflected contribution. A highlight and a white screen are different workloads A small highlight can use high local drive while much of the panel remains dark. A largely white picture drives many more elements at once. The display can reduce permitted drive under that larger load. Dell documents picture-pattern-dependent luminance on specified OLED laptop panels. The general relationship is developed in automatic brightness limiting ; the exact curve belongs to the product and its mode. For an Emby movie, a bright snow scene can therefore have different sustained brightness from a small bright lamp in an otherwise dark scene. This is a panel-output relationship, not evidence that the player has changed the encoded video bitrate. Brightness should be described with its picture area and duration. A peak figure from a small patch cannot be applied unchanged to an entire screen. A fast pixel still displays timed movie pictures Fast response reduces the time a transition spends between its old and new level. It does not add source pictures. A 24-fps film still contains a new source picture roughly every 41.7 milliseconds. Repeating each picture evenly on a high-refresh display preserves that sampling. An uneven repeat pattern can still cause judder . Holding a picture’s light while the eye tracks a moving object can also produce persistence blur, even if the initial pixel transition is very fast. Black-frame insertion explains one way a display can shorten the illuminated interval. See Also LCD and LED-backlit displays Automatic brightness limiting Display response time and motion blur Black-frame insertion and display persistence References LG: OLED emission and LCD backlighting Dell: OLED luminance and display-pattern loading VESA: DisplayHDR performance criteria

articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.title: Projectors and the viewing surface | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.keywords: Projectors and the viewing surface A projector forms a picture through an imaging engine and optics onto a viewing surface whose size, reflectance and ambient illumination affect the visible result. A projector does not end its picture path at an internal panel. Its imaging engine and lens put light onto a screen or other surface, which then sends some of that light toward the viewer. The viewing surface and room therefore participate in the displayed picture. A projector with the same settings can produce a different visible result after its image is enlarged or the room lights are changed. Illumination and imaging do different jobs A lamp, LEDs or lasers supply illumination. An imaging arrangement controls the picture carried by that light. Epson’s 3LCD description separates light into red, green and blue paths, modulates them through their LCD panels and recombines them. DLP uses controlled micromirrors; TI also documents optical-actuator arrangements that create shifted sub-images. “Laser projector” identifies the light source, not a unique pixel technology or a guarantee about contrast. The imaging engine, optics and drive arrangement still determine important picture properties. Lumens and screen luminance are different quantities A lumen figure concerns luminous flux. Screen luminance, commonly expressed in cd/m² or nits, describes light leaving the surface in a viewing direction. To connect them, the screen’s area and reflection need assumptions. Consider an original ideal model: 2,000 lumens reach a uniformly illuminated four-square-metre screen. The screen reflects 80% of incident light. Reflection is diffuse, following an ideal Lambertian relationship. Illuminance is flux divided by area. Luminance for this model is illuminance multiplied by reflectance and divided by π: Illuminance = 2000 / 4 = 500 lux Luminance = 500 × 0.8 / π = 127.324 cd/m² Doubling both picture dimensions gives four times the area. The same flux then produces 125 lux and 31.831 cd/m² in this model. Real screens can direct light differently; projector output can be nonuniform, and the usable output depends on the selected picture mode. The calculation is not a conversion rule for every advertised lumen value. It explains why enlarging the Emby movie’s projected image can reduce its brightness without changing the video stream. Room light raises the dark floor Assume a second original model has projected white at 100 cd/m² and projected black at 0.1 cd/m². In the absence of ambient contribution, their ratio is 1000:1. If the room adds a uniform one cd/m² of reflected luminance to both areas: Visible white = 100 + 1 = 101 cd/m² Visible black = 0.1 + 1 = 1.1 cd/m² Contrast = 101 / 1.1 = 91.818:1 The white changes little proportionally; the black changes greatly. Raising projector output is consequently not equivalent to removing ambient light. A screen with directional properties can change which room light reaches the viewer. Its orientation and viewing geometry then become part of the result. The simple diffuse model above deliberately excludes those effects. The input mode is not the final optical detail A projector can accept a source larger than its physical imaging grid and resample it. Some arrangements create multiple shifted positions during a frame. Native resolution separates the physical imager from accepted input and temporally addressed screen positions. Lens focus, alignment and the screen also affect whether fine detail survives. A keystone correction can resample the picture to compensate for geometry. That correction cannot add optical focus or make every source position map directly onto an imaging element. HDR needs a target suited to the projected image An HDR input describes an intended signal interpretation. The projector and screen must still map that signal into their usable luminance and contrast. A mastering peak is not a command to produce the same measured luminance on every projected screen. Tone mapping addresses the adaptation; display peak brightness explains the conditions needed to describe its target. See Also Native display resolution HDR display capabilities Display peak brightness Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References Epson: 3LCD projection technology TI: DLP display technology, including optical pixel shifting SID/ICDM: Information Display Measurements Standard

articles/display-av/characteristics/tech.keywords: Overview: Display technologies Display technologies produce light and visible images through different panel or projection mechanisms.
