articles/display-av/connections/AV-DSC.h.title: Display Stream Compression (DSC) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/AV-DSC.h.keywords: Display Stream Compression (DSC) Display Stream Compression encodes the display-link picture representation to reduce transport demand under a supported source/sink configuration. Display Stream Compression , or DSC , reduces the amount of picture data carried by a compatible display connection. It operates at a different point from the HEVC or AV1 encoding of an Emby movie. The client ordinarily decodes the movie first, prepares an output presentation, then an implemented display-link path can encode that presentation with DSC. Two compression layers belong to different routes Stored/network movie encoding -> media decoder -> presentation pictures -> supported DSC display-link encoding -> display-link decoding -> display output DSC does not rewrite the source movie or directly reduce the server’s network bitrate. Its purpose is the local display transport. VESA publishes the DSC specification and describes its performance as visually lossless. HDMI and DisplayPort have their own supported arrangements for carrying a DSC representation. A rate reduction can change feasibility Consider an original active-data budget with thirty bits per pixel, a 3840 × 2160 presentation and 120 picture occurrences per second: Uncompressed active data = 3840 × 2160 × 120 × 30 = 29.859840 Gbit/s Under a declared threefold reduction, the modeled compressed active rate is: 29.859840 / 3 = 9.953280 Gbit/s The reduction is substantial, but this exercise omits transport overhead and all particular DSC mode constraints. It is not proof that a real twelve-Gbit/s path carries the mode. The selected compressed bits-per-pixel target, format, slice arrangement, buffering and implementation limits still need to be accepted. Source and sink must agree on the configuration A DSC encoder and decoder need the relevant picture and compression parameters. Slicing organizes the picture into regions processed under the selected configuration. Support for one DSC arrangement does not promise every picture extent, color representation or slice layout. A receiver, converter or dock can also constrain which compressed representation passes through it. An intermediate device may forward an accepted compressed stream or reconstruct and generate another output, depending on its implementation. The route should identify which role it actually performs. A cable does not add a missing DSC decoder to a display. Visually lossless is a quality description Visually lossless does not mean that every reconstructed sample is mathematically identical to the original under every mode. That distinction matters when describing display-link data, but it should not be confused with the quality choices of the movie’s own codec. A heavily compressed source can have visible artifacts before the DSC stage is reached. The DSC specification defines its coding behavior and configurations. Actual display performance and compatibility remain properties of the implemented route. For an Emby session, changing a network transcoding bitrate and enabling a supported DSC output solve different capacity problems. One concerns media delivery; the other concerns the presentation signal sent to the display. See Also DisplayPort video links HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode Video Bit Depth References VESA: Standards and public DSC resources VESA DisplayPort: Technical FAQ HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview

articles/display-av/connections/AV-Recei.title: AV receivers in the video path | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/AV-Recei.keywords: AV receivers in the video path An AV receiver in the picture route accepts an upstream display signal, handles its audio/control roles and produces a downstream signal whose capabilities form a second connection constraint. When a player connects through an AV receiver, the path contains two picture connections: player to receiver, then receiver to display. The receiver is not just a length of cable. It receives an upstream signal, can use its audio and other information, and produces the downstream connection. Each side has its own requirements The player’s output must fit the receiver input. The receiver’s output must fit the TV input. Both installed cable paths must carry their selected signals. Capability information presented upstream can represent an arrangement involving the receiver’s own features and the connected display. It is not always a byte-for-byte copy of what the TV would advertise directly. EDID develops those declarations. The receiver’s particular port and mode remain relevant. An unchanged pass-through exercise Use three invented mode labels: A : a chosen 1080p60 SDR mode. B : a chosen 4K60 eight-bit mode. C : a chosen 4K60 ten-bit PQ mode. Suppose the player can produce A/B/C; the receiver input accepts A/B/C; the receiver output supports only A/B; the TV accepts A/B/C. For this unchanged pass-through model: Player {A,B,C} ∩ Receiver input {A,B,C} ∩ Receiver output {A,B} ∩ TV input {A,B,C} = {A,B} The TV’s support for C does not make C available across the whole route. A receiver implementing format conversion can have a different relationship, with input C transformed into another accepted output. That would be a changed presentation, not unchanged pass-through. The model above deliberately excludes such conversion. Audio can leave before the video reaches the TV For a client connected to the receiver, the receiver can consume the HDMI audio while forwarding an implemented video output. It does not need the TV to return that same audio over ARC. In another topology, the Emby app runs on the TV or an external player connects directly to the TV. The audio system then needs a route from TV to receiver, such as ARC or eARC . These arrangements can expose different audio-format limits. The receiver decoding a codec at one input does not prove the TV returns that codec unchanged through every route. Bitstream passthrough also needs the actual codec and endpoint relationship, separate from video mode support. Picture processing can change the route A receiver may scale, overlay its interface, convert a format or forward an accepted signal. Its selected operating behavior determines whether picture samples and signaling are preserved. HDR and variable-refresh features need the corresponding downstream behavior. A receiver successfully forwarding an ordinary SDR mode does not establish its support for a different HDR or VRR mode. For protected output, an HDCP-capable receiver can have a repeater role. Authentication and downstream topology are another part of the connection rather than a video-codec decoder requirement. A direct connection is a useful comparison Keeping the same source and requested output while comparing direct player-to-TV with player-to-receiver-to-TV changes the intermediate route. If only the direct arrangement works, the observation narrows the problem to the added ports, links, capability handling or receiver behavior. It does not yet identify which one failed. See Also HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) EDID: display capability declarations HDCP and protected display links Audio Bitstream Passthrough References HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview HDMI LA: Enhanced Audio Return Channel DCP: HDCP specifications

articles/display-av/connections/displayp.title: DisplayPort video links | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/displayp.keywords: DisplayPort video links DisplayPort carries presentation streams over a negotiated link with separate lane/rate, stream-format and capability relationships. DisplayPort transports a prepared presentation signal from a source toward a display. Like HDMI, it describes the local display connection rather than the compressed movie delivered by Emby Server. Its link has an implemented lane count and rate. The picture streams carried through that link have their own timing and sample-format requirements. The main link and AUX path serve different work The main link carries the presentation stream. The AUX relationship supports control and capability operations such as reading relevant device information and establishing the link. A source needs both suitable stream properties and a usable trained link. Reading a display’s declarations does not prove that the main link is carrying the intended signal successfully. EDID supplies display declarations within the appropriate arrangement; other DisplayPort capability information also participates. Four lanes do not all use the same rate or coding Use two original four-lane arithmetic exercises: Declared link Gross lane total Coding-only ceiling Four HBR3 lanes at 8.1 Gbit/s each 32.4 Gbit/s 25.92 Gbit/s after 8b/10b expansion Four UHBR20 lanes at 20 Gbit/s each 80 Gbit/s 77.575758 Gbit/s after 128b/132b expansion These ceilings remove only the stated channel-coding expansion. They are not complete active-picture capacity calculations. VESA’s DisplayPort FAQ gives 77.37 Gbit/s as the maximum payload for its stated four-lane UHBR20 arrangement. Additional transport accounting explains why the simple 80 × 128/132 ceiling is a different number. The requested mode also has timing, color precision, chroma and possibly DSC requirements. Gross rate alone does not prove a particular uncompressed mode fits. The edition does not identify every feature The current VESA FAQ discusses DisplayPort 2.1b, including that certification can encompass devices without UHBR rates. Its product feature declarations are therefore still needed. “DisplayPort 2.1b” cannot be expanded into “this exact port always supplies four UHBR20 lanes.” The actual source, sink, cable and implemented path determine the selected configuration. A laptop’s integrated output and a separate graphics card can expose different link resources even if their marketing descriptions use the same edition name. Adapters introduce another interface A DisplayPort-to-HDMI converter receives one transport and generates another. Its accepted DisplayPort mode and produced HDMI mode are separate constraints. A passive dual-mode arrangement and an active protocol converter are not the same mechanism. Which route is present belongs to the device/adapter specification. Likewise, a dock can share link resources between several displays or other traffic. A mode working on one direct display does not prove that an expanded dock topology retains the same budget. USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode develops the connector and lane-allocation relationship. The stream is the local presentation An Emby client can keep a high-resolution desktop output while playing lower-resolution content within it. The DisplayPort stream then describes that desktop presentation. See Also USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode Display Stream Compression (DSC) HDMI video transport Variable refresh rate (VRR) References VESA DisplayPort: Technical FAQ VESA: Standards and public DSC resources

articles/display-av/connections/displayp.title: USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/displayp.keywords: USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode uses a supported USB-C connection arrangement to carry DisplayPort signaling, with lane allocation and adapters determining the available presentation path. A USB-C connector can support several kinds of connection. DisplayPort Alt Mode is one defined arrangement that uses the supported connector/cable path for DisplayPort signaling. The connector’s shape alone does not establish that the port, cable or adapter provides that arrangement. Protocol support has to be present VESA defines DisplayPort Alt Mode for USB Type-C in collaboration with the USB ecosystem. A supporting source and connected device establish an appropriate mode and lane arrangement. A charging-only or data-only path can have the same connector shape without exposing the required video route. Power delivery capability is also not a substitute for DisplayPort capability. For an Emby client connected to a screen through USB-C, identify the source port’s actual video support, the cable and the device at the other end. Lane allocation can change the display budget A supported arrangement can assign all four high-speed lanes to DisplayPort, or use a two-lane DisplayPort arrangement alongside other supported data use. Take an original HBR3 exercise with 8.1 Gbit/s per DisplayPort lane and 8b/10b channel coding: Four DP lanes: 4 × 8.1 × 8/10 = 25.92 Gbit/s Two DP lanes: 2 × 8.1 × 8/10 = 12.96 Gbit/s These are coding-only ceilings before other transport requirements. The two-lane arrangement has half the four-lane budget under these declared assumptions. This does not identify the policy of every dock. Its negotiated mode, lane rate, compression and internal processing need their own evidence. A display’s USB hub may influence the chosen arrangement in a product that shares those resources. A resolution supported through a dedicated DisplayPort connection can consequently have different conditions through its USB-C hub route. Several displays can share one upstream resource A dock using one upstream DisplayPort link for multiple streams must fit their combined transport demand into its usable resource. If one original stream needs twelve units of a declared twenty-unit budget, adding another identical stream would require twenty-four. Both cannot fit unchanged under that model. The model omits packet overhead and is not a dock benchmark. It shows why “supports this mode on one screen” does not imply “supports this mode on every output simultaneously.” DSC or a different mode can change the demand if the complete path implements it. The number of physical output sockets does not create extra upstream capacity. Three USB-C video routes should be named accurately Route Presentation relationship DisplayPort Alt Mode Uses an established alternate-mode lane/signaling arrangement DisplayPort tunneling Carries a display transport through a supported interconnect’s tunneling route USB graphics device Produces display output through an implemented USB graphics/data arrangement The application, driver and hardware requirements differ. A USB-C-to-HDMI device can also perform an active conversion after receiving DisplayPort. These routes are not interchangeable merely because the connectors fit. See Also DisplayPort video links Display Stream Compression (DSC) HDMI handshakes and black screens References VESA: DisplayPort over USB-C VESA DisplayPort: Technical FAQ VESA: Standards and public DSC resources

articles/display-av/connections/displayp.title: Overview: DisplayPort connections | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/displayp.keywords: Overview: DisplayPort connections DisplayPort carries video through supported link and connector arrangements, including USB-C alternate-mode paths. A USB-C connection can expose a DisplayPort route under the applicable alternate-mode arrangement. The connector, lane allocation and receiving path still need their own context. articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.title: HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.keywords: HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL HDMI link bandwidth depends on the selected timing, sample format and TMDS or FRL transport arrangement rather than on the movie’s compressed bitrate. A movie’s compressed bitrate is not the bandwidth of its display connection. Once the client has decoded and prepared pictures, the output link must transport a defined presentation mode. For HDMI, TMDS and FRL use different transport arrangements. Resolution, refresh, sample precision and chroma all contribute to the requested work. Start with active picture samples An original uncompressed RGB model has three components per pixel. Its active sample rate is: width × height × refresh × 3 × component bits At 3840 × 2160, sixty Hz and eight bits per component, this gives 11.943936 Gbit/s. Ten-bit components at the same active geometry give 14.929920 Gbit/s. Doubling the refresh to 120 Hz doubles those active rates. A 4K120 ten-bit RGB model consequently has 29.859840 Gbit/s of active samples. These values omit timing and transport overhead. They are a starting point, not the cable rate required by a qualified HDMI mode. TMDS adds timing and coding relationships Traditional TMDS uses three data channels and a separate clock relationship. In the basic eight-bit-per-component RGB exercise, each data channel transmits ten-bit symbols. Use an original declared sixty-Hz timing with totals of 4400 × 2250: Pixel clock = 4400 × 2250 × 60 = 594,000,000 Hz Eight-bit RGB TMDS data rate = 594,000,000 × 3 × 10 = 17.82 Gbit/s The active picture remains 3840 × 2160, but the timing totals include intervals beyond its active samples. That is why the active 11.943936-Gbit/s calculation does not equal the TMDS wire rate. For the same declared RGB/4:4:4 timing, a ten-bit Deep Color exercise scales the data rate by 10/8 : 17.82 × 10/8 = 22.275 Gbit/s That exceeds a declared 18-Gbit/s TMDS route even though the eight-bit exercise fits below it. YCbCr 4:2:2 has its own packing rules. Its requested transport rate should not be derived by blindly applying this RGB Deep Color formula. FRL has another link organization Fixed Rate Link packetizes the presentation over an implemented lane/rate configuration. AMD’s HDMI transmitter documentation distinguishes its FRL path, including forward-error-correction parity and 16b/18b coding, from its TMDS path. For an original four-lane, twelve-Gbit/s-per-lane exercise: Gross rate = 4 × 12 = 48 Gbit/s Coding-only ceiling = 48 × 16/18 = 42.666667 Gbit/s The second value removes only that coding expansion. It is not a claim of 42.666667 Gbit/s of usable active picture payload: packet/control and error-correction relationships still need accounting. HDMI LA’s current HDMI 2.2 overview specifies an upper bandwidth of 96 Gbit/s. That specification maximum does not establish the lane/rate implementation of every source, receiver or display input. A source and sink use a supported actual configuration. A higher edition number is not a replacement for its feature and mode declarations. Chroma and link compression change the request Reducing chroma sampling can lower the amount of color-detail information carried by a picture. It changes the representation; it is not simply another cable with the same picture data. Chroma subsampling describes that spatial relationship. HDMI packing and mode rules determine how the selected format is transported. DSC compresses the display-link representation under a supported arrangement. It is separate from the movie’s HEVC/AV1 compression. Both endpoints and any intermediate path must accept the required DSC configuration. Using a compressed or subsampled mode can consequently make a requested output feasible under a different bandwidth condition, while retaining its own format and interoperability constraints. Establish feasibility for the whole route First identify the exact output: active dimensions, refresh, timing, sample format, precision and whether DSC is used. Then establish the actual transmitter, input/output ports, intermediate devices and cable capability. A receiver can accept one signal and expose another link constraint toward the TV. Finally, distinguish an advertised mode from successful active operation. Link establishment, format interpretation and sustained transport still need to succeed. A movie playing at thirty Mbit/s over the network can ask for the same HDMI mode as another playing at ten Mbit/s. If both are presented through the same desktop mode, their display-link request can be identical. See Also HDMI video transport HDMI cable categories Display Stream Compression (DSC) Chroma Subsampling Video Bit Depth References HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview AMD/Xilinx: TMDS encoding and serialization reference AMD PG350: HDMI TMDS/FRL transmission and coding CTA: CTA-861 digital-interface standard Intel: HDMI Deep Color ratios, versioned FPGA guide

articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.title: HDMI cable categories | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.keywords: HDMI cable categories HDMI cable categories identify tested transport capabilities and certification scopes, independently of the features implemented by connected devices. HDMI cable names describe transport capability and, for the relevant categories, certification. They are not a list of features that the cable can add to the connected electronics. The requested output mode must fit the devices and the particular cable path together. Official categories have different scopes The following summarizes HDMI LA’s public category descriptions checked in October 2026: Cable category Published scope relevant here Standard HDMI Earlier 720p/1080i applications High Speed HDMI Up to 10.2 Gbit/s Premium High Speed HDMI Certified up to 18 Gbit/s Ultra High Speed HDMI Up to 48 Gbit/s Ultra96 HDMI Up to 96 Gbit/s Ethernet variants and specific certification programs have their own definitions. The exact official name and certification label are more useful than a vague “4K cable” claim. A resolution label is incomplete because refresh, precision, chroma and link compression can change the mode’s transport requirements. Capability does not add device features A 96-Gbit/s-capable cable does not make an eighteen-Gbit/s transmitter send at 96 Gbit/s. Nor does it supply a missing HDR, VRR or eARC implementation in a connected device. The cable can support the requested electrical transport while the source or sink still lacks the requested operation. HDMI bandwidth develops that complete mode relationship. eARC also needs compatible return-audio ports and capabilities. The installed cable is the relevant instance Certification applies within its defined model/length scope. A long installation, extension, adapter or switch adds a different signal path from a short direct connection. An active or optical assembly can have a designated source/display direction and additional power or installation requirements. Its physical fit does not establish correct orientation. This does not mean every long cable fails or every short cable works. It means the full installed path should be identified. Compare one output request at a time For an Emby playback comparison, keep the same source and selected output mode while changing the cable path. That tests the transport variable more clearly than simultaneously changing resolution, refresh and HDR state. A path that works at one mode but fails at a higher-rate mode provides useful evidence about the requested transport. It does not prove that the movie’s compressed bitrate caused the failure. See Also HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL HDMI handshakes and black screens HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) References HDMI LA: Cable categories and certification HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview

articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.title: HDMI video transport | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/connections/hdmi/AV-.keywords: HDMI video transport HDMI video transport carries a selected presentation signal between source and sink, with accompanying audio and signaling distinct from the compressed media delivered to the player. In a typical Emby setup, the server delivers encoded media to the client. The client decodes and prepares a presentation, then its HDMI output sends a selected display signal to a TV or receiver. The cable ordinarily carries that presentation signal, not the original movie container or its HEVC/AV1 bitstream. Two connections carry different representations Connection Representation in the ordinary playback route Emby Server → client Encoded media through the chosen delivery method Decoder → renderer Reconstructed picture resources and their timing/color meaning Client HDMI output → display input Selected picture timing, sample representation, audio and signaling The network bitrate and HDMI link rate therefore describe different data. For an original 3840 × 2160, sixty-picture/second RGB exercise with eight bits per component, active picture samples alone require: 3840 × 2160 × 60 × 3 × 8 = 11,943,936,000 bits/second This is about 11.944 Gbit/s before the transport’s timing, coding and other overhead. A source file encoded at twenty Mbit/s is about 597 times smaller by those two declared rates. The calculation is an active-sample model, not an HDMI mode qualification. Link bandwidth adds the transport relationships. The selected signal has several properties A mode needs more than a resolution label: Property Example question Picture timing Which dimensions, refresh rate and timing totals are selected? Sample representation RGB or YCbCr, with which chroma arrangement and precision? Color interpretation Which primaries, transfer function and range describe the output? Link arrangement Which supported TMDS or FRL configuration carries it? Companion information Which audio and required signaling are supplied? A device can use a high-resolution output for a lower-resolution movie because the client scales the picture into its established output mode. Conversely, delivering a 4K movie does not prove that the client sends a 4K HDMI signal. The selected local mode may be smaller. Source, sink and intermediate devices participate The output device is the HDMI source for this connection. The receiving input is its sink. A receiver or switch can add another input/output relationship. Capability information helps the source choose a mode, while the link must successfully establish and carry that choice. A mode supported by the TV alone may not survive an intermediate device or a particular port arrangement. EDID describes declarations. AV receivers explains the two-link route. Handshakes separates mode choice from active signal progress. Picture transport has separate companion functions HDMI can carry audio alongside the video presentation. ARC/eARC provides an additional return-audio relationship from a TV toward an audio system. CEC carries control messages. HDCP addresses protected-link authentication. HDR signaling communicates relevant output interpretation. See Also HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL HDMI cable categories EDID: display capability declarations HDMI HDR signaling HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) References HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview CTA: CTA-861 digital-interface standard AMD PG350: HDMI TMDS/FRL transmission and coding

articles/display-av/Display-Frame-to-Scr.title: The path from decoded frames to the screen | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/Display-Frame-to-Scr.keywords: The path from decoded frames to the screen A displayed picture results from decoding, presentation scheduling, color processing, output transport and the display’s own light-producing response. A movie can Direct Play from Emby Server and still pass through several transformations before its pictures become light. Direct Play describes delivery of the original media to a compatible client. The client then decodes and presents it through its device’s display system. That distinction matters when a movie plays without buffering but has uneven motion, incorrect colors or a short blackout at startup. Those symptoms can arise after the server has delivered the right bytes. A picture changes representation along the route The decoder reconstructs a picture in a memory layout such as YCbCr planes. A renderer prepares it for the presentation surface: perhaps scaling it, converting its color representation, composing subtitles or placing it inside the app interface. The operating system can combine that surface with other windows. An output engine produces the selected display signal. A connected TV or monitor receives that signal and can apply additional processing before driving its pixels. These operations can occur on dedicated hardware, GPU processing or other implemented paths. Frame surfaces describe the storage and ownership relationships; a compatible decoder surface is not automatically a finished display signal. For example, a 1920 × 1080 source shown on a 3840 × 2160 panel needs a spatial mapping somewhere. If the client sends 1080p, the display may scale it. If the client sends 2160p, scaling occurs earlier. The panel’s resolution alone does not identify the scaler. Four different clocks meet at presentation Clock or interval What it describes Programme timestamps When each picture belongs in the movie Decode/processing completion When its usable result becomes ready Presentation/refresh schedule When the display system can select or scan that result Pixel response and light emission When the visible output changes A picture with a presentation timestamp of ten seconds is not required to spend ten seconds in the decoder. The player uses a playback clock to relate programme time to the current presentation deadline. Likewise, “60 Hz” describes a refresh schedule, while “24 fps” describes source-picture timing. A player must map one to the other. Frame-rate matching develops that mapping. The audio clock can also guide synchronization. Delaying video while audio advances creates another relationship to manage; increasing server throughput does not automatically correct it. Ready, selected and visible are different moments Consider an original simplified 60-Hz model. Refresh boundaries occur at 0, 16.667 and 33.333 milliseconds. Picture A becomes usable at 10 ms. Assume the presentation system selects A at the next boundary, then scans the picture progressively from top to bottom over one refresh interval: Event Model time A becomes ready 10 ms A is selected for scanout 16.667 ms Centre of A is scanned 25 ms Bottom of A is scanned 33.333 ms If the centre pixels have a declared four-millisecond transition after their new drive begins, their modeled response point is 29 ms. Ready-to-centre-response time is therefore nineteen milliseconds. This exercise assumes a continuous scan, no extra queued pictures, no TV processing delay and the stated response interval. A real panel may buffer, scan differently, illuminate in pulses or have transitions that differ by color level. It is a timing explanation, not a latency measurement. An extra presentation queue can add time before selection. Display processing can add time after reception. A quoted pixel response does not include either automatically. Color interpretation travels with the picture The source’s transfer function, primaries, matrix and range guide its interpretation. The renderer and output system need a compatible destination representation. The display needs the intended signal interpretation. Ten-bit storage does not, by itself, make the result HDR. A PQ picture interpreted through an SDR transfer function can look wrong even though the decoder reconstructed its values correctly. Display color management explains the application/OS relationship. HDMI HDR signaling separates source metadata, sink capability and the signal actually being sent. Evidence should identify its stage An Emby playback report showing Direct Play establishes the delivery choice. A hardware decoder report establishes a reconstruction path. The operating system’s selected output mode describes the display connection. A TV’s signal information describes what that input recognizes. Together these observations locate the route. None replaces all the others. When a mode change produces a startup blackout, the useful question is whether the output is being re-established at that moment. When a pan has regular uneven steps, the useful question is whether source pictures receive equal display durations. A stall while the next programme interval is unavailable is a different observation again.
