articles/display-av/input/Input-Bluetoot.title: Bluetooth remote controls | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/input/Input-Bluetoot.keywords: Bluetooth remote controls A Bluetooth remote delivers supported control data over a paired wireless relationship, with its profile, host mapping and application context determining available actions. A Bluetooth remote communicates through a supported wireless/profile relationship rather than relying solely on an optical path to an infrared receiver. Pairing establishes part of that relationship. The host still needs to understand the remote’s control representation and deliver useful events to the application. Connection is one layer of compatibility Layer Relationship to establish Wireless connection Remote and host can establish the supported link Profile/service Host understands the device’s implemented control arrangement Input mapping Reports become appropriate host controls Application context The app recognizes the event in its current view Bluetooth SIG’s HID over GATT Profile defines one supported way to carry HID control data over Bluetooth LE. Other Bluetooth HID or vendor-specific arrangements can differ. A remote being connected does not prove that a voice control, proprietary shortcut or every media key has a mapping in every host. One handset can contain more than one path A handset can use infrared for a power command while using Bluetooth for navigation. The TV’s power action may consequently work even when the paired navigation route is unavailable. The reverse can also occur: navigation reaches the paired host while a power action aimed at another receiver does not. For Emby, identify which device receives each particular control. A TV remote forwarding an event to an external player introduces an additional host or CEC relationship. Reports still need state and context A held control can produce continuing state. The application decides whether that means one action, repeated navigation or a continuous operation. After a disconnection, stale held-state information should not be treated as a fresh press on a newly available device. The host/app’s reconnection handling supplies that policy. HID describes how a report’s declared meaning becomes usable input. Gamepad input develops analog state and threshold decisions. Emby’s keyboard and remote support concerns the later application actions. A useful comparison checks one named button from connection through host recognition to the focused app response. See Also Human Interface Devices (HID) Infrared remote controls Gamepad input for media navigation References Bluetooth SIG: HID over GATT Profile 1.2 USB-IF: HID class and usage specifications

articles/display-av/input/Input-Gamepads.title: Gamepad input for media navigation | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/input/Input-Gamepads.keywords: Gamepad input for media navigation Gamepad input exposes button and axis state that a media application maps into navigation and playback actions with appropriate thresholds, repetition and focus handling. A gamepad supplies buttons, sticks and other control state. A media app can map that state into focus movement, selection, seeking and playback actions. The device’s connection and the application’s mapping are separate. A controller working in a game does not establish its behavior in every Emby view. Values and physical layout need their own meaning The W3C Gamepad Working Draft describes button values and axes, along with a canonical standard mapping when the browser recognizes a matching layout. A standard mapping relates reported indices to physical control positions. It does not mean that every controller uses the same printed letters or that an app must assign the same action to every position. Unrecognized layouts can expose another ordering. Native apps can use platform-specific APIs and mappings. Input kind Example application policy Button transition Activate selection or toggle playback once Direction held Move focus with an intended repeat schedule Stick displacement Convert analog movement into navigation or seeking Reconnection Rebuild available-device and held-state context A dead zone can reject small centre noise Use an original one-axis model with input x between −1 and 1 and a dead zone of 0.2: y = 0, if |x| ≤ 0.2 y = sign(x) × (|x| − 0.2) / 0.8, otherwise The model maps input 0.1 to zero, 0.5 to 0.375 , −0.5 to −0.375 and the endpoints to ±1. This is a teaching policy, not an Emby default or a requirement of the W3C draft. Two-dimensional stick processing can use a radial or another dead-zone arrangement instead. The purpose is to prevent small resting variation from being interpreted as deliberate movement. Hysteresis separates entering and leaving an action A navigation decision near one threshold can chatter if the axis repeatedly crosses it. An original policy enters a positive navigation state at 0.6 and leaves it below 0.4 . Sample Input State after sample 1 0.55 Rest 2 0.65 Positive navigation entered 3 0.58 Positive navigation retained 4 0.45 Positive navigation retained 5 0.35 Rest 6 0.70 Positive navigation entered again The gap between the thresholds prevents small fluctuations from repeatedly starting/stopping the action. The modeled sequence has two entries into navigation. An app can then choose a timed repeat while the navigation state remains active. That repeat policy is another decision, not an extra physical press. A held button needs edge handling If a player polls not pressed, pressed, pressed, pressed, not pressed , a toggle should not necessarily run on every pressed sample. Detecting the transition makes one initial action possible. Retaining the state allows different behavior for a control intended to repeat or remain continuous. Focus changes and disconnected devices also need context. A press already held before a new view opens should not automatically be interpreted as a fresh selection in that view. Emby’s mapping is an application feature Emby documents an enhanced gamepad feature with an overview of assigned controls and a way to examine their recognition on the supported app route. That supplies app-specific context rather than a universal mapping for all clients. Check the particular app’s control view and current navigation/playback context. See Also Human Interface Devices (HID) Bluetooth remote controls References W3C: Gamepad specification USB-IF: HID class and usage specifications USB-IF: HID Usage Tables 1.7

articles/display-av/input/Input-HID.html.title: Human Interface Devices (HID) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/input/Input-HID.html.keywords: Human Interface Devices (HID) Human Interface Device reports describe controls through declared report layouts and usages, which a host interprets before applications assign actions. HID , Human Interface Device, provides a structured way to describe and report controls. Its use includes keyboards, pointers, gamepads and media-control devices. The report’s declared layout and usages tell a host what its fields mean. The receiving application then gives those controls an action in its own context. A descriptor describes; a report supplies state A report descriptor defines properties such as field sizes, ranges, collections and usages. An input report supplies values using that established layout. Reading a byte as an arbitrary key number without its descriptor can give the wrong meaning. The same bit pattern can represent a button, an axis value or padding under different layouts. The USB HID class specification defines its USB contract. Other transports, including supported Bluetooth profiles, can carry HID-related report arrangements through their own contracts. Usage pages qualify the control identifier USB-IF’s Usage Tables place controls into usage pages. The Consumer page has identifier 0x0C ; its Play/Pause usage is 0xCD . Those identifiers describe a control meaning, not the label painted on every handset or a guarantee that every host/application exposes it. A keyboard key and a Consumer Play/Pause control are consequently different declarations even when an application maps both to a playback action. An original one-bit report model This readable teaching object defines one media-control field: { "usagePage": 12, "usage": 205, "logicalRange": [0, 1], "inputBits": 1, "paddingBits": 7 } It is not a native HID report descriptor or a device capability capture. The decimal identifiers correspond to the Consumer/Play-Pause meanings above. For this original declared one-byte arrangement, with the control in the least significant bit: Report byte Declared control state 00 Not asserted 01 Asserted Seven other bits are padding in this model. A real descriptor can define more controls, report IDs and other layouts; the host must parse that actual declaration. An assertion is not an instruction to toggle continuously Polling an asserted report several times does not necessarily mean the user pressed the button several times. For an original sequence 00, 01, 01, 00 , the control has one transition from unasserted to asserted. A toggle action can therefore run once rather than once per asserted sample. A navigation action can intentionally use a repeat policy. A continuous analog action can use another policy again. HID reports provide input meaning/state; application behavior decides the operation. The focused route determines the result The operating system can consume a media control globally or route it to an application. A UI view can also assign a control differently while a movie is playing than while the user browses a library. For Emby, a device recognized as HID is only early evidence. The host event, app focus and current action mapping determine whether a press actually pauses, navigates or does something else. Keyboard and remote support describes the app’s control surface. Gamepad input adds axis values and mapping decisions beyond a single media button. See Also Bluetooth remote controls Infrared remote controls Gamepad input for media navigation References USB-IF: HID class and usage specifications USB-IF: HID Usage Tables 1.7 Bluetooth SIG: HID over GATT Profile 1.2

articles/display-av/input/Input-Infrared.title: Infrared remote controls | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/input/Input-Infrared.keywords: Infrared remote controls An infrared remote sends coded light pulses to a compatible receiver, whose decoding and key mapping determine the input delivered to an application. An infrared remote sends modulated light carrying an encoded command. The receiver must detect that signal, interpret its protocol and map the resulting command into a usable host input. A handset’s button label does not directly call an Emby function. Light modulation and commands have different timing Many consumer arrangements use a modulated carrier whose bursts and gaps encode the command. The exact protocol determines the message structure. For an original 38-kHz carrier exercise: Carrier period = 1 / 38,000 second = 26.316 microseconds That period is not the duration of a complete button message. A message uses a sequence of carrier bursts and gaps across a longer interval. A receiver designed for the wrong carrier/protocol can fail before the application receives any meaningful key. Infrared also needs a usable optical path; the receiver’s view and surrounding light conditions can affect detection. Reception, decoding and key mapping are separate stages The Linux remote-controller documentation provides a concrete implementation example. Some hardware supplies raw timings for software decoding; other hardware supplies decoded scancodes. A scancode identifies the received command within its protocol/device context. A keymap assigns a host key meaning. The focused app then interprets that host input. The same handset can therefore work differently through two receivers or host mappings. Repeated reports need an action policy A held key can produce repeated protocol reports. Some arrangements synthesize a release after an appropriate timeout rather than receiving a separate physical release message. Use an original logical-state exercise: Reported button state: 0, 1, 1, 1, 0 Rising-edge actions: 1 A toggle action triggered by every observed 1 would run three times. Triggering the initial transition runs once. Navigation can intentionally repeat while a button remains held; Play/Pause usually needs a different repeat policy. The protocol decoding alone does not choose the application’s desired behavior. A TV remote may take another route onward If the TV receives the infrared command and forwards a supported CEC control , the external Emby player receives that later route rather than the original optical pulses. If a USB IR receiver is connected to the player, the host may expose mapped input directly through its input system. Emby’s keyboard and remote documentation describes application-side control context. Identifying the original receiver, host event and focused view makes an input problem more precise than saying only that the remote is compatible. See Also Human Interface Devices (HID) Bluetooth remote controls HDMI-CEC control and device addressing References Linux: Remote-controller decoding and input events USB-IF: HID class and usage specifications

articles/display-av/motion/Display-Black.title: Black-frame insertion and display persistence | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/Display-Black.keywords: Black-frame insertion and display persistence Black-frame insertion or timed dark intervals reduce visible picture persistence by interrupting illumination between presentations. A display can shorten how long a picture remains illuminated by inserting dark intervals or timing its light output into shorter pulses. Black-frame insertion , often abbreviated BFI , is one name for this kind of persistence-reduction behavior. The purpose is to change when light is visible, not to add missing source pictures. A held picture and a light pulse In an original exact sixty-Hz exercise, one picture interval lasts 16.667 ms. Route A illuminates the picture continuously for that interval. Route B illuminates it for the first 8.333 ms and remains dark for the second 8.333 ms. A tracking eye receives the held object for less time on Route B. In a simple persistence model, that can reduce tracking smear. An LCD implementation can time its backlight while its pixel state is retained. An emissive implementation can drive its own dark/light pattern. The product’s actual mechanism, timing and motion processing determine the result. Average light changes with duty cycle Assume a declared 200-cd/m² level whenever the picture is illuminated, with ideal zero light during the dark interval. The half-duty route has time-average luminance: 200 × 0.5 = 100 cd/m² To restore 200 cd/m² time-average light under the same ideal half-duty schedule, the illuminated level would have to be 400 cd/m². A four-millisecond pulse per sixty-Hz interval has duty fraction 4/16.667… = 0.24 . At the same 200-cd/m² illuminated level, its modeled time average is 48 cd/m². Real output limits, pulse shape and other processing can prevent simple compensation. Peak brightness and sustained brightness consequently remain relevant. A dark interval does not create another movement sample If a 24-fps movie is repeated on a faster output, several illumination pulses can show the same source position before the next source picture arrives. A tracking eye can then perceive separated images of that one held position. The exact result depends on pulse timing, tracking and source motion. Motion interpolation addresses a different question: it estimates intermediate positions between source pictures. BFI changes the emission pattern of the presented pictures. Frame-rate matching also remains relevant. Equal source-picture duration and short emission persistence are independent properties. Timing and comfort belong to the selected mode Dark intervals can introduce visible flicker or alter brightness, and the response depends on the mode and viewer. A feature name does not establish a suitable pulse rate or duty cycle for every situation. For an Emby comparison, preserve the scene and source cadence while identifying the output timing and the actual illumination feature. That makes it possible to distinguish shorter persistence from interpolation, sharper pixel transitions or a changed repeat schedule. See Also Display response time and motion blur Display refresh rate Judder and uneven picture cadence Display peak brightness References VESA: ClearMR motion blur, overshoot and measurement context SID/ICDM: Information Display Measurements Standard

articles/display-av/motion/Display-Judde.title: Judder and uneven picture cadence | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/Display-Judde.keywords: Judder and uneven picture cadence Judder is perceived uneven movement associated with irregular picture presentation durations or cadence, distinct from pixel-transition blur. A pan can look uneven even when all source pictures arrive and decode successfully. If neighbouring pictures remain on screen for different durations, movement advances with an irregular rhythm. This cadence contribution is commonly described as judder . Equal source steps, unequal display holds Use an original film-motion exercise. An object moves ten picture pixels between each of four source pictures: positions 0, 10, 20 and 30. At exact 24 fps, each intended source interval is 41.667 ms. On a fixed sixty-Hz grid, alternating three/two refresh holds give durations of 50 and 33.333 ms. The apparent step rates associated with a ten-pixel advance become: 10 / 0.050 = 200 pixels/second 10 / 0.033333… = 300 pixels/second The average fits the programme timing, but the neighbouring holds do not. A long steady pan can make the rhythm especially visible. Using an exact 120-Hz grid with five refreshes per source picture gives equal 41.667-ms holds. Frame-rate matching develops this correction. Removing unequal holds does not add temporal detail An evenly presented 24-fps source still jumps between only twenty-four source samples per second. A fast or sharply exposed motion can look stepped even with perfect equal-duration playback. A display can estimate intermediate pictures through motion interpolation. That changes the sequence and can introduce its own artifacts around occlusions or fine moving structures. Repeating the source evenly preserves the original samples. Interpolating tries to create additional ones. They are different results. Three similar-looking symptoms Observation Relationship to investigate Regular three/two rhythm during pans Source/output cadence ratio Long isolated hold or sudden jump Late, missing or dropped picture; processing or delivery progress Soft trail or blurred moving edge Recorded motion blur, pixel transitions or display persistence A repeated presentation is not always an error. Repetition is necessary when an output refreshes more often than source pictures change. The issue is whether the resulting durations fit the intended cadence. For an Emby comparison, preserve the same programme interval while identifying exact source rate, output mode and interpolation settings. That distinguishes a cadence change from a decoder or network problem. A fast pixel response can make the discrete source steps clearer rather than eliminate them. It changes how quickly the display reaches each picture’s light values, not when the source created those pictures. See Also Frame-rate matching at the display Display response time and motion blur Black-frame insertion and display persistence Dropped video frames during playback References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization VESA: Standards and public DSC resources

articles/display-av/motion/Display-Respo.title: Display response time and motion blur | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/Display-Respo.keywords: Display response time and motion blur Display response time measures a defined transition in pixel output, while motion clarity also depends on picture timing, illumination persistence and processing. When a display is driven to a new pixel level, its output does not necessarily reach that level instantly. Response time measures a specified part of that transition. The measurement needs a starting level, destination level and threshold definition. A quoted number without those conditions gives only a partial description of motion. Transition, delay and persistence are different times Quantity What it describes Processing/input delay Time before a new picture begins affecting the output Pixel transition time Time spent changing between specified light levels Illuminated persistence How long the picture’s light remains visible within its presentation Source-picture interval Time between samples created by the content A “one-ms response” does not establish one-ms input-to-light delay. A display can buffer a picture before driving a fast pixel. A fast transition also does not imply that the picture is illuminated only briefly. A curve needs a defined measurement interval Consider an original normalized transition from zero toward one: L(t) = 1 − exp(−t / 2), with t in milliseconds The two-millisecond parameter is a time constant, not a measured gray-to-gray result. The model reaches 10% at approximately 0.210721 ms and 90% at 4.605170 ms. Its 10%-to-90% interval is: t90 − t10 = 2 × ln(9) = 4.394449 ms It reaches 99% at 9.210340 ms, so reaching 90% is not the same event as completing the entire asymptotic transition. The equation is a teaching model. Real response depends on the display technology, source/destination levels, drive policy and temperature, and need not have this shape. A fast initial crossing can hide overshoot An implementation can drive a transition aggressively so it reaches the target earlier. If its light output then exceeds the intended level before settling, the moving object can acquire a bright or dark inverse trail. Use a separate original sampled trace: Model time Normalized output 0 ms 0 2 ms 1.15 4 ms 1.05 6 ms 1 The early crossing of one does not mean all later samples are correct. The maximum overshoot is 15% relative to this unit target. VESA’s ClearMR material treats motion blur and overshoot/undershoot as relevant visual behavior. A transition-time figure alone cannot describe those artifacts completely. The trace above is not an overdrive setting or a measurement of a panel. Eye tracking exposes another blur mechanism Suppose an ideal pixel changes instantly, then holds a picture’s light for the whole 16.667-ms interval of an exact sixty-Hz output. As the eye tracks an object moving at an original declared 960 screen pixels per second, the object’s held position moves across the retina during that interval. A simple uniform-hold estimate is: 960 × (1 / 60) = 16 pixels of tracking smear If illumination lasts only four milliseconds under otherwise ideal conditions: 960 × 0.004 = 3.84 pixels This model excludes the camera’s blur, pixel transition shape, eye dynamics and multiple image pulses. It explains persistence as a separate contribution, not a complete prediction of perceived blur or a ClearMR score. Black-frame insertion develops how the illuminated interval can be shortened. Movies include their own motion sampling A 24-fps movie can have substantial camera-exposure blur and only twenty-four distinct source samples per second. A fast display cannot reconstruct motion information that was never supplied. Judder concerns another relationship: unequal presentation durations can add a repeated rhythm to those samples. For Emby playback, compare the same scene while identifying source cadence, output mode and display processing. A panel response difference, an interpolation change and an uneven repeat schedule can all alter movement, but through different mechanisms. See Also OLED displays LCD and LED-backlit displays Judder and uneven picture cadence Black-frame insertion and display persistence References VESA: ClearMR motion blur, overshoot and measurement context SID/ICDM: Information Display Measurements Standard Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization

articles/display-av/motion/index.html.title: Overview: Motion on a display | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/index.html.keywords: Overview: Motion on a display Motion on a display depends on presentation cadence, pixel transitions and optional visibility-control techniques. Judder describes a timing experience; response time describes a transition; black-frame insertion changes when the picture is visible. Refresh and synchronization govern another part of that motion path. This branch gives those effects distinct explanations so several forms of blur or unevenness are not merged into one symptom. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Refresh and synchronization Refresh and synchronization connect frame presentation to a display's update schedule. Judder Judder is perceived uneven movement associated with irregular picture presentation durations or cadence, distinct from pixel-transition blur. Display response time Display response time measures a defined transition in pixel output, while motion clarity also depends on picture timing, illumination persistence and processing. Black-frame insertion Black-frame insertion or timed dark intervals reduce visible picture persistence by interrupting illumination between presentations. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization

articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.title: Frame-rate matching at the display | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.keywords: Frame-rate matching at the display Frame-rate matching selects a display timing compatible with the source cadence so source pictures can receive regular presentation durations. A player needs to place each source picture onto the available presentation schedule. Frame-rate matching selects an output timing that makes that relationship regular. Matching can use the source rate itself or a suitable integer multiple. A 24-fps film does not require the physical display to refresh only twenty-four times per second. Why sixty refreshes are awkward for twenty-four pictures Take an original exact-rate exercise. Twenty-four source pictures per second need to occupy sixty refresh intervals: 60 / 24 = 2.5 refreshes per source picture A fixed presentation cannot hold every picture for half an additional refresh. A common repeat schedule alternates three and two intervals. At sixty Hz, those holds are 50 and 33.333 milliseconds. The intended source interval is 41.667 milliseconds. The average duration is right, while each neighbouring hold differs. At 120 Hz: 120 / 24 = 5 refreshes per source picture 5 / 120 = 1 / 24 second Every picture can receive the same duration without synthesizing another source picture. That removes the unequal-repeat contribution to judder . It does not remove the discrete motion sampling already present in twenty-four-fps footage. Exact rates matter beyond the rounded label Consider a 24000/1001 -fps movie presented with one source picture per refresh on an exact 24-Hz grid. The source interval is 1001/24000 seconds; the display interval is 1/24 seconds. The difference per source picture is: 1001/24000 − 1/24 = 1/24000 second = 0.041667 ms After 1000 pictures, that difference totals one exact 24-Hz refresh interval: 41.667 milliseconds. If the programme speed stays unchanged, the presentation system must accommodate the growing mismatch. It can make a repeat/drop or another scheduling correction according to its implementation. This exercise does not predict the exact moment a particular player performs that correction. Using 24000/1001 Hz, or its exact fivefold multiple 120000/1001 Hz, removes this particular clock mismatch. “24” and “120” in a menu can be rounded displays of a more precise mode, so the actual rate is the useful evidence. Fractional frame rates explains the source conventions. Other source rates need their own mapping Exact source Example fixed output Even repeat count 24 fps 120 Hz 5 25 fps 50 Hz 2 30 fps 60 Hz 2 50 fps 100 Hz 2 60 fps 120 Hz 2 The table is arithmetic, not a promise that a connected TV exposes every mode. Resolution, color representation, link capability and the device’s mode list constrain which choices exist. Variable-frame-rate content has a changing source interval. One fixed repeat count cannot describe its whole sequence. A variable presentation arrangement or timed repeats may be needed. Changing playback speed is another solution with another result A player can sometimes conform source timing to a nearby rate by changing programme speed. Conforming 24000/1001 fps to 24 fps requires a speed ratio of 1001/1000 , a 0.1% increase. That avoids this cadence drift by changing playback duration. Audio must participate in the intended timing relationship; maintaining pitch can require additional processing. It is not the same result as preserving programme timing and correcting an occasional presentation interval. An explanation of smooth motion should state which choice occurred. Motion interpolation is another distinct option. It estimates additional pictures rather than simply repeating the original ones evenly. Emby switching needs a supported local route Emby’s documented Display Control feature detects available display rates and can switch rates when enabled on its supported application route. Its options depend on the GPU, connection, resolution and color mode. That is a local output-mode operation. It does not require the server to turn the movie into a different source frame rate merely because the client changes its display timing. A mode change can briefly re-establish the connection, producing a blackout. Quick Media Switching addresses a narrower supported rate-change case; it does not make every resolution or HDR change seamless. See Also Display refresh rate Judder and uneven picture cadence Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Quick Media Switching (QMS) References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview

articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.title: Display refresh rate | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.keywords: Display refresh rate Display refresh rate describes how often the output refreshes or scans pictures, independently of how often the source contains a new picture. A refresh rate of sixty hertz describes sixty refresh occurrences per second under that output mode. The interval is the reciprocal of the rate. It is a display timing property. The source’s frame rate describes when its own pictures occur. The refresh interval sets a presentation grid Declared fixed refresh One interval 24 Hz 41.667 ms 50 Hz 20 ms 60 Hz 16.667 ms 120 Hz 8.333 ms A higher refresh rate provides more presentation opportunities. What is shown at those opportunities depends on the player, source and display processing. Repeating a picture preserves its source identity A 24-fps source on an exact 120-Hz presentation grid can hold each source picture for five refreshes. The display refreshes 120 times per second, but the source still supplies twenty-four distinct pictures. A display using motion interpolation can synthesize intermediate pictures. That is another operation, with an estimate of movement between source samples. It is not implied by selecting a 120-Hz mode. An interface animation, a game and a movie can therefore use the same output refresh while having different picture-update behavior. Fractional modes are different clocks The rate 60000/1001 is approximately 59.940 Hz, not exactly 60. The rate 24000/1001 is approximately 23.976 fps, not exactly 24. Their ratio is 2.5, so that particular source/output pair needs uneven picture repetition unless another mechanism changes the presentation schedule. By contrast, 120000/1001 divided by 24000/1001 is exactly five. Rounded labels can hide this useful relationship. Frame-rate matching develops both integer repetition and small clock mismatches. Refresh is not pixel response A refresh can progressively scan rows rather than make the entire panel change at one instant. Pixel transitions then have their own response and illumination timing. A quoted one-millisecond response does not turn a sixty-Hz output into a thousand-Hz refresh mode. Conversely, a high refresh rate does not guarantee that every pixel transition settles before the next update. For Emby playback, the selected output mode, source cadence and presentation behavior establish the motion schedule. The display’s response time and persistence determine additional visible properties. See Also Frame-rate matching at the display Vertical synchronization (VSync) Variable refresh rate (VRR) Video Frame Rate References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization VESA: Standards and public DSC resources

articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.title: Variable refresh rate (VRR) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.keywords: Variable refresh rate (VRR) Variable refresh rate allows a supported display route to vary presentation intervals within a defined operating range. Variable refresh rate , or VRR , lets a supported output vary the interval between refresh occurrences rather than using one fixed cadence throughout. This can align presentation more closely with when new pictures become ready. Source, display, transport and application must all participate in the supported arrangement. A variable interval still has limits For an original example, suppose the accepted variable range is 48–120 Hz. The reciprocal intervals are: Fastest interval = 1000 / 120 = 8.333 ms Slowest interval = 1000 / 48 = 20.833 ms Picture-readiness intervals of 12, 16 and 20 ms fit inside that declared interval range. An interval of 30 ms does not. This is an invented range, not a specification of every VRR screen. A product’s range can depend on its mode and connection. HDMI VRR and DisplayPort Adaptive-Sync provide related presentation capabilities through their respective interfaces. Certification of motion performance and exposure of a transport feature also have different evidence scopes. A low source rate can require repeated refreshes An exact 24-fps movie has 41.667 ms between source pictures. That is outside the example’s 20.833-ms maximum refresh interval. An implemented low-rate compensation arrangement could refresh the same picture twice at 48 Hz. Each interval is 20.833 ms, while the source picture lasts 41.667 ms in total. The repeated refresh does not create another movie picture. It maintains the display timing while retaining the source-picture duration. This exercise illustrates a possible relationship. The hardware/software route must actually implement the repetition or another supported policy; merely advertising a VRR range does not establish that behavior. Regular film timing is a different use from irregular rendering A game can finish pictures at irregular times. A fixed-rate movie already has a defined programme cadence. For movie playback, an exact compatible fixed mode may give regular presentation without requiring arbitrary interval variation. A VRR feature is therefore not a universal prerequisite for smooth film motion. It also does not remove motion blur recorded by the camera, the source’s limited temporal sampling or the display’s pixel/emission response. Frame-rate matching develops the film cadence question. QMS uses a supported variable-refresh mechanism for a specific rate-switching purpose. The application route decides what is used A display supporting VRR does not force every browser or native player to use it. The operating system’s presentation mode, API flags and application integration determine the active route. Microsoft documents those requirements for its DXGI implementation. They should not be generalized into a setting recipe for every platform. See Also Vertical synchronization (VSync) Frame-rate matching at the display Quick Media Switching (QMS) Display refresh rate References HDMI LA: Variable refresh rate VESA DisplayPort: Technical FAQ Microsoft: Variable refresh rate displays VESA: Standards and public DSC resources

articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.title: Vertical synchronization (VSync) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.keywords: Vertical synchronization (VSync) Vertical synchronization coordinates presentation with display refresh boundaries to avoid showing incompatible picture updates within a scan. A display can scan a picture progressively. If the presented image changes partway through that scan, one part can come from an older picture and another from a newer picture. A moving edge can then appear discontinuous at the boundary: a tear line . Vertical synchronization, or VSync , coordinates updates with the refresh schedule so the intended picture is presented coherently. The scan and the update need a relationship Imagine an original sixty-Hz scan beginning with picture A. Halfway down the screen, the output starts reading picture B, whose moving object has shifted. The top rows contain A’s position; the bottom rows contain B’s. The mismatch belongs to presentation within the scan, not necessarily to corrupted decoding. A synchronized arrangement selects or schedules the new picture at an appropriate refresh boundary. Its buffering and presentation rules determine the concrete handoff. A ready picture can wait For an original fixed sixty-Hz grid, let refresh boundaries occur at 0, 16.667, 33.333 and 50 ms. Assume each ready picture is selected at the next boundary, with no additional queue: Ready time Selected boundary Modeled wait 10 ms 16.667 ms 6.667 ms 17 ms 33.333 ms 16.333 ms 34 ms 50 ms 16 ms A picture arriving just after a boundary can wait nearly an interval. Additional queued pictures or display processing can add time again. This model explains boundary waiting; it is not a benchmark of VSync latency. Actual operating systems expose different queue and presentation arrangements. Microsoft’s DXGI Present documentation, for example, gives synchronization-interval semantics for its presentation models. Their flags and queue behavior are part of that specific contract. Coherent scanout does not guarantee smooth cadence A perfectly coherent sequence can still hold film pictures for uneven durations. Twenty-four source pictures fitted to sixty fixed refreshes commonly need three/two interval repetition. VSync prevents a particular scan/update mismatch. Frame-rate matching addresses the source-to-output timing ratio. Similarly, if the next usable picture is late, the system can continue showing the previous one. That can produce a visible pause or repeat without a tear line. Decoder readiness, presentation deadlines and the chosen queue policy remain relevant. For Emby playback, a regular uneven pan, a single missed deadline and a picture torn during scanout are different observations. VRR has an API-specific presentation contract A variable-refresh route can schedule an output update around picture readiness within its supported range. It still needs synchronization and valid picture selection. Microsoft’s documented DXGI VRR route requires particular tearing-capability flags and sync-interval settings. The word “tearing” in that API permission is not, by itself, evidence that every presented picture will contain a visible tear. The actual output mode, supported variable range and presentation behavior determine the result. VRR explains why those conditions matter. See Also Variable refresh rate (VRR) Judder and uneven picture cadence Display refresh rate Dropped video frames during playback References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization Microsoft: Variable refresh rate displays

articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.title: Overview: Refresh and synchronization | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/motion/refresh-synch.keywords: Overview: Refresh and synchronization Refresh and synchronization connect frame presentation to a display's update schedule. The source cadence and the screen's refresh schedule must form a presentation arrangement. Frame-rate matching, VSync and VRR address different parts of that relationship. Their pages explain the timing decision, including what varies and what remains fixed in the selected mode. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Display refresh rate Display refresh rate describes how often the output refreshes or scans pictures, independently of how often the source contains a new picture. Frame-rate matching Frame-rate matching selects a display timing compatible with the source cadence so source pictures can receive regular presentation durations. Vertical synchronization (VSync) Vertical synchronization coordinates presentation with display refresh boundaries to avoid showing incompatible picture updates within a scan. Variable refresh rate (VRR) Variable refresh rate allows a supported display route to vary presentation intervals within a defined operating range. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft: DXGI presentation and synchronization HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview HDMI LA: Variable refresh rate

articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.title: HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.keywords: HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) HDMI Audio Return Channel sends supported audio from a TV toward an audio system over a designated return-audio connection. ARC , Audio Return Channel, provides an audio path from a TV toward a compatible audio system through designated HDMI ports. The word “return” describes its direction relative to the ordinary video/audio connection from an external source toward the TV. The TV can be the audio source If the Emby app runs on the TV, the TV already owns the playback’s audio output. ARC can carry an implemented audio representation from that TV to a receiver or soundbar. It does not require the TV app to send a movie video signal out to the receiver. The TV is showing its own presentation while returning audio. An external player connected directly to the TV creates another case: the TV receives the player’s audio and then must produce or forward a representation accepted by its return-audio route. Direct receiver input is a different path If the external player connects to the AV receiver first, the receiver can consume the ordinary upstream HDMI audio before forwarding video to the TV. That arrangement does not require ARC for that player’s audio. Switching between these topologies can therefore change available formats even when the receiver and TV are the same devices. AV receivers develops the two-picture-link arrangement. Codec support and return transport both matter ARC commonly carries stereo PCM and supported compressed formats. It does not provide the same multichannel linear-PCM/high-bitrate transport capability as eARC. A receiver supporting a codec at an ordinary HDMI input does not establish that the TV can pass that codec through its ARC output. The TV’s input handling, selected output representation and the return endpoints all participate. An Emby source can be decoded to PCM, passed as an accepted compressed bitstream or converted according to its implemented route. Those choices have different transport requirements. Bitstream passthrough separates the codec representation from the path carrying it. The designated endpoints must participate ARC uses compatible return-audio ports and the corresponding setup/control relationship. An arbitrary HDMI input on the TV is not necessarily its ARC endpoint. CEC-based control is commonly part of ARC arrangements, while the picture transport and control settings remain their own operations. Device labels and documented behavior should identify the actual supported route. Enhanced ARC expands the return-audio capability through a different supported arrangement. Its presence on one end alone does not convert an ARC-only counterpart into an eARC receiver. See Also HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) AV receivers in the video path HDMI-CEC control and device addressing Audio Bitstream Passthrough References HDMI LA: Enhanced Audio Return Channel HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview Sony: ARC and eARC audio-format distinction

articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.title: HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.keywords: HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) Enhanced Audio Return Channel expands the supported TV-to-audio-system transport and capability relationship beyond conventional ARC. eARC , Enhanced Audio Return Channel, provides a higher-capability audio return path from a TV toward an audio system. It addresses the same general TV-origin direction as ARC, through an implemented eARC arrangement. Its greater transport capability is useful when the TV needs to return multichannel PCM or supported high-bitrate compressed audio. The returning representation determines the work An Emby app on the TV can produce audio for its connected sound system. An external player connected to the TV can also supply audio that the TV must handle before returning it. The resulting return representation might be PCM or a compressed bitstream. Those alternatives have very different data rates. HDMI LA documents eARC support for multichannel uncompressed audio and relevant high-bitrate formats. Sony’s receiver material similarly distinguishes multichannel PCM and certain high-bitrate formats from conventional ARC transport. An eight-channel PCM exercise For an original PCM payload with eight channels, 48,000 samples per second and twenty-four bits per sample: 8 × 48,000 × 24 = 9,216,000 bits/second For a separate stereo sixteen-bit payload at the same sample rate: 2 × 48,000 × 16 = 1,536,000 bits/second The first is six times the second. Both calculations describe raw sample payload, excluding framing, clocks and transport overhead. This does not establish the limit of a specific port. It explains why returning decoded multichannel audio is a different request from returning stereo PCM. Transport capacity does not supply a decoder An audio system still needs to understand the representation it receives. A TV still needs the required input, app/output processing and pass-through behavior. An eARC label consequently does not prove that every source codec is forwarded unchanged. The TV can support different input and output combinations, and a particular app can expose a narrower route. For a source that has already been decoded to multichannel PCM, the audio system is not being asked to decode that original compressed codec again. For bitstream output, its decoder support remains relevant. The representation is therefore useful evidence alongside the return mode. Object-audio names need their carrier An object-audio presentation can reach an audio system through different supported encoded arrangements. A family name such as Dolby Atmos does not alone identify whether the current carrier is a streaming compressed representation, a high-bitrate representation or another implemented output. That is why “Atmos works” on one title is not proof that every Atmos-bearing source will traverse the same TV path. The source format, app handling, return representation and receiver’s reported input together identify the actual operation. Bitstream passthrough develops that codec/transport separation. The negotiated route can have a different fallback An eARC-capable endpoint paired with an ARC-only counterpart may use an implemented ARC fallback. That does not retain all eARC transport capabilities. The designated ports, cable path and supported capability exchange must participate in the chosen arrangement. A converter or extractor can introduce another processing boundary. See Also HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) AV receivers in the video path HDMI cable categories Audio Bitstream Passthrough Audio Channel Order References HDMI LA: Enhanced Audio Return Channel HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview Sony: ARC and eARC audio-format distinction

articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.title: Overview: Audio return channels | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/audio-retu.keywords: Overview: Audio return channels HDMI audio return channels provide defined routes for audio to travel back from the television side of a connection. ARC and eARC address an audio direction different from the ordinary source-to-screen video path. Their discovery, capability and transport arrangements differ. The two pages explain that return relationship before a particular audio format or receiver setup is assessed. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) HDMI Audio Return Channel sends supported audio from a TV toward an audio system over a designated return-audio connection. HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) Enhanced Audio Return Channel expands the supported TV-to-audio-system transport and capability relationship beyond conventional ARC. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References HDMI LA: Enhanced Audio Return Channel

articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDCP.ht.title: HDCP and protected display links | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDCP.ht.keywords: HDCP and protected display links HDCP authenticates supported display-link participants and protects audiovisual transport under the applicable content and output policy. HDCP , High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection, addresses protected audiovisual transmission over supported display interfaces. Its participants authenticate under the applicable protocol before protected output is established. This is a display-link relationship. It is different from decoding the movie’s video codec or choosing an Emby network-delivery method. The participants have defined roles Role Responsibility in the protected route Transmitter Sends protected audiovisual output under the implemented protocol Receiver Authenticates and receives that output Repeater Participates upstream while maintaining the required downstream protection/topology relationship DCP publishes interface-specific HDCP specifications and related material. Protocol revision, interface and device role need to accompany a claim of support. An AV receiver can consequently add more than a video-bandwidth constraint. Its protected upstream and downstream arrangements must be valid for the chosen route. Authentication is separate from mode declarations A source can read a display declaration and select an otherwise supported picture mode before another required stage fails. HDCP is not simply an EDID flag that makes the chosen connection valid. It includes an active protocol relationship, with appropriate participant and topology checks. If protected presentation is required by the actual content/output policy, a failure can prevent visible output or produce an application-specific error. The symptom alone does not identify the exact stage. HDMI handshakes separates capability exchange, transport establishment and protected-output progress. Codec support answers another question A TV accepting an HDCP-protected HDMI picture signal is not being asked to decode the original movie’s HEVC stream through that input. The client ordinarily performs media decoding before producing the display signal. Its codec capability and the link’s protected-output capability therefore have different scopes. A codec error in Emby and an authenticated-display-link error can both interrupt playback while belonging to different parts of the route. Delivery DRM and output protection can be connected A protected media system can decrypt/license media within its implemented playback environment and apply an output policy to the resulting presentation. That policy can require a suitable protected display route. Playback DRM and browser EME describe earlier application/delivery relationships. They do not replace the output-link protocol. Likewise, the mere existence of HDCP hardware does not establish which policy the current source or application requires. See Also AV receivers in the video path HDMI handshakes and black screens DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) and browser key sessions References DCP: HDCP specifications Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata

articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-CE.title: HDMI-CEC control and device addressing | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-CE.keywords: HDMI-CEC control and device addressing HDMI-CEC carries device-control messages on a control path whose addressing and application handling remain distinct from HDMI picture and audio transport. HDMI-CEC , Consumer Electronics Control, carries control messages between participating HDMI devices. It can support actions such as input selection, standby or forwarded user controls through an implemented arrangement. It does not carry the movie’s picture samples, and it does not by itself decide which action an Emby app performs. A separate control relationship Function Relevant path Picture/audio presentation Selected HDMI transport Return audio Supported ARC/eARC relationship Device-control messages CEC App navigation Host input handling and application mapping A picture working over HDMI does not prove that the source, receiver and TV all expose the desired CEC control behavior. CEC can also reach a device without the target application using the resulting event. The control message and the app action are separate stages. Physical and logical addresses answer different questions A physical address describes location in the HDMI topology. A logical address identifies a participating device role on the CEC control bus. Use this original topology illustration: TV: 0.0.0.0 Receiver on TV input 2: 2.0.0.0 Player on receiver input 1: 2.1.0.0 The player could also have a logical playback-device address. That logical address is not obtained by treating 2.1.0.0 as the same number. The labels above illustrate the hierarchical physical relationship. They are not a captured device report or a promise of address assignments on every installation. The source’s visible physical-address context can change when it moves to another port or receiver arrangement. A remote press still needs an application route One possible control sequence is: TV receives remote input -> TV sends supported CEC user control -> external player handles the message -> host/app maps it to an action The external player can expose that event as an input key or handle it through another platform-specific interface. The app then decides what the action means in the current view. Volume can be consumed by an audio device rather than forwarded to the player’s navigation. A standby action belongs to device state rather than to a media-seek command. For Emby playback, identify which device receives the original remote input and which device is supposed to perform the action. Support is specific to the command and route A vendor’s control label may cover a set of CEC features, not every possible command. Firmware, adapter and receiver behavior can also affect the path. The public Linux CEC interface illustrates that kernel/device handling and userspace control can have different responsibilities. Other platforms expose their own routes. See Also HDMI Audio Return Channel (ARC) Infrared remote controls Bluetooth remote controls Human Interface Devices (HID) References Linux: HDMI CEC introduction HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview Linux: CEC physical-address topology Linux: CEC protocol and logical-address roles

articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-Ha.title: HDMI handshakes and black screens | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-Ha.keywords: HDMI handshakes and black screens HDMI establishment involves capability exchange, a compatible output choice, transport progress and any required signaling/protection relationships whose failures can produce similar visible symptoms. A black screen describes what the viewer sees, not which operation failed. The player may be unable to obtain capabilities, establish its selected transport, satisfy an output policy or deliver a correctly interpreted picture. “HDMI handshake” is often used for this whole establishment process. It is more useful to separate the relationships inside it. Connected, configured and carrying pictures are different states A source can detect a connected sink before it has selected a working mode. It can read EDID before its selected high-rate transport succeeds. A trained link can still need correct interpretation or protection handling. Observation What it supports Connected-device indication A relevant connection/detection state EDID data read Capability information was obtained Compatible mode selected The source chose a declared/implemented output Transport becomes ready Relevant link-establishment progress Protected-output requirement satisfied The applicable authentication/policy stage progressed Sink recognizes current signal Input recognized timing/interpretation Visible picture advances Later presentation progress These are useful stages of evidence. They need not appear in every platform’s log, and no single row proves every later row. A startup mode change can create a temporary gap An Emby app can begin playback in a different rate or HDR state from its interface. The local output then has to establish the selected presentation. During that transition, the display may temporarily have no usable current picture. A short blackout that occurs once at the output change is a different observation from periodic blackouts during an otherwise stable mode. Frame-rate matching explains the rate choice. QMS covers a narrower supported same-resolution rate-switch case rather than every possible transition. An original dependency trace Consider a teaching model in which the route needs readable capabilities, a chosen mode, usable transport and successful required protection before its first protected picture is shown. Model event Declared time Connection detected 0 ms Capability read completed 30 ms Compatible mode chosen 40 ms Transport ready 120 ms Required protection ready 170 ms First intended picture visible 200 ms The 200-ms duration is invented. The table is not a universal HDMI ordering rule or a benchmark: real operations can overlap, retry or have different dependencies. The model’s visibility condition is an intersection of required states. If capability reading succeeds at 30 ms but transport never becomes ready, the first condition is true and the complete route is still incomplete. If protection is not required by the actual content/output policy, that particular gate is absent. The model should follow the real policy rather than assume every movie uses the same gate. An absent requirement is different from a failed requirement Use this original readable state object: { "capabilitiesReady": true, "modeSelected": true, "transportReady": false, "signalInterpretationReady": true, "protectionRequired": false, "protectionReady": false } It is a teaching state, not a native HDMI report or Emby log. Its simplified prerequisite condition is: capabilitiesReady AND modeSelected AND transportReady AND signalInterpretationReady AND (NOT protectionRequired OR protectionReady) The condition fails because transport is not ready. Protection being false is not another failure in this case, because that requirement is absent. If transport becomes ready while the other declared states remain unchanged, all modeled prerequisites pass. Actual picture submission and later presentation must then progress too; the prerequisite result is not a captured visible frame. Separating an unused stage from an unsuccessful required stage prevents an irrelevant status from becoming the diagnosis. Mode changes alter more than one request “4K” does not specify the complete signal. Refresh rate, pixel clock/timing totals, precision, chroma, HDR interpretation and DSC can change its requirements. A route that carries an eight-bit SDR mode can fail a higher-rate ten-bit request. A receiver can preserve ordinary video but constrain the required HDR or protected-output relationship. HDMI bandwidth develops the transport request. AV receivers develops the additional input/output boundaries. The correct comparison records the actual mode on both sides, not just the movie’s resolution. A controlled comparison changes one relevant boundary Use an original comparison matrix: Case Preserved context Deliberate change A Player, source, output request and TV input Baseline indirect receiver route B Same source/player/output request Direct player-to-TV route C Baseline topology and source Lower declared output rate/precision D Baseline source/topology/output mode Another known cable path If B works while A fails, the added intermediate route is relevant. That observation still includes the receiver’s ports, second cable and capability handling; it does not isolate one component yet. If C works while A fails, the request matters. It may have changed electrical rate, format or another interpretation, so identify exactly which property changed. If D differs, the installed transport path is relevant under the preserved mode. A cable result at a lower mode should not be reported as a test of the higher one. These are diagnostic relationships, not instructions to change a user’s system without context. Audio and video can advance through different paths A receiver may extract upstream audio while downstream picture transport or interpretation is failing. A TV can also recognize a connected device without displaying its intended picture. Audio continuing is therefore useful evidence that some work progressed. It does not prove that the picture signal reached the final display correctly. Likewise, the server showing Direct Play establishes original-media delivery, not the later HDMI link’s state. For Emby playback, separate server/client progress, the chosen local output and the final sink’s observations. A network stall prevents new programme data from reaching presentation; a display-link blackout can occur while that data is already available. Repeated interruptions need their own timing context Record whether the event follows a rate/HDR/input change, occurs at a regular interval or appears unpredictably while the mode stays stable. A reported new mode at every interruption suggests a different relationship from a stable-mode link that repeatedly loses progress. Application, receiver and display evidence should be aligned to the same event. The useful report contains source/client context, exact topology, before/after output modes and the first stage known to have stopped progressing. That gives the black screen a location in the route instead of treating its appearance as a diagnosis. See Also EDID: display capability declarations HDCP and protected display links HDMI HDR signaling AV receivers in the video path HDMI link bandwidth: TMDS and FRL Quick Media Switching (QMS) References HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata AMD PG350: HDMI TMDS/FRL transmission and coding DCP: HDCP specifications

articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-QM.title: Quick Media Switching (QMS) | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/AV-HDMI-QM.keywords: Quick Media Switching (QMS) Quick Media Switching uses a supported HDMI variable-refresh mechanism to reduce interruption during compatible frame-rate changes at a retained resolution. Quick Media Switching , or QMS , addresses a specific interruption: a supported HDMI source changes the video presentation rate while retaining the applicable resolution and other compatible signal conditions. It uses a supported variable-refresh mechanism to avoid the ordinary blackout associated with re-establishing that rate change. Rate changes can have a narrower scope than mode changes A trailer can have a different source cadence from the feature that follows it. Without a suitable seamless-switch route, the source can either preserve a fixed output cadence or change its output mode and allow the link/display to re-establish. QMS gives a supported arrangement another option for the relevant rate-switch case. Original switch exercise Relation to the published QMS scope 3840 × 2160 at 24 Hz → same resolution at 60 Hz, otherwise compatible A rate-change case to examine for QMS support 1920 × 1080 → 3840 × 2160 Resolution changes; the basic QMS promise does not establish seamless operation SDR presentation → PQ/HDR presentation Other interpretation/mode changes; QMS alone does not establish seamless operation The table illustrates scope, not tested devices. VRR and QMS are related but distinct claims HDMI LA describes QMS using a VRR mechanism. That does not mean every device exposing VRR implements the required QMS feature or every player uses it. The source, display and any intermediate receiver need the compatible route. Application/OS integration also determines which output change is actually requested. Frame-rate matching explains why the player might want a rate change. VRR explains the underlying variable timing relationship. The observed switch is the useful evidence For an Emby transition, record the before/after output rates, resolution and HDR state. A blackout involving several simultaneous mode changes cannot be attributed to QMS rate handling alone. An app’s refresh-rate switching support is not automatically a declaration that it uses QMS on every compatible TV. A stable-rate presentation also cannot demonstrate a rate-switch feature because no such switch occurred. See Also Frame-rate matching at the display Variable refresh rate (VRR) HDMI handshakes and black screens References HDMI LA: Quick Media Switching HDMI LA: Variable refresh rate HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview

articles/display-av/signaling/capability.title: CTA-861 capability blocks | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/capability.keywords: CTA-861 capability blocks CTA-861 capability structures extend display declarations with defined video, audio, color and metadata information used by consumer digital-interface routes. An EDID base block cannot express every useful consumer display feature on its own. CTA-861 defines additional timing and signaling relationships, including structures that can appear in a CTA extension of the display declaration. These structures can describe video, audio and relevant color/metadata capabilities. Each block has a defined meaning; treating the whole extension as a single “HDR supported” switch loses information. Data blocks have boundaries A CTA extension identifies its structure and provides a region for data blocks, alongside other defined information. A data-block header encodes a tag and a payload length. An extended-tag block uses a further byte to identify its particular kind. A parser must respect those lengths before interpreting bytes. A flag read from the wrong offset can give an apparently plausible but unrelated capability. The referenced Linux parser checks the HDR static metadata block’s extended tag and minimum payload length. It then reads the EOTF and static-metadata descriptor flags at their defined positions. A small original HDR capability fragment Consider this synthetic four-byte data block: E3 06 0C 01 Byte Meaning in this fragment E3 Extended-tag block with three payload bytes 06 HDR static metadata extended tag 0C EOTF capability bits: PQ and HLG in this exercise 01 Static metadata descriptor Type 1 capability The fragment is an original teaching input. It is not a complete CTA extension, complete EDID or captured device capability. The EOTF field is a bit set: more than one supported interpretation can be declared. It is not the numeric value of the currently active signal’s EOTF. Likewise, the Type 1 capability bit is not a list of that movie’s mastering luminances. Additional optional fields and other blocks have their own definitions. CTA’s HDR static metadata extension standard supplies the specification reference; the public parser provides a concrete implementation reference for the displayed byte relationships. A truncated fragment must stop the interpretation Remove the final byte from the teaching fragment: E3 06 0C E3 still declares three payload bytes, but only two follow it. The parser cannot obtain the missing Type 1 capability field from this fragment. Reading the first byte of a following block as though it completed this one would merge unrelated structures. The original four-byte fragment fits its stated boundary; the three-byte fragment fails that boundary check. The length check precedes interpretation of the flags. This is why a useful capability parser validates structure as well as recognizing a familiar tag. Related declarations answer different questions Video timing information describes accepted presentation timings. Audio descriptors can specify format/channel/rate properties. Colorimetry, chroma-format and metadata structures add other constraints. A supported audio codec name does not establish every channel count or sample rate. A supported video timing does not imply every color precision or chroma arrangement at that timing. The selected HDMI/DisplayPort transport also has to carry the required combination. The source cannot safely manufacture a universal mode by collecting unrelated positive flags from several blocks. Capability is not current output A TV can declare that it accepts PQ while a client currently sends an SDR presentation. It can also accept a format that the source or an intermediate device cannot produce on the chosen route. For Emby playback, source-file color tags, path-visible CTA declarations and the active display signal remain separate observations. EDID explains where the declaration is read. HDMI HDR signaling explains how the source describes the output it actually sends. See Also EDID: display capability declarations HDMI HDR signaling HDMI video transport HDMI Enhanced Audio Return Channel (eARC) References CTA: CTA-861 digital-interface standard CTA: HDR static metadata extensions Linux: EDID parser, pinned v6.12 format reference Linux: HDMI HDR field definitions, pinned v6.12

articles/display-av/signaling/capability.title: EDID: display capability declarations | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/capability.keywords: EDID: display capability declarations EDID is a structured display-capability declaration that a source reads to learn supported timings and related properties, potentially through an intermediate device. A source needs to know which presentation formats a connected display path says it can accept. EDID , Extended Display Identification Data, provides a structured declaration for that purpose. It is capability information, not a live picture of the display’s current output or a measurement of every advertised property. The declaration belongs to the visible connection path A directly connected TV can expose its EDID to the player. A receiver, switch or converter can instead supply an upstream declaration appropriate to its own role and the downstream display. The player reads the information it can actually see on that path. Adding an intermediate device can therefore change the available mode list without changing the TV itself. An EDID also does not supply the player’s output capability. A source can use only combinations implemented by its own output route. Base data and extension data have defined structure A conventional EDID base block is 128 bytes. It contains identity/version fields, display characteristics and timing-related information. A count indicates additional 128-byte extension blocks. Extensions can carry further structures, including CTA-861 capability blocks . A base block with one declared extension consequently describes a 256-byte base-plus-extension arrangement. The recognizable base header is: 00 FF FF FF FF FF FF 00 Seeing that header alone does not validate the rest of the data. Version rules, field bounds, extensions and their contents still need parsing. The Linux EDID parser referenced here supplies a version-pinned, public implementation example. Its behavior is evidence of that parser’s checks, not a substitute for all requirements of the VESA standard. A checksum checks bytes, not claims The EDID block checksum condition makes the sum of its 128 bytes equal zero modulo 256. For an original reduced arithmetic exercise, assume the first 127 bytes sum to 1617: 1617 mod 256 = 81 Checksum byte = (256 − 81) mod 256 = 175 = AF hexadecimal (1617 + 175) mod 256 = 0 This is a checksum exercise, not a complete valid EDID block or a real device dump. Changing one earlier byte by one without changing the checksum would make the new remainder one. That can reveal a data-integrity inconsistency. A checksum that passes does not prove that every capability is physically implemented, that the chosen cable works or that HDR brightness was measured accurately. It establishes a byte-level relationship. The source chooses from compatible possibilities Use an original readable capability exercise: { "sourceModes": ["1080p60-sdr", "2160p60-sdr", "2160p24-pq"], "pathDeclaredModes": ["1080p60-sdr", "2160p24-pq"], "selectedMode": "2160p24-pq" } The overlapping modes are the source/path intersection. The selection is one choice within it. This object is a teaching descriptor, not native EDID syntax or a captured operating-system report. The real mode includes precise timing, sample representation and other requirements hidden by these short labels. A listed PQ mode also does not say that the current source is actively sending PQ. HDR signaling separates the sink declaration from the output signal. The active route needs additional evidence After selecting a mode, the source must establish its actual transport. Link rate, sample format, training and any protected-output requirements remain part of the route. The screen can then apply its own processing and brightness controls. EDID may contain information relevant to those choices, but it does not become a physical luminance measurement merely by being reported through an API. For Emby playback, the media’s source resolution and HDR tags are another layer again. The client may scale or map that source into a selected output mode. A useful report records the media properties, the path-visible declarations and the active output separately. Connection changes can invalidate an earlier assumption A hot-plug event, input switch or changed receiver arrangement can make the source re-evaluate the visible display information. A cached mode from an earlier direct connection may not describe the new path. If a mode disappears after adding a receiver, compare the declarations and supported output arrangements at the changed boundary. If a listed mode produces a black screen, successful declaration parsing has already answered only the first part of the question. HDMI handshakes develops the later stages and the evidence that separates them. See Also CTA-861 capability blocks HDMI handshakes and black screens AV receivers in the video path Native display resolution References VESA: Standards and public DSC resources Linux: EDID parser, pinned v6.12 format reference Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata

articles/display-av/signaling/capability.title: HDMI HDR signaling | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/capability.keywords: HDMI HDR signaling HDMI HDR signaling communicates relevant interpretation of the active output picture, separately from HDR metadata in the source and HDR capabilities declared by the sink. HDR information appears at several stages of playback. A source file describes its encoded picture; a display declaration describes accepted inputs; output signaling describes the presentation actually being sent. Keeping those stages separate avoids a common misunderstanding: a movie being HDR does not guarantee that every later stage is currently carrying the same HDR representation. Three descriptions, three scopes Information What it describes Source color tags and mastering/content metadata Interpretation and creation/content context of the encoded media Sink capability, including relevant CTA blocks What the connected path declares it can accept Output signal and applicable InfoFrames Interpretation/information supplied with the active presentation CTA’s static HDR extension defines EDID capability information and a relevant HDR metadata InfoFrame relationship. Capability and output information have different directions and purposes. CTA-861 blocks develops the declaration side. A compatible display can still receive SDR This original readable example describes one valid kind of adapted route: { "source": {"transfer": "PQ", "primaries": "BT.2020"}, "sink": {"acceptsPQ": true}, "output": { "transfer": "SDR", "primaries": "BT.709", "toneMapped": true } } It is a teaching descriptor, not a native HDMI packet or captured Emby report. The sink could accept PQ, yet the selected route sends an SDR target after tone mapping. The source’s PQ tags should not then be copied blindly as though they described unchanged PQ output. The active output must describe the values actually being presented. Otherwise the display may interpret an adapted SDR picture through the wrong transfer/color relationship. The renderer and output system must agree A decoder reconstructs picture values in their encoded interpretation. A renderer can scale, convert or tone-map those values. The presentation/output system then establishes the appropriate surface and signal interpretation. A PQ-tagged source interpreted as SDR can look wrong without any missing video bytes. A surface carrying changed values but retaining a stale interpretation can also be wrong. Display color management explains those responsibilities. The server’s Direct Play decision establishes the original media delivery choice, while local client output preparation still needs its own correct route. Metadata is not a measurement of the current panel Mastering display metadata describes a creation context. Content-light information describes properties of the content. Sink declarations can provide target information within their defined scope. None is automatically a measurement of the light emitted by the panel at that moment. A TV reporting HDR recognition is useful evidence that its input identified a relevant signal arrangement. Its tone mapping, local dimming and brightness limits still determine the actual output. An AV receiver or converter can also affect whether the required signaling reaches the display. Successful ordinary video transport through that device does not establish preservation of every HDR packet or format. See Also CTA-861 capability blocks HDR display capabilities Video Color Tags and Signaling HDR10 Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session References CTA: HDR static metadata extensions CTA: CTA-861 digital-interface standard HDMI LA: HDMI 2.2 specification overview Linux: Connector properties, EDID and HDR metadata
