articles/display-av/signaling/index.html.title: Overview: Capability negotiation and signaling | Emby Learn
articles/display-av/signaling/index.html.keywords: Overview: Capability negotiation and signaling Display signaling coordinates capabilities, protection, control and other functions around the carried video signal. An EDID exchange, an HDCP check and a CEC command perform different jobs. Audio return and quick mode switching add further negotiated relationships. This area separates those functions, providing useful checkpoints for a black screen or an unexpected mode change. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Capability exchange Capability exchange describes the signal formats a receiving path reports and the metadata used to interpret them. articles/general-concepts/Graphs.html.title: What is a graph? | Emby Learn
articles/general-concepts/Graphs.html.keywords: What is a graph? In media software, a graph is a set of nodes and the edges that connect them, not a chart. What nodes and edges stand for depends on the application. The word graph has two common meanings that are easy to confuse: In everyday language and school mathematics, a graph is a chart : a plot that shows how values relate, such as bitrate over time or the curve of a function. Most pictures labelled "graph" show this kind. In computer science and discrete mathematics, a graph is a structure of connected elements . This is the meaning behind terms such as filter graph and the one used throughout this documentation. The two have little in common beyond the name. A chart places values on axes. A graph in the second sense has no axes, and the position of its elements on a drawing carries no meaning. Definition A graph consists of a set of nodes (also called vertices) and a set of edges , where each edge connects two nodes. That is all the definition requires: a graph records which elements are connected, not where they are or what they look like. In a directed graph , each edge leads from one node to another. Drawings show the direction with arrows. Graphs in media software are usually directed, because data or decisions proceed from one element to the next. Boxes and arrows are a common way to draw a graph, but the drawing is only one presentation of it. Software holds graphs as data, and an FFmpeg filtergraph, for example, is written as a single line of text. The definition does not say what nodes and edges stand for; each application decides that. Reading any graph therefore starts with two questions: what does a node represent, and what does an edge mean? Processing graphs: edges carry media In a media processing graph, nodes are operations, and each edge carries the output of one operation to the input of another. A conceptual video processing path. The arrows between operations show data dependencies, not how long each operation takes. A decoder turns encoded packets into pictures. A scaler resizes them, and a compositor places a logo on each picture. The logo arrives through a second edge from its own source. An encoder turns the result back into an encoded stream. Three shapes recur in such graphs. A chain connects operations one after another, like the decoder, scaler and encoder. A join combines several inputs into one result, like the compositor. A split sends one output to several destinations, for example to produce a full-size picture and a thumbnail from the same decoded frame. Edges also determine what kind of data travels between operations: packets before the decoder and after the encoder, pictures in between. An output can only be connected to an input that accepts its data. For this reason, nodes have defined inputs and outputs, called pins in DirectShow and pads in GStreamer. Where a graph begins and ends depends on the software. An FFmpeg filtergraph works on decoded pictures or audio samples, so in the illustration only the scaler and the compositor belong to it. A DirectShow filter graph also includes sources, decoders and renderers. The filter graph article explains how order, formats and branching affect the result, and the transcoding pipeline shows what surrounds the filtergraph. Decision graphs: edges connect choices Emby Server's Expert Mode uses a graph for a different purpose: choosing which transcoding configuration handles an operation. Its nodes do not process media. A GPU node, for example, stands for a device used with a particular configuration, so the same physical GPU can appear as several nodes. The edges change meaning accordingly. They describe how choices are considered, not how media moves. Several GPU nodes in the graph are alternatives for an attempt, not a picture passing through several GPUs in turn. Drawn on screen, a processing graph and a decision graph can look alike. The difference lies only in what their nodes and edges stand for. articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.title: The hardware decode-filter-encode pipeline | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.keywords: The hardware decode-filter-encode pipeline A hardware video pipeline connects encoded input, decoded surfaces, picture transformations and encoded output through compatible devices, memory formats and completion dependencies. A hardware video pipeline must connect the output of each stage to a usable input for the next . Finding a decoder and encoder is only the beginning: picture layout, memory location, device context, transformations and timing also have to fit. This is the hardware view of the broader transcoding pipeline . Its central objects are compressed packets at the ends and decoded picture surfaces between the stages. Define the source and target first Imagine an original conversion exercise: Source: 3840 × 2160 HEVC Main 10, HDR, 4:2:0. Target: 1920 × 1080 H.264, SDR, 8-bit 4:2:0. Selected subtitle: must be painted into the delivered video. The decoder reconstructs the source picture. Scaling changes its spatial size; tone mapping prepares the intended SDR relationship; subtitle composition adds the selected presentation. The encoder creates the target compressed video. A successful decode query addresses the source configuration. A successful encode query addresses the target. Neither query, alone, establishes the transformations and handoffs between them. Compressed packets become picture surfaces The decoder consumes codec data and produces reconstructed picture information. A hardware path commonly represents that output through device-associated surfaces. A surface carries or refers to storage with a defined picture layout. The consumer needs to know dimensions, format, planes, row pitch and memory context, alongside the media's timing and colour interpretation. For an original ideal, unpadded 4K 4:2:0 layout whose samples occupy sixteen-bit storage: 3840 × 2160 × 1.5 samples per pixel × 2 bytes per sample = 24,883,200 bytes per picture A ten-bit sample occupying sixteen-bit storage still has ten bits of image precision. Storage size and precision describe different properties. The original 1080p 8-bit 4:2:0 target layout needs 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes per picture before padding. Spatial scaling and storage conversion both contribute to that difference. Actual hardware surfaces can have alignment, tiling, compression and additional allocation requirements. The arithmetic explains data scale without assigning an allocation size to a specific driver. The filter needs a usable input A GPU filter may accept surfaces from one hardware context and require particular formats. Another filter may operate on CPU-accessible frames. In the example, a picture-sized subtitle operation might be available through the selected device path, or the application might use a CPU renderer. In the latter case, the application needs a suitable transfer or mapping arrangement for the frame, performs the composition and prepares the next stage's required input. Handoff Requirement Decoder to device filter Accepted surface format, context and completion state Device to CPU filter CPU-usable layout and the needed data access CPU result to hardware encoder Accepted input layout and device-accessible storage Device filter to encoder Compatible processed surface and ownership/timing The implemented route decides which handoffs occur. The same named hardware decoder can feed different filters in two sessions. Operation order matters as well. Painting an overlay before scaling scales the painted overlay with the picture. Painting it after scaling uses destination-picture coordinates. Hardware execution does not remove that relationship. Frame traffic is larger than the delivery bitrate The declared 4K layout above, at thirty pictures per second, represents: 24,883,200 × 30 = 746,496,000 bytes per second If a model downloads every complete picture to CPU-accessible memory and uploads an equally sized result, the two transfer payloads total: 746,496,000 × 2 = 1,492,992,000 bytes per second For comparison, a compressed source averaging 20 Mbit/s carries 2,500,000 bytes per second before overhead. Its compressed delivery rate is not the rate of full-picture traffic. The transfer model deliberately assumes the same picture size both ways. A route that scales before transfer, changes layout or shares suitable storage has different traffic. The point is to calculate the route actually being discussed. Completion and reuse are different permissions Submitting a decode operation can return before the picture is ready. A filter must wait for the producer's relevant completion before reading it. The consumer can then continue using the surface after decoding has finished. Reusing that storage for a new picture too early can overwrite a reference, a filter input or an encoder input. An original ownership timeline makes this visible: Model event Time Permission established Decoder finishes writing surface A 4 ms Consumer may read the finished picture Filter finishes reading A and writing B 7 ms Its use of A can end Encoder finishes consuming B 12 ms Its use of B can end The example does not claim those are device timings. It separates producer completion from completion of all downstream uses. Codec references create another reason to retain a decoded surface. A picture can remain useful for reconstructing later pictures even after it has been displayed or passed to an encoder. Pool ownership must account for those references. Overlap changes the throughput calculation Independent stages can work on different pictures at once. Their single-picture service times add for a serial route, while a well-filled overlapped pipeline has a different steady-state throughput limit. With original stage costs of 3 ms decode, 8 ms filter and 5 ms encode, serial service is sixteen milliseconds. Under an ideal independent-overlap model, the eight-millisecond filter stage limits the filled pipeline to 125 pictures per second. That model omits transfer, synchronization, startup, queues and shared-device contention. It is useful for locating the limit implied by its assumptions, rather than reporting a hardware benchmark. First output and filled-pipeline progress Use the same declared 3/8/5-millisecond stage costs, with four pictures already available and one worker per independent stage. Each later stage starts only when its input is ready and its own previous job has finished. Picture Decode interval Filter interval Encode interval Encoded output ready A 0–3 ms 3–11 ms 11–16 ms 16 ms B 3–6 ms 11–19 ms 19–24 ms 24 ms C 6–9 ms 19–27 ms 27–32 ms 32 ms D 9–12 ms 27–35 ms 35–40 ms 40 ms The first picture needs sixteen milliseconds through all three stages. Once work fills the route, subsequent outputs arrive eight milliseconds apart because the filter controls the available processing slots. The decode worker can finish C before the filter has finished B. That result needs retained storage while it waits. More asynchronous work therefore introduces queue and ownership requirements as well as potential overlap. If input pictures arrive more slowly, or stages share an execution resource, this modeled schedule changes. Its distinction between first-output latency and filled-pipeline progress remains useful when interpreting the corresponding observed quantities. articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.title: Fixed-function media engines | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.keywords: Fixed-function media engines Fixed-function media engines implement specialized video operations within a device, using dedicated processing paths rather than executing the entire job as general-purpose GPU shader work. A fixed-function media engine is a specialized processing path designed for particular video tasks. A decoder reconstructs supported compressed pictures; an encoder creates a supported compressed representation. Such blocks can be part of a discrete GPU or an integrated system-on-chip. They are distinct from the general-purpose compute and graphics resources beside them. Different blocks answer different questions Resource Work to associate with it Dedicated decoder Supported compressed-video reconstruction Dedicated encoder Supported video compression Video processor Supported picture-processing operations Programmable compute/graphics Application-defined transformations and rendering NVIDIA's NVDEC and NVENC documentation explicitly identifies dedicated decode and encode engines. Intel's Quick Sync and Apple's media-engine specifications likewise distinguish media work from general CPU or GPU-core counts. A chip can offer one decode capability and a different encode capability. The fact that a compressed format can be decoded does not establish an encoder for that format. Specialized hardware exposes specific configurations The engine implements operations within its supported configuration range. Relevant properties can include codec profile, bit depth, chroma format, dimensions and the encoded tools in use. A newer graphics architecture or higher shader count is therefore not a substitute for its media capabilities. Two products with different graphics performance can have similar dedicated media blocks, while products sharing a marketing family can differ in which blocks are present. For an Emby conversion, the input decoder and output encoder are selected against different requirements. Their connection is developed in the hardware pipeline . The engine operates inside a software-controlled job The application still locates and parses the resource, submits work, manages picture storage and coordinates completion. A dedicated media operation can also use adjacent processing for preparation or optional analysis. For example, decoded pictures can be processed by a GPU shader before reaching an encoder. A hardware encoder's input might need layout conversion. That adjacent work belongs to the route actually implemented. Task-manager categories should consequently be interpreted by their engine scope. A video-decode workload can be active while a general 3D category remains quiet. Conversely, a busy compute category can describe filtering rather than compressed-video decoding. articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.title: GPU compute and video processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.keywords: GPU compute and video processing GPU compute processes picture data with programmable parallel work whose layout, colour interpretation and completion requirements connect it to the surrounding media pipeline. A GPU can run programmable work over picture data: scaling, colour transformations, composition and other algorithms. The application supplies the processing logic and the GPU executes suitable work in parallel. This is a different role from a dedicated decoder , which reconstructs compressed pictures. The GPU-processing step usually starts from a usable picture representation produced by decoding or another filter. Picture operations expose parallel work Many operations can calculate an output pixel from an input neighborhood independently of other output pixels. That gives the GPU a large set of related tasks. A scaling filter, for example, maps each output coordinate into the source and obtains the needed samples. An overlay operation combines source picture and overlay information. Dependencies and memory traffic still depend on the chosen algorithm. Consider a conceptual 1920 × 1080 output dispatched in 16 × 16 tiles: Horizontal tiles = ceil(1920 / 16) = 120 Vertical tiles = ceil(1080 / 16) = 68 Threads = 120 × 68 × 256 = 2,088,960 Output pixels = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 Extra threads = 15,360 The dispatch covers 1088 rows. Its final eight rows fall outside the output picture. An original conceptual kernel therefore includes a bounds decision: x, y = this thread's output coordinate if x >= width or y >= height: return output[x, y] = transform(input, x, y) The expression is pseudocode, not a real CUDA or Metal API. It illustrates how dispatch geometry and the picture's bounds cooperate. The processor needs the right picture meaning A hardware surface can have several planes, padded rows or a device-specific layout. A filter must use the representation its interface actually accepts. Colour meaning is another input. Transfer function, range, matrix and primaries determine what the stored values represent. A texture format describing channel storage does not supply all those properties. For HDR-to-SDR conversion, a processing path needs the intended tone-mapping relationship , not just a faster way to change sample numbers. Producer and consumer work need an order GPU launches and media operations can complete asynchronously. A filter cannot read a picture still being written by its decoder, and an encoder cannot consume a result still being written by the filter. Streams, command dependencies and completion objects coordinate those uses. A host API returning quickly can mean work was queued; it does not necessarily mean the transformed picture is ready. An Emby session can therefore use a hardware decoder, programmable GPU filtering and a hardware encoder while still having CPU-side coordination. The route describes the work of each stage. Order affects the visible result Scaling a picture after painting a subtitle scales the painted text along with it. Scaling first and composing the subtitle in output coordinates can produce a different text size and edge appearance. Similarly, applying a colour operation to nonlinear stored values can produce a different result from processing in a suitable linear-light representation. GPU execution accelerates the selected algorithm; it does not select the intended image operation on the application's behalf. articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.title: Overview: Processing building blocks | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/building-.keywords: Overview: Processing building blocks Hardware media processing combines engines and programmable operations within a decode, filter and encode sequence. A fixed-function decoder, an encoder and a GPU compute operation perform different work. The pipeline connects their inputs and outputs, including any stages handled elsewhere. These building blocks provide a more useful description than treating every operation on a graphics device as the same kind of acceleration. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> The decode-filter-encode pipeline A hardware video pipeline connects encoded input, decoded surfaces, picture transformations and encoded output through compatible devices, memory formats and completion dependencies. Fixed-function media engines Fixed-function media engines implement specialized video operations within a device, using dedicated processing paths rather than executing the entire job as general-purpose GPU shader work. GPU compute and video processing GPU compute processes picture data with programmable parallel work whose layout, colour interpretation and completion requirements connect it to the surrounding media pipeline. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References FFmpeg: Hardware devices and processing NVIDIA SDK 13.1: NVDEC programming guide NVIDIA CUDA: Asynchronous execution and streams

articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: AMD VCN generation capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: AMD VCN generation capabilities AMD VCN capability tables separate codec directions, sample configurations and product-specific engine availability, including exceptions within one named generation. AMD's VCN tables describe both a media-generation feature set and product-specific availability. Their codec rows need to be read together with the product notes. A VCN version alone is not a complete encoder or decoder query. Published codec progression The pinned AMD AMF reference labels all its displayed codec rows as 4:2:0 . Selected AV1 and HEVC entries are: Reference group HEVC decode/encode precision AV1 decode AV1 encode VCN 2.0 Listed 8/10-bit paths Not listed Not listed VCN 3.0 / 3.1 Listed 8/10-bit paths Listed 8/10-bit Not listed VCN 4.0 Listed 8/10-bit paths Table lists 8/10/12-bit Listed 8/10-bit VCN 5.0 Listed 8/10-bit paths Table lists 8/10/12-bit Listed 8/10-bit These are the source's grouped declarations. Exact profile/level, dimensions, implementation and product exceptions refine their use. The kernel's product/IP table can express more specific component revisions than the vendor summary group. Preserve each source's version scope rather than forcing their labels to be identical. A product note can remove the encoder assumption The same AMD reference identifies Navi24 RX 63xx/64xx/65xx entries as decode-only , while other VCN 3.0 products have a different arrangement. That note means a generation-row encoder declaration should not be copied unconditionally onto those products. Their actual decoding formats also need the exact product/interface evidence. An Emby conversion requiring new compressed video therefore asks for an available encoder, not merely a VCN label. Instance count and codec availability are separate The reference lists different numbers of VCN instances for products. It also states that its AV1 encoder is supported on one VCN instance, except the noted Strix Halo arrangement where both support it. Two physical instances consequently do not automatically establish two AV1 encoding resources. Codec operation and instance-specific availability remain distinct. The broader session discussion explains why those hardware resources are also different from a count of sustainable playback clients. Actual software selects the usable route AMF or another implemented interface supplies the usable operation, surface representation and driver context. The target encoder and source decoder can require different formats. For a supported AV1 source-to-H.264 output job, the source needs the appropriate AV1 reconstruction while the target needs H.264 encoding. The filters and picture lifetimes connect those two operations. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: How to read a hardware codec support matrix | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: How to read a hardware codec support matrix A hardware codec matrix relates a particular device or implementation to operation-specific codec, format and resource capabilities whose headings, legends and footnotes define the answer. A support matrix answers a specific media-operation question . The useful result is a relationship among device, codec configuration, direction and the source's stated scope. Before using a check mark to explain an Emby session, identify which operation the session needs. Turn the source and target into separate questions Consider an original conversion from 4K HEVC Main 10, 4:2:0 input to 1080p H.264 8-bit, 4:2:0 output. The source needs HEVC reconstruction. The target needs H.264 encoding. Its scaling, colour processing and subtitle choices are additional requirements. An invented two-device example makes that separation visible: Declared capability Device A Device B HEVC Main 10, 4:2:0 decode at the chosen 4K size Yes No H.264 8-bit, 4:2:0 decode Yes Yes H.264 8-bit, 4:2:0 encode at the chosen 1080p size Yes Yes Both offer the output encoder. Only A offers the selected source decoder under these declarations. This does not prevent a supported software decoder from supplying the input on B. It means the proposed hardware-only input path was not established. Format qualifiers in the claim Codec family is one field. Profile, bit depth, chroma subsampling, dimensions, level and relevant picture-order/tool support can refine the answer. HEVC 4:2:0 ten-bit decoding does not answer HEVC 4:2:2 ten-bit decoding. A supported 1080p configuration does not identify an arbitrary 8K limit. Likewise, a supported storage surface such as P010 describes the decoded-picture representation used by the next stage. It is not the same field as the compressed profile or a guarantee of HDR-to-SDR processing. Use the legend rather than inventing a binary meaning Intel's pinned Media Driver table distinguishes: Symbol Meaning in that source D Hardware decoding E Its hardware/low-power encoding path Es Hardware plus shader-based encoding Blank No declaration in that cell of that table The source also separates Full-Feature and Free-Kernel builds. Combining their rows into one “yes” can lose a real implementation distinction. From Meteor Lake, the source documents consolidation of the encoding entrypoint arrangement. An API entrypoint spelling is consequently not a universal physical-engine classification across all generations. A blank in an implementation table should be retained as “not listed here,” with its build, version and product scope. Another hardware or API reference can have a different question and scope. Check the exact chip and variant NVIDIA's current matrix lists several GTX 1650 variants with different NVENC generations and HEVC B-frame support. A Turing family label alone does not resolve that difference. Its Ampere A100 entry is another concrete example: it has decoder resources while the encoder table reports zero NVENC. Treating a powerful architecture name as proof of an encoder would give the wrong answer. AMD's table similarly marks selected Navi24 products as decode-only despite their VCN-family context. The exact row and its footnotes are therefore useful facts, not cosmetic details. Engine count, session policy and capacity are different columns Several physical encoders can improve aggregate available work. They do not necessarily give a one-engine-per-client limit or override a software session policy. NVIDIA SDK 13.1 describes a twelve-session combined system limit for non-qualified cards and a resource-limited policy for qualified cards. That policy is another scope from codec support or an engine count. Actual media demand, filters and memory determine whether a permitted workload can keep up. Concurrent encoder sessions develops those distinctions. Preserve the implementation context A manufacturer hardware reference, a driver feature table and a live API query describe different layers. The application also needs an integration that uses the exposed path. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Arc Alchemist media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Arc Alchemist media capabilities Arc Alchemist’s documented media implementation adds AV1 encoding alongside supported decoding, with source/target formats and driver build determining the usable route. Arc Alchemist is important for Intel media workloads because its documented path includes AV1 encoding as well as decoding. The selected source can therefore differ from the target codec while each operation uses an appropriate media capability. Intel Media Driver places Alchemist in its DG2/ATSM group. Preserve the direction and build declaration Selected pinned entries are: Configuration row Full-Feature Free-Kernel AVC D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit 4:2:2 D/E D/E AV1 10-bit D/E E The AV1 Full-Feature cell contains both directions. The Free-Kernel cell in this snapshot supplies E rather than the same complete D/E declaration. Intel's separate Arc A-Series hardware reference lists AV1 8/10-bit, 4:2:0 decode support. The hardware reference and implementation-build table answer related but different questions. New output encoding changes the representation choice In an original conversion exercise, a HEVC Main 10 source can be decoded and prepared for AV1 output through compatible selected operations. Alternatively, an AV1 source can be prepared for H.264 output. Those examples require different source and target queries. They do not mean that an existing compressed segment can switch codec by changing its label. The receiving client still needs the chosen output format. An Emby server offering AV1 output to a client without a usable AV1 playback path has not established end-to-end compatibility. Processing and resources remain separate requirements A decode/encode declaration does not add every desired scaling, tone-mapping or subtitle route. The selected filters need compatible pictures and completion relationships between the stages. A discrete adapter can also introduce transfer costs if the application uses CPU-side processing or another adapter's resources. The actual frame route, output dimensions and source properties determine the workload. An advertised engine or codec entry does not give a fixed number of complete 4K sessions. Query the installed implementation The application needs a compatible runtime/driver and integration for the selected operation. A build-dependent AV1 row illustrates why those details should be retained alongside the product identity. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Elkhart Lake and Jasper Lake media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Elkhart Lake and Jasper Lake media capabilities Elkhart Lake and Jasper Lake expose a documented low-power Intel media feature set whose AVC, HEVC and VP9 operations differ from newer AV1-capable implementation columns. Elkhart Lake and Jasper Lake combine modest general-purpose CPU resources with a dedicated Intel media path. CPU-core performance and media support need to be read separately. Intel's Media Driver groups these platforms in its EHL/JSL column. Identify the declared codec operations Selected rows in the pinned implementation table are: Configuration row Full-Feature build Free-Kernel build AVC D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit D/E D/E VP9 10-bit D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit 4:2:2 D D AV1 10-bit Not listed Not listed The rows preserve direction and sample configuration. A HEVC 4:2:2 decode declaration is a different fact from encoding that configuration. D/E also uses the source's operation legend. It does not say that an Emby build exposes every listed operation, profile limit or filter combination. HEVC and AV1 sources make different demands For an original selected-source comparison, assume a movie's compatible H.264 audio/video route and a HEVC Main 10 video route are both implemented on the device. Dedicated reconstruction can avoid asking the CPU to perform all of that video work. An otherwise similar AV1 source requires its own decoder. The EHL/JSL snapshot does not list the AV1 rows, while Tiger Lake-related columns do. A newer codec source can therefore change the CPU path or source-selection result without changing the server's device name. Xe-LP media capabilities explains the next relevant comparison. General CPU and media processing still cooperate Container parsing, audio handling and server coordination remain general software work. A CPU-side subtitle or colour operation can also introduce a different frame path after supported decoding. For an Emby server on a low-power system, these remaining stages can be significant even when decoding and encoding are supported by the media path. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Kaby Lake media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Kaby Lake media capabilities Kaby Lake’s media capabilities provide important AVC and ten-bit HEVC decoding paths, with encoding classifications and exposed features dependent on the documented software implementation. Kaby Lake is an important Intel generation for reconstructing mainstream HEVC Main 10 video. The supported integrated media path can decode the ten-bit source pictures needed by many HDR files. Decoding those pictures and preparing an SDR output are separate work. The latter still needs the selected tone-mapping and other picture operations. Use the KBLx column with its legend Intel Media Driver groups Kaby Lake with related platforms in its KBLx column. These selected entries come from the pinned implementation snapshot: Configuration row Full-Feature build Free-Kernel build AVC D/E/Es D/E HEVC 10-bit D/Es D VP9 10-bit D D AV1 10-bit Not listed Not listed D identifies decoding, E the source's hardware/low-power encoding path, and Es hardware-plus-shader encoding. Intel's separate 2024 hardware reference likewise classifies the 7th/8th-generation HEVC encoder under its hardware-plus-shader row. Describing every listed HEVC operation as one pure fixed-function path would erase that distinction. A ten-bit HDR input needs a complete picture route Imagine an Emby conversion taking HEVC Main 10 input and delivering an 8-bit H.264 SDR target. The selected source decoder is one requirement. The picture route needs the intended HDR-to-SDR relationship , output dimensions and selected subtitle handling before the target encoder receives its pictures. Main 10 decode support does not apply those transformations automatically. A software or device-based filter choice determines the actual intermediate path and its frame access. The processor SKU must provide the media resource A processor product without enabled processor graphics does not supply this integrated media path merely because its CPU architecture belongs to the generation. Another discrete adapter is a separately identified resource. The installed runtime/driver and application need a usable route to the selected device. An older Media SDK description and a current driver matrix have their respective implementation scopes. Retain the operation that matters to the session For Kaby Lake source compatibility, HEVC Main 10 decode and AV1 decode are different questions. The selected table declares the former and does not list the latter. For output, the AVC and HEVC rows have different classifications. Choosing the actual target codec and implementation therefore changes the route being assessed, even with the same source file. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Xe2 media capabilities: Lunar Lake and Battlemage | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Xe2 media capabilities: Lunar Lake and Battlemage Lunar Lake and Battlemage have separate Intel driver columns whose format/direction declarations include AV1 and differ from earlier groups in selected HEVC and VP9 rows. Lunar Lake and Battlemage appear as separate LNL and BMG columns in the pinned Intel Media Driver table. Their selected entries provide a useful example of how a newer media path can change several capabilities rather than merely extend one list. The graphics-family term Xe2 supplies architectural context. The operation and its implementation declaration remain the specific media evidence. Compare selected rows directly In this snapshot the displayed rows agree between LNL and BMG: Configuration row LNL and BMG: Full-Feature / Free-Kernel MTLx comparison AVC D/E in both D/E HEVC 10-bit D/E in both D/E HEVC 10-bit 4:2:2 D/E in both D AV1 10-bit D/E in both D/E VP9 10-bit D in both D/E The entries retain the source's D/E legend. They describe the named driver rows, not a completed native profile/configuration test or every application's exposed output. A newer column is not simply a superset The VP9 ten-bit row is a concrete example: the snapshot lists decoding for LNL/BMG while MTLx includes an encoding entry. A workload that specifically needs VP9 output therefore asks a different question from one decoding VP9 input. Replacing the source/target with AV1 gives another declared operation set. This matters when comparing an Emby job or a prepared-media workflow. The target codec is part of the comparison, not merely a consequence of the graphics-generation label. Chroma needs its own query A HEVC Main 10, 4:2:0 source and a ten-bit 4:2:2 source are different encoded configurations. Their usable API profiles, picture formats and output constraints need to match the requested direction. The source table provides the selected declarations to investigate. The runtime's native capability and initialization results establish the usable detailed configuration. Keep integrated and discrete resources identified Lunar Lake and Battlemage also have different product/resource arrangements. The selected driver/device context, picture storage and consumers determine whether processing remains on compatible resources or needs another handoff. An application can use the shared interface family without using the same frame route on both products. Driver-dependent capabilities develops the implementation side of that comparison. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Xe-LP media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Xe-LP media capabilities Xe-LP-era Intel media paths include AV1 decoding in the documented full-feature implementation, while AV1 encoding belongs to later specified media groups. The Xe-LP-era Intel media path is relevant to AV1 source decoding . It should be assessed separately from the ability to create AV1 output. For practical matrix interpretation, the pinned Media Driver identifies explicit TGLx and DG1/SG1 groups. TGLx includes its listed Tiger Lake-related platforms; DG1/SG1 identifies the separate listed product group. AV1 decode and encode are separate steps These selected TGLx entries retain the table's build distinction: Configuration row Full-Feature Free-Kernel AVC D/E/Es D/E HEVC 10-bit D/E/Es D/E VP9 10-bit D/E D/E AV1 10-bit D Not listed The AV1 entry is decode-only in the Full-Feature declaration. The DG1/SG1 AV1 row likewise gives a full-feature decoding declaration rather than an encoder. Intel's published hardware reference lists AV1 8/10-bit, 4:2:0 decoding for its stated Xe MAX and 11th-generation-related product scope. These are source-specific references, not a promise for every device carrying a similar graphics label. A source can use AV1 while output uses H.264 An Emby conversion can reconstruct an AV1 source using a supported selected path, prepare its pictures and encode H.264 output. That does not require an AV1 encoder. Conversely, selecting AV1 output needs another encoder capability that the displayed TGLx rows do not supply. Arc Alchemist introduces an explicitly different AV1 encode declaration in the compared implementation matrix. The backend build is part of the result The table's AV1 Full-Feature and Free-Kernel cells differ. An installed package therefore needs its actual implementation/build context preserved when comparing an observed query with the source table. The device, selected backend, requested source profile and usable output surface describe the route. A profile absent from one implementation's query is not repaired by pointing at another build's row. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: Intel Xe-LPG media capabilities: Meteor Lake and Arrow Lake | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: Intel Xe-LPG media capabilities: Meteor Lake and Arrow Lake Meteor Lake and Arrow Lake use the documented MTLx media implementation group, whose AV1 and encoding-interface declarations need to be interpreted at their own format and software scope. Intel Media Driver groups Meteor Lake and its listed Arrow Lake platforms in the MTLx column. That implementation grouping is useful for relating a product to the table's specific media declarations. The general graphics-generation name and the driver group have different roles. The exact processor/graphics SKU still identifies the physical resource. Selected MTLx rows Configuration row Full-Feature Free-Kernel AVC D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit D/E D/E HEVC 10-bit 4:2:2 D D VP9 10-bit D/E D/E AV1 10-bit D/E D/E The selected AV1 row contains decoding and encoding. The HEVC 4:2:2 row gives decoding rather than an equivalent encoder declaration. Consequently, a list of supported codec names would lose a useful difference. Profile, chroma and direction establish the requested operation. The encoding interface convention changes The pinned source notes that, from Meteor Lake, the earlier low-power and shader encoding entrypoint arrangement is consolidated into a unified encoding entrypoint using its documented hardware path. An application-visible VAEntrypointEncSlice name therefore cannot be classified as “shader encoding” solely because an older group used that entrypoint for a different arrangement. The group, source legend and implementation revision need to accompany the interpretation. Integrated media is still a pipeline resource For an Emby source/target exercise, AV1 input and H.264 output need two selected operations. An AV1 output choice is another valid target question under a compatible implemented route. Scaling, HDR-to-SDR preparation and subtitle composition remain separate picture operations. Their usable route depends on the selected implementation and frame representation. Shared/integrated memory also retains bandwidth, surface and synchronization costs. CPU-core or graphics-core counts do not measure those media-engine resources directly. Connect the product to the implementation The MTLx platform list provides a grouping for the displayed table, rather than a guarantee that every application exposes every row. Runtime/device selection and actual query/init results establish the executing route. Xe2 supplies a useful next comparison because some chroma-direction and encoding declarations change again. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: NVIDIA Ada Lovelace media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: NVIDIA Ada Lovelace media capabilities Ada Lovelace media implementations include AV1 encoding on the specified products, with codec tools, engine counts and input/output constraints belonging to their exact matrix rows. Ada Lovelace adds a documented NVIDIA AV1 output-encoding path on the specified products, alongside AV1 reconstruction. That changes the set of possible source/target combinations, provided the application and receiver can use the selected representation. A named product gives concrete feature scope Selected GeForce RTX 4090 matrix entries include: Property Declaration NVENC generation / physical count Eighth / two NVDEC generation / physical count Fifth / one AV1 4:2:0 encoding Yes AV1 8/10-bit decoding Yes HEVC ten-bit and B-frame encoding Yes Listed H.264/HEVC 4:2:2 encoding columns No The absence in the selected 4:2:2 columns is distinct from ordinary 4:2:0 support. The requested sample configuration should remain visible in the claim. AV1 output needs a compatible receiver An original Emby conversion exercise takes HEVC Main 10 input and prepares AV1 output. A supported source decoder, picture route and AV1 encoder establish the server-side operations. The receiving app still needs the chosen AV1 profile, packaging and presentation path. A server encoder capability does not configure the client's decoder. The reverse direction—AV1 input to H.264 output—selects another encoder while retaining AV1 reconstruction. Two encoders describe physical work resources The RTX 4090 count of two NVENC units is useful for aggregate processing capacity under the documented workload and driver behavior. It does not mean two clients are the only permitted workload, or that a twelve-session system policy becomes twenty-four. Physical units, permitted active sessions and sustainable media throughput are different quantities. Concurrent sessions develops that distinction with a checked original workload example. Preserve the coding choices in a quality comparison AV1, HEVC and H.264 use different representations and tool sets. Comparing outputs needs the same prepared source interval, target dimensions/cadence, achieved rate and declared encoder configuration. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: NVIDIA Ampere media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: NVIDIA Ampere media capabilities Ampere-family media capabilities differ between graphics and compute-oriented chips, with AV1 decoding and encoder presence requiring the exact product’s published row. Ampere graphics products make AV1 decoding relevant to many NVIDIA media routes. Compute-oriented Ampere products can have a different decoder architecture and no encoder. The exact chip/product must accompany the family name. The RTX 3080 and A100 rows answer different questions Selected current matrix facts are: Property GeForce RTX 3080 NVIDIA A100 NVENC resources One, seventh-generation entry Zero NVDEC resources One, fifth-generation entry Five, fourth-generation entry AV1 decoding Yes, 8/10-bit entries No in the listed entries AV1 encoding No No HEVC ten-bit encoding Yes No NVENC path in this row NVIDIA SDK 13.1 also states that GA100's NVDEC architecture corresponds to the Turing decoder architecture. That supports the exact-chip distinction shown in the matrix. More general-purpose compute resources do not change which codec hardware is present. Input and output can use different formats On a supported RTX 3080 route, an AV1 source can be reconstructed into pictures and prepared for H.264 or HEVC output. This uses an AV1 decoder and a different target encoder. It does not require AV1 encoding, which the selected encoder row does not supply. For A100, pointing at the RTX 3080's AV1 or NVENC entry would identify another product's capability. A conversion needing that operation must establish a different usable route. Engine count is not a complete-session estimate Five decoder resources on A100 describe its published media hardware. They do not create a video encoder, nor do they calculate the CPU/filter/output requirements of a complete session. A graphics product's single encoder can likewise support permitted work through its actual capacity and session policy rather than one fixed client per physical engine. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: NVIDIA Blackwell media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: NVIDIA Blackwell media capabilities Blackwell’s documented media additions include H.264/HEVC 4:2:2 paths and H.264 ten-bit features, with exact product resources and SDK/driver exposure defining the usable configuration. Blackwell's documented NVIDIA media additions include H.264 and HEVC 4:2:2 encoding/decoding paths and ten-bit H.264 features. These are specific format changes, beyond another entry for ordinary eight-bit 4:2:0 video. NVIDIA introduced these capabilities in its SDK 13.0 Blackwell material. The current SDK and product matrix establish their updated software and device scope. Chroma and precision are separate dimensions A 4:2:2 picture retains chroma at a different spatial sampling relationship from 4:2:0. Ten-bit storage precision is another property. For an original ideal 1920 × 1080 picture, 4:2:0 has 1.5 samples per pixel across its planes, while 4:2:2 has two. If each sample occupies two bytes of storage: 4:2:0 = 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 × 2 = 6,220,800 bytes 4:2:2 = 1920 × 1080 × 2 × 2 = 8,294,400 bytes The calculation concerns ideal unpadded picture storage. It does not give a compressed bitrate. NVIDIA's Blackwell material names NV16 and P210 among its semiplanar encoder input formats for the relevant 4:2:2 paths. A product row defines its resource count The GeForce RTX 5090 matrix lists three ninth-generation NVENC units and two sixth-generation NVDEC units. Those are different operation resources. The same row includes its 4:2:2 encoding columns and AV1 encode/decode entries. A Blackwell architecture label is not a rule that every product must contain those same counts. The exact selected row remains part of the evidence. Source and target profiles need software exposure A new device feature needs an application wrapper, SDK/runtime and driver path that expose the requested profile and picture format. A program compiled with an older interface can therefore fail to offer a configuration present in the hardware reference. Its accepted input-surface layout is also another required link. For an Emby source using ten-bit 4:2:2, the server's actual decoder, filters and target encoder establish the executing route. The feature addition is relevant to the source query, while the observed initialization supplies the implemented answer. Keep the pipeline’s picture work explicit Scaling, colour interpretation, subtitle composition and output packaging remain separate operations. An accepted 4:2:2 decoder does not choose those transformations automatically. The format and resource relationships described by frame surfaces connect the new codec configurations to their consumers. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: NVIDIA Pascal media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: NVIDIA Pascal media capabilities Pascal-family NVIDIA products have SKU-specific decode and encode resources, with selected HEVC capabilities and important encoder-presence exceptions in the published matrix. Pascal introduced media capabilities useful for mainstream H.264 and HEVC work, but the exact NVIDIA product is important. The family name alone does not establish that the device even includes an encoder. The current matrix supplies both feature columns and physical engine counts for named products. Use a concrete Pascal example For the GeForce GTX 1080 Ti row, selected entries include: Property Published declaration NVENC generation / count Sixth generation / two NVDEC generation / count Third generation / one HEVC ten-bit encoding Yes HEVC 4:2:0 ten-bit decoding Yes HEVC B-frame encoding No AV1 encode/decode No in the selected rows These facts concern the named product and matrix scope. Ten-bit encoding and picture-order tools are different feature questions. The two encoders are physical resources. They are not a rule that the server can run exactly two playback clients. A smaller Pascal product exposes a different role The GeForce GT 1030 entry reports zero NVENC, while its decoder table lists a decode resource and its supported configurations. A GT 1030 can therefore participate in applicable reconstruction work without supplying the same target-encoding route as the GTX 1080 Ti. That is a concrete hardware-presence distinction, rather than a driver setting that adds the missing encoder. An Emby session needing a new video representation would need another usable encoder path. Codec tools remain separate columns A published HEVC encoder does not supply every HEVC profile, chroma format or coding tool. The selected row's absent HEVC B-frame feature illustrates that refinement. Preset and rate-control comparisons should preserve the actual supported tool set. A setting with the same label on another generation can run under a different available feature set. Hardware encoding explains why rate, prepared pictures and implementation choices must be held together in a picture-quality comparison. Source reconstruction and target compression form the route A supported HEVC Main 10 input can still need scaling, SDR preparation or subtitle processing before H.264 output. An AV1 source asks for a decoder not established by the selected Pascal rows. articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.title: NVIDIA Turing media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/generatio.keywords: NVIDIA Turing media capabilities Turing-family NVIDIA products include differing encoder implementations, so selected codec tools and engine generation must be read from the exact product row. Turing is a useful example of why an architecture label cannot replace the exact media-engine row. NVIDIA's current matrix lists GTX 1650 variants with different NVENC generations and HEVC B-frame support . The product variant determines the feature evidence. Compare the published variants Selected encoder entries are: Named matrix row NVENC generation HEVC B-frame encoding GTX 1650 GDDR5 Sixth No GTX 1650 GDDR6: listed sixth-generation variant Sixth No GTX 1650 GDDR6: listed seventh-generation variant Seventh Yes GTX 1650 SUPER Seventh Yes RTX 2060 / 2070 Seventh Yes All of those rows carry the Turing family context, but the encoder declarations differ. A product description omitting the relevant variant therefore leaves part of the encoder question unresolved. HEVC tools and bit depth are different properties The selected RTX 2060 entries include HEVC ten-bit encoding and the listed B-frame feature. Those are separate capabilities: one concerns sample representation, the other a picture-coding/order tool. The encoder still needs a suitable profile, input surface, dimensions and configuration. Its accepted output choices do not identify the decoder used for the source. AV1 needs its own operation The selected Turing encoder and decoder rows do not list AV1 as supported. A supported HEVC input or H.264 output does not supply an AV1 decoder or encoder. An Emby AV1 source can consequently need another reconstruction route. A HEVC-to-H.264 session asks a different pair of supported operations. Ampere gives the next useful AV1 decode comparison, including another exact-chip exception. Relate the variant to the actual encoder The selected runtime/device and initialized encoder establish which implementation the job uses. A copied feature list for a different GTX 1650 variant would not explain a missing tool on this one. The resulting picture and rate-control choices can then be compared within the relevant encoder's supported set. articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.title: Hardware decoding and software decoding | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.keywords: Hardware decoding and software decoding Hardware and software video decoding reconstruct encoded pictures through different execution paths while preserving the stream’s configuration, reference and presentation requirements. A video decoder reconstructs pictures from the selected encoded stream. A software decoder performs that implementation's work through CPU execution; a hardware decoder submits suitable work to an exposed hardware decoding path. Both need the stream's actual configuration and picture dependencies. The container must first be parsed so the decoder receives the appropriate encoded data. Match the encoded configuration Codec family is one property of the query. Hardware support can also depend on profile, chroma format, bit depth, dimensions and relevant coding features. Use an original teaching decoder that accepts HEVC Main/Main 10, 4:2:0, within its declared dimension range: Selected stream Result under the invented declaration HEVC Main 10, 4:2:0, 1920 × 1080 Within the stated configuration HEVC 4:2:2, same dimensions Chroma configuration does not match HEVC Main 10 beyond its maximum dimensions Dimension limit does not match Another codec family A separate support query is needed The table is not a real device matrix. It explains why one HEVC source can enter a hardware path while another needs a different decoder. An Emby session's actual source properties and active decoder identify which case was exercised. An enabled setting describes permission or preference; the selected runtime path describes execution. References determine reconstruction order Compressed video can use pictures that refer to other pictures. A decoder needs those references before reconstructing the dependent pictures. An original four-picture model uses an encoded/decode order of I0, P3, B1, B2 and a presentation order of I0, B1, B2, P3. In this model the two B pictures use I0 and P3 as references. The hardware/driver or application manages the required decoded-picture storage according to the chosen interface. A reference picture cannot be overwritten while later decoding still needs it. Some APIs expose pictures in presentation order; others expose lower-level completion and ordering responsibilities. V4L2 stateless decoding , for example, gives the application an explicit role in reference state. Reconstruction and later processing are separate Choosing a decoder does not re-encode the source. For supported conforming input, decoding implements its reconstruction rules. Visible differences can arise elsewhere: output bit depth or range conversion, deinterlacing, scaling, colour processing or display handling. A comparison should keep those later operations consistent before attributing a difference to the decode implementation. Likewise, a decoder's output format matters to the next stage. A hardware frame may remain in device-associated storage, while a software decoder usually gives the application a CPU-oriented picture layout. Fallback changes a route, not the movie’s identity An application can choose a software path when its usable hardware path cannot decode the selected configuration. That can change CPU demand and subsequent memory handling while preserving the source and intended programme timeline. A CPU filter after hardware decoding needs the appropriate access or transfer. Conversely, software-decoded pictures can be prepared for a hardware encoder. The full decode-filter-encode route determines those costs. articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.title: Hardware encoding and software encoding | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.keywords: Hardware encoding and software encoding Hardware and software video encoders create a new compressed representation using different execution paths and supported configuration, rate-control and coding-tool choices. An encoder creates a new compressed video representation from prepared pictures. A hardware encoder uses an exposed hardware encoding path; a software encoder implements its selected coding work through CPU execution. The decision concerns the output representation. It is separate from which decoder reconstructed the input. Choose the output before comparing implementations The encoder must fit the target codec, dimensions, bit depth, chroma format and supported coding tools. Its rate-control and latency choices shape how it spends bits and buffers pictures. Choice What it describes Codec/profile Target compressed-video configuration Picture dimensions and cadence Prepared pictures to be represented Rate control How the encoder manages bitrate or quality objectives Preset/tuning Implementation-specific processing and coding choices Reordering and lookahead Available analysis and picture-order behavior An Emby H.264-to-H.264 conversion still uses another encode when it changes the representation. Matching codec family names at the input and output does not establish stream copying . Equal bitrate does not mean equal picture quality Encoders can choose different predictions, quantization and other coding decisions for the same pictures. Their supported tools and preset meanings also differ. A useful comparison holds the programme interval and target constraints together: Preserve Why it matters Same prepared source pictures Avoids comparing different scaling or tone mapping Same output codec and picture configuration Avoids spending bits on a different representation Comparable achieved output rate Nominal settings can produce different actual rates Declared latency/analysis constraints Some choices need additional buffering Identified implementation and preset Preset names are not universal quality units The result should be assessed on representative content, including motion and texture. Hardware execution is not a predetermined quality score, and a “slow” label from one software encoder is not a matching mode in another encoder. Output rate and duration describe stored payload For an original example with a known average encoded-video rate of 5,000,000 bit/s over 1800 seconds: 5,000,000 × 1800 / 8 = 1,125,000,000 bytes That is 1.125 GB of video payload in decimal units. Audio, packaging and transport add other bytes. The calculation assumes the achieved average rate. A maximum-rate constraint or a quality-target setting does not automatically make the output average equal to that number. Accepted input and completed output are different events An encoder can accept pictures into a queue before output appears. Analysis, frame reordering and asynchronous hardware completion can separate those events. The application must retrieve generated bitstream data and retain input storage for as long as the encoder needs it. At the end, draining obtains remaining output that may have been delayed. articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.title: What hardware acceleration does for media | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/Hardware-.keywords: What hardware acceleration does for media Media hardware acceleration assigns supported decoding, picture processing or encoding work to specialized device paths within a larger playback or conversion pipeline. Media hardware acceleration changes where particular processing work is performed . A supported video decoder can reconstruct pictures using a media engine; a processor can scale or transform those pictures; an encoder can create a new compressed representation. In an Emby video-conversion session, these are separate opportunities. The server still coordinates source access, selected streams, timing and delivery. Start with the work the session requires A Direct Play session does not need the server to decode and encode the video merely because acceleration is enabled. Its receiving player still performs its own decoding and presentation. A conversion session instead has a specific input and target. Its work can include decoding, scaling, colour processing, subtitle composition and encoding. Supported hardware paths can take responsibility for particular stages. Work Possible execution path Encoded video reconstruction Specialized decoder or CPU implementation Picture transformations Media processor, GPU compute or CPU filter New compressed video Specialized encoder or CPU implementation File/session and output coordination Application and operating-system work An acceleration API is how the application reaches a suitable device path. The API name, hardware block and codec name describe different parts of that relationship. The saved work depends on the affected stages Use an original serial-cost model for one picture: Stage Initial cost Cost after selected acceleration Decode 12 ms 3 ms Filter 8 ms 8 ms Encode 20 ms 5 ms Other coordination 4 ms 4 ms Total 44 ms 20 ms These are invented service costs. They do not describe overlap, actual GPU timings or a real Emby session. The modeled improvement is 44 / 20 = 2.2 . Accelerating only decoding gives a different result: 3 + 8 + 20 + 4 = 35 milliseconds, or about 1.257 times the original rate. The example makes the remaining work visible. Once the expensive encoder is faster, the unchanged filter and coordination account for a larger share of the total. Hardware support is a configuration question A usable decoder needs the selected codec configuration, including relevant profile, bit depth, dimensions and picture format. An encoder needs the target configuration. The stages also need compatible memory and processing relationships. A device can decode the source but lack the requested encoder or filter path. A driver can expose one operation while the application's build uses another interface. Those are specific configuration facts, rather than one device-wide acceleration switch. Emby's hardware overview identifies its platform routes. The hardware pipeline develops how successful stages are connected into a useful result. Capacity is measured across the complete job A faster video stage can free CPU time, shorten conversion or make concurrent work possible. The useful result depends on the rest of the selected pipeline and the delivered media deadline. articles/hardware-acceleration/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Media hardware acceleration Media hardware acceleration uses supported device engines and software interfaces to perform parts of a playback or conversion pipeline. A GPU name does not describe the entire media path. Decoding, filtering and encoding can use different engines, and the software must reach those engines through a compatible interface with suitable picture formats. The building-block and interface topics establish those relationships. Generation pages explain how capabilities differ, while pipeline topics show why transfers, synchronization or another stage can limit the benefit. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: AMD Advanced Media Framework (AMF) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: AMD Advanced Media Framework (AMF) AMD AMF is a component framework that connects media applications to supported AMD decoding, encoding and processing paths with defined memory and asynchronous data-flow behavior. Advanced Media Framework , or AMF , is AMD's media component framework. It gives an application supported decoding, encoding and processing operations while coordinating their memory and device relationships. AMF is software. VCN, UVD and VCE are media-engine names that can appear beneath the framework in different hardware generations. Components preserve the media-stage roles Component role Input and output to recognize Video decoder Selected encoded stream to decoded surfaces Video encoder Prepared pictures to compressed output Video converter/processor Picture configuration to another supported picture configuration Application Container access, selection, stage coordination and delivery AMD's video-decoder documentation states that container demultiplexing belongs to the application. A supported AMF decoder therefore needs the selected codec data rather than automatically interpreting every container file. The components share a framework but keep their own configuration and result contracts. A decoder success does not report an encoder's target capabilities. Device memory is configured in context An AMF context connects components to their supported memory/device arrangement. A surface or buffer has a specific representation and ownership lifecycle. The public API supports interoperability arrangements through appropriate graphics/compute interfaces. The usable options depend on the selected implementation, platform and runtime. For an Emby path, the relevant facts are the initialized component, selected device, actual source/target properties and intervening processing. The AMF label provides one layer of that route. Input acceptance and output readiness use separate calls SubmitInput() supplies data to a component. QueryOutput() obtains its produced data. A component may need several inputs or asynchronous work before an output is ready. Result Scoped interpretation AMF_OK Successful result under the method's contract AMF_INPUT_FULL Submission cannot accept more under its current queue/resource state AMF_REPEAT The output query should be tried later under its processing contract AMF_EOF The documented drain has reached its output end Some components can return AMF_OK with no output object when data is not ready. The application checks the data result as well as the status. An original trace can therefore be: Submit input A -> accepted Submit input B -> accepted Submit input C -> INPUT_FULL Retrieve completed output -> queue/resources can advance Retry input C -> accepted The trace models backpressure. It does not report actual queue depth or a decoder error. Retrying C should preserve the same intended input rather than silently discard it. Draining completes already submitted work At an input end, a component may still hold media needed for delayed output. Drain() requests completion of that submitted work according to the component contract. The application retrieves remaining output until the drain's completion indication. It does not treat the first empty output query as proof that the whole job has finished. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: AMD Unified Video Decoder (UVD, legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: AMD Unified Video Decoder (UVD, legacy) UVD names AMD’s legacy dedicated video-decoder family, while related identifiers can persist in software interfaces that run on later supported devices. Unified Video Decoder , or UVD , is AMD's legacy dedicated video-decoder family. Its role is reconstruction of supported compressed video into pictures. AMD's 2017 multimedia presentation identifies UVD as the decoder and VCE as the encoder. Later hardware uses VCN-family media blocks, while older UVD terminology remains useful in documentation and software identifiers. Recognize the hardware role Name in the older architecture Role to associate with it UVD Supported video reconstruction VCE Supported video compression Graphics/compute resources Programmable processing and graphics work This is a role distinction. The accepted codecs, profiles and formats depend on the actual UVD generation and exposed driver path. A UVD decoder's output can be used for playback or another encoding stage. Decode support alone does not establish the target encoder. Component identifiers can preserve old names AMD's current AMF decoder documentation still uses names such as AMFVideoDecoderUVD_H264_AVC . That is a component identifier supplied to the framework. Its spelling is not a report that the device contains a particular old UVD block. The application creates a supported component through its runtime and device context. The current documentation also uses HW-prefixed identifiers for other decoder configurations. Both styles belong to the public software interface rather than a universal naming rule for physical media hardware. Interpret an older acceleration description by stage An older Emby-related discussion might mention UVD decoding and an AMD encoder in the same conversion. The first name concerns the input reconstruction stage; the second concerns newly created output. The selected device and source configuration establish what could actually be decoded. The intervening picture operations and encoder establish the rest of the route. VCN and AMF provide the hardware-family and software-interface context for reading those names in newer stacks. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: AMD Video Coding Engine (VCE, legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: AMD Video Coding Engine (VCE, legacy) VCE names AMD’s legacy video-encoding engine family, separating compressed-output creation from source decoding and from the software framework controlling the job. Video Coding Engine , or VCE , is AMD's legacy video-encoding engine family. It creates compressed output from suitable pictures. Older AMD architectures distinguish VCE encoding from UVD decoding. Later supported media-engine families can use VCN, while application and driver interfaces provide the software route to the relevant operation. Encoding begins after usable pictures exist A video-conversion job needs a decoder for its selected input and an encoder for its selected output. An older VCE description concerns the second role. For an original H.264-to-H.264 example, the input is decoded to pictures and then encoded into another H.264 representation. That is different from passing the existing encoded stream through unchanged. The output codec label alone does not identify which operation occurred. The mapping or initialized encoder supplies that evidence. Framework and engine are different layers Evidence Fact it describes VCE in a hardware description A legacy media-engine family AMF in an application description A media component/API route H.264 in the output A compressed-video format Selected device and initialized component Execution context for the operation Output bitrate/preset Choices for the new representation An AMF framework name does not establish that every supported device uses an old VCE block. Conversely, a VCE hardware entry does not guarantee that every modern application exposes its operation. Rate and picture choices remain encoder choices The supported codec configuration and encoding tools belong to the actual engine/interface combination. Generation, driver and application support determine the usable target. An Emby acceleration discussion can therefore be read by preserving the decoder, prepared picture configuration and output encoder separately. That keeps a legacy engine label from becoming a claim about the whole session. The AMF article describes current component coordination, including the distinction between accepted input and completed output. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: AMD Video Core Next (VCN) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: AMD Video Core Next (VCN) VCN is AMD’s video-engine family associated with supported media decoding and encoding operations, distinct from its graphics architecture and the software API used to access it. VCN is AMD's video-engine family. It describes media hardware beneath the application and driver interfaces that expose supported decoding and encoding operations. An application can reach applicable AMD media paths through AMF or another supported platform interface. The VCN name belongs to the hardware layer rather than to a container or video codec. Graphics and media IP have their own versions AMD's Linux hardware-component table lists graphics, display, video and DMA components in separate columns. Those versions identify different blocks within a product. For example, its RAVEN/PICASSO entry associates a graphics-core version with VCN 1.0; CARRIZO/STONEY uses the earlier VCE/UVD pair. The distinction identifies a component family, rather than supplying a complete media support or performance table. A graphics-generation number should therefore not be substituted for the media IP version. Likewise, a product-name number alone does not establish a particular decode/encode configuration. The exposed operations are queried separately Source reconstruction and target compression have different requirements. A device can accept one compressed input while offering another set of output encoders. In an Emby conversion exercise, HEVC Main 10 input and H.264 output need separate decode and encode paths, with a usable picture-processing relationship between them. The software runtime and driver expose those operations to the application. Current hardware information, implementation capability and the actual selected media configuration cooperate in the answer. Legacy software names can outlive the old block name AMF's current decoder documentation still includes UVD-prefixed component identifiers for several codecs. A component name can remain stable while the implementation uses a different supported hardware generation. This mirrors a broader API pattern: names preserve compatibility with application code. Reading an identifier as a hardware-probing result would confuse the software contract with the selected physical device. The UVD article explains the legacy decoder name, while AMF explains the component interface. The complete job still has picture and memory work VCN's codec operation can cooperate with GPU processing, driver services or CPU-side application work. Scaling, subtitle composition and colour transformations belong to their selected processing path. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Android MediaCodec and buffer ownership | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Android MediaCodec and buffer ownership MediaCodec exposes Android codec components through configured input/output buffers or surfaces whose ownership, timing and state determine how media is processed. MediaCodec is Android's interface to codec components. An application selects and configures a decoder or encoder, supplies its inputs and handles its outputs through the component's supported buffer or surface arrangement. The interface can expose hardware-accelerated and software implementations. Its name alone does not identify the selected component. Select the operation and configuration The application needs an appropriate component for the media type and operation. Decoder and encoder selection are separate questions. MediaCodecInfo describes properties including supported types and, on applicable API versions, whether a component reports hardware acceleration or software-only operation. The declared hardware attribute comes from the device implementation; observed processing supplies another kind of evidence. A selected HEVC decoder still needs support for the actual profile, dimensions, sample format and other required features. An Android Emby player and an Android-hosted server can request different media work through that platform. Buffer ownership lets the codec make progress The application obtains an available input buffer, fills it with valid encoded data or picture input as appropriate, then returns it to the codec through its queueing contract. Output availability establishes another ownership stage. After processing or rendering the output, the application releases the output buffer back to the component. Event Permission or progress Input buffer becomes available Application may prepare that offered buffer Input is queued Codec may consume it Output becomes available Application can handle the reported output Output is released Its retained use can end under the contract Android's documentation warns that holding buffers can stall component progress. An empty output queue and a pool exhausted by retained outputs are different states. Surface-based paths avoid treating every result as an ordinary CPU byte array. Their consumer and presentation lifetimes still need the supported interface behavior. Media time has a declared unit A codec sample's presentationTimeUs uses microseconds. It is a programme-time coordinate, rather than the wall time at which a callback happened. For an original 25-fps sequence: One picture interval = 1 / 25 second = 40,000 microseconds Picture 0: 0 us Picture 1: 40,000 us Picture 2: 80,000 us Those times retain the intended presentation schedule even if decoding produces the pictures ahead of playback. Synchronous and asynchronous modes have different rules Synchronous processing obtains available buffers through dequeue operations. Asynchronous processing receives availability through configured callbacks and follows its corresponding state model. In the documented asynchronous arrangement, a flush requires a subsequent start() to resume the Running state and input callbacks. Old buffer indices or callbacks need their validity context; they are not permanent storage identifiers across arbitrary reconfiguration. An output-format change also supplies a new interpretation for subsequent output. Dimensions, format and surface requirements should be related to that changed state rather than inferred from the original configure call.
