articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: OpenMAX IL components, ports and state | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: OpenMAX IL components, ports and state OpenMAX IL defines a multimedia component interface whose ports, buffer exchanges and asynchronous state transitions coordinate supported processing implementations. OpenMAX Integration Layer , or OpenMAX IL , defines a component interface for multimedia processing. A decoder, encoder or another processor presents ports, configuration, state and buffer-exchange behavior through that contract. Khronos now lists OpenMAX among its inactive standards. The published interface remains useful for interpreting existing implementations and older OMX-named media routes. Ports describe the component’s data relationship An input port accepts the media type configured for it; an output port supplies the component's resulting type. A decoder's compressed input and picture output have different configurations. The application or a suitable tunnel between components coordinates the buffers. Compatible ports and implementations determine whether those objects can be shared. An OMX component name identifies an implementation interface. It does not guarantee that all its operations use dedicated hardware or that it accepts every profile of a codec. The component state controls valid work Some central states in the specification are: State Role in the lifecycle Loaded Component exists with its configuration-stage context Idle Operational resources and enabled-port requirements are established Executing Component performs the supported processing Pause Processing is paused under the interface's state rules A requested transition has conditions. For example, the move to Idle can depend on the enabled ports' required buffers being supplied. Sending a state-change command is therefore different from receiving its completion event. The client must not treat a queued command as proof that the new state's operations are already permitted. Buffers return through defined callbacks EmptyThisBuffer submits an input buffer, while its corresponding EmptyBufferDone callback reports the return of that buffer under the contract. The output side similarly uses FillThisBuffer and FillBufferDone . Completing an input use does not universally mean that exactly one final output has already appeared: decoding, buffering and frame-order behavior can give a more complex relationship. The caller preserves the buffers and handles their lifecycle until the interface returns the relevant use. An exposed route is implementation-specific OpenMAX IL standardizes a contract, not a requirement that every current operating system or device must use it. Modern Android MediaCodec implementations can have other platform backends. Emby's documentation includes OpenMAX/OMX in its platform-route context. A particular version/build and initialized component establish whether a session actually exercises that interface. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Rockchip Media Process Platform (RKMPP) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Rockchip Media Process Platform (RKMPP) Rockchip MPP connects supported codec implementations, buffer management and hardware abstraction to a compatible Rockchip platform and kernel interface. Rockchip Media Process Platform , commonly called MPP or RKMPP , supplies media software, codec handling and hardware abstraction for supported Rockchip platforms. The public project connects its media interface and buffer management to codec/parser work, a hardware abstraction layer and the relevant kernel path. It is a distinct application integration from simply finding a V4L2 codec device. Packets, frames and buffers describe different objects Object Role MppPacket Encoded-stream input or output context MppFrame Picture properties and the associated frame result/input MppBuffer Backing memory/resource representation MppBufferGroup An arrangement for managing suitable buffers Those objects preserve the difference between compressed data and reconstructed pictures. The container's selected stream has to reach the codec with the appropriate packet and timing information. Hardware support depends on the actual SoC, codec configuration and software stack. A repository listing a SoC does not make every older and newer Rockchip product interchangeable. Visible dimensions do not define the allocation Use an original linear 8-bit 4:2:0 picture with visible dimensions 1920 × 1080, horizontal stride 2048 and padded vertical height 1088: Allocation model = 2048 × 1088 × 1.5 = 3,342,336 bytes Visible unpadded picture = 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes The first value describes this declared padded layout. It is not a universal MPP allocation formula for tiled, compressed or other pixel formats. The consumer uses the actual frame's layout and buffer size. Reading every row as 1920 contiguous bytes would ignore the declared padding and misplace later rows. Information changes require a prepared output context A decoder can discover or change picture information as it parses the stream. MPP reports the relevant information-change condition so the client can establish suitable output resources. Rockchip's guide describes allocation modes and, where applicable, an external buffer group. The MPP_DEC_SET_INFO_CHANGE_READY control tells the decoder that the required reset/resource preparation for that condition is ready. A deliberate wait at this boundary need not mean the hardware stopped understanding the codec. It can mean the client has not yet supplied the output-resource relationship needed to continue. Release the result after its consumers finish The client retains picture buffers for downstream display, filtering, reference or encoding use. When those uses end, it returns/releases resources under the configured allocation mode. A compatible exported/shared-resource route can avoid an application-level copy, while another consumer may require a different layout. DMA-BUF sharing explains the Linux resource boundary. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Metal for video processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Metal for video processing Metal exposes Apple GPU graphics and compute work used to process suitable picture textures, with CoreVideo interoperability, layout and synchronization connecting it to media sessions. Metal is Apple's graphics and compute interface. A media application can use it to process or render suitable picture data produced by its media path. Compressed-video reconstruction and compression belong to their selected media implementations. Metal adds programmable work around the prepared pictures. CoreVideo can supply picture storage VideoToolbox and related media paths use pixel-buffer representations. CoreVideo's Metal texture-cache interface can expose compatible pixel-buffer data as suitable Metal textures. A texture view describes access to particular picture storage. The actual compatibility depends on the pixel-buffer attributes, storage and requested texture format. This route can avoid an application manually copying every pixel into an unrelated allocation when suitable shared resources are available. One picture can have several planes Consider an original, unpadded 1920 × 1080 NV12 picture: Plane Dimensions Stored channels per element Payload Luma 1920 × 1080 1 byte 2,073,600 bytes Interleaved chroma 960 × 540 2 bytes 1,036,800 bytes Complete picture — — 3,110,400 bytes An appropriate texture representation can expose the luma through a single-channel eight-bit view and chroma through a two-channel eight-bit view. The half-sized chroma plane contains paired chroma values. It is not a second smaller full-colour picture. The layout example assumes compatible linear unpadded storage; real pixel buffers expose their actual row layout and supported resource arrangement. Texture format does not provide the whole colour description Sampling an eight-bit channel tells the shader how values are stored. Video range, matrix, primaries and transfer function determine how those values should be interpreted. A YUV-to-RGB operation needs that interpretation, and an HDR transformation needs the intended output relationship. Otherwise a fast GPU operation can faithfully compute the wrong picture transformation. The GPU-processing explanation develops operation and coordinate order independently of the execution API. Completion preserves picture ownership Metal command work can proceed asynchronously. The source pixel buffer and texture-related resources need suitable lifetimes through their consumers' use. A following encoder needs a completed, accepted picture representation. Releasing or rewriting storage while the GPU is still reading it violates the intended data relationship. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Apple silicon media engines | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Apple silicon media engines Apple silicon includes specialized media resources whose codec directions and software exposure are distinct from CPU, GPU and Neural Engine counts. Apple silicon includes specialized media resources alongside CPU, GPU and other processing blocks. The media-engine specification identifies different capabilities from the general core counts. Applications reach those capabilities through supported platform media interfaces such as VideoToolbox . Use the exact chip’s published roles Apple's Mac mini 2024 specification provides a concrete example for M4 and M4 Pro. It lists a video decode engine, video encode engine, ProRes encode/decode engine and AV1 decode, alongside hardware-accelerated H.264, HEVC and ProRes-family entries. Published field What it describes CPU cores General CPU execution resources GPU cores Graphics/compute resources Neural Engine Its separate acceleration role Media Engine entries Listed codec and specialized media roles Memory bandwidth The chip's stated shared memory-system capability The field names make the scope visible. A larger GPU-core number is not, by itself, a count of video encoders. Preserve the codec direction A specification's decode entry establishes a reconstruction capability in its stated scope. It should be read separately from its encoding entries. In the cited M4/M4 Pro example, AV1 is explicitly listed as decode. That entry supports the decoding question; it does not serve as evidence for an AV1 output encoder. An Emby source and target can use different formats. Each needs a suitable exposed implementation for its own operation, while scaling, tone mapping and other preparation have their own requirements. Unified memory still has data movement A shared memory architecture can avoid the separate host/device allocation and transfer arrangement found in some discrete-device routes. Processing still reads and writes picture data, and consumers still need compatible layouts and completion dependencies. Use an original ideal 1920 × 1080 8-bit 4:2:0 layout: it has 3,110,400 bytes per picture. At sixty pictures per second, one full read represents 186,624,000 bytes per second. A modeled full read and full write double that traffic. Those are unpadded layout calculations, not memory measurements on an Apple device. They explain why a shared addressable picture still has a bandwidth cost when processed. Platform interfaces determine the exercised path The operating-system media stack selects supported implementations for the actual configuration. Metal can process suitable decoded pictures while media-engine operations perform supported compression or reconstruction. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Apple VideoToolbox | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Apple VideoToolbox VideoToolbox provides Apple-platform compression and decompression sessions whose selected implementation, pixel buffers and completion behavior define the media-processing path. VideoToolbox supplies low-level video compression and decompression services on Apple platforms. Applications configure sessions, submit suitable media data and receive their outputs. The selected session implementation and media configuration determine the actual path. The framework name alone describes the interface being used. A session has defined media input and output A decompression session accepts suitably described compressed samples and produces decoded picture data. A compression session accepts suitable pictures and creates compressed output. Apple's media stack uses Core Media sample/format/timing objects and CoreVideo pixel buffers around those roles. Object or stage Meaning to retain Compressed sample Encoded data with its media description and timing Decompression session The selected reconstruction path CVPixelBuffer Picture storage, layout and relevant attachments Compression session The selected new-output encoding path Compressed output Data that still needs the intended packaging/delivery The objects keep the media operation and its surrounding timing/storage context together. Hardware preference and selected execution are different facts Apple provides controls for hardware selection and properties for observing the selected path. Its decoder documentation describes a “require hardware” specification that can make creation fail when a suitable hardware decoder cannot be provided. An encoder can be configured to enable hardware, then its actual selected hardware use can be queried through kVTCompressionPropertyKey_UsingHardwareAcceleratedVideoEncoder . An original interpretation table illustrates the distinction: Request/result context What has been established Hardware allowed or enabled A selection preference/permission Session successfully created An accepted session configuration Actual selected-use property reports hardware Hardware use for that queried session Required hardware cannot be supplied Creation fails under that requirement The table contains no measured session. It explains why a request and an observation should not be substituted for each other. Pixel layout and interpretation travel together A CVPixelBuffer describes picture storage, including dimensions, pixel format and row layout. Attachments can carry colour interpretation. A downstream processing stage needs the actual pixel layout and the meaning of its values. An encoder configured for another layout can require a supported conversion. For a native Emby playback or conversion comparison, preserve the input/output media configuration alongside the selected platform path. That identifies whether a visible change belongs to decoding, colour processing, scaling or output encoding. Completion governs reuse Compression and decompression can involve asynchronous work. Output callbacks and session operations have their own completion contracts; returning from submission does not grant unlimited permission to overwrite the input storage. A decoded pixel buffer used by another GPU operation must likewise remain valid until that operation is finished with it. Metal integration provides the picture-processing part of that route. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: How media APIs connect applications to hardware | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: How media APIs connect applications to hardware A media acceleration API connects an application’s requested video operation to a compatible runtime, driver and device configuration with defined buffers and completion behavior. An acceleration API turns an application's requested media operation into work on a supported device path. Between the call and the hardware are implementation and driver layers that define how configurations, buffers and completion are represented. This is why the API, runtime and media engine need to be identified separately. The call passes through an implementation The application calls an interface it was built to use. A library or dispatcher can select an implementation, which communicates through the relevant driver path to the device. A development SDK supplies interfaces and development material. The usable execution path also needs the runtime/driver and the exposed hardware operation. Installing development headers does not add a missing hardware decoder. Emby's platform documentation provides product context for supported routes. The device capabilities are then a separate configuration question. A query describes an operation and its conditions This original readable capability example is a teaching structure, not the wire format of a vendor API: { "device": "model-adapter-A", "operation": "decode", "codec": "hevc", "profile": "Main 10", "chroma": "4:2:0", "bitDepth": 10, "maximumWidth": 3840, "maximumHeight": 2160, "outputLayout": "P010" } It describes one decoded-video path. It does not describe encoding, every video filter or the availability of another adapter. An output encoder needs its own target query. A filter needs its accepted input/output relationship. A complete job combines those compatible operations rather than treating the first successful query as a device-wide “yes.” Buffers and completion are part of the interface The API exposes or accepts frame storage under a defined memory model. Some paths use system memory, others device surfaces, and others can import compatible shared resources. The consumer needs the correct device and frame context, layout and completion dependencies. A surface handle meaningful to one context is not automatically usable by an unrelated context. Asynchronous calls also need their specified completion behavior. An accepted operation can still be working after control returns to the CPU. Several names can describe one route Name category Example of the fact it conveys Codec The compressed format being processed API The interface used to request processing Runtime/backend The implementation of those calls Driver The device/operating-system execution path Media engine The hardware carrying out the specialized work Application wrapper The integration selected by the media program An Intel media operation can be exposed through Intel VPL or through a supported VA-API path. The interfaces differ while the underlying hardware can overlap. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Intel Media SDK (legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Intel Media SDK (legacy) Intel Media SDK is a discontinued media software interface whose names remain in older Intel acceleration stacks and logs, distinct from the hardware generations those stacks use. Intel Media SDK provided interfaces for accelerated video decode, encode and processing on supported Intel media hardware. Older applications, distribution packages and logs can still describe that software stack. Intel has discontinued the project and directs users toward its successor library, now called Intel VPL . “Legacy” here describes the software project, not the age of every device an application might use. API names preserve the operation roles The SDK uses MFX-prefixed interfaces. Names in an older source or trace can identify the intended stage: Legacy interface family Role MFXVideoDECODE Encoded input to decoded pictures MFXVideoVPP Picture processing MFXVideoENCODE Prepared pictures to encoded output MFXVideoCORE Shared session/core services Those roles explain why a log can name several Intel media operations in one conversion. Decode and encode remain different stages even when both are accessed through the same SDK family. The installed stack contains several parts An application built against a media interface needs a compatible implementation and driver path at execution time. Development headers and sample projects are another layer. An older package name can therefore describe the API dependency without identifying the exact active graphics driver or physical engine. Changing a library package alone does not add a codec feature to the device. Conversely, newer physical hardware can require a software stack different from the one assumed by an old application build. QSV wrapper names do not date the entire route Suppose an original log names an h264_qsv encoder and MFX-related initialization. That identifies an Intel-oriented H.264 encoding route at the shown stage. It does not report which decoding operation preceded it, the surface format supplied by its filters or the complete version of every runtime component. Those facts need their own log/configuration context. The qsv name remains meaningful in software that uses successor interfaces as well. A stable wrapper name is useful for recognizing the family of the operation while API/runtime versions identify the particular stack. The successor keeps the task categories Intel VPL continues the decode, encode and video-processing roles with its current API and implementation-selection model. The dispatcher discussion shows how matching implementations and sessions are selected. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Intel Quick Sync Video (QSV) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Intel Quick Sync Video (QSV) Intel Quick Sync Video is the name for Intel’s dedicated media-acceleration capabilities, reached through supported software and driver paths for decoding, processing and encoding. Intel Quick Sync Video , often shortened to QSV , names Intel's dedicated media-acceleration capabilities. Applications reach those capabilities through a supported media software and graphics-driver path. Quick Sync is not an encoded-video format. An H.264 stream remains H.264 when a QSV encoder creates it. Separate the hardware name from the software interface Intel's current Video Processing Library, formerly called oneVPL, is one software route to decode, encode and video processing. Older applications and logs can refer to Intel Media SDK. Linux's Intel Media Driver also exposes supported operations through VA-API. Those software names identify interfaces and implementations. They should not be read as separate brands of compressed media. For an Emby session, the selected platform route and runtime matter alongside the physical device. A QSV option does not identify every stage of the conversion by itself. Input and output use different capabilities Use an original selected-source example: Stage Requirement Decode Accept the selected HEVC Main 10 source Process Prepare the target picture size/colour/subtitle presentation Encode Create the selected H.264 output Package Put the encoded output on the intended delivery path The decoder and encoder need different supported configurations. Hardware HEVC decoding does not establish hardware HEVC encoding, and an H.264 encoder does not decode the source on its own. The example is a route to reason about, not a statement that every Quick Sync device supports those source and processing choices. Device generations and exact products expose different media capabilities. Dedicated media and general CPU resources are different On an integrated Intel graphics device, the media engine is part of the processor's graphics/media system. CPU cores still run application, operating-system and other media work. A software-only encoder can make CPU-core resources prominent. A Quick Sync encode instead relies on its suitable media path, with driver, memory and supporting-work requirements of its own. Adding CPU cores does not proportionally duplicate a particular dedicated media engine. Likewise, general graphics capability is a different resource from its codec engine. Integrated memory can reduce the need for a discrete-device transfer arrangement, but the application still has surface layout, access and completion responsibilities. A mixed route is a defined combination A session can use QSV decoding, a CPU-only filter and QSV encoding. Another can keep its supported picture processing within a compatible device path. The relevant question is which operation received which frame representation. Intel video processing develops the processor role; the hardware pipeline explains the frame handoffs. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Intel VPL and the oneVPL name | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Intel VPL and the oneVPL name Intel VPL is the media library interface and dispatcher used to select supported Intel video implementations and coordinate decode, encode and processing sessions. Intel's Video Processing Library , now called Intel VPL , provides interfaces for media decoding, encoding and processing. oneVPL is the earlier name still found in repositories, packages and application build descriptions. Intel's current overview explicitly describes that naming change and identifies VPL version 2.x as the successor API to the discontinued Media SDK project. The dispatcher finds a usable implementation The dispatcher lets an application enumerate and filter available implementations before creating a session with a selected implementation. Some central names in the public API are: API operation Role MFXLoad Create the loader MFXCreateConfig Create a filter configuration MFXSetConfigFilterProperty Apply an implementation-selection property MFXEnumImplementations Inspect matching implementations MFXCreateSession Load and initialize a selected implementation MFXUnload End the loader's lifecycle These are roles, not a complete sequence that can ignore error results or object ownership. Enumerated descriptions have a specified release function, and session/loader lifetimes must follow the API contract. A matching implementation answers the stated selection Consider an original candidate-selection exercise: Candidate Hardware implementation Decoder Encoder A Yes Declared HEVC Main 10 Declared H.264 B Yes Declared H.264 Declared H.264 C Hypothetical unmatched implementation Other configuration Other configuration If the application needs the declared HEVC input and H.264 output, A fits these stated codec requirements. B's hardware label does not add the missing HEVC declaration. The table is invented selection data. It is not a VPL capability dump, product list or promise that a particular implementation is installed. Additional conditions can include adapter, dimensions, surface formats and video-processing support. A filtered result becomes useful only when the requested operation can be initialized with its actual configuration. A session coordinates media work and resources A created session supplies a media implementation context. Decode, encode and VPP use their own configuration and data-flow contracts inside the supported interface. Video work can be asynchronous. The application must arrange usable surfaces, retrieve outputs and use completion/synchronization appropriately. Loading the dispatcher library establishes an earlier software stage than completing a media operation. This distinction matters in an Emby-related log or build description. A reference to libvpl or oneVPL explains a software dependency; the selected decoder, encoder and actual media properties identify the executing job. Legacy compatibility is a software-stack question Older Media SDK interfaces, runtimes and applications are not made identical to a VPL version-two application by changing a filename. The transition involves the application's interface use and the installed implementation/driver path. Intel's legacy project is no longer maintained. The Media SDK article explains why its names remain useful for interpreting older stacks without treating them as another media-engine generation. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Intel video processing (VPP) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Intel video processing (VPP) Intel VPP processes decoded pictures into a requested output picture configuration, coordinating supported transformations, output cadence and surface completion. VPP is Intel's video-processing stage: it accepts pictures and produces pictures with a requested configuration. It sits between reconstruction and compression in a typical decode-process-encode route. Scaling, format conversion and other supported transformations belong here. The following encoder creates the compressed output. Query an input/output relationship A processor needs more than a list of filter names. Its configuration describes input and output picture size, storage format, cadence and the selected processing operations. For an original scaling exercise, a 1920 × 1080 input becomes 1280 × 720. The width and height ratios are both two-thirds, while picture area becomes four-ninths: 1280 / 1920 = 720 / 1080 = 2/3 (1280 × 720) / (1920 × 1080) = 4/9 A compatible input surface must also be available in the accepted memory/context arrangement. Whether a particular combined operation is exposed is a runtime/device query. In an Emby route, a QSV decoder, VPP stage and QSV encoder can describe three cooperating operations. A CPU filter inserted between them changes their picture handoffs. Output cadence can change the number of pictures Use an original duplicate-cadence model that turns three progressive input pictures at 30 fps into six output pictures at 60 fps over the same 0.1-second interval. Input picture Input presentation time Two output presentation times A 0 0 and 1/60 s B 1/30 s 2/60 and 3/60 s C 2/30 s 4/60 and 5/60 s The pictures are duplicated in this model. It does not claim interpolation or an Intel default. The output encoder receives six picture occurrences and their sixty-fps timeline, while the represented interval remains 0.1 seconds. Other operations, including deinterlacing, can have different input/output relationships. Frame-rate conversion describes the presentation consequences separately. The output loop must honor the result Intel's public VPP procedure describes asynchronous processing and return values that inform the next operation: Result Relevant meaning in the documented processing loop MFX_ERR_NONE Successful step; follow its output and completion contract MFX_ERR_MORE_SURFACE Additional output-surface handling is needed for the current input relationship MFX_ERR_MORE_DATA The operation needs further input, or draining has reached its specified end condition In the documented asynchronous loop, usable output is synchronized before it is consumed. A successful submission and a completed output surface are separate stages. A multiple-output transformation can therefore require another output surface while retaining the current input. Advancing the input unconditionally after every call can lose an intended output occurrence. These status names are API results, not picture-quality categories. Processing order defines the intended picture A selected overlay painted before scaling changes size with the picture. An overlay applied after scaling uses the output coordinate system. A colour conversion likewise needs the input's actual range, matrix and transfer interpretation. Picture storage and colour/timing metadata must stay coherent across the stage. A format conversion changes the representation it was configured to change; it does not infer every desired HDR presentation policy from the VPP name. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: DRM PRIME and DMA-BUF frame sharing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: DRM PRIME and DMA-BUF frame sharing DRM PRIME and DMA-BUF let compatible Linux subsystems exchange references to frame storage while layout, synchronization and ownership determine how the shared picture may be used. DMA-BUF lets compatible Linux subsystems exchange references to allocated buffer storage. DRM PRIME provides related sharing interfaces in the Direct Rendering Manager. Here DRM means the graphics subsystem, not digital-rights-managed media. The sharing mechanism concerns memory resources, while protected-playback licensing is another subject. Share a resource reference with a compatible consumer A producer can export a buffer through the supported mechanism. A consumer can import a reference to that storage through its compatible interface. The process exchanges a resource handle, not a complete self-describing movie. The consumer still needs the picture's layout and the context in which those bytes should be interpreted. For example, a decoder can produce suitable storage that another processor or encoder imports. Their accepted formats, layout modifiers and device relationships determine whether this handoff is usable. Plane geometry is part of the picture Consider an original 1920 × 1080, 8-bit NV12 layout. Its luma and interleaved chroma rows each have a declared 2048-byte pitch: { "format": "NV12", "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "layout": "LINEAR", "bufferLabel": "model-buffer-A", "allocationBytes": 3317760, "planes": [ { "objectIndex": 0, "offset": 0, "pitch": 2048 }, { "objectIndex": 0, "offset": 2211840, "pitch": 2048 } ] } This is a teaching descriptor, not a native DRM struct or valid exported file descriptor. The luma occupies 1080 rows and the chroma occupies 540: Luma bytes = 2048 × 1080 = 2,211,840 Chroma bytes = 2048 × 540 = 1,105,920 Total = 3,317,760 The chroma plane begins after the declared luma storage. Its paired chroma values cover the half-resolution chroma geometry while its row pitch remains the declared byte stride. An unpadded layout would have 3,110,400 bytes. The modeled padding adds 207,360 bytes, about 6.667%. Assuming width equals pitch would give the wrong row addressing and chroma offset. A real import also needs the actual supported format/modifier relationship. A tiled or compressed layout cannot be interpreted as this linear example just because its visible dimensions match. Handles have a process context A file descriptor is a handle in the process that owns it. Sending its printed integer as ordinary metadata does not transfer another process's usable reference. Through an appropriate supported handle-transfer path, another process can receive its own descriptor referring to the same underlying resource. The two integer values can differ while the backing storage relationship is shared. Likewise, a DRM-local handle and an exported DMA-BUF descriptor have different scopes. The relevant export/import operation establishes the relationship. The illustrative buffer label above avoids pretending that a particular integer descriptor is live on the reader's machine. Sharing needs completion and ownership A consumer cannot read a picture while its producer is still writing the data it needs. An earlier producer completion also does not prove a later consumer has finished. Use an original timeline: Model interval Operation Storage relationship 0–4 ms Producer writes picture A Consumer waits for the relevant completion 4–7 ms Consumer reads A Producer preserves A's storage After 7 ms Consumer use ends Reuse additionally requires no other outstanding owner/reference The kernel describes implicit and explicit synchronization arrangements. Fences communicate completion in their stated scope; the participating interfaces need a coherent way to honor those dependencies. A resource remaining allocated is not the same fact as its last write being complete or all readers being finished. CPU coherence is another preparation CPU mapping of a DMA buffer can require cache-coherency handling. The kernel's userspace documentation brackets CPU access with the appropriate DMA_BUF_IOCTL_SYNC start/end operations. Waiting for a transfer or fence does not universally perform every needed CPU-cache preparation. Conversely, cache preparation is not a substitute for coordinating an outstanding producer or consumer under an explicit synchronization arrangement. A GPU-to-GPU route that does not need CPU sample access can have a different set of requirements from a CPU filter reading the same picture. Import/export is evidence of a handoff A shared-resource path can avoid an application's explicit full-picture copy when the resources and consumers are compatible. The use of DMA-BUF or PRIME alone does not prove that the entire job avoided layout conversions, staging or other memory traffic. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: V4L2 memory-to-memory codecs | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: V4L2 memory-to-memory codecs A V4L2 memory-to-memory codec transforms application-supplied buffers through paired source and destination queues whose formats, ownership and state define the media operation. A V4L2 memory-to-memory codec receives application-supplied buffers, transforms their media and returns destination buffers. The device interface pairs source and destination queues, with negotiated formats describing the operation. “Memory-to-memory” describes the data route. The device can use specialized hardware to perform its supported transformation. OUTPUT is the device’s source queue V4L2 names these queues from the device interface's perspective: Operation OUTPUT queue CAPTURE queue Decode Encoded stream data supplied to the device Decoded pictures returned from it Encode Raw pictures supplied to the device Encoded stream data returned from it For decoding, therefore, the movie's compressed input enters OUTPUT. CAPTURE is not necessarily a camera: it is where the application receives the result of this memory-to-memory operation. The multi-planar variants use the same source/destination distinction with their applicable buffer structures. Negotiate each queue’s format A stateful decoder accepts supported encoded stream data and manages its decoding state through the driver/device path. The application negotiates encoded OUTPUT and suitable decoded CAPTURE formats. The selected encoded configuration can constrain the possible decoded layouts and dimensions. A capability result for one coded format should not be transferred to every other format on the device. The driver can learn actual picture information from the bitstream and report a source-change event. The application then establishes the appropriate CAPTURE layout and buffers for the changed picture configuration. This is why a placeholder size set before the stream's headers arrive is not always the final output-surface requirement. Queueing transfers ownership The application prepares a buffer and queues it. It then follows the interface's completion/dequeue relationship before treating that buffer as available again. An original decoder trace distinguishes source and destination: Queue encoded buffer E0 on OUTPUT Device consumes E0 under its stream/decoding state Return E0 to the application Decoded picture P0 becomes available on CAPTURE Application passes P0 to its next consumer Return P0 for reuse after the required consumer/reference use The trace is conceptual, not a required one-input/one-output ordering. A decoder can retain picture dependencies, buffer several inputs and reorder output for presentation under its documented stateful contract. Returning an encoded source buffer proves that buffer's relevant use can end. It does not universally prove every resulting decoded picture has already been consumed downstream. Changes and end-of-stream have their own state A new picture configuration can require CAPTURE queue/resource changes while the encoded-stream side has its own continuing state. Drain handling likewise obtains delayed output under the device's specified end behavior. Closing input immediately after the last bytes can lose the distinction between input completion and final decoded output. The application follows the driver's supported state machine. For an Emby deployment on embedded Linux, the usable route needs an application integration for the exposed interface, formats and device. A kernel codec device existing does not identify which interface a particular server build actually uses. Stateless decoding describes another V4L2 contract with explicit application-maintained picture state. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: V4L2 stateless decoding and the Request API | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: V4L2 stateless decoding and the Request API V4L2 stateless decoding makes the application supply per-picture decoding state, references and encoded data through requests that bind the operation’s controls and buffers. A stateless decoder interface makes the application supply the decoding state needed for each picture. The application parses the encoded stream, tracks relevant references and submits the required controls and buffers with the decoding request. The hardware still reconstructs pictures. The interface moves responsibility for supplying consistent codec state to the client. Stateless does not remove picture dependencies Inter-predicted pictures can still need earlier reconstructed pictures. A stateless interface makes those relationships explicit inputs rather than assuming the device maintains the entire coded stream's state on the application's behalf. The Linux kernel contrasts this with the stateful decoder contract, where the application provides encoded stream data and obtains pictures under the driver/device's stateful behavior. Responsibility Stateless-interface role Container and bitstream parsing Client supplies the selected encoded picture and codec parameters Reference-picture bookkeeping Client supplies the relevant reference state Request binding Controls and encoded input belong to the intended operation Reconstruction Device performs the supported requested decoding Output ordering and lifetime Client follows the interface's completion/reference rules This is an application/device contract. It does not describe whether a particular embedded processor exposes a compatible decoder. References identify usable reconstructed storage Use an original four-picture model: Picture Target surface References in this model I0 A None P3 B A B1 C A and B B2 D A and B The reconstruction order is I0, P3, B1, B2. Their intended presentation order is I0, B1, B2, P3. A and B are decoded pictures used to reconstruct later pictures. The model keeps those references in storage while B1 and B2 need them. This readable request fixture illustrates one relationship: { "request": "model-R-B1", "codedPicture": "B1", "targetSurface": "C", "referenceSurfaces": ["A", "B"], "parameters": { "bitDepth": 8, "chroma": "4:2:0" } } It is not a V4L2 ABI structure or captured request. Real codec controls supply substantially more specific data. The fixture makes the target, references and picture parameters belong to the same declared operation. The Request API binds controls and buffers A media request groups the relevant work so controls do not accidentally describe another queued picture. If the encoded data for B1 were paired with parameters or references for a different picture, completing the request would not make that mismatch meaningful. The application must construct a consistent operation before queueing it. The request lifecycle includes preparing its data, queueing the request and waiting for its defined completion. Modifying an already queued operation is a different state from building the next request. For an original conceptual state model: Build request -> bind controls and encoded input -> queue Queued operation -> completion observed -> suitable reuse/reinitialization The model deliberately avoids a native ioctl recipe. The kernel Request API specifies allocation, control association, queueing and reinitialization behavior for actual clients. Completion does not free every reference A reconstruction operation finishing establishes progress for that operation. A decoded picture can remain a reference for another outstanding picture and can also be in use by a display or filter consumer. In the four-picture model, A cannot be overwritten as a new target while B1 or B2 still needs it. Finishing presentation of I0 is insufficient evidence that A has no remaining decoding use. The kernel's stateless-interface guidance explicitly requires preserving reference resources while relevant decoding still needs them. The client also follows its consumers' ownership contracts. This is why the number of buffers required can exceed the number of pictures immediately waiting for display. Output must be related to the programme timeline The client combines decoded results with the intended presentation timing and ordering. Completion order, decode order and display order have different meanings. A pending P3 result can be needed as a reference before B1 is reconstructed, while P3 is presented after B2. Choosing the next displayed picture solely by the order in which the reconstruction calls were made would mishandle that model. Packet timestamps provide the broader timing context. The Request API coordinates an operation; the application's media state places its result in the programme. A seek establishes a new reference context A jump to another programme position can require new parser and decoded-reference state. The client resolves a suitable access point and reconstructs the pictures needed for the requested destination. In the declared four-picture model, submitting B2 alone cannot provide the A and B references it names. A reference label retained from another source or a replaced decoder context is not proof that suitable reconstructed storage exists for this new request. The client therefore has to relate each reference to the active stream and decoded-picture context. A source change can also alter dimensions or codec parameters, requiring its new output/configuration relationship. This explains a specific kind of restart cost: a hardware block can reconstruct the new pictures quickly once given a consistent request, while the application still needs to establish the correct encoded access and reference sequence. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Video Acceleration API (VA-API) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Video Acceleration API (VA-API) VA-API exposes video decode, encode and processing operations through profile/entrypoint configurations implemented by a selected device driver backend. VA-API , the Video Acceleration API, exposes supported video operations through a selected implementation and device. Its configuration combines a codec/profile, an operation entrypoint and other attributes. The interface covers decoding, encoding and video processing. A particular backend supplies the operations available for its supported hardware and software configuration. A profile and an entrypoint form a useful query A profile identifies a coded configuration. An entrypoint identifies the requested operation within the API. This original readable capability fixture illustrates the distinction: { "device": "model-render-node", "profiles": [ { "profile": "VAProfileHEVCMain10", "entrypoints": ["VAEntrypointVLD"] }, { "profile": "VAProfileH264High", "entrypoints": ["VAEntrypointVLD", "VAEntrypointEncSlice"] } ] } Under this invented declaration, the HEVC entry supplies a decoding operation; the H.264 entry supplies separate decode and encode operations. It does not declare HEVC encoding or any processing filter. The fixture is not actual vainfo output or an Emby device response. The published API identifiers show why one profile name should not be interpreted as every possible operation. The backend implements the operation Libva supplies the interface layer and backend arrangement. Driver backends connect it to the appropriate hardware/driver stack. The loaded backend and selected device therefore matter to the query. Two configurations using the VA-API interface can expose different results. In Emby's Linux documentation , VA-API identifies an available family of acceleration routes. The actual initialized profile/entrypoint and source/target properties identify a session's operations. Surfaces provide the picture relationship A context uses appropriate picture surfaces and parameter buffers for the selected operation. A decoder's usable output must fit a later processor or encoder. The API exposes configuration and surface attributes as well as profile lists. Bit depth, dimensions and accepted surface layout are additional facts a pipeline needs. Video processing has its own capabilities and input/output relationships. Decode support does not, by itself, supply HDR conversion or every overlay operation. Submission and completion have different stages The application supplies the necessary picture parameters and codec data using the configured context. The driver-backed operation can still be executing after its submission is accepted. A consumer needs suitable synchronization before it reads the result. Surface ownership also continues while later stages or decoding references still use that storage. Libva's thread-safety documentation separates safe API implementation from the application's responsibility to synchronize operations on shared objects. A thread-safe library does not arrange every application-level media dependency automatically. Frame sharing adds the resource-transfer boundary when another compatible interface consumes the pictures. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: VA-API driver backends | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: VA-API driver backends A VA-API backend implements the interface for a supported device and driver stack, so loader selection, hardware identity and backend capabilities determine the usable media path. A VA-API driver backend implements VA-API calls for a supported device and software stack. Libva provides the interface/loader layer; the selected backend provides device-specific acceleration behavior. This separation explains why having libva installed is an earlier condition than successfully decoding a chosen video. Identify each layer Layer Fact to preserve Application Interface/build and operation it requests Libva API and backend-loading layer Backend Selected implementation and version Device/driver stack Actual adapter and exposed kernel/device context Media operation Profile, entrypoint, format and dimensions A capability report belongs to that combined context. A profile list copied from another machine is not a query of this backend/device pair. Intel backend names are implementation names Intel's current Media Driver repository uses the iHD backend name. Its earlier Intel VA-API driver uses i965 and is now archived. Name Relevant role iHD Intel Media Driver backend i965 Earlier Intel VA-API backend project HEVC Main 10 A codec/profile configuration VAEntrypointVLD A selected decode entrypoint The backend names are not codec formats or universal generation labels. Their supported products and operations belong to their documented implementations. Intel's current repository describes LIBVA_DRIVER_NAME and driver-search-path configuration for its stack. Those settings influence selection; they do not manufacture support for hardware outside that implementation. Device paths identify access points A Linux render-node path such as /dev/dri/renderD128 identifies a device access node in that environment. The numeric suffix is not an Intel, AMD or NVIDIA model specification. The process must open the intended node and use its compatible backend. Which adapter it denotes should be established from the system's device information rather than inferred from “128.” No device node was opened for this article. Process context is part of a comparison An interactive diagnostic and Emby Server's process can have different environment, library search, device access or selected adapter context. A successful report from one context establishes its result. Comparing it with another process requires retaining those selection and access facts. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Video Decode and Presentation API for Unix (VDPAU) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Video Decode and Presentation API for Unix (VDPAU) VDPAU provides Unix video decoding, mixing and presentation interfaces with defined surface types and driver-backed capability relationships. VDPAU stands for Video Decode and Presentation API for Unix. It gives media applications interfaces for supported decoding, picture mixing and presentation through an appropriate implementation. The API name describes an application/driver contract rather than an encoded-video format. The interface separates surface roles API role Relationship Decoder Selected compressed configuration to video surfaces Video mixer Process/combine supported picture information Output surface A representation suitable for the relevant output operations Presentation queue/target Arrange supported output presentation The decoder needs actual profile support. The mixer and surface configuration have their own supported properties. The driver implementation connects these objects to the device. A documented function name does not imply that every implementation supplies every feature. Mixing is another picture-processing stage A video mixer can perform supported processing and composition on suitable surfaces. Deinterlacing and other operations require their own capability and configuration. The output picture is therefore the result of both reconstruction and the selected later operations. A visible difference should not automatically be attributed to the decoder if mixer configuration changed too. This is the same stage separation developed in the hardware pipeline , applied to VDPAU's object model. Decode support answers a different question from encoding VDPAU's decode/mixing/presentation interfaces are not a generic output-encoding API. A conversion job needs a separately available encoder and a compatible way to supply it with prepared pictures. A supported VDPAU decoder can consequently participate in a larger route without identifying the entire conversion stack. Device and display integration define the environment An application establishes the relevant VDPAU device and presentation arrangement through its supported platform integration. The resources and capabilities belong to that context. For an Emby-related Unix discussion, identify whether the actual app/route uses VDPAU, VA-API, NVDECODE or another interface. Similar underlying hardware can be exposed through different software contracts. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Overview: Linux | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Overview: Linux Linux media interfaces connect codec operations, driver backends and picture-sharing mechanisms. A VA-API path depends on its backend, and V4L2 codec arrangements have their own stateful or stateless relationships. VDPAU supplies another video interface; DRM PRIME and DMA-BUF concern picture sharing across components. This group keeps those layers visible when diagnosing a working decoder with a difficult downstream handoff. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Video Acceleration API (VA-API) VA-API exposes video decode, encode and processing operations through profile/entrypoint configurations implemented by a selected device driver backend. VA-API driver backends A VA-API backend implements the interface for a supported device and driver stack, so loader selection, hardware identity and backend capabilities determine the usable media path. Video Decode and Presentation API for Unix (VDPAU) VDPAU provides Unix video decoding, mixing and presentation interfaces with defined surface types and driver-backed capability relationships. V4L2 memory-to-memory codecs A V4L2 memory-to-memory codec transforms application-supplied buffers through paired source and destination queues whose formats, ownership and state define the media operation. V4L2 stateless decoding and the Request API V4L2 stateless decoding makes the application supply per-picture decoding state, references and encoded data through requests that bind the operation’s controls and buffers. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: NVIDIA CUDA in media processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: NVIDIA CUDA in media processing CUDA provides NVIDIA GPU compute and device-memory interfaces used for programmable picture processing and interoperability around dedicated video engines. CUDA supplies programming and device-memory facilities for NVIDIA GPU compute. Media applications can use it to transform decoded pictures and connect suitable device resources to dedicated video engines. NVDEC and NVENC are separate specialized engines. A CUDA context or frame label can participate in their route without meaning that general compute cores perform the entire compressed-video operation. A media route contains several kinds of work Role Media task NVDEC Supported source reconstruction CUDA processing Programmable picture operations and associated memory work NVENC Supported target compression Host application Resource parsing, submission, timing and output coordination The combination depends on the implemented pipeline. A hardware decoder can also have post-processing and output-layout preparation defined by its API. A device frame changes the filter input A CUDA hardware frame describes picture data through the applicable device/frame context. A CUDA-capable filter needs a compatible layout and device relationship. This original FFmpeg command illustrates a selected route for an SDR, 16:9 source with MP4-compatible AAC audio: ffmpeg -hwaccel cuda -hwaccel_output_format cuda -i input-sdr.mp4 -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -vf scale_cuda=1280:720 -c:v h264_nvenc -c:a copy output.mp4 The command was not run. It assumes the device and FFmpeg build expose the required paths. The requested hardware-frame output supplies the filter path with device-associated pictures. scale_cuda produces the selected size, and h264_nvenc encodes the prepared output. Audio copying is another selected operation. This example does not implement HDR-to-SDR colour processing. Its declared SDR input makes the demonstrated scaling route a defined subject. A CPU-only filter requires a compatible CPU-accessible frame. Adding that operation can introduce a transfer or mapping and a subsequent preparation for hardware encoding. Asynchronous submission needs dependencies CUDA work can be queued into streams. Returning control to the CPU is different from completing all queued work. Use an original three-operation model for one picture: Operation Model interval Produce the input picture 0–4 ms Read input and write processed result 4–7 ms Consume the result 7–12 ms The intervals illustrate required dependencies, not actual GPU timings. Starting the second operation at two milliseconds would violate this model's input-readiness condition. Work in a stream has its documented ordering relationship. Dependencies across streams need suitable synchronization rather than a guess based on how quickly the host calls returned. Those relationships also govern when picture storage can be reused. Layout and meaning remain application inputs Device memory can contain planar, semiplanar or other layouts. Pitch, plane offsets and sample format determine how data is addressed. Colour and media-time information determine how it should be interpreted. A CUDA kernel needs the intended operation on those values. Its execution facility does not infer a tone-mapping policy or decide which subtitle should be painted. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: NVDEC and CUVID API names | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: NVDEC and CUVID API names NVDEC names NVIDIA’s decoding engine while CUVID and NVDECODE names persist in software interfaces, library symbols and media-program wrappers that reach its supported decode paths. NVIDIA video decoding appears under several related names. NVDEC names the dedicated engine. NVDECODE API names its software interface, while CUVID remains visible in function, header and library names. Reading those names at their own levels avoids inventing separate codec formats or hardware blocks. Current interfaces retain CUVID symbols The SDK 13.1 guide still documents these names: Name Role cuviddec.h and nvcuvid.h Decoder-interface headers cuvidCreateDecoder Create the selected decoder cuvidDecodePicture Submit picture reconstruction cuvidMapVideoFrame Obtain the traditional mapped/post-processed output cuvidUnmapVideoFrame Release that mapped output nvcuvid.dll or libnvcuvid.so Platform library naming in the documented stack The names are part of the software contract. Seeing cuvid in a trace does not establish that the application is using a separate ancient decoder engine. The NVDEC article develops the surface and ownership behavior behind those calls. A media program can expose different wrappers An application can integrate dedicated codec wrappers with cuvid-related names, or use a hardware-acceleration path that describes its device frames as CUDA. For example, h264_cuvid names a H.264 decoding wrapper in builds that provide it. A -hwaccel cuda option requests a supported hardware-acceleration arrangement under the media program's own configuration. These names do not replace the actual source codec. H.264 remains H.264, and HEVC needs its own suitable decode configuration. They also do not identify the encoder. A later h264_nvenc name concerns the H.264 output encoding stage. Device context and engine execution are different facts A decoder API can use a CUDA context and expose CUDA-addressable output. That makes the picture useful to GPU processing or a compatible encoder. The compressed reconstruction can still be carried out by NVDEC's specialized hardware. A CUDA memory/interface label and a compute-engine activity counter have different scopes. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: NVIDIA NVDEC | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: NVIDIA NVDEC NVDEC is NVIDIA’s dedicated video-decoding engine, exposed through a decoder API that reconstructs supported encoded streams and makes decoded surfaces available to later processing. NVDEC is NVIDIA's dedicated video-decoding engine. Its supported path reconstructs compressed video and supplies decoded picture data for processing, presentation or encoding. The NVDECODE API is the software interface to that role. Its surrounding parser, memory and device work explains what happens before and after the hardware decode. Demuxing, parsing and decoding are separate responsibilities A container reader finds the selected encoded stream. A bitstream parser identifies the picture information and sequence configuration needed by decoding. The decoder reconstructs pictures from those inputs. NVIDIA's supplied parser is a software component; an application can use an appropriate other parser. A supported NVDEC operation does not parse every media container automatically. An Emby conversion can therefore perform CPU-side container and stream work while NVDEC carries out the selected picture reconstruction. Query the selected encoded configuration The decoder API exposes hardware capability queries. Relevant conditions include codec, bit depth, chroma format and dimensions, along with the requirements documented for the selected path. A positive query for one format does not answer the target encoder query. Decoded HEVC pictures can later be encoded as H.264, but those are different device operations. The hardware generation and exact device matter to supported configurations. This article describes the engine/interface relationship rather than assigning one codec matrix to all NVIDIA products. Decoded and mapped output surfaces have different roles NVDEC maintains decoded-picture storage used for reconstruction and references. The application obtains a usable output representation through the relevant API path. In the documented traditional path, cuvidMapVideoFrame() waits for the relevant decoding, prepares the configured output format and returns an output device pointer and pitch. The documentation describes processing and a copy to an output surface in that mapping path. Thus “map” should not automatically be read as “nothing moved or changed.” It is an API operation with specified output semantics. SDK 13.1 also documents other input/output interoperability paths with their own constraints. Consumers keep storage in use After mapping, a consumer can process the output picture or pass a suitable representation to another stage. cuvidUnmapVideoFrame() releases the mapped output for reuse under the API's lifecycle. An original four-surface model illustrates the resource effect: Event Mapped outputs still in use Four outputs mapped and retained 4 Next output requested without release No unused slot under this model Consumer completes two and releases them 2 Two available slots can be reused 2 slots available The pool size is an invented model, not an NVDEC default. Its lesson is ownership: finishing reconstruction does not mean every consumer has finished with the storage. Decode-reference storage has an additional lifetime. An earlier picture can still be needed to reconstruct later pictures even after presentation has moved on. Queue placement affects host-side progress Mapping in the traditional path can block while the relevant decode completes. Calling it on the same host thread that submits further decoding can prevent that thread from supplying more work during the wait. NVIDIA documents producer/consumer coordination as one way to separate those responsibilities. The design must still preserve the picture's reference and output lifetimes. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: NVIDIA NVENC | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: NVIDIA NVENC NVENC is NVIDIA’s dedicated video-encoding engine, creating a supported compressed representation from prepared input pictures through its encoder API. NVENC is NVIDIA's dedicated video-encoding engine. It takes suitable prepared pictures and creates the selected compressed video representation. Source reconstruction belongs to NVDEC or another decoder. Scaling, tone mapping and subtitle preparation belong to the selected processing route. Configure the representation being created The encoder needs a supported target codec configuration, picture dimensions, input surface representation and encoding choices. Capability queries identify the features available through the selected hardware/API path. Preset, tuning, rate control and picture-order choices then describe how the implementation should create that output. A setting name belongs to this encoder's contract; it is not a universal quality unit shared by every encoder. An Emby log naming h264_nvenc identifies a NVIDIA-oriented H.264 encoder wrapper. The preceding decoder and filters still need their own evidence. Prepared input can require adjacent work NVENC is distinct from CUDA compute cores, while its input and optional processing can involve other GPU work. SDK 13.1, for example, describes preparation of traditional pitch-linear input and an alternative compatible block-linear CUDA-array path. The documented layouts have different preparation requirements. This provides a concrete reason to keep the engine and its surrounding route separate. A compute activity counter can describe input preparation or another filter while the dedicated encoder performs compression. The input lifetime extends through consumption The application supplies or registers suitable input storage and retrieves the encoder's generated output through the chosen API mode. Consider an original selected timeline: Picture Input accepted at wall time Output ready at wall time Programme presentation time A 0 ms 8 ms 0 s B 1 ms 11 ms 1/30 s C 2 ms 14 ms 2/30 s The times are invented. They show input acceptance, output readiness and media timestamps as three different coordinates. An input picture cannot be overwritten merely because submission returned. Its storage remains subject to the encoder's ownership/completion contract. Generated output also needs to be obtained and passed to the output packaging stage. Analysis or frame reordering can add other relationships between inputs and bitstream availability. The application follows the mode supported on its platform rather than assuming one notification mechanism everywhere. Output still needs media packaging NVENC creates encoded video, not the entire server session. The application combines encoded output with selected audio, timing and the intended container or streaming delivery. A session using NVENC can consequently wait for an upstream filter or for output coordination. The pipeline explanation connects that encoder work to the pictures and delivery deadlines around it. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Overview: NVIDIA | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Overview: NVIDIA NVIDIA media technologies distinguish video decoding, video encoding and general GPU computation. NVDEC and NVENC name different media-engine roles. CUDA supplies a programmable compute route, while CUVID appears in related decoding API terminology. The pages here connect those names to the operation being performed and the picture data exchanged with the rest of the pipeline. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> NVIDIA NVDEC NVDEC is NVIDIA’s dedicated video-decoding engine, exposed through a decoder API that reconstructs supported encoded streams and makes decoded surfaces available to later processing. NVIDIA NVENC NVENC is NVIDIA’s dedicated video-encoding engine, creating a supported compressed representation from prepared input pictures through its encoder API. NVIDIA CUDA CUDA provides NVIDIA GPU compute and device-memory interfaces used for programmable picture processing and interoperability around dedicated video engines. NVDEC and CUVID API names NVDEC names NVIDIA’s decoding engine while CUVID and NVDECODE names persist in software interfaces, library symbols and media-program wrappers that reach its supported decode paths. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References NVIDIA SDK 13.1: NVDEC programming guide NVIDIA SDK 13.1: NVENC programming guide NVIDIA CUDA: Asynchronous execution and streams

articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Overview: Platform media APIs | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Overview: Platform media APIs Platform media APIs provide operating-system or device-family routes to supported video operations. A Windows, Linux or embedded media path has its own interface, memory and driver relationships. Those contracts determine how an application submits work and receives pictures. The platform branches describe the available routes before a codec-support or data-transfer result is interpreted. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Windows Windows video interfaces connect applications to supported decoding, processing or transform operations. Linux Linux media interfaces connect codec operations, driver backends and picture-sharing mechanisms. Android and embedded systems Android and embedded media interfaces expose platform-specific codec and processing relationships. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: OpenCL for media processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: OpenCL for media processing OpenCL runs programmable work on supported compute devices through contexts, memory objects and command queues, with explicit capability and completion relationships for picture processing. OpenCL is a programmable compute interface. A media application can use it to transform suitable picture data, with operations such as scaling, composition or colour processing expressed as kernels. A dedicated video decoder or encoder is another operation. An OpenCL filter can sit between those stages without making OpenCL itself a compressed-video codec API. Select a device and usable resources The application selects a platform/device and creates the relevant context. Its kernels and memory objects need the capabilities exposed by that implementation. Image support, accepted image formats, memory limits and interoperability extensions are specific queries. The common API does not mean every supported device exposes every optional feature. The current unified specification covers current and earlier versions. A version string should be interpreted together with the feature queries required by the application's particular processing route. Command dependencies make the picture ready Commands can be queued without the host waiting for all device work to finish. Events let the application express the dependencies needed by later commands. An original data-flow trace is: Prepare input -> event W Run picture kernel, waiting for W -> event K Read or hand off the result, waiting for K -> event R The labels are conceptual events, not live OpenCL handles. They express that a kernel must not read unfinished input and that a consumer must not use an unfinished result. An in-order queue has its specified ordering behavior; an out-of-order arrangement needs the applicable dependencies. Merely creating several queues does not synchronize their shared memory automatically. Completing the host's enqueue call therefore establishes submission, while the relevant completion event establishes device progress. A picture representation has an allocation cost For an original 1280 × 720 output represented as four 32-bit floating-point channels: 1280 × 720 × 4 channels × 4 bytes = 14,745,600 bytes This is a selected intermediate representation, not the encoded-video bitrate or a requirement that all OpenCL filters use float RGBA. The device's maximum allocation size constrains a particular memory object. Total global memory constrains a larger set of live allocations. Passing one limit does not establish that every pool and intermediate needed by the pipeline fits simultaneously. Interoperability connects another memory contract An application can import or share suitable resources when the device and relevant extension path support it. The consumer still needs the actual layout and completion/ownership rules. A hardware-decoded surface does not become a usable OpenCL image simply because both are associated with a GPU. Another processing route might require transfer, format preparation or a different implementation.
