articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Vulkan for media processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Vulkan for media processing Vulkan exposes device queues, image resources and programmable processing whose formats, synchronization and ownership determine how pictures move through a compatible media pipeline. A media application can use Vulkan to run programmable picture work and manage suitable GPU image resources. Queues, command buffers, formats and synchronization make the data relationship explicit. Vulkan graphics or compute support is distinct from Vulkan Video , whose extensions expose particular codec operations. Picture processing uses a defined device path The application selects a physical device and supported queue arrangement. It creates or imports images accepted for the required uses, then records the processing commands. A filter needs the actual picture format and intended colour interpretation. An image's storage format does not infer an HDR-to-SDR policy or select which subtitle to compose. An Emby-related Vulkan processing route therefore needs an implemented filter and compatible resources, alongside a usable device/driver interface. Ordering and visibility describe different requirements Consider an original model with an input producer during 0–4 ms, compute processing during 4–7 ms and another consumer during 7–11 ms. The compute stage begins after the relevant input write. The final consumer begins after the compute result is available. An execution dependency establishes an order between operations. The applicable memory dependency and resource state establish how accesses to the produced data become valid for the consumer. The host issuing those commands in that textual order is not, by itself, a complete synchronization strategy across independent queues. Resources have a permitted usage and state A picture image must support its requested usage and format. The chosen arrangement can require appropriate layout transitions and access scopes. A resource prepared for one operation should not be silently treated as valid for every later operation. A decoder-output use, a shader read/write use and a presentation use can have different requirements. Vulkan exposes the concepts needed to describe those relationships. A filter implementation supplies their concrete sequence for its selected resources. Queue families can add an ownership boundary When operations use different queue families, the applicable sharing/ownership arrangement must be maintained. Synchronization between the operations and ownership of the resource are related parts of a valid handoff. External resource import/export has further compatibility and synchronization conditions. It establishes a specific sharing relationship rather than a universal proof that no copies occurred anywhere. Frame surfaces and contexts develop those resource identities independently of the particular API. See Also Vulkan Video profiles, queues and sessions OpenCL for media processing GPU compute and video processing Hardware frame surfaces and GPU contexts Zero-copy video pipelines and the boundary being avoided References Khronos Vulkan: Queues Khronos Vulkan: Synchronization and cache control Khronos Vulkan: Video coding specification FFmpeg: Hardware and software filters

articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Vulkan Video profiles, queues and sessions | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Vulkan Video profiles, queues and sessions Vulkan Video exposes supported codec operations through video profiles, queue capabilities, session resources and codec-specific picture parameters. Vulkan Video adds supported compressed-video operations to Vulkan through video-related extensions. It combines a codec operation, a video profile, suitable queue support and configured resources. The application still supplies the selected encoded media and the codec-specific information needed for the operation. A profile describes the operation and media A Vulkan video profile includes the decode or encode operation, chroma subsampling and component bit depths, with codec-specific profile information provided through the relevant extension structures. This original readable fixture expresses one request: { "operation": "decode", "codec": "h265", "profile": "Main 10", "chroma": "4:2:0", "lumaBitDepth": 10, "chromaBitDepth": 10, "codedWidth": 3840, "codedHeight": 2160 } It is a teaching object, not a native Vulkan structure or captured capability response. A HEVC Main 10 decode request is different from a H.264 encode request. The existence of the latter does not satisfy the former. Capability is an intersection The application checks the relevant device extensions, queue-family video operations and profile-specific capabilities. It then establishes supported picture/reference formats and resource requirements. Condition Fact needed Codec operation extension The required operation is exposed Queue support The selected family can execute it Video profile The implementation accepts the requested configuration Coded extent and references The operation fits its limits Picture/resource formats Results and references have accepted storage Application integration Codec parameters and dependencies are supplied correctly A general graphics or compute queue does not automatically promise those video capabilities. Sessions and pictures retain separate roles A video session represents an operation/profile context and its implementation's required session memory. Session-parameter objects can supply reusable codec information. Decoded-picture-buffer resources and output picture resources describe picture storage used by reconstruction and later consumers. Their formats and whether output/reference storage can coincide follow the implementation's queried capabilities. A session successfully existing does not make an arbitrary picture resource compatible with it. The client supplies codec interpretation A media implementation locates the selected stream, parses required codec information and supplies the codec-specific operation data. The video-coding API does not read an arbitrary MKV or MP4 filename and construct the complete playback route automatically. Reconstruction order, references and programme timing still need their intended relationships. Reference pictures must stay usable while later operations need them. Synchronization connects reconstruction, processing and encoding uses of the resulting images. Standardized operations need actual implementation The specification defines the contract for an exposed codec operation. The required extension/profile/format set must still be implemented by the driver and used by the application. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Overview: Portable GPU processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Overview: Portable GPU processing Portable GPU interfaces offer programmable processing or defined video operations under their own resource contracts. OpenCL and general Vulkan processing are distinct from Vulkan Video's codec-operation interfaces. Each route needs suitable resources, picture representations and synchronization. Comparing them starts with the work required, rather than assuming one portable API exposes every fixed-function media engine. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> OpenCL for media processing OpenCL runs programmable work on supported compute devices through contexts, memory objects and command queues, with explicit capability and completion relationships for picture processing. Vulkan for media processing Vulkan exposes device queues, image resources and programmable processing whose formats, synchronization and ownership determine how pictures move through a compatible media pipeline. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Overview: Vendor media technologies | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Overview: Vendor media technologies Vendor media technologies expose decoding, encoding or processing through particular engines and software interfaces. Intel, NVIDIA, AMD and Apple organize their media technologies differently. Within one vendor's terminology, an engine and the API that reaches it can also be separate concepts. The grouped pages keep those names attached to the work and interface they describe. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Intel Intel media interfaces connect video engines and processing facilities to supported application operations. articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Direct3D 11 video acceleration (D3D11VA) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Direct3D 11 video acceleration (D3D11VA) Direct3D 11 video acceleration uses driver-backed video interfaces and texture resources to reconstruct supported encoded pictures and connect them to compatible consumers. D3D11VA identifies a Direct3D 11 video-acceleration path. Its video interfaces let media software request supported decoding work and manage the resulting pictures through Direct3D resources. A Direct3D 11 graphics device is the context for that work. The application's video configuration still needs a supported decoder arrangement. Negotiate the decoder configuration The media path establishes an appropriate decoder profile, output format and configuration for the source. The driver exposes those possibilities through the video interfaces. A successfully created general Direct3D device does not answer whether the selected codec profile and picture representation can be decoded. Microsoft's Media Foundation integration describes sharing the Direct3D device through a DXGI device manager. A decoder component can then obtain the relevant device access and allocate suitable picture resources. The decoder, its output views and its textures belong to that compatible context. The application supplies the picture work The decoding interface uses codec-specific parameters and compressed buffers. A media implementation parses the selected stream and submits the necessary reconstruction information. Microsoft's documented flow brackets picture submissions with decoder-frame operations and submits the required buffers. It reuses DXVA decoding structures for supported codec profiles while using Direct3D 11's device/resource interfaces. Container parsing and selection remain earlier responsibilities. A driver-backed decoder does not turn a movie filename into a complete playback session. Consumer lifetime controls texture reuse A decoded texture can be passed to a suitable renderer or processor. The decoder's completion makes the picture ready for that use; it does not prove the consumer is finished. An original ownership model has a picture written during 0–4 ms and read by a consumer during 4–7 ms. Rewriting the same storage at 5 ms would conflict with that declared consumer use. The times are invented, but the required ownership order is the useful relationship. Microsoft describes tracking released samples so the pipeline can distinguish available surfaces from surfaces still in use. A CPU-only processing stage can introduce another memory/access path. A compatible GPU consumer can preserve the device-resource relationship instead. A device change can invalidate the old arrangement The selected device can change or become unavailable. A pipeline then needs to recreate the appropriate decoder/resources and renegotiate configuration for the new context. Retaining an old texture pointer does not establish that it remains a valid input in a newly selected context. Device identity and resource lifetime belong together. See Also DirectX Video Acceleration (DXVA2) Media Foundation transforms and processing state The hardware decode-filter-encode pipeline How media APIs connect applications to hardware Hardware decoding and software decoding References Microsoft: Direct3D 11 decoding in Media Foundation Microsoft: About DXVA 2.0 Microsoft: Hardware Media Foundation transforms FFmpeg: Hardware devices and processing

articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: DirectX Video Acceleration (DXVA2) | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: DirectX Video Acceleration (DXVA2) DXVA2 exposes Windows video-acceleration services through which a software media implementation submits supported decoding or processing work to a driver-backed device. DirectX Video Acceleration 2.0 , or DXVA2 , gives Windows media software access to supported hardware video operations through the graphics-driver path. A software codec can parse and coordinate a stream while asking the accelerator to perform specified reconstruction work. “Software component” therefore need not mean that every operation executes on CPU cores. The decoder and accelerator cooperate Responsibility Part of the route Stream/codec interpretation Media implementation supplies the needed codec information Configuration Application and driver establish a supported acceleration arrangement Reconstruction work Driver-backed decoder device performs the requested operation Surface handling The pipeline manages output storage and consumer use The decoder needs a supported profile/configuration and suitable output surfaces. Encoded data alone is not a complete acceleration request. DXVA2 also includes video-processing services. Its video acceleration should not be mistaken for a generic API that exposes every vendor encoder. Device configuration and picture storage are linked A usable hardware path must accept the selected encoded configuration and output format. Media software then supplies the codec-specific buffers and picture relationships required by that path. The decoded surfaces have device and lifetime context. A renderer or later processor needs a suitable relationship to those resources; a CPU consumer can require another representation or access arrangement. Those are part of the hardware pipeline , rather than properties supplied by the DXVA2 name alone. Direct3D 11 uses a related but different interface Windows also exposes video decoding through Direct3D 11. Microsoft's documentation identifies shared DXVA decoding data structures while describing a different device and resource interface. Consequently, a log or setting that distinguishes dxva2 from d3d11va is distinguishing software paths. Both names can refer to acceleration, but their resource/context arrangements are not interchangeable labels. See Also Direct3D 11 video acceleration (D3D11VA) Media Foundation transforms and processing state Hardware decoding and software decoding How media APIs connect applications to hardware References Microsoft: About DXVA 2.0 Microsoft: Direct3D 11 decoding in Media Foundation Emby: Hardware acceleration on Windows

articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.title: Media Foundation transforms and processing state | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/interface.keywords: Media Foundation transforms and processing state A Media Foundation transform is a Windows media-processing component whose negotiated types, input/output state and resource context determine its decoding, encoding or processing role. A Media Foundation transform , or MFT , is a Windows media-processing component. The same component model can represent a decoder, encoder or picture-processing operation. The label describes an interface contract. Its actual implementation and device/resource context determine where the work runs. Media types define the transformation A transform negotiates the media types it accepts and produces. A decoder accepts encoded input and produces pictures; an encoder accepts suitable pictures and produces compressed output. Transform role Relationship Decoder Encoded configuration to accepted picture representation Processor One picture configuration to another Encoder Prepared pictures to selected compressed output The negotiated output must fit the next consumer. A decoded 10-bit picture format and an encoder expecting another format can need a suitable processing step between them. The transform framework coordinates those types; it does not make every proposed connection valid. A type must fit both sides of the connection An original negotiation model makes the cross-stage requirement concrete: Component Accepted input Offered output Decoder Selected encoded video NV12 or P010 Processor NV12 NV12 or BGRA Encoder NV12 Selected compressed output The compatible route through these declarations uses NV12 from decoder to processor and NV12 from processor to encoder. Selecting P010 from the decoder would not fit this processor's declared input. Selecting BGRA from the processor would not fit this encoder's declared input. The existence of each individual component does not repair either connection. These are invented capability sets, not a Media Foundation enumeration. They illustrate how negotiation chooses a complete relationship rather than independently choosing a preferred format at every stage. The pipeline can select another processor or explicitly add an appropriate conversion when supported. That changes its negotiated route and resource requirements; it should not silently reinterpret P010 or BGRA bytes as NV12. Synchronous input/output state has backpressure The basic processing model exposes ProcessInput() and ProcessOutput() . Their results tell the caller whether another input can be accepted or whether output needs handling. This original synchronous trace illustrates the relationship: ProcessInput(A) -> accepted ProcessInput(B) -> MF_E_NOTACCEPTING ProcessOutput() -> completed result available ProcessInput(B) -> accepted ProcessOutput() -> MF_E_TRANSFORM_NEED_MORE_INPUT The trace is a model, not an actual COM call sequence. It preserves B when the first attempt could not accept it. MF_E_NOTACCEPTING can describe a state that needs output progress, rather than an unsupported codec. MF_E_TRANSFORM_NEED_MORE_INPUT says that this output request needs further input under the transform's current processing state. The application interprets status, output data and the negotiated contract together. One accepted input does not universally promise exactly one immediately available output. Asynchronous transforms have another scheduling contract Media Foundation also provides an asynchronous processing model. Hardware MFTs have documented asynchronous and dynamic-format requirements. The caller follows event/readiness rules appropriate to that model rather than blindly using a synchronous polling loop. A host call returning and a media operation finishing can occur at different times. This lets queued work proceed while the application performs other coordination. The input and output resources still need valid ownership through their consumers' use. A software component can coordinate hardware decoding Microsoft's D3D11 decoder-integration documentation calls the codec-facing component a software decoder while the driver-backed decoder device performs accelerated reconstruction. That illustrates why component implementation, registered hardware-MFT category and execution of a particular media operation are different facts. An MFT name alone should not be read as a CPU-utilization measurement. A suitable device manager and decoder configuration connect that component to Direct3D resources. The resulting pictures still need compatible downstream types and context. A format change propagates to consumers A source or transform can change its output picture configuration. The application needs to establish the new accepted types and resource requirements with the affected pipeline. A different dimension or surface format can require new buffers or a different next-stage configuration. Continuing to interpret the new output using the old assumptions can make an otherwise supported source fail downstream. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Why hardware acceleration can still use the CPU | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Why hardware acceleration can still use the CPU CPU activity during accelerated media processing can come from unaccelerated stages, host coordination and concurrent work, so its meaning depends on the complete selected workload. Hardware acceleration assigns supported work to particular device paths. The application and other media stages still have work on the CPU. A high overall CPU number therefore needs a workload explanation before it becomes evidence that hardware decoding or encoding failed. Identify the CPU’s tasks Work Possible CPU contribution Container and packet handling Source reads, parsing and stream selection Audio processing Selected decode, channel processing or encoding Subtitle/picture work A selected CPU renderer or filter Device coordination Submission, queues, callbacks and resource handling Delivery Packaging, temporary output and request handling Other server activity Concurrent jobs and library/system work NVIDIA's decoder documentation, for example, separates its software parser from the dedicated reconstruction engine. An application can consequently perform CPU parsing while NVDEC is doing its selected decode work. Small per-picture work can accumulate Use an original model with eight milliseconds of CPU work per picture at thirty pictures per second: 0.008 CPU seconds × 30 pictures = 0.24 CPU seconds per wall second If the modeled work uses one core at a time, it is about 24% of one core's time. Four equivalent independent jobs request 0.96 core-seconds per wall second. On an ideal eight-core total-time denominator, that is 12% aggregate CPU time. The actual reporting convention, scheduling and extra work determine a real utilization display. The numbers are invented. They show why a per-picture cost, a per-core percentage and a machine-total percentage should not be interchanged. Observation scope by stage Evidence What it establishes Hardware encoder successfully initialized Selected output encoder path Hardware decoder produces pictures Selected reconstruction progress CPU filter appears in the graph A picture-processing path needing its CPU contract Total CPU utilization is high Combined activity under that reporting interval Conversion falls below playback rate Deficit somewhere in the complete producer route A hardware encoder name does not prove every upstream operation used hardware. Conversely, total CPU utilization does not erase a successfully running hardware stage. Preserve the compared workload An Emby session with a newly selected burn-in subtitle can introduce CPU picture work while keeping the same hardware decoder and encoder. Changing simultaneous jobs or output dimensions also changes demand. Compare the same source, selected tracks, target and job count before assigning the difference to acceleration. Transcoding logs supply operation and progress evidence that can be related to the observation interval. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Driver-dependent media capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Driver-dependent media capabilities A usable media capability depends on the hardware and the driver/runtime/application path that exposes a particular operation and picture configuration. Hardware can implement a media operation while a particular software path does not expose or use its complete configuration. The driver/runtime and application integration connect physical capability to a usable session. This makes a capability claim more specific than “the GPU supports HEVC.” Identify the layers in the claim Evidence Scope Manufacturer hardware table Listed product’s stated hardware capability Driver feature table Operation exposed by that implementation/build Native API query Selected device/context and requested configuration Application build Interfaces and features integrated by the program Initialized session Configuration the actual runtime accepted Observed result Output/progress through the selected route A failure at one layer should be related to that layer rather than silently replacing every other result. A backend-build example is visible in the source Intel's pinned Media Driver table separates Full-Feature and Free-Kernel rows. Its TGLx AV1 ten-bit entry supplies D in Full-Feature while leaving the Free-Kernel declaration blank. DG2/ATSM likewise has differing AV1 direction declarations between those builds. That is a concrete implementation distinction. It can coexist with a hardware reference listing AV1 capability for the relevant product. The application must use the actual installed backend and exposed operation. Copying another build's feature list does not create that operation. Interfaces require compatible versions and resource contracts A new codec/profile feature can require interface definitions, runtime support and application integration. A newer physical engine alone does not make an older wrapper supply those structures. Surface formats and interoperable resource paths can change as well. The usable decoder and its next consumer need a matching accepted picture relationship. This is particularly relevant to new chroma/bit-depth paths and explicitly queried video operations such as Vulkan Video. A process comparison preserves selection An original example has an interactive tool selecting adapter A and a full-feature backend, while the server process selects adapter B or another backend path. Their different profile results describe different contexts. Both reports can be accurate for their own selection. Library search, environment, device access and process identity are also part of the route. Those facts should be established before concluding that a supported stream became corrupt. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Hardware acceleration in Emby Server | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Hardware acceleration in Emby Server Emby Server’s accelerated conversion uses supported selected decode, picture-processing and encode paths whose source/target, runtime and resource evidence establish the actual session route. Emby Server uses a media-conversion route appropriate to the selected source, tracks, client and output constraints. Hardware acceleration can supply supported operations within that route. Emby lists hardware-accelerated transcoding as an Emby Premiere feature. Feature availability, usable device/runtime capability and the actual session's work are separate conditions. Establish whether the server needs new video A Direct Play session uses the original representation. Enabling acceleration does not require the server to decode and re-encode video that the client can use directly. A Direct Stream session can preserve video while adapting packaging or another stream. Audio conversion in that session is different from a newly encoded video representation. When video conversion is required, the selected source decoder, picture operations and target encoder form the route. Treat settings as selection input The server's configured acceleration preferences and detected paths influence selection. They do not report that a given source profile and target were successfully initialized. A device can support HEVC Main 10 reconstruction while another requested profile or filter needs another path. A target encoder has its own capability and resource requirements. Emby's platform documentation supplies high-level route context. Some public lists and setup remarks reflect older versions, so the actual server build, available settings and current runtime result should accompany an investigation. This page explains the technology and evidence, rather than prescribing one forced setting for every platform. Work through a selected original session Imagine an original source with 4K HEVC Main 10 video, AC-3 audio and a subtitle that the client cannot present separately. The target is 1080p H.264 SDR with stereo AAC. Requirement Operation to establish Source HEVC pictures Supported selected decoder Smaller SDR presentation Appropriate scale/colour processing Painted subtitle Selected composition path H.264 video output Supported target encoder Stereo AAC Selected audio preparation Streaming resources Output packaging and delivery One route could use hardware reconstruction, CPU-specific picture work and hardware encoding. Another could use compatible device picture processing. The active route, not the enabled setting alone, establishes those handoffs. The example does not claim a particular private Emby planning algorithm or captured session. Distinguish availability, initialization and progress Observation Stage it supports Device/path appears as available Detected or exposed selection context Decoder/encoder configuration accepted Successful initialization at that stage Mapped/processed pictures become available Picture-path progress Encoded output advances Producer progress through the selected target Client presents the next interval Later delivery and receiver progress A source/output codec label can appear in both copying and re-encoding scenarios. Stream-operation mappings identify the difference. A process called transcoding can also perform packaging or other-stream adaptation. The name of the process is less specific than its actual selected operations. Relate playback information and the relevant log Playback information relates source properties, selected output and session observations. A conversion log records input, mappings, filters and progress in the relevant job context. The public TranscodingInfo model includes decoder/encoder and hardware-related fields. Their interpretation belongs to that session and reporting stage, rather than a whole-server guarantee for every file. Source codec/profile, dimensions, bit depth, selected tracks, target constraints and server/runtime versions help explain why a different path was selected. Progress clocks can locate a later wait Successful hardware initialization establishes the configured stage, while producer, receiver and viewer progress describe later boundaries. Use an original common-origin programme-time model: Wall-clock observation Server-ready position Client-received position Viewer position 50 seconds 120 seconds 95 seconds 90 seconds 60 seconds 150 seconds 100 seconds 100 seconds The producer advanced thirty media seconds in ten wall seconds, giving a modeled 3x rate over this interval. The client’s usable lead fell from five seconds to zero while the viewer advanced at 1x. In this example, fast server output coexists with client starvation at the final boundary. A stall alone would not show that the hardware encoder stopped working. The model stops at that first starvation point and assumes the received intervals are continuous and usable. A real record needs common timestamp origins and the actual readiness/receipt observations. After a seek or a replaced conversion job, an output timestamp can have another origin. Relating a new log's zero to the programme position is necessary before comparing its progress with the viewer’s current time. Change one relevant input in a reproduction A useful original comparison is: Case Preserved context Changed input A Source, client, target limit, programme interval Baseline track selection B Same as A Subtitle requiring another processing path C Same as A A source variant with another encoded profile B can change picture processing while leaving decoder support intact. C can change reconstruction requirements while keeping the title the same. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Concurrent encoder sessions, policy and capacity | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Concurrent encoder sessions, policy and capacity Concurrent encoding is constrained by session policy, supported configurations and available processing/memory resources, with encoder sessions differing from client count and physical engine count. An encoder session is a configured encoding operation with its own input/output and resource state. It is different from a playback client and from a physical encoder unit. Several constraints cooperate: whether the session is permitted, whether its configuration is supported, and whether the combined workload has enough capacity and memory. Count encoding operations, not just viewers Selected media work New video-encoding operations in this example Direct Play of original video 0 Copied video with converted audio 0 One new video representation 1 A job creating two video representations 2 The table counts declared video-encoding work, not every process or audio operation. An application can implement its configured representations with additional internal details. A server with several clients can therefore have fewer video encoders than clients. Conversely, another processing job can add encoder work without another viewer. A physical unit is a work resource A device can schedule several sessions through its available media engines. The physical count does not impose a universal one-session-per-engine rule. Engine count is useful for aggregate work under the actual implementation, workload and driver scheduling. Decoder, filtering and memory resources can limit the complete route separately. NVIDIA’s published policy has a system scope SDK 13.1 distinguishes qualified and non-qualified products. It describes qualified products as resource-limited and gives twelve simultaneous encoding sessions per system across all non-qualified cards combined . This is the referenced policy as checked on 11 October 2026, not a timeless limit for every driver version or a policy for other vendors. For an original two-card example: Card A: 7 sessions Card B: 5 sessions Combined: 12 sessions A new session on either card would make the combined count 13. Adding another non-qualified card does not make that stated combined policy twenty-four. A qualified card's resource-limited sessions have the separate scope described by the source. Permission does not calculate sustained speed Use an original declared encoder capacity of 120 prepared pictures per second for one defined configuration. Four independent thirty-fps sessions request 120 pictures per second, leaving no modeled spare capacity. Five request 150, beyond the declared capacity even though five is below twelve. The rates are invented. Changing codec, resolution, preset, preprocessing or device clock changes the relevant measured capacity. The selected pipeline also has source decoding, filters and delivery. A fast encoder cannot consume pictures that a slower upstream stage has not prepared. Memory and lifetime add another constraint Each session can retain inputs, references, analysis state and output buffers. Their combined live memory must fit the usable resource budget. The GPU-memory example shows two individually valid jobs exceeding a combined budget. A policy allowing those sessions does not change that allocation result. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Mixed hardware and software filtering | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Mixed hardware and software filtering A mixed video-processing route connects hardware and CPU operations through the picture representations each consumer accepts, with operation order and transfer placement affecting the result and cost. A conversion can combine hardware decoding, CPU filtering, GPU processing and hardware encoding. Each stage needs a representation it can use, and the route must preserve the intended picture transformation. “Hardware acceleration enabled” does not choose one universal arrangement for those filters. Start from the selected operation A source can need scaling, colour processing and subtitle composition. The selected application has implementations for those operations with particular input/output contracts. A CPU-only renderer needs a CPU-usable picture. A device filter needs an accepted surface format/context. The result then needs to fit the next consumer. Three original arrangements are: Route Processing relationship A Hardware decode → device processing → hardware encode B Hardware decode → copy-back → CPU processing → hardware encode input C Hardware decode → device scale → CPU-specific operation → hardware encode input Each describes the chosen consumers, not a ranking that all sources and operations must share. Stage location changes the transferred picture Assume an ideal 4K 4:2:0 picture with sixteen-bit sample storage: 24,883,200 bytes. If a compatible route scales and prepares a 1080p eight-bit picture before CPU access, that selected representation has 3,110,400 bytes. At thirty pictures per second, the modeled download payload changes from 746,496,000 to 93,312,000 bytes per second. That is an eightfold payload difference for these declared representations. It omits driver padding and other operations. The CPU operation must still accept the smaller representation and preserve the intended algorithm. Reducing data is useful only when it remains the right input. Coordinates make the order visible Use an original 1920 × 1080 source scaled to 1280 × 720, a ratio of two-thirds. An overlay painted with height 48 source-coordinate units before scaling becomes 32 destination units. A 48-unit overlay painted after scaling remains 48 destination units: Before scale: 48 × 2/3 = 32 After scale: 48 These are geometric models, not measured fonts. They show why moving an operation across another stage can change the visible result even when both routes run faster. Colour processing likewise needs its intended value interpretation. A selected nonlinear-to-linear transformation and a tone-mapping operation cannot be replaced by arbitrary byte-format conversion. Cross-stage completion protects the data The device producer must finish the picture the CPU or another device reads. The CPU result must be available before another encoder consumes it. The input and output allocations also remain live through codec references and outstanding consumers. A synchronization event and a resource's final release answer different questions. Compatible shared storage can avoid a particular copy. An unsupported CPU filter can still require another representation despite successful hardware decoding and encoding. The slow stage limits the filled route An original independent-overlap model gives stage capacities of 120 pictures/s decode, 25 pictures/s filter and 90 pictures/s encode. The filter limits the model to 25 pictures/s. Doubling the encoder to 180 does not change that minimum. Improving the filter to 60 moves the limit to 60, subject to the other stated assumptions. A 30-fps target exceeds the original 25-picture/s producer model. Existing buffer reserve can cover a temporary deficit, but sustained production needs the complete route to keep up. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Overview: Hardware pipelines and their limits | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Overview: Hardware pipelines and their limits Hardware pipeline behavior depends on picture transfers, synchronization, shared resources and the stages actually accelerated. A fast engine can still wait for data or another stage. Mixed software and hardware filtering, session limits and driver-dependent behavior affect the whole operation. This branch follows those relationships into Emby's processing path, including the CPU work that can remain when media engines are active. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Frame memory and transfers Frame memory and transfer paths determine how processing stages share, copy and retain pictures. Concurrent encoder sessions Concurrent encoding is constrained by session policy, supported configurations and available processing/memory resources, with encoder sessions differing from client count and physical engine count. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Copy-back video pipelines | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Copy-back video pipelines A copy-back video path makes hardware-decoded pictures available in a CPU-oriented representation so software consumers can process them before later delivery or encoding. A copy-back route gives a CPU-oriented consumer access to pictures reconstructed by a hardware decoder. The application obtains a suitable system-memory representation, applies the selected software work and supplies the next stage. Hardware decoding remains hardware decoding. The copy-back describes a later picture handoff. A CPU consumer can be the reason A selected subtitle renderer, colour transform or other filter may need CPU-accessible picture data. A device surface is not necessarily that accepted input. The route can therefore be: Hardware decode -> suitable CPU picture -> software processing -> compatible hardware-encoder input -> compressed output The preparation back into a device path is needed only when that chosen consumer requires it. A software encoder can use another relationship. Calculate the sizes at each boundary Use an original model that downloads an ideal 4K 4:2:0 picture with sixteen-bit sample storage, then prepares a 1080p 8-bit 4:2:0 result on the CPU. At thirty pictures per second: Transfer Bytes per picture Declared payload per second 4K picture to CPU 24,883,200 746,496,000 1080p result to encoder path 3,110,400 93,312,000 Combined — 839,808,000 The upload is smaller because the model's output has both a quarter of the spatial area and half the sample storage width. This calculation omits padding, intermediate copies, transfer overhead and compression. It does not establish an actual PCIe or integrated-memory measurement. Moving the processor changes the boundary If a compatible device filter scales before CPU access, the downloaded picture can be smaller. If the software filter requires original-size samples, that change can alter its intended result. The algorithm's input and coordinate meaning therefore matter alongside the transfer size. A subtitle painted before scaling is not always equivalent to painting it afterward. Likewise, a processing step can change storage format. The next encoder must accept the prepared result rather than infer its layout from the previous decoder. A transfer has readiness and ownership The CPU consumer needs a completed usable picture and any required memory-access/coherency arrangement. The producer storage also remains live while decoding references or other consumers need it. An upload or imported encoder input has its own completion/lifetime contract. Submitting the prepared picture does not give immediate permission to overwrite it. Keep the retained benefit visible A copy-back session can reduce CPU reconstruction work while leaving substantial CPU filtering and transfer coordination. It is not necessarily equivalent to a fully software route. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Hardware frame surfaces and GPU contexts | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Hardware frame surfaces and GPU contexts A hardware frame surface represents picture storage within a device/context relationship, with layout, timing, ownership and completion determining how another stage may use it. A hardware frame surface represents picture storage associated with a particular media device/context. It is more than a codec name or a width/height pair. The next stage needs a valid way to access the actual picture and preserve its interpretation, timing and lifetime. A frame has several relationships Relationship What the consumer needs Device/context A compatible route to the selected storage Pixel representation Format, planes, dimensions and row layout Picture interpretation Colour range, matrix, transfer function and primaries Programme timing Intended presentation/decode context Readiness Relevant producer completion Ownership Remaining references and consumers A frame handle meaningful to one context is not automatically a usable input in an unrelated context. Another adapter or interface may need a supported import, transfer or newly prepared resource. Coded storage can exceed the visible picture Consider an original P010-style 4:2:0 layout for a visible 3840 × 2160 picture. Samples use sixteen-bit storage, the declared pitch is 8192 bytes, and the padded storage height is 2176. The luma and chroma planes have this declared geometry: Luma = 8192 × 2176 = 17,825,792 bytes Chroma = 8192 × 1088 = 8,912,896 bytes Total 26,738,688 bytes The ideal unpadded geometry would occupy 24,883,200 bytes. The example's row and height padding add 1,855,488 bytes. This is a declared linear layout model. It is not a formula for every tiled, compressed or driver-specific surface. The visible width identifies picture samples to present. Pitch identifies how storage rows are addressed. A consumer using one as the other can misread the picture even when its codec and visible dimensions are correct. Sample precision is not allocation width A ten-bit sample can occupy sixteen bits of storage. The unused storage bits do not become additional source-image precision. Changing a surface format can therefore change memory demand without creating more image information. An intermediate four-channel float representation has another storage cost again. The accepted formats must fit both sides of a handoff. A processor offering BGRA does not automatically satisfy an encoder that accepts only the selected NV12 configuration. Readiness and release occur at different times Use an original picture A timeline: Event Model time Established relationship Decoder finishes writing A 4 ms The relevant result can become ready to read Filter finishes its A use 7 ms That filter use can end Decoder finishes the last declared dependent-picture use 9 ms That decoding-reference use can end If no other uses remain, nine milliseconds is the model's earliest reuse point. Reusing at seven would overlook the reference use. These are invented times. They make the two kinds of retention visible: a downstream consumer and a future decode dependency can both keep a surface live. A pool coordinates several pictures The producer needs available storage for new results while other surfaces remain retained. A filled pool can delay submission even when the hardware operation itself is fast. An API can return a mapped or reference-counted object, but the application still follows its relevant completion and release contract. A reference count preventing deallocation does not by itself say the last write is finished. At a format or device-context change, the application establishes a compatible new resource arrangement. Old handles and strides retain their old context rather than becoming valid merely because the next picture has the same title. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: GPU memory limits in video processing | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: GPU memory limits in video processing Video-processing memory demand comes from distinct live picture allocations, codec references, queues and intermediates whose layouts and lifetimes must fit the selected device’s usable limits. Video processing stores reconstructed pictures, not only compressed packets. Reference frames, pending outputs, filter results and encoder inputs can keep several pictures live at once. The usable memory limit is therefore a property of the selected layouts, allocation identities and lifetimes within the actual device path. A surface costs more than its compressed packet Use the original padded 4K P010-style layout developed in frame surfaces : 26,738,688 bytes per surface. In binary units: 26,738,688 / 1,048,576 = 25.5 MiB per surface A twenty-Mbit/s encoded source does not replace that picture allocation with twenty million bits for every decoded second. Compression and reconstructed storage have different representations. Intermediate float/RGBA pictures, driver-specific padding, tiling or staging can introduce other costs. Count distinct allocations Several references or views can point to the same backing storage. Summing every visible handle as a new full allocation can overcount. An original owner-set example is: Decode-reference uses: A, B, C, D Queued-stage uses: C, D, E Encoder uses: D, F There are nine owner entries, but six distinct backing labels: A through F. At 25.5 MiB each, six allocations cost 153 MiB. Counting all owner entries independently would report 229.5 MiB. The real implementation can also create separate result or staging allocations. The correct identity comes from the actual resource relationship; matching labels in this example only illustrate the distinction. A pool and its other live work share the budget Consider a declared 512-MiB budget for one processing route, with 96 MiB of other live allocations: Pool choice Picture allocations Other live memory Modeled total 16 surfaces 408 MiB 96 MiB 504 MiB 18 surfaces 459 MiB 96 MiB 555 MiB The first fits this budget with eight MiB remaining. The second does not. These values are invented teaching inputs. They are not total VRAM or a recommendation for a decoder's buffer count. More buffering extends storage lifetimes A reference picture must remain available until dependent reconstruction ends. A filter input or encoder input remains retained until the relevant consumer finishes. More asynchronous work can increase overlap but also increase the number of pictures waiting or still in use. A decoder can consequently run out of available surface slots before a global byte-allocation limit is reached. The pool's capacity and the device's memory budget are different constraints. Concurrent jobs have combined demand For another original model, each job uses ten of the same surfaces plus forty MiB of other distinct live work: Per job = 10 × 25.5 + 40 = 295 MiB Two independent jobs = 590 MiB Under the declared 512-MiB budget, one fits and two do not. Shared resources or another layout would change the accounting. A permitted encoder session count does not grant additional memory for those jobs. Concurrent sessions separates that policy from capacity. Peak demand is a timeline Counting every allocation ever created is another kind of overcount. The important constraint is which backing allocations remain live together. Use an original model with the same 25.5-MiB pictures and a temporary 96-MiB processing allocation: Observation Live picture allocations Temporary memory Total Start A, B, C 0 MiB 76.5 MiB Processing begins A, B, C, D 96 MiB 198 MiB A and B end; E is created C, D, E 96 MiB 172.5 MiB C, D and temporary work end E 0 MiB 25.5 MiB Five distinct pictures occur during the model, but they never all coexist with the temporary allocation. Its peak is 198 MiB, not the 223.5 MiB sum of every picture ever created plus temporary storage. This model assumes the ended allocations are actually freed. Returning a surface lease to an existing pool can instead make a slot reusable while the pool retains its backing memory. A lower queue occupancy then does not necessarily reduce allocated bytes. The distinction explains why a workload can stop using a picture without immediately returning all associated memory to the device budget. A real account needs both live consumers and the allocator/pool retention policy. Limits can apply at several scopes An API can expose a maximum individual allocation, supported image extents or a session's reference/working-memory requirements. The application's route also competes with other live device use. A product's advertised total memory is therefore not identical to the free budget available for this exact pipeline. articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.title: Zero-copy video pipelines and the boundary being avoided | Emby Learn
articles/hardware-acceleration/pipelines.keywords: Zero-copy video pipelines and the boundary being avoided A zero-copy claim identifies a picture handoff that avoids a particular data copy, while compatible storage, processing and synchronization determine the remaining pipeline traffic. Zero-copy is useful when its boundary is specified. A pipeline can avoid copying a picture from device memory to CPU memory, or avoid a duplicate device allocation at one handoff, without eliminating every memory operation in the job. The question is which data would otherwise be copied, between which resources, and whether the actual consumer can use the producer's storage. Compare the actual handoff Three original routes illustrate different claims: Route Selected picture handoff A Decoder surface is directly usable by the compatible device consumer B Pictures stay on the GPU, but are copied/converted into another device allocation C Pictures are prepared in CPU-accessible memory for a CPU-only consumer Route A can avoid the particular intermediate copy. B avoids a device-to-host transfer but still has device-side picture traffic. C supplies a different consumer requirement. The route label should describe those objects, rather than conclude “zero bytes moved” from a hardware-decoder name. Compatible storage is the prerequisite The next stage must accept the actual layout, device/context and picture format. Shared backing storage is useful only through a supported consumer relationship. A buffer import can establish a reference to the same allocation. It does not fix an unsupported tiling modifier, pixel format or queue/context relationship. Likewise, a processor needing another output format can create a new result allocation even if its input was imported without a copy. The handoff into the processor and the processor's own write are different operations. Avoided transfers can have a large payload For an original ideal 4K 4:2:0 picture using sixteen-bit sample storage, each frame has 24,883,200 bytes. At thirty pictures per second, a modeled full download and same-sized upload carry: 24,883,200 × 30 × 2 = 1,492,992,000 bytes per second Avoiding those two transfers removes that declared payload from that route. It does not make decoding, filtering or encoding stop accessing their picture data. A scaling operation still samples input and writes output. A codec still uses references and reconstructed pictures. Those operations have their own traffic and caching behavior. An API’s mapping contract matters The traditional NVDEC mapping path documented in SDK 13.1 prepares and copies a decoded result into an output representation. Calling the operation “map” does not make it a no-movement proof. The same SDK documents an opaque block-linear output path into application-provided CUDA arrays, plus compatible NVENC array input. Under its stated supported conditions, that arrangement avoids specified intermediate preparation/copies. Those are concrete interface relationships. A media program needs integration for the selected path before its session can claim that result. Linux DMA-BUF/DRM PRIME likewise supports sharing resources. The DMA-BUF article develops the layout, handle and completion context needed by that sharing. Shared input can produce several new outputs Consider an original route where a processor reads the decoder's P010 surface directly. It writes a prepared NV12 main picture and a separate preview result. The decoder-to-processor input avoids an additional copy under this declared compatible relationship. The processor still has to create its changed results. For ideal unpadded output layouts: 1920 × 1080 NV12 main output = 3,110,400 bytes 320 × 180 NV12 preview = 86,400 bytes Combined result storage = 3,196,800 bytes per occurrence At 30 occurrences/second = 95,904,000 bytes/second of result writes That write payload excludes the processor's input reads, codec references and other traffic. It exists even though the input handoff shared storage without an extra copied picture. The preview is also another consumer/resource path. Its completion and release can differ from those of the main encoder. Releasing one branch does not establish that every use of the shared input or result storage ended. This makes a boundary-specific zero-copy claim compatible with substantial useful processing and several live output allocations. Shared use retains synchronization and lifetime A consumer cannot read unfinished producer output or overwrite a resource still used by another stage. Zero-copy sharing can increase the importance of preserving that exact storage through its consumers. A larger pool can keep more pictures live so stages overlap. It has a corresponding memory cost, even when the handoffs avoid a copy. State the measurable claim For an Emby processing route, identify the producer surface, consumer format, actual import/transfer operations and CPU-versus-device stages. “Decoder-to-encoder avoids a full-picture CPU round trip” is a defined claim when supported by the actual route. “Everything uses the GPU, therefore there are no copies” omits the device-local preparation and filter writes that still need examination. articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Overview: Audiobooks | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Overview: Audiobooks Audiobook organization relates files and chapters to a particular edition and narrated performance. A long listening work can be split into many tracks or stored with an internal chapter structure. Its edition and narrator can also distinguish it from another recording of the same book. The topics here connect those identities to the navigation and grouping the listener expects. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Audiobook organization Audiobook organization relates a narrated edition to its ordered audio resources, descriptive credits and navigation without equating chapters with files. Audiobook editions An audiobook edition identifies a particular narrated presentation whose reader, language, text selection and timeline can differ from other versions of the same book. Audiobook narrators A narrator credit identifies who performs a particular audiobook presentation separately from the author and other contributors to its text or production. articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Audiobook chapter structure | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Audiobook chapter structure Audiobook chapter structure relates narrative divisions and navigation markers to resource-local timelines that may not share the same file boundaries. A chapter can mean a division in the written work, a navigation point in an audio resource, or a file selected by a player. Those meanings often coincide in a well-prepared audiobook, but none automatically guarantees the others. For a listener, the important questions are which passage a chapter names and where that passage begins in the represented narration. Three chapters, two files Use the original 90-minute edition of The Lantern Keeper : Narrative chapter Position in this narration Duration 1, The Door 0:00–20:00 20 minutes 2, The Lamp 20:00–53:00 33 minutes 3, The Return 53:00–90:00 37 minutes Now divide the storage into two 45-minute files. The split lies inside chapter 2: File 1 ends 25 minutes into chapter 2. File 2 begins with the final eight minutes of chapter 2, then chapter 3 starts at its local minute 8. Calling the whole second file “chapter 3” would lose that distinction. These are known boundaries in a fictional model, not a chapter detector or actual book recording. Translate a position using resource offsets For whole-book minute 61, first locate the resource interval. It lies in File 2, whose whole-book start is minute 45: file 2 local position = 61 - 45 = 16 minutes chapter 3 local position = 61 - 53 = 8 minutes Both coordinates are correct. They identify different origins. For chapter 3's start, the File 2 marker is at 53 - 45 = 8 minutes . A marker at local minute 53 would lie outside the 45-minute second file. The inverse is equally important. A stored resume value of 16:00 in File 2 becomes book minute 61 only when the resource's offset is known. Applying that number to another part or another narrated edition is a different operation. Chapter metadata refers to the resource A single-file audiobook can carry chapter metadata at each navigation position. Multiple file formats provide representations for such information. MP4-based audiobook resources can use chapter structures understood by compatible readers. The .m4b suffix supplies a customary resource label; it does not identify which chapter representation is present or whether an app will expose it. ID3's chapter extension defines CHAP frames for chapter information and CTOC frames for tables of contents. Chapter element identifiers connect the table to the chapter frames. They are local identifiers within the tag, not global book identifiers. An illustrative single-file representation of the same narration would use: Chapter element Start in milliseconds End in milliseconds c1 0 1,200,000 c2 1,200,000 3,180,000 c3 3,180,000 5,400,000 The table is field arithmetic, not complete encoded ID3 frames. Twenty minutes is 20 × 60 × 1,000 = 1,200,000 milliseconds . A chapter field in milliseconds must not be read as the 100-nanosecond ticks used by some playback interfaces. The table of contents can supply an ordered relationship among c1, c2 and c3. A chapter label such as The Return describes content; its element ID supplies the local reference; its start value supplies a timeline position. Narrative divisions need accurate navigation evidence A file can have navigation points every ten minutes without those points being the book's narrative chapters. Conversely, a named chapter can contain sub-sections worth navigating independently. A table of contents can therefore represent hierarchy rather than only a flat numbered list. The structures and display behavior depend on the reader. Format capability and app support are separate questions. Emby's audiobook documentation describes embedded chapter/track and disc numbering for resource organisation. That concerns the represented sequence; it should not be read as a promise that every chapter frame in every supported audio container produces identical app navigation. A different edition changes the map Dane Rowan's reading can place The Return at minute 67 instead of minute 53. The title can still identify the same narrative chapter, while every marker value needs its edition's own timeline. An abridged edition can remove a chapter or combine passages. Retaining the old numbers and elapsed-time values then creates apparently precise navigation to the wrong content. articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Audiobook editions and narrated versions | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Audiobook editions and narrated versions An audiobook edition identifies a particular narrated presentation whose reader, language, text selection and timeline can differ from other versions of the same book. The same book can be read by different narrators, translated, abridged or presented as a dramatized production. An audiobook edition identifies the particular presentation the listener is choosing. A new codec is a technical representation change. A new reader or a different text selection can change the performance and its timeline. Fictional edition of The Lantern Keeper Reader Text selection Duration in this example E1 Nora Hale Unabridged 90 minutes E2 Nora Hale Abridged 60 minutes E3 Dane Rowan Unabridged 105 minutes The durations are invented. A shorter recording does not alone prove abridgement: reading pace, pauses and other presentation choices also affect length. Text and performance are related identities An unabridged label describes the intended text coverage for the represented edition. It does not establish that two readings have identical pauses, pronunciation, introductions or chapter times. An abridged presentation changes what is included. A dramatization can change speakers and adapt the text into another form. Those choices matter even when all versions retain the underlying book title. A translation adds another textual relationship before the narration is considered. Two English encodes of E1 can correspond to the same performance; an English and French reading cannot be aligned merely by matching their title labels. Schema.org's audiobook description has separate author/reader, edition, language and abridgement concepts. Those fields illustrate the information a description may preserve; they are not a list of dedicated fields guaranteed in every Emby app. Publication identifiers select products An ISBN identifies a publication's edition and format in the ISBN system. It is not an audio hash or a location within a narrated performance. A catalogue's book/work identity can be broader still. Thus an identifier can help distinguish a published audiobook product without supplying any timing correspondence to another narration. Conversely, a recording re-encoded from FLAC to AAC can preserve its performance while changing bytes and technical properties. Emby's book documentation describes library resource recognition. A library can recognise two files under familiar book names while still needing enough edition context to explain which narration each file represents. Chapter anchors reveal different pacing For E1, story chapter 3 begins at minute 53. For E3 it begins at minute 67 in this original example. Those known boundaries identify the same structural place in the text at different performance times. A position eight minutes after E1's chapter-3 start is book minute 61. Adding eight minutes to E3's boundary yields minute 75, but that is only an elapsed-time guess. Dane Rowan can spend a different amount of time on each sentence, so equal time since the chapter start does not establish the same spoken passage. Preserving the chapter gives a meaningful broad continuation point. Preserving an exact passage requires more detailed correspondence between the text and each performance. Multiplying a whole-book percentage by the destination runtime supplies neither. Labels should distinguish what the listener hears A useful edition description includes the reader, language and abridgement or adaptation status when those distinguish available choices. Nora Hale, unabridged conveys a different decision from AAC, 128 kbit/s . The performance label and technical source label can both be retained. That lets a listener choose E1's narration and then use a suitable resource representation, while E3 remains a different reading rather than an unexplained “higher-duration version.” See Also Audiobook narrators and reader credits Audiobook chapter structure Resume positions and playback timelines Media item identity References Schema.org: Audiobook, author and reader roles International ISBN Agency: What an ISBN identifies Emby: Audiobook naming Emby: Book naming and media types

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Audiobook narrators and reader credits | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Audiobook narrators and reader credits A narrator credit identifies who performs a particular audiobook presentation separately from the author and other contributors to its text or production. The narrator performs an audiobook's spoken presentation. The author created its text. One person can do both, but the roles remain different. For the fictional The Lantern Keeper : Person Credit Elin Ward Author Nora Hale Reader of edition E1 Dane Rowan Reader of edition E3 Ivo Reed Translator of another textual edition Searching for Elin Ward's books and searching for Nora Hale's readings traverse different relationships. Replacing the author with the reader because the audio has an Artist field erases the first route. One reader or a cast A single narrator can voice several characters. That does not make each character another person credited as a narrator. A full-cast production can have several performers assigned to different roles. It can also have a distinct narrator who supplies connecting prose. Retaining contributor names and roles makes that description intelligible without guessing from the number of names printed on the cover. A character name is a role label. The performer's identity remains another field. The distinction is the same one used in cast and crew credits . Metadata conventions need a role interpretation Schema.org uses readBy for a person who reads an audiobook, separately from its author relationship. Audio taggers may instead use inherited artist/performer fields or additional descriptive fields. Their presence does not establish one universal audiobook-role convention. Emby's audiobook organisation uses descriptive information accompanying the resources. The imported fields and app presentation determine how reader credits are exposed. Where a description offers a compact credit such as read by Nora Hale , that qualified text preserves more meaning than a bare list of author and reader names. See Also Audiobook editions and narrated versions Album artists and track artists Cast and crew credits Multi-valued metadata fields References Schema.org: Audiobook, author and reader roles Emby: Audiobook naming MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Audiobook organization | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Audiobook organization Audiobook organization relates a narrated edition to its ordered audio resources, descriptive credits and navigation without equating chapters with files. An audiobook is a narrated edition of a text, represented by one or more ordered audio resources. The author, narrator, edition and resource sequence all matter to how the library describes and plays it. The fictional novella The Lantern Keeper can be stored in one 90-minute audio file or in two 45-minute files. Those two storage arrangements do not, by themselves, define two different books. Files and chapters have different boundaries Arrangement Resource organisation Chapter navigation One file for the whole narration One resource timeline Needs embedded or otherwise associated chapter points One file per narrative chapter File boundaries coincide with chapter boundaries File selection can help locate chapters Several storage-sized parts Parts divide the recording for convenience Narrative chapters can cross a part boundary The third case is common enough to make “one file equals one chapter” an unreliable assumption. Calling a 45-minute part Chapter 2 can misdescribe it if it contains the end of one narrative chapter and the start of another. The .m4b extension commonly labels an MP4-based audiobook resource. It does not, by itself, prove that the file contains a correct chapter map. An MP3 can also carry chapter information through suitable metadata. Edition-level fields hold the sequence together A book title supplies the human-readable name. Edition context supplies language, narrator, abridgement and publication information. File/track positions supply the playback sequence. They have separate jobs. An illustrative directory communicates storage clearly: Elin Ward/ The Lantern Keeper — Nora Hale, unabridged/ Part 01.mp3 Part 02.mp3 This is an original descriptive layout, not a promise that every phrase becomes a dedicated imported field. Emby's audiobook naming documentation describes organisation and embedded chapter/track numbering; its Book Naming guide supplies the content-type context. Embedded titles and positions remain important when filenames are shortened, copied or changed. In a multi-disc source, the disc coordinate can qualify a restarted track counter. Alphabetical file sorting alone can put Part 10 before Part 2. Keep contributor roles visible Elin Ward wrote the book. Nora Hale reads this edition. A translated edition can add a translator. Those roles should not collapse into an unexplained Artist label. Some metadata conventions inherit fields originally designed for music. A reader interpreting them needs to know whether an artist-like field carries the author, narrator or album-level grouping credit. Narrator credits explains why that choice matters. An edition label also helps distinguish two recordings of the same text. A work title can remain unchanged while the narration language, performed duration or abridgement changes. Continuing a multipart narration A resume value of 16:00 in Part 02 corresponds to book minute 61 in the original two-part example: the first part contributes 45 minutes. The file-local position remains 16:00. Replacing the narration with another reader's edition changes the timing correspondence. A percentage through one performance does not automatically locate the same passage in another. A chapter identifier and a known textual location can provide better context than an unqualified elapsed-time value. Chapter structure develops the resource-local and whole-book coordinates using the same three-chapter example. See Also Audiobook editions and narrated versions Audiobook narrators and reader credits Audiobook chapter structure Resume positions and playback timelines References Emby: Audiobook naming Emby: Book naming and media types Schema.org: Audiobook, author and reader roles ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Overview: Books and spoken audio | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Overview: Books and spoken audio Book and spoken-audio libraries organize long-form works through editions, parts and navigable reading or listening structures. An audiobook, podcast episode and electronic book expose different kinds of structure. Narration, chapters, series relationships and page or archive organization influence how the work is identified and navigated. This area connects those models to the corresponding content, including comic archives. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Audiobooks Audiobook organization relates files and chapters to a particular edition and narrated performance. Podcasts Podcast catalogues connect a series and its feed to individually identified episode content. Electronic books An electronic book packages a publication’s text, layout and resources while catalogue identity, reading order and reader-generated pages remain distinct. Comic book archives A comic book archive packages page-image resources and optional descriptive metadata whose archive format, reading order and page roles require separate interpretation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C: EPUB 3.3 Emby: Book naming and media types

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Comic book archives: CBZ and CBR | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Comic book archives: CBZ and CBR A comic book archive packages page-image resources and optional descriptive metadata whose archive format, reading order and page roles require separate interpretation. A comic archive commonly stores a sequence of page images in one archive resource. CBZ conventionally uses ZIP; CBR uses RAR. The archive organises stored entries, while a comic reader interprets which images to display and in what sequence. Those are different jobs. Renaming a RAR archive to .cbz changes a filename, not its compression format. Archive, page image and presentation Layer Question it answers ZIP or RAR container How are the entries stored and retrieved? JPEG, PNG or another page-image format How is each picture encoded? Comic metadata Which issue, contributors and page roles are described? Reader presentation Which page, spread, direction and zoom are shown? Repackaging page entries can preserve their image bytes. Resizing or recompressing those images changes another layer. A reader's zoom changes the displayed view without rewriting the stored pages. Page order needs an agreement An original filename set demonstrates the issue: 1.jpg 2.jpg 10.jpg Simple lexical order places 10.jpg before 2.jpg . A natural-number sort can instead interpret the numbers. Zero-padded names make the intended sequence explicit for many lexical readers: 001.jpg 002.jpg 010.jpg An archive's internal entry order, filename order and metadata page order are not necessarily the same. The reader's actual policy determines which evidence it uses. Nested directories can introduce further grouping, so the complete paths matter as well as the basenames. A cover image can be part of the page sequence. Advertisements, title pages and double-page spreads can also be deliberate entries. Counting only story pages need not equal counting all stored images. Metadata describes the issue and its pages ComicInfo.xml is one used metadata convention, documented by the Anansi Project. An original small fragment is: <ComicInfo> <Title>The First Crossing</Title> <Series>Harbour Stories</Series> <Number>7</Number> <PageCount>3</PageCount> <Pages> <Page Image="0" Type="FrontCover" /> <Page Image="1" Type="Story" /> <Page Image="2" Type="Story" DoublePage="true" /> </Pages> </ComicInfo> Issue number 7 identifies a position in the described series. Image index 0 identifies a page resource in this page model. The first visible page can therefore be the cover of issue 7, not “issue 0” or “story page 7.” A double-page indication describes a spread role. It does not require every reader to display the same two-screen layout. A wide page image, page metadata and viewport policy each contribute to presentation. The fragment is an original descriptive example. Its presence does not guarantee that every library or reader imports all its fields. Image quality affects reading Small text and line art can be sensitive to source resolution and compression. Enlarging a low-resolution page does not recover missing lettering detail. Cropping a spread can remove part of the panel sequence. Image orientation and the reader's handling of it also matter. Metadata that directs a rotation is different from rewriting the stored pixels. Emby's Book Naming documentation includes CBR and CBZ among book resources. That recognition does not specify every reader's sorting, metadata or spread behavior. The archive format, ordered image resources and described page roles provide the information needed to interpret the publication. See Also Electronic books and reading resources Image resolution Image orientation Unicode metadata References PKWARE: ZIP file format specification RARLAB: RAR 5 archive format Anansi Project: ComicInfo fields Emby: Book naming and media types

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Electronic books and reading resources | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Electronic books and reading resources An electronic book packages a publication’s text, layout and resources while catalogue identity, reading order and reader-generated pages remain distinct. An electronic book is a publication represented by digital resources. Its title, author and edition describe the publication. The file format determines how text, images, styling and reading order are packaged. A reading system turns that information into the pages or views a person sees. That last step explains why a book's identity can remain the same while its displayed page count changes. Reflow and fixed presentation A reflowable publication allows text to adapt to the reading area and chosen font. Increasing the font size fits fewer words into each screenful; narrowing the reading area changes line breaks. A fixed-layout publication preserves an intended page composition. Enlarging it normally changes the scale or viewport rather than repaginating its text into another sequence.
