Observation What it can mean Page 42 becomes page 57 after a font change Reader-generated pagination changed The same chapter and passage remain visible Content location can remain stable A printed page number appears in the text or navigation The publication has supplied another numbering context A fixed page is cropped or zoomed Viewport and scale changed, not the publication's reading sequence A screen page number is therefore not a universal identifier for a passage in every reader. It needs its pagination context. EPUB packages relationships, not just files EPUB 3 uses web-based content and a defined container/package structure. An original illustrative resource layout is: mimetype META-INF/container.xml EPUB/package.opf EPUB/nav.xhtml EPUB/text/opening.xhtml EPUB/text/return.xhtml EPUB/styles/book.css EPUB/images/cover.jpg The container information identifies the package document. The package describes publication resources and default reading order. Individual content documents reference styling and other resources. A random ZIP containing HTML is not automatically a conforming EPUB. EPUB imposes additional structure and packaging requirements, including the special mimetype resource and its storage rules. The manifest and spine answer different questions The following original fragment focuses on two package relationships. Surrounding publication metadata and other required resources are omitted: <package xmlns="http://www.idpf.org/2007/opf" version="3.0" unique-identifier="book-id"> <manifest> <item id="ending" href="text/return.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml" /> <item id="opening" href="text/opening.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml" /> </manifest> <spine> <itemref idref="opening" /> <itemref idref="ending" /> </spine> </package> The manifest lists resources by identity. The spine references them in the intended order: opening, then ending. The fact that the manifest lists ending first does not prescribe that as the reading sequence. Likewise, sorting filenames in the archive is not a substitute for resolving the spine. Navigation can provide a chapter menu, while the spine defines the default progression through content. Those functions can agree without being identical. The excerpt is well-formed XML, not a complete valid EPUB package. A package that references a missing content document can remain syntactically readable while failing to resolve its publication resources. Locations should refer to content A chapter/document reference can locate a broad part of the publication. A structural fragment or a scheme such as EPUB CFI can refer more precisely to content within it. Such a reference is more useful for carrying a reading position across a font or viewport change than an unqualified screen-page number. It still belongs to a particular document structure and publication context. Revising the text can require correspondence or recovery rather than blindly reusing an old offset. ISBN supplies edition/format identity in a publication system. It does not encode a paragraph position or determine how a reader paginates that edition. Catalogue, container processor and reader A library can catalogue a book file, extract descriptive metadata or offer the resource for use elsewhere. A reading system has additional work: interpret its content documents, layout, navigation and supported interactive features. The EPUB reading-system specification explicitly distinguishes container processing from complete reading-system behavior. This helps explain why recognising an EPUB is a different capability from rendering its full publication. Emby's Book Naming guide lists recognised electronic-book formats and library conventions. Format recognition should be understood in that resource/catalogue scope; available reading behavior depends on the consuming app or workflow. For the original package fragment, a reader resolves the opening content before the ending content. The same publication can then produce different screen pages in a narrow phone view and a wide desktop view while preserving that reading order. See Also Audiobook editions and narrated versions Comic book archives: CBZ and CBR Media item identity Unicode metadata References W3C: EPUB 3.3 W3C: EPUB Reading Systems 3.3 IDPF: EPUB Canonical Fragment Identifiers 1.1 International ISBN Agency: What an ISBN identifies Emby: Book naming and media types PKWARE: ZIP file format specification

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Overview: Podcasts | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Overview: Podcasts Podcast catalogues connect a series and its feed to individually identified episode content. A feed supplies more than a current list of audio URLs. Series information and episode identifiers help a consumer recognize continuing content as the feed changes. These pages explain those relationships, which matter when an episode moves, is republished or appears in several observations. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Podcast series A podcast series relates published episode records to a show identity while feeds, release ordering and downloaded audio supply different parts of the catalogue. Podcast RSS feeds A podcast RSS feed publishes show and episode metadata with media enclosure references that clients can discover separately from downloading or playing the media. Podcast episode identifiers A podcast episode identifier preserves a published item’s identity across descriptive and delivery changes without equating that identity with a filename or media hash. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library setup

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Podcast episode identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Podcast episode identifiers A podcast episode identifier preserves a published item’s identity across descriptive and delivery changes without equating that identity with a filename or media hash. An episode identifier lets a client recognise a published programme after its title, description or media location changes. It supplies continuity that a display title cannot. RSS calls the field guid . Despite the name, its value need not be a UUID. RSS defines it as a string; when isPermaLink="false" , the reader should not assume it is a web address. The original Harbour Notes example uses: <guid isPermaLink="false">harbour-notes:episode:001</guid> The text is an invented opaque key. A publisher needs an appropriate uniqueness scope; a client retains the relevant feed/subscription context as well as the key. The locator can change while the episode stays the same Observation GUID Media locator Meaning in this original model Initial publication episode:001 Host A / file A First observed record Title correction and host migration episode:001 Host B / file B Updated record for the same identified episode Same programme reintroduced under another GUID episode:099 Host B / file B Another published identity requiring interpretation The table abbreviates the invented keys and locators. It is not a real feed history. A client that keys records by stable GUID can update the second row without creating another episode. If it keys only by locator, the migration can look like a new programme. If a GUID changes, an identifier-based client can treat the third row as another record even when the media bytes agree. Actual duplicate handling can use more evidence. The table explains the identity boundary rather than predicting every client's result. Stability supports continuity Apple Podcasts requires episode GUIDs that do not change. This is a concrete example of an ecosystem relying on identifier persistence. A corrected title should not force a viewer's listened state to become unrelated to the episode. A signed delivery URL can change for access reasons without being a useful programme identifier. A filename can change when the recording is downloaded to another device. A GUID supplied as a permalink has different declared behavior. RSS's default isPermaLink value is true; explicitly false is important when the key is not a usable episode page URL. Episode identity is not byte or timeline identity A stable published identity can accompany a replacement audio resource. A publisher may correct audio or change inserted material while retaining the programme record. A complete-file hash would notice changed bytes, but it answers a resource question. A resume value needs the corresponding media timeline. If the replacement inserts a minute before the saved point, retaining the episode identity does not supply an automatic timestamp conversion. For a downloaded episode added to an Emby library, the file's catalogue identity and the publisher's GUID can be separate relationships. A reliable workflow preserves whichever context it needs rather than assuming the local path reconstructs the publisher's identifier. See Also Podcast RSS feeds Podcast series and episode organisation Media item identity Resume positions and playback timelines References RSS Advisory Board: RSS 2.0 specification Apple Podcasts: RSS feed requirements

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Podcast RSS feeds | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Podcast RSS feeds A podcast RSS feed publishes show and episode metadata with media enclosure references that clients can discover separately from downloading or playing the media. A podcast feed is a document that describes a show and its published episodes. It normally contains references to media rather than the media bytes themselves. A client reads the feed to discover an episode, then retrieves the referenced resource when it needs a download or playback. RSS 2.0 supplies a general syndication structure. Podcast ecosystems add conventions and requirements around audio/video enclosures, artwork, episode roles and delivery. A small original feed This example uses a fictional show, episode and non-operational example host: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <rss version="2.0"> <channel> <title>Harbour Notes</title> <link>https://example.invalid/harbour-notes</link> <description>Conversations about journeys by water.</description> <item> <title>The First Crossing</title> <description>A conversation with the harbour pilot.</description> <guid isPermaLink="false">harbour-notes:episode:001</guid> <pubDate>Sat, 10 Oct 2026 08:00:00 +0000</pubDate> <enclosure url="https://media.example.invalid/harbour-01.mp3" length="36000000" type="audio/mpeg" /> </item> </channel> </rss> The channel fields describe the show. The item fields describe one episode. The enclosure points to that episode's media. There is no MP3 payload embedded in this XML. The fixture demonstrates base RSS structure; it is not a submitted feed or a complete claim of compatibility with every podcast directory. Three enclosure fields, three meanings Attribute in the example Meaning url The media locator to retrieve length Declared size in bytes: 36,000,000 type Declared media type: audio/mpeg The length is not 36 million seconds or a playback duration. Dividing a byte size by an assumed bitrate can produce an estimate, but the feed's enclosure length alone does not establish the recording's timing. Likewise, the MIME type is a declaration about the resource. A client can use it to choose handling, while technical inspection provides evidence about the actual bytes and streams. The episode's web-page link, if supplied, has another role from its enclosure URL. A page describing the programme is not automatically the audio resource. XML syntax and feed meaning The example's element names are case-sensitive. Text characters that have XML syntax meaning must be represented appropriately: an ampersand in literal text needs an entity such as & . A document can be well-formed XML while omitting required RSS channel information or declaring an enclosure that does not exist. XML parsing establishes syntax; RSS validation establishes document structure; media retrieval establishes another dependency. Podcast-specific requirements add further distinctions. Apple Podcasts, for example, documents stable episode identifiers and enclosure/delivery requirements. Those requirements belong to that ecosystem; they are more specific than merely being able to parse RSS. Additional namespaced elements can describe concepts that base RSS does not define. A namespace identifies their vocabulary. A reader that does not understand a particular extension cannot necessarily use its semantic detail just because the XML is well-formed. Discovery and retrieval can fail independently A feed can be readable while its media host is unavailable. Its episode description can remain visible while a download fails. Conversely, an existing local download can play while the publisher's current feed cannot be fetched. A hosting or delivery change can also update the locator without creating a new episode identity. Episode identifiers explains why the media URL and GUID must not be treated as interchangeable fields. For clients that seek or inspect remote resources, delivery behavior matters. Apple documents support for HEAD and byte-range requests in its podcast requirements. A server returning an episode's full bytes for ordinary download is not the same capability as serving an efficient requested byte range. Those network operations do not alter the episode's story identity. They concern access to its current media representation. Polling updates a published view Reading a feed periodically reveals what the publisher currently exposes. It need not enumerate every episode ever published. A shortened feed can omit older records even when a client still has their downloads or history. Updating a subscription therefore requires retaining identity and state beyond the current document when that is part of the client's intended model. Treating every omitted old item as proof that its local recording vanished confuses publication view with storage inventory. An Emby scan of downloaded resources answers a storage/catalogue question. Polling the publisher's RSS answers a publication-discovery question. A workflow can connect them, but they do not become the same operation because both can reveal a new episode. See Also Podcast series and episode organisation Podcast episode identifiers Technical analysis of library media Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References RSS Advisory Board: RSS 2.0 specification Apple Podcasts: RSS feed requirements

articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.title: Podcast series and episode organisation | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/books-spo.keywords: Podcast series and episode organisation A podcast series relates published episode records to a show identity while feeds, release ordering and downloaded audio supply different parts of the catalogue. A podcast series supplies the shared identity and description for published episodes. An episode record describes one programme; its media resource contains the sound or video. A feed distributes those records so a client can discover additions and updates. For the fictional Harbour Notes , the chain is: show: Harbour Notes -> episode: The First Crossing -> published media reference -> downloaded audio resource The show's title and artwork describe the series. The episode's title and description describe its content. The download's file size and codec describe the stored resource. Publication order and listening order Programme pattern Useful starting order Additional context Independent weekly conversations Newest release may be most relevant Topics remain independently understandable A continuing documentary story Story sequence may begin at episode 1 Season and episode relationships matter A feed mixing full episodes and trailers Role-aware selection A trailer is not another full story episode Revised or reissued programmes Publisher identity and edition context A new date need not mean a new underlying story A feed can list recent items first without prescribing that as the story's intended sequence. A serial production can require earlier episodes even when a newly published item is easy to discover. A show can also expose different distributions: a public feed, an alternate-language edition or another programme selection. Sharing branding does not prove their episode records and audio are identical. Downloaded and listened are separate states A client may know an episode is published but not have downloaded it. It may have a local file that is still unplayed. It may retain listening progress while an old download has been removed. These states answer different questions. Subscription discovery finds published records. Resource availability establishes whether playback can access the media. User history describes what this listener has done. A locally stored episode brought into an Emby library has a resource and descriptive context. Recognising that audio does not, by itself, recover its original feed, subscription state or stable publisher episode identifier. Those relationships need to be retained by the workflow that supplies the resource. Episode descriptions evolve A publisher can correct a title or synopsis while keeping the episode identity. The identifier lets a client recognise the updated record rather than relying entirely on a display title. The RSS feed carries the discovery and media-reference information. The actual codec and playable duration still come from the media resource; a show-level description cannot supply them. See Also Podcast RSS feeds Podcast episode identifiers Series, seasons and episodes User-specific playback history References RSS Advisory Board: RSS 2.0 specification Apple Podcasts: RSS feed requirements Emby: Library setup

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Overview: Library concepts | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Overview: Library concepts Library concepts describe how a catalogue identifies, groups and presents media independently of its physical file layout. A folder tree is one way to store a collection; a library adds item identities, content models and relationships that can span that tree. Collections and playlists then organize items for different purposes. These concepts explain what the viewer is navigating before any particular movie, album or series convention is applied. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is a media library? A media library is a catalogue that relates media resources to descriptive information, browsing views and playback state. Library content models A library content model determines which entities and relationships a catalogue expects to find in a media collection. Virtual library organization Virtual library organization builds browsing views from catalogue relationships without requiring the media files to share the same folder layout. Media item identity Media item identity distinguishes a catalogue entry, the work or episode it describes, and the particular resources that can play it. Collections A media collection groups catalogue items by a chosen relationship without requiring their files to share a directory. Playlists A playlist stores an ordered sequence of media references whose entries can differ from the distinct media items they point to. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library setup Emby API: Item information Emby: Collections Emby API: Playlist entries

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Media collections | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Media collections A media collection groups catalogue items by a chosen relationship without requiring their files to share a directory. A collection gives a selection of library items a name and a shared place to browse. It can represent a film series, a director retrospective or a personally curated theme. The important resource is the membership relationship: each listed member still refers to its own catalogue item. For example, Night Ferry can belong to a River stories collection and a Director retrospective . Its film description need not be copied into two independent movie records. Collection Members in this fictional example Reason for grouping River stories Night Ferry, The Lockkeeper Subject chosen by the curator Director retrospective Night Ferry, Platform Nine A credited director Harbour Trilogy Harbour I, Harbour II, Harbour III A series of related films The first two are interpretations of a catalogue; the third could correspond to a provider's recognized movie collection. The file paths do not determine any of these memberships. The group can have its own description A collection's title, overview and artwork describe the group. A movie's title, synopsis and poster describe the member. That distinction lets a collection introduce a retrospective without rewriting every film's synopsis. The group can also be incomplete. Owning two films from a three-film collection does not imply the third resource exists. A provider's collection membership describes a catalogue relationship; the library's available members describe what this server can present. Emby supports both manual collections and automatic movie collection creation from imported information. The Collections support page describes those controls. A meaningful automatic group relies on the imported relationship, rather than inferring a franchise from every shared word in a title. Automatic and curated membership answer different questions Membership basis What it is trying to express Why it may change Imported provider relationship A collection recognized by that catalogue Provider corrections, matching changes or refresh behavior Manual selection The curator's intended set Someone edits the membership Search/filter result Items satisfying current field conditions Fields or filtering conditions change A collection named Films set by the sea may intentionally include a documentary and a drama. It need not coincide with any provider's franchise model. Imported franchise information is equally unlikely to know that this viewer has chosen a special weekend programme. A playlist is useful when that programme needs a playback sequence. A collection primarily says “these belong together”; a playlist makes ordering and individual entries part of the selection. The distinction remains useful even if an app can play all members of a collection. Removing a membership and deleting a media item are different concepts. The former changes the group's contents; the latter affects the resource or its catalogue entry. See Also Virtual library organization Media playlists Film franchises in a media library References Emby: Collections Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Library content models | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Library content models A library content model determines which entities and relationships a catalogue expects to find in a media collection. A content model tells a library what kinds of things exist and how they fit together. A television model expects series, seasons and episodes. A movie model expects films and their playable sources. A music model needs relationships among tracks, albums and credited artists. This affects recognition, metadata scope and browsing. It is more consequential than choosing a different icon for the same pile of files. One directory, two interpretations Imagine this fictional directory: Harbour Watch (2020)/ Season 1/ Harbour Watch S01E01.mkv Harbour Watch S01E02.mkv Under an episodic model, the outer name supplies series context and the two files represent children within a season. A series poster belongs to the parent; an episode still and episode title belong to one child. The number 01 only makes sense within its season and series. Under a general video model, the same paths might simply identify two independent videos. Their shared directory does not, by itself, establish which catalogue series they are episodes of. That reading may suit personal footage, but it loses relationships needed for season browsing and next-episode selection. Emby's library setup documentation describes content types and the limited mixed-content option. A mixed folder does not make all of the specialized models equally available: the server still needs sufficient structure to interpret each resource. Entities have different scopes Observation A useful entity relationship What goes wrong if flattened Twelve episodes belong to one series Episode → season → series The series is repeated as twelve unrelated titles Two encodes represent the same cut Media sources → one movie item The movie appears twice instead of offering a source choice One album has several tracks Track → album, with artist credits Album identity is confused with each track's performer A trailer promotes a feature Supplement → parent movie A short promotional video is mistaken for another full movie These are explanatory relationships, not an Emby schema definition. Public models such as Schema.org's Movie and TVSeries describe some of the same distinctions; Emby's item API exposes its own item types, parent relationships and media-source information. A parent entity need not be a playable file. A series page represents the show and organizes episodes. Conversely, one playable file may cover more than one episode . “One object equals one file” cannot describe both cases. Matching needs a model before it needs a title A catalogue search for a film named The Crossing asks a different question from a search for the episode with that title in Harbour Watch . For the episode, the series identity, season and selected episode order supply much stronger context than the title alone. Technical properties do not resolve that meaning. A probe can establish that a file contains 42 minutes of H.264 video; it cannot infer from the codec whether the resource is an episode, a concert or a home video. The same principle applies to field inheritance. A series overview describes the series, not every episode's plot. A shared studio credit may be relevant at the series level, while an episode guest credit belongs to a specific episode. Copying all parent data to all children creates plausible-looking but inaccurate descriptions. Physical nesting is evidence, not the entire model Folders and filenames help communicate relationships, but a catalogue can also express associations that have no corresponding storage directory. Genres, credits and collection memberships cross those boundaries. A content model combines those descriptive relationships with the resource structure instead of requiring every view to reproduce the disk layout. For the Harbour Watch directory, the decisive result is an episode associated with the correct series and season. Its codec is a property of the playable source; the parent relationship gives the programme its place in the catalogue. See Also What is a media library? Series, seasons and episodes Media item identity References Emby: Library setup Schema.org: Television series relationships Schema.org: Movie relationships Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Media item identity | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Media item identity Media item identity distinguishes a catalogue entry, the work or episode it describes, and the particular resources that can play it. “What is the same movie?” has several answers. Two titles may describe the same work. Two encodes may preserve the same cut. Two paths may lead to identical bytes. Two server entries may nevertheless have separate internal identities. A useful identity decision begins by stating which of those things should be the same. Without that scope, a duplicate check can collapse an extended edition into a theatrical release, or preserve two accidental copies as if they were different films. Four identities in one movie library Consider the fictional film Night Ferry : Scope Example identifier What it identifies Catalogue work A movie provider's qualified movie ID The film record in that provider's catalogue Edition Theatrical or extended cut A particular editorial version of the work Media resource Source F1, with its path and stream details One playable representation of an edition Server item Item M1 on server S1 An entry through which this server presents the movie The labels M1, S1 and F1 are invented for this explanation. They are not a proposed database layout. Two encodes of the theatrical cut can share a work identity and edition identity while having different resource identities. The extended cut can share the work identity while differing in content and timeline. A provider that has only one film record may not supply a separate ID for every cut. In Emby's API, an item has an Id and can expose ProviderIds and MediaSources . The source information has its own Id , Path and technical description. These fields express distinct purposes. The presence of an ID does not promise that it survives every import, deletion, server rebuild or change of storage layout. A title is a label, not a primary key A title can change with language, preferred presentation or correction. Two unrelated works can also have the same title and year. Even a title/year pair is matching evidence rather than a universal identifier. A provider identifier must retain its namespace and entity type. The number 12345 from one provider is not equivalent to 12345 from another. A series ID is not an episode ID, even when an interface presents both as numbers. The library's own item ID has another scope. It identifies the object used by that server API, not a global catalogue work. Copying an item ID into another independent server is not a dependable way to identify the same film there. This matters for history transfer. A source-server ID can locate the old record; a qualified provider ID can help locate a candidate on the destination. The transfer still has to account for entity type and edition. A resume point needs an even more precise match because it refers to a particular timeline. What a fingerprint proves Different identity checks answer different questions: Evidence Useful conclusion Remaining uncertainty Same path string The stored locator text agrees The bytes may have been replaced; the path may resolve differently on another machine Same file size and modification time A cheap change signature agrees Different content can share both values Same cryptographic hash over complete files Extremely strong evidence of byte equality The files' catalogue meaning still needs interpretation Similar audio/video fingerprint Portions may contain the same perceptual content Another cut, excerpt or re-encode may also match Same provider work ID Both descriptions refer to that provider's work record Edition, encode and local-item relationships can still differ SHA-256, specified in the Secure Hash Standard, hashes a byte sequence. Changing a container tag or artwork attachment can change the complete-file hash without changing the film's pictures and sound. Re-encoding the same cut will ordinarily change it too. A byte comparison is excellent for identifying copied files; it is the wrong test for deciding whether two encodes should be alternate sources of one movie. Likewise, similarity is useful evidence rather than an automatic merge decision. A trailer contains excerpts from the feature. An audio fingerprint could find shared passages, but that does not make the trailer another full version of the film. Identity continuity after a change Suppose F1 moves from Disk A to Disk B. The underlying cut can remain the same while the path changes. A catalogue may update a locator, or may recognize a removed resource and a new resource through other evidence. The resulting item/history behavior depends on its reconciliation rules. Replacing F1 with a corrected encode introduces another case. The same work and cut may remain, but duration, stream indexes, seek previews or cached analysis may need updating. Replacing it with an extended cut changes the timeline as well: retaining a 70-minute resume value does not preserve the same scene. For a migration, the meaningful question is therefore more detailed than “Did the title appear?” It is whether the destination preserved the intended work match, source relationships and viewer state at the right scope. Emby's metadata manager discusses how identifying information can affect library behavior; its documentation should guide product-specific correction workflows. A practical identity test For two entries, state the intended relationship before looking for matching evidence: Same bytes: compare the actual resources, not just the posters. Same cut, different encode: compare edition and timeline, then technical differences. Same work, different cut: retain the edition distinction even if a provider ID agrees. Related work or supplement: express that relationship instead of treating it as sameness. See Also Provider identifiers Media identification Movie editions and cuts Alternate media versions Duplicate library entries User-specific playback history References Emby API: Item information Emby API: BaseItemDto Emby API: MediaSourceInfo NIST: Secure Hash Standard, FIPS 180-4 Emby: Metadata manager

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: What is a media library? | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: What is a media library? A media library is a catalogue that relates media resources to descriptive information, browsing views and playback state. Put two encodes of a movie on a disk and the file manager shows two files. A media library can present one movie, offer a choice of versions, attach its poster and synopsis, and remember where a particular viewer stopped. The library supplies the relationships that a directory listing does not. In Emby, a configured library brings one or more physical folders into a browsing area with a content type. The folders contain the resources; the server builds a catalogue from what it finds. That distinction explains how films spread across two disks can appear together without copying them onto one disk. The diagram is an original conceptual model. It does not reproduce Emby's database tables. What the catalogue adds A file has a path, a size and encoded streams. A library item has meaning: a movie, an episode, a song or a photograph. Its metadata can supply names, credits and relationships. Technical analysis supplies details such as duration and audio tracks. Those descriptions make different questions possible. “What is in this directory?” asks about storage. “Which unwatched dramas were released in the 1990s?” asks about catalogue fields and a viewer's history. A poster grid answers the second kind of question even when its items occupy unrelated directories. The item also connects browsing to playback. Choosing a movie leads to an available media source; selecting a subtitle track refers to that source's streams. An attractive catalogue entry and a playable resource are separate pieces of the same system. Three changes, three different results Add another encode. The bytes on disk increase. If the new file is recognized as an alternate version, the movie count need not increase. The item gains another source. Add a movie to a collection. Its grouping changes. Its file can remain exactly where it was, and the movie can still appear in the main movie view. Collections add membership rather than another copy of the film. Disconnect a disk. A stored description does not make its media readable. Depending on the server's scan and availability behavior, an entry may remain temporarily or change during reconciliation. Its poster is evidence that an item was catalogued, not evidence that every source is currently reachable. See Also Library content models Virtual library organization Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References Emby: Library setup Emby API: Item information

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Media playlists | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Media playlists A playlist stores an ordered sequence of media references whose entries can differ from the distinct media items they point to. Consider this short listening sequence: Entry Media item Duration Start in the sequence P1 Track A 3:20 0:00 P2 Track B 2:40 3:20 P3 Track A again 3:20 6:00 The programme lasts 9:20. It contains three entries but only two distinct songs. That difference is central to a playlist: an entry is an occurrence in a sequence, while an item is the media that occurrence refers to. A list model can represent repeats; the editing and playback behavior of a particular server or app determines whether it retains them. Emby's playlist-items API distinguishes a returned item's identity from its PlaylistItemId . That provides context for operations on a playlist occurrence rather than on the song itself. Order is part of the meaning Moving P3 before P2 changes the listening sequence without changing either audio file. Removing P1 can leave the later occurrence of Track A in a list that supports repeated entries. Deleting Track A's resource affects both references. This is different from a collection , where the primary statement is membership. A playlist can express a concert set, a sequence of exercises or a particular introduction to an artist. Its arrangement can be as important as the chosen items. A reference still needs to resolve A playlist may refer to local files by path, or to server catalogue items by ID. A file path is portable only where the same path meaning exists. A server item ID is meaningful only in the relevant server catalogue. An exported list can therefore preserve its labels while losing the ability to locate the resources elsewhere. Some formats include both descriptive information and a location. The XSPF specification also provides identifiers and alternative location information to help resolve tracks. Those format capabilities explain why a playlist is more than a line of display text; they do not establish which formats Emby imports in every version. A stored song title alone is an especially weak locator. Two performances can have the same title, and a translated or corrected label can change. Media identity remains important even for a small list. Saved playlist and playback queue The saved playlist describes the reusable sequence. The active queue describes the present playback session. Shuffling or skipping entries can affect the queue without necessarily editing the saved playlist. Likewise, a queue can contain an item added for this session that was never part of the stored list. These states can diverge while both remain correct. The listener may want today's shuffled order and still expect tomorrow's playback to start with the original programme. Whether an interface saves a queue change is a product behavior, so the meaningful distinction is the state being changed. Availability is evaluated at playback time. A referenced item can be temporarily unreachable, removed, or inaccessible to the current user. The sequence may still be intact as a description even when one entry cannot be played. See Also Media collections Media item identity References Emby API: Playlist entries XSPF version 1 playlist specification

articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.title: Virtual library organization | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/concepts/.keywords: Virtual library organization Virtual library organization builds browsing views from catalogue relationships without requiring the media files to share the same folder layout. A virtual view organizes what the catalogue knows. It can gather films from several disks, show titles by genre, or place the same movie in two collections. The storage directory does not have to reproduce each of those arrangements. Suppose three fictional movies occupy these locations: Movie Physical source Relevant description Night Ferry Disk A, Movies/2020 Drama; a river journey Platform Nine Disk B, Archive/2018 Drama; a railway story Mountain Road Disk A, Movies/2022 Documentary; a journey A Late-night drama collection might contain Night Ferry and Platform Nine. A Journeys collection might contain Night Ferry and Mountain Road. Night Ferry has two memberships and still only one physical source in this example. Membership, filtering and sorting do different work A collection records an association: these items belong together. A genre view selects items whose genre field matches a value. A sort changes the order of the selected results. Changing Night Ferry's genre can therefore change a genre view without changing a manually chosen collection membership. Changing its sort title can move it within a view without changing either membership or location. This is why virtual organization depends on consistent metadata. If two descriptions use Science Fiction and Sci-Fi as unrelated values, an interface may expose two groups. The physical folders cannot repair that semantic mismatch; the catalogue needs a way to align the labels. Emby merges the contents of a library's configured paths into a virtual display. Its movie documentation also distinguishes metadata-based browsing from the Folders view, which exposes the physical organization. Both can be useful: the former answers questions about the films, the latter about where the resources are stored. A display boundary is not automatically an access boundary Arrangement Its main purpose Separate question Physical directory Locate resources Can the server read it? Configured library Define a catalogue area and its content interpretation Which users can access that library? Collection or genre view Group or select catalogue items Are the underlying items accessible to this viewer? Playlist Specify a sequence of item references Can each entry be played now? An attractive Children's favourites collection describes an editorial choice. The name alone does not establish an access policy. Actual visibility depends on the server's user and content rules. Virtual organization makes changing perspectives inexpensive: a film can be part of a franchise, a director retrospective and a personal weekend selection at once. Those are relationships to the same item, so editing its description need not require finding and updating three copied files. See Also Media collections Library content models Faceted browsing References Emby: Library setup Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby: Collections

articles/libraries-collections/history/i.title: Overview: Playback history | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/i.keywords: Overview: Playback history Playback history records user-specific observations and state across media items and sessions. Watched status, a resume position and a play count describe different aspects of a user's activity. Next-episode selection can use that state together with the series model. This group explains those relationships so one user's view of the collection is not mistaken for a permanent property of the media file. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Watched status Watched status records a user’s played classification for a media item separately from its resume position or a complete record of viewed content. Resume positions A resume position is a saved media-time location that needs the correct user, item and source timeline to continue playback meaningfully. Play counts A play count is an accumulated application-defined measure whose interpretation depends on the events and state rules used to update it. User-specific playback history User-specific playback history relates viewing state to a viewer and media identity while shared catalogue descriptions remain separate. Next-episode selection Next-episode selection combines an intended episode sequence, user state and resource availability to choose a continuation candidate. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: Item information Emby API: Next Up episodes

articles/libraries-collections/history/L.title: Next-episode selection | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/L.keywords: Next-episode selection Next-episode selection combines an intended episode sequence, user state and resource availability to choose a continuation candidate. “Next episode” can mean the next story in sequence, the next available unwatched item, or the partly watched episode that the viewer should finish first. These meanings often agree, but the differences explain many apparently odd continuation choices. A selection needs three kinds of evidence: the intended episode order , this viewer's state, and the available resources. Incrementing a filename's number considers only part of the first. A worked continuation set Use this original fictional sequence: Sequence position Item This user's state Resource available 1 S01E01 Played Yes 2 S01E02 Played Yes 3 S00E01, a bridge special Played Yes 4 S01E03 Unplayed, resume 12:10 Yes 5 S01E04 Unplayed No 6 S01E05 Unplayed Yes A policy that continues an unfinished episode would select S01E03 at its saved point. That selection occurs before deciding what to do about the missing S01E04. This diagram is a teaching model, not Emby's Next Up algorithm or a measured app result. Missing and later are different properties After S01E03 is marked played, two reasonable policies diverge: Preserve story succession: identify S01E04 as next and communicate that its resource is missing. Choose the next playable candidate: omit unavailable resources and offer S01E05. The second policy can make playback convenient while skipping narrative content. The first can retain continuity while offering nothing playable immediately. The decision concerns availability and intended behavior, not whether the episode numbering was parsed correctly. A filtered catalogue can create a similar effect. An episode absent from one user's accessible candidates is not necessarily absent from storage. The selection's user and library scope therefore matter. Specials supply placement, not arithmetic The bridge special in the example belongs after E02 despite its season-zero coordinate. A numeric season/episode sort would place it elsewhere. A defined placement relationship is needed to include it in the intended story sequence. Television specials explains that distinction. A selection can choose to include relevant specials while excluding supplementary programmes; both decisions require knowing their roles. Likewise, an alternate episode order can reorder the stories or change their segmentation. “Next number” has meaning only within the arrangement actually represented by the catalogue and files. Continuation is not general discovery A newly added episode can be recent without being the next story for this viewer. A recommendation can suggest a different series without continuing the current one. An upcoming catalogue description can have no local playable resource yet. Emby's Next Up API returns episode candidates in a user context and exposes series and parent filtering. That interface establishes the feature's scope; it does not publish every detail of eligibility and ranking. See Also Understanding episode order Television specials Watched status Resume positions and playback timelines References Emby API: Next Up episodes Emby: Ordering television specials Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/history/L.title: Media play counts | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/L.keywords: Media play counts A play count is an accumulated application-defined measure whose interpretation depends on the events and state rules used to update it. A play count stores an accumulated number associated with media use. Its exact meaning depends on the application's update rules: a playback start, sufficient progress, completion, an imported value or an explicit state update can be relevant in different systems. The field name alone does not define which rule applies. Emby's user-item model exposes a nullable PlayCount separately from played status and the last-played date. Value or field What can be concluded Count 3 The stored counter is three under the system's rules Count 0 A zero was supplied or retained Missing/null count No count value was supplied at this interface Last-played date One latest recorded date, if available Played flag A current played classification Treating null as zero erases the difference between “known zero” and “not supplied.” A total cannot reconstruct its events A count of three does not tell us whether the events occurred yesterday, across three years, or before a history import. It cannot reveal how much of the programme was viewed or which source was used. Even count 3 plus one last-played date leaves the earlier dates unknown. Those events require a separate history record if an application wants to reconstruct them. Consider a fictional migration that imports count 3 for a film seen elsewhere. The number can faithfully preserve a previous counter without proving three local streaming sessions occurred on this server. The useful comparison keeps the definition Play counts can help a listener find frequently revisited music or contribute evidence to a recommendation system. Comparing them is meaningful only when the counting conventions and scope agree. A counter for one user differs from a household total. A song-play definition differs from a film-completion definition. A change in event rules can also make an old and new count difficult to compare directly. The public Emby API exposes both played-state operations and user-data updates, but their existence does not specify every automatic counter transition. For a precise interpretation, use the relevant implementation/version's behavior rather than equating the counter with completed screenings. See Also Watched status User-specific playback history Recommendation systems for media References Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: Updating user item data Emby API: Marking an item as played

articles/libraries-collections/history/L.title: Resume positions and playback timelines | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/L.keywords: Resume positions and playback timelines A resume position is a saved media-time location that needs the correct user, item and source timeline to continue playback meaningfully. A resume position identifies a location on a media timeline. It is useful only with the context needed to interpret it: the viewer, the catalogue item and the represented source or edition. A value of 36:30 means “36 minutes 30 seconds into this timeline.” It does not mean the viewer spent that long watching, and it is not a wall-clock time. A stored value and its unit Emby's user-item model exposes PlaybackPositionTicks . Its playback-progress model reports PositionTicks with item and media-source information. The tick convention uses 100-nanosecond units, or ten million ticks per second. For a fictional position of 36:30: 36 × 60 + 30 = 2,190 seconds 2,190 × 10,000,000 = 21,900,000,000 ticks The reverse calculation divides by 10,000,000, then formats 2,190 seconds as 36:30. A tick count does not become milliseconds merely because it is an integer. Value Meaning 21,900,000,000 ticks 2,190 seconds under this convention 2,190,000 milliseconds The same interval in another unit 36:30 A human-readable location A calendar timestamp An instant when an event happened, not this location The unit's fine resolution does not prove that playback or saved state is accurate to 100 nanoseconds. The player, reporting frequency and media timestamps impose their own practical precision. The server saves reported state A player knows its current location during playback. A server can save only the information it receives and accepts. Imagine this original reporting sequence: A progress update at media position 36:10 reaches the server. Playback continues to 36:30. The app disappears before its final update is received. The last known saved point can remain 20 seconds behind the viewer's stopping point. That result does not require a codec error: the state report was simply older than the final player state. The times and lost report are fictional. They do not specify an Emby reporting interval, retry policy or failure rate. A normal stop report can provide a more recent position. Repeated or delayed reports require session-aware handling so that old state does not accidentally replace newer state. The public API describes report fields; it does not fully specify the server's conflict-resolution algorithm. Seeking is a second source of difference Even with the correct saved value, a decoder may need to begin reading before the requested picture. Compressed video often uses earlier reference pictures, so random access can start at an appropriate keyframe or access point . A player can decode forward and discard earlier output to reach the target, or choose a nearby practical position depending on the playback path. Reading from an earlier access point and having an older saved resume point are different mechanisms, even if both appear as “it resumed too early.” Container timestamp origins and time bases add another conversion boundary. A stored media location must be interpreted against the relevant source timeline rather than copied as a raw packet timestamp. Elapsed viewing time is another quantity Pause for ten minutes and the wall clock advances while the media position stays still. Play at double speed and 20 minutes of media can advance in about ten minutes of uninterrupted wall-clock playback. Seek forward and the media position jumps without viewing the skipped passage. A resume value therefore describes where to continue, not how much content was consumed. Watched status and viewing-duration analytics need their own definitions. A source change can invalidate correspondence Two encodes of an unchanged sequence can have corresponding locations, but a different cut may not. In the edition example , a 13-minute insert moves the scene at theatrical minute 70 to extended minute 83. The number 70 remains valid in the new file while referring to the wrong scene. Changing a multipart representation can also require converting between a whole-feature time and a part-local time. Removing opening material changes subsequent offsets. No work-level provider ID supplies those mappings. See Also Watched status User-specific playback history Movie editions and cuts Multipart movies and file stacking Time Bases Video Keyframes and Random Access References Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: Playback progress reporting Microsoft: TimeSpan tick units Emby API: MediaSourceInfo FFmpeg: Seeking and media processing

articles/libraries-collections/history/L.title: User-specific playback history | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/L.keywords: User-specific playback history User-specific playback history relates viewing state to a viewer and media identity while shared catalogue descriptions remain separate. A movie's title and runtime describe the media. Its watched flag and resume position describe a viewer's relationship to that media. Two people can therefore browse the same catalogue item while seeing different progress. Emby's item API can return user-context information, and its user-data operations include a user identity as well as an item identity. That is a separate scope from shared descriptive metadata. The matrix is an original conceptual example. It does not specify Emby's database keys or every rule by which multiple versions share state. A shared description, several personal states Change Relevant scope Correct the movie's original title Catalogue description Record Dana's stopping point Dana's playback state for the relevant media Record Noor's played classification Noor's playback state Replace the source with another cut Resource/edition identity and any dependent state Change the displayed sort order A presentation preference or query A shared catalogue correction does not mean both users stopped at the same position. A personal played flag does not change the film's credits. Resource and presentation grouping can also affect state scope. If several versions share a logical media identity or history association, selecting a different source need not create an independent personal history record. A different cut still presents the timeline correspondence problem , even when the work-level watched classification is shared. The viewer is not the device Using the same account on a television and a phone gives the server a common user context. Switching devices need not mean switching histories. Conversely, two people using one account report into that shared context. The server sees the account association, not a guaranteed identification of the person holding the remote. A household can therefore observe progress changes caused by another person using the same login without any cross-account error. The account model explains the scope; it does not promise that every offline or disconnected state change becomes immediately available elsewhere. A device can display cached state, and the server can retain an older point until a new report arrives. Concurrent sessions need a state decision Suppose Dana's television reports minute 42 of a movie while the phone still has an older session at minute 20. Accepting a later-arriving phone message blindly would move the apparent resume point backwards. An application must decide how report/session context affects saved state. The public playback model includes session and source identifiers, but the field list does not completely define the server's conflict policy. The example identifies the problem rather than claiming how every Emby version resolves it. This is also why an accumulated state record is not a complete session log. A last-played date and a current resume point can describe the latest retained state while leaving previous sessions unreconstructable. Moving history requires two matches A transfer between independent catalogues needs to establish: Which destination user represents the source viewer. Which destination media identity corresponds to the source item. Matching only the movie title leaves ambiguity between works and editions. Matching only a source-server item ID assumes an identity that may have no meaning on the destination. Qualified provider IDs can help with work matching, while edition and timeline evidence remain necessary for resume values. A played classification can sometimes be meaningfully transferred at work level. A position at 36:30 needs a corresponding timeline. The two state fields can therefore require different matching precision. See Also Watched status Resume positions and playback timelines Media play counts Media item identity References Emby API: Item information Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: Playback progress reporting Emby API: Updating user item data Emby: Metadata manager

articles/libraries-collections/history/L.title: Watched status | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/history/L.keywords: Watched status Watched status records a user’s played classification for a media item separately from its resume position or a complete record of viewed content. Watched status is a classification attached to a viewer and item: the system treats that item as played or unplayed. It drives choices such as unwatched filters and progress indicators. It is separate from the current resume point and from a detailed record of which passages were actually viewed. Emby's public user-item model exposes Played alongside PlaybackPositionTicks , PlayCount and LastPlayedDate . Those fields describe different aspects of state. Information Question it answers Played flag Is this item classified as played for this user? Resume position Where might this user continue? Play count What accumulated count does the system retain? Playback event log, if present Which events were recorded, and when? A catalogue item can be classified as seen because a viewer watched it elsewhere or explicitly marked it played. Emby's API includes a separate “mark played” operation; the classification need not originate from playing the local resource to its end. Final position is not viewed coverage Consider a fictional 60-minute programme. A viewer watches its first two minutes, seeks to minute 55, watches one minute and stops. The final position is 56:00, or about 93.33% of the duration. The viewed material totals three minutes, only 5% of the programme. A policy based on reaching a position near the end could classify this differently from a policy based on actual coverage. The example explains the difference; it is not Emby's completion threshold or a reproduction of its watched-state algorithm. A progress report describes a position and session state, not a proof that every intervening second was viewed. Classification can be an intentional correction Marking a film played can be useful when migrating an existing collection or recording that it was seen on another service. Marking it unplayed can express a new viewing intention. Neither action rewrites the movie's content. A manual correction should therefore be understood as a change to viewer state. It does not supply a forensic account of a screening, or a reliable measure of viewing time. A replay also introduces a new resume position without changing the historical fact that the person has seen the film before. How a product updates its played flag during replay depends on its state rules; the two concepts remain distinct. See Also Resume positions and playback timelines Media play counts User-specific playback history References Emby API: UserItemDataDto Emby API: Marking an item as played Emby API: Playback progress reporting

articles/libraries-collections/index.htm.title: Overview: Libraries and media collections | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Libraries and media collections A media library connects stored files to catalog entries, content relationships and user-specific playback state. Files on disk and items in a library are related views of a collection. A catalog adds identities, series and album relationships, editions and other organization that a directory listing alone does not provide. This area explains those models for movies, television, music, books and personal media. Scanning topics describe how the server observes and analyzes sources; history topics describe state that belongs to individual users. The distinction helps when a file is found under the wrong title, two versions appear separately, or a rescan is expected to recover more than the source can supply. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Library concepts Library concepts describe how a catalogue identifies, groups and presents media independently of its physical file layout. Movies and related videos Movie organization relates editions, alternate files, franchises and supplementary videos to the intended catalogue item. Television and episodic media Television library structure connects series, seasons, episode identities and the files representing them. Music libraries Music library models connect works, recorded performances, releases, credits and associated media. Books and spoken audio Book and spoken-audio libraries organize long-form works through editions, parts and navigable reading or listening structures. Personal media Personal media organization attaches useful catalogue context to home videos and photographs. Playback history Playback history records user-specific observations and state across media items and sessions. Library scanning and media analysis Library scanning observes accessible sources and updates the catalogue through discovery and media analysis. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.title: Overview: Editions and versions | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.keywords: Overview: Editions and versions Editions, versions and multipart structures describe different relationships among files associated with a movie. A different cut changes the edition; another encoding can provide a version of the same content; a split feature can require several parts. Those arrangements call for different catalogue and playback relationships. The three pages here establish the intended relationship before the files are grouped or selected. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Movie editions A movie edition identifies a particular cut or presentation of a film whose content and timeline may differ from other releases. Alternate media versions Alternate media versions provide different playable representations of a catalogue item, each with its own technical properties and resource identity. Multipart movies A multipart movie divides one intended feature across sequential resources whose local timelines must be interpreted as parts of a whole. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships

articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.title: Alternate media versions | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.keywords: Alternate media versions Alternate media versions provide different playable representations of a catalogue item, each with its own technical properties and resource identity. One movie can have several playable sources: a 1080p encode for a small display, a 4K HDR encode, or a source with another audio presentation. An alternate version gives the library another way to play the item. The catalogue item and its sources have different jobs. The item supplies the film's identity and browsing description. Each source supplies the actual container, streams, duration and location used for playback. Compare the whole source The fictional sources below represent the same 108-minute cut: Source Video presentation Average total bitrate assumed for this example Approximate bytes from bitrate × duration A 1080p SDR 12 Mbit/s 9.72 GB B 2160p HDR 35 Mbit/s 28.35 GB C 1080p SDR, lower bitrate 6 Mbit/s 4.86 GB The estimates use decimal units and a constant average total bitrate: bytes = bits per second × 6,480 seconds ÷ 8 . They are arithmetic examples, not measurements or quality scores. Source B contains more pixels and uses more bytes under these assumptions. Whether it is the most useful source depends on the receiving display, supported video/audio formats and available delivery bandwidth. Bitrate alone cannot establish visual quality, and a 4K label cannot establish whether the source is HDR or SDR. Emby's movie naming documentation describes recognized multi-version grouping. The API's MediaSourceInfo describes individual sources. Neither a filename suffix nor a display label replaces the technical information discovered from the media. Track selections belong to the chosen source Suppose source A has English audio at stream index 1 and French audio at index 2. Source B might have English at index 2 and a commentary at index 3. The number 2 is an index within a particular representation, not a global identifier for French. The same issue applies to subtitles and chapters. Their availability, indexes and timings can differ between versions. A player switching sources needs to interpret the target source's tracks rather than copying an old index without context. The public playback-progress model includes both item and media-source identifiers. That distinction makes sense: knowing which movie is playing does not, by itself, identify which resource's streams and timeline are in use. The useful label names the choice A label such as 1080p SDR — stereo or 4K HDR — surround helps a viewer understand what changes. A label such as final-v2 records production history without conveying the available presentation. If two sources are different cuts , a cut label belongs in that choice too. Their shared work identity does not make their timestamps interchangeable. For two encodes of the same sequence, equal scene timing is a reasonable thing to verify; it is not guaranteed simply because both were grouped under one poster. See Also Movie editions and cuts Media item identity Streams and Tracks Bitrate References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Emby API: Playback progress reporting

articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.title: Movie editions and cuts | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.keywords: Movie editions and cuts A movie edition identifies a particular cut or presentation of a film whose content and timeline may differ from other releases. The theatrical cut and an extended cut can tell different versions of the same film. Their scenes, pacing and duration may differ even when a metadata provider describes both with one movie record. An edition identifies that content or presentation; an encode identifies how a representation was compressed and packaged. A new encode does not automatically make a new cut. Conversely, the same codec and resolution do not establish that two files contain the same edition. Change between two files Likely relationship Information needed to distinguish them 1080p and 4K encodes of one cut Alternate technical representations Resolution, codec, colour format and source quality Theatrical and extended cuts Different editorial editions Cut label, scene correspondence and duration Restored transfer with the same scene sequence A changed presentation, possibly the same cut Restoration/master information and actual content Censored release with replaced material An edition difference Region/release context and sequence differences Labels such as Director's cut , Unrated or Restored describe release claims. Their exact meaning depends on the release; they do not specify a universal transformation of the film. Why a timestamp belongs to a cut Imagine an original fictional film lasting 108 minutes. An extended edition inserts 13 minutes of new material at the original 35-minute point and otherwise preserves the sequence. Its duration becomes 121 minutes. In this deliberately simple model: Before the insertion: extended time = theatrical time After the insertion: extended time = theatrical time + 13 minutes A scene at theatrical minute 20 remains at extended minute 20. A scene at theatrical minute 70 moves to extended minute 83. An insertion boundary needs the same care as any edit boundary: the time just before the insert and the corresponding scene just after it are different positions. The model is an original illustration, not an Emby timeline-conversion algorithm. Real cuts can remove, reorder or replace scenes, so correspondence may require multiple segments or may not exist for a particular passage. Percentage is not scene identity A resume point at 70 minutes is about 64.81% of the 108-minute cut. Taking 64.81% of the extended duration produces approximately 78:26. The corresponding scene is at 83:00, so the proportion-based guess lands about 4 minutes 34 seconds early. Preserving elapsed time produces a different error: 70:00 in the extended version is 13 minutes before the corresponding scene. Both values are numerically valid playback positions. Neither means “continue at the same moment in the story.” This is why resume positions , chapter markers and timed subtitles need the correct source timeline. A shared movie ID cannot supply a missing edit map. Edition-dependent material Several assets that look like movie metadata are actually tied to the represented edition. Subtitles refer to dialogue and its presentation times. An insert may shift later cues; replacement dialogue may require different text. Merely changing one global offset cannot fix a cut with several edits. Chapters refer to the actual sequence and timing. The same chapter name can occur at different positions, and a deleted scene can remove a chapter altogether. Seek previews and intro/credit markers are derived from particular media. If the new file changes the sequence, a cache created for the old edition can show the wrong pictures or identify the wrong interval. Technical runtime describes the resource. A provider's general movie runtime may describe another release. Comparing both values can reveal a mismatch, but it cannot determine the cut without more evidence. Equal runtimes can conceal different content Two releases can last 108 minutes while exchanging a scene, replacing an opening logo, changing credits or applying speed conversion alongside other edits. Duration agreement is evidence of a possible match, not proof of identical sequence. Likewise, duration differences are not always editorial. Different frame-rate playback of the same sequence can alter total time without adding scenes. A comparison needs both the content and its time interpretation. An edition label is therefore useful when it describes something a viewer would want to choose. A label containing only HEVC answers a technical question; a label containing Extended cut answers a content question. If both differ, recording both distinctions makes the choice understandable. Edition identity in a library A provider may describe the film as one work while the local library retains several sources or separately presented editions. These are different modelling decisions. Grouping cuts together makes work-level browsing convenient; preserving distinct edition identity helps retain edition-specific history and assets. Emby's movie naming guide describes multi-version presentation and notes limitations when it is used for different cuts. That is a reason to consider the relationship deliberately rather than to assume a version label creates an independent edition model. For the fictional example, the informative description is “extended cut, with a 13-minute insert after minute 35,” not just “another file of Night Ferry.” The former explains why the timeline changes; the latter cannot tell a player, a subtitle author or a viewer which position remains meaningful. See Also Alternate media versions Media item identity Resume positions and playback timelines Chapter Markers References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Schema.org: Movie relationships

articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.title: Multipart movies and file stacking | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/ed.keywords: Multipart movies and file stacking A multipart movie divides one intended feature across sequential resources whose local timelines must be interpreted as parts of a whole. A multipart movie stores the beginning and continuation of one feature in separate resources. Both parts are needed to represent the intended film. That is different from alternate versions , where each source is another way to play the item. “Part” can also occur in the title of a sequel. Harbour Part II is a separate work; two files named as the first and second segments of Night Ferry may be one divided work. The catalogue has to interpret the relationship, not just notice the word. Two clocks in the second file Take a fictional stack with these durations: Resource Local duration Position in an ideal combined timeline Part 1 54:00 0:00 to 54:00 Part 2 62:00 54:00 to 116:00 Assume no overlapping scenes, omitted material or duplicated credits. The ideal combined length is 54 + 62 = 116 minutes . For a combined position of 75:00, subtract the duration of the preceding part: part 2 local position = 75:00 - 54:00 = 21:00 This arithmetic describes a conceptual combined timeline. A particular Emby app may expose or play a stack differently; recognizing the library relationship does not promise a seamless joined stream or the same resume UI everywhere. A subtitle cue at 21:00 in part 2 belongs at combined minute 75 in this model. A chapter marker at 21:00 has the same scope issue. Treating either as minute 21 of the whole film sends the viewer to the first part. The boundary has content as well as time A real split can include an intermission, repeated opening material or overlapping scenes. Adding file durations then measures playback of the stored parts, not necessarily the continuous feature's narrative length. For example, if part 2 repeats the last 30 seconds of part 1, the concatenated resources include those seconds twice. A player cannot determine the intended editorial boundary from the filenames alone. The resource relationship must be distinguished from a decision to trim or join content. Technical transitions matter too. The second file can have a different audio-track order, different codec parameters or timestamps beginning again near zero. “The same stream index in both files” does not guarantee the same language or commentary. Joining bytes without interpreting the containers and streams is not equivalent to playing the parts sequentially. How a library recognizes the relationship Emby's naming guide documents stacking markers such as part1 and part2 for resources held together in one movie folder. A simple illustrative form is: Night Ferry (2020)/ Night Ferry (2020)-part1.mkv Night Ferry (2020)-part2.mkv The guide also sets constraints on the contents of a stacked movie folder. The support documentation is the authority for accepted structures and playback-specific workflows. The essential interpretation is sequential resources, one intended feature . It affects counting, duration, track scope and resuming. If the files actually represent two complete cuts, the correct relationship is alternatives; if they represent two films, each needs its own work identity. See Also Alternate media versions Movie editions and cuts Chapter Markers References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby API: MediaSourceInfo FFmpeg: Seeking and media processing

Several files can belong to one movie, while similarly named files can represent different cuts or catalogue records. Extras and trailers introduce further relationships around the feature.
