articles/libraries-collections/movies/Li.title: Duplicate library entries | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/Li.keywords: Duplicate library entries Duplicate library entries require comparing catalogue identity, edition and actual resource relationships rather than relying on matching titles or posters. Two identical-looking posters can represent an accidental duplicate, two useful encodes, two cuts, or two different works that were matched incorrectly. The display is evidence about presentation, not proof that the underlying resources are interchangeable. The first useful question is therefore “What is duplicated?” It may be the bytes, the work description, a storage route or only the visible label. Four situations that look similar Observation Possible relationship Evidence that resolves it Different paths, equal complete-file hashes Copied resources Byte equality plus confirmation of the represented work Different bytes, same cut and timeline Alternate encodes Edition, scene sequence and technical comparison Same provider movie ID, different sequence Different cuts of one work Edition and timeline comparison One resource reachable through two configured routes Repeated catalogue exposure Resolved paths, storage mappings and library scope The routes in the diagram are explanatory choices, not an automatic Emby deduplication algorithm. A collection can also make a movie appear in more than one browsing context without duplicating either the item or file. Count the underlying item identities and resources before treating repeated visibility as an error. Byte equality and semantic equality A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is a compact fingerprint of bytes. Matching hashes over the complete files provide extremely strong evidence that the resource contents agree. Different paths can still locate such copies. A hash difference is less informative. Retagging a file, changing its container packaging or re-encoding it can change the complete-file bytes while preserving the same cut. A hash cannot answer whether two different resources should be grouped as alternate versions . Names and provider IDs operate at the other end of the evidence scale. They describe or identify catalogue entities. Two cuts can share a movie ID, while two unrelated films can acquire the same poster after a bad match. An identity mistake must be corrected at the descriptive layer before a resource relationship can be assessed confidently. Investigating two entries Suppose two entries named Night Ferry appear in a library. One offers a 108-minute 1080p source; the other offers a 121-minute 4K source. The difference in resolution suggests a possible version relationship. The difference in runtime raises another question. In this fictional case, checking the sequence reveals that the longer source contains a 13-minute insert. The entries describe two cuts, not just a higher-resolution copy. That distinction affects the proposed result. A work-level presentation might collect both choices under one film. It should still retain the cut labels and recognize that resume positions , subtitles and derived previews can differ. Collapsing resource identity would lose useful information even if the browsing grid became less crowded. Now suppose both resources instead have the same complete-file hash. The explanation is likely copied bytes or overlapping exposure, but the current catalogue state still matters. Which item does each playlist refer to? Where is viewer history associated? Are the records in different configured library contexts? Those relationships can outlive the superficial poster duplication. Why refreshing the picture is not a duplicate test A metadata refresh can change a description or image. It cannot turn two files into one, nor establish their scene correspondence merely by retrieving a shared work record. Conversely, changing a path can alter recognition while leaving the film's work identity unchanged. Library scanning has to reconcile that resource change with the catalogue. Reappearance after a scan can reflect unresolved storage or identity evidence rather than a stubborn artwork cache. See Also Media item identity Alternate media versions Movie editions and cuts Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation Media identification References NIST: Secure Hash Standard, FIPS 180-4 Emby API: BaseItemDto Emby: Metadata manager Emby: Movie naming and media relationships

articles/libraries-collections/movies/Li.title: Film franchises in a media library | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/Li.keywords: Film franchises in a media library A film franchise relates distinct works through a shared series or setting while retaining each film’s identity and possible viewing orders. A franchise connects distinct films. Each film still has its own release history, credits and playable editions. Calling three films a trilogy describes a relationship among works; it does not turn them into three parts of one continuous movie resource. The relationship can be a direct sequel, a prequel, a spin-off or a shared setting. A remake may reuse a title while starting another continuity. Describing the connection is more useful than merging the titles under one movie identity. Which order does the collection express? Consider this entirely fictional series: Film Release year Position in its story chronology Harbour: The Last Voyage 2004 3 Harbour: First Tide 2007 1 Harbour: The Crossing 2012 2 Release order is Last Voyage → First Tide → The Crossing . Story chronology is First Tide → The Crossing → Last Voyage . Alphabetical title order produces yet another arrangement. Neither release nor story order is inherently the best introduction. A prequel can assume knowledge supplied by an earlier release, while a returning viewer may want the events in chronological order. The title First Tide does not carry a machine-readable promise about that choice. A collection can gather the works. A playlist can record an intended viewing sequence. Keeping the two purposes distinct lets the library offer a franchise page without implying a universal viewing order. Catalogue boundaries and fictional boundaries A metadata provider's collection is a specific catalogue entity. TMDB, for example, has collection identifiers separate from movie identifiers. A broader franchise can encompass more than one such group, television spin-offs or works in different continuities. An imported group therefore describes that provider's association. It does not automatically enumerate every licensed work sharing the setting, nor does it establish that the library has every member available. In Emby, automatic movie collections can use imported collection information, while manual collections can represent a broader or personal selection. The Collections documentation explains the product behavior. Choosing a shared collection name does not replace the individual films' provider identities. Preserve the kind of connection A library description benefits from saying sequel to , prequel to or remake of rather than only related to . These relationships answer different questions and can coexist. A prequel can belong to the same series and precede another work's events while having been released years later. Each Harbour film can then have its own editions , ratings and viewing history, while the collection or playlist supplies the chosen relationship among them. See Also Media collections Media playlists Metadata relationships References Emby: Collections TMDB API: Collection identity Schema.org: Movie relationships

articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.title: Overview: Supplementary videos | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.keywords: Overview: Supplementary videos Supplementary movie videos attach supporting material such as extras and trailers to a feature. An interview or trailer can belong with a movie without being another version of its main programme. The association and presentation role determine how that video should appear in a library. These topics explain those roles so supplementary material stays recognizable beside the feature. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Movie extras Movie extras are supplementary resources whose role and relationship to a feature distinguish them from another complete movie version. Movie trailers A movie trailer is a promotional video associated with a work or release, with its own edit, language, resource and playback role. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby: Trailer naming

articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.title: Movie extras and supplementary videos | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.keywords: Movie extras and supplementary videos Movie extras are supplementary resources whose role and relationship to a feature distinguish them from another complete movie version. An extra supplies material around a feature: an interview, a deleted scene, a making-of programme or another supplementary video. Its role explains why it appears with the movie even though it has its own duration and streams. Resource Relationship to the feature Useful description Deleted scene Material omitted from a represented cut Scene name, duration and relevant cut Making-of video Describes production Subject, participants and production context Interview A contribution about the film or its creators Interviewee and topic Featurette A short programme about an aspect of the work Subject rather than only “extra 4” Trailer Promotes a release Trailer version and language These videos can be playable resources without being alternate full versions of the film. A 6-minute deleted scene does not offer another way to watch the 108-minute feature. The parent relationship carries meaning A video called Location tour could accompany almost any movie. Its association with Night Ferry tells the library where it belongs. Its own title tells the viewer what it contains. Borrowing the feature's synopsis would obscure that distinction. Edition scope can matter. A deleted scene from the theatrical release may already be present in an extended cut. Calling it an “extra for the film” is broadly reasonable, but claiming it is absent from every edition would be wrong. Likewise, a restoration documentary may describe a specific remaster rather than the original production. Emby's movie naming guide describes recognized supplementary folders and associations. Those conventions express the parent relationship; they do not infer an extra's precise subject from its technical format. Commentary can be a track An audio commentary often accompanies the feature's pictures as another audio stream within the movie source. It then belongs to the source's track selection , with timing aligned to that version of the feature. A separate filmed commentary or interview is a supplementary video. Treating both as the same resource type hides a practical difference: one changes the sound while the film continues, and the other starts another programme. See Also Movie trailers Movie editions and cuts Media item identity References Emby: Movie naming and media relationships Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.title: Movie trailers | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/movies/su.keywords: Movie trailers A movie trailer is a promotional video associated with a work or release, with its own edit, language, resource and playback role. A trailer is its own edited video, assembled to promote a film or release. It can use excerpts, titles, music and shots that do not appear in precisely that form in the feature. Its relationship to the film is promotional, not an alternate full-film representation. Several trailers for one film can all be legitimate: Label What may differ Teaser Shorter edit or an earlier campaign Theatrical trailer The main promotional edit for a release International trailer Edit, title cards, dubbing or release information Restored-release trailer Promotion of a later presentation of the same work The trailer's audio and text language can differ from the available movie source. Selecting the film's French audio does not automatically produce a French trailer. A local trailer is a stored media resource. A remote trailer reference points to another service or location whose availability and delivery behavior can change. A catalogue can therefore know about a trailer without possessing an independent local copy. Emby documents local associations using a trailer suffix or a trailer folder in its Trailer Naming guide . The relevant idea is that a short promotional resource belongs to the movie without becoming another movie entry. Association and pre-roll use A trailer on the movie's detail page helps a viewer decide what to watch. A trailer played before another feature forms part of a pre-roll programme. The same resource can serve both purposes, but the association and playback decision are separate. Emby's Cinema Intros describes using trailers and custom intros before the feature. A library's trailer association alone does not prescribe that sequence. A custom ident or codec introduction can appear in pre-roll without being a movie trailer at all. Because the trailer is an independent edit, its duration and played state do not establish that the viewer finished the feature. They describe a different playback event. That resource boundary keeps promotional browsing from being confused with watching the film. See Also Movie extras and supplementary videos Alternate media versions References Emby: Trailer naming Emby: Cinema Intros Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.title: Overview: Albums and credits | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.keywords: Overview: Albums and credits Album organization uses artist roles, compilation relationships, disc numbering and detailed musical credits. A track performer and an album artist need not be the same role. Compilations and multi-disc releases add grouping rules, while classical credits often distinguish several contributors to the work and performance. These pages describe the relationships needed to present an album coherently. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Album artists Album-artist metadata supplies album-level credit and grouping context independently of each track’s performer credit. Compilation albums A compilation album brings selected recordings into one release whose shared album context differs from the performer credits of individual tracks. Multi-disc albums A multi-disc album uses disc and track coordinates to organize several media within one release without turning each disc into an unrelated album. Classical music credits Classical music credits preserve the distinct roles of composer, conductor, ensemble, soloist and other contributors at work, recording and release scopes. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Music naming and tags MusicBrainz: Classical style

articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.title: Album artists and track artists | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.keywords: Album artists and track artists Album-artist metadata supplies album-level credit and grouping context independently of each track’s performer credit. Harbour Sessions is credited to Mira Vale at album level. On one track she performs alone; on another she is joined by the Harbour Quartet. The album can retain one album-level credit while the tracks describe their different performers. That is the purpose of separating album artist from track artist . The first supplies album context. The second describes the credit attached to a particular track. Fictional track Album artist Track artist River Lights Mira Vale Mira Vale Night Crossing Mira Vale Mira Vale with Harbour Quartet Morning Tide Mira Vale Mira Vale Changing the album-artist value to match each track's guests can turn one intended album into several grouping contexts. Keeping the track credits distinct preserves the guests without losing the album's shared description. Emby's music documentation describes album and album-artist consistency as relevant to grouping. The embedded fields supply this meaning even when all three files already occupy one folder. A field name can be a convention Tag formats do not all use the same physical field names: Common album-artist mapping Storage convention ID3v2 TPE2 Vorbis comments ALBUMARTIST Common iTunes-style MP4 metadata aART Picard documents these mappings. The ID3 definition of TPE2 is band/orchestra/accompaniment; its widespread album-artist use is a tagging convention layered on that field. A tag editor's friendly “Album artist” label is therefore an interpretation of stored data, not a universal string appearing identically in every format. A composer field answers another question. A classical album can credit a composer, conductor, orchestra and soloist in different roles. Classical credits develops those scopes. Display text and contributor identities The credit Mira Vale with Harbour Quartet is readable presentation text. A structured model can retain Mira Vale and Harbour Quartet as separate contributor identities, plus the joining phrase with . Treating the whole display string as a single artist can create a synthetic catalogue identity. Splitting it at every space or punctuation mark loses the joining phrase and can damage actual names. Multi-valued tags can carry several contributors, subject to the tagger and reader's conventions. Emby documents a supported separator for its music artist values. A comma inside a name is not automatically evidence of two people. See Also Compilation albums Classical music credits Music releases and album editions Multi-valued metadata fields References Emby: Music naming and tags MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions

articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.title: Classical music credits | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.keywords: Classical music credits Classical music credits preserve the distinct roles of composer, conductor, ensemble, soloist and other contributors at work, recording and release scopes. A classical recording can involve a composer who wrote the work, a conductor who led the performance, an ensemble, several soloists and an arranger. The album cover may print all their names together. A useful library preserves what each person or group did. Putting every name into one artist field can display the names while losing the relationships that make them meaningful. One performance, several roles Consider an entirely fictional recording of Mara Fen's River Suite : Contributor Role Scope of the credit Mara Fen Composer The musical work Leon Ash Conductor This recorded performance Harbour Orchestra Ensemble This recorded performance Mira Vale Soloist, violin The relevant performed passages Ivo Reed Arranger The represented arrangement of the work Mara Fen remains the composer when another orchestra records the suite. Leon Ash's conducting credit belongs to this performance, not to every realization of the work. Mira Vale may perform in only one movement, so copying her soloist credit indiscriminately to every track can misdescribe the recording. A conductor and an orchestra are also separate identities. Joining them into “Leon Ash and Harbour Orchestra” as a synthetic single artist would make it difficult to find other performances by the same orchestra under another conductor. Work titles can contain a hierarchy The suite contains two movements, Arrival and Night Crossing . A display title such as River Suite: II. Night Crossing combines the larger work and movement label. A richer model can retain the movement as a work related to the suite. That supports questions like “Which recordings of Night Crossing do I have?” without relying on identical punctuation in every track title. The movement number is a position within the work. It is not necessarily the release track number. A release containing another work first could place movement II at track 5, and a single track could contain both movements. Similarly, a catalogue or opus number identifies work context. It does not locate a file or select the performing ensemble. Titles, work identifiers and recording identities need their own scopes. Artist is interpreted by a catalogue convention There is no single classical artist string that answers all of these questions: Who composed the music? Which orchestra performs it? Who conducts? Which soloist is featured? How is the issued album credited? MusicBrainz's classical track-artist guideline uses the composer for the track artist, while performer relationships carry the performance detail. Other tagging and presentation workflows may prefer a performer-led artist display. Reading Artist as “the audible performer” without knowing the convention can therefore produce the wrong conclusion. This is not resolved by declaring one role irrelevant. The library needs both the work's creators and the recording's performers. A presentation can emphasize one role while retaining the others as structured fields or relationships. Tags offer several role fields Picard's mappings include separate composer and conductor fields as well as artist and album artist. ID3v2.4 also defines structured musician and involved-person credit frames, alongside simpler text fields. Information to retain Why a generic artist list is insufficient Composer identity The composition survives changes of performer Conductor identity The role differs from instrument performance Ensemble identity The group may recur with different conductors Soloist and instrument Several people can have different performing roles Arrangement A version of the work can use another contributor's treatment Album-level credit Describes the issued product's presentation The reader must actually understand those fields for them to affect a particular interface. A tag's presence and a browsing facet's availability are different parts of the workflow. In Emby's tag-based music organisation, stable album fields help keep a release together. That album grouping should not force every movement's detailed credits to become identical. An album of several composers can share one album context while retaining each work's own composer field. Preserve a credit before simplifying its display A compact label such as Fen / Ash / Harbour Orchestra can work on a small screen if the underlying fields retain their roles. The same string is poor exchange data when no one can determine which name belongs to which role. The work's original title and a translated display title present another boundary. Changing the visible language should not create a new composer or performance identity. Multi-valued metadata explains the corresponding distinction between a readable list and separately identified contributors. For the River Suite example, a composer query should relate both movements to Mara Fen; a conductor query should select Leon Ash's performance; a violin-soloist query should retain the passages credited to Mira Vale. These are three different routes through the same catalogue, made possible by retaining the roles instead of only the names. See Also Musical works and compositions Music recordings and track occurrences Album artists and track artists Cast and crew credits Multi-valued metadata fields References MusicBrainz: Classical style MusicBrainz: Classical track artist convention MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions MusicBrainz: Work

articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.title: Compilation albums | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.keywords: Compilation albums A compilation album brings selected recordings into one release whose shared album context differs from the performer credits of individual tracks. A compilation selects recordings into an issued album. The performers can change from track to track while the release remains one product. These three track occurrences are an excerpt from the fictional Evening Selection : Track Track artist Album Album artist 7, River Lights Mira Vale Evening Selection Various Artists 8, Signal Ivo Reed Evening Selection Various Artists 9, Last Ferry Harbour Quartet Evening Selection Various Artists Various Artists is the album-level credit chosen in this example. It is not the performer who sang or played every track. How the album can split Suppose the first two files instead copy their performers into the album-artist field. A grouping model using album title and album artist sees three different contexts, despite the shared directory and album name. The diagram is a simple explanatory model, not Emby's complete album-key algorithm. Emby's music documentation does establish the relevance of consistent album and album-artist fields to compilation grouping. Changing all track artists to Various Artists would make those labels consistent at the wrong scope. It discards useful information about who performs Signal and Last Ferry . The album-artist field supplies the shared context without replacing those credits. Compilation is a role, not an identifier A compilation flag can tell a reader or tagger that an album has compilation status. It does not identify the particular release product, nor resolve conflicting album IDs. A compilation can also feature only one primary artist—for example, a collection of recordings previously issued by that artist. “Several artists” and “compilation” are overlapping concepts, not exact synonyms. The recordings themselves can keep their original identities. The River Lights studio audio may also occur on Harbour Songs . Its occurrence on Evening Selection has another track number, album context and cover without requiring a new recording merely because it was selected again. Keep the product's sequence A compilation's sequencing can be intentional. Sorting by performer rearranges the programme; sorting by its release track positions preserves the issued sequence. If the product spans two discs, the disc and track pair identifies that position. Album identity, album-level credit and the ordered occurrences together describe the compilation, while the track credits continue to describe its contributors. See Also Album artists and track artists Music recordings and track occurrences Music releases and album editions References Emby: Music naming and tags MusicBrainz: Release MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping

articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.title: Multi-disc albums | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/alb.keywords: Multi-disc albums A multi-disc album uses disc and track coordinates to organize several media within one release without turning each disc into an unrelated album. A two-disc release normally restarts track numbering on its second disc. The two track 1 values are not duplicates: their coordinates are disc 1, track 1 and disc 2, track 1 . The disc coordinate qualifies the track coordinate, just as a season qualifies an episode number. Sorting the pair In this separate original five-track product, disc 1 has three tracks and disc 2 has two: Product position Disc Track 1 1 1 2 1 2 3 1 3 4 2 1 5 2 2 Sorting by track number alone can interleave the discs: 1/1, 2/1, 1/2, 2/2, 1/3. Sorting by disc and then track preserves the product sequence. For disc 2 track 1, the product position is 3 + 1 = 4 because three tracks precede that disc. That flattened position is derived from this particular product's track counts; it is not a universal replacement for the disc/track pair. Disc position and total are different values Common tag mappings include ID3 TPOS for part-of-set and TRCK for track position, or Vorbis DISCNUMBER and TRACKNUMBER . Tagging conventions can also retain total-disc and total-track information. A value such as 2/2 in a part-of-set field means disc 2 of a two-disc set. It does not mean “two tracks,” and the track total for disc 2 can differ from the total for disc 1. The tag format and tagging software determine how these values are encoded. Emby's music library reads the embedded information; naming a folder Disc 2 is storage evidence, not a substitute for consistently represented album and position fields. One release can own several media A common album title and album-level credit can remain the same across both discs. The disc coordinate then distinguishes their positions within the release . Appending Disc 2 to the album title can deliberately create a separate presentation, but it also changes the album label. If the intended model is one product, that distinction is better carried by the medium coordinate. Product identity still matters when a single-disc original and a two-disc expanded edition share a title. Disc numbers distinguish the media within an edition; they do not, by themselves, distinguish the editions. The music can cross the packaging boundary A long work can continue across a disc change. A continuous concert can be divided into several tracks. The medium boundary and the composition boundary need not coincide. Gapless playback concerns the transition between the encoded resources. Disc/track metadata concerns ordering. Correct numbering can deliver the intended next track without proving that decoder delay and padding were handled correctly at the boundary. Gapless playback explains that separate mechanism. See Also Music releases and album editions Album artists and track artists Gapless playback Audiobook chapter structure References Emby: Music naming and tags MusicBrainz: Release MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions

articles/libraries-collections/music/ind.title: Overview: Music libraries | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/ind.keywords: Overview: Music libraries Music library models connect works, recorded performances, releases, credits and associated media. An album title, a recording and a musical work identify different parts of a music catalogue. Artist roles, disc structure and lyrics add further relationships around them. The branches below explain those distinctions so the library's grouping reflects what the files represent, rather than only matching their visible names. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Works, recordings, and releases Works, recordings and releases distinguish the composition, captured performance and published edition of music. Albums and credits Album organization uses artist roles, compilation relationships, disc numbering and detailed musical credits. Music video cataloguing Music video cataloguing identifies an audiovisual production and relates it to music credits without equating it with the sound recording alone. Lyrics Lyrics can accompany music as untimed text or as content associated with positions on the playback timeline. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Music naming and tags

articles/libraries-collections/music/Lib.title: Music video cataloguing | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/Lib.keywords: Music video cataloguing Music video cataloguing identifies an audiovisual production and relates it to music credits without equating it with the sound recording alone. A music video combines sound with a particular visual production. Its soundtrack can use a familiar studio recording while its pictures, editing and production credits identify another resource. The fictional song River Lights illustrates several possibilities: Video Sound relationship Video relationship Promotional film Uses the studio recording A staged and edited audiovisual production Concert clip Captures a live performance A recording of that concert presentation Lyric video May reuse the studio recording Another visual presentation with rendered words These videos can express the same musical work without being identical recordings. The promotional film and lyric video can even share the same sound while having different video content. IFPI's music-video identifier guidance makes that distinction explicit: a music-video recording has an identity separate from a sound recording, including when the latter supplies its soundtrack. Credits describe different contributions The songwriter and composer belong to work context. Musicians and vocalists describe the represented performance. A video director, editor or cinematographer describes the audiovisual production. Copying the audio track's credits can therefore supply useful music information while leaving the video's production unexplained. A video title plus artist also may not distinguish several edits of the same promotion. Useful edition labels describe the actual choice: original promotional edit , live at the harbour or lyric video . Codec/resolution labels describe alternate technical sources of one production instead. Album associations need a reason A video can promote an album, feature a song later included on several products, or represent a performance never issued on that album. An album relationship is not established solely by a soundtrack match. Emby's Music Naming documentation describes music-video libraries and artist/album associations. Those associations help connect browsing contexts. The video still needs its own audiovisual description. A rendered lyric video is also distinct from timed lyric data . Its text is part of the video image. A sidecar lyric timeline gives an app text and timing that it can render separately. See Also Music recordings and track occurrences Musical works and compositions IMVDb music-video metadata Alternate media versions References Emby: Music naming and tags IFPI: Identifying music-video recordings IFPI: International Standard Recording Code

articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.title: Overview: Lyrics | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.keywords: Overview: Lyrics Lyrics can accompany music as untimed text or as content associated with positions on the playback timeline. A lyric sheet and a synchronized lyric display contain related words but different timing information. LRC provides one representation for attaching that timing. The pages here separate the textual content from the cue relationship used to follow the song during playback. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Unsynchronized lyrics Unsynchronized lyrics store readable song text without timestamps that align its lines or words to playback. Synchronized lyrics Synchronized lyrics associate text with media-time positions so that a renderer can select the words or lines appropriate to playback. LRC files LRC is a text-file convention that prefixes lyric text with playback timestamps, with parser-dependent extensions for metadata and finer timing. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Music lyrics

articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.title: LRC lyric files | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.keywords: LRC lyric files LRC is a text-file convention that prefixes lyric text with playback timestamps, with parser-dependent extensions for metadata and finer timing. An LRC file stores timed lyrics as readable text. In a common simple form, a bracketed timestamp precedes the lyric line it starts. The file remains separate from the audio, so a player needs both an association with the track and a parser that understands the convention. This is an original example for a fictional song: [ar:Mira Vale] [ti:River Lights] [00:12.40]River lights [00:20.00]Carry us home [00:28.25]Lift the sail [00:40.00][01:10.00]Into the morning The artist/title fields are descriptive tags. They are not playback events. The final physical line describes the same text starting at two different times. Timestamp fractions and millisecond conversion For [00:12.40] : 0 × 60 + 12 + 40 / 100 = 12.40 seconds 12.40 × 1,000 = 12,400 milliseconds The .40 represents forty hundredths of a second under this two-decimal convention, not forty milliseconds. Parsers can also encounter other fractional precision; the actual number of digits matters. Timestamp Position in seconds 00:12.40 12.40 00:28.25 28.25 01:10.00 70.00 LRC minutes are elapsed media minutes. They are not an hour/minute clock display, and the timestamps do not encode a calendar date. One stored line can yield several cue occurrences Expanding the final example line produces separate cues at 40 and 70 seconds. The file has four physical lyric lines but five timed occurrences. A reader can sort the expanded cues by time before display. Keeping the text only once while ignoring its second timestamp loses the repeated verse. Treating every bracket as another lyric line also confuses descriptive fields with time values. Synchronized-lyrics software such as Kid3 documents importing/exporting simple and enhanced LRC. Enhanced variants can carry finer timing than whole lines. The parser's supported variant matters; an unfamiliar tag or extension does not automatically have the same meaning in every application. Correcting a timeline is a content operation A missing 500-millisecond delay can be applied as a timestamp edit: the first cue becomes 12.90 seconds and the second becomes 20.50 seconds. That example adds 0.50 seconds directly to the cue positions. An offset metadata tag is another convention. Its support and sign interpretation should be established for the reader being used rather than assumed to be equivalent to those edited cue times everywhere. Changing a file extension from .txt to .lrc does not create timestamps. Likewise, timing for a studio recording may need more than a constant correction for a live version. Synchronized lyrics works through a drift example. File association and text encoding A sidecar needs to resolve to the intended track; a title-only association can become ambiguous when several recordings share a song title. Emby's Music Lyrics documentation describes supplied lyric companions, while the actual server/app support determines which representation can be displayed. See Also Synchronized lyrics and music timelines Unsynchronized lyrics Unicode metadata References KDE Kid3: Synchronized lyrics and chapters ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions Emby: Music lyrics

articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.title: Synchronized lyrics and music timelines | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.keywords: Synchronized lyrics and music timelines Synchronized lyrics associate text with media-time positions so that a renderer can select the words or lines appropriate to playback. Synchronized lyrics pair text with positions on a particular recording's media timeline. A renderer can use those positions to show the current line or word, and to recover the correct text after the listener seeks. The association is with media time, not with the wall clock. Pausing the audio should not make the lyrics run ahead. Four lines on a timeline Use this original fictional cue set: Media position Text 12.40 seconds River lights 20.00 seconds Carry us home 28.25 seconds Lift the sail 40.00 seconds Into the morning One simple display model chooses the latest cue whose time is no later than the current media position. Under that rule, position 26 seconds selects Carry us home . Seeking backwards to 15 seconds selects River lights . Before 12.40 seconds, no lyric line has started. This is an explanatory selection rule, not a claim about a specific app's rendering algorithm. A cue containing only a start time also does not supply an explicit end time. A renderer's policy determines whether it retains the line until the next cue, clears it during silence, or uses additional interval information. Granularity changes what can be displayed A line cue says when the line starts. It cannot establish when the second word or final syllable is sung. Word or syllable timing supplies more detailed boundaries. That enables a karaoke-style progression, but it requires more timing evidence. Dividing the line's duration evenly among its words assumes a rhythm that the performance may not have. ID3's SYLT frame associates text fragments with timestamps and identifies the timestamp unit. Its definitions distinguish milliseconds from MPEG audio-frame counts. A number stored as frame count cannot be interpreted as milliseconds without conversion. Plain USLT text has no such timeline. LRC is another timed-text representation, usually encountered as a sidecar. Playback state supplies the clock If playback pauses at 26 seconds, the relevant position remains 26 seconds. If the listener resumes, the media clock advances again. If playback speed changes, the lyric positions still identify moments in the recording, while the time needed to reach them changes. Seeking introduces a direct jump in position. A renderer should resolve the cue from the destination position rather than waiting for every skipped lyric event to arrive. An output delay can introduce another clock boundary: the reported playback position and the sound heard from an audio device may not be perfectly aligned. A renderer may need an appropriate synchronization policy. Changing the lyric file to compensate for one device's delay can make it wrong on another playback path. Another recording needs another correspondence The same words can be sung with a different introduction, tempo or verse sequence. A lyric timeline for one recording is not automatically valid for a live performance or radio edit of the same work. An extra 1.5-second introduction would call for a constant shift in this simple example: new cue time = old cue time + 1.5 seconds Every cue moves by the same amount. But a duration change distributed through the performance creates drift as well. Imagine a version whose correspondence follows this deliberately simple model: new cue time = 1.5 + 1.02 × old cue time At 12.40 seconds, the corresponding time is 14.148 seconds. At 40.00 seconds, it is 42.30 seconds. Adding only 1.5 seconds leaves the first cue 0.248 seconds early and the later cue 0.80 seconds early. The model assumes a uniform timing change. A live performance with pauses, reordered verses or omitted words needs more detailed correspondence. Two anchors reveal the uniform change For two established matching points, the slope is: (42.30 - 14.148) / (40.00 - 12.40) = 1.02 Subtracting 1.02 × 12.40 from 14.148 gives the 1.5-second intercept. This separates a constant offset from proportional drift rather than trying to correct both with one slider. Two points do not validate every intermediate verse. Additional matching points can reveal whether the uniform model actually fits or whether a local edit interrupts it. Emby's supplied-lyrics feature is described in Music Lyrics . The specific file parser and app determine which timing granularity is usable. The underlying correspondence remains recording-specific: the four original lines can be reused as words, while their timing must match the audio actually being played. See Also Unsynchronized lyrics LRC lyric files Music recordings and track occurrences Resume positions and playback timelines Subtitle time offsets References ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions KDE Kid3: Synchronized lyrics and chapters Emby: Music lyrics

articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.title: Unsynchronized lyrics | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/lyr.keywords: Unsynchronized lyrics Unsynchronized lyrics store readable song text without timestamps that align its lines or words to playback. Unsynchronized lyrics are readable words without an accompanying performance timeline. They can be shown as a verse or full song text while the audio plays, but the data does not say when a particular line is sung. For a fictional song, the text might be: River lights Carry us home Lift the sail Into the morning The four lines have an order and line breaks. They have no timestamps. A reader can scroll through them; a player cannot derive dependable word highlighting merely by knowing the song's duration. Where the text lives Representation Relationship to the media Text sidecar Separate file associated with a track ID3 USLT frame Text embedded in an audio tag Another format's lyrics field A format-specific embedded description Text painted into a video Pixels in the audiovisual presentation The ID3 USLT frame can qualify text with a language and content descriptor. That allows distinct text entries without pretending they are a timed sequence. The format's encoding also matters for accented or non-Latin characters. Emby's Music Lyrics documentation describes displaying supplied sidecar lyrics. That is a natural use for untimed text: adding a readable companion does not require modifying the actual song audio. The text should match what is sung A translated text, a studio verse and a live performance's changed verse can all be useful, but they describe different content. Their labels should preserve that distinction. Correcting a spelling error changes the lyric text. Adding timestamps changes its representation into synchronized lyrics . Rewriting the audio is another operation entirely. For the original verse above, timing begins only when someone supplies evidence such as “River lights starts at 12.40 seconds.” The line breaks themselves never contained that fact. See Also Synchronized lyrics and music timelines LRC lyric files ID3v2 audio tags Unicode metadata References Emby: Music lyrics ID3v2.4: Native frame definitions MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping

articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.title: Overview: Works, recordings, and releases | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.keywords: Overview: Works, recordings, and releases Works, recordings and releases distinguish the composition, captured performance and published edition of music. Two performances of one composition are different recordings. One recording can then appear on several releases, and related editions can share a release-group relationship. These distinctions make credits and identifiers easier to interpret when a collection contains compilations, reissues or several performances of the same work. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Musical works A musical work identifies a composition or other created musical material independently of the recordings and releases that express it. Music recordings A music recording identifies distinct recorded audio that can occur on several releases and be encoded in multiple local resources. Music releases A music release identifies an issued product and its media, track occurrences and release context rather than only the album’s general title. Release groups A MusicBrainz release group gathers related release products under a common album or release concept while retaining each product’s identity. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References MusicBrainz: Work MusicBrainz: Recording MusicBrainz: Release MusicBrainz: Release group

articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.title: Musical works and compositions | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.keywords: Musical works and compositions A musical work identifies a composition or other created musical material independently of the recordings and releases that express it. Three musicians can perform the same composition at different tempos, with different instruments and on different occasions. A library that knows only the song title can list those performances; a catalogue that also knows the work can explain why they belong together. The work is the created musical material. A recording is a particular recorded realization. A release makes recordings available in an issued product. These identities answer different questions. The composition has its own credits In an original example, Mara Fen composes River Lights , Ivo Reed writes its lyrics, and Mira Vale records a performance. A later recording by the Harbour Quartet still relates to the composition, while its performers and production credits differ. Question Relevant scope Who composed River Lights? Work Who wrote its lyrics? Work Who sings on this recorded version? Recording and performance credits Which album includes this track? Release and track occurrence Which codec is in the local file? Playable resource Setting every one of those fields to Mira Vale would make a convenient artist label while erasing the composition's authorship. A composer need not be a performer, and an instrumental performance need not contain the work's lyrics. Larger works can contain smaller works A symphony, suite or opera can organize constituent movements or numbers. The fictional River Suite contains Arrival and Night Crossing as movements: The diagram is an original relationship model. A movement's title can be shared by its recordings without making the movement itself an audio file. One recorded track can also cover more than one work, as with a medley, so work-to-track relationships are not restricted to one work per file. An ordinary collection of songs is not automatically a single composite composition. The album's track sequence and the work's authored structure are separate evidence. Identifiers retain that scope MusicBrainz assigns entity identities to works and relates them to recordings and credited contributors. The International Standard Musical Work Code, or ISWC, identifies a musical work. Neither identifies the bytes of a particular MP3 or the product edition of an album. A work title alone is weaker evidence. Two unrelated compositions can share the same title, while one composition can have alternate titles. Matching therefore needs context such as creators and catalogue identity. Emby's music library reads embedded tags, as described in Music Naming . Composer and other descriptive fields can preserve useful work information even when a particular browsing interface does not expose the complete work graph. A title like River Suite: II. Night Crossing communicates a hierarchy to a person; explicit work relationships make that hierarchy usable as data. See Also Music recordings and track occurrences Classical music credits MusicBrainz identifiers Metadata relationships References MusicBrainz: Work CISAC: International Standard Musical Work Code Emby: Music naming and tags

articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.title: Music recordings and track occurrences | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.keywords: Music recordings and track occurrences A music recording identifies distinct recorded audio that can occur on several releases and be encoded in multiple local resources. A familiar song can have a studio recording, a live recording and a remix. They may express the same work , but they contain different recorded audio. That difference matters when a listener chooses a performance, looks up credits or matches a local file. A recording can also appear more than once without becoming a different recording every time. The original album, a compilation and a reissue can all contain occurrences of the same studio audio. Recording, track and file Use the fictional River Lights studio recording R-A: Object Example What changes Recording R-A, Mira Vale's studio version Recorded audio identity Track occurrence Disc 1 track 2 of Harbour Songs Position and credit in that release Another track occurrence Track 7 of Evening Selection Another release context Local file A FLAC encode of the first occurrence Encoded bytes, tags and storage Another local file An AAC encode of the same audio Technical representation Here R-A is an invented explanatory key. An actual MusicBrainz recording ID has its own identifier syntax. The two occurrences can have different track numbers and album artwork while referring to the same recording. Copying the second occurrence's album fields onto the first would preserve the audio match and lose the release context. What makes recorded audio different? A new performance changes the recording. A remix changes the presented mix of recorded material. An edit can change the sequence or remove a passage. Merely compressing unchanged audio into another format changes a resource representation. MusicBrainz's recording model places its audio identity after editing/mixing and before final mastering, so mastering alone does not create a new recording in that catalogue's terminology. This is a catalogue convention, not a universal assertion that every remaster sounds identical. A remaster can change dynamics, level or tonal balance while preserving that recording relationship. For a listener comparing releases, those presentation differences still matter. The release identity can retain them. ISRC supplies another identifier scope for recorded sound and music video. Assignment follows its own rules. A MusicBrainz entity and an ISRC field are related catalogue evidence; neither is a hash of the local file. The audio match leaves another question Suppose a fingerprint matches the studio recording R-A. That is useful evidence about which audio was represented. It cannot decide whether the local track was obtained from Harbour Songs or Evening Selection when both contain that recording. Release-specific evidence—album identity, track list, disc/track position and product identifiers—resolves the remaining question. Duration can help distinguish an edit but is not sufficient to identify a release by itself. Emby's tag-based music organisation makes that distinction practical. Recording and release identifiers can supply precise context, while album, album-artist and track fields describe the occurrence the library should present. A match that gets the recording right but rewrites the album incorrectly has solved only one part of the identity problem. See Also Musical works and compositions Music releases and album editions Media item identity Acoustic fingerprinting MusicBrainz identifiers References MusicBrainz: Recording IFPI: International Standard Recording Code MusicBrainz: Release Emby: Music naming and tags

articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.title: Music releases and album editions | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.keywords: Music releases and album editions A music release identifies an issued product and its media, track occurrences and release context rather than only the album’s general title. An album name often describes a family of releases: an original CD, a later reissue, a download and an expanded edition. A release identifies a particular issued product within that family. It provides the context for which tracks, artwork and edition information belong together. This is the identity needed when the question is “Which album edition is in my library?” rather than “Which recording is playing?” Two products called Harbour Songs Consider these fictional products: Property Release P1 Release P2 Display title Harbour Songs Harbour Songs Edition Original Expanded Medium One CD Two-disc set Disc 1 Three original track occurrences The same three track occurrences Disc 2 None Two live tracks and a demo Release year 2020 2025 Cover Original design Revised edition design The shared title is meaningful. So are the different track list and product contexts. If the library combines all six track occurrences into one unexplained album, it becomes difficult to determine which release the viewer is browsing. MusicBrainz models a release as an issued product with identifying properties and one or more media. Its release group describes the broader album concept. The products above can belong to one group while retaining distinct release identities. A track is an occurrence in that product Imagine the studio recording of River Lights appears as P1 disc 1 track 2 and also as track 7 of a compilation. Those positions belong to track occurrences on releases. The recording's identity does not encode “track 2.” A release track can have a printed title or credit that differs from a general recording description. The occurrence retains what this product presents. The audio can still refer to the same recording. The relation can be pictured as: release P1 -> medium 1 -> track position 2 -> studio recording R-A -> composition River Lights Each step adds context. The playable file is a representation of that audio with embedded tags describing the desired occurrence and product. Its path does not replace the entire chain. Product evidence needs interpretation A catalogue can use release events, label/catalogue information, barcodes, track lists and explicit release IDs to distinguish products. Each clue has a scope and limitations. A barcode can be useful product evidence, but reissues or catalogue practices can make it less decisive than expected. A printed catalogue number needs its label context. A region/date pair can distinguish an issuance while leaving other properties unresolved. A complete track-list match is stronger than a single title, but an expanded edition may intentionally reuse the original disc. Matching only that disc can therefore leave both P1 and P2 plausible. A recording fingerprint has a similar limit. It can match R-A accurately while both products contain R-A. Release matching requires evidence about the product, not only about its constituent audio. What the local tags need to preserve Descriptive field Job in the library Album title Human-readable product/album label Album artist Album-level credit or grouping context Disc and track numbers Position within the represented release Release identifier Explicit catalogue product identity, when supplied Recording identifier Identity of the recorded audio Release-group identifier Broader album concept The exact storage names depend on the tag format. Picard's mapping documentation distinguishes these identifier and position fields across formats. A recording ID placed into the album-ID field does not become a valid release identifier merely because both values resemble UUIDs. Emby's Music Naming documentation explains its tag-based music organisation and identifies album IDs as relevant when same-named albums need distinction. That does not define the server's complete private album-key algorithm. It does explain why consistent product-level evidence matters. An edition mismatch can hide behind good audio tags Suppose disc 1 is tagged as the original album while disc 2 retains the expanded release ID and a slightly different album-artist spelling. The audio and individual song titles may all be correct. The album relationship is inconsistent. A useful investigation asks which product each file is supposed to represent, then compares the fields that carry that meaning. Renaming every directory to Harbour Songs leaves the contradictory embedded identity intact. Conversely, appending “Disc 2” to every album title can create two album labels when the intended product is one two-disc release. Multi-disc albums explains how the disc coordinate supplies that distinction without replacing release identity. Keeping P1 and P2 separate lets the original artwork and three-track list describe one product, while the revised artwork and extra disc describe the other. The shared album concept remains available through the release-group relationship. See Also Music release groups Music recordings and track occurrences Multi-disc albums Album artists and track artists MusicBrainz identifiers Release dates References MusicBrainz: Release MusicBrainz: Release group Emby: Music naming and tags MusicBrainz Picard: Tag mapping

articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.title: Music release groups | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/music/wor.keywords: Music release groups A MusicBrainz release group gathers related release products under a common album or release concept while retaining each product’s identity. A release group answers a broad album question: “Which album concept do these products belong to?” A release answers the narrower question: “Which issued product is this?” The original and expanded Harbour Songs products can therefore belong to one release group. Their different disc counts, artwork and release events remain properties of the individual releases . MusicBrainz uses release group as a defined catalogue entity. Each release belongs to one such group in its model. A personal group of favourite albums, a genre view or a playlist is a different kind of association. Identity Suitable question Release group G1 Which overall Harbour Songs album concept? Release P1 Which original issued product? Release P2 Which expanded issued product? Medium 2 of P2 Which disc within the expanded product? The labels are invented keys for this example. A disc within a multi-disc product is not automatically another release or release group. Broad matching and precise matching A group-level match can be enough to discover album information or relate editions in a catalogue. It cannot select the exact product's track list when those editions differ. For example, using G1 to identify P2 still leaves unanswered whether the library should contain three tracks on one medium or an additional disc. A release ID can resolve that product question; a group ID cannot substitute for it. The same issue appears with dates. The broad album concept and a 2025 expanded product can legitimately carry different release contexts. Overwriting the expanded product's date with a group's original-release context erases the edition distinction. Reading an album ID Tagging software can store both release and release-group identifiers. The field name matters because the UUID's text does not announce its entity type. An Emby library reading embedded album information needs consistent release evidence for the product being presented. The group relationship explains why several products are related, while the release description preserves which one the files represent. See Also Music releases and album editions Music recordings and track occurrences Media collections MusicBrainz identifiers References MusicBrainz: Release group MusicBrainz: Release Emby: Music naming and tags

articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Overview: Personal media | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Overview: Personal media Personal media organization attaches useful catalogue context to home videos and photographs. A private recording may have no corresponding film or programme entry in an online catalogue. Dates, locations, albums and the owner's own descriptions can instead supply the useful organization. This branch explains how that context relates to home-video and photographic collections. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Home video cataloguing Home video cataloguing describes personal recordings, events and derived edits while preserving the distinct origins and dates of their media resources. Photo organization Photo organization uses album relationships, capture times and location information to make a collection navigable. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library setup

articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Home video cataloguing | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Home video cataloguing Home video cataloguing describes personal recordings, events and derived edits while preserving the distinct origins and dates of their media resources. A home video often needs information that no commercial movie catalogue can supply: who or what it depicts, where the event took place, and which recording or edit the resource represents. A title such as IMG_0428 locates a camera file. A description such as Harbour trip — arrival at the jetty tells a viewer why it is worth opening. Both can be retained instead of using one field to do every job. Event, recording and edit An original personal-media example has three resources: Resource Content relationship Original tape recording Captures several parts of the harbour trip Digitised full recording Represents that tape's recorded sequence as a digital resource Twelve-minute edited film Selects and rearranges material from the recording The edit is not simply a smaller encode of the full recording. Its sequence and timeline differ. A resume point or chapter list for the digitised tape cannot be copied into the edited film without correspondence. In an Emby library, the content model provides the context for recognising the resources. The descriptive title and event information supply personal meaning that a codec probe cannot derive. Four dates can all be correct Date in the example What it describes Approximately 1988 The depicted trip and original recording, if that is the known evidence 2020 Digitisation of the tape 2026 Creation of the twelve-minute edit A later copy timestamp This stored copy's filesystem history Replacing the approximate event year with the exact 2026 export date would make the metadata more precise while describing the wrong event. Container date fields also need interpretation. A creation value can reflect a digital resource's production or another writer's convention. It does not necessarily recover the date when an old tape's pictures were recorded. A timecode is another coordinate altogether. It can identify a location within the recording or production timeline; it is not, by itself, the calendar date of the event. Description should identify the passage A long recording can contain several events or camera segments. Chapter names such as Arrival , Boat launch and Evening return make those portions easier to find than generic minute counters. A derived short edit can carry a summary of its selection, while the source description retains the fuller recording context. An association such as edited from recording T1 expresses provenance without claiming identical content. Where the exact date or person identity is uncertain, a qualified description preserves that uncertainty. “Harbour trip, probably summer 1988” has a different evidential meaning from an invented timestamp of 1 January 1988 at midnight. Preserve source context when making another representation Re-encoding can preserve the depicted event while changing resource bytes and technical properties. Editing can change both presentation and sequence. A catalogue description benefits from identifying which operation the new resource represents. Embedded metadata or associated descriptive records can preserve information beyond the filename. Whether a library imports a particular field depends on its readers; the file's technical stream information and its personal description remain separate evidence. articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Overview: Photo organization | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Overview: Photo organization Photo organization uses album relationships, capture times and location information to make a collection navigable. The time a file was copied is not necessarily the time its photograph was taken. Capture metadata and geolocation describe another context, while albums express an organizational choice. These distinctions help group and sort personal pictures without reducing their history to the current file path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Photo albums A photo album groups picture resources by an intended selection or arrangement while physical folders, image identity and derived copies remain separate. Photo capture dates A photo capture date describes when an image was made, with clock, offset, precision and provenance needed to distinguish it from digitisation, editing or file-copy times. Photo geolocation Photo geolocation describes a coordinate and its context, including reference directions and uncertainty, separately from the place depicted or the location of a stored file. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library setup ExifTool: Exif date and GPS field definitions ExifTool: GPS fields and reference directions

articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Photo albums and picture membership | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Photo albums and picture membership A photo album groups picture resources by an intended selection or arrangement while physical folders, image identity and derived copies remain separate. A photo album gathers pictures for a purpose: a trip, a person, an event or a chosen visual sequence. The membership explains which pictures belong together. Their file locations explain where the stored resources are found. The same harbour photograph can belong to Summer trip and Boats without requiring another original capture. In a library such as Emby, storage structure and catalogue browsing supply context for picture organisation. Whether a particular album is represented by a folder, a catalogue group or another application feature depends on the workflow. Selection is different from location Meaning Original example Physical folder Camera imports / July Event selection Summer trip Subject selection Boats Curated sequence Departure, crossing, arrival Derived export A small copy for display Moving a picture to another directory changes its storage location. Changing its album membership changes a selection. Neither operation inherently changes what the photograph depicts. An album title also describes the group. It should not replace every member's caption with the same words. A picture of the jetty can retain Waiting for the ferry while its album supplies the trip context. One capture can have several resources A camera original, an edited version and a resized export can depict the same captured moment. They differ as resources and can differ visually. An album intended to show finished pictures may choose the edited version. An archive-oriented selection may retain the original. Displaying both can be deliberate, but the relation should be understandable rather than appearing as accidental repeated pictures. A smaller export can also omit descriptive metadata retained in the source. The album membership and caption in one catalogue do not automatically travel inside every exported image. Order can tell a story A capture-date sort can reconstruct a broad event sequence if the clocks and date fields agree. A deliberate album order can instead introduce the location, then show an activity, then finish with a portrait. Capture dates are evidence for chronological arrangement. Subject labels and location metadata provide other perspectives. None alone supplies the curator's intended visual progression.
