articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Photo capture dates and camera clocks | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Photo capture dates and camera clocks A photo capture date describes when an image was made, with clock, offset, precision and provenance needed to distinguish it from digitisation, editing or file-copy times. A photograph can have several legitimate dates: capture, digitisation, editing and copying. They describe different events. A newly copied file can depict a much older moment. Choosing a date for album ordering therefore requires knowing what the field means, not merely selecting the newest or most precise-looking timestamp. A date needs an event scope Information Intended event Capture date/time Making the original image Digitisation date/time Creating a digital representation, such as scanning a print Metadata or resource modification time A later editing or writing operation Filesystem creation time Creation of this stored filesystem object Catalogue import date Adding the resource to that catalogue Exif, XMP and IPTC can represent relevant descriptive dates, with different field structures and semantics. A scanner or editor's output date does not reconstruct the original exposure simply because it appears inside an image file. For an old print scanned in 2026, taken around 1988 and digitised in 2026 can both be correct descriptions. They should remain separate. Local time and offset An Exif-style original-time example is: DateTimeOriginal: 2026:07:14 18:30:00 OffsetTimeOriginal: +02:00 SubSecTimeOriginal: 250 The local clock value describes 18:30. Its offset makes the corresponding UTC instant 16:30. The subsecond string supplies .250 seconds in this example, so the combined local value is 18:30:00.250. Subseconds express additional precision. They do not prove that the camera clock was calibrated to millisecond accuracy. A DateTimeOriginal value without offset information supplies a local clock reading but not, by itself, a unique UTC instant. The computer's current time zone is not evidence that the camera was in that zone when the image was made. Two cameras at the same event Take these original fictional observations: Camera Recorded local clock Known fixed offset Converted UTC clock A 18:30:00 +02:00 16:30:00Z B 09:32:00 −07:00 16:32:00Z The nine-hour local-clock difference mostly reflects offsets. After conversion, a two-minute difference remains. If independent event evidence establishes that B's clock was two minutes fast, applying that known correction aligns the observed moment at 16:30Z. Merely changing its offset would confuse clock error with time-zone interpretation. The diagram assumes the offsets and clock error are known. It is not an automatic date-repair procedure or a claim about real photographs. For a combined album, preserving the recorded clock, established offset and applied correction makes the ordering explainable. Rewriting all dates without that provenance loses the evidence needed to revisit the decision. Calendar days can differ for the same instant A local capture at 23:45 on 14 July with a fixed UTC−04:00 offset corresponds to 03:45Z on 15 July. The instant is the same, but its local and UTC calendar dates differ. A trip album grouped by the photographer's local day can reasonably retain 14 July. A global chronological index can use the UTC instant. Neither grouping should silently claim that its calendar-day interpretation is the only date carried by the photograph. An offset also does not identify a time-zone region or all of its historical clock rules. The same offset can be used in several places, and one place can use different offsets at different times. GPS time supplies another observation GPS date/time fields can describe a UTC positioning fix. That timestamp has its own event scope. It should not automatically replace the exposure time unless the relationship between fix and capture is established. A nearby GPS observation can help with interpretation, but coordinates alone do not prove the camera's clock setting or exact exposure instant. Photo geolocation explains the corresponding location scopes. Video resources add another date convention. Container creation fields can have UTC semantics while some devices write values differently. Reading software's interpretation needs to preserve that distinction; applying the current machine zone blindly can create another error. Approximate knowledge should retain its precision A family record may establish only a year or month. Inventing 1 January at midnight fills a missing value while making a false claim of precision. A qualified description, an appropriate partial-date representation or an explicit uncertainty record can retain the actual knowledge. The supported metadata fields and reader determine how that information is stored and displayed. Copying or exporting an image can preserve, transform or omit its date metadata depending on the workflow. In a catalogue, the interpreted capture date should remain associated with its evidence rather than being replaced by whichever filesystem timestamp happened to change last. See Also Exif photo metadata XMP metadata Photo albums and picture membership Photo geolocation and coordinate metadata Release dates References CIPA: Exif 3.1 specification, DC-008-2026 ExifTool: Exif date and GPS field definitions IPTC Photo Metadata specification ExifTool: QuickTime metadata definitions

articles/libraries-collections/personal-.title: Photo geolocation and coordinate metadata | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/personal-.keywords: Photo geolocation and coordinate metadata Photo geolocation describes a coordinate and its context, including reference directions and uncertainty, separately from the place depicted or the location of a stored file. A photograph's geolocation supplies a coordinate associated with the image. That can describe where the camera was, a subject location or a later assigned descriptive place, depending on the field and provenance. It is unrelated to the filesystem path. Moving a picture from a laptop to a server changes storage, not the depicted scene's geographical location. Magnitude and direction work together Common Exif GPS coordinates store degree, minute and second magnitudes with separate latitude and longitude reference directions. For an original illustrative coordinate: Latitude: 51 degrees, 30 minutes, 0 seconds; N Longitude: 0 degrees, 7 minutes, 12 seconds; W Convert the magnitude to decimal degrees: latitude = 51 + 30/60 + 0/3600 = 51.5 longitude = 0 + 7/60 + 12/3600 = 0.12 North is positive latitude; west is negative longitude in this signed representation. The resulting pair is 51.5, −0.12 . The diagram uses invented example records rather than measured photographs. Reference Sign in the decimal pair North latitude Positive South latitude Negative East longitude Positive West longitude Negative Dropping the W reference turns −0.12 into +0.12 and places the point on the other side of the reference meridian. The coordinate's numeric magnitude alone was not enough. Latitude, longitude and altitude are different axes Latitude measures the north/south position; longitude supplies east/west position. Reversing them produces a different point, even when both values remain within allowed numeric ranges. An altitude field has another reference. In a common Exif representation, a magnitude of 12 metres with the below-sea-level reference describes −12 metres under that convention. The number 12 alone does not establish which side of the reference surface is meant. A complete position also needs its coordinate-system context. Exif provides relevant GPS fields, and representations can carry a map datum. A reader should not infer an arbitrary local grid or an altitude reference merely from three numbers. Camera location and depicted location A photograph taken across a river can show a landmark on the opposite bank. The camera coordinate and the landmark coordinate are different locations. IPTC distinguishes location created from location shown. A human-readable place name can also be broader than a point: a region, city, harbour or venue. Converting a point into a place label is a lookup or interpretation. It can choose a nearby feature or administrative area, while the original coordinate continues to carry its numeric meaning. A label such as Harbour does not establish an exact camera position. A location field is still a descriptive claim. It can be captured automatically, added from a track log or entered later. Its provenance tells a catalogue how the claim was obtained; the pixels alone do not certify it. Precision and accuracy are separate Displaying six decimal places expresses small numeric increments. It does not prove that the positioning fix was accurate at that scale. A fix can be uncertain, stale or deliberately approximate. Exif GPS metadata can include a horizontal-positioning error field. Retaining available uncertainty is more informative than extending the displayed decimal string. The coordinate pair 0,0 is a real numerical position. It must not automatically stand for “location missing.” Absence and an actual zero coordinate need distinct representations. A derived image can retain the location A resized export can preserve the original location metadata even though the visible image becomes smaller. Another export can omit it. The picture's visual appearance does not reveal which metadata survived. A catalogue may also retain a location in an external descriptive record while the exported file has none. Reading the exported resource and reading the original catalogue then answer different questions. For an album grouped by place, the point or qualified place description provides evidence for membership. Capture dates provide another event dimension. The storage folder continues to locate the image bytes, while those descriptive fields explain where and when the photographed event belongs. articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Overview: Media analysis and previews | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Overview: Media analysis and previews Media analysis and preview generation derive technical information or navigation aids from source content. A probe describes the media streams; intro detection identifies a content relationship; seek previews provide pictures associated with playback positions. Each operation derives a different result and has its own workload. These pages connect that derived information to the source it was analyzed from. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Technical analysis of library media Technical media analysis inspects a resource’s container, streams and timing to supply playback facts independently of its catalogue description. Intro detection Episode intro detection estimates a recurring introduction interval whose start and end markers must belong to each episode’s actual timeline. Seek-preview thumbnails Seek-preview thumbnails are time-indexed small images that help a viewer locate scenes without decoding full video interactively for every seek position. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation Emby: Intro Skip W3C: Media Fragments URI 1.0

articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Episode intro detection | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Episode intro detection Episode intro detection estimates a recurring introduction interval whose start and end markers must belong to each episode’s actual timeline. Intro detection finds an interval that appears to be a programme's recurring introduction. The useful output is a pair of markers on each episode's timeline: where the introduction starts and where it ends. A fixed rule such as “skip the first minute” cannot describe every show. An episode can begin with a recap or a variable-length cold open before reaching the familiar title sequence. Another episode can start that sequence immediately. Recurrence survives a time shift One possible class of detection approach compares content-derived features across episodes. An audio fingerprint, for example, summarizes aspects of the signal so that a matching passage can be located without requiring complete-file byte equality. Research such as Haitsma and Kalker's audio-fingerprinting paper develops robust signal matching. It is background for the concept, not evidence that Emby implements that paper's algorithm. A file hash answers another question. Two independently encoded episodes have different bytes even when they share an opening sequence. A complete-file SHA-256 equality test is not a detector for the repeated portion. An original matching example Suppose each ten-second block is represented by an invented integer label. Six matching labels occur in both episode sequences: Shared labels: 2, 7, 4, 1, 9, 3 Episode A: shared run begins at block 4 Episode B: shared run begins at block 10 Block numbering starts at zero. Under this deliberately coarse model: Episode Candidate start Candidate end, exclusive Candidate duration A 4 × 10 = 40 seconds (4 + 6) × 10 = 100 seconds 60 seconds B 10 × 10 = 100 seconds (10 + 6) × 10 = 160 seconds 60 seconds The labels are synthetic. No audio was fingerprinted, and a ten-second block is not a claimed Emby analysis resolution. The example demonstrates how correspondence can survive an offset; it does not establish that the matched passage is a real introduction. Matching, boundaries and semantic role Finding repeated content supplies a candidate. Determining usable boundaries is another problem. An opening song may remain similar while the final title card changes. Dialogue may overlap its beginning. A short fade can make the perceptual boundary differ from the first confidently matched block. A detector needs enough evidence to avoid cutting into preceding dialogue or stopping partway through the opening. The interval's role also needs interpretation. Recaps can repeat clips; a broadcaster ident can recur; a scene may be reused later. “Found in several episodes” does not by itself mean “safe to skip as an introduction.” A useful model combines recurrence with context such as location within episodes and consistency across related programmes. The exact features, thresholds and exclusion rules vary by implementation. Neither the synthetic block model nor a general fingerprinting reference supplies Emby's private decisions. Seasons provide related comparison material A title sequence can change between seasons. Grouping unrelated episodes together could make the wrong recurrence appear dominant or leave the intended opening unsupported by enough comparisons. Emby's Intro Skip documentation describes season-based analysis and requires at least two episodes for detection in a season. It also describes background processing and app choices for using the resulting markers. Those documented product behaviors are separate from the explanatory matching model above. Even within a season, an episode may have a special opening or no recurring sequence. A missing marker can be an accurate result rather than an indication that the entire library scan failed. Detection does not remove the media The server can retain markers describing an interval. An app can then offer a button, skip automatically, or ignore those markers according to supported behavior and user choice. Skipping normally moves playback to the end marker; it does not require editing the original video or deleting the opening from storage. The interval remains part of the resource and can still be played. The public marker model distinguishes intro-start and intro-end markers from ordinary chapters. For the toy candidate in episode A, the pair would retain 40 seconds as the start and 100 seconds as the end. A single chapter named “Opening” supplies only a location unless additional interval information is defined. Markers are source-dependent Replacing an episode with another cut can shift its opening. Trimming a recap changes the start offset. A differently segmented combined programme can put a later episode's introduction inside a larger resource. The marker values must therefore remain associated with the timeline they describe. If the resource changes, reuse needs valid correspondence or new analysis. A retained series title and poster cannot establish that old intervals still match. See Also Series, seasons and episodes Technical analysis of library media Movie editions and cuts Chapter Markers References Emby: Intro Skip Haitsma and Kalker: A Highly Robust Audio Fingerprinting System (ISMIR 2002) Emby API: Playback progress reporting FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation

articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Technical analysis of library media | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Technical analysis of library media Technical media analysis inspects a resource’s container, streams and timing to supply playback facts independently of its catalogue description. Technical analysis asks what a particular media resource contains. It can identify a container, enumerate streams, read codec parameters and interpret timing information. Those facts support track selection, duration displays and playback decisions. A catalogue provider answers another question: which movie, episode or recording does the resource represent? A correct film synopsis cannot establish that the local file contains HEVC rather than H.264, or that its second audio track is present. Probing reads structured evidence FFprobe is a useful reference tool for this distinction. Its documented options can expose format, stream and chapter information: ffprobe -v error -show_format -show_streams -show_chapters -of json "movie.mkv" This is a read-only inspection command, not a requirement to process a library or change the file. The information available depends on the format, resource and analysis performed. The following hand-authored fragment illustrates output fields. It is not a measurement from an actual movie: { "streams": [ { "index": 0, "codec_type": "video", "codec_name": "h264", "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "avg_frame_rate": "24000/1001", "time_base": "1/24000" }, { "index": 1, "codec_type": "audio", "codec_name": "aac", "sample_rate": "48000", "channels": 6 } ], "format": { "duration": "6480.000000", "size": "9720000000" } } There are two streams with different roles. The audio channel count belongs to the audio stream; the video dimensions belong to the video stream. The format duration and size describe the resource-level example. Derive quantities at the right scope From the illustrative format values: 9,720,000,000 bytes × 8 ÷ 6,480 seconds = 12,000,000 bits per second = 12 Mbit/s average total bitrate That average includes everything counted in the file size, not only the video elementary stream. A separately reported video bitrate can therefore differ without contradiction. Variable bitrate also means the instantaneous delivery demand can exceed the average. The video's frame-rate ratio is approximately 23.976 frames per second. Its time base says one timestamp unit is 1/24,000 second. These are not the same property. For a hypothetical constant-frame-rate sequence with that frame rate, an interval of 1,001 such timestamp units represents one frame interval: 1,001 ÷ 24,000 seconds . The time base alone does not prove constant frame cadence or supply every frame's actual timestamp. Reading headers is not decoding the entire programme A probe can read container structures and enough stream data to identify relevant parameters. More detailed packet or frame analysis can inspect other evidence. Successfully displaying a stream list does not prove that every later packet is intact or every picture can be decoded. Likewise, an extension is only a naming clue. An MKV can carry several possible video and subtitle formats. The actual stream descriptions provide stronger evidence than the suffix. A duration can be declared in container information, derived from timestamps, or unavailable at the inspected scope. In incomplete recordings or resources with different stream endpoints, one reported number may not cover every question. Missing information should remain missing rather than being silently treated as zero. Descriptive tags and playback facts Container tags can carry titles and language labels. These are descriptive claims accompanying the stream; they are not conclusions that audio speech was recognized in that language. Colour-transfer metadata can describe an intended signal interpretation. Its presence is different from visually judging a frame. A six-channel audio stream supplies a count; more detailed layout information is needed to determine the channel positions. Emby's MediaSourceInfo exposes source-level information used by clients. A product can normalize or derive fields when importing probe data, so its displayed value is not necessarily a verbatim copy of every tool field. Analysis supports a playback decision A file can be valid and still require conversion for a particular device, display or delivery path. Codec/profile support, subtitles, audio capabilities and available bandwidth contribute to that decision. For the illustrative source, the resulting decision starts with H.264 video at 1920 × 1080, six-channel AAC audio and an average resource bitrate of 12 Mbit/s. The receiving playback path then determines which of those properties it can use directly and which require conversion. See Also Streams and Tracks Time Bases Bitrate Video Keyframes and Random Access Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation Emby API: MediaSourceInfo FFmpeg: Seeking and media processing

articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Seek-preview thumbnails | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Seek-preview thumbnails Seek-preview thumbnails are time-indexed small images that help a viewer locate scenes without decoding full video interactively for every seek position. A seek-preview thumbnail is a small picture associated with a position on a video timeline. When the viewer scrubs through the progress bar, the app can display the nearby indexed picture instead of repeatedly opening and decoding the full-resolution video at each pointer movement. The preview is an aid to locating content. It does not change the main video's resolution or guarantee that playback will begin on exactly the frame shown. A time lookup selects an image Assume an original preview set with samples at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 seconds. A lookup policy that chooses the latest sample at or before the requested time maps 42 seconds to the 40-second image. A policy choosing the nearest sample could differ at another position—for example, 47 seconds could select the 50-second image. The sampling interval and selection policy together determine the preview's temporal approximation. A chapter thumbnail is associated with a chapter point. A regular seek-preview set samples across the timeline. The same image can serve both roles in a particular system, but chapters and regular samples do not inherently have the same positions or count. More samples cost more work and storage For the fictional 108-minute movie, duration is 6,480 seconds. Sample at time zero and then at fixed intervals strictly before the end: Interval Sample count Assumed average image size Image-payload total 10 seconds 648 12,000 bytes 7.776 MB 5 seconds 1,296 12,000 bytes 15.552 MB The values use decimal units and the deliberately fixed average image size. Real images compress differently, and archive/index overhead adds further bytes. Halving the interval doubles the count under these assumptions. It improves temporal granularity, but it also increases extraction, encoding and storage work. The count does not imply that every source frame has to be decoded independently from scratch: sequential extraction can reuse decoded progression, while repeated random seeks have different costs. BIF archives store images with a time index A BIF archive packages preview images with index information. Roku's specification describes a header, time/offset entries and image data. The indexed timestamp is interpreted with a timestamp multiplier; the offsets locate the image bytes. Emby uses BIF resources for video previews. A current Emby team discussion describes storage either alongside media or in the server's metadata area. Packaging many pictures in one archive explains why the viewer can have hundreds of preview images while the file manager shows one .bif resource. Consider this original index arithmetic for three hypothetical image payloads , not a validated BIF file: Entry Timestamp value Time with 1,000 ms multiplier Absolute byte offset Image 0 0 0 seconds 96 Image 1 10 10 seconds 1,096 Image 2 20 20 seconds 2,296 End sentinel 0xffffffff End-of-data entry 3,196 A 64-byte header and four 8-byte index entries occupy 96 bytes. The assumed payload lengths are 1,000, 1,200 and 900 bytes. Subtracting consecutive offsets recovers those lengths; the final entry supplies the endpoint for the last image. These values illustrate two distinct coordinates: time selects an entry; byte offset locates its payload . Neither coordinate is a pixel position inside an image. A sprite sheet uses spatial coordinates instead Another design packs thumbnails into a larger image, called a sprite sheet, and indexes the rectangle for each time. Suppose a sheet has three columns and two rows of 320 × 180 tiles. Sample 4, counted from zero, occupies column 1 and row 1: column = 4 mod 3 = 1 row = floor(4 / 3) = 1 x = 1 × 320 = 320 y = 1 × 180 = 180 A spatial fragment can express that rectangle as: sheet.jpg#xywh=320,180,320,180 W3C's Media Fragments specification defines this pixel-rectangle notation. The example is a generic sprite design, not a claim that Emby uses this delivery format. The sketches are original illustrations, not captured film frames. Extraction needs a usable picture A requested timestamp can fall between random-access points. The decoder may start from an earlier access point and decode forward to obtain the intended picture. That is different from simply choosing a nearby keyframe as the preview; each approach has a different time/cost trade-off. The extracted frame then needs appropriate scaling and display interpretation. Aspect-ratio mistakes distort the image. An HDR source may need a suitable conversion for an SDR preview presentation. A black frame can be the correct sample at one instant but an unhelpful way to recognize a scene. These are content-processing choices. The availability of a preview file does not establish which extraction or colour-conversion algorithm produced it. Previews belong to the source timeline An archive created for one cut can remain numerically well-formed after the movie is replaced, while its images depict the wrong moments. A 13-minute insert shifts later content without necessarily changing the path. Regeneration or valid correspondence is then needed at the resource level. A metadata refresh that changes the movie's synopsis does not, by itself, prove the preview cache was regenerated. Storing previews beside the media likewise does not guarantee they correspond to a newly replaced file. articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Overview: Library scanning and media analysis | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Overview: Library scanning and media analysis Library scanning observes accessible sources and updates the catalogue through discovery and media analysis. A scan connects what the server can currently observe with the records already in its library. Incremental work can focus on changes, while analysis derives information or previews from the media itself. The branches here separate source observation from the later processing that enriches a catalogue entry. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Library scanning Library scanning discovers media resources and reconciles their recognized identities, descriptions and availability with the catalogue. Incremental library scans Incremental library scans reuse unchanged catalogue work while identifying the resources and dependent results affected by observed changes. Media analysis and previews Media analysis and preview generation derive technical information or navigation aids from source content. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library setup Microsoft: FileSystemWatcher event behavior

articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Incremental library scans | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Incremental library scans Incremental library scans reuse unchanged catalogue work while identifying the resources and dependent results affected by observed changes. An incremental scan limits repeated work by using what the catalogue already knows. It tries to identify additions, changes and removals, then updates the affected items and derived results. Unchanged resources can reuse previous analysis. Incremental does not necessarily mean “look only at one directory.” A scan can enumerate a whole root while avoiding expensive reanalysis of files whose chosen change signatures agree. Discovery scope and recomputation scope are different quantities. An original snapshot comparison Suppose a scanner records a path, size and modification timestamp for each resource: Path label Previous size/time signature New observation Initial decision in this model A 1,000 bytes / time 1 Same Reuse B 2,000 bytes / time 1 2,500 bytes / time 2 Changed C None 700 bytes / time 2 Added D 900 bytes / time 1 Absent under a reachable root Missing The tiny sizes are invented signatures, not movie sizes. Under these observations, one previous resource can be reused, one needs change handling, one is new and one is no longer present. Now repeat the scan against the same settled observations. There are no new signature changes. A well-defined incremental model should not keep inventing a fresh addition of C each time. That property—repeating the same reconciliation without creating additional changes—is useful when reasoning about retries. A cheap signature is not proof of byte identity A replacement can retain the same size and timestamp. Backup restores, coarse timestamp resolution and deliberate metadata preservation can produce that result. The model would classify it as unchanged even if the bytes differ. A complete cryptographic hash provides much stronger byte evidence, but obtaining it requires reading the complete resource. That can be expensive across large media collections or remote storage. Hash equality also says nothing by itself about whether two differently encoded resources represent the same cut. These are different trade-offs: Change evidence Work needed Useful limit Path/name Directory information Cannot establish content continuity Size and timestamp File attributes Can miss changes that preserve both Complete-file hash Read all bytes Strong byte evidence, not catalogue-work identity Media analysis Inspect relevant structures or content Cost and meaning depend on the analysis performed No single row supplies every kind of identity. Media item identity explains why the distinctions matter. Notifications trigger inspection; they do not replace it Real-time monitoring receives operating-system notifications of changes. An incremental reconciliation can use those notifications to decide what to inspect. It can also run after periodic enumeration without receiving any notification. Microsoft documents that filesystem notifications can be duplicated and that their buffers can overflow. An event stream is therefore not a perfect ledger of every final resource state. A rename or complex operation can also produce several notifications. A file-created event does not establish that a long copy has finished. Software may need to coalesce activity, recheck the file or defer dependent work until a usable resource is observed. Emby's library documentation describes real-time monitoring on supported filesystems. That establishes a product capability; the original diagram above does not reconstruct its debounce, retry or queue implementation. Changed resources invalidate dependent results Suppose a video is replaced at the same path with an extended cut. Recognizing the change is only the first step. Technical stream information may need reprobe. Seek previews and intro markers were derived from the old timeline. Any retained correspondence for a resume value needs assessment. A movie title retrieved from a work-level provider can remain correct while all those resource-specific facts change. This is a dependency problem. In a conceptual cache: resource version -> stream analysis -> timeline previews -> content-derived markers Reusing the descriptive movie record does not justify reusing every derived resource result. Conversely, retagging only a descriptive field need not require recomputing every video-derived result in a model that can distinguish those dependencies. A product chooses its own invalidation rules and signatures. The model explains the required relationships, not a promise that every small edit has an identical cost in Emby. Reachable absence differs from failed observation A periodic scan can recover a missed notification by observing a settled directory. But an unreachable root still supplies incomplete evidence. Treating all its previous items as confirmed deletions would equate “could not inspect” with “inspected and found absent.” The system's actual response belongs to its retention and error policy. For understanding the result, keep discovery success, resource availability and confirmed removal as distinct states. articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.title: Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/scanning/.keywords: Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation Library scanning discovers media resources and reconciles their recognized identities, descriptions and availability with the catalogue. A library scan compares available resources with the catalogue the server already holds. It discovers additions, notices changes, interprets names and structure, and updates the represented items according to the product's reconciliation rules. That can involve much more than listing filenames, but it need not mean decoding every second of every film. Discovery, descriptive metadata retrieval, technical probing and derived analysis are related operations with different purposes. From a path to a described item An explanatory pipeline is: This is a conceptual dependency diagram. It is not Emby's internal scheduler or an assertion that its tasks run in this exact sequence. Discovery finds entries within configured roots and supported resource structures. It needs to determine which are media, supplementary files, directories or other material. Interpretation gives the resource a role. A season/episode filename, a movie folder, a trailer association or an embedded music tag can supply clues. The configured content model provides context. Reconciliation compares the observed resource with existing catalogue state. A newly observed path, a changed resource and a no-longer-observed path call for different decisions. Enrichment adds descriptions and technical facts. A provider lookup supplies catalogue information; a probe inspects the actual resource. Neither operation substitutes for the other. Derived work can create previews or detect recurring intervals. It depends on media content and may be scheduled or completed separately from the basic catalogue update. The phases explain why a new entry can appear with a filename-derived title before its final poster or analysis is available. A usable path and a completed description are different milestones. A before-and-after inventory Use this original observation set: Resource Previous observation Current observation Question for reconciliation A Present Present, unchanged signature Can existing analysis be reused? B Present Present, changed signature Which technical or derived facts became stale? C Absent Present What entity and source does it represent? D Present Not found under a reachable root Was it removed or moved? E Present Its root could not be read Is availability unknown rather than confirmed absent? A signature here means the scanner's chosen change evidence, not necessarily a complete-file hash. Incremental scans explains the trade-off between cheap change detection and certainty. The final two rows are especially important. A reachable directory that no longer contains D supplies different evidence from a failed attempt to read E's entire disk. “Not observed” is a result; its cause determines how much can be concluded. Actual retention/removal behavior belongs to the server's implementation and settings. A move can appear as a disappearance and an addition. Preserving the original logical identity then requires sufficient evidence to relate the two observations. The same title alone is not necessarily sufficient. A file can appear before it is complete During a copy, a resource may already have its final-looking name while its size is still growing. Container headers can be incomplete, or essential index information can arrive later. A probe at that moment can fail or discover only a provisional description. A change notification tells a scanner that something happened. It does not certify that the final media is complete and ready. Rechecking, observing stability or using a deliberate publish/rename workflow are possible ways for software to handle that dependency; they are not universal guarantees supplied by the filesystem. Likewise, a readable directory does not establish that every file can be opened. Resource-level permissions and transient errors can differ from directory enumeration. These distinctions help interpret a scan that has found a title but has not yet supplied a dependable duration or stream list. Scan, refresh and extraction answer different questions Operation Primary question Discover/reconcile library resources What media is present, changed or missing? Refresh descriptive metadata What catalogue fields should be retrieved or updated? Probe a source What streams and technical properties does this resource contain? Extract seek previews Which small pictures represent its timeline? Detect episode intros Which interval appears to be a recurring introduction? A metadata refresh may act on an already known item without discovering another path. Replacing a poster does not establish that cached stream analysis matches a newly replaced video. Finishing enumeration does not establish that preview extraction has finished. Emby's Library Setup , metadata manager and scheduled-task documentation describe the corresponding product controls. The Learn distinction is about the work they request, rather than their click paths. Why scan duration varies The cost depends on the number of directory entries, storage latency, how much analysis can be reused and which new work is required. Many small files can be expensive to enumerate even if their total byte count is low. A few large files may be cheap to identify but costly to decode for content-derived analysis. Provider access contributes another cost: a new match can require network requests that an unchanged, already described item does not. Image retrieval and background extraction add further dependencies. A completed scan therefore has a defined scope. It is useful to ask which catalogue reconciliation finished and which derived tasks remain, rather than treating one percentage as a universal measure of every library operation. articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Overview: Episode ordering | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Overview: Episode ordering Episode ordering conventions assign positions to programmes according to a particular catalogue or release arrangement. The same programme can have one position in an aired order and another on a DVD release. Absolute numbering supplies a different sequence again. A match needs the intended convention as well as the numbers, which explains how an apparently valid episode label can identify the wrong content. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Understanding episode order Episode order maps a series arrangement and its season or episode coordinates to the actual episodes represented by media resources. Aired episode order Aired episode order assigns episode coordinates according to a catalogue’s broadcast or release arrangement for a television series. DVD episode order DVD episode order describes an episodic release arrangement that can change numbering, grouping or segmentation relative to broadcast order. Absolute episode numbering Absolute episode numbering assigns series-wide ordinal positions whose relationship to season coordinates depends on a defined episode sequence. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB API: Television episode groups Emby: Television naming

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Absolute episode numbering | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Absolute episode numbering Absolute episode numbering assigns series-wide ordinal positions whose relationship to season coordinates depends on a defined episode sequence. Absolute numbering gives each episode one position across a series, rather than restarting the episode counter within each season. It is useful when resources or viewers use a continuous sequence. The number still belongs to a defined arrangement: “episode 15” is not a complete identity without the series and ordering agreement. A worked season conversion Assume this original catalogue arrangement: Season Regular episodes Absolute interval 1 12 1–12 2 10 13–22 3 8 23–30 With the same regular-episode sequence in both schemes, season 2 episode 3 has absolute number: episodes in earlier seasons + episode within this season 12 + 3 = 15 To convert absolute 15 back, find the interval containing it. That is 13–22, so subtract the preceding twelve episodes: 15 - 12 = 3 . The result is S02E03. The boundaries matter. Absolute 12 is S01E12, absolute 13 is S02E01, and absolute 23 is S03E01. An assumed “ten episodes per season” formula would be wrong for this catalogue. The arithmetic assumes the same sequence If another order rearranges the episodes, season counts alone cannot perform the conversion. The actual episode must first be resolved through an order mapping . Specials can change the agreement too. Suppose a special is inserted between regular absolute episodes 12 and 13. A sequence that includes it assigns 13 to the special and shifts the next regular episode to 14. A scheme that excludes specials retains 13 for that regular episode. Both sequences can be internally consistent. The integer 13 cannot tell a library which agreement the resource's filename uses. Combined or recut programmes add another complication: one ordinal might refer to a programme covering two episodes from another arrangement. A one-to-one number conversion then loses the segmentation relationship. Numbering is a catalogue property Absolute numbering does not change the media's codec, timing or stream structure. A filename like Harbour Watch 015.mkv supplies a clue about an intended ordinal; it does not state the catalogue's season partition or special-inclusion rules. Emby's TV Naming guide is the reference for recognized resource naming. Bringing series-wide numbers into a seasonal library requires an appropriate catalogue interpretation or a verified mapping; continuous numbering is not a promise that every integration will infer that mapping from a bare number. See Also Understanding episode order Series, seasons and episodes Television specials References TheTVDB: API season types and alternate orders Emby: Television naming TVmaze API: Episode dates and alternate lists

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Aired episode order | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Aired episode order Aired episode order assigns episode coordinates according to a catalogue’s broadcast or release arrangement for a television series. Aired order describes the sequence a catalogue assigns to a show's broadcast or initial release arrangement. It is commonly the default numbered arrangement, but the word aired does not supply a universal ordering rule independent of that catalogue. TheTVDB's API documentation says its default order is generally aired order. That describes a catalogue convention. It does not imply that every broadcaster, region or later release used the same sequence. Production and broadcast can disagree A fictional show supplies this example: Story Production position Broadcast coordinate Arrival 1 S01E01 The Missing Boat 2 S01E03 Night Signal 3 S01E02 Production position describes the making or intended production sequence. Broadcast coordinate describes the aired arrangement. A production code printed on a script is therefore not automatically a filename-ready episode number. The distinction explains why story continuity can appear unusual under aired order without the library having misread the files. A network can change the release sequence; the catalogue can accurately record that sequence. An air date supplies evidence, not the complete key Two episodes can be released on the same day. A streaming season can be released as a batch. A programme can have several regional air dates. Sorting dates alone may therefore leave ties or select the wrong release context. An aired coordinate typically retains season and episode position, while a date field records a release event. Both can be useful without being interchangeable. For daily programmes, a date-based episode may supply a better naming clue than an enormous season counter. The date still needs the series and catalogue context to locate the right entry. Recognizing a correct aired match If a local file contains Night Signal and the catalogue's aired arrangement assigns it S01E02, then that coordinate is consistent with its story. If the file was named from a DVD arrangement that calls The Missing Boat E02, the same coordinate text can lead to a different match. The decisive check is the episode identity and content, not whether the number looks plausible. Understanding episode order works through that translation in detail. See Also Understanding episode order DVD episode order Date-based episodes TheTVDB References TheTVDB: API season types and alternate orders TVmaze API: Episode dates and alternate lists Emby: Television naming

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: DVD episode order | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: DVD episode order DVD episode order describes an episodic release arrangement that can change numbering, grouping or segmentation relative to broadcast order. DVD order names a catalogue arrangement associated with an episodic disc release. It can differ from broadcast order because episodes were rearranged, grouped into different seasons or presented as combined programmes. The label describes the release arrangement, not the encoded file format. An MKV extracted from a DVD can retain DVD numbering. A DVD-Video resource can contain episodes that the catalogue numbers in aired order. Changing the container does not choose the episode order. Disc numbers are storage coordinates Disc label What it establishes What it does not establish Season 1, disc 2 A disc in that particular box set Catalogue season 2 Programme 3 on disc 2 A selectable programme on that disc Series-wide episode 3 Bonus disc A supplementary resource grouping A provider's season-zero episode identities Disc layouts can include menus, multiple programmes and extras. Their physical positions are not a universal series-numbering system. A catalogue's DVD arrangement can instead assign explicit season/episode coordinates. In the fictional Harbour Watch example, The Missing Boat is DVD S01E02 and aired S01E03. Matching its file as aired E02 would retrieve the wrong story even though the disc extraction and filename parsing succeeded. One DVD programme can represent two episodes Suppose a DVD programme contains two 22-minute stories in a 44-minute resource. A broadcast catalogue may describe those stories separately. A DVD arrangement may describe their combination. This is not only a permutation. The relationship between the resource and catalogue episodes has changed. TheTVDB's multi-segment policy explicitly addresses combined DVD entries, illustrating why the chosen catalogue can have different episode entities across orders. A filename range can describe coverage of two episodes in a library that supports that relationship. It does not provide the exact point inside the video where the second episode begins. Multi-episode files explains that distinction. Match the release before translating numbers The useful evidence is the release's actual episode sequence, story titles and segmentation, plus the catalogue arrangement that describes them. A general “DVD” label may be insufficient if another region's box set has a different cut or programme layout. A correct series identity narrows the candidates, but a coordinate still needs its arrangement. Translation works by resolving the actual episode and finding its coordinate under the target order; a universal offset between aired and DVD numbering does not exist. Emby's TV naming documentation describes supported resource naming. Provider arrangements still need representation in the integration being used. For The Missing Boat, the mapping remains concrete: resolve the DVD programme's story, then associate it with aired S01E03 if that is the target catalogue arrangement. See Also Understanding episode order Aired episode order Multi-episode files TheTVDB References TheTVDB: Multi-segment episodes and DVD orders TheTVDB: API season types and alternate orders TVmaze API: Episode dates and alternate lists Emby: Television naming

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Understanding episode order | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Understanding episode order Episode order maps a series arrangement and its season or episode coordinates to the actual episodes represented by media resources. Episode order is the agreement that makes an episode number meaningful. It specifies which episode occupies a particular position in a series arrangement. Aired order, DVD order and absolute numbering can assign different coordinates to the same material. This is why a filename can be recognized perfectly while its title, synopsis and thumbnail are wrong. The parser may read S01E02 correctly, but the metadata lookup interprets that coordinate under a different agreement from the one used to name the file. Four stories, two arrangements The fictional show Harbour Watch has four episode stories. The labels A–D below are stable keys invented for this example; they do not stand for real provider IDs. Story key Episode title Aired coordinate DVD coordinate A Arrival S01E01 S01E01 B The Missing Boat S01E03 S01E02 C Night Signal S01E02 S01E03 D Departure S01E04 S01E04 Aired sequence: A → C → B → D . DVD sequence: A → B → C → D . The bytes of story B do not change when its coordinate changes from aired E03 to DVD E02. What changes is the arrangement used to locate it. Now take a DVD-derived file named Harbour Watch S01E02.mkv . Its pictures and dialogue contain The Missing Boat —story B. A lookup under aired order asks for story C. The resulting synopsis can be internally correct for aired E02 and still be wrong for the local resource. Choosing “sort by episode number” cannot repair this. Both interpretations already have a number 2; the problem is which episode the number refers to. Resolve identity through the arrangement A reliable interpretation follows a chain: Establish the series. Distinguish the original show from a reboot or another show with the same name. Establish the arrangement. Determine which order the file's numbers use. Interpret the coordinate. Resolve season and episode number within that arrangement. Associate the resource. Confirm that the resolved episode matches the file's actual story. Present the desired sequence. Display or play the identified episodes using the intended ordering. The sequence matters. A correct series ID narrows the catalogue, but it does not automatically select an appropriate alternate order. A correct coordinate under the wrong arrangement produces the wrong child identity. In the worked example, translating DVD E02 into aired order requires two lookups: DVD S01E02 -> story B story B -> aired S01E03 Changing 02 to 03 is the last step, not the rule. Another show could map DVD E02 to aired E07, move it to another season, or leave it unassigned in the target arrangement. For a whole collection, an explicit mapping is safer to reason about than a constant offset. A permutation can cross in both directions: B moves from 2 to 3 while C moves from 3 to 2. Adding one to every number would corrupt the other stories. Sorting and identification are separate operations Sorting takes already identified items and chooses their display order. It can put correctly matched episodes in release-date order, title order or another supported presentation. Identification determines which episode an item represents. It establishes the description and relationships on which sorting operates. Confusing these operations produces several misleading fixes: Change What it can do What it cannot establish by itself Change display sort Rearrange identified items Correct a wrong episode match Rename a coordinate Supply another naming clue Prove which story the file contains Select another metadata order Interpret coordinates under another arrangement Guarantee a one-to-one match for a recut release Correct provider identity Associate the right catalogue entity Supply missing boundaries inside a combined resource An ordering field in a product model is evidence that the product represents some order information. It does not imply every catalogue alternate arrangement is exposed, or that changing that field remaps every existing asset and history record automatically. Alternate releases can change the episodes themselves Some alternatives are simple permutations like A, C, B, D. Others change segmentation. Imagine the DVD contains one 44-minute programme combining A and B, while the aired catalogue describes two 22-minute episodes. The relationship is now: DVD programme X -> aired episode A + aired episode B There is no single aired coordinate that fully represents X. A multi-episode relationship , a catalogue record for the combined programme, or some other explicit representation is needed. Treating X as only A loses B; treating the file as two independent full-length resources pretends a boundary exists that the player may not know. TheTVDB documents alternate season types and orders that can include differently cut episodes. Its multi-segment policy also describes combined DVD episodes. These are concrete reasons why “choose DVD order” is not universally equivalent to rearranging the same episode records. A recut can go further by moving scenes between programmes. Then matching a title or total runtime is insufficient. The resource's release context and actual content must establish which catalogue description applies. Specials have identity and placement A special often has a coordinate such as S00E03 while its intended viewing position is between two regular episodes. The special's catalogue group and its place in a sequence answer different questions. Putting every season-zero item before season one is one possible numeric sort, not a universal narrative order. An introductory special, a later holiday episode and a retrospective can require different placements. Television specials develops that relationship separately. Absolute numbering has another agreement: one series-wide sequence instead of a season/episode pair. It still needs a defined order and rules about specials. The integer alone does not tell us how the catalogue partitions seasons. What an order correction can affect A wrong match can attach the wrong title, synopsis, credits and episode thumbnail. Correcting only the visible title leaves the deeper association unresolved. Viewer state also has an identity scope. A played flag for story B should not become a played flag for story C just because both occupy coordinate E02 in different arrangements. A resume value additionally needs the correct resource timeline. The same reasoning applies to introductory markers and extracted previews. This does not require a universal recipe for changing every Emby installation. The TV Naming documentation describes supported naming relationships, while provider and server capabilities determine which orders can be selected or represented. The conceptual requirement is to preserve series, arrangement, episode identity and resource correspondence throughout the change. For the four-story example, success is easy to describe: The Missing Boat continues to identify story B, its local resource remains associated with B, and the chosen display sequence puts it in the intended place. An attractive row labelled “Episode 2” is not enough to establish those results. See Also Aired episode order DVD episode order Absolute episode numbering Multi-episode files TheTVDB References TheTVDB: API season types and alternate orders TheTVDB: Multi-segment episodes and DVD orders TMDB API: Television episode groups Emby: Television naming Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Overview: Television and episodic media | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Overview: Television and episodic media Television library structure connects series, seasons, episode identities and the files representing them. An episode's place in a series is not always captured by one season-and-number label. Specials, date-based programmes and anthology structures add context, while one file can contain several episodes. This area establishes those models and the ordering conventions used to connect the source to the intended programme. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Series hierarchy A series hierarchy organizes episodic media by parent series and season while retaining each episode’s identity and playable resources. Episode ordering Episode ordering conventions assign positions to programmes according to a particular catalogue or release arrangement. Television specials A television special has its own episode identity whose catalogue grouping can differ from its intended position among regular episodes. Multi-episode files A multi-episode file stores material for several episodes in one media resource, requiring a distinction between catalogue coverage and internal playback boundaries. Date-based episodes Date-based episode naming identifies a programme by a catalogue-associated release date whose series and broadcast context remain part of the match. Anthology series An anthology series groups stories under a shared series identity while narrative continuity may occur at episode or season level. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Television naming Emby: Ordering television specials

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Anthology series | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Anthology series An anthology series groups stories under a shared series identity while narrative continuity may occur at episode or season level. An anthology series gives distinct stories a shared television identity. What continues can be the format, theme or presentation rather than the same characters and plot. There are different levels of narrative continuity: Pattern What remains connected Where the story normally develops Episode anthology Series format or theme Within individual episodes Season anthology Series identity and presentation Across the episodes of one season Continuing serial Series and continuing narrative Across seasons as well as episodes These are descriptive patterns, not content-type settings. A catalogue still needs to identify the actual series and its children. A season title can name a story Imagine the fictional anthology Coastal Lives . Season 1, The Lighthouse , tells one six-episode story. Season 2, The Harbour , has a different cast and tells another eight-episode story. The season titles communicate narrative scope. They do not necessarily establish two unrelated television series. If the chosen catalogue represents both under Coastal Lives , retaining that series identity makes its season relationships and provider matching coherent. A personal collection can bring together favourite anthology stories across shows without changing their original episode identities. That is a collection relationship , not a reason to assign every selected episode to a fabricated common series. Independence does not erase order For an episode anthology, many episodes may be understandable in isolation. Release order still supplies their catalogue coordinates. Selecting a different story because the number was interpreted under the wrong order remains a metadata error. For a season anthology, the within-season order can be essential even when seasons can be watched independently. “The seasons are unrelated” does not imply “every episode is interchangeable.” Emby's TV Naming documentation describes the series/season context used to recognize episodic resources. The relevant catalogue evidence determines whether a named story is a season, an episode, a separate series or a related film. Narrative similarity alone cannot select that entity type. See Also Series, seasons and episodes Understanding episode order Film franchises in a media library Metadata relationships References Schema.org: Television series relationships TheTVDB: API season types and alternate orders Emby: Television naming

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Date-based episodes | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Date-based episodes Date-based episode naming identifies a programme by a catalogue-associated release date whose series and broadcast context remain part of the match. For a daily programme, a date can be a clearer label than a season and episode counter. A resource named Evening Harbour 2026-10-09.mkv communicates the intended programme date directly. Emby's TV Naming guide documents date forms. The naming clue still needs the series and catalogue context: the date is not a global episode ID. Release date and recording instant Suppose a fictional programme begins at 23:30 on 9 October under a fixed UTC−04:00 offset: Representation Value Local start 2026-10-09 23:30, UTC−04:00 The same instant in UTC 2026-10-10 03:30Z Local programme date 2026-10-09 Adding four hours changes the calendar date without changing the event. Using the UTC date as the programme's catalogue date would select the next day in this example. A provider can define the programme date in its broadcast or release context. That field should not be replaced automatically with the machine's recording date, file creation time or upload date. A recording copied the next morning still depicts the previous night's programme. Release dates explain the broader distinction between calendar dates and time instants. One date can yield several candidates A series might release two programmes on one day, or have separate editions associated with that date. TVmaze's episodes-by-date interface returns a set of episodes, illustrating why a date lookup need not produce exactly one candidate. A matching process may need another clue: the edition title, guest/topic information or a provider episode identity. Those clues should resolve the candidate rather than assume a filename suffix is a universally supported tie-breaking convention. Date found on a resource Appropriate interpretation Known catalogue air/release date Strong date-based matching clue for that series Recording-start timestamp Evidence about capture, requiring broadcast-context interpretation Filesystem creation time Evidence about this stored copy Date embedded in an arbitrary title A label that may need confirmation See Also Aired episode order Understanding episode order Release dates References Emby: Television naming TVmaze API: Episode dates and alternate lists Microsoft: TimeSpan tick units

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Multi-episode files | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Multi-episode files A multi-episode file stores material for several episodes in one media resource, requiring a distinction between catalogue coverage and internal playback boundaries. A multi-episode file contains material corresponding to more than one episode. It might preserve a double-length broadcast, a disc programme combining two stories, or a recording that runs through several episodes. The library needs to express what the file covers. A player additionally needs to know where each episode begins if it is to start a particular episode inside that resource. Those are separate kinds of information. One range, one resource An illustrative Emby naming form is: Harbour Watch S01E01-E02.mkv The TV Naming guide documents ranges for multiple episodes within the same season. The name expresses coverage of episodes 1 and 2. It does not change the container, create another file or insert a timestamp for the start of episode 2. The diagram describes an original coverage model, not the exact item layout used by every server version. A boundary must come from other evidence Assume the fictional resource contains story A from 0:00 to 22:00 and story B from 22:00 to 45:00, with no extra material at the boundary. Position within the resource Corresponding story position 12:00 Story A, 12:00 22:00 Story B begins 40:30 Story B, 18:30 45:00 Resource end The third row subtracts B's known start: 40:30 - 22:00 = 18:30 . Splitting the total duration in half would instead place the boundary at 22:30. That guess is wrong by 30 seconds because the stories have unequal lengths. Production logos, credits or interstitial material can produce further differences. A chapter marker may identify a useful start, but “chapter 2” is not automatically “episode 2.” A feature can have many chapters, and a combined programme can have none. Exact episode boundaries require appropriately scoped metadata or content analysis, rather than a number extracted from the filename. Metadata coverage can differ from programme segmentation A catalogue may represent the broadcast as one combined episode, or describe its component stories separately. A disc release can choose another segmentation again. TheTVDB's multi-segment policy illustrates why both combined and separated arrangements exist. A range against one arrangement is therefore not automatically a range against another. If the same file covers DVD programme X but aired episodes A and B, the mapping needs those actual entity relationships. Emby's public item model includes an end index as well as an initial index. That can describe a numbered span. It does not by itself promise that the file contains corresponding internal chapter boundaries or that every app exposes independent playback of each covered episode. The inverse of a multipart resource Resource relationship Catalogue meaning One file contains two episodes Several episode identities or a covered span share a resource Two files contain one movie Sequential parts collectively represent one intended feature Two files encode one episode Alternative playable representations of an episode All three can involve the same number of filenames, but their playback logic differs. For alternatives, choose one complete representation. For sequential parts, traverse the necessary resources. For a combined resource, locate the relevant content within one timeline. History and subtitles need that timeline A file-relative resume point of 40:30 is unambiguous for the resource. Reporting it as 40:30 of story B would be wrong under the worked boundary. Treating the range as two ordinary independent 45-minute episodes would be wrong for a different reason: it invents two full resources. Timed subtitles also normally refer to the combined file's presentation time unless a specific representation translates them. A cue at file minute 23 belongs after the second story begins in the example; subtracting 22 minutes only makes sense when converting to B's local timeline. See Also Understanding episode order DVD episode order Multipart movies and file stacking Chapter Markers References Emby: Television naming TheTVDB: Multi-segment episodes and DVD orders Emby API: BaseItemDto FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Series, seasons and episodes | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Series, seasons and episodes A series hierarchy organizes episodic media by parent series and season while retaining each episode’s identity and playable resources. A television library needs to know both which show an episode belongs to and where it fits within that show's chosen arrangement. The usual series → season → episode hierarchy supplies that context. The hierarchy describes catalogue entities. The episode's actual media is another layer: one episode may have several encodes, and one file may contain several episodes. The number is qualified by its parents S01E02 identifies a position within a season and series arrangement. Thousands of shows have that coordinate. It is not a global episode identifier. Entity Fictional example Describes Series Harbour Watch (2020) The show as a whole Season Season 1 under the chosen order A grouping of the show's episodes Episode Season 1, episode 2 One episode in that arrangement Media source An MKV encode of that episode The playable representation Even within one series, a coordinate can change meaning under another episode order . The parent series identity resolves which show is meant; the selected order resolves how its seasons and numbers map to episodes. A show title plus its first-release year helps distinguish similarly named series and reboots. A provider ID supplies a more explicit catalogue match. Neither a familiar title nor the fact that files occupy the same drive establishes the correct series parent. Folder structure communicates the relationship A directory layout can make the intended parents clear: Harbour Watch (2020)/ Season 1/ Harbour Watch S01E01.mkv Harbour Watch S01E02.mkv Season 2/ Harbour Watch S02E01.mkv Emby's TV Naming guide describes recognized structures. A season folder is useful storage evidence, but a season entity and a season directory are not identical concepts. A catalogue can organize by season when the numbering supplies that context, subject to the product's supported library conventions. That distinction also explains why moving an episode file does not, in itself, change the television work it represents. The scanner must reconcile the path and naming evidence with the entity relationship. Description belongs at the right level A series overview introduces the premise. A season overview can describe a particular run or story arc. An episode overview describes that episode's events. A guest actor can appear on one episode without being a regular cast member for every season. Artwork has the same scopes. The series poster identifies the show; a season poster can identify one run; an episode thumbnail depicts or represents a particular episode. Incorrect parent assignment can therefore produce a credible series poster with the wrong episode synopsis and image below it. Parent counts also answer different questions. A season with ten catalogued episode descriptions does not necessarily have ten local playable files. One combined resource could cover two episodes, while another described episode could be unavailable. Specials add a further distinction between catalogue storage and viewing placement. A special can be grouped separately and still belong between two regular episodes in an intended sequence. The hierarchy tells us which entities exist; their ordering and availability determine how a viewer moves through them. See Also Library content models Understanding episode order Television specials References Emby: Television naming Schema.org: Television series relationships Emby API: BaseItemDto

articles/libraries-collections/televisio.title: Television specials | Emby Learn
articles/libraries-collections/televisio.keywords: Television specials A television special has its own episode identity whose catalogue grouping can differ from its intended position among regular episodes. A special is episodic material that a catalogue groups outside the regular season sequence. It can be an introductory programme, a holiday story, a bridge between seasons or a retrospective. Many television catalogues use season zero for such entries. That provides a place to identify and browse them. It does not mean every special should be watched before season one. Identity and placement are two coordinates In this fictional example, special S00E03 belongs between regular episodes S01E03 and S01E04: The special's identity is its entry in the special group. Its placement is a relationship to the regular sequence. Sorting solely by season number places the whole special group first; sorting solely by E03 could mix unrelated groups. Neither rule captures the illustrated placement. Emby's special-ordering documentation describes metadata that can position specials relative to regular seasons and episodes. This separates their catalogue identity from the timeline in which they should appear. The exact available behavior depends on the represented metadata and app. Special role A plausible viewing placement What its number alone establishes Introductory programme Before the regular story begins Its coordinate within the chosen special group Bridge episode Between two regular seasons The same limited grouping coordinate Holiday story Within an existing season's sequence No universal holiday/date placement Retrospective After the relevant stories No guarantee of spoiler-safe order These are illustrative placements, not provider-assigned rules for all specials. A catalogue special is not every extra A making-of video can be a numbered episode in a provider's catalogue, or it can be a local supplementary resource without such an episode record. Both are useful ways to describe it, but they have different identity evidence. Assigning an arbitrary special number does not establish that the provider uses the same number. A later metadata match could resolve to an unrelated programme if the coordinate and catalogue disagree. The local title and role remain important. A resource called The Making of Night Signal describes a documentary about an episode; it is not necessarily another cut of that episode. Placement affects continuation If a viewer finishes S01E03, an intended sequence that includes the bridge special may choose S00E03 before S01E04. A sequence excluding supplementary material can choose the regular episode directly. The difference is a selection policy, not a change to the special's identity. Watched state adds another dimension: a special already seen by this user can be handled differently from an unseen one. That is why next-episode selection needs catalogue order, availability and user state together. See Also Series, seasons and episodes Understanding episode order Next-episode selection References Emby: Ordering television specials Emby: Television naming Emby API: BaseItemDto TVmaze API: Episode dates and alternate lists

articles/live-tv/channels/identity/index.title: Overview: Channel identity | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/identity/index.keywords: Overview: Channel identity Channel identity connects broadcast services and multiplexes to the names or numbers presented in a lineup. The number shown in a guide can be a logical label rather than a direct physical tuning frequency. Service identifiers and multiplex membership provide another layer of identity. These topics explain the mapping that connects a visible channel entry to the programme stream the source actually supplies. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Broadcast multiplexes A broadcast multiplex combines several service/component data streams into one defined transport/acquisition context, with shared capacity and signaling linking the selected programme to its packets. Service identifiers Broadcast service identifiers locate a programme within its defined network/transport/source context, independently of component PIDs and viewer-facing channel labels. Virtual channel numbers Virtual channel numbers provide viewer-facing labels mapped through defined signaling or source information to the physical transport and programme actually acquired. Channel lineups A channel lineup is a source-contextual inventory of service identities, labels and access/media locations that must be associated separately with guide descriptions. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts DVB: Service Information specification ATSC: A/65 PSIP specification ATSC: A/65:2013 channel and transport fields Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits

articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Li.title: Channel lineups and source identity | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Li.keywords: Channel lineups and source identity A channel lineup is a source-contextual inventory of service identities, labels and access/media locations that must be associated separately with guide descriptions. A channel lineup is an inventory of services exposed by a source. It connects channel identities and presentation labels to the route used to acquire media. An Emby guide adds programme descriptions through another association. The lineup and guide are related inputs, not the same database. Number and name are not always unique selection keys Use an original combined inventory: Source Source channel key Display number Name A news-main 101 Harbour News B region-news 101 Estuary News A cinema-main 205 Harbour Cinema A key made only from display number 101 cannot distinguish the first two entries. The declared composite identities (A, news-main) and (B, region-news) can. These are invented entries, not a scanned lineup. A backend or tuner interface can use another representation, but its own selection scope needs to remain intact. The guide join can be wrong while media works Suppose (A, news-main) correctly supplies Harbour News, yet its guide association points to a fictional estuary.news guide channel. The media source can work while the programme descriptions belong to the wrong station. Changing the video decoder would not fix that data association. Emby’s channel mapping documentation addresses the source-to-guide relationship. An extended M3U tvg-id can assist that association through the implementation’s interpretation. Its display name/number and stream URL still have separate roles. Presentation changes need not change acquisition Renaming an entry, ordering the lineup or applying a display tag can alter how it is presented without replacing its underlying source key. A source change—such as updated service identifiers or a new stream URL—affects another part of the route. It must be reflected in the appropriate source data rather than inferred from a label edit.
