Likewise, hiding a lineup entry does not establish that a currently owned acquisition has been released. Resource lifetime belongs to the actual active use and source contract. An inventory is not proof of current media A stored catalogue can retain a channel that is temporarily unavailable, has moved or requires an access path the current source cannot supply. A successful inventory request and a successful media request therefore need separate observations. Programme descriptions can also update on another schedule. The stable source identity connects those observations. It makes it possible to report that one named service’s media changed while retaining or correcting its independent guide association. See Also Extended M3U channel lists Broadcast service identifiers Virtual channel numbers References SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits Emby: Channel-to-guide mapping

articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Mu.title: Broadcast multiplexes | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Mu.keywords: Broadcast multiplexes A broadcast multiplex combines several service/component data streams into one defined transport/acquisition context, with shared capacity and signaling linking the selected programme to its packets. A broadcast multiplex combines several data streams into one transmission/transport context. A receiver can acquire that shared context before selecting the programme the viewer requested. The RF carrier, multiplex and selected programme are therefore related but different objects. Programme tables connect service selection to packets Use this original readable MPEG-TS-style model: { "transportStreamId": 10, "services": [ {"programNumber": 101, "pmtPid": 256, "videoPid": 512, "audioPid": 513}, {"programNumber": 102, "pmtPid": 257, "videoPid": 768, "audioPid": 769} ] } It is not a native table or a captured transport. The PAT relationship associates a programme number with its programme-map PID. The corresponding PMT identifies the relevant components. Selecting programme 101 is not the same operation as filtering arbitrary packets with PID 101. MPEG-TS programme tables develops that structure in detail. Each service can have several audio, subtitle and other components beyond the simplified video/audio pair shown here. Capacity is shared over time Consider an original twenty-six-Mbit/s transport-budget exercise, with two Mbit/s reserved for other declared work: Observation News demand Cinema demand Other work Combined 1 6 Mbit/s 12 Mbit/s 2 Mbit/s 20 Mbit/s 2 10 Mbit/s 8 Mbit/s 2 Mbit/s 20 Mbit/s 3 4 Mbit/s 18 Mbit/s 2 Mbit/s 24 Mbit/s All three observations fit the budget. News peaks at ten and Cinema at eighteen, but those peaks do not coincide in this sample. Adding their independent maxima plus other work would give thirty Mbit/s. That is not the continuously observed total. Statistical multiplexing can exploit differing demands under an implemented allocation policy. It still needs to keep the actual transmitted result within its capacity and constraints. A coincident burst needs another decision If News and Cinema both request their modeled peaks at once, demand becomes thirty Mbit/s against twenty-six. The excess is four Mbit/s. Under an original two-Mbit queue assumption: Time to fill from empty = 2 Mbit / 4 Mbit/s = 0.5 second The queue can postpone the consequence, not carry that excess indefinitely. Rate allocation, buffering or another defined policy must resolve the demand. This is a producer/budget model, not a measurement of an RF multiplex. Actual transmission framing, stuffing and scheduling have their own rules; unused slots can have a representation rather than making the RF carrier disappear. Shared acquisition is not automatic shared output A full recovered multiplex contains several services, but a source API may expose only one selected programme per acquisition request. A backend can redistribute several services from one acquisition only when the implemented hardware/interface and selection route permit it. Tuner concurrency contrasts full-multiplex sharing, same-service sharing and independent requests. A common reception fault can affect several services If the common acquired data becomes unusable, several programmes can be affected. A later fault in one component or client conversion can instead affect a narrower result. Preserving the service/PID and common-acquisition relationship helps distinguish a shared transport problem from an isolated media-stream problem. See Also Broadcast service identifiers Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts DVB: Service Information specification Linux: Digital TV demultiplexer and MPEG-TS filters

articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Se.title: Broadcast service identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Se.keywords: Broadcast service identifiers Broadcast service identifiers locate a programme within its defined network/transport/source context, independently of component PIDs and viewer-facing channel labels. A television service needs an identity the receiving system can use to select its media. That identity is not necessarily the number shown in the guide or the PID of its video packets. Its scope is part of its meaning. The same service ID can exist in two contexts DVB service identity uses the appropriate original-network, transport-stream and service relationship. Consider two original entries: [ {"originalNetworkId": 1, "transportStreamId": 10, "serviceId": 101}, {"originalNetworkId": 1, "transportStreamId": 20, "serviceId": 101} ] Both have service ID 101, but they identify different transport/service contexts. A key made from the service ID alone would collide. These are readable teaching tuples, not native SI bytes or a real broadcaster inventory. A backend can also add its own source identity when services from several origins are combined. The provider-specific mapping should preserve that provenance. A PID identifies component packets in a transport In an original programme 101, video PID 512 and audio PID 513 identify two components. They are not alternative spellings of programme 101. PAT/PMT relationships connect the programme to its component descriptions. Multiplexes and programme tables develop that selection. Component PIDs also have transport scope. A PID reused on another transport is not automatically the same media component. ATSC has its own identity relationships ATSC PSIP links virtual-channel information to the relevant transport and programme. Its fields include channel_TSID and program_number, with source identity information serving other defined associations. Those names should be interpreted within A/65, rather than copying a DVB tuple rule as though every broadcast family uses identical signaling. Virtual channel numbers explains the viewer-facing major/minor label. Guide and presentation keys serve another purpose Identifier Purpose in the selected arrangement Broadcast service/programme identity Select the programme in its transport context Component PID Select or identify encoded component packets Source/backend channel key Address a service through that source interface Display channel number/name Present the channel to the viewer Guide channel identifier Associate programme descriptions with the source channel An M3U tvg-id is a channel-list identifier. It need not equal a DVB service ID numerically. For Emby, the adapter/source connects its stable key to the actual service. The guide mapping then joins a different description source to that channel. Changing a display label while retaining the selection key need not change the programme. Dropping the key’s context can instead select another service that happens to reuse the same short number. See Also Broadcast multiplexes Virtual channel numbers Channel lineups and source identity MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References DVB: Service Information specification ATSC: A/65:2013 channel and transport fields SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API

articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Vi.title: Virtual channel numbers | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/identity/TV-Vi.keywords: Virtual channel numbers Virtual channel numbers provide viewer-facing labels mapped through defined signaling or source information to the physical transport and programme actually acquired. A virtual channel number is a viewer-facing label connected to service identity through the applicable signaling/source arrangement. In the ATSC major/minor form, 7.1 does not mean the receiver necessarily tunes physical RF channel 7. One RF transport can have several familiar labels Use this original mapping: Display label Physical RF label Transport ID Programme number 7.1 RF22 100 3 7.2 RF22 100 4 12.1 RF31 200 8 The first two display channels share a physical acquisition context while selecting different programmes. The table is fictional and its RF labels are not a frequency plan. ATSC A/65’s virtual-channel information associates the display labels with relevant transport/programme fields. A receiver uses those relationships rather than interpreting the displayed number as an RF tuning command. The label can remain while the physical route changes If the first service moves from RF22 to another compatible acquired transport, the receiver/backend needs updated tuning and signaling information. The displayed identity can remain 7.1 under the applicable updated mapping. A familiar label does not prove that cached physical parameters are still correct. Conversely, editing a label in a media-server interface need not change where the source actually tunes. Service identifiers and lineups separate those operations. Major/minor labels should not become floating-point values Consider 7.2 and 7.10. Their major number is seven; their minor numbers are two and ten. They are not decimal fractions 7.2 and 7.1. An original major/minor ordering therefore gives: 7.2 7.10 Lexical ordering of strings can put 7.10 before 7.2 . Converting them to floating-point values can erase the distinction between 7.10 and 7.1 . The appropriate data representation retains both components or the exact source label according to the interface contract. The source context still belongs to the channel Two different sources can both expose a label such as 7.1 without representing one interchangeable acquisition. HDHomeRun’s API uses GuideNumber in its defined lineup context. Emby’s source key and guide association connect that visible number to the intended programme. See Also Broadcast service identifiers Channel lineups and source identity ATSC 1.0 broadcast television HDHomeRun network tuner routes References ATSC: A/65 PSIP specification ATSC: A/65:2013 channel and transport fields SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API

articles/live-tv/channels/index.html.title: Overview: Channels and reception | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/index.html.keywords: Overview: Channels and reception Channel identity and reception describe which programme service is selected and whether its delivered data are usable. Selecting the intended service and receiving it correctly are separate stages. A lineup or service identifier supplies identity, while signal measurements and reception errors describe the actual delivery. This group keeps those stages visible when a channel is missing, mislabelled or unreliable. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Channel identity Channel identity connects broadcast services and multiplexes to the names or numbers presented in a lineup. Reception quality Reception quality describes the signal conditions and data errors affecting a received television service. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/live-tv/channels/reception/inde.title: Overview: Reception quality | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/reception/inde.keywords: Overview: Reception quality Reception quality describes the signal conditions and data errors affecting a received television service. Signal strength and signal quality measure different properties. Uncorrectable errors describe a later result after the reception and correction path has done its work. Reading those observations together is more informative than selecting one high-looking signal number as proof of reliable programme delivery. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Signal strength TV signal strength is a receiver-reported input-level measurement or estimate whose units, calibration and observation context determine its interpretation. Signal quality TV signal quality describes receiver-specific digital-recovery measurements such as carrier/noise, modulation-error or correction-related observations rather than input power alone. Uncorrectable reception errors Uncorrectable reception errors indicate data the receiver’s defined correction stage could not recover, with counter scope and later media dependencies determining their significance. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux: Digital TV property scales and statistics Linux: Frontend counter and signal-statistic semantics

articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-R.title: Uncorrectable reception errors | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-R.keywords: Uncorrectable reception errors Uncorrectable reception errors indicate data the receiver’s defined correction stage could not recover, with counter scope and later media dependencies determining their significance. Error protection can correct some received-data damage, but it has defined limits. An uncorrectable reception error reports an integrity problem the receiver’s stated correction stage could not resolve. Its count is not automatically a count of damaged movie frames. The reporting unit, stage and interval need to be identified first. Corrected input and bad output are different results An earlier-stage error can be repaired before the receiver emits usable data. An uncorrectable block or transport error instead concerns information that remains unreliable at its declared output stage. Receiver APIs report different measures: bits, blocks, transport flags, continuity-related observations or derived quality indices. The device’s definition establishes what one increment means. SiliconDust’s diagnostic material, for example, separates RF, transport and network fields. Linux’s frontend documentation likewise gives statistic availability and counter/stage semantics. Cumulative values need interval differences Use an original counter exercise: Observation Error-block counter Total-block counter At 0 s 1000 500,000 At 10 s 1012 600,000 The interval has twelve additional error blocks among 100,000 additional blocks: Error rate = (1012 − 1000) / 10 = 1.2 error blocks/s Block-error fraction = 12 / 100,000 = 0.00012 = 0.012% Dividing the whole lifetime count 1012 by only the latest interval’s blocks mixes different scopes. If the counter later becomes three after a reset or resource change, its difference from 1012 is not a meaningful negative number of reception errors. The continuity/reset context must be re-established. The table is invented, not a tuner measurement. The same interval count can hide different timing Twelve errors spread across ten seconds and twelve errors concentrated within one-tenth of a second have the same ten-second total. Their effects on required tables, media packets or picture reconstruction can differ. A short burst can damage a critical entry point or reference relationship, while another interval may affect different components. A coarse average therefore does not describe which data was affected or when the first visible problem occurred. Transport discontinuity can arise later A source can emit recovered packets correctly while the network or receiving process loses some of them. Later packet gaps are not automatically proof of uncorrectable RF errors. For MPEG-TS, continuity observations also need packet/PID context and the applicable rules, including payload, discontinuity indications and resets. A raw counter jump should not be called a physical reception fault solely because the final picture broke. MPEG-TS programme tables develops the component context. The source’s reception and output observations, then the server’s arrival observations, locate the missing-data boundary. A boundary-specific observation narrows the location Use an original ten-second comparison for one declared component and continuous counter context: Model observation Result Receiver uncorrectable-error delta 0 Relevant source-output continuity gaps 0 Same component’s server-arrival continuity gaps 5 Under the model’s payload/continuity assumptions, the first new gap appears between the observed source output and server arrival. A later visible artifact does not turn the receiver’s zero delta into five RF errors. This does not identify the exact network or receiving-process cause. It identifies the boundary containing the first observed loss. Another model with errors already present at the source output would locate a different starting point. The table is invented and assumes the same packet/component context at both observations. No tuner or network capture was made. One unreliable reference can affect later pictures Consider this original simplified prediction model: Picture Reference Declared input state I0 None Usable P1 I0 Its coded payload is damaged P2 P1 Its own payload is usable P3 P2 Its own payload is usable I4 None Usable independent entry Assume this model has no successful concealment and every dependency on an unreliable reference remains unreliable. P1 is affected by its own payload. P2 and P3 are then affected by their reference chain even though their own modeled payloads are usable. I4 can restore an independent usable context. A receiver’s one error increment cannot therefore be translated directly into one damaged presentation picture. The association depends on which packets/components and prediction state were affected. Real codecs and decoders can conceal, recover or propagate damage differently. The table is a dependency exercise, not an executed bitstream or a guarantee about a particular client. Buffering and transcoding operate on the supplied data A larger client reserve can absorb arrival variation when usable media eventually arrives. It cannot reconstruct arbitrary programme information that the source never recovered. A transcoder can also encounter or conceal upstream damage and encode a result containing it. Its selected encoder being hardware-accelerated does not establish that the original input was error-free. See Also TV signal quality and decoding margin TV signal strength Dropped video frames during playback MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References Linux: Frontend counter and signal-statistic semantics SiliconDust: RF, transport and network diagnostic fields ATSC: A/78 transport-stream verification scope

articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-S.title: TV signal quality and decoding margin | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-S.keywords: TV signal quality and decoding margin TV signal quality describes receiver-specific digital-recovery measurements such as carrier/noise, modulation-error or correction-related observations rather than input power alone. A receiver can report a strong input while having difficulty distinguishing the wanted digital signal. Signal quality concerns that recovery relationship rather than raw received level alone. The exact field might represent carrier/noise, modulation error, an implementation index or another measurement. Its meaning and scale must accompany the value. Several metrics have different referents Observation Relationship described Carrier/noise ratio Wanted carrier power relative to the relevant noise measurement Modulation error ratio (MER) Reference-symbol energy relative to error-vector energy Pre-correction error observation Errors at the declared earlier decoding stage Post-correction/symbol integrity Relevant recovered-output accuracy Relative quality index The receiver’s defined normalized/derived reporting scale SiliconDust distinguishes strength, signal quality and symbol quality for its own receiver reports. Those percentages should not be silently used as universal measurements for every tuner. Linux’s frontend statistics likewise identify scale and stage availability rather than requiring every device to expose every statistic at all times. Two original ratio exercises If a declared wanted carrier has power 100 and measured noise has power one: C/N = 10 × log10(100 / 1) = 20 dB In a separate original constellation exercise, mean reference-symbol energy is one and mean error-vector energy is 0.001: MER = 10 × log10(1 / 0.001) = 30 dB The two numbers compare different defined quantities. The error-vector measurement can include distortion as well as noise. These are mathematical inputs, not measured frontend data or a threshold for any broadcast configuration. A margin needs a specified reference Assume an original receiver/configuration model requires eighteen dB by its declared quality rule. Observation Model measurement Margin relative to declared rule 1 20 dB +2 dB 2 22 dB +4 dB 3 17 dB −1 dB 4 19 dB +1 dB 5 21 dB +3 dB The third observation is below this model’s reference. A real failure result cannot be inferred from it without the actual modulation/coding, receiver, measurement method and time behavior. A percentage threshold copied from another device or delivery system does not establish that reference. Error correction changes the useful observation Consider an original interval with 1200 reported errors among one million earlier-stage bits, and zero reported errors among 800,000 later-stage bits. The earlier observed ratio is 0.12%. The later counter reports no errors at its own defined stage in that interval. That is consistent with an implemented correction route producing usable output despite earlier errors. It does not prove the exact number of corrected information bits by subtracting counters from different stages. A second declared interval has forty later-stage errors among 800,000 bits: 40/800000 = 0.00005 , or 0.005%. These are readable counter exercises. Real devices can report estimated bit ratios, uncorrectable blocks or other measures, with different meanings and availability. Unavailable is not a measured zero Consider an original readable observation: { "cnr": {"state": "not-available"}, "uncorrectableBlocks": { "state": "available", "value": 0, "intervalSeconds": 1 } } The first field supplies no CNR measurement. The second supplies a zero count under its own stated interval. Treating both as numeric zero would invent a CNR result. A genuine zero-dB power ratio means equal numerator and denominator, which is a very different assertion from no measurement. Availability can depend on the receiver’s acquisition stage or supported statistics. Its reported state needs to travel with the value. The packet/media path can add other failures Reception quality is upstream of the source’s delivered media. A clean recovered output can still experience network loss or a later conversion problem. Conversely, increasing a client buffer cannot recreate broadcast information that the receiver failed to recover. Uncorrectable errors develops counter intervals and later picture dependencies. The same source identity and observation interval connect the receiver measurement to the media affected by it. See Also TV signal strength Uncorrectable reception errors DVB-T2 terrestrial television Over-the-air television References Linux: Digital TV property scales and statistics Linux: Frontend counter and signal-statistic semantics SiliconDust: Signal strength, quality and symbol quality DVB: TR 101 290 measurement definitions

articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-S.title: TV signal strength | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/channels/reception/TV-S.keywords: TV signal strength TV signal strength is a receiver-reported input-level measurement or estimate whose units, calibration and observation context determine its interpretation. Signal strength describes a received input level reported or estimated by the receiver. Its unit and calibration belong to the implementation. It is different from how accurately the digital data is recovered. A strong unwanted contribution or a distorted input can make a large level reading without making the programme usable. Calibrated power uses a reference dBm expresses power relative to one milliwatt: P(mW) = 10^(dBm / 10) An original −70-dBm level is 10^-7 mW. At −60 dBm, it is 10^-6 mW: ten times the power. The negative values are not negative physical power. They describe a power smaller than the reference. A real receiver’s reported level can be calibrated or estimated through its frontend behavior. The field’s documentation should identify that scope. A relative percentage needs its own scale Use an original readable report: { "metric": "strength", "scale": "relative", "value": 32768, "declaredMaximum": 65535, "physicalCalibration": null } Under that declared normalization: 100 × 32768 / 65535 = 50.000763% The object is not a native frontend query or a device capture. Its ratio produces a relative percentage, not a physical power conversion. Without a calibrated mapping, fifty percent cannot be assigned a universal dBm value. Nor must another receiver’s fifty-percent reading represent the same input level. Linux frontend statistics distinguish declared scale types and unavailable measurements. SiliconDust’s strength/quality descriptions give another product-specific interpretation. Gain can raise signal and noise together For an original linear-power model, let wanted signal power be 100 units and noise power one unit. Their ratio is 100, or twenty decibels. Multiplying both by four gives signal 400 and noise four. The strength has increased while the ratio remains 100. If the amplifier then adds four more noise units under this model, the result is signal 400 divided by noise eight: ratio fifty, approximately 16.99 dB. These are invented values. They do not recommend a real amplifier, gain or receiver input level. The calculation explains why “more strength” and “better recoverable data” need separate evidence. The recovered output answers the next question Signal quality describes other reception/error-margin observations. Uncorrectable errors describe a later integrity result at a defined stage. For Emby playback, the relevant input reading belongs to the source receiver. A client displaying a damaged picture is observing a later stage that can include reception, network delivery and media processing. See Also TV signal quality and decoding margin Uncorrectable reception errors Over-the-air television References Linux: Digital TV property scales and statistics Linux: Frontend counter and signal-statistic semantics SiliconDust: Signal strength, quality and symbol quality

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/index.html.title: Overview: Live television fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/index.html.keywords: Overview: Live television fundamentals Live-TV fundamentals distinguish continuing programme delivery from the physical or network source supplying it. Over-the-air, cable, satellite and IPTV routes reach the viewer through different source arrangements. Their shared deadline is that programme data continue arriving along a live timeline. These pages establish the source vocabulary before tuning, reception or recording behavior is examined. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is live TV? Live TV presents a channel’s continuing programme timeline as new media arrives, with acquisition, delivery and buffering determining what a viewer can currently watch. Over-the-air television Over-the-air television carries broadcast signals through radio propagation to a compatible receiver, which recovers the selected services for playback. Cable television Cable television distributes services through an operator’s cable network using a defined transmission and access arrangement that a compatible source must expose to the playback system. Satellite television Satellite television reception selects a compatible transponder and satellite-input arrangement before recovering programme services and their access/coding requirements. IPTV IPTV delivers television services through IP networks, with channel discovery, session access and media transport determining the stream a playback system can acquire. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Live TV setup and source roles RFC 8216: HLS media-playlist semantics ITU-R: BT.1306 digital terrestrial transmission systems DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification DVB: DVB-S satellite transmission specification ITU-T: Y.1901 IPTV service requirements

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Cable.h.title: Cable television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Cable.h.keywords: Cable television Cable television distributes services through an operator’s cable network using a defined transmission and access arrangement that a compatible source must expose to the playback system. Cable television is delivered through an operator’s distribution network. Its programme services can be carried in digital RF multiplexes or through other implemented operator arrangements. An Emby source needs a compatible path to the actual media. The presence of a cable connection does not establish that every service is exposed as an ordinary playable tuner stream. A cable carrier and its services differ A digital RF channel can contain several encoded programme services. Frequency and modulation locate the carrier; service information identifies which programme is requested. Description Example role RF frequency/modulation Tuner acquisition Multiplex/transport identity Recovered carrier’s data context Service/programme identifier Selected media within that context Operator channel number The lineup’s viewer-facing label Guide channel identifier Programme-description association Changing a service’s viewer-facing number need not change its frequency or media components. Modulation does not describe access permission QAM describes a modulation arrangement. Clear QAM describes relevant cable services that are unencrypted, under a compatible reception path. A cable network can contain protected services as well as clear ones. Recovering their RF data does not establish a supported decryption and playback route. Encrypted channels separates acquisition, entitlement and the implemented protection path. A subscription relationship and a generic QAM tuner are not interchangeable pieces of that route. DVB-C is another specifically defined cable transmission system; the service’s actual coding and access properties remain additional information. A box output is already another representation An operator box can receive and process a service, then emit a prepared HDMI presentation. That output is different from the encoded service feed exposed by a tuner/backend. The box’s video output capability does not prove that its original service can be acquired through an unrelated server interface. Likewise, an HDMI display signal does not carry the original movie container in the ordinary presentation path. HDMI video transport develops that later representation. Emby needs the source and its identity A supported cable tuner or backend can supply the channel inventory and media acquisition interface. Guide mapping then associates those source channels with programme descriptions. Availability is specific to the operator, region, source hardware and implemented access route. A manufacturer’s Clear QAM example is not a declaration that every cable provider currently sends those services. See Also DVB-C cable television Clear QAM cable television Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths Channel lineups and source identity References DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification SiliconDust: CableCARD protected-channel path requirements Hauppauge: WinTV-quadHD models 1609 and 1698

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-IPTV.ht.title: IPTV and internet-delivered live channels | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-IPTV.ht.keywords: IPTV and internet-delivered live channels IPTV delivers television services through IP networks, with channel discovery, session access and media transport determining the stream a playback system can acquire. IPTV uses Internet Protocol networks to deliver television services. The term does not name a single codec, container or channel-list format. ITU-T describes an IPTV service framework with defined network/service requirements. In everyday media-server discussion, “IPTV” is also used more broadly for live channels supplied through internet-accessible stream URLs. The actual delivery arrangement is the useful technical description. Finding a channel and receiving its media differ Layer Question Channel discovery/list Which service is available, and how is it addressed? Access/session Can this client/server establish the provider’s supported request? Transport/packaging Continuous stream, segments or another implemented route? Media representation Which encoded video/audio tracks are present? Playback preparation What can the chosen Emby client consume? A readable channel list can succeed while the subsequent stream request fails. A successful connection can also return an error page rather than usable media. An HTTP status and the returned payload answer different parts of the request. Permitted sessions still need transport capacity Consider an original network exercise with four channel streams at eight Mbit/s each: 4 × 8 = 32 Mbit/s of media payload If the declared usable path budget is thirty Mbit/s, the unchanged streams cannot all fit continuously, even if the provider permits four sessions. Three such streams need twenty-four Mbit/s and leave six under this simplified budget. Actual overhead and time-varying rates need additional accounting. Connection limits concerns a different constraint from bitrate. Lowering client-facing video bitrate after server conversion does not necessarily reduce the original provider stream entering the server. A channel list is not a media timeline An extended M3U channel list can associate names and identifiers with source URLs. The URL can lead to another representation, such as an HLS playlist. An HLS media playlist describes segments and their sequence for one presentation. The fact that both kinds of text use related playlist notation does not make their entries have the same meaning. Extended M3U lists develops the channel attributes used by an Emby source. The provider’s actual access and stream requirements remain separate. The receiving location matters When Emby Server acquires the source, its route to the provider supplies the incoming media. The client’s route to Emby is another connection. A stream that works directly in one app does not prove the server uses the same network path, request context or supported protection arrangement. See Also Extended M3U channel lists IPTV connection limits HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description References ITU-T: Y.1901 IPTV service requirements Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits RFC 8216: HLS media-playlist semantics

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Live.ht.title: What is live TV? | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Live.ht.keywords: What is live TV? Live TV presents a channel’s continuing programme timeline as new media arrives, with acquisition, delivery and buffering determining what a viewer can currently watch. A live channel has a continuing programme timeline. New media becomes available as that timeline advances, rather than the player opening a complete movie whose entire duration is already stored. The programme itself can be a live event, a prerecorded film or a scheduled repeat. “Live TV” describes the channel’s delivery and schedule relationship, not necessarily when its pictures were captured. The viewer is behind several arrival points An Emby route can acquire a channel from a tuner or compatible internet source, prepare its media for the selected client and retain some recent content for presentation. Consider an original common-origin timing exercise: Observation at wall time 100 s Programme position Broadcaster’s current position 100 s Last usable position received by the server 98 s Position the viewer is presenting 90 s The viewer is ten seconds behind the broadcaster. Two seconds belong to source arrival; another eight separate the received position from presentation. If the viewer pauses for five seconds while acquisition continues, the declared received position can become 103 s while presentation remains at 90 s. The lag is now fifteen seconds, and the received reserve is thirteen. The model assumes continuous usable intervals and a common time origin. Real timestamps can need mapping between broadcaster, receiver and presentation clocks. A larger playback buffer can deliberately increase delay while protecting against short arrival variations. Two clients using different preparation and buffering routes can consequently show the same event at different moments. Starting a channel requires a usable entry point A source being selected is not the same event as the first picture becoming visible. An RF route needs suitable tuning/demodulation, service information and the intended encoded components. A compressed-video decoder also needs enough initialization/reference information to begin reconstructing usable pictures. A segmented internet route can wait for an appropriate playlist/segment boundary. The client then needs its own presentation reserve. These stages explain why a channel can take time to start even when sustained delivery later keeps up. TV tuners develops acquisition; HLS develops one segmented delivery arrangement. Channel media and guide descriptions are different inputs A channel source supplies the media path and its identity. Guide data describes what is scheduled and when. An attractive guide entry does not establish that the corresponding source can currently be acquired. A working stream can also exist with missing or mismatched programme descriptions. Emby’s Live TV setup connects sources, guide data and channel mapping as separate parts of the supported route. A recording changes what remains available A stored recording can preserve an interval that has already passed. Its later playback need not stay near the advancing channel. Pausing live presentation instead requires the earlier interval to remain accessible through an implemented buffer or recording arrangement. If the source provides only the newest content and no retained history, an arbitrary backward seek cannot recover an interval that was never kept. The source timeline continues in both cases. What changes is the retained media the viewer can address. See Also Over-the-air television IPTV and internet-delivered live channels TV tuners and service acquisition How a media server delivers playback References Emby: Live TV setup and source roles SiliconDust: Record-engine live TV sharing API RFC 8216: HLS media-playlist semantics

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-OTA.htm.title: Over-the-air television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-OTA.htm.keywords: Over-the-air television Over-the-air television carries broadcast signals through radio propagation to a compatible receiver, which recovers the selected services for playback. Over-the-air television reaches a receiver through radio transmission. An antenna collects a mixture of signals; the tuner and demodulator select a compatible broadcast carrier and recover its data. The receiver then identifies the television service and its media components. The antenna does not deliver a decoded movie directly to Emby. One RF carrier can contain several services A digital broadcast can multiplex several programmes into one carrier. The receiver tunes that carrier, while later processing selects the requested programme and component streams. Broadcast multiplexes describes this sharing. A displayed channel number is another label, so “channel 7.1” need not mean that the receiver tunes physical RF channel 7. The applicable regional delivery system also matters. ATSC, DVB-T/T2, ISDB-T and DTMB define different reception arrangements. A receiver supporting one is not made compatible with the others simply by attaching an antenna. Reflections change the received signal Radio energy can arrive through a direct path and reflected paths with different delay and amplitude. Some transmission arrangements provide a guard interval and receiver processing intended to handle delayed copies. For an original timing exercise, assume an OFDM arrangement with a declared 200-microsecond guard interval: Model reflected-path delay Relation to that declared interval 80 μs Within it 240 μs Beyond it The first comparison addresses timing only. It does not prove successful reception: amplitude, synchronization and the implemented receiver still matter. The second illustrates why an echo can exceed the assumed timing protection. These are invented conditions, not a prediction for a particular transmitter or home. DVB-T develops one guard-interval mechanism; other delivery systems need their own interpretation. Acquisition and decoding have separate evidence Stage Useful observation RF/front end Appropriate carrier and reception state Demodulated output Recovered data with its error/correction context Service selection Intended programme and component identifiers Media decoding Supported actual video/audio representation Client presentation Usable pictures and audio advance A frontend lock does not identify the video codec by itself. Nor does a decoder error prove that the RF signal is weak. For Emby, the tuner/backend supplies the recovered media through its supported interface. Server/client preparation then follows the chosen playback route. More RF power is not always more usable information Noise, interference and receiver distortion affect whether symbols can be distinguished. A larger strength reading can coexist with worse digital recovery. Signal strength measures a different property from signal quality . Their scales and time intervals should be read at the receiver that produced them. When several services share a carrier, a reception problem can affect more than one of them at once. Their common RF acquisition is the useful relationship to investigate. See Also ATSC 1.0 broadcast television DVB-T terrestrial television ISDB-T terrestrial television TV signal quality and decoding margin Broadcast multiplexes References ITU-R: BT.1306 digital terrestrial transmission systems ATSC: A/53 Part 2, RF transmission specification DVB: DVB-T framing, coding and modulation specification

articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Satelli.title: Satellite television reception | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/fundamentals/TV-Satelli.keywords: Satellite television reception Satellite television reception selects a compatible transponder and satellite-input arrangement before recovering programme services and their access/coding requirements. Satellite reception begins with a dish and a compatible input arrangement that delivers the wanted radio signal to a tuner. A demodulator then recovers data from the selected transponder signal. The programme chosen by the viewer is a later selection within that recovered data. The LNB changes the frequency range The low-noise block downconverter, or LNB, receives a satellite-band signal and converts a selected input range into an intermediate-frequency range suitable for its receiver path. Use an original difference-frequency model: Declared received frequency = 11,900 MHz Declared local oscillator = 10,600 MHz Difference frequency = 1,300 MHz The tuner’s input in this model is at 1300 MHz, not the original 11900-MHz satellite frequency. Real LNB arrangements specify their bands, oscillator choices and switching behavior. The numbers do not identify an actual satellite or installation. Transponder selection is not programme selection Selection Property involved Satellite/input route Which dish/feed or distribution path reaches the receiver Transponder signal Frequency, polarization, symbol rate and transmission arrangement Programme service Identifier and encoded components within the recovered data Several programme services can share one transponder stream. DVB-S and DVB-S2 define related but different transmission/coding arrangements. The selected programme’s video and audio codecs are another layer. A demodulator supporting DVB-S2 does not itself promise the application can decode every service carried there. Shared input selection can constrain concurrency In an original shared-input exercise, two tuners depend on one upstream path that can expose only one of two input states, A or B, at a time. One requested transponder needs state A; another needs B. Having two tuners does not make those mutually exclusive input states simultaneously available. An installation using separate suitable feeds or another supported distribution arrangement can have a different relationship. Its physical routing and receiver capabilities determine the actual constraint. Tuner concurrency distinguishes simultaneous acquisition resources from the number of requested programmes. A received service may have another access requirement A transponder can contain unencrypted or protected services. Correct tuning and signal recovery do not replace the required supported access/protection route. An Emby backend can expose a compatible service through its implemented interface; it must first be able to acquire and supply that service. The client then needs its actual media representation. See Also DVB-S satellite television DVB-S2 satellite television Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths References DVB: DVB-S satellite transmission specification DVB: DVB-S2 satellite specification Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/guides/formats/index.ht.title: Overview: Guide sources and formats | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/formats/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Guide sources and formats Guide sources and formats encode programme schedules and supporting service information through different conventions. XMLTV, supplied guide data and broadcast service-information tables expose different source and field arrangements. A consumer must connect them to its channel identities and clock context. The pages here describe that representation before the server turns it into a displayed schedule. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> XMLTV XMLTV represents channel identities and programme listings in XML, with format-specific timestamps and episode-number systems that a guide importer must interpret. Emby guide data Emby guide data supplies supported regional programme listings whose lineup selection, station mapping and loaded horizon determine the guide shown by the server. DVB Service Information DVB Service Information describes broadcast services, programme events and timing context through tables that a receiver must collect, interpret and associate with the selected service. ATSC PSIP ATSC PSIP connects virtual-channel identity with event descriptions, table-discovery information and a GPS-based system clock in the ATSC 1.0 broadcast environment. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup DVB: Service Information specification catalogue ATSC: A/65 PSIP specification ATSC: A/65:2013 virtual-channel, event and time tables

articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-DVB-S.title: DVB Service Information and broadcast guides | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-DVB-S.keywords: DVB Service Information and broadcast guides DVB Service Information describes broadcast services, programme events and timing context through tables that a receiver must collect, interpret and associate with the selected service. A DVB transport stream carries more than audio and video. Service Information , commonly called DVB-SI , describes the services and events available in the broadcast environment. A receiver can use that information to build a station list and guide. The resulting descriptions must stay associated with the right service while table sections repeat and change. For Emby, the final guide still depends on its configured source and supported backend/importer. Broadcast SI existing in the multiplex does not prove that a particular integration exposes it as Emby guide data. Different tables answer different questions The Service Description Table identifies and describes services. The Event Information Table supplies programme events. Network and time tables provide other context, including delivery descriptions and the clock interpretation used by receivers. Media selection still uses programme/component information such as the MPEG-TS programme tables . An event title is not a video-stream PID. The catalogue currently identifies EN 300 468 V1.20.1, dated September 2026, as the published SI specification. An event belongs to a service context This invented readable projection retains the relevant identities: { "originalNetworkId": 1, "transportStreamId": 10, "serviceId": 101, "eventId": 37, "startUtc": "2026-10-12T18:00:00Z", "durationSeconds": 1800, "title": "Harbour Evening" } The projection is not the binary layout of an EIT section. It makes the association visible: event 37 describes an airing on service 101 within the declared network/transport context. Another service can have an event numbered 37 as well. Taking the event number alone loses which station it describes. Replacing the service context with the viewer’s display number can also lose information. Service identifiers develops that broadcast context. The guide importer must preserve it, or translate it into an equally unambiguous internal identity. Now and next do not imply a full schedule EIT present/following and EIT schedule are separate classifications. Actual-transport and other-transport information have distinct table identities too. A receiver can collect current/following events while having little or no longer schedule data. It might also receive descriptions about another transport without currently acquiring that transport’s media. These distinctions explain a useful observation pattern: Collected information What the receiver can reasonably present Service description only Station label without programme schedule Present/following events Current and next entries for the relevant service Additional schedule sections Further airings within their supplied coverage The actual amount depends on the transmitted sections and what the receiver retains. RF lock does not establish that every schedule section has been collected. A table revision has several parts A sectioned table may need several sections before its full current contents are available. Repeated reception of section zero does not stand in for a missing section one. Consider an original assembly exercise: Observation Version Section Declared last section First arrival 31 0 1 Repeated arrival 31 0 1 Completing arrival 31 1 1 Changed table begins 0 0 1 The first two rows have the same collected section set: only zero. The third completes that version’s two-section set. The fourth belongs to a changed wrapping version and must not be combined casually with the old section one. Version identity is scoped to the table/subtable context. A numerically larger version is not always newer, and identical version numbers on unrelated services do not identify the same data. See Also Broadcast service identifiers Broadcast multiplexes DVB-T2 terrestrial television Electronic programme guides References DVB: Service Information specification catalogue ETSI: EN 300 468 V1.20.1, DVB Service Information Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup

articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-Emby-.title: Emby guide data and lineup selection | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-Emby-.keywords: Emby guide data and lineup selection Emby guide data supplies supported regional programme listings whose lineup selection, station mapping and loaded horizon determine the guide shown by the server. Emby guide data supplies programme listings for the supported locations. Emby’s current setup documentation identifies the United States, Canada and United Kingdom and places guide configuration alongside source setup and channel mapping. The guide service supplies descriptions and schedules. Your tuner or IPTV source supplies media. Choosing a guide does not add a television subscription or change what the source can acquire. The region selects a station inventory A provider lineup describes stations associated with a location or service. Two nearby inventories can share many familiar names while differing in local affiliates, regional feeds or additional stations. Suppose a fictional source receives Harbour News and Hill News near a market boundary. A selected guide includes Harbour News but only the neighboring market’s Valley News. Source station Selected guide result Harbour News Appropriate schedule available Hill News No corresponding station Valley News Guide station exists, but source does not receive it Downloading that guide again does not create Hill News’s absent schedule. Emby documents multiple guide configurations and manual station selection for cases where one inventory does not cover the received lineup. A station with the same network brand can still have a different regional schedule. The match needs the intended station/feed, not merely a recognizable logo or channel number. The channel association is the last join Emby attempts automatic matches and permits selecting the guide provider and station manually. Channel mapping develops the identity relationship. A complete provider inventory can therefore coexist with an incorrectly displayed guide if the source was matched to another station. Conversely, a correctly mapped station can have incomplete entries in the supplied data. Separating those cases gives a more useful question than “Is the guide broken?”: is the desired station absent, is its association wrong, or are its supplied programmes incomplete? Loaded days and fresh revisions are different Emby’s DVR settings include a loaded-guide horizon. Its current documentation describes an automatic choice based on channel count as well as a configurable number of days. A longer horizon exposes more future entries only where they are available. It increases the amount of schedule data the server handles; it does not make the provider publish later days or resolve recent changes more quickly. Freshness asks when the displayed schedule last incorporated a relevant revision. Coverage asks which stations and time intervals it contains. These can change independently. For a programme moved from 20:00 to 20:15, extending the guide by another week does not by itself correct tonight’s stale start. The updated event must reach the provider, be loaded and be used by the relevant recording plan. Schedule changes follows that sequence. See Also Electronic programme guides Mapping source channels to guide stations Programme schedule changes and recording plans References Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup Emby: Source-to-guide channel mapping Emby: DVR settings and recording paths

articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-PSIP..title: ATSC PSIP: virtual channels, events and time | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-PSIP..keywords: ATSC PSIP: virtual channels, events and time ATSC PSIP connects virtual-channel identity with event descriptions, table-discovery information and a GPS-based system clock in the ATSC 1.0 broadcast environment. PSIP , the Program and System Information Protocol, helps an ATSC 1.0 receiver turn a physical broadcast into familiar virtual channels and programme descriptions. A displayed number such as 7.1 is only one part of that relationship. The receiver also needs the source identity used by event tables, the programme selected for media and the timing context used to place events in the guide. The channel number connects to two paths The Virtual Channel Table, or VCT, describes virtual channels. Its programme association helps connect the channel to its media; its source_id connects it to guide events. That makes it possible for the picture and schedule to fail independently. The media selection can work while the event association or clock interpretation is wrong. Virtual channel numbers explains why 7.1 does not directly specify an RF frequency. Table discovery precedes event interpretation The Master Guide Table, or MGT, identifies relevant table types and their delivery locations. Event Information Tables, or EITs, carry scheduled events. Extended Text Tables can add longer descriptions. The System Time Table, or STT, supplies clock context. An original teaching projection combines a few of those relationships: { "vct": {"major": 7, "minor": 1, "programNumber": 3, "sourceId": 23}, "mgt": {"eventTablePid": 7680}, "eit": {"sourceId": 23, "eventId": 17, "startsAfterReferenceSeconds": 600}, "stt": {"referenceClock": "GPS", "gpsUtcOffsetSeconds": 18} } These simplified keys are explanatory rather than native A/65 field layouts. The EIT’s source 23 matches the VCT’s source 23. Programme three remains the separate media selection. The MGT location tells the receiver where to collect the event table; it is not the event’s episode identity. The eighteen-second offset is a declared teaching value. A receiver uses the offset actually supplied by the relevant system-time context. Event numbers have a scope An ATSC event identifier belongs to its virtual-channel/event-table context. It does not become a global episode identifier merely because it is called an ID. A repeat of the same television episode can be another airing. Another channel can also use an equal event number for unrelated content. Matching a future recording therefore needs the relevant channel, event/time context and the application’s translated identity. Programme identifiers distinguishes those airings from episode and series identities. Table revision markers are scoped too. A/65’s guidance specifically warns against treating the MGT’s EIT/ETT version information as a simple version for a time slot without retaining the table delivery context. GPS seconds are not Unix seconds PSIP’s system and event start counts use the GPS epoch of 6 January 1980. Unix time has another epoch. Interpreting one count as the other produces a large date error before local time zones enter the calculation. The GPS-to-UTC offset must also be applied. Only then can the resulting instant be displayed in a chosen local zone. An event six hundred seconds after the system-time reference is ten minutes later on the same interpreted clock. That relative difference survives a common offset correction. Giving the absolute event a local display time additionally requires the correct epoch and conversion. Guide time zones develops local clock changes; those are separate from the GPS/UTC distinction. This PSIP explanation concerns A/65 in the ATSC 1.0 environment. ATSC 3.0 uses its own signaling system. See Also ATSC 1.0 broadcast television Virtual channel numbers Programme identifiers: airings, episodes and series Guide time zones and clock changes References ATSC: A/65 PSIP specification ATSC: A/65:2013 virtual-channel, event and time tables ATSC: A/69:2009 PSIP implementation guidelines

articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-XMLTV.title: XMLTV listings: channels, programmes and time | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/formats/TV-XMLTV.keywords: XMLTV listings: channels, programmes and time XMLTV represents channel identities and programme listings in XML, with format-specific timestamps and episode-number systems that a guide importer must interpret. An XMLTV file contains television listings. It gives a guide importer channel identifiers, programme times and descriptive fields; it does not contain the television video. A file can be downloaded successfully, parse as XML and still produce the wrong guide. The useful checks extend from XML structure to channel references, timestamp meaning and the particular metadata fields the importer uses. A small complete listing This original document describes one fictional channel and two adjacent airings: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <tv generator-info-name="Learn example"> <channel id="harbour.news"> <display-name>Harbour News</display-name> </channel> <programme start="20261012180000 +0000" stop="20261012183000 +0000" channel="harbour.news"> <title lang="en">Harbour Stories</title> <sub-title lang="en">The First Crossing</sub-title> <episode-num system="xmltv_ns">0.0.</episode-num> </programme> <programme start="20261012183000 +0000" stop="20261012184000 +0000" channel="harbour.news"> <title lang="en">Coast Weather</title> </programme> </tv> Both programme elements refer to the channel’s id . Their position in the file does not give them that association; the identifier does. The display name is a human label. Renaming it while retaining harbour.news need not change the identity. Changing the ID requires the programme references and any relevant source-to-guide mapping to remain consistent. XML validity does not establish a correct join The XMLTV DTD gives programme start and channel attributes required status; stop is optional. It describes the permitted element arrangement, including channel elements before programmes. Its channel-reference rule is described in comments rather than enforced as a DTD ID/IDREF relationship. A structural validator therefore cannot prove that every programme has the intended station. For the fixture, three semantic checks add useful evidence: The declared channel ID is unique. Both programme references match that ID. The first stop equals the second start after time conversion. Now change only the second programme’s channel to harbour.weather . The document can remain structurally valid while that entry no longer belongs to the declared channel. The importer might accept an undeclared channel reference according to its own policy, but it cannot infer that the author meant Harbour News. Emby associates imported guide stations with source channels through channel mapping . A matching XMLTV ID is useful within that process; it is not the media URL itself. The timestamp is not a local display string In 20261012180000 +0000 , the date/time portion is 12 October 2026 at 18:00, with a zero UTC offset. The XMLTV convention assumes UTC when no explicit time zone is supplied. Explicit numeric offsets make the intended interpretation easier to inspect. Thus these values describe the same instant: XMLTV timestamp UTC instant 20261012180000 +0000 18:00 UTC 20261012200000 +0200 18:00 UTC Displaying 18:00 UTC in a plus-two-hour zone produces 20:00 local time. Treating the original digits as local time first and then applying another conversion shifts the event incorrectly. XMLTV allows reduced precision and some named zone forms. Those permissions do not guarantee identical acceptance by every importer. This example deliberately uses full date/time values and explicit numeric offsets. A missing stop also needs interpretation. Inferring it from the next entry can be convenient, but a missing or overlapping next entry changes that inference. The listed content length is another field; it is not automatically the exact transmission interval including breaks. Episode numbers carry a numbering system The fixture’s xmltv_ns value 0.0. means season one, episode one, with the part unspecified. The numeric positions use zero-based indexing. Compare: <episode-num system="xmltv_ns">1.4.</episode-num> <episode-num system="onscreen">S02E05</episode-num> Here the first representation denotes season two, episode five. The second is presentation text in the onscreen system. They can describe the same episode, but the digits cannot be parsed with the same indexing rule. A missing component is unknown rather than zero. An unspecified episode must not silently become episode one. Programme identifiers explains why episode identity also differs from an airing ID. Fields such as episode identity, repeat/new indicators and descriptions improve series matching when the source and importer support them. A provider can omit those fields even while supplying a valid schedule. Diagnose the first wrong interpretation Start with an actual affected airing: its channel reference, original start/stop, interpreted UTC interval and final station association. These observations show whether the discrepancy began in the file, time conversion or mapping. A global time shift can hide one symptom while moving correctly interpreted events as well. Replacing every channel display name similarly leaves an incorrect reference key untouched. See Also Electronic programme guides Extended M3U channel lists Programme identifiers: airings, episodes and series Guide time zones and clock changes References XMLTV: Version-pinned listings DTD and field semantics Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup Emby: Source-to-guide channel mapping

articles/live-tv/guides/index.html.title: Overview: Electronic programme guides | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/index.html.keywords: Overview: Electronic programme guides Electronic programme guides connect channel identity with scheduled events, source data and time conventions. A guide entry needs the right channel and the right time interpretation before it can support a recording decision. Programme IDs and schedule changes add further relationships as the listing evolves. This branch explains those mappings so a correct-looking title is not mistaken for a fully matched recording event. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is an EPG? An electronic programme guide associates stations and time intervals with programme descriptions, supplying the schedule information used for browsing and programme-based recording. Guide sources and formats Guide sources and formats encode programme schedules and supporting service information through different conventions. Channel mapping Channel mapping associates a selectable source service with the corresponding guide station, preserving station and provider context when names or numbers are ambiguous. Programme identifiers Programme identifiers distinguish series, episodes and scheduled airings within a provider or broadcast context, enabling reliable joins without treating titles or local IDs as universal keys. Guide time zones Guide time zones determine how supplied date/time values become absolute instants and local display times, including repeated or missing clock times around daylight-saving changes. Programme schedule changes Programme schedule changes revise the station, time or content associated with an airing, requiring the loaded guide and recording plan to be evaluated separately. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup Emby: Source-to-guide channel mapping Emby developer documentation: Programmes, timers and series timers ETSI: EN 300 468 V1.20.1, DVB Service Information Microsoft: DateTimeOffset and time-zone rules RFC 3339: Internet timestamps and numeric offsets

articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Channel-Mappi.title: Mapping source channels to guide stations | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Channel-Mappi.keywords: Mapping source channels to guide stations Channel mapping associates a selectable source service with the corresponding guide station, preserving station and provider context when names or numbers are ambiguous. A source can deliver Harbour News while the guide describes Estuary News. The media acquisition succeeded; the source channel was associated with the wrong guide station. Channel mapping is that association. It connects the service a viewer can tune with the programme schedule intended for that service. Keep both sides of the association Use these invented identities: { "sourceChannel": {"source": "A", "key": "news-main", "number": "101"}, "guideStation": {"provider": "P", "key": "harbour.news"}, "mapping": {"A/news-main": "P/harbour.news"} } The source channel’s key selects media within source A. The guide station’s key selects descriptions within provider P. Display number 101 is a label, not the complete identity of either side. If another source B exposes a different station also numbered 101, it needs its own association. Merging on the display number alone can attach the same schedule to two unrelated media sources. Similarly, another guide provider can have its own harbour.news key. Retaining provider context prevents an equal local key from silently switching datasets. A name match can look convincing Suppose two guide entries are named “Harbour Network,” one for the coast feed and one for an inland feed. Both can have the right logo and many of the same programmes. They may differ during regional news, advertising breaks or delayed airings. A single familiar programme at one time is therefore weaker evidence than several distinctive slots. A useful comparison includes: Comparison Identity information it adds Local/regional news Which station or feed is present A time-delayed programme Whether this is the intended time-shifted variant Several adjacent slots Whether the schedule alignment persists Provider station key Which descriptive inventory was actually selected The television number, name, region and feed variant are matching evidence. None should overwrite a stable source key merely to make the label look right. Emby exposes the guide choice Emby attempts automatic matches and allows selecting the guide provider and station manually. Its channel mapping documentation describes that configuration. The important consequence is conceptual: correcting the guide association does not retune the underlying source or change its video codec. It changes which descriptions belong to the selected channel. With extended M3U lists , a tvg-id can assist that association. Its meaning depends on the configured guide/importer; the ID must actually correspond to the intended station in that data. A mapping correction affects future decisions Programme-based recording begins from guide events. If an event belongs to the wrong mapped station, its title and interval can describe something other than the media that will be acquired. For example, Harbour News carries a local programme at 18:00 while the incorrectly associated guide advertises a drama. A request created from that drama’s guide row still needs a concrete source channel. The mismatch can yield a perfectly readable recording of the wrong programme. After a correction, the guide can describe the intended station while a previously created timer retains older information according to its own update rules. Inspect the intended airing, selected channel and requested interval together. A mapping error, a time-zone error and stale programme data can all make a guide look wrong. The first changes which station’s schedule is attached; the second changes interpreted instants; the third leaves an outdated revision. Their corrections act on different inputs. articles/live-tv/guides/TV-EPG.html.title: Electronic programme guides | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/TV-EPG.html.keywords: Electronic programme guides An electronic programme guide associates stations and time intervals with programme descriptions, supplying the schedule information used for browsing and programme-based recording. You can have a clear live picture and an empty guide. The video arrived through a working source, but the server has no usable programme description associated with that channel and time. An electronic programme guide , or EPG , supplies those descriptions: what is scheduled, on which station and when. A grid is one way to present the data. Search results, programme detail pages and recording choices are other views of the same schedule. Three inputs meet in a guide row The source lineup identifies the service Emby can acquire. A guide station identifies the schedule to display. A programme entry identifies an airing within that schedule. For example, a fictional source exposes (A, news-main) . Its selected guide station is harbour.news . That station has an airing called Harbour Evening from 18:00 to 18:30 UTC. The programme title does not tune the source. The source key does not provide the episode description. Channel mapping supplies the association between the two inventories. This separation explains three different symptoms: Observation Association or input to examine Correct channel, no programme entries Guide coverage, loaded schedule and station mapping Correct channel, another station’s programmes Source-to-guide station mapping Correct programme descriptions, unavailable picture The channel’s media acquisition and delivery A guide entry can remain readable during a source outage because it is descriptive data, not a test of the current stream. “Now” selects an interval Use these original adjacent entries for one station: Programme UTC interval Harbour Evening [18:00,18:30) Coast Weather [18:30,18:40) At 18:29:59, the first entry applies. At 18:30:00, the second applies. The half-open convention includes each start and excludes its end, avoiding an artificial overlap at the shared boundary. XMLTV explicitly uses this convention when both start and stop are supplied. A receiver or imported guide still needs to interpret its particular data format correctly. The guide’s “current programme” comes from the schedule and clock comparison. The media can be delayed by acquisition, distribution or playback buffering; the picture on screen may still belong to the previous interval. Live TV develops that continuing media timeline. A schedule entry can become a recording request Choosing Record supplies the intended programme and channel to the recording workflow. Emby’s developer documentation distinguishes programmes, individual timers and persistent series timers. The resulting timer must retain acquisition times and an actual source selection. Its programme association adds useful identity and descriptions; creating that association does not reserve every resource or prove that the programme was captured. A later schedule update can move the airing. A successful recording can also include material before or after its nominal interval through padding. The guide interval, requested capture interval and resulting stored media therefore have different boundaries. The visible horizon is finite A guide only shows events supplied by its provider and loaded by the server. An empty week beyond that horizon does not establish that the station has stopped broadcasting. Increasing the loaded horizon can expose more future airings when the provider has supplied them. It cannot create missing entries or update a stale source.
