articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Guide-Time-Zo.title: Guide time zones and clock changes | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Guide-Time-Zo.keywords: Guide time zones and clock changes Guide time zones determine how supplied date/time values become absolute instants and local display times, including repeated or missing clock times around daylight-saving changes. On a clock-change morning, “02:30” can identify two different moments. A guide or recording timer that retains only those clock digits has lost information needed to choose the intended airing. Consider Europe/Berlin on 25 October 2026. These original XMLTV timestamps have equal local digits and different offsets: 20261025023000 +0200 -> 2026-10-25T00:30:00Z 20261025023000 +0100 -> 2026-10-25T01:30:00Z The instants are an hour apart. The first belongs to the summer-time occurrence of 02:30; the second belongs to the standard-time occurrence. Convert each supplied value to an instant A numeric offset expresses local time minus UTC. To obtain UTC, subtract that offset. Supplied date/time Offset Interpreted UTC 25 October, 02:30 +02:00 25 October, 00:30 25 October, 02:30 +01:00 25 October, 01:30 The offset is part of the supplied value. Discarding it and applying the server’s current zone instead can map both entries to one moment or select the wrong occurrence. XMLTV has its own timestamp convention: absent an explicit zone, UTC is assumed. That convention must not be replaced with “whatever the server considers local.” Other formats can have different requirements; RFC 3339 timestamps use an explicit offset or Z in their complete form. The end can look earlier while elapsed time is positive Take this original interval spanning the same rollback: start: 20261025025000 +0200 -> 00:50 UTC stop: 20261025021000 +0100 -> 01:10 UTC elapsed: 20 minutes Subtracting the local clock labels would suggest minus forty minutes. Converting both endpoints first gives the correct positive twenty minutes. The capture system needs elapsed time between instants. A guide display needs the appropriate local label for each instant. Those are related calculations with different inputs. The same issue affects padding. Adding ten elapsed minutes to an absolute endpoint is straightforward. Adding ten to a bare local label near a transition needs the zone’s rules and a policy for ambiguous or missing results. Spring creates a missing interval In Europe/Berlin on 29 March 2026, the local clock advances from 01:59 to 03:00. A bare local time of 02:30 does not occur in that zone on that date. An offset-bearing value can still identify an instant mathematically. It does not necessarily describe a valid local civil time under the claimed zone rules. For example, “02:30 with +01:00” resolves to 01:30 UTC, which Berlin displays as 03:30 after that transition. If the author intended Berlin’s wall clock, the supplied label and rules disagree. A parser accepting the timestamp therefore establishes syntax and offset arithmetic, not that the provider chose a valid civil time for a named zone. An offset is not a zone rule +01:00 tells you an offset at a particular instant. Europe/Berlin identifies a set of civil-time rules that can choose different offsets at other instants. A programme scheduled for the same local clock time next month can consequently have a different UTC time. Carrying today’s offset into every future event loses the transition. IANA maintains the Time Zone Database as jurisdictions change their rules. Microsoft’s DateTimeOffset and TimeZoneInfo documentation likewise distinguishes an offset-bearing instant from a named zone and its adjustments. This is also why a recurring “every Monday at 20:00 local” rule differs from “every 168 hours after this instant.” The former follows civil labels; the latter follows elapsed time. A weekly local rule can have a 169-hour interval For another original Europe/Berlin example, compare 20:00 local on 18 October and 25 October 2026. Before rollback, the first is 18:00 UTC. After rollback, the second is 19:00 UTC. The local weekly labels are seven calendar days apart, but their absolute separation is 169 hours. Adding exactly 168 elapsed hours to the first instant reaches 19:00 local on the second date. A recurring manual timer intended for 20:00 local therefore needs the named-zone rules or separately supplied event instants. Repeating a fixed elapsed interval expresses a different intent. Programme-based recording instead receives the particular scheduled airing’s time. A bare weekday/time preference in a series rule is an eligibility input; the airing still supplies a concrete instant. Keep the interpretation stages visible A useful guide/timer path retains: The original supplied timestamp and its declared convention. The interpreted absolute instant. The interval calculations and recording deadlines. The display zone used for the viewer’s local labels. Server and client can display different local times for the same instant without disagreeing about the recording. Conversely, matching labels on two machines do not prove that they agree about the instant. Emby’s public timer contract identifies start and end dates in UTC. The timer is therefore easier to assess by comparing interpreted instants with its requested capture interval, rather than comparing only a screenshot’s clock labels. A constant shift fixes only a constant error If all events are uniformly two hours late because an importer treated UTC digits as local time, correcting that interpretation addresses the cause. Applying an extra fixed shift after a correct conversion instead changes every intended instant. It can appear helpful during one offset period and become wrong after a transition. Compare an affected event’s original value, interpreted UTC and displayed local time. If those are consistent but a recording starts late, acquisition delay or an outdated schedule belongs elsewhere in the explanation. articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Programme-IDs.title: Programme identifiers: airings, episodes and series | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Programme-IDs.keywords: Programme identifiers: airings, episodes and series Programme identifiers distinguish series, episodes and scheduled airings within a provider or broadcast context, enabling reliable joins without treating titles or local IDs as universal keys. “Programme ID” can mean several different things. It may identify a scheduled airing, the episode being aired or a series containing that episode. Those identities support different decisions. A timer needs an airing and time. A series rule needs series membership. Duplicate detection usually needs the content identity and an assessment of what was already captured. One episode can have two airings Use this original inventory: Object Identity Meaning Series P/series/HARBOUR Harbour Stories Episode P/episode/CROSSING The First Crossing Monday airing P/airing/A100 That episode on station N at 18:00 Wednesday repeat P/airing/A240 That episode on station N at 21:00 There are two airings but one episode. Recording both airings would produce two captures of the same intended content, although their edits, reception and completeness can differ. Replacing the airing ID with the episode ID loses the ability to distinguish the two scheduled requests. Replacing the episode ID with the airing ID prevents a simple identity comparison from recognizing the repeat. The namespace belongs in the key Provider-local values can collide: [ {"provider": "P", "kind": "episode", "id": "42", "title": "The First Crossing"}, {"provider": "Q", "kind": "episode", "id": "42", "title": "Harbour Storm"}, {"provider": "P", "kind": "airing", "id": "42", "title": "Coast Weather"} ] The string 42 appears three times. Each complete (provider, kind, id) key describes a different object. A server can translate supplied keys into internal IDs. That translation does not make equal raw IDs from unrelated providers interchangeable. Provider identifiers develops the broader namespace principle. Television adds an explicit scheduled-airing dimension. Broadcast event identity is another representation DVB event IDs are allocated within service definitions; ATSC event IDs belong to their virtual-channel/EIT context. They describe broadcast events rather than automatically supplying a provider’s persistent episode identity. The associated service/source and relevant table/time context matter. A display number is not a complete replacement for that context, and a reused event number should not be treated as a permanent global key. Emby exposes programme and timer identities along with separate channel, series and provider-related properties. Use the identity appropriate to the decision rather than assuming every field containing “Id” has the same lifetime. Episode coordinates need their numbering convention XMLTV’s xmltv_ns convention uses zero-based season, episode and part coordinates. Thus 1.4. denotes season two, episode five, with part unspecified. An onscreen label such as S02E05 is a different representation. A missing coordinate is unknown; it does not mean the first episode. Even known season/episode coordinates require the intended series and order. Two series can each have a season-two episode-five, and alternative episode orders can use different coordinates for the same content. Missing identity changes the confidence of the decision A title can help a viewer find a programme, but identical titles occur across episodes, remakes and daily broadcasts. A changed title can also describe the same content. When a trusted content ID is absent, matching may need several pieces of metadata and an explicit policy for uncertain results. False matches skip wanted recordings; failed matches capture repeats. articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Schedule-Chan.title: Programme schedule changes and recording plans | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/guides/TV-Schedule-Chan.keywords: Programme schedule changes and recording plans Programme schedule changes revise the station, time or content associated with an airing, requiring the loaded guide and recording plan to be evaluated separately. A recording can be scheduled correctly and still miss the end of a programme that moves later. The original request was based on one schedule revision; the broadcast followed another. The relevant question is which revision reached each stage before its decision deadline. A fifteen-minute move exceeds ten-minute end padding Use an invented airing on one station: Revision Programme interval, UTC Original listing 20:00–21:00 Revised listing 20:15–21:15 The original timer asks for five minutes before and ten minutes after the original listing. Its capture interval is therefore 19:55–21:10. If that timer remains unchanged, it covers only 20:15–21:10 of the revised programme: fifty-five of sixty minutes. The final five minutes lie outside the requested interval. Padding reduced the loss from fifteen minutes to five. It did not identify the new end. A timer reconciled to the revised listing with the same padding would request 20:10–21:25. That is another interval and another resource demand. The revision has to travel through several stages A broadcaster or provider first produces the changed information. The server loads it. A recording planner then decides what to do with a request already associated with that airing. These can happen at different times. A freshly displayed guide does not by itself prove that an existing timer now has matching boundaries. Consider the original event identity P/airing/A100 : { "airing": "P/airing/A100", "loadedGuide": {"revision": 2, "start": "20:15", "end": "21:15"}, "timer": {"basedOnRevision": 1, "captureStart": "19:55", "captureEnd": "21:10"} } These short UTC labels are a same-date teaching projection, not an Emby API object. The mismatch is visible even though the airing ID is unchanged. The application’s rules determine whether the timer follows the programme, retains a manual interval or requires another action. Emby’s public API distinguishes programme-associated and manual timers; it does not establish every reconciliation policy from the presence of an ID. A moved airing can change conflicts The revised end at 21:25 may overlap another request that previously fit. Updating the guide association and checking capacity are separate decisions. Suppose a second recording needs an independent source acquisition from 21:10. The original first timer ended at that boundary. The revised first timer now overlaps it for fifteen minutes. That conflict must be evaluated under the actual source sharing and priority rules. Updating metadata cannot make an unavailable resource appear. Recording conflicts develops those intervals and assignments. Recording padding explains the extra margins. Missing from an update does not always mean cancelled A refreshed guide can be a full snapshot, a partial update or a shorter horizon. An event absent from a partial response might simply be outside its returned range. In an original comparison, revision one covers 18:00–24:00 while the next response covers only 18:00–20:00. The absence of a 21:00 airing from the second response does not establish its cancellation. A planner needs the provider’s update semantics and coverage before treating absence as deletion. Otherwise, shortening a request window can erase valid future intent. Station changes and split/merged programme entries add identity questions too. Keeping only a title and start time makes a move resemble a different programme; assuming equal titles always identify one airing can merge unrelated entries. A changed guide still describes a plan A programme may overrun without a timely listing revision. A schedule-based timer then has no new endpoint to follow. Some broadcast signaling can describe event running status, but whether a configured backend and recorder uses it is another implemented capability. Its existence is not a universal guarantee that Emby will extend every live programme automatically. articles/live-tv/index.html.title: Overview: Live TV and recording | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/index.html.keywords: Overview: Live TV and recording Live television joins a continuing source with reception, programme information and time-sensitive playback or recording. Live TV has a moving deadline: data continue arriving whether the viewer or recorder is ready for them or not. A successful recording depends on more than a timer entry; the source, reception, guide information and storage path must cooperate during the intended interval. The fundamentals and standards describe the broadcast signal. Tuner and channel topics explain how it reaches the server, programme guides identify what should be recorded, and recording topics explain concurrency, padding and time shifting. In Emby, those stages provide useful checkpoints for a missing channel, a late start or an incomplete recording. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Live television fundamentals Live-TV fundamentals distinguish continuing programme delivery from the physical or network source supplying it. Broadcast standards Digital television standards define signal, service and delivery conventions for particular broadcast systems. Tuners and television sources Live-TV sources connect a tuner, backend or channel resource to the server's available programme streams. Channels and reception Channel identity and reception describe which programme service is selected and whether its delivered data are usable. Electronic programme guides Electronic programme guides connect channel identity with scheduled events, source data and time conventions. Recording and time shifting Live-TV recording connects scheduled intent with source allocation, stored output and a completed recording lifecycle. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/live-tv/recording/index.html.title: Overview: Recording and time shifting | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/index.html.keywords: Overview: Recording and time shifting Live-TV recording connects scheduled intent with source allocation, stored output and a completed recording lifecycle. A timer describes intended work; the recording still needs its source and destination during the relevant interval. Scheduling, lifecycle and time-shifting topics cover different parts of that relationship. Together they explain how a requested programme becomes stored media or remains available through a live buffer. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Digital video recording Digital video recording retains media from a live source for later playback, with source acquisition, storage completion and library presentation forming distinct stages. Scheduling and conflicts Recording scheduling combines timers, series rules, resource conflicts and padding around programme boundaries. Recording lifecycle A recording lifecycle covers completion, duplicate recognition, retention and processing after capture. Time shifting Time shifting separates the viewer's playback position from a continuing live source through retained media. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup

articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/ind.title: Overview: Recording lifecycle | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/ind.keywords: Overview: Recording lifecycle A recording lifecycle covers completion, duplicate recognition, retention and processing after capture. Recorded content has a history beyond the timer that created it. The server may need to recognize a duplicate, distinguish an incomplete result or apply a retention rule. Post-processing is another operation on that result, so each page identifies the lifecycle decision and the evidence it uses. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Duplicate recording detection Duplicate recording detection compares intended content identities and existing capture outcomes so repeat airings can be skipped without confusing different episodes or incomplete recordings. Recording retention Recording retention determines which captured artifacts remain under count, protection and active-use policies, while successful storage reclamation remains a separate outcome. Incomplete recordings An incomplete recording lacks part of the intended programme coverage, even when its remaining container parses, its media plays and a recording item is visible. Recording post-processing Recording post-processing transforms or reorganizes captured media after acquisition, requiring output validation and a consistent publication step before replacing the usable original. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby plugin API: SeriesTimerInfo recording rules Emby plugin API: TimerInfo identity, UTC dates and padding Emby: DVR settings and recording paths

articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.title: Duplicate recording detection and episode identity | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.keywords: Duplicate recording detection and episode identity Duplicate recording detection compares intended content identities and existing capture outcomes so repeat airings can be skipped without confusing different episodes or incomplete recordings. A repeat airing can be a second opportunity to capture the same episode. Duplicate detection decides whether that opportunity adds something wanted or merely creates another copy. The decision depends on what “same” means and on whether the earlier recording is adequate. Equal titles and equal content are different tests Consider four invented airings: Airing Display title Content key A100 Harbour Stories P/episode/E1 A240 Harbour Stories P/episode/E1 A250 Harbour Stories P/episode/E2 A300 Coast Weather Unknown A100 and A240 describe the same intended episode. A250 has the same series title but another episode. A300 cannot be given a stable episode identity from its title alone. A title-only rule merges E1 and E2 incorrectly. An airing-ID-only rule fails to recognize that A100 and A240 repeat E1. A useful content key retains its provider/type scope. Programme identifiers explains that distinction. Existing does not necessarily mean sufficient Use these original prior-capture records: [ {"content": "P/episode/E1", "outcome": "complete"}, {"content": "P/episode/E2", "outcome": "partial"}, {"content": null, "title": "Coast Weather", "outcome": "complete"} ] Under a declared teaching policy, a complete matching content key suppresses a repeat, a partial match remains eligible for replacement and an unknown key requires another decision. Candidate Result under that policy Repeat of E1 Skip: adequate matching capture Repeat of E2 Keep eligible: prior capture partial Another Coast Weather Identity uncertain The table illustrates policy rather than claiming Emby uses these exact outcome strings or completeness tests. An application can instead prioritize avoiding duplicates, filling gaps, obtaining a better-quality edition or retaining every airing. Those choices have different expected results. Numbering and edition affect identity Season/episode coordinates need the correct series and episode order. A missing episode number is unknown rather than episode one. A two-part airing, an edited repeat and a combined multi-episode programme add further distinctions. They can belong to the same story without being interchangeable captured artifacts. Likewise, identical bytes provide strong evidence of equal artifacts, but do not identify another encoding of the same episode. Content metadata and byte equality answer different questions. The library check is one input to a series rule Emby’s series-rule contract includes skipping episodes in the library. The usefulness of that option depends on the identity information available for the airing and existing item. If the guide supplies only a series title, confidently distinguishing individual daily episodes becomes harder. If an existing item was misidentified, a correct future airing can be skipped for the wrong reason. See Also Programme identifiers: airings, episodes and series Series recording rules and future airings Understanding episode order Provider identifiers References Emby plugin API: SeriesTimerInfo recording rules Emby plugin API: TimerInfo identity, UTC dates and padding XMLTV: Version-pinned listings DTD and field semantics

articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.title: Incomplete recordings and missing programme intervals | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.keywords: Incomplete recordings and missing programme intervals An incomplete recording lacks part of the intended programme coverage, even when its remaining container parses, its media plays and a recording item is visible. A recording can play from beginning to end and still be incomplete. The player can present every retained packet successfully while the file lacks the opening, a middle interval or the programme’s ending. Completeness concerns what wanted media was captured. Playability concerns whether the retained media can be read and decoded. One hour with three missing intervals Use an original expected programme interval [0,3600), measured in seconds from its start. Suppose usable retained media covers: { "wanted": [0, 3600], "usableIntervals": [[90, 1200], [1260, 3510]] } All intervals are half-open. The recording starts ninety seconds late, loses sixty seconds in the middle and ends ninety seconds early. The retained intervals last 1110 and 2250 seconds, totaling 3360 seconds: fifty-six minutes of wanted coverage. The span from the first retained point to the last is 3420 seconds, or fifty-seven minutes. That larger extent includes the sixty-second internal gap. Neither number equals the wanted sixty minutes. A duration shown by a player can reflect container timestamps and its handling of discontinuities. It is not automatically a measurement of complete programme coverage. Each missing part has a different boundary Missing part Observation to compare Opening Requested start, scheduler attempt and first usable acquisition Middle gap Source media progress, reception errors and stored progress during the interval Ending Requested end, actual programme end and final usable stored media A late acquisition can miss the beginning without any later source errors. A reception failure can damage the middle while the timer continues running. An early stop can be deliberate under a conflict policy or follow an outdated scheduled end. Recording timers separates the start deadline from the first usable media. Reception errors explains why one counter does not identify every later loss. File size alone cannot identify the missing minutes Under a deliberately constant ten-Mbit/s payload, the fifty-six captured minutes in the model contain 4.2 GB of media bytes. A complete hour at an average of approximately 9.333333 Mbit/s also contains 4.2 GB. Equal size therefore does not establish equal coverage when rates differ. Conversely, a larger partial recording can include more streams, padding or higher-rate material than a smaller complete one. This calculation excludes container and filesystem overhead. Its point is the ambiguity: bytes need their rate and timeline context before they become a duration estimate. A successful retry does not fill the earlier gap If the source returns at second 1260, the new packets can supply later media. They do not supply the absent [1200,1260) interval unless some other retained/source history makes it available. Joining the later capture to the earlier file can improve usability. The join still needs compatible stream descriptions and coherent timestamps. Simply concatenating bytes is not a general container repair. A decoder can conceal some damaged pictures, and remuxing can rebuild or change packaging. Neither operation reconstructs programme content that was never received from any available source. A repeat airing or another complete capture can provide a replacement. That is a new source of the missing content rather than evidence that the original recording was complete. Closure is another independent property A recorder may retain all wanted media but fail to finalize a container or catalogue entry. That is a completion/packaging problem with potentially recoverable data. It may also finalize a clean container around only the partial intervals in this example. A successful close does not add those missing minutes. articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.title: Recording post-processing and verified replacement | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.keywords: Recording post-processing and verified replacement Recording post-processing transforms or reorganizes captured media after acquisition, requiring output validation and a consistent publication step before replacing the usable original. Post-processing can change a recording’s container, encoding, programme boundaries or location after capture. Those operations have different effects on the media and on the files that other parts of the server can use. Emby provides an optional recording post-processing hook. A hook launches configured work; it does not establish that the resulting artifact is complete, correctly identified or suitable for every client. Choose what is actually being changed Operation Media consequence Remux Repackage selected compressed streams without decoding and re-encoding them Transcode Decode and encode the selected media, potentially changing its representation Cut/edit Change the retained timeline, subject to the chosen edit method Move Change location; container and elementary media can remain unchanged Stream selection matters even in a remux. Keeping only video and one audio track can omit wanted subtitles or another language without performing a lossy video encode. A precise cut can also require more work than copying whole compressed packets. Decodable entry points and dependencies determine whether the requested boundary can be retained without re-encoding. Container seeking supplies that navigation context. A precise cut has a dependency boundary Use an original simplified video model with independent entry pictures at zero, four and eight seconds. The desired clip begins at second three and ends at seven. Starting copied video at four omits the first wanted second. Retaining the independent picture at zero and all of its following dependency chain also retains three seconds before the wanted beginning. The requested cut lies between independent entry points. A decoder can begin at the preceding entry, reconstruct the intervening pictures and discard presentation before second three; producing a new independently decodable start then requires an appropriate encoding/edit strategy. This exercise assumes those declared dependency points and omits reordering. It does not identify the actual nearest safe cut in an unspecified codec stream. Audio adds another boundary. A packet spanning the wanted cut can contain samples on both sides. Selecting whole packets and selecting exact samples are different operations; timestamp normalization must keep the chosen audio and video aligned. A container change alone does not redefine those dependencies. The output requirements need to state whether extra lead-in, a shifted cut or re-encoding is acceptable before a successful process can be judged. Process success is one observation Here is an original validation exercise: { "processExitCode": 0, "inputStreams": ["video", "audio-en", "audio-de", "subtitle"], "requiredStreams": ["video", "audio-en", "subtitle"], "outputStreams": ["video", "audio-en"], "outputReadable": true, "timelineCheckPassed": true } The process reports success, and the output is readable. The required subtitle is absent, so this declared replacement policy rejects it. The check needs the intended output, not an assumption that every input stream must always be copied. If the user deliberately wanted only video and English audio, the requirements would be different. Other meaningful checks can include usable duration/coverage, expected codecs, language/default flags and seeking. A larger file or a zero exit status does not substitute for those properties. Keep a usable artifact while building the candidate Overwriting the original pathname while producing output exposes a partial file to readers and leaves fewer recovery options if the job fails. A separate candidate allows the existing artifact to remain available while the replacement is created and checked. Publishing the accepted candidate is then its own operation, coordinated with library metadata and active readers. The storage path determines the available publication guarantees. Microsoft documents that a cross-volume move behaves as a copy followed by source deletion; it is not one instantaneous same-volume pathname change. Copy-and-delete replacement can expose partial destinations if interrupted. Likewise, flushing application buffers, completing a container and durable storage are separate conditions. A publication design must use the guarantees of its actual filesystem and write path. A retry needs the intended input generation Suppose job J1 transforms generation G1 of a recording. Before it publishes, another operation replaces the current artifact with G2. J1’s late result should not silently overwrite G2 merely because both use the same display title or final pathname. The job needs to compare the input generation it processed with the artifact it is now replacing. An original decision fixture makes that check explicit: { "jobInputGeneration": "G1", "currentGeneration": "G2", "candidateValidated": true, "publishAllowed": false } Validation passed for J1’s candidate, but its input is stale for this replacement. A retry with an unchanged job identity and input generation can also detect an already-published result rather than creating another independently named copy. The exact job/catalogue mechanism belongs to the implementation. Temporary storage can exceed the final saving Use a separate original budget: an input of 5 GB, a candidate of 3 GB and 1 GB of working files. While all three coexist, they occupy nine decimal GB. Even though the final candidate is two GB smaller than the input, the job needs four GB beyond the original during this modeled peak. If the candidate fails validation, retaining the original avoids turning a formatting problem into missing content. Recording retention should account for the owners and publication state before reclaiming either artifact. articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.title: Recording retention and storage ownership | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/lifecycle/TV-.keywords: Recording retention and storage ownership Recording retention determines which captured artifacts remain under count, protection and active-use policies, while successful storage reclamation remains a separate outcome. A rolling recording collection keeps recent episodes while making room for new ones. Retention expresses which recordings should remain; it also needs a reliable way to turn deletion decisions into actual storage changes. A “keep three” preference is only fully defined once ordering, protected items and active uses have been addressed. A count needs a declared policy Use this original inventory, ordered from oldest to newest: Recording Size Protected Active use R1 2 GB Yes No R2 3 GB No No R3 4 GB No No R4 3 GB No Yes R5 5 GB No No For this teaching exercise, keep the newest three, retain protected items additionally, and defer removal while an item has an active use. The newest set is R3, R4 and R5. Adding protected R1 produces four retained items. R2 is the only current deletion candidate. The initial collection contains seventeen decimal GB. If removing R2 successfully reclaims its three GB under the declared storage model, fourteen remain. This policy permits exceptions to exceed the nominal count. A different implementation can define how protected items contribute to its limit; the setting name alone does not choose that rule. Retention and recording eligibility are separate A series rule can want an airing and later apply retention to its completed result. Deleting an old artifact does not inherently delete the continuing series intent. It can, however, change a later “skip episodes already in the library” decision. A now-absent episode may be eligible again under that policy. A retained history of previous capture and a presently available file are also different inputs. A recorder might use either when suppressing repeats according to its configured rules. A candidate is not reclaimed capacity The selection stage identifies R2. The removal stage still needs to succeed against the actual destination, permissions and current ownership. An active viewer, post-processing job or other open use can prevent or defer removal on some storage paths. Another path can remove a name while an existing open use continues retaining storage. Those behaviors depend on the filesystem and access contract. The important observations are therefore distinct: Observation What it establishes Selected for deletion Policy chose the item Removed from library display Catalogue visibility changed Storage operation succeeded The particular removal operation completed Available space increased Capacity was actually reclaimed on that volume Filesystem allocation, shared extents, delayed reclamation and storage reservations can make byte accounting differ from a sum of displayed file sizes. Coordinate the artifact’s owners Post-processing can temporarily retain an original and a replacement together. Retention should apply to the intended artifact state rather than deleting an input while its owner still needs it. The library also needs a consistent view after removal. A stale item can remain listed even when its path has disappeared; rescanning/catalogue reconciliation addresses that association. Emby exposes recording retention concepts in its public series/timer contracts. A rolling collection deliberately removes older content under a policy; a backup has the different purpose of preserving recoverable copies. articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/in.title: Overview: Scheduling and conflicts | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/in.keywords: Overview: Scheduling and conflicts Recording scheduling combines timers, series rules, resource conflicts and padding around programme boundaries. A single event timer and a continuing series rule select work differently. Their requests can overlap, and padding extends the interval for which resources are needed. These topics make the selection and timing rules explicit before a late start or conflict is attributed to the recorder. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Recording timers A recording timer retains a selected channel, intended time interval and recording options so the server can attempt acquisition at the required deadline. Series recording rules A series recording rule retains matching and retention preferences for a series, producing individual recording requests as eligible airings become available in the guide. Recording conflicts A recording conflict occurs when requested capture intervals cannot all be assigned compatible acquisition or processing resources under the implemented sharing and priority rules. Recording padding Recording padding expands the requested capture interval before and after a listed programme, trading additional source and storage use for coverage of timing uncertainty. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby developer documentation: Programmes, timers and series timers Emby plugin API: TimerInfo identity, UTC dates and padding Emby: DVR settings and recording paths

articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.title: Recording conflicts and feasible resource assignments | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.keywords: Recording conflicts and feasible resource assignments A recording conflict occurs when requested capture intervals cannot all be assigned compatible acquisition or processing resources under the implemented sharing and priority rules. Two programmes can fit neatly beside each other in a guide and still compete for the same source. Their actual recording intervals include padding, acquisition lifetimes and any other overlapping consumers. A recording conflict means the requested uses cannot all obtain the compatible resources they require. The programme grid is only the starting input. Expand the programme intervals first Use these original recordings, with minutes measured from 20:00 UTC: Request Acquisition key Nominal interval Pre/post padding Requested interval A M1 [0,30) 2 / 3 min [-2,33) B M2 [30,60) 2 / 3 min [28,63) C M3 [29,40) 0 / 0 min [29,40) Assume two otherwise compatible resources, one independently acquired key per resource, and no sharing between these three keys. A and B have no nominal overlap. Their padded intervals overlap from minute 28 to 33. Adding C raises demand to three during minutes 29 through 33. Interval Active requested acquisitions [-2,28) A [28,29) A, B [29,33) A, B, C [33,40) B, C [40,63) B Only [29,33) exceeds the declared two-resource capacity. Looking at a programme’s total duration or average daily workload would miss that four-minute conflict. Sharing changes the resource key Now suppose A and C are services in the same multiplex and the route explicitly supports one shared full-multiplex acquisition. The simultaneous requests still number three. Their required acquisition keys become M1 and M2, so two suitable resources can serve the interval under that different policy. Same-service sharing would not give the same result if A and C are different programmes. A backend redistributing one service does not automatically expose the full multiplex. Tuner concurrency develops the distinctions. The sharing behavior must be established by the actual route, not inferred from equal station names or tuner marketing counts. A sufficient count still needs a compatible assignment Consider a separate original allocation: { "resources": [ {"id": "F1", "accepts": ["M1", "M2"]}, {"id": "F2", "accepts": ["M1"]} ], "required": ["M1", "M2"], "validAssignment": {"F1": "M2", "F2": "M1"} } Both resources are free, and two acquisitions are wanted. A greedy choice of F1 for M1 strands M2 because F2 cannot acquire it. The listed assignment succeeds by preserving the less flexible resource for M1. If F1 instead accepts only M1, no assignment can serve M2 regardless of priorities. Eligibility can include delivery-system support, input arrangement, provider/source restrictions or the resource’s current ownership. It is a condition of the assignment, not an extra resource created after counting. A feasible assignment must last across time The allocator can know about later demand before it arrives. Choosing a free compatible resource for the first request can still strand a future recording. Use a separate original case with the same F1/F2 eligibility. M1 is wanted from minute zero to thirty; M2 is wanted from ten to twenty. Assigning M1 to F1 at zero leaves F2 idle, but F2 cannot supply M2 when minute ten arrives. The free count then remains one while the required compatible resource is occupied. Assigning M1 to F2 from the outset leaves F1 available for M2 during [10,20). Both captures can continue without moving either acquisition. Moving an already active M1 capture from F1 to F2 at minute ten requires a source handoff. It may need overlap or reacquisition and can create a gap; it is not equivalent to the uninterrupted initial assignment. The planned decision therefore needs the resource eligibility and requested lifetimes together. A count at each instant is a useful capacity test, but does not by itself choose which continuing acquisition owns each resource. Priority chooses the consequence For the original three-key conflict, a policy might keep A and B and delay C until minute 33. C then misses its requested first four minutes, from 29 to 33. Keeping B and C instead can end A at minute 29. That removes A’s tail padding and one minute of its nominal programme. Keeping A and C can delay B, losing part of B’s requested beginning. Those are different losses. “Highest priority wins” describes a choice between them; it cannot make the excluded acquisition available. If padding is optional under the chosen policy, removing A’s tail after minute 30 reduces the conflict. It does not remove the three-key overlap from minute 29 to 30 because B is still using its start padding while A and C contain nominal programme material. Removing all margins leaves at most two nominal acquisitions in this original request set. That resolves the modeled capacity conflict while giving up the protection those margins supplied. A replacement airing can solve another problem If the guide supplies a suitable repeat, recording it later can satisfy the viewer’s episode intent without serving the conflicting airing. That requires reliable episode identity and an acceptable replacement. The later recording does not recover minutes from the original source retrospectively. It obtains another airing of the intended content. Recheck when the inputs change A schedule revision, larger padding or another viewer can alter the active intervals. A source failure or incompatible input can shrink the eligible pool. Source acquisition, IPTV session limits, media preparation and storage throughput can each constrain a recording route. A warning about one does not establish that the others were exhausted too. articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.title: Recording padding and programme coverage | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.keywords: Recording padding and programme coverage Recording padding expands the requested capture interval before and after a listed programme, trading additional source and storage use for coverage of timing uncertainty. A programme listing says 20:00–21:00. The broadcast might begin slightly early or continue beyond the listed end. Recording padding requests extra capture around the nominal interval. It adds a fixed margin; it does not discover the programme’s actual boundaries. Draw the capture and programme intervals together Use two minutes of start padding and five of end padding: { "listed": {"startMinute": 0, "endMinute": 60}, "padding": {"beforeMinutes": 2, "afterMinutes": 5}, "actualProgramme": {"startMinute": -1, "endMinute": 68} } Minutes are measured from 20:00 on the same date. The requested capture is [-2,65), or 19:58–21:05. The actual programme runs [-1,68), lasting sixty-nine minutes. Capture includes its first sixty-six minutes and misses the final three. One captured minute precedes the actual programme. That is a useful improvement over recording only [0,60), but it does not provide complete coverage in this case. If the programme instead ends at minute 64, the same padding contains it. The result depends on the actual uncertainty, not simply on padding being enabled. Margins have a reason and a cost Start padding can cover an early broadcast and leave room for acquisition to become usable. End padding can cover a late finish. Those are different uncertainties and need not use equal values. Sports and live events can have a larger uncertain ending than a fixed-length recorded programme. Even a large chosen margin remains finite. An updated guide can provide a better nominal interval. Extending padding indefinitely is not a substitute for correcting a systematically wrong time conversion or station mapping. “Requested” is not always “available” Emby documents default start/end padding with per-recording choices. Its public timer contract also distinguishes padding values and whether pre/post padding is required. The implementation decides how optional margins interact with competing recordings. If a margin is dropped to resolve a conflict, compare the actual captured interval with the programme before deciding whether any wanted material was lost. A required margin expresses a stronger request. It still cannot make an unavailable source or unwritable destination work. Back-to-back programmes on one station can share a continuous acquisition only through a route that implements that behavior. The two output recordings and their owners still need the appropriate individual lifetimes. Added minutes consume actual resources In a constant ten-Mbit/s payload exercise, sixty minutes require 4.5 GB of media bytes. Adding the two/five-minute margins increases that to 5.025 GB, an extra 525 MB. These are decimal units and exclude other overhead. The acquisition also lasts seven minutes longer. At schedule boundaries, the extra source lifetime can overlap another request even when the nominal programmes do not. Recording conflicts shows that overlap explicitly. articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.title: Recording timers and acquisition deadlines | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.keywords: Recording timers and acquisition deadlines A recording timer retains a selected channel, intended time interval and recording options so the server can attempt acquisition at the required deadline. A recording timer is a saved request to acquire a particular source during a particular interval. It contains more intent than an alarm that rings when the guide’s programme begins. The server needs to know what to open, when usable capture should start and end, and which options apply to that request. The requested interval includes margins Use this original same-date UTC descriptor: { "channel": "A/news-main", "airing": "P/airing/A100", "programmeStart": "2026-10-12T20:00:00Z", "programmeEnd": "2026-10-12T21:00:00Z", "prePaddingSeconds": 120, "postPaddingSeconds": 300 } The nominal programme lasts sixty minutes. Subtracting the pre-padding and adding the post-padding gives a requested capture interval of 19:58–21:05, lasting sixty-seven minutes. This is an explanatory descriptor. Emby’s public TimerInfo contract has its own channel/programme IDs, UTC date fields and padding properties. The programme association supplies useful descriptions and identity. The source selection must still resolve to the intended service. An acquisition command is not the first usable picture Suppose the request says usable capture should begin at 19:58:00. In a separate original startup model, waking takes twenty seconds, source acquisition takes four and the first usable media entry point takes two. If all three stages are serialized, they require twenty-six seconds. Beginning preparation at 19:57:34 reaches the modeled usable point at 19:58:00. Beginning those stages at 19:58:00 reaches it at 19:58:26 instead. The clock alarm was on time, but the requested first twenty-six seconds were not yet available to write. These times are declared teaching inputs. A real implementation may keep a source warm, perform some work concurrently or use another preparation strategy. The distinction still matters: a scheduled start, a source-open attempt and the first useful captured packet are different observations. A manual timer has different update intent A request created from a guide programme can retain that programme association. A manual request can specify a channel and interval without programme information. Emby’s developer documentation explicitly allows missing programme information for timers. A client displaying them therefore needs the saved interval and channel even when no programme object is available. A moved guide event creates another policy question. Should the request follow the associated programme or preserve the explicit interval? Schedule changes develops the consequences without assuming one universal answer. A series rule is different again: it can generate many individual timers as future matching airings become known. Persisting intent does not guarantee execution The saved timer can survive longer than an application screen, but capture still needs a running scheduler, usable source and writable destination at the deadline. Emby documents an option to wake the server for scheduled recordings. Whether that succeeds also depends on the machine and platform’s supported wake path. The setting alone is not evidence that a particular sleeping server resumed. When a start is missed, distinguish three times: the requested capture start, the scheduler’s actual attempt and the first usable stored media. A late attempt and an on-time attempt with slow acquisition have different causes, even if both produce a short recording. See Also Programme schedule changes and recording plans Recording padding and programme coverage Recording conflicts and feasible resource assignments Guide time zones and clock changes References Emby developer documentation: Programmes, timers and series timers Emby plugin API: TimerInfo identity, UTC dates and padding Emby: DVR settings and recording paths

articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.title: Series recording rules and future airings | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/scheduling/TV.keywords: Series recording rules and future airings A series recording rule retains matching and retention preferences for a series, producing individual recording requests as eligible airings become available in the guide. A viewer chooses “Record series” because they want future episodes without creating every timer manually. The saved intent must therefore outlive the currently visible guide. A series recording rule describes which future airings are wanted. Individual timers represent the concrete recordings produced from that rule and the schedule currently known. The rule survives the guide horizon Suppose an original series, Harbour Stories, has two airings in this week’s loaded guide. Creating two timers covers only those entries. A persistent rule can also select next week’s matching airings after they are supplied and loaded. Before that happens, the rule can exist without timers for unknown future dates. The absence of a timer beyond the guide horizon does not prove that the series rule was deleted. The programme information required to create that timer is not present yet. Matching combines several conditions Emby’s public series-timer reference exposes concepts such as series identity, days/time preferences, new-only recording, skipping episodes already in the library and keeping a limited number of recordings. Those settings answer separate questions. Series membership selects the content family; channel/time conditions select eligible airings; new/repeat and existing-episode information can narrow that set further. Here is a deliberately small candidate set for an original rule: { "rule": {"series": "S", "station": "N1", "newOnly": true, "skipInLibrary": true}, "airings": [ {"id": "A101", "series": "S", "station": "N1", "episode": "E2", "isNew": true, "inLibrary": false}, {"id": "A102", "series": "S", "station": "N1", "episode": "E3", "isNew": null, "inLibrary": false}, {"id": "A103", "series": "S", "station": "N2", "episode": "E2", "isNew": true, "inLibrary": false}, {"id": "A104", "series": "S", "station": "N1", "episode": "E4", "isNew": true, "inLibrary": true} ] } These keys are a teaching model. For this exercise only, new-only accepts an explicit true value; unknown new/repeat status does not pass that condition. Airing Result under the declared rule A101 Eligible A102 New/repeat status unknown A103 Wrong selected station A104 Episode already marked present Changing the unknown-status policy can admit A102. Disabling the station restriction can admit A103. Turning off the existing-episode condition can admit A104. A missing timer therefore needs its eligibility inputs inspected before being blamed on resource capacity. Conversely, passing the filter only establishes that the airing is wanted; it can still encounter a recording conflict . “New” and “not recorded” mean different things A guide’s new/repeat indicator describes the supplied airing metadata. A programme new to the viewer can be marked as a repeat. The library check asks whether matching content is already present according to the implementation’s identity and library rules. That is separate from the broadcaster’s repeat classification. A previous failed or partial capture adds another question: does the policy regard that item as sufficient existing content? Duplicate recording detection develops the confidence needed for that decision. The same episode can also air on several stations or at several times. Selecting one eligible airing does not require treating the others as different episodes. Keep the rule and its outcomes separate A rule has a continuing lifetime; generated timers have individual intervals and statuses. Editing or deleting one timer can have different meaning from changing the persistent rule. The application defines how exceptions, cancelled airings and later guide revisions affect that relationship. Inspect both the saved rule and the relevant generated timer when a single episode behaves unexpectedly. Retention acts later still. It controls which captured artifacts remain, rather than deciding whether an airing belongs to the series in the first place. articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.title: Overview: Time shifting | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.keywords: Overview: Time shifting Time shifting separates the viewer's playback position from a continuing live source through retained media. The live edge advances as new programme data arrive. A buffer or recording can retain earlier data so the viewer can pause, rewind or chase a programme still being captured. These pages relate the available retained interval to the viewer's position and to the ongoing source. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Time-shift buffers A time-shift buffer retains a bounded portion of an advancing live stream so playback can pause or rewind within media that has not yet been evicted. The live playback edge The live playback edge is the newest usable position in a particular delivery path, which remains behind acquisition and publication stages and can require additional playback margin. Chase playback Chase playback reads an ongoing recording before capture finishes, coordinating a growing usable endpoint with the reader’s position and the recording’s final completion state. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: DVR settings and recording paths RFC 8216: HLS playlist mutability, retention and live playback Emby developer documentation: Programmes, timers and series timers

articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.title: Chase playback while a recording grows | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.keywords: Chase playback while a recording grows Chase playback reads an ongoing recording before capture finishes, coordinating a growing usable endpoint with the reader’s position and the recording’s final completion state. A programme is still being recorded, but its beginning is already stored. Chase playback lets a viewer start that retained beginning while the recording continues to grow. The reader is following a moving usable endpoint. That differs from playing a completed file whose endpoint is fixed. The writer and viewer advance independently Use an original recording that has 600 seconds of usable media when the viewer is at 480: Wall time from this observation Usable recorded endpoint at 1× capture Viewer at 1× playback 0 s 600 480 120 s 720 600 240 s 840 720 The gap remains 120 seconds. Normal-speed playback does not catch a writer advancing at the same speed. If the viewer instead runs at 1.5×, the gap closes at 0.5 seconds per wall second. It reaches the moving endpoint after 240 seconds, at media position 840. Seeking closer to the endpoint closes the gap immediately by skipping content. Faster playback retains more of that content while taking time to catch up. Only usable written media belongs to the endpoint Bytes at the physical end of a growing file may include an incomplete container unit or a picture lacking the entry-point information the reader needs. The writer therefore needs to expose a usable extent, not merely a filename and current byte count. The chosen container/index and media route determine how a reader discovers new data and seeks within it. A segmented representation can publish complete pieces as they become ready. This original HLS example contains three completed six-second segments: #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:3 #EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:EVENT #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6 #EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0 #EXTINF:6, recording-0.ts #EXTINF:6, recording-1.ts #EXTINF:6, recording-2.ts It exposes eighteen seconds so far. Its EVENT type permits appending to the existing presentation, and the absence of ENDLIST means no final endpoint has been declared. This playlist is a protocol teaching example, not a claim that every Emby ongoing-recording route uses this representation. Emby’s actual app, backend and media path establish the supported growing-recording behavior. Reaching the current endpoint can mean waiting For an original abstract state model: [ {"reader": 18, "usableEnd": 18, "finalized": false, "result": "wait-for-progress"}, {"reader": 18, "usableEnd": 18, "finalized": true, "result": "finished"} ] The reader position and usable endpoint are equal in both rows. The finalization state changes the meaning. A player treating temporary lack of new data as permanent completion stops too early. A player waiting forever after a confirmed final endpoint fails in the other direction. The implementation can wait for progress, refresh a playlist, retry a read or report a stalled recording according to its route. That state needs to distinguish a healthy writer, an interrupted source and a confirmed completion. Stopping capture fixes a different boundary Suppose the modeled recording finally stops with 900 seconds of usable media. Once completion is confirmed, the endpoint remains 900 while the viewer can continue toward it. For an HLS representation, ENDLIST indicates that no further segments will be added. A growing file uses its own completion signal and finalized structure. The scheduled guide ending is not that signal. Capture can include padding, stop early or continue after a programme overrun. The actual retained endpoint belongs to the recording result. Persistent capture differs from a sliding live window A time-shift buffer can evict earlier media as new data arrives. A chaseable recording must retain the earlier region the reader is permitted to access under its recording lifecycle. Another owner, post-processing job or retention action can still change availability. A shared display title does not keep the underlying artifact alive. articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.title: The live playback edge and delivery delay | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.keywords: The live playback edge and delivery delay The live playback edge is the newest usable position in a particular delivery path, which remains behind acquisition and publication stages and can require additional playback margin. “Go live” moves playback toward the newest position the current route can use. It does not move the viewer to the physical event before its media has been acquired, prepared and delivered. There are several edges, depending on which stage is observed. Name the edge being compared Use this original common-origin snapshot: Stage Latest usable media position Event/source reference 500 s Acquired source media 480 s Server’s published media 474 s Client’s loaded usable media 468 s Currently presented 450 s The viewer is fifty seconds behind the reference. Eighteen seconds of loaded media lie ahead of its presentation. The eighteen-second client reserve is not the entire fifty-second delay. Earlier stages account for another thirty-two seconds before the client’s latest loaded position. A guide’s “now” label describes its schedule/clock interpretation; it does not measure these media positions. A published edge advances in usable pieces In a segmented route, a completed segment can become available after the source has already produced part of the next one. The latest published endpoint consequently advances in steps. Here is an original HLS live playlist, with the first segment declared to start at media time 324: #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:3 #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6 #EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:54 #EXTINF:6, segment-54.ts #EXTINF:6, segment-55.ts #EXTINF:6, segment-56.ts #EXTINF:6, segment-57.ts #EXTINF:6, segment-58.ts #EXTINF:6, segment-59.ts Its six segments span thirty-six seconds, ending at 360. The sequence number identifies the first listed segment; it does not by itself give a wall-clock time. The URIs are fictional relative references. No ENDLIST marker declares a final endpoint. The client expects updates rather than treating 360 as the completed programme duration. Starting at the newest segment gives little reserve RFC 8216 recommends that ordinary live playback without another instructed start should not choose a segment starting less than three target durations from the playlist end. In this six-second-target example, that margin is eighteen seconds. A start at 342 meets it; the newest segment begins at 354 and leaves only six seconds of listed media. The extra margin helps absorb publication and delivery variation. Choosing a very recent start can reduce delay while increasing the risk of reaching data that has not been published yet. This is the conventional HLS recommendation being illustrated. Other protocols and explicitly designed low-latency paths have their own timing rules. Seeking and catching up move differently A seek near the usable edge skips intervening programme content. Faster playback can reduce the gap while still presenting that content. For an original gap of thirty seconds, assume the edge advances at normal speed and playback runs at 1.25 times that speed. The gap shrinks at 0.25 seconds per wall second, so catching it takes 120 seconds if the conditions remain unchanged. Normal-speed playback retains the gap. Pausing increases it. A player must settle into an appropriate live rate or margin after catching up. Chase playback develops the corresponding case where the advancing endpoint belongs to an ongoing retained recording. See Also What is live TV? articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.title: Time-shift buffers and the retained live window | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/time-shifting.keywords: Time-shift buffers and the retained live window A time-shift buffer retains a bounded portion of an advancing live stream so playback can pause or rewind within media that has not yet been evicted. Pausing live TV usually stops the viewer’s position while acquisition continues. A time-shift buffer retains earlier media so the viewer can resume behind the advancing channel. The retained history is finite. A pause can outlast it even while the source and recorder continue working normally. A byte limit is not a fixed number of minutes For an original constant-payload model, let capacity be 360 MB, with MB meaning a million bytes. Retained payload rate Time fitting 360 MB 4 Mbit/s 720 s 8 Mbit/s 360 s 12 Mbit/s 240 s 16 Mbit/s 180 s The calculation is time = capacity × 8 / rate . It excludes container overhead, allocation and additional retained data. At eight Mbit/s, one second uses one MB in this model. At twelve Mbit/s, the same byte limit holds four minutes rather than six. Variable bitrate makes the retained duration change as older low-rate and high-rate material enters or leaves the window. A configuration expressed in time and one expressed in bytes can therefore impose different effective limits. The oldest retained point moves during a pause Assume a full six-minute window at eight Mbit/s and a common media-time origin. Initially the newest usable point is 600 seconds, the oldest retained point is 240 and the viewer is at 540. Time after pausing Newest point Oldest retained point Paused viewer 0 s 600 240 540 300 s 900 540 540 360 s 960 600 540 After five minutes, the viewer reaches the modeled retention boundary. After six, that original position is sixty seconds older than the retained window. Continuing source acquisition does not preserve every earlier second. The eviction policy removed old media to respect the capacity. A real buffer can operate on segment/file boundaries, with its own active-reader rules. Some routes pin data in use, exceed a soft limit or force a playback move instead. Those are implementation choices rather than effects that follow from the word “buffer.” Segment sizes affect eviction This original chunk inventory has four six-second segments: { "capacityMB": 18, "segments": [ {"id": 10, "durationSeconds": 6, "sizeMB": 6}, {"id": 11, "durationSeconds": 6, "sizeMB": 9}, {"id": 12, "durationSeconds": 6, "sizeMB": 3}, {"id": 13, "durationSeconds": 6, "sizeMB": 6} ] } Together they require 24 MB. Under a whole-segment oldest-first policy, removing segment ten leaves eighteen MB and eighteen seconds. Removing an arbitrary six MB from the middle would not describe the same contiguous history. Segment retention needs to preserve the chosen timeline and the index/playlist that exposes it. HLS represents one such media window using an ordered playlist. Its live-playlist rules permit removal from the beginning under specified conditions; an append-only EVENT playlist has different semantics. Stored bytes need a decodable entry point Suppose another retained interval begins at media time 120, but its first usable independent video entry point is at 126. A player asked to begin at 120 may need earlier dependencies that are no longer present. The earliest independently decodable point is later than the earliest retained byte. The required initialization data, timestamps and audio alignment also need to remain available. A time-bar position alone is not a guarantee that every representation can begin cleanly at that exact point. Seeking develops those dependencies. The live edge examines the opposite boundary: the newest safely usable presentation. Rewind history and playback reserve have different jobs A client’s forward playback reserve holds media ahead of its current presentation so it can absorb delivery variation. A source/server time-shift buffer can retain media behind the live position for rewind. They can both contain bytes, but increasing one does not automatically expand the other. A viewer can have ample old history while the client has too little upcoming data for smooth playback. Emby’s DVR settings include a live-stream buffer limit. The actual source/backend and app route establish how that setting relates to pause, rewind, eviction and storage. A permanent recording retains a separately intended capture under its recording/retention policy. Starting one after earlier live media has already been discarded cannot manufacture that lost history. See Also What is live TV? The live playback edge and delivery delay Chase playback while a recording grows Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References Emby: DVR settings and recording paths RFC 8216: HLS playlist mutability, retention and live playback FFmpeg: Stream copying, transcoding and stream selection

articles/live-tv/recording/TV-DVR.html.title: Digital video recording: from live source to stored media | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/recording/TV-DVR.html.keywords: Digital video recording: from live source to stored media Digital video recording retains media from a live source for later playback, with source acquisition, storage completion and library presentation forming distinct stages. A digital video recorder, or DVR, turns arriving television media into a stored presentation that can be watched later. The programme listing supplies the intent and description; the media source supplies what is actually recorded. The retained file may contain compressed streams from the source or media prepared by the chosen recording route. Recording does not inherently mean decoding every picture and encoding it again. Emby’s DVR settings connect recording paths, padding, buffering and optional later processing. From a request to retained media A simplified recording path has several stages: The timer identifies the intended channel and interval. Acquisition needs a compatible available source. The recorder then receives and writes usable media, preserving the container and stream information required to read it later. The file becomes a library item through another association with metadata, images and the recording path. A visible library entry does not by itself establish that every requested second was captured. These are different results: a planned recording, an open source, advancing media, advancing stored bytes and a readable completed artifact. Storage follows the retained payload For an original constant-payload exercise, let the recorded stream use ten Mbit/s for sixty minutes: 10,000,000 bits/s × 3,600 s ÷ 8 = 4,500,000,000 bytes = 4.5 GB Here GB means a billion bytes. Container overhead, extra retained streams and filesystem allocation are excluded. Adding two minutes before and five after extends capture to sixty-seven minutes. Under the same deliberately constant payload, the result becomes 5.025 GB. The rate describes what is written, not necessarily the channel’s complete RF multiplex or the smaller stream an app receives later. A full-multiplex source can carry other services that the recorder discards before writing; a playback conversion can produce another bitrate after recording. Variable bitrate requires integrating the actual rate over time. A file size divided by an assumed rate gives only an estimate of captured duration. Stopping and completing are different conditions When the requested interval ends, acquisition stops. The recording route can still need to finish a container, flush writes and make its metadata consistent. A stream-oriented container and a container requiring finalized indexing can expose different growing-file behavior. Container seeking describes how those structures affect navigation. The application’s successful status is a workflow result. A readable file is a media result. Durable storage is another property of the write/flush and storage path. Neither filename nor timer creation proves all three. An incomplete recording can remain useful even after a late start, source gap or early stop. The stored result needs its actual coverage considered rather than simply being classified by whether a file exists. Playback is a later compatibility decision Emby presents recordings through the media playback system. An app can receive the stored streams directly, in another container or after transcoding according to its capabilities. A recording that was inexpensive to capture can therefore require substantial processing to play on a particular client. Conversely, transcoding during playback does not change which earlier programme intervals were saved. See Also What is live TV? Recording timers and acquisition deadlines Incomplete recordings and missing programme intervals Chase playback while a recording grows References Emby: Live TV sources and guide setup Emby: DVR settings and recording paths Emby developer documentation: Programmes, timers and series timers Microsoft: FileStream.Flush and buffered writes FFmpeg: Stream copying, transcoding and stream selection

articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/index..title: Overview: Source capacity | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/index..keywords: Overview: Source capacity Source capacity determines which live-TV streams or subscriptions can be active at the same time. Two playback or recording requests can compete for the same source resource even when each works alone. Tuner concurrency and IPTV connection limits describe different forms of that shared capacity. Their pages identify the resource and accounting rule behind a refused or conflicting request. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Tuner concurrency Tuner concurrency depends on simultaneous compatible acquisitions and the implemented sharing policy, which can differ from the count of viewers, recordings or services. IPTV connection limits IPTV connection limits constrain a provider or source’s permitted concurrent sessions, independently of stream bitrate and client-facing playback count. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux: Digital TV frontend API Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits

articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/TV-IPT.title: IPTV connection limits | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/TV-IPT.keywords: IPTV connection limits IPTV connection limits constrain a provider or source’s permitted concurrent sessions, independently of stream bitrate and client-facing playback count. An IPTV source can impose a concurrent connection/session limit. That limit belongs to the provider’s or source interface’s defined policy. It is not automatically the number of Emby users, the number of entries in an M3U file or a bitrate budget. Count the sessions the policy actually counts Use an original two-session policy with these states: Session State in the model S1 Acquiring News S2 Acquiring Cinema S3 New Sport request S1 and S2 fill the declared allowance. Opening S3 independently would require three sessions, so it cannot be admitted unchanged under the two-session policy. The model is not a statement of any real provider’s terms. Different services can count connections at different scopes and can retain closed sessions for a defined release interval. Channel switching can create temporary overlap Suppose S1 remains counted until time twelve, while its replacement S3 is requested at time ten. S2 is still counted throughout. Between ten and twelve, accepting the replacement before releasing the old session would produce three counted sessions. After twelve, only S2 and S3 remain, so the count returns to two. The steady-state result fits while the transition does not. A route can need an explicit stop/release/start policy rather than assuming that a channel change is one instantaneous event. The exact release semantics come from the actual source. Closing a client-facing player is not proof that its upstream session has already ceased to count. Sharing changes viewer-to-session mapping An implemented server route can acquire News once and redistribute that media to several compatible clients. Three viewers of that acquisition could then depend on one upstream session. If each viewer opens a separate provider session, the count is three instead. The displayed programme being identical does not establish the chosen policy. Tuner concurrency develops similar resource-key distinctions. An IPTV session count and a physical RF tuner count are different constraints even when a server presents both as television sources. Bitrate does not remove a session gate Two one-Mbit/s sessions still count as two under this declared policy. One twenty-Mbit/s session still counts as one. Lowering an Emby client target can reduce outgoing traffic or conversion work, but it does not automatically reduce the count or bitrate of original provider acquisitions. Emby’s M3U source documentation includes a simultaneous-stream-limit setting. Its configured limit should represent the intended source policy; it does not create extra permitted provider sessions. Release follows the remaining users If two clients share S1, one closing should not release the upstream source while the other still needs it. When the last dependent use ends, the route can request release according to its source contract. A reconnect/retry that opens another independent session before accounting for the old one changes the resource count. The current active lifetimes, not the number of visible playback windows alone, explain that demand. See Also IPTV and internet-delivered live channels Extended M3U channel lists Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition Playback stalls and unavailable next media References Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits SiliconDust: Record-engine live TV sharing API

articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/TV-Tun.title: Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/capacity/TV-Tun.keywords: Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition Tuner concurrency depends on simultaneous compatible acquisitions and the implemented sharing policy, which can differ from the count of viewers, recordings or services. A tuner count describes acquisition resources, not automatically the number of clients that can watch television. Several clients can use one acquired source only if the route implements the relevant sharing. Different programmes on the same RF multiplex add another question: does the source/backend expose the whole multiplex or only independently acquired programme streams? Three policies have different resource keys Declared policy One acquisition is keyed by Independent request Each viewer/recording request Shared same service A compatible service/source combination Shared full multiplex A compatible RF/multiplex acquisition supplying the required services Same-service sharing and full-multiplex sharing are different capabilities. A backend able to redistribute one programme to several clients does not thereby supply different programmes from the same carrier through one acquisition. The full key can include input route and physical-layer configuration. Matching only a frequency label is not always sufficient. Five original requests Use this invented request set, with times measured in seconds from a common origin: Request Use Service Multiplex Interval A Viewer News M1 [0,20) B Recording Weather M1 [5,15) C Viewer Cinema M2 [10,30) D Recording Sport M3 [15,25) E Another viewer News M1 [7,12) Intervals are half-open: a use ending at fifteen does not overlap a use starting at fifteen merely because their boundary is equal.
