The labels do not represent real broadcasts, user timers or Emby API data. The peak depends on what can actually share Between ten and twelve seconds, A, B, C and E are active: Four requests. Three distinct services: News, Weather and Cinema. Two distinct multiplexes: M1 and M2. Under full-multiplex sharing, two suitable acquisition resources can supply that interval. Under same-service sharing, three are required. Under independent acquisition, four are required. At fifteen seconds, B has ended and D has started. A, C and D now require M1, M2 and M3. Even the ideal full-multiplex policy needs three acquisition resources then. Across the complete exercise, the peaks are four requests, three service acquisitions and three multiplex acquisitions. A two-resource model still has a conflict Assume two compatible resources and the declared full-multiplex policy. Demand is: Interval Required multiplex acquisitions [0,5) 1 [5,7) 1 [7,10) 1 [10,12) 2 [12,15) 2 [15,20) 3 [20,25) 2 [25,30) 1 The conflict is fifteen through twenty seconds. If D waits until twenty, it can acquire M3 when A releases M1, but its first five requested seconds have not been captured by that delayed route. A policy that rejects, delays or interrupts a request must choose which consequence is intended. Resource arithmetic does not decide that priority. Actual recording rules, padding and other source consumers can change the intervals. This model isolates acquisition demand rather than claiming a real scheduler result. A shared source stays live while any use remains A and E share News under the same-service policy. E ending at twelve does not release the acquisition while A still needs it through twenty. For a full-multiplex route, B also uses M1 until fifteen. Resource release must consider every remaining dependent service/use. This is why the ownership lifetime matters alongside the count. Releasing the acquisition on the first client disconnect can stop another client; retaining it after the last dependent use can leave a resource unnecessarily occupied. Backend adapters develops the interface/lifetime boundary. RF sharing can increase other work Suppose an original full-multiplex output uses twenty Mbit/s for M1 and twenty-four for M2. The two-acquisition interval then brings forty-four Mbit/s to the server. If the selected programme payloads are News six, Weather two and Cinema ten Mbit/s, their combined service payload is eighteen. The full-multiplex route uses fewer RF acquisitions under the stated assumptions while carrying more incoming data. Selection/filtering location and network capacity therefore remain separate considerations. Neither rate includes transport overhead, and neither describes a measured tuner. A compatible assignment is another condition A free-resource count can be sufficient numerically while a careless assignment still fails. For a separate original two-resource exercise: Resource Eligible modeled acquisitions F1 M1 or M2 F2 M1 The required acquisitions are M1 and M2. Assigning M1 to F1 first leaves F2 unable to acquire M2. A valid assignment instead places M2 on F1 and M1 on F2. Both demands then have distinct compatible resources. { "resources": [ {"id": "F1", "eligible": ["M1", "M2"]}, {"id": "F2", "eligible": ["M1"]} ], "required": ["M1", "M2"], "assignment": {"F1": "M2", "F2": "M1"} } The object is a teaching matching model, not native capabilities or a tuner-allocation report. Eligibility can represent supported input/configuration differences in a real route. This separate example does not change the five-request model’s assumption that its resources are otherwise compatible. It adds the reason that counting alone cannot choose a working assignment. The implementation establishes the policy A vendor’s direct stream interface, its record engine and a separate backend can expose different sharing behavior. SiliconDust’s record-engine API, for example, documents automatic tuner sharing for its defined live-TV route; that statement should not be generalized to every direct source request or every Emby backend. The relevant question is which source operation is opened and how its data is redistributed. A shared channel name or two requests beginning at the same time is not proof of shared acquisition. Finally, all counted resources must support the requested delivery system and input arrangement. An occupied tuner, an incompatible frontend or a mutually exclusive shared satellite input can reduce the available pool before client conversion capacity is considered. See Also Broadcast multiplexes Network TV tuners IPTV connection limits Concurrent encoder sessions, policy and capacity References Linux: Digital TV frontend API Linux: Digital TV demultiplexer and MPEG-TS filters SiliconDust: Record-engine live TV sharing API SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API

articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/index..title: Overview: Tuner hardware | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/index..keywords: Overview: Tuner hardware Tuner hardware receives television signals and exposes programme data through a supported local or network interface. A tuner must match the signal and provide a usable route to the server. Network tuners place part of that route on another device; named product families add their own supported interfaces. These pages connect the receiving hardware and its interface to Emby's source path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> TV tuners A TV tuner and frontend select and recover a compatible broadcast data path, while demultiplexing and media decoding perform later service and picture/audio operations. Network TV tuners A network TV tuner performs broadcast acquisition in a separate device and exposes channel/control and media interfaces over a supported local network route. HDHomeRun HDHomeRun exposes model-specific broadcast reception through a network source whose channel inventory, stream acquisition and diagnostic fields have separate scopes. Hauppauge tuners Hauppauge tuner integration depends on the specific receiving model, region, host driver/application route and exposed service resources. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux: Digital TV frontend API Emby: Hauppauge integration on Windows

articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Hau.title: Hauppauge TV tuner routes | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Hau.keywords: Hauppauge TV tuner routes Hauppauge tuner integration depends on the specific receiving model, region, host driver/application route and exposed service resources. Hauppauge makes tuner devices with different interfaces and regional reception capabilities. The particular model and variant matter before its services can be exposed to Emby. A product-family name is not a complete list of supported broadcast systems. Similar names can have different receiving variants The following are explicitly scoped manufacturer examples: Published example Described arrangement WinTV-quadHD models 1609/1698, cited US product page Four PCIe tuners for the listed ATSC/Clear QAM uses Cited DVB-T/T2/C quadHD guide Four receivers for the listed DVB arrangements The manufacturer documents those variants separately. An ATSC/QAM specification should not be silently applied to a DVB version because both use the quadHD name. These are product-description facts, not a benchmark or a statement that every current Hauppauge device has four resources. Emby’s documented Windows route uses another layer Emby’s Hauppauge setup describes its Windows integration through the installed WinTV/driver arrangement and configured channel data. That means the path contains hardware, the host software/interface and Emby’s source integration. A device physically present in the computer is only the first condition. The documentation includes version-specific and historical setup details. The relevant current model/application requirements should be read in their own support context, rather than treating one old minimum as a universal requirement for every host. Resource count and current availability differ Under an original exclusive-use model, a four-resource device with one resource already owned by another application leaves three available. A new request must also use a resource compatible with the required delivery system. Four total resources do not establish four resources for an unspecified standard. Tuner concurrency explains why recording, viewing, channel scanning and other consumers can interact with the acquisition pool. Receiving a service does not supply every later operation The US example’s Clear QAM support concerns unencrypted cable reception. It should not be expanded into support for arbitrary protected cable services. Similarly, recovering a transport does not identify whether the media must be copied or converted for an Emby client. The selected service’s actual video/audio components answer that later question. See Also TV tuners and service acquisition Live TV backend adapters Clear QAM cable television References Hauppauge: WinTV-quadHD models 1609 and 1698 Hauppauge: DVB-T/T2/C quadHD variant guide Emby: Hauppauge integration on Windows

articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-HDH.title: HDHomeRun network tuner routes | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-HDH.keywords: HDHomeRun network tuner routes HDHomeRun exposes model-specific broadcast reception through a network source whose channel inventory, stream acquisition and diagnostic fields have separate scopes. HDHomeRun is a family of network TV sources. A compatible model recovers broadcast services and exposes channel/media interfaces that another application can use. Emby’s HDHomeRun integration concerns that supported source route. Discovery, channel inventory and a playable service are separate results. The model determines the reception resources HDHomeRun products have different broadcast-system and resource arrangements. A general brand name does not identify ATSC, DVB or CableCARD support for every model. The manufacturer lists particular ATSC 3.0-receiving models, but that alone is not a statement that every tuner resource or every protected service is usable by every third-party app. The exact device and its exposed capabilities belong with the source description. Inventory and acquisition use different operations The public HTTP API describes channel information such as GuideNumber, GuideName and relevant tags. A listed channel number identifies a request in that source’s lineup. Its media request then needs available acquisition resources, a supplied programme and any required supported access path. A channel’s presence in the lineup does not prove that its current request returns usable video. One HTTP status can describe several failures The manufacturer documents a more specific error header alongside HTTP status. Its API gives these relevant distinctions: API condition Published response context Unknown virtual channel 404 No available tuner 503, with the corresponding tuner-use reason Requested programme not found/authorized in the described interval Can produce 503 Required content-protection path not requested Can produce 503 For an original illustrative response: HTTP status: 503 X-HDHomeRun-Error: 805 The published meaning of 805 is “All Tuners In Use.” This fragment is not a captured response. A bare 503 is consequently too broad to identify that cause on its own. A source can be discoverable and its lineup readable while this later media request cannot proceed. Diagnostic fields locate another boundary Manufacturer diagnostic family Role RF lock/strength/quality Reception context Transport error counters Recovered-data integrity context Filtered/output bitrate Data selected or emitted by the source Network packet/output information Later delivery progress Signal strength and quality develop their interpretation. A report should retain the field’s scale and observation interval. An RF error already present in the recovered transport differs from a continuous source output whose packets fail to arrive at Emby Server. Protected services require their supported end-to-end route The manufacturer’s CableCARD protection documentation describes particular supported protected-channel arrangements. It is not a promise that a generic HTTP client or third-party media server can consume every protected channel. Likewise, supporting ATSC 3.0 reception does not itself establish a protected-service path in Emby. The receiving model, selected service, exposed interface and actual access/media requirements determine which operation reaches the client. Encrypted TV channels develops those gates separately. See Also Network TV tuners Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths Channel lineups and source identity References SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API SiliconDust: RF, transport and network diagnostic fields SiliconDust: ATSC 3.0 receiving models SiliconDust: CableCARD protected-channel path requirements

articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Net.title: Network TV tuners | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Net.keywords: Network TV tuners A network TV tuner performs broadcast acquisition in a separate device and exposes channel/control and media interfaces over a supported local network route. A network TV tuner receives broadcast signals in one device, then exposes a supported control/media interface to another device over the network. The network connection changes where acquisition occurs. It does not remove the need for the tuner’s RF path to recover the selected broadcast. The route has two delivery boundaries A tuner can be reachable for discovery or channel-list requests before it has successfully acquired the wanted service. Likewise, its control interface and media stream can have different request and resource conditions. A channel appearing in a list is evidence of inventory. Usable encoded bytes arriving are evidence of acquisition/delivery progress. HDHomeRun provides a specific product/API example. Other network tuners can expose different supported interfaces. Incoming and outgoing traffic differ For an original model, suppose two different source services each arrive at twelve Mbit/s: Incoming source media = 2 × 12 = 24 Mbit/s If Emby produces two client presentations at four Mbit/s each, their outgoing media totals eight Mbit/s. Those values belong to different boundaries. Reducing the outgoing target does not automatically reduce the original tuner streams entering the server. The model excludes overhead and sharing. A full-multiplex output or an implemented shared acquisition would have another input relationship. Capacity lives in several places The source has finite compatible tuning resources. Its interface can also limit sessions or selected outputs. The local network must carry the exposed stream, and the server/client path needs its own preparation capacity. A new client can share an existing acquisition only if the implemented route provides that sharing. Having the same channel name in two clients is not sufficient evidence. Tuner concurrency distinguishes those policies. An RF fault and a network fault can resemble each other Unusable data can arise before the source produces its stream or after it begins sending packets. Blocked reception and network loss can both interrupt the final picture. Receiver RF/error observations describe the earlier boundary. Tuner packet/output statistics and server arrival describe later ones. If the tuner’s usable output remains continuous but the server receives gaps, that is different evidence from the tuner already reporting uncorrectable reception errors. The observation needs the same interval and source identity to connect the stages. See Also HDHomeRun network tuner routes Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition Broadcast multiplexes How a media server delivers playback References SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API SiliconDust: RF, transport and network diagnostic fields Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Tun.title: TV tuners and service acquisition | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/hardware/TV-Tun.keywords: TV tuners and service acquisition A TV tuner and frontend select and recover a compatible broadcast data path, while demultiplexing and media decoding perform later service and picture/audio operations. A TV tuner selects a radio-frequency input path. Its associated demodulation/frontend arrangement recovers data under a supported transmission system. That is different from decoding compressed video into pictures. A product can combine several functions, so its actual exposed interface matters more than the word “tuner” alone. Acquisition, selection and decoding Function Result Tuning/front-end setup Selected carrier and supported input configuration Demodulation/error handling Recovered broadcast data Demultiplexing Requested programme/component data Media decoder Reconstructed pictures or audio samples Renderer/client delivery Prepared presentation through the chosen route Linux’s frontend and demux interfaces provide concrete examples of this separation. A demux can filter MPEG transport packets by PID through supported hardware or software handling. A tuner device can instead expose already selected service streams through another vendor/backend API. The function boundary should follow that interface. RF lock can precede a usable first picture Use an original absolute startup timeline: Model event Time since request Relevant RF lock achieved 150 ms Needed service tables available 350 ms First decodable video entry point available 900 ms Prepared output available 1100 ms Client presents the picture 1600 ms The first picture occurs at 1600 ms, not at the 150-ms lock observation. A compressed-video decoder can need initialization and a suitable reference/entry point. Tables and programme components also have to be identified. Client buffering adds another stage. These times are invented and assume the displayed sequence. Real operations can overlap or use another arrangement; the table is not a tuner speed benchmark. The exposed output changes the server’s task A full multiplex output contains more than the viewer’s requested programme. The backend/application must select the corresponding components and retain required signaling. A selected-service output has already performed some selection. The downstream route still needs to interpret its media and timing. MPEG-TS programme tables develops the associations. Multiplexes explains the shared-carrier resource. A device’s one-channel HTTP interface and its full-transport interface can therefore support different acquisition/sharing arrangements. Hardware capability is not the whole application route The driver and installed backend must expose the device under the server’s actual host context. A device recognized by one local application does not prove another process owns the same usable interface. Other applications can also consume finite acquisition resources. Two physical tuners with one already occupied do not leave two free under an exclusive-use model. Tuner concurrency develops that resource accounting. Several frontends need their individual capabilities A multi-tuner product can expose separate resources, and those resources need not all support identical delivery systems. The relevant count is the number available for the requested configuration. A total socket or tuner number cannot be substituted for a particular standard’s usable acquisition count. See Also Network TV tuners Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition TV signal quality and decoding margin MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References Linux: Digital TV frontend API Linux: Digital TV demultiplexer and MPEG-TS filters SiliconDust: RF, transport and network diagnostic fields

articles/live-tv/sources/index.html.title: Overview: Tuners and television sources | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/index.html.keywords: Overview: Tuners and television sources Live-TV sources connect a tuner, backend or channel resource to the server's available programme streams. A source can be a local tuner, a network tuner, an adapter or a listed network resource. Capacity and access conditions then determine which programmes can be obtained concurrently. This branch separates that source relationship from reception quality and from the guide entry describing the programme. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Tuner hardware Tuner hardware receives television signals and exposes programme data through a supported local or network interface. Live TV backend adapters A Live TV backend adapter connects Emby to an external acquisition/service interface, translating source identities and operations while the backend retains its own hardware and resource responsibilities. Extended M3U channel lists An extended M3U channel list associates source URLs with channel labels and attributes, while actual stream access and programme timing remain separate operations. Source capacity Source capacity determines which live-TV streams or subscriptions can be active at the same time. Encrypted TV channels An encrypted television service needs a supported acquisition, entitlement/protection and media path; recovering its broadcast data alone does not provide playable programme content. Clear QAM Clear QAM refers to relevant unencrypted digital cable services carried through a compatible QAM reception path, rather than to every cable channel or every QAM system. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Live TV backend adapters Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits RFC 8216: HLS media-playlist semantics ATSC: A/360 security and service protection DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification

articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Backends.htm.title: Live TV backend adapters | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Backends.htm.keywords: Live TV backend adapters A Live TV backend adapter connects Emby to an external acquisition/service interface, translating source identities and operations while the backend retains its own hardware and resource responsibilities. A Live TV backend adapter gives Emby a supported interface to another system that acquires and manages television services. The adapter is not the RF receiver itself. It translates operations and identifiers across the boundary between Emby and a standalone backend. Ownership is split across the route An external backend can own tuner configuration, channel scans, service selection and finite acquisition resources. The adapter exposes the relevant catalogue and media operations in a form Emby can use. Emby’s Live TV plugin documentation explicitly distinguishes the plugin from the standalone application it depends on. Adding an adapter does not necessarily create or configure that backend. The actual plugin/backend version pair must expose the operations needed for the selected service. A channel label needs a stable backend key Use an original translation exercise: { "embyChannelKey": "sourceA:news", "displayName": "Harbour News", "backendServiceKey": "mux10:service101", "openOperation": "open-selected-service" } The adapter uses the backend key to request the service. Changing only the displayed name does not need to change that key. The object is a readable teaching model, not an Emby API payload or a captured backend report. An adapter that mistakenly requests another key can supply the wrong programme even while the catalogue and network connection both work. Service identifiers develops the underlying identity scope. Catalog access and media access can fail independently The backend can return channel metadata while a later request lacks a free compatible tuner, current service data or required supported access. A successful catalogue call does not make these later conditions true. Likewise, a backend stream can be usable while a chosen Emby client needs additional media preparation. A useful stage distinction is: Observation Boundary established Catalogue returned Inventory/identity interface Acquisition allocated Backend resource selection Usable media begins arriving Selected-service production/delivery Client output advances Later server/client presentation This ordering gives an error a position rather than treating every failure as a missing plugin. A shared acquisition needs explicit lifetime rules In an original sharing model, viewers A and B both use one backend acquisition. Its consumer count is two. A closing its request reduces the count to one. The acquisition cannot be released solely because A ended; B still needs it. When B ends, the count becomes zero and the model can release the resource. If the adapter opens an independent acquisition for each viewer, its count and resource use have a different relationship. A shared display name does not prove shared acquisition. Cancellation, disconnects and retries also need to preserve the backend’s ownership semantics. Otherwise a resource can remain held after its intended consumer has gone away or be released while another still needs it. Tuner concurrency develops the demand side of this relationship. The backend can perform preparation before Emby sees the stream A backend might expose a full multiplex, a selected encoded programme or an already prepared representation. The adapter contract should identify which one it supplies. If preparation has already happened upstream, a later Emby “direct” delivery choice describes that received representation. It does not imply the original broadcast went through no earlier selection or conversion. See Also TV tuners and service acquisition Network TV tuners Tuner concurrency and shared acquisition References Emby: Live TV backend adapters Linux: Digital TV frontend API Linux: Digital TV demultiplexer and MPEG-TS filters

articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Clear-QAM.ht.title: Clear QAM cable television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Clear-QAM.ht.keywords: Clear QAM cable television Clear QAM refers to relevant unencrypted digital cable services carried through a compatible QAM reception path, rather than to every cable channel or every QAM system. QAM describes modulation. Clear QAM , in the relevant digital-cable context, distinguishes unencrypted services that can be recovered through a compatible source without an additional programme-decryption stage. The word “clear” does not supply a reception standard, media decoder or guarantee that a provider offers those services. Modulation and access are independent properties Property What it identifies QAM arrangement How symbol alternatives carry data through the selected carrier Clear/encrypted status Whether the service has the relevant protection layer Programme/service identity Which media within the transport is selected Codec/profile How its picture/audio components are reconstructed A receiver’s “QAM locked” indication concerns acquisition. It is not automatically an access result for every programme carried there. Several services can differ on the same carrier Use an original inventory exercise: Carrier Service Declared access state Q1 News Clear Q1 Cinema Protected Q1 Weather Clear The three services share the carrier label, but their access states differ. Finding Q1 does not make Cinema clear. The labels are fictional. They are not a discovered channel list or a report of any operator. Broadcast multiplexes develops the carrier/service distinction. The full source route still has requirements An applicable tuner must support the modulation and regional arrangement, identify the service and expose usable media through its driver/backend. A clear service can still carry a codec/profile the selected Emby client does not consume unchanged. Being unencrypted removes one access gate; it does not make all other gates true. DVB-C is a defined cable transmission system. A generic Clear QAM label should not be substituted for a precise receiving-system specification. Availability belongs to the operator’s current service Hauppauge’s cited US product material explicitly presents Clear QAM as dependent on availability from the cable provider. Its applicable tuner support is a device fact, not a universal channel-lineup fact. Emby’s source receives what the supported route actually supplies. The channel identity and its playable clear representation are the relevant result, rather than a cable connection being present by itself. See Also Cable television DVB-C cable television Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths Hauppauge TV tuner routes References Hauppauge: WinTV-quadHD models 1609 and 1698 SiliconDust: CableCARD protected-channel path requirements DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification

articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Encrypted-Ch.title: Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/TV-Encrypted-Ch.keywords: Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths An encrypted television service needs a supported acquisition, entitlement/protection and media path; recovering its broadcast data alone does not provide playable programme content. A receiver can discover a television service and recover its transmitted data while the selected application still has no usable path to its protected content. An encrypted channel adds an access/protection relationship to the acquisition and media-decoding route. These conditions should be evaluated separately. The gates have different responsibilities Gate Question Reception/delivery Can the source obtain the intended service data? Entitlement Is access available under the applicable service arrangement? Implemented protection path Can the actual source/software/client carry out the required supported operation? Media decoding Can the recovered video/audio representation be consumed? Required presentation path Does the later output meet the actual playback requirements? A scan can identify a name or service descriptor without passing all later gates. Two original access cases Model case Service found Entitled Supported protection path Playable data established A Yes Yes No No B Yes Yes Yes Depends on the remaining media/output stages Case A explains why a valid subscription or device pairing is not by itself an application capability result. Case B supplies that access prerequisite without proving every later decoder or presentation condition. These are invented diagnostic states, not claims about a provider or product. Protection support can be an end-to-end arrangement ATSC A/360 defines security/service-protection mechanisms within its scope. Cable conditional-access and product delivery arrangements have other defined contracts. SiliconDust’s CableCARD documentation describes particular supported protected-channel playback paths. It does not declare that every ordinary network stream client supports them. A service working in a manufacturer’s application therefore cannot automatically be used as evidence for a different generic server/client route. The actual protected representation and interface need their own support. Encryption is not a video codec HEVC, H.264 or another codec describes picture reconstruction from an appropriate encoded representation. Supporting that decoder does not establish the required protected-service access. Likewise, HDCP concerns a protected display-link relationship. It is not a universal replacement for the earlier broadcast/service protection stage. If reception succeeds but playable data is not exposed, a different client bitrate or video encoder does not solve the missing access path. Clear reception is a distinct case Clear QAM describes relevant unencrypted cable services. It should not be generalized into a promise about all services on the same cable network. For Emby, the useful source result is the playable representation actually supplied by the supported interface. A channel-list entry, RF lock and account status describe different prerequisites before that result. See Also Clear QAM cable television ATSC 3.0 broadcast television HDHomeRun network tuner routes DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths HDCP and protected display links References ATSC: A/360 security and service protection SiliconDust: CableCARD protected-channel path requirements SiliconDust: HDHomeRun channel and HTTP API

articles/live-tv/sources/TV-M3U.html.title: Extended M3U channel lists | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/sources/TV-M3U.html.keywords: Extended M3U channel lists An extended M3U channel list associates source URLs with channel labels and attributes, while actual stream access and programme timing remain separate operations. An extended M3U channel list can describe live sources through text entries: a channel label and attributes are associated with the following source URL. Emby’s M3U tuner documentation describes accepting this source inventory through a file or downloadable list. Reading the list and acquiring its channels are separate operations. Two original channel entries #EXTM3U #EXTINF:-1 tvg-id="harbour.news" tvg-name="Harbour News" tvg-chno="101" tvg-group="News",Harbour News https://tv.example.net/live/news #EXTINF:-1 tvg-id="harbour.cinema" tvg-name="Harbour Cinema" tvg-chno="205" tvg-group="Films",Harbour Cinema https://tv.example.net/live/cinema The hosts, identifiers and entries are fictional. No endpoint was requested. The negative duration placeholder is a live-channel-list convention in this teaching example, not the duration of an actual programme or an HLS media-segment instruction. Extended IPTV attributes are conventions interpreted by an implementation; they are not all defined by one universal normative M3U standard. Attributes have different roles Attribute Documented Emby role relevant here tvg-id Channel identity tvg-name Channel name tvg-chno Channel number tvg-group Channel group/tag relationship tvg-shift A guide-time offset when specifically applicable The label after the comma is another presentation name in the entry. The URL on the next line supplies the source location. A parser must preserve quoted attribute values containing spaces. Splitting the metadata line on every space would break tvg-name="Harbour News" into unrelated pieces. Guide matching can use the channel identity, while the number and name control other aspects of presentation. Renaming “Harbour News” does not inherently change harbour.news . A quoted comma is not the metadata boundary Use a separate original metadata-line exercise: #EXTINF:-1 tvg-id="harbour.news" tvg-name="Harbour News, Coast",Harbour News, Coast The comma inside the quoted tvg-name belongs to that attribute value. The comma after the closing quote separates metadata from the presentation label. A naive split at the first comma would stop inside the quoted attribute. A parser of this declared example must track the quote state before choosing the boundary. The intended attribute value and presentation label are both “Harbour News, Coast”; the identity remains harbour.news. This is a text-parsing exercise, not a report that every playlist implementation accepts every extension convention. A channel URL is not a successful media response The list can be syntactically readable while a source later needs a supported request context, authorization or available session. An expired or changed URL can fail independently of the channel’s display metadata. A successful HTTP response can also contain an error document rather than the intended encoded media. IPTV connection limits adds another condition. The number of entries in a list does not establish the permitted number of simultaneously opened channels. HLS playlists describe another object An HLS media playlist describes media segments and their sequence for a presentation. The two entries above describe different channel sources, not two consecutive segments of one movie. A channel URL could lead to an HLS presentation whose own playlist then supplies the media timeline. RFC 8216 defines the HLS semantics; HLS playlists develops their use. Sharing #EXTM3U notation does not make all channel-list attributes into HLS tags. Identity should survive presentation edits An original parser of the example should retain two identities: harbour.news and harbour.cinema , with their corresponding numbers and URLs. Changing the first display label to “Harbour News HD” while retaining its identity leaves it the same source entry under that declared model. Changing the identity or URL instead changes a different relationship. See Also IPTV and internet-delivered live channels Channel lineups and source identity IPTV connection limits HLS playlists: variants, media order and live windows References Emby: M3U tuner properties and stream limits RFC 8216: HLS media-playlist semantics

articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/index.ht.title: Overview: ATSC family | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/index.ht.keywords: Overview: ATSC family ATSC generations define distinct broadcast and service arrangements that require corresponding receiver support. ATSC 1.0 and ATSC 3.0 are separate system generations. A familiar channel name does not make their transmission and receiver requirements interchangeable. The two pages describe those arrangements so service availability and tuner capability can be assessed under the appropriate standard. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> ATSC 1.0 ATSC 1.0 uses the A/53 television system, including its terrestrial 8-VSB transmission and MPEG transport/service relationships, with PSIP providing relevant channel information. ATSC 3.0 ATSC 3.0 is a layered terrestrial television system using a different physical and delivery architecture from ATSC 1.0, with service coding and protection remaining additional compatibility conditions. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts ATSC: A/53 Part 2, RF transmission specification ATSC: A/300 system standard and current edition ATSC: A/300:2026-04 system specification

articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/TV-ATSC1.title: ATSC 1.0 broadcast television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/TV-ATSC1.keywords: ATSC 1.0 broadcast television ATSC 1.0 uses the A/53 television system, including its terrestrial 8-VSB transmission and MPEG transport/service relationships, with PSIP providing relevant channel information. ATSC 1.0 is associated with the A/53 digital television system. Its terrestrial transmission uses 8-VSB , while later processing recovers and selects programme services in the transport. The RF modulation, transport tables and encoded picture format are different parts of the route. Eight signal levels do not mean eight programmes The “8” in 8-VSB concerns eight symbol-level alternatives in its modulation arrangement. Eight alternatives can label three bits because: 2³ = 8 That arithmetic does not give the useful programme bitrate. Framing, synchronization, coding and error protection must also be included in a real transmission calculation. It is a conceptual alphabet, not an ATSC waveform generator or a reconstruction of the complete coded signal. A compatible frontend recovers the broadcast data. The television application then needs the intended service and its actual media components. A transport can carry several programme services An MPEG transport can contain several programmes, with tables associating programme numbers with component streams. Broadcast multiplexes explains that sharing. The PAT and PMT relationships are developed in MPEG-TS programme tables . One tuned carrier therefore need not correspond to one item in the viewer’s channel list. ATSC PSIP supplies additional information, including the relationship between virtual channel labels and transported programmes. A major/minor label such as 7.1 is not itself an RF frequency. Virtual channel numbers develops that identity mapping. A/53 separates transport from video and audio A/53 includes several parts rather than one undifferentiated “ATSC format.” Its video and audio parts have their own scope. MPEG-2 video and AC-3 are familiar ATSC 1.0 representations, but a universal “ATSC 1.0 can only carry MPEG-2 video” claim would miss later transport work. ATSC’s current catalogue includes the Part 3:2023-02 rollup incorporating AVC signal transport. That does not mean every station uses AVC or every legacy receiver decodes it. It means the component representation must be read from the actual service and the supported receiving/playback profile. Emby receives the recovered service A supported tuner/backend exposes the selected encoded programme to Emby. Client compatibility and any needed preparation follow from its actual video/audio streams. ATSC reception alone does not guarantee that the current client can consume every recovered representation unchanged. ATSC 3.0 is a different system architecture and waveform, so it should not be described as a codec option that an ATSC 1.0-only frontend gains merely by updating its media player. See Also ATSC 3.0 broadcast television Virtual channel numbers MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS Over-the-air television References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts ATSC: A/53 Part 2, RF transmission specification ATSC: A/65 PSIP specification

articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/TV-ATSC3.title: ATSC 3.0 broadcast television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/atsc/TV-ATSC3.keywords: ATSC 3.0 broadcast television ATSC 3.0 is a layered terrestrial television system using a different physical and delivery architecture from ATSC 1.0, with service coding and protection remaining additional compatibility conditions. ATSC 3.0 is a layered system designed differently from ATSC 1.0. ATSC describes the suite as largely incompatible with its predecessor, rather than as another video-codec choice for the same receiver. A working route needs compatible acquisition hardware and implemented service delivery, media and access support. Physical reception is the first layer ATSC 3.0 uses an OFDM-based physical arrangement with signaling and configured data paths. The receiver has to recover that system before a television application can handle the delivered service. A frontend that can demodulate ATSC 1.0’s 8-VSB signal is not automatically an ATSC 3.0 receiver. A media-decoder update does not by itself supply the different RF demodulation. The broad device model also needs precision: some products can have tuners with different supported capabilities. A “four-tuner” count need not mean four identical ATSC 3.0 acquisition resources. IP transport is not the same as unrestricted internet access ATSC 3.0 uses IP-based delivery relationships in its broadcast system. Service signaling identifies how the applicable media components are obtained and synchronized. That does not turn every broadcast service into an ordinary public website URL. The data can arrive through the RF path, and the receiver/app must implement the relevant service discovery and delivery arrangement. ATSC A/331 describes those signaling/delivery relationships. Broadcast and broadband components can also participate in a supported service architecture. The physical, protocol/management and application/presentation layers are organized by the A/300 system specification. Its dated normative references should be read together when describing a particular edition. Reception, access and decoding form separate conditions Consider these original diagnostic cases: Model case RF acquisition Service delivery Supported access Media decoding A Yes Yes Yes Yes B Yes Yes No Not established C Yes Yes Yes Required audio decoder unavailable Case A satisfies the declared prerequisites. Case B cannot be made playable simply by improving the antenna. Case C can have correctly recovered video data while lacking the needed audio route. These are teaching conditions, not reports from any tuner or Emby installation. Protection is another implemented relationship. A/360 defines security and service-protection mechanisms; available source devices, software and approved service paths still determine whether a selected protected service can be supplied. Encrypted channels develops that distinction without treating a subscription, a tuner lock or a generic media-server interface as interchangeable. Picture and audio properties belong to the service The system can support newer media and presentation capabilities, but a station’s actual service can choose a particular resolution, video profile, audio representation and feature set. An ATSC 3.0 label consequently does not prove that every programme is 4K or HDR. The “4K” in a receiver model likewise does not describe every received channel. When a service uses Dolby AC-4 , the playback path needs the corresponding implemented audio handling. The broadcast label alone is not an audio-decoder capability result. A network tuner adds another delivery boundary An ATSC 3.0-capable source can recover a service and expose it to another application through an implemented local interface. That interface needs to supply a representation the receiving server/app can use. Support demonstrated in the manufacturer’s own app does not automatically establish the same path in every third-party application. This is especially relevant when protection or media preparation belongs to a specific end-to-end arrangement. See Also ATSC 1.0 broadcast television Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths HDHomeRun network tuner routes MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description Dolby AC-4 Audio References ATSC: A/300 system standard and current edition ATSC: A/300:2026-04 system specification ATSC: A/331 signaling and delivery ATSC: A/360 security and service protection

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/index.htm.title: Overview: DVB family | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/index.htm.keywords: Overview: DVB family DVB delivery standards adapt digital television to terrestrial, cable or satellite transmission conditions. DVB-T and T2 address terrestrial delivery, DVB-C addresses cable, and DVB-S or S2 address satellite. Those environments lead to different transmission and receiver relationships. The individual pages explain the selected standard before a service or reception problem is interpreted. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DVB-T DVB-T specifies terrestrial television transmission using an OFDM-based carrier arrangement, framing and error protection before programme services are selected from recovered data. DVB-T2 DVB-T2 defines a second-generation terrestrial transmission arrangement with its own coding, framing and physical-layer-pipe configuration requirements. DVB-C DVB-C specifies a digital cable transmission arrangement whose QAM modulation and framing recover service data before access and media decoding are established. DVB-S DVB-S defines a satellite transmission system using QPSK and specified framing/error-protection relationships before programme services are recovered. DVB-S2 DVB-S2 specifies second-generation satellite framing, modulation and error protection, with the selected configuration determining the required reception and transport relationships. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References DVB: DVB-T framing, coding and modulation specification DVB: DVB-T2 specification and EN/TS evolution DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification DVB: Service Information specification DVB: DVB-S satellite transmission specification DVB: DVB-S2 satellite specification

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-C..title: DVB-C cable television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-C..keywords: DVB-C cable television DVB-C specifies a digital cable transmission arrangement whose QAM modulation and framing recover service data before access and media decoding are established. DVB-C defines framing, channel coding and modulation for digital cable systems. Its QAM arrangement lets a receiver recover data from a compatible cable carrier. It does not, by itself, describe whether a programme is encrypted or which video codec it contains. More constellation alternatives label more bits QAM uses amplitude/phase relationships represented by a constellation of possible symbol points. For an original mapping exercise: Alphabet Alternatives Bits needed to label a point 64-QAM 64 6 256-QAM 256 8 At a declared five million symbols per second, the raw label rates are thirty and forty Mbit/s respectively. These calculations omit error coding, framing and other transmission structure. They are not the useful programme capacity of an installed cable service. Point separation affects recovery Consider an original ideal square-constellation model normalized to the same unit mean symbol power. An eight-by-eight grid with odd levels −7 through 7 has mean unnormalized energy 42. A sixteen-by-sixteen grid with odd levels −15 through 15 has mean energy 170. Their normalized adjacent-point distances are: 64-point grid: 2 / √42 = 0.308607 256-point grid: 2 / √170 = 0.153393 The denser alphabet places neighbouring alternatives closer under this normalization. Noise or distortion can consequently move a received point toward another decision region more easily. This is a geometric teaching model, not a measured error threshold or a complete DVB-C receiver simulation. Coding and the actual receiver/channel also influence recovery. The service can have an access requirement A demodulator recovering a cable transport has answered the transmission question. It has not necessarily established a usable protected-service path. Clear QAM addresses relevant unencrypted cable services. Encrypted channels addresses the additional access/protection relationship. Those conditions should not be inferred merely from a QAM modulation label. Emby needs the selected recovered components The source/backend identifies the programme and supplies its encoded streams. Client/server preparation then depends on their actual representations. See Also Cable television Clear QAM cable television Encrypted TV channels and supported playback paths Broadcast service identifiers References DVB: DVB-C framing, coding and modulation specification DVB: Service Information specification

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-S..title: DVB-S satellite television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-S..keywords: DVB-S satellite television DVB-S defines a satellite transmission system using QPSK and specified framing/error-protection relationships before programme services are recovered. DVB-S specifies a digital satellite transmission arrangement. It uses QPSK with its defined channel coding and framing to carry recoverable data through the satellite link. The programme selected by an Emby viewer is contained in that recovered data, not defined by the modulation name. Four symbol alternatives QPSK has four phase alternatives in its symbol alphabet. Four labels need two bits because 2² = 4 . The diagram concerns symbol alternatives. It does not depict four television programmes, four tuners or a complete channel’s useful bitrate. Symbol rate and information rate differ For an original twenty-million-symbol/second exercise: Raw point-label rate = 20,000,000 × 2 = 40,000,000 bits/s If a declared inner coding relationship has information fraction two-thirds, its coding-only information ceiling is: 40,000,000 × 2/3 = 26,666,667 bits/s, approximately Outer error protection, framing and other structure still require accounting. The second value is not a complete DVB-S programme-capacity calculation. A more redundant coding arrangement gives some transmitted work to protection rather than new information. The usefulness of that tradeoff depends on the received channel and receiver. The transponder needs a complete tuning description Frequency, input route, polarization and symbol/configuration information identify the required acquisition. A frequency alone can be insufficient if another needed parameter or upstream input state is wrong. Satellite reception explains downconversion and shared-input constraints. Several services can share a recovered transponder transport. Later programme and component selection determines which media Emby receives. DVB-S2 changes the transmission/coding arrangement DVB-S2 has a second-generation definition with additional modulation/coding relationships. It is not simply an instruction to decode the same DVB-S stream with HEVC. See Also DVB-S2 satellite television Satellite television reception Broadcast multiplexes References DVB: DVB-S satellite transmission specification DVB: DVB-S2 satellite specification

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-S2.title: DVB-S2 satellite television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-S2.keywords: DVB-S2 satellite television DVB-S2 specifies second-generation satellite framing, modulation and error protection, with the selected configuration determining the required reception and transport relationships. DVB-S2 defines a second-generation satellite transmission system. Modulation, coding and framing jointly describe how data is carried and protected; the selected combination matters to the receiver. A programme’s resolution or codec is another part of the service. Modulation and coding must be read together DVB-S2 includes specified modulation alternatives and powerful coding arrangements. A modulation/coding combination is often described as a MODCOD. The symbol alphabet determines how many alternatives can be represented. Coding determines how transmitted work relates to information and protection. Neither should be treated as a universal useful bitrate on its own. Two declared configurations Use a common original twenty-Msymbol/s rate: Model configuration Bits per point label Declared information fraction Coding-only ceiling QPSK, two-thirds 2 2/3 26.666667 Mbit/s 8PSK, three-quarters 3 3/4 45 Mbit/s For the second row, 20 × 3 × 3/4 = 45 . The ceiling excludes framing, pilots and other transport accounting. The configurations are teaching inputs, not a measured transponder or a prediction that a receiver can recover both equally well. An eight-phase alphabet places phase alternatives closer than a four-phase alphabet under a corresponding constant-radius model. The actual channel and coding determine the usable error margin. A larger information fraction also allocates a different share of transmitted work to redundancy. More potential information is not automatically more reliable recovery. Configuration support belongs to the actual frontend The required delivery system and its selected modulation/coding/input arrangement must be exposed by the hardware and driver/backend route. A source supporting a subset of DVB-S2 configurations does not thereby support every later extension or profile. The base DVB-S2 and related extension specifications have their own scopes. A failed acquisition should therefore retain the actual requested parameters rather than only the family name. Media properties come after recovery A DVB-S2 service can carry a chosen video/audio representation. The transmission label does not say that every programme is HD, 4K or HEVC. For Emby, the backend supplies the selected recovered service, then server/client compatibility determines whether it can be copied or needs conversion. See Also DVB-S satellite television Satellite television reception TV signal quality and decoding margin References DVB: DVB-S2 satellite specification Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-T..title: DVB-T terrestrial television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-T..keywords: DVB-T terrestrial television DVB-T specifies terrestrial television transmission using an OFDM-based carrier arrangement, framing and error protection before programme services are selected from recovered data. DVB-T is a terrestrial digital television transmission system. Its standard defines how broadcast data is framed, coded and modulated for reception, rather than naming one video codec. The receiver recovers that data before selecting and decoding a programme service. Many subcarriers carry one transmission arrangement DVB-T uses OFDM, organizing data across many subcarriers. Their frequency/time relationship lets the receiver distinguish the intended symbols within the configured transmission. Delayed copies from radio propagation affect reception. The transmitted symbol arrangement includes a guard interval intended to help accommodate relevant delay relationships. The receiver still needs suitable synchronization and a sufficiently recoverable signal. A guard interval is not a guarantee against every reflection, interference source or receiver limitation. Guard time occupies part of the symbol interval Use an original timing model with 800 μs of useful symbol interval and 200 μs of guard: Total interval = 800 + 200 = 1000 μs Useful-time fraction = 800 / 1000 = 0.8 Guard-time fraction = 200 / 1000 = 0.2 If the guard were instead 100 μs with the same useful interval, the useful-time fraction would be 800/900 = 0.888889 . These values illustrate a timing tradeoff, not a complete DVB-T bitrate calculation. Carrier allocation, modulation, coding, pilots and other structure also affect useful data. The larger declared guard has a larger timing allowance for delayed copies but a smaller useful-time fraction. Actual receiver/channel behavior determines whether the protection is adequate. The recovered programme has other properties After reception, the route identifies the intended service and its component PIDs through transport/signaling relationships. MPEG-TS programme tables explains that selection. The resulting video/audio codecs determine the later decoding request. An Emby tuner/backend can recover a DVB-T transport while a selected client still needs preparation for a particular service format. RF support and media-decoder support should therefore remain separate results. DVB-T2 is another transmission system DVB-T2 changes the physical/framing/coding arrangement and introduces its own configuration/profile relationships. A DVB-T-only frontend does not gain that demodulation merely because the server can decode a newer video codec. See Also DVB-T2 terrestrial television Over-the-air television TV signal quality and decoding margin Broadcast multiplexes References DVB: DVB-T framing, coding and modulation specification Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-T2.title: DVB-T2 terrestrial television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/dvb/TV-DVB-T2.keywords: DVB-T2 terrestrial television DVB-T2 defines a second-generation terrestrial transmission arrangement with its own coding, framing and physical-layer-pipe configuration requirements. DVB-T2 is a second-generation terrestrial transmission system with a different reception/framing/coding arrangement from DVB-T. Its receiver requirements cannot be reduced to “the channel uses a newer video codec.” A frontend must support the applicable physical configuration before the service’s media reaches Emby. A physical-layer pipe is not a TV channel number A physical-layer pipe , or PLP, carries data through a defined physical-layer arrangement. Different pipes can use appropriate coding/modulation relationships within the transmission. The programme service selected by the viewer is another identity. A PLP identifier is neither the service identifier nor the viewer-facing channel number. Use this original readable configuration: { "deliverySystem": "DVB-T2", "plps": [ {"id": 0, "serviceLabels": ["Harbour News"]}, {"id": 1, "serviceLabels": ["Harbour Cinema", "Harbour Weather"]} ], "selectedPlpId": 0 } The model selects the pipe containing News. It does not establish acquisition of Cinema merely because both pipes belong to the same broadcast arrangement. This is a teaching object, not native DVB signaling, a receiver query or a real broadcaster lineup. Reception and selection have separate prerequisites A receiver can establish a relevant RF state while still lacking the requested pipe/configuration. Conversely, recovering the selected pipe does not by itself identify which programme and component streams the application needs. The complete route relates: Compatible RF configuration -> selected physical-layer data path -> recovered service transport -> intended programme/components -> media decoding and presentation Linux’s frontend interface illustrates that delivery-system and substream-related parameters have defined scopes. Hardware/driver support determines which selections are exposed through that particular implementation. An Emby backend supplies the recovered service through its own supported interface; it does not automatically eliminate a missing physical selection capability. Profiles and document editions need their scope DVB’s published specification page explains the evolution of EN 302 755, including T2-Base/T2-Lite terminology and the accompanying TS 102 755 work. Those document/profile relationships should accompany claims about features. A broad DVB-T2 label does not prove that an installed receiver supports every option or profile combination. The separate implementation guidelines explain system choices and receiver context. They are useful alongside the normative framing/coding specification. The media format remains another condition A recovered service can carry video/audio with its own codec and profile requirements. Supporting the DVB-T2 waveform does not supply every required media decoder. If a receiver exposes the wanted service but Emby’s selected client cannot consume its audio unchanged, that is a later compatibility problem. If the source never recovers the wanted data path, an audio conversion cannot fix the earlier acquisition. See Also DVB-T terrestrial television TV tuners and service acquisition TV signal quality and decoding margin Broadcast service identifiers References DVB: DVB-T2 specification and EN/TS evolution DVB: DVB-T2 implementation guidelines Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/standards/index.html.title: Overview: Broadcast standards | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/index.html.keywords: Overview: Broadcast standards Digital television standards define signal, service and delivery conventions for particular broadcast systems. ATSC, DVB, ISDB-T and DTMB describe different broadcast families. Their definitions affect how a compatible tuner and receiver obtain programmes from the signal. This group gives each family its own context before the channel and guide information carried with it is interpreted. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Digital television standards Digital television standards define interoperable transmission, transport, signaling and media relationships whose supported combination determines a receiving and playback route. ATSC family ATSC generations define distinct broadcast and service arrangements that require corresponding receiver support. DVB family DVB delivery standards adapt digital television to terrestrial, cable or satellite transmission conditions. ISDB-T ISDB-T defines segmented terrestrial transmission with layer/configuration relationships, while regional media profiles and the selected service determine later playback requirements. DTMB DTMB is a terrestrial television transmission system defined by GB 20600, with its specific framing, coding and modulation required before service media can be recovered. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts ATSC: A/300:2026-04 system specification ARIB: STD-B31 terrestrial transmission standard ITU-R: BT.1306 digital terrestrial transmission systems

articles/live-tv/standards/TV-Digital-St.title: Digital television standards and compatibility layers | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/TV-Digital-St.keywords: Digital television standards and compatibility layers Digital television standards define interoperable transmission, transport, signaling and media relationships whose supported combination determines a receiving and playback route. A digital television service crosses several compatibility layers. A broadcast-standard label often names a transmission arrangement, while the recovered service also needs transport/signaling, media decoding and any applicable access support. This is why a tuner can recognize a signal without the complete Emby playback route working. The layers perform different work Layer Responsibility RF transmission How the receiver acquires symbols/data from the carrier Framing and error protection How data boundaries and correction relationships are established Service transport/signaling How the intended service and components are identified Media coding How pictures and audio are reconstructed Access and presentation How the implemented authorized route produces usable output The standard families place these responsibilities in different document structures. ATSC A/53 has distinct transmission, transport, video and audio parts. ATSC 3.0 has an explicitly layered suite. DVB has transmission, coding and service-information specifications. A positive result at one layer is not the whole result Use an original readable prerequisite model: { "rfCompatible": true, "serviceLocated": true, "accessPathAvailable": true, "videoDecoderAvailable": true, "audioDecoderAvailable": false } Under a model requiring all five conditions, the complete audio/video route fails despite compatible RF reception. The object is not a native tuner query or captured Emby report. It illustrates separate conditions; a real system can expose a different set of stages and error messages. The inverse distinction matters too. A media decoder supporting HEVC does not teach an RF frontend to demodulate an unfamiliar broadcast waveform. Related standards need their own names ATSC 1.0 and ATSC 3.0 have fundamentally different reception/system arrangements. DVB-T and DVB-T2 describe terrestrial transmission generations. DVB-C , DVB-S and DVB-S2 address their defined cable/satellite arrangements. ISDB-T and DTMB define other terrestrial systems. These links lead to the separate subjects. A generic “digital tuner” description cannot replace the actual supported delivery systems. Regions and editions add context Transmission standards can be used with regional media profiles and operational choices. An installed service’s codec, precision, audio and protection properties should therefore be established independently of a broad national or family label. A newer specification edition also does not prove that an older device exposes every feature. The actual hardware/driver/backend implementation determines what reaches Emby. Containers and codecs explains the corresponding distinction after acquisition: carrying a component in a supported transport is different from reconstructing that component’s media. See Also ATSC 1.0 broadcast television ATSC 3.0 broadcast television DVB-T terrestrial television DVB-T2 terrestrial television ISDB-T terrestrial television DTMB terrestrial television Containers and Codecs References ATSC: A/53 system, transport, video, audio and transmission parts ATSC: A/300:2026-04 system specification DVB: Specification catalogue ITU-R: BT.1306 digital terrestrial transmission systems

articles/live-tv/standards/TV-DTMB.html.title: DTMB terrestrial television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/TV-DTMB.html.keywords: DTMB terrestrial television DTMB is a terrestrial television transmission system defined by GB 20600, with its specific framing, coding and modulation required before service media can be recovered. DTMB , Digital Terrestrial Multimedia Broadcasting, is a terrestrial transmission system defined by GB 20600. ITU’s terrestrial-system material identifies its distinct transmission arrangement. It is not another name for DVB-T, nor a video codec that a media server selects after receiving any digital RF signal. Framing and modulation need a compatible receiver The standard addresses how data is framed, coded and modulated for transmission. Its single-carrier/multicarrier arrangements and synchronization structure need their own receiver support. Linux’s frontend parameter documentation provides examples of relevant DTMB mode and guard identifiers: Identifier family Role C1 / C3780 Applicable transmission-mode distinctions PN-related guard identifiers Defined synchronization/framing-related selections Delivery-system declaration Whether the frontend exposes the required system Those API names describe an implementation contract. They are not a complete dump of the DTMB specification or proof that every tuner implementing the API supports it. A guard or framing identifier taken from another terrestrial system should not be silently assumed to have the same meaning. A media decoder is a later resource Consider an original compatibility exercise: { "frontendDeliverySystems": ["DVB-T", "DVB-T2"], "requestedDeliverySystem": "DTMB", "clientVideoDecoderAvailable": true } The frontend’s declared set does not include the requested system. The positive client-decoder flag cannot recover missing RF data. The object is readable teaching data, not a native query or a real product capability report. In the reverse case, a compatible receiver can recover a programme whose audio or video still needs another decoder or preparation route. These conditions have different positions in the chain. The standard label does not supply every service property The recovered transport and selected service establish the actual encoded components. The transmission standard’s scope should not be expanded into a universal resolution, bitrate or codec for every programme. For an Emby source, hardware/driver/backend support must first expose a usable service. Playback then depends on the supplied media and the chosen client. See Also Digital television standards and compatibility layers Over-the-air television TV tuners and service acquisition References SAMR: GB 20600-2006 standard catalogue ITU-R: BT.1306 digital terrestrial transmission systems Linux: Digital TV frontend API

articles/live-tv/standards/TV-ISDB-T.htm.title: ISDB-T terrestrial television | Emby Learn
articles/live-tv/standards/TV-ISDB-T.htm.keywords: ISDB-T terrestrial television ISDB-T defines segmented terrestrial transmission with layer/configuration relationships, while regional media profiles and the selected service determine later playback requirements. ISDB-T uses a segmented terrestrial transmission arrangement. The familiar thirteen-segment structure describes the physical transmission organization, not a count of thirteen TV programmes. Layers can use different supported configurations. Regional service and media profiles add another part of the receiving/playback relationship. One central segment can have a separate role DiBEG describes One-Seg as a partial-reception arrangement using the central segment, with the other twelve available for the broader service arrangement. Linux’s frontend properties also distinguish layer segment counts and partial reception. Those are implementation parameters, not viewer-facing channel numbers. Use an original assignment: Model layer Segments Declared symbol-label bits Declared information fraction A 1 2 1/2 B 12 6 3/4 C 0 — — The segment counts sum to thirteen. The table is an invented configuration exercise, not a broadcaster’s transmitted parameters. Segment count does not equal information share Assume each modeled segment contributes 100,000 useful symbol occurrences per second, with other overhead excluded. The layer ceilings become: A = 1 × 100,000 × 2 × 1/2 = 100,000 bits/s B = 12 × 100,000 × 6 × 3/4 = 5,400,000 bits/s Layer A has one-thirteenth of the segment count but one-fifty-fifth of the modeled information total, about 1.82%. The difference comes from the declared modulation/coding choices. A real capacity calculation needs the actual symbol arrangement, pilots, guards, coding and other structure. One-Seg is consequently not a rule that one-thirteenth of every full service’s bitrate becomes available to a partial receiver. Transmission and regional media profiles differ ARIB STD-B31 addresses the defined transmission system. DiBEG’s harmonization material distinguishes transmission, media coding and other service requirements across participating regional arrangements. An ISDB-T RF label should therefore not be expanded into one universal video/audio codec claim for every country and service. An Emby source has to expose the wanted recovered programme, while the client needs its actual encoded components. Correct layer reception and a supported media decoder are separate conditions. The selected service still needs identity The receiver’s physical/layer configuration identifies the acquired data path. Service and component identifiers locate the wanted programme within it. See Also Over-the-air television Digital television standards and compatibility layers TV signal quality and decoding margin References ARIB: STD-B31 terrestrial transmission standard DiBEG: Segmented terrestrial delivery and One-Seg DiBEG: International harmonization documents

articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.title: ASF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.keywords: ASF Container Advanced Systems Format stores synchronized audio, video, and metadata in an object-based container associated with Windows Media. The Windows Media file extensions WMV and WMA often sit above an ASF package. Advanced Systems Format stores descriptions, timed media packets, and optional navigation as identified objects. ASF objects begin with a GUID identifying their kind and a size indicating their extent. A reader can recognize the descriptions it implements and use the object size to navigate through the structure. Top-level object What the reader obtains Header File properties, stream descriptions, and optional metadata Data Encoded media in packets Index objects Time-based access to packet positions Initialize, then deliver packets The Header appears first and describes the source and its streams. The stream properties identify the media representations and setup needed to decode them. Global properties include information such as packet counts, size conventions, and duration. The Data object follows. Its packets have parsing information and payloads associated with one or more streams. Packet presentation timing helps organize their delivery. A reader routes the appropriate payloads to video or audio decoding rather than asking a decoder to consume ASF object headers. This separation explains a readable Windows Media file whose picture still needs conversion for an Emby app: the server can identify the ASF structure and its codec, while the receiving framework may need a different encoded representation or package. How a later position is found An index can map a requested time to a useful packet position. Without appropriate index information, finding that time can involve more reading or scanning. Sequential playback and fast random access consequently exercise different parts of the same package. A new mux can change the packet organization, timing description, and navigation while copying suitable encoded media. Descriptive tags require their own destination representation. The copied codec name describes the media branch, not every ASF object retained by the output. Recognized content and protected content ASF can also describe content-protection information. Recognition lets software explain what kind of resource it has encountered; obtaining usable media may additionally require an authorized decryption path. An object parser or a new filename does not supply that authorization. For an older collection, follow this sequence: Header interpretation, Data reading, source decoding, and the particular output needed. It places a failure at an actual boundary instead of attributing it broadly to “Windows Media.” See Also Containers and Codecs Packet Timestamps Container Indexes and Seeking References Microsoft: ASF file structure Microsoft ASF Specification 1.20.06: archived download catalogue

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: AIFF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: AIFF Container Audio Interchange File Format stores sampled audio and supporting information in a chunk-based file structure originally defined by Apple. An AIFF stores sample descriptions and sound data in separate chunks. Its outer FORM structure identifies the format; COMM describes the audio, and SSND holds its sound data and positioning fields. Chunk Reader use COMM Obtain channels, sample-frame count, precision, and sample rate SSND Locate the actual sound samples, accounting for its offset information MARK, where present Read named positions in the recording Descriptive/instrument chunks Interpret additional recording or instrument information The reader follows sizes through the chunk structure. It does not infer where samples begin solely from the filename or one assumed header length. Interpret the bytes in the declared order Original AIFF PCM stores multibyte values in big-endian order: the most significant byte comes first. For a positive 16-bit value of 291, hexadecimal 0123, the stored bytes are 01 followed by 23. Swapping their interpretation produces hexadecimal 2301, or 8,961, a very different sample. This does not give big-endian audio a sound-quality advantage. It specifies how bytes represent the same numbers. A proper conversion into a little-endian PCM arrangement swaps storage order as required while preserving the decoded values. For stereo, one sample frame contains a value for each channel. If COMM reports 44,100 sample frames at 44.1 kHz, the audio lasts one second. At 16 bits per channel, the uncompressed sample data occupies 44,100 × 2 × 2 = 176,400 bytes, before container structures. AIFF-C describes more encodings AIFF-C extends the description with an encoding identifier, allowing compressed audio and further representations. The extra letter therefore changes what the reader must interpret, rather than simply naming a smaller version of the same original PCM layout. To compare an AIFF master with a WAV listening copy in an Emby collection, compare decoded format, rate, channel layout, and complete duration. A conversion preserving those samples can still write different bytes and different tags because the destination structures differ. An accurate sample comparison begins after each container and byte arrangement has been interpreted. Comparing the raw file bytes would conflate the sample values with their storage order, headers, and descriptive chunks. See Also WAV and RIFF PCM Sample Formats CAF: Core Audio Format References Apple Audio Interchange File Format 1.2: original specification mirror Apple: AIFF file type

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: CAF: Core Audio Format | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: CAF: Core Audio Format Apple Core Audio Format uses extensible chunks and 64-bit size fields to store audio, packet descriptions, and metadata. A recording can outgrow a classic 32-bit chunk length, and compressed audio can contain packets whose byte sizes vary. Core Audio Format (CAF) describes both the large-file storage and the packet information needed to interpret such audio. CAF uses 64-bit chunk size fields. The Audio Description identifies the encoding, sample rate, channel count, and packet/sample conventions. The Audio Data holds the actual content. Other chunks can supply layout, markers, metadata, and a Packet Table. When a fixed calculation is enough For ordinary PCM with a known number of bytes per sample frame, the reader can translate a frame index into a data offset by multiplication.
