The same logic works for packets when their byte length and frame count are fixed and known. Variable packets require more information. Suppose three invented encoded packets occupy 180, 240, and 190 bytes. Their data offsets from the start of this packet sequence are 0, 180, and 420 bytes. A reader cannot locate packet 3 by multiplying one assumed length by two; it needs the intervening sizes or equivalent indexing information. Packet Bytes Start offset 1 180 0 2 240 180 3 190 420 CAF's Packet Table provides packet descriptions as needed for variable-size or variable-duration arrangements. The description and table together let the reader locate and count the audio it will decode. Decoded frames and valid frames A compressed codec can produce initial priming frames and trailing remainder frames beyond the intended recording. CAF can describe those alongside the number of valid frames. For an illustrative 48 kHz case, suppose three packets decode 1,024 frames each, with 256 priming frames and 256 remainder frames. The valid recording contains 3,072 − 256 − 256 = 2,560 frames, lasting approximately 53.333 ms. The encoded packet count alone would instead suggest 64 ms. These fields describe which reconstructed samples belong to the presentation. They are not another codec compressing the audio a second time. The production file and its listening copy CAF's size and packet conventions are useful in capture or editing workflows, including arrangements where data continues to be written. Its description can carry different encodings, so the playback requirements come from the actual encoding and layout inside. If a CAF production source is to be used in an Emby collection, preserve its intended valid audio interval when making a more convenient listening copy. Compare the decoded start and end, channels, and sample format—not just the nominal packet duration. Keeping the valid-frame accounting explains why a correct copy can differ in stored structure while containing the same intended sound. See Also WAV and RIFF AIFF Container PCM Sample Formats References Apple Core Audio Format Specification 1.0

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: DSDIFF: DFF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: DSDIFF: DFF Container Philips DSDIFF stores DSD audio or its losslessly compressed DST representation with properties and optional production information. A DSDIFF file, usually named .dff, carries either raw DSD or a losslessly compressed representation called DST . The format reader must identify which path applies before it can supply the one-bit audio sequence. The file's Form DSD structure contains a format-version description and sound properties. Those properties identify sample rate, channels, and a compression type. Raw DSD data and DST data occupy different sound-data structures. Declared sound type Route to the DSD sequence DSD Read and interpret the stored one-bit data arrangement DST Read compressed frames and decode them back into DSD DST is Direct Stream Transfer, not a PCM conversion. Its lossless decoding reconstructs the DSD it encoded. Converting that result to PCM is another operation after the storage representation has been interpreted. A DST frame has time even when its bytes vary The Philips specification relates a DST frame to 1/75 second. At a DSD64 rate of 2,822,400 one-bit samples per second, that interval contains 37,632 bits, or 4,704 bytes, per channel before compression. Stereo therefore corresponds to 9,408 raw bytes for that interval. DST can encode that interval in a different number of bytes according to the signal. A reader uses frame structure and, where present, indexing to navigate compressed data; it cannot derive every frame's address from one constant compressed size. This is the same distinction between represented duration and stored length that appears in many variable-size encodings, applied here to a one-bit signal. Production descriptions surround the sound DSDIFF can carry channel descriptions, markers, comments, and edited-master information. These describe the source or intended production use; they do not constitute a second soundtrack. DSF uses different channel blocking and its specified ID3v2 tagging arrangement. Translating raw DSD between these containers can preserve the signal while changing its byte arrangement and descriptive structures. Where the source uses DST, producing raw DSF also needs lossless DST decoding first. A conversion that preserves the sound but loses the album descriptions has preserved one layer and changed another. Likewise, a listening copy in PCM has changed the audio representation even when it retains all the titles and markers. For an Emby source, note DSD versus DST, rate, channel layout, valid duration, and the delivered output path. These properties establish which reading and decoding stages are required. They explain the work far more precisely than the shared description “a DSD file.” See Also DSF: DSD Stream File Lossy and Lossless Compression Media Probing Direct Stream Digital (DSD) References Philips DSDIFF Specification 1.5: original PDF mirror

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: DSF: DSD Stream File | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: DSF: DSD Stream File Sony DSF stores raw DSD audio in channel blocks together with an optional ID3v2 metadata section. A DSF , or DSD Stream File, stores Direct Stream Digital audio as channel blocks plus a format description and optional tags. Its sample count is especially useful because the final stored block may include padding. Sony's specification describes a DSD header, a fmt description, a data chunk, and an optional ID3v2 metadata area at the end. The header supplies the file size and a pointer to the metadata; the format description supplies channel arrangement, sampling frequency, and sample count. Block padding in a one-second DSD recording Take an illustrative stereo DSD source at 2,822,400 one-bit samples per second per channel. Its unpadded audio needs: 2,822,400 ÷ 8 = 352,800 bytes per channel per second The stereo total is 705,600 bytes. DSF groups the data into 4,096-byte blocks for each channel, with a block for one channel followed by a block for the other before the next block group. One second requires ceil(352,800 / 4,096) = 87 blocks per channel. Those blocks occupy 356,352 bytes per channel, or 712,704 for stereo. The difference, 7,104 bytes across both channels, is final-block padding in this simplified one-second example. Container headers and optional tags add further bytes. Quantity Reader interpretation Sampling frequency How many one-bit sample instants occur per second Sample count How many of those instants belong to each channel Channel type and count Which channel sequences are present Block size How the channel data is arranged in storage The reader stops presenting according to the valid sample count. Dividing the whole padded file size by an assumed audio rate would overestimate its duration. Bits in a byte are part of the storage convention Eight successive one-bit samples are packed into a byte. The format's representation fields specify how the bits are interpreted; reversing their order changes their time sequence, even though it does not change the number of bytes. A package conversion must respect the bit and channel arrangement rather than treat the data as PCM integers. DSDIFF arranges DSD differently. A converter can translate that arrangement while preserving the DSD sequence. Converting DSD to PCM instead constructs a different sample representation and requires audio-processing work. Tags do another job DSF's optional ID3v2 area can describe artist, album, title, or artwork. It is located through the header pointer, independently of the samples' duration. A music library's title information can therefore change without changing the stored one-bit signal. For an Emby session, distinguish reading this source from the subsequent output. The actual route may preserve DSD or convert it for the app and device. The DSF header explains what was stored; the delivered format explains what the next stage receives. See Also DSDIFF: DFF Container Audio Sample Rate Media Probing Direct Stream Digital (DSD) References Sony DSF File Format Specification 1.01: original PDF mirror ID3v2.4.0: main structure

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: Overview: Audio-oriented containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: Overview: Audio-oriented containers Audio-oriented containers organize sample data and associated information for particular recording and playback workflows. An audio file's packaging can matter even when its decoded sound is familiar PCM or DSD. Chunk structures, metadata and format conventions affect how the stream is identified and read. This group covers the audio-focused containers below, keeping their stored structure distinct from the signal representation they carry. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> WAV and RIFF WAV usually stores audio in a RIFF WAVE structure containing a format description, sample data, and optional metadata chunks. AIFF Audio Interchange File Format stores sampled audio and supporting information in a chunk-based file structure originally defined by Apple. CAF Apple Core Audio Format uses extensible chunks and 64-bit size fields to store audio, packet descriptions, and metadata. DSF Sony DSF stores raw DSD audio in channel blocks together with an optional ID3v2 metadata section. DSDIFF (DFF) Philips DSDIFF stores DSD audio or its losslessly compressed DST representation with properties and optional production information. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: WAV and RIFF | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: WAV and RIFF WAV usually stores audio in a RIFF WAVE structure containing a format description, sample data, and optional metadata chunks. A WAV reader needs to find both how the audio is represented and where its data starts . The familiar RIFF/WAVE structure gives it separately identified chunks for those jobs. RIFF begins with an overall chunk size and a file type, here WAVE. Child chunks have their own four-character identifiers, sizes, and contents. The reader advances using those sizes and required alignment rather than assuming every WAV has a fixed-length header. Chunk or description What it supplies fmt Encoding, channel count, sample rate, and sample/block properties data Encoded or uncompressed audio bytes Additional chunks Metadata, markers, or other information WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE, where used A richer format description, including speaker roles and valid sample precision Byte layout of 48 kHz stereo PCM Suppose fmt describes two-channel, 48 kHz, signed 16-bit linear PCM . Each channel sample occupies two bytes, so one sample frame—one value for each channel—occupies four bytes. The stored sequence is commonly interleaved: left, right, then left, right for the next sample instant. 48,000 sample frames/s × 2 channels × 2 bytes = 192,000 bytes/s Once the reader locates data, advancing 192,000 bytes covers one second of this particular PCM arrangement. The format fields make that inference possible. A compressed WAV uses its own block and decoding rules instead; .wav is not synonymous with these PCM parameters. The bytes occupied by a sample and its useful precision WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE can distinguish the container size for one sample value from the number of valid bits. For example, 20 meaningful bits can occupy a 24-bit, three-byte storage unit. Here “sample container” means the space occupied by one value, not a media-file container such as WAV. For multichannel sound, a speaker-position mask describes which roles the channels occupy. Six values per sample frame alone do not establish whether they represent the expected speaker order . The encoding, precision, and channel roles together tell the audio pipeline how to interpret them. Why data does not always start at byte 44 A minimal PCM WAV layout is often associated with a 44-byte header. Extra metadata, an extended format description, or other chunks can move the beginning of data. A tool extracting samples by a hard-coded offset can consequently treat header bytes as sound or omit the first samples. The same principle applies to size limits. Classic RIFF chunk lengths are 32-bit, giving a practical limit around 4 GiB. RF64 adds conventions for larger files; a reader needs those conventions rather than just a familiar extension. CAF uses another large-file-oriented design. For a WAV imported into Emby, the useful source description includes the encoding, actual sample format, channel roles, rate, and complete duration. These fields explain the sound's stored organization and the amount of data the chosen playback route will need. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Channel Order AIFF Container CAF: Core Audio Format Linear PCM (LPCM) References Microsoft: RIFF and WAVE file structure Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: extensible wave format descriptors

articles/media-files/containers/AVI-Cont.title: AVI Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/AVI-Cont.keywords: AVI Container Audio Video Interleave stores audio and video chunks in a RIFF-based file structure with stream headers and optional indexes. An AVI reader first learns the streams, then reads alternating chunks of their data. Audio Video Interleave uses the RIFF chunk structure, with AVI as its file type. A RIFF chunk contains a four-character ID, a size, and data. LIST chunks group child chunks. The size lets a reader advance over a section instead of interpreting every byte as media; alignment rules can add a padding byte for odd-sized data. AVI structure Information used by the reader hdrl list File and stream descriptions Stream header/format descriptions Track timing conventions and codec setup movi list Media chunks assigned to the streams idx1 or OpenDML indexes Media locations and information used for navigation Chunk IDs connect payloads to stream descriptions A media chunk's ID associates it with a stream and a data kind. The reader uses that stream's header and format description to interpret the payload, then passes compressed video to its decoder. AVI can therefore hold different codecs, including MPEG-4 Part 2 or DV , without AVI itself defining their compression. The timing model also comes from the stream description and chunk sequence. It predates the flexible per-sample composition conventions of some newer formats. Writers and readers have developed extensions and conventions to accommodate different encoded arrangements; those details matter when handling an unusual legacy file. The same opening, two different seeks A reader can scan a readable movi list sequentially. To jump into a long movie, a useful index gives it the corresponding chunk locations and restart information. If navigation is absent or damaged, the opening can still play while the reader spends much longer finding a later location. OpenDML extensions provide additional indexing and larger-file arrangements using RIFF/AVIX structures. A large AVI is therefore not simply a classic small AVI with more bytes; the reader must follow the applicable extended organization. A remux of intact streams can write different indexes in a new package. It need not reconstruct pictures to improve navigation. If a particular media chunk is damaged, rebuilding the index only supplies a better route to that damaged data. For an Emby file comparison, distinguish a sequential-read result from a seek result and record the detected codec and legacy format properties. The source's age does not name a failure stage; chunk interpretation, navigation, and decoding do. See Also Container Indexes and Seeking Codec Identifiers and FourCC Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Microsoft: AVI RIFF File Reference FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/containers/index.ht.title: Overview: Common containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Common containers Media container families define different ways to package tracks, metadata and navigation information. An extension is a useful clue about packaging, not a complete inventory of the encoded content. The families below differ in the structures and conventions they use, and some impose narrower combinations than a general-purpose container. Their individual pages connect those choices to inspection, seeking and playback compatibility. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Matroska family Matroska and WebM share a container foundation while defining different permitted media combinations and conventions. ISO base media and QuickTime ISO base media and QuickTime formats use related structural ideas to organize timed media and its supporting metadata. AVI Audio Video Interleave stores audio and video chunks in a RIFF-based file structure with stream headers and optional indexes. ASF Advanced Systems Format stores synchronized audio, video, and metadata in an object-based container associated with Windows Media. MPEG systems MPEG systems containers multiplex timed elementary streams in arrangements suited to different storage and delivery conditions. Ogg Ogg encapsulates codec packets in pages that support continuous delivery, logical streams, and codec-specific timing. Audio-oriented containers Audio-oriented containers organize sample data and associated information for particular recording and playback workflows. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.title: Overview: ISO base media and QuickTime | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.keywords: Overview: ISO base media and QuickTime ISO base media and QuickTime formats use related structural ideas to organize timed media and its supporting metadata. MP4 and MOV files expose relationships among track descriptions, timing and stored media through structured container elements. Their shared history does not make every file interchangeable. The pages here distinguish the applicable format definitions and the media information a reader needs before judging a particular file's compatibility. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> MP4 and the ISO base media file format MP4 is a container derived from the ISO base media file format that stores encoded media with track descriptions and timing. QuickTime (MOV) QuickTime MOV stores timed media and presentation information in an atom-based container that predates the ISO base media file format. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Apple: chunk offsets Apple: QuickTime File Format

articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.title: MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.keywords: MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format MP4 is a container derived from the ISO base media file format that stores encoded media with track descriptions and timing. You drag the playback position forward in an Emby movie. The player now needs pictures and sound for a new time, but an MP4 file is a sequence of bytes. How does it get from that time request to the right encoded data? An MP4 carries the media together with descriptions of its tracks, timing, and data locations. Following a seek makes the purpose of those descriptions visible. The example below uses a conventional nonfragmented layout. Logical layout of a simple conventional file. The boxes contain descriptions and data; their drawn widths do not represent actual byte sizes. 1. Identify the selected track and its decoder configuration The reader first needs to know which video and audio tracks are selected, how they are encoded, and how to configure their decoders. The movie description in the moov box contains the track information. Within each track, a sample-description table such as stsd identifies the coding arrangement and its configuration. H.264 video and AAC audio are common in MP4, but the filename extension does not select a codec for every track. The actual sample entry supplies that identification. A sample here is a coded media unit in the file-format sense. A coded audio sample can represent many decoded PCM amplitude samples. The reader needs the encoded unit's size and timing, then the audio decoder expands it into the corresponding sound. 2. Relate the requested time to a usable starting sample The track has timing information for its samples. A conventional stts table describes their durations on the decoding timeline; ctts , when required, supplies offsets for the presentation timeline. These can differ because predicted pictures may need to be decoded in a different order from the order in which they appear on screen. The reader uses that information to relate the requested time to the track's samples. For video with reference dependencies, it also needs a suitable starting point. A sync-sample table such as stss , where present, provides information about access points, while the codec's rules determine the required reconstruction path. If that starting point is earlier than the requested picture, the decoder reconstructs the necessary intervening pictures. The player can then begin presentation at the intended position. Audio is located on its corresponding timeline so that both tracks reach the same presentation time. This is why a seek does more than multiply the movie's average bitrate by the number of elapsed seconds. Encoded sample sizes vary, several tracks can be interleaved, and a requested picture may depend on data from an earlier point. 3. Turn the selected sample into a byte location Sample-to-chunk information such as stsc describes how the track's samples are grouped into chunks. A chunk-offset table, stco or co64 , gives the chunks' locations in the file. Sample-size information such as stsz supplies the size of each coded unit. Consider a small constructed example. The reader has chosen sample 15 as its starting sample. The tables establish that chunk 5 begins at byte offset 40,000 and contains samples 13 through 16: Sample in chunk 5 Encoded size Calculated start offset 13 1,000 bytes 40,000 14 1,500 bytes 41,000 15 900 bytes 42,500 16 1,100 bytes 43,400 To locate sample 15, add the lengths of the preceding samples in that chunk: 40,000 + 1,000 + 1,500 = 42,500 The reader can now obtain 900 bytes beginning at that offset. It did not need to decode samples 13 and 14 merely to discover where sample 15 was stored. Their lengths and the chunk location supplied the navigation information. That byte lookup is separate from the decoder's reference requirements established in step 2. Locating a coded picture does not make it independently decodable. The tables get the right data to the right decoder; the codec determines how that data reconstructs a picture. 4. Decode the data and restore the presentation order The selected samples are passed to the configured decoder in the necessary order. Decoded pictures are presented using their presentation times, and decoded audio is placed on the same presentation timeline. For the user, the result is a new playback position. Underneath, the reader has connected four pieces of information: track configuration → timing and access point → byte locations → decoded presentation . A damaged table can break that chain even when much of the encoded media remains intact. A wrong offset directs the reader to the wrong bytes; missing configuration can prevent decoding; incorrect timing can affect duration, ordering, or synchronization. Each failure concerns a different relationship in the file. A small dictionary for the file structure MP4 organizes information into boxes , each with a size and type. Some boxes contain others, producing a hierarchy. The ISO base media file format defines the shared structure on which MP4 is built. Box or table What to look for ftyp Brands declaring file-format conventions moov Movie and track descriptions mdat Stored media data stsd Sample coding descriptions and configuration stts / ctts Decode durations and presentation offsets stsc / stsz Sample grouping and sizes stco / co64 Chunk locations stss, where present Sync-sample information The shared ancestry with QuickTime explains many familiar structures in MOV and MP4. The specific file conventions and supported coding arrangements still determine how a reader uses them. What changes when the layout changes? In a conventional file, the main description can be placed after the bulk media data. A sequential reader then needs access to that later description before it can interpret the presentation. Fast start moves the description earlier and updates affected offsets. It makes navigation information available sooner. Fragmented MP4 supplies initialization data followed by descriptions and media for successive fragments. The lookup information for later samples arrives with those fragments, which suits segmented delivery and media still being produced. The conventional table walkthrough above therefore does not describe every fragmented-file lookup. For an Emby item, inspect the packaging actually delivered to the app as well as the stored file. A server-prepared stream may organize the same encoded media differently. If the playback problem concerns duration or seeking, follow the timing and location descriptions. If the descriptions lead to the correct data but decoding fails, inspect the selected codec and its configuration. That follows the same chain the reader uses to reach the requested playback position. articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.title: QuickTime: MOV Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.keywords: QuickTime: MOV Container QuickTime MOV stores timed media and presentation information in an atom-based container that predates the ISO base media file format. A phone recording can appear portrait even when its stored picture raster is landscape. A production export can be enormous while a phone file with the same MOV extension is small. These observations make sense once QuickTime MOV is read as a presentation structure around media, rather than one codec. The format uses atoms , each identifying a kind of data and its size. Movie descriptions contain track and timing information; media-data atoms contain the encoded samples. This design was the basis for ISO base media formats , although their file types and conventions remain distinct. Sample timing and track edit lists A track describes its media type and sample representation. Sample tables identify encoded samples, how long they last, and where they live. The reader finds the bytes and hands them to the appropriate decoder. A movie can also use an edit list to relate media time to presentation time. A track may begin after an initial empty interval, or present a range beginning partway through its stored media. Reading every sample from media time zero need not reproduce the presentation described by those edits. Information layer What it changes Coded samples The reconstructed pictures or sound Sample timing and location When samples belong and where their bytes are read Track edits Which media range maps onto the movie timeline Display transformation How the reconstructed track is placed or oriented These layers can change independently. Copying coded samples preserves one of them, not necessarily the complete presentation. The portrait phone example Suppose the coded raster is 1920 × 1080 and the track describes a 90-degree display rotation. The decoder reconstructs the landscape raster. Applying the transform gives a portrait arrangement whose displayed dimensions exchange width and height. A conversion can bake the rotation into newly encoded pixels, or preserve the raster and transfer appropriate orientation information . Copying only the picture bytes while losing the transform produces a sideways result. That error arises after successful decoding, in how the decoded track is presented. An editing master has different data demands A MOV can hold ProRes or other production media that spends much more data per second than a compact delivery encode. This serves editing and preservation of production information. The same container can also hold a camera's compressed delivery-like video. For an Emby source, inspect the actual codec, data rate, track edits, and orientation. Those properties explain why one MOV is straightforward to deliver while another benefits from a smaller viewing copy. An input that merely needs new packaging follows a different transformation from one whose pictures are resized, rotated into pixels, or newly compressed. The movie structure records how the media should be assembled. Following it explains both the sound/picture timing and the visible orientation of the final presentation. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Streams and Tracks Video Rotation Metadata References Apple: QuickTime File Format

articles/media-files/containers/matroska.title: Overview: Matroska family | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/matroska.keywords: Overview: Matroska family Matroska and WebM share a container foundation while defining different permitted media combinations and conventions. Matroska can organize multiple kinds of tracks and supporting information in one container. WebM builds on that foundation with a more constrained format definition. Comparing the two is useful when a familiar-looking file needs to work in a particular player or delivery environment; the track codecs remain part of that decision. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Matroska (MKV and MKA) Matroska stores multiple encoded tracks, timing information, and optional chapters and attachments in an extensible media container. WebM WebM is a constrained Matroska-based container designed for web delivery of encoded video and audio. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification WebM Project: container guidelines

articles/media-files/containers/matroska.title: Matroska: MKV and MKA | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/matroska.keywords: Matroska: MKV and MKA Matroska stores multiple encoded tracks, timing information, and optional chapters and attachments in an extensible media container. A film's main picture, original soundtrack, translation, commentary, and subtitles can all share one Matroska file. The container keeps their descriptions and timing separate so the viewer can choose a combination without duplicating the picture. .mkv usually denotes video; .mka usually denotes audio without video. Both use the Matroska family. To understand what a reader does with either one, follow its structure from descriptions to media. Elements describe other elements Matroska uses EBML , a binary system of identified elements. An element has an ID, an encoded size, and data. Some elements contain a number or text; others contain child elements. The reader uses the known size and type to move through this hierarchy. An EBML header identifies the document convention. The Matroska Segment contains the presentation's major structures. This is a hierarchy inside the format, not a claim that the whole movie is one network segment. Segment component Reader's use Info Overall timing scale and segment information Tracks Codec, configuration, and properties of each media component Clusters Groups of timed media blocks SeekHead Locations of major elements Cues Timeline entries used to find media efficiently Chapters, Tags, Attachments Navigation, description, and supporting resources The design permits optional elements a reader does not implement to be skipped by their declared size. Required interpretation still depends on the document version and the relevant component. Extensibility means the structure can evolve; it does not make every possible new feature behave identically in old software. Reading one video block and the accompanying sound The Tracks element identifies a video track and its CodecID. The codec mapping explains where decoder setup is stored and how the block's payload represents encoded units. A codec-private field may contain initialization information the decoder needs before processing media. The reader then encounters Clusters containing blocks assigned to track numbers. Blocks from video and audio can be interleaved in file storage. Their track identities let the demuxer build separate sequences for decoding. A cluster has a timestamp and a block has a relative timestamp. With an illustrative TimestampScale of 1,000,000 nanoseconds per tick, a cluster at 12,000 ticks and a block offset of 40 ticks represent: (12,000 + 40) × 1,000,000 ns = 12.040 seconds This example assumes the ordinary unit track scale. The block's place among file bytes is not itself its presentation time: a nearby audio block can use a different offset and contain a different amount of sound. Selecting an English soundtrack tells the reader which audio track's blocks to deliver. It does not delete the German or commentary blocks stored in the file. That distinction is useful in Emby when a change in selected sound or subtitles changes processing even though the same MKV video remains selected. Looking up a scene To seek, a reader can use Cues to find a suitable cluster or block location near the requested time, then decode from a usable video random-access point. SeekHead serves another lookup role by locating top-level structures such as Tracks or Cues. A pointer to a structure and a pointer from media time to data are different kinds of index. The seeking walkthrough explains why the decoder may reconstruct preceding pictures before showing the desired one. A Cue supplies a useful address; it does not remove dependencies in the compressed video. Information outside the timed blocks A font attachment supplies a file that a subtitle renderer may use. A cover image can be another attachment. These resources are not timed sound or picture streams, so preserving the main tracks during a remux does not automatically preserve them. Ordinary chapters label points in a fixed timeline. Ordered editions can instead define ranges and references that compose a different sequence. Tags describe the file or particular objects. Together these features explain why a file's meaning is richer than a list of copied video and audio packets. For a repackaged copy, compare the intended presentation components: selected tracks and language descriptions, timing, usable seeking, chapters, and supporting resources. Matroska's structure makes those individually describable, and an inspection can establish which of them the output actually retained. See Also Streams and Tracks Codec Support in Containers Matroska Attachments Matroska Ordered Chapters How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification RFC 8794: Extensible Binary Meta Language Matroska codec mappings

articles/media-files/containers/matroska.title: WebM Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/matroska.keywords: WebM Container WebM is a constrained Matroska-based container designed for web delivery of encoded video and audio. A WebM recording uses the same kind of EBML element hierarchy as Matroska, with a constrained set of media and feature conventions suited to web delivery. WebM gives the reader a more specific contract than “some Matroska tracks.” WebM component Reader's job EBML header and WebM document type Establish which container conventions apply Track descriptions Identify codec and initialization information Clusters and timed blocks Supply each component's encoded data at its media time Cues, when present Locate suitable media positions for seeking The project guidelines enumerate VP8/VP9 video with Vorbis/Opus audio. Modern writers also handle AV1 : the pinned FFmpeg n8.1 WebM codec map explicitly includes it. That is useful when a newer file reports AV1 while an older summary of the format mentions only VP8 and VP9. Browser decoding and synchronized presentation A reader parses the document type and Tracks information. It creates a video decoding path for the declared codec and an audio path for Opus or Vorbis . Cluster blocks supply encoded packets and presentation timing. The playback framework schedules the reconstructed pictures and samples together. The HTTP response's media type and codec parameters can identify this combination before the reader has parsed the complete source. The combination must still match the actual bytes. A declaration of VP9 does not convert an AV1 track into VP9, and the receiving framework needs the appropriate decoder. An Emby library source can be opened and repackaged on the server or delivered in its original arrangement. Identify the selected output when comparing a browser's behaviour with another app: decoding the source on a server and decoding it in the browser are different routes. What changing an MKV into WebM involves Suppose an MKV contains H.264, AAC, an ASS subtitle, and attached fonts. Changing the extension does not change its document declaration, codec mappings, or feature set. A real conversion must choose a WebM-compatible representation for each component it retains. If the input video is already AV1 and the soundtrack already Opus, a writer supporting that combination can instead copy suitable encoded media into WebM. It recreates the allowed structure and setup; it does not need to recompress the sound and picture merely because the file's name changes. The distinction is between meeting the destination's contract and doing new coding work. The general Matroska format can retain a broader range of original components, while WebM provides a narrower delivery arrangement. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Media MIME Types Codec Support in Containers AV1 Video Opus Audio References WebM Project: container guidelines Matroska codec mappings FFmpeg n8.1: WebM codec mappings

articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.title: Overview: MPEG systems | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.keywords: Overview: MPEG systems MPEG systems containers multiplex timed elementary streams in arrangements suited to different storage and delivery conditions. A transport stream and a program stream both carry related media streams, but their packaging serves different environments. Transport-stream packetization and programme identification are especially relevant to continuing broadcast or network sources. These pages explain the container choice before moving into the codecs carried inside it. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> MPEG transport stream (TS and M2TS) MPEG transport stream interleaves encoded media and programme information in small fixed-size packets suited to continuous delivery. MPEG program stream MPEG program stream multiplexes related encoded streams into variable-size packs for storage and playback in comparatively reliable environments. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-T H.222.0 (04/2025): MPEG systems

articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.title: MPEG Program Stream | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.keywords: MPEG Program Stream MPEG program stream multiplexes related encoded streams into variable-size packs for storage and playback in comparatively reliable environments. An older MPG movie and the video objects on a DVD can organize media through MPEG program stream (PS) . This systems layer arranges encoded components for synchronized playback; it does not define their picture compression. PS uses packs , which contain a pack header and packetized elementary-stream data. Unlike the fixed small packets of transport stream , pack and PES organization is suited to a comparatively reliable source such as stored media. Pack clocks, PES timestamps, and stream identifiers The reader identifies the pack structure and its systems clock information. It then examines PES packet headers to identify components and obtain timestamps where supplied. Payload belonging to video is routed to video decoding, while audio payload is routed to an audio decoder. Information Role in this process Pack header and system timing Describe the multiplex's delivery timing Stream identifiers Distinguish components or private-data arrangements PES PTS/DTS, when present Schedule presentation and decoding Encoded payload Supplies the codec's media data Stream identifiers do not all imply one universal codec choice. DVD, for example, defines additional conventions for private-stream audio and subpictures. The systems reader must understand the relevant arrangement before the appropriate codec receives its bytes. Reading order and viewing order Interleaving puts pieces of different components within the package. Their timestamps associate them with a shared schedule. The file reader does not need to play the entire video portion before the entire audio portion; it supplies queues for both so the player can present them together. A component's timestamps and codec setup can therefore be essential when copying its elementary data into another package. Preserving only payload while losing timing is not the same as preserving the presentation. What a DVD adds around VOB media DVD-Video uses constrained program-stream-based video objects, commonly stored in VOB files. A title can span several such files and use navigation that chooses cells or angles. Its IFO descriptions supply title and programme-chain organization outside the ordinary act of decoding a VOB's packets. Opening one VOB demonstrates that its media can be read. It does not resolve the disc's intended complete title. Joining filenames in order similarly follows storage naming rather than the navigation that selected the presentation. When preparing a disc-derived source for an Emby library, the useful boundary is the intended title and its selected components. A remux can retain their encoding while writing a new timed package, after the source's presentation choices have been resolved. See Also MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS DVD-Video File Structure Packet Timestamps References ITU-T H.222.0 (04/2025): MPEG systems FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.title: MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.keywords: MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS MPEG transport stream interleaves encoded media and programme information in small fixed-size packets suited to continuous delivery. A receiver can join a television transmission after it has already started. MPEG transport stream (TS) gives it repeated descriptions and small identifiable packets so it can find the wanted components in that ongoing sequence. Every basic TS packet occupies 188 bytes . A minimum four-byte header includes synchronization, a PID identifying the packet's role, and control fields describing its payload and continuity. An optional adaptation field can carry additional timing or signalling; the remaining space carries payload. Stored framing schematic. Widths do not represent byte proportions. Find the boundaries, then find the programme A reader looks for the synchronization pattern at the expected packet spacing and validates the packet structure. One apparent matching byte in arbitrary data is less useful than a sequence consistent with the format. The PID identifies a component locally within the multiplex. PAT and PMT give those identifiers meaning: the PAT points to a programme's PMT, and the PMT identifies its video, audio, subtitles, and programme clock reference. Several programmes can share one transport sequence. Selecting one service follows the PIDs described for that programme. It does not mean that every packet in the file is part of the selected presentation. A complete multiplex recording can include other services or signalling as well. A picture can span many packets Media is commonly wrapped in PES , a packetized elementary-stream layer. A PES packet carrying video can be spread across many 188-byte transport packets. The reader reassembles those bytes and their timing before supplying encoded video to a decoder. A transport-packet boundary is therefore different from a picture boundary. Losing one packet can remove part of an encoded picture or its setup, with consequences for that picture and any following dependent pictures. The continuity counter helps observe delivery at the PID level. For packets carrying payload it advances modulo 16, so 15 followed by 0 is an ordinary wrap. An unexpected jump can signal missing data, while duplicates, adaptation-only packets, and declared discontinuities require their specific rules. The counter is a local consistency aid, not a complete decode test. Keep the programme clock and picture schedule separate PCR observations help the receiver follow the programme clock. PTS and DTS in the media timing describe when results are presented and encoded data is decoded. Arrival order, clock recovery, and picture presentation are related jobs with different information. If a broadcast changes components or resets timing, the descriptions and discontinuity handling determine how the receiver continues. A stored recording preserves those events; putting the packets onto disk does not silently turn them into a conventional movie timeline. Why M2TS occupies 192 bytes per stored unit Blu-ray M2TS prefixes each TS packet with four more bytes, including arrival-time information. It therefore stores 192-byte units while retaining the 188-byte transport packet inside. A reader must account for the prefix before interpreting TS headers. Changing .ts to .m2ts does not add that framing. Conversely, a properly repackaged copy can remove or add the outer framing while retaining suitable encoded media. For an Emby recording, a useful comparison starts with the selected programme and its components, then examines timing or packet loss at the affected moment. Remuxing can build more convenient file navigation and a coherent selected presentation. It cannot supply media bytes that reception never recorded. See Also MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT Packet Timestamps MPEG Program Stream Blu-ray File Structure References ITU-T H.222.0 (04/2025): MPEG systems Blu-ray Disc Association: BD-ROM audiovisual application white paper, March 2005 (original PDF mirror) FFmpeg n8.1 MPEG-TS reader and packet handling

articles/media-files/containers/Ogg-Cont.title: Ogg Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/Ogg-Cont.keywords: Ogg Container Ogg encapsulates codec packets in pages that support continuous delivery, logical streams, and codec-specific timing. An Ogg file is made of pages, but a decoder consumes codec packets. Understanding that distinction explains how a small audio packet, a large setup packet, and timing information can all share one file. Vorbis and Opus are coding formats carried through their own Ogg mappings. Ogg supplies the page structure around them; it does not make their decoding rules interchangeable. Assemble a packet from page segments A page contains a header, a segment table, and payload. The segment table uses lengths up to 255 bytes to describe how portions of packets occupy the payload. A length below 255 terminates a packet; longer packets use continued segments and can cross a page boundary. For an invented 600-byte packet fitting on one otherwise empty page, segment lengths 255, 255, and 90 describe its data. The fixed 27-byte header and three-byte segment table add 30 bytes, producing a 630-byte page in this simplified example. Page information Reader use Capture pattern and flags Recognize boundaries and continuation/start/end conditions Stream serial number Associate pages with one logical stream Page sequence number Follow its ordering Checksum Detect inconsistent page bytes Granule position Interpret completed media position through the codec mapping The decoder sees the reassembled packet, not the Ogg header and segment lengths. Where a packet spans pages, the reader retains its partial bytes until it is complete. A granule position becomes audio time The granule field's meaning comes from the codec mapping. Ogg Opus uses a 48 kHz sample-count coordinate even when an implementation outputs audio at another supported rate. The Opus header's pre-skip tells the reader how many initial decoded samples should be discarded. Take a simple stream with ordinary initial positioning, 48,000 decoded samples represented at the final granule position, and an illustrative pre-skip of 312. The presented length is: (48,000 − 312) ÷ 48,000 = 0.9935 seconds The subtraction is not missing audio caused by the container. It is the mapping's way to exclude initial codec delay from the intended output. End-position rules can similarly trim extra decoded samples at the end. The encoded packet duration and presented duration can therefore differ for a legitimate reason. Logical streams can end before the physical file Chaining ends one logical stream and begins another, with new headers and identity. A continuous radio archive can consequently contain several linked portions within one physical file. A reader following only the first logical stream can report or play a shorter result than one following the complete chain. For an Emby source with an unexpected duration or failure at a transition, record the codec, its header timing, and whether the file contains a chain. It targets the actual page/packet/timeline relationship rather than treating .ogg as a complete description of the sound. See Also Streams and Tracks Container Indexes and Seeking Containers and Codecs Vorbis Audio Opus Audio References RFC 3533: Ogg encapsulation format RFC 7845: Ogg encapsulation for Opus

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Overview: Container structure | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Overview: Container structure Container structures organize encoded streams, timing, track information and navigation within a media file. A player needs more than a sequence of compressed bytes. It needs to identify the streams, locate useful starting points and relate their data to presentation time. This branch explains the container structures that supply those relationships, as well as the overhead and failure cases that arise when packaging is incomplete or damaged. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is a media container? A media container organizes encoded streams and the information needed to find, identify, and time them. Types of media containers Media containers use different structures to serve stored files, continuous transport, and segmented delivery. Multiplexing and demultiplexing Multiplexing combines media tracks into one organized source, while demultiplexing separates them for playback or processing. Elementary streams An elementary stream contains one coded media component before it is combined with other components in a container. Timing and navigation Container timing and navigation connect packet clocks, playback positions, seek indexes and chapter locations. Codec identifiers and FourCC Codec identifiers tell a container reader how to interpret a track's encoded data and its packaging. Codec support in containers A valid container and codec combination needs both a defined storage mapping and software that implements it. Track and programme descriptions Track and programme descriptions identify available content and provide context for selecting or routing it. Container overhead Container overhead is the space used to organize and describe media in addition to its encoded picture and sound. Damaged and incomplete media files A damaged media file can lose container structure, timing, or encoded content, with different consequences for recovery. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Codec Identifiers and FourCC | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Codec Identifiers and FourCC Codec identifiers tell a container reader how to interpret a track's encoded data and its packaging. A report can show HEVC as the codec name and hvc1 as its codec ID. The first names the compression system. The second identifies a particular representation of that system inside the container. The reader uses this identifier to choose the correct mapping: which configuration record to parse, how encoded units are delimited, and which placement conventions apply. It is more like a parser's dispatch key than a marketing name. Container field Example Reader interpretation MP4 sample-entry type avc1 AVC samples with the corresponding configuration and storage convention MP4 sample-entry type hvc1 or hev1 HEVC samples with different parameter-set carriage rules Matroska CodecID V_MPEG4/ISO/AVC Matroska's defined mapping for AVC AVI video identifier A FourCC such as XVID A registered or implemented compressed-video representation FourCC means four-character code. Spaces and case can form part of the literal value. MP4 uses four-character sample-entry types, while the Matroska example is a longer string. An inspection tool's friendly display name can conceal that distinction, so retain the literal identifier when reporting a parsing problem. Where hvc1 and hev1 carry HEVC parameter sets An HEVC decoder needs parameter sets describing the sequence and pictures: VPS , SPS , and PPS . Encoded slices refer to that setup information. The container mapping establishes where the reader obtains it. For hvc1, the parameter sets must be supplied through the sample entry's HEVC configuration; they are not carried as in-band parameter-set units in samples. The hev1 representation permits parameter sets in samples as well as the configuration record. A reader expecting one arrangement can consequently behave differently with the other, although both tracks report HEVC. Retagging hev1 as hvc1 is therefore an assertion about the stream's organization. A correct conversion checks the configuration and sample contents and satisfies the new convention. Editing four characters alone does not move setup information out of samples or ensure that all required parameter sets are available in the configuration record. From identifier to decoder requirements After identifying the mapping, the reader can expose dimensions, profile , level , bit depth, and other configuration to a decoder. That is the next stage of interpretation. The identifier routes the track to a coding family; the configuration describes the actual demands within that family. This is useful in an Emby case where two HEVC files with apparently matching dimensions take different paths. Include the literal codec ID and setup properties in the comparison. It separates a packaging convention from a difference in decoded sample format or decoder resource requirements. See Also Containers and Codecs Codec Support in Containers Media Probing Video Codec Profiles Video Codec Levels and Tiers References MP4 Registration Authority: codec sample-entry codes Matroska codec mappings Microsoft: video FOURCC identifiers ISO/IEC 14496-15:2024: NAL-structured video carriage in ISO BMFF

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: What Is a Media Container? | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: What Is a Media Container? A media container organizes encoded streams and the information needed to find, identify, and time them. Imagine extracting a film's encoded picture bytes and soundtrack bytes into two separate files. To play them together, software still needs to know which decoders to use, when each piece belongs, and how to find the point you ask to watch. A container supplies the organization around those components. The jobs are shared across container families; the arrangement of bytes differs. A file reader typically obtains three kinds of information. Track descriptions identify encoded components and their configuration. Media storage divides or groups their data so it can be read. Timing and navigation connect the groups with positions in the presentation. Subtitle timing beside video and audio Suppose a dialogue subtitle should appear from 12.4 to 14.0 seconds. The file must identify it as a subtitle component, store its text or bitmap, and associate it with those times. The video for that scene and its sound are other components. Reading them from one file does not make their internal encodings the same. The container reader extracts the chosen components and passes them to the appropriate decoder or renderer. The playback system schedules their results against a shared presentation time. That is how several differently encoded sequences become one viewing experience. Additional information can describe the track's language, name a chapter, or carry a font used by the subtitle renderer. These objects do not all behave like timed media: an attached font is a supporting file, while a subtitle event has a presentation interval. A seek asks a different question from ordinary reading Reading sequentially asks for the next data. Seeking to 12 minutes asks where data for that time lives and where decoding can restart. A container's index or sample tables can map time to locations. Codec dependencies then determine whether earlier pictures must also be decoded. MP4 commonly describes stored samples through tables; Matroska groups media in clusters and can index them with Cues. The general job is the same, even though a reader follows different structures. For Emby, this distinction makes a packaging change useful when the selected streams already suit an app but their container reader does not. Remuxing recreates those descriptions and data arrangements in another format. Decoding the picture is a separate job, so the encoded picture can travel unchanged through a new container. See Also Containers and Codecs Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Container Indexes and Seeking References RFC 9559: Matroska media container format

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Codec Support in Containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Codec Support in Containers A valid container and codec combination needs both a defined storage mapping and software that implements it. A muxer needs more than the encoded bytes of a soundtrack. It needs a codec mapping telling it how to describe those bytes in the chosen container. A mapping supplies a codec identifier, a place for decoder configuration, boundaries for encoded units, and any timing or initialization rules particular to that codec. The corresponding reader follows the same rules in reverse. For example, AAC in Matroska has an A_AAC identifier and defined configuration handling. AAC in MP4 has an audio sample entry and its own configuration representation. Copying the sound between them can retain the coded audio while translating those surrounding descriptions. A proposed output with three tracks Suppose a source has H.264 video, AAC sound, and a subtitle track. The destination is WebM. First ask whether the destination defines acceptable mappings for the selected components. WebM's video/audio conventions cover a constrained collection, rather than all the mappings available in Matroska. The H.264/AAC pair cannot simply be relabelled as WebM. At that point there are distinct choices: keep an accommodating container, or convert the encoded components to formats the destination supports. A subtitle that does not fit introduces its own choice to omit, convert, render, or use another package. Those are content and processing decisions, not a failed compression of the movie. Check Evidence that answers it Format mapping exists The container's specification or registration and applicable carriage rules Writer implements it The muxer's documented support for this combination Reader implements it The app or playback framework's container and mapping support Decoder handles the track The codec, configuration, and resource limits available in that path These checks are ordered because each solves a different problem. A registered MP4 code tells developers how a representation is identified; it does not install that representation in an older writer or reader. Why one conversion can combine copying and encoding If a different destination accepts the video mapping but needs another audio format, the video branch can be a copy while the audio branch decodes and re-encodes. Emby can similarly choose a delivery route based on the selected combination rather than one global “supported file” label. A useful before/after record lists the selected components and the treatment of each. It makes an absent commentary track or a changed subtitle visible, even when the main video was copied successfully. See Also Codec Identifiers and FourCC Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Containers and Codecs References Matroska codec mappings WebM container guidelines MP4 Registration Authority: codec sample-entry registrations

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Container Overhead | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Container Overhead Container overhead is the space used to organize and describe media in addition to its encoded picture and sound. A transport packet makes the cost of organization visible. A basic MPEG-TS packet occupies 188 bytes . Its minimum header occupies four, leaving at most 184 for the remaining packet data. minimum header fraction = 4 ÷ 188 = approximately 2.128% To carry a simplified one million payload bytes using full 184-byte payload spaces requires ceil(1,000,000 / 184) = 5,435 packets. Those packets occupy 1,021,780 bytes. Their headers occupy 21,740 bytes, and the final packet has 40 bytes of otherwise unused space in this simplified accounting. This is a worked minimum-header example, not a total overhead prediction for a real TS. Actual adaptation fields, programme tables, packet filling, and other structures change the allocation. Repeated costs and one-time costs Organizational cost How it contributes Track descriptions and codec setup Usually a small amount compared with a long movie Per-packet framing Repeats as more media packets are stored Timing, sample tables, and seek indexes Grows with the media organization Padding or reserved space Allocates space for layout or later updates These bytes are container overhead : information or space needed around the encoded media. The encoded video and soundtrack have their own sizes before this additional packaging is considered. Packaging savings versus removed media Suppose a remux copies the same selected video and audio into a format with different packet grouping and index structures. The whole output can have fewer bytes even though its decoded picture and sound are unchanged. The difference belongs to packaging. Now remove a 384 kb/s soundtrack lasting two hours. That eliminates 345.6 MB of encoded content, not merely overhead. Similarly, removing a large font or cover attachment changes stored resources. To understand a size difference, account for selected components before comparing the organizational cost. Overall file bitrate includes container bytes because it divides total file size by duration. A network transfer adds HTTP, transport, and link costs outside the file. An Emby delivery estimate therefore needs to identify whether a rate describes encoded streams, the whole packaged file, or network traffic. The distinction prevents a shorter remux from being mistaken for a better video encode: fewer organization bytes and a changed representation of the picture are different improvements. See Also File Size and Duration MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems RFC 9559: Matroska data structure

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Types of Media Containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Types of Media Containers Media containers use different structures to serve stored files, continuous transport, and segmented delivery. Where can the reader start, and what information is available then? This question explains many structural differences between media containers. Reading situation Information the format must provide Structural approach A complete stored file Where its samples are and how they are timed Tables or indexes covering stored content A receiver joining a transmission What programmes and streams are currently being sent Repeated identification and timing information A presentation that is still being produced Enough setup and timing for each newly available part Initial setup followed by successive media groups A conventional MP4 can use a complete set of sample descriptions and locations. If its reader can request any file position, it can read that information and then fetch the relevant ranges. Fast-start placement makes initialization convenient for readers obtaining bytes from the beginning. A television receiver has a different starting point. It may join an MPEG transport stream after the programme began. Repeated programme tables let it discover the components currently present, while packet framing lets it find boundaries in a continuing transmission. The reader does not need to wait for a final movie-wide table. Fragmented MP4 supplies track setup followed by descriptions of successive sample groups. The complete duration and future samples need not be known when the beginning is delivered. Matroska similarly carries media through clusters and has specific arrangements for file and live uses . Storage and delivery are two independent choices Recording transport packets onto disk creates a file, but preserves the packets' structure. Sending a stored MP4 over HTTP makes it a network-delivered resource, but preserves its file tables unless it is repackaged. “File format” and “streaming format” are therefore not two exclusive bins. The distinction becomes visible in an Emby session. An original stored container may be read on the server while a different package is written for the app. To understand startup or a seek, identify both the source arrangement and the delivered arrangement. The useful comparison is between concrete tasks: initialize from the available bytes, identify selected tracks, locate a requested time, and handle material that has not finished arriving. Format-specific pages explain the structures used to perform those tasks; this classification connects the structures to the reading situations that motivated them. See Also What Is a Media Container? Container Overhead Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Apple: QuickTime file structure ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems Matroska streaming specification

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Damaged and Incomplete Media Files | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Damaged and Incomplete Media Files A damaged media file can lose container structure, timing, or encoded content, with different consequences for recovery. A recorder stops unexpectedly after writing several gigabytes. The size proves that bytes were written, but leaves a more useful question open: which information had been written when it stopped? A player needs descriptions of the media, a way to locate and time it, and the encoded content itself. Damage to these parts produces different failure patterns. Observation A possible missing part Reader cannot initialize the file Essential track setup or sample descriptions Opening plays, but jumps take a long time Useful navigation entries Repeated failure at one scene Encoded packets or structure around that location Apparent duration exceeds actual playback Final media data is absent although earlier descriptions remain The observations identify which stage to investigate; they do not uniquely name a fault. An unfinished conventional MP4 A writer can accumulate media in mdat and finish the moov description later. If interruption leaves no usable moov, the reader may lack codec setup, sample sizes, locations, or timing needed to interpret the existing data. There can be abundant payload without an ordinary file reader being able to separate it into the right samples. A routine remux needs a reader to supply usable streams first. It cannot simply invent the missing descriptions. Specialized recovery can sometimes use information from the recording setup or another matching file, but the reliability depends on the exact source and writer. Complete earlier groups can survive A fragmented MP4 with usable initialization and complete earlier fragment descriptions can leave those earlier groups interpretable after an interruption. The last partial group may still be unusable. A transport recording or suitable Matroska writing arrangement likewise distributes information differently from a final-table-dependent file. This is a structural reason for differing recovery behaviour. The extension alone does not specify when the particular recorder committed its essential information. Navigation damage and media damage have different limits If a reader can scan intact streams and timing, a new mux can write indexes that were missing or broken. That can repair navigation without changing the encoded movie. If some media bytes are absent or corrupted, a decoder may stop, conceal errors, or recover at a later usable point. Rebuilding an index does not restore the original picture or sound for that gap. A checksum can detect an inconsistency where provided; it does not supply a replacement payload. For a failing Emby item, separate storage access from media interpretation first. A server that cannot read a path has not yet tested the container. If the bytes are accessible, compare initialization results with probing and decoding near the repeatable failure. Unsupported decoding can also fail on an intact file, so the codec and failure stage belong in the evidence. A repair should be evaluated by what it recovered: track setup, full expected duration, the affected scene, and normal seeking. This is more informative than observing that the repaired output now has a recognized extension. See Also Media Probing Container Indexes and Seeking Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References FFmpeg formats: fragmentation and interrupted output Matroska: streaming and incomplete-length segments

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Elementary Streams | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Elementary Streams An elementary stream contains one coded media component before it is combined with other components in a container. After a demuxer opens a movie, the video decoder receives encoded video rather than the entire movie file. That one coded component is an elementary stream . Its codec syntax describes how to reconstruct the media; the outer container supplies additional presentation organization. For AVC/H.264, the elementary data contains units such as sequence configuration, picture configuration, and coded slices. The decoder interprets these to reconstruct pictures and maintain the reference state needed for later pictures. The elementary stream is thus structured data, even without a container around it. Encoded picture, packetized picture, transport packets These three layers are easy to confuse: Layer What is added or described Elementary stream Codec configuration and encoded media syntax Packetized elementary stream, PES MPEG systems framing that can include presentation and decoding timestamps MPEG transport packets Small fixed-size units carrying pieces of PES data or signalling, identified by PID A PES packet can span many transport packets. Neither boundary necessarily marks one independently displayed picture. Demultiplexing transport stream removes the delivery structure to recover the appropriate component and its timing. What happens when the component is extracted? Consider variable-frame-rate video whose first pictures are meant to appear at 0, 40, and 100 milliseconds. An extraction that retains only coded picture data may lose the container's distinction between the 40-millisecond and 60-millisecond gaps. If a later tool assumes evenly spaced 25 fps pictures, it would schedule them at 0, 40, and 80 milliseconds instead. Whether timing survives depends on the codec data, extraction format, and writing tool. The example shows why “the encoded picture bytes were copied” and “the presentation was preserved” are different observations. A container also carries language, track selection, subtitles, and chapters outside the video elementary stream. Extracting video alone omits those components by definition. For a usable Emby library copy, remuxing into a suitable container normally retains more of the presentation than a raw extraction does. Framing can change without picture decoding An AVC unit needs an identifiable boundary. One packaging convention prefixes a start code; another prefixes a byte length. A bitstream filter can translate that framing and move configuration to the required place. It does not need to reconstruct and re-encode each picture to do so. When investigating an extracted source, ask which layer the tool wrote and which information that layer actually retains. That makes a missing timeline or track description an identifiable result of extraction, rather than a mysterious change in the codec. See Also Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Packet Timestamps Streams and Tracks References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems FFmpeg: bitstream filters and framing conversions

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Multiplexing combines media tracks into one organized source, while demultiplexing separates them for playback or processing. A video encoder and an audio encoder produce different sequences. A multiplexer , or muxer, writes those sequences into one package. A demultiplexer , or demuxer, reads the package and routes the data back to its component streams. Illustrative interleaving. These media packets are distinct from network packets, and their sizes and durations need not match. Why alternate the stored data? Suppose a film stored all its video first and all its audio at the end. To play the opening, a reader would need bytes near the beginning for picture and bytes much later for sound. A reader obtaining the file only from front to back would not have the opening audio when it needed it. Interleaving puts portions of related streams near one another. The muxer can write an upcoming group of video and audio, then another group, while preserving each stream's own timestamps. It does not make audio packets and video frames share one fixed duration. It arranges their storage to make nearby media time practical to read. A demuxer parses the surrounding headers and obtains stream identifiers, encoded bytes, timestamps, and configuration. It sends each encoded component to a matching decoder. The file's alternating storage order is therefore turned into several queues, rather than decoded as one undifferentiated sequence. Trace a remux Take an MKV with one video, two soundtracks, and subtitles. A remux selecting video and Audio 1 follows this sequence: Read Matroska track descriptions and blocks. Identify the selected tracks and retain their encoded data and timing. Translate configuration, timestamp units, or framing where the destination requires it. Write the new container's descriptions, sample storage, and navigation information. Audio 2 is absent because of selection, not because the main picture was recompressed. A chapter list or font attachment needs its own preservation decision because it is not one of the two selected encoded streams. Stream copy skips picture reconstruction and new video encoding. It can still alter bytes around the encoded units. For example, AVC units may be stored with start codes in one arrangement and length prefixes in another; translating those delimiters leaves the encoded picture information intact. For an Emby Direct Stream route, this is how compatible video can be delivered in a package the app expects. If audio is also converted, its branch passes through an audio decoder and encoder while the video branch remains a copy. An effective comparison lists the intended output components first, then verifies their content and timing. It checks what the muxer was asked to write rather than assuming that an unchanged video codec implies an unchanged whole presentation. See Also Streams and Tracks Elementary Streams Codec Support in Containers References FFmpeg: processing flow and stream copy

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Overview: Timing and navigation | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Overview: Timing and navigation Container timing and navigation connect packet clocks, playback positions, seek indexes and chapter locations. A position in a media file is not automatically a position on the playback clock. Timestamps and time bases describe when data belong; indexes describe how to find a useful place to resume decoding, and chapters attach named navigation points. Together these topics explain how a player reaches the requested moment rather than merely opening a byte offset. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Packet timestamps Packet timestamps tell a playback pipeline when encoded media must be decoded and when the resulting content should be presented. Time bases A time base defines the duration of one timestamp tick so integer media timestamps can be converted to real time. Container indexes and seeking A container index connects points on the media timeline to file locations so a player can seek efficiently. Chapter markers Chapter markers give named navigation points within a media presentation without splitting it into separate files. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Chapter Markers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Chapter Markers Chapter markers give named navigation points within a media presentation without splitting it into separate files. A concert recording can remain one continuous video while offering a menu of songs. Chapter markers attach names to positions in its timeline. Illustrative chapter Stored position in seconds Opening — 00:00 0 The journey — 12:40 760 Finale — 48:15 2,895 Choosing The journey asks the player to seek to 760 seconds. The ordinary chapter entry does not create a separate clip or make that picture independently decodable; normal index lookup and decoder restart still apply. The name, start time, and any end time are chapter information. A preview image is another object. A player can generate it from the picture near a chapter position or obtain navigation previews through a separate process. Storing a chapter title does not store the corresponding image. An edit moves the landmarks If a new version removes the first 30 seconds before The journey, its new position becomes 730 seconds, or 12:10. Copying the old 12:40 marker unchanged would land 30 seconds late. Chapter preservation after an edit therefore involves mapping positions to the new timeline, not just copying chapter names. A simple remux that preserves the timeline can retain those positions more directly. Inspecting the chapter list establishes which entries the output actually contains. Matroska can also define ordered editions that choose ranges and alter the sequence being played. That is a different use of chapter structures. For an ordinary scene or song list, the useful model is a named position in one fixed presentation.
