See Also Container Indexes and Seeking Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe References Matroska chapter specification

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Container Indexes and Seeking | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Container Indexes and Seeking A container index connects points on the media timeline to file locations so a player can seek efficiently. Move the playback slider to a scene and the player receives a time, not a file address. Seeking must turn that time into readable bytes and then rebuild enough decoding state to produce the requested picture. Conceptual seek. Random-access positions and index detail depend on the actual codec and container. A target at 10 minutes and 3 seconds Suppose a simplified index records usable video restart positions at 600 and 605 seconds. The viewer requests 603 seconds. The reader chooses the earlier suitable position, 600 seconds, and obtains its location in the file. In Matroska, a Cue can identify a timestamp, track, and location within the segment, typically referring to a cluster holding a video random-access point. The reader follows that reference, parses the cluster's blocks, and supplies the relevant encoded data to the decoder. It then decodes forward. Pictures before the requested moment can be reconstructed without being shown; they establish the reference state required by later pictures. Once the requested time is reached, normal presentation resumes. Part of the seek Question answered Timeline lookup Which earlier usable entry covers 603 s? Container lookup Where are its bytes and selected tracks? Input read Can the storage or server deliver those bytes promptly? Decoder restart What references or preroll must be reconstructed? Output scheduling Which decoded picture and audio samples should first be presented? At an illustrative 25 fps, three seconds contain 75 picture intervals. This gives a sense of the forward-decoding work in the example; a real restart depends on dependencies and preroll, not just multiplying the requested gap by frame rate. What an index changes Without suitable entries, a reader may scan media to discover timestamps and restart positions. An index avoids much of that search. It is navigation information about the media, so adding it can improve a slow seek without recompressing the pictures. Chapters answer a different question: they give names to times. “Scene 4 starts at 603 seconds” still needs this byte lookup and decoding process. An HTTP reader can request a byte range corresponding to the seek rather than fetch the whole prefix. A server transcoding for an Emby app may instead restart source reading and conversion, then generate new output around the desired time. These paths put the same time request through different combinations of storage, network, and processing. Compare where the delay occurs. A reader spending time scanning a source has a different problem from one that locates the bytes quickly but cannot fetch or decode them fast enough. A readable file with missing navigation can often be remuxed to create new indexes. An unreadable or damaged payload needs a response directed at the media itself. See Also Packet Timestamps Chapter Markers Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Matroska: cues and seeking recommendations Matroska: random access points

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Packet Timestamps | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Packet Timestamps Packet timestamps tell a playback pipeline when encoded media must be decoded and when the resulting content should be presented. A decoder and a viewer can need pictures in different orders. If picture B predicts from C, the decoder must reconstruct C before B even when the viewer should see B first. Decoding timestamps (DTS) and presentation timestamps (PTS) describe these two schedules. Follow this simplified three-picture group. Each displayed picture lasts 40 milliseconds, and C is a reference used to decode B. Packet read in decode order DTS PTS Decoder action A 0 ms 40 ms Reconstruct A and retain it C 40 ms 120 ms Reconstruct C, retain it, and defer its display B 80 ms 80 ms Reconstruct B using its references The viewer's order is A at 40 ms, B at 80 ms, then C at 120 ms. The compressed packet order is A, C, B. The presentation offset in this invented example gives the decoder time to build the required reference state; it is not a universal delay used by a codec. The queue is part of the mechanism At decode time 40 ms, C is ready but does not yet belong on screen. It waits in a decoded-picture buffer. At 80 ms, B is reconstructed and can be presented before the retained C. The decoder must keep pictures for two potentially different reasons: later prediction and later presentation. Sorting the compressed packets by PTS would send A, B, C to the decoder. B would then arrive before its reference C. The output schedule is a reason to reorder reconstructed pictures, not a reason to reorder dependent compressed input blindly. For video with no such reordering, DTS and PTS may coincide. Audio also uses presentation timing, while its packet duration tells the scheduler how much decoded sound that packet contributes. Comparing picture and sound A video PTS and an audio PTS can be integers on different time bases . On a 90,000-tick scale, 90,000 means one second; on a 48,000-tick scale, 48,000 means the same moment. Synchronization compares the converted time, not the raw numbers. If sound is consistently 200 ms late in an Emby session, an offset is one possibility. If the difference grows through the programme, durations, resampling, or an incorrectly interpreted clock can be involved. Those are different timing patterns, so the symptom guides which relationships to inspect. Containers need not store two literal fields on every packet. They can describe decode durations and composition offsets from which a reader derives the schedules. Inspection tools report the resulting timestamps through their own packet model. Reading a warning in context PTS can move backwards in the file's decode order, as 120 → 80 ms does here. That is normal reordering. A DTS moving backwards where the receiving muxer expects an ordered decode timeline has another meaning. Timestamp resets in a continuing recording, missing durations, and discontinuities can also need explicit handling. A useful packet inspection keeps DTS, PTS, duration, time base, stream identity, and the playback symptom together. Replacing all times with consecutive values would erase the information that makes this example display correctly. See Also Time Bases Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Container Indexes and Seeking References FFmpeg: AVPacket timestamp definitions Apple: QuickTime time-to-sample and composition timing

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Time Bases | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Time Bases A time base defines the duration of one timestamp tick so integer media timestamps can be converted to real time. A timestamp is a counter. Its time base tells you how much time one count represents: seconds = timestamp × time base For a time base of 1/90,000 second per tick, a counter value of 45,000 represents half a second. An audio clock counting at 48,000 ticks per second uses 24,000 for that same moment. Tick duration Counter Converted time 1/90,000 s 45,000 0.5 s 1/48,000 s 24,000 0.5 s 1/1,000 s 500 0.5 s Frame rate chooses the gaps, not the counter's units At 25 frames per second, consecutive evenly spaced pictures are 0.04 seconds apart. On a 90,000-tick clock they can advance by 3,600 ticks each. The clock's time base remains 1/90,000; the picture rate is 25 fps. At 30,000/1,001 fps, the gap on that clock is 90,000 × 1,001 / 30,000 = 3,003 ticks. Keeping the rational values avoids treating the rounded display label 29.97 as the exact rate. Variable-frame-rate pictures can use different gaps on one unchanged clock. A counter that advances irregularly is therefore not itself evidence that the time base changed. Rescaling into another container Suppose an audio component advances by 1,024 samples on a 48 kHz clock. Its packet starts are: Source ticks Exact start in milliseconds Nearest millisecond counter 0 0 0 1,024 21.333… 21 2,048 42.666… 43 3,072 64 64 Rescaling preserves the represented time as closely as the new integer units permit. The resulting millisecond gaps are 21, 22, and 21, not one fixed rounded gap. Multiplying a rounded 21 ms duration three times would give 63 ms instead of the correct 64 ms. This is why rescaling absolute positions or using careful rational accumulation matters. The rounding error is bounded by the destination's resolution; it should not accumulate as if every packet independently shortened the programme. A finer destination clock can represent more of the original positions exactly. ffprobe exposes both raw counters and converted fields such as pts_time. For an Emby timing investigation, the converted positions show how audio and video align. Keep any start offsets as part of that comparison: a counter's zero is a convention, while the relative schedules determine synchronization. See Also Packet Timestamps Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe References FFmpeg: stream time-base definitions

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Overview: Track and programme descriptions | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Overview: Track and programme descriptions Track and programme descriptions identify available content and provide context for selecting or routing it. Language labels and default flags help describe a track, while MPEG transport-stream tables identify programmes and their component streams. That information guides interpretation and selection without replacing the player's own policy. This branch is useful when the file's available tracks differ from the language or programme the viewer expected. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Track language metadata Track language metadata identifies the language of an audio or subtitle track for display and selection. Default track flags Default track flags provide selection hints that players interpret alongside language, accessibility, and user preferences. MPEG-TS program tables (PAT and PMT) PAT and PMT describe which transport-stream packets belong to each programme and what media those packets carry. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Default Track Flags | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Default Track Flags Default track flags provide selection hints that players interpret alongside language, accessibility, and user preferences. Consider these audio descriptions in an MKV: Track Language Role Default eligibility Main soundtrack English Main programme Yes Translation German Main programme Yes Director commentary English Commentary No The default flag helps a player form an automatic choice. In Matroska it describes eligibility for default selection; it is not a universal command to play one numbered track. More than one language can be eligible. A viewer preferring German can therefore have a suitable default candidate even while English is also marked default. The player combines the file's information with its own selection policy, user preferences, accessibility choices, and any remembered or manual choice. Why “default English” can still be the wrong choice Two English tracks satisfy the language preference in the example, but their roles differ. The commentary flag, title, and default eligibility help distinguish them. Marking commentary default just because its language is English blurs the intended automatic choice. A title containing “Default” is plain descriptive text. It does not set the structured flag. Likewise, removing a default flag does not remove the track: a user may still select the component explicitly. Subtitles use another kind of hint Default and forced subtitle flags answer different questions. A default subtitle may contain the full dialogue. A forced track commonly supplies text needed with the chosen soundtrack, such as a sign or a brief exchange in another language. The forced designation describes the intended selection role; it does not inspect or shorten the subtitle contents. If a full-dialogue track is marked forced, all its events remain in the track. A player following that hint may show far more text than the author intended. For an Emby selection comparison, start with the actual track combination: effective language, main versus commentary/accessibility role, default eligibility, and subtitle intent. Then compare the user's relevant preferences and whether the session has retained a manual selection. This explains a difference between two apps without assuming either has simply ignored the file. Correcting these descriptions normally edits the container metadata. The encoded soundtrack and subtitle events can remain the same; what changes is the information automatic selection receives. See Also Track Language Metadata Streams and Tracks References RFC 9559: Matroska track flags and default selection Matroska element specification: track flags

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT PAT and PMT describe which transport-stream packets belong to each programme and what media those packets carry. Join a television transport stream halfway through a programme. Packets are arriving with many different PIDs , or packet identifiers. The receiver needs to learn which identifiers belong to the selected service before it can choose video and sound. The discovery route begins with the Program Association Table (PAT) on PID 0. It maps programme numbers to the PIDs carrying their Program Map Tables (PMTs) . Each PMT then describes that programme's components. Programme 7 and the nonzero PIDs are an example. The PAT's PID 0 is defined by MPEG systems. Programme discovery: PAT, PMT, and component PIDs Filter packets on PID 0 and assemble the PAT section. Find programme 7's entry: its PMT is carried on PID 0x0100. Filter that PID and assemble the PMT. Read its components: video at PID 0x0101 and audio at PID 0x0102 in this example. Use the stream descriptions and descriptors to route those components to the appropriate decoders. The transport headers identify packets, while tables describe what their identifiers mean. A PID is an address within this multiplex, not a globally meaningful name for an audio codec. Another recording can use different PIDs for the same kinds of component. A table section can occupy more than one transport packet. The receiver assembles it using section framing and can check its CRC before accepting the description. Repetition lets receivers discover the structure after joining, and table versions distinguish updated descriptions from repeats of the same information. A clock and several component timelines The PMT also names the PID carrying the programme clock reference (PCR) . Here it is the video PID. PCR observations help a receiver relate packet delivery to the programme's clock; PTS and DTS then schedule presentation and decoding of the media against timing derived from that system. PCR need not be on a separate stream with its own pictures or sound. It can be carried in an adaptation field of packets that also belong to a media PID. That separates the clock's role from the audio/video payload's role. When the programme changes A service can add an audio component or change its assigned PID. A receiver observing the updated PMT can adjust the set of streams it follows. A short examination containing an old table, or not enough repeated signalling, can give an incomplete view. This is useful when inspecting a television recording for Emby. A transport file can preserve multiple programme groupings, and the first video found is not automatically the wanted service. Programme-aware inspection follows the same hierarchy: programme identity, its component PIDs and descriptions, then the properties of the selected media. The programme number is a systems grouping. The film or episode name displayed in a library is descriptive information at another layer. See Also Streams and Tracks Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Media Probing References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems FFmpeg n8.1 MPEG-TS demuxer: PAT and PMT parsing

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Track Language Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Track Language Metadata Track language metadata identifies the language of an audio or subtitle track for display and selection. An Emby audio selector can offer two tracks called English even though one is the main film and the other is commentary. Language metadata answers which language a track represents; it does not describe the track's role. Value encountered in a report Interpretation eng English in ISO 639-2 deu or ger German terminology/bibliographic ISO 639-2 codes pt-BR Portuguese with the Brazil region subtag in BCP 47 und Undetermined language A machine-readable tag helps selection software compare a component with the viewer's preferences. A human-readable title supplies extra description such as “Commentary” or “Stereo.” Both can appear together, and neither needs to be copied into the other. Where regional detail fits A BCP 47 tag can identify language and optional attributes such as script or region. The hyphen separates subtags; pt-BR is not a new unrelated language code. This richer form is useful where a distinction between regional variants matters to the viewer. Containers use different language fields. Matroska has a legacy field and a LanguageIETF field for BCP 47. When LanguageIETF is present, it takes precedence under the specification. Updating only the legacy code can thus leave the effective language unchanged for a reader using the newer field. That gives a concrete explanation for a misleading edit: the track title now says “English,” its old field says eng, but its LanguageIETF field still identifies German. The visible title and the machine-readable effective tag describe different things. Comparing two selection results For each relevant audio or subtitle track, collect its effective language, title, and role/selection flags . Then compare them with the user's audio and subtitle preferences. This isolates a language mismatch from a commentary-role mismatch. Subtitles describe the language of their displayed text, which can differ from the soundtrack. The library's original-language metadata describes the work as a whole; it need not match every available translation. A metadata edit can correct the description without decoding the sound. It does not translate the recorded dialogue. Reading the fields after the edit establishes that the intended description, including any higher-precedence field, is now the one the software receives. See Also Streams and Tracks Default Track Flags Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo References Library of Congress: ISO 639-2 language codes RFC 5646: language tags Matroska: language-code fields and precedence

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Overview: Bitrate and file size | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Overview: Bitrate and file size Bitrate, duration and data units connect the amount of encoded media to its storage and delivery requirements. Bitrate is a rate, while file size is an accumulated amount. Duration connects them, but a varying rate means that one moment's demand need not match the whole file's average. These pages make the units and observation intervals explicit, which helps when estimating storage or comparing a media rate with network capacity. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Bitrate Bitrate measures how much encoded data represents each second of media. Bitrate variation Bitrate variation describes how the amount of encoded data changes across the running time of a media source. Digital media data units Bits, bytes, and decimal or binary prefixes express different amounts of media data. File size and duration Average bitrate and running time provide a practical estimate of a media file's size. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Bitrate Bitrate measures how much encoded data represents each second of media. Bitrate measures data against media time. At an average rate of 10 Mb/s, ten seconds of content accounts for 100 million bits, or 12.5 MB. It need not take ten seconds to download those bytes. That distinction gives a transfer graph and a media report different meanings. A connection delivering 25 Mb/s can fetch ten seconds of this simplified content in four seconds. The player can then consume those stored bytes over the following ten seconds. Reported rate The data being counted Video bitrate Encoded picture data Audio bitrate One encoded soundtrack Overall file bitrate All file bytes divided by presentation duration Transfer rate Data arriving per second of real elapsed time What is included in a movie's rate? Imagine a file with 8 Mb/s of video and two 384 kb/s soundtracks. The streams total 8.768 Mb/s, before container structures and other content. A presentation that sends only the selected soundtrack has a different stream total: 8.384 Mb/s. Whether the complete file or a selected set of tracks crosses a connection depends on delivery. This is why an Emby source's overall rate and its delivered stream rate can legitimately differ even without changing the video encoding. Using an average For storage, multiply the average by duration and divide by eight to change bits to bytes. Ten minutes at an exact overall average of 10 Mb/s occupies 750 MB. File size and duration develops this calculation for a complete file. For playback, the average hides changes through the presentation . Pictures with more encoded data consume the buffer faster than simpler pictures. A rate measured over one second and a rate measured across the whole film summarize different intervals. Bitrate is consequently a useful data budget, not a measurement of resolution or a quality score. To judge the encoding, compare the reconstructed pictures or sound. To judge delivery, compare data demand over time with arrival and available buffering. See Also Bitrate Variation File Size and Duration Digital Media Data Units References FFmpeg: overall bitrate and stream information NIST: metric prefixes

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Bitrate Variation | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Bitrate Variation Bitrate variation describes how the amount of encoded data changes across the running time of a media source. A film's encoded data can be unevenly distributed. In this constructed example, each interval represents four seconds of media: Encoded media rates in four-second intervals. These are illustrative allocations, not network measurements. The four intervals contain 24, 48, 96, and 24 megabits. That is 192 megabits over 16 seconds, giving a whole-example average of 12 Mb/s. The same average could describe a much flatter allocation. How the buffer absorbs a bitrate burst Now give the connection an uninterrupted 18 Mb/s arrival rate and start the simplified calculation with an empty playback buffer. Assume playback consumes data at each interval's listed rate and the reader can fetch ahead. Interval Media consumes Connection supplies Change in buffered data Buffer after interval First four seconds 24 Mb 72 Mb +48 Mb 48 Mb Next four seconds 48 Mb 72 Mb +24 Mb 72 Mb Demanding four seconds 96 Mb 72 Mb −24 Mb 48 Mb Final four seconds 24 Mb 72 Mb +48 Mb 96 Mb The demanding interval uses data faster than it arrives, but it finishes successfully because earlier intervals stored enough data. The 24-megabit deficit consumes 3 MB of that reserve. This calculation omits finite buffer capacity, headers, request delays, and variable throughput. Its purpose is to expose the causal relationship: arrival minus consumption changes the reserve . In a real finite file the reader also stops requesting once it has obtained the remaining content; the final row is a notional continuing-arrival calculation. Seeking changes the starting state Start directly at the demanding interval instead. Without its earlier reserve, the same 18 Mb/s connection cannot supply the whole 24 Mb/s interval in real time. The player must accumulate data before presenting it, obtain it faster, or use a lower-demand output. That explains why a movie can play smoothly from the beginning yet pause after a seek, or buffer around the same busy scene in an Emby session. The important quantities are the delivered media's demand, available arrival rate, and reserve at that moment. A peak must also have a measurement interval. One unusually large frame, four demanding seconds, and a ten-minute high-rate section put different demands on a buffer. A single peak number loses that duration information. See Also Bitrate File Size and Duration References FFmpeg: encoder bitrate and rate-control options

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Digital Media Data Units | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Digital Media Data Units Bits, bytes, and decimal or binary prefixes express different amounts of media data. Symbol Meaning Typical media use b bit Network and media bitrate B byte: eight bits File size and transfer amount /s per second A rate rather than an amount To convert bits per second to bytes per second, divide by eight. 100 Mb/s ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB/s , before transmission overhead. Look up the prefix Unit Number of bytes MB, megabyte 1,000,000 MiB, mebibyte 1,048,576 GB, gigabyte 1,000,000,000 GiB, gibibyte 1,073,741,824 Decimal prefixes use powers of 1,000; binary prefixes use powers of 1,024. One billion bytes is 1 GB , or approximately 0.931 GiB . Both describe the same file length. Convert a streaming rate into an amount At an average of 8 Mb/s , the stream uses approximately 1 MB each second , or 60 MB each minute . For a longer interval, multiply the byte rate by the number of seconds. Bitrate and file size versus duration develop that calculation. See Also Bitrate File Size and Duration References NIST: prefixes for binary multiples NIST: SI prefixes and their use

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: File Size and Duration | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: File Size and Duration Average bitrate and running time provide a practical estimate of a media file's size. Start with the streams you intend to store. For a two-hour film, suppose video averages 10 Mb/s and each of two soundtracks averages 384 kb/s. bytes = average bits per second × seconds ÷ 8 There are 7,200 seconds in two hours. The video therefore contributes 10,000,000 × 7,200 ÷ 8 = 9,000,000,000 bytes. Stored component Average rate Bytes over two hours Decimal GB Video 10 Mb/s 9,000,000,000 9.0000 Audio 1 384 kb/s 345,600,000 0.3456 Audio 2 384 kb/s 345,600,000 0.3456 Streams combined 10.768 Mb/s 9,691,200,000 9.6912 Container structures, subtitles, attachments, and tags add their own bytes. An embedded image adds storage without adding running time. The stream sum estimates the largest contributions; an overall file average already includes all the stored bytes used in its calculation. Work the relationship in either direction If a finished two-hour file is exactly 9.8 billion bytes, its overall average is: 9,800,000,000 × 8 ÷ 7,200 = approximately 10.889 Mb/s A file half as long at that same size has twice the overall average. A larger size can thus mean a longer presentation, more tracks, or more data per second; the division tells you which of these quantities you are comparing. Decimal and binary units change the displayed number, not the underlying bytes. The 9.6912 GB stream sum is about 9.026 GiB. Always establish the units before comparing an encoder estimate with a file browser's display. When the calculation exposes another problem Some inspection tools obtain overall bitrate by dividing file size by reported duration. If a two-hour source is mistakenly reported as one hour, that derived bitrate doubles. Repeating the same calculation cannot independently confirm either value. That is useful when Emby or an inspection report shows a surprising rate. Compare the duration evidence with the expected presentation and track timestamps. A damaged or incomplete file can have intact headers yet a different amount of actual media. For planning a target size, choose the duration and complete data budget first. For examining an existing file, use the measured size and a trustworthy duration. Local variation affects delivery and buffering, while this calculation accounts for the total. See Also Bitrate Digital Media Data Units Container Overhead References FFmpeg: duration and total bitrate fields

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Contai.title: Containers and Codecs | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Contai.keywords: Containers and Codecs A container organizes media streams, while codecs define how their picture and sound data are encoded. A file ending in MP4 may carry H.264 video with AAC sound. Another MP4 may carry HEVC with different audio. To understand the difference, follow the data through the player rather than treating the file as one indivisible format. Stage What enters What comes out Container reader, or demuxer Bytes from the MP4 Encoded packets belonging to separate tracks Video decoder Encoded video and its configuration Reconstructed pictures Audio decoder Encoded audio and its configuration Sound samples Playback scheduling Pictures, samples, and timestamps Synchronized presentation The container defines the package: how tracks are described, how their data is stored, and how their time and location are represented. A codec defines an encoded representation and the corresponding decoding rules. H.264 and AAC do different jobs inside the same package. Changing the package Suppose the video already suits the receiving app, but the app expects different packaging. A remux reads the input container and writes a new one. It copies encoded video packets through this route: input container → demuxer → encoded video → muxer → output container There is no picture reconstruction in that route. The output file's bytes differ because its headers, indexes, timestamps, or framing differ, while the encoded picture information can be preserved. Codec configuration may have to move from one header convention to another. That is still distinct from decoding and recompressing the pictures. The destination must have a defined way to store the chosen tracks. An audio track may fit while a subtitle format does not, so preserving the movie's picture is only one part of preserving its contents. Changing the representation If the app needs a different video codec, the route becomes: encoded video → decoder → pictures → encoder → new encoded video The encoder makes new coding decisions from reconstructed pictures. This costs processing time and, with lossy settings, introduces another compression generation. Resizing or filtering also acts on these decoded pictures. An audio-only conversion follows the same idea for sound while allowing video packets to be copied. The result can therefore involve transcoding without re-encoding the picture. That distinction explains why some Emby playback conversions need little video processing and others need substantial decoding, filtering, and encoding. For a concrete source, write down the selected tracks separately: container, video codec, audio codec, and subtitles. Then compare those with the delivered stream. The question becomes which stage changed, rather than whether the file was broadly called “converted.” See Also What Is a Media Container? Media File Extensions Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References FFmpeg: processing flow and stream copy

articles/media-files/fundamentals/index..title: Overview: Media file fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/index..keywords: Overview: Media file fundamentals Media-file fundamentals distinguish the stored object, its encoded tracks and the terms used to describe its contents. Before investigating playback, it helps to separate three questions: what kind of file is this, what does it carry, and how much data does it require? Container names, codec names and track descriptions answer different parts of that description. The topics here establish those distinctions, including the units behind bitrate and size and the meaning of lossy or lossless compression. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is a media file? A media file stores the data and instructions a player needs to reproduce recorded sound, pictures, or both. Containers and codecs A container organizes media streams, while codecs define how their picture and sound data are encoded. Streams and tracks A media track is a separately described sequence of video, audio, subtitles, or other data within a media source. Media file extensions A media file extension is a naming convention that hints at the file's format without proving its contents. Media MIME types A media MIME type labels the kind of content delivered by a protocol such as HTTP. Bitrate and file size Bitrate, duration and data units connect the amount of encoded media to its storage and delivery requirements. Lossy and lossless compression Lossless compression preserves the encoded input exactly, while lossy compression permits changes to reduce the amount of data. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: What Is a Media File? | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: What Is a Media File? A media file stores the data and instructions a player needs to reproduce recorded sound, pictures, or both. Press Play on a film and several things begin together: the first picture appears, sound starts, and subtitles arrive at their appointed moments. A media file stores the material for those events and enough information to organize them. An illustrative collection of components, rather than a byte map of a particular format. Follow one moment in that film. The file reader locates some encoded video data, identifies its codec, and passes it to a decoder. The decoder reconstructs a picture. Separately, an audio decoder produces samples for the same part of the soundtrack. Timestamps tell the playback system when to present each result. Reading bytes, reconstructing media, and scheduling playback are different jobs. The container supplies the organization around the encoded content. It can describe several tracks , so choosing a commentary soundtrack changes the audio sequence without duplicating the picture. A subtitle track supplies timed text or images; chapter information supplies named positions within the presentation. Information for playing and information about the film Consider an item in an Emby library titled Example Film . A poster and a plot summary help you choose it. A video resolution of 1920 × 1080, an English audio tag, and a duration of 01:42:00 help software handle the source. These descriptions answer different questions. Information Describes Where it can come from Encoded picture and sound The recorded media The file's payload Codec, timing, and track properties How to reproduce it Headers, container structures, or examination of the data Film title, cast, and synopsis The work represented by the file Embedded tags, local metadata, or a library provider A library can identify the work correctly while the file's audio language is missing. Conversely, a technically readable file can have no useful film title at all. This is why media probing and library identification are separate operations. A file also separates stored order from viewing order. It may alternate chunks of audio and video rather than keep one uninterrupted run of each. The reader extracts those pieces and their timing; the player assembles the experience. When you inspect a file, its track list and timestamps reveal more of that organization than its filename does. See Also Containers and Codecs Streams and Tracks Media Probing How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures References Matroska: basic container concepts

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Media File Extensions | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Media File Extensions A media file extension is a naming convention that hints at the file's format without proving its contents. A file extension is the part of a name after its final dot. It helps software choose an application or decide which files to examine. Some endings describe containers, while others conventionally identify one audio coding family. Filename Usual interpretation Movie.mkv Matroska video container Recording.mov QuickTime container Song.mp3 MPEG Layer III audio file Movie.strm A text pointer to another media source Consider a downloaded film named Movie.mp4. Changing that name to Movie.mkv alters the directory entry; its internal headers and media bytes stay the same. A real container conversion reads those bytes and writes new packaging. The two operations affect different parts of the stored item. If the ending disagrees with inspection , use the detected format to establish what the file actually is. Some readers examine its signature and open it despite the name; filename-based discovery can make a different choice. A second naming issue arises when extensions are hidden. A text editor may save Movie.strm.txt while the file browser displays Movie.strm. The full filename reveals why it is treated as ordinary text rather than a media pointer . Reading the internal format and viewing the full name resolve different kinds of naming mistake. See Also Containers and Codecs Media MIME Types Media Probing References Apple: QuickTime file format introduction

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Lossy and Lossless Compression | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Lossy and Lossless Compression Lossless compression preserves the encoded input exactly, while lossy compression permits changes to reduce the amount of data. Take four invented digital sample values: 100, 101, 101, 100 One way to describe them is to store the first value and then the differences: 100, +1, 0, −1 . Reconstruction adds each difference to the previous result: 100, then 101, then 101, then 100. Nothing was approximated. A compressor can exploit such predictable differences to use fewer bits, while retaining a reversible description. That is the essential bargain of lossless compression . The exact representation differs among codecs, but a correct decoder recovers the encoder's input samples. FLAC , for example, predicts audio samples and codes the remaining differences without discarding them. What changes when approximation is allowed? Now round the invented inputs to the nearest multiple of four: Input Rounded output Output minus input 100 100 0 101 100 −1 101 100 −1 100 100 0 The resulting constant sequence may be easier to describe. However, decoding it yields four values of 100. It gives no way to determine that the middle two were originally 101. Several possible inputs have become the same output. This is a simplified example of lossy approximation, not the full operation of an audio or video codec. Real codecs apply coding tools, predictions, transforms, and models that decide which changes are worthwhile. The video compression walkthrough follows those stages. A changed numerical value may have little visible or audible effect, so lossiness and an obvious defect are different judgments. Locate the lossless boundary in a conversion Consider this route: MP3 file → MP3 decoder → PCM samples → FLAC encoder → FLAC decoder The two PCM sequences surrounding FLAC can match exactly. They are still the samples reconstructed from MP3, including changes made when that MP3 was encoded. A lossless stage preserves its own input; it cannot infer an earlier input that no longer exists. A resampler, a volume adjustment, or a pixel-format conversion before the lossless encoder introduces another boundary. To test the lossless codec itself, compare the samples immediately before encoding with those immediately after decoding in the same representation. Comparing entire files also includes containers and tags, which may differ even with identical samples. For an Emby collection, copying the encoded source or remuxing its tracks can preserve an existing lossy representation without adding a new coding generation. Re-encoding reconstructs samples and produces a new encoded representation; a lossless encoding stage can retain their values exactly. The useful question is which representation you want to preserve and at which stage you are comparing it. See Also Containers and Codecs Bitrate How Video Compression Works References RFC 9639: FLAC format and compression definitions

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Media MIME Types | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Media MIME Types A media MIME type labels the kind of content delivered by a protocol such as HTTP. When a player fetches a resource over HTTP, the response can include: Content-Type: video/mp4 This is a media type , commonly called a MIME type. It describes the response body. The URL may have no extension, and the bytes may be delivered dynamically, so the HTTP label has a job independent of the filename. The first part, video, is the broad category; mp4 is the subtype. A parameter adds information whose meaning is defined for that type. Media type What the response represents video/mp4 MP4-family content with video audio/mp4 MP4-family audio without video audio/mpeg MPEG audio application/vnd.apple.mpegurl An HLS playlist describing other resources From a playlist to media bytes A streaming player can first receive an HLS playlist with the playlist media type. It reads that text to find media locations. A later request obtains an actual media segment whose type describes its own container. These responses participate in one presentation but contain different kinds of data. Emby can similarly deliver a package different from the library file. The Content-Type belongs to the response being sent, so it should describe that output rather than simply repeat the source's extension. Making the track description more precise RFC 6381 defines a codecs parameter for supported media types. An MP4 type can, for example, be accompanied by codecs="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2" . The first token describes an AVC track: the hexadecimal profile value 64 means 100, the compatibility byte is 00, and the level value 28 means 40. The second identifies MPEG-4 audio object type 2, AAC-LC. These are declarations about encoded tracks within the package. That precision helps a browser or playback framework choose a decoding path before reading all the media. The byte contents still need to agree with the declaration. Merely changing the label cannot change an AVC profile or turn one audio codec into another. A useful HTTP investigation follows the resource sequence: which request returned the playlist, which returned media, which Content-Type each response supplied, and which codecs the actual tracks use. It distinguishes a wrong label from wrong media and from a reader that lacks the required decoding path. See Also Media File Extensions Containers and Codecs References RFC 6838: media type specifications and registration RFC 6381: codecs and profiles parameters IANA media types registry

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Streams and Tracks | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Streams and Tracks A media track is a separately described sequence of video, audio, subtitles, or other data within a media source. Here is a possible track list for one film: Track in the file Contents Selected for this viewing? Video The film's picture Yes Audio 1 English 5.1 soundtrack Yes Audio 2 German stereo soundtrack No Audio 3 English commentary No Subtitle 1 English dialogue subtitles Optional Each track is a separately described sequence. The picture can be paired with any of the soundtracks because their timestamps refer to the same presentation. Switching languages chooses another audio sequence; it does not require another copy of the video. Stream often means the same component when discussing a file. It emphasizes the sequence of packets extracted from that track. A “network stream” can instead mean the whole delivery, including a container holding several such components. What is inside an audio track? The English 5.1 track contains six audio channels : five main speaker roles and a low-frequency effects channel. A channel describes one component of the sound being decoded together. It is not a separately selectable soundtrack. At a sample rate of 48 kHz, one second of decoded 5.1 audio contains 48,000 sample values for each of six channels. The decoder produces those channels together from one encoded audio track. Selecting commentary changes tracks; changing the receiver's speaker layout changes what happens to channels within the selected track. Selection changes the work, even with the same picture An Emby session playing Audio 1 may use a different audio output path from one playing Audio 2. The German stereo track may already suit the output, while a surround track might need downmixing or a codec conversion. The video sequence remains the same. Subtitle selection is another independent choice. A timed text sequence can be rendered by the app; a selected subtitle that the route cannot render separately may need to be incorporated into the video. The complete session therefore depends on the chosen combination, not every track stored in the source. A track description normally includes a codec, technical properties, language, and sometimes a title and selection flags . “English commentary” in a title is separate from the language code . Those fields help distinguish two soundtracks with the same language. When comparing a remux with its original, match tracks by these descriptions. Inspection tools may renumber the output after a track is removed, so “track 2” can refer to different content in the two files. See Also What Is a Media File? Track Language Metadata Default Track Flags Understanding Audio in Media References FFmpeg: stream descriptions

articles/media-files/index.html.title: Overview: Media files and containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/index.html.keywords: Overview: Media files and containers Media files combine encoded tracks with container structures that organize playback, timing and metadata. A filename such as Film.mkv identifies a kind of packaging; it does not tell you every codec, language or subtitle track inside. A useful description of the file separates its container, its streams and the information that lets a player find and present them. The fundamentals establish that vocabulary. Container and packaging topics explain the structures behind seeking, delivery and alternate tracks, while inspection tools reveal what a particular file actually contains. Playlists and references cover the related case where a small file points to media elsewhere. These distinctions help explain why two similarly named files can take different playback paths in Emby. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media file fundamentals Media-file fundamentals distinguish the stored object, its encoded tracks and the terms used to describe its contents. Container structure Container structures organize encoded streams, timing, track information and navigation within a media file. Common containers Media container families define different ways to package tracks, metadata and navigation information. File packaging details Media packaging details shape how a container stores, exposes or references the content needed for playback. Media inspection Media inspection reads the properties and stream structure needed to understand a particular file. Playlists and media references Playlists and media references describe locations or playback organization rather than storing the complete referenced media. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/inspection/index.ht.title: Overview: Media inspection | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Media inspection Media inspection reads the properties and stream structure needed to understand a particular file. A playback investigation becomes more concrete when it starts with the file's reported tracks, codecs, timing and metadata. Probing tools expose that information at different levels of detail. This group introduces the inspection process and the MediaInfo and ffprobe views used to turn a filename into useful technical evidence. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media probing Media probing examines a source to identify its container, streams, and technical properties before playback. Media stream inspection with MediaInfo MediaInfo presents a file's container, stream formats, and technical tags in a readable report. Media stream inspection with ffprobe ffprobe inspects containers, streams, chapters, and packet timing without converting the media. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.title: Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.keywords: Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe ffprobe inspects containers, streams, chapters, and packet timing without converting the media. ffprobe is FFmpeg's inspection tool. Its value is that the question controls what is reported: whole-source information, individual streams, programmes, chapters, encoded packets, or decoded frames. With ffprobe installed, start with a structured description: ffprobe -v error -show_format -show_streams -show_chapters -of json "Movie.mkv" The format section concerns the source as a whole. Each stream section concerns one component. Chapters describe named positions. The report is written as JSON without creating a converted movie. Field Interpretation format_name Detected reader/format family; related formats may share a name index, codec_type, codec_name Which component the following properties describe time_base Seconds represented by one integer timestamp tick tags and disposition Descriptive fields and selection roles duration and bit_rate Values for the section's scope, potentially calculated or estimated Move from a summary to a timing question Suppose video stutters around ten minutes. This command requests a short packet examination near that source position: ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -read_intervals "600%+5" -show_packets -show_entries packet=pts_time,dts_time,duration_time,flags,pos,size -of json "Movie.mkv" v:0 selects the first video component, not every stream. The interval requests a seek near 600 seconds followed by about five seconds of reading. Seeking may begin at a nearby usable point, and the relative interval is measured from the actual found position. Treat the returned timestamps as the evidence of the range actually read. The packet fields connect decode and presentation time with byte position, size, and flags. In reordered video, PTS can move backwards in decode order while DTS advances. That is a meaningful pattern rather than an automatic corruption diagnosis. A programme question uses another view For a television transport recording, add -show_programs to the summary request. Programme entries show how streams are grouped. A global stream index and a programme number answer different identity questions; they should not be confused when several services occupy one file. Packets and frames ask different things of the tool -show_packets reports encoded packet information obtained by the reader. -show_frames asks for information about decoded frames and can involve decoder work. A successful packet report does not establish that all picture data decodes, while decoding a selected interval still does not test the rest of a long recording. For Emby investigation, use the exact source and record which tracks the session selected. The useful progression is a summary to identify the source, then a narrower packet or frame question that corresponds to the observed failure. Missing optional JSON fields mean no value was emitted; they should not silently become zero in a comparison or script. See Also Media Probing Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo Packet Timestamps MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References ffprobe documentation

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.title: Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.keywords: Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo MediaInfo presents a file's container, stream formats, and technical tags in a readable report. An Emby playback question often starts with “this is a 4K MKV.” MediaInfo can turn that shorthand into a description of what the file actually asks a reader and decoder to handle. Use a detailed presentation such as Tree or Text, then read from the outside inward. The General section describes the package; each Video, Audio, or Text section describes a component inside it. Section Details to retain for a playback comparison General Format, duration, file size, and overall rate Video Codec, profile, dimensions, sample format, and color information Each Audio Codec, channels, sample rate, language, and title Each Text Subtitle format, language, and selection information Menu, where detected Chapter or navigation positions Format versus Codec ID: HEVC and hvc1 Imagine the video section says Format: HEVC and Codec ID: hvc1. HEVC names the compression system, while hvc1 identifies the container representation . They describe different layers of one track. Now add Main 10 and 3840 × 2160. That suggests a 10-bit-capable HEVC profile and a particular raster, but leaves frame rate, level, precise sample format, and the receiving decoder path to examine. Rather than collecting one label, build the complete description that explains a difference between files. A second file with the same General format can have a different video profile, a different soundtrack, or different subtitles. The section boundaries keep those differences visible. Choose the component that actually played If the source contains English surround audio and English stereo commentary, retain both descriptions and identify the session's selection. A report for the unselected surround track cannot explain the processing of the commentary track. The same principle applies to subtitles. Their format can change rendering or conversion work even when the video is identical. Keeping the relevant sections in a text report is more useful than a screenshot of only resolution and filename. HDR fields describe the source information that MediaInfo detected. The display's current output mode is measured elsewhere. In a comparison between direct and converted playback, first establish the source's signaling, then obtain evidence about the delivered output and display. Understand the report's scope MediaInfo can show declared values, calculated values, or information derived by analyzing media. Different field names, rounding, or analysis versions can explain some disagreements with another inspector. The report is also not an exhaustive decode of the entire file. For a repeatable failure at a scene, retain the report as the source description and add the failing position and selected playback route. Packet or frame inspection can then examine the particular timing or decoding question that the summary cannot answer. See Also Media Probing Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe Codec Identifiers and FourCC HDR Metadata References MediaInfo: features and report contents MediaInfo: analysis and display questions

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-Pr.title: Media Probing | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-Pr.keywords: Media Probing Media probing examines a source to identify its container, streams, and technical properties before playback. Before a player can construct a playback path, it must discover the source's contents. Probing turns bytes and structures into a description: container, components, codec setup, timing, and useful technical properties. Information can come from a declared field, an observation, or a calculation. These have different evidential strength. Stored metadata, observed properties, and estimates The reader starts by recognizing the input format from signatures and structure. It parses descriptions of tracks and codec identifiers where the container supplies them. It may then inspect encoded data, or decode a limited portion, to obtain properties that are absent from the initial descriptions. A file-oriented container might already state its tracks in an early header. A transport stream may require observing repeated programme tables and enough packets to discover every component. An audio stream that begins after the first video packet can therefore appear only after more analysis. Result in a report Possible source of the value Track language A container tag Picture dimensions Codec configuration or examined pictures Duration Stored timing, observed timestamps, or an estimate Overall bitrate Reported information or file size divided by duration A calculated bitrate is not independent confirmation of the duration used in the division. A missing field can mean that the analyzer lacked evidence to report it, rather than that the property is zero. Why analysis limits exist Inspecting more data takes time and input reads. FFmpeg exposes controls such as probesize for the amount of probing data and analyzeduration for stream analysis. On a continuing or unusual source, enough analysis can reveal components or configuration missed by a smaller examination. The tradeoff is startup work and latency. More analysis is useful when discovery is incomplete. It is not a substitute for every kind of validation. A two-hour file can initialize successfully while containing a corrupt packet much later; inspecting its beginning does not exercise that packet. This distinction matters in Emby: source probing informs technical media details and playback decisions, while library providers identify the film or episode. An accurate poster and synopsis can coexist with incomplete stream discovery. For an unexplained report, compare MediaInfo and ffprobe on the same actual source. Keep whether a value is declared, observed, or estimated in the interpretation. If failure repeats at a known scene, examine that part and its decoding separately from the successful initialization report. See Also Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References FFmpeg format options: probing limits MediaInfo: technical information displayed

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-A.title: AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-A.keywords: AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) ADTS frames AAC audio with repeated headers containing synchronization, frame length, and core decoding information. An ADTS reader can find and delimit AAC audio as it reads from a file or continuing input. Audio Data Transport Stream surrounds audio data with repeated header information rather than relying on one movie-wide sample table. The header includes a synchronization pattern, MPEG/profile information, a sampling-frequency index, channel configuration, and the length of the framed unit. That lets the reader obtain the next boundary and basic setup from the stream. Walk three framed units Consider a simple single-raw-data-block case with no CRC. Each header is seven bytes, and the invented audio payloads contain 100, 120, and 90 bytes. ADTS unit Framed length Start byte relative to the sequence First 107 0 Second 127 107 Third 97 234 The reader validates the first header, reads its declared 107-byte unit, then checks the next expected header at byte 107. After another 127 bytes, the third begins at 234. The complete three-unit sequence occupies 331 bytes. In a common CRC-protected single-block arrangement, the header includes the additional protection field and occupies nine bytes. Arrangements with several raw data blocks have further details, so the seven-byte example should not be applied indiscriminately. Validating successive structures distinguishes a real framing sequence from one matching byte pattern inside unrelated data. The reader's work is boundary discovery and setup interpretation before audio decoding. How those bytes acquire audio time For ordinary AAC-LC units with 1,024 samples at 44.1 kHz, each represents approximately 23.220 ms. Three units represent 3,072 samples, or approximately 69.660 ms, despite their different byte lengths. Advanced AAC tools can change the relationship between the declared core and the final output. HE-AAC , for example, can reconstruct a higher-rate output from its core. The header fields are part of a complete interpretation, not a reason to discard signalling carried elsewhere in the audio syntax. Within a larger transport or a different file ADTS is not MPEG transport stream . TS can carry ADTS-framed audio as one component, adding its programme identification and systems timing around it. In MP4, encoded audio can instead be stored as samples whose configuration and timing are described by the container. Translating the package reads ADTS framing, retains applicable encoded audio, and writes the destination setup. An Emby delivery route can therefore change how AAC arrives without necessarily recompressing the soundtrack. See Also AAC Stream Packaging AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS HE-AAC Audio References ISO/IEC 13818-7:2006: MPEG-2 AAC ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio FFmpeg: aac_adtstoasc bitstream filter

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-L.title: AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-L.keywords: AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) LATM packages MPEG-4 audio and configuration information in a multiplex structure that can be carried over several delivery transports. A source described as AAC/LATM combines an audio coding format with a multiplex structure. The receiver first interprets LATM's configuration and payload arrangement, then supplies the encoded audio to the appropriate decoder. Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex groups audio data and the information needed to interpret it. LOAS , Low Overhead Audio Stream, can provide synchronization and length framing around that multiplex. They are different layers, not two names for one AAC codec. Layer Reader's operation LOAS, when used Find the framed LATM data in a continuing byte sequence LATM Interpret multiplex setup, payload boundaries, and configuration reuse AAC coding Reconstruct the sound from encoded audio units TS or RTP carriage Obtain this component through the outer delivery structure Configuration reuse and receiver state RFC 6416 describes a LATM audioMuxElement carrying payload and, in its in-band configuration mode, a useSameStreamMux indication. A StreamMuxConfig describes how the audio and its configuration are arranged. An initial element can supply configuration A and its audio. A following element can indicate that the previous setup is reused and carry the next payload without a complete repeat of A. The receiver retains A and applies it while parsing and decoding that next payload. This saves repeated descriptions, but makes retained setup part of the receiving state. If the reader joins after A and receives only reuse indications, it needs the applicable configuration before it can interpret those payloads. Repeating configuration periodically helps a receiver joining or recovering from loss. If the stream changes to configuration B, the reader must follow the new description rather than continue using A. A change near a programme transition is therefore meaningful evidence when sound begins failing at that point. Configuration can arrive elsewhere LATM over RTP can use out-of-band setup supplied through session description. That route does not need to repeat the same configuration within every audioMuxElement. The delivery convention establishes how the receiver obtains it. This is why stripping a supposed fixed header from every packet is not a general LATM-to-ADTS conversion. A converter needs to parse the multiplex, recover setup and encoded units, and write the destination's actual conventions. Some audio configurations cannot be represented by the same simple ADTS fields as another stream. For an Emby recording, compare the coding variant, multiplex/configuration handling, and output package. Reading AAC from one wrapper and reading it from LATM are different input paths to potentially the same audio decoder. The configuration trace explains a startup or transition failure more precisely than treating every AAC-labelled source as identical. See Also AAC Stream Packaging AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS References ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio RFC 6416: MPEG-4 Audio transport and LATM

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-S.title: AAC Stream Packaging | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-S.keywords: AAC Stream Packaging AAC audio can use several framing and container conventions that carry its encoded data and decoder configuration in different ways. An AAC decoder needs encoded audio units and configuration . Packaging decides where it obtains the unit boundaries, object type, sampling information, and channel description. Packaging Setup and boundaries ADTS Repeated transport headers surrounding audio data MP4/M4A Track setup plus sample sizes and timing in the container LATM Multiplex configuration and audio payload structure Follow one ordinary AAC-LC stereo stream at 44.1 kHz from ADTS into MP4. The audio units can stay encoded while the descriptions around them change. Translate the setup In this AAC-LC case, an ADTS header's profile value is 1, which maps to MPEG-4 audio object type 2. Its sampling-frequency index is 4, meaning 44,100 Hz, and channel configuration 2 represents stereo. The writer constructs an AudioSpecificConfig for the destination track. For this simple case, the object type, frequency index, channel configuration, and basic general-audio flags form the familiar two-byte value 0x12 0x10. The decoder receives that setup from the track description rather than deriving it from a repeated ADTS header. Those bytes describe this particular AAC configuration. HE-AAC and other variants can need additional signalling and have core and output properties that differ; they must be parsed in their own terms rather than forced into this two-byte example. Translate each unit's surrounding structure The converter reads an ADTS frame length, separates the header from its encoded audio, and writes the audio unit as a destination sample. It records that sample's size and duration through the container's structures. If an invented frame has a seven-byte unprotected header and 100 bytes of audio, the destination sample can hold those same 100 audio bytes. The original framed unit occupied 107 bytes. The MP4 also adds its own track and sample metadata, so removing seven bytes per unit does not by itself predict the total file-size difference. No sound has yet been decoded in this route. FFmpeg's aac_adtstoasc filter performs this sort of header/configuration translation for applicable inputs. What is preserved? The coded sound can be preserved while framing, setup location, and timing description change. A raw source may also lack the album tags or chapter information supplied by a more general container. These are distinct pieces of the result. For an Emby source comparison, record the AAC variant and how it is supplied to the decoder. A successful packaging-only route can avoid a new lossy audio generation; a route requiring another audio representation instead passes through decoded samples and an encoder. See Also AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) M4A and M4B File Conventions Elementary Streams AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC Audio References ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-7:2006: MPEG-2 AAC FFmpeg: aac_adtstoasc bitstream filter

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/index.title: Overview: AAC transport formats | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/index.keywords: Overview: AAC transport formats AAC transport formats frame and describe coded audio for the container or delivery system carrying it. AAC identifies the audio coding family; it does not uniquely identify the surrounding stream arrangement. ADTS and LATM package or describe AAC data in different ways, while other containers carry AAC through their own structures. This branch helps distinguish a codec-support question from the framing needed to locate and decode its data. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> AAC stream packaging AAC audio can use several framing and container conventions that carry its encoded data and decoder configuration in different ways. Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) ADTS frames AAC audio with repeated headers containing synchronization, frame length, and core decoding information. Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) LATM packages MPEG-4 audio and configuration information in a multiplex structure that can be carried over several delivery transports. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-7:2006: MPEG-2 AAC

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Blu-.title: Blu-ray File Structure | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Blu-.keywords: Blu-ray File Structure A Blu-ray movie presentation uses playlists, clip descriptions, and transport-stream media files within a BDMV directory structure. A Blu-ray feature can reuse some clips across different cuts and languages. Its BDMV structure keeps the stored media separate from the playlist selecting which ranges form a presentation. Simplified directory relationships. Optional directories and application details are omitted. PLAYLIST contains .mpls descriptions. CLIPINF contains .clpi clip information and access descriptions. STREAM contains the .m2ts encoded media. The playlist uses clip identities and ranges; the clip information helps the reader obtain suitable positions in the corresponding stream. Playlist time mapped to three clip ranges Take an invented feature playlist with these entries: Clip Source range Length Position in the presentation 00010 10–70 s 60 s 0–60 s 00020 0–600 s 600 s 60–660 s 00030 5–95 s 90 s 660–750 s The viewer sees 750 seconds, or 12 minutes 30 seconds. A request for presentation time 700 seconds falls into clip 00030 at source time 5 + (700 − 660) = 45 seconds. The reader resolves that clip's information, locates the relevant M2TS data, and begins decoding from an appropriate access point. It then maps the chosen source interval into the presentation's clock. The stored clip's complete duration is not the same as its selected contribution here. Another playlist could use an alternate middle clip or different ranges while reusing the opening and ending. Its scene sequence can differ even if the largest individual stream file is shared. Entry logic surrounds the playlist index.bdmv and movie-object information provide presentation entry and navigation. Interactive BD-J material can implement further application behaviour. Reading one playlist's video is a narrower task than executing the entire disc's menus and application. A reader selecting the actual feature should therefore identify the intended playlist or disc navigation choice. File size and duration can be clues, but cannot uniquely distinguish reused clips, alternative cuts, or different branching arrangements. Create a self-contained feature A remux must follow the selected playlist, obtain each requested range, and write an output timeline with the chosen audio and subtitles. Chapter positions need to map to that assembled timeline rather than remain unrelated clip-local times. For Emby, a disc presentation and a linear MKV/MP4 feature are different source forms. Library organization gives their context, while the playlist trace explains why copying one M2TS can produce the wrong movie. Preserving encoded streams is valuable only after the requested ranges and sequence have been identified. See Also MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS Disc Images: ISO Files Chapter Markers References Blu-ray Disc License Office: format specifications Blu-ray Disc Association: BD-ROM audiovisual application white paper, March 2005 (original PDF mirror)

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Disc.title: Disc Images: ISO Files | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Disc.keywords: Disc Images: ISO Files A disc image stores a volume and its filesystem as a file, preserving a disc presentation rather than replacing it with a single encoded movie. Mount an ISO image and a file browser can show a disc's folders. The operation interprets a stored volume; it has not yet selected a movie, separated its tracks, or decoded its pictures. A conventional .iso image commonly stores the logical data sectors of a disc as one file. The extension does not guarantee that the contained filesystem is ISO 9660: UDF or a bridge arrangement can also be present. Sectors, files, playlists, and encoded media Layer Reader operation Image and volume Obtain logical sectors and recognize the filesystem Filesystem Resolve names such as VIDEO_TS or BDMV into file locations Disc presentation Select a title, playlist, branches, and media ranges Media containers Read VOB or M2TS timing and encoded components Codecs Reconstruct the chosen picture and sound Each layer supplies information to the next. A volume can mount successfully while a particular contained file is damaged. A media stream can decode successfully while an incorrect playlist produces the wrong feature. What preserving an image retains Keeping the volume can retain directory structure, menus, extras, several cuts, and relationships between files. It preserves a disc-shaped source rather than merely one movie's selected tracks. A filesystem can describe a file through sector locations or extents. The image reader resolves those locations when another reader requests the named file. Copying an individual M2TS or VOB removes that outer filesystem context but still leaves the disc presentation choices to consider. A feature remux goes further: it follows the intended DVD title or Blu-ray playlist , obtains selected media, and writes a new linear container. Its output can preserve the encoded feature while omitting menus and extras. The difference is a selected presentation, not simply a different spelling of the same image. Access and protection remain at their boundaries Mounting supplies a way to access stored bytes. It does not authorize decryption of protected media. A disc-aware playback path and an ordinary movie-file reader also perform different jobs; a decoder accepting the underlying codec does not supply the filesystem and navigation stages by itself. For an Emby library, identify and organize the actual source form. If an image reports the wrong title or duration, inspect the contained disc structure and selected presentation before judging codec conversion. An image's completeness is tested by its content and readability, not by a successful mount alone. This layered view places a missing file, wrong playlist, damaged stream, or unavailable decoder at the stage that actually failed. See Also DVD-Video File Structure Blu-ray File Structure Types of Media Containers References ECMA-119, 6th edition: ISO 9660 volume and file structure ECMA-167, 3rd edition: volume and file structure ECMA TR/71: DVD read-only disk file system specifications Blu-ray Disc License Office: format specifications

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/DVD-.title: DVD-Video File Structure | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/DVD-.keywords: DVD-Video File Structure DVD-Video combines VOB media files with IFO navigation information and backup files inside a VIDEO_TS directory. Open a VIDEO_TS folder and its files describe a DVD presentation at several levels. The filesystem locates files; DVD navigation selects a title and its sequence; the VOB media supplies encoded picture, sound, and subpictures. Example filename or type Role VIDEO_TS.IFO Disc-level manager information, including title relationships VTS_01_0.IFO Information for title set 1 and its programmes/navigation .BUP Backup of corresponding IFO information VTS_01_0.VOB, where present Menu video objects for that title set VTS_01_1.VOB and subsequent numbered parts Title-set video objects containing media The filename sequence describes storage organization. It is not itself an instruction to play every VOB as an independent movie. Choose a title and resolve its sequence A DVD-aware reader obtains disc-level information and follows the selected title into its title set. Within that structure, programme chains (PGCs) describe an ordered route through programmes and cells of video objects. Cells identify playable ranges; navigation can select angles, branches, and the route to follow. Think of a simple invented chain as ranges A, C, and E from the stored objects. The player follows those ranges in order even if range B is physically between A and C on the disc. A linear concatenation of all stored bytes would instead include B. Both readers might decode valid MPEG media while presenting different content. A chapter, or part-of-title entry, identifies a navigation starting point within the title's structure. It is not necessarily a VOB filename boundary. A film can cross numbered VOB parts in the middle of a scene while its chapter begins elsewhere. Decode the selected media Within the chosen video objects, program-stream-based packaging supplies the timed encoded components. The reader needs the intended soundtrack and subpicture descriptions as well as the video. DVD navigation and timing connect those pieces into the selected presentation. Menu execution is another part of the disc experience. A DVD player can follow navigation commands and maintained state, whereas a file converter often resolves one selected title into a conventional linear output. Those are different consumer jobs applied to the same disc. Folder, image, or a selected movie A complete copied folder retains the file relationships. An image additionally retains the volume/filesystem around them. A remuxed feature instead writes the chosen title's components and timeline into one movie container, usually without reproducing the disc's menu logic. For an Emby collection, use the movie organization guidance and identify which of these source forms is present. A lone VOB may initialize normally while representing only part of the intended feature. Title selection and scene order need to be resolved before evaluating whether the encoded video was preserved. The public references describe filesystem and reader behaviour; the licensed DVD-Video Book is the format's detailed specification.
