The distinction keeps a useful structural explanation separate from claims to have reproduced the complete navigation standard. See Also MPEG Program Stream Disc Images: ISO Files Chapter Markers References ECMA TR/71: DVD read-only disk file system specifications DVD Forum: DVD-Books, Part 3 DVD-Video Book (bibliographic citation in RFC 9559) VideoLAN libdvdread: IFO, menu VOB, and title VOB lookup FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/inde.title: Overview: Disc structures and images | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/inde.keywords: Overview: Disc structures and images Disc structures and images preserve media files together with the organization used by a disc-based playback system. A DVD or Blu-ray title can involve several files and navigation structures. An ISO image preserves a disc-shaped storage arrangement rather than converting that title into one ordinary movie track. These pages explain what is stored so a disc folder, image and extracted media file are not mistaken for the same playback object. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DVD-Video file structure DVD-Video combines VOB media files with IFO navigation information and backup files inside a VIDEO_TS directory. Blu-ray file structure A Blu-ray movie presentation uses playlists, clip descriptions, and transport-stream media files within a BDMV directory structure. Disc images (ISO) A disc image stores a volume and its filesystem as a file, preserving a disc presentation rather than replacing it with a single encoded movie. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ECMA TR/71: DVD read-only disk file system specifications ECMA-119, 6th edition: ISO 9660 volume and file structure

articles/media-files/packaging/index.htm.title: Overview: File packaging details | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/index.htm.keywords: Overview: File packaging details Media packaging details shape how a container stores, exposes or references the content needed for playback. Two files using the same general format can be arranged differently. Metadata placement, fragmentation, attachments or disc structures can change how a reader starts, navigates or obtains the media. These topics explain those packaging choices rather than assuming that the extension captures the whole playback arrangement. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> MP4 packaging MP4 packaging choices affect media segmentation, startup access and the conventions used for audio-only files. Matroska features Matroska attachments and ordered chapters add supporting assets and navigation relationships beyond ordinary media tracks. MP3 files and MPEG audio frames An MP3 file stores MPEG Layer III audio frames together with optional tags and information for duration and seeking. AAC transport formats AAC transport formats frame and describe coded audio for the container or delivery system carrying it. Disc structures and images Disc structures and images preserve media files together with the organization used by a disc-based playback system. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.title: Overview: Matroska features | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.keywords: Overview: Matroska features Matroska attachments and ordered chapters add supporting assets and navigation relationships beyond ordinary media tracks. Some Matroska files carry resources alongside their tracks or describe a playback order through chapters. Those features can affect subtitle appearance and how segments are presented, even when the principal video and audio codecs are unchanged. The pages below explain the stored feature and the reader support it requires. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Matroska attachments Matroska attachments embed supporting files such as fonts and cover images alongside the timed media tracks. Matroska ordered chapters Matroska ordered chapters define a presentation sequence that can reuse or rearrange ranges from one or more segments. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification

articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.title: Matroska Attachments | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.keywords: Matroska Attachments Matroska attachments embed supporting files such as fonts and cover images alongside the timed media tracks. A subtitle sign that fitted neatly in one player can wrap or shift in another even when its text and position commands are identical. The missing information may be the font file , carried as a Matroska attachment. An attachment is an embedded supporting resource rather than a timed media stream. Matroska supplies its filename, media type, identifying information, and bytes. The renderer or library decides how to use that resource. Attached resource Consumer TrueType/OpenType font Subtitle renderer needing its faces and metrics Cover image Software using embedded artwork Other file A consumer implementing that particular resource use From a named typeface to positioned text A styled subtitle requests a font family, style, size, and positioning. The renderer finds an appropriate font face and uses its glyph shapes and metrics to calculate text layout. The attachment's filename is not necessarily the same as the family name embedded inside the font. For an invented layout example, a line has 110 pixels of available width. One font's glyph advances total 96 pixels; a fallback's total 120. The first can remain on one line while the second needs wrapping or a different layout. That change comes from font metrics, not from a different subtitle sentence. Embedding the intended font gives a renderer a way to reproduce the requested face without relying on a separate system installation. The result still follows the renderer's layout and supported style commands. Fonts at the app or server subtitle renderer In a route where the Emby app renders subtitles, the subtitle data and usable supporting resources need to reach that rendering stage. In a server burn-in route, the server's renderer needs them before it combines the result with the pictures. The attachment is needed at the consumer, not merely somewhere earlier in the system. A remux selecting video, sound, and subtitles can omit attachments if they are not selected or supported. The video codec and subtitle text can survive while the intended font disappears. Comparing only the timed track list will miss that change. Cover artwork likewise lives at a different layer from the library's stored poster choices. An image attached to the movie and an image chosen for a library role can both exist without being the same record. To explain a changed subtitle, compare the requested family/style, available attachments, fallback chosen, and the location of rendering. It follows the information that actually determines the layout. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Streams and Tracks Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification MKVToolNix: mkvmerge manual

articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.title: Matroska Ordered Chapters | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.keywords: Matroska Ordered Chapters Matroska ordered chapters define a presentation sequence that can reuse or rearrange ranges from one or more segments. An ordered edition in Matroska can describe what should play, rather than merely name positions in a fixed movie. Its chapter ranges form a virtual timeline using material from the current segment or referenced segments. Conceptual linked-segment presentation. The numerical example below uses the same opening/body/ending arrangement. Assemble the edition's clock Suppose three stored segments contain an opening, an episode body, and an ending. An ordered edition requests these ranges: Source range Selected length Position in the played edition Opening: 0–90 s 90 s 0–90 s Body: 0–1,200 s 1,200 s 90–1,290 s Ending: 0–90 s 90 s 1,290–1,380 s The resulting presentation lasts 1,380 seconds, or 23 minutes. Each range has source coordinates and a place in the concatenated output. The next episode can reference the same opening and ending while selecting a different body. A seek to 430 seconds in this edition falls inside the body. Its corresponding body-source position is 430 − 90 = 340 seconds. A reader must resolve that range and then perform a normal seek within the referenced media. Seeking directly to source time 430 would land at a different scene. The references are part of the presentation Segment links identify the target through its unique segment identifier. The reader needs to locate the matching media and initialize its tracks; the chapter range alone contains no encoded picture or sound. Copying the body file while leaving behind the shared opening and ending can thus leave an otherwise readable body with unresolved presentation dependencies. The body has not necessarily lost bytes. The edition has lost access to requested ranges in other media. Another edition could omit the opening and present 1,290 seconds instead. The same stored body then occupies a different position in the output timeline. An edition's duration is therefore a result of its chosen ranges, not simply the physical file's linear duration. What a flattened movie needs To produce a self-contained movie, a converter must follow the selected edition, obtain every range, and map their audio/video timing onto one output timeline. It must also handle decoding restart and transitions at the range boundaries. Copying only the body's streams skips that assembly step. This explains an Emby item whose linear media plays but differs from an ordered-edition-aware desktop player. Compare which edition was followed and whether linked segments were resolved before comparing codecs. The requested presentation may be different even though the stored picture data is identical. Ordinary chapters only offer named destinations in a fixed sequence. Ordered editions add source-range selection and timeline assembly; those are the mechanisms that distinguish this feature. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Chapter Markers Packet Timestamps References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification MKVToolNix: mkvmerge manual

articles/media-files/packaging/MP3-Files.title: MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/MP3-Files.keywords: MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames An MP3 file stores MPEG Layer III audio frames together with optional tags and information for duration and seeking. An MP3 file commonly stores a sequence of MPEG Layer III audio frames, with optional descriptive and navigation information around or within that sequence. Reading those frames is a different job from interpreting a general movie container with several soundtracks. Each MPEG frame has a four-byte header describing such properties as MPEG version, layer, bitrate choice, sample-rate choice, and channel mode. The reader validates the fields and successive boundaries before passing frame data to the audio decoder . One frame's duration and length For MPEG-1 Layer III, one frame represents 1,152 sample frames per channel. At 44.1 kHz, that is 1,152 / 44,100 = approximately 26.122 ms. For an ordinary 128 kb/s frame at that rate, the byte-length calculation is: floor(144 × 128,000 / 44,100) + padding byte = 417 or 418 bytes The padding-byte choices keeps the long-term stored rate aligned with the specified rate. Equal audio duration therefore need not mean exactly equal stored length, even in this constant-bitrate example. Information Question it answers Frame header Which encoding parameters and boundary size apply? Frame count How much nominal decoded audio is represented? Optional Xing/VBRI data What duration or navigation summary was written? ID3 metadata What names, descriptions, or artwork accompany the recording? Encoder delay and end padding can require separate trimming information when interpreting the intended presented duration. Counting nominal frame samples and accounting for that valid interval are related but distinct steps. Why a frame boundary is not always a clean cut Layer III's bit reservoir allows encoded main data associated with a frame to occupy available space in earlier frames. Side information tells the decoder where that data begins relative to the present frame's main data. Starting at an arbitrary visible header can therefore leave the decoder without bytes needed for the first audio it tries to reconstruct. A reader can need preceding frame data; cutting a file at that boundary does not necessarily create a clean independent excerpt. This is a packing mechanism within the encoded stream, not a second audio track. Its purpose is to share the data allowance across varying coding demands. Tags and timing belong to different interpretations ID3 also calls its individual metadata records “frames.” An ID3 title frame carries text, while an MPEG audio frame represents sound. A music library can identify a file incorrectly because of its ID3 records even though the sound decodes normally. For variable-bitrate audio, dividing the whole file by one observed frame's bitrate can misstate duration. Readers can instead examine frame information and optional summaries. In an Emby music case, keep title/tag problems separate from seek or duration problems: they lead to different structures in this same file. See Also Containers and Codecs Container Indexes and Seeking Bitrate Variation MP3 Audio References ISO/IEC 11172-3:1993: MPEG-1 Audio RFC 5219: MP3 frame structure and bit reservoir ID3v2.4.0: main structure FFmpeg n8.1 MPEG audio header decoding

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/Fragm.title: Fragmented MP4 | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/Fragm.keywords: Fragmented MP4 Fragmented MP4 distributes timing and sample descriptions across successive media fragments after an initial track description. A conventional MP4 can describe the samples of a complete movie in tables. Fragmented MP4 describes newly available groups of samples as the presentation proceeds. A writer can commit each group before the whole recording exists. Common conceptual layout. Optional boxes, size differences, and additional fragments are omitted. Initialization supplies track identities, time scales, and codec setup. Successive moof boxes describe movie fragments; accompanying mdat boxes hold their encoded media. This divides global track setup from information about the current samples. Sample times and byte offsets inside a fragment Take an invented fragment for a video track whose clock uses 30,000 ticks per second. Let its base decode time be 60,000 ticks. Each of three samples lasts 1,000 ticks, and their byte sizes are 800, 500, and 650. For this example there is no picture reordering, so the presentation offsets are zero. Assume a 120-byte moof followed by an eight-byte mdat header. A sample run uses a data offset of 128 from the moof's beginning with movie-fragment-relative addressing. Sample Decode time Time in seconds Byte start relative to moof 1 60,000 2.0000 128 2 61,000 2.0333… 928 3 62,000 2.0666… 1,428 The reader obtains the time base from initialization, the base decode time from the track fragment, and durations/sizes from the sample run or its declared defaults. Cumulative durations produce the next decode positions; cumulative sizes produce the next byte addresses. The three media samples total 1,950 bytes. The fragment ends at relative byte 2,078 in this simplified layout, and its next decode time is 63,000 ticks, or 2.1 seconds. This is concrete work the fragment description performs: it turns one group's bytes into identified, scheduled samples. Real fragments can contain multiple tracks and runs, defaults, composition offsets, and additional boxes. The reader follows the applicable fields rather than assuming every fragment uses these invented sizes. Initialization and restart are separate dependencies A media-only segment needs the associated track setup. Even after setup is available, a video sample may predict from an earlier picture. Beginning at a suitable random access point supplies a usable decoding restart; storing a moof in front of arbitrary samples does not itself create one. The browser Media Source Extensions byte-stream note defines initialization and media-segment requirements for that path. HLS defines another fMP4 carriage convention. Those requirements build on ISO BMFF rather than describing every possible fragmented file arrangement. Stored fragments and delivered segments Fragments can occupy one physical file or several resources. A streaming playlist can identify separate initialization and media resources; another reader can traverse successive moof/mdat pairs in one file. Fragmentation is the internal description method, while the delivery system chooses how those groups are obtained. In an Emby session, the original library file can be read into such an output arrangement. It is the delivered initialization and fragments the app follows, even if the source was MKV or a conventional MP4. Fast start solves another initialization problem by moving one conventional movie description early. Fragmentation instead keeps adding group descriptions as samples become known. That distinction explains its usefulness for ongoing recording and segmented delivery. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format MP4 Fast Start Container Indexes and Seeking References ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format W3C ISO BMFF byte stream format: 23 July 2024 Group Note RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming, media segment formats

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/index.title: Overview: MP4 packaging | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/index.keywords: Overview: MP4 packaging MP4 packaging choices affect media segmentation, startup access and the conventions used for audio-only files. A reader may need container information before it can interpret the media bytes. Fast-start placement and fragmentation address that relationship in different ways, while M4A and M4B names describe common audio-file conventions. The linked topics distinguish physical organization from the codec and content-type assumptions often attached to an MP4-family filename. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Fragmented MP4 Fragmented MP4 distributes timing and sample descriptions across successive media fragments after an initial track description. MP4 fast start MP4 fast start places the movie description before the bulk media data so a sequential reader can initialize playback earlier. M4A and M4B file conventions M4A and M4B are audio-oriented filename conventions for MP4-family files, with M4B commonly indicating audiobook content. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format ISO/IEC 14496-14:2020: MP4 file format

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/M4A-M.title: M4A and M4B File Conventions | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/M4A-M.keywords: M4A and M4B File Conventions M4A and M4B are audio-oriented filename conventions for MP4-family files, with M4B commonly indicating audiobook content. A music album and a spoken book can use the same MP4-family audio structure. M4A commonly identifies audio such as music; M4B commonly identifies a book-oriented use, often with chapters. The file still needs a coded audio track. An M4A can contain AAC or Apple Lossless , so the extension does not prescribe one audio representation. Layer in an audiobook experience Information involved Encoded sound Audio codec, sample rate, channels, and timing Book navigation Chapter names and positions Library description Book, author, cover, and organization Listening history The user's position in a particular item Chapter markers and a resume position at 37:12 An uninterrupted book track can carry a chapter list without being split into separate sound files. A chapter at 30:00 names a position within that track. If a listener stops at 37:12, the playback/library system can retain 2,232 seconds as that user's position. On resuming, the system requests the corresponding source time. The container's sample navigation gets it to the encoded data. Chapter descriptions can supply names near that point, while the user's remembered position supplies the specific resume request. These are different records used together. Changing .m4a to .m4b changes a filename convention; it does not add the chapter list or populate listening history. A particular app may use the convention to classify the item, but the underlying data still has to exist. Preserve the right book information in a conversion MP4/QuickTime supports different chapter representations. A converter that retains the sound may omit the chapter representation another reader expects. Compare chapter names and exact positions alongside decoded sound and duration. If an introduction is removed, later chapter positions and any retained listening position need interpretation against the edited timeline. An audio-preserving remux with unchanged timing is a different operation from such an edit. For Emby, audiobook organization supplies the library context for this book experience. The file's track and chapters describe the recording; the item's metadata and playback records describe how it is presented and used. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Chapter Markers Media File Extensions Apple Lossless (ALAC) AAC-LC Audio References ISO/IEC 14496-14:2020: MP4 file format Apple AVFoundation: M4A file type Apple Audio Toolbox: M4B file type Apple: QuickTime File Format

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/MP4-F.title: MP4 Fast Start | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/MP4-F.keywords: MP4 Fast Start MP4 fast start places the movie description before the bulk media data so a sequential reader can initialize playback earlier. A reader receiving an MP4 from beginning to end needs the movie description before it can interpret its samples. Fast start places that description ahead of the bulk media data. A conventional writer may finish its moov box after writing mdat, because only then are all the sample locations and timing known. The resulting file is complete and usable for readers that can seek to the description, but a sequential reader encounters the payload first. Simplified before/after layouts. Box widths are not file-size proportions. What actually moves? Suppose an illustrative layout has 24 bytes of file-type information followed by an eight-byte mdat header. The first media sample begins at byte 32, and a completed moov of 100,000 bytes sits after the media. Move that moov between the file-type box and mdat, keeping the other relevant sizes unchanged. The first sample now starts at byte 100,032. A later chunk previously at byte 1,050,032 moves to 1,150,032. The sample bytes themselves are the same. The chunk-location tables must be rewritten to reference the new addresses. Moving a block of metadata without updating its stored offsets would give the reader a valid-looking table that points at the wrong bytes. Changed by this operation Retained by this operation moov placement and affected chunk offsets The coded media samples The order in which a sequential reader encounters setup The codec's picture/sound representation Actual rewriting can also need larger offset fields or layout adjustments. The numerical example isolates the relocation mechanism rather than prescribing every writer's result. Sequential transfer and byte-range access For a purely sequential transfer of a 250 MB file at 5 MB/s, trailing setup could remain unavailable until roughly 50 seconds of data has been received. In the simplified early-moov layout, reading 100 kB at that rate takes roughly 0.02 seconds; codec setup, required media, and request latency still add startup work. A byte-range-capable reader can instead fetch the trailing description directly and then request the needed media. It need not transfer the 250 MB prefix to reach moov. Fast-start placement therefore changes one access pattern more than another. For an Emby session, establish whether the app receives this original file layout or a repackaged output. Fragmented delivery supplies initialization and successive sample descriptions through its own arrangement. The useful result of fast start is earlier availability of the instructions for reading the movie. Its offsets and encoded samples explain that result; no new picture encoding is required. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Fragmented MP4 Container Indexes and Seeking References ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: Overview: Playlists and media references | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: Overview: Playlists and media references Playlists and media references describe locations or playback organization rather than storing the complete referenced media. A small text file can select tracks, describe an ordering or point a player toward another source. Its contents may depend on paths and resources outside the file itself. M3U, PLS, CUE and STRM topics explain those different reference roles, which helps when a playlist opens successfully but the item it points to cannot be reached. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> M3U playlists An M3U playlist is a text file that lists media locations and can add descriptive information for each entry. PLS playlists A PLS playlist uses numbered text fields to list media locations, titles, and optional durations. CUE sheets A CUE sheet describes track boundaries and metadata for referenced disc-image or audio files. Media pointer files (STRM) A STRM file is a small text pointer that lets Emby associate a library item with a media URL or file path. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: CUE Sheets | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: CUE Sheets A CUE sheet describes track boundaries and metadata for referenced disc-image or audio files. One long audio recording can represent an album with several songs. A CUE sheet describes their positions and names while the sound remains in the referenced file. FILE "Concert.wav" WAVE TRACK 01 AUDIO TITLE "Opening" INDEX 01 00:00:00 TRACK 02 AUDIO TITLE "Second song" INDEX 01 04:30:00 FILE identifies the recording. TRACK starts a disc-track description, TITLE names it, and INDEX 01 identifies its main start. The example does not create a second audio stream or a separate sound file. Convert the position before using it CUE time is minutes:seconds:frames at 75 CD frames per second . Those frames are units of disc time, not video pictures or milliseconds. seconds = minutes × 60 + seconds field + frames ÷ 75 CUE value Calculation Time 04:30:00 4 × 60 + 30 270 s 04:30:30 270 + 30/75 270.4 s 04:30:74 270 + 74/75 270.9866… s For 44.1 kHz PCM, one 1/75-second disc frame corresponds to 588 sample frames per channel. The 04:30:30 position therefore corresponds to 270.4 × 44,100 = 11,924,640 sample frames. This relationship explains how a disc-oriented boundary can become a precise location in the decoded recording. Turning a boundary into individual songs A splitter uses a track's start and the next applicable boundary to select a region of the referenced audio. It writes separate outputs and associates each with the track's descriptions. In contrast, a player interpreting the CUE can offer those regions without physically splitting the long file. INDEX 00 can describe a pregap position before INDEX 01. Handling that interval is a disc-layout decision: assigning it to the preceding output, the following output, or a separate region produces different file boundaries. Read the actual indexes when the exported songs have unexpected starts or gaps. This CUE “track” is a region of a recording, unlike a separately selectable movie audio track . For an Emby music collection, establish whether the chosen reader uses those regions or sees the source as one long recording. If the audio is edited, the positions need to be mapped onto the new timeline. If its filename changes, the FILE reference needs to identify the new location. These operations preserve different relationships: one concerns time and the other concerns access to the recording. See Also Chapter Markers M3U Playlists References libcue: CUE parser grammar libcue: minutes, seconds, and frame conversion

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: M3U Playlists | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: M3U Playlists An M3U playlist is a text file that lists media locations and can add descriptive information for each entry. Open this M3U playlist and the reader sees an ordered set of media locations, with optional descriptions immediately before them: #EXTM3U #EXTINF:180,Opening song Music/Opening.flac #EXTINF:240,Second song Music/Second.flac #EXTM3U identifies the extended convention. Each #EXTINF line supplies a duration in seconds and a display title for the following location. The title is descriptive; the path is what the reader must open to obtain the sound. Relative paths resolve from the playlist folder If the playlist is stored in a folder called Concert, Music/Opening.flac conventionally refers to Concert/Music/Opening.flac. Moving only the playlist into another folder changes that relationship. An absolute location instead identifies its destination independently of the playlist's folder. Opening the text succeeds before opening the media. A list can therefore display both song titles even if one referenced file is missing. That gives two distinct stages to test: parsing entries and obtaining each entry's content. M3U8 commonly denotes UTF-8 text. That convention determines how text characters are represented; it does not turn every M3U8 into one particular kind of streaming presentation. What HLS adds to the family An ordinary music list describes an order of independent items. HLS gives playlists protocol-specific meanings: a media playlist lists timed segments of one presentation, while a multivariant/master playlist describes alternative streams. Tags govern durations, sequence updates, and other playback behaviour in addition to locations. The reader must interpret the appropriate conventions, rather than merely follow every path as a new song. Emby's M3U tuner guidance concerns a channel list and its source descriptions, another distinct use of related text syntax. When inspecting a playlist, first identify its job. Then read the actual location associated with the failing entry and the base location used to resolve it. The playlist organizes access; the referenced resource supplies the codec and container data. See Also PLS Playlists Media Pointer Files: STRM References VideoLAN: M3U playlist reader implementation RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming playlists

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: PLS Playlists | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: PLS Playlists A PLS playlist uses numbered text fields to list media locations, titles, and optional durations. A radio station's small PLS download can contain only an address and descriptive text. A playlist reader opens that address to obtain the ongoing audio; the downloaded text is not the recording. The syntax associates fields through a shared entry number: [playlist] File1=Music/Opening.mp3 Title1=Opening song Length1=180 File2=Music/Second.mp3 Title2=Second song Length2=240 NumberOfEntries=2 Version=2 File1, Title1, and Length1 describe one entry. The second group describes another. Length values conventionally use seconds; −1 commonly represents an unknown duration, such as a continuing radio source. Reading an entry The reader obtains the location from FileN and uses TitleN for its description. Replacing “Opening song” with a new title changes how the entry is displayed, not what plays. Replacing File1 changes its destination even if the visible title remains unchanged. For a local relative path, the playlist's location supplies the base relationship. Keeping the playlist and its referenced Music folder together preserves that relationship when the collection moves. A remote location instead needs the relevant network access each time playback obtains it. A conversion to M3U writes the locations in that format's sequence and translates useful titles or lengths. Renaming .pls to .m3u does not perform this parse-and-write operation. PLS is useful to recognize when a media shortcut opens in a desktop player but is mistaken for a saved song. The contents of FileN identify the actual source; its availability and format can then be examined separately from the playlist text. See Also M3U Playlists Media Pointer Files: STRM References VideoLAN: PLS playlist reader implementation

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: Media Pointer Files: STRM | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: Media Pointer Files: STRM A STRM file is a small text pointer that lets Emby associate a library item with a media URL or file path. A STRM file lets an Emby library item point to media stored elsewhere. The pointer is small because it stores a location; the movie's encoded tracks remain at that destination. The library description, the pointer, and the media are three different objects. Follow the address through the system. Emby recognizes the named library item and reads its text pointer. The media-opening path obtains the referenced source. That source is then examined for its tracks and delivered through an appropriate playback route. The STRM documentation defines the supported pointer contents and organization. Two addresses that look similar can return different data A website's video page supplies HTML and player code. The player can make another request for the actual movie or a streaming playlist. A pointer needs the media location supported by the opening path, rather than an arbitrary webpage that happens to display a video. Similarly, a shared-file path is interpreted from the environment that opens it. A drive letter visible on an administrator's desktop may not exist for a server service. A network path can identify the same source more clearly, but access still depends on that process's credentials and connectivity. This is a location-resolution question before any codec is decoded. What is preserved when the library is copied? Copying the STRM file preserves its text address. Copying local library descriptions can preserve the displayed item. Neither operation copies the distant recording. The pointer's storage size therefore does not represent the movie's size, and an offline copy of the pointer does not provide offline movie bytes. If the destination changes or an expiring address stops granting access, the item can remain visible while playback can no longer obtain its source. Update the address relationship or source availability; the library's retained title is not evidence that the media was fetched. A useful failure trace follows the same boundaries: recognized item, readable pointer, resolved address, returned media rather than HTML, then source initialization . Once the actual media is obtained, its container and selected tracks determine the playback work just as they do for an ordinary local source. See Also What Is a Media File? M3U Playlists References RFC 3986: URI syntax

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.title: Overview: Cover and branding artwork | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.keywords: Overview: Cover and branding artwork Cover and branding artwork provide distinct visual identities for catalogue items and their presentation surfaces. A portrait poster, a wide backdrop and a transparent logo are intended for different compositions. Embedded cover art adds another storage relationship. The pages here explain those roles, helping identify whether an unexpected image comes from selection, aspect ratio or the source supplying the asset. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Posters A poster is a principal identification composition whose title, imagery and aspect relationship need to remain useful at the library's display size. Backdrops A backdrop is a background composition associated with media that must remain useful under crop, interface overlays and the chosen display environment. Transparent logos A transparent logo retains title or branding pixels and coverage as a layer that can be composed over the library's chosen background. Embedded cover art Embedded cover art carries image resources inside media metadata, with picture type, encoding and selection determining which image reaches the library. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB: Image configuration and paths RFC 9639: FLAC metadata

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.title: Media backdrops | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.keywords: Media backdrops A backdrop is a background composition associated with media that must remain useful under crop, interface overlays and the chosen display environment. A backdrop supplies visual context behind other interface content. A detailed scene can look attractive on its own while competing with the title, controls or descriptive text drawn over it. The composition includes the interface An original wide scene has a prominent subject on its right side and relatively quiet space on the left. Placing text in that quiet area can retain both recognition and readable foreground content. This is an original layout experiment, not an Emby screenshot or a mandatory safe-area specification. Text readability can depend on local image contrast, an overlay treatment and the actual type size. The backdrop's image resolution does not establish those relationships by itself. Cropping changes the useful region A narrow screen can retain another portion of a wide backdrop than a widescreen presentation. A subject near the edge may be removed, while a centered crop can preserve another image better. Image resizing develops contain/cover geometry. The selected app's layout decides which operation is used. A wide backdrop should not automatically be turned into a portrait poster; its composition and missing title treatment can have been authored for another role. One work can have several background resources Emby's image-type documentation describes backdrop use and the possibility of clients alternating backgrounds. Those resources remain images associated with the same entity. The order/selection of that set is different from movie playback order. A stale or wrong backdrop can also concern cached artwork rather than a wrong video file. Keep the image's entity, language/text treatment and chosen role with its source. That makes an artwork correction specific to the background being presented. See Also Media artwork roles Media posters Transparent media logos Image resizing References TMDB: Image configuration and paths Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.title: Embedded cover art | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.keywords: Embedded cover art Embedded cover art carries image resources inside media metadata, with picture type, encoding and selection determining which image reaches the library. A media file can carry cover images in its metadata structures. Their bytes form image resources associated with the item; they are not additional sound samples. The enclosing tag describes the picture Representation Relevant boundary ID3v2 APIC Picture type, MIME information, description and image bytes FLAC PICTURE metadata Structured picture information and encoded image payload MP4 cover metadata Cover entries interpreted through that metadata convention The actual image still needs a matching image decoder. A tag reader locating an APIC frame does not itself decompress its JPEG or PNG payload. Several pictures need a selection rule ID3's attached-picture types distinguish, among other roles, front and back covers. A file can consequently contain more than one legitimate image. Selecting the first encountered picture can pick a back cover or another role. An integration should retain the type and relevant description where its model uses them. In Emby music, compare the actual embedded candidates with the selected library image. A provider's album artwork and the file's embedded front cover can both be available sources under another selection policy. Image bytes have their own cost An original file might carry encoded pictures of 60,000 and 80,000 bytes . Their combined image payload is 140,000 bytes , before tag/block overhead. Those bytes contribute to file size and retrieval but do not increase the audio's sample count. A whole-file bitrate calculation includes them; a codec-only audio rate has another scope. Decoded image memory also depends on its image grid and output representation, not simply on this encoded byte total. Metadata preservation is independent of audio copying A rewrite can retain coded audio while replacing or omitting cover metadata. The sound payload can remain the same while the whole-file checksum changes. An extraction or conversion therefore needs a picture-preservation decision as well as an audio decision. Keep role, image type and selected resource together when assessing the resulting cover. See Also ID3v2 audio tags MP4 metadata atoms Vorbis comments Media artwork roles JPEG images References ID3.org: ID3v2.4 frame definitions RFC 9639: FLAC metadata TagLib: MP4 metadata interface

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.title: Media posters | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.keywords: Media posters A poster is a principal identification composition whose title, imagery and aspect relationship need to remain useful at the library's display size. A poster serves as an identification image for a work or release presentation. Its composition can combine a title, recognisable imagery and credits arranged for a portrait-shaped space. Layout must survive the intended view Consider an original 600 × 900 poster. That 2:3 ratio is an illustrative choice, not a rule that every poster must obey. To fill a wide 16:9 rectangle by centered cropping, only 600 × 337.5 source units remain. The retained vertical interval is 281.25–618.75 . A title anchored near y = 90 lies outside that interval. Enlarging the crop does not bring the title back. A purpose-made backdrop can therefore serve the wide view better than a poster converted solely by cropping. A browsing tile changes legibility A 600 × 900 source reduced to 200 × 300 has one-third of each dimension and one-ninth of its sample count. Small credit lettering and fine texture may cease to be useful at that size. The source's nominal resolution and its composition answer different questions. More pixels help sampling, while large clear title shapes and suitable contrast help recognition. Emby's image roles and views supply the product context. The actual app layout determines how the selected poster is fitted and presented. The image still belongs to an identity An alternate-language title or edition branding can be deliberate. A poster for a remake with the same name can instead be the wrong entity. Compare work/edition relationship and artwork language before solving the issue as a resize problem. A selected smaller asset can be suitable if it matches the intended presentation and has adequate detail. A large unrelated poster remains unrelated at every display size. See Also Media artwork roles Media backdrops Artwork language selection Image resizing References TMDB: Image configuration and paths Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.title: Transparent media logos | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/cove.keywords: Transparent media logos A transparent logo retains title or branding pixels and coverage as a layer that can be composed over the library's chosen background. A transparent logo is a title/branding layer intended to sit over another image or page background. Its transparent positions let that destination remain visible. One layer meets several backgrounds An original logo can be presented over a dark backdrop and a light panel without importing a rectangular background colour of its own. The example uses a generated graphic and local GDI+ composition. It illustrates a resource relationship rather than an Emby screen capture. A painted white rectangle in an opaque image is not equivalent to alpha. Image transparency develops that distinction. Emby's logo role is commonly composed over other artwork. The selected image therefore needs useful coverage through the actual resource and presentation route. Edges retain colour and coverage Antialiased lettering uses intermediate coverage around its contours. Filtering that colour/alpha relationship inconsistently can create a dark or coloured halo. Converting the logo into an ordinary opaque photo commits it to a background. A later page cannot recover the original transparent edge from those flattened pixels alone. Use the intended file/processing convention, rather than assuming every four-component buffer has the same alpha interpretation. Canvas and visible lettering have different bounds A 900-pixel-wide transparent canvas can contain lettering occupying only 600 pixels. A view fitting the complete canvas consequently gives the lettering less visible space than a tightly bounded resource. Cropping unused transparent margins changes the canvas relationship while preserving the visible shape. The app's placement and scaling must still be considered. Text belongs to a language presentation A title logo can contain localized wording. Selecting a French poster and an English logo can create a mixed presentation even when both assets refer to the right work. Artwork language selection connects that text treatment to role and source identity. A textless logo or branding mark needs a deliberate neutral interpretation rather than a language guessed from the audio file. See Also Media artwork roles Media backdrops Image transparency PNG images Artwork language selection References Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles Fanart.tv: Legacy v3 artwork metadata

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/inde.title: Overview: Artwork and preview images | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/inde.keywords: Overview: Artwork and preview images Artwork roles identify which image belongs in a particular library or playback presentation. A poster, backdrop and preview frame serve different purposes even when all are ordinary image files. Role, dimensions and language influence how an application selects and presents them. This area connects cover and branding assets with the thumbnails used to recognize or navigate the actual programme. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media artwork roles An artwork role describes an image's presentation purpose and entity relationship, separately from its file format, dimensions or source. Cover and branding artwork Cover and branding artwork provide distinct visual identities for catalogue items and their presentation surfaces. Preview thumbnails Preview thumbnails associate representative pictures with an episode or a navigable point within media. Artwork language selection Artwork language selection chooses among role- and identity-matched resources using visible-text language, neutral/unknown status and the application's fallback policy. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB: Image configuration and paths TMDB: Image language filtering RFC 4647: Language matching

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/Meta.title: Artwork language selection | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/Meta.keywords: Artwork language selection Artwork language selection chooses among role- and identity-matched resources using visible-text language, neutral/unknown status and the application's fallback policy. Artwork language usually concerns text visible in the image, such as a localized title. It need not match the original spoken language, a subtitle track or the app's menu language. Filter the intended role before comparing size An original candidate set for one movie is: Candidate Role Text language Dimensions P1 Poster French 600 × 900 P2 Poster English 1200 × 1800 P3 Backdrop French 1920 × 1080 P4 Poster Textless/neutral 900 × 1350 For a French poster request with a minimum width of 500 pixels, P1 matches the role and language and has adequate width. P2 has more pixels but another textual presentation; P3 has the requested language but another role. The criteria's order belongs to the selected policy. This table is a teaching example, not a reconstruction of Emby's internal ranking. Textless and unknown are different observations A deliberately textless image can serve several audiences. An image with no known language label may still contain words. Provider interfaces represent these states through their own conventions. Legacy Fanart v3 documents 00 for textless artwork; TMDB's image interface supports additional language filtering including a null representation. Do not reinterpret those markers as ordinary BCP 47 tags without their source meaning. Language tags explains the general language model. A fallback should preserve its purpose If P1 is absent, an original policy can prefer the neutral poster P4 before another language's title image. Another product policy can choose differently. The selected value should remain identifiable as a fallback. A French movie title in metadata does not automatically translate an English poster or logo. In Emby, library/provider choices and the selected app presentation determine the available combination. A localized title and an artwork resource are separate selections even when they share an intended language. Cache and refresh retain context Reusing a previously selected English poster after a language change can concern cached/retained artwork rather than a wrong work match. Compare the candidate set, intended role/language and selected resource. Image replacement also has its own operation in Metadata Manager . Obtaining translated text does not prove that an existing image was replaced in the same operation. See Also Language tags for metadata Localized titles Media artwork roles Fanart.tv The Movie Database (TMDB) References TMDB: Image language filtering Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles Fanart.tv: Legacy v3 artwork metadata RFC 4647: Language matching

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/Meta.title: Media artwork roles | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/Meta.keywords: Media artwork roles An artwork role describes an image's presentation purpose and entity relationship, separately from its file format, dimensions or source. Artwork identifies or supports a media presentation. Its role describes where and why an image is used, rather than which decoder opens its bytes. Purposes have their own resources Role Purpose Poster A principal portrait-style identification image Backdrop A wider background behind the interface Transparent logo A compositable title/branding layer Embedded cover An image carried inside a media file Episode image An image associated with an episode Chapter image A preview associated with a programme position Embedded describes carriage, so an embedded image still needs its intended cover or other presentation role. Role, format and dimensions differ A JPEG can be a poster or backdrop. A PNG can be a transparent logo or an opaque rectangle. Width alone does not decide the entity or role. The selected image should also belong to the right movie, series, season, episode or album relationship. A high-resolution image for another edition or episode can be technically valid and visually unsuitable. Emby's image-type documentation describes role-aware views and applicable fallbacks. That product context is distinct from a provider's resource labels. A fallback serves a missing slot A view can use a primary image where its preferred role is absent. That supplies something to display; it does not transform the composition into an equally suitable poster, logo and background. The app's fitting/cropping rules can change what remains visible. A title near the top of a portrait poster can disappear when a centered wide crop is applied. Keep selected role and available fallback separate when evaluating the result. Selection combines several requirements Identity, role, language, dimensions, alpha and the available source all contribute. A larger wrong-language image need not be preferable to a smaller adequate match. Artwork language selection develops that choice. Image resizing explains what happens after a resource is selected. See Also Media posters Media backdrops Transparent media logos Artwork language selection How metadata providers work References TMDB: Image configuration and paths Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.title: Overview: Preview thumbnails | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.keywords: Overview: Preview thumbnails Preview thumbnails associate representative pictures with an episode or a navigable point within media. An episode thumbnail helps identify a programme; a chapter thumbnail represents a position used for navigation. Both may be derived from media, but they attach to different library relationships. Catalogue identity and navigation position give each kind of preview its own association. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Episode thumbnails An episode thumbnail is associated with a particular episode presentation or record, which can differ from series artwork and locally extracted frame previews. Chapter thumbnails A chapter thumbnail associates a rendered frame preview with a programme position, requiring the selected source, time mapping and image derivative to remain coherent. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB: Image configuration and paths FFmpeg: Container metadata options

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.title: Chapter thumbnails | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.keywords: Chapter thumbnails A chapter thumbnail associates a rendered frame preview with a programme position, requiring the selected source, time mapping and image derivative to remain coherent. A chapter image previews a programme position. It belongs to a particular media source and timeline as well as to the library item. This is a different relationship from the one selected episode image used for browsing. A position needs a corresponding picture An original programme can have chapter positions at 0, 45, 90 and 135 seconds . A derived image set associates each chosen position with a rendered picture and its image resource. The chapter label and the image can be correct only if they refer to the same source/time mapping. Another edit of the film can change that correspondence while retaining its work title. Seek access and target time are different In an original constant-rate model, picture PTS is n/24. A target at 46 seconds corresponds to picture 1104 . Suppose the usable earlier seek point is at 45 seconds , picture 1080 . The target lies 24 picture intervals later. The decoder can begin at the access point and continue toward the required presentation. That does not mean the picture at the access point is already the target image. This simple model describes timing, not measured decoder work. Real prediction, reordering and seek behavior depend on the stream and processing route. Presentation time selects the visible result A packet's decode order or arrival time can differ from its picture's presentation time. Packet timestamps explains those boundaries. A frame preview should represent the selected programme position, not merely whichever decoded packet happened to be reached first. A crop or colour conversion then affects the image produced from that picture. Regeneration follows source and recipe changes Replacing a local file with another cut can leave old chapter previews associated with the work. The old pictures may still look plausible while referring to another timeline. A different image recipe can also require updated derivatives. Keep selected source/version, chapter position and processing context together when comparing an Emby preview with the current video. A small cached image is the result of this derivation; it is not itself evidence that the current video's chapter mapping was re-evaluated. See Also Episode thumbnails Packet Timestamps Time Bases Image thumbnail generation References Matroska: Tag targets and semantics FFmpeg: Container metadata options

articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.title: Episode thumbnails | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/artwork/prev.keywords: Episode thumbnails An episode thumbnail is associated with a particular episode presentation or record, which can differ from series artwork and locally extracted frame previews. An episode image identifies or previews one episode. It can come from a catalogue asset or from a chosen local frame, depending on the route. A series poster describes another level of the library hierarchy. The image source has an identity Candidate source Association to check Provider episode image Selected episode record Local extracted frame Selected video and programme position Series artwork fallback Series relationship, not an episode-specific scene Correctly matching the series does not resolve every episode order. A recut release can divide the story differently, so a provider's episode 3 image may depict scenes outside the local part 3. The TheTVDB article develops that ordering context. Emby's TV naming documentation supplies the product's identification workflow. The useful still is a presentation choice A frame at a fixed offset can fall on a black transition, credits or an unrepresentative scene. A catalogue-selected image can serve recognition better, but it still needs to describe the intended episode. There is no universal rule that the first or central frame makes the best thumbnail. Identity and image selection answer different questions. Fitting can change what remains visible An episode image can have the programme's aspect or another supplied composition. The client tile and generated derivative can crop or fit it. A readable subject in the original can disappear at the smaller crop. Thumbnail generation explains the source/derivative boundary. A set of time-position previews serves navigation within the episode; chapter thumbnails explains that other relationship. One selected episode image does not encode every scene position. See Also TheTVDB Media artwork roles Chapter thumbnails Image thumbnail generation References TheTVDB: Official v4 API documentation and season types TMDB: Image configuration and paths

articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/in.title: Overview: Finding related media | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/in.keywords: Overview: Finding related media Metadata-driven discovery uses indexed values and relationships to support search, browsing and recommendations. Search and faceted browsing offer different ways to narrow a collection. Relationships can connect related works or people, while recommendation systems apply another selection model. This group shows how those experiences depend on the metadata available to the library and the interpretation applied to it. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Search indexing A search index derives lookup structures from selected metadata fields, with analysis, field scope, positions and ranking determining which items a query returns. Faceted browsing Faceted browsing narrows a defined item set through structured field membership, with combination rules and count scope explaining available choices. Metadata relationships Metadata relationships connect identified entities through directed, qualified meanings such as edition, credit and artwork association rather than through shared display wording alone. Recommendation systems A recommendation system generates and ranks eligible media candidates using content, behavior or other signals, then evaluates whether the chosen presentation serves the intended discovery goal. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References SQLite: FTS5 indexing and queries Unicode UAX 15: Normalization forms W3C SKOS: Concepts and labels Google: Recommendation systems

articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.title: Faceted browsing | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.keywords: Faceted browsing Faceted browsing narrows a defined item set through structured field membership, with combination rules and count scope explaining available choices. A facet filters items using a structured property such as genre, year or language. Its choices and counts refer to a defined item set. Start with a small explicit dataset These are original fictional records: Item Genre Year Language A Drama 2020 fr B Comedy 2020 en C Drama 2019 en D Documentary 2020 en E Drama 2020 en F Drama 2021 fr G Drama Unknown en A Drama filter selects A, C, E, F, G . A 2020 filter selects A, B, D, E . Applying both with AND leaves A and E . Adding language en leaves E . The result comes from membership in all selected sets, not a substring search over a rendered description. AND and OR describe different operations Within the genre facet, choosing Drama OR Comedy yields A, B, C, E, F, G . Combining that union with year 2020 leaves A, B, E . A product can use another selection rule. The useful description names which choices are OR alternatives and which facets must all match. For a multi-valued genre field, one item can belong to several choices. Counting each choice separately can legitimately exceed the number of distinct items. Counts can describe the current context After selecting Drama and 2020, the two remaining items have language counts fr: 1, en: 1 . Those differ from the complete dataset's language counts. They answer how many items could match within the current genre/year context. A self-excluding facet policy calculates a facet's options using the other filters while omitting its own active filter. With language en also active, the current result is E; the language facet can still show fr: 1 and en: 1 because it computes against Drama + 2020. That is a coherent way to offer alternatives, not proof of a bad count. An all-filters-applied policy would answer another question. Unknown values need an explicit place G has no known year. A 2020 constraint does not establish it as a match, and replacing Unknown with an invented year would corrupt the source. A browse policy can offer an unknown category, omit it from the year choices, or use another documented representation. Its count should retain that scope. In the Drama set, original year counts are 2019: 1, 2020: 2, 2021: 1, Unknown: 1 . Count the intended entity once Several files or joined credit rows can describe one library item. Counting those rows as separate movies can inflate a facet. The selected identity level matters: works, editions and local resources can have different useful totals. Deduplication should preserve that level rather than merely deduplicate equal titles. For Emby browsing, compare the selected library/eligible items, active filters, combination rules and displayed counts. This model does not prescribe the app's facet algorithm; it supplies the evidence needed to interpret the result. See Also Multi-valued metadata fields Genre taxonomies Search indexing for media metadata Missing metadata References W3C SKOS: Concepts and labels SQLite: FTS5 indexing and queries

articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.title: Recommendation systems for media | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.keywords: Recommendation systems for media A recommendation system generates and ranks eligible media candidates using content, behavior or other signals, then evaluates whether the chosen presentation serves the intended discovery goal. A recommendation proposes something useful to discover within an eligible media set. It can use descriptive features, known relationships, viewing behavior or a combination. The result depends on what the system is trying to help the viewer do: find a familiar style, explore something different, continue a collection or discover an unseen work. Generate candidates, score them, then choose a presentation Candidate generation narrows the pool. Scoring estimates a particular relationship or preference signal. A later selection/reranking stage can apply availability, diversity or presentation constraints. Those stages answer different questions. A high score among candidates does not explain why another item never entered the pool. The eligible set can also depend on the selected library and viewer context. A discovery result and a playback/source choice remain separate operations. Content similarity has a declared feature model For an original example, use three binary features: Drama, Railway, Night . An invented viewer profile is [1, 1, 0] . Candidate Feature vector A [1, 1, 0] B [1, 0, 1] C [0, 0, 1] Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of vector lengths. For A, the dot product is 2 and both lengths are √2, giving 1 . For B, the dot product is 1 with the same lengths, giving 0.5 . For C, the dot product is zero, giving 0 . The numbers express similarity in this feature model. They are not probabilities of enjoyment and not an Emby score. Other feature weights or representations can change the ordering. A genre tag is only one kind of evidence. Contributor relationships, plot topics and other supported features can add another view of relatedness. Behavior can supply another signal Consider these fictional viewing sets: Viewer Observed items U1 A, B U2 A, C U3 A, C Overlap with U2/U3 can supply a reason to consider C for U1, even though C has no overlap with the simple content profile above. That observation does not establish a universal preference rule. A recorded play can represent curiosity, shared-device use or an abandoned viewing, rather than an explicit approval. A behavior model therefore needs a definition of its observations and target. Completion, replay, explicit feedback and item exposure are different signals. Exposure affects the observed numbers Suppose candidate X was shown 100 times and received 10 selections, while Y was shown 10 times and received 2. Raw selection counts favor X. The observed selection rates are 10% and 20% respectively. Y's rate is based on fewer observations. The comparison does not prove a causal preference or a stable advantage; it shows why the denominator and observation context matter. A system that mostly shows already popular items gathers more data about them. Using those counts without considering exposure can reinforce its original presentation choices. Evaluate a stated discovery target An original held-out example treats C and E as the known relevant future items. A ranked list [C, D, E] contains two relevant items among three: Precision@3 = 2/3. Recall@3 = 2/2 = 1. These metrics describe that defined relevance set. They do not establish enjoyment, novel discovery or suitability of every item absent from the set. Using future behavior in the feature preparation for an earlier recommendation can leak the answer into the evaluation. A time-coherent comparison keeps the available evidence separate from the later outcome. New items and viewers need another route An item with no viewing observations can still have content metadata. A new viewer can still have explicit preferences or choose a starting item. Those inputs supply a cold-start path without pretending that nonexistent behavior was measured. A mixed design can use different evidence where each is available. Incorrect identification can contaminate both routes: the wrong synopsis changes content features, and merged/split item identities change recorded behavior. Diversity changes the final selection If A and another near-identical candidate both score highest, choosing only those can repeat the same narrow signal. A policy can retain A and include B to offer another facet of the profile. That is a tradeoff in the intended discovery experience, not necessarily a scoring error. The selection goal should make it assessable. For Emby-related discovery, evaluate the actual feature/behavior source, candidate set and selected result. The primary references describe recommendation designs; this original example does not assert which proprietary or plugin algorithm an installed server uses. See Also Metadata relationships Genre taxonomies Faceted browsing Media identification References Google: Recommendation systems Google: Content-based filtering Google: Collaborative filtering

articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.title: Metadata relationships | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.keywords: Metadata relationships Metadata relationships connect identified entities through directed, qualified meanings such as edition, credit and artwork association rather than through shared display wording alone. A metadata relationship connects entities with a meaning. “Directed by”, “edition of” and “poster for” are different links even when all are drawn as lines. Together, the entities and their relationships form a graph . An original graph preserves the levels Suppose local file F1 represents edition E1 of work W1. Another edition E2 belongs to W1, person P1 directs W1, and image I2 is a poster for E2. Source Relationship Target F1 Represents E1 E1 Edition of W1 E2 Edition of W1 W1 Directed by P1 I2 Poster for E2 F1 is not the catalogue work itself. Its codec or byte checksum describes another level than W1's title and credits. Direction determines the query To find other editions of F1's work, follow F1 to E1, then E1 to W1, then the edition relationships back to E2. To find other works by P1, use the director relationship in the appropriate direction. That query does not mean “other files with the same printed artist name”. A work related through an actor edge can answer another discovery question than a work related through a director edge. Qualifiers retain the actual responsibility Cast and crew credits develops person, role, character and ordering. A bare person-to-work line can lose those distinctions. Relationships can also have a source, applicable time or release context. A series credit and an episode guest credit need not make the same claim. Stable identities help prevent two people with equal names from being merged, while alternate labels can remain attached to one known entity. Asserted and derived links have different evidence A provider can explicitly state that an edition belongs to a work. A local process can derive a tentative relationship from title/year similarity. Those are different provenance histories. Similarity alone should not silently be stored as an unquestioned identity equivalence. An Emby library can expose useful associations without implementing the exact graph shown here. The conceptual levels explain why a recording match, a movie match and a file-version match support different related-data choices. Relatedness can drive discovery without collapsing identity A recommendation can use shared contributors, categories or edition relationships. The resulting “related item” is still another entity, not a duplicate merely because it shares some features. Keeping typed links makes that result explainable: another film by the director, another edition of the work, or another resource for the selected edition are three concrete relationships. See Also Provider identifiers Cast and crew credits Media identification Recommendation systems for media References Schema.org: Movie relationships Schema.org: Qualified roles W3C SKOS: Concepts and labels

articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.title: Search indexing for media metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/discovery/Me.keywords: Search indexing for media metadata A search index derives lookup structures from selected metadata fields, with analysis, field scope, positions and ranking determining which items a query returns. A reader searching for River Station can mean the title, while another search can mean any item mentioning a river or station. A useful search route needs a defined relationship between that query and the metadata fields it examines. An index prepares derived structures for that work. It is a representation of selected metadata, not another catalogue identity. An original corpus makes the lookup visible Consider these fictional records: Item Title Overview D1 River Station night train at station D2 Station Road river journeys D3 Quiet River river river night For this example only, the analyzer lowercases the English text and splits its words. That deliberately simple rule is not a universal multilingual tokenizer. A field-aware inverted index can retain entries such as: Field and term Item/position relationships title:river D1 at 0; D3 at 1 title:station D1 at 1; D2 at 0 overview:river D2 at 0; D3 at 0 and 1 overview:station D1 at 3 Instead of rereading every title for each term, the query can consult the relevant posting lists. The index's layout/compression and query engine determine its actual cost. Field scope changes the answer Across both fields, river occurs in all three items and station in D1/D2. An AND query returns D1 and D2 . Restricted to title, river has D1/D3 and station has D1/D2. Their intersection returns D1 only . Those results answer different questions correctly under the declared rules. D2's overview mentions river, so it belongs to the wider search even though its title is Station Road. A filename, person name or tag can form another field. Deciding which fields participate is part of the query contract, not merely a cosmetic label around one universal string. Phrase matching needs positions Both title words occur in D1 with river immediately before station. That supports the phrase River Station . The reversed phrase Station River is not present. Keeping only membership sets loses this order information. It can support AND queries but cannot distinguish that phrase by itself. Stop-word processing adds another choice. If an analyzer removes by from River by Station , retaining original position gaps lets the engine distinguish that wording from an adjacent River Station phrase. Renumbering every surviving token as adjacent can erase the distinction. The field boundary matters too: the last word of a title and first word of an overview should not accidentally become one phrase merely because an index concatenated fields. Ranking is separate from membership A query can first produce matching candidates, then order them. In an original presence-based score model for station: score = 3 if present in title + 1 if present in overview. D1 scores 4 , D2 3 , and D3 0 . The weights express this example's title preference; they are not an Emby score. More elaborate methods can account for term frequency, corpus frequency and document length. The linked BM25 reference documents one such similarity family. Repetition should not automatically be treated as independent evidence of relevance without the method's stated policy. A numerical score is not necessarily a probability that the viewer intended that work. Display ordering and an exact identifier lookup also serve different tasks. Analysis needs a text policy Unicode metadata explains canonical normalization and the value of preserving the display title while deriving a comparison key. Case folding, punctuation treatment, stemming and transliteration can improve some searches while changing distinctions. English word splitting cannot simply be assumed suitable for every script or for opaque provider identifiers. The query and indexed fields need compatible analysis. Lowercasing only the query while retaining case-sensitive postings can produce missed matches even when the title looks correct in the library. Updates must reach the derived representation If a title changes but its postings remain unchanged, the displayed item can be correct while searches still find its old wording. Replacing a resource at a path can likewise leave another version's derived technical fields. A coherent update removes or replaces obsolete index entries and installs the new analyzed values. The source record and index need a usable version relationship; rebuilding the same old source data does not discover a missing correction. In Emby, compare the imported field, selected search scope and actual returned items. The source/analysis/index/query boundaries identify what is being tested. This article does not infer that Emby's media search uses SQLite FTS5, Lucene or the illustrated weights. The result pool has its own scope Search can operate on a particular library, media type or eligible set. Ranking then orders that set rather than making every indexed item available to every viewer. A count computed over all records can disagree with a scoped result count legitimately. Faceted browsing develops those filters and the importance of counting distinct items. The complete observation is therefore the source data, field analysis, query semantics, eligible set and ranking. A visible title alone does not describe every one of those decisions. See Also Unicode metadata Sort titles Faceted browsing Metadata relationships References SQLite: FTS5 indexing and queries Lucene 10.3.1: BM25 similarity Unicode UAX 15: Normalization forms

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/index.title: Overview: Metadata fields and localization | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/index.keywords: Overview: Metadata fields and localization Metadata fields represent values and relationships whose meaning depends on type, vocabulary and context. A release date, genre and cast credit answer different questions about an item. Repeated values and localization add structure beyond a single display string. This branch gives those fields their own context, so inconsistent sorting or grouping can be traced to the representation rather than only to its visible label. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Multi-valued metadata fields A multi-valued metadata field preserves several entries with an applicable order, role and identity policy instead of treating every value as one punctuation-delimited string. Text and localization Text and localization rules connect character representation, language context and display or sorting choices. Release dates A release date describes a particular event with territory, edition and precision context rather than one universal timestamp for a work. Genre taxonomies A genre taxonomy organizes classification concepts and their labels or relationships, allowing consistent membership beyond matching display strings. Content ratings A content rating is a classification within a named scheme and release/territory context, distinct from an audience or critic opinion score. Cast and crew credits A credit relates a person or organization to a work through a role, optional character and presentation order, retaining identity beyond the printed name. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Xiph: Vorbis comment header TMDB: Release dates and certifications RFC 3339: Internet timestamps W3C SKOS: Concepts and labels

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.title: Cast and crew credits | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.keywords: Cast and crew credits A credit relates a person or organization to a work through a role, optional character and presentation order, retaining identity beyond the printed name.
