A credit is a relationship between a contributor and a work. It can retain a role, a character played and an order used for presentation. The printed name is a label for that relationship, not necessarily a unique person identifier. Identity and responsibility occupy different fields An original credit model could contain: Person key Printed name Role Character P1 Alex Baker Actor Conductor P1 Alex Baker Director — P2 Alex Baker Actor Station master P1 has two responsibilities. P2 is another invented person who happens to share the same name. Deduplicating every Alex Baker line loses both distinctions. A more useful key considers the person and the qualified relationship being represented. A character is another presentation relationship The actor's name and the character's name serve different purposes. A cast display can show both without treating the character as a separate actor record. The same performer can also portray several characters. Flattening those descriptions into an arbitrary separator string can make later imports ambiguous. Multiple-valued fields develops why list boundaries and qualifiers should survive serialization. Credit order has meaning too Cast order can reflect a supplied presentation rather than alphabetic ordering or importance inferred by the library. Crew can be grouped by responsibility. An original ordered sequence of three credits contains more information than an unordered set of their names. Sorting the printed names for convenience changes that sequence. In Emby, compare the imported people/role information with the selected provider or local record. The pinned NFO parser has actor handling, but recognizing one input form does not imply that every provider credit category maps identically. Attach the credit to the intended work A series-level credit, an episode guest appearance and a particular music-video production can describe different scopes. Copying series credits into every episode can imply participation not established by those records. Metadata relationships explains how directed, qualified links retain that context. A useful correction identifies the contributor, role, work and source instead of changing a printed name until the list looks plausible. See Also Multi-valued metadata fields Metadata relationships Provider identifiers NFO metadata files References Schema.org: Qualified roles Schema.org: Movie relationships Emby NFO parser: 21 July 2026 snapshot

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.title: Content ratings | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.keywords: Content ratings A content rating is a classification within a named scheme and release/territory context, distinct from an audience or critic opinion score. A content rating describes a classification under a particular scheme. A community rating of 8/10 describes an opinion score. The two values should not be used as if they answer the same question. Labels belong to their schemes Example Context PG-13 U.S. MPA film classification TV-PG U.S. television guideline label 8/10 An opinion-score scale A similar-looking PG component does not make the movie and television labels identical contracts. Their schemes and applicable descriptors supply the meaning. A useful record retains scheme, territory and the relevant release or presentation context. A film's classification can differ across territories or editions. Descriptors can supply more context Some schemes accompany the broad category with information about the reason/content. That is another part of the classification relationship, not a second critic score. Preserving only an unqualified display string can discard the source/territory context used for a later comparison. In Emby, Metadata Manager documents parental-rating fields as inputs to configured access behavior. Accurate identity and imported classification consequently matter beyond the displayed label. Missing and unrated are different states An absent field can mean that the selected source did not supply a usable classification. An explicitly recorded unrated status is another claim. Neither should be guessed from a genre such as Family. A provider failure also does not establish a low classification. The server's configured handling of unknown or overridden values belongs to its product rules. The metadata itself supplies evidence, rather than a universal allow/block flag. Corrections need the intended release A classification for a differently edited version can be accurate for that version while unsuitable for the local presentation. Compare the identity, territory, edition and source before replacing the field. Do not make a cross-scheme conversion merely because two labels contain similar words. The source's defined scheme and the application's supported policy determine the usable relationship. See Also Missing metadata Conflicting metadata The Open Movie Database (OMDb) Genre taxonomies References MPA: Movie rating categories TV Parental Guidelines: Television content labels TMDB: Release dates and certifications

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.title: Genre taxonomies | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.keywords: Genre taxonomies A genre taxonomy organizes classification concepts and their labels or relationships, allowing consistent membership beyond matching display strings. Genre labels help readers browse works with related styles or traditions. A taxonomy can organize those classification concepts, their labels and any defined broader/narrower relationships. A concept can have several labels An original vocabulary model is: Concept key English label French label C1 Drama Drame C2 Mystery Mystère C1's labels name one classification concept. Counting Drama and Drame as unrelated categories because the strings differ can split the same intended membership. A vocabulary can also define preferred and alternate labels. Deciding that Sci-Fi and Science Fiction are synonyms requires that vocabulary relationship, rather than a universal rule to merge every similar string. Membership can overlap A mystery drama can belong to both C1 and C2. That does not require two copies of the movie. A browse view that counts each genre independently can therefore have category totals greater than the number of distinct works. Faceted browsing develops the corresponding set arithmetic. In Emby, compare imported genre entries with the selected browse/filter result. A display list can be localized or curated while the intended classification remains stable. Genre, subject and rating answer different questions Railway can be a useful subject keyword for a story without being a universal film genre. A parental classification describes another relationship; it does not automatically replace Drama or Mystery. A recommendation system can use several such features, but their meanings should remain explicit. Combining them into one label string makes later filtering harder to interpret. Vocabularies can change A provider, an editorial catalogue and a user's personal organization can use different category granularity. A broader concept and a more specific subgenre need not be contradictions. SKOS supplies a reference model for concepts and labels; it does not mandate that every media library implement the full model. The relevant decisions are which vocabulary the entries belong to, how aliases/localized labels are mapped and what membership a query tests. See Also Multi-valued metadata fields Faceted browsing Search indexing for media metadata Content ratings References W3C SKOS: Concepts and labels DCMI: Metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.title: Multi-valued metadata fields | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.keywords: Multi-valued metadata fields A multi-valued metadata field preserves several entries with an applicable order, role and identity policy instead of treating every value as one punctuation-delimited string. A field can contain several artists, genres, languages or credits. Its representation needs to retain the entries and the relationships that give them meaning. Consider the single name Baker, Alex . Splitting every comma would turn one entry into two people. Lists, sets and qualified records differ Representation Meaning to preserve Ordered credit list Entry order and join/presentation context Genre set Membership under the chosen vocabulary Repeated tag values Several source values for a named field Qualified person credits Person identity plus role/character/order The same person can be both actor and director. Deduplicating by person name alone can erase one valid responsibility. A creator sequence and a subject-keyword bag can likewise have different ordering semantics. The serialization should not make those choices accidentally. A punctuation string loses boundaries An original structured artist list might be: ["Baker, Alex", "North / South"] A comma- or slash-joined export requires a defined escaping/separator convention if it is meant to be read back. Without one, the reader cannot distinguish real punctuation from a separator. Vorbis repeated entries, ID3 version-specific value conventions and XML repeated elements provide different representations. A converter must interpret the source's semantics before producing the target. In Emby, compare the source list with the imported artist/genre/credit field. Several values visibly joined in the app do not prove that they were stored as one indivisible string. A merge policy changes membership Take existing genres [Drama, Railway] and incoming values [Drama, Mystery] . Operation Result Replace Drama, Mystery Stable deduplicated union Drama, Railway, Mystery Blind append Drama, Railway, Drama, Mystery Repeating the union leaves the same membership. Repeating blind append accumulates duplicates. Replacement can remove deliberate local classification; union can retain a stale label. Precedence develops that decision. The field's purpose and operation decide which result is appropriate. Filtering uses entries, not display punctuation A genre filter can test membership in the structured set. A person filter should refer to the intended identity and credit context, rather than find an arbitrary substring in a rendered credit line. Keep source entries and display formatting separate. That lets a library change its presentation without silently changing which people or categories the item belongs to. See Also Cast and crew credits Vorbis comments Metadata precedence Faceted browsing References Xiph: Vorbis comment header Schema.org: Qualified roles DCMI: Metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.title: Release dates | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/Metad.keywords: Release dates A release date describes a particular event with territory, edition and precision context rather than one universal timestamp for a work. A film or album can be released through several events. A premiere, regional theatrical opening and later physical edition need not share one date. Name the event before choosing the year For an invented film: Event Date Context Premiere 2020-02-20 Initial public presentation Theatrical release 2020-05-12 One territory Theatrical release 2020-06-19 Another territory Physical edition 2021-01-05 Later distribution event A displayed year of 2020 and a physical-release year of 2021 can both be valid within their fields. They are not automatically competing identities. TMDB's release-date interface provides event types and country context. In Emby, the displayed item date/year reflects the applicable source and selected field representation. Preserve precision that is actually known Supplied information What is known 2020 Year only 2020-05 Year and month 2020-05-12 Calendar day A full timestamp with offset A specified clock/instant relationship Substituting January 1 for a known year can make unknown precision look like a verified date. A library may use a sorting convention, but that convention should remain distinguishable from the source's claim. These partial values illustrate metadata precision; they are not all complete RFC 3339 timestamps. A calendar date and an instant differ A release announced for a particular day can be a calendar-date relationship. A timestamp at midnight UTC describes an instant that may fall on another calendar day in another time zone. Converting every date through a timestamp pipeline can therefore shift the displayed release day without improving the source fact. The field's data type and event meaning determine whether time-zone conversion is appropriate. Sorting selects a relationship Sorting by first release, local release, edition issue or date added can produce different useful sequences. Date added describes a library activity rather than a release event. When two sources disagree, compare event, territory, edition and precision through conflicting metadata . Choosing a date with the right scope is more informative than forcing every record to agree on one year. See Also Conflicting metadata The Movie Database (TMDB) TheTVDB Sort titles References TMDB: Release dates and certifications RFC 3339: Internet timestamps DCMI: Metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.title: Overview: Text and localization | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.keywords: Overview: Text and localization Text and localization rules connect character representation, language context and display or sorting choices. A translated title and a sort title can legitimately differ from the original display name. Language tags identify context, while Unicode describes the stored characters. These pages distinguish those roles so a library can preserve the intended text and still organize it appropriately for the viewer. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Unicode metadata Unicode metadata represents text through defined characters and encodings, while normalization, search keys and locale ordering are separate transformations. Language tags A language tag identifies a linguistic presentation with applicable language, script, region and extension information, while selection and fallback remain separate policies. Localized titles Localized titles provide language- or region-associated labels for one work, independently of its original title and scoped catalogue identity. Sort titles A sort title is a presentation-order key that can differ from the displayed title, with locale, numeric and tie-breaking policies determining the resulting sequence. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Unicode UAX 15: Normalization forms RFC 5646: Language tags TMDB: Language and region requests RFC 4647: Language matching Unicode CLDR: Locale collation

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.title: Language tags for metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.keywords: Language tags for metadata A language tag identifies a linguistic presentation with applicable language, script, region and extension information, while selection and fallback remain separate policies. A metadata language choice can affect which title or overview a viewer receives. A language tag describes that presentation; it does not identify a different film or translate its audio. Subtags carry different information Example Interpretation en English en-US English with a United States region context zh-Hant Chinese in traditional script zh-Hant-TW Chinese, traditional script, Taiwan region context Language, script and region are related but distinct. The region does not universally tell a reader which script or spoken dialect every resource contains. BCP 47 defines the tag structure. A conventional casing such as en-US helps readability, while the defined comparison rules are not a case-sensitive identity of movie records. A field's language needs its own scope The language of an overview, the original language of a work, and a local audio track's language can differ. Copying one into another changes what the field claims. A translated title does not prove that the chosen video has that language track. An artwork-language value may instead describe text visible in a poster. In Emby, distinguish the library's descriptive-language context from subtitle preferences and the app's interface language. Provider conventions need interpretation A provider may accept a language-region request, a narrower language code or a special neutral marker. Those contracts should not be rewritten as if every string were a valid BCP 47 tag. For example, a legacy artwork marker can identify textless content using a provider-specific value. Unknown language and deliberately textless artwork also need not mean the same thing. Keep the source convention with its mapped meaning. Matching and fallback are chosen operations RFC 4647 defines language matching approaches. A concrete application still decides its available set, desired range and fallback behavior. An original library policy could try a requested fr-CA title, then available fr, then a designated original title. That is a useful example, not a required fallback chain for every provider or Emby installation. A script-sensitive request should preserve its purpose. Falling from a traditional-script request to any Chinese string can choose a presentation the viewer did not intend. Localized titles shows how those alternatives retain one underlying entity while supplying different labels. See Also Localized titles Unicode metadata Artwork language selection Subtitle language preferences References RFC 5646: Language tags RFC 4647: Language matching TMDB: Language and region requests

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.title: Localized titles | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.keywords: Localized titles Localized titles provide language- or region-associated labels for one work, independently of its original title and scoped catalogue identity. A film can have several valid labels associated with different audiences. An original title and a localized release title describe the same work through different wording. One entity can supply several labels For an invented work: Label role Example Original title La Gare English presentation The Station French presentation La Gare Provider identity One selected movie reference The English wording is not another provider entity merely because its characters differ. Conversely, a different film named The Station remains a different work. Title disambiguation explains that distinction. Selection needs an available-language set A library can choose a title using requested language, supplied alternatives and a fallback policy. If an exact fr-CA label is absent but fr is present, one policy can select fr; another can retain the original title according to its rules. The result should keep its source/language relationship. Filling a requested English field with an original French label without describing the fallback can make the record misleading. Emby's library context and configured metadata sources govern the product route. A user's interface language does not by itself establish that every item has been fetched anew in that language. A cache must retain the presentation request An original conceptual key includes entity and requested language. If a lookup cached only the entity ID, a later request can reuse the earlier language's label accidentally. A stale title and a wrong identity are then different problems. The file can remain matched to the intended movie while displaying a label from another presentation request. Preserve edits with their purpose A user can deliberately choose a local title, an edition suffix or another useful display label. Metadata Manager documents editing and protecting fields through refresh. A provider title correction should be assessed against that purpose. The original label, localized label and selected display value can coexist in a structured record rather than being flattened into one supposedly authoritative string. See Also Language tags for metadata Sort titles Title disambiguation The Movie Database (TMDB) References DCMI: Metadata terms TMDB: Language and region requests RFC 4647: Language matching

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.title: Sort titles | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.keywords: Sort titles A sort title is a presentation-order key that can differ from the displayed title, with locale, numeric and tie-breaking policies determining the resulting sequence. A sort title controls presentation order without necessarily replacing the displayed title. A library can show The Station while ordering it under Station . The examined Emby NFO parser maps sorttitle separately from the item name. That provides a concrete distinction between display wording and an ordering field. Removing an article is a language decision Display title Original illustrative sort key The Station Station A River River Station II Station II This example uses English presentation rules. Applying the same article-removal list to every language can remove genuine title content or leave another language's article untouched. An explicit authored sort title can retain that decision. It should not be treated as another work identifier. Collation adds an ordering context An original locale experiment uses the strings A, Z, Å . An English collation can place Å with the A group; Swedish places Å after Z. The illustrated results use a recorded runtime's Intl.Collator with explicit locales. They are not a measurement of Emby's current sort routine. Code-point order, normalized byte order and human language collation need not produce the same sequence. Unicode metadata develops the preceding normalization boundary. Numeric ordering is another choice Lexical ordering can place Station 10 before Station 2 , because it compares the first differing character. A numeric-aware collation can instead compare the number values and place 2 first. That option should not silently reinterpret opaque provider IDs as numeric title fragments. Its useful scope is the chosen display-order key. Equal keys need a stable tie-break Two entries can legitimately have the same sort title. A stable secondary criterion, such as another defined field and ultimately an item identity, can make pagination consistent. Without a coherent ordering, moving through pages can repeat or miss entries when equal-key positions change. The ordering model and current dataset determine that behavior. For Emby, compare the displayed title, available sort field and selected view's order. Editing only the display name need not change a deliberately retained sort key. See Also Localized titles Unicode metadata NFO metadata files Search indexing for media metadata References Unicode CLDR: Locale collation Emby NFO parser: 21 July 2026 snapshot

articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.title: Unicode metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/fields/text-.keywords: Unicode metadata Unicode metadata represents text through defined characters and encodings, while normalization, search keys and locale ordering are separate transformations. Metadata text can contain several scripts, combining marks and punctuation. Correct representation begins with interpreting the file's bytes using the specified encoding. The word café also demonstrates a second boundary: equivalent visible text can use different character sequences. One visible word, two stored sequences Representation Code points UTF-8 bytes c a f followed by U+00E9 4 5 c a f e followed by U+0301 5 6 The second sequence uses an ordinary e plus a combining acute accent. For these strings, NFC normalization produces the composed form; NFD produces the decomposed form. A byte comparison before normalization can therefore report inequality even though the intended text agrees. A hash of the file's bytes remains a byte relationship; it should not be reinterpreted as a normalized-title identity. Decoding comes before normalization A decoder chooses characters from bytes. Normalization then transforms a character sequence under its defined rules. If UTF-8 bytes were interpreted through the wrong encoding and became garbled characters, normalization generally cannot infer the original bytes and repair that mistake. It acts on the characters it receives. ID3v2's text-encoding information and Vorbis's UTF-8 value contract provide concrete input boundaries. A library needs the right one before applying any search-oriented text transformation. Compatibility folding can discard distinctions NFKC can map the circled digit ① to ordinary 1 . That can be useful in a chosen comparison policy, but it changes a distinction present in the original title. Canonical normalization, case folding, punctuation removal and transliteration are different operations. They should not all be called “make it Unicode”. An opaque provider identifier also has its own comparison contract. A presentation-oriented normalization policy should not rewrite every identifier in the record. Preserve the title and derive a useful key A library can retain the authored text for display while deriving another key for searching. The search key can normalize or fold selected differences to improve candidate recall. That does not make the resulting strings unique work IDs. Two distinct films can share the same normalized title. For Emby metadata comparisons, separate source bytes, decoded text, imported display value and any search/sort representation. A correct database title can still be presented with a different font; a missing glyph is a rendering issue rather than proof of bad decoding. Alphabetical order adds locale rules Unicode code-point order is not a universal human alphabetical order. Locale collation can place accented letters differently and can apply case or numeric options. Sort titles develops that relationship with an original locale example. Normalizing a title does not by itself choose the language's sorting policy. See Also Language tags for metadata Sort titles ID3v2 audio tags Vorbis comments Unicode in subtitles References Unicode UAX 15: Normalization forms Unicode CLDR: Locale collation ID3.org: ID3v2.4 frame definitions Xiph: Vorbis comment header

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Overview: External identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Overview: External identifiers External identifiers name entries within a particular provider or catalogue namespace. An identifier is meaningful within the system that assigned it. IMDb and MusicBrainz IDs connect to different kinds of catalogue records, and a provider ID should retain that context when it travels through a file or library. The pages here explain the record being identified rather than treating every ID as a universal title key. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Provider identifiers A provider identifier names a record within a provider's namespace and entity model, independently of a local file path or displayed title. IMDb identifiers IMDb identifiers distinguish catalogue title and person records, with published dataset fields preserving the keys as strings and recording entity relationships separately. MusicBrainz identifiers MusicBrainz identifiers are UUID-shaped keys for distinct music entities, so recording, release and release-group references must retain their intended scope. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects MusicBrainz: Recordings

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: IMDb identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: IMDb identifiers IMDb identifiers distinguish catalogue title and person records, with published dataset fields preserving the keys as strings and recording entity relationships separately. IMDb uses identifiers for catalogue entities rather than relying on display titles as unique keys. Its published datasets expose title keys as tconst and person keys as nconst . A title key does not determine the title type Title identifiers commonly have a tt prefix; person identifiers have nm . Those are different reference roles. Published field/context What it represents tconst A title's identifier titleType The title's category, such as film, series or episode nconst A person identifier Episode parentTconst Reference from an episode to its parent series The tt prefix alone does not distinguish a movie from a series or episode. That meaning is supplied by the record and its relationships. An episode's identifier and its series identifier are not interchangeable, even when the library normally displays the series title first. Preserve the complete string Treat the identifier as a string. Removing its prefix or leading zeroes changes the textual key; assuming every identifier has one permanent numeric width can also make a parser reject later records. An original shape illustration is tt followed by digits , not a claim that those digits encode year, genre or popularity. The identifier can anchor a selected match while the record's primary and original titles provide different descriptive labels. A localized display name need not change the associated title entity. Reference the intended library entity For an Emby movie, series or episode, a provider key should describe the entity being edited. Attaching a parent series key to an episode as if it were the episode's own identity collapses that relationship. Provider identifiers explains why the provider namespace still accompanies the string. Metadata Manager documents the product's matching/editing context. See Also Provider identifiers Title disambiguation Media identification References IMDb: Published dataset identifier and title fields

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: MusicBrainz identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: MusicBrainz identifiers MusicBrainz identifiers are UUID-shaped keys for distinct music entities, so recording, release and release-group references must retain their intended scope. A MusicBrainz Identifier , or MBID, is a UUID-shaped reference to a MusicBrainz entity. It is not a hash of an audio file and does not contain a readable artist/title description. Shape and entity scope belong together An invented UUID-shape example is: 11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555 This demonstrates textual form only; it is not supplied as a MusicBrainz lookup for a real artist or release. Entity Meaning needed for matching Artist A credited artist entity Recording An audio recording relationship Release A particular issued product/edition Release group The broader grouping of related releases Work A musical-work relationship The key's spelling does not tell the reader which field it belongs in. Preserve the associated entity context instead of treating every music UUID as an interchangeable album ID. One recording can have several release contexts Take an invented recording, Platform Lights . It appears as track 2 on a standard album and track 5 on a later compilation. Matching that recording identifies an audio relationship. It does not decide which release's cover, date, barcode or track order belongs to the local album. A release group can collect several issued releases of the broader album concept. The standard and deluxe releases can share that group while having different product details and track lists. A track belongs to its release/medium context and references a recording. Keeping those levels separate avoids using a track position as if it were an intrinsic property of the recording. A fingerprint supplies evidence, not every identifier An acoustic match can help identify recorded audio. It need not establish the physical or digital edition from which the file came. Combine that evidence with release tags, artist credits, track lists and other appropriate product information. Acoustic fingerprinting develops that separation. Different encodings can share an audio relationship while having different byte hashes. An MBID does not verify that two local files have identical encoded content. Merges can preserve earlier references MusicBrainz documents redirects when entities are merged, and one entity can consequently have more than one associated MBID. A redirect is a provider-defined identity relationship, not permission to discard entity type. For Emby music matching, distinguish recording/artist references from release or release-group context. Music naming documentation provides the product's local library guidance; the provider's model explains why a plausible UUID in the wrong field can still select the wrong metadata. See Also Provider identifiers Acoustic fingerprinting Media identification Descriptive metadata References MusicBrainz: Recordings MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects MusicBrainz: Release groups MusicBrainz: Releases

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Provider identifiers | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Provider identifiers A provider identifier names a record within a provider's namespace and entity model, independently of a local file path or displayed title. A provider identifier refers to a record in a particular catalogue. The useful key includes its namespace and entity context , not just the printable value. A value is only one part of the reference Consider this invented key model: (provider namespace, entity type, identifier string) Reference Interpretation Provider A, movie, "42" A movie record in A Provider B, movie, "42" Another provider's movie record Provider A, series, "42" A potentially different entity class in A Local library, item, "42" A server's own item relationship The identical string does not establish that those references point to the same thing. A catalogue's actual API determines which entity classes share or separate identifier namespaces. A local path is another kind of address. Renaming a file need not change its associated work, and one work can have several local file versions. Keep opaque keys as keys Identifiers can contain prefixes, leading zeroes or UUID punctuation. Converting them into integers or stripping characters for cosmetic reasons can change the reference. The key generally should not be reverse-engineered into a title, release date or quality judgment. A large numeric value does not imply a higher-resolution movie. IMDb and MusicBrainz show concrete schemes. Their values have different forms and entity models. Identity and descriptive values can change independently A provider can correct a title without creating a new work. A record merge can also introduce redirects or another canonical relationship under that provider's rules. Those changes need a defined interpretation. A stored old identifier does not become the key to an unrelated record merely because its display text changed. The selected record still needs the intended scope. A valid music release identifier placed into a field intended for a recording can make subsequent lookup use the wrong entity. An Emby item has several identity relationships A library item can have a server-local identity, provider references and one or more media resources. They serve different actions. In Emby, Metadata Manager is the documented place for reviewing a match and its related fields. Compare the provider namespace and entity being corrected, rather than replacing every identifier with the same number. A provider work ID also does not prove an exact edition match for subtitles. Subtitle release matching considers the extra timing and content evidence. See Also IMDb identifiers MusicBrainz identifiers Media identification Metadata precedence References IMDb: Published dataset identifier and title fields MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Overview: Identification and matching | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Overview: Identification and matching Media identification connects a source item to the intended catalogue entry using names, identifiers and other matching evidence. Two works can share a title, and one work can appear under several names. Identification therefore needs enough context to distinguish the intended entry. External IDs and fingerprints supply particular evidence, while missing or conflicting metadata describe the cases where that evidence is incomplete or disagrees. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media identification Media identification associates a local resource with the intended work or catalogue entity using content context, search evidence and scoped identifiers. Title disambiguation Title disambiguation uses type, date, people and naming context to distinguish entities that share similar or identical display titles. External identifiers External identifiers name entries within a particular provider or catalogue namespace. Acoustic fingerprinting Acoustic fingerprinting derives a compact audio-content representation that a matching system can compare with known recordings, independently of filenames and byte checksums. Missing metadata Missing metadata is a field-level absence whose cause can lie in the source, acquisition, parsing, mapping or selection rather than in one universal refresh failure. Conflicting metadata Conflicting metadata requires comparison of entity, field meaning, scope, version and provenance before selecting or correcting the displayed value. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects MusicBrainz: Release groups FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation W3C PROV Model Primer

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Acoustic fingerprinting | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Acoustic fingerprinting Acoustic fingerprinting derives a compact audio-content representation that a matching system can compare with known recordings, independently of filenames and byte checksums. Acoustic fingerprinting builds a compact representation from audio content. A matching system compares that representation with indexed references to help identify recorded material. This makes it useful when a filename or title tag is missing or misleading. It supplies another kind of evidence alongside descriptive matching. Decode, describe, compare, identify A pipeline first obtains audio samples, then computes its fingerprint representation. A lookup compares it with known reference data and returns candidate relationships or match evidence. Chromaprint's library accepts decoded, uncompressed audio; its documentation explicitly separates fingerprint calculation from reading encoded file formats. A tool supplying it with samples therefore needs an appropriate decode path. Fingerprint generation and provider lookup are also different operations. Computing a fingerprint locally does not inherently assign an artist, release or MusicBrainz identifier. A landmark experiment makes timing consistency visible One approach identifies useful time-frequency landmarks and compares hashed relationships. Avery Wang's ISMIR paper describes a landmark-based audio search design. For an original simplified experiment , suppose three matched landmark keys occur at these positions: Landmark key Query time Candidate A time Candidate A offset hA 2 s 12 s 10 s hB 3 s 13 s 10 s hC 5 s 15 s 10 s All three support the same displacement: the query excerpt begins ten seconds into candidate A. Another candidate contains the same three simplified keys at 12, 20 and 28 seconds. Its offsets are 10, 17 and 23 seconds . It has isolated key matches without one consistently supported alignment. The experiment illustrates why agreement in time helps reject accidental feature matches. It does not implement the paper's hashing, feature selection or a production confidence threshold. A real system needs enough useful evidence, tolerance appropriate to its representation and a policy for ambiguous or weak matches. Short, repetitive or heavily altered audio can challenge those decisions. Fingerprints and file hashes answer different questions A byte checksum evaluates encoded bytes under a specified checksum algorithm. Changing the container or codec normally changes those bytes. An acoustic representation instead describes chosen features of decoded content. A robust implementation can retain useful similarity across some encoding differences. Its invariances are design choices: a scheme tolerant of compression is not automatically tolerant of every pitch, speed, mix or noise change. Chromaprint documents a particular design for near-identical audio and related uses. It should not be presented as identical to the landmark experiment above or as an unrestricted recognition solution for any short noisy recording. A recording is not an album edition A recognized recording can appear on an original album, a compilation and later issued products. An acoustic relationship alone does not identify which release's artwork, track number or release country belongs to the local album. MusicBrainz identifiers keep recording, release and release-group relationships distinct. Use accompanying release metadata and track-list context where the action needs that level of identity. An acoustic match also does not establish that two files are byte-identical, fully undamaged or equally high quality. The evidence concerns the features that were compared. Apply the evidence at its actual boundary For an Emby music-identification comparison, distinguish supported local tags, any fingerprint-capable integration and the catalogue relationship finally selected. This article explains fingerprint technology; it does not declare that every Emby installation performs the illustrated analysis automatically. A useful match record names the algorithm/service context, supplied audio segment, candidate entity and relevant evidence. See Also Media identification MusicBrainz identifiers Provider identifiers Technical media metadata References Avery Wang: An Industrial-Strength Audio Search Algorithm, ISMIR 2003 AcoustID: Chromaprint inputs and fingerprinting Chromaprint: Algorithm scope and implementation MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects MusicBrainz: Releases

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Conflicting metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Conflicting metadata Conflicting metadata requires comparison of entity, field meaning, scope, version and provenance before selecting or correcting the displayed value. Two differing values are not automatically contradictory. They may describe different entities, events, languages or resource versions. A useful conflict comparison first asks whether the values are meant to answer the same question. Test scope before choosing a winner Differing values Relationship to examine Original title and translated display title Different valid labels for one work Festival year and regional release year Different release events 20:15 at offset +02:00 and 18:15 UTC Same instant in different representations Source video width 1280 and current width 1920 Different encode/file versions Film synopsis and same-title series synopsis Different entities or a mistaken match Camera capture time and file-copy time Different activities For the timestamp example, subtracting two hours from 20:15 yields 18:15 UTC. Replacing both strings with one without retaining the offset can instead remove useful context. Likewise, changing a translated title to match the original title can discard a deliberate presentation choice while doing nothing to improve identity. Genuine competing claims need provenance If two sources disagree about the same release event, both should be tied to their source and scope. Check whether one reflects a correction, a different edition, a parse/mapping error or unsupported inference. The provenance article explains those annotations. Retrieval time alone does not make the newly fetched claim authoritative: it may be an older catalogue value copied into a fresh response. A technical claim can be verified against the intended current file. A descriptive claim may instead require the relevant catalogue or release evidence. They do not share one universal proof method. Identity errors have broad consequences A wrong provider match can install a consistent title, synopsis, date and cast set for the wrong work. The fields agreeing with one another does not prove they belong to the local resource. In that case, correcting only the display title leaves the underlying relationship unresolved. Identification develops how the intended entity is selected. A correct identity with two local title candidates is a different problem: precedence can determine which presentation value remains. Keep a correction specific In Emby, review the entity and fields being edited through Metadata Manager , using its documented persistence controls where appropriate. Record why the selected value fits the intended scope. A correction can preserve both an original and a localized label, retain two different event dates in their proper fields, or replace an old probe result. It need not erase every difference to make the record useful. See Also Metadata provenance Metadata precedence Title disambiguation Exif photo metadata References W3C PROV Model Primer DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms IMDb: Published dataset identifier and title fields

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Media identification | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Media identification Media identification associates a local resource with the intended work or catalogue entity using content context, search evidence and scoped identifiers. Identification connects a local media resource to an intended entity. For a film, that may be a catalogue's movie record. For music, a recording and an issued album release can require different identities. The encoded file's checksum identifies its byte content under that checksum algorithm. It does not, by itself, identify the film title in a provider's catalogue. Generate candidates, then assess the match Consider an invented filename suggesting The Station , 2020, in a movie library. A title search returns: Candidate Title Year Entity type A The Station 2020 Film B The Station 2020 Television series C The Station 1982 Film Title wording alone cannot choose among them. Year and media-type context support A in this example. A search result is a candidate, not a completed identification. After selection, a scoped provider identifier can retain the chosen relationship while descriptions and artwork are obtained. If the filename's year is wrong, a rigid exact-year rule can reject the intended work. Matching evidence needs an appropriate interpretation rather than an assumption that every local label is authoritative. More specific clues can resolve ambiguity For episodes, the series identity and ordering context matter alongside a number in the filename. For music, artist, track listing, release information and supported acoustic fingerprints can supply other evidence. Title disambiguation develops name/date clues. Provider identifiers explain the namespace and entity relationship of the chosen key. The algorithm and confidence policy belong to the implementation. The example above is an evidence comparison, not a reconstruction of Emby's internal matching score. Work identity does not describe every representation A standard and extended film edit can share a catalogue work identity while having different timelines. A dubbed encode can add another audio presentation. Technical probing describes the actual streams; it should not be replaced with properties guessed from the work's provider page. In music, one recording can appear on several releases with different track positions or artwork. A recording match alone therefore does not establish an album edition. The appropriate identity level depends on the action: finding a synopsis, choosing release artwork and aligning subtitles can require different additional evidence. No public match is a valid outcome A personal home video may have no commercial catalogue record. It can still have a local title, date, description and technical properties. For Emby, library context , naming guidance and Metadata Manager provide the documented identification/editing workflow. See Also Title disambiguation Provider identifiers Acoustic fingerprinting Conflicting metadata Technical media metadata References IMDb: Published dataset identifier and title fields MusicBrainz: Identifier model and redirects MusicBrainz: Releases

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Missing metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Missing metadata Missing metadata is a field-level absence whose cause can lie in the source, acquisition, parsing, mapping or selection rather than in one universal refresh failure. A blank overview in the library establishes that the displayed record lacks that overview. It does not identify where the information was lost or whether the source ever contained it. Locate the missing field's boundary Observation Possible boundary Provider has no record for a home video No applicable descriptive source Selected provider record has no overview Field absent at the source Resource could not be obtained Acquisition did not supply usable data Sidecar contains the field but uses an unsupported mapping Import does not create that library field Correct value is a rejected candidate Selection/protection policy Current source differs from a cached or earlier record Version/freshness relationship These cases call for different evidence. Repeating the same request cannot create a provider record that does not exist or add support for an unrecognized property. A successful download also does not establish successful field import. Readability, syntax and mapping come after acquisition. Ask a field-specific question For a missing title, inspect the relevant identity and descriptive source. For missing video dimensions, inspect the selected file and probe information. For a missing photo capture time, inspect the source's capture record rather than substituting its copy timestamp. A resource can have correct technical metadata with no public catalogue match. A provider can supply a complete synopsis for an item whose local file cannot be read. The meaning of “metadata missing” becomes useful only after identifying its scope. Unknown and deliberately cleared differ A source may omit a field because it has no claim. A user can also intentionally clear an incorrect value. Precedence explains why those states need different handling during a partial update. Filling every blank from a low-confidence candidate can produce a visually complete but inaccurate library. Leaving an unknown field empty retains the distinction between evidence and a guess. Refresh targets a particular cause Emby's Metadata Manager documents missing-data and replacement refresh behavior. A suitable operation can obtain new provider information when that is the missing boundary. If the match points to the wrong work, correct identification first. If a local descriptive record is not associated with the item, resolve that relationship. If the field is not supported by the applicable reader, another refresh of the same record will still encounter that mapping limit. Keeping the field, source/entity, observed acquisition/import result and selected state together makes the next action concrete. See Also Media identification Technical media metadata Metadata precedence Metadata provenance Sidecar metadata References DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation Adobe: XMP specifications and storage model

articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.title: Title disambiguation | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/identificati.keywords: Title disambiguation Title disambiguation uses type, date, people and naming context to distinguish entities that share similar or identical display titles. A title is a presentation label. Several unrelated works can use it, while one work can have several localized or release-specific titles. Similar wording creates different ambiguities Situation Additional evidence Original film and later remake share a name Release context, year and creator credits Film and television series share a name Entity type and series/episode relationships Two musical works share a title Composer, artist or recording/release context One film has localized titles A known shared entity and language/region relationship The first cases distinguish different entities. The last case can describe alternate labels for the same entity. A title-comparison operation should not treat all of them as duplicates. For the fictional movie candidate table in identification , a 2020 film and a 2020 series remain different even though the words and year match. Dates are evidence with a scope A film can have festival, theatrical, regional and later release dates. An album release group's original issue and a particular reissue can likewise have different dates. A year mismatch may indicate another work, another edition, incomplete information or a mistaken local label. Investigate its meaning before changing every record to make the strings equal. More precise data is useful only when it describes the same event. A file's copy date is not a more accurate version of a film's first-release year. Search normalization does not create identity Search can ignore case, punctuation or equivalent character encodings to find useful candidates. Removing a year suffix or punctuation can improve recall. That normalization is not proof that the results are one work. Transliteration and translation can also change wording considerably while preserving a known relationship. Once a match is established, a provider-scoped identifier carries a more specific reference than the displayed title. The local title can then remain localized or curated without forcing a new identity whenever the wording changes. In Emby, a title edit and a provider-ID correction have different consequences. Metadata Manager supplies the documented editing workflow; the evidence determines whether the required change concerns presentation, matching or both. See Also Media identification Provider identifiers Descriptive metadata Conflicting metadata References IMDb: Published dataset identifier and title fields MusicBrainz: Release groups DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/index.html.title: Overview: Metadata and discovery | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/index.html.keywords: Overview: Metadata and discovery Metadata describes media and supplies the identities, artwork and relationships used to organize and discover a collection. A title, poster and episode number are statements about a media item, not the item's encoded picture or sound. Those statements can come from the file, a nearby sidecar, an online provider or a user's own corrections. The topics below explain how identifiers connect those sources, how conflicting values are resolved, and how local formats preserve them. Artwork, localization and discovery build on that information. For an Emby library, the important question is often which source supplied a value and why that source was matched to this item. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Understanding metadata Metadata fundamentals distinguish descriptive and technical information, its storage location and the rules for choosing among sources. Identification and matching Media identification connects a source item to the intended catalogue entry using names, identifiers and other matching evidence. Metadata services Metadata services supply catalogue information or artwork through provider-specific coverage, identities and interfaces. Local metadata formats Local metadata formats store descriptive or technical information within media files or nearby companion files. Metadata fields and localization Metadata fields represent values and relationships whose meaning depends on type, vocabulary and context. Artwork and preview images Artwork roles identify which image belongs in a particular library or playback presentation. Finding related media Metadata-driven discovery uses indexed values and relationships to support search, browsing and recommendations. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Overview: Audio tags | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Overview: Audio tags Audio tags store metadata in defined structures associated with an audio file or stream. ID3v1, ID3v2 and Vorbis comments use different field and storage conventions. Their treatment of text and repeated values affects what an application can read or preserve. These pages connect the tag representation to the album, artist and other information displayed in a music library. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> ID3v1 ID3v1 stores a fixed 128-byte trailing metadata record, while ID3v1.1 reuses part of its comment space for a track number. ID3v2 ID3v2 organizes audio metadata into identified frames with version-specific sizes, text encodings and structured payloads rather than a fixed set of trailing fields. Vorbis comments Vorbis comments store length-prefixed UTF-8 name/value entries with case-insensitive field names and support for repeated values, within the enclosing codec's metadata structure. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Xiph: Vorbis comment header RFC 9639: FLAC metadata

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: ID3v1 audio tags | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: ID3v1 audio tags ID3v1 stores a fixed 128-byte trailing metadata record, while ID3v1.1 reuses part of its comment space for a track number. ID3v1 appends a small fixed-size metadata block to an audio file. Its familiar use is MP3 tagging. The reader can check the final 128 bytes for the TAG marker rather than discovering a variable-length set of frames. Fixed positions define the fields Byte offsets, inclusive Field Capacity 0–2 TAG marker 3 bytes 3–32 Title 30 bytes 33–62 Artist 30 bytes 63–92 Album 30 bytes 93–96 Year 4 bytes 97–126 Comment 30 bytes 127 Genre code 1 byte The capacities sum to 128 including the marker. A 1000-byte toy file would place this block at byte offset 872 . The genre byte refers to a code list; it is not a one-character genre name or a modern open list of several genres. A title cannot exceed its reserved space An original ASCII capacity example contains 31 characters: 123456789012345678901234567890X Only its first 30 bytes fit the title field. Padding fills unused space for shorter values, but it cannot enlarge the field. Encoding interpretation also matters. The format's small legacy fields should not be assumed to provide the same Unicode signaling as ID3v2. A byte capacity and a count of user-visible characters are different quantities. Version 1.1 trades comment space for a track number ID3v1.1 uses 28 comment bytes, a zero separator byte, and the remaining byte before the genre for track information. It remains a 128-byte block. That is a constrained extension, not a flexible new set of arbitrary named fields. Rich credits, long descriptions and multiple values need another representation. Another tag can coexist with it A file can carry richer ID3v2 information as well as a trailing v1 record. If the two disagree, a reader's supported version and selection rules affect the displayed title. For Emby music, compare the actual tag records with the imported field rather than assuming the title came from the filename. ID3v2 develops the variable frame representation and its text-encoding boundary. See Also ID3v2 audio tags Unicode metadata Multi-valued metadata fields MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames References ID3.org: ID3v1 and v1.1

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: ID3v2 audio tags | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: ID3v2 audio tags ID3v2 organizes audio metadata into identified frames with version-specific sizes, text encodings and structured payloads rather than a fixed set of trailing fields. ID3v2 stores identified information frames in a tag associated with audio. A frame names its kind of information and describes its own payload length and flags. That makes it possible to carry much more than ID3v1's fixed title/artist/album slots. The tag version defines how the frames are read A tag header identifies ID3, major/revision version, flags and body size. A frame then has an identifier, size information and flags before its payload. Common frame ID Role TIT2 Title information TPE1 Artist/performer information TALB Album information TRCK Track-position information APIC Attached picture COMM Structured comment For Emby music, retain the tag version and the frame's meaning when comparing a file with its imported title, album or artist values. Music naming provides the product context. Version 2.3 and 2.4 are not byte-identical contracts. For example, the tag-header size uses synchsafe encoding, but v2.3 frame sizes use ordinary big-endian integers while v2.4 frame sizes use synchsafe integers. Treating every four-byte size as the same integer can put the next frame boundary in the wrong place. Synchsafe integers reserve a bit in each byte A four-byte synchsafe value carries seven useful bits per byte: value = b0 × 2²¹ + b1 × 2¹⁴ + b2 × 2⁷ + b3. For 00 00 02 00 , that gives 256 . Interpreting those bytes as a normal big-endian integer instead gives 512 . The version and field definition determine which interpretation applies. The bit pattern alone is not a complete size parser. One original title tag can be read end to end For a small ID3v2.4 tag carrying only the UTF-8 title Café , with no extra header, padding, unsynchronisation or footer: Tag header: 49 44 33 04 00 00 00 00 00 10 TIT2 frame header: 54 49 54 32 00 00 00 06 00 00 Payload: 03 43 61 66 C3 A9 The title's UTF-8 text occupies five bytes . Its encoding byte makes a six-byte payload . Adding the ten-byte frame header makes 16 bytes of tag body , represented by 00 00 00 10. The ten-byte tag header gives 26 bytes total . This is an original minimal tag example. A complete reader also handles applicable flags, version rules and other frames; parsing this case is not a conformance suite. Not every payload is plain text APIC carries an image-related structure including encoding, MIME description, picture type, a description and picture data. COMM likewise has more structure than a bare string. Scanning the entire tag for printable characters can mix descriptions with binary bytes or lose the attached image's role. Embedded cover art develops that selection. Text frames can also have version-specific multiple-value conventions. A slash that a legacy application uses as a separator can occur in real wording, so blindly splitting every field changes its meaning. See Also ID3v1 audio tags Unicode metadata Embedded cover art Multi-valued metadata fields References ID3.org: ID3v2.4 tag structure ID3.org: ID3v2.4 frame definitions

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Vorbis comments | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Vorbis comments Vorbis comments store length-prefixed UTF-8 name/value entries with case-insensitive field names and support for repeated values, within the enclosing codec's metadata structure. Vorbis comments represent metadata as named UTF-8 entries. The comment structure includes a vendor string and a list of entries with explicit byte lengths. The vendor identifies the writing implementation's context; it is not automatically the track's artist or album. A field can have repeated entries An original example is: ARTIST=Ana artist=Bo TITLE=A=B ARTIST and artist identify the same field name under the format's case-insensitive ASCII name rule. The two values can describe two entries. The first equals sign separates name from value. In TITLE=A=B, the title value is A=B , not merely A. Entry UTF-8 bytes in the whole name=value entry ARTIST=Ana 10 artist=Bo 9 TITLE=A=B 9 Lengths count bytes, not a generic character count. A non-ASCII value can occupy more UTF-8 bytes than its displayed letters suggest. The inner lengths have a defined byte order A four-byte unsigned length precedes the vendor bytes; another count describes the number of entries; each entry has its own four-byte length. These integers use the format's little-endian order. With vendor Demo and the three entries above, the original inner-content model occupies: 4 + 4 + 4 + (4 + 10) + (4 + 9) + (4 + 9) = 52 bytes. This excludes the enclosing codec/packet framing. It is a small structural example rather than a complete encoded audio file. The enclosing format still matters Vorbis's comment header has its packet relationship and framing bit. FLAC carries a corresponding comment structure in a metadata block with its own outer rules; it does not copy every Ogg/Vorbis packet byte. Recognizing the same comment concepts therefore does not mean the whole files share one metadata offset or packet layout. Mapping preserves list and field meaning An Emby music reader can import supported named values into its library model. Keeping a repeated artist list separate from album-artist or performer meaning remains necessary. Multiple-valued fields explains why joining those names into a single string and later splitting punctuation can lose information. Supported input semantics and the library's selected representation determine the result. See Also Multi-valued metadata fields Unicode metadata ID3v2 audio tags FLAC Audio References Xiph: Vorbis comment header RFC 9639: FLAC metadata

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Overview: Container metadata structures | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Overview: Container metadata structures Container metadata structures attach descriptive information to media through the container's own elements and conventions. MP4 atoms and Matroska tags provide different places and structures for metadata. A familiar field name in an inspection tool can conceal those storage differences. This group explains the underlying container representation, which helps when information survives one remuxing or editing operation differently from another. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> MP4 metadata atoms MP4 metadata uses structured boxes and metadata conventions whose keys, payload types and scope must be interpreted separately from the coded media streams. Matroska tags Matroska tags associate named values with specified targets such as tracks or the broader resource, retaining scope, language and default-value relationships. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References FFmpeg: Container metadata options

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Matroska tags | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Matroska tags Matroska tags associate named values with specified targets such as tracks or the broader resource, retaining scope, language and default-value relationships. Matroska tags can describe particular targets within a media resource. A tag is not necessarily a global label for the entire file. A target establishes which entity receives the value Consider an original conceptual hierarchy: Tag Targets TrackUID: 12 SimpleTag TagName: TITLE TagString: Director commentary Here, the title belongs to the targeted track. It should not automatically replace the movie's displayed title. The hierarchy names the relevant concepts; it is not an encoded EBML file or a complete tag-interchange XML document. Track identity and menu position differ A TrackUID identifies a track relationship in the resource. A player's “audio track 2” can be a selection ordinal in its current menu. Those values should not be substituted for one another. A remux can alter ordering while retaining another identity relationship, or recreate track identities while preserving the audio content. Value Scope Global title tag Applicable broader target Track-targeted title A particular track Track selection index A consumer's selection context Provider work identifier An external catalogue relationship For Emby, the source target and imported field explain whether “Director commentary” belongs in an audio-track label or the library's work title. Languages and defaults can coexist A tag can carry language/default information. Several title values can therefore be intentional alternatives rather than duplicate corruption. The consumer needs a selection rule and the intended scope. Flattening all values into one string loses those relationships; selecting the first encountered value can choose an unintended language. Language tags explains the wider language-identification concepts. The applicable Matroska field/version determines its precise representation. Moving containers can change tag mapping Another container may not provide the same target/value organization. A converter must decide what to retain and how to map it. Preserving the video/audio packets does not inherently preserve every descriptive target. See Also Embedded metadata Multi-valued metadata fields Language tags for metadata Matroska: MKV and MKA Streams and Tracks References Matroska: Tag targets and semantics

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: MP4 metadata atoms | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: MP4 metadata atoms MP4 metadata uses structured boxes and metadata conventions whose keys, payload types and scope must be interpreted separately from the coded media streams. MP4 packages media and associated descriptions through boxes, often called atoms in related terminology. The movie's coded tracks and a descriptive title occupy different structures. One common tag convention uses ilst An illustrative iTunes-style hierarchy is: moov udta meta ilst ©nam data The visible key ©nam is commonly associated with a title in that convention. Other keys describe artist information or cover artwork. Example key Conventional role ©nam Title ©ART Artist aART Album-artist relationship covr Embedded cover data These labels name a metadata convention. They should not be read as a promise that every MP4 uses this hierarchy or every reader exposes the same fields. Other metadata arrangements use another contract Keyed metadata can use a key table and namespace relationship instead of interpreting every entry as one familiar ilst key. FFmpeg documents an option to write mdta metadata. A reader supporting one arrangement can still fail to map another arrangement into the expected library title. Renaming a file does not convert those boxes. The payload also has a type. A string, number and picture bytes need their appropriate interpretation rather than one blanket “decode every data box as text”. The description does not replace stream properties A title or album tag can describe the work represented by an M4A or video file. Track/sample structures establish the actual codec, duration and media layout. For Emby, compare the descriptive atom the file carries with the imported field and the selected media source. Correct playback and correct title import can succeed independently. A rewrite has preservation choices A remux can retain coded media while changing which metadata boxes are copied or rewritten. An export can produce a useful new audio file while omitting embedded artwork or custom fields. Embedded cover art explains the picture-selection boundary; Unicode metadata develops the text-decoding boundary. See Also Embedded metadata Embedded cover art MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Unicode metadata References TagLib: MP4 metadata interface TagLib: MP4 tag implementation FFmpeg: Container metadata options

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Overview: Local metadata formats | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Overview: Local metadata formats Local metadata formats store descriptive or technical information within media files or nearby companion files. Local information can travel with a collection and remain available independently of an online lookup. Its representation depends on the format: NFO sidecars, audio tags, container structures and photo standards have different fields and conventions. The linked branches explain how those stored values become useful library information. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> NFO files A media-library NFO is an associated metadata record, commonly XML, whose supported fields, item type and association determine what is imported or saved. Audio tags Audio tags store metadata in defined structures associated with an audio file or stream. Container metadata structures Container metadata structures attach descriptive information to media through the container's own elements and conventions. Photo metadata standards Photo metadata standards describe capture details, editorial information and extensible properties around an image. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C XML 1.0 syntax

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: NFO metadata files | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: NFO metadata files A media-library NFO is an associated metadata record, commonly XML, whose supported fields, item type and association determine what is imported or saved. A media-library NFO stores information associated with an item outside its video or audio payload. Many such records use XML. The same extension can also occur on ordinary text-information files, so the suffix alone does not establish a usable metadata record. The record needs the intended item An original illustrative pair is: The Station (2020).mkv The Station (2020).nfo Association depends on the applicable reader's naming/location rules. A well-formed movie record beside the wrong file can still import a wrong title and identity. Emby's naming documentation provides the product context. Kodi's linked reference documents its own convention; its precedence rules should not automatically be attributed to Emby. XML carries typed field meanings Here is an original small movie record. The identifier value is invented for illustration, not supplied as a match to a real film: <movie> <title>The Station & the River</title> <originaltitle>The Station</originaltitle> <sorttitle>Station and the River</sorttitle> <year>2020</year> <uniqueid type="tmdb">424242</uniqueid> <genre>Drama</genre> <genre>Railway</genre> </movie> The XML escape preserves an ampersand in text. The named identifier retains a provider scope. Repeated genre elements express several values rather than one title-like string. In the examined 21 July 2026 public Emby NFO parser, title/localtitle maps into the item name, originaltitle and sorttitle have separate destinations, and uniqueid uses its type attribute as a provider relationship. The source also has genre and actor handling. This is evidence of that source revision's mappings. A complete input still needs the appropriate item reader and installed version. Reading and saving are different operations A reader imports supported values into the library. The current values can then reflect local data, providers and edits under precedence . A saver serializes a supported representation later. A database edit does not inherently prove that a sidecar has already been updated, and editing the sidecar does not prove the library has reread it. That distinction explains an old file value alongside a new displayed value without inventing a failed XML parser. A round trip needs a preservation decision An application can recognize some fields while ignoring others. Saving its model back out may reproduce only mapped fields, reorder lists or select one localized presentation. Unsupported data can therefore disappear even when the resulting XML remains valid. A title/identifier preserved through a round trip does not establish preservation of every credit, language variant or playback-state field. Keep the source record and its association available when comparing those operations. XML syntax, supported mapping and selected library values are three separate results. See Also Sidecar metadata Metadata precedence Provider identifiers Metadata providers in Emby Server References Emby NFO parser: 21 July 2026 snapshot Kodi: Movie NFO field reference W3C XML 1.0 syntax

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Overview: Photo metadata standards | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Overview: Photo metadata standards Photo metadata standards describe capture details, editorial information and extensible properties around an image. Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata and XMP serve related but distinct purposes. A photograph can carry more than one of these representations, with overlapping information that an application must interpret. Their pages explain the field context needed to understand dates, authorship, location and other image properties. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Exif Exif specifies image-associated capture and presentation records, including camera information, capture-time context, orientation and applicable location data. IPTC Photo Metadata IPTC Photo Metadata defines descriptive and contextual photo properties whose meanings remain distinct from their XMP, legacy or other storage representations. XMP XMP defines an extensible metadata model and RDF/XML serialization whose namespaced properties can be embedded in resources or carried in associated sidecars. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: Exif photo metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: Exif photo metadata Exif specifies image-associated capture and presentation records, including camera information, capture-time context, orientation and applicable location data. Exif records information associated with an image's capture and presentation. It can describe camera/exposure facts, capture time, orientation and applicable location information. CIPA's current catalogue identifies Exif 3.1, published 30 January 2026 . The linked tag reference documents ExifTool's interpretation of specific fields; it is implementation documentation alongside the standard's publisher reference. Capture and filesystem dates describe different events Information Event or relationship DateTimeOriginal Original image capture context Applicable subsecond/offset fields Additional precision and time-zone context Image modification metadata A recorded image-related modification Filesystem creation/modification time Activities involving this stored file Copying a photograph can change filesystem timestamps without changing the depicted event. Exporting another format can also create a new file today from a capture made years earlier. A library timeline needs a deliberate selection of the date's meaning, rather than assuming every property called “created” names the camera exposure. An offset can turn a clock reading into an instant For an invented record: DateTimeOriginal: 2024:07:01 20:15:00 OffsetTimeOriginal: +02:00 the corresponding UTC instant is 2024-07-01 18:15:00Z . Without usable offset context, the original clock reading should not automatically be treated as UTC. A camera clock can also have been set incorrectly; correctly parsing its text does not independently verify the real capture event. Keep any retained precision and offset meaning coherent during conversion. Removing an offset while retaining the same clock numbers changes how a later reader may place the photo. Location components need their reference Coordinates can be described using rational degree/minute/second components and direction references.
