An invented latitude of 25 degrees, 30 minutes, 0 seconds , with a south reference, corresponds to: −(25 + 30/60 + 0/3600) = −25.5 degrees. The components alone do not convey the sign. The associated reference supplies that interpretation. Other capture/location fields have their own units and meaning. A descriptive place shown in the picture is not automatically the camera's measured location. Orientation can be presentation data Exif uses the familiar orientation relationship described in image orientation . A stored grid and its transform work together to establish the intended direction. Removing the record without normalizing a sideways stored image can change its displayed appearance. Rotating the samples but keeping the old transform can instead cause another rotation. A photo conversion therefore needs both pixel and metadata decisions. In Emby, distinguish the original record, the applicable library/image reader's supported fields and the generated or displayed result. Exif is also not the same function as IPTC descriptions or an ICC colour profile . Those records can coexist while supplying different kinds of interpretation. See Also Image orientation IPTC Photo Metadata XMP metadata Metadata provenance Camera raw images References CIPA: Exif 3.1 and current imaging standards ExifTool: Exif tag interpretation reference Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification Adobe DNG 1.7.1.0 specification

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: IPTC Photo Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: IPTC Photo Metadata IPTC Photo Metadata defines descriptive and contextual photo properties whose meanings remain distinct from their XMP, legacy or other storage representations. IPTC Photo Metadata supplies defined meanings for photographic descriptions and context. The reference here is IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1 . Those meanings are useful for personal photo collections as well as professional image workflows. Describe one photograph with several roles For an invented railway-platform photograph: Property role Example information Title/name Platform at dawn Headline First departure after the storm Description An account of the depicted scene Keywords Railway, dawn, platform Creator credit The photographer's identity Location information The appropriate created or depicted location The title is a concise name, while a description can provide more context. Keywords provide additional discovery labels; they should not automatically replace a complete caption. Creator, credit and rights-related properties also have distinct semantic roles. Keeping them in their defined fields retains more useful meaning than concatenating all text into one description. Created location and shown location can differ A photographer standing on one bank can photograph a landmark on the opposite bank. The camera location and the depicted landmark location then describe different places. IPTC distinguishes Location Created from Location Shown in the Image . A GPS capture position can be relevant to the first relationship without fully naming every location shown. This distinction can matter for browsing a travel collection. A person interested in pictures of the landmark need not be searching for the exact place where the camera stood. A semantic field is separate from its storage mapping For Emby, the relevant boundary is which defined properties the applicable reader imports and how they map to the library's fields. A standard defining a property does not establish that every property has a product mapping. XMP explains the packet and structured-value side of that relationship. IPTC properties have specified representation mappings, including XMP and legacy IIM relationships where applicable. “IPTC data” should not be treated as one independent photo-file extension. An image can carry descriptive properties in a metadata packet, and supported workflows can also use associated records. Different storage representations need coherent values where they express the same property. A conversion that preserves visible pixels can omit those descriptions. Conversely, copying a packet onto another image can retain valid syntax while assigning the wrong description to that image. See Also XMP metadata Exif photo metadata Descriptive metadata Metadata provenance References IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1 Adobe: XMP specifications and storage model

articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.title: XMP metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/local-format.keywords: XMP metadata XMP defines an extensible metadata model and RDF/XML serialization whose namespaced properties can be embedded in resources or carried in associated sidecars. XMP, the Extensible Metadata Platform , defines a metadata model and its serialization. A packet can be embedded in a supported resource or carried in an associated sidecar. The XML text is a representation of structured properties. Its readability does not by itself establish that every consumer recognizes their meaning. Model, serialization and storage are separate Layer Responsibility Data model Properties and their structured values RDF/XML serialization How that model is written as XML Schema/namespace Identity and meaning of named properties File embedding or sidecar association Where the serialized record is carried Adobe's specifications separate the core model, additional properties and storage in files. This explains why a .xmp sidecar and an embedded packet can use the same metadata model while having different association/preservation behavior. Namespaces identify properties A prefix such as dc is a convenient local abbreviation for a namespace. The property's identity depends on the namespace and local name, not on a universal requirement to spell that prefix identically in every document. Here is an original small packet with an invented creator and description: <x:xmpmeta xmlns:x="adobe:ns:meta/"> <rdf:RDF xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"> <rdf:Description rdf:about="" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/"> <dc:creator> <rdf:Seq><rdf:li>Ana Lee</rdf:li></rdf:Seq> </dc:creator> <dc:subject> <rdf:Bag><rdf:li>railway</rdf:li><rdf:li>dawn</rdf:li></rdf:Bag> </dc:subject> <dc:description> <rdf:Alt> <rdf:li xml:lang="x-default">Platform at dawn.</rdf:li> <rdf:li xml:lang="en">Platform at dawn.</rdf:li> <rdf:li xml:lang="fr">Quai à l'aube.</rdf:li> </rdf:Alt> </dc:description> </rdf:Description> </rdf:RDF> </x:xmpmeta> The namespace URIs are identifiers in the syntax, not instructions to download a schema or image from those addresses. Structured values retain distinctions The default description appears first and is repeated with its actual English language qualifier; the French alternative remains a separate value. The creator sequence represents ordered entries. The subject bag represents a collection whose ordering does not carry that same meaning. The description alternatives retain language qualifiers. Flattening those values into one string can lose ordering, element boundaries or language context. A generic XML parser finding text does not perform the schema-aware mapping automatically. Properties can additionally use defined structures and types. A supported edit instruction and a descriptive keyword are not interchangeable just because both are inside the same packet. Reconcile overlapping records deliberately The same image can carry Exif, IPTC-related properties and XMP. Applicable storage/reconciliation rules help keep overlapping claims coherent when they refer to the same fact. That is different from blindly making all similarly named date fields equal. Capture time, export time and filesystem time can describe different events. For an Emby resource, keep packet validity, supported property mapping and selected library values as separate observations. A well-formed external packet still needs a recognized association and reader; a mapped value can then interact with provider or edited values through precedence . See Also IPTC Photo Metadata Exif photo metadata Embedded metadata Sidecar metadata Camera raw images References Adobe: XMP specifications and storage model Adobe: XMP data types IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1

articles/metadata-discovery/services/ind.title: Overview: Metadata services | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/ind.keywords: Overview: Metadata services Metadata services supply catalogue information or artwork through provider-specific coverage, identities and interfaces. A provider can help identify a work, enrich its description or supply a particular kind of artwork. Those roles do not always belong to one service. This area explains the provider relationship and the named services before connecting them to Emby's configured metadata sources. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How metadata providers work A metadata provider connects library requests to a catalogue or resource source through identification, retrieval, mapping and selection. Movie and television databases Movie and television metadata services organize their own records and interfaces for programme identification and description. MusicBrainz MusicBrainz supplies structured music catalogue entities and relationships through separate search, lookup and browse operations. Fanart.tv Fanart.tv provides role-specific artwork associated with movie, television and music identities, with versioned response structures and language information. IMVDb IMVDb identifies music-video records separately from audio recordings; an archived integration illustrates how artist and song-title evidence were mapped into video metadata. Metadata providers in Emby Server Emby's metadata route combines supported local readers, remote providers, field selection and optional saving, with library context and installed integrations determining the available operations. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB: API v3 overview RFC 9110: HTTP semantics MusicBrainz: Search, lookup and browse API

articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.title: Fanart.tv | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.keywords: Fanart.tv Fanart.tv provides role-specific artwork associated with movie, television and music identities, with versioned response structures and language information. Fanart.tv supplies artwork associated with media identities. A returned logo, backdrop or cover has a presentation role; it is not simply another interchangeable picture of the same dimensions. Emby's image management documentation names Fanart.tv among image sources. The applicable integration and selected library determine how those resources are requested and used. The identity comes from an appropriate namespace Media relationship Key context to retain Movie artwork Supported movie-provider reference Television artwork Intended series reference Music artist artwork Artist MBID Album artwork Applicable release-group relationship Passing a recording MBID where artist artwork is requested can target the wrong kind of entity even though both keys have UUID form. An image provider's record can therefore complement descriptive catalogues rather than establish local identity from scratch. Role and language narrow the candidate A wide backdrop supports a different layout from a transparent title logo. Its language information can also concern visible text in the artwork rather than the spoken language of the video. Legacy v3 documentation uses 00 for textless artwork. That is a provider convention, not a universal BCP 47 language tag. Other interfaces can represent neutral/unspecified language differently. Artwork language selection separates those cases and the fallback policy used to select a resource. Versioned structures need versioned readers The current API documentation distinguishes v3, v3.1 and v3.2 response shapes. Its music album structure changes from a map keyed by release-group ID to an array with an explicit release_group_id. A client treating that array as the old map can lose the relationship without any problem decoding the actual image bytes. The request/response version is part of the data contract. Additional timestamps and dimension information also belong to those documented versions; they should not be assumed present in every older response. Preview and selected image are different resources A small preview is useful for choosing among candidates. The chosen asset can then be retrieved in the form needed for presentation. Keeping that distinction avoids treating a preview's dimensions as the master asset's dimensions. Role, language, identity and resource variation together describe the artwork that actually reaches the library. See Also Media artwork roles Artwork language selection Provider identifiers Metadata providers in Emby Server References Fanart.tv: Current API and image roles Fanart.tv: Legacy v3 artwork metadata

articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.title: IMVDb music-video metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.keywords: IMVDb music-video metadata IMVDb identifies music-video records separately from audio recordings; an archived integration illustrates how artist and song-title evidence were mapped into video metadata. A music video is a video work associated with a song and performers. An audio recording can accompany several visual versions: an official narrative video, a live performance or another edit. IMVDb's music-video identity should therefore be kept separate from an album or audio-recording reference. The visual work needs its own relationship Information Useful scope Song title and performing artist Matching evidence Audio recording identity Recorded-audio relationship Music-video record The intended visual work/version Video-production credits Responsibilities for that production Local encode The particular media representation Identical artist/title words do not prove that two local videos are the same production. Their visual content and version can matter alongside catalogue evidence. A concrete archived integration The examined source is an archived IMVDb provider for Emby, pinned to 2 October 2018 . It declares a music-video metadata interface and distinguishes search by artist/title from retrieval by a selected IMVDb identifier. Its reader consumes fields such as id , song_title , year and artist-name data. That is direct evidence of the historical mapping. It does not establish that all production credits or every artist in a record were imported. A field visible on a provider's catalogue and a field consumed by one integration are different observations. Cast and crew credits explains how responsibilities and identity need to remain structured. Retain the music-video key A provider-specific video identifier can anchor the selected visual record while MusicBrainz relationships describe the associated music. The keys should not be copied into each other's fields simply because both concern the same song. For an Emby library, the intended content type, local title/artist evidence and available integration form the actual route. A descriptive record still needs to belong to the music video being played. Current availability needs current evidence The publisher's developer pages did not yield readable content during this source check. That observation does not establish permanent service closure. This page uses the dated implementation to explain the relationship and its observed fields. It does not claim that every current Emby installation includes that provider or that a live IMVDb request succeeded. The linked publisher documentation is the place for a current interface check. See Also MusicBrainz Provider identifiers Cast and crew credits How metadata providers work References IMVDb: Publisher developer documentation Archived IMVDb integration: 2 October 2018 snapshot

articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.title: MusicBrainz | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.keywords: MusicBrainz MusicBrainz supplies structured music catalogue entities and relationships through separate search, lookup and browse operations. MusicBrainz organizes music information into entities such as artists, recordings, releases, release groups and works. Its relationships let a library describe more than one title string attached to an audio file. Three operations ask different questions Operation Original example question Search Which artists or releases match these words? Lookup What does this known entity identifier describe? Browse Which releases are related to this known artist or recording? Searching by an album name can produce several candidate releases. Selecting an MBID gives a particular reference for later lookup; browsing then explores connected records. The distinction matters when the library already has a reliable identifier. Repeating a broad name search can reintroduce ambiguity that the selected identity had resolved. Recording and release data serve different actions An invented recording, Platform Lights , appears on a standard album and a compilation. Both releases refer to its audio relationship, but each can have its own track order, credits and product information. MusicBrainz identifiers explains those entity levels. A fingerprint-assisted recording match does not necessarily choose the album release whose cover belongs to the local files. In Emby music matching, local tags and the selected provider relationship should agree at the intended level. Music naming guidance gives the product context; the provider model explains the meanings of those references. Related information is not always in one response A lookup can request supported related information through the API's inclusion mechanisms. Browse and search also have their own result sets and pagination relationships. A short response can consequently be complete for its requested shape while omitting data that another operation would retrieve. Absence from that one response does not prove the catalogue lacks the relationship. A useful integration retains the request scope with the response, including entity, requested additions and language/format context where applicable. A catalogue reference is separate from a media resource MusicBrainz metadata describes music relationships; it is not the local encoded song. Artwork retrieval also has an associated-resource boundary, and the correct release or release group matters there. Imported descriptions can coexist with embedded cover art and edited library values. Matching the catalogue entity is the basis for selecting related data, rather than an instruction to replace every existing resource. See Also MusicBrainz identifiers Acoustic fingerprinting How metadata providers work Embedded cover art References MusicBrainz: Search, lookup and browse API MusicBrainz: Entity identifiers

articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.title: Metadata providers in Emby Server | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.keywords: Metadata providers in Emby Server Emby's metadata route combines supported local readers, remote providers, field selection and optional saving, with library context and installed integrations determining the available operations. An Emby library can obtain information through local records and configured remote sources. The selected content type gives those operations an entity context, such as movie, episode or music item. Readers, providers and savers occupy different boundaries Role Work Local reader Recover supported fields from an associated resource Remote provider Search or retrieve catalogue information Image provider Supply artwork candidates/resources Selection/merge Determine current library values Saver Serialize supported library data to a chosen output The public NFO source exposes parsing of title, original title, sort title and scoped identifiers. Its presence demonstrates an implementation, not that every imaginable NFO field has a mapping in every installed version. Reading a sidecar also is not a guarantee that a later database edit has been written back into it. Refresh names an operation Metadata Manager documents refreshing missing information versus replacing metadata, with a separate image-replacement choice. It also describes protection through field or item locks. That separates three questions: whether a source was consulted, whether it supplied a usable candidate, and whether the selected operation allowed that candidate to replace an existing value. Precedence develops a field-level model. The actual provider/library configuration supplies the product-specific ordering and behavior; this page does not invent one universal priority list. Correct identity before comparing descriptions A wrong match can yield internally consistent title, synopsis, date and artwork for another work. Rearranging provider priority does not make that record describe the local film. Conversely, a correct identity can yield different localized labels or edition artwork. Compare the field's intended scope rather than treating every differing string as a bad match. Inspect the boundary that is missing If text was imported but artwork is absent, inspect the image reference/retrieval/selection. If a local field remains in its file but is absent in the library, inspect association and mapping. If an edited value reappears after refresh, compare selected operation and protection state. A current investigation uses the server/integration version and the relevant library configuration. These observations make the documented editing workflow specific without turning Learn into a duplicate click-by-click setup guide. See Also How metadata providers work NFO metadata files Metadata precedence Missing metadata Media artwork roles References Emby NFO parser: 21 July 2026 snapshot TMDB: API v3 overview MusicBrainz: Search, lookup and browse API

articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.title: How metadata providers work | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/Met.keywords: How metadata providers work A metadata provider connects library requests to a catalogue or resource source through identification, retrieval, mapping and selection. A provider supplies catalogue information or related resources to a library. The useful route begins with the intended entity and ends with selected library fields or images. A poster can be missing even when the film's synopsis is present. Those outputs may depend on different requests, resources and selection rules. From a hint to a selected record A title/year search produces candidates. Choosing one establishes a provider-scoped identity ; a subsequent lookup can obtain its description, dates, credits and associated references. Stage Result Candidate search Possible matches Identification Selected catalogue entity Record retrieval Source fields and related references Field mapping Values recognized by the library model Selection Current values after applicable precedence A successful search is evidence about candidates. It does not mean the full record has already been imported. Artwork is a related retrieval A record may contain an image path or an asset identifier rather than the image bytes. The integration obtains a usable image resource, chooses its role/language/size and associates it with the item. That gives several explanations for a synopsis with no poster: the matched source has no suitable asset, a reference did not yield bytes, the requested role/language was unavailable, or another image-selection decision applied. Artwork providers can also use another catalogue's identity to find their assets. Those namespaces need a coherent cross-reference, not a guess based on equal-looking numbers. Mapping retains meanings, not just strings A provider's original title, translated title and sort label can occupy different fields. An episode record can refer to a parent series without being that series itself. The integration must preserve those distinctions. A valid response can still be mapped into an unsuitable field or attached to the wrong local entity. In Emby, Metadata Manager and the library's configured providers describe the product workflow. Precedence explains why a received candidate need not replace a protected or deliberately selected value. A cache has a context An original conceptual lookup key could include provider, entity type, identifier and requested language. Reusing a French response for an English request because only the numeric ID was retained loses that context. Cached data also has acquisition/version history. Reading it today is different from obtaining a new response today. A missing-field refresh and a replacement operation can use the results differently. These are interface relationships, not a universal cache-key or refresh algorithm. They let a comparison identify whether the missing boundary is identity, retrieval, field mapping or selection. See Also Media identification Provider identifiers Metadata precedence Metadata providers in Emby Server Media artwork roles References TMDB: API v3 overview MusicBrainz: Search, lookup and browse API RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.title: Overview: Movie and television databases | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.keywords: Overview: Movie and television databases Movie and television metadata services organize their own records and interfaces for programme identification and description. TMDB, TheTVDB and OMDb maintain distinct catalogue relationships and service contracts. A title or identifier accepted by one service does not automatically select the same record in another. Their pages describe the relevant coverage and identity model so a metadata match can be investigated at its source. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> The Movie Database (TMDB) TMDB supplies movie, television, person and image metadata through distinct catalogue entities and language-aware API requests. TheTVDB TheTVDB supplies television and movie records whose series, season-type and episode relationships preserve the ordering context used for matching. The Open Movie Database (OMDb) OMDb exposes title search and record retrieval with distinct query parameters, IMDb references and a separately documented poster service. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References TMDB: API v3 overview TheTVDB: API information

articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.title: The Open Movie Database (OMDb) | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.keywords: The Open Movie Database (OMDb) OMDb exposes title search and record retrieval with distinct query parameters, IMDb references and a separately documented poster service. OMDb, The Open Movie Database, offers a web API for movie and related title information. Its publisher distinguishes searching a set of candidates from retrieving a particular record. Query parameters express different questions Parameter Documented purpose s Search by title wording i Retrieve using an IMDb title identifier t Retrieve using title wording type Narrow the title category y Supply release-year context plot Select a short or full plot representation An integration with an uncertain title can first search candidates. A known identifier can instead support a more specific lookup. The result's interpretation still needs the entity context. A series and an episode have related descriptions without being interchangeable title records. External keys retain their namespace OMDb accepts IMDb title references. That relationship does not make the two services identical or make every response field originate from one universal catalogue. For an Emby comparison, keep the selected provider, the lookup identity and the returned record together. IMDb identifiers explains the key's form and scope. A localized library title or a user edit can then coexist with that identity. It need not be replaced merely to make the display wording match the search hint. A content label and an opinion score differ A response can provide descriptive ratings-related information. A parental/content classification and an audience or critic score answer different questions. A score of eight on a ten-point opinion scale is not an age threshold. Content ratings develops the scheme/territory context needed for the other kind of label. Posters have another retrieval boundary The publisher documents a poster service separately from ordinary descriptive queries. A successful record response therefore does not prove that the applicable poster retrieval is available or has succeeded. Emby's Metadata Manager exposes image selection independently of the displayed title and overview. When only the image is missing, compare that asset route with the successful descriptive lookup rather than treating both as one failed search. See Also IMDb identifiers How metadata providers work Content ratings Media posters References OMDb: Search and record parameters

articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.title: TheTVDB | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.keywords: TheTVDB TheTVDB supplies television and movie records whose series, season-type and episode relationships preserve the ordering context used for matching. TheTVDB supplies television and movie catalogue information. For episodic media, series identity and episode ordering belong together. A local “episode 3” needs its series and ordering context before it becomes a useful catalogue reference. Series and episodes have distinct identities Relationship What it answers Series record Which programme? Season type/order Which arrangement of episodes? Season and episode position Where in that arrangement? Episode record Which described episode entity? Local media file Which encoded presentation is being played? A series identifier cannot replace an episode's own identity. The numbering is a relationship, not a globally unique title key. Alternate ordering can describe different cuts The official v4 documentation supports multiple season types. It explains that alternate arrangements can include recut episodes rather than merely rearranging an unchanged set. Consider an invented programme whose original release has three long episodes. Another release edits the same story into six shorter parts. Part 3 of the shorter release need not contain the same scenes as original episode 3. Local evidence Identification implication Same series title Shared programme context Different ordering type Another episode arrangement Different count/duration Possible split or recut presentation Known scene boundaries Evidence for the actual local episode This matters for summaries, episode images and subtitles. Correctly identifying the series alone cannot establish the local file's episode timeline. Images belong to their described entity Series artwork and an episode still serve different roles. An episode image is not necessarily a frame extracted from the local encode; it can be a catalogue asset attached to the episode record. Emby's TV naming guidance supplies the product's identification context. The provider's order and the actual library/integration settings determine which relationship is used. See Also Media identification How metadata providers work Episode thumbnails Provider identifiers References TheTVDB: Official v4 API documentation and season types TheTVDB: API information

articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.title: The Movie Database (TMDB) | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/services/mov.keywords: The Movie Database (TMDB) TMDB supplies movie, television, person and image metadata through distinct catalogue entities and language-aware API requests. TMDB, The Movie Database, supplies catalogue data for movies, television and people, together with associated images. Its API v3 documentation treats those as distinct resources. Retain the entity context Catalogue resource Intended relationship Movie A movie record Television series A series record Season/episode A position and entity within the applicable TV structure Person A credited person Image reference A related asset, not the movie identifier itself A movie lookup and a TV lookup using the same printable number should not be treated as the same entity relationship. In Emby, selecting the right match is therefore more specific than pasting a numeric value into an unspecified field. Provider identifiers develops that namespace/scope model. A request can ask for translated text TMDB documents language-region requests such as en-US and pt-BR . The requested presentation can affect returned descriptive fields while preserving the underlying entity. An original comparison might ask for one selected movie's English and Portuguese title/overview. If one field lacks a translation, the response or integration's fallback behavior becomes part of the result; the documentation does not promise that every field is localized. Names, original language and translated descriptions also have different meanings. Changing the metadata request language does not change the spoken language of the local video. An image path is not the downloaded artwork TMDB's image documentation combines configuration information with an image's file path and a chosen size. The path associated with a movie is consequently only part of a usable image reference. The resulting resource still needs retrieval and association with the intended poster, backdrop or other role. A smaller image variation is a derivative of the asset, not another catalogue film. Emby's image management exposes selected artwork. Artwork language selection considers language as another choice alongside role and size. Dates describe particular release events TMDB provides release-date/certification information with release types such as premiere, theatrical, digital and physical. One displayed year is a library presentation of that richer event information. The release-date article explains how country, event type and precision prevent different valid dates from being mistaken for an identity error. See Also How metadata providers work Provider identifiers Localized titles Artwork language selection Release dates References TMDB: API v3 overview TMDB: Language and region requests TMDB: Image configuration and paths TMDB: Release dates and certifications

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Overview: Understanding metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Overview: Understanding metadata Metadata fundamentals distinguish descriptive and technical information, its storage location and the rules for choosing among sources. A title supplied by a provider and a codec reported by a probe describe different aspects of the same item. Embedded and sidecar locations answer another question: where that information was stored. Provenance and precedence then explain why a value was accepted, retained or replaced in the library. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What is metadata? Metadata records information about a media resource or the work it represents, allowing a library to identify, describe, organize and present it. Descriptive metadata Descriptive metadata expresses the identity, content and context of a work or resource for discovery and presentation rather than specifying how its samples are decoded. Technical media metadata Technical media metadata describes the encoded resource, tracks and presentation properties recovered by parsing, probing or analysis. Embedded metadata Embedded metadata is stored within the media resource's own structure and can describe different scopes such as a file, track, image or catalogue relationship. Sidecar metadata A metadata sidecar stores associated information outside the media resource, relying on a defined association and schema rather than being part of the image or media payload. Metadata provenance Metadata provenance records the sources and activities responsible for values or derived resources, making identity, corrections and later refresh results easier to assess. Metadata precedence Metadata precedence is the field- and operation-dependent policy for selecting among local, provider, derived and edited candidate values. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1 FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation W3C PROV Model Primer

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Descriptive metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Descriptive metadata Descriptive metadata expresses the identity, content and context of a work or resource for discovery and presentation rather than specifying how its samples are decoded. Descriptive metadata answers questions such as what is this, who made it, and what is it about? It supplies meaningful labels and relationships for browsing a library. Fields express different meanings For an invented film record: Field Example value Meaning Title The Station Name used for presentation Creator credit An invented director credit Responsibility for the work Description A story about a remote railway stop Account of the content Release year 2020 A date claim within a release context Identifier A named provider's record key Reference to a catalogue entity The title is useful wording, while the identifier refers to an entity. Treating them as the same key can merge remakes, adaptations or unrelated same-title works. A date also needs its intended scope. Production year, first release and a later regional release can be different facts about related material. A record can have several legitimate presentations A work may have an original title and several localized titles. An artist credit can name several contributors with a specified order or join wording. A photograph can have multiple subject keywords. Those distinctions should remain structured where the model supports them. Flattening every list into one comma-separated string can make it difficult to distinguish a punctuation mark inside a name from a separator between contributors. Descriptions can also vary by source and editorial purpose. A brief browsing summary and a detailed catalogue annotation need not be identical to describe the same work accurately. Personal media has a description too A home photo may have no public movie-provider record. Its caption, creator, capture context and subjects can still make it discoverable. IPTC Photo Metadata supplies relevant semantic fields for images. Their value does not depend on a provider recognizing a commercial title. For Emby, descriptive information shapes the displayed library and search/browsing context. Correcting it should be assessed separately from probing codecs and dimensions. See Also What is metadata? Title disambiguation Provider identifiers IPTC Photo Metadata Technical media metadata References DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Embedded metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Embedded metadata Embedded metadata is stored within the media resource's own structure and can describe different scopes such as a file, track, image or catalogue relationship. Embedded metadata travels inside the media file. “Embedded” describes its storage relationship; it does not establish the meaning, correctness or precedence of every contained value. One file can carry several scopes Example record Intended scope A track's language description That particular stream A movie title tag The represented work or applicable target An image orientation tag The intended image presentation A colour profile Interpretation of image samples A provider identifier A catalogue reference for its specified entity A reader must interpret the record according to its format, field and target. Copying an album title into every track title would retain the words while changing their meaning. Matroska tags can identify targets rather than describe only a single flat file record. Photo formats can similarly carry several metadata/resource structures with different responsibilities. Container preservation is not the same as field use A remux or export can retain coded media while changing its metadata carriage. Another conversion can preserve readable tags but change picture dimensions or colour representation. An output needs records consistent with those changes. Keeping a pre-crop dimension or old orientation interpretation beside newly transformed pixels can misdescribe the result. The orientation example shows why physically rotating a grid and retaining its old transform can cause a second rotation later. Import creates another representation of the record A library can read supported embedded fields into its database and then combine them with provider or user data. That database presentation is a new layer, not the original file rewritten in memory. For Emby, distinguish the embedded record, the field the server reads and the displayed library value. Provenance and precedence explain how those layers can differ without assuming every possible embedded field has an Emby mapping. A tag can remain present in the file while the library does not import it, maps it into a different field, or selects another candidate value. Editing the library display also need not change the source file. See Also Sidecar metadata Technical media metadata Metadata provenance Exif photo metadata XMP metadata References Matroska: Tagging specification Adobe: XMP specifications and storage model Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: What is metadata? | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: What is metadata? Metadata records information about a media resource or the work it represents, allowing a library to identify, describe, organize and present it. A movie file can have a technical identity as bytes and streams, while the film has a title, creators and release history. A media library needs useful information about both. Metadata records that information. It lets a library show something more meaningful than a list of file paths and lets playback decisions use properties of the actual resource. The described thing matters Consider an invented film called The Station and one encoded copy: Fact What it describes Display title and cast The film/work Provider's title identifier A catalogue record for that work Resolution and video codec A particular media representation Audio language and track title A stream within that representation Local path and file size A stored resource Artwork's dimensions A related image resource These scopes should not be collapsed into one universal item identifier. Two editions of a film can share descriptive facts while having different timelines and technical properties. Records make library actions possible Descriptive metadata supports browsing by title, people, dates or other meaningful properties. Technical metadata helps characterize the selected file and its streams. Identification connects the resource with an intended work or catalogue entity. Metadata can come from embedded records, sidecars, external providers or user edits. The record's meaning depends on its field and vocabulary. A language code, an orientation tag and a release date are not interchangeable strings merely because all can be serialized as text. In Emby, library setup establishes the content context, while the Metadata Manager exposes descriptive editing. Those functions rely on different kinds of information being attached to the correct resource or library entity. A correction changes a particular layer Changing a display title does not rename the spoken dialogue inside the video. Editing a language label does not translate an audio track. Correcting an orientation description can change how an image is displayed without rotating its stored samples. Likewise, replacing a media file can change its technical properties while the film's title remains valid. The useful question is which entity and field an operation updates. Provenance records where values came from; precedence explains how candidate values can become the currently displayed record. See Also Descriptive metadata Technical media metadata Embedded metadata Sidecar metadata Media identification References DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms Matroska: Tagging specification

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Metadata precedence | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Metadata precedence Metadata precedence is the field- and operation-dependent policy for selecting among local, provider, derived and edited candidate values. A media item can receive values from file tags, local records, remote catalogues and user edits. Precedence determines which candidate becomes the current value. The decision can depend on the field and the operation. Treating every refresh as “the newest source wins” loses important distinctions. Decide what is eligible before ranking it A proposed value first needs to describe the intended entity and field. A movie year from a same-title television series is not a useful competing movie value simply because that source has high priority. Likewise, an audio track's language and a work's original language have different scope. A correct value in one field can be incorrect if copied into the other. Eligibility can also depend on parsing, supported mapping and completeness. The absence of a usable candidate is different from a low-ranked candidate. An original field-level merge model Suppose an invented library policy preserves deliberate title edits, probes technical dimensions from the selected file and permits a provider to fill missing descriptions: Field Existing state Incoming candidate Illustrative result Display title User-edited and protected Provider's standard title Keep the protected title Video width Old encode: 1280 Current probe: 1920 Use the current file's value Overview Missing Matched provider's overview Fill it Genre list Local curated list Another provider's list Apply the chosen replace/merge rule Capture time Camera time without known zone File-copy timestamp Keep their distinct meanings This is a teaching policy, not a published Emby source-order table . It illustrates why one blanket priority list cannot answer all the decisions. A field can also retain its provenance : choosing the provider overview should not relabel the user-edited title as provider-authored. Missing, blank and clear are not synonyms An absent field can mean that a source did not supply a claim. An empty string can mean incomplete input, or it can be the representation of a deliberate clear operation under a particular schema. A merger needs a rule for that distinction. Treating every absent field as a request to erase the existing value can remove useful data during a partial update. Ignoring every explicit clear can make it impossible to remove an incorrect description. Lists add another choice. Replacing a list, appending values and computing a deduplicated union produce different results. A union can retain stale or contradictory entries that were meant to be removed. A scalar title normally needs selection rather than concatenating all candidates into a longer title. The field's meaning guides the operation. Trace one partial update For an original policy experiment, assume the existing record has a protected title, an absent overview, and the genre list [Drama, Railway] . A matched incoming source supplies an ordinary title, an overview, and [Drama, Mystery] . The merge can proceed field by field: Verify that the incoming record refers to the intended entity. Reject the batch as a match source if it belongs to the same-title series instead. Keep the existing title because this experiment treats that protected edit as ineligible for replacement. Accept the overview because the existing field is absent and this candidate supplies it. Apply the declared genre-list rule rather than treating it as a scalar string. Under replace , the result is [Drama, Mystery]. Under a stable union , it is [Drama, Railway, Mystery]. If Railway was an outdated provider label, union retains it; if it was deliberate local classification, replacement removes it. Neither operation is intrinsically the right answer without the field policy. Now consider an incoming update that contains no overview field. In this experiment, that absence preserves the current overview. A separately recognized explicit-clear operation removes it. Recording which operation occurred makes the two outcomes distinguishable. A successful repeated update should also avoid accumulating duplicate list entries. A stable deduplicated union yields the same three labels on the second application; blindly appending the incoming two strings does not. The example is deliberately explicit about entity, protection, absence and list semantics. It is not an implementation of Emby’s internal merge algorithm. Refresh has a declared purpose An operation that searches for missing information has different intent from one that replaces existing metadata. Technical probing and provider fetching are also different activities. Emby's Metadata Manager documentation describes refresh modes and protecting changes using field or item locks. Its controls establish concrete product behavior; the actual library/provider configuration and operation determine the applicable combination. Learn's conceptual model does not infer an undocumented universal ordering of every Emby reader and provider. When evaluating a change, keep the selected operation, field state and relevant source candidates together. Identity mistakes survive good merge rules A precisely applied policy can still install the wrong synopsis if the item was matched to another film. Correcting that requires an identity decision, not merely moving the same bad provider response higher in the source order. Similarly, a correct work-level title does not prove that a chosen poster belongs to the intended edition or language. Related records need the right scope before their values are selected. A useful comparison records the existing value and protection state, the incoming value and source/entity, and the result. That makes a surprising refresh explainable as a field decision rather than as an unexplained failure to “keep metadata”. See Also Metadata provenance Conflicting metadata Missing metadata Media identification Embedded metadata References W3C PROV Model Primer DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Metadata provenance | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Metadata provenance Metadata provenance records the sources and activities responsible for values or derived resources, making identity, corrections and later refresh results easier to assess. A library can display a title that differs from the filename, an embedded tag and a provider's current title. Provenance makes that difference explainable by recording where the selected information came from and what produced it. It answers a history question. It does not automatically decide which source should win. Record sources at the field's scope An invented record can have this source history: Field Selected information Source/activity Display title The Station — restored edition A user correction Video width 1920 pixels Probe of the selected file version Release year 2020 A provider record for the matched work Photo caption Platform at dawn An imported descriptive record Calling the entire item “provider metadata” hides that combination. A later title refresh might change only one relationship, while the technical width still belongs to the local file. Useful annotations can include source identity, the source's entity/field, retrieval or edit time and any transformation. They should distinguish a value copied directly from one computed or translated. This is an explanatory record model, not a claim that Emby persists every annotation shown in the table. Derived images have a history too Suppose a raw capture produces an edited JPEG, which then produces a browsing thumbnail. The thumbnail's crop and colour appearance can come from the export and the later image operation. A difference from the raw preview may therefore result from the chosen development, rather than from changing a caption field. A trace should identify which source version supplied the derivative. Retaining only the path can become ambiguous if another image replaces the file at that path. The W3C PROV model supplies vocabulary for entities, activities and responsible agents. A practical library record can apply those ideas without implementing every part of that formal model. Retrieval time is not the media's event time A metadata fetch performed today can return a release date decades earlier. A thumbnail generated today can depict a capture made years ago. Similarly, an old cached response can be read today without being newly obtained from its provider. Separate acquisition, edit, derivation and described-event times when assessing freshness. A single “last updated” date cannot always answer all those questions. A correction needs a source and a policy A user may deliberately select a localized title or repair a mistaken match. Its source history explains why it differs from the next provider response. Precedence decides how that new candidate interacts with the selected value. In Emby, documented field/item locks provide a concrete persistence mechanism, described in Metadata Manager . Those controls are selection behavior; the justification for the correction belongs to its provenance. Keeping the two concepts distinct helps explain whether a surprising change came from a new source, a different entity match, or a changed rule for choosing among existing values. See Also Metadata precedence Conflicting metadata Provider identifiers Image thumbnail generation References W3C PROV Model Primer DCMI: Dublin Core metadata terms

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Sidecar metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Sidecar metadata A metadata sidecar stores associated information outside the media resource, relying on a defined association and schema rather than being part of the image or media payload. A sidecar stores related information beside a resource rather than inside it. For example, a raw-photo workflow can use an XMP file associated with the camera file: Capture-0042.raw Capture-0042.xmp These are invented names illustrating association. The reader's supported naming and lookup rules decide how it connects them. Association and schema solve different problems Requirement Question Association Which media resource or entity does this file describe? Syntax/schema How are fields represented and what do they mean? Version relationship Does the record still describe the current resource? Merge policy How does it interact with other metadata candidates? A syntactically valid sidecar can still be attached to the wrong copy. Sharing a basename can be useful evidence within a naming convention, but it is not a universal content fingerprint. The format also determines whether the record contains descriptions, applicable edit instructions or other information. A sidecar's existence does not make every field meaningful to every media library. For Emby, supported local metadata is an input to the applicable library reader. Metadata Manager describes editing and refresh behavior; it does not imply that every external XMP property or every sidecar convention is imported. The useful comparison keeps source association, supported field mapping and the displayed record separate. External storage permits a different editing boundary Writing a sidecar can leave the media payload unchanged. That is useful when a workflow wants to retain a master while recording additional description or supported processing instructions. The output appearance changes only when an application actually reads and applies those instructions. A player ignoring a raw-development recipe can show a prepared preview instead. Conversely, a database-only title edit is not automatically an update to the sidecar. There are separate read, merge and write-back operations. Moves and duplicates need a coherent relationship Moving a media file without its sidecar can lose the external context. Replacing the media while keeping an old sidecar can preserve a relationship to the wrong source version. A duplicate basename in another folder introduces another association context. Copying just the metadata into that folder should not be assumed to transfer correct capture or identity information to unrelated media. See Also Embedded metadata XMP metadata Metadata provenance Metadata precedence Camera raw images References Adobe: XMP specifications and storage model Adobe: XMP data types

articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.title: Technical media metadata | Emby Learn
articles/metadata-discovery/understandin.keywords: Technical media metadata Technical media metadata describes the encoded resource, tracks and presentation properties recovered by parsing, probing or analysis. Technical metadata characterizes a particular media resource and its streams. It can include container/codec identification, dimensions, duration, track layout and applicable presentation signaling. A provider's synopsis cannot establish those properties of the local file. They come from that resource's structure or analysis. File, stream and presentation have different properties Scope Example properties File/container Packaging, size, contained streams Video stream Codec/profile, sample dimensions, timing and colour signaling Audio stream Codec, sample rate, channel description Subtitle stream Coding, language/role description, applicable timing Image Sample grid, orientation and colour interpretation Some information is declared in headers, some inferred, and some measured by reading more of the resource. A short probe and a full analysis need not establish the same level of detail. For example, a declared language can be readable metadata without proof that every spoken passage uses that language. A valid codec identifier also does not establish that the entire bitstream is undamaged. Average file rate includes everything in the file Take an invented resource of 210,000,000 bytes lasting 600 seconds : 210000000 × 8 / 600 = 2,800,000 bits/s , or 2.8 Mb/s . That whole-file average includes its audio, subtitles, packaging and other stored material. It should not automatically be copied into a field describing the video's average bitrate. Peak delivery demand has another relationship to time. A short high-rate section can matter for streaming even when the full-file average is modest. Bitrate develops that distinction. Replacing the resource can invalidate old observations A new encode of the same film can have another resolution, track set or timeline. Retaining the film's descriptive identity may be appropriate; retaining old stream details can be wrong. In Emby, compare the actual selected media source with the technical data exposed for it. If a playback description reports a missing track or an old resolution, establish whether it refers to the updated file or another version before editing unrelated descriptive fields. Technical renewal and provider refresh answer different questions. The first recovers the resource's properties; the second seeks descriptive information about the associated work. See Also Descriptive metadata Streams and Tracks Bitrate Missing metadata Image resolution References FFmpeg: ffprobe documentation Matroska: Tagging specification

articles/networking/access/identity/inde.title: Overview: Identity and sessions | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/identity/inde.keywords: Overview: Identity and sessions Identity and session concepts distinguish authentication evidence, account scope and permission decisions. A user label names a claimed account; authentication establishes the accepted identity under the server's contract. Authorization then evaluates an operation, and a login session has its own continuing state. These concepts explain why a successful sign-in is useful evidence without being permission for every later request. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media server authentication Media-server authentication verifies credential evidence for a requested account, while user/device labels and later operation permissions have separate roles. Media server authorization Media-server authorization evaluates whether an established user context may perform a specific operation on the requested resource under the applicable policy. Server user identity Server user identity associates a local account with its state and policy within one server, separately from display labels, device identity and optional Connect linkage. Login sessions A login session retains accepted account evidence for subsequent requests, with token scope, validity and revocation separate from application-window or playback-session state. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby developer documentation: User authentication and tokens Emby: Server-local users

articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.title: Media server authentication and credential evidence | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.keywords: Media server authentication and credential evidence Media-server authentication verifies credential evidence for a requested account, while user/device labels and later operation permissions have separate roles. A client names a user and describes its device. The server still needs evidence that the request is entitled to act as that account. Authentication evaluates that credential relationship. It precedes deciding which library or operation the account is allowed to use. Labels describe a claim A user ID, display name and device ID can identify intended objects in a request. They are not secret proof merely because they are unique. An original reduced decision is: { "requestedUser": "U1", "deviceLabel": "Living Room", "credentialValid": false, "authenticatedUser": null } The user and device labels are present, but the declared verifier result is false. No authenticated account follows from those labels alone. The fields are explanatory outcomes, not native Emby authentication input. A login establishes evidence for later requests Emby’s developer documentation describes user authentication and a successful result with an access token. Later requests carry that token under the documented protocol. The application serializes credential information in its request body. HTTPS protects the transport to the validated endpoint; application-body text and plaintext transmission over an unprotected connection are different concepts. A token then represents the accepted relationship according to its scope/lifetime. It needs protection as credential material, rather than being treated like a harmless device label. A displayed user still needs authentication The documented public-user list supports login-screen presentation. Its presence identifies selectable accounts; it does not establish that a viewer has authenticated as one. The same documentation says authentication is still required when the displayed user’s HasPassword value is false. The intended protocol result matters, rather than inferring access from a missing password prompt. A client can consequently show the correct account image while failing to establish its valid request context. The server and account scopes belong together An account on one server is not automatically the same account on another. A token accepted by server A should not be sent as proof to unrelated server B merely because the user’s displayed name matches. Emby’s documented token storage guidance associates it with the server ID. User identity develops that scope. NIST’s authentication guidance supplies broader verifier/session concepts. It is not a claim that every Emby authentication route implements a particular government assurance level. Successful authentication leaves an authorization question A valid U1 request can still be denied administration, deletion or access to another user’s library scope. Authorization evaluates those operations. Login sessions follows persistence and revocation of the established evidence. See Also Media server authorization and operation-specific access Server user identity and scoped account state Login sessions, tokens and revocation HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity References Emby developer documentation: User authentication and tokens NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authentication and session concepts Emby: Server-local users Emby: Server and account security

articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.title: Media server authorization and operation-specific access | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.keywords: Media server authorization and operation-specific access Media-server authorization evaluates whether an established user context may perform a specific operation on the requested resource under the applicable policy. A user logs in successfully and can play a film, yet cannot delete it or open server administration. The credential relationship is valid; the operations have different permissions. Authorization evaluates the action and resource under the established user context. Ask about the particular operation Use this original policy matrix for U1: Operation Resource Declared result Browse Family library Allow Play A permitted family item Allow Delete That same item Deny Administer Server configuration Deny The same authenticated account appears in every row. “Authenticated” is not one universal allow flag for all later operations. Emby’s user, content-access and parental-control documentation identifies these separate policy areas. Actual implemented routes must enforce their relevant policy. Keep the resource and user in the decision An original reduced request is: { "authenticatedUser": "U1", "resource": "Family/Item7", "operation": "delete", "canPlay": true, "canDelete": false, "decision": "deny" } The model denies deletion even though playback is allowed. Reusing only the canPlay result would select the wrong permission. A decision also needs the resource’s actual library/folder/rating context. A client-written display label should not replace the server’s authoritative object association. Enforce policy at the operation boundary Filtering a list in the client improves presentation but is not sufficient authorization for a later direct resource request. The server needs the applicable checks when the operation is attempted through its supported path. A trusted session identifies the user; it does not bypass resource policy. Conversely, a hidden UI button is not evidence that the backend denied an attempted operation. Those are separate observations. This is an access-control principle and teaching model, not a claim that live behavior was tested on a particular Emby version. Several policy inputs can combine Library/folder access, rating/tag restrictions, remote-access conditions and administrative capability can affect different operations. A request can satisfy one condition while failing another. Library permissions and rating restrictions develop those content decisions. The server’s storage identity also differs from the application user. The process being able to read a file does not give every authenticated user permission to request it. An allowed request still needs a working media result Authorization can permit playback while an absent file, incompatible output or network failure prevents presentation. That failure does not retroactively mean the user was unauthorized. An application should preserve the difference between policy denial and unavailable/failed media processing. See Also Media server authentication and credential evidence Library access permissions and the user’s media scope Rating-based restrictions and unknown metadata Server user identity and scoped account state References Emby: Server-local users Emby: Library and channel access Emby: Rating, tag and access-schedule controls Emby developer documentation: User authentication and tokens

articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.title: Login sessions, tokens and revocation | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.keywords: Login sessions, tokens and revocation A login session retains accepted account evidence for subsequent requests, with token scope, validity and revocation separate from application-window or playback-session state. A signed-in app can make many requests without resending the password each time. The session/token mechanism retains accepted evidence according to the server’s protocol and policy. Closing the app and ending that evidence are different events. An access token belongs to the intended server Emby’s developer documentation describes returning an access token after successful authentication and using it on subsequent HTTP requests. It also describes storing the token with the server ID. An equal account name on another server does not make that token appropriate there. An illustrative token label such as T1 in a model is not a usable credential. Actual token contents should be treated as authentication material. Session validity can include several conditions Use an original policy projection: { "issuedAtSeconds": 0, "absoluteLifetimeSeconds": 3600, "lastActivitySeconds": 100, "idleLifetimeSeconds": 600, "nowSeconds": 701, "revoked": false } The absolute deadline is 3600. The idle deadline is 700. At the stated observation time 701, the idle condition has expired even though the absolute one has not. These durations are invented. They do not claim Emby uses a one-hour or ten-minute default. NIST’s session guidance supplies the broader distinction between session conditions and the proof that originally established them. A protocol can instead retain revocable tokens under another lifetime design. Explicit logout and process exit differ Emby’s documented logout operation revokes the applicable access token. The documentation distinguishes that from closing the app and retaining the token for later use. A process/window exit can therefore leave server-side accepted evidence intact. An app reopened later still needs the server’s current validity result rather than assuming its saved token is permanently accepted. A password or policy change has its defined server behavior too. The application should not invent one universal revocation rule from the UI action’s name. A rejected token can arrive over a valid connection An HTTPS connection can be valid while a later request receives an authentication rejection because its token is invalid or revoked. The transport result and session result are independently meaningful. Repeatedly changing a certificate would not repair an actually rejected token. The documented protocol identifies a 401 response as a context for returning to the authentication flow. A playback session is another object An active player can have media position, stream state and remote-control information. Those are not the same thing as the login evidence authorizing its requests. Several playback operations can use one accepted user session, and a client can retain login evidence while no video is playing. Authorization also remains current for each requested operation. Session persistence identifies the account relationship; it does not turn one earlier successful play into permission for every later resource. See Also Media server authentication and credential evidence Server user identity and scoped account state Media server authorization and operation-specific access HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity References Emby developer documentation: User authentication and tokens NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authentication and session concepts Emby: Server and account security

articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.title: Server user identity and scoped account state | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/identity/Netw.keywords: Server user identity and scoped account state Server user identity associates a local account with its state and policy within one server, separately from display labels, device identity and optional Connect linkage. Two servers can each have an account named Alex. They are not one account merely because the displayed names match. An Emby server’s local user identity owns that server’s account state and policy relationships. A complete identity retains server scope Use this original inventory: Server Local user ID Display name A U1 Alex B U1 Alex A U2 Family The first two raw user IDs match too, but the complete keys (A,U1) and (B,U1) refer to different local objects. [ {"serverId": "A", "userId": "U1", "name": "Alex"}, {"serverId": "B", "userId": "U1", "name": "Alex"} ] The example values are fictional rather than native returned Emby IDs. A client’s saved token and selected server should retain that same scope. Names and devices have another lifetime A renamed user can keep its local identity and associated state. A recreated account with an equal display name can be another object. A device identifier describes a client/device relationship, not the user’s entire identity. Several users can use one television, and one user can use several devices. The current request/session supplies which account is active. The hardware’s friendly label does not select that account’s permissions by itself. Personal media state belongs to the account context Watched progress, favorites and recommendations can vary by user on the same server. User history describes that state. The shared media item and each account’s personal association are different records. A permission change can alter which items the user sees without changing the underlying shared library object. A metadata correction can change the item while the personal relationship remains scoped to the relevant user/item identities. Connect linkage adds an association Emby documents optional linking of a local user with a Connect identity. That assists sign-in and server location. The local account remains the server’s policy/state object. A central identity link does not merge all local accounts into one universal library permission set. See Also Media server authentication and credential evidence Emby Connect and the path to the selected server User-specific playback history Library access permissions and the user’s media scope References Emby: Server-local users Emby developer documentation: User authentication and tokens Emby developer documentation: Item identity, ratings and user state

articles/networking/access/index.html.title: Overview: User identity and access | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/index.html.keywords: Overview: User identity and access Media-server access connects accepted identity and session state with the rules governing requested resources. Reaching the server is followed by another decision: who is making the request and what that identity may do. Sessions supply a continuing authentication relationship, while library and rating rules govern particular media access. The two branches keep identity evidence separate from the resource decision. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Identity and sessions Identity and session concepts distinguish authentication evidence, account scope and permission decisions. Media access rules Media-access rules apply account and resource policies to particular libraries or rating-related content. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/networking/access/rules/index.h.title: Overview: Media access rules | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/rules/index.h.keywords: Overview: Media access rules Media-access rules apply account and resource policies to particular libraries or rating-related content. A viewer's permitted library set and a rating restriction describe different policy inputs. Unknown or incomplete rating information can also require an explicit rule. These pages explain the resource decision without confusing it with the server process's filesystem permissions or the mere existence of an item in the catalogue. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Library access permissions Library access permissions scope which media an application user may request, with library/folder policy separate from the server process’s filesystem access and client presentation choices. Rating-based access restrictions Rating-based restrictions compare supplied content metadata within the configured rating scheme and unknown-content policy, adding a distinct condition to other library and account access rules. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Library and channel access Emby: Rating, tag and access-schedule controls

articles/networking/access/rules/Network.title: Library access permissions and the user’s media scope | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/rules/Network.keywords: Library access permissions and the user’s media scope Library access permissions scope which media an application user may request, with library/folder policy separate from the server process’s filesystem access and client presentation choices. One shared server library can provide different users with different media access. The server retains its collection; the user’s applicable policy determines the permitted scope. Library and folder choices can combine Use this original reduced policy: { "user": "U1", "allowedLibraries": ["L1"], "allowedFolders": ["L1/Family"], "requests": ["L1/Family/Item7", "L1/Other/Item8", "L2/Family/Item9"] } For this exercise, a request must satisfy both its library membership and selected folder scope. Request Library condition Folder condition Model result L1/Family/Item7 Pass Pass Allow L1/Other/Item8 Pass Fail Deny L2/Family/Item9 Fail Outside selected L1 scope Deny The complete folder key retains the library. Reusing only the label Family would incorrectly merge different collection contexts. Emby’s content-access documentation describes library and channel selections, with folder-level access for libraries containing multiple configured paths. Its folder-based reference explains the shared-library/different-user-view role. The server’s filesystem identity is another boundary The Emby process needs the appropriate storage access to scan/read the relevant media. That operating-system identity is different from the application user U1. A readable file can still lie outside U1’s permitted library scope. A permitted U1 request can also encounter storage the process cannot presently read. The first is an application-policy issue; the second is an availability/operating-system access issue. Granting every user library access does not repair a missing mount or server-side read failure. A client view is a presentation of the policy Removing a card, favorite or library shortcut in one app does not establish that the corresponding resource request is denied by the server. The policy needs to be applied at the relevant operation boundary. A later direct playback request has its own resource and user context. Likewise, hiding a library is different from removing its indexed items or deleting its physical media. Other content rules still have inputs A library permission can pass while rating/tag restrictions exclude an item. A permission to play can coexist with a denial of deletion or administration. Authorization develops those operation distinctions. Rating restrictions follows the metadata-dependent content check.
