See Also Media server authorization and operation-specific access Rating-based restrictions and unknown metadata Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References Emby: Library and channel access Emby: Folder-based access control Emby: Server-local users

articles/networking/access/rules/Network.title: Rating-based restrictions and unknown metadata | Emby Learn
articles/networking/access/rules/Network.keywords: Rating-based restrictions and unknown metadata Rating-based restrictions compare supplied content metadata within the configured rating scheme and unknown-content policy, adding a distinct condition to other library and account access rules. A rating restriction uses the item’s interpreted rating metadata. It does not inspect every scene and discover its suitability automatically. The chosen rating system and handling of unknown metadata belong in the policy. Compare ranks within the intended scheme Use an original fictional system called LearnBands: { "scheme": "LearnBands", "allowedMaximumRank": 1, "blockUnknown": true, "items": [ {"id": "A", "rank": 0}, {"id": "B", "rank": 2}, {"id": "C", "rank": null} ] } Under this declared comparison, A passes, B exceeds the threshold and C fails the unknown-content rule. Item Interpreted rank Block unknown Permit unknown A 0 Allow Allow B 2 Deny Deny C Unknown Deny Allow Changing blockUnknown to false changes C’s branch. It does not assign C a known low rating. This is an invented rank model. National and provider rating schemes have their own identifiers and interpretations; their labels should not be compared as one global alphabetical or numeric order. Unrated is a separate decision Emby’s parental-control documentation describes a maximum rating and separate options for unrated content. A threshold alone therefore does not define every unknown case. Missing, unrecognized and incorrectly mapped metadata can produce different inputs to the actual implementation. An unrated item is not evidence that the content is suitable for every viewer. It says the relevant metadata did not yield a rating under that interpretation. Metadata correction can change the result Emby item information includes an OfficialRating property and other content fields such as tags. If the item was misidentified or its rating is stale, the access result can reflect that wrong metadata while the physical video remains unchanged. Content ratings develops the provenance and scheme context. A parental limit cannot correct an incorrectly supplied item identity by itself. Tags and libraries add separate conditions Emby documents additional tag-based restrictions and library/channel access controls. A permitted rating does not override a denied library scope. A permitted library does not remove the relevant rating/tag check. The exact combination belongs to the configured product policy. The simplified rank exercise illustrates one condition rather than proving all routes of a particular server enforce a complete set. Account selection is part of the boundary The relevant user must be active for the intended restriction to apply. A shared device’s friendly name is not the account context, and UI filtering is not a substitute for server operation policy. See Also Library access permissions and the user’s media scope Media server authorization and operation-specific access Content ratings References Emby: Rating, tag and access-schedule controls Emby developer documentation: Item identity, ratings and user state Emby: Library and channel access

articles/networking/addressing/index.htm.title: Overview: IP addressing | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/index.htm.keywords: Overview: IP addressing IP addressing identifies interfaces and network relationships under particular address scopes and configuration rules. An address can belong to a local subnet, a public route or a loopback context. IPv4, IPv6, CIDR notation and DHCP reservations describe different properties of that arrangement. These pages help interpret the address the server or app is actually using rather than treating every visible address as equally reachable. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> IP addresses An IP address identifies an addressable interface or endpoint within a particular address family and scope, with routing and service selection determining whether Emby can be reached there. IPv4 IPv4 carries packets between 32-bit source and destination addresses, with routing, packet lifetime and fragmentation separate from the transport service carried inside. IPv6 IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses with explicit scope and interface context, allowing several addresses and routes that a client must interpret when reaching a server. Private and public addresses Private, shared, local and special-purpose address ranges have different routing roles, and a globally assigned address still needs a permitted service path to be reachable. Subnets and CIDR notation CIDR notation specifies how many leading address bits form a prefix, defining address membership and the specificity used to choose matching routes. DHCP reservations A DHCP reservation binds a chosen server-side client identity to a stable address allocation while the client continues obtaining its network configuration through DHCP. Loopback addresses Loopback addresses reach the requesting host’s own network stack, making localhost useful for same-host access while proving little about another device’s server path. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 791: Internet Protocol RFC 8200: IPv6 specification RFC 1918: Private IPv4 address allocation RFC 4632: CIDR addressing and aggregation RFC 2131: DHCP leases and client binding RFC 1122: Internet host communication requirements

articles/networking/addressing/Network-C.title: Subnets, CIDR and matching routes | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-C.keywords: Subnets, CIDR and matching routes CIDR notation specifies how many leading address bits form a prefix, defining address membership and the specificity used to choose matching routes. The /24 in 192.168.50.0/24 means that the first twenty-four address bits form the prefix. It does not mean twenty-four devices. The remaining eight IPv4 bits give 256 address combinations in that prefix. Prefix length is the information missing when someone describes a network only as “192.168.50.” A /25 boundary cuts the final byte in half Use the original address 192.168.50.20 with a /25 prefix. The mask is 255.255.255.128. The first three bytes are entirely prefix bits. In the last byte, only the high bit belongs to the prefix: address last byte: 20 = 00010100 mask last byte: 128 = 10000000 AND result: 0 = 00000000 prefix: 192.168.50.0/25 There are seven remaining bits, giving 128 addresses from 192.168.50.0 through 192.168.50.127. Now consider 192.168.50.200. Its final byte has the high bit set, so it belongs to 192.168.50.128/25. Prefix being compared .20 and .200 in the same prefix? 192.168.50.0/24 Yes The relevant /25 subdivisions No The first three dotted numbers match in both cases. Only the actual prefix tells you whether the local grouping matches. Prefix membership does not require a .0 ending A prefix need not end on an eight-bit boundary. The same calculation works for /23, /26 or any other supported length. For example, a /23 has 512 IPv4 combinations. The aligned 192.168.50.0/23 block includes both the 192.168.50.* and 192.168.51.* ranges. Writing 192.168.50.20/24 as an interface address retains the host’s .20 value and its prefix length. A normalized network-prefix representation uses 192.168.50.0/24. Those strings describe related objects, not interchangeable host destinations. Total combinations differ from ordinary host allocation For IPv4, total combinations are 2^(32 - prefix length) : Prefix Total combinations Interpretation in this example /24 256 Ordinary LAN often reserves network/broadcast values /25 128 Same ordinary-LAN reservation convention /31 2 RFC 3021 point-to-point use can use both endpoints /32 1 One address, useful as a host-specific route “Subtract two” is therefore not a universal address-count rule. IPv6 applies the same prefix-bit idea to 128 bits. A /64 contains 2^64 address combinations; IPv4’s ordinary network/broadcast subtraction does not carry over unchanged. More specific matching routes win first Use this original reduced route table: { "destination": "192.168.50.200", "routes": [ {"prefix": "0.0.0.0/0", "path": "default", "metric": 10}, {"prefix": "192.168.50.0/24", "path": "lan", "metric": 20}, {"prefix": "192.168.50.128/25", "path": "vpn", "metric": 500} ], "selectedPath": "vpn" } All three prefixes include the destination. The /25 is the longest matching prefix and selects the VPN path in this exercise, despite its larger metric. Metric comparison is a later choice among otherwise competing route candidates according to the implementation. A low-metric default route does not automatically override every more-specific route. A mistaken narrow route can therefore capture only some addresses in what looked like one LAN. VPN routing develops that overlap. Routing and Emby’s classification use prefixes for different decisions The operating system uses routes to decide how to send traffic. Emby’s LAN Networks setting uses specified ranges in its local/remote policy classification. An incorrect /16 instead of /24 can include 256 times as many address combinations. That can broaden the application classification without extending the actual network or creating a route. See Also IP addresses and reachable interfaces Private, public and special-purpose IP addresses VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling References RFC 4632: CIDR addressing and aggregation RFC 3021: IPv4 /31 point-to-point prefixes RFC 4291: IPv6 addressing architecture Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/addressing/Network-D.title: DHCP reservations and stable server addresses | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-D.keywords: DHCP reservations and stable server addresses A DHCP reservation binds a chosen server-side client identity to a stable address allocation while the client continues obtaining its network configuration through DHCP. A port-forward or saved app connection needs a stable destination. If the server’s DHCP allocation changes, an otherwise correct reference can keep pointing to the old address. A DHCP reservation asks the DHCP server to allocate a chosen address to a particular client binding. The client still uses DHCP Address arrangement Where the address choice is maintained Ordinary dynamic allocation DHCP server’s pool and lease policy Reservation DHCP server’s client-to-address binding Manual static configuration The client/interface configuration With a reservation, the client can still obtain its address and other options through the DHCP exchange. This differs from typing the address, prefix, router and DNS settings into the client manually. The DHCP server needs a consistent allocation policy so the reserved value is not also handed to another client. Emby’s connectivity documentation points to a DHCP reservation as a way to stabilize the server’s local address. The binding belongs to a client identity This original reduced allocation model uses explicit client keys: { "reservations": {"client-A": "192.168.50.20"}, "requestClient": "client-B", "reservedMatch": false, "dynamicOffer": "192.168.50.42" } Client B does not match client A’s reservation. Keeping the computer’s display name unchanged does not alter that comparison. A DHCP server can identify clients through client identifiers and/or hardware-address-related bindings according to its implementation. A router’s user interface may expose a MAC-based reservation. Replacing the adapter, changing its exposed identity or using another interface can therefore need a different binding. “This is the same computer” is not necessarily the identity the DHCP server compares. A stable choice still has a lease lifecycle For an original twenty-four-hour lease using the usual default fractions, renewal begins around hour twelve and rebinding around hour twenty-one if renewal has not succeeded. The lease expires at twenty-four. Successful renewal extends the binding’s valid lifetime. A client cannot keep using an expired allocation indefinitely merely because a reservation exists in a configuration screen. The timer details and actual allocation behavior belong to the DHCP implementation. The reservation supplies a preferred stable choice within that process. Stabilize the references that use the address A port-forward rule targets the internal address. A DNS record or discovery advertisement can report it. A cached app entry can retain it. Changing the binding does not automatically rewrite every separate reference or immediately move an already leased client to the new value. See Also IP addresses and reachable interfaces Port forwarding and the complete inbound path DNS resolution, record types and cached answers References RFC 2131: DHCP leases and client binding Emby: Connecting from client apps

articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.title: IP addresses and reachable interfaces | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.keywords: IP addresses and reachable interfaces An IP address identifies an addressable interface or endpoint within a particular address family and scope, with routing and service selection determining whether Emby can be reached there. An Emby server address tells the client where to send IP traffic. It is not a permanent device identity or a complete description of the service to request. One machine can have several useful addresses, and only some of them may be reachable from a particular client. A machine can expose several address contexts Use this original inventory: Interface or context Example address Intended reach Ethernet LAN 192.168.50.20 Its routed/local private realm VPN interface 10.8.0.1 The configured tunnel realm IPv6 interface 2001:db8:50::20 Documentation example of an IPv6 address Loopback 127.0.0.1 or ::1 The requesting host’s own network stack The IPv6 value uses the documentation prefix; it is not a publicly reachable example server. A client on the Ethernet LAN might use the first address. A VPN client needs the relevant routes. Another device’s loopback address refers to that other device. The service adds another part of the endpoint An address plus a transport protocol and port identifies the intended listener. A URL additionally names the application scheme and resource path. Two services can share one IP address by listening on different ports. TCP and UDP can also use the same numeric port independently. If a client reaches 192.168.50.20 but uses the wrong port, the address itself may be correct. Network ports explains the next part of the selection. An address can outlive or change before a saved reference A DHCP lease can change, an interface can disconnect, or an IPv6 prefix can be renumbered. A saved connection entry may still contain the earlier value. The server’s identity can remain the same through that change. The old address can eventually belong to another machine. A DHCP reservation stabilizes a selected allocation through the DHCP server’s binding policy. A hostname provides another indirection, whose records must also remain correct. Listening and advertising are separate A server can listen on an address or wildcard interface selection and report a particular address to clients. These observations need to agree with the route a client can use. The wildcard 0.0.0.0 in a listener configuration means a binding choice, not a destination address to type into a remote app. IPv6 has its corresponding unspecified address. Emby’s reported local-address setting addresses the advertisement side of that relationship. Changing an advertised address does not make an otherwise unreachable interface appear on the client’s network. See Also IPv4 packet addressing and forwarding IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability Subnets, CIDR and matching routes Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints References RFC 791: Internet Protocol RFC 4291: IPv6 addressing architecture Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.title: IPv4 packet addressing and forwarding | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.keywords: IPv4 packet addressing and forwarding IPv4 carries packets between 32-bit source and destination addresses, with routing, packet lifetime and fragmentation separate from the transport service carried inside. An IPv4 address such as 192.168.50.20 contains four eight-bit values. Together they form a 32-bit address. The dotted form is readable notation for those bits. It does not tell you the subnet size, the service port or whether another network has a route to the address. Four bytes describe one address For this original value: 192.168.50.20 11000000 . 10101000 . 00110010 . 00010100 Each displayed number lies from zero to 255. Prefix length supplies the separate network grouping used by CIDR . An address beginning with 192 does not automatically have a particular “class C” subnet in a modern configured network. The actual prefix and routes determine the boundary. Routers preserve the final destination while selecting each hop A packet for an off-link server is sent first to the chosen router on the local link. The link-layer frame is addressed to that next hop; the IP destination remains the intended server. At another hop, the frame’s local addressing changes again. Ordinary routing does not need to replace the final destination with every router’s address. NAT is a separate operation that can rewrite IP/transport endpoint fields. Address translation develops that added state. Packet lifetime is not a playback timer IPv4’s TTL bounds forwarding lifetime. Routers decrement it, and a packet cannot keep circulating indefinitely. This original reduced projection assumes one decrement at each listed router: { "initialTtl": 64, "routerHops": 3, "remainingTtl": 61 } It does not describe sixty-one seconds of movie buffer. A forwarding-lifetime value and media presentation time have different purposes. Packet size belongs to the chosen path In a declared 1500-byte IP packet with a minimum twenty-byte IPv4 header, 1480 bytes remain for the carried transport and its data. If that transport is UDP with its eight-byte header, the application payload is 1472 bytes under those assumptions. Options, tunnels or a smaller path limit change the result. Fragmentation can divide an IPv4 datagram, but all required pieces must arrive for reassembly. Losing one fragment can consequently lose the larger datagram’s usable result. See Also IP addresses and reachable interfaces Subnets, CIDR and matching routes NAT and address/port translation state IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability References RFC 791: Internet Protocol RFC 1122: Internet host communication requirements RFC 1918: Private IPv4 address allocation RFC 5737: IPv4 documentation address blocks

articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.title: IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-I.keywords: IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses with explicit scope and interface context, allowing several addresses and routes that a client must interpret when reaching a server. These two strings can describe the same IPv6 address: 2001:0db8:0050:0000:0000:0000:0000:0020 2001:db8:50::20 Leading zeroes can be omitted in a group, and one run of zero groups can be compressed with :: . The shorter text still identifies the same 128 bits. This address uses the documentation prefix. It illustrates notation, not a reachable Emby server. Several addresses can belong to one interface An IPv6 interface can have a link-local address plus other addresses with different uses and lifetimes. Address category Intended context Link-local, such as fe80::… Communication on the relevant local link Unique local, from the locally assigned ULA space Communication within the configured private routing realm Global unicast allocation Potential wider routing under its actual prefix and policy Loopback ::1 The requesting host itself An address being present does not establish that a particular app has a route to it. The advertised address needs to suit the receiving client’s context. Link-local destinations need a link context The address fe80::20 can occur on different links. A machine with Ethernet and a VPN therefore needs to know which link is intended when using such a destination. A zone identifier, often an interface name or local index, supplies that context in supporting interfaces. Its value is local to the requesting machine: one device’s interface number is not a portable global label. RFC 9844 is the current referenced user-interface specification and obsoletes RFC 6874. Actual browser/app input support still needs to be established by the implementation. A bare link-local address copied from the server is consequently a poor universal endpoint for unrelated remote clients. The URL has another delimiter requirement An IPv6 address literal in a URL authority uses brackets so the address’s colons do not become confused with a port separator: https://[2001:db8:50::20]:8920/ Here 8920 is the explicit service port. The example assumes the chosen service provides HTTPS on that port; the notation does not enable TLS or create a listener. Hostnames and URLs develops that complete endpoint. Wider addressing does not choose an access policy IPv6 can provide routed global addresses without the IPv4 address-sharing translation familiar in many homes. Inbound traffic still depends on routes, gateway policy, host firewall and service binding. ULA routing can connect selected private sites or VPNs. It does not provide a normal public-internet route merely because its addresses have the IPv6 width. Neighbor Discovery and router information also have their own roles. IPv6 uses multicast rather than IPv4-style broadcast for many link operations; an application cannot simply reuse an IPv4 broadcast discovery exchange unchanged. A hostname can offer both families An A record can supply IPv4 while an AAAA record supplies IPv6. Either family can have a working route, a broken route or a stale endpoint. A client can try them in a chosen order or use connection concurrency. Having a valid AAAA answer alone does not prove that the matching listener and return path work. See Also IP addresses and reachable interfaces Private, public and special-purpose IP addresses Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References RFC 8200: IPv6 specification RFC 4291: IPv6 addressing architecture RFC 5952: IPv6 text representation RFC 9844: Entering IPv6 zone identifiers RFC 4861: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery RFC 4193: Unique local IPv6 addresses RFC 3849: IPv6 documentation prefix

articles/networking/addressing/Network-L.title: Loopback addresses and the meaning of localhost | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-L.keywords: Loopback addresses and the meaning of localhost Loopback addresses reach the requesting host’s own network stack, making localhost useful for same-host access while proving little about another device’s server path. A browser on the server opens http://localhost:8096/ successfully. The same text entered on a phone does not reach that server. The hostname stayed the same. The machine interpreting it changed. Localhost belongs to the requester Loopback traffic stays within the requesting host’s network stack. IPv4 reserves 127.0.0.0/8 for loopback; 127.0.0.1 is the familiar example. IPv6 uses ::1. Requester Destination localhost refers to Browser on the Emby machine That machine’s network stack Browser on the phone The phone’s network stack Proxy with its own network namespace The proxy’s namespace-local stack The phone does not interpret localhost as “the Emby server I was thinking about.” It needs an address or name for a reachable server endpoint. A loopback connection tests a short path An on-server success can establish that a listener and application operation work through that local path. It does not exercise the LAN interface, remote device route or inbound firewall policy for another machine. If the service binds only to loopback, remote clients cannot reach that listener through the server’s LAN address. An all-interface binding is a different selection, still subject to service and firewall policy. Emby’s connectivity documentation uses localhost for local dashboard access and separately identifies the address other devices can use. A proxy changes which process is the requester A same-host reverse proxy may reach Emby through loopback while accepting client connections on another interface. That is a deliberate two-connection path. If the proxy instead lives in another machine or isolated network namespace, its loopback destination is no longer the Emby machine’s stack. It needs the appropriate origin endpoint in that context. Reverse proxies develops those independent sides. Wildcard and loopback have different meanings A listener bound to 0.0.0.0 is expressing an IPv4 binding choice across interfaces. It is not the IPv4 loopback address, and it is not a destination to advertise to a phone. Similarly, IPv6’s unspecified :: and loopback ::1 have different roles. Whether one wildcard listener also accepts another address family depends on its socket/platform settings. See Also Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints References RFC 1122: Internet host communication requirements RFC 4291: IPv6 addressing architecture IANA: Special-purpose IPv4 address registry Emby: Connecting from client apps

articles/networking/addressing/Network-P.title: Private, public and special-purpose IP addresses | Emby Learn
articles/networking/addressing/Network-P.keywords: Private, public and special-purpose IP addresses Private, shared, local and special-purpose address ranges have different routing roles, and a globally assigned address still needs a permitted service path to be reachable. A private address can work perfectly inside a home and still be meaningless as an outside client’s destination. Its scope belongs to the private routing realm using it. The other common mistake is to call every address outside the private ranges “public.” Several other ranges have special purposes. The three private IPv4 blocks RFC 1918 reserves: Prefix Included address range 10.0.0.0/8 10.0.0.0–10.255.255.255 172.16.0.0/12 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 192.168.0.0/16 192.168.0.0–192.168.255.255 These addresses can be reused by unrelated homes and organizations. A route for your home’s 192.168.50.20 must select your private realm, not somebody else’s equal address. The boundary around 172 is important: 172.20.1.1 is inside RFC 1918 space, while 172.40.1.1 is outside that block. The first displayed number alone is insufficient. Non-private does not imply an ordinary public destination Other range Purpose 100.64.0.0/10 Shared address space, commonly associated with carrier-grade NAT 127.0.0.0/8 IPv4 loopback 169.254.0.0/16 IPv4 link-local communication 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 Documentation examples The current IANA special-purpose registry distinguishes properties such as forwarding and global reachability. It provides more precise context than one “not private” test. The documentation blocks used in these Learn examples stand in for outside address labels in invented topologies. They are not actual public services to contact. A global allocation still needs a complete path A globally assigned destination can lack a route, be filtered, have no listener at the selected port or reject the application request. NAT can translate a household’s private IPv4 endpoints to an outside allocation. The translation does not add a user account, TLS certificate or permission to view a library. Similarly, an address range being private is not a security boundary by itself. Private networks can be interconnected or accessed through tunnels; the configured policies determine what traffic is allowed. IPv6 has its own categories IPv6 has loopback, link-local, unique local and globally routed categories. Locally assigned ULA prefixes use the fd portion of fc00::/7 and are intended for private routing rather than normal global-internet reachability. The documentation prefix 2001:db8::/32 is another special-purpose range. See Also NAT and address/port translation state Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References RFC 1918: Private IPv4 address allocation RFC 6598: Shared IPv4 address space RFC 4193: Unique local IPv6 addresses IANA: Special-purpose IPv4 address registry RFC 5737: IPv4 documentation address blocks RFC 3849: IPv6 documentation prefix

articles/networking/boundaries/index.htm.title: Overview: Network boundaries | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Network boundaries Network boundaries constrain routes, visibility and forwarding across interfaces or execution environments. A guest network, VLAN, container namespace or second interface can change the path an application sees. Multicast adds its own forwarding and listener relationships. This area identifies the boundary involved so a successful connection on one side is not treated as evidence of the same access on another. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Guest network isolation Guest isolation applies a network’s chosen policy to guest clients and destinations, allowing internet access without necessarily permitting local media-server or discovery paths. VLANs A VLAN identifies a bridged network context through port and tag handling, with routing and policy required for communication between separately defined realms. Multicast routing Multicast delivery uses receiver membership and forwarding context to copy group traffic onto selected paths, with link-local discovery retaining its own scope rules. Container network modes A container’s network mode selects the namespace and forwarding relationship that owns its service listener, with published ports and discovery behavior depending on the actual implementation. Multiple network interfaces Multiple network interfaces add address, listener, route and advertisement choices whose independent selection determines the server path seen by each client. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Client connection paths RFC 4632: Prefixes and route specificity RFC 9776: IGMPv3, replacing RFC 3376 Docker: Bridge network driver

articles/networking/boundaries/Network-C.title: Container network modes and reachable service endpoints | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/Network-C.keywords: Container network modes and reachable service endpoints A container’s network mode selects the namespace and forwarding relationship that owns its service listener, with published ports and discovery behavior depending on the actual implementation. Emby can listen successfully inside a container while another device cannot reach that listener. The container’s address and namespace are part of the network path. A host address, container address and published endpoint are related but distinct selections. Bridge networking adds another address realm Use this original reduced Docker-style bridge arrangement: { "hostAddress": "192.168.50.20", "containerAddress": "172.18.0.2", "containerTcpPort": 8096, "publishedHostTcpPort": 45096 } The service belongs to the container’s TCP listener at 8096. The declared published endpoint makes a separate host-port association at 45096. Another device using the host’s port 8096 is not selecting this model’s published 45096 endpoint. Publishing does not make an absent container listener ready. The host/gateway route and policy still need to permit the intended path. Container localhost identifies its own namespace A client process inside another isolated namespace interprets localhost there. It does not automatically identify Emby’s container or the Docker host. User-defined bridge networks can provide their own container-name/service relationships. A proxy’s upstream needs the endpoint available in the proxy’s actual namespace. An EXPOSE declaration describes container/service metadata; port publication is a separate operation. Host networking changes the ownership model In host mode, the container uses the host network stack under the supported implementation. The service therefore competes for the host’s listener ports rather than obtaining an independently translated published port. Docker documents host networking for Linux and an opt-in Docker Desktop implementation. The Desktop arrangement has its documented layer-four limitations; it should not be generalized into identical low-level behavior on every platform. Port publishing is not the same mechanism in host mode. A conflicting host listener can consequently prevent the desired service from binding. Discovery needs its own reachable scope A TCP publication can make manual application access work without relaying a local broadcast or multicast into the container’s context. A host-mode or another network design can expose a different discovery path. The supported driver, platform and interface selection determine the actual result. Emby discovery remains a separate exchange from the later media listener. Bind intent and actual exposure are separate observations A published port can target selected host addresses. Loopback-only and all-interface intent describe different scopes. Docker’s documentation also identifies version-specific behavior, so a displayed bind value should not replace checking the intended implementation’s actual reachability. See Also Loopback addresses and the meaning of localhost Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References Docker: Bridge network driver Docker: Host network driver Docker: Published port behavior Emby: Client connection paths

articles/networking/boundaries/Network-G.title: Guest network isolation and permitted paths | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/Network-G.keywords: Guest network isolation and permitted paths Guest isolation applies a network’s chosen policy to guest clients and destinations, allowing internet access without necessarily permitting local media-server or discovery paths. A guest phone can browse the internet while being unable to reach the home’s Emby server. Internet access and access to another local device are separately permitted paths. Guest network isolation describes the policies that separate guest clients from selected peers or other network realms. A guest label does not specify every rule Use this original reduced policy: { "guestRealm": "192.168.80.0/24", "serverRealm": "192.168.50.0/24", "internetAllowed": true, "serverRealmAllowed": false, "guestPeerAllowed": false, "localDiscoveryRelayed": false } The four flags describe this teaching arrangement. A product’s actual guest mode can implement another combination. A DHCP lease and valid default route can therefore coexist with a denied server connection. Peer isolation and inter-network policy are different boundaries Client isolation can restrict communication between stations on a wireless network. Routing/firewall policy controls traffic between different network realms. A guest SSID can use its own VLAN and routed boundary, or another supported arrangement. Merely naming it “guest” does not reveal that topology. Likewise, a shared wireless name does not prove that two devices have an unfiltered layer-two path. Discovery can be filtered independently A broadcast/multicast discovery exchange can be absent while a permitted manual unicast connection works. In the declared policy, discovery is not relayed and the server realm is denied. Typing the server’s private address cannot override either network rule. A configured exception for one server service can instead make manual access possible while keeping peer traffic and discovery restricted. A public server endpoint can select another path A guest client might use a public-facing hostname rather than the private server address. Gateway loopback/translation and the policy’s enforcement point then determine the resulting path. A rule before destination translation and a rule on the final inside destination can see different endpoint context. Intentional publication of a service can also permit a path that direct LAN access does not. Port forwarding and NAT loopback identify those stages. Network reach and account access remain independent A guest device reaching the Emby listener still needs the intended authentication and media permissions. A permitted network exception is not permission to administer the server. See Also VLANs, tagged links and routed policy Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints How a home media network carries an Emby stream References Emby: Client connection paths IEEE: 802.1Q bridges and bridged networks IEEE: 802.11 working-group scope

articles/networking/boundaries/Network-M.title: Multicast membership, routing and local scope | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/Network-M.keywords: Multicast membership, routing and local scope Multicast delivery uses receiver membership and forwarding context to copy group traffic onto selected paths, with link-local discovery retaining its own scope rules. A multicast sender targets a group rather than individually opening one connection to every receiver. The network needs to know which paths have interested listeners. That forwarding problem has separate link-layer and routed parts. A bridge can select interested output ports Use this original reduced snooping model: { "group": "239.1.2.3", "incomingPort": 1, "candidateEgress": [2, 3, 4, 5], "listenerPorts": [2, 4], "multicastRouterPorts": [5], "expectedEgress": [2, 4, 5] } The declared policy sends toward the known listeners and multicast-router port. It excludes candidate port three and the incoming port. This is a teaching policy with explicit inputs. Real snooping behavior also needs its defined group, query, aging and exceptional/control-message rules. Snooping does not install a routed multicast path A bridge observing membership helps decide which ports receive traffic within its bridged realm. A router connecting realms needs multicast forwarding state and appropriate routing behavior. PIM sparse mode is one cited routing architecture; it is not created merely by enabling a bridge’s snooping option. The return/member-control messages also need to reach the relevant querier/router. Missing or expired membership information can change forwarding while ordinary unicast still works. Membership can include source selection A group label alone need not describe every permitted sender. Source-filtering can ask for particular source/group relationships or exclude sources under its protocol rules. The IPv4 IGMPv3 and IPv6 MLDv2 references define those membership roles. Current RFC 9776 and RFC 9777 replace the older RFC 3376 and RFC 3810 references. A receiver’s membership declaration, the bridge’s learned port state and the router’s forwarding state are different observations. Local discovery has another scope Routable multicast for an application group does not automatically relay mDNS’s link-local exchange or Emby’s local broadcast discovery. Their destinations, scope and application semantics differ. A discovery reflector/proxy can provide additional behavior under its own rules. Similarly, decrementing a packet’s forwarding lifetime can make a routed path unavailable even when group membership exists. The relevant lifetime and scope must permit that hop. Group visibility is only a candidate relationship A discovered service address still needs a usable unicast route and application access when the later connection begins. See Also Multicast DNS and local-link naming SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations VLANs, tagged links and routed policy Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References RFC 9776: IGMPv3, replacing RFC 3376 RFC 9777: MLDv2, replacing RFC 3810 RFC 7761: PIM sparse-mode multicast routing RFC 4541: Multicast snooping considerations RFC 6762: Multicast DNS local-link scope

articles/networking/boundaries/Network-M.title: Multiple network interfaces and selected server paths | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/Network-M.keywords: Multiple network interfaces and selected server paths Multiple network interfaces add address, listener, route and advertisement choices whose independent selection determines the server path seen by each client. An Emby machine can have Ethernet, Wi-Fi and a VPN interface at the same time. It can listen through more than one address while using one selected route for a particular reply. The address advertised to an app and the interface chosen by the operating system answer different questions. A route chooses the reply destination path Use this original reduced inventory: { "addresses": { "ethernet": "192.168.50.20", "wifi": "192.168.60.20", "vpn": "10.8.0.1" }, "routes": [ {"prefix": "192.168.50.0/24", "path": "ethernet"}, {"prefix": "10.8.0.0/24", "path": "vpn"}, {"prefix": "0.0.0.0/0", "path": "wifi"} ] } A reply to 192.168.50.30 matches the Ethernet /24. A reply to 10.8.0.6 matches the VPN /24. Another destination can use the Wi-Fi default under this model. A low-cost/default path does not replace a more-specific route merely because both interfaces are active. Listening has its own interface context A listener can bind to a particular address or a supported wildcard selection. The choice establishes where the service can accept traffic. It does not tell the route table to send every reply through that same physical interface. The source address, policy routing and platform/socket behavior can add further context. An asymmetric path can encounter a gateway lacking expected state or a policy that rejects it. “Both interfaces are connected” is not enough to establish a working round trip. Advertisement must suit the receiving client An app on the Ethernet realm may not have a route to the server’s VPN address. Reporting the VPN address can therefore produce a discovery candidate the app cannot use. Emby’s documented local-address override concerns the endpoint it presents to clients. It does not install a client route or change every operating-system binding decision. A hostname can also have several address answers. The client’s family/address choice needs to be retained when comparing outcomes. Several links do not automatically aggregate one flow Having two one-Gbit/s interfaces does not make every individual stream a two-Gbit/s connection. Aggregation, failover, multipath or another selected implementation can define additional behavior. The ordinary route model chooses a path for its particular destination/context. A measurement tool binding to an interface can help isolate a declared path, but the resulting test still needs its actual addresses and routes identified. Observe all four selections together For a missing or misclassified Emby connection, retain the advertised endpoint, accepting listener, chosen return route and client context the application interprets. See Also IP addresses and reachable interfaces Subnets, CIDR and matching routes VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context References RFC 4632: Prefixes and route specificity Emby: Network and secure-connection settings ESnet: iperf3 invocation and direction

articles/networking/boundaries/Network-V.title: VLANs, tagged links and routed policy | Emby Learn
articles/networking/boundaries/Network-V.keywords: VLANs, tagged links and routed policy A VLAN identifies a bridged network context through port and tag handling, with routing and policy required for communication between separately defined realms. A physical switch can carry several separate bridged network contexts. VLANs identify those contexts through port membership and, on appropriate links, frame tags. The separation is a link-layer relationship. IP prefixes and routed access policy add other decisions. A tag carries several fields Use this original 802.1Q-style field fragment: 81 00 60 2A 08 00 Here 81 00 identifies the tag type, 60 2A is the chosen tag-control information and 08 00 is the enclosed IPv4 EtherType. The tag-control exercise has priority value three, drop-eligibility value zero and VLAN ID forty-two: {"priority": 3, "dropEligible": 0, "vlanId": 42, "tagControl": 24618} The calculation is (3 << 13) | (0 << 12) | 42 = 0x602A . VLAN ID occupies twelve bits; priority and drop-eligibility are separate fields. The fragment omits the rest of the Ethernet frame. It is not an emitted packet or a switch command. Untagged frames still need a port context An access-style port can associate untagged traffic with its configured VLAN. A trunk-style link can carry permitted tagged contexts toward another VLAN-aware device. The port’s handling of untagged traffic and its default/PVID context are configuration facts. Removing a tag does not make the frame belong simultaneously to every bridged network. Two connected ports can therefore carry different realms while sharing one switch chassis. VLAN and IP subnet have related but distinct roles An IP subnet can be assigned to a VLAN-backed realm. The VLAN tag identifies the bridged context; the prefix identifies address membership and route matching. An original server on VLAN ten with 192.168.50.20/24 and a client on VLAN twenty with 192.168.80.30/24 needs an appropriate routed path between the realms. Sharing an upstream cable does not create direct same-link address resolution between them. A router provides another policy boundary An inter-VLAN router can select and forward the packet toward the server realm. Firewall policy can permit one service while denying other operations. Guest isolation can use that arrangement. Multicast routing adds membership/scope behavior that ordinary unicast routing does not supply by itself. A VLAN ID is not a user credential or media permission. The reachable Emby operation still has its account policy. Retain the tagged and untagged observations For a missing server path, identify the client’s port/SSID realm, carried tags, allowed trunk contexts, routed destination and return policy. See Also Subnets, CIDR and matching routes Guest network isolation and permitted paths Multicast membership, routing and local scope Quality of service, classification and scheduling References IEEE: 802.1Q bridges and bridged networks RFC 4632: Prefixes and route specificity

articles/networking/fundamentals/index.h.title: Overview: Home network fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/networking/fundamentals/index.h.keywords: Overview: Home network fundamentals Home-network fundamentals connect addressing and transport with the local or remote route a media request uses. A connection needs a destination address, a usable path and an appropriate transport endpoint. Local and remote requests can meet different conditions along that path. The addressing and transport branches establish those layers before discovery, router rules or streaming performance are investigated. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How a home media network works A home media network carries requests and media between Emby Server and client apps through local links and any routed boundaries in their selected path. Local and remote connections Local and remote connections describe the path and client-address context used to reach Emby, which can differ from a device’s physical location or the hostname it uses. IP addressing IP addressing identifies interfaces and network relationships under particular address scopes and configuration rules. Transport protocols and ports Transport protocols and ports identify how applications exchange data and which endpoint receives it. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Connecting from client apps RFC 791: Internet Protocol Emby: Network settings and reported addresses RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation

articles/networking/fundamentals/Network.title: How a home media network carries an Emby stream | Emby Learn
articles/networking/fundamentals/Network.keywords: How a home media network carries an Emby stream A home media network carries requests and media between Emby Server and client apps through local links and any routed boundaries in their selected path. A television app asks Emby Server for a presentation. The server prepares the selected media and sends it back over the connection the app established. Within a home, that path can be much shorter than “up to the internet and back.” The devices, link arrangement and chosen endpoint determine where the traffic goes. Trace the local stream Use this original network: Device Address Connection Emby Server 192.168.50.20 Ethernet to a switch TV app 192.168.50.30 Wi-Fi through an access point Router 192.168.50.1 Connects this LAN to other networks Assume both end devices use the same ordinary IPv4 /24 LAN, and the access point bridges Wi-Fi to the switch. The app’s packets for 192.168.50.20 go over Wi-Fi, through the access point and switch, to the server. They do not need the router’s internet-facing connection. A household “router” box can contain a router, switch and wireless access point together. Traffic passing through its switch or Wi-Fi hardware is not necessarily being routed to the internet. Address resolution selects a local next hop An IPv4 host uses its address/prefix and routes to decide whether the destination is on its local link. For an ordinary local destination, ARP resolves the link-layer address needed to send the frame. For an off-link destination, the host instead sends the frame toward the selected router. The IP destination remains the remote host; the next-hop frame address identifies the router for that link. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery for its corresponding link relationships. The underlying distinction is the same: the final IP destination and the next hop are different roles. Subnets and routes develops the prefix calculation. The media request and media payload have different sizes Selecting a title, requesting a playlist and reporting playback state can involve small messages. Delivering the media usually accounts for much more traffic. An app showing posters and browsing a library has therefore established some successful communication, not a measurement of sustained streaming capacity. A media request can also choose another resource URL or begin a different connection. Server delivery explains what the server prepares. The network transports that result; it does not decide whether the video must be transcoded merely because the TV uses Wi-Fi. A Wi-Fi association is only one completed step The TV can join its access point yet lack a permitted path to the server. A guest network, separate routed segment or client-isolation rule can change the topology. Established observation Remaining question TV joined Wi-Fi Does its segment permit the server path? Name resolved Is the returned address reachable from this client? Connection established Does the requested application operation succeed? Short request succeeded Can the route sustain the selected media delivery? Emby’s connectivity documentation separates local access from external reachability. Knowing which boundary the request actually crosses makes those checks more precise. See Also Local and remote connections to Emby IP addresses and reachable interfaces DNS resolution, record types and cached answers Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints References Emby: Connecting from client apps RFC 791: Internet Protocol RFC 4861: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery RFC 826: Ethernet address resolution

articles/networking/fundamentals/Network.title: Local and remote connections to Emby | Emby Learn
articles/networking/fundamentals/Network.keywords: Local and remote connections to Emby Local and remote connections describe the path and client-address context used to reach Emby, which can differ from a device’s physical location or the hostname it uses. A phone sitting beside the server can use a public-looking hostname. A phone outside the home can reach a private server address through a VPN. Physical location, the destination URL and the client address observed by Emby are different pieces of information. Compare the actual paths Consider these original cases: Client’s situation Chosen destination Path On the server LAN 192.168.50.20 Direct local path On the same LAN A hostname resolving to the gateway’s outside endpoint Possible NAT loopback path Away, connected through a VPN 192.168.50.20 Routed tunnel into the server network The second case needs the router’s supported return-to-inside behavior. The third needs tunnel routes and an allowed return path. A private destination written into a remote phone’s app does not become reachable until its network has a route to that private realm. Emby also classifies client addresses Emby’s network settings include LAN Networks, used when applying local/remote bandwidth and access controls. That classification is an application decision based on the relevant client-address context. Declaring a prefix local does not install an operating-system route, extend Wi-Fi or create a port mapping. If a VPN client has address 10.8.0.6, the administrator may intend it to count as local under a particular access policy. The VPN can be fully routed while that classification still needs to match the intended policy. Conversely, marking a very broad range local can change how genuinely external clients are treated. The prefix should represent the actual intended address realm. Translation can change what the server observes A tunnel can preserve a VPN client’s source address, or a gateway can translate it. A reverse proxy makes its own upstream connection to Emby. Suppose an original proxy at 192.168.50.10 forwards a request from an outside client. The origin’s socket peer is the proxy. Additional trusted metadata can describe the earlier client, but it needs the correct trust interpretation. Forwarded client addresses develops that distinction. Seeing a private socket address does not by itself establish that the original viewer was on the home LAN. A hostname can select another path at home With split DNS , one hostname can resolve to a local destination at home and an external destination elsewhere. With another configuration, the same outside address may be used from both locations. Those are different connection paths even though the URL text matches. They can also have different ports, encryption endpoints and intermediaries. See Also Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints NAT loopback and same-network public endpoints VPN access and the routed path to a media server Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context References Emby: Network settings and reported addresses Emby: Connecting from client apps RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation

articles/networking/index.html.title: Overview: Networking and remote access | Emby Learn
articles/networking/index.html.keywords: Overview: Networking and remote access Media networking connects addressing, routing, transport security, delivery performance and the access policies applied to a request. Reaching an Emby server involves several decisions before playback begins: finding its address, choosing a route, establishing the connection and presenting acceptable identity evidence. Continuing playback then depends on the rate and consistency of data delivery. The topics below distinguish home-network behavior from remote reachability, and connection security from user authorization. Performance and network-boundary pages explain why a reachable server can still have a slow stream or an isolated client. Keeping those questions separate makes each observed failure more informative. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Home network fundamentals Home-network fundamentals connect addressing and transport with the local or remote route a media request uses. Names and discovery Network names and discovery mechanisms help an application find the destination it needs to contact. Routers and remote reachability Router and intermediary behavior determines how a request reaches the server and what its successive connection legs mean. Connection security Connection security relates protected transport, endpoint identity and browser-enforced request boundaries. Network performance Network performance describes useful delivery over time through the links and shared resources carrying a stream. Network boundaries Network boundaries constrain routes, visibility and forwarding across interfaces or execution environments. User identity and access Media-server access connects accepted identity and session state with the rules governing requested resources. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/networking/names/discovery/inde.title: Overview: Service discovery | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/discovery/inde.keywords: Overview: Service discovery Service discovery exchanges information about available destinations within each protocol's defined scope. mDNS, SSDP and Emby's discovery mechanism use different messages and relationships. Their results help locate a service; they do not replace the connection or access checks needed to use it. This group explains why discovery can work on one network segment and produce a different result across a boundary. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Multicast DNS (mDNS) Multicast DNS resolves specified names on a local link through participating responders, with DNS-based service discovery adding service-instance and endpoint information. SSDP discovery SSDP discovers UPnP candidates through advertisements and searches, returning service-description locations whose later accessibility must be evaluated separately. Emby server discovery Emby’s documented local discovery exchange uses a UDP broadcast to find server identity and an advertised address, followed by a separate application connection. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 6762: Multicast DNS Emby developer documentation: UDP server discovery

articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.title: Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.keywords: Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints Emby’s documented local discovery exchange uses a UDP broadcast to find server identity and an advertised address, followed by a separate application connection. An Emby app can discover a server locally without the user typing its address. The documented exchange asks a local UDP service for server information. That information identifies a connection candidate. The client still needs to reach the advertised application endpoint. The documented request is specific to Emby Emby’s developer documentation specifies UDP port 7359 and the query text: who is EmbyServer? This is a distinct exchange from mDNS and SSDP. Opening their ports or receiving their descriptions does not make this query equivalent. The broadcast belongs to the relevant local network context. A routed path to the server does not automatically forward the local broadcast across every subnet or VPN. Identity and address have different jobs The documented reply contains Address, Id and Name. This original projection uses fictional values: { "Address": "http://192.168.50.20:8096", "Id": "learn-server-A", "Name": "Harbour Library" } The address tells the app where it can attempt a connection. The ID identifies the server, while the name is a human label. A name change need not be an address change. A DHCP change can alter the endpoint while the server identity stays the same. Two servers can also have equal friendly names. Treating that label as the complete identity can select the wrong instance. A reply can advertise an unusable address A server with several interfaces can report an address suited to one network but not the receiving client’s realm. Advertising loopback is a particularly clear error: a phone interprets that destination as its own local stack. Another case is an address on a VPN or isolated interface that the client cannot route to. Emby’s local-address setting concerns the advertised endpoint. The chosen value needs to describe a reachable interface/service path for the intended clients; it does not create that route by itself. Compare discovery and direct connection separately Observation Useful interpretation No discovery, manual endpoint works Broadcast/reply/discovery processing may be the missing stage Discovery works, endpoint connection fails Candidate arrived; the advertised service path still failed Correct endpoint, wrong server identity The client selected another server or stale association Correct server reached, user request rejected Application access is a later stage These outcomes do not require changing a video codec or transcoding setting. They precede usable media delivery. See Also UDP datagrams and application delivery policy Loopback addresses and the meaning of localhost SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations Emby Connect and the path to the selected server References Emby developer documentation: UDP server discovery Emby: Connecting from client apps Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.title: Multicast DNS and local-link naming | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.keywords: Multicast DNS and local-link naming Multicast DNS resolves specified names on a local link through participating responders, with DNS-based service discovery adding service-instance and endpoint information. A supporting device can resolve a name such as library-box.local by asking participants on its local link instead of consulting one authoritative internet DNS server. Multicast DNS , or mDNS , uses DNS-like messages with local-link delivery and its own coordination rules. The multicast destination identifies participants The familiar IPv4 destination is 224.0.0.251 on UDP port 5353; the IPv6 link-local multicast equivalent is ff02::fb. Participants can answer for the names and records they advertise. Name conflict detection and record lifetimes matter because unrelated devices might otherwise try to use the same local label. A central household DNS record with a .local suffix does not guarantee that every client will ask that DNS server. A client implementing .local multicast resolution can select another mechanism. The home.arpa convention provides a separately specified home-network naming context. Service discovery adds more than a host address DNS-Based Service Discovery, defined separately in RFC 6763, can associate a service type with instances, a target host and a port. This original reduced generic example shows the joins: { "serviceType": "_https._tcp.local.", "instance": "Library Demo._https._tcp.local.", "srv": {"target": "library-box.local.", "port": 8920}, "address": {"name": "library-box.local.", "type": "A", "value": "192.168.50.20"} } The service instance is not itself the host’s address. The SRV target needs its relevant address lookup, and the port belongs to the service endpoint. These are explanatory fields, not wire DNS packets or a claim that Emby advertises this service instance. The local link is a real boundary A client and server on different VLANs or on a routed VPN can have a permitted unicast connection while local multicast discovery does not cross between them. Moving the unicast packet route does not automatically relay every discovery message. A configured reflector/proxy can supply additional behavior, with its own scope and policy. Conversely, relaying discovery can make an address visible without giving the client a working route to that address. The later endpoint still needs to be usable in the receiving realm. Discovery is not server authentication A supplied name or service description identifies a candidate endpoint. It does not prove who controls the later application service. For HTTPS, the application’s peer/certificate checks supply another identity stage. Access to Emby also needs the intended server/user relationship. Emby server discovery uses its own documented UDP exchange. Sharing a home network and UDP transport does not make that exchange identical to mDNS. See Also DNS resolution, record types and cached answers SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints VPN access and the routed path to a media server References RFC 6762: Multicast DNS RFC 6763: DNS-Based Service Discovery RFC 8375: The home.arpa special-use domain

articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.title: SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/discovery/Netw.keywords: SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations SSDP discovers UPnP candidates through advertisements and searches, returning service-description locations whose later accessibility must be evaluated separately. SSDP helps a UPnP control point find devices and services. A device can advertise its presence, and a client can search for a matching type. The discovery exchange describes a candidate. Using that candidate requires a later request to its advertised location. A search has a target and response window This original readable search example targets UPnP root devices: M-SEARCH * HTTP/1.1 HOST: 239.255.255.250:1900 MAN: "ssdp:discover" MX: 2 ST: upnp:rootdevice USER-AGENT: LearnOS/1.0 UPnP/2.0 Example/1.0 It shows the relevant fields rather than an emitted UDP packet. Actual wire framing and complete protocol requirements belong to the cited UPnP architecture. The multicast destination is UDP port 1900. The search target ST selects what the control point is asking for. MX gives the specified response window used by this multicast search. Matching devices can spread their responses through that interval rather than all answering at once. The response points toward another resource A matching search response can include a LOCATION URL for the device description. The control point then obtains that description and interprets its device/service information. For an invented generic device, a location might be http://192.168.50.40:5000/description.xml . Receiving that text proves the discovery reply arrived. It does not prove the client can connect to TCP port 5000 or obtain the expected XML there. A description can also contain service control and event locations. Those are subsequent application endpoints, not the same UDP discovery transaction. Advertisements have lifetimes A device can send availability advertisements, refresh them and indicate departure. Cache age tells a control point how long the advertised candidate remains valid under that exchange. In an original lifetime exercise, an advertisement received at second zero has maximum age 1800 seconds. A valid refresh at second nine hundred with the same age moves the declared expiry to second 2700. A departed or expired candidate should not remain equivalent to a freshly observed service. A saved UI entry can outlive the discovery cache as another application state. Scope and transport permissions can differ A network can permit ordinary server connections while filtering multicast searches or their replies. Guest isolation and routed boundaries can create that distinction. Even when discovery is relayed, the advertised location must be meaningful to the receiving client. A private address from another realm can be visible but unusable. SSDP is also distinct from mDNS and Emby’s own discovery . They use different multicast/broadcast destinations, messages and service descriptions. Successful SSDP does not establish the other exchanges worked. See Also Multicast DNS and local-link naming Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints UPnP port mapping and gateway control UDP datagrams and application delivery policy References OCF: UPnP Device Architecture 2.0 IANA: Service names and transport-protocol port numbers

articles/networking/names/dns/index.html.title: Overview: DNS and naming | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/dns/index.html.keywords: Overview: DNS and naming DNS and hostname conventions connect service names and URLs with the addresses used in a particular network view. The same name can resolve differently inside and outside a home network. Dynamic DNS and split DNS address different relationships between that name and its changing or scoped addresses. These pages also distinguish the hostname from the rest of a URL, which includes the scheme, port and resource path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DNS DNS resolves typed questions about names through authoritative data and caches, with address answers providing only one stage of a server connection. Dynamic DNS Dynamic DNS updates a name’s address records when the represented endpoint changes, while caches and the actual inbound network path retain independent lifetimes. Split DNS Split DNS supplies different answers for a name under different resolver views, allowing one server hostname to select local and external endpoints without changing its other URL components. Hostnames and URLs A server URL combines scheme, host, optional port and resource path, while hostname resolution and relative-reference rules determine distinct later selections. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 2308: DNS negative caching RFC 2136: Dynamic DNS updates RFC 9499: DNS terminology and views RFC 3986: URI structure and relative references

articles/networking/names/dns/Network-DD.title: Dynamic DNS and a changing server address | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/dns/Network-DD.keywords: Dynamic DNS and a changing server address Dynamic DNS updates a name’s address records when the represented endpoint changes, while caches and the actual inbound network path retain independent lifetimes. A household connection can receive a new outside address while its preferred server hostname stays the same. Dynamic DNS , or DDNS , updates the relevant records so that hostname can lead to the new endpoint. The update changes descriptive DNS data. It does not move an existing connection or create a missing inbound route. Four times identify the transition Use this original timeline, with documentation address labels: { "oldAddress": "198.51.100.12", "newAddress": "203.0.113.44", "cacheFetchedAt": 90, "cachedTtlSeconds": 300, "addressChangedAt": 100, "authoritativeUpdateAcceptedAt": 110 } Times are seconds from one common origin. The original cache expires at second 390. From second 110, newly obtained authoritative data can describe the new address. The already cached positive answer can remain valid for another 280 seconds in this ordinary cache model. An updater’s successful response therefore establishes one stage of the transition. It is not a push notification that replaces every client’s retained answer. The updater must report the intended endpoint A server behind a home gateway has a private LAN address as well as the gateway’s outside endpoint. Behind another translation layer, the gateway’s WAN address can itself be shared or private. Updating a public-facing hostname to the wrong layer’s address can make the DNS operation succeed while producing an unusable destination for outside clients. The source of the address observation and the intended connection path must agree. Carrier-grade NAT explains why the outside translation may not be under household control. IPv4 and IPv6 records change separately Changing an A record does not automatically change an AAAA record. The two address families may also have different lifetimes or reachability. A newly correct IPv4 answer alongside a stale IPv6 answer can produce different app outcomes according to the family selected. Similarly, changing a CNAME target introduces the lifetimes of the alias and relevant target records. The hostname remaining visually unchanged does not collapse those records into one universal cache item. Update protocol and provider interface are different layers RFC 2136 defines DNS UPDATE. A commercial or self-hosted DDNS interface can instead accept an authenticated API request and perform its own DNS changes. An accepted provider request, publication of the authoritative record and later recursive lookup are separate observations. The implementation determines how promptly they converge. This distinction is useful without copying a provider’s credential-bearing update URL into a diagnostic record. Recheck the service destination after the name transition Emby can advertise a configured external domain. The remote URL still needs the intended scheme and port, and the new address must lead through the actual route, mapping and listener. A correct new DNS answer cannot supply an inbound mapping inside somebody else’s carrier gateway. It can accurately name an endpoint that remains unreachable. See Also DNS resolution, record types and cached answers Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Emby Connect and the path to the selected server References RFC 2136: Dynamic DNS updates RFC 1034: DNS concepts and facilities RFC 1035: DNS records and protocol Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/names/dns/Network-DN.title: DNS resolution, record types and cached answers | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/dns/Network-DN.keywords: DNS resolution, record types and cached answers DNS resolves typed questions about names through authoritative data and caches, with address answers providing only one stage of a server connection. In https://media.example.net:45000/ , the hostname is media.example.net. A normal address lookup asks DNS for address records for that name. The lookup does not test port 45000, complete TLS or log into Emby. Those stages use the chosen answer later. Address records have types An A record supplies an IPv4 address; an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. A CNAME identifies another name to follow rather than directly supplying an address. This original reduced answer set uses documentation addresses: { "name": "media.example.net", "records": [ {"type": "A", "value": "198.51.100.12", "ttlSeconds": 300}, {"type": "AAAA", "value": "2001:db8:50::20", "ttlSeconds": 300} ] } The name and address labels are invented. They are not endpoints to query or contact. Ordinary A/AAAA resolution leaves the URL’s scheme, port and path intact. Other DNS record types can include service information, such as the port in an SRV record, when the client implements that discovery method. The resolver can answer from a cache The client normally uses a resolver. That resolver can obtain information from authoritative DNS data and retain it for its supplied lifetime. A cached answer is not a fresh measurement of the destination server. It describes the name-to-record relationship last obtained under the cache rules. Consider a teaching timeline where an A answer is cached at second zero with a three-hundred-second TTL. At second one hundred, the authoritative record changes to another address. A resolver retaining the original positive answer can still supply it before its expiry at three hundred. Another resolver asking after the change can supply the newer value. Both can follow the stated caching model while giving different answers. Special stale-answer mechanisms and local overrides have additional rules; this example isolates an ordinary unexpired positive cache. No address and no connection are different failures Result Meaning to examine NXDOMAIN The queried name does not exist under the answer’s context Name exists, requested record type absent No matching data for that type Resolver timeout No timely usable resolution response Address returned, connection fails The later route/service path failed For example, an absent AAAA record does not establish that an A record is absent. A returned A address followed by a refused TCP connection is not a DNS-name failure. DNS can use UDP and TCP; current implementation requirements include TCP support. “DNS is just UDP port 53” omits useful behavior, especially for responses requiring another transport exchange. A missing-name answer can be cached too Negative caching retains an applicable negative result under its supplied lifetime rules. Creating the missing record does not force every resolver to ask again immediately. Use this original reduced name case: { "negativeFetchedAt": 0, "negativeTtlSeconds": 120, "nameCreatedAt": 30, "queryAt": 60 } At second sixty, the model’s unexpired negative cache can still answer that the name is absent. Its stated expiry is second 120, ninety seconds after the authoritative name was created. A lookup that never produces an address has not reached the TCP listener. Restarting the media decoder cannot replace that retained name result. The exact negative cache key and lifetime depend on the response type and DNS rules. NXDOMAIN and absence of one record type must retain their different meanings. The numbers above are declared inputs rather than a captured resolver response. An alias and target have separate record lifetimes Suppose an original CNAME maps media.example.net to gateway.example.net for six hundred seconds, while the target A answer has a three-hundred-second TTL. The alias can remain correct after the target address changes. Once the target A cache expires, that record can be obtained again without waiting for the unchanged alias to expire too. Conversely, changing the alias itself leaves its earlier unexpired CNAME answer applicable under the ordinary cache model. “The DNS cache” is therefore not one timer attached to the entire displayed URL. Different address families can select different paths A client can receive both address families and choose, order or race connection attempts. Happy Eyeballs describes one concurrency strategy intended to improve connectivity. The IPv4 and IPv6 answers can lead to different routing, listener or firewall outcomes. Seeing one working browser does not identify which family another app attempted. Keep the name question and endpoint result separate For a failed Emby connection, retain the actual name, record type, returned address and selected endpoint. That makes a stale record different from a missing listener or an application rejection. See Also Dynamic DNS and a changing server address Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability References RFC 2308: DNS negative caching RFC 1034: DNS concepts and facilities RFC 1035: DNS records and protocol RFC 9499: DNS terminology and views RFC 7766: DNS transport over TCP RFC 8305: Happy Eyeballs connection concurrency

articles/networking/names/dns/Network-Ho.title: Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/dns/Network-Ho.keywords: Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint A server URL combines scheme, host, optional port and resource path, while hostname resolution and relative-reference rules determine distinct later selections. A hostname is one component of a server URL. Copying only the name can discard information the client needs to reach the intended service.
