Take this original endpoint: https://media.example.net:45000/emby/ Component Value Role Scheme https Requests the HTTPS application scheme Host media.example.net Name used to select/resolve the endpoint Explicit port 45000 Destination service port Path /emby/ Resource/base location at that service The endpoint is an invented example. DNS resolves the hostname’s relevant records; it does not normally replace all the other URL components. Omitted ports have scheme defaults Without an explicit port, HTTP uses its default 80 and HTTPS its default 443. Removing :45000 therefore changes the requested destination service in this example. An Emby listener on a customized port does not become available at the scheme default merely because the client uses a familiar hostname. Likewise, writing an https scheme does not make a plaintext listener perform TLS. Scheme and service behavior have to agree. IPv6 address literals need brackets Compare the original literal form: https://[2001:db8:50::20]:8920/emby/ The brackets distinguish the IPv6 address’s internal colons from the separator before port 8920. The value uses the IPv6 documentation prefix. A limited-scope IPv6 address can additionally need a requesting-interface context. Current RFC 9844 describes that user-interface problem; implementation support must be checked separately from an ordinary globally scoped bracketed literal. Relative references use the current base Use a base URL of https://media.example.net/emby/ : Reference Resolved URL path login /emby/login /login /login ../login /login The leading slash starts from the origin root. It does not retain the application’s /emby prefix. A reverse proxy can forward the initial page successfully and still expose broken later navigation if generated links, redirects or resource URLs disagree about the public base path. Reverse proxies follows both sides of that relationship. Name conventions carry resolution context A .local name has multicast-DNS semantics in supporting clients. The home.arpa domain is specified for local home-network naming. An ordinary external domain uses its configured DNS arrangement. These conventions do not guarantee that every TV app resolves names through the same operating-system path. See Also DNS resolution, record types and cached answers Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path References RFC 3986: URI structure and relative references RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 9844: Entering IPv6 zone identifiers RFC 8375: The home.arpa special-use domain Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/names/dns/Network-Sp.title: Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/dns/Network-Sp.keywords: Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints Split DNS supplies different answers for a name under different resolver views, allowing one server hostname to select local and external endpoints without changing its other URL components. The same server hostname can lead to a local endpoint at home and an outside endpoint when the viewer is away. Split DNS makes that choice in the name-resolution view rather than asking every user to keep two hostnames. One name, two answers This original reduced view model uses documentation data for the outside label: { "name": "media.example.net", "views": { "homeResolver": {"type": "A", "address": "192.168.50.10"}, "outsideResolver": {"type": "A", "address": "198.51.100.12"} } } The answer depends on the resolver/view that handles the query. Physical location alone does not force the home answer if the client uses another DNS path. The inside endpoint can be the server itself or an appropriate local proxy. It must implement the service the client’s unchanged URL requests. Address selection does not rewrite the URL’s port Suppose the public URL is: https://media.example.net:45000/ Outside, the gateway maps TCP 45000 to the server’s configured HTTPS listener at 8920. Now make the inside A answer point directly to that server at 192.168.50.20. The home client still requests port 45000. Ordinary A-record resolution does not substitute 8920, so the direct inside path fails if nothing listens on 45000 there. A local proxy or listener using the requested port can provide the intended inside endpoint. Alternatively, the connection design can use separate URLs. The DNS answer alone cannot choose between those arrangements. The hostname remains the requested identity Changing the resolved address does not replace media.example.net in the URL. In HTTPS, the client still needs the service’s certificate/authentication context to satisfy that name. A consistent hostname can therefore preserve the requested identity across two address paths. It does not guarantee that both endpoints were configured consistently. Path prefixes matter too. If one endpoint serves an application under a prefix and the other expects another path, the same URL can select a different resource arrangement even with correct address resolution. Network changes can leave an old view cached A phone can obtain the home answer and then move onto mobile data while retaining it. That private address may no longer be reachable from the new network. The reverse transition can retain the outside answer at home. It then depends on the outside/hairpin path rather than automatically using the local one. DNS explains record lifetimes. Resolver selection and VPN-provided DNS can also change which view supplies the next answer. Split DNS and NAT loopback solve different parts Split DNS can supply an inside endpoint so the client avoids sending the connection to the outside gateway mapping. NAT loopback instead makes that outside endpoint usable from the inside. One can work while the other is absent. See Also DNS resolution, record types and cached answers NAT loopback and same-network public endpoints VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path References RFC 9499: DNS terminology and views RFC 1034: DNS concepts and facilities Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/names/index.html.title: Overview: Names and discovery | Emby Learn
articles/networking/names/index.html.keywords: Overview: Names and discovery Network names and discovery mechanisms help an application find the destination it needs to contact. A configured hostname can be resolved through DNS, while discovery can obtain information through another protocol exchange. Those mechanisms have different scopes and dependencies. The two branches explain how an app learns about an Emby server before ordinary connection and authorization checks begin. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DNS and naming DNS and hostname conventions connect service names and URLs with the addresses used in a particular network view. Service discovery Service discovery exchanges information about available destinations within each protocol's defined scope. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Overview: Capacity and delivery quality | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Overview: Capacity and delivery quality Delivery capacity and quality describe data rate, delay, variation and loss in the direction a media operation uses. Upload capacity matters on the sending side, while throughput describes what was delivered during an interval. Latency, jitter and packet loss add timing or reliability information that an average rate can hide. These topics give those quantities separate meanings before they are related to playback reserve. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Network throughput Network throughput measures delivered work over a stated interval and accounting layer, with chronological delivery determining whether media deadlines can be met. Upload bandwidth Upload bandwidth limits the server-side egress used by remote streams and competing traffic, with payload peaks and accounting overhead affecting the total demand. Network latency Network latency describes delay through a stated direction and path, combining serialization, propagation, processing and waiting rather than indicating throughput alone. Network jitter Network jitter is variation in packet delay under a specified metric, with reordering and deadline effects determined by the actual timing sequence. Packet loss Packet loss counts absent delivery under a specified observation and threshold, while recovery, burst shape and media dependencies determine the application consequence. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework Emby: Network and secure-connection settings RFC 7679: One-way delay metric RFC 3393: IP packet delay variation RFC 2680: One-way packet loss metric

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Network jitter and changing packet delay | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Network jitter and changing packet delay Network jitter is variation in packet delay under a specified metric, with reordering and deadline effects determined by the actual timing sequence. Equal-spaced sends need not arrive equally spaced. Waiting, contention and path behavior can change the delay from packet to packet. The word jitter needs a stated metric. Packet-delay variation, arrival-spacing variation and a tool’s smoothed estimator are not interchangeable numbers. Calculate delay before its variation Use this original common-clock trace: { "sendMs": [0, 20, 40, 60], "arrivalMs": [20, 45, 95, 87] } The one-way delays in send-sequence order are twenty, twenty-five, fifty-five and twenty-seven ms. Consecutive signed delay differences are +5, +30 and -28 ms. Under this exercise’s chosen mean-absolute-difference statistic, the result is twenty-one ms. That twenty-one-ms figure does not assert every tool called “jitter” would report the same statistic. Changing delay can reverse arrival order Packet three is sent at forty and arrives at ninety-five. Packet four is sent later, at sixty, but arrives earlier at eighty-seven. Reordering therefore occurs without either packet being absent. An ordered transport can retain the later sequence data until the earlier missing position arrives. Packet loss describes another observation; a late packet needs a defined threshold before it is counted as lost by a particular measurement. A larger target can absorb this declared variation Suppose a reduced playout model needs each packet at its send time plus fifty ms, with no other processing. The third deadline is ninety ms, but that packet arrives at ninety-five: five ms late. The other three pass their stated deadlines. Using fifty-five ms instead gives deadlines 55, 75, 95 and 115. All four arrivals meet them in this ideal model, including the third exactly at its boundary. The extra delay improves tolerance to this trace. It also increases the chosen playout delay; it does not accelerate arrival. A real media pipeline needs decode, buffering and usable-entry-point margins too. Exact boundary arrival is not a safe universal operating target. Keep the clock and selection rule with the number A one-way variation measurement needs meaningful endpoint timing. A statistic also needs the selected packets, interval and treatment of missing/late entries. A whole-test average can hide brief delay excursions. The maximum delay in this four-packet trace is fifty-five ms while its average is 31.75. See Also Network latency, delay components and round trips Packet loss, recovery and media deadlines Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Measuring the actual streaming delivery path References RFC 3393: IP packet delay variation RFC 7679: One-way delay metric RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Network latency, delay components and round trips | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Network latency, delay components and round trips Network latency describes delay through a stated direction and path, combining serialization, propagation, processing and waiting rather than indicating throughput alone. A request can use little data and still take time to reach its response. The relevant quantity is delay through the path, not only how many bits the link could carry each second. A one-way delay has several components Use this original packet-path model: { "packetBytes": 1500, "linkMbitPerSecond": 100, "propagationMs": 20, "processingMs": 8, "queueMs": 12 } Putting 1500 bytes onto the stated one-hundred-Mbit/s link takes 0.12 ms. Adding the other declared components gives 40.12 ms one-way. Increasing that serialization rate alone would change only the 0.12-ms component in this model. It would not remove the twenty-ms propagation or twelve-ms queue. For another explicitly chosen packet size, 500 bytes on a one-Mbit/s link takes four ms. Byte size and link rate belong in the arithmetic together. Round-trip time measures both directions If the modeled forward delay is 40.12 ms and the return delay fifteen ms, their network round trip is 55.12 ms before additional endpoint-response work. Dividing that round trip by two gives 27.56 ms. It does not recover the actual forty-ms forward delay because the path is asymmetric. A real one-way measurement also needs an appropriate time reference across endpoints. Unsynchronized clocks can make timestamp subtraction misleading. The cited IP performance metrics distinguish the measurement definition from the timing data used to estimate it. Startup can wait for several serial exchanges For an original eighty-ms round-trip path, four strictly serial request/response waits contribute 320 ms before their other processing. A page or playback startup can combine name lookup, connection establishment, authentication, metadata and media preparation. Some work can overlap; other steps depend on an earlier result. The reduced four-exchange exercise does not claim an exact Emby startup sequence. It explains why setup delay can accumulate while each individual message is small. A playback reserve changes tolerance to delay Once an app has usable media ahead of its presentation, it can continue through some delivery waiting. That is different from removing the network latency itself. Interactive controls can remain visibly delayed even while buffered playback is smooth. A seek or new stream can also require data not covered by the earlier reserve. See Also Network jitter and changing packet delay TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery Bufferbloat and standing queue delay Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References RFC 7679: One-way delay metric RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Packet loss, recovery and media deadlines | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Packet loss, recovery and media deadlines Packet loss counts absent delivery under a specified observation and threshold, while recovery, burst shape and media dependencies determine the application consequence. Five packets can be missing from a hundred in several different patterns. The count is the same, but the recovery and timing consequences need not be. Packet loss describes absence under the measurement’s sent-set, observation point and waiting rules. State which deliveries were expected Use this original packet-ID exercise: { "sentCount": 100, "scatteredMissing": [10, 30, 50, 70, 90], "burstMissing": [10, 11, 12, 13, 14] } Both cases have five missing IDs and a five-percent loss fraction. The burst has a contiguous missing run of five; the scattered case’s longest missing run is one. A transport recovery process can react differently to those sequences. The final percentage alone loses their chronological shape. Late and missing need a threshold A receiver observing no packet yet cannot know whether it will arrive later. A measurement defines when its waiting ends and how the packet is classified. A media deadline can be shorter than a transport’s eventual recovery time. A packet arriving after that deadline can be useless for the intended presentation even while it is eventually delivered. Retain the observation time and threshold when comparing loss reports from different tools or layers. Link retries and transport retries are separate A wireless link can retry a frame before the transport receives the data. A retransmitted TCP range can recover missing bytes later still. Those observations should not be merged into one count without a definition. Many link retries can reduce useful airtime even when the receiver eventually obtains every transport byte. TCP’s ordered stream also retains later data behind a missing position. UDP leaves the application protocol to choose its own recovery and ordering behavior. A packet is not a video frame Encoded pictures, audio units and container structures can span packets. One lost packet can affect several dependencies; another can be recovered before the decoder notices any missing input. Concealment and independent entry points change the visible result. The number of absent transport packets does not directly equal a number of lost video frames. A visible frozen picture can consequently involve transport waiting, unrecovered media data or another stage. Playback buffering connects retained usable input with presentation timing. Observe the direction and layer that failed Loss in the request/acknowledgment direction can affect forward delivery too. A gateway counter and client capture can also refer to different points. See Also TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery UDP datagrams and application delivery policy Network jitter and changing packet delay Wi-Fi signal quality, noise and useful airtime Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References RFC 2680: One-way packet loss metric RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Network throughput and useful delivery rate | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Network throughput and useful delivery rate Network throughput measures delivered work over a stated interval and accounting layer, with chronological delivery determining whether media deadlines can be met. A connection reports a high average rate, but playback stalls during a short slow interval. Both observations can be correct. Throughput describes work delivered over time. Its meaning depends on which bytes were counted, where they were counted and which interval was used. State the accounting layer A negotiated PHY/link rate, transmitted transport bytes and useful media bytes are different quantities. Protocol headers, repeated transmissions, acknowledgments and other traffic consume resources without all becoming new usable movie bytes. A sender’s count can also differ from the receiver’s successfully delivered count. For a useful payload comparison, divide the relevant delivered bytes by the observation interval and retain the units. Eight bits form one byte; decimal Mbit/s and MB/s differ by that factor. A six-second average hides the first deficit Use this original receiver-side payload trace: { "intervalSeconds": 2, "usefulBytes": [2000000, 10000000, 10000000], "mediaMbitPerSecond": 20, "initialReserveMbit": 16 } The three interval rates are eight, forty and forty Mbit/s. Total useful data is twenty-two decimal MB, or 176 Mbit. Over six seconds, the average is approximately 29.333333 Mbit/s. That average exceeds the twenty-Mbit/s media consumption rate. During the first interval, however, the deficit is twelve Mbit each second. Assume continuous usable delivery within each interval and no other delay. The initial sixteen-Mbit reserve is exhausted after 16/12 seconds, about 1.333333 seconds. The first interval lasts two seconds. The later high rates cannot retrospectively supply bytes before that first missed deadline. The selected path sets another ceiling For an original series of links with available useful capacities of 1000, 100 and 200 Mbit/s, the slowest stated link bounds continuous end-to-end capacity at one hundred. That bound assumes no other limiting work. Storage, media preparation, transport windows or receiver consumption can reduce achieved delivery further. A fast speed-test endpoint can use a different path from the Emby server, especially for remote playback. Aggregate rate and one stream differ Several parallel connections can use more aggregate capacity than one flow under their transport/window behavior. A headline measured with many flows is not automatically the rate an individual media request obtains. Likewise, changing the media representation can reduce required payload without increasing the path’s delivery capability. See Also Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams Ethernet link speeds and end-to-end capacity TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery ESnet: iperf3 invocation and direction

articles/networking/performance/capacity.title: Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/capacity.keywords: Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams Upload bandwidth limits the server-side egress used by remote streams and competing traffic, with payload peaks and accounting overhead affecting the total demand. During remote playback, the household running Emby sends media outward. Its upload direction can be the narrow part of the route even when the viewer has a fast download connection. The available egress is shared by the active streams and other outgoing work. Add the concurrent demand at one boundary Use an original twenty-five-Mbit/s boundary budget: { "capacityMbitPerSecond": 25, "streamPayloadsMbitPerSecond": [6, 8, 4], "otherPayloadMbitPerSecond": 5, "declaredExtraPerPayloadFraction": 0.1 } The media payloads total eighteen Mbit/s. Adding the other payload gives twenty-three. For this arithmetic exercise only, allow an additional tenth of those payload bits at the same constrained boundary. The accounted requirement becomes 25.3 Mbit/s, exceeding the twenty-five-Mbit/s budget. The added fraction is a teaching assumption, not a universal protocol-overhead percentage. A comparison using already measured useful capacity should not count the same overhead twice. Per-stream limits do not create one aggregate allowance Emby documents its internet streaming bitrate limit as a per-stream control. If three streams each use a ten-Mbit/s allowance, their allowed aggregate can reach thirty before other traffic. A ten-Mbit/s per-stream setting does not mean the entire server sends at most ten. Concurrent-stream limits and per-user controls add their own policy. They do not increase the physical egress capacity. Peak intervals still need delivery room A variable-rate presentation can require more data during some intervals than its whole-programme average. The client can absorb some variation through available media reserve. Several viewers can also request bursts at similar times, while backups or uploads compete at the same gateway. The budget therefore needs the active timeline rather than only a sum of long averages. Congestion develops the queue when arrivals exceed service. Measure the direction the stream actually uses A remote client’s download test to a nearby commercial endpoint does not measure the Emby household’s outgoing path. The useful comparison places the sender, receiver and direction on the actual route. A direct local stream can avoid the internet uplink entirely; a remote path cannot assume that local capacity. See Also Network throughput and useful delivery rate Network congestion and competing arrival rates Quality of service, classification and scheduling Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection References Emby: Network and secure-connection settings RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery

articles/networking/performance/index.ht.title: Overview: Network performance | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Network performance Network performance describes useful delivery over time through the links and shared resources carrying a stream. A negotiated link rate, a useful throughput measurement and a delayed packet describe different observations. Wireless conditions and traffic queues can change those observations while the destination remains reachable. This branch connects delivery quality, link types and measurement to the timeline a media player depends on. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Capacity and delivery quality Delivery capacity and quality describe data rate, delay, variation and loss in the direction a media operation uses. Wireless links Wireless link behavior depends on radio conditions, frequency use and the paths sharing available airtime. Ethernet link speeds Ethernet link speed describes negotiated link-layer operation, while frame overhead, duplex and slower intermediate links determine its relationship to useful end-to-end media delivery. Powerline networking Powerline networking carries data over electrical wiring through a shared channel whose usable rate depends on the supported PHY/link family and changing path conditions. Congestion and traffic management Congestion and traffic management describe how shared demand creates queues and how delivery is scheduled. Measuring network capacity for streaming A streaming-capacity measurement must use the intended endpoints, direction, protocol and workload, retaining interval and receiver-side progress before testing the actual Emby presentation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery ITU-T G.9960: Wireline home-network PHY and architecture RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/Network-.title: Ethernet link speeds and end-to-end capacity | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/Network-.keywords: Ethernet link speeds and end-to-end capacity Ethernet link speed describes negotiated link-layer operation, while frame overhead, duplex and slower intermediate links determine its relationship to useful end-to-end media delivery. A “gigabit” adapter can connect through a path containing a slower port or negotiated link. The label on one component is only one part of the route. Retain each negotiated link Use an original path inventory: Link Declared negotiated rate Server to switch 1000 Mbit/s Switch uplink 100 Mbit/s Viewing device link 1000 Mbit/s The one-hundred-Mbit/s link is the lowest declared rate. Faster end links do not raise its continuous service capacity. A cable, port, transceiver or negotiation result can account for a rate differing from a component’s maximum advertised capability. Useful payload has an on-wire budget Use an original full-size untagged frame exercise: { "ipPacketBytes": 1500, "ipv4HeaderBytes": 20, "tcpHeaderBytes": 20, "ethernetFrameBytes": 1518, "preambleAndStartBytes": 8, "interFrameGapBytes": 12, "linkMbitPerSecond": 1000 } The IP packet contains 1460 bytes of TCP payload under the minimum-header assumptions. The frame and stated timing allowance occupy 1538 byte-times. The conditional payload rate is 1000 × 1460 / 1538 , approximately 949.285 Mbit/s. This omits tags, options, encryption/application framing, reverse traffic, loss and other work. It explains the accounting difference rather than predicting a real Emby transfer at that rate. Full duplex describes two directions A one-Gbit/s full-duplex link supports its declared operation in each direction. It is not a two-Gbit/s one-direction payload path. Requests and acknowledgments use a return direction with its own work. A switch’s aggregate fabric capacity also differs from one port’s rate. Link-up is another observation from clean delivery A link can negotiate and remain up while errors, drops or another path bottleneck reduce useful progress. The client’s decode and server’s preparation/storage can limit playback further. Throughput follows the delivered bytes after those constraints. See Also Network throughput and useful delivery rate How a home media network carries an Emby stream Wireless backhaul and repeated airtime References IEEE: 802.3 Ethernet specifications RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/Network-.title: Measuring the actual streaming delivery path | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/Network-.keywords: Measuring the actual streaming delivery path A streaming-capacity measurement must use the intended endpoints, direction, protocol and workload, retaining interval and receiver-side progress before testing the actual Emby presentation. Start with the path whose result matters: the Emby sender, the actual viewing device or a suitable receiver beside it, and the direction in which the media travels. A test to another internet endpoint can be useful context, but it measures another path. Describe the question before running a test A useful observation record includes: Input Why it belongs with the result Sender and receiver Selects the path Data direction Identifies which upload/download resources are used Address family and endpoint Retains IPv4/IPv6 and proxy/VPN differences Protocol and connection count Distinguishes one-flow and aggregate behavior Duration and interval results Exposes transient deficits Other active traffic Records the sharing context For remote playback, data normally leaves the Emby household toward the viewer. A measurement in the opposite direction can miss that uplink constraint. A controlled receiver test has its own service iperf3 uses an explicitly established client/server measurement arrangement. It does not turn the Emby application port into an iperf receiver. An original illustrative invocation is: iperf3 -c receiver.example.net -R -t 20 -i 1 The example assumes an appropriate measurement receiver has been arranged. The reserved hostname is not a real target, and the command was not run. The reverse flag makes data travel from the measurement server to the invoking client. That can represent a media-server-to-viewer direction when those roles are deliberately placed on the intended path. A normal client-to-server test has another direction. Do not label one “upload” without identifying whose side is being described. Preserve receiver-side intervals Consider original useful payload results over two-second intervals: { "secondsPerInterval": 2, "receivedBytes": [10000000, 1000000, 10000000] } The interval rates are forty, four and forty Mbit/s. The whole-test average is twenty-eight. A twenty-Mbit/s presentation can fit that average yet experience a sixteen-Mbit/s deficit during the slow interval. Its current usable reserve determines whether that interval can be tolerated. Sender and receiver reports can differ in what reached the observation boundary. Use the appropriate receiver-side useful data for a delivery claim. Translate a slow interval into required reserve For the separate stated twenty-Mbit/s presentation, the four-Mbit/s interval has a sixteen-Mbit/s deficit. Over two seconds, it consumes thirty-two Mbit of existing usable reserve: four decimal MB. A player with only sixteen Mbit available at that interval’s start can absorb one second under a constant within-interval rate assumption. A forty-Mbit reserve can absorb two and a half seconds, leaving eight after this two-second interval. Those are conditional arithmetic results, not a fixed recommended buffer size. Real transfers arrive in bursts, and received bytes need their media/container/decoder context before they become usable presentation reserve. The example gives an interpretable question for a test: did the observed deficit exceed the reserve actually available at that point? The twenty-eight-Mbit/s whole-test average cannot answer that chronological question alone. Change one path input for an informative comparison A wired receiver near the viewing location can help separate one wireless segment from the rest of the route. Comparing local and remote delivery can identify an internet-path constraint. A different IPv4/IPv6 result, tunnel selection or proxy path changes the question too. Retain those endpoint inputs rather than treating every result as one universal property of “the network.” Repeated measurements can reveal time-dependent contention. They still describe their measured workload and interval, not every future household condition. Preserve what a changed result can attribute Suppose the same original sender obtains eighty Mbit/s at a wired receiver near the TV, while that TV location’s wireless path has repeated low intervals. That comparison supports examining the changed wireless segment. It does not by itself identify signal, contention, backhaul or driver behavior as the cause. A local result and a remote result also change more than distance: they can change endpoint family, gateways, upload capacity and proxy/tunnel use. An attribution needs those differences stated. A repeatable test record should therefore keep both the controlled change and the other conditions that remained comparable. That makes a useful hypothesis different from assuming any faster alternative proved one particular device was faulty. Then test the actual presentation A synthetic transfer omits media preparation, container/playlist requests, encryption/application behavior and client decoding/rendering work. A real Emby presentation needs its playback mode, selected media rate, server progress and client reserve observed alongside network delivery. A server failing to produce data is different from a path failing to carry already available data. Emby’s remote bitrate controls express demand policy; they are not a throughput measurement. Transcode speed supplies another potential production limit. See Also Network throughput and useful delivery rate Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams Network jitter and changing packet delay Ethernet link speeds and end-to-end capacity Transcoding speed, fps and media time References ESnet: iperf3 invocation and direction RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework RFC 7679: One-way delay metric RFC 2680: One-way packet loss metric Emby: Network and secure-connection settings

articles/networking/performance/Network-.title: Powerline networking and a variable shared channel | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/Network-.keywords: Powerline networking and a variable shared channel Powerline networking carries data over electrical wiring through a shared channel whose usable rate depends on the supported PHY/link family and changing path conditions. Powerline adapters can carry network traffic over a building’s electrical wiring. To the attached Ethernet devices, a pair can provide another link in the server path. The electrical communication channel has its own modulation, error handling and shared-resource behavior. The label describes a PHY family and capability The cited G.hn references describe wireline home-network PHY and data-link roles. Other powerline families have their own protocols; a generic “powerline” label does not establish interoperability. Advertised or observed property What it describes Maximum PHY capability A supported physical operation under its defined conditions Current link indication The device’s present interpreted link state/rate Useful transferred media bytes Application delivery over the actual path Ethernet socket rate Another attached link’s negotiated capability Those quantities should be kept separate. A fast Ethernet socket does not remove a slower electrical segment. The electrical path can vary Wiring layout, coupling, connected loads and interference can change the available channel. Signal processing can alter its usable carriers/coding and retry behavior. A nearby wall socket is not necessarily the same communication path as another nearby socket. The actual supported adapter and electrical arrangement determine the result. A long average can hide short service changes Use this original reduced payload service: { "intervalSeconds": 4, "availableMbitPerSecond": [60, 30] } Equal four-second intervals average forty-five Mbit/s. A fifty-Mbit/s media demand still exceeds both that average and the second interval’s available service. A lower demand can fit the average yet need buffer tolerance during a dip. The time trace and usable-media reserve determine that relationship. This exercise is not a claimed powerline benchmark or a conversion from an advertised adapter number. Measure its place in the complete route Compare a transfer over the intended adapter path with an appropriate reference path using the same sender, receiver and direction. That separates the electrical segment’s effect from server preparation, remote upload capacity or receiver performance. Streaming-path measurements develops those observation boundaries. See Also Network throughput and useful delivery rate Network jitter and changing packet delay Packet loss, recovery and media deadlines Measuring the actual streaming delivery path References ITU-T G.9960: Wireline home-network PHY and architecture ITU-T G.9961: Wireline home-network data link RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/traffic/.title: Overview: Congestion and traffic management | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/traffic/.keywords: Overview: Congestion and traffic management Congestion and traffic management describe how shared demand creates queues and how delivery is scheduled. When offered work exceeds a link's service rate, data wait or are discarded according to the queueing arrangement. Bufferbloat concerns excessive waiting; QoS concerns applicable scheduling or classification. These topics explain those mechanisms while keeping management choices distinct from creating additional physical bandwidth. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Network congestion Network congestion occurs when competing offered work exceeds a path’s service over time, producing queued delay, drops or sender adaptation under the implemented policy. Bufferbloat Bufferbloat is excessive standing queue delay under load, where retained work can keep link utilization high while delaying interactive and media-control traffic. Quality of service (QoS) Quality-of-service policy classifies traffic and schedules limited service, with markings and priority meaningful only under the policies that interpret them. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery RFC 8289: Controlled Delay, an Experimental AQM reference RFC 2474: Differentiated Services field

articles/networking/performance/traffic/.title: Bufferbloat and standing queue delay | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/traffic/.keywords: Bufferbloat and standing queue delay Bufferbloat is excessive standing queue delay under load, where retained work can keep link utilization high while delaying interactive and media-control traffic. A movie transfer uses most of the link, and opening a small page or seeking suddenly feels slow. The bulk rate can remain high while small requests wait behind a large standing queue. Bufferbloat describes that excessive queued delay. Convert bytes ahead into waiting Use an original FIFO model: { "bytesAhead": 5000000, "serviceMbitPerSecond": 20 } Five decimal MB is forty Mbit. At twenty-Mbit/s service, clearing that work takes two seconds before other delay components. A very small new request does not escape the two seconds just because its own serialization needs little time. Doubling the service to forty would halve the conditional wait. Adding another five MB of queued work would instead double it at the original rate. A burst and a standing queue have different evidence An original short sojourn-time sample set is 0.5, 40, 0.8 and 0.6 ms. Another is 40, 50, 45 and 42 ms. The first trace includes one excursion while returning near a low delay. The second keeps even its minimum at forty ms. A maximum alone emphasizes the excursion. Evidence about sustained minima/time behavior can distinguish persistent waiting from a brief queue that drains. These are teaching observations, not a full CoDel decision trace or a real queue measurement. Reducing every buffer is not the entire design Useful buffers absorb bursts and rate variation. Removing that capacity indiscriminately can create other losses or underutilization. Active queue management can signal/drop under its defined policy to control excessive queue behavior. Flow scheduling can keep one bulk flow from monopolizing all queued service. RFC 8289 and RFC 8290 describe Experimental CoDel/FQ-CoDel designs. Their configured/implemented behavior and the sender’s response determine the actual outcome. The queue’s location matters A household router cannot directly manage every queue in an ISP, wireless hop or another client. A shaping arrangement can choose a controlled local service point when its assumptions about the real bottleneck are appropriate. A changing bottleneck rate or another unobserved queue can defeat a simplistic fixed-rate estimate. For Emby, smooth buffered presentation and delayed controls can coexist. The former uses already retained media; the latter waits for a new operation’s path. See Also Network congestion and competing arrival rates Network latency, delay components and round trips Quality of service, classification and scheduling Proxy buffering, progress and timeout clocks References RFC 8289: Controlled Delay, an Experimental AQM reference RFC 8290: Flow Queue CoDel, an Experimental scheduling reference RFC 7679: One-way delay metric

articles/networking/performance/traffic/.title: Network congestion and competing arrival rates | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/traffic/.keywords: Network congestion and competing arrival rates Network congestion occurs when competing offered work exceeds a path’s service over time, producing queued delay, drops or sender adaptation under the implemented policy. A path can have a ready link and reachable server while several senders offer more work than it can serve. The excess must wait, be rejected or change through the senders’ behavior. That resource mismatch is the basis of network congestion . A queue integrates arrival minus service Use this original fluid model: { "serviceMbitPerSecond": 20, "firstArrivalMbitPerSecond": 30, "reducedArrivalMbitPerSecond": 10, "capacityMbit": 40, "initialQueueMbit": 0 } During the first phase, the queue grows ten Mbit each second. It reaches forty Mbit after four seconds. If arrival then falls to ten while service remains twenty, the queue drains at ten Mbit/s and becomes empty after another four seconds. The exercise assumes continuous rates and one FIFO work budget. It is not an implementation of a router queue or TCP congestion algorithm. Waiting follows the work already ahead At forty Mbit queued and twenty-Mbit/s service, clearing the work ahead takes two seconds under this model. A small new packet can therefore wait much longer than its own serialization time. The delay belongs to queued work, not merely the packet’s size. A larger buffer allows more excess to wait. It does not increase the twenty-Mbit/s service rate. Finite capacity creates another decision If thirty continues arriving after the queue reaches capacity, the original excess rate remains ten Mbit/s. The implementation can drop traffic, apply backpressure at another layer, mark congestion where supported, or take another defined action. It cannot store unbounded excess in the finite stated capacity. Transport senders can react to loss/marking and timing feedback. That reaction has its own delay and policy; it is not instantaneous agreement between every sender. Several application uses share the constrained stage Remote video, backups, photo uploads and other traffic can compete at a household uplink. Wireless airtime can add another shared resource before that link. A per-stream media cap can reduce one demand. It does not reserve all remaining service from other uses or convert a congested aggregate into an unconstrained path. Upload bandwidth adds the active payloads. QoS explains another choice about sharing service between traffic classes. Queue management addresses delay as well as utilization A path can keep transmitting at a high useful rate while maintaining a large standing queue. That produces a different experience for interactive operations. Bufferbloat develops that persistent waiting. CoDel and FQ-CoDel are cited Experimental references for relevant queue-management ideas; the arithmetic here does not claim their full algorithm or behavior on an unspecified gateway. See Also Bufferbloat and standing queue delay Quality of service, classification and scheduling Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery References RFC 9293: TCP byte-stream delivery RFC 8289: Controlled Delay, an Experimental AQM reference RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/traffic/.title: Quality of service, classification and scheduling | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/traffic/.keywords: Quality of service, classification and scheduling Quality-of-service policy classifies traffic and schedules limited service, with markings and priority meaningful only under the policies that interpret them. A congested path must choose which work receives its limited service. Quality of service , or QoS , describes classification and handling policies used to make those choices. A policy can improve one use’s delay or share. It cannot create the capacity that the path lacks. A class allocation spends one finite budget Use this original twenty-Mbit/s service model: { "capacityMbitPerSecond": 20, "classes": [ {"name": "interactive", "demand": 1, "allocation": 1}, {"name": "media", "demand": 6, "allocation": 6}, {"name": "bulk", "demand": 20, "allocation": 13} ] } The demands total twenty-seven; allocations total twenty. The stated policy serves interactive and media demand while the bulk class receives thirteen of its requested twenty. Another policy can distribute the shortfall differently. Its desired result depends on the intended classes and operations. Priority needs a bounded interpretation Strict priority for a high-demand class can leave lower classes without service. If the first class alone continuously offers more than the link can serve, a priority label does not preserve a guaranteed share for everyone else. Weighted or reserved service policies express another design, with their own admission and scheduling conditions. For a remote Emby presentation, one bulk file operation and one interactive control message can need different handling. The appropriate policy still has to identify their actual traffic at its enforcement point. Markings identify a requested class The Differentiated Services field includes a six-bit DSCP and separate ECN bits. An original field exercise chooses DSCP forty-six and ECN value two: (46 << 2) | 2 = 186 = 0xBA The ECN bits are not another part of the DSCP number. The cited Expedited Forwarding reference supplies a defined behavior context for its codepoint. A marker in a packet does not prove that every gateway, ISP or wireless link honors the same policy. Boundaries can ignore, rewrite or classify it differently. Classification is an implementation decision Rules can use endpoints, protocols, application context or other available evidence. Encryption can limit direct payload inspection; a port number alone can group several distinct operations. Classifying all HTTPS as “video” can therefore miss other uses and combine unrelated demand. Flow scheduling and queue management can add another distinction within a class. Bufferbloat explains why low-delay handling also needs the work waiting ahead considered. See Also Network congestion and competing arrival rates Bufferbloat and standing queue delay Upload bandwidth and simultaneous remote streams References RFC 2474: Differentiated Services field RFC 3246: Expedited Forwarding behavior RFC 8290: Flow Queue CoDel, an Experimental scheduling reference

articles/networking/performance/wireless.title: Overview: Wireless links | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/wireless.keywords: Overview: Wireless links Wireless link behavior depends on radio conditions, frequency use and the paths sharing available airtime. A strong-looking signal can coexist with interference or an inefficient shared path. Frequency-band characteristics and wireless backhaul add context beyond the client-to-access-point link. The pages here identify those radio and topology relationships before a streaming result is attributed to signal strength alone. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Wi-Fi signal quality Wi-Fi signal quality combines received signal, interference/noise, selected radio behavior and airtime use, so RSSI alone does not predict useful media throughput. Wi-Fi frequency bands Wi-Fi frequency bands provide different spectrum and propagation contexts, while permitted channels, device capability and actual channel conditions determine the usable link. Wireless backhaul Wireless backhaul carries access-point traffic toward the rest of the network, with repeated use of a shared radio resource affecting end-to-end capacity. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-R P.525: Free-space attenuation RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/performance/wireless.title: Wi-Fi frequency bands and link conditions | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/wireless.keywords: Wi-Fi frequency bands and link conditions Wi-Fi frequency bands provide different spectrum and propagation contexts, while permitted channels, device capability and actual channel conditions determine the usable link. “Use 5 GHz” is incomplete as an explanation of a media link. The band changes its spectrum and propagation context, but the devices, chosen channel and surrounding traffic still matter. Frequency and wavelength are related For these rounded teaching frequencies, use an approximate wave speed of three hundred million metres per second: Frequency Approximate wavelength 2.4 GHz 12.5 cm 5 GHz 6 cm 6 GHz 5 cm These are representative frequency values rather than a list of legal Wi-Fi channels. For the same distance and stated free-space link assumptions, changing 2.4 to 5 GHz adds approximately 6.375 dB of calculated free-space attenuation. Changing 2.4 to 6 GHz adds approximately 7.959 dB. The comparison uses twenty times the logarithm of the frequency ratio. It holds the other declared terms constant. Walls, multipath, antenna gain, permitted power and device behavior can change an indoor result. The free-space comparison should not be promoted into a universal rule about how many rooms a band covers. Spectrum and permitted operation are separate inputs Bands can offer different channel arrangements and width choices. Availability and power rules depend on the jurisdiction and operation type. An app, access point and client also need compatible capability. A “Wi-Fi” label alone does not establish that a particular device can use 6 GHz. Channel width and modulation/spatial-stream choices affect the PHY rate. The band name is not itself the throughput value. Band and Wi-Fi generation are different dimensions A generation/specification family can support operation in more than one band, with specific amendments and certified capability defining the actual options. The IEEE 802.11 references identify the standards family and current base publication context. They do not supply a capability declaration for an unspecified TV. Likewise, a newer access point cannot give an older client radio capabilities it does not have. Compare the actual link at the viewing location A less congested channel, different width or another propagation path can produce a useful change. That result needs to be evaluated through the actual client’s route and delivered rate. See Also Wi-Fi signal quality, noise and useful airtime Wireless backhaul and repeated airtime Network throughput and useful delivery rate References IEEE: 802.11 working-group scope IEEE: 802.11-2024 publication notice ITU-R P.525: Free-space attenuation

articles/networking/performance/wireless.title: Wi-Fi signal quality, noise and useful airtime | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/wireless.keywords: Wi-Fi signal quality, noise and useful airtime Wi-Fi signal quality combines received signal, interference/noise, selected radio behavior and airtime use, so RSSI alone does not predict useful media throughput. A television shows a strong Wi-Fi signal yet streams poorly. Received signal strength describes one radio observation; interference, retries and shared airtime can still limit the useful result. Signal and noise must share a reference Use these original dBm observations: { "cases": [ {"signalDbm": -55, "noiseDbm": -85}, {"signalDbm": -55, "noiseDbm": -65} ] } Both cases have the same received signal level. Their modeled signal-to-noise differences are thirty and ten dB. Thirty dB represents a thousandfold power ratio; ten dB represents tenfold. These are ratio calculations under the stated common measurement reference, not real receiver captures. A device’s strength percentage may use its own scale. It should not be treated as a calibrated SNR or a universal conversion to a supported bitrate. The radio chooses an operating representation Modulation, coding, channel width, spatial streams and supported capabilities influence the selected PHY behavior. Changing channel conditions can change those choices. A higher reported rate describes a particular link operation. It is not a measurement of continuous new media bytes delivered through the whole path. Different clients can have different antenna arrangements and supported radio options at the same physical location. Retries consume useful airtime For an original reduced exercise, transmitting sixty Mbit at a selected three-hundred-Mbit/s data rate takes 0.2 seconds of data airtime. If the same complete payload must be transmitted twice before success, the modeled data airtime becomes 0.4 seconds. Its useful-payload ceiling becomes 150 Mbit/s before other overhead. Actual Wi-Fi access, acknowledgments and retry units add their own behavior. The calculation isolates why repeated transmission can reduce useful rate even with an unchanged strength display. Other clients and interfering transmissions can also occupy or defer use of the channel. Strong RSSI does not reserve that airtime for Emby. The two directions can behave differently The access point’s received client signal and the client’s received access-point signal are separate observations. Transmit power, antenna behavior and local noise can differ at the two ends. A strong downlink observation does not prove the return direction carrying requests and acknowledgments is equally usable. Wireless backhaul adds another link behind the access point. Its resources can be the bottleneck even when the TV’s immediate radio link is healthy. Retain useful-delivery evidence For a Wi-Fi playback discrepancy, keep the actual client/link, relevant signal/noise interpretation, retries/airtime, selected rates and delivered-media progress together. See Also Wi-Fi frequency bands and link conditions Wireless backhaul and repeated airtime Packet loss, recovery and media deadlines Network throughput and useful delivery rate References IEEE: 802.11 working-group scope IEEE: 802.11-2024 publication notice Cisco: Wireless signal and noise context ITU-R P.525: Free-space attenuation

articles/networking/performance/wireless.title: Wireless backhaul and repeated airtime | Emby Learn
articles/networking/performance/wireless.keywords: Wireless backhaul and repeated airtime Wireless backhaul carries access-point traffic toward the rest of the network, with repeated use of a shared radio resource affecting end-to-end capacity. An access point can give the television a good nearby signal while reaching the wired server through another wireless hop. That second hop is its wireless backhaul . The stream must traverse both links. If they use one shared airtime resource, each delivered payload consumes that resource again. Two shared hops add their airtime Use this original idealized exercise: { "payloadMbit": 100, "firstHopMbitPerSecond": 300, "secondHopMbitPerSecond": 150, "sharedAirtimeResource": true } The first transmission needs one third of a second. The second needs two thirds. Their serialized data airtime totals one second for one hundred Mbit of delivered payload. The ideal useful rate is therefore one hundred Mbit/s before protocol overhead and competing traffic. For rates C1 and C2 in this shared-resource model, the ceiling is 1 / (1/C1 + 1/C2) . With equal three-hundred-Mbit/s hops it becomes 150. With the declared unequal hops it becomes one hundred, rather than automatically half of either single reported rate. Independent resources allow another pipeline Suppose the two hops can use independent radio resources and forward a long stream concurrently. Its continuous ideal rate can then approach the slower one-hundred-fifty-Mbit/s hop, after accounting for pipeline startup and other work. That is another resource model. Separate channel labels do not alone establish complete independence. Shared hardware, interference and device scheduling can create other contention. Likewise, a product’s use of a dedicated backhaul capability needs its actual configuration and client path checked. Several clients share the backhaul too The backhaul can carry traffic for multiple viewers, library browsing and other devices. Their payloads consume its available service, while each client-facing link adds its own airtime demand. A capacity estimate for one isolated client is therefore different from an estimate while several rooms stream. A changing backhaul link can also alter the end-to-end path while the TV’s immediate RSSI stays almost unchanged. A wired backhaul removes this particular repeated-radio model An Ethernet connection between access point and the rest of the network can move that hop onto another resource. It still has a negotiated link rate, switch path and other demand. It does not eliminate every possible bottleneck or fix an application access failure. See Also Wi-Fi signal quality, noise and useful airtime How a home media network carries an Emby stream Network throughput and useful delivery rate Network congestion and competing arrival rates References IEEE: 802.11 working-group scope IEEE: 802.11-2024 publication notice RFC 2330: IP performance metrics framework

articles/networking/routers/index.html.title: Overview: Routers and remote reachability | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/index.html.keywords: Overview: Routers and remote reachability Router and intermediary behavior determines how a request reaches the server and what its successive connection legs mean. Address translation, firewall decisions, VPN routes and reverse proxies act at different points in a request's path. Identifying those points locates which part of a remote path is being observed. Emby Connect adds another server-location relationship within that broader connectivity context. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Address translation and port mapping Address translation and port mapping relate internal endpoints to the addresses and routes visible elsewhere. Firewalls A firewall applies traffic policy to packet and connection context, with addresses, ports, interfaces, direction and tracked state contributing to different reachability outcomes. VPN routing VPN access and routing place media connections within a selected tunnel and its surrounding network paths. Reverse proxy behavior Reverse proxies forward requests through distinct client-facing and server-facing connections. Emby Connect and server connectivity Emby Connect associates a central sign-in with permitted server accounts and helps clients locate the selected server, while media connections still use the server’s actual reachable endpoint. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft: Windows Firewall traffic and profile policy Emby: Emby Connect and direct server connections

articles/networking/routers/nat/index.ht.title: Overview: Address translation and port mapping | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Address translation and port mapping Address translation and port mapping relate internal endpoints to the addresses and routes visible elsewhere. One home router, two translation layers and a carrier-managed translation boundary create different reachability conditions. Loopback and UPnP mappings address further cases within that arrangement. These topics explain which endpoint is exposed and which device controls the relevant mapping. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Network address translation (NAT) NAT rewrites endpoint addressing across network realms, with address/port translation retaining state that associates outside traffic with the intended inside flow. Port forwarding Port forwarding maps a selected inbound endpoint to an internal service, with address stability, firewall policy and service readiness determining whether the complete request can succeed. Double NAT Double NAT places two translation boundaries in a connection path, requiring their endpoint mappings and state to compose before outside traffic can reach an internal server. Carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) Carrier-grade NAT places subscriber traffic behind an operator-controlled translation layer, so household gateway settings do not necessarily provide an outside inbound service mapping. NAT loopback NAT loopback lets an inside client use an outside mapped endpoint for an inside service, with compatible translation and return routing keeping the client’s expected peer consistent. UPnP port mapping UPnP gateway port mapping asks a compatible gateway to maintain an inbound endpoint association, with granted mapping details and lifetime distinct from complete server reachability. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation RFC 6598: Shared IPv4 address space RFC 4787: UDP NAT behavior and hairpinning Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings Carrier-grade NAT places subscriber traffic behind an operator-controlled translation layer, so household gateway settings do not necessarily provide an outside inbound service mapping. Your home router can have a WAN address that is not the address outside services see. Another translation layer may stand between the household gateway and the internet. With carrier-grade NAT , or CGNAT , that layer is operated by a provider and can share an outside IPv4 allocation among subscribers. The shared range is not RFC 1918 private space RFC 6598 reserves 100.64.0.0/10 for shared addressing. It spans 100.64.0.0 through 100.127.255.255. It is distinct from the three familiar RFC 1918 blocks. Looking only for 10. , 172.16–31. and 192.168.* can therefore miss this context. Use an original topology: Layer Address label Emby server inside the home 192.168.50.20 Home gateway’s provider-facing side 100.64.12.3 Provider’s outside side 198.51.100.12 The last value is a documentation stand-in, not an actual public endpoint. The presence of a shared-range address is evidence of that address realm. An address comparison alone does not fully identify every intermediary or provider policy. The household controls only its own mapping A household rule can translate an arriving request at 100.64.12.3 to the internal server. It cannot make outside traffic arrive there through the operator’s gateway unless that earlier layer provides the required path. An ordinary dynamic-DNS update can correctly point to the provider’s outside address while leaving no subscriber-specific inbound association. Dynamic DNS changes the descriptive record. It does not allocate an external transport endpoint in the provider’s translator. Shared allocations also share outside port resources The provider can distinguish subscriber flows through ports and other state. A public-facing IPv4 address alone does not select one subscriber’s home server. Outbound requests and their replies can work because appropriate translation state exists. A new inbound request for an Emby listener needs a separate supported association and permitted path. This is the same broad distinction as double NAT , with the important added question of who can control the outer layer. Another route needs its own prerequisites Possible connection designs include an operator-provided public allocation or supported mapping service, routed IPv6 where both ends and policies support it, or a VPN/tunnel arrangement that supplies a reachable intermediary. These are different capabilities, not settings that every connection necessarily offers. Each still needs its return route, service and access policy. Emby Connect helps clients locate their selected server. Its documented direct-connection role does not itself create an operator-controlled inbound mapping. Compare the relevant layer’s observation A gateway’s displayed WAN address, an outside address observation and the endpoint advertised to apps describe different positions in the path. They should be compared for the same address family and connection context. A VPN or different outgoing interface can make another observation represent a different route. See Also Private, public and special-purpose IP addresses Double NAT and two translation boundaries Dynamic DNS and a changing server address VPN access and the routed path to a media server References RFC 6598: Shared IPv4 address space RFC 6888: Carrier-grade NAT requirements RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation IANA: Special-purpose IPv4 address registry

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: Double NAT and two translation boundaries | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: Double NAT and two translation boundaries Double NAT places two translation boundaries in a connection path, requiring their endpoint mappings and state to compose before outside traffic can reach an internal server. An internet gateway can have another router behind it. If both translate between different address realms, the server’s path crosses double NAT . A working rule on the inner router then describes only part of an outside connection. Name the two inside-facing realms Use this original topology: Outer gateway: outside documentation address 198.51.100.12, inside interface 192.168.1.1. Inner router: WAN-side address 192.168.1.2, inside interface 192.168.50.1. Emby service: 192.168.50.20:8920. The inner router’s WAN is still inside the outer gateway’s realm. It is not the public-facing endpoint in this exercise. The two mappings compose This original reduced map chain targets a declared internal HTTPS listener: { "protocol": "tcp", "outerMap": { "from": {"address": "198.51.100.12", "port": 45000}, "to": {"address": "192.168.1.2", "port": 45000} }, "innerMap": { "from": {"address": "192.168.1.2", "port": 45000}, "to": {"address": "192.168.50.20", "port": 8920} } } The outer destination becomes the inner rule’s arriving endpoint. Protocol, address and port need to match at that boundary. If the outer gateway sends to 192.168.1.3, the inner router at .2 never receives the request. If it sends to .2:45001 while the inner rule matches 45000, the endpoint also fails to compose. Adding only the inner rule leaves the outer inbound stage unresolved. Outbound success can hide the second boundary An inside client initiating an internet request can create state at both translating gateways. Replies then follow those associations back. That successful browsing path does not demonstrate an unsolicited inbound Emby request has a matching path through both gateways. The return path also needs the correct state and routing context. An asymmetric return through another gateway can fail despite correct-looking inbound rule text. Another Wi-Fi box need not be another NAT A device operating as a bridge/access point can extend a link without adding a translating routed realm. A device operating as a router can instead create another subnet and policy boundary. The physical presence of two boxes is not sufficient evidence of double NAT. Changing that operating mode has broader network effects; this explanation identifies the path rather than prescribing a mode change. Control of the outer layer matters If the outer translation belongs to an ISP, the household may not have the ability to install its mapping. Carrier-grade NAT develops that case. See Also NAT and address/port translation state Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings How a home media network carries an Emby stream References RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation RFC 5382: TCP NAT behavioral requirements Emby: Connecting from client apps

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: NAT and address/port translation state | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: NAT and address/port translation state NAT rewrites endpoint addressing across network realms, with address/port translation retaining state that associates outside traffic with the intended inside flow. Many home IPv4 networks use private addresses internally and one outside address at the gateway. Network address translation , or NAT, connects those address realms by rewriting relevant packet fields. The common address-and-port form, NAPT, lets several inside flows share one outside address while retaining different associations. Two equal source ports can become distinct outside flows Use this original teaching table. The outside addresses are documentation labels: Inside source Remote destination Translated outside source 192.168.50.30:51000 203.0.113.10:443 198.51.100.12:62000 192.168.50.31:51000 203.0.113.10:443 198.51.100.12:62001 Both clients selected source port 51000. Their different inside addresses distinguish their original flows; the gateway’s chosen outside ports distinguish these two translated flows. A reply for outside port 62000 can be translated back to the first inside endpoint under this model. Port 62001 belongs to the second. The actual mapping key and reuse behavior depend on protocol and gateway implementation. Equal outside port values can have additional context in other policies. The return association has to remain available An original reduced state entry is: { "protocol": "tcp", "inside": {"address": "192.168.50.30", "port": 51000}, "outside": {"address": "198.51.100.12", "port": 62000}, "remote": {"address": "203.0.113.10", "port": 443} } This is explanatory state, not a router configuration or captured connection. The translation changes the packet’s endpoint representation. Return traffic needs to traverse a gateway that has the applicable association or another supported configured mapping. Changing the path to a gateway without that state can break the flow even though both gateways can route ordinary packets. A reply is different from a new outside request The clients’ outbound operations created the relevant associations. A new outside viewer asking for an Emby service has not necessarily created such inside-originated state. A port-forward supplies an explicit inbound mapping for the selected service. It is a different intent from allowing replies to an outbound client connection. Mapping behavior and filtering behavior are also distinct. A translation can identify the inside endpoint while another policy rejects the incoming traffic. Address translation does not define the application identity The translated outside address can represent several clients. A server observing it cannot recover each viewer’s private endpoint simply from that address. Likewise, a gateway’s translation does not authenticate an Emby user or encrypt an HTTP session. Those operations belong to other layers of the path. Address translation is not required merely because a connection uses IPv6; routed IPv6 has its own reachability and firewall conditions. State has a lifetime Mappings can expire, be removed or disappear after a gateway restart. A client’s saved URL can remain unchanged while that traffic state changes. See Also Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Double NAT and two translation boundaries Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings NAT loopback and same-network public endpoints References RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation RFC 2663: NAT terminology RFC 4787: UDP NAT behavior and hairpinning RFC 5382: TCP NAT behavioral requirements

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: NAT loopback and same-network public endpoints | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: NAT loopback and same-network public endpoints NAT loopback lets an inside client use an outside mapped endpoint for an inside service, with compatible translation and return routing keeping the client’s expected peer consistent. A server URL works from mobile data but fails when the same phone rejoins home Wi-Fi. If the name still resolves to the gateway’s outside endpoint, the home request now needs a path back inside. NAT loopback , also called hairpin NAT, supplies that return-to-inside behavior. The final service is inside even though the selected endpoint looks outside Assume an original mapping from the documentation outside endpoint 198.51.100.12:45000 to a declared server listener at 192.168.50.20:8920. A LAN client at 192.168.50.30:51234 sends toward the outside endpoint. The gateway must recognize and redirect that traffic to the inside service rather than treating it only as an ordinary internet-bound request. The remote-client mapping and the inside-client hairpin behavior are related capabilities. A gateway supporting one does not prove the other is enabled or usable. The return route must preserve the expected peer Suppose the gateway changes only the destination and leaves the client’s original LAN source unchanged. The server then sees a request from its local neighbor 192.168.50.30. It can send a direct local reply from 192.168.50.20:8920, bypassing the gateway’s reverse translation. The client, however, began a flow to 198.51.100.12:45000. A reply from the different inside endpoint does not match that expected peer under this simple connection model. The routing topology therefore matters alongside the destination rewrite. One design also translates the inside source Here is an original complete endpoint exercise: { "protocol": "tcp", "original": { "source": "192.168.50.30:51234", "destination": "198.51.100.12:45000" }, "insideLeg": { "source": "192.168.50.1:61000", "destination": "192.168.50.20:8920" }, "serverReply": { "source": "192.168.50.20:8920", "destination": "192.168.50.1:61000" }, "clientReply": { "source": "198.51.100.12:45000", "destination": "192.168.50.30:51234" } } The gateway’s inside address and chosen source port make the server return through it. Its state then reverses the appropriate fields so the client receives a reply from the endpoint it selected. These are explanatory fields, not configured rules or captured packets. A gateway can implement another valid hairpin design; the example isolates the return-route requirement. The server may observe a translated client In this design, the origin’s socket peer is 192.168.50.1 rather than the original LAN client address. That can affect application address classification, logs or per-address policy. It is another reason to keep path and observed peer separate. An application cannot infer every earlier address simply from the translated socket peer. Split DNS can select a direct inside endpoint instead A home resolver can return a suitable local destination for the same hostname, avoiding this outside/hairpin route. That split-DNS design still needs the same requested scheme, port and path to work at its inside endpoint. Replacing only the address can leave a port mismatch. See Also Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints Port forwarding and the complete inbound path NAT and address/port translation state Local and remote connections to Emby References RFC 4787: UDP NAT behavior and hairpinning RFC 5382: TCP NAT behavioral requirements RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: Port forwarding and the complete inbound path | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Port forwarding maps a selected inbound endpoint to an internal service, with address stability, firewall policy and service readiness determining whether the complete request can succeed. A remote app targets an outside address and port. A port-forward rule tells the gateway which internal service should receive the matching inbound traffic. The rule identifies a translation destination. It is one stage of the connection path. The rule matches more than a number This original HTTPS-listener exercise uses an outside documentation address: { "protocol": "tcp", "outside": {"address": "198.51.100.12", "port": 45000}, "inside": {"address": "192.168.50.20", "port": 8920} } Assume the selected internal service actually implements HTTPS on 8920. The mapping does not create or enable that listener. Arriving destination Match under this declared rule? TCP, shown outside address, port 45000 Yes UDP, same address and numeric port No TCP, same address, port 45001 No The remote URL consequently selects the outside port, while the gateway forwards to the different internal port. The target address must still identify the server If 192.168.50.20 moves to another device or the server obtains .42 instead, the stored rule can remain structurally correct while targeting the wrong host. A DHCP reservation helps keep the intended allocation stable. It does not automatically repair an earlier rule after renumbering. The target must also be reachable from the gateway on the relevant internal route. Another routed segment can add its own policy and return-path conditions. Every following stage still has a result After translation, the host firewall must permit the intended traffic and the selected listener must be ready. The service then performs its application and user-access checks. A working gateway rule with no listener can produce a refused or failed connection. A working listener reached through a wrong URL scheme can fail at the protocol stage. A valid connection can still receive an application rejection. Emby’s network settings distinguish local listener ports from reported public ports. Reporting 45000 does not prove the router has this rule, and a router rule does not prove Emby is listening at its target. A successful inside test takes another path A LAN client connecting directly to 192.168.50.20:8920 does not exercise the outside mapping. A LAN client using the outside address instead needs NAT loopback or another supported path. That is why “it works at home” and “the outside route works” are separate observations.
