With double NAT , another gateway can sit before the one whose rule was inspected. Both boundaries need a coherent path rather than an extra rule at only the inner router. See Also NAT and address/port translation state DHCP reservations and stable server addresses Double NAT and two translation boundaries Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References RFC 3022: Traditional NAT and address/port translation RFC 5382: TCP NAT behavioral requirements Emby: Network settings and reported addresses Emby: Connecting from client apps

articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.title: UPnP port mapping and gateway control | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/nat/Network-.keywords: UPnP port mapping and gateway control UPnP gateway port mapping asks a compatible gateway to maintain an inbound endpoint association, with granted mapping details and lifetime distinct from complete server reachability. Automatic port mapping gives an application a way to request an inbound mapping from a compatible gateway. UPnP discovery first helps locate the gateway service; a later control operation requests the mapping. Finding a gateway and changing its traffic association are different operations. The request identifies a concrete service destination The standardized WANIPConnection service describes port-mapping operations. Their roles include the external port, protocol, internal client/port and mapping lifetime. Use this original reduced granted result: { "gateway": "G1", "protocol": "TCP", "externalPort": 45000, "internalClient": "192.168.50.20", "internalPort": 8920, "acceptedAtSeconds": 100, "grantedLeaseSeconds": 600 } It is explanatory JSON, not a SOAP request or native gateway reply. The exercise assumes the mapping was granted with the shown details. That result says G1 maintains the declared TCP association. It does not say an internal listener was created or another external gateway accepted a corresponding rule. A granted lifetime needs an owner In this model, six hundred granted seconds from time one hundred gives expiry at seven hundred. Continued use requires the appropriate supported renewal or another valid lifetime arrangement. Observation Meaning Gateway service discovered A control candidate was located Mapping request accepted The gateway accepted its declared mapping operation Current entry/lifetime confirmed The association is presently represented there Outside service request succeeds The complete connection path worked A router restart, changed allocation or expired lease can invalidate a mapping while a client retains the old server URL. Exact lifetime rules vary by service version and implementation. A request’s desired duration should not be substituted for the duration actually granted. The gateway’s policy controls exposure A port-mapping service changes the inbound reachability of a selected endpoint. Which clients can request it and which destinations it permits are gateway-control policy decisions. UPnP device/service versions and their protection capabilities are documented in the OCF catalogue. A particular household device’s implemented policy is a separate fact. A discovery advertisement alone does not authenticate every later control operation. Emby can attempt this separate stage Emby’s network documentation describes automatic mapping through UPnP when the gateway supports and permits it. A successful local operation still leaves the internal firewall, service readiness and any upstream translation boundary to evaluate. Under double NAT , G1 can be only the inner router. With CGNAT , the household’s mapping result does not establish a corresponding operator-controlled path. See Also Port forwarding and the complete inbound path SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations Double NAT and two translation boundaries Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings References UPnP Forum via OCF catalogue: WANIPConnection:2 mapping service OCF: UPnP Device Architecture 2.0 Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/Network-Emby.title: Emby Connect and the path to the selected server | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/Network-Emby.keywords: Emby Connect and the path to the selected server Emby Connect associates a central sign-in with permitted server accounts and helps clients locate the selected server, while media connections still use the server’s actual reachable endpoint. Emby Connect lets a user use a central sign-in and locate servers whose local accounts have been associated with that user. The server’s media still needs a reachable connection path. Connect sign-in and playback are separate operations. Location assistance and media delivery have different destinations Emby’s documentation states that client connections go directly to the Emby server rather than passing the media through Emby Connect. That explains an otherwise puzzling result: the Connect service can be reachable while a particular household server is not. The server can be powered off, advertise an outdated endpoint or sit behind a missing inbound mapping. Successfully obtaining its location does not resolve those path failures. A candidate is not a completed connection Use this original reduced state model: { "connectSignInSucceeded": true, "serverAssociationFound": true, "candidate": {"serverId": "learn-server-A", "url": "https://media.example.net:45000/"}, "serverConnectionSucceeded": false } These fields are explanatory rather than a native Connect API response. The fictional hostname was not queried. The first two successes establish the association stage. The false final condition belongs to the selected server’s connection path. DNS , port forwarding and CGNAT explain distinct reasons that path can remain unavailable. The server’s local user relationship still matters The server administrator associates a Connect username with a local server account. That account’s server-side access remains a separate relationship from the central username. A central sign-in does not make every listed server’s library accessible without its intended account/permissions. Removing or changing the local association can also change access while the Connect identity remains the same. The documentation recommends retaining a local account password as part of the account setup. This page explains the relationship rather than changing any account. Server identity can survive endpoint changes A friendly name is a display label. An endpoint can change after address allocation or network configuration changes. The intended server identity can remain stable through both. A client holding an old candidate can therefore need updated location information while the user’s server association is still valid. Local discovery supplies another location mechanism in its network scope. Connect supplies central assistance for the associated servers; neither candidate alone proves the later media service request succeeded. See Also Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints Dynamic DNS and a changing server address Carrier-grade NAT and control of inbound mappings Local and remote connections to Emby References Emby: Emby Connect and direct server connections Emby: Connecting from client apps Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/Network-Fire.title: Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/Network-Fire.keywords: Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state A firewall applies traffic policy to packet and connection context, with addresses, ports, interfaces, direction and tracked state contributing to different reachability outcomes. A firewall decides which traffic its policy permits. The decision can depend on protocol, addresses, ports, direction, interface, application context and previously tracked connection state. It can allow one Emby path while blocking another to the same machine. Start with the packet context that reaches this boundary An outside packet can have its destination rewritten by a router before the host firewall sees it. A VPN or proxy can change its source representation as well. The rule therefore needs to match the context at the boundary where it is enforced, not only the endpoint originally entered into the app. A host listening on 8920 and a gateway mapping to 8920 are not evidence that the host’s inbound policy permits the arriving source. A reduced stateful policy Use this original first-match teaching model: { "rules": [ {"trackedState": "established", "action": "allow"}, {"family": "ipv4", "transport": "tcp", "sourcePrefix": "192.168.50.0/24", "destinationPort": 8920, "inputInterface": "lan", "action": "allow"} ], "otherwise": "drop" } These are not executable firewall rules. The tracked state is supplied by the model’s connection tracker, not accepted from a client-written header. For a new TCP connection from 192.168.50.30 arriving on lan for port 8920, the second rule matches. A new connection from 10.8.0.6 does not match the source prefix, even if a VPN route delivers it successfully. A new IPv6 connection also does not match this explicit IPv4 rule. It needs its own applicable policy or another rule in a real implementation. Established return traffic has another relationship A stateful tracker can associate later traffic with an already permitted flow. The policy can then handle appropriate return packets without describing every automatically selected client-side port as a permanent inbound service. A completely new request for another service is different. An equal source address or a claim inside an HTTP header does not make it part of an established flow. A gateway restart or expired state can also change how later packets are classified. Stateless packet filters operate with another rule context. The existence of stateful behavior in one device should not be generalized to every boundary. Profiles and interfaces can change which rules apply Windows Firewall has network profiles and application/rule context. Other systems can attach rules to interfaces, zones or chains with their own precedence. A server can therefore behave differently through Ethernet, Wi-Fi, a VPN interface or another address family while the application itself is unchanged. Two observed paths Possible policy distinction to retain Loopback versus another device Local stack versus network ingress LAN versus VPN source Source range and input interface IPv4 versus IPv6 Address family and separate applicable rules Direct client versus reverse proxy Observed socket peer and trusted metadata context This table identifies inputs, not a claim that any one product uses the simple model’s first-match ordering. A rejected connection does not identify every earlier stage DNS can return the right address and routing can deliver the packet before the firewall drops it. A different case can fail before any packet reaches that firewall. A refused TCP connection can instead come from an endpoint with no suitable listener or an explicit rejection. A timeout can have several causes, including silent filtering and missing return traffic. The observation’s location matters. Emby’s connectivity documentation describes the host-firewall stage without treating a disabled firewall as a necessary diagnostic step. Application access comes after permitted transport The firewall can permit the TCP service while Emby rejects a user or requested operation. Those results are not contradictory. Forwarded client addresses explains why trusted proxy metadata must also be interpreted at the right layer. A network-policy decision and an application’s reported client identity should not be collapsed into one unqualified “allowed address.” See Also Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints Port forwarding and the complete inbound path IPv6 addressing, scope and reachability Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context References Microsoft: Windows Firewall traffic and profile policy Netfilter project: Connection-tracking state and tools Emby: Connecting from client apps Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/proxy/index..title: Overview: Reverse proxy behavior | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/proxy/index..keywords: Overview: Reverse proxy behavior Reverse proxies forward requests through distinct client-facing and server-facing connections. The proxy receives one request and performs another operation toward the origin. Forwarded-address information preserves selected context, while buffering and timeouts affect delivery behavior. These pages explain those independent connection legs and the evidence needed to interpret a proxy-mediated Emby request. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Reverse proxies A reverse proxy accepts a public-facing application request and makes a separate upstream request, translating endpoint and resource context according to its configured policy. Forwarded client addresses Forwarded client-address metadata describes an earlier request path only when interpreted through trusted proxy context, separately from the origin’s actual socket peer. Proxy buffering and timeouts Proxy buffering and timeout settings control progress between independent upstream and downstream connections, with finite storage and idle clocks distinct from a movie’s total duration. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 7239: Forwarded HTTP metadata and trust RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol

articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.title: Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.keywords: Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context Forwarded client-address metadata describes an earlier request path only when interpreted through trusted proxy context, separately from the origin’s actual socket peer. When a reverse proxy contacts Emby, the socket peer Emby sees is that proxy. The original viewer can be represented in forwarded metadata, but the origin needs a reason to trust the representation. A header and a transport observation are different evidence. Keep the socket peer as a separate value Use this original chain, with documentation addresses standing for external nodes: { "socketPeer": "192.168.50.10", "forwardedFor": ["198.51.100.77", "203.0.113.40"], "trustedProxies": ["192.168.50.10", "203.0.113.40"], "selectedClient": "198.51.100.77" } The origin’s direct peer is the inside proxy. The earlier edge proxy is another explicitly trusted node. The remaining address represents the client under this declared model. The fields are an explanatory projection. They are not a native Forwarded or X-Forwarded-For parser result from a running server. Walk only through established trust For this exercise, begin at the observed peer. If it is not a trusted proxy, ignore its address-chain claims. If it is trusted, walk the supplied chain from the nearest end toward the earlier client, continuing only through the nodes the policy trusts. Select the first nontrusted address reached. NGINX documents a related recursive real-IP interpretation using trusted sources and the last nontrusted supplied address. Actual products have their own configuration and supported header formats. Now prepend a forged 198.51.100.5 to the original chain. The model still stops at 198.51.100.77. Choosing the leftmost value unconditionally would instead accept the forged prefix. This assumes the trusted proxies supply the expected chain semantics and protect the relevant hop context. Trusting an address label without a controlled path is insufficient. Direct origin access is another input Suppose a direct client at 198.51.100.77 contacts the origin and supplies a header claiming 127.0.0.1. Under the model, that socket peer is not a trusted proxy, so the claim does not replace it. A header cannot make an external request originate from the origin’s loopback stack. A real deployment’s direct-access and proxy trust policy determine how this boundary is enforced. RFC 7239 explains why forwarded fields cannot be assumed correct merely because they arrived. Parse the declared header format before classifying addresses Forwarded and X-Forwarded-For are different representations. RFC 7239 defines structured Forwarded parameters; an IP-list interpretation is not a complete parser for that format. An original readable header example is: Forwarded: for="[2001:db8:50::77]";proto=https;host=media.example.net, for=203.0.113.40 The first for value is a quoted, bracketed IPv6 address. The commas separate forwarded elements, while semicolons separate parameters within an element. The source values are documentation data. The standard also allows unknown and obfuscated node identifiers. Those values can describe a forwarding step without yielding a concrete client IP for address classification. They must not silently become a loopback or private-address value. Equivalent IPv6 spellings can identify the same address bits. A trust policy comparing unnormalized text can mistakenly distinguish them; syntax validation and canonical address interpretation precede the membership decision. Neither successful parsing nor a valid IP range establishes provenance. The observed peer and trusted forwarding path still determine whether the interpreted value can influence the application’s decision. Address and scheme metadata affect application decisions The interpreted original address can affect logs, local/remote classification, limits or address filters. A forwarded scheme/host can affect generated external links and redirects. Those uses need consistent provenance. Misclassifying an earlier outside client as the inside proxy can produce a different policy result from the intended one. Emby exposes forwarded-header interpretation in its network settings. That documented role does not establish that every arbitrary chain or direct-origin path is trustworthy. Preserve the chain when investigating a discrepancy The socket peer, received header values, trusted-proxy set and selected interpretation explain the decision together. Recording only the final displayed address loses the evidence needed to tell a legitimate translated client from an incorrectly accepted claim. Local and remote connections follows the classification built on that context. See Also Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path Local and remote connections to Emby Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state References RFC 7239: Forwarded HTTP metadata and trust NGINX: Trusted sources and recursive client-address interpretation Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.title: Proxy buffering, progress and timeout clocks | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.keywords: Proxy buffering, progress and timeout clocks Proxy buffering and timeout settings control progress between independent upstream and downstream connections, with finite storage and idle clocks distinct from a movie’s total duration. A proxy can receive media from Emby faster than its client consumes it. It can also spend time waiting for the next upstream bytes while the client waits for delivery. The two sides have different progress observations. Buffering coordinates their rates; timeouts bound a selected kind of waiting. A finite buffer temporarily absorbs unequal rates Use this original constant-rate model: { "upstreamMbitPerSecond": 12, "downstreamMbitPerSecond": 8, "availableBufferMbit": 24, "initialBufferedMbit": 0 } The queue grows by four Mbit each second. With no other changes, its twenty-four-Mbit capacity is reached after six seconds. At that point, the proxy cannot continue retaining the same excess indefinitely. It needs another permitted storage destination, reduced upstream progress, a dropped/failed transfer or another implemented policy. If upstream flow is backpressured toward the client’s eight-Mbit/s consumption, the earlier twelve-Mbit/s rate no longer describes continuous received progress. Buffering changes where work can wait A proxy can buffer response data in memory and, under its configured rules, temporary files. That can let the upstream operation progress independently for a while. With another forwarding policy, upstream reads remain more directly tied to downstream consumption. Smaller retained storage does not automatically make the complete application faster; it changes where rate mismatch is absorbed. The origin, proxy and client can each have their own buffers. A media player’s presentation reserve is not the same queue as a proxy’s response buffering. A read timeout is not necessarily a whole-response deadline NGINX’s documented proxy_read_timeout applies between successive upstream read operations rather than to the total response duration. Its documented default is sixty seconds. Use this original timing exercise: { "readTimeoutSeconds": 60, "successfulReadTimes": [0, 55, 110, 165], "nextDataTime": 230 } Each completed gap is fifty-five seconds, so the declared idle threshold is not exceeded during those reads even though the response has already lasted 165 seconds. After the read at 165, the next data is delayed until 230, a sixty-five-second gap. Under this reduced clock model, the deadline at 225 arrives before that next data. Increasing a timeout changes tolerance for that waiting. It does not make the missing bytes arrive sooner. The selected clock matters Connect time, upstream response reads, upstream writes and downstream client progress can have separate timeout settings and causes. An upstream that stops producing media differs from a client that stops accepting it. Both can eventually stop the overall operation, but the relevant clock and queue observations are different. A WebSocket or another long-lived exchange can also need its own progress/keepalive handling. Successful ordinary-page delivery does not establish every long-lived path’s behavior. Locate the stalled side before interpreting the result For an Emby stream that starts and later fails through a proxy, retain upstream progress, downstream progress, buffered work and the timeout that expired. A 60-second read-idle setting should not be interpreted as “movies must be shorter than sixty seconds.” The timing exercise shows how a much longer healthy response and a shorter stalled interval produce different results. See Also Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery Buffering, ready media and playback reserve HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) References NGINX: HTTP proxy buffering, headers and timeouts NGINX: WebSocket proxying RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol RFC 9110: HTTP semantics

articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.title: Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/proxy/Networ.keywords: Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path A reverse proxy accepts a public-facing application request and makes a separate upstream request, translating endpoint and resource context according to its configured policy. A reverse proxy can accept a client connection at a public hostname and forward the application request to Emby through another endpoint. There are two service-facing connections: client to proxy, and proxy to origin. Success on one side does not establish success on the other. The public and upstream endpoints can differ Use this original reduced arrangement: { "publicBase": "https://media.example.net/emby/", "proxyAddress": "192.168.50.10", "upstreamBase": "http://192.168.50.20:8096/", "removeRequestPrefix": "/emby" } These fields describe a model, not executable proxy settings. The public connection uses HTTPS with its scheme-default port; the declared upstream connection uses another scheme and explicit port. The proxy can perform TLS termination on the public side. The origin side has its own transport and security properties. Public HTTPS does not by itself describe every later hop. The origin’s socket peer is the proxy’s upstream endpoint. Forwarded addresses can describe the earlier client only within the relevant trust policy. Request paths need a consistent transformation An original client request to /emby/api/item is transformed to /api/item under this model’s stated prefix removal. That works only if the origin expects that path. Retaining the prefix would produce another upstream resource name. The application can also have its own base-path behavior. Applying both an application prefix and an incompatible proxy rewrite can duplicate or remove path segments unexpectedly. A successful first page can hide the problem until a later media, script or API URL uses another form. Response references need the public base too Consider three generic references in a response, resolved against https://media.example.net/emby/ : Returned reference Client destination path login /emby/login /login /login http://192.168.50.20:8096/login A different explicit origin The client resolves those references; it does not know that the proxy administrator intended the /emby prefix. An absolute inside address can be unusable from outside. A root-relative link can leave the public prefix. A hostname-correct redirect can still choose an unintended scheme or port. URL structure explains that resolution. Proxy redirect rewriting and the application’s original-host/base-URL interpretation must describe a coherent public service. Request headers describe another context A proxy can send an upstream Host value reflecting the public host or its chosen origin arrangement. Forwarded metadata can describe an original scheme, host or client address. The origin should interpret that context according to the actual trusted proxy path. A client-written header is not evidence that the request traversed the intended proxy. Emby’s network settings include a reverse-proxy secure-connection mode and header interpretation. The relevant application behavior must match the configured forwarding design, rather than assuming any header creates the needed route. Long-lived or upgraded operations have their own forwarding behavior A proxy that returns a small ordinary HTTP response can still handle streaming, range requests or an upgraded connection differently. WebSocket proxying, for example, involves specific handling for the upgrade and hop-by-hop headers. It is not guaranteed by serving the web app’s initial HTML successfully. Likewise, buffering and timeout clocks govern progress over the separate sides. These can explain an operation that starts correctly and later stalls. See Also Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context Proxy buffering, progress and timeout clocks Port forwarding and the complete inbound path References RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 3986: URI structure and relative references NGINX: HTTP proxy buffering, headers and timeouts NGINX: WebSocket proxying Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/routers/vpn/index.ht.title: Overview: VPN routing | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/vpn/index.ht.keywords: Overview: VPN routing VPN access and routing place media connections within a selected tunnel and its surrounding network paths. A tunnel can provide a route to a private server, but the traffic still follows the configured routing decisions. Split tunneling determines which destinations use that route and which use another path. The pages here trace which destinations use the tunnel and which follow another route. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> VPN access to a media server VPN access adds a tunnel path into a network, while destination routes, return routes, name resolution and service policy determine whether a media server is usable through it. VPN routing and split tunneling VPN routing determines which destination prefixes use a tunnel, with route specificity, overlapping address realms and DNS policy separate from the tunnel’s connected state. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 4301: IPsec policy and tunnel architecture RFC 4632: CIDR addressing and aggregation

articles/networking/routers/vpn/Network-.title: VPN access and the routed path to a media server | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/vpn/Network-.keywords: VPN access and the routed path to a media server VPN access adds a tunnel path into a network, while destination routes, return routes, name resolution and service policy determine whether a media server is usable through it. A VPN can provide a path from an outside device into the server’s network. “Tunnel connected” establishes that tunnel’s connection state, not that every desired private service is now reachable. The application’s request still has a destination, route and return path. The inner destination differs from the tunnel peer Use an original example with a VPN client address 10.8.0.6 and Emby service address 192.168.50.20. The inner request targets the private server. The outer tunnel traffic targets the VPN gateway through whatever underlay path its protocol uses. The tunnel can protect its carried traffic according to its protocol and policy. Authentication to that tunnel is still different from authorization to use the Emby server. RFC 4301 describes one IPsec policy/tunnel architecture. Other VPN technologies implement their own details. Both directions need a route This original reduced routed model preserves the VPN client’s source address: { "clientAddress": "10.8.0.6", "serverAddress": "192.168.50.20", "clientRoutes": [{"prefix": "192.168.50.0/24", "path": "vpn"}], "serverReturnRoutes": [{"prefix": "10.8.0.0/24", "path": "vpn-gateway"}] } The client’s request can enter the tunnel because the server destination matches its route. The server’s reply can reach the VPN client because another route identifies that client realm. If the server instead sends replies to a gateway that lacks the relevant return path, the initial request can arrive while the connection still fails. A gateway can translate the VPN client source as another design. That changes what Emby observes and which return association it uses; it is not the same source-preserving model. Names need the appropriate resolution path A private hostname can require a resolver available inside the VPN. A public hostname can resolve to a public endpoint even when the private tunnel path exists. The actual resolved address determines which destination route applies. “DNS works” needs its returned address and view retained, especially with split DNS . The tunnel has a packet-size budget For an original arithmetic exercise, let the underlay allow a 1280-byte packet and let the chosen tunnel add eighty bytes. The declared inner packet budget is then 1200 bytes. This is a teaching overhead assumption, not an IPsec or product measurement. Media delivery can stall when larger packets cannot traverse the effective path and the required size discovery/recovery fails. A successful small request does not measure that larger-packet behavior. Routed access does not extend every broadcast A permitted unicast route to 192.168.50.20 can work without carrying Emby’s local discovery broadcast . A layer-two extension or an explicit discovery relay is another capability, with its own scope. It should not be inferred from ordinary routed VPN connectivity. See Also VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling Subnets, CIDR and matching routes Firewalls, traffic rules and connection state Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints References RFC 4301: IPsec policy and tunnel architecture RFC 4632: CIDR addressing and aggregation Emby: Network settings and reported addresses Emby: Connecting from client apps

articles/networking/routers/vpn/Network-.title: VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling | Emby Learn
articles/networking/routers/vpn/Network-.keywords: VPN routing, overlapping prefixes and split tunneling VPN routing determines which destination prefixes use a tunnel, with route specificity, overlapping address realms and DNS policy separate from the tunnel’s connected state. A connected VPN does not automatically receive every packet. The client’s routes and policy select which destinations use it. Split tunneling sends selected traffic through the tunnel while other traffic follows another path. A full-tunnel design has a broader selection, but still needs the tunnel’s own outer connection to remain reachable. Select the route for the actual destination Use this original reduced client table: { "routes": [ {"prefix": "0.0.0.0/0", "path": "ordinary-gateway", "metric": 10}, {"prefix": "192.168.50.0/24", "path": "vpn", "metric": 50} ], "serverDestination": "192.168.50.20", "otherDestination": "203.0.113.80" } Under longest-prefix matching, the server uses the VPN /24. The outside documentation destination uses the ordinary default route. The lower metric on that default does not override the more-specific /24. Metrics are compared within the relevant competing-route context. Equal private ranges can describe different places Suppose the visiting network also uses 192.168.50.0/24. The server’s home address and a visiting local address can now have equal numeric text. Add a second matching /24 route through the local interface with metric ten. In this deliberately simple tie policy, that local route wins over the VPN /24 at metric fifty. The request can then head toward the visiting realm instead of the home server. No amount of successful tunnel authentication changes what the chosen local route means. A prefix is an address grouping; it is not a global site identifier. Reusing RFC 1918 ranges makes overlapping private realms possible. A more-specific destination can change the choice For a separate model, add a route for 192.168.50.20/32 through the VPN. That host route is longer than either /24 and selects the tunnel for that one address even with metric one thousand. This illustrates specificity, not a universal configuration prescription. Some systems also use routing tables, policy rules or interface-bound sockets beyond this reduced model. The chosen route still needs a reachable tunnel destination and permitted return path. A host route cannot distinguish two services simultaneously wanted at the same numeric address without another separation strategy. A broad tunnel route needs an underlay path One full-tunnel model can use the two half-space prefixes 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1. Together they match the IPv4 address space more specifically than an ordinary /0 default. The tunnel peer itself is also an IP destination. An outer packet accidentally routed into the tunnel it is supposed to carry creates a dependency problem. This original carrier exception makes the intended separation explicit: { "fullTunnelPrefixes": ["0.0.0.0/1", "128.0.0.0/1"], "peerAddress": "198.51.100.12", "peerRoute": {"prefix": "198.51.100.12/32", "path": "underlay"} } The /32 keeps that peer on the underlay in this model. Actual clients can implement another appropriate mechanism; the numerical exception is not a packet capture or a native route command. DNS policy is another selection Routing a media address through the VPN does not determine which resolver supplies that address. A client can use a tunnel resolver, local resolver, encrypted resolver or application-specific resolution arrangement. The resolver’s traffic then has its own route. Split DNS can deliberately supply another address depending on the chosen view. See Also VPN access and the routed path to a media server Subnets, CIDR and matching routes DNS resolution, record types and cached answers Local and remote connections to Emby References RFC 4632: CIDR addressing and aggregation RFC 4301: IPsec policy and tunnel architecture RFC 9499: DNS terminology and views

articles/networking/security/browser/ind.title: Overview: Browser security boundaries | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/browser/ind.keywords: Overview: Browser security boundaries Browser security boundaries govern when a page can request or read resources from another connection or origin. Mixed-content rules concern insecure resources in a secure-page context. Same-origin policy and CORS concern a different relationship: which responses the page is allowed to read. Their pages explain those gates without assuming that browser permission also authorizes the operation on the server. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Mixed content in browsers Mixed-content processing governs insecure subrequests made by a secure browser page, with request type, upgrade policy and local-network features separate from CORS and server reachability. Same-origin policy and CORS The same-origin policy and CORS govern script access across browser origins, with preflight, credentials and allowed responses separate from the server’s authentication and authorization. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C: Mixed Content RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and origins

articles/networking/security/browser/Net.title: Same-origin policy, CORS and readable responses | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/browser/Net.keywords: Same-origin policy, CORS and readable responses The same-origin policy and CORS govern script access across browser origins, with preflight, credentials and allowed responses separate from the server’s authentication and authorization. A browser can receive an application response yet refuse to expose it to the requesting script. CORS is one mechanism that decides whether an applicable cross-origin response can be read. The server’s own decision to authenticate or authorize the request is another stage. Origin means scheme, host and port Compare these original URLs with https://media.example.net/ : Other URL Same origin? https://media.example.net/library Yes https://media.example.net:443/ Yes, using the scheme-default port https://media.example.net:8920/ No http://media.example.net/ No https://app.example.net/ No Paths select resources within an origin. Changing a path alone does not create another origin, while a different scheme or effective port does. Two hostnames resolving to the same IP do not become one origin. The browser uses the requested URL identity, not an assumption that the addresses share a physical machine. A preflight checks the intended method and headers A request using a nonsafelisted header such as Authorization can require a preflight before the later application request proceeds. This original reduced descriptor shows the permission inputs: { "origin": "https://app.example.net", "target": "https://media.example.net/api/item", "method": "GET", "requestHeaders": ["authorization"], "requiresPreflight": true } The browser’s OPTIONS exchange describes the intended cross-origin method/header use. An appropriate preflight result is not itself the authenticated GET operation or proof that the requested item is permitted. The later request and response still need their own applicable CORS and application results. Preflight and application results are two exchanges An original readable preflight fragment for the descriptor above is: OPTIONS /api/item HTTP/1.1 Host: media.example.net Origin: https://app.example.net Access-Control-Request-Method: GET Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization A corresponding reduced successful permission fragment is: HTTP/1.1 204 No Content Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.net Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization Access-Control-Max-Age: 120 These illustrate relevant fields with a generic resource path; they are not captured packets or an executed Emby endpoint. Actual framing and all applicable protocol requirements remain in their specifications. The permission result lets the browser proceed with the stated cross-origin GET/header combination. The later GET can still return 401 if its credential evidence is invalid. With appropriate response CORS fields, the script can read that authentication rejection. By contrast, a successful application response lacking the applicable response permission can remain unreadable to the script. Preflight permission and readable application result need separate evidence. The preflight permission cache is distinct from caching the application resource itself. Its key/context and lifetime concern permitted method/header use; retaining permission does not mean the requested media response or account authorization is cached as successful. Credentials restrict the allow-origin relationship For an original credentialed-response policy: { "requestOrigin": "https://app.example.net", "credentialsMode": "include", "allowOrigin": "*", "allowCredentials": true, "readableByScript": false } Under the Fetch rules, the wildcard allow-origin value is not sufficient for this credentialed result. The response needs the appropriate explicitly allowed origin and other applicable checks. Allowing credentials does not mean every origin should receive a credentialed response. The permitted origin is a policy input, and different requests can require different cache/context handling. The object is an explanatory projection, not a suggested server configuration. Some requests can be sent without preflight A qualifying simple request can go to another origin before the browser checks whether the script may read its response. A failed readable-response result therefore does not prove that the server received no request. This matters for operations that change state. CORS is not a replacement for server authentication, authorization or defenses appropriate to state-changing requests. The browser’s read boundary and the service’s operation policy protect different relationships. Likewise, CORS does not constrain a native app or command-line client through the same browser mechanism. Credential mode does not force every cookie to be sent A request configured to include credentials still follows the browser’s applicable cookie/security rules. The cookie scope and other browser policy can affect whether any credential is actually attached. Likewise, an Authorization header is a separate explicitly supplied credential mechanism. A preflight allowing that header does not create its value or decide that the server should accept it. The observable request therefore needs its actual credential presence kept separate from the application’s requested credential mode and the response’s allow-credentials declaration. Media elements and script access can have different requirements Displaying a resource through a media/image element and reading or manipulating it from script are not always the same operation. A native Emby app, a server-hosted web app and a hosted web client can consequently expose different connection behavior. The actual request mode, page origin, credentials and resource use belong in the comparison. Mixed-content and local-network-access processing can reject a request at another gate before a CORS response becomes relevant. The failing exchange identifies the stage A preflight rejection, server-side 401/403, TLS failure and unreadable successful response identify different stages. See Also Mixed content and a browser’s secure-page boundary Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint Media server authentication and credential evidence Browser media playback and its loading paths References WHATWG: Fetch and CORS processing RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and origins Chrome: Local Network Access permission Emby: Client connection paths

articles/networking/security/browser/Net.title: Mixed content and a browser’s secure-page boundary | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/browser/Net.keywords: Mixed content and a browser’s secure-page boundary Mixed-content processing governs insecure subrequests made by a secure browser page, with request type, upgrade policy and local-network features separate from CORS and server reachability. An HTTPS web page can load correctly while a later request to a plaintext HTTP media server is refused by the browser. The page and subrequest have different security contexts. The browser evaluates that relationship before ordinary application code can use the result. A secure page can choose an insecure subresource Use this original reduced case: { "page": "https://app.example.net/", "request": "http://media.example.net/api/status", "kind": "scripted-fetch", "upgradePolicy": false, "localNetworkExemption": false } The request is an active scripted fetch to an ordinary HTTP endpoint. Under the stated base mixed-content processing, it is blocked rather than becoming a successful readable response. This is a policy exercise, not a browser capture. The example names are reserved, and the data explicitly excludes additional exemptions. Resource types and upgrade policies matter The Mixed Content specification distinguishes processing that can upgrade certain requests from processing that blocks insecure requests. Request context Relevant behavior to examine Script/API fetch from a secure page Blocking or an applicable explicit policy/exception Eligible image/audio/video request Automatic upgrade rules and actual secure endpoint Request to an IP-literal host Its separate eligibility/exemption context Navigation to another page Navigation policy, distinct from fetching a subresource The table identifies different contexts rather than promising one outcome in every browser release. A content-security policy can also request upgrades. It changes the selected URL scheme; it does not make an HTTP listener understand TLS. An upgrade preserves some endpoint choices Suppose an eligible original poster URL is: http://media.example.net:8096/poster.jpg An upgrade to https retains the explicit port 8096. It does not automatically select Emby’s other HTTPS listener at 8920. The secure version can therefore fail even though the HTTP poster worked separately. The endpoint has to provide the requested protected service. Local-network access has another browser policy Local/private destinations can trigger additional browser rules or permissions. Chrome’s published Local Network Access material describes a permission introduced in Chrome 142 and specific local-request behavior. That feature can interact with mixed-content handling; it should not be treated as a universal rule shared by every TV app and browser. Loopback and potentially trustworthy local contexts also have defined exceptions. A result for localhost should not be generalized to every plaintext private server address. Retain the actual browser/version, page origin, subrequest URL and relevant permission/policy when identifying this stage. CORS controls another decision CORS governs whether the browser can expose an applicable cross-origin response to the requesting script. It does not cause an earlier blocked mixed-content request to become an ordinary secure resource. A server adding an allow-origin header cannot create TLS on its HTTP listener. Similarly, a working TLS endpoint can still reject or fail a CORS request. Same-origin and CORS follows that readable-response boundary. Hosted and server-hosted web apps can have different origins A hosted Emby web page and a web app served directly by the chosen server start from different page origins. They can consequently exercise different subrequest relationships even when the viewer selects the same media. Emby’s connectivity documentation identifies secure hosted-web access as a context to examine. The relevant evidence is the browser’s actual blocked/selected request and its security reason, not only the server’s ability to answer another standalone HTTP connection. articles/networking/security/certificate.keywords: Overview: Certificate validation and lifecycle Certificate validation and lifecycle connect public identity evidence, trust paths, requested names and deployed certificate state. A certificate has to fit the requested service identity and lead through an acceptable validation path. Renewal also has to produce the certificate actually served to a new connection. These topics separate certificate contents, trust, name matching and deployment lifecycle so each observed failure can be located. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> TLS certificates A TLS certificate binds public-key and service-identity information within a signed certificate structure whose usage, validity and trust must be evaluated by the client. Certificate trust chains A certificate trust chain links endpoint evidence through valid issuer relationships to a client-trusted anchor, with path validation separate from service-name matching. Certificate hostnames Certificate hostname validation compares the requested service identity with appropriately typed certificate names, keeping wildcard scope and direct IP identities distinct. articles/networking/security/certificate.title: Certificate renewal, ACME and deployed results | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/certificate.keywords: Certificate renewal, ACME and deployed results Certificate renewal obtains and deploys successor TLS evidence through distinct validation, issuance, installation and endpoint-reload stages, which ACME can automate in part. A certificate renewal job reports success, yet a TV still receives an expired certificate. The new artifact may have been issued correctly while the public TLS endpoint continues serving its predecessor. Renewal needs an observed deployment result as well as an issuance result. ACME coordinates an order and identifier validation ACME provides a protocol for a client to request certificate issuance from a supporting authority. The client supplies the desired identifiers and completes the required authorization/challenge process. HTTP-01 demonstrates control through a prescribed HTTP resource. DNS-01 demonstrates control through the prescribed DNS TXT information. Their validation paths and requirements differ. The certificate’s public key comes through a signing request. The server’s private key and the ACME account key have separate roles; identifier validation does not turn either into a public DNS record. ACME success is not proof that an Emby listener or reverse proxy has loaded that certificate. The served generation can remain old Use this original reduced deployment state: { "issuedGeneration": "C2", "installedGeneration": "C2", "servedGeneration": "C1", "reloadSucceeded": false, "newHandshakeChecked": false } The new file is present, but the modeled endpoint did not activate it. A subsequent new handshake is the observation that can establish what clients now receive. A file copied to the direct Emby listener also does not update a different public reverse proxy. The job must address the TLS endpoint the client actually contacts. The chain and matching private key need to be deployed coherently. Replacing only the leaf can leave another path-validation problem. Renewal timing follows the actual lifetime For a declared ninety-day teaching certificate, choosing renewal at sixty days leaves thirty days of remaining lifetime. A sixty-day fixed schedule applied to a forty-five-day certificate instead reaches the certificate fifteen days after expiry. 90-day lifetime - renewal at day 60 = 30 days remaining 45-day lifetime - renewal at day 60 = 15 days too late The arithmetic is a model, not a recommended universal renewal policy. Derive timing from the actual certificate, authority/client behavior and renewal information rather than assuming every artifact retains a historical lifetime. Public-trust policy is changing As checked on 12 October 2026, the cited CA/Browser Forum requirements limit subscriber certificates issued from 15 March 2026 until 15 March 2027 to a maximum two hundred days. That maximum is not a promise that an individual authority issues certificates for two hundred days. Providers can choose shorter lifetimes. Let’s Encrypt’s current published plan moves its default to sixty-four days in February 2027 and forty-five days in February 2028. Those future changes should not be described as an already universal forty-five-day default in October 2026. The current policy references provide the dated context; an automation should observe its issued artifact and authority’s supported renewal mechanisms. Validation and deployment can fail independently A DNS challenge can fail because the required record has not reached the validation context. An HTTP challenge can reach another listener or path. An accepted challenge can still be followed by a failed issuance or artifact retrieval. After issuance, permissions, key pairing, format, destination and reload behavior form another sequence. An existing application connection can also retain its already negotiated TLS session while new connections see another certificate generation. A new-handshake check identifies the deployed evidence rather than merely reusing an earlier connection. Keep useful evidence for each stage Retain the requested identifiers, authorization/order outcome, issued certificate expiry, deployment destination and certificate observed at the intended endpoint. Emby’s direct secure listener and a proxy installation have different artifact/reload arrangements. Their successful output is the intended leaf/chain/key relationship made visible to clients, not simply a renewal command ending with a successful status. See Also TLS certificates, public keys and endpoint evidence Certificate trust chains and path validation TLS termination and independent connection legs DNS resolution, record types and cached answers References RFC 8555: Automated Certificate Management Environment CA/Browser Forum: Current TLS Baseline Requirements CA/Browser Forum: TLS Baseline Requirements 2.2.5 Let's Encrypt: Current and planned certificate lifetimes Emby: Network and secure-connection settings

articles/networking/security/certificate.title: TLS certificates, public keys and endpoint evidence | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/certificate.keywords: TLS certificates, public keys and endpoint evidence A TLS certificate binds public-key and service-identity information within a signed certificate structure whose usage, validity and trust must be evaluated by the client. A TLS certificate gives a client evidence about a public key and the identities that key is permitted to represent. An issuer’s signature protects that certificate information within its certificate structure. The client still needs to decide whether the evidence is appropriate for the service it requested. Inspect the roles of the fields This original readable projection contains several relevant properties: { "keyId": "K1", "issuer": "Intermediate I", "dnsNames": ["media.example.net"], "notBefore": "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z", "notAfter": "2026-12-30T00:00:00Z", "isCa": false, "extendedUsage": ["serverAuth"] } The projection is not an encoded X.509 certificate or a claim that its signature was verified. Property Question it helps answer Public key Which key participates in endpoint authentication? Issuer/signature Which issuer attests to the certificate contents? Subject Alternative Name Which service identities are presented? Validity interval At what times is this certificate valid? Basic constraints and usage Is it appropriate for this role? The key label K1 stands for a public key in this exercise. The actual private material is a separate artifact. A copied certificate is insufficient to act as the endpoint The server proves control of the matching private key during the relevant TLS authentication process. Possessing only the public certificate does not provide that proof. Likewise, a private key paired with the wrong certificate public key cannot complete the intended certificate/key relationship. Certificate export formats can bundle the leaf, chain and private key together for installation. The bundle’s contents and permissions must be understood as distinct from a public certificate file. Emby’s direct secure-listener documentation describes a PKCS #12 installation artifact. That is a server-configuration role, not proof that every supplied bundle has the required chain or matching key. Validity is evaluated at the client’s clock The declared descriptor spans ninety days. At 12 October 2026 it is within that interval; before its notBefore or after notAfter it is not. A wrong device clock can consequently produce a different validation outcome even when the endpoint serves the same certificate bytes. Time validity is only one check. It does not establish the requested name, trusted issuer path, appropriate usage or relevant revocation/status result. A certificate has a lifecycle beyond file creation Issuance creates an artifact. Installation chooses which endpoint serves it. Renewal obtains a successor. Replacement/reload makes that successor visible on new handshakes. These events can occur at different times. A successfully created file can remain unused while an app still sees the previous certificate. See Also Certificate trust chains and path validation Certificate hostnames and the requested service identity Certificate renewal, ACME and deployed results HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity References RFC 5280: Certificate profiles and path validation RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 handshake and protected records RFC 9525: Service identity in TLS Emby: Network and secure-connection settings

articles/networking/security/certificate.title: Certificate trust chains and path validation | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/certificate.keywords: Certificate trust chains and path validation A certificate trust chain links endpoint evidence through valid issuer relationships to a client-trusted anchor, with path validation separate from service-name matching. A server normally presents its endpoint certificate and the relevant intermediate certificates. The client tries to build an acceptable path from that leaf evidence to an anchor it already trusts. A list of certificates sent by the server is therefore input to validation. It is not automatically a trusted chain. Begin with the client’s anchor Use an original path: Server leaf L -> Intermediate I -> Root R Client trust anchors: R Each arrow in this graph represents an issuer relationship whose signature and constraints must be checked. L is the endpoint certificate; I is permitted to issue the relevant child certificate; R is the declared anchor for this client. Trust starts with the client’s chosen anchor policy. A self-signed root received over the same untrusted connection cannot grant itself trusted status merely by validating its own signature. Otherwise, an arbitrary endpoint could create a root and declare its own evidence acceptable. The path needs the intermediate relationships Consider this original reduced input: { "leaf": {"id": "L", "issuer": "I"}, "availableIssuers": [{"id": "R", "issuer": "R"}], "trustedAnchors": ["R"], "pathComplete": false } The client trusts R, but it cannot directly bridge L’s issuer I to that root with the supplied data. Sending R again does not replace the missing I. The client needs an appropriate intermediate from its available sources. Some implementations can use cached or retrieved intermediates. Another TV/app may have no such source available. A browser succeeding with a previously cached I therefore does not prove the server supplied a complete usable chain to every client. Signature relationships are necessary but not sufficient A certificate claiming issuer I needs a valid issuer-signature relationship to the relevant key. Matching the issuer’s display text alone does not verify that relationship. Path processing also checks constraints and usage appropriate to the chain. Intermediate basic constraints, certificate-signing key usage, permitted path length and name constraints can affect whether a path is acceptable. A certificate chain can therefore have apparently connected issuer names while still failing validation. This page’s readable objects omit signatures and detailed constraint processing. They explain the graph and prerequisites, rather than implementing RFC 5280’s complete validation algorithm. An intermediate constraint applies to its descendants Consider a separate original constraint exercise. Intermediate I1 is a CA, can sign certificates and has a path-length limit of zero. It issues either the endpoint leaf L directly or another non-self-issued intermediate I2, which then issues L. Descendants beneath I1 Subordinate CA count Fits the declared zero limit? Endpoint leaf L 0 Yes Intermediate I2, then L 1 No The endpoint leaf is not another CA certificate in that count. A valid signature by I1 therefore does not automatically permit an extra issuer level. Name constraints add another kind of permitted scope. An issuer can restrict the relevant names in descendant certificates even while the cryptographic issuer relationships are connected. Both the path and permitted naming need the complete prescribed processing. These reduced cases explain what a constraint can exclude. Self-issued exceptions, policy processing and the complete validation state remain in RFC 5280 rather than being implemented by this table. Time and service identity add independent checks Relevant certificate validity intervals must be appropriate at the validation time. Revocation/status handling and algorithm policy also belong to the client’s validation context. The final server identity must match the requested service . A path to a trusted root with a certificate for another hostname does not establish the identity of media.example.net. An original decision table makes the independence explicit: Declared path result Declared requested-name result Suitable endpoint identity in this simplified model Valid Match Passes these two prerequisites Valid Mismatch Fails the service identity Incomplete Match Fails the path prerequisite The first row still leaves other required checks to their real validation process. The same issuer key can have alternative certificate paths A cross-signed issuer can have certificate representations leading toward different roots. Equal issuer labels alone do not identify which representation the client received or selected. Use this original key/issuer graph, with all omitted signature relationships assumed valid for the exercise: { "leaf": { "id": "L", "issuerKey": "KI" }, "issuerCandidates": [ { "id": "I-old", "publicKey": "KI", "issuer": "R-old" }, { "id": "I-new", "publicKey": "KI", "issuer": "R-new" } ], "trustedAnchors": [ "R-old" ], "selectedPath": [ "L", "I-old", "R-old" ] } The leaf’s signature can be checked with the same modeled issuer key KI in either branch. The available certificates then lead toward different root anchors. A client trusting only R-old has a candidate through I-old; receiving only I-new does not supply that old-root path unless the client can obtain the other applicable certificate separately. Another client may trust R-new and prefer the other branch. A server transmitting one chain and a client constructing its usable path therefore have related but distinct choices. The graph’s key labels do not verify actual signatures. They make the reason for alternative paths visible without claiming that a root name or fingerprint by itself establishes trust. Different clients can start from different anchor sets Operating systems, embedded devices and app-specific TLS libraries can carry different trust stores and update lifecycles. A path ending at R can be acceptable to a client trusting R and unavailable to another whose anchor set lacks it. An alternative served/cached chain can also lead to another supported anchor. The useful comparison is the actual served leaf/intermediates, the path built by the failing client and its relevant validation result. “The root is trusted on my laptop” identifies that laptop’s context. Deployment includes the chain actually served A renewed leaf file can be installed alongside an old or missing intermediate set. A public proxy and direct Emby listener can serve different certificate chains. See Also TLS certificates, public keys and endpoint evidence Certificate hostnames and the requested service identity Certificate renewal, ACME and deployed results References RFC 5280: Certificate profiles and path validation RFC 9325: TLS and DTLS deployment guidance RFC 9525: Service identity in TLS

articles/networking/security/certificate.title: Certificate hostnames and the requested service identity | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/certificate.keywords: Certificate hostnames and the requested service identity Certificate hostname validation compares the requested service identity with appropriately typed certificate names, keeping wildcard scope and direct IP identities distinct. A client requests https://media.example.net/ . The certificate must present an appropriate identity for media.example.net under the client’s service-validation rules. The address obtained from DNS can change without changing that requested DNS name. Match the requested name to typed certificate evidence Use this original reduced descriptor: { "dnsNames": ["*.example.net"], "ipAddresses": [] } The DNS identity is a wildcard for one leftmost label. Under the stated RFC 9525 rule: Requested host Match to this DNS wildcard? media.example.net Yes tv.example.net Yes example.net No room.media.example.net No The wildcard is the complete leftmost label and matches one label. It is not an arbitrary substring pattern. An IP-literal URL asks for an IP identity Now request https://192.168.50.20/ . The original certificate projection has no IP address identity, so its DNS wildcard does not satisfy that direct IP request. Even if media.example.net resolves to that IP, the two URL forms retain different reference identities. Reverse lookup of an address should not silently replace the name the client actually requested. Likewise, equivalent IPv6 spellings identify the same address bits when checking an IP identity. DNS wildcard matching is another operation. Current RFC 9525 uses appropriately typed presented identities and prohibits using free-form Common Name text as the service identifier. A familiar subject label does not replace the relevant SAN evidence. SNI helps select a certificate before the HTTP request A client can send the intended DNS name in the TLS handshake’s server-name indication. A shared TLS endpoint uses that context to choose a certificate/virtual service. The later HTTP Host information is application data inside the established connection. It cannot retroactively make an already rejected certificate handshake succeed. A proxy’s default certificate or missing name selection can therefore produce a mismatch even when its HTTP routing would have selected the correct application later. Keep identity through local and remote DNS paths With split DNS, media.example.net can resolve to an inside or outside endpoint. Both need certificate evidence appropriate to the unchanged hostname. An internal address answer does not turn the requested name into an IP-literal identity. A different TLS termination endpoint can, however, serve another certificate. See Also Certificate trust chains and path validation Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint Split DNS and location-dependent server endpoints TLS termination and independent connection legs References RFC 9525: Service identity in TLS RFC 5280: Certificate profiles and path validation RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and origins

articles/networking/security/index.html.title: Overview: Connection security | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/index.html.keywords: Overview: Connection security Connection security relates protected transport, endpoint identity and browser-enforced request boundaries. HTTPS can protect a connection while the client still needs to validate the intended endpoint. TLS termination locates that protection on a particular leg, and browser rules add another boundary around requests made by a page. This branch gives those checks their own context instead of treating one secure URL as proof of the whole path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HTTPS and TLS HTTPS uses TLS to protect an HTTP connection and verify the intended peer, with routing, handshake validation and application login forming distinct stages. Certificate validation and lifecycle Certificate validation and lifecycle connect public identity evidence, trust paths, requested names and deployed certificate state. TLS termination TLS termination identifies the endpoint that decrypts protected records and handles the resulting application data, with any forwarded connection carrying its own protection and peer identity. Browser security boundaries Browser security boundaries govern when a page can request or read resources from another connection or origin. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 handshake and protected records

articles/networking/security/Network-HTT.title: HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/Network-HTT.keywords: HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity HTTPS uses TLS to protect an HTTP connection and verify the intended peer, with routing, handshake validation and application login forming distinct stages. A client can reach the server’s IP address and still fail before it receives an Emby login response. TCP established a connection, but TLS could not establish the intended protected peer relationship. HTTPS carries HTTP through TLS. Its protection belongs to that particular connection between the client and the TLS endpoint. The protected channel has several properties TLS negotiates cryptographic parameters and establishes traffic keys. Its protected records provide confidentiality and integrity for the application bytes carried through the channel. In the usual certificate-authenticated server case, the endpoint also proves control of the relevant private key. The client checks the certificate’s path, intended use and requested service identity according to its validation rules. Those checks make encryption meaningful for the service the app intended to reach. Exchanging encrypted records with an arbitrary unverified endpoint is a different result. The port number participates in service selection. Calling a listener 443 or 8920 does not make a plaintext service perform TLS. Public certificate and connection keys have different roles The certificate supplies public-key and identity information signed by its issuer. It is not the private key itself. TLS 1.3 normally derives traffic secrets through its handshake, including ephemeral key agreement in the common certificate-based case. Bulk application records then use the negotiated symmetric protection. The certificate key helps authenticate the handshake. It is not a rule that every movie byte is encrypted directly with the certificate’s public key. A public certificate can therefore be inspected without revealing the server’s private key. Its validity still needs to be evaluated for the actual connection. Setup delay includes protocol round trips Use an original simplified timing exercise: { "roundTripMs": 40, "tcpSetupRoundTrips": 1, "tls13SetupRoundTrips": 1, "resumption": false, "earlyData": false } Under these stated assumptions, TCP setup takes forty ms and the TLS 1.3 setup phase another forty. The modeled client reaches its application-request point after eighty ms. DNS, loss/retransmission, certificate processing and media startup are excluded. TLS can also use other handshake paths, and HTTP/3 has its own QUIC integration. The arithmetic explains why a high-throughput connection can still have measurable setup time. It is not a benchmark or a universal delay added to every segment during an already established connection. Certificate identity follows the requested service A client using media.example.net checks the appropriate certificate name for that request. Resolving the name to a private or public IP does not automatically change its requested DNS identity. Connecting directly to an IP literal instead asks for the corresponding IP identity. Certificate hostnames develops the matching rules. An unexpired certificate can still have the wrong name, an unsuitable usage or no trusted path. The failure is more specific than “HTTPS is broken.” Emby authentication is a later operation TLS server authentication identifies the protected service endpoint. Emby’s user authentication identifies the account making the later application request. A valid HTTPS connection can deliver a rejected login or access-denied response correctly. Conversely, a blocked TLS handshake never reaches that application decision. Emby can terminate TLS itself through its configured secure listener, or a reverse proxy can provide the public TLS endpoint. TLS termination identifies which connection leg is protected in each arrangement. See Also TLS certificates, public keys and endpoint evidence Certificate hostnames and the requested service identity TLS termination and independent connection legs Mixed content and a browser’s secure-page boundary References RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 handshake and protected records RFC 9325: TLS and DTLS deployment guidance RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and origins Emby: Network and secure-connection settings

articles/networking/security/Network-TLS.title: TLS termination and independent connection legs | Emby Learn
articles/networking/security/Network-TLS.keywords: TLS termination and independent connection legs TLS termination identifies the endpoint that decrypts protected records and handles the resulting application data, with any forwarded connection carrying its own protection and peer identity. In a proxied connection, the certificate seen by the viewer can belong to the proxy’s TLS endpoint. Emby can receive a separate request from that proxy. TLS termination is the point where a protected TLS connection ends and its records are decrypted for the endpoint’s application processing. Compare the connection arrangements Arrangement Public connection Origin-side relationship Direct Emby TLS Client validates Emby’s TLS endpoint No application reverse-proxy leg in this model Proxy termination Client validates proxy endpoint Proxy makes a separately configured request to Emby TLS pass-through Intermediary forwards the protected connection The final TLS endpoint still authenticates/decrypts it A pass-through intermediary can route connections without behaving like an HTTP reverse proxy that rewrites the decrypted request. A terminating proxy, in contrast, can interpret HTTP and make a new upstream request. It becomes an application and trust boundary. Public HTTPS does not describe the origin leg Use this original two-leg projection: { "clientToProxy": {"tls": true, "requestedName": "media.example.net"}, "proxyToOrigin": {"tls": false, "endpoint": "192.168.50.20:8096"} } The public leg is protected under the stated model. The inside leg carries another connection whose TLS flag is false. Choosing re-encryption for the upstream would create another TLS session. The proxy must then validate the intended origin’s evidence under its own policy; accepting any upstream certificate would not establish that peer’s identity. Each certificate follows its own requested name The viewer can validate media.example.net while the proxy requests another internal origin name. Those are different reference identities. Sharing one displayed server name or copying a certificate file does not decide the appropriate name on every leg. SNI, certificate selection and the configured upstream host each need their intended context. Certificate names develops that validation. Forwarded metadata explains another application context A terminating proxy can describe the original scheme, host or client through headers. The origin’s socket peer still belongs to the upstream connection. Emby’s reverse-proxy secure-connection mode relates to that application arrangement. It does not cryptographically extend the public TLS session through the origin’s separate leg. See Also Reverse proxies and the two-sided server path Forwarded client addresses and trusted proxy context HTTPS and TLS: transport protection and peer identity References RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 handshake and protected records NGINX: Separate proxy connection and TLS behavior Emby: Network and secure-connection settings RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and origins

articles/networking/transport/index.html.title: Overview: Transport protocols and ports | Emby Learn
articles/networking/transport/index.html.keywords: Overview: Transport protocols and ports Transport protocols and ports identify how applications exchange data and which endpoint receives it. An IP address reaches a network destination; a port identifies a transport endpoint within that context. TCP and UDP provide different delivery behavior. This group establishes those distinctions before a connection error or a media-rate problem is assigned to the application. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Network ports A network port selects a transport endpoint within an addressed host, with listener binding and connection context separating services that share an IP address. TCP TCP supplies an ordered reliable byte stream, recovering missing transport data while leaving message structure, encryption and successful media decoding to higher layers. UDP UDP carries bounded datagrams without supplying TCP-style ordering or retransmission, allowing each application protocol to define its own response to loss and timing. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol RFC 2018: TCP selective acknowledgments RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol

articles/networking/transport/Network-Po.title: Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints | Emby Learn
articles/networking/transport/Network-Po.keywords: Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints A network port selects a transport endpoint within an addressed host, with listener binding and connection context separating services that share an IP address. An IP address gets traffic to the addressed network context. A port helps select the service within it. For example, a server can expose its web service and another application through the same interface address while using different destination ports. One listener can accept many client connections Use this original reduced TCP inventory: { "listener": {"address": "192.168.50.20", "port": 8096}, "clients": [ {"address": "192.168.50.30", "port": 51000}, {"address": "192.168.50.31", "port": 51000} ] } Both clients target the same server port. Their equal client-side port values are distinguished by their different addresses. For this exercise, the flow keys include transport, source address/port and destination address/port. The server’s listener can accept both separate flows rather than allocating a new destination service number for every viewer. The transport protocol is part of the selection TCP port 8096 and UDP port 8096 belong to different transport namespaces. Equal numbers do not make them the same service or turn UDP data into a TCP connection. Endpoint property What it selects Address family and destination address The addressed interface/network context TCP or UDP The transport protocol Destination port The relevant listener/service Application request The operation or resource within that service Emby’s familiar HTTP and optional HTTPS listener choices are configurable. Its local discovery exchange uses a separate UDP service. A service using a number that is often associated with HTTPS still needs to implement TLS; the number alone does not encrypt its traffic.
