Client-side ports have their own lifetime The client operating system often chooses a temporary source port. It helps identify that connection locally and in any translation state along the route. The IANA registry separates system, user and dynamic/private port-number ranges. An operating system’s actual automatic allocation range and policy need not equal one simplistic fixed range on every platform. A retained connection and another new connection can use different source numbers while targeting the same Emby endpoint. A public number can differ from the local listener An original forwarding example might map TCP outside port 45000 to the server’s configured local HTTPS port 8920. The remote URL must select 45000, while the internal service still listens on 8920. Merely changing the port Emby reports publicly does not install that router mapping. Likewise, changing a local listener does not automatically update every app entry, proxy upstream or gateway rule. See Also TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery UDP datagrams and application delivery policy Port forwarding and the complete inbound path Hostnames, URLs and the complete server endpoint References IANA: Service names and transport-protocol port numbers RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol Emby: Network settings and reported addresses

articles/networking/transport/Network-TC.title: TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery | Emby Learn
articles/networking/transport/Network-TC.keywords: TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery TCP supplies an ordered reliable byte stream, recovering missing transport data while leaving message structure, encryption and successful media decoding to higher layers. TCP carries an ordered stream of bytes. If data is lost or arrives out of order, the transport can recover the missing portion and present the bytes in order to the application. That reliable stream is useful for HTTP requests and media delivery. Reliability does not mean every byte arrives before the viewer’s playback deadline. A missing middle holds up a later tail Use this original simplified receive trace: [ {"arrivalMs": 0, "offset": 0, "data": "ABCD"}, {"arrivalMs": 10, "offset": 8, "data": "IJKL"}, {"arrivalMs": 35, "offset": 4, "data": "EFGH"} ] Offsets are relative byte positions in a teaching stream. They are not wire sequence numbers from a TCP capture. After the first arrival, the application can receive ABCD. After the second, IJKL is present but the intervening EFGH is missing. Only after the third arrival is the complete ordered prefix ABCDEFGHIJKL available. The later tail waited twenty-five milliseconds in this model. A media buffer can absorb some such delay; an empty playback reserve cannot present missing input merely because later bytes have arrived. Acknowledging the tail does not remove the gap For the original trace, the cumulative contiguous byte boundary is four after both the first and second arrivals. It becomes twelve after the missing middle arrives. Selective acknowledgment can describe received ranges beyond that contiguous boundary when the option is supported. An original range [8,12) reports the retained IJKL tail while the cumulative boundary remains four. That information can help the sender recover the missing range without treating every later byte as absent. It does not make the application receive IJKL ahead of the missing middle in the ordered stream. A duplicate arrival of ABCD also does not deliver a second ABCD to the byte-stream consumer. Sequence context recognizes those bytes as already received; duplication in a network trace and duplication in application media are different observations. The example omits wire sequence origins, options, timers and the chosen loss-recovery algorithm. Its purpose is to expose which bytes are received, which missing interval needs recovery and which contiguous prefix is usable. TCP does not preserve application message boundaries An application can write a request in several operations, and the receiver can read it in different-sized operations. Transport segment boundaries and application read boundaries are not a universal record format. HTTP, a framed binary protocol or another application layer defines where its messages begin and end. Likewise, a video frame is not normally “one TCP packet.” One encoded picture can span transport data, while one received block can contain several media units. Two different windows constrain sending The receiver advertises how much additional data its receive capacity can accommodate. Congestion control separately limits the sender’s permitted in-flight work according to the path’s behavior. For an original simplified budget, let the receive allowance be 64 KiB and the congestion allowance 16 KiB. The smaller allowance constrains the stated in-flight data budget to 16 KiB before other details. Increasing the receive buffer alone does not raise that sixteen-KiB congestion allowance. Conversely, a large path allowance cannot make an application consume a full receive buffer faster. This reduced comparison illustrates separate constraints; it is not a throughput benchmark or a complete TCP window calculation. In-flight capacity and round-trip time constrain progress Continue with an original fixed-window exercise: { "receiveWindowBytes": 65536, "congestionWindowBytes": 16384, "alreadyInFlightBytes": 4096, "roundTripSeconds": 0.05 } KiB means 1024 bytes. With the stated smaller 16-KiB limit, four KiB already in flight leaves at most twelve KiB of additional allowance in this simplified comparison. If a steady sender can keep only 16 KiB unacknowledged over a fifty-millisecond round trip, the window/round-trip calculation gives 327,680 bytes per second, or 2.62144 Mbit/s. This excludes other overhead and assumes the stated window remains fixed. That can be far below a link’s advertised capacity. Increasing only the receiver’s 64-KiB window does not change the smaller congestion limit in this exercise. Real congestion control adjusts its permitted work, acknowledgments can change over time, and application pauses can leave capacity unused. The arithmetic is a conditional ceiling rather than a prediction for a particular server. It explains why link speed and actual transport progress need different observations. An acknowledgment is not a playback result TCP acknowledgments describe the transport’s received byte progress. They do not establish that Emby accepted a request, the client parsed the media, or the screen displayed a frame. A successfully delivered error response is also successful byte delivery. Application status needs its own interpretation. TCP itself does not provide the HTTPS certificate/peer authentication used by TLS. Reliable delivery, connection identity and encrypted application transport are different properties. Playback buffering follows the retained media after transport delivery. QUIC, covered by its own specification, can provide different stream-loss coordination over UDP rather than inheriting TCP’s single ordered byte stream. See Also UDP datagrams and application delivery policy Network ports, listeners and connection endpoints Buffering, ready media and playback reserve HTTP range requests for media resources References RFC 2018: TCP selective acknowledgments RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol RFC 9110: HTTP semantics RFC 9000: QUIC transport over UDP

articles/networking/transport/Network-UD.title: UDP datagrams and application delivery policy | Emby Learn
articles/networking/transport/Network-UD.keywords: UDP datagrams and application delivery policy UDP carries bounded datagrams without supplying TCP-style ordering or retransmission, allowing each application protocol to define its own response to loss and timing. UDP gives an application datagrams: bounded messages addressed to a destination IP and UDP port. It does not turn those messages into one automatically recovered ordered byte stream. The protocol above UDP decides what a missing, repeated or late datagram means. Message boundaries survive delivery, when delivery succeeds Use this original application-message exercise: { "sentIds": [1, 2, 3], "receivedIds": [3, 1, 1] } Message two is missing. Message one appears twice, and three arrived first. The application can use its declared IDs to recognize those conditions. UDP itself does not resend message two or reconstruct the sent order. The useful policy depends on the content. A discovery query might be repeated; an old timing update might be discarded in favor of a newer one; a reliable transfer protocol can request missing data. A datagram still has a size budget UDP’s ordinary header occupies eight bytes. In a declared 1500-byte IPv4 packet with a minimum twenty-byte IP header, 1472 bytes remain for the application payload. With the forty-byte IPv6 base header and no extensions, the corresponding value is 1452 bytes. Those are header arithmetic examples, not a promise that every internet route accepts a 1500-byte packet. Tunnels and path limits can reduce the usable size. Dividing a large application message into several datagrams also requires a policy for identifying and assembling the pieces. Losing one piece may invalidate the complete message. A retry needs a request meaning Repeating a discovery request can elicit another description of the same service. Repeating an operation that changes state can require duplicate detection or another idempotent design. A timeout therefore belongs to the application’s request lifetime. It can decide when to retry or report failure, but cannot prove why no response arrived. The request can be filtered, the response can be filtered, the service can be absent, or the route can simply have lost a datagram. “Uses UDP” does not mean “unreliable application” QUIC uses UDP as its underlying transport while defining its own reliable streams, loss recovery and security. A protocol’s end-to-end behavior must therefore be read at the appropriate layer. UDP describes the datagram service, not all guarantees built above it. Emby’s local server discovery , mDNS and SSDP use different messages and destinations despite sharing UDP. A rule or observation for one discovery protocol is not automatically evidence about the others. See Also TCP: an ordered byte stream for media delivery Multicast DNS and local-link naming SSDP discovery, advertisements and service locations Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints References RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol RFC 791: Internet Protocol RFC 8200: IPv6 specification RFC 9000: QUIC transport over UDP

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-AVI.title: AVIF images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-AVI.keywords: AVIF images AVIF defines AV1-coded images within an image-file container, with specified colour, alpha and derived-image arrangements beyond the capabilities of a video decoder alone. AVIF uses AV1 image coding within an image-file format. Its reader must recover the intended picture and interpret the file's presentation information. The reference here is AOM AVIF 1.2.0 , a Final Deliverable dated 16 October 2025 . That version context matters when describing newer derived-image features. Coding and file presentation describe different boundaries A conventional AV1 image item provides coded picture samples. The file describes how those items and their properties belong to the image presentation, including applicable colour and auxiliary information. A successful AV1 video playback test therefore does not fully test an app's AVIF image path. The video route can use different parsing, decoder configuration, memory and output preparation. For Emby artwork/photos, identify what the server image processor and receiving app actually exchange. That delivered representation determines the remaining rendering requirements even when the original source used AVIF. Precision depends on the representation Ordinary AV1 image items use their applicable 8-, 10- or 12-bit coding. AVIF 1.2.0 also defines sample-transform derived images that can combine item information to extend sample precision beyond that ordinary range. Consequently, “all AVIF images are limited to twelve bits” is not an accurate description of the full referenced format. A reader supporting ordinary coded items does not necessarily implement every derived-image feature. Observation What it establishes File recognized as AVIF Container identification Main coded item decodes That item/configuration can be recovered Derived/auxiliary information interpreted Additional presentation requirements can be fulfilled Result presented correctly Colour, alpha and geometry agree with the selected output path These observations are useful separately when comparing an original photo and a browsing derivative. Colour and transparency need their intended output Higher precision allows finer numerical levels. HDR also requires appropriate colour/luminance interpretation and display handling; bit depth alone does not make it HDR. An alpha-bearing presentation can additionally require a compatible auxiliary path. Converting it into an opaque JPEG commits the output to a background, rather than retaining independently compositable transparency. See Also HEIF and HEIC images HDR still images Image transparency AV1 Video References AOM AVIF 1.2.0, Final Deliverable of 16 October 2025 ISO/IEC 23008-12:2025: High Efficiency Image File Format

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-Cam.title: Camera raw images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-Cam.keywords: Camera raw images A camera raw resource retains sensor-derived samples and interpretation metadata that a development process turns into a chosen viewable photograph. A camera raw file retains sensor-derived image information for later interpretation. A rendered JPEG from the same capture is one chosen photographic result. The raw resource leaves more of that rendering decision to the development process. It can also contain a ready-made preview. Showing that preview and developing the sensor data are different operations, even when a viewer labels both as opening the same file. Sensor samples need an interpretation A common colour-filter-array sensor measures one filtered colour component at each position. An illustrative Bayer tile is: Column 0 Column 1 Row 0 Red Green Row 1 Green Blue The development process estimates a full colour representation from the sampled arrangement. Those neighboring measurements are not four complete RGB pixels already waiting to be copied into a display image. This is one common arrangement, not a definition of every camera. DNG also describes linear raw representations, including data that already has been demosaiced. Black and white levels establish a working range Take an invented fourteen-bit sample with black level 512 , white level 15,872 and stored value 8192 . A simple normalization gives: (8192 − 512) / (15872 − 512) = 7680 / 15360 = 0.5. The useful range is not automatically zero through the largest fourteen-bit integer. The interpretation data describes how that camera representation relates to the working image. White balance can apply different component gains. A normalized component of 0.5 multiplied by gain 2 becomes 1 in this model. Further tone/colour decisions determine the rendered output. Clipping values early can discard distinctions that a later development would have used. The arithmetic is a teaching example, not a complete camera calibration or a DNG decoder. Real development can additionally apply sensor corrections, active-area geometry and specified operations. Development chooses an appearance Exposure adjustments, white balance, demosaicing, noise treatment, colour conversion and tone rendering affect the output photograph. Two applications can use the same capture while choosing different processing or reading different edit instructions. An embedded preview often represents a camera or earlier application's choices. A raw developer may instead use another recipe. A difference between them need not mean that one decoded a corrupted file. The raw resource's Exif and other records provide capture/interpretation information. An XMP sidecar can hold applicable editing or descriptive data without replacing the sensor payload. Raw, DNG and compression are separate labels Camera-specific raw formats can have different structures. DNG supplies a documented format built on TIFF-related organization, with additional required interpretation fields. Raw does not mean universally uncompressed. A particular format/setting can use reversible or lossy coding, and a DNG resource can contain different supported raw representations. The representation and coding choice determine what is retained. Nor does raw automatically describe a finished HDR image. Sensor range must still be developed and encoded into a presentation with the intended brightness and colour interpretation. Sensor storage and developed RGB have different sizes For an invented 24-million-position mosaic with one fourteen-bit sample per position, ideal bit-packed storage is 24,000,000 × 14 / 8 = 42,000,000 bytes . A buffer using sixteen-bit storage for each sample is 48,000,000 bytes . After development into three-component, sixteen-bit RGB, the same position count has an ideal payload of 144,000,000 bytes . This difference follows from component/storage representation; it is not a measurement of a camera file’s encoded size. Compression, previews, metadata and working buffers add other relationships. A compact raw file can therefore require much more memory during development without representing a different capture resolution. Keep the master and the viewing derivative distinct A rendered derivative can be useful for a photo library that needs a directly presentable image. Generating it selects dimensions, orientation, colour space and appearance; it does not replace the raw resource's editing possibilities. For an Emby source, identify whether the observed image is an embedded preview, a prepared export or an output from a raw-capable processing route. That distinction explains what was actually presented without assuming that every server/app combination develops every camera raw variant. See Also TIFF images HDR still images ICC color profiles Exif photo metadata XMP metadata References Adobe DNG 1.7.1.0 specification Adobe: Understanding digital raw capture

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-GIF.title: GIF images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-GIF.keywords: GIF images GIF uses indexed-colour image data and control records that can provide binary transparency and timed changes to a shared presentation canvas. GIF stores image positions as indices into a colour table. A table can contain up to 256 entries . A file can use local colour tables for different images, so that limit should not be described as a universal maximum for all colours ever shown by an entire animation. The index names a palette entry An invented palette might be: Index Defined colour Use 0 Background colour Filled positions 1 Dark lettering Caption shape 2 Bright marker Moving indicator Decoding index 1 recovers the entry's colour; the index itself is not an RGB component value. Reducing a photographic source to an indexed palette can introduce colour grouping or dithering before the GIF's reversible coding. An exact decoding of those indices cannot recover the earlier photographic samples. Transparency skips destination positions A transparent-index declaration identifies positions that leave the existing destination unchanged. It supplies binary treatment rather than a full set of fractional alpha values around an edge. A soft translucent logo converted into that model may need a different edge representation or a chosen background. The result can retain recognizable lettering while changing how it integrates with an Emby page. An animation develops a canvas over time A later image can cover only a rectangle within the logical canvas. The control information includes a delay and disposal behavior, determining whether earlier drawn content remains or is replaced/restored after presentation. For an invented sequence with delays 2, 3 and 5 hundredths of a second , the nominal loop duration is 0.10 seconds . A consumer's scheduling and delay policy can affect the observed playback. The animated-image article shows why a small frame rectangle is not necessarily a complete standalone picture. A gallery thumbnail needs a reconstructed canvas at a selected instant, rather than blindly saving the latest rectangle. See Also Animated images Image transparency PNG images WebP images References GIF89a specification

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-HEI.title: HEIF and HEIC images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-HEI.keywords: HEIF and HEIC images HEIF is an image-container framework with item relationships and presentation properties; HEIC commonly identifies HEVC-based usage rather than a separate universal image codec. HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format , describes image-file organization. It is a container framework rather than one compression algorithm. HEIC commonly refers to HEVC-based HEIF usage. ISO/IEC 23008-12:2025 is the image-file-format edition linked here. A concrete file's brands, coding and item properties determine what a reader needs. The file can describe relationships between images An item-oriented resource can designate a principal image and relate other items to it, such as a thumbnail or an auxiliary image. Properties and references help the reader interpret which items form the intended presentation. A thumbnail's small dimensions do not make it the authoritative master. An auxiliary image may have another purpose, such as coverage or additional interpretation; it should not automatically appear as a second ordinary photograph. The container also supports defined derived-image arrangements. Recovering the principal presentation can therefore involve relationships and transformations as well as one coded payload. Codec and presentation requirements meet at the reader Requirement What it answers Container parsing Which image and associated items belong to the presentation? Picture decoding How are the coded samples recovered? Property interpretation Which dimensions, transforms and colour description apply? Output preparation What representation reaches the app/display? A device's HEVC video engine answers only part of picture decoding. It does not establish that an app's photo reader understands all item relationships, metadata or rendering properties. AVIF uses an AV1-based image format within related file-format architecture. Changing a filename from HEIC to AVIF does not replace its coded image data. In an Emby library, compare the source image with the particular generated or delivered resource. That comparison identifies whether the chosen path retained the intended main picture, rather than inferring full-container preservation from one successful preview. An export chooses what to retain A conversion to a single ordinary JPEG can create a useful shareable photo while retaining less of a multi-item source. It must decide which presentation to render, how to handle orientation, whether to preserve metadata and how to represent colour/HDR. See Also AVIF images Image orientation HDR still images MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format References ISO/IEC 23008-12:2025: High Efficiency Image File Format AOM AVIF 1.2.0, Final Deliverable of 16 October 2025

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-JPE.title: JPEG images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-JPE.keywords: JPEG images Common JPEG photo files use block-transform lossy coding, while the wider JPEG 1 standard includes additional coding modes and file-interchange conventions. JPEG is commonly used for photographic still images, including library artwork. The usual JPEG photo route uses lossy transform coding. JPEG 1's broader standard also defines other modes, so “every JPEG is inherently lossy” is too broad. A photo's gradual tones often tolerate some reduced precision. Thin lettering and sharp graphic edges can make the same coding changes much easier to see. Blocks become frequency coefficients The common DCT-based route divides component samples into 8 × 8 blocks and expresses each block through coefficients. Those coefficients describe a constant contribution and variations at different spatial frequencies. Quantization reduces their precision before further coding. Coefficients that become zero can be represented efficiently; their discarded detail cannot be reconstructed from the encoded result. For a small invented coefficient example: Original coefficient Quantization step Quantized integer Reconstructed coefficient 112 8 14 112 −17 10 −2 −20 3 5 1 5 1 5 0 0 The table illustrates round/divide/multiply arithmetic rather than a full JPEG block. Reconstruction retains some values exactly and changes others. Strong reduction can make neighboring blocks disagree visibly or create ringing around edges. These effects are different from blur already present in the photographed scene. Chroma and alpha are separate choices A common photographic representation reduces chroma sampling relative to luma. Chroma subsampling explains that representation and why fine coloured text can be sensitive to it. The ordinary JPEG photo path does not supply a PNG-style alpha channel. A transparent logo converted to that path must use some background or another presentation arrangement. For a rectangular poster this can be appropriate; for a floating logo it changes the design. Exif and an ICC profile can accompany JPEG picture data. They describe capture/orientation and colour interpretation respectively. Removing those records can change downstream presentation without changing the compressed image coefficients. Sequential and progressive describe scan organization A sequential JPEG supplies its coded components in the relevant sequential scan arrangement. A progressive JPEG supplies coefficient information in stages, allowing an increasingly complete reconstruction. Progressive organization does not inherently change the final dimensions or make the image lossless. Its browsing benefit depends on a consumer presenting intermediate scans and on how data reaches that consumer. An Emby route may decode and generate a new artwork image before the app receives it. In that case, the original source's scan arrangement and metadata are distinct from the delivered derivative's properties. A high quality setting is not a reversible-edit guarantee Encoder quality labels influence choices such as quantization, and sometimes subsampling through additional options. Their interpretation belongs to the encoder. Even a high setting does not establish exact recovery of the original editing buffer. After another resize or edit, decoding and re-encoding commonly quantizes the new result again. Keeping the master separates archive quality from the particular small JPEG useful for a browsing tile. See Also Image compression PNG images Exif photo metadata ICC color profiles References JPEG committee: JPEG 1 coding modes and specifications ITU-T T.81: JPEG coding requirements and guidelines CIPA: Exif 3.1 and current imaging standards ICC.1:2022: Profile architecture, format and data structure

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-PNG.title: PNG images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-PNG.keywords: PNG images PNG stores losslessly coded raster samples with optional transparency, colour information, metadata and, in the current specification, frame-based animation. A transparent logo or a diagram with sharp edges often benefits from preserving its prepared samples exactly. PNG supplies lossless image coding rather than the usual JPEG photo quantization. Prediction can be reversible For an invented eight-bit grayscale row containing 10, 13, 15, 18 , store the first byte and then differences from the previous byte: Original: 10 13 15 18 Differences: 10 3 2 3 Recovered: 10 13 15 18 Adding each difference back to the already recovered byte reconstructs the row. A real PNG filter operates on bytes with specified arithmetic and predictors; compression then codes that reversible representation. This explains why prediction is different from rounding several values to one level. The example intentionally uses a one-byte-per-pixel row; it is not a complete PNG file. Chunks describe different parts of the resource Information Example chunk role Grid and sample representation IHDR Coded image data IDAT Palette, where applicable PLTE Additional transparency, where applicable tRNS ICC colour profile iCCP Exif record eXIf Animation control and frames acTL, fcTL, fdAT Some transparency is carried directly in alpha-bearing samples rather than tRNS. Choosing an indexed representation can also require palette preparation before encoding. The current Third Edition W3C Recommendation, dated 24 June 2025 , includes animated PNG and HDR colour signaling. An old summary that treats PNG as universally static and SDR misses those defined uses. A lossless derivative can still differ from its master If a source is cropped, resized, palette-reduced or converted to another colour space, PNG can retain the resulting samples exactly. It cannot reverse those earlier operations. For an Emby artwork comparison, examine the original and the delivered derivative. A correctly decoded logo can have lost alpha during a conversion, and a high-precision master can have been reduced before the final lossless save. See Also Image compression Image transparency Animated images HDR still images References W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-TIF.title: TIFF images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-TIF.keywords: TIFF images TIFF organizes image data through tagged directories, allowing different sample layouts, compression choices and multiple image representations within one file. TIFF is a tagged image-file structure. An image directory describes how its associated samples are stored and interpreted. The format is useful for varied imaging workflows because those descriptions need not all select one fixed pixel layout or compression method. A directory tells the reader how to find samples The file header establishes byte order and leads to image-directory information. Tags describe dimensions, sample representation and the locations of image data, which can be organized in strips or tiles. Tag responsibility Example information Shape Width and image length Components Bits/sample and samples/pixel Interpretation Photometric meaning, orientation Storage Compression and strip/tile offsets Associated resources Applicable colour profile or additional metadata The reader uses those descriptions together. Finding a TIFF header does not make every variant a directly readable RGB photo. Compression is a choice within the file A TIFF representation can use uncompressed samples or an applicable compression scheme. Losslessness depends on that scheme and on changes made before encoding. High precision and an ICC profile serve different purposes too: one provides numerical sample capacity, while the other helps interpret colour. A large sixteen-bit file is not automatically HDR or correctly colour managed. For an Emby image route, the relevant question is whether its reader can decode the selected sample/compression arrangement and present the intended image. A generic “TIFF supported” statement is less specific than that combination. Several images need a selection rule Directories can describe multiple pages or representations. One may be a preview, another the principal image, or several may be document pages. That structure is not automatically a timed animation. A thumbnail generator needs to choose the intended image/page, apply its orientation and colour interpretation, then derive the browsing view. DNG builds on TIFF-related structures while adding raw-camera requirements. Its raw processing involves further interpretation rather than simply treating every directory as a finished photograph. See Also Raster images Image orientation ICC color profiles Camera raw images References Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification Adobe DNG 1.7.1.0 specification

articles/photos-images/formats/Image-Web.title: WebP images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/Image-Web.keywords: WebP images WebP packages lossy or lossless image coding in a RIFF container that can also describe alpha, colour/metadata and animation. WebP combines image coding with a RIFF-based file structure. Its lossy and lossless routes represent different choices; an extension alone does not identify which was used. Read the container's roles Part Meaning RIFF / WEBP identification Recognizable file packaging VP8 image data Lossy coded picture VP8L image data Lossless coded picture Extended structure Additional image features Alpha, ICC, Exif or XMP data Coverage and associated interpretation/metadata Animation records Canvas, timed frames and applicable composition behavior The extended structure can bring these features together. The reader needs the features present in the particular resource, rather than merely recognizing a VP8-based picture. Lossless image coding also needs a defined input representation. It does not restore a previous full-resolution or higher-precision master that was changed before the encoder received it. For Emby photos and artwork, compare that delivered resource with what the app can display. A video decoder accepting VP8 does not by itself prove that the same app implements WebP's still-image container, alpha or animation path. Compare the same prepared image Consider a photograph and a transparent title logo. The photo's useful result may tolerate lossy coding. The logo may instead need precise lettering and smooth alpha edges. A meaningful comparison retains the same output dimensions and required colour/alpha behavior, then assesses appearance and encoded size. A codec's quality number and another encoder's identically named number do not establish equivalent output. Conversion can also flatten alpha or discard metadata independently of the coding mode. A visually acceptable still thumbnail does not imply preservation of an animated WebP source's whole presentation. A browsing derivative is a separate resource A server-side image route can decode a source, resize it and encode another format for the app. The source's WebP features then matter at the decoding boundary; the output format's features matter at the receiving boundary. See Also Image compression Image transparency Animated images JPEG images References Google: WebP container specification Google: WebP lossless bitstream specification

articles/photos-images/formats/index.htm.title: Overview: Image formats | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/formats/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Image formats Image formats define how pictures, supporting metadata and sometimes multiple images are stored and interpreted. JPEG, PNG and the other formats below make different choices about compression, transparency, animation and metadata. Some names identify a container or a camera-oriented representation rather than one finished display image. The individual pages describe those arrangements so a filename can be connected to the decoder and presentation it needs. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> JPEG Common JPEG photo files use block-transform lossy coding, while the wider JPEG 1 standard includes additional coding modes and file-interchange conventions. PNG PNG stores losslessly coded raster samples with optional transparency, colour information, metadata and, in the current specification, frame-based animation. WebP WebP packages lossy or lossless image coding in a RIFF container that can also describe alpha, colour/metadata and animation. GIF GIF uses indexed-colour image data and control records that can provide binary transparency and timed changes to a shared presentation canvas. TIFF TIFF organizes image data through tagged directories, allowing different sample layouts, compression choices and multiple image representations within one file. HEIF HEIF is an image-container framework with item relationships and presentation properties; HEIC commonly identifies HEVC-based usage rather than a separate universal image codec. AVIF AVIF defines AV1-coded images within an image-file container, with specified colour, alpha and derived-image arrangements beyond the capabilities of a video decoder alone. Camera raw images A camera raw resource retains sensor-derived samples and interpretation metadata that a development process turns into a chosen viewable photograph. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-T T.81: JPEG coding requirements and guidelines W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 Google: WebP container specification GIF89a specification ISO/IEC 23008-12:2025: High Efficiency Image File Format AOM AVIF 1.2.0, Final Deliverable of 16 October 2025

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.title: Image compression | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.keywords: Image compression Image compression reduces encoded storage through reversible coding or lossy representation changes, while decoded dimensions and downstream processing remain separate. Compression changes the encoded representation of an image to use fewer storage bytes. Lossless coding allows exact reconstruction of its input samples. Lossy coding replaces some information with a representation judged useful at a smaller size. Exact reconstruction has a specific starting point Suppose an editor resizes a photograph from 6000 × 4000 to 1200 × 800, then saves the smaller samples losslessly. Decoding can exactly recover the 1200 × 800 result. It cannot recover the discarded original grid. Palette conversion and colour/precision reduction can introduce similar earlier changes. A lossless final codec does not undo them. Boundary What can change Preprocessing Dimensions, crop, colour representation or precision Lossy coding Information represented by the encoded samples/coefficients Lossless coding Byte arrangement while retaining its specified input Decode and display Reconstructed samples, then presentation processing Quantization groups different values together Take an invented scalar quantizer that rounds each value to a multiple of 16: Input Stored index: round(input / 16) Reconstructed value 101 6 96 107 7 112 109 7 112 113 7 112 Three different inputs lead to 112. The decoder cannot determine which was originally supplied. This model explains irreversible grouping; it is not a complete JPEG, WebP or AVIF encoder. Real codecs can apply quantization to transformed coefficients and use other prediction/coding steps. Image content affects size A flat-colour diagram contains different redundancy from textured foliage or sensor noise. Consequently, an equal dimension and codec setting do not imply an equal file size. A comparison should keep the source, output dimensions, colour/alpha requirements and encoder context explicit. A “quality 80” label is an implementation setting, not a universal perceptual scale shared by codecs and applications. Decoded memory remains related to the output sample grid and buffer representation. A small 24-megapixel file can still require a large pixel buffer when an Emby image-processing route opens it. Repeatedly editing and re-encoding lossy derivatives can introduce additional loss. Retaining a suitable master and generating the needed browsing derivative from it avoids making a previous small preview the input for every later version. See Also JPEG images PNG images WebP images AVIF images Raster images References JPEG committee: JPEG 1 coding modes and specifications W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 Google: WebP lossless bitstream specification

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.title: Image orientation | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.keywords: Image orientation Orientation metadata describes a transform from stored image rows and columns to the intended visual direction, including reflections as well as rotations. A camera can store its photo as a landscape-shaped pixel grid while recording that the intended viewing direction is portrait. A viewer honoring that orientation shows it upright; a viewer using only the stored rows and columns can show it sideways. Eight transforms describe more than rotation The familiar TIFF/Exif orientation values identify the following transforms from stored samples to a normalized display: Value Transform 1 Identity 2 Reflect horizontally 3 Rotate 180° 4 Reflect vertically 5 Transpose across the main diagonal 6 Rotate 90° clockwise 7 Reflect across the other diagonal 8 Rotate 90° counterclockwise Reflections account for the extra cases beyond the four right-angle rotations. Values 5–8 exchange the visual width and height. Rotate the sample grid once For this stored grid: A B C D E F a 90° clockwise display becomes: D A E B F C A stored 6000 × 4000 image with orientation 6 therefore has an upright visual shape of 4000 × 6000. Its sample count remains 24 million. A thumbnail generator should base its fitting/cropping decision on that intended shape. Treating it as landscape before applying orientation can choose the wrong crop or fit. A normalized derivative has a new orientation state A process can physically rotate/reflect the samples into their intended direction and write the result with orientation 1. Keeping the old orientation 6 after performing that rotation asks the next viewer to rotate it again. Another process can preserve the stored grid and its original tag. Both strategies can be valid if every subsequent stage knows which state it receives. The same requirement applies to an embedded preview: it needs a coherent relationship between its own pixels and any applicable orientation information. An upright preview alone does not prove that the larger source has been normalized. For Emby photo/artwork comparisons, inspect the source, generated derivative and displayed output separately. Exif explains where orientation belongs alongside capture information. See Also Exif photo metadata Image thumbnail generation Image resizing Raster images References Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification CIPA: Exif 3.1 and current imaging standards Adobe DNG 1.7.1.0 specification

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.title: Raster images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.keywords: Raster images A raster image describes a rectangular grid of samples whose dimensions, component representation and colour interpretation determine the decoded picture. A raster image represents a picture on a grid. Its width and height count positions in that grid; each position has samples describing colour, brightness or other components. Read a grid before enlarging it In this invented three-column, two-row picture, each letter stands for a distinct pixel: Column 0 Column 1 Column 2 Row 0 A B C Row 1 D E F An enlargement can draw every source pixel as a large square. Those squares reveal the sampling grid; the original file does not contain a larger detailed letter or shape inside each position. A vector description instead specifies shapes or paths that can be rasterized at a chosen output size. Rendering a vector logo into a PNG produces a raster derivative with a particular grid. Pixel, component and byte are different units An RGB pixel has red, green and blue components. With eight bits per component, each has 256 possible stored levels. An RGBA representation adds alpha for transparency. The representation can instead use grayscale, palette indices, higher precision or another arrangement. A palette index is a reference to an entry, not three directly stored colour components at that position. For tightly packed RGB at 6000 × 4000 and eight bits per component: 6000 × 4000 × 3 = 72,000,000 bytes. That is 24 million pixels and 72 million component bytes. RGBA needs 96,000,000 bytes in the same ideal model. Actual image buffers can also contain row padding and additional working copies. Compressed bytes are another representation A photo file may be far smaller than its decoded pixel buffer. Its decoder reconstructs the sample grid from encoded data; a gallery then resizes, converts or presents that grid. This helps explain why loading many large photos can consume memory even when their files look modest. Thumbnail generation can use a smaller derivative for the visible tile rather than retaining every full-resolution decoded picture. The grid alone does not identify the colour space. ICC profiles and other colour signaling explain how the component values should be interpreted. The file's descriptive title and camera tags are separate metadata . See Also Image resolution Image transparency Image compression ICC color profiles References W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.title: Image resolution | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.keywords: Image resolution Image resolution includes pixel dimensions and their relationship to presentation size; megapixels and pixel-density metadata describe different quantities. A photograph measuring 6000 × 4000 pixels contains 24,000,000 pixel positions: 24 megapixels . That count says how large its sample grid is. It does not describe the scene's sharpness, lens quality or compression history. Dimensions matter alongside the total A 6000 × 4000 image has a 3:2 aspect ratio. Another image with 8000 × 3000 dimensions has the same 24-megapixel count but a much wider composition. Cropping the first image to 6000 × 3375 creates a 16:9 picture with 20.25 megapixels . It removes 625 rows in total; it does not squeeze the original picture into that shape. Operation on the 6000 × 4000 source Result Retain the whole grid 24 MP, aspect 3:2 Crop to 6000 × 3375 20.25 MP, aspect 16:9 Resize to 3000 × 2000 6 MP, same 3:2 aspect Change density metadata only Pixel grid remains 6000 × 4000 Halving each dimension quarters the number of pixels. This is why a useful browsing preview can require much less decoded memory than the original. Density describes a physical-size relationship At 300 pixels per inch, 6000 × 4000 pixels corresponds to approximately 20 × 13.33 inches . At 150 pixels per inch, the same samples correspond to 40 × 26.67 inches . Changing that density label does not create another 24 million samples. Resampling to meet a physical-size/density target is a separate operation. Screen presentation also has its own scaling and device-pixel ratio. A gallery tile's layout width does not necessarily equal the number of physical display pixels used to draw it. The resizing article develops that output-grid decision. More stored pixels need not mean more recovered detail Upscaling can create a larger grid and smoother-looking edges. It cannot restore scene detail that was never captured. Blur, missed focus or strong compression can remain apparent in a large file. In an Emby photo or artwork view, distinguish the original dimensions, the server's generated image and the app's presentation size. A blurry small preview enlarged on screen does not establish that the full-resolution source is blurry too. See Also Raster images Image resizing Image thumbnail generation Video Resolution References Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.title: Image transparency | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/Imag.keywords: Image transparency Transparency tells a compositor how an image contributes over a background, using alpha or a format-specific transparent index rather than an ordinary background colour. A logo placed on a dark page can carry an unexpected white rectangle. The white pixels may be part of the image, while the intended design needed transparent background positions. Transparency describes how the source contributes to a composition. A checkerboard in an image editor is usually a visualization of transparent regions, rather than the background that every viewer will receive. Coverage changes the result over each background For an opaque destination, a straight-alpha blend in a declared numerical domain is: result = alpha × source + (1 − alpha) × background. Take a white source sample with value 1 and coverage 0.25: Background sample Calculation Result 0, black 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 0 0.25 0.4, gray 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 0.4 0.55 1, white 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 1 1 The same image edge therefore produces different final pixels on different backgrounds. This is arithmetic in the stated working domain; perceptual display brightness also depends on colour encoding. A transparent index and an alpha channel have different scope An indexed format can designate an entry as transparent. GIF's transparent index leaves those destination positions unchanged. It does not provide arbitrary fractional coverage for each palette colour. An alpha-capable image can retain intermediate values around an antialiased edge. PNG's colour samples are stored unassociated with alpha. A processing buffer may use premultiplied samples instead, so the decoder/compositor boundary must preserve the convention. The subtitle overlay example develops the corresponding straight/premultiplied calculations. They apply to image layers as well as captions. Flattening commits to a background Flattening the white edge above onto black produces a gray sample of 0.25. Saving that result without alpha makes the gray edge permanent. Placing it on a white page later cannot recover the original white source and its coverage from that single value. This is why an Emby logo and a rectangular photographic backdrop have different image requirements. The intended layer needs useful alpha through the source, any generated derivative and the app's composition. Resizing introduces another boundary. Filtering colour and alpha inconsistently can pull hidden background colours into the edge and create a fringe. A suitable process keeps their relationship coherent, then encodes the result in the output format's required convention. See Also PNG images GIF images WebP images Image resizing Subtitle overlay filtering References W3C Compositing and Blending Level 1 W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 GIF89a specification

articles/photos-images/fundamentals/inde.title: Overview: Digital image fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/fundamentals/inde.keywords: Overview: Digital image fundamentals Image fundamentals describe the pixel grid, transparency, orientation and compression behind a digital picture. A picture's dimensions identify its stored grid, while transparency and orientation affect how that grid is presented. Compression changes the way the image data are represented and can affect retained detail. These topics establish those properties before an image format or display operation is examined. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Raster images A raster image describes a rectangular grid of samples whose dimensions, component representation and colour interpretation determine the decoded picture. Image resolution Image resolution includes pixel dimensions and their relationship to presentation size; megapixels and pixel-density metadata describe different quantities. Image transparency Transparency tells a compositor how an image contributes over a background, using alpha or a format-specific transparent index rather than an ordinary background colour. Image orientation Orientation metadata describes a transform from stored image rows and columns to the intended visual direction, including reflections as well as rotations. Image compression Image compression reduces encoded storage through reversible coding or lossy representation changes, while decoded dimensions and downstream processing remain separate. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 W3C Compositing and Blending Level 1

articles/photos-images/index.html.title: Overview: Photos and images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/index.html.keywords: Overview: Photos and images Digital images have pixel, format and metadata properties that influence their appearance, size and presentation. A photograph's visible appearance depends on more than its dimensions. Encoding can discard detail, transparency can change compositing, and orientation information can change how stored pixels are displayed. The fundamentals explain the image signal, the format pages describe its packaging and compression, and presentation topics connect it to the screen. These distinctions matter for photographs and for the posters, backgrounds and previews displayed around an Emby library. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Digital image fundamentals Image fundamentals describe the pixel grid, transparency, orientation and compression behind a digital picture. Image formats Image formats define how pictures, supporting metadata and sometimes multiple images are stored and interpreted. Image presentation Image presentation turns stored picture data into a sized, color-interpreted and sometimes animated or HDR display result. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.title: Animated images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.keywords: Animated images An animated image changes a shared canvas through timed frame data and composition/disposal rules, rather than necessarily storing independent full-size pictures. An animated image presents changes over time using an image format's frame and control structure. GIF, APNG and animated WebP provide related capabilities with different syntax and rules. Reconstruct the canvas, not just the latest rectangle Take an invented six-cell canvas. A first frame draws a marker in the leftmost cell; the next draws a marker in the third cell. Stage Keep earlier content Clear earlier marker before next draw After first draw A . . . . . A . . . . . After second draw A . B . . . . . B . . . The second frame's rectangle can contain only B. Whether A remains visible depends on the applicable disposal/composition behavior. A transparent position in an update does not universally mean “erase the existing canvas here”. It may leave that destination unchanged. Some format operations also restore a previously saved canvas region. The reader must apply the source format's actual rules. Time belongs to the composed presentation Frames carry or inherit durations in the format's time model. A loop's nominal duration is the sum of its applicable frame intervals, rather than the number of frames divided by an assumed video frame rate. For original intervals 0.10, 0.20 and 0.15 seconds , one traversal lasts 0.45 seconds . Repeating it twice nominally lasts 0.90 seconds , apart from any additional scheduling or loop policy. A consumer can schedule very short delays differently or choose to suppress animation. That is separate from correctly recovering the frame rectangles and their canvas positions. A still preview needs an instant and a reconstructed state Choosing “frame 2” can be ambiguous. Its encoded rectangle may be only an update, while its visible canvas includes earlier retained content. A thumbnail generator should obtain the intended composed state at a selected time. A default still image defined by a format can also have a different relationship to the animation sequence. For an Emby image path, distinguish the animated source, any server-generated still derivative and the app's handling of the delivered resource. A static tile can be an intentional derivative even when the original contains valid animation; an incomplete tile can instead result from extracting an update without reconstructing its canvas. See Also GIF images PNG images WebP images Image thumbnail generation References GIF89a specification W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 Google: WebP container specification

articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.title: HDR still images | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.keywords: HDR still images An HDR still presentation combines suitable image samples and luminance/colour interpretation with an output path that can render the intended brightness range or a defined fallback. An HDR photograph can represent and present brightness relationships beyond a chosen SDR reproduction. Its meaningful properties include the samples, their colour/luminance interpretation and how the output path renders them. Capturing a wide range of scene light and storing a finished HDR presentation are different tasks. A raw capture or a high-precision TIFF can supply useful information without being a directly displayable HDR image. Capture and presentation make different decisions A raw development or a merge of bracketed exposures can recover scene information across a range of light levels. The photographer still chooses exposure, appearance and an output representation. An SDR export maps that result into an SDR reproduction. An HDR export can retain another brightness relationship using a suitable encoding or gain-map arrangement. Increasing bit depth supplies more numerical levels. It does not identify which values mean SDR white, HDR highlights or a particular transfer function. Two useful representation routes A directly interpreted HDR image uses appropriate sample encoding and colour/luminance description. Its reader needs to decode and interpret that representation, then render for the actual output. A gain-map arrangement relates a base rendition to another appearance using an additional spatial map and metadata. A compatible consumer can combine them according to the supported reconstruction and available output headroom. A base-only consumer can receive the designated base presentation when that arrangement permits it. Android's Ultra HDR v1.1 reference specifies one JPEG-based gain-map packaging. Adobe's resources describe its gain-map design and the ISO 21496-1 standardization relationship. These are concrete arrangements, rather than a guarantee that every file called HDR stores the same fields. A gain is a relationship between renditions For an original, simplified one-channel, zero-offset model, let base linear sample B = 0.5 , full gain G = 4 , and reconstruction weight w between 0 and 1: output = B × Gʷ. Weight w Calculation Linear result 0 0.5 × 4⁰ 0.5 0.5 0.5 × 4⁰·⁵ 1 1 0.5 × 4¹ 2 Here, 1 denotes the model's chosen SDR-white reference. The reconstructed highlight can rise above it as more of the gain is applied. Real specified gain maps define how map samples, metadata, offsets, channels and display capacity determine the operation. This table illustrates the multiplicative relationship; it is not a complete gain-map decoder, and w is not a claim about a particular display's brightness setting. Thumbnail generation can choose a different rendition An image converter that reads only a designated SDR base may produce a useful SDR thumbnail while omitting the map. A later HDR-capable viewer cannot reconstruct the lost source relationship from that derivative alone. Another converter can reconstruct the HDR appearance, then intentionally create an SDR result through tone mapping. Simply clipping every value above 1 merges distinct highlights into one level; HDR-to-SDR tone mapping develops the alternative mapping. Cropping/resizing also needs a coherent relationship between the image and any spatial auxiliary map. Carrying an unchanged map alongside differently cropped base samples can make their positions disagree. Output headroom belongs to the full route The app's decoding, colour handling, operating-system surface and display presentation all contribute to the observed result. A display with HDR capability does not cause an image decoder to recover missing gain-map data or automatically repair wrong colour signaling. For Emby photos/artwork, compare the selected original, delivered representation and final appearance. Determine whether that route preserved the intended HDR information, chose an SDR derivative, or lost part of the relationship during conversion. A sound SDR fallback is another authored result, not necessarily evidence of a failed capture. It should retain useful scene relationships for its intended output rather than rely on a filename or bit-depth label to communicate the whole presentation. See Also AVIF images HEIF and HEIC images PNG images ICC color profiles Camera raw images How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References Adobe: HDR gain maps and specification resources Android: Ultra HDR image format v1.1 AOM AVIF 1.2.0, Final Deliverable of 16 October 2025 W3C PNG Third Edition, Recommendation of 24 June 2025 ICC.1:2022: Profile architecture, format and data structure

articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.title: ICC color profiles | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.keywords: ICC color profiles An ICC profile describes a colour relationship used by a colour-management process to interpret source samples and prepare values for a destination. Two applications can decode the same RGB sample values and show different colours if they interpret those values differently. An ICC profile describes a colour relationship for a colour-management process; it is not another set of photographic pixels. The application needs to use the description at the relevant processing boundary. Merely carrying the profile in the file does not perform a conversion. Source and destination have different roles A source profile describes how the supplied image values relate to a defined colour interpretation. A destination profile describes the target's corresponding relationship. The conventional ICC architecture connects transforms through a profile connection space , based on specified CIE colour representations. This allows source and destination descriptions to be combined. The profile's fields can describe curves, matrices or lookup-based relationships as applicable. ICC.1:2022 defines the referenced version-4 profile format. This architecture is broader than assuming every file uses one simple RGB matrix. Assignment changes meaning; conversion changes representation Suppose a file contains the sample triplet (128, 64, 32) interpreted using source profile A. Operation Sample numbers Intended effect Assign profile B without transforming Remain (128, 64, 32) Interpret those numbers according to B Convert from A to B Can change Express the source colours in B's representation Remove the profile Remain, unless another operation changes them Leave the reader to its applicable fallback interpretation Assigning a different label cannot by itself preserve the original colour meaning. Conversion attempts to preserve or suitably map that meaning, within the target's limits. This is also why attaching an sRGB label to arbitrary wide-gamut values is different from converting those values into sRGB. The label says what the numbers mean; it does not silently calculate the required replacement numbers. A destination may not contain every source colour If a source colour is outside the target gamut, exact reproduction in that target is unavailable. The transform's rendering policy determines how it maps that colour. Different policies can prioritize different reproduction relationships. The useful comparison includes the actual source profile, destination, intent and display environment, rather than judging only whether an ICC chunk exists. A source profile also is not a universal creative correction. It does not remove blur, recover clipped detail or know which artistic look the photographer intended. Derivatives need a coherent new description An image-processing route may convert samples to a selected output colour space and encode a browsing derivative. That output needs colour signaling consistent with the new numbers. Keeping the old source profile after changing the representation can mislabel the derivative. Discarding the profile while leaving the original numbers can instead invite a different fallback interpretation. For Emby photos/artwork, examine the original resource, server-generated image and app/operating-system presentation. A difference can arise where the profile was ignored, converted inconsistently or replaced, even though image decompression itself succeeded. Precision and HDR are related but independent More sample precision can help represent intermediate colour values with less rounding. It does not identify a source profile, and a profile is not automatically an instruction that every display should show HDR highlights. The HDR still-image article adds luminance interpretation, gain maps and output headroom to that chain. Resizing also distinguishes averaging encoded values from averaging light; a coherent colour label does not specify every arithmetic choice performed earlier. See Also HDR still images Raster images Image resizing How Video Color Is Represented References ICC.1:2022: Profile architecture, format and data structure ICC: Frequently asked questions about colour management W3C CSS Color 4: Colour spaces and conversion algorithms

articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.title: Image resizing | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.keywords: Image resizing Image resizing reconstructs a source image onto a new sample grid, with fit/crop policy, filtering, colour domain and alpha handling affecting the result. A 4000 × 3000 photograph does not have the same shape as a 400 × 400 browsing tile. A resize request must first decide whether to retain the whole picture or fill the tile by cropping. Those geometry decisions come before choosing how the source samples contribute to each output pixel. Contain and cover solve different requirements For contain , use the smaller dimension scale: min(400/4000, 400/3000) = 0.1. The picture becomes 400 × 300 , leaving 100 vertical pixels of unused tile space. A centered arrangement leaves 50 above and 50 below. For cover , use the larger scale, 400/3000 = 2/15. The scaled picture is approximately 533.33 × 400 . A centered crop removes approximately 66.67 scaled pixels from each side. An equivalent source-space description keeps a 3000 × 3000 square, removing 500 source columns from each side, then scales that square to 400 × 400. Real implementations choose integer sizes and rounding. The calculations above describe ideal geometry; they do not specify an Emby crop algorithm. Output pixels correspond to source neighborhoods One common pixel-centre mapping for uniform scale s places output column j at source coordinate: x = (j + 0.5) / s − 0.5. At scale 0.2, the first two output centres correspond to source x = 2 and 7 . This gives a phase relationship between the grids. It does not itself define the filter or its neighborhood. Nearest-neighbor chooses a source sample. Bilinear and other scaling kernels combine samples with specified weights. Downscaling also needs an appropriate reduction of detail above the output grid's useful spatial frequency. Thin patterns expose aliasing Imagine alternating black and white source columns. Selecting every second column can produce all black or all white depending on the starting phase. The original pattern had equal contributions from both. A suitable averaging/reconstruction process can instead produce a representative gray at the smaller scale. This is why a thumbnail can show moiré, false patterns or vanished thin lines even though its dimensions are mathematically correct. Sharper-looking filters can also create edge overshoot/ringing. The useful choice depends on the source content and intended result, rather than on a universal ranking of kernel names. Average light and average encoded values differ Consider two sRGB samples: black at 0 and white at 1. Averaging their encoded values gives 0.5, which corresponds to approximately 0.214 in linear light . Averaging their linear-light values gives 0.5 light units. Re-encoding that result as sRGB yields approximately 0.735 , or 188 on a rounded eight-bit scale. Direct encoded averaging instead gives about 128 . These are defined numerical models using the sRGB conversion equations. They do not assert that every image library resizes in linear light. The working domain is part of the operation's meaning. Transparent edges need coherent filtering Colour hidden under zero alpha can enter an interpolation if colour and coverage are filtered independently without suitable treatment. That can produce a dark or coloured fringe when the resized logo is placed over a page. A process can use an appropriate premultiplied working representation while filtering, then write the output in the file format's required convention. The transparency article explains why a flattened edge cannot be repaired simply by changing its later background. Consider two source pixels in a declared linear numerical domain: transparent black (colour 0, alpha 0) and opaque white (colour 1, alpha 1) . Averaging their straight colour and alpha separately gives colour 0.5 and alpha 0.5. Over black, that produces only 0.25 . Averaging premultiplied values instead gives premultiplied colour 0.5 and alpha 0.5. Its equivalent straight colour is 1, so the result over black is 0.5 . Over white, the first method yields 0.75, while the coherent white edge yields 1. Halfway edge Over black Over white Independently averaged straight colour/alpha 0.25 0.75 Premultiplied working interpolation 0.5 1 These values explain the dark fringe in this specific two-pixel model. Colour-domain choice remains an additional question; premultiplying does not itself convert encoded samples into linear light. In an Emby comparison, examine the source, generated image dimensions/crop and final app scaling. A good server derivative can still be stretched or enlarged at the presentation stage; a sharp original can already have been reduced into an unsuitable crop before it reaches that app. See Also Image resolution Image thumbnail generation Image transparency How Video Scaling Works Nearest-Neighbor Video Scaling Bilinear Video Scaling References W3C CSS Color 4: Colour spaces and conversion algorithms W3C Compositing and Blending Level 1

articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.title: Image thumbnail generation | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/Imag.keywords: Image thumbnail generation Thumbnail generation creates a smaller viewing derivative from a selected, oriented and interpreted source image, with cache identity determining when that derivative remains valid. A thumbnail is a separate, smaller image useful for browsing. It may come from an embedded preview or be generated from a principal image. Displaying the original in a small layout box does not necessarily create that derivative or reduce the original's decoding work. Match the useful output grid An invented 300-layout-pixel-wide tile on a display using two device pixels per layout pixel can use a 600-pixel-wide derivative. For a 3:2 photograph, that is 600 × 400 . Compare it with a 6000 × 4000 source: Representation Pixels Ideal tightly packed RGB bytes Original 24,000,000 72,000,000 600 × 400 derivative 240,000 720,000 The derivative has one percent of the source's pixels in this example. Encoded sizes have their own compression relationship. Producing the thumbnail may still require decoding a larger image or using a codec-specific reduced-resolution path. A small delivered file does not establish low peak memory during generation. Select and interpret before choosing the crop A raw or multi-image resource may contain a preview different from its master. First choose which picture supplies the intended appearance. Apply a coherent orientation state, then establish its visual dimensions. A portrait photo stored as a landscape grid can otherwise receive a landscape crop before its direction is resolved. The generation route also needs colour interpretation and an appropriate resize/crop policy. Alpha and animation add their own requirements: a logo may need coverage retained, while an animated source needs a selected reconstructed canvas. A cache entry represents a particular derivation An original conceptual cache identity could contain: source identity + source version + target dimensions + crop policy + orientation/colour processing + output format This is an explanatory model, not a documented Emby cache-key schema. If the source changes but the cached derivative is reused, a viewer can continue to show an old rotation, crop or image. If the image-processing rules change, the same source version may also need a new derivative. That separates stale preview from wrong master . In an Emby comparison, identify the original and the actual delivered image before treating the displayed result as evidence that the master was not edited. A thumbnail has a different preservation role An embedded preview can be convenient without reflecting the latest external editing recipe. A generated thumbnail can omit descriptive records that remain in the master. Keep that distinction when moving or rebuilding a library. A cache is replaceable derivation work; the source image and metadata needed to reproduce the intended presentation carry a different value. See Also Image resizing Image orientation Camera raw images ICC color profiles Metadata provenance References Adobe DNG 1.7.1.0 specification Adobe: TIFF Revision 6.0 specification ICC.1:2022: Profile architecture, format and data structure

articles/photos-images/presentation/inde.title: Overview: Image presentation | Emby Learn
articles/photos-images/presentation/inde.keywords: Overview: Image presentation Image presentation turns stored picture data into a sized, color-interpreted and sometimes animated or HDR display result. A thumbnail is a derived picture, while a color profile supplies interpretation for the picture's samples. Animation and HDR still images add further presentation relationships. This branch separates those operations, helping explain a changed appearance without assuming that the source pixels themselves were rewritten. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Image resizing Image resizing reconstructs a source image onto a new sample grid, with fit/crop policy, filtering, colour domain and alpha handling affecting the result. Image thumbnail generation Thumbnail generation creates a smaller viewing derivative from a selected, oriented and interpreted source image, with cache identity determining when that derivative remains valid. ICC color profiles An ICC profile describes a colour relationship used by a colour-management process to interpret source samples and prepare values for a destination. Animated images An animated image changes a shared canvas through timed frame data and composition/disposal rules, rather than necessarily storing independent full-size pictures.
