articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.title: Overview: Playback diagnostics | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.keywords: Overview: Playback diagnostics Playback diagnostics capture the active media path and enough context to reproduce or explain its result. Emby playback information and a transcoding log expose different views of a session. A reproducible case connects those observations to the particular source, app and operation. This branch explains how to read that evidence together, including the distinction between a requested operation and the result it actually produced. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Reading Emby playback information Emby playback information relates source, selected streams, output processing and session observations whose meanings depend on their measurement scope. Reading a transcoding log A transcoding log records process configuration and progress whose inputs, stream mappings, output stages and final events need to be interpreted in their own scopes. Reproducing a media playback problem A playback reproduction preserves a defined source, session context and observation interval so that a controlled change can test a specific media-processing or delivery hypothesis. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: TranscodingInfo FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress Emby: Log files

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.title: Reading Emby playback information | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.keywords: Reading Emby playback information Emby playback information relates source, selected streams, output processing and session observations whose meanings depend on their measurement scope. Playback information becomes useful when each field is attached to the part of the session it describes. Source properties, selected tracks, generated output, player observations and conversion reasons are different scopes. A 4K source and a 720p session output can both be reported correctly. A copied video stream and converted audio can also coexist. An original video-copy/audio-conversion fragment The following hand-authored fragment uses public Emby session property names and readable conversion-reason names. It is not a captured API response: { "IsVideoDirect": true, "IsAudioDirect": false, "VideoCodec": "h264", "Width": 1920, "Height": 1080, "VideoBitrate": 8000000, "AudioCodec": "aac", "AudioBitrate": 192000, "AudioChannels": 2, "TranscodeReasons": [ "ContainerNotSupported", "AudioCodecNotSupported", "AudioChannelsNotSupported" ] } In the described original case, the video is preserved while selected audio is prepared as stereo AAC. The reasons identify several relevant mismatches; they do not say that playback failed. Emby's public model exposes separate video/audio direct-handling fields and conversion information. The exact fields shown by a particular app or diagnostic surface can vary. Source and output should be compared deliberately Question Relevant information What is stored in the library resource? Source/container and source stream analysis Which streams did the viewer choose? Source-qualified audio/subtitle selection What representation is being delivered? Output/container and stream processing information Why was another path chosen? Capability/limit decisions and reason context What happened at the player? Player state, buffer and presentation observations Matching source and output codec strings does not establish stream copying. The same codec can be encoded again. Stream handling or mapping supplies stronger evidence. Conversely, a process using conversion infrastructure can preserve video while converting audio. That is the Direct Stream relationship developed in the example. Reasons and results differ A reason such as unsupported container can explain selection of a successful adapted path. An unsupported selected audio presentation can explain another stream's conversion. A direct-play error can describe a fallback after an attempted path. That needs event order as well as the final session information. One reason need not describe every relevant condition. An incomplete field or absent observation should remain incomplete rather than becoming an invented proof of compatibility or zero resource use. Several progress clocks can appear The viewer's programme position, server conversion position, received-media ranges and processing speed answer different questions. A converter at programme minute 30 while playback is at minute 20 can have produced ahead. It does not prove the player has ten minutes buffered or that the viewer watched thirty minutes. Likewise, a percentage of conversion completion is not watched coverage. Source duration and output-origin mapping can influence how progress coordinates are interpreted. Transcoding speed explains media-time versus wall-time units. A conversion log supplies more direct stream-operation and event evidence. Keep the session context The source, app/player path, selected tracks, requested position and observation time belong with the fields. A source change or restarted job can supply another context. See Also Direct Play in Emby Direct Stream in Emby Video transcoding in Emby Transcoding speed, fps and media time Dropped video frames during playback References Emby API: TranscodingInfo Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Emby API: TranscodeReason Emby API: Playback progress reporting Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.title: Reproducing a media playback problem | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.keywords: Reproducing a media playback problem A playback reproduction preserves a defined source, session context and observation interval so that a controlled change can test a specific media-processing or delivery hypothesis. A useful reproduction defines the session that produced the observation. The title alone leaves source version, tracks, app, starting point, limits and activity uncontrolled. A controlled comparison changes a specified input while retaining enough context to interpret the resulting media plan and symptom. An original three-case worksheet Assume source F1 has compatible video, stereo AAC at audio index 2, six-channel AC-3 at index 1, and bitmap subtitles at index 6. Assume the target needs packaging adaptation, cannot use that AC-3 presentation, and needs bitmap subtitles rendered into video. Case Changed request relative to A What the comparison tests A Baseline: audio 2, no subtitle Video/audio copy with packaging adaptation B Audio 1 replaces audio 2 Additional audio conversion C Subtitle 6 is selected; audio stays 2 Additional picture rendering and video encoding These are declared hypotheses for the example capabilities, not observed Emby results. The actual source and app may support another plan. The resulting pipeline is allowed to change: that is the consequence being examined. Holding the output mode artificially fixed would remove the effect of the input change. Keep the context that matters Context Reason to retain it Work/episode and edition Distinguishes different content under one title Media source identity and technical facts Identifies the actual represented streams Audio/subtitle choices Defines selected content and processing requirements App/player and output route Defines the receiving capability context Requested position Distinguishes startup, seek and a difficult source interval Applicable rate/format conditions Explains another output plan Delivery/storage path Identifies relevant access and retrieval context Competing activity and cold/warm state Describes shared load and reusable work This is an experiment description, not a requirement to exhaustively vary every item before understanding a problem. It selects the evidence relevant to a specific hypothesis. Observation and explanation should remain separate “The playhead stopped near minute 12” is an observation. “The network caused it” is an explanation that needs relevant evidence. A conversion log can establish stream handling and progress. A client observation can establish received ranges or presentation behavior. The artifacts should be related to the same session and time interval. An output-mode change after selecting another track supplies evidence that the media plan changed. It does not alone prove that the original symptom was caused by that plan. Repeats also have a state A repeat may reuse opened resources, analysis or generated data. Competing activity can change. The same nominal request can therefore have another cold/warm context. A problem disappearing on one repeat is useful evidence about that run. It is not automatically a permanent fix or proof of one particular cache mechanism. A reproducible observation should retain what occurred, when, and under which relevant state. Reading playback information and reading a conversion log explain the artifact scopes that make the comparison assessable. See Also Reading Emby playback information Reading a transcoding log Track selection and playback plans Media source selection for playback Playback error categories and evidence scopes References Emby: Log files Emby: Transcoding Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest Emby API: Playback progress reporting

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.title: Reading a transcoding log | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/dia.keywords: Reading a transcoding log A transcoding log records process configuration and progress whose inputs, stream mappings, output stages and final events need to be interpreted in their own scopes. A conversion log describes a process and its observations. The most useful reading connects input, selected streams, handling, output and event order rather than treating every codec name or warning as the conclusion. The excerpts below are original illustrations. They were not captured from an Emby session or an executed FFmpeg job. Begin with the input and intended selection This example selects the first video and audio streams and requests video copying with AAC audio output: ffmpeg -i source.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -c:v copy -c:a aac -ac 2 -b:a 192k output.mp4 Input and output options have a scope. The source name identifies a resource locator; the map identifies which of its streams is selected; codec options identify requested handling for the relevant output streams. A described input could contain: Input #0, matroska,webm, from 'source.mkv': Stream #0:0: Video: h264, yuv420p, 1920x1080, 24 fps Stream #0:1: Audio: ac3, 48000 Hz, 5.1, 384 kb/s That is source information. It does not establish the output audio codec or channel count. If the source contains other tracks, their presence is different from their selection. A source-qualified map avoids inferring “first English audio” from a generic integer in another representation. The mapping supplies operation evidence For the original video-copy/audio-conversion case: Stream mapping: Stream #0:0 -> #0:0 (copy) Stream #0:1 -> #0:1 (ac3 (native) -> aac (native)) The video mapping says copy. The audio mapping names decoding/encoding implementations. Both streams participate in the same output process while taking different operations. An output description can then be: Output #0, mp4, to 'output.mp4': Stream #0:0: Video: h264, yuv420p, 1920x1080, 24 fps Stream #0:1: Audio: aac, 48000 Hz, stereo, 192 kb/s The selected audio has changed from six-channel AC-3 to stereo AAC. The video mapping supplies the evidence that its H.264 representation is preserved; the matching H.264 label alone does not. Same codec names can conceal another video encode A separate original mapping example is: Stream #0:0 -> #0:0 (h264 (native) -> h264 (libx264)) The input and output codec family are both H.264, but this mapping describes decoding and another encode. It is different from the copy mapping. A filename containing “transcode” also does not decide the operation. The server can use conversion infrastructure for remuxing or audio preparation. Requested options and actual mapping are more precise evidence. Encoder and decoder names describe stages. A named hardware encoder, where present, does not establish how every upstream filter ran or whether all picture data stayed in one memory domain. Filters connect another kind of data An original graph fragment could contain: [0:v:0]scale=1280:720[vout] The filter uses decoded pictures and labels its output vout. An output map consuming that label is another relationship from directly mapping an input stream-copy path. Dimensions in an output description can help confirm the requested result, but a configured output header is still not proof that valid media was generated through the entire programme. A format or graph-initialisation error can occur before useful output. A later error can interrupt an otherwise successful start. The event timing matters. Interpret progress with its clock and units In a separate original 24-fps video-encoding example: frame=1440 fps=48 time=00:01:00.00 speed=2.00x If that output progress was accumulated over 30 wall seconds, 1,440 output frames represent sixty media seconds, giving a 2x rate. The media progress time is not the wall-clock duration. After a seek or another timestamp-origin choice, an absolute-looking time also needs its initial context before differences are computed. Frame counters do not universally prove how many source pictures were decoded. Stream copying, cadence conversion and multiple outputs can give counters different scopes. Transcoding speed supplies the unit reasoning. A quiet progress interval can be throttling or a wait. It can also reflect a blocked or failed stage. The surrounding events and positions distinguish them. The final event changes the interpretation A process can be stopped because playback ended, the viewer sought elsewhere or another job replaced it. A terminated process does not automatically imply an accidental failure. Conversely, earlier output configuration and a few successful progress lines do not prove complete success. Final process status, the generated output and the player's observed result supply additional evidence. Even a completely successful output process does not prove that the player retrieved or presented its media. Playback information and request/player observations connect that later part of the path. Correlate the relevant job A library can have several sessions and several log files. The source identity, selected tracks, process/session context and timestamp interval connect the log to the observed problem. Wall-clock time zones or skew can also affect cross-device correlation. A line labelled 10:00 on one device is not automatically simultaneous with another device's 10:00 without clock context. Emby's Log Files documentation describes the product's log artifacts and access workflow. The technology reading here asks what each artifact establishes. articles/playback-streaming/behavior/ind.title: Overview: Understanding playback behavior | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/ind.keywords: Overview: Understanding playback behavior Playback behavior links visible symptoms to observations of the stages involved in a media session. A late start, a stall and a dropped frame describe different results. Diagnostic information can then show which source, conversion or delivery path was active. This group pairs those symptom definitions with ways to capture evidence, so the investigation follows the actual session rather than one assumed cause. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Playback symptoms Playback symptoms describe distinct failures or limits in starting, continuing and presenting media. Playback diagnostics Playback diagnostics capture the active media path and enough context to reproduce or explain its result. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Overview: Playback symptoms | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Overview: Playback symptoms Playback symptoms describe distinct failures or limits in starting, continuing and presenting media. When does the problem appear: before playback, while data are arriving, or while frames are presented? Startup delay, stalls, quality limits and dropped frames point to different observations. The pages here give each result a precise meaning before an underlying cause is selected. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Playback startup delay Playback startup delay is the wait before useful presentation, produced by the session’s control, resource, processing, delivery and player-readiness dependencies. Playback stalls A playback stall occurs when the next required presentation cannot progress because media or another dependency is not ready, requiring evidence from the affected stage. Playback quality limits Playback quality limits constrain the chosen delivery representation through applicable rate, format and presentation conditions rather than promising one fixed visual quality. Dropped video frames Dropped playback frames are pictures not presented as intended, with counter origin and observation interval needed to distinguish client timing from source or conversion changes. Playback error categories Playback errors identify observations at planning, access, processing, delivery or player stages, with their namespace and event context needed for interpretation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: Playback information negotiation Emby API: TranscodingInfo Emby: Transcoding FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Dropped video frames during playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Dropped video frames during playback Dropped playback frames are pictures not presented as intended, with counter origin and observation interval needed to distinguish client timing from source or conversion changes. A dropped playback-frame observation concerns pictures not presented as intended. It can occur even while media continues to arrive and audio/playback time advances. The first question is where the counter was measured. A player-side count is different from a conversion process's output-frame policy or a damaged source sequence. Availability and presentation can disagree A player may have enough received media while decoding, compositing or output scheduling cannot meet every picture's deadline. That differs from a stall caused by unavailable next media. Late or discarded pictures can make motion uneven without proving the network buffer was empty. Conversely, network starvation can stop progress without a useful frame-drop counter explaining the cause. Compare counters over a defined interval Use original cumulative observations: Snapshot Total video frames counted Dropped frames counted A 1,000 10 B 2,000 50 The recent interval contains 1,000 counted frames and 40 drops, a ratio of 4%. The lifetime ratio at B is 50 / 2000 = 2.5% . These ratios describe different observation intervals. A cumulative counter that stays nonzero after a problem disappears is not evidence that it is still increasing. The example assumes the same counter epoch and scope. A reset, new source or new player object can invalidate a simple subtraction. The counter's owner matters The W3C Media Playback Quality draft defines player-oriented frame counters. A 2022 Emby app-developer explanation identifies the discussed dropped-frame information as coming from the player. Neither reference promises identical fields or instrumentation in every app. A log's encoded-frame count is another observation. An encoder or cadence-conversion policy can intentionally omit or duplicate frames while producing a valid target sequence. A picture skipped because the user sought elsewhere also differs from a picture missed during intended continuous presentation. Observation Appropriate scope Player frame drops Player decoding/presentation path and its counter definition Cadence conversion output Requested frame-rate transformation Missing/corrupt source data Input validity and decoder evidence Seek jump Requested timeline change Relate the interval to the actual workload Source parameters, client app/player, display/output path and competing activity can change presentation load. A “supported” codec configuration does not alone establish smooth output throughout the session. See Also Playback stalls and unavailable next media Client playback capabilities Video Frame Rate Frame-Rate Conversion Reading Emby playback information References W3C draft: Media Playback Quality Emby app developer: Player-side dropped frame count (2022) WHATWG: HTML media playback FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Playback error categories and evidence scopes | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Playback error categories and evidence scopes Playback errors identify observations at planning, access, processing, delivery or player stages, with their namespace and event context needed for interpretation. Playback can fail before a media plan exists, while accessing a resource, during conversion, during retrieval or inside the player. Those failures need different evidence. An error message describes an observation at one of those stages. Its code or wording is not automatically the original cause. Keep the namespace with the code Example observation Namespace and meaning HTTP 403 This HTTP request was forbidden HTTP 404 This request did not find an available target resource Browser MediaError code 3 A decoding-stage media error in the HTML media model Browser MediaError code 4 The selected source was unsuitable in that model Emby NoCompatibleStream A playback-information error identifying no compatible offered stream A conversion-reason identifier Evidence about why another media plan was selected The browser's number 3 has no universal meaning for a native player's unrelated error namespace. An HTTP status also concerns a particular request, not every aspect of the catalogue item. Emby's public playback-information response defines its own error vocabulary. Its conversion-reason model describes another kind of state. Identify the failing boundary A denied source access can prevent any conversion. A writable-output failure can interrupt a converter that decoded the input correctly. A delivery request can fail after the server generated usable media. A browser decode error supplies evidence about the player's stage. It does not, by itself, prove which packet or resource property caused it. The source representation, received data and decoder context still matter. Likewise, “no compatible stream” does not prove the original file is corrupt. The available plan can fail to meet the requesting client's constraints even when the source is valid. A reason is not always a failure A container or audio mismatch can lead to a successful Direct Stream plan. An unsupported video presentation can lead to a successful replacement video. Conversion-reason information therefore explains a decision; it should not automatically be counted as a failed playback. A later fallback after an attempted original path introduces another event. Its reason and the final successful mode need the order of observations rather than one flattened label. Aborts and interruptions need context A user cancellation, seek-triggered job replacement or deliberate session stop can end a request or process. An exit or aborted operation is not automatically evidence of an accidental playback failure. Conversely, a process can have started and printed output configuration before failing to deliver any useful interval. The earlier messages do not establish successful presentation. Retain enough evidence to test a cause The relevant record includes the affected stage, timestamp/clock context, source and selected tracks, the actual request or process, and what the player did next. Playback information , conversion logs and a controlled reproduction supply complementary evidence. Their value comes from relating observations to the same session and boundary. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Playback stalls and unavailable next media Reading Emby playback information Reading a transcoding log Reproducing a media playback problem References Emby API: Playback information negotiation Emby API: TranscodeReason WHATWG: HTML media playback IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and ranges Emby: Log files

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Playback quality limits and output constraints | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Playback quality limits and output constraints Playback quality limits constrain the chosen delivery representation through applicable rate, format and presentation conditions rather than promising one fixed visual quality. A playback limit describes a constraint on the selected representation. It does not guarantee one visual quality, nor require the encoder to fill the permitted rate exactly. The relevant constraints can come from the client request, delivery context, user/server policy and the media configuration. Their applicability needs the actual session context. An original set of applicable caps Assume an invented planner applies all four limits below and chooses their minimum: Applicable cap in the model Value Player/profile limit 12 Mbit/s Server delivery policy 8 Mbit/s User policy 6 Mbit/s Current app request 4 Mbit/s Under that declared policy, the effective ceiling is 4 Mbit/s. Seeing a server setting of 8 does not make the other stated constraints disappear. This is not a specification of Emby's complete precedence or network-classification algorithm. Its public request/profile models and transcoding documentation do establish that rate constraints participate in a session decision. A ceiling and a target are different quantities If an existing compatible source uses 3.192 Mbit/s in the original source-selection example, a 4 Mbit/s ceiling does not require padding it to four. If a conversion is requested, the actual achieved average can depend on rate control and content. A maximum, a target average and a constant-quality control have different meanings. A combined-stream budget also differs from a video-only rate. With a nominal 4 Mbit/s combined budget and 192 kbit/s audio, 3.808 Mbit/s remains before any additional packaging allowance. Allocating the entire four to video would ignore the audio contribution. Output dimensions and compression interact Reducing dimensions can change the number of samples encoded per picture. At a fixed delivery rate, that changes the encoder's allocation problem, but it does not supply a universal visual-quality score. A suitable lower-resolution presentation on a small display can be useful. Enlarging it later cannot recover spatial detail that the preparation removed. Codec efficiency, content motion/texture, cadence and encoder decisions all matter. “More Mbit/s” is not a complete comparison across different sources or output formats. The encoding quality articles explain the underlying controls. The playback limit is the session constraint that makes a particular output necessary or permissible. Source information and displayed output A library item can report 4K source video while a session delivers a 720p conversion. Those values describe different resources in the path. The target may also have a different colour presentation or channel layout. A change to bitrate alone does not establish whether scaling, tone mapping or audio preparation occurred. Another encode can reduce additional visible degradation relative to a less suitable encode. It cannot reconstruct information already absent from the source. Raising a maximum does not automatically retrieve another master or edition. A limit should be assessed in its context A source or track change can alter the selected plan. A client-request change can affect the effective conditions. A conservative or incomplete capability observation can produce a different available path. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Media source selection for playback Video transcoding in Emby Video Bitrate Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video How Video Scaling Works References Emby: Transcoding Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest Emby API: DeviceProfile FFmpeg: Codec options

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Playback stalls and unavailable next media | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Playback stalls and unavailable next media A playback stall occurs when the next required presentation cannot progress because media or another dependency is not ready, requiring evidence from the affected stage. A stall is a failure to make the next required playback progress when it should occur. The missing dependency can be media arrival, server output, resource access, decoder readiness or another part of the path. A waiting indicator describes the player's state. It does not identify the cause by itself. Three positions can tell different stories Use an original common-origin model: server-ready position = 120 + 2 × wall seconds client-received position = 110 + 0.75 × wall seconds intended playback position = 100 + 1 × wall seconds At the start, the client has ten media seconds ahead of playback. The server's output progresses quickly, but the client's arrivals progress at only 0.75x. At wall second 40, received and intended playback positions both reach programme second 140. The client has exhausted the stated reserve while the server-ready position is already 200. The model ends at that first starvation point. Afterward, uninterrupted intended playback cannot continue under the assumptions; a real player must wait or apply another recovery policy. The server-ready value is not proof of client receipt. Nor does client receipt guarantee a decoded picture's presentation deadline. Locate the missing dependency Observation Useful question Server output stops advancing while active work is required Is production blocked, failing or too slow? Server output advances but arrivals do not Which retrieval/delivery dependency is holding up the client? Received media is present but presentation cannot progress Is decoding, output initialization or another player dependency unresolved? Sound continues but pictures are visibly uneven Are pictures missing presentation deadlines rather than the whole playhead waiting? The last case can be dropped video frames , a different observation from an exhausted continuous media reserve. A source-read interruption can eventually propagate through several queues. The visible symptom can occur later than the original failure because earlier buffers temporarily cover the gap. Recovery introduces another interval A player can wait for reserve, retry retrieval, select another representation or stop with an error. Those behaviors have different evidence and policies. Changing to a lower output rate can reduce delivery demand. It cannot correct a missing resource or automatically repair corrupt input. Changing server conversion speed cannot establish that a client's current route can carry the chosen output. An intentional pause in playback and a deliberate producer throttle also differ from a stall. Their state and positions should be retained in the observation record. Compare the same session context Source, tracks, app, requested position and competing activity all influence the path. A successful test with different subtitles or another source is not the same workload. The original plot isolates one cause: slower client arrival than consumption despite faster server production. A real example needs the relevant position/rate observations before that explanation can be assigned. See Also Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Dropped video frames during playback Playback error categories and evidence scopes Reading Emby playback information References WHATWG: HTML media playback Emby API: TranscodingInfo Emby API: Playback progress reporting

articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.title: Playback startup delay | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/behavior/sym.keywords: Playback startup delay Playback startup delay is the wait before useful presentation, produced by the session’s control, resource, processing, delivery and player-readiness dependencies. Startup delay is the wait before the viewer receives useful picture and sound. It includes dependencies that a steady encoding-speed number does not describe. The measurement also needs endpoints. Time from pressing Play to the first presented picture differs from time from the first media request to its first received bytes. Name the measured interval Endpoint What it observes User requests playback The viewer's initial action Session plan becomes available Control/selection work has progressed First media bytes arrive Delivery has started First decodable picture is ready Codec/input dependencies are satisfied First picture is presented The player has scheduled visible output Those milestones can be separated by input access, initialization, processing, buffering or player state. A request that has returned successfully does not, by itself, establish that a picture has been shown. An original store-and-forward example Assume this deliberately serial workflow: Work before presentation Assumed wall time Session control 0.2 seconds Source access/inspection 0.3 seconds Processing initialization 0.7 seconds Produce one six-second output interval at 2x 3.0 seconds Retrieve its 36-million-bit payload at 12 Mbit/s 3.0 seconds Initial player decoding/presentation preparation 0.2 seconds The total is 7.4 seconds. The example assumes 6 Mbit/s output and a whole-interval dependency. It is not a claim that Emby always waits for six-second segments or serializes those stages. Another path can overlap production and retrieval, expose usable data earlier, or need a different initial reserve. Those changes alter the dependency chain rather than contradicting the arithmetic. Steady speed does not erase initial work The producer in the example runs at 2x. It still needs initialization and the stated first-output interval before the next dependency can begin. A pipeline can therefore start after a noticeable wait and then maintain a comfortable lead. Conversely, a quick first frame can be followed by stalls if sustained arrival cannot keep up. Codec look-ahead, reference-picture requirements and output-container information can contribute to initial readiness. The exact contribution depends on the represented streams and implementation. Cold and warm observations A first request may need source opening, inspection or another cache-dependent operation that a later request can reuse. Comparing a cold request with a warm one changes more than elapsed time. A useful test records that state. A repeat becoming faster is evidence about the repeated context, not proof of one specific cache mechanism. A changed audio/subtitle choice can also alter the planned work. “The same movie started faster” is incomplete without the source, tracks, client and requested position. The player has its own start conditions The player can wait for data, decoder/output initialization or another readiness condition. The server cannot infer all those conditions merely from having written output. A seek can create a similar dependency chain at another point in the programme. Seeking distinguishes destination readiness from the original startup interval. See Also How a transcoding pipeline works Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Reading Emby playback information Reproducing a media playback problem References Emby API: Playback information negotiation FFmpeg API: Send/receive encoding and decoding FFmpeg: Container and segment formats WHATWG: HTML media playback

articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.title: Overview: DLNA playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.keywords: Overview: DLNA playback DLNA playback uses discovery, media descriptions and device-specific compatibility information to connect a source with a receiver. A DLNA receiver needs both a reachable resource and a representation it can interpret. Device profiles describe the relevant compatibility relationship rather than changing the receiver's hardware. These pages connect that information to media selection and delivery through a DLNA path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DLNA media playback DLNA media playback uses interoperable media and UPnP AV roles to discover content, select a renderer and establish a supported media-delivery path. DLNA device profiles A DLNA device profile describes identification and media-handling rules used to offer a representation compatible with a particular receiving path. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: DeviceProfile

articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.title: DLNA media playback and UPnP AV roles | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.keywords: DLNA media playback and UPnP AV roles DLNA media playback uses interoperable media and UPnP AV roles to discover content, select a renderer and establish a supported media-delivery path. DLNA media playback combines media-format interoperability with network roles used to discover and control presentation. Its UPnP AV architecture separates the source of content, the presentation device and the controlling application. A device being discovered establishes part of the network interaction. The selected resource must still fit the renderer's media and access requirements. Roles can share a physical device Role Main responsibility Media server Expose content descriptions and media resources Media renderer Present the selected media Control point Discover, browse, select and control the relevant devices These are logical roles. A television can combine browsing controls and rendering, while another arrangement can use a phone as the control point. In a common HTTP arrangement, the control point supplies a selected media resource to the renderer's supported transport control, and the renderer retrieves the resource from the server. The controller need not relay every movie byte. UPnP AV provides named services for those responsibilities, including ContentDirectory, AVTransport, RenderingControl and ConnectionManager. Their presence and supported actions belong to the actual device implementation. A content description includes resource information This original selected DIDL-Lite fragment describes one fictional video resource: <DIDL-Lite xmlns="urn:schemas-upnp-org:metadata-1-0/DIDL-Lite/" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:upnp="urn:schemas-upnp-org:metadata-1-0/upnp/"> <item id="movie-1" parentID="0" restricted="1"> <dc:title>Harbour Evening</dc:title> <upnp:class>object.item.videoItem</upnp:class> <res protocolInfo="http-get:*:video/mp4:*" duration="00:02:00">https://media.example.invalid/demo.mp4</res> </item> </DIDL-Lite> protocolInfo identifies a transport/network/content-format/additional-information relationship. In this selected example, http-get and video/mp4 describe the offered retrieval and content type; the asterisks are part of the protocol-information syntax. The description is not the movie's encoded samples. An XML parser accepting it does not prove that the hypothetical MP4 is valid or that its video/audio configuration matches a renderer. A real DLNA resource can carry additional profile and capability information. The server's device profile can help choose an appropriate offered representation. Browsing and presentation use different paths The control point can browse successfully while the renderer cannot reach the named media address. The renderer may also accept the address but reject the encoded configuration. These observations belong to different stages: Device discovery. Content-description retrieval. Resource and renderer selection. Transport/control action handling. Media retrieval and presentation. An Emby server can expose or adapt media for the relevant receiving path where its DLNA integration is available. Direct Stream and video conversion remain stream-operation choices, separate from the discovery mechanism. One item can offer several media resources A catalogue item can describe more than one resource for the same content. One resource might carry the original representation while another offers a different compatible representation. For an original example, assume a two-minute item offers these alternatives: Resource Offered representation A MP4, H.264/AAC, 5 Mbit/s nominal combined rate B MP4, H.264/AAC, 2 Mbit/s nominal combined rate The item title and catalogue identity remain the same. The selected resource establishes which media bytes and configuration the renderer will receive. Its content-type label alone does not distinguish the nominal rates or prove support for every encoded configuration. Resource metadata, device capability and actual presentation need to be related to the selected alternative. An Emby device profile can participate in offering a suitable resource. Keeping item identity and resource choice separate also explains why two successful browses of the same title can lead to different delivered media. See Also DLNA device profiles and declared media constraints Playback remote control and reported session state Controller and receiver connectivity Direct Stream in Emby Casting and screen mirroring: where playback happens References OCF: UPnP AV devices and service specifications UPnP AV Architecture version 2 Emby API: DeviceProfile Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.title: DLNA device profiles and declared media constraints | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/dlna.keywords: DLNA device profiles and declared media constraints A DLNA device profile describes identification and media-handling rules used to offer a representation compatible with a particular receiving path. A DLNA device profile describes rules for a receiving media path. It helps the server identify the intended device context and offer media that fits the stated constraints. The profile declares compatibility information; it does not install another decoder in the receiving device. Identification and media rules do different work Emby's public DeviceProfile model includes identification and media-handling structures such as DirectPlayProfiles, TranscodingProfiles and CodecProfiles. Responsibility Question addressed Device identification Which receiving context should these rules describe? Direct-play rules Which offered source configurations can be used directly? Codec conditions Which limits apply within an encoded format? Conversion rules Which output representation can satisfy the receiving path? Response-related information How is the offered resource described for the receiver? Recognizing a television name and establishing support for a particular audio/video configuration are separate tasks. The model is also used in broader Emby playback negotiation. A namespace named DLNA should not be interpreted as proof that every profile instance belongs to a DLNA session. Work through an explicit invented profile Assume a teaching profile accepts: MP4 packaging. H.264 video up to 1920 × 1080 and thirty pictures per second. AAC audio up to two channels. A defined supported subtitle path. These are invented constraints, not a recommended Emby profile or a claim about a television. Selected source Mismatch under those rules Candidate operation MP4, 1080p24 H.264, stereo AAC None in the stated components Preserve the source Matroska, same video/audio Packaging Remux into a suitable MP4 arrangement MP4, same video, six-channel AC-3 Selected audio Prepare compatible audio while preserving video MP4, 4K60 H.264, stereo AAC Video dimensions/cadence Create a suitable video representation The table links each declared mismatch to an operation at the affected scope. A session can have several mismatches and need a combined output plan. Subtitles add another selected requirement. A profile satisfying video and audio does not establish that every subtitle can be rendered separately. A more permissive declaration changes what is offered If a profile says the receiver accepts a source it cannot actually use, the server can preserve an incompatible representation. If the profile understates support, the server can do unnecessary conversion. Both cases are possible because the declaration and the device's observed capability are different evidence. A successful result with one ordinary H.264 file also does not establish support for every profile, bit depth, cadence or container combination. The experiment needs the selected configuration that the rule describes. Relate an adjustment to the observed operation For an Emby investigation, preserve the matched device context, selected source/tracks and the server's resulting stream operations. Then compare the offered representation with the receiver's actual result. Playback information can establish whether video was preserved or encoded; the renderer observation establishes whether it could use the result. See Also DLNA media playback and UPnP AV roles Client playback capabilities What determines playback compatibility? Remuxing media containers Video transcoding in Emby References Emby API: DeviceProfile UPnP AV Architecture version 2 Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/casting/inde.title: Overview: Casting and remote playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/inde.keywords: Overview: Casting and remote playback Casting and remote playback separate control, media delivery and presentation across participating devices. The device that selects a film need not be the device that decodes or displays it. Casting, mirroring and remote control arrange those responsibilities differently. The protocol pages and connectivity topic identify the controller, receiver and server relationships needed to understand where an operation failed. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Casting and screen mirroring Casting and screen mirroring send presentation to another device through different media paths, with receiver playback or sender-screen transmission changing resource and processing requirements. Google Cast Google Cast connects a sender application to a receiver application that manages the selected media presentation and its resource-loading path. AirPlay AirPlay provides supported media-output and screen-mirroring routes whose sender, application and receiver choices determine how the presentation reaches another screen or audio device. DLNA playback DLNA playback uses discovery, media descriptions and device-specific compatibility information to connect a source with a receiver. Playback remote control Playback remote control sends commands to a selected playback session while reported state and actual media presentation establish what the receiving player did. Controller and receiver connectivity Remote playback depends on separate discovery, control and media-retrieval paths whose reachability and access contexts can succeed or fail independently. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Google Cast: Sender and receiver APIs Apple: AirPlay video streaming and screen mirroring Emby API: Remote control Google Cast: Discovery troubleshooting IETF RFC 6762: Multicast DNS

articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.title: AirPlay media presentation and screen mirroring | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.keywords: AirPlay media presentation and screen mirroring AirPlay provides supported media-output and screen-mirroring routes whose sender, application and receiver choices determine how the presentation reaches another screen or audio device. AirPlay can present supported media on another device and can also mirror a sender's screen. Those are different modes: choosing a receiver for video within an app is not necessarily the same operation as choosing Screen Mirroring. The app, sender platform and receiver determine which route is available and how that presentation behaves. Identify the selected mode User-visible arrangement Presentation being requested App-based video output The app's supported video presentation on a selected receiver Audio-output selection Audio through a supported remote output Screen Mirroring A representation of the sender's displayed screen Apple documents app-based video streaming and screen mirroring separately. It also states that some video apps might not support AirPlay. This means that operating-system support for AirPlay does not by itself establish support in a particular Emby app or media path. The specific app/version and available output option supply that evidence. A matched video can still produce different output Imagine an original comparison using the same source and subtitle selection. In screen mirroring, the phone first presents the video and subtitle on its displayed surface. The mirrored result can therefore contain that subtitle as part of the screen image. In an app-based media-output path, the app and receiver integration determine how video, audio and subtitle presentation are supplied. Seeing a subtitle on the phone before the switch does not establish that a separate subtitle track was delivered to the receiver. Picture dimensions can differ for the same reason. A mirrored screen includes the sender's composition and scaling, while another media-output route can prepare the programme using its own presentation path. The casting and mirroring comparison develops those media-route consequences. Receiver selection is one stage of connectivity Apple's documented consumer workflow for iPhone/iPad video streaming and mirroring uses the sender and compatible receiver on the same Wi-Fi network. This describes that workflow rather than every possible managed or peer-to-peer deployment. A receiver appearing in the output list establishes availability for selection under the current environment. Subsequent activation, media presentation and ongoing sender behavior are additional observations. If video fails after selection, preserve the mode that was chosen, the application, source and tracks, and whether any picture or audio actually started. That context distinguishes a missing app route from a failed session on an offered route. Controller behavior and media behavior need separate observations A pause command, a sender screen change and an output-route change can affect the active session differently. A mirroring session continues to depend on its screen source; an app-based media session follows its supported output integration. articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.title: Casting and screen mirroring: where playback happens | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.keywords: Casting and screen mirroring: where playback happens Casting and screen mirroring send presentation to another device through different media paths, with receiver playback or sender-screen transmission changing resource and processing requirements. Casting often makes one device a controller for playback on another. Screen mirroring sends a representation of the sender's displayed surface to a receiver. Both put a picture on another screen, but they can move media through different paths. Identifying that path explains which device needs the codec, where subtitles are rendered and which connection carries most of the media traffic. Receiver playback can leave the phone out of the media path In a typical media-casting arrangement, the controller tells a receiver what to play. The receiver then obtains the programme resource from its origin and performs playback. An Emby phone app can act as the controller while Emby Server delivers the selected representation to the receiver. The phone's ability to play the original source does not establish the receiver's compatibility. Mirroring includes the sender's presentation Screen mirroring captures or otherwise produces a representation of the sender's displayed surface. The receiving device presents that transmitted result. A movie originally encoded in one format can therefore be decoded on the sender, composed with its interface and subtitles, and transmitted as another representation. Scaling, display timing and the mirroring path can affect what reaches the larger screen. Property Receiver media playback Screen mirroring Primary media preparation Receiver's selected media path Sender presentation plus mirroring path Content represented Programme resource and selected features Sender's displayed surface Subtitle handling Receiver or delivered subtitle/video path Can be part of the captured displayed result Sender activity Controller lifecycle Ongoing screen/presentation source This comparison describes two arrangements. Products such as AirPlay offer multiple modes, so the visible brand or output button alone does not establish which arrangement is active. A picture-quality change needs a path explanation If an Emby cast receiver needs a lower-rate compatible representation, the server can change the delivered media. That is different from mirroring a high-resolution source after the phone has already scaled it into a smaller displayed surface. Likewise, a mirrored subtitle visible on the phone can appear as pixels in the transmitted screen. Receiver playback can instead select a separate subtitle rendition or require burn-in based on the receiver's capabilities. Recording the actual source, selected tracks and receiving mode makes those differences understandable. The sender's lifecycle follows its role A receiver pulling media can continue independently of individual controller interactions, subject to its application/session policy. A mirroring path needs its active sender presentation. A controller disappearing can still end a receiver session if that receiver's policy says to stop. Continued playback after a phone screen turns off is therefore evidence about a particular session, not a universal rule for all casting. Controller and receiver connectivity separates discovery, control and media retrieval so each route can be examined directly. articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.title: Google Cast and receiver-side media playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.keywords: Google Cast and receiver-side media playback Google Cast connects a sender application to a receiver application that manages the selected media presentation and its resource-loading path. Google Cast connects a sender app to a receiver app. The sender manages the user's interaction; the receiver manages presentation on the receiving device. For media casting, the receiver's playback path is the one that needs to obtain and use the selected programme resources. Emby's Chromecast documentation describes its casting integration. The receiver's load sequence A sender initiates or joins a Cast session and supplies a media load request through the supported application integration. A receiver can interpret or customize that request before its player loads the media. The receiver then retrieves the relevant resource, prepares its media path and reports playback status. Sender commands can request play, pause, seek and other supported behavior. A content identifier in a load request need not be the final direct resource URL. A custom receiver can resolve or alter the request under its own integration. Google's Web Receiver message-interception API is one documented mechanism for that behavior. Device and application capabilities both matter Google's media documentation separates container support, encoded-media configurations and device-specific limits. It also distinguishes facilities that need additional receiver integration. One concrete example is its published device list: third-generation Chromecast's stated H.264 path goes up to 1080p60, while Google TV Streamer lists additional video configurations including AV1. Those entries should not be flattened into “all Chromecast devices support the same formats.” Context Requirement to establish Receiver model Relevant decoding and output capabilities Receiver application Supported delivery, tracks and playback integration Selected source Actual codec configuration and packaging Audio/subtitle choice Additional selected media requirements Origin access Receiver can obtain the needed resources The sender's successful local playback establishes a different media path. Emby Server may supply an adapted representation for the receiver even when the phone played the original. Resource access belongs to the receiver The receiver must reach the addresses it uses. A server-local file path or a phone-only address is not automatically meaningful there. A Web Receiver also has the relevant web loading context. For script-managed delivery, cross-origin behavior can affect its requests. A phone's authenticated fetch does not prove that a separate receiver request has the same access state. Seeing the device in a Cast chooser establishes discovery. Successfully connecting a session establishes additional control communication. Neither observation, by itself, proves media-resource retrieval. Relate status to actual presentation Observation Evidence supplied Receiver appears in the chooser Discovery under the current environment Receiver application starts Session/application activation Load request is handled Receiver accepted that request stage Media bytes are obtained Retrieval succeeded for those resources Playback status advances Receiver reports progress in its playback context See Also Casting and screen mirroring: where playback happens Controller and receiver connectivity What determines playback compatibility? articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.title: Controller and receiver connectivity | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.keywords: Controller and receiver connectivity Remote playback depends on separate discovery, control and media-retrieval paths whose reachability and access contexts can succeed or fail independently. A controller finding a receiver is one successful interaction in a remote-playback session. The receiver still needs control communication and access to the resources it will present. Keeping discovery , control and media retrieval separate explains many apparently contradictory casting results. Three paths can have different endpoints Path Purpose Discovery Locate an offered receiving device or service Control/session communication Activate a receiver and request actions Media retrieval Obtain the programme, initialization and supporting resources Discovery can use local-network mechanisms such as multicast service discovery. Media retrieval commonly uses unicast HTTP connections to a media origin. Their successful paths need not be identical. For example, an original arrangement can have this result: Interaction Result Controller discovers receiver Succeeds Controller establishes receiver session Succeeds Controller obtains media from origin Succeeds Receiver obtains media from origin Fails The first three results do not contradict the fourth. They involve a different initiating device or protocol path. Addresses belong to the requesting device's context Suppose a controller can obtain a resource at: http://127.0.0.1:8096/media/example.mp4 This fictional locator points to loopback on the device making the request. Passing it unchanged to another receiver makes the receiver ask its own loopback address, not the controller's. A server's local file path has a similar scope problem. The receiver needs a resource locator meaningful and reachable in its own environment. Names also require receiver-side resolution. A hostname known on the controller need not resolve identically on another network segment or device. Shared wireless access is useful context, not complete evidence The documented consumer casting workflow often places devices on the same local network. A shared network name alone does not establish communication among every connected device: guest isolation, multicast handling, addressing and routed access can differ. Google's discovery documentation treats receiver discovery as a distinct troubleshooting stage. That supports a focused investigation of whether discovery reaches the intended devices before drawing conclusions about the movie's codec. The network topology is equally relevant when a controller can browse Emby Server remotely while the receiver tries another server address. Identify the address each device actually uses. A reachable resource still needs the right access context Successful TCP/HTTP reachability does not establish that a request is authorized or permitted through the receiving web player's loading rules. A Web Receiver fetching across origins needs the applicable Fetch/CORS behavior. Session-specific resource access must also remain valid for the receiver's request. An authenticated controller's success is scoped to that controller request. In segmented playback, the initial description, initialization, media and selected subtitle resources can each require access. Loading one playlist is not proof that all its resolved references can be obtained. See Also Google Cast and receiver-side media playback AirPlay media presentation and screen mirroring DLNA media playback and UPnP AV roles Playback remote control and reported session state Browser media playback and its loading paths What determines playback compatibility? articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.title: Playback remote control and reported session state | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/casting/Play.keywords: Playback remote control and reported session state Playback remote control sends commands to a selected playback session while reported state and actual media presentation establish what the receiving player did. Playback remote control lets one application request actions from another playback session. Play, pause, seek, track selection and volume operate on that receiving player's supported state. The controller can remain outside the media-delivery path. A pause command can travel through a server while movie bytes travel from the media origin directly to the receiver. Commands and status form a feedback path Stage What it establishes Controller forms a command Intended action and target session Command reaches the supported handler Receipt at that stage Player changes state Receiver-side action Updated state is reported Feedback available to the controller Programme presentation changes The user's observed result An HTTP response acknowledging a request does not, alone, describe the picture currently on screen. A receiver can need more media preparation before a requested seek becomes visible. Target the session that can accept the action Emby's remote-control API documentation describes selecting controllable sessions and supported commands. A client can filter sessions by the relevant user's control context. A discovered receiver and a currently controllable playback session are therefore different concepts. Sessions can end or be replaced; a command for an old session need not control the new one. Track selection also belongs to a particular source/session context. An audio-stream number from one source should not be assumed to identify the same language in another. Absolute actions and toggles have different intent Consider an original state example starting in Playing: Intent applied twice Result in the simplified state model Pause Paused, then still Paused Toggle play/pause Paused, then Playing The table models requested state meanings, not the retry contract of a particular HTTP API. It explains why a controller that repeats a toggle after uncertain feedback can undo the action it wanted. A useful user interface reconciles intended state with reported state. A delayed status message also needs its session and ordering context so it does not overwrite a newer observation incorrectly. Seek coordinates need their unit Emby exposes seek positions in ticks for the relevant remote-control operation. One second is ten million ticks. For an original request targeting programme second 95: 95 × 10,000,000 = 950,000,000 ticks That value is a media-time destination. It is not an HTTP byte offset or a wall-clock timestamp. The receiving player still resolves the seek through its media and decoding path. articles/playback-streaming/conversion/i.title: Overview: Conversion pipelines | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/i.keywords: Overview: Conversion pipelines Media conversion connects source decoding, optional processing and output encoding into a working representation. Conversion is a pipeline with dependencies between its stages. Picture or audio formats must match across those connections, and temporary output must remain available while the player consumes it. This branch separates the operations from their performance and capacity questions, including conversion performed outside a live playback session. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How a transcoding pipeline works A transcoding pipeline connects resource access, selected stream processing, timestamp handling and output packaging so that a new media representation can be delivered. Pipeline stages Conversion stages reconstruct, process and encode media through defined input and output relationships. Transcoding performance and capacity Transcoding performance compares pipeline progress and shared resource demand with the deadlines of active playback. Transcode temporary files Transcode temporary files hold generated session output whose size, availability and lifecycle differ from both the original media and the client’s playback buffer. Offline media conversion Offline media conversion prepares another media representation before playback, separating production time from the later session’s delivery deadlines. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References FFmpeg API: Send/receive encoding and decoding Emby: Transcoding IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Overview: Transcoding performance and capacity Transcoding performance compares pipeline progress and shared resource demand with the deadlines of active playback. A real-time operation needs to produce usable output quickly enough for the presentation. Processing speed, throttling and concurrent work affect that progress in different ways. These topics connect observed rate and waiting behavior to the pipeline stage or shared resource that sets the limit. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Real-time transcoding Real-time transcoding must supply usable media at the rate playback consumes it, with temporary buffer lead covering only finite production deficits. Transcoding speed Transcoding speed compares produced media-time progress with wall time, while fps, bitrate and completion describe different quantities. Transcode throttling Transcode throttling limits work produced ahead of playback by pausing or reducing a producer whose output lead is already sufficient. Transcoding bottlenecks A transcoding bottleneck is the limiting processing or delivery dependency under the actual workload, which may differ from the most visible utilisation counter.
