articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Transcoding bottlenecks | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Transcoding bottlenecks A transcoding bottleneck is the limiting processing or delivery dependency under the actual workload, which may differ from the most visible utilisation counter. A bottleneck is the dependency that limits the current job. It can be decoding, filtering, encoding, resource access, transfers or delivery. A prominent CPU or GPU percentage is an observation, not a complete identification of that dependency. The useful question is what prevents the next required usable media interval from becoming available in time. A three-stage model Assume original independent stage capacities for one specified picture format and workload: Stage Service capacity Ideal per-picture service time Decode 120 pictures/s 8.33 ms Filter 30 pictures/s 33.33 ms Encode 90 pictures/s 11.11 ms If the stages can overlap with sufficient buffering and do not share another limiting resource, steady throughput cannot exceed the slowest stage: 30 pictures/s. For a 24-fps output, that is 30 / 24 = 1.25x . The example has some idealised processing reserve, not a guarantee of smooth playback. Latency adds while overlapped throughput can differ A picture still needs the relevant work at each stage. The ideal sum of the listed service times is about 52.78 ms, before additional waits or buffering. If pictures were processed strictly one at a time through all three stages, that sum would yield about 18.95 pictures/s. Overlap lets different pictures occupy different stages, producing the higher steady 30-picture/s result. Thus reciprocal stage rates are useful for this defined model, but “the pipeline is 30 fps” does not mean every picture completes the whole dependency chain in 33.33 ms. An upgrade can leave the limit in place Doubling decode capacity from 120 to 240 pictures/s leaves the filter at 30. The ideal steady result stays 30. Raising filter capacity to 60 changes the result to 60. Raising it to 150 leaves encoding at 90 as the new limit. The limiting stage moves as capacities change. These are arithmetic outcomes for the assumed model, not measured improvements from buying a component or changing an Emby setting. Shared resources break simple independence Stages can compete for CPU cores, memory bandwidth or accelerator resources. A hardware decode path and hardware encode path can still require a filter in another memory domain. For an ideal 24,883,200-byte picture buffer, two full-picture transfers per frame at 24 fps would move about 1.194 GB/s. Actual transfer volume and memory layout vary. The point is that copied decoded data has another scale from the source's compressed bitrate. A graph that avoids a particular transfer can change that work. A utilisation counter alone does not establish whether a transfer was avoided. Likewise, a blocked output writer can slow the whole process while an encoder appears idle. Faster encoding cannot make an unavailable temporary directory writable or fix a constrained delivery path. Compare rates in compatible units Storage/network rates in bytes or bits per second cannot be compared directly with pictures per second without the relevant media representation. A source read rate concerns its encoded bytes. A picture transfer concerns raw surfaces. Output delivery concerns the generated encoded representation. Each conversion to “media seconds ready per wall second” needs the corresponding size/rate context. Total CPU usage can also hide a single saturated worker or serial dependency. Low overall usage is not proof that no CPU-bound stage exists. See Also How a transcoding pipeline works Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Concurrent playback workloads Media filter graphs Transcode temporary files and generated output References FFmpeg API: Send/receive encoding and decoding FFmpeg: Media filters Emby API: TranscodingInfo FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Concurrent playback workloads | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Concurrent playback workloads Concurrent playback capacity depends on the combined resource demands and timing of the actual session plans rather than only on a stream count. A stream count says how many sessions exist. It does not say what work they require. A copied original source, an audio-only conversion and an HDR picture conversion have different processing and delivery demands. Capacity needs the combined plans and their relevant shared resources. An original resource-demand model Let one unit represent each resource's available capacity. Use these invented per-session demand fractions: Session type CPU Video encoder Storage Network A, lighter picture conversion 0.15 0.20 0.05 0.08 B, filter-heavy conversion 0.45 0.40 0.10 0.15 D, original-source playback 0.01 0.00 0.04 0.12 The values are not benchmarks. They assume independent linear demand on the stated resources, solely to illustrate capacity reasoning. One B plus two A sessions totals 0.75 CPU, 0.80 encoder, 0.20 storage and 0.31 network. It fits each declared unit capacity. Two B plus three A sessions demand 1.35 CPU and 1.40 encoder, even though storage and network demand remain below one unit. A demand above one means the model requests more than the available service. It is not a claim that an observed utilisation percentage can physically exceed 100%. The most constrained sum controls the result Unused network capacity cannot substitute for missing encoder service. Likewise, a powerful encoder does not create additional storage throughput. Four D sessions in the same model require no video encoder demand but still add CPU, storage and network work. Direct Play is therefore a lighter conversion path, not zero shared-resource demand. The media source matters too. Selecting another existing compatible representation can change both conversion and delivered bitrate. The resulting workload should be assessed for the selected session plan. Starts and seeks are bursts Several steady sessions can be healthy while simultaneous startup creates more contention. Opening resources, initialising codecs, preparing first output and filling buffers concentrate work in another interval. Seeking can introduce another burst or restart. A previously comfortable buffer lead does not necessarily describe the newly requested destinations. Throttling can reduce unnecessary future production after enough lead exists. It does not eliminate the need to obtain the first usable intervals for sessions that start together. Real workloads need more evidence than linear addition Actual stages can share engines, threads, memory paths or scheduling policies. Content difficulty varies over time, and a job's active demand can change when its output is throttled. The original fractions provide a transparent model, not a universal estimator of how many Emby sessions a system supports. Observed tests need the actual sources, selected tracks, processing paths and time intervals. See Also Transcoding bottlenecks Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Direct Play in Emby Transcode throttling and producer lead Media source selection for playback References Emby API: TranscodingInfo Emby API: DeviceProfile Emby API: MediaSourceInfo FFmpeg API: Send/receive encoding and decoding

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Real-time transcoding must supply usable media at the rate playback consumes it, with temporary buffer lead covering only finite production deficits. Real-time transcoding needs to produce usable media soon enough for its playback deadlines. At ordinary speed, the viewer consumes about one second of media per second of wall time. A production path that sustains less than that rate loses ground. A prepared buffer can delay the resulting stall. It cannot make a persistent production deficit disappear. Production rate is media time divided by wall time If a job produces 60 seconds of usable output in 30 seconds, its average rate is 2 media seconds per wall second, commonly described as 2x. That result concerns the specified output and measured interval. It does not automatically predict another resolution, filter graph or concurrent workload. A pipeline also needs to produce all the data required for presentation. Having video ready while required audio or output packaging is delayed does not supply a complete playable interval. A thirty-second lead can drain Use an original simplified model: buffer lead Q(t) = Q(0) + (production rate - consumption rate) × t Assume the initial lead is 30 media seconds, production is 0.75 media seconds per wall second, and consumption is 1. The lead decreases by 0.25 seconds each second. Wall time since playback starts Remaining lead 0 seconds 30 seconds 40 seconds 20 seconds 80 seconds 10 seconds 120 seconds 0 seconds The model assumes a single relevant ready-data buffer and steady rates. Actual playback has several queues and can use recovery policies. After the buffer empties, uninterrupted playback is no longer supported by these assumptions. Adding a larger initial lead changes the waiting time. It does not change the negative slope. Playback rate changes the deadline At 1.5x playback, consumption is 1.5 media seconds per wall second. A producer at 1.2x then has a deficit of 0.3. With the same 30-second initial lead, the model reaches zero in 30 / 0.3 = 100 wall seconds . Calling 1.2x “faster than real time” without specifying playback rate hides that deficit. A deliberate pause in playback changes consumption instead. A deliberate transcode throttle changes production when enough lead exists. Neither is equivalent to an overloaded converter that cannot meet active demand. Server output is not client-ready media Suppose a server produces at 2x but the delivery path supplies 3 Mbit/s for a constant 6 Mbit/s representation. The simplified delivery rate is only 0.5 media seconds per wall second. A client buffer with 15 media seconds then drains in 30 wall seconds at ordinary playback. Fast conversion has not fixed the delivery constraint. Likewise, sufficient network goodput does not fix a slow client decoder or display path. Playback stalls and dropped frames describe different symptoms. Capacity needs margin over the tested interval Difficult source portions can cost more than easy ones. Storage, transfers and concurrent jobs can change the available service rate. A short high-speed sample therefore supplies evidence about that sample, rather than proof of sustainable capacity for every session. For a live source, the future input is not available in advance. An engine that could process stored media at 4x cannot create four future seconds of a real-time source before those seconds arrive. See Also Transcoding speed, fps and media time Transcoding bottlenecks Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Playback stalls and unavailable next media Transcode throttling and producer lead References FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress FFmpeg API: Send/receive encoding and decoding Emby API: TranscodingInfo FFmpeg: Container and segment formats

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Transcoding speed, fps and media time | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Transcoding speed, fps and media time Transcoding speed compares produced media-time progress with wall time, while fps, bitrate and completion describe different quantities. A speed multiplier compares media-time progress with wall time. Frames per second counts frame processing at a particular point. Encoded bitrate counts bits per media second. They are different units. Confusing them can make a normal or deliberately idle job appear too slow, or make a high frame-processing count look faster than it really is. An original progress excerpt frame=1440 fps=48 time=00:01:00.00 speed=2.00x Assume this excerpt describes a 24-fps output that produced 60 media seconds over 30 wall seconds: 1440 frames / 24 frames per media second = 60 media seconds 60 media seconds / 30 wall seconds = 2x The excerpt is an illustration, not a captured server log. Actual field availability and calculation details depend on the tool/version and output context. The output cadence determines the fps conversion Source cadence Output cadence Processing count rate Corresponding rate in the stated simple case 24 fps 24 fps 48 output frames/s 2x 24 fps 30 fps 60 output frames/s 2x About 59.94 fps About 29.97 fps About 59.94 output frames/s About 2x Dividing the second row's 60 by the source 24 would yield 2.5. That is not the output-media progress represented by the specified 30-fps output. Variable cadence and multiple outputs can need a more careful timestamp-based interpretation. A frame counter alone does not provide every timeline origin or duration. time is a media coordinate A progress time generally concerns output media progress, not the elapsed wall clock. Starting from another source position, copying timestamps or using another output origin can complicate the comparison. A diagnostic should establish the context and compare progress over a known wall-time interval. A source position of minute 20 is not evidence that the process ran for twenty minutes. Likewise, fps is not Mbit/s. A job can have high fps while producing a large output rate that overwhelms delivery. Active speed and waiting time A producer can intentionally pause after getting ahead. During that interval, little new media is produced. Averaging the quiet period with active processing gives another number from the engine's active speed. In an original idealised cycle, a producer active at 4x for one quarter of the wall time can average 1x over the full cycle. That can meet ordinary playback demand while avoiding conversion of the entire source immediately. A low recent progress value therefore needs the surrounding state: active conversion, throttling, input wait, output wait or failure. The value alone does not distinguish those causes. See Also Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Transcode throttling and producer lead Reading a transcoding log Video Frame Rate Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress FFmpeg: Time, duration and frame-rate conventions Emby API: TranscodingInfo

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Transcode throttling and producer lead | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Transcode throttling and producer lead Transcode throttling limits work produced ahead of playback by pausing or reducing a producer whose output lead is already sufficient. A converter can run faster than the viewer consumes its output. Throttling avoids producing unlimited future work when sufficient output already exists ahead of playback. It can therefore create bursts of processing followed by quiet periods without changing the selected output codec, resolution or rate-control target. Two positions define producer lead In a simple model: producer lead = ready output position - playback position If ready output reaches programme second 150 while playback reaches second 120, that model has a thirty-second lead. The lead describes a production relationship. It does not prove that those thirty seconds have reached the client, survived its buffer policy or been decoded. A server queue and a player queue are different places. An Emby team explanation from 2016 describes pausing when the producer is sufficiently ahead and resuming as playback catches up. That is evidence for the mechanism's purpose, not a specification of current thresholds or every implementation detail. An original high/low-threshold cycle Assume an invented producer that runs at 4x when active. Playback consumes at 1x. The model pauses at a thirty-second lead and resumes at a ten-second lead. Using separate stop and restart thresholds is called hysteresis. It avoids toggling immediately at one shared boundary. During active production, lead grows at 4 - 1 = 3 seconds per wall second . Growing by twenty seconds therefore takes about 6.67 wall seconds. While paused, the same twenty seconds drain in twenty wall seconds. The cycle lasts about 26.67 seconds, of which the producer is active for 6.67. Its idealised active fraction is one quarter. This is a calculation for the stated model, not an Emby performance measurement. Quiet is different from unable A paused producer with adequate ready output is behaving differently from an active producer that sustains only 0.75x and is losing lead. The first can resume before its chosen reserve is exhausted. The second needs a capacity or workload change to become sustainable. A CPU percentage or one recent speed sample does not distinguish those states by itself. Throttling also does not mean the player is being intentionally paused. The intended result is ongoing playback using already prepared media while future production rests. A seek changes the needed region If the viewer seeks beyond the produced interval, the old lead no longer describes the data required at the destination. A playback path may need to resume or restart production from another location. That can introduce a new wait even when the converter had been comfortably ahead of the old position. Seeking during streaming develops the destination dependencies. The chosen high/low values trade reserve against produced work and storage. Longer lead can prepare more future data; shorter lead can avoid generating output never viewed. Neither value creates processing capacity or network throughput. Output remains a separate configuration Pausing production is a scheduling decision. Reducing video bitrate or picture size is an output-representation decision. Both can affect load, but they solve different problems. See Also Transcoding speed, fps and media time Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Transcode temporary files and generated output References Emby team: Transcode throttling mechanism (2016) Emby: Transcoding Emby API: TranscodingInfo

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Overview: Pipeline stages | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Overview: Pipeline stages Conversion stages reconstruct, process and encode media through defined input and output relationships. Decoding turns a coded stream into a usable signal representation. Filters operate on that representation, and encoding produces a coded result for storage or delivery. A filter graph connects those operations explicitly, which helps explain why a stage can work alone yet fail within the chosen sequence. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Decoding Decoding reconstructs pictures or audio samples from encoded stream data, with configuration, dependencies and timing determining when usable frames become available. Encoding Encoding creates an encoded stream from prepared pictures or samples, with output configuration and rate-control decisions determining its compatibility, size and processing cost. Media filter graphs A media filter graph connects decoded-frame transformations through defined input/output relationships whose order, format and branching affect the result. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References FFmpeg API: Decoding FFmpeg API: Encoding FFmpeg: Media filters

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Decoding media streams | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Decoding media streams Decoding reconstructs pictures or audio samples from encoded stream data, with configuration, dependencies and timing determining when usable frames become available. A decoder turns encoded data into reconstructed pictures or audio samples. It needs the relevant codec configuration and valid input data; it may also need reference information from other parts of the stream. That makes decoding a different operation from reading a container's stream list. A probe can identify a codec without reconstructing every later picture. Packets are not necessarily displayed frames A demuxer supplies encoded packets. A decoder supplies frames in its output representation. The relationship need not be one packet in, one frame out. A packet can contribute partial data, supply configuration or contain data associated with several outputs. A decoder can retain input while waiting for dependencies and can later produce buffered output. FFmpeg's send/receive API documents this decoupled relationship. It is a useful reference for why a program must handle “input accepted, no frame yet” without treating every such result as a decoding failure. Decode order can differ from presentation order In an original illustrative picture sequence: Picture label Presentation position Dependency purpose I0 0 Starting independently coded picture B1 1 A picture using surrounding reference context B2 2 Another picture using surrounding reference context P3 3 Later reference picture A decoder can need P3 before reconstructing B1 and B2. The encoded/decode sequence can therefore be I0, P3, B1, B2 , while presentation remains I0, B1, B2, P3 . The shorthand is not a complete H.264 or HEVC bitstream specification. Packet timestamps and reference dependencies supply the real ordering context. A player presenting the pictures immediately in decode order would show the wrong sequence. Correct reconstruction and correct scheduling are both needed. Audio frames carry sample intervals For an original example, a decoded audio frame containing 1,024 samples per channel at 48,000 samples per second covers: 1024 / 48000 = 0.021333... seconds That is about 21.33 milliseconds. It is a specified example frame size, not a universal property of every audio codec or profile. Several channels share that interval while carrying their separate samples. A six-channel frame does not last six times longer merely because it contains six sets of samples. The raw sample representation can use different formats and channel layouts. A processing stage must interpret those properties rather than treating every decoded byte as the same kind of PCM. Decoding needs memory and state Reference pictures and reordered output can occupy buffers. Input configuration changes can require a different decoder state. Hardware decoding can produce frames in an accelerator's surface representation rather than immediately accessible software arrays. Those details affect initialisation and transfers to later filters. The codec name alone does not tell a pipeline how much buffering or movement is required. At the end of input, a decoder can still hold delayed output. Draining that state is different from receiving a new packet. A program that stops at the last input packet without handling delayed frames can truncate valid output. A decode result has a scope Successfully reconstructing one frame proves something about that inspected data. It does not validate every later packet, the output display path or a server's ability to sustain the requested rate. An unavailable hardware decoder, malformed input and a slow but valid decoder also describe different failures or limitations. Playback error categories separates those observations. In Direct Play the client still performs relevant decoding. In a server-side picture conversion, the server decodes before filtering and encoding another representation. articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Encoding a new media representation | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Encoding a new media representation Encoding creates an encoded stream from prepared pictures or samples, with output configuration and rate-control decisions determining its compatibility, size and processing cost. An encoder creates a new stream representation from prepared pictures or audio samples. A video encoder does not simply relabel the source's compressed packets. It makes new coding decisions for the pictures it receives. If H.264 is decoded and then encoded into H.264 again, the codec family remains the same while the stream representation changes. The input is already prepared An encoder receives pictures or samples in a format it can use. Their dimensions, cadence, channel layout and other properties have been established or transformed by upstream work. Requirement Relevant output property The player accepts another codec/configuration Encoded format and parameters The picture was scaled Output dimensions Audio was mixed to stereo Output channel presentation Delivery has a rate constraint Rate-control/output policy A cadence change was requested Encoded picture timing/cadence Encoding cannot make a wrongly selected commentary track become the intended main programme. It can faithfully encode the samples it was given while the selection remains wrong. Rate, quality and time interact A bitrate target constrains one aspect of the output. The quality obtainable under that constraint depends on content, dimensions, cadence and the encoder's decisions. A constant-quality approach aims at another control variable and lets size/rate vary. An encoder preset can alter the amount of search or analysis. These choices affect work and compression efficiency; they are not interchangeable names for one quality slider. The existing rate-control and preset articles develop those subjects. Here the important boundary is that their decisions occur when a new encoded representation is created. A lossy mode approximates reconstructed input. A lossless mode has another preservation objective and can carry different rate/compatibility consequences. The mere presence of an encoder does not define one universal percentage of quality loss. Encoder output still needs packaging A video encoder can supply encoded packets and configuration. A muxer writes the container or delivery package that carries them. That is why “the encoder supports H.264” and “the target path accepts this MP4 resource” are different statements. Container structure, selected audio, subtitle handling and timing remain relevant outside the encoder. The send/receive model can also have delayed output. An encoder can buffer input for its decisions, then produce packets later. Initial output latency and sustained encoding throughput need their own measurements. Hardware identifies a stage A named hardware video encoder describes a supported implementation path for that stage. It does not establish that the decoder or filters use the same accelerator, that all frames remain in one memory domain, or that the complete job is fast enough. A pipeline can use hardware encoding after software picture processing. Another can move surfaces between devices. Bottlenecks depend on those complete relationships. articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.title: Media filter graphs | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/p.keywords: Media filter graphs A media filter graph connects decoded-frame transformations through defined input/output relationships whose order, format and branching affect the result. A filter graph connects media transformations. Its edges carry pictures or samples in compatible representations; its nodes perform operations such as scaling, mixing or rendering. Order and connectivity are part of the meaning. A collection of enabled options does not, by itself, describe how their outputs reach the next stage. A source can feed two branches This original FFmpeg-style graph expression splits one decoded video input and scales the branches to two sizes: [0:v:0]split=2[a][b];[a]scale=1280:720[main];[b]scale=320:180[small] The labels connect outputs to later inputs. In this example: Label Relationship 0:v:0 The selected video input context a and b Outputs of the split main The 1280 × 720 branch output small The 320 × 180 branch output The expression is not an executed conversion. Downstream encoders, output mappings and resource packaging are another part of the job. One branch producing preview-sized pictures does not make the main programme 320 × 180. The connections determine which result reaches which output. A graph output also needs to be consumed by the intended path rather than merely declared. Operation order can change the result Suppose the source picture is 1920 × 1080 and the destination is 1280 × 720. The size ratio is 2/3. If a 48-pixel-high text overlay is painted before scaling, its geometric height scales to 32 pixels. If the picture is scaled first and a 48-pixel overlay is painted afterward, the output overlay remains 48 pixels high. Those are different presentations even though both graphs contain the same broad operations. The calculation is a geometry model; actual font rasterization and filter behavior can introduce additional detail. Colour processing has a similar ordering issue. An overlay must have an appropriate signal interpretation at the point where it joins the pictures. A graph cannot assume every input already uses the same range, transfer function or pixel format. Filters require usable representations A scaling filter operates on picture data, not on opaque copied video packets. That is why a stream-copy path cannot also perform ordinary picture scaling. Connected filters can impose requirements on dimensions, sample format, colour or memory domain. The graph implementation may need an explicit or negotiated format conversion between them. A mismatch can cause initialisation failure even when every named filter exists individually. The failure concerns the connection between representations, not merely a missing codec. Branching changes workload Splitting a decoded frame can avoid decoding the same source twice in a suitable graph. It does not make every downstream operation free: each branch can still need filtering, buffers and encoding. A preview branch and a full-resolution branch have different amounts of picture data. They can also compete for shared processing or transfer resources. Likewise, a hardware encoder after the graph does not establish how the graph's filters ran. Software filters, accelerator filters and surface transfers remain distinct work. The complete pipeline supplies that context. See Also What is a graph? articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.title: Offline media conversion and prepared versions | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.keywords: Offline media conversion and prepared versions Offline media conversion prepares another media representation before playback, separating production time from the later session’s delivery deadlines. Offline conversion produces another media representation before the viewer starts using it. The work can take longer than the programme's duration without interrupting a live viewing session. A prepared version can then be selected as an existing source. That shifts when the conversion happens; it does not remove the later requirements for access, delivery, decoding and presentation. Prepared and session-generated output Question Prepared representation On-demand playback conversion When is the encoding work done? Before playback is requested During the playback job Which deadline governs production? The preparation workflow The session's consumption needs How is the output retained? As an intended resource with its own lifecycle As generated session output under delivery policy Can another session reuse it? If made available and selected appropriately Depends on implementation and representation context A download of the original file is a different operation from converting it. A client can also store a converted version for offline use, but storage location and conversion are separate decisions. A defined original conversion example For an SDR, 16:9 source, this illustrative command requests 720p H.264 video and stereo AAC: ffmpeg -i source.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -vf scale=1280:720 -c:v libx264 -b:v 6M -c:a aac -b:a 192k -ac 2 prepared.mp4 It was not executed for an actual media file. The named encoders and format must be available in the tool being used. The command also does not implement an HDR-to-SDR colour conversion. The selected input streams become a new output set. Extra audio, subtitles, chapters and attachments require their own decisions rather than being assumed to survive every preparation command. Conditional time and storage estimates If a 108-minute programme is processed at an average 2x, the ideal processing-time estimate is 54 minutes. If its average combined output rate is 6.192 Mbit/s over 6,480 seconds: 6,192,000 × 6,480 / 8 = 5,015,520,000 bytes That is about 5.016 GB in decimal units before additional packaging effects. An encoder's bitrate target does not guarantee that exact average rate or file size, and conversion speed can vary across the content. These estimates explain the dependencies without claiming an actual benchmark. A prepared source still needs a meaning The representation should retain which work, episode and edition it represents. A smaller encode of the same cut is different from an abridged or edited version. Its own streams, indexes and timing need analysis. Selecting audio index 2 from the old source can be wrong if the prepared resource has another stream set. A corresponding resume position also needs the represented timeline. Preserving scene timing is useful when an encode preserves the sequence; changes to introductions, cadence interpretation or editorial content can require another association. Preparation changes the later trade-off A compatible prepared resource can reduce per-session conversion work while adding retained storage and preparation time. A representation made for one target can still need another plan on a different player path. articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.title: Transcode temporary files and generated output | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.keywords: Transcode temporary files and generated output Transcode temporary files hold generated session output whose size, availability and lifecycle differ from both the original media and the client’s playback buffer. A playback conversion can create generated output for the session: media chunks, container initialization data, indexes or playlists. Those resources differ from the original library media and from data the player has already received. Their lifecycle belongs to the conversion/delivery job. A file's existence on the server does not mean it is a permanent alternative edition or a usable interval currently buffered at the client. Ready media occupies bytes Assume an original constant-average output of 6.192 Mbit/s. Preparing 120 seconds of output represents: 6,192,000 bits/s × 120 s / 8 = 92,880,000 bytes Under an additional six-second-segment assumption, one interval carries about 4,644,000 payload bytes and twenty intervals cover those 120 seconds. These are arithmetic assumptions, not Emby segment or throttle defaults. Container overhead, indexes, bitrate variation and any retained earlier data add other space. If the model also retains thirty seconds behind playback, that adds about 23,220,000 payload bytes. Retaining past output and producing future output are different contributors to the stored set. Server output and player buffer A generated interval can exist on disk before the player requests it. The player can also retain data after its corresponding server-side resource is no longer needed under a suitable lifecycle policy. A progress bar based on media position, a list of generated files and the player's buffered ranges therefore describe different states. A filename also does not prove a completed usable resource. A process can have created a file while still writing it, and a dependent index may not yet expose it. The temporary directory has an owner Emby's Transcoding documentation describes its temporary location as writable scratch space that the server manages and cleans. It is a dedicated generated-output area, with a lifecycle different from source storage. Access failures, full storage or a blocked writer can prevent usable output even when the video encoder itself is working. Several sessions can also combine their write/read demands. The cleanup responsibility matters because files in that location are not ordinary archival library assets. Output still required by an active session needs to remain available under the applicable implementation policy. A seek can require another output region A seek beyond prepared media can cause new generation from another source location. Older intervals might become irrelevant to the request, but their actual deletion/reuse behavior depends on the delivery implementation. Generated output does not make the whole original programme seekable under every player path. Seeking needs resource, access-point and timeline context as well. See Also Transcode throttling and producer lead Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Concurrent playback workloads How a transcoding pipeline works References Emby: Transcoding FFmpeg: Container and segment formats IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.title: How a transcoding pipeline works | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/conversion/P.keywords: How a transcoding pipeline works A transcoding pipeline connects resource access, selected stream processing, timestamp handling and output packaging so that a new media representation can be delivered. A transcoding pipeline forms a graph of connected operations that use different kinds of data. The input is a stored or incoming media resource. Some stages handle compressed packets; others need reconstructed pictures or audio samples. The output is encoded media packaged for a playback path. Understanding those boundaries explains both what a conversion changes and where its time or memory cost can arise. A concrete conversion plan Take an original fictional 108-minute source with 4K HEVC HDR video, six-channel AC-3 audio and a text subtitle. The chosen target is 1280 × 720 H.264 SDR, stereo AAC and separately usable subtitle text. The plan contains three different stream paths: The diagram describes dependencies. Emby may schedule, fuse or accelerate operations differently. The video needs a new picture presentation and encoding. The audio needs a new channel/codec presentation. The text does not need to become video pixels in this plan. If the target instead requires subtitle burn-in, those pixels become another input to picture processing. From resource bytes to selected packets The resource reader obtains input bytes. A demuxer interprets the container and exposes its streams and packet timing. Selection decides which streams contribute to the output. This matters when several audio tracks or subtitle types are present. Decoding the wrong audio track successfully still produces the wrong programme. A correct pipeline starts with the intended resource and track identities. The demuxer can also provide format information, chapters and codec configuration. Those descriptions help initialise downstream stages. They are not the decoded pictures themselves. Boundary Data at that point Resource access Container or incoming delivery bytes Demuxed video/audio Encoded packets and associated timing/configuration Decoder output Reconstructed video pictures or audio samples Picture/audio filters Frames in the formats those filters require Encoder output A newly encoded stream representation Muxer/packager output Bytes organised for the delivery resource A compatible stream-copy branch can bypass reconstruction and encoding. It still needs valid selection, timing and output packaging. Reconstruct before changing pictures or samples A decoder interprets compressed data. It can need reference pictures, codec configuration and enough input before it produces a usable output frame. Picture filters then operate on a suitable decoded representation. For the example, colour/range conversion and scaling prepare the SDR 720p pictures. Their exact algorithms are separate subjects; the important pipeline fact is that their inputs and outputs are picture data. Audio takes another branch. A decoder supplies samples; channel processing prepares the stereo presentation; the audio encoder produces AAC. Video and audio therefore can have different costs and buffering while sharing one output timeline. The separately delivered text keeps its timing association. It does not pass through the video encoder merely because the video is being transcoded. Decoded data changes the memory scale A compressed stream at 35 Mbit/s represents about 4.375 MB/s in decimal units. Its decoded picture data can be far larger. Assume an ideal unpadded 3840 × 2160, 4:2:0 picture stored in 16-bit containers per sample: 3840 × 2160 × 1.5 samples per pixel × 2 bytes per sample = 24,883,200 bytes per picture At 24 pictures per second, that layout represents 597,196,800 bytes per second of picture buffers. Five such buffers occupy 124,416,000 bytes. These are layout calculations, not measured Emby memory use. Actual surfaces can use other layouts, alignment, compression or memory domains. A processing step can also require an intermediate representation different from the decoder's output. The calculation explains why transfers between processing stages can matter even when the encoded bitrate seems small. A hardware decoder and hardware encoder do not automatically eliminate every movement of picture data between them. Encode the prepared representation The video encoder receives the prepared pictures and creates a stream meeting the target configuration. The output resolution, cadence, colour interpretation and rate-control choices describe this new representation. The audio encoder does the corresponding job for its prepared samples. A muxer can then interleave the encoded outputs, retain needed configuration and write the chosen container or delivery package. An encoder does not normally produce a complete MP4 merely because it produces H.264 packets. The packaging stage supplies the container structures. Likewise, a successful mux cannot rescue an upstream branch that never produced valid data. Preserve a timeline across the stages Each stage needs to retain or deliberately transform presentation timing. Audio and video clocks must refer to the intended programme moments, even if their packet cadence differs. Suppose playback is requested from programme minute 10. An original simplified delivery model can start its new output clock at zero while retaining an association with source second 600: programme time = output time + 600 seconds Output second 12 then represents programme second 612. Copying an unqualified output timestamp into a user resume record would lose that association. Another path may retain source-origin timestamps instead. The example explains why the mapping matters; it does not specify every Emby timestamp policy. Seeking develops the access-point and timing dependencies. The first picture and sustained throughput are different results Before output can be used, resource access, parsing, decoder initialisation and any needed reference data must be available. Filters and encoders can introduce additional startup buffering. The output path then needs enough usable packaged data for the player. After startup, stages may overlap. One stage can decode later pictures while another encodes earlier ones. That can improve steady throughput without making the first frame's entire dependency chain disappear. A pipeline can therefore have noticeable startup delay and then run faster than real time. It can also start quickly but lose ground during difficult portions. Real-time capacity and startup delay describe those different observations. See Also What is a graph? articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.title: Overview: HLS delivery | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.keywords: Overview: HLS delivery HLS delivery connects playlists with the media segments and timeline information they describe. A playlist describes which resources belong to a presentation and how they are organized; the segments carry the media. A player uses both as the stream advances or changes representation. These pages explain the HLS relationship before a missing segment or stale playlist is treated as an encoding problem. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) HTTP Live Streaming describes a media presentation through playlists that direct a player to successive media intervals and, when offered, alternative representations. HLS playlists HLS playlists describe representation choices or ordered media intervals, with tags carrying duration, initialization, publication and continuity information. HLS media segments HLS media segments carry timed media intervals whose packaging, initialization and decoding dependencies determine how a player can enter and assemble the stream. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational)

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.title: HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.keywords: HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) HTTP Live Streaming describes a media presentation through playlists that direct a player to successive media intervals and, when offered, alternative representations. HTTP Live Streaming , usually called HLS , lets a player discover a media presentation through playlists and retrieve its media over HTTP. An .m3u8 resource usually contains text describing other resources. It is a starting point for playback rather than a video codec. HLS can carry the output of an Emby session, but its presence does not identify whether video was copied, audio was converted or video was newly encoded. Those are stream-operation decisions . A playlist leads to the media An HLS presentation may begin with a multivariant playlist, called a Master Playlist in RFC 8216. It describes available variant streams and associated rendition groups. A chosen variant leads to a media playlist, which identifies successive media intervals. A simple presentation can start directly at a media playlist. No multivariant layer is needed when the player is being given one sequence. A typical request journey is: Obtain the starting playlist. Select a suitable variant and associated tracks when alternatives exist. Read the selected media playlist. Obtain required initialization and media resources. Prepare and present samples while retrieving later media ahead. These are responsibility boundaries, not a required one-request-at-a-time schedule. A player can overlap retrieval, parsing and presentation. The details of the text appear in HLS playlists . Format, track and quality are separate choices HLS does not mean “H.264 in a Transport Stream.” Its media formats include fragmented MP4 and other defined arrangements. The receiver still needs support for the actual container, encoded streams and selected presentation features. Property Example question Delivery protocol Is this presentation described using HLS? Media packaging Are the intervals fragmented MP4 or another supported format? Video encoding Can the receiver decode this H.264 or HEVC configuration? Rendition selection Which audio language or subtitle rendition was chosen? Representation selection Does another suitable quality cover the same programme time? An alternate language is a rendition choice. Moving to a lower-rate video representation is an adaptation choice. Merely listing multiple languages does not create a bitrate ladder. A server can publish HLS for a single session-specific conversion. In that case the player may receive one representation, even though HLS can also describe several. Adaptive bitrate streaming requires additional alternatives and selection behavior. A finite presentation and a growing presentation publish differently A complete on-demand media playlist can describe the whole sequence and indicate that no more segments will be added. A live media playlist changes as new intervals become available; older intervals may leave its published window. A player of the changing presentation needs refreshed information. It cannot obtain future media simply by predicting a filename. Publication controls which intervals are available and which timing context accompanies them. HLS low-latency extensions add mechanisms such as partial segments and more responsive playlist retrieval. They are developed in Low-latency streaming . RFC 8216 is an informational 2017 publication describing protocol version 7; it is a useful baseline rather than a complete account of later extensions. See Also HLS playlists: variants, media order and live windows HLS media segments and initialization Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection Common Media Application Format (CMAF) Low-latency streaming and the live presentation delay Direct Stream in Emby References IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational) Apple: HTTP Live Streaming Apple: Enabling Low-Latency HLS Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.title: HLS playlists: variants, media order and live windows | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.keywords: HLS playlists: variants, media order and live windows HLS playlists describe representation choices or ordered media intervals, with tags carrying duration, initialization, publication and continuity information. An HLS playlist is a text description that helps the player choose or locate media. Its tags give meaning to the resource names: duration, track associations, initialization, continuity and whether further intervals can appear. Reading it as a list of filenames misses the relationships needed for playback. Representation choices come before interval choices This original multivariant example offers two H.264/AAC variants. The rates and dimensions are teaching inputs, not Emby defaults: #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:7 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1728000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2" 720/main.m3u8 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3328000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2" 1080/main.m3u8 The URI following each EXT-X-STREAM-INF line identifies that variant's media playlist. It does not identify the first video segment. BANDWIDTH describes a peak segment-rate requirement for the variant's playable combinations under the HLS definition; it is not a promise of the client's measured download speed. RESOLUTION gives the stated video dimensions, and CODECS describes the encoded formats the client may encounter. A real ladder must use values appropriate to its actual media. Choosing a bandwidth number because it looks like a desirable quality label can mislead the selection policy. A media playlist establishes order and duration The selected media playlist can instead look like this original on-demand example: #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:7 #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6 #EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:120 #EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD #EXT-X-MAP:URI="init.mp4" #EXTINF:5.500, segment-120.m4s #EXTINF:6.000, segment-121.m4s #EXTINF:4.500, segment-122.m4s #EXT-X-ENDLIST Each EXTINF describes the duration of the media segment named after it. These three intervals total sixteen seconds. Within this simple timeline, their cumulative boundaries are 0, 5.5, 11.5 and 16 seconds. EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6 is not a command to make every interval exactly six seconds long. The HLS constraint compares each media-segment duration, rounded to the nearest integer, with the target duration. The example's values satisfy that limit. EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:120 gives the first listed segment's sequence number. The following segments are 121 and 122. The first displayed interval can begin at programme time zero in this fictional complete presentation even though its sequence number is 120. Sequence identity and media time are different coordinates. EXT-X-MAP supplies the initialization-resource locator for these fragmented MP4 segments. EXT-X-ENDLIST indicates that no more media segments will be added. The VOD playlist type gives additional publication rules for a completed, unchanging presentation. Resource names have a base Relative locators are resolved against the playlist containing them. If the media playlist is at: https://media.example.invalid/demo/720/main.m3u8 then segment-120.m4s refers to the same /demo/720/ directory. It does not automatically inherit the directory of a separately loaded multivariant playlist. This address is a fictional URI-resolution example; no server was contacted. A player or receiver must be able to retrieve each resolved resource using the relevant access context. Receiving the initial playlist does not transfer all its named media along with it. A live window can move without renumbering retained segments Imagine two snapshots of an original six-second-interval live presentation: Snapshot First sequence Listed intervals Earlier 120 120, 121, 122 Later 121 121, 122, 123 The second snapshot has removed 120 and added 123. Segments 121 and 122 retain their sequence identities. A client comparing those values can distinguish retained media from newly advertised media. In this example each window advertises eighteen seconds, but the later window covers a later programme interval. An unchanged number of rows does not mean publication has stopped. The player also needs discontinuity context when relevant. If a removed interval carried a discontinuity marker, a rolling playlist cannot simply lose the information that establishes the remaining segments' continuity sequence. A playlist answers a publication question A playlist shows which resources the publisher describes at that snapshot. It does not establish that the client has fetched them, that their contents match the description or that their decoder configuration is supported. These observations help interpret a real session: Observation Evidence it supplies A variant is listed An offered representation and its declared attributes A segment appears An advertised media interval The same sequence remains after reload Retained interval identity in the published window A segment request completes Retrieved resource bytes The player advances through that interval Successful preparation and presentation See Also HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) HLS media segments and initialization Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection Live streams and on-demand streams Stream discontinuities and timeline changes References IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational) Apple: HTTP Live Streaming IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and range requests

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.title: HLS media segments and initialization | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/hls.keywords: HLS media segments and initialization HLS media segments carry timed media intervals whose packaging, initialization and decoding dependencies determine how a player can enter and assemble the stream. An HLS media segment carries a described interval of the presentation. The media playlist identifies it and gives its duration. The player retrieves its bytes, interprets their packaging and uses the samples on the intended timeline. A segment's filename does not identify the video codec or prove that the media is self-contained. Two packaging arrangements HLS supports specified media-segment formats. Two common video arrangements are MPEG-2 Transport Stream and fragmented MP4. Arrangement Where important interpretation information appears Transport Stream Transport-stream structure, programme information and encoded-stream configuration Fragmented MP4 Initialization track descriptions plus media-fragment timing and sample data A .ts segment can carry encoded video and audio within transport-stream packets. “TS” names the container arrangement rather than H.264, HEVC or another video encoding. For fragmented MP4, a schematic relationship is: Initialization: ftyp + moov (track and sample descriptions) Media: moof (fragment metadata) + mdat (sample bytes) This is a selected-box sketch, not a complete valid file. The ISO BMFF byte-stream reference and HLS specification define additional structure and constraints. The HLS EXT-X-MAP tag names the applicable initialization resource. Downloading a later media fragment does not replace the need to know how its track identifiers and encoded configuration should be interpreted. Independent entry is a stronger property A segment boundary is a delivery boundary. A suitable video random-access point is a decoding property. If pictures near a boundary depend on earlier pictures, the player may need prior encoded data or start at another suitable access point. A publisher advertising EXT-X-INDEPENDENT-SEGMENTS asserts that the segments satisfy the protocol's independence requirement. It cannot create independence simply by adding the tag to an arbitrary split. This distinction explains why packaging and encoding are often coordinated. Segment boundaries intended for quality switching or seeking need appropriate timing and decoding relationships. Video keyframes explains the underlying access-point concepts. Splitting does not require another encode A delivery job can package copied encoded video into segments while preserving its picture representation. That is compatible with an Emby Direct Stream session. Alternatively, a converter can generate a new representation and package its output in the same delivery format. The resulting resource names can look similar in both cases. The evidence of copying or encoding lies in the stream operations , not in a .m4s or .ts suffix. Media duration and byte size vary independently A segment lasting four seconds can be much larger than its neighbor of the same duration. Scene complexity and encoding decisions determine payload size. The playlist duration helps establish the timeline; actual byte arrival helps determine whether the next interval is available in time. Separate video, audio and text resources can also have different interval boundaries. A subtitle cue may span a video-segment boundary, while an audio stream uses its own sample cadence. The player assembles their presentation relationships rather than requiring all resources to be identical little files. When track configuration or timing changes, discontinuity handling supplies the boundary context needed to continue interpreting later media.
