articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.title: Overview: HTTP file delivery | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.keywords: Overview: HTTP file delivery HTTP file delivery exposes media bytes through progressive access or requests for particular ranges. A player can receive the beginning of a file while more data are still arriving, or ask for a range needed at another position. Those request patterns serve different parts of startup and seeking. The pages here relate the HTTP exchange to the file structure the player must interpret. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Progressive download Progressive download plays a media resource while its bytes are still arriving, using container information and buffered data to prepare the next presentation. HTTP range requests An HTTP range request asks for selected bytes of a resource representation, allowing a media player to retrieve the regions needed for container analysis or playback. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and range requests

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.title: HTTP range requests for media resources | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.keywords: HTTP range requests for media resources An HTTP range request asks for selected bytes of a resource representation, allowing a media player to retrieve the regions needed for container analysis or playback. A player can need bytes near the end of a file before it has downloaded the middle. HTTP range requests let it ask for a selected part of a resource representation. This helps obtain indexes, resume transfers and retrieve the encoded data around a seek destination . The coordinates are byte offsets. The server is not being asked to “play minute twenty” by a Range header. Inclusive byte intervals An original illustrative exchange requests part of a million-byte resource: GET /media/example.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Range: bytes=100000-199999 HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 100000-199999/1000000 Content-Length: 100000 Offsets begin at zero, and both endpoints are included: 199999 - 100000 + 1 = 100000 bytes The Content-Range describes where the response body belongs in the complete representation. The Content-Length describes the response body length here, not the full movie size. Neither number establishes the duration represented by those bytes. Two further forms have different meanings: Request range Requested portion of a 1,000,000-byte representation bytes=900000- From offset 900,000 through the end: 100,000 bytes bytes=-65536 The final 65,536 bytes: offsets 934,464–999,999 bytes=0-0 The first single byte A suffix request can help a parser obtain information stored near the end. Its usefulness depends on the container layout and the player, not just on the fact that the request is accepted. The response decides what actually arrived A range request is a request for optional server behavior. The player must interpret the response status and fields rather than assume the server sent the selected interval. Response Meaning relevant to media retrieval 206 Partial Content The response supplies a selected range or ranges 200 OK The server can be supplying the complete representation instead 416 Range Not Satisfiable The requested range cannot be satisfied for the selected representation For a simple unsatisfiable byte-range response, Content-Range: bytes */1000000 can communicate the current complete length. A requested start beyond that length does not identify a bad codec; it identifies a mismatch between the requested coordinates and the resource. Accept-Ranges: bytes advertises range support. Its absence alone is not a rule that a client can never attempt a byte-range request. The response remains the evidence of what happened. Container indexes connect bytes to time To reach a presentation time, the player first needs a mapping from media timing to sample locations and usable decoding access points. It can then retrieve the associated byte regions. Variable bitrate, interleaving, headers and dependencies make that mapping more complicated than multiplying duration by average bitrate. Suppose an index maps a target to video data at offset 700,000 and an earlier suitable decoding point at 680,000. Starting the retrieval at 680,000 is consistent with eventually presenting the requested later picture. Those offsets are invented teaching inputs, not a rule about Emby's file seeking. A segmented presentation can also describe byte ranges within one larger object. A URL-addressable segment and a separate physical file are therefore not always the same thing. Ranges must belong to one representation Combining the first portion of one file revision with the last portion of another can corrupt the reconstructed byte sequence. HTTP validators, including entity tags, help establish representation identity. If-Range lets a client make a conditional range request: when its validator no longer matches, receiving the complete representation allows it to start from consistent content. The identity matters for generated media as well as library files. A changed conversion session or replaced resource can have different bytes even when its display title is identical. Successful retrieval of several independent ranges is useful only when those ranges fit the representation the parser is assembling. See Also Progressive download and playback before completion Seeking during streaming HLS media segments and initialization Packet Timestamps References IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and range requests WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.title: Progressive download and playback before completion | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/htt.keywords: Progressive download and playback before completion Progressive download plays a media resource while its bytes are still arriving, using container information and buffered data to prepare the next presentation. A movie does not have to arrive completely before the player shows its first picture. With progressive download , the player obtains a media resource over HTTP and presents the part for which it already has enough information and data. Retrieval and viewing overlap. This is a delivery arrangement. In an Emby Direct Play session, a player may receive the original media this way. The term does not say whether the resource is a library original or a prepared version. The player needs more than the first bytes A media container describes how encoded streams, their timestamps and their locations relate. The player uses that information to find samples, initialize decoders and schedule presentation. For an ordinary MP4, the moov box carries movie and track information, including sample tables. If that information is near the beginning, a player can discover the layout early. If it is at the end, startup may require retrieving that part first. An HTTP range request can allow this without transferring everything preceding it. FFmpeg's faststart option for suitable non-fragmented MP4 output moves the index information toward the beginning. It changes packaging; it does not reduce the encoded video's bitrate or add codec support to the receiving device. Fragmented delivery organizes initialization and media differently. The consequence is practical: two files with the same codecs and bitrate can start differently because the information needed to interpret their bytes appears in different places. Arrival and viewing run on different clocks Consider an original simplified example: a 600-second resource contains 450,000,000 bytes of media and packaging, and the connection sustains 12,000,000 bits per second. 450,000,000 × 8 / 12,000,000 = 300 seconds to transfer 450,000,000 × 8 / 600 = 6,000,000 bits per media second on average If bytes needed for each next interval arrive in time, the transfer can finish halfway through a ten-minute viewing. The player may nevertheless start much earlier, after establishing its initial buffer reserve . This calculation assumes a stable useful transfer rate. Real media sizes vary by scene, and retrieval can be interrupted or scheduled in bursts. Knowing the average rate does not identify how much usable media exists before the next gap. Observation What it describes Bytes already received Transfer progress for the resource Buffered media intervals Time ranges the player has retained for use Current playback position The programme moment being presented Complete local copy A storage result, if the application retains the entire resource A player may discard earlier bytes or cease retrieval after playback stops. A progress bar approaching the end is therefore not evidence that the app has created a permanent offline copy. A jump can start another retrieval Seeking changes which portion is useful next. A player that supports the file layout and server range behavior can request the container information and encoded data needed around the destination rather than waiting for all intervening bytes. The required region can begin before the requested picture because decoding may need an earlier access point. That relationship is developed in Seeking during streaming . A jump to a later scene can consequently create a new request and a short readiness wait even though the first part of the movie was already playing. See Also HTTP range requests for media resources Segmented streaming and addressable media intervals Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Direct Play in Emby Containers and Codecs References IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and range requests FFmpeg: Container formats and fragmented MP4 WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/ind.title: Overview: Streaming delivery | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/ind.keywords: Overview: Streaming delivery Streaming delivery connects media representations, transport requests and player buffers across a playback timeline. Delivery can expose a file progressively or supply a sequence of media segments. Adaptive selection, discontinuities and live timing add further relationships to that sequence. This area explains those transport arrangements and the buffering or seeking behavior around them. Keeping delivery separate from conversion helps identify whether the player lacks incoming data or the server has not yet produced it. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HTTP file delivery HTTP file delivery exposes media bytes through progressive access or requests for particular ranges. Segmented streaming Segmented streaming presents media as a sequence of addressable intervals whose timing and initialization information let a player retrieve and assemble the programme. HLS delivery HLS delivery connects playlists with the media segments and timeline information they describe. Adaptive bitrate streaming Adaptive bitrate streaming selects among suitable representations of the same programme timeline to balance presentation quality, delivery capacity and playback reserve. MPEG-DASH MPEG-DASH describes timed media representations and their addressable segments in a Media Presentation Description that a player uses for HTTP delivery and adaptation. Common Media Application Format (CMAF) CMAF constrains segmented media tracks and their relationships so compatible delivery systems can use shared addressable media objects for timed presentation and switching. Low-latency streaming Low-latency streaming reduces the delay between an event and its presentation by coordinating encoding, early media availability, delivery and player buffering. Live streams and on-demand streams Live and on-demand streams differ in when programme media exists and remains available, shaping timeline discovery, seeking, pausing and the meaning of the live position. Stream discontinuities A stream discontinuity marks a change in media timing or configuration that requires the player to interpret the following interval in a new continuity context. Buffering Buffering retains media ahead of use, with continuity, readiness and consumption rate determining how much playback reserve the stored data actually provides. Seeking during streaming Seeking resolves a requested media-time destination through available ranges, resource access and decoding dependencies before presentation resumes. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational) ISO/IEC 23009-1:2026: DASH presentation and segment formats ISO/IEC 23000-19:2024: CMAF Apple: Enabling Low-Latency HLS IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and ranges

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection Adaptive bitrate streaming selects among suitable representations of the same programme timeline to balance presentation quality, delivery capacity and playback reserve. Adaptive bitrate streaming lets a player choose different representations of the same programme as conditions change. A lower-rate representation generally needs fewer delivered bits for the next media interval. A higher-rate representation can provide more picture information when delivery and decoding can sustain it. The player needs alternatives it can use at corresponding programme times. A single stream whose server-side encoder was assigned a bitrate at startup is a different arrangement. A ladder provides real alternatives Imagine an original ladder with total nominal media rates of 2, 4 and 8 Mbit/s. Each representation covers the same programme, with aligned four-second intervals. For this simplified example, audio is included in those totals. Representation Nominal rate Four-second payload at that rate Low 2 Mbit/s 1 MB Middle 4 Mbit/s 2 MB High 8 Mbit/s 4 MB The player is choosing the encoded representation for an interval. It is not instructing an existing eight-Mbit/s segment to become smaller while keeping the same bytes. Actual segment sizes vary, and a published rate attribute has the meaning defined by its manifest format. The table deliberately uses constant-rate payload estimates to make the scheduling arithmetic visible. Throughput is evidence for a decision A player's useful download throughput is calculated from a particular transfer and timing interval. Request setup, connection reuse, cache hits and pauses can affect how that observation should be interpreted. An original teaching policy might choose the highest supported ladder rate no greater than 70% of a six-Mbit/s throughput estimate: 6 × 0.70 = 4.2 Mbit/s selection budget Highest ladder rate within 4.2: 4 Mbit/s The margin leaves room for uncertainty and changing conditions. It is not a standard HLS requirement, a dash.js default or an Emby setting. A real policy can also consider how much media is buffered, recent fluctuations, decoder load and the cost of changing quality. The dash.js primary documentation provides a concrete implementation example with throughput and buffer-based rules, plus additional rules that can influence selection. Those mechanisms establish that adaptation is a player policy, not one fixed rule prescribed by a manifest. A throughput sample needs a measurement interval An original one-MB payload has eight million bits. Assume its active byte transfer takes two seconds and request/setup adds another 0.2 seconds. Active payload rate = 8,000,000 / 2 = 4,000,000 bit/s Whole-request rate = 8,000,000 / 2.2 ≈ 3,636,364 bit/s Both calculations describe the same request with different intervals. A policy needs to know which observation its estimator uses and how request overhead affects the next interval. Shorter media intervals can make that overhead more significant relative to payload time. A period deliberately spent idle between requests also should not be silently mixed into an unrelated active-transfer measurement. The dash.js throughput reference describes implementation-specific measurement and averaging options; the calculation here does not assign it one universal formula. The buffer explains why adaptation helps Use an original serial-retrieval model with eight seconds of ready media before the next request. Playback consumes one media second per wall second. Each completed request contributes a four-second interval, and its entire payload becomes usable at completion. No extra request delay, overhead or stall occurs in these three steps: Request Selected rate Useful throughput Retrieval time Ready reserve after completion First 4 Mbit/s 6 Mbit/s 2.667 s 9.333 s Second 4 Mbit/s 2.5 Mbit/s 6.400 s 6.933 s Third 2 Mbit/s 2.5 Mbit/s 3.200 s 7.733 s For the second request: Payload = 4 media seconds × 4 Mbit/s = 16 Mbit Retrieval = 16 / 2.5 = 6.4 wall seconds New reserve = 9.333... - 6.4 + 4 = 6.933... seconds The connection slowed after the earlier estimate. Reserve covered the unexpectedly long transfer. The following request uses the lower-rate representation and arrives in less time than it contributes, so reserve grows again. This model illustrates a delayed response to changed conditions. It does not simulate an actual player's estimator, request abandonment or incremental fragment use. A policy that always spends the full latest measured rate has little room for a worse next interval. A policy that always selects the lowest quality protects reserve at the expense of presentation quality. Adaptation manages that tradeoff across the viewing, including the time required to learn that conditions changed. Switching needs a compatible timeline The next selected representation must continue at the intended programme moment. Suitable access points, timing alignment, codec configuration and the receiver's switching capabilities determine whether that transition works. Changing from one representation at time twelve to another whose next interval begins at fourteen creates a gap. Switching to an incompatible codec configuration can require reinitialization or may not be supported by that player path at all. Packaging conventions such as CMAF can constrain tracks into suitable switching sets. Manifest labels alone do not repair a mismatch between the actual encoded tracks. Buffered material also affects when the viewer sees the change. If the player retains several intervals of the former quality, a newly requested lower-rate interval can appear later on the playhead. Some implementations can replace buffered material under particular policies; others continue presenting what they already have. Quality controls can act at different places An app's “Auto” choice can mean automatic source selection, a negotiated session bitrate, an adaptive player policy or another app-specific behavior. Its label alone does not show which mechanism operates. In Emby, playback information , the delivery manifest and the actual representation requests provide different pieces of that evidence. A server quality limit can constrain which output is offered. A client-switchable ladder additionally requires alternative representations for the same session timeline. See Also HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Playback quality limits and output constraints Media source selection for playback Low-latency streaming and the live presentation delay References DASH-IF dash.js: Adaptive bitrate settings DASH-IF dash.js: Throughput calculation IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational) DASH-IF: Restricted timing model (2024 snapshot)

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Buffering, ready media and playback reserve | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Buffering retains media ahead of use, with continuity, readiness and consumption rate determining how much playback reserve the stored data actually provides. A buffer stores media for later use. Playback reserve is the portion that can support the upcoming presentation without waiting for additional work. Those are related but different quantities. A player can retain thirty seconds of media in total and still have only two seconds before a gap. A server can have output on disk that the player has not received. Several queues can exist at once Location What can be retained Source reader Input bytes awaiting container/stream processing Server conversion path Frames or encoded output waiting for the next stage Generated output storage Media produced ahead of the viewing position Client input buffer Received media for later decoding Client presentation queues Decoded pictures or samples waiting for their deadlines A reserve measure needs to identify the queue and the readiness being counted. “Buffered for sixty seconds” without that scope can conceal the distinction between generated output, received data and decoded presentation. Emby's production position and the client's reported playback position describe useful session state. Their difference does not directly measure every client queue. A ready-media model For an original simple model, count contiguous usable media seconds ahead of consumption: change in reserve = arriving ready-media rate - consumption rate Assume ordinary playback at one media second per wall second and an initial ten-second reserve. Wall-time interval Ready-media arrival rate Reserve change 0–20 seconds 1.5 media seconds/s Ten seconds gained 20–30 seconds No new ready media Ten seconds used 30–50 seconds 0.5 media seconds/s Ten seconds used The reserve rises from 10 to 20, returns to 10, then reaches zero at wall second 50. The graph assumes steady consumption until the first empty point. After that point, uninterrupted playback no longer follows the model; a player must wait, recover or choose another policy. A larger initial reserve can postpone starvation. It cannot make a sustained arrival deficit disappear. Stored ranges can have a gap Suppose an original received-data view contains media intervals 0–10 and 40–60 seconds. Playback is at second 8. There are thirty seconds stored across the intervals, but only two seconds remain before the next gap. The latest stored endpoint is 60; subtracting the playback position gives 52, which incorrectly counts the missing interval as reserve. HTML media playback exposes buffered ranges rather than requiring one universal continuous interval. Seeking, fetching policy and discarded data can produce another set over time. The range still describes a media-time availability view, not a promise that every picture can start independently at every point. Codec configuration and reference dependencies remain relevant to seeking . Bytes need their rate context At a constant 6 Mbit/s, five media seconds represent 30 million payload bits. Before playback starts, a path supplying 8 Mbit/s would take an ideal 3.75 seconds to fetch that amount. Once playback starts, some arrivals replace consumed data rather than increasing reserve. Assuming the same constant media rate, the net ready-media gain is 8/6 - 1 , about one third of a media second per wall second. Variable bitrate changes the conversion between byte inventory and media-time reserve. A five-second low-complexity passage can occupy fewer bytes than another five-second passage. A bitrate burst can exhaust a finite byte inventory Use another original model: average demand is 6 Mbit/s over a sixteen-second cycle, made of four seconds at 12 Mbit/s and twelve seconds at 4 Mbit/s. The arithmetic average is: (4 × 12 + 12 × 4) / 16 = 6 Mbit/s A constant 8 Mbit/s delivery rate exceeds that average. But during the 12 Mbit/s burst, an initial twelve-million-bit buffer loses four million bits per second and reaches zero after three seconds. The burst is four media seconds long, so the stated reserve is insufficient for uninterrupted presentation of that interval. The model stops at its first empty point; a real stalled player does not keep consuming nonexistent bytes. This is why an average-rate comparison and a finite buffer need to be considered together. It is not an Emby network estimate or a measured movie bitrate trace. Buffer policy changes waiting and resource use Waiting for more initial data can increase startup delay while providing another reserve. Retaining more received media can support later navigation but uses memory or storage. Discarding old data changes the available range set. A pause in playback reduces consumption and can allow reserve to grow. A producer throttle can reduce arrivals when sufficient server-side output exists. Those controls apply at different points in the path. None of these queue changes establishes decoder compatibility or repairs an unavailable resource. They manage when usable data is retained and consumed. See Also Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Transcode throttling and producer lead Playback stalls and unavailable next media Seeking during streaming Playback startup delay References WHATWG: HTML media playback IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and ranges Emby API: TranscodingInfo IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Common Media Application Format (CMAF) | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Common Media Application Format (CMAF) CMAF constrains segmented media tracks and their relationships so compatible delivery systems can use shared addressable media objects for timed presentation and switching. Common Media Application Format , or CMAF , defines constrained segmented media tracks and how suitable tracks form a presentation. It builds on the ISO Base Media File Format, adding relationships intended for interoperable delivery, decoding and switching. CMAF does not itself define the playlist, player or delivery protocol. That separation allows a delivery system to describe compatible media using HLS or DASH. Shared media, different descriptions A publisher can create compatible CMAF media objects and describe them in both HLS playlists and a DASH MPD. The descriptions remain different, while the addressable media resources can be shared. For a service offering both delivery systems, this can avoid keeping two separate copies of identically encoded and packaged media. The shared objects must actually satisfy the relevant constraints. Matching filename extensions does not establish that two independently packaged outputs are interchangeable. Layer What it supplies Encoded video or audio Compressed pictures or samples CMAF track and media objects Constrained packaging, timing and track relationships HLS playlist or DASH MPD Resource discovery and presentation information Player Selection, retrieval, preparation and presentation This explains why “CMAF support” is not a complete compatibility statement. The receiver still needs the actual encoding configuration, delivery description and other selected features. A switching set coordinates alternatives Alternative encodings intended for seamless switching need compatible boundaries and timeline relationships. CMAF defines constraints and profiles for tracks, switching sets and presentations. An original example has two video alternatives covering the same intervals, one at 720p and one at 1080p. If both have a suitable switching boundary at programme second twelve, the player can continue with the other alternative from that moment. If one alternative instead has a usable boundary at thirteen, describing it as another quality does not create the missing second. The track relationship must be established during encoding and packaging. A fragment is not a synonym for a complete movie. Track initialization describes how later samples are interpreted. Timed media objects then supply those samples, and the delivery description relates them to the presentation. Chunks can become available before a longer interval is complete Lower-latency delivery can make smaller units available while a larger media interval is still being produced. A player capable of incremental receipt and preparation can work closer to the live publication edge. CMAF chunks provide a media organization that such delivery can use. The delivery protocol must also expose availability early enough, and intermediaries must avoid holding all bytes until the larger object completes. A six-second interval divided into twelve half-second units does not by itself promise half-second end-to-end delay. Encoding, publication, transfer, buffer policy and rendering contribute their own delays. Low-latency streaming works through that distinction. Identify the constraints behind the label An ordinary fragmented MP4 already has initialization and fragment structure. CMAF adds specific constraints, media profiles, brands and cross-track relationships; arbitrary fragmented output is not automatically a conforming CMAF presentation. ISO/IEC 23000-19:2024 is the published base edition referenced here. Its media and presentation constraints give the CMAF label a more specific meaning than fragmented MP4 alone. See Also HLS media segments and initialization MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection Low-latency streaming and the live presentation delay Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery References ISO/IEC 23000-19:2024: CMAF Apple: CMAF with HTTP Live Streaming DASH-IF: Restricted timing model (2024 snapshot) W3C Group Note: ISO BMFF byte stream format

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description MPEG-DASH describes timed media representations and their addressable segments in a Media Presentation Description that a player uses for HTTP delivery and adaptation. MPEG-DASH describes a media presentation that a player can retrieve over HTTP. Its Media Presentation Description , or MPD , identifies timing, available tracks and representations, and how to locate their media segments. DASH is a delivery and presentation-description system. “DASH” on its own does not name a video codec, a DRM system or an Emby playback mode. The presentation hierarchy Three useful levels organize the media: Level Role in the presentation Period A programme interval with its own presentation context AdaptationSet A group of related media alternatives, such as a video group or an audio-language group Representation A particular encoded alternative within that group A video AdaptationSet can offer different rates or dimensions for corresponding content. An audio AdaptationSet can represent a separate selected track. The player combines the suitable selected components on the intended timeline. Several Periods can describe consecutive programme contexts. They are not necessarily just “the low, medium and high versions”: those alternatives belong at a different level. A template resolves resource names This original selected XML excerpt describes a twelve-second static video presentation with two representations and four-second media intervals: <MPD xmlns="urn:mpeg:dash:schema:mpd:2011" type="static" minBufferTime="PT1.5S" mediaPresentationDuration="PT12S"> <Period start="PT0S"> <AdaptationSet contentType="video" mimeType="video/mp4"> <SegmentTemplate timescale="1000" duration="4000" startNumber="1" initialization="init-$RepresentationID$.mp4" media="$RepresentationID$-$Number$.m4s" /> <Representation id="low" bandwidth="2000000" width="1280" height="720" codecs="avc1.4d401f" /> <Representation id="high" bandwidth="4000000" width="1920" height="1080" codecs="avc1.640028" /> </AdaptationSet> </Period> </MPD> The fictitious resources and omitted audio/profile details make this an addressing example, not a complete validated streaming package. timescale="1000" gives the template duration a unit of one thousand ticks per second. Therefore duration="4000" means four seconds, not four thousand seconds. For the high representation, initialization resolves to init-high.mp4 . With startNumber="1" , the first three media names are high-1.m4s , high-2.m4s and high-3.m4s . In this simple zero-origin example they cover 0–4, 4–8 and 8–12 seconds. The bandwidth values describe representations. They do not give the network speed that a particular viewer will obtain when requesting those resources. Sample time needs a presentation mapping Other presentations use explicit segment timelines and nonzero sample origins. A raw timestamp then needs its timescale and offset before it becomes a programme position. For an original conversion exercise, assume: Period start: 20 programme seconds. Sample timestamp: 900,000 ticks. Presentation time offset: 450,000 ticks. Timescale: 90,000 ticks per second. Time within Period = (900000 - 450000) / 90000 = 5 seconds Programme position = 20 + 5 = 25 seconds The sample value alone represents ten seconds in its raw unit. Treating that as the final programme position would miss both the offset and the Period start. The public DASH-IF timing guideline develops these relationships under its stated restricted interoperability model. It is a 2024 snapshot of implementation guidance, separate from the full ISO standard. Static and dynamic presentations expose different availability A static MPD describes a bounded presentation. A dynamic MPD can describe media becoming available as time advances, with a moving availability window and updated presentation information. For live delivery, a locator is useful only while the resource is available. Wall-clock mapping, the publication window and the player's intended delay from live all affect which interval it should request. Live streams and on-demand streams develops those viewing consequences. The MPD supplies information for adaptation, but the player supplies the selection policy. Two DASH players can choose differently from the same offered representations because their estimators, buffer states or device constraints differ. articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Stream discontinuities and timeline changes | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Stream discontinuities and timeline changes A stream discontinuity marks a change in media timing or configuration that requires the player to interpret the following interval in a new continuity context. A stream discontinuity marks a boundary where the following media needs a changed interpretation. Its timestamp sequence, track configuration or other properties may differ from what preceded it. A network delay between continuous segments is a delivery problem. A discontinuity can instead be intentional programme structure, such as switching sources or inserting another sequence. A local timestamp can restart at a continuous programme position Consider two original ten-second intervals: Interval Local sample-time range Intended programme range A 0–10 seconds 0–10 seconds B 0–10 seconds after a timestamp reset 10–20 seconds If the player interpreted B using A's unchanged local-time mapping, B's samples would appear to return to programme time zero. The intended programme continues forward. A selected HLS media-playlist excerpt can mark that boundary: #EXTINF:10.000, a.ts #EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY #EXTINF:10.000, b.ts This is an original boundary illustration, not a complete playlist or generated pair of media files. HLS requires discontinuity signaling for specified changes, including the timestamp sequence. The marker tells the client that the previous continuity assumptions no longer suffice. It does not give an instruction to display duplicate pictures or erase ten seconds of programme time. Configuration can change at the same boundary A transition can also involve different track identifiers, encoded configuration or packaging context. The player may need new initialization or decoder preparation. For example, switching from one input source to another can introduce a timestamp reset and different codec parameters. The client must know both how to interpret the new sample timing and how to prepare the encoded samples. A valid marker alone does not guarantee seamless operation. The new representation still needs to be supported, correctly described and available early enough. A gap in intended programme coverage remains a gap even when the boundary is signaled. In DASH, Period boundaries provide presentation context for changes. Period timing and cross-period continuity have their own model; a new Period should not be treated as a literal spelling variant of an HLS tag. Wall-clock time is another mapping Programme continuity does not imply continuity of raw sample timestamps, and neither directly gives the clock time at which the event occurred. A publication can provide a programme-to-wall-clock relationship. That helps compare captures, live delay or parallel tracks. A timestamp reset then needs the correct context to keep those relationships meaningful. If a log prints sample time zero twice, identifying the continuity context can explain why the second zero belongs later in the programme. Subtracting the values without that context would report an apparent backward jump. Rolling playlists need the retained context Imagine a live playlist with a discontinuity before segment 200. A later window begins at 201, after the segment carrying the marker has left the list. The client still needs to distinguish this continuity context from an earlier one. HLS uses EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY-SEQUENCE to retain the relevant sequence context as older discontinuity tags leave a rolling playlist. That value is separate from EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE , which identifies the first media segment's sequence number. Their roles should not be combined into one “stream position” counter. Relate the observation to the boundary Observation Interpretation to investigate Media sample timestamps reset at a signaled boundary Changed continuity context A request takes longer, with otherwise continuous media Delivery timing and reserve New initialization or codec parameters appear Configuration transition The intended programme ranges leave a hole Missing programme coverage Presentation resumes after decoder preparation Receiver handling of the transition In Emby, a seek or new conversion job can also restart an output timestamp origin. Relating playback information and conversion logs to the affected job distinguishes a new output origin from a fault in one continuous media sequence. articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Live streams and on-demand streams | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Live streams and on-demand streams Live and on-demand streams differ in when programme media exists and remains available, shaping timeline discovery, seeking, pausing and the meaning of the live position. An on-demand stream starts from programme media that already exists. A live stream publishes media as a programme unfolds. The delivery can use the same protocol in both cases, while availability and timeline behavior differ. This distinction explains why live seeking can have a moving boundary and why “go live” is more than jumping to the last byte in a file. Compare what is available Question Completed on-demand presentation Live presentation with a rolling window Does later programme media already exist? Normally yes Future programme media does not yet exist Does the description need new intervals? A completed description can remain stable New availability must be communicated Can the earliest available position move? Normally fixed for the resource Older intervals can leave the window What does pausing do? Holds a position in existing media Publication can advance while the position stays still Live delivery can retain a large seekable window or very little. A recording can retain media beyond the streaming window. These are separate resource and product decisions. The live edge has a publication context Use an original snapshot whose available programme interval is 90–120 seconds. A viewer is presenting programme second 108: Delay behind the advertised end = 120 - 108 = 12 seconds If the capture clock has already reached programme second 123, three seconds of programme time have not yet reached this availability boundary. Capture-to-presentation delay is then: 123 - 108 = 15 seconds The two results measure different endpoints. “Twelve seconds behind live” is ambiguous until the reference is identified. A player usually selects a suitable position behind the newest available media so it has enough reserve and dependencies for reliable presentation. The last advertised sample is not automatically the best immediate starting position. A paused playhead can fall out of the window Assume the example's rolling window continues to retain thirty seconds while publication advances at one programme second per wall second. After ten paused seconds, it covers 100–130. Position 108 remains available, but it is now twenty-two seconds behind the end. After thirty paused seconds, it covers 120–150. Position 108 is outside that advertised window. Resuming from the old position requires some other retained resource or a policy that chooses another available position. The original pause did not delete the programme. It allowed the publishing system's availability boundary to advance beyond what this delivery path still exposes. Seeking needs availability as well as an access point An on-demand seek uses a destination inside the resource's duration and resolves the relevant data and decoding dependencies. A live seek first needs to establish whether that destination is still available. The player then needs the appropriate playlist or manifest information, initialization and suitable encoded access point. A visible time slider can describe seekable availability rather than fully downloaded media; buffered and seekable ranges are different observations. In an Emby live-TV session, the delivery window, the server's temporary session output and any retained recording therefore have different meanings. A temporary conversion resource is not inherently a permanent recording of everything that has passed. Ending publication changes the task Once a programme ends, a publisher can mark that no more intervals will appear. It may also publish a stable complete resource for later viewing. A final rolling snapshot containing only the last thirty seconds does not suddenly become the complete earlier programme. To create an on-demand asset covering the whole event, the publisher must retain and describe that complete media range. articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Low-latency streaming and the live presentation delay | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Low-latency streaming and the live presentation delay Low-latency streaming reduces the delay between an event and its presentation by coordinating encoding, early media availability, delivery and player buffering. Live latency is the delay between a programme event and the viewer seeing or hearing it. Low-latency streaming reduces that delay across the whole path, including when media becomes available and how far behind it the player chooses to stay. A converter running faster than real time can help keep up with the programme. Its processing speed does not measure how old the displayed picture is. Choose the two endpoints An event can be timed at camera capture, encoder input or publication. At the receiving end, a measurement can stop at byte arrival, decoder output or actual presentation. These produce different latency numbers. For viewers, capture-to-presentation is usually the meaningful experience. A server's “output is ready” timestamp accounts for only part of that path. The startup delay is another quantity: the wait after a playback request until useful presentation begins. A live player can start in one second while presenting a programme picture ten seconds old. Several delays add to the picture's age Consider two original, deliberately simplified serial budgets: Component Longer-delay arrangement Earlier-availability arrangement Capture/ingest 0.04 s 0.04 s Encoding 0.18 s 0.18 s Publication wait 4.00 s 0.25 s Discovering newly available media 0.25 s 0.05 s Transfer 0.30 s 0.30 s Chosen player reserve 6.00 s 1.00 s Final preparation/presentation 0.08 s 0.08 s Total 10.85 s 1.90 s These inputs are explanatory delays for one model, not typical HLS or Emby values. Real stages can overlap, and delay varies with where an event falls within an interval. The model keeps encoding unchanged. Most of the improvement comes from publishing usable media earlier and retaining less intentional delay at the player. Making the encoder twice as fast would affect only its 0.18-second contribution here. Earlier media requires an earlier delivery path If the publisher waits until a complete six-second interval exists, no receiver can obtain its first usable part four seconds before that publication. Producing shorter intervals or exposing partial media removes part of that wait. Low-Latency HLS adds several coordinated mechanisms: Mechanism Contribution Partial segments Describe smaller media units before their parent segment is complete Blocking playlist reload Let a playlist response wait for the requested new availability rather than force repeated empty polling Preload hints Identify a resource expected to become available next Delta updates Reduce repeated playlist information Rendition reports Help relate availability across alternatives These features work together with the publisher, origin, intermediaries and player. A cache that waits for the whole object before forwarding it can restore a delay that the packager intended to remove. CMAF is useful for organizing incrementally available media. It does not supply the discovery or request policy by itself, and a delivery system must coordinate media timing and availability with its description. A smaller reserve buys less time through an interruption For a simple player with one second of usable reserve, a 1.4-second period with no useful arrivals can exhaust that reserve after one second. With six seconds initially available, the same interruption leaves 4.6 seconds. The longer reserve improves tolerance while increasing how far behind the newest usable media the presentation remains. Low-latency policies manage that tradeoff rather than abolish it. A player can recover by pausing to rebuild reserve, moving closer to the new live position, or changing its playback rate within its supported policy. Those choices affect continuity, omitted programme time and live delay differently. Measure the part that changed When assessing an Emby live session, identify the capture or programme-time reference, the currently presented moment, the server's ready-output position and the receiver's buffered position. That separates a producer struggling to keep up from a player deliberately maintaining a reserve. A lower transfer time with unchanged publication and reserve can improve one component while leaving most of the picture's age intact. The delay budget shows where an observed improvement can enter the result. See Also Live streams and on-demand streams HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) Common Media Application Format (CMAF) Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Playback startup delay Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines References Apple: Enabling Low-Latency HLS Apple: HTTP Live Streaming DASH-IF: Restricted timing model (2024 snapshot) ISO/IEC 23000-19:2024: CMAF

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Seeking during streaming | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Seeking during streaming Seeking resolves a requested media-time destination through available ranges, resource access and decoding dependencies before presentation resumes. Seeking asks a playback path to resume at a particular media-time destination. That can require selecting another resource interval, fetching data, initialising a decoder and producing new output before the requested picture is available. The requested time and the point where reading or decoding begins need not be identical. The destination can depend on earlier data Assume an original source with known suitable random-access points at seconds 40, 44, 48 and 52. A request targets second 46.25. A path can begin decoding at 44 and process forward to the destination. For a constant 24-fps sequence, the positions are separated by: (46.25 - 44) × 24 = 54 frame intervals This counts intervals between the stated positions, not a universal packet or decode-frame count. Real codec dependencies, timestamp cadence and access-point types supply the actual work. Some paths present near an available access point; others decode forward and discard preceding output to reach a more precise target. A nearby presentation and an exact-target presentation are different behaviors. Buffered and seekable are different ranges A position can be seekable through resource retrieval even when it is not currently buffered at the player. Conversely, received data does not prove that every location is an independently decodable starting point. A stored on-demand resource can offer destinations across its available timeline. A live stream can expose a moving retained window. A requested old position outside that window needs another archive or cannot be resolved through that current live resource. The HTML media model distinguishes seekable and buffered ranges. Those concepts help explain why a progress bar's current received interval is not a complete map of every possible destination. HTTP uses bytes, not media seconds An original HTTP example requests part of a million-byte resource: Range: bytes=400000-499999 HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 400000-499999/1000000 Content-Length: 100000 The inclusive byte endpoints yield 499999 - 400000 + 1 = 100000 bytes . There is no timestamp in those fields. A container index or other media interpretation must relate the requested playback time to useful resource data. Multiplying a timestamp by an average bitrate is not a generally exact seek map for variable-rate, multi-stream media. The example was not sent to a server. It illustrates the byte contract defined by HTTP range semantics. Segmentation adds another coordinate A delivery path can fetch a segment covering the destination interval. The segment's identity and its internal presentation times are different coordinates again. A segment boundary does not by itself prove independent decoding. The format, initialization data and access-point properties determine whether the chosen data can begin a useful decode sequence there. HLS includes explicit independent-segment semantics rather than making independence a universal consequence of every boundary. Fetching the right segment can therefore be necessary while still leaving decoder preparation before the target picture. Conversion can need a new output region A server may have generated output far ahead of the old playback position while having nothing ready for a new destination elsewhere. The old lead does not describe the newly requested interval. A conversion path can restart or resume work for that region. Input access, filter/encoder state and output packaging can then contribute to seek delay. The resulting output may have another clock origin. In an original mapping that starts output at zero for the requested 46.25-second destination: programme position = output position + 46.25 seconds Output second 2 corresponds to programme second 48.25. Another path can retain source timestamps instead. Reporting progress needs the relevant association, not an unqualified copy of one output clock. Other selected streams must align Audio and subtitles also need the requested programme context. Starting video at the destination while using unrelated old audio or subtitle timing does not produce a correct continuation. Resource changes add another problem: a saved time from another cut can identify a different scene. Resume positions develop that identity/timeline relationship. See Also Video Keyframes and Random Access Packet Timestamps Time Bases Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Transcode temporary files and generated output Resume positions and playback timelines References WHATWG: HTML media playback IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and ranges IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest

articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.title: Segmented streaming and addressable media intervals | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/delivery/Pla.keywords: Segmented streaming and addressable media intervals Segmented streaming presents media as a sequence of addressable intervals whose timing and initialization information let a player retrieve and assemble the programme. Segmented streaming gives a player a sequence of addressable media intervals. Instead of treating a programme as one long download, the player discovers and retrieves the intervals needed next, keeps enough ahead for playback, and advances through their timeline. HLS and MPEG-DASH use this approach. A segmented delivery path can carry copied source streams or newly encoded output from an Emby conversion pipeline . Segmentation describes how that output is organized and delivered. The interval is the useful unit An original twelve-second example has three four-second intervals: Segment Programme interval Encoded payload A 0–4 seconds 2 MB B 4–8 seconds 5 MB C 8–12 seconds 3 MB Their durations match; their sizes do not. The middle scene may simply take more encoded bits. At a useful transfer rate of 16 Mbit/s, ignoring headers and other delays, these payloads take 1, 2.5 and 1.5 seconds to obtain. Each still contributes four seconds of media. The player's reserve depends on how those arrivals compare with consumption, including interruptions between requests. A segment locator can identify a separate object or a byte range inside a larger object. A segment also need not contain both video and audio: separate tracks can be addressed independently and combined by the player. Initialization supplies the meaning of the bytes Encoded samples require configuration. In fragmented MP4 delivery, an initialization resource supplies track descriptions and related information, while later media fragments provide timed samples. A player entering the presentation midway needs the relevant initialization as well as the chosen later media. Possessing segment C's bytes alone does not necessarily give it all the information needed to interpret them. The initialization resource is reusable while its configuration remains applicable. A boundary that changes the configuration can require another initialization resource and corresponding player handling. Continuity comes from timing and dependencies Request completion order is not programme order. A player can retrieve future data ahead of time, then present samples according to their timestamps. Separate audio and video paths likewise depend on their intended time relationship rather than on which HTTP request completes first. Decoding dependencies cross another boundary. If a video segment begins with pictures that depend on earlier pictures, entering at that boundary may require an earlier access point. A presentation that advertises independently decodable segments makes a stronger promise than one that merely provides segment URLs. Stream discontinuities mark changes that need additional interpretation. A new timestamp origin or track configuration is different from a network gap between two otherwise continuous segments. Short intervals create more scheduling opportunities More frequent boundaries can provide earlier opportunities to change representation or react to a seek. They also increase object and scheduling activity. For an original ten-minute programme, four-second intervals mean 150 media intervals per track; one-second intervals mean 600. That is four times as many intervals, before accounting for initialization, playlist updates, parallel tracks or retries. The numbers describe this example, not prescribed segment durations. Adaptive bitrate streaming additionally needs usable alternatives for the same programme moments and a selection policy. A single-representation segmented stream still has segments, while a server that changes its encoder settings for a new session has not automatically supplied a client-switchable ladder. See Also HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) MPEG-DASH and its media presentation description Common Media Application Format (CMAF) Adaptive bitrate streaming and representation selection Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Stream discontinuities and timeline changes References IETF RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (informational) DASH-IF: Restricted timing model (2024 snapshot) W3C Group Note: ISO BMFF byte stream format FFmpeg: Container formats and fragmented MP4

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Overview: Playback compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Overview: Playback compatibility Playback compatibility relates the source representation to the capabilities of the receiving app and its environment. A codec name is one part of compatibility, alongside the stream's properties, packaging and the interfaces the player uses. The receiving environment determines which of those combinations it can handle. These pages establish the evidence needed before choosing direct delivery or a conversion path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What determines playback compatibility? Playback compatibility depends on the selected source and tracks, decoding and presentation capabilities, delivery constraints and the actual playback environment. Client playback capabilities Client playback capabilities describe the media configurations a particular player path can accept and present rather than a universal list attached to a device name. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: DeviceProfile W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Client playback capabilities | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Client playback capabilities Client playback capabilities describe the media configurations a particular player path can accept and present rather than a universal list attached to a device name. A client capability describes a playback configuration: a container/delivery path, codec parameters, picture dimensions and cadence, selected audio presentation, and any relevant subtitle handling. It is more precise than “this model of television plays video.” The app, operating system, decoder and connected output path participate in that configuration. Two apps on one device need not expose the same capabilities. Different kinds of evidence Evidence What it supplies Hardware support specification What a media engine is designed to process App/profile declaration What the application tells a planner it can handle Configuration query A response about a particular described media configuration Successful observed playback Evidence that this tested session worked Smooth observed presentation Evidence about timing and load during that session A hardware specification cannot guarantee that a browser uses that engine. A successful short sample does not test every format variation. A capability report is still useful: it narrows which media plan is sensible before the full programme is attempted. Emby's DeviceProfile model represents several distinct kinds of media constraints. A planner can use such information alongside the selected source and session request. A query needs actual parameters The W3C Media Capabilities draft takes configuration information such as type, codec/content type, dimensions, bitrate and frame rate. Its result distinguishes supported, smooth and power-efficient expectations. For example, asking about one 1080p configuration supplies different evidence from asking about a 4K, higher-frame-rate configuration. Changing only the display label while leaving the query parameters unchanged would not test the second case. These are predictions or declarations about a configuration, not a live network-speed measurement. The working-draft interface also does not imply that every Emby client uses it for every decision. Output paths matter A surround codec that can be passed to an external receiver may need another presentation when listening through stereo headphones. A display change can alter HDR output behavior. A selected subtitle can require a renderer that another app lacks. The source's stream facts remain the same; the usable client path has changed. That is why a capability result should retain context such as app/player, relevant output route and chosen media parameters. Unknown is not the same as unsupported A missing field or an untested configuration supplies incomplete evidence. Software can respond conservatively, try a fallback, or obtain more information. Those policies differ from a proven decoding limitation. A fallback after a playback failure supplies another kind of evidence. Emby's public conversion-reason vocabulary includes direct-play errors as well as format/property mismatches. The named reason identifies what the planner observed or decided; it is not a complete diagnosis of the underlying failure. Playback compatibility combines these capability observations with the actual source, selected tracks and delivery limits. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Media source selection for playback Track selection and playback plans References Emby API: DeviceProfile W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest Emby API: TranscodeReason

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: What determines playback compatibility? | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: What determines playback compatibility? Playback compatibility depends on the selected source and tracks, decoding and presentation capabilities, delivery constraints and the actual playback environment. “Supports H.264” answers one part of a playback question. A source also has a container, codec parameters, resolution, frame rate, colour presentation and selected audio/subtitle streams. The delivery path adds its own constraints. Compatibility is the agreement among those properties and the particular player environment. A file extension or a device's product name cannot represent the whole agreement. The checks intersect For a fictional playback environment, assume that MP4, H.264 8-bit 1080p and stereo AAC are accepted, and that the chosen delivery limit is 12 Mbit/s. These are invented conditions, not a support promise for a named Emby app. Selected source Relevant result under those assumptions MP4, accepted video, stereo AAC, within limit Fits the stated original-playback conditions Another container, accepted video/audio Packaging can be the remaining mismatch Accepted video, selected AC-3 audio not accepted by this path Audio needs another supported representation Higher-resolution or unsupported video parameters Video processing can be needed Subtitles that must be rendered into pictures The video pixels must change A real decision can involve more conditions and more available alternatives. The table explains why a single successful check cannot imply success for the whole source. Codec names omit parameters A codec family can contain several profiles, levels, bit depths, chroma formats and reference-picture requirements. A decoder's support can be narrower than the family name. The chosen delivery path also matters. A native player and a browser on the same computer can use different container parsers, decoders and subtitle renderers. Hardware capability alone does not establish that both applications expose it in the same way. Emby's public profile model separates container, codec and subtitle profiles. Its conversion-reason identifiers likewise distinguish several kinds of mismatch. That structure reflects the need for more than one generic “supported” flag. The selected tracks change the problem Suppose a source contains compatible stereo AAC and another surround track that this path cannot use. Selecting stereo can produce one media plan; selecting the surround track can produce another. Similarly, a text subtitle that the app renders separately differs from a bitmap subtitle that must be burned into video . The second operation changes the pictures, even when the original video codec was already accepted. Track selection is therefore evidence about the current session. Merely listing every format present in a file does not tell us which one caused the observed path. Acceptance, smoothness and presentation A representation can be accepted by a decoder but too demanding to present smoothly under current load. It can decode while the display path needs another colour interpretation, or while an audio output route has different capabilities. The W3C Media Capabilities draft distinguishes support from predicted smoothness and power efficiency for a specified configuration. Those are different answers; the API is not proof of current network throughput or perfect behavior throughout a particular movie. Changing the bitrate setting can request another representation, but it does not create decoder support for an unsupported codec. Conversely, upgrading a decoder does not make a slow delivery path faster. Match the evidence to the session The useful compatibility description identifies the actual source, selected tracks, app/player path and limits. If any of those change, the earlier result may no longer describe the same test. See Also Client playback capabilities Direct Play in Emby Direct Stream in Emby Video transcoding in Emby Containers and Codecs Subtitle delivery in Emby References Emby API: DeviceProfile Emby API: TranscodeReason Emby: Playback methods W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Overview: From server to player | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Overview: From server to player Server-to-player delivery selects a media source and a representation compatible with the requested playback path. What is being sent, and which parts of the source are being changed? Compatibility and media-source selection establish the options, while Emby's playback modes describe the resulting route. Remuxing, stream copying and track selection give that route more precise meaning than a general statement that the server is streaming a file. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How a media server delivers playback Media-server playback combines a session decision about sources and tracks with a media-delivery path that may preserve or convert the selected streams. Playback compatibility Playback compatibility relates the source representation to the capabilities of the receiving app and its environment. Emby playback modes Emby playback modes describe different combinations of source delivery, repackaging and media conversion. Remuxing Remuxing places existing encoded streams into another container or delivery package without re-encoding those streams. Stream copying Stream copying passes selected encoded stream data to an output path without decoding and re-encoding its pictures or samples. Media source selection Media source selection chooses a playable representation by evaluating edition identity, source properties, client conditions and session preferences. Track selection Track selection chooses the actual audio and subtitle content for a source, affecting both user presentation and the media processing required by the playback path. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby API: Playback information negotiation FFmpeg: Container and segment formats FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress Emby API: MediaSourceInfo

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Overview: Emby playback modes | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Overview: Emby playback modes Emby playback modes describe different combinations of source delivery, repackaging and media conversion. Direct Play, Direct Stream and transcoding name different playback routes. The useful comparison identifies which streams remain in their encoded form, which packaging changes and which media must be converted. Their pages connect those changes to the selected source and the receiving app's needs. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Direct Play in Emby Direct Play uses the original media representation for the selected playback session while the client performs its normal decoding and presentation work. Direct Stream in Emby Direct Stream preserves the encoded video while adapting delivery packaging or other selected streams to the receiving playback path. Transcoding in Emby Emby video transcoding creates a new encoded video representation when the selected source needs another format, bitrate or picture presentation for playback. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Direct Play in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Direct Play in Emby Direct Play uses the original media representation for the selected playback session while the client performs its normal decoding and presentation work. Direct Play uses the source media representation without server-side media conversion. The receiving playback path can handle the selected source under the session's relevant constraints. That can still involve sending the resource from Emby Server. Some client environments can access a filesystem source directly, as Emby's Playback Methods describes. Direct Play is a media-processing category, not a promise that every app reads a network share itself. The work is distributed Server or source side Player side Locate and access the resource Interpret the received container Supply bytes through the chosen path Decode selected compressed streams Maintain the playback session Buffer and synchronise presentation Receive relevant progress reports Render pictures, audio and subtitles The player does not draw compressed H.264 packets directly onto the display. It reconstructs pictures from them. Likewise, compressed audio must be decoded or delivered through a suitable bitstream output path. Compressed delivery and decoded frames have different rates Consider an original constant-rate example carrying 8 Mbit/s over the delivery path. That is 1,000,000 bytes per second in decimal units. An ideal tightly packed 1920 × 1080, 8-bit 4:2:0 decoded picture occupies: 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes At 24 pictures per second, those ideal picture buffers represent 74,649,600 bytes per second. Actual memory layouts can add alignment and padding. These figures are not measurements of an Emby device. They show why the network and decoded-frame processing rates describe different work. A client can have demanding decoding/display work even when the server does not encode replacement video. The session still needs compatible conditions The original container and selected stream presentation must work through the chosen player path. A bitrate constraint, unsupported audio choice or required subtitle rendering can change the media plan. The relevant evidence is the actual session, rather than a poster's title or a general device capability list. Compatibility explains how those conditions fit together. Original media and final presentation Using the original representation does not bypass the client's presentation choices. The player can scale a picture to its display, apply an appropriate colour/output interpretation or render separately supplied subtitles. Those client-side operations do not make the server's session a video transcode. The Direct Play label describes preservation of the delivered media representation; the player still has to produce a useful presentation from it. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Direct Stream in Emby Client playback capabilities Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References Emby: Playback methods Emby API: MediaSourceInfo FFmpeg API: Decoding IETF RFC 9110: HTTP semantics and ranges

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Direct Stream in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Direct Stream in Emby Direct Stream preserves the encoded video while adapting delivery packaging or other selected streams to the receiving playback path. Direct Stream preserves the source's encoded video while adapting something else needed by the playback path. That can be container/delivery packaging, selected audio or subtitle handling. Emby's mode name and the general technical word transcoding therefore have different scopes. An audio track can be transcoded within a session whose video remains copied and whose product mode is Direct Stream. A mixed-stream example Assume a fictional MKV source contains H.264 video at 8 Mbit/s, AC-3 audio at 384 kbit/s and a text subtitle. The target path accepts the video but needs AAC stereo audio and another delivery package. Selected component Operation in this example H.264 video Copy encoded video into the chosen delivery representation AC-3 audio Decode, prepare stereo samples and encode AAC Text subtitle Supply a supported text representation through the chosen subtitle path Container/delivery package Repackage the selected output streams The diagram is an explanatory media plan, not Emby's complete scheduling or selection algorithm. The video avoids a new video-encoding generation. The audio does not: its encoding and possibly channel presentation change. “No video re-encode” is therefore more precise than “nothing was converted.” Packaging can change without reconstructing pictures A muxer writes encoded packets into a supported output container or streaming package. Required bitstream framing or codec configuration can also differ between representations. Those changes do not necessarily require decoding and re-encoding the pictures. Bitstream filters and stream copying explain that distinction. They also explain why a copy path does not promise complete-file byte equality. Changing packaging still requires work: access, packet processing, interleaving and output delivery. Direct Stream should not be interpreted as “the server does nothing.” Audio conversion cannot remove the video's bitrate If the example's audio changes from 384 to 192 kbit/s, the nominal combined stream rate changes from 8.384 to 8.192 Mbit/s, before any packaging overhead. That helps with the audio mismatch but leaves the 8 Mbit/s video intact. It cannot create a 6 Mbit/s total representation just by choosing another container or reducing audio. If a substantially lower video rate is required, another source or video transcode is a different plan. Process names and stream operations A server may use the same conversion executable and session infrastructure for remuxing, audio conversion and video encoding. A transcode log or temporary output can therefore exist for a video-copying session. The useful log evidence is the selected stream mapping and output handling. A video copy operation differs from a named video encoder even when both are launched by the same process. Emby's public session information separates video and audio handling. Reading those stream-level facts alongside the mode explains the otherwise puzzling combination “Direct Stream, with converted audio.” See Also Remuxing media containers Stream copying and encoded packet handling Video transcoding in Emby Track selection and playback plans Subtitle delivery in Emby References Emby: Playback methods FFmpeg: Bitstream filters FFmpeg: Container and segment formats Emby API: TranscodingInfo

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Video transcoding in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Video transcoding in Emby Emby video transcoding creates a new encoded video representation when the selected source needs another format, bitrate or picture presentation for playback. In Emby's video-transcoding mode, the server produces a replacement encoded video representation for the playback session. It decodes the source pictures, performs any required picture processing, and encodes the output. The video codec name can remain the same. H.264 video encoded again at another bitrate or resolution is still a new video representation. What requires another representation? Session requirement Possible video work Source codec or parameters are unusable in this path Encode an accepted video format/configuration Delivery needs a lower video bitrate Produce another rate-controlled representation Picture dimensions must change Scale decoded pictures before encoding An HDR source needs an SDR server output Apply suitable colour/range processing and encode the result Subtitles must become picture content Render subtitle pixels before video encoding These operations describe different reasons to use the same broad conversion pipeline . They do not imply that every session needs every stage or filter. Emby's Transcoding documentation identifies format, bitrate and subtitle handling among the reasons a session can need conversion. The actual plan depends on the source, selected tracks and client context. A same-codec example Take an original fictional source with 1920 × 1080 H.264 video and a target requiring 1280 × 720 H.264 at a lower rate. Property Source Requested output in this example Codec family H.264 H.264 Picture dimensions 1920 × 1080 1280 × 720 Frame cadence 24 fps 24 fps Video representation Existing encoded stream Newly encoded stream The matching codec labels do not make this a stream copy. The dimensions and encoding decisions have changed. A lossy output adds another approximation of the reconstructed pictures. Its result depends on the output dimensions, bitrate/rate control, encoder and content complexity. Copying the original video would preserve its encoded representation but would not perform the requested scaling or rate reduction. Other streams can take another path A session that encodes replacement video can still copy compatible audio. It can supply subtitles separately, convert them to another supported form, or burn them into the pictures if that is required. Thus the mode does not imply that all tracks were encoded. The per-stream operations explain which content and technical properties changed. Likewise, a Direct Stream session can convert audio while preserving video. Looking only for any occurrence of the word “transcode” obscures that distinction. Requirements and capacity are different questions Selecting an appropriate output plan does not establish that the server can produce it fast enough under current load. Decoding, filtering, encoding, storage and delivery all contribute to the result. Hardware can accelerate supported parts of a pipeline, but a hardware encoder does not automatically accelerate every filter or remove transfer costs. The bottleneck article develops a simple capacity example. A lower requested bitrate can reduce delivery demand while adding server processing. A compatible original source can reduce conversion demand while requiring more network throughput. These are different constraints rather than a universal ranking of modes. The source remains the source On-the-fly playback conversion ordinarily creates session output without replacing the original library resource. Its technical output description should therefore remain separate from the source description.
