For the 1080p-to-720p example, source media information can correctly report 1920 × 1080 while playback information reports the 1280 × 720 output. Those values describe different points in the same session. See Also How a transcoding pipeline works What determines playback compatibility? Direct Stream in Emby Playback quality limits and output constraints Subtitle burn-in How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References Emby: Playback methods Emby: Transcoding Emby API: TranscodeReason FFmpeg: Codec options FFmpeg API: Encoding

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Remuxing media containers | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Remuxing media containers Remuxing places existing encoded streams into another container or delivery package without re-encoding those streams. Remuxing changes how encoded streams are packaged. A demuxer reads their packets from the source, and a muxer writes the selected streams into the output container or delivery representation. The pictures need not be reconstructed and encoded again. That makes remuxing different from changing the video's resolution or reducing its encoded bitrate. Preserved media, new package Part of the resource Possible result Encoded picture/audio content on copied paths No new encoding generation Container headers and indexes Written for the output format Packet framing and codec configuration May need a compatible representation Selected stream set Can differ from the complete source set Chapters, attachments and descriptive metadata Depend on selection and output-format support A new file hash is expected when the container bytes change. It does not prove the pictures were re-encoded. Conversely, retaining a codec label does not prove a remux. H.264 could have been encoded again into another H.264 stream. The actual stream operation is the relevant evidence. The destination must represent the streams A container is not a universal wrapper for every possible stream. Its format and the receiving parser impose requirements. Codec data may need another framing convention. FFmpeg's bitstream-filter documentation describes transformations that can prepare encoded data for a destination without decoding pixels. Those are different from picture filters such as scaling or subtitle rendering. Timing also needs correct interpretation. Writing another container can change time bases or timestamp origins while preserving intended presentation. Copying integers without accounting for their units would be a timing error, not a normal guarantee of remuxing. A pure remux and a mixed job If video and selected audio are both copied, the job can be a pure remux of those media streams. If video is copied while audio is decoded and encoded into AAC, the job combines video repackaging with audio transcoding. Emby's Direct Stream category can include that mixed case. The product mode describes the video-preserving delivery plan; the individual stream operations supply the more detailed technical description. Source features need another scope check A Matroska attachment, chapter structure or subtitle track may have no identical representation in the destination. A remux can therefore preserve copied picture content while producing a resource with a different set of accompanying features. The word “remux” in a filename is only a label. Stream mapping, format properties and the represented metadata establish what the actual resource retained. See Also Stream copying and encoded packet handling Direct Stream in Emby Containers and Codecs Packet Timestamps Matroska Attachments References FFmpeg: Container and segment formats FFmpeg: Bitstream filters Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: How a media server delivers playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: How a media server delivers playback Media-server playback combines a session decision about sources and tracks with a media-delivery path that may preserve or convert the selected streams. When someone presses Play, a media server needs to know which resource to use, which tracks the viewer wants, where playback should begin and what the receiving app can handle. Delivering bytes is one part of that exchange. The same catalogue movie can therefore produce different playback sessions. A television may use its original source, while a phone receives another representation of the selected content. The diagram is a dependency model, not Emby's internal call sequence. A session chooses more than a title Selection or constraint Why it matters Media source Defines the actual container, streams and timeline Audio track Can change codec, language and channel requirements Subtitle track and presentation Can use separate text, embedded data or rendered pixels Requested starting position Can require seeking or producing output from another point Client capabilities Describe what this playback path can accept Delivery limits Constrain the representation that can be sent Emby's public playback-information interface exposes source, track and capability context. Its result supplies media-source information in a playback session. A catalogue title alone cannot identify all those choices. Consider a fictional source with supported video but unsupported selected audio. The video might remain compressed exactly as supplied while the audio is converted. Selecting another audio track could change that decision without changing the movie. The media path has its own work Direct Play uses the original media representation. Direct Stream preserves video while adapting packaging or other selected streams. Video transcoding produces a new encoded video representation. These product modes describe useful categories, but their consequences are clearest when the selected video, audio and subtitle paths are considered separately. A process can copy one stream and convert another. The server still has to access the source and supply the chosen delivery path. For generated output it may need to produce data ahead of playback. The receiving player then buffers, demultiplexes, decodes and presents the content. The client always has a presentation job Direct Play does not mean that compressed pictures can be drawn without decoding. It means the server has not needed to replace the media representation for this session. The player still interprets the container, reconstructs pictures and samples, synchronises them and sends them to display and audio output. That distinction explains why a session can be cheap for the server and demanding for the client. It also explains why a healthy server-side conversion does not prove that the receiving app presents every frame smoothly. State reports describe the session The player can report its media position and session information. Saved history then uses those reports at the relevant user/item scope. A report that playback reached minute 20 does not establish how many bytes are currently buffered or how much of the movie has been converted on the server. Resume positions explain the timeline association. Playback information helps distinguish the observations made at the different parts of the delivery path. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Media source selection for playback Track selection and playback plans Direct Play in Emby Direct Stream in Emby Video transcoding in Emby References Emby API: Playback information negotiation Emby: Playback methods Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Emby API: Playback progress reporting

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Media source selection for playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Media source selection for playback Media source selection chooses a playable representation by evaluating edition identity, source properties, client conditions and session preferences. A movie item can offer several playable sources. Selecting one defines the actual streams and timeline for the session. It is a different decision from selecting the catalogue title. The useful source depends on what the viewer intends to watch and what the playback path can handle. Three sources, one fictional cut Assume these sources represent the same 108-minute cut: Source Video Audio Nominal total rate F1 1080p H.264 SDR, 8 Mbit/s AC-3, 384 kbit/s 8.384 Mbit/s F2 4K HEVC HDR, 35 Mbit/s Surround audio, 640 kbit/s 35.640 Mbit/s F3 720p H.264 SDR, 3 Mbit/s Stereo AAC, 192 kbit/s 3.192 Mbit/s Now assume an invented target path accepts F3's configuration and has a 5 Mbit/s limit. F3 is an existing representation that fits those assumptions. F1 would need another plan to reduce the rate; F2 adds other video/output requirements. This does not establish Emby's actual ranking or the best source for every device. It demonstrates why “highest resolution” is not a complete selection rule. First preserve the intended content Two sources under one movie description may be different editions . A director's cut and a theatrical cut should not be treated as interchangeable merely because one uses an easier codec. The viewer's intended edition or presentation comes before a technical preference in an identity-conscious model. Once the intended content is established, its available representations can be evaluated. A remembered resume position also needs the relevant timeline. Selecting an extended cut cannot recover a scene correspondence from the shared movie ID alone. Then compare the complete representation Container, video parameters, colour presentation, audio choices and subtitles all contribute. A compatible video track can still have another selected stream that needs conversion. The public Emby media-source model retains source-specific identifiers, stream information and delivery possibilities. Playback requests can also specify a media-source identity. Those fields let a session refer to a representation rather than only to the movie item. Available possibilities are not a guarantee that every request will succeed. Current access, selected tracks and client conditions still participate in the observed session. Track choices belong to that source F1 could have French audio at index 2 while F3 has a commentary at index 2. Moving the integer without checking the target source would select the wrong content. Likewise, chapter positions and subtitle timing can differ between sources. A change of source requires interpreting the destination representation's information. See Also Alternate media versions Movie editions and cuts What determines playback compatibility? Client playback capabilities Track selection and playback plans References Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest Emby API: DeviceProfile Emby API: Playback information negotiation

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Stream copying and encoded packet handling | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Stream copying and encoded packet handling Stream copying passes selected encoded stream data to an output path without decoding and re-encoding its pictures or samples. Stream copying selects encoded stream data and passes it toward an output without rebuilding and re-encoding the corresponding pictures or samples. It is not the same as a filesystem copy. A file contains container structures and possibly several media streams; a stream-copying job can choose only some of them and write another container. One command can use two operations An original illustrative FFmpeg command is: ffmpeg -i source.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -c:v copy -c:a aac delivery.mp4 The command illustrates option meaning, not an executed conversion or a guarantee that every source can be written this way. Option Meaning in the example -map 0:v:0 Select the first video stream from input 0 -map 0:a:0 Select the first audio stream from input 0 -c:v copy Use the video stream-copy path -c:a aac Encode the selected audio with the named AAC encoder delivery.mp4 Choose the output resource/container context The video avoids a video encoder. The audio does not avoid an audio encoder. Looking only at the executable's name cannot distinguish those operations. Packets and frames are different objects An encoded packet carries data that a decoder interprets. A decoded video frame contains reconstructed picture samples. A raw audio frame contains samples suitable for processing and presentation. A stream-copy path works on encoded data. A scale, deinterlace or subtitle-painting operation works on pictures and therefore needs another path through decoding and encoding. That boundary explains why adding -vf scale=1280:720 is not a way to scale a video while keeping -c:v copy . The requested operations require incompatible data representations on that stream. Copying does not mean identical file bytes The output muxer writes its own container headers, indexes and packet layout. A bitstream filter can alter encoded framing or associated configuration without producing a new compressed picture generation. Thus an output hash can differ while the copied media preserves its encoded picture information. A subtitle/image attachment can also be excluded simply because it was not mapped. Codec names and duration agreement are insufficient evidence of stream copying. The mapping and selected codec-handling path are more direct evidence. Selection survives as output scope Stream identifiers and indexes belong to their input or output representation. The first input audio stream does not have to remain stream index 1 after another set of streams is selected and written. A playback diagnostic should therefore relate output streams back to the chosen input mapping. An output track numbered 0 is not automatically the input track numbered 0. Remuxing describes the packaging job around these copied streams; Direct Stream describes Emby's relevant video-preserving session category. See Also Remuxing media containers Decoding media streams Encoding a new media representation Streams and Tracks Packet Timestamps References FFmpeg: Processing, mapping and progress FFmpeg: Bitstream filters FFmpeg: Container and segment formats

articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.title: Track selection and playback plans | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/from-server/.keywords: Track selection and playback plans Track selection chooses the actual audio and subtitle content for a source, affecting both user presentation and the media processing required by the playback path. A source can contain several audio and subtitle streams. The viewer selects content, not just a codec: language, commentary, accessibility role and subtitle purpose can all matter. Those choices also change what the playback path must handle. A source with several English tracks Use this original stream inventory: Source-local index Role Language Representation 0 Video Not an audio-language choice H.264 1 Main audio English Six-channel AC-3 2 Main stereo audio English Stereo AAC 3 Main audio French Stereo AAC 4 Commentary English Stereo AAC 5 Full subtitles French SRT text 6 Forced subtitle material English PGS bitmap Language alone cannot distinguish indexes 2 and 4. Their content roles differ. Channel count and codec information cannot establish that role either; descriptive evidence is needed. Emby's playback request model includes audio and subtitle selection indexes alongside source context. Those coordinates refer to a particular representation. Present is different from selected An unsupported stream somewhere in a file is different evidence from an unsupported stream selected for the session. A player may ignore unselected tracks if its container path allows that. Suppose the target accepts the video and stereo AAC but not the six-channel AC-3 presentation. Choosing index 1 calls for audio handling different from choosing index 2. The library item and video stream remain the same. Similarly, selecting SRT that can be delivered as supported text differs from selecting bitmap material that the chosen path must render into video. The second choice can require replacing the video representation. Flags supply clues with a scope A default disposition can indicate an intended default track within the resource. It does not know every user's language or whether the user wants commentary. A forced-subtitle flag describes intended use of the marked material. It does not guarantee that every player interprets the flag identically or that the stream's metadata is correct. Remembered user choices and app policies supply another layer of selection. A diagnostic needs the actual chosen stream rather than guessing from the first listed track or a flag. Changing source changes the coordinate system Index 2 on another source can refer to different content. Output stream indexes can also change after mapping and repackaging. A track choice should therefore be associated with source identity and checked against its stream description. Copying an index alone can turn “English main audio” into “English commentary” without causing a codec error. For the original inventory, a test record should say source F1, audio index 2, French SRT index 5 . “The movie works with English” leaves the selected role and subtitle path unresolved. See Also Streams and Tracks Subtitle track selection What determines playback compatibility? Direct Stream in Emby Subtitle burn-in Media source selection for playback References Emby API: MediaSourceInfo Emby API: PlaybackInfoRequest Emby API: DeviceProfile FFmpeg: ffprobe inspection

articles/playback-streaming/index.html.title: Overview: Playback and streaming | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/index.html.keywords: Overview: Playback and streaming A playback session connects source access, compatibility decisions, optional conversion, delivery and player presentation. Pressing Play starts a chain of operations. The server must locate a readable source, select a supported representation and deliver data at a useful rate; the player must decode, buffer and present that data. The branches below expose different parts of that chain. Conversion topics explain changes to media, streaming topics explain its transport, and player or casting topics explain which device performs the final work. Diagnostic topics connect those mechanisms to observed symptoms, so a pause is investigated at the stage that actually ran short of data or processing capacity. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> From server to player Server-to-player delivery selects a media source and a representation compatible with the requested playback path. Conversion pipelines Media conversion connects source decoding, optional processing and output encoding into a working representation. Streaming delivery Streaming delivery connects media representations, transport requests and player buffers across a playback timeline. Players and playback environments Playback environments determine which media interfaces, device resources and delivery routes an application can use. Casting and remote playback Casting and remote playback separate control, media delivery and presentation across participating devices. Understanding playback behavior Playback behavior links visible symptoms to observations of the stages involved in a media session. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: Overview: Browser playback | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: Overview: Browser playback Browser playback uses web media interfaces and browser policies within the device's available decoding environment. An HTML media element, a Media Source Extensions pipeline and a codec-detection result answer different questions about playback. Browser policy can also govern when presentation starts. These topics connect the exposed web interfaces to actual media handling rather than treating a successful capability query as a complete playback test. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Browser media playback Browser media playback combines web application logic, browser media APIs, permitted resource loading and the available decoding and presentation path. HTML media elements HTML audio and video elements expose media playback controls, asynchronous state and time ranges whose meanings distinguish resource loading from presentation readiness. Media Source Extensions (MSE) Media Source Extensions lets an application append supported encoded media byte streams to a browser playback path while coordinating buffering, timing and asynchronous updates. Browser codec detection Browser codec detection queries a particular resource or byte-stream configuration, producing support predictions whose scope differs from observed playback. Browser autoplay restrictions Browser autoplay restrictions govern when media may begin without suitable user interaction, making a playback request’s promise result part of the player’s state. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C Working Draft: Media Source Extensions

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: Browser autoplay restrictions and playback permission | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: Browser autoplay restrictions and playback permission Browser autoplay restrictions govern when media may begin without suitable user interaction, making a playback request’s promise result part of the player’s state. A browser can refuse to begin media without an appropriate user interaction, even when the resource and codecs are supported. Autoplay restrictions govern permission to start, including circumstances involving audible media. This explains why a video can be ready while its player still presents a Play button. Requesting playback is an action with a result The HTML autoplay attribute expresses a request; the browser's applicable policy determines whether automatic presentation can begin. Muted and audible media can be treated differently. Chrome's documented policy is one concrete example: it distinguishes muted autoplay from audible autoplay and considers factors such as user interaction and permitted embedded playback. Other browsers and embedded views have their own applicable behavior. A player should react to the result of its start request. This original example assumes video is the selected media element and the functions update the application's visible controls: async function requestStart() { try { await video.play(); showPlayingControls(); } catch (error) { showPlayButton(error.name); } } The code does not claim playback is running merely because it called play() . If the promise rejects, the app can expose a usable action and retain the error context. Separate permission from media preparation Observation Question it raises play() rejects with NotAllowedError Was playback permitted under the applicable policy? The user clicks Play and presentation starts Did that interaction provide the required permission? The resource request fails Could the media be obtained? A decoder reports failure after data is obtained Could this encoded media be prepared? Playback starts and later stalls Is the next required media ready? A NotAllowedError is not a codec identifier. Conversely, a user gesture does not repair an inaccessible resource or an unsupported encoding. In an Emby Web session, this distinction can prevent a ready-but-paused player from being mistaken for slow transcoding. The server can already have useful output while the browser is waiting for permission to present it. Embedded playback has another context An embedded player can be affected by its embedding page's permission policy. User interaction in one frame is not a universal instruction that every unrelated frame must start audible media. Applications need to preserve the intended interaction and examine the actual promise result. A successful user-triggered start can update the controls immediately; a rejected start should leave the user an action that corresponds to the browser's state. See Also HTML media elements, state and time ranges Browser media playback and its loading paths Playback error categories and evidence scopes Playback startup delay References WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback Chrome: Autoplay policy and play promises

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: Browser media playback and its loading paths | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: Browser media playback and its loading paths Browser media playback combines web application logic, browser media APIs, permitted resource loading and the available decoding and presentation path. A browser player uses the browser's media facilities inside a web application. The application chooses a resource or delivery path, while the browser performs supported media parsing, decoding and presentation. The operating system may contribute decoders or output facilities, but a format available to a native application is not automatically exposed through every browser media API. Two ways to supply the media A web player can assign a media resource directly to an HTML media element . The browser then manages the supported resource-loading path. Alternatively, application JavaScript can fetch encoded media and feed it through Media Source Extensions . A library can use that arrangement to implement segmented delivery and adaptation over the browser's underlying media engine. Path What the application supplies Direct media resource A resource locator and player configuration Script-managed MSE Encoded byte-stream data, append scheduling and media-selection logic A browser with native HLS resource support can interpret an HLS URL through its own path. A browser using an HLS JavaScript library may instead receive suitable media through MSE. The same protocol label can therefore conceal different loading and compatibility requirements. Resource access and script access have different rules Opening a media URL successfully is useful evidence that a particular navigation or loading route can access it. It does not establish that another web page's JavaScript may read its response. Consider a fictional web app served from one origin and a media resource served from another. Direct media-element playback can work in circumstances where a script cannot read the cross-origin response. A script-managed player using Fetch needs the appropriate cross-origin response behavior, including credential handling when applicable. This is a loading-path issue, separate from whether the downloaded encoded pictures could be decoded. A permissive container parser does not change the browser's origin rules. The same distinction matters for cast receivers implemented as web applications: the phone's successful request and the receiver's allowed request have different origins and access contexts. The supported configuration is the selected one Browser playback depends on more than a codec family name. Container and byte-stream format, profile, dimensions, cadence, selected audio and text handling all participate. A browser can accept a simple MP4 resource without accepting an arbitrary MP4 byte sequence through MSE. A chosen MSE byte-stream format has its own initialization and fragment structure. For an Emby Web session, the server can adapt the selected media to the path the app and browser can use. That can mean packaging changes, audio conversion or video conversion depending on the actual incompatibility. Diagnose the stage that produced the observation Observation Stage to examine Media resource request is refused Loading and access context Script cannot read a cross-origin response Fetch/CORS behavior for that request MSE append reports an error Byte-stream interpretation and append state play() rejects before presentation starts Promise result, including policy or loading failure Pictures begin and then drop Decode/presentation timing and available media An autoplay restriction can prevent an otherwise supported source from starting without the required interaction. A codec prediction can report a plausible configuration before any actual resource has been fetched. See Also HTML media elements, state and time ranges Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery Browser codec detection and capability predictions Browser autoplay restrictions and playback permission Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) and browser key sessions Native media players and their playback engines References WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback W3C Working Draft: Media Source Extensions WHATWG: Fetch and cross-origin requests W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: Browser codec detection and capability predictions | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: Browser codec detection and capability predictions Browser codec detection queries a particular resource or byte-stream configuration, producing support predictions whose scope differs from observed playback. A browser support query asks whether a described media configuration is plausible for a particular playback path. It is useful input for a web app deciding which representation to request. The question needs enough detail to distinguish the path and the encoded configuration. “Can this browser play H.264?” leaves much of that question unspecified. Start with the resource or byte-stream path An original direct-resource query can look like: document.createElement("video").canPlayType( 'video/mp4; codecs="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"' ); canPlayType() can return an empty string, "maybe" or "probably" . These express a support assessment for the described type, not a completed decoding test. A separate MSE query asks about its appendable byte-stream path: MediaSource.isTypeSupported('video/mp4; codecs="avc1.4d401f"'); An app must first establish that the relevant API is available. A positive result does not make arbitrary ordinary-file bytes valid MSE fragments. A fuller configuration asks a more useful question The Media Capabilities API describes dimensions, cadence and bitrate alongside the media type: const prediction = await navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({ type: "media-source", video: { contentType: 'video/mp4; codecs="avc1.4d401f"', width: 1280, height: 720, bitrate: 2000000, framerate: 30 } }); This original example asks about a specific video configuration. The result includes supported , smooth and powerEfficient assessments. Input Meaning in the example type The media-source path, rather than a file path width and height Encoded picture dimensions bitrate 2,000,000 bits per second framerate Thirty pictures per second The query does not measure a private media file or the current server connection. Its power-efficiency prediction is also not a live wattmeter. These examples were not run against a particular browser or device. They illustrate the API questions; an app needs its own availability and error handling. Keep selection and observation together A supported video configuration does not describe a separately chosen unsupported audio track. A media-source prediction does not establish another browser's direct-resource behavior. A changed output route or application version can alter the relevant playback conditions. For an Emby Web session, useful evidence combines the declared configuration with the selected source/tracks and the observed loading, decoding and presentation result. That gives a capability report a concrete scope. See Also Client playback capabilities Browser media playback and its loading paths Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery What determines playback compatibility? Dropped video frames during playback References WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback W3C Working Draft: Media Source Extensions W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities Google Cast: Supported media

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: HTML media elements, state and time ranges | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: HTML media elements, state and time ranges HTML audio and video elements expose media playback controls, asynchronous state and time ranges whose meanings distinguish resource loading from presentation readiness. HTML's <video> and <audio> elements are the browser's interfaces for media playback. They expose controls, timing and state while the browser handles its supported decoding and presentation path. An element can exist in the page before it has usable media. The distinction between requesting playback and being ready to present matters throughout its API. A small element still has asynchronous work This original example supplies a video resource and requests browser controls: <video controls preload="metadata" playsinline> <source src="/media/example.mp4" type="video/mp4"> </video> controls asks for the browser's player controls. preload="metadata" expresses a loading preference; it is not a guarantee that exactly a fixed number of bytes will be fetched. playsinline encourages presentation within the element's area and does not add codec support. The browser still needs to select and access the source, interpret its format, initialize the required media path and prepare presentation. A scripted play() request returns a promise. Code can respond to its resolution or rejection and keep the visible controls consistent with the result. The promise is associated with starting playback, not with obtaining a permanent complete copy of the resource. Three range properties answer different questions A media element exposes normalized time ranges for several observations: Property Question answered buffered Which media-time intervals are currently retained as buffered data? seekable Which intervals can currently be targeted by seeking? played Which intervals have been played? An on-demand resource can be seekable across much of its duration while only a small portion is buffered. A live resource can have a moving seekable window. The ranges can also have gaps. Consider an original snapshot: currentTime: 8 buffered: [0, 10] and [40, 60] seekable: [0, 120] played: [0, 8] The immediate buffered interval ends at ten, leaving two seconds before its next gap. Summing the buffered intervals gives thirty stored media seconds, while subtracting the playhead from the last buffered end gives fifty-two. Those latter calculations answer different questions. A seek to fifty can land in another buffered interval. A seek to ninety can still be allowed by the seekable range while requiring retrieval and preparation of additional data. Readiness is different from network activity The element's network state concerns resource loading. Its readiness state concerns how much usable media information exists around the current position. Loaded metadata can establish properties such as dimensions or duration when available. It does not mean a future picture is already ready. Download activity can continue while presentation proceeds, and a player can consume buffered media while making no new request. Events expose changes in those states, not a fixed universal story for every source. For example, waiting identifies a presentation wait related to readiness, while ended belongs to reaching the playback end under the relevant state. A stalled live publication and a completed resource have different contexts for interpretation. The media clock is a programme coordinate currentTime is a position on the media timeline. It is not the elapsed wall time since the user pressed Play. Pausing, seeking and playback-rate changes separate those values further. A browser can also report picture-presentation counters through a separate interface. Those counters relate to dropped video frames , rather than to the sum of played intervals. See Also Browser media playback and its loading paths Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery Browser autoplay restrictions and playback permission Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Seeking during streaming Dropped video frames during playback References WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback Chrome: Autoplay policy and play promises W3C Working Draft: Media Source Extensions

articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.title: Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/brow.keywords: Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery Media Source Extensions lets an application append supported encoded media byte streams to a browser playback path while coordinating buffering, timing and asynchronous updates. Media Source Extensions , or MSE , lets a web application supply encoded media to the browser's playback engine. The application can fetch and select media intervals; the browser interprets a supported byte stream and performs decoding and presentation. This is a useful boundary for a JavaScript HLS or DASH player. The JavaScript library can implement delivery and adaptation without implementing the video decoder itself. The application chooses what to supply A MediaSource is attached to a media element. The application adds one or more SourceBuffer objects for supported encoded-media configurations and appends data to them. Application responsibility Browser media responsibility Interpret the delivery description Interpret an accepted media byte-stream format Select tracks or representations Maintain coded media and playback state Fetch the required bytes Decode supported samples Schedule appends and removals Present the selected timeline through the media element Retrieval, appending and presentation proceed at different times. A completed download is input for the append process, not proof that the samples have become playable. Encoded bytes need the expected structure A SourceBuffer is created with a supported media type and codec description. That is more precise than saying that the browser “supports MP4.” For the ISO BMFF MSE byte-stream format, initialization supplies track and sample descriptions. Later media fragments supply fragment metadata and sample data. An arbitrary portion cut from the middle of an ordinary MP4 is not automatically a valid appendable fragment. A player entering at another programme position therefore needs the appropriate initialization, timed media and decoding dependencies. A representation change can also require compatible configuration or supported reconfiguration. The CMAF and HLS media segment pages develop the packaging relationships. MSE supplies the browser API boundary through which suitable bytes enter. Appends are asynchronous operations appendBuffer() begins processing the supplied data. During an update, SourceBuffer.updating is true, and incompatible overlapping operations can fail. A client needs a queue or another ownership arrangement to coordinate updates. This original helper illustrates one serialized append. It assumes that the caller exclusively controls an existing, attached SourceBuffer and that the MediaSource is in an appropriate state. The supplied values are byte data, not resource URLs: function appendOne(buffer, bytes) { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { function clean() { buffer.removeEventListener("updateend", done); buffer.removeEventListener("error", failed); buffer.removeEventListener("abort", failed); } function done() { clean(); resolve(); } function failed(event) { clean(); reject(new Error("Append failed: " + event.type)); } buffer.addEventListener("updateend", done); buffer.addEventListener("error", failed); buffer.addEventListener("abort", failed); try { buffer.appendBuffer(bytes); } catch (error) { clean(); reject(error); } }); } await appendOne(sourceBuffer, initializationBytes); await appendOne(sourceBuffer, firstMediaBytes); The second call waits for the first operation to finish successfully. A synchronous exception or an asynchronous error/abort rejects the helper's promise and removes its listeners. This selected example does not create a MediaSource, fetch data, choose codecs, retry operations or coordinate a complete player's queue. Its purpose is to show why returning from appendBuffer() is different from completing an append. Byte arrival, append completion and media readiness These three boundaries can advance separately. Initialization can append successfully while supplying no programme pictures at all. A later append can supply only part of a fragment or encoded sample, leaving the parser waiting for more bytes. Imagine a selected four-second interval arriving in two pieces. In this original model, the first piece contains fragment information and an incomplete first sample; the second completes the required media. No complete sample exists before that second piece. Event Accumulated input Ready programme interval in the model Initialization append completes Track configuration None First media-piece append completes Headers and partial sample data None Second media-piece append completes Required interval data is complete 0–4 seconds An update can finish processing the input it was given without making the entire intended media interval ready. Conversely, a suitable incremental byte stream can make some samples usable before the complete larger resource has arrived. This is why an application's downloaded-byte counter, its append queue and the media element's buffered ranges describe different state. A player needs to preserve both the byte-stream parsing context and the programme-time relationships while more data arrives. Media timestamps decide where samples belong In timestamp-based segments mode, the media carries timestamps that establish sample placement. timestampOffset can transform the placement under the API's rules. For an original simplified example, assume a valid media fragment has local presentation timestamps covering 0–4 seconds. With a suitable offset of twelve seconds, its intended placement becomes 12–16: Presentation placement = local presentation time + offset 0 + 12 = 12 4 + 12 = 16 These numbers are programme-time relationships. Appending the bytes at wall-clock second fifty does not place the movie interval at programme second fifty. sequence mode has different grouping behavior. The application must use the selected mode consistently rather than assume that every new append automatically belongs immediately after the last picture it saw. Separate audio and video buffers also need compatible timing. Receiving audio first and video later can still produce synchronized output when their timestamps describe the same programme moments. Retained media has a lifecycle Long sessions can accumulate coded media that the player no longer needs. remove() lets an application request removal of ranges, coordinated with update state and decoding dependencies. Buffer capacity is not a universal fixed number of seconds. Encoded byte size, tracks, browser implementation and device conditions matter. A QuotaExceededError at append time belongs to that resource/state context; requesting the same bytes again without changing the relevant condition need not solve it. Removal can reduce retained data, while seeking or adaptation can create new retrieval and append work. A player must preserve the media and dependencies needed around the current and intended next positions. End the source only when the presentation permits it For a completed on-demand presentation, a player can signal the end of the supplied stream when the relevant SourceBuffers have finished updating and the MediaSource state permits it. A live presentation still expecting new media has a different lifecycle. A decoder error, append error, exhausted delivery window and normal completion therefore have different evidence. In an Emby Web session, relating the media-element state to actual fetch and append results helps locate the stage at which the next usable interval stopped becoming available. articles/playback-streaming/players/inde.title: Overview: Players and playback environments | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/inde.keywords: Overview: Players and playback environments Playback environments determine which media interfaces, device resources and delivery routes an application can use. The same source can meet different conditions in a native app, browser, external player or television. Mobile and offline use add another resource or availability context, while protected media introduces its own access path. This branch identifies the environment before interpreting a reported playback capability. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Native media players A native media player uses application and platform media components to retrieve, decode and present content within an operating system’s playback environment. Browser playback Browser playback uses web media interfaces and browser policies within the device's available decoding environment. External players External-player playback hands a media resource from one application to a separate player whose access, track choices and reporting form a distinct playback path. Smart TV playback limitations Smart TV playback limits belong to the selected model, application media path and output configuration, with container, codec, cadence and track handling contributing separately. Media playback on mobile devices Mobile media playback combines a device-specific decoding path with changing delivery, power, application lifecycle and audio-output conditions. Offline playback Offline playback uses media and required supporting resources retained on the viewing device before the session, while preserving a compatible representation and catalogue context. Protected media Protected media playback connects encrypted content with the authorization and platform mechanisms needed to present it. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Android Media3: Supported formats and decoder paths Emby: Playback methods Emby: Download options W3C Recommendation: Encrypted Media Extensions (2017)

articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.title: External players and the application handoff | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.keywords: External players and the application handoff External-player playback hands a media resource from one application to a separate player whose access, track choices and reporting form a distinct playback path. An external player is a separate application that receives a media resource from the library app. It then performs playback using its own engine and output configuration. This changes the playback path. It can also change which application owns controls, track selection and progress reporting. A handoff transfers a defined resource A caller can supply a file path, a media URL or another supported handoff representation. The external player must be able to use what it receives. Resource supplied Access requirement Local file path The file exists in the external player's filesystem context Network path The receiving process can reach and access that share HTTP media resource The player can obtain the resource using the relevant access context Session-specific output The resource remains valid for the intended playback lifecycle A path meaningful on Emby Server's machine is not automatically meaningful on a different client. The same printed directory name can refer to different storage, or no storage, on the receiver. A media URL also has its own lifetime and access requirements. Handoff needs to preserve the usable context, not just a title or catalogue identifier. Player options become part of the session This original mpv illustration asks a player to open a fictional file at a start position: mpv --start=120 "example.mkv" The command was not executed. It demonstrates that resource identity and a starting position are separate inputs. The external player can have its own audio, subtitle, decoding and output preferences. If the caller does not convey a selected track through a supported mechanism, the player may choose according to its own defaults. Consequently, comparing integrated and external playback requires the same source and intended tracks. A successful external run with a different subtitle selection does not exercise the same processing requirements. Playback progress needs a return path Starting a process proves that a launch occurred. Its exit proves that it ended. Neither observation reports which programme intervals were presented. For a library app to update resume state accurately, an integration needs suitable progress or final-position feedback and a mapping to the correct item/source timeline. A prepared version with different opening material can have a different local time for the same scene. Merely copying its final counter into the original source's resume position can therefore misplace the next start. See Also Native media players and their playback engines Media source selection for playback Track selection and playback plans Reproducing a media playback problem Resume positions and playback timelines References mpv: Player manual and command interface Emby: Playback methods Emby API: Remote control

articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.title: Media playback on mobile devices | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.keywords: Media playback on mobile devices Mobile media playback combines a device-specific decoding path with changing delivery, power, application lifecycle and audio-output conditions. A mobile player operates in a changing environment. Network reachability, audio route, foreground state and available decoding resources can change while the same programme is playing. These changes affect different stages. A pause for audio focus, a slow media transfer and a decoder missing presentation deadlines need different evidence. A session has more than a handset name Condition Playback consequence to examine Wi-Fi or cellular delivery path Reachability, useful throughput and variation Selected encoded representation Transfer demand and decoding work Built-in audio or another route Output format, channels and route changes Foreground/background state Applicable application and platform lifecycle Other audio activity Audio focus and interruption behavior A mobile device with hardware decoding for a codec still needs its application to use a compatible container and sample configuration. The native-player path determines how that media reaches the decoder. Representation size has a practical transfer cost For an original ninety-minute planning example, suppose the selected representation averages 4 Mbit/s video plus 128 kbit/s audio. Ignoring packaging and transport overhead: Duration = 90 × 60 = 5400 seconds Combined rate = 4,000,000 + 128,000 = 4,128,000 bit/s Bytes = 5400 × 4,128,000 / 8 = 2,786,400,000 That is about 2.786 GB in decimal units. A lower representation changes the delivered byte demand; a smaller screen alone does not cause the already encoded original to become smaller. A rate limit can also help maintain reserve on a variable connection. The relevant choice includes source detail, target dimensions and decoding path, as well as the useful transfer rate. Playback quality limits explains those constraints. Audio focus controls who is heard Mobile platforms coordinate audio from multiple applications. Android's audio-focus model, for example, communicates whether an app may present audio and how it should respond when another activity takes focus. Navigation directions can temporarily reduce music volume; another app can interrupt or replace the audible activity. Platform and app behavior determine the response. In that situation, Emby Server can continue to have useful media ready while the mobile player pauses or changes audio presentation. A server conversion log is not the sole source of evidence for the audible interruption. Background state changes the application environment Switching apps or locking the device changes lifecycle conditions. The platform's permitted background behavior and the application's selected presentation mode determine what can continue. A video, a background music session and a picture-in-picture session can therefore have different supported behavior on the same device. Naming the platform is not enough to establish that every app implements those modes identically. When the app resumes, it may continue from retained media, request more data or reestablish session state. Record whether the programme position, delivery path or output route changed around the transition. For planned travel without a dependable connection, offline playback moves media acquisition before viewing. The prepared local representation still needs to fit the mobile player's actual decoding and presentation path. See Also Native media players and their playback engines Client playback capabilities Playback quality limits and output constraints Offline playback and prepared local media Buffering, ready media and playback reserve Casting and screen mirroring: where playback happens References Android Media3: Supported formats and decoder paths Android: AudioFocusRequest Apple: AVPlayer-based playback in AVKit Emby: Download options

articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.title: Native media players and their playback engines | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.keywords: Native media players and their playback engines A native media player uses application and platform media components to retrieve, decode and present content within an operating system’s playback environment. A native media player runs as an application in the device's operating-system environment. Its playback engine coordinates media retrieval, parsing, decoding, timing and output, while the app supplies library navigation and controls. The native app and its playback engine are related components. They need not be the same piece of software. A visible app sits over several responsibilities A player can use platform media frameworks, include its own parsing or decoding components, or combine both. Android Media3 ExoPlayer provides one public example: container and delivery support belongs to the player library, while its default sample decoders come from the platform. Included software-decoder extensions can change that arrangement. Apple AVKit supplies playback user-interface components over AVFoundation and related media facilities. These are examples of how native playback is layered, rather than a universal blueprint for Emby apps. Component Typical responsibility Application Source selection, controls, account and library context Playback engine Resource loading, stream parsing, track selection and scheduling Decoder path Converting encoded pictures or samples to usable media Platform output Display timing, audio routing and device integration An application can customize one layer without replacing every layer beneath it. Two apps can expose different media paths Suppose a device has a hardware decoder for a particular video format. Player A's engine can parse the selected container and submit that video configuration to the decoder. Player B's engine cannot accept that container arrangement. A may play the original source while B needs another package from the server, even though the same physical decoder exists on the device. Another difference can be subtitle rendering. One app can draw the selected text subtitle directly; another may need a supported subtitle representation or video with the subtitle already painted into it. The video decoder's capabilities alone do not answer that question. The actual intersection appears in client playback capabilities . “Native” describes the application environment rather than a complete support list. Output integration affects the result Native playback can use platform facilities for audio focus, background presentation, hardware surfaces or display output. These facilities have their own state and route requirements. Changing from built-in speakers to a different audio output can alter the usable channel configuration. Changing the app's playback engine can alter container, subtitle or hardware-decoding behavior. The source file can remain identical throughout. See Also Browser media playback and its loading paths External players and the application handoff Client playback capabilities Decoding media streams Media playback on mobile devices Smart TV playback limitations and player paths References Android Media3: Supported formats and decoder paths Apple: AVPlayer-based playback in AVKit Emby API: DeviceProfile Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.title: Offline playback and prepared local media | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.keywords: Offline playback and prepared local media Offline playback uses media and required supporting resources retained on the viewing device before the session, while preserving a compatible representation and catalogue context. Offline playback uses a representation retained on the viewing device before the session begins. It removes the need to retrieve the programme's media continuously from the server during that viewing. The app still needs suitable local media, required supporting resources and enough context to identify what the user is playing. Preparation, transfer and local readiness are different states Emby's download options distinguish downloading to supported apps or targets and describe conversion before transfer when a job requests it. A converted job can be ready on the server while the target app is not yet running or reachable. State What has been established Job selected A target and requested representation are defined Conversion finished The prepared media exists at that stage Transfer finished The intended media bytes reached the target Local playback ready The app can locate and use its required resources Offline presentation The local session is actually presenting media A catalogue image or title visible in the app establishes navigation metadata. It does not prove that the programme bytes have been retained. The chosen local version has its own requirements A download can contain an original source or a converted representation. The selected version must match the target player's actual decoding and presentation capabilities. Audio and subtitle choices also matter. A locally retained video does not supply an external subtitle that was never included. A chosen language may be absent if another audio track was the one retained. For segmented content, local readiness includes the relevant description and initialization plus the required media intervals. Downloading only a starting manifest does not make its remote references available without a connection. Android Media3's download architecture is a public example of managing selected tracks and a local cache for playback. It illustrates the resource relationships rather than claiming that every Emby app uses that library. Estimate the stored media you actually selected An original storage exercise uses two complete titles of sixty and ninety minutes. Their selected local representations average 2 Mbit/s video plus 128 kbit/s audio, before overhead: Combined rate = 2,128,000 bit/s Sixty-minute title = 3600 × 2,128,000 / 8 = 957,600,000 bytes Ninety-minute title = 5400 × 2,128,000 / 8 = 1,436,400,000 bytes Total = 2,394,000,000 bytes The result is 2.394 GB in decimal units. It is a conditional estimate from the selected average rates and durations, not a guaranteed encoder output size. The space calculation should also include other retained tracks, descriptions and overhead. A source-sized original and a lower-rate prepared version can have substantially different storage demands. Local viewing still belongs to a programme timeline The local player can record progress while disconnected. Reconnecting allows an application, where supported, to reconcile that state with the library item. A local prepared version may preserve the original timeline or may have different material. Source identity and time correspondence determine whether a local position can be reused directly as the original source's resume position. See Also Offline media conversion and prepared versions Media playback on mobile devices Media source selection for playback Resume positions and playback timelines DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths References Emby: Download options Android Media3: Downloading media W3C Recommendation: Encrypted Media Extensions (2017)

articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.title: Smart TV playback limitations and player paths | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/Play.keywords: Smart TV playback limitations and player paths Smart TV playback limits belong to the selected model, application media path and output configuration, with container, codec, cadence and track handling contributing separately. A smart TV's display resolution is only one part of its media capability. The selected app must obtain and parse the media, reach an appropriate decoder path, handle the selected tracks and present the result through the configured outputs. That is why playback from a USB interface, a browser-style app and another media app can differ on one television. Model limits and application paths are separate facts Manufacturer specifications commonly separate video codec, profile, resolution, cadence, bitrate and permitted containers. Their scope can depend on model generation and product group. Samsung's 2025 video documentation provides a concrete example: its 25TV_BASIC1 discussion distinguishes H.264 UHD decoding from the MSE path, which is limited there to FHD. Samsung's AVPlay guide separately describes a product media API for capabilities beyond its HTML5 path. The useful lesson is the documented distinction between paths. It does not establish which path a particular Emby TV app uses or transfer the same limits to another TV model. Evidence Question it answers Panel resolution What the display surface can show Model-specific decoder specification Which stated encoded configurations a documented device group supports Application media API Which path the app can use to submit media Actual selected source and tracks Which requirements this session presents Output route Where picture and audio are being presented A four-K panel can display a scaled lower-resolution input. The visible output size does not by itself reveal the encoded size the app decoded. Preserve the source when comparing paths Use an original comparison with a 4K video source and two audio tracks: stereo AAC and a different surround format. One playback route chooses AAC; another chooses surround. If the second route triggers conversion, the comparison has changed both the application path and selected audio. It does not isolate the video's 4K capability. The same issue occurs with subtitles. A supported text-rendering path can leave video untouched, while a selected subtitle requiring burn-in adds a video-processing requirement. Compatibility is the intersection for those selected components. A broad “the TV supports the codec” statement leaves packaging and track choices unresolved. Audio output can introduce another constraint The TV's built-in speakers, an attached receiver and another output route can accept different audio configurations. The app's decoder and audio-routing behavior determine what reaches that route. A codec entry in a television specification is therefore not a complete promise of multichannel passthrough through every connector and app. To understand the observed session, preserve the selected track and the actual output configuration together. See Also What determines playback compatibility? Client playback capabilities Browser media playback and its loading paths Native media players and their playback engines Video transcoding in Emby Subtitle delivery in Emby References Samsung: Playback using AVPlay Samsung: 2025 TV video specifications Android Media3: Supported formats and decoder paths Emby: Playback methods

articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.title: Overview: Protected media | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.keywords: Overview: Protected media Protected media playback connects encrypted content with the authorization and platform mechanisms needed to present it. Encryption makes the stored or delivered bytes dependent on an accepted decryption path. DRM systems coordinate additional policy and licensing relationships, while EME exposes a browser interface into supported protection systems. The pages here distinguish those roles from ordinary codec or network compatibility. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> DRM-protected media DRM-protected playback combines encrypted media with a compatible key system, usable authorization and the required processing and output conditions. Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) Encrypted Media Extensions provides browser APIs for selecting a supported key system and coordinating key sessions needed for encrypted media playback. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C Recommendation: Encrypted Media Extensions (2017)

articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.title: DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.keywords: DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths DRM-protected playback combines encrypted media with a compatible key system, usable authorization and the required processing and output conditions. DRM-protected media needs more than the decoder for its video or audio codec. The receiving path must also support the applicable protection system and hold usable authorization for the encrypted samples. This creates another layer in playback compatibility. A codec, container and network can all work while protected presentation remains unavailable. Media and authorization have different roles Component Role Encoded media The compressed pictures or audio samples Media encryption Protects the selected media data Key system and decryption component Interprets protection information and manages usable keys License or authorization response Supplies system-specific authority and conditions for using keys Playback/output path Meets the required preparation and output conditions A key identifier is not the key itself. A media description can identify encryption or a required key without granting the receiving application permission to decrypt it. Browsers use Encrypted Media Extensions to connect an application to supported key systems. Native players have platform-specific protected-media integration. Neither arrangement makes every key system available everywhere. A positive codec result leaves another question Use an original four-case comparison: Supported encoded configuration Usable protected-playback authorization Result to investigate Yes Yes Continue checking the actual media and output path Yes No Protection-system, license or authorization readiness No Yes Encoded configuration or player-path compatibility No No Both sets of requirements remain unresolved The first row is not a guarantee of the complete session. It establishes two prerequisites while delivery, initialization and presentation still have their ordinary work to do. For an Emby media-server comparison, possessing an encrypted resource does not establish a supported path for decoding or creating another representation. Conversion requires the relevant usable input path; a server's ordinary codec support does not supply a provider's key-system authorization. HTTPS protects a different boundary HTTPS protects communication between endpoints. Media encryption can keep samples protected within the resource after it has been delivered. Downloading an HTTPS-served, unprotected MP4 produces ordinary usable media bytes once the permitted transfer is complete. Downloading protected sample data leaves that protection in place. Conversely, a failed HTTPS connection concerns resource access or transport. It does not by itself identify a DRM license failure. A useful diagnosis records the stage that produced the error. Key readiness can change over time Protected playback can require a license exchange after the application encounters initialization data. A key might be pending, usable, expired or restricted by the output context. The EME model exposes key-status information such as usable , expired and output-restricted . Their presence gives the app scoped evidence about protected-media readiness. A restricted output status should not be interpreted as “the codec is absent.” Authorization lifetime, renewal and output conditions belong to the applicable protection system and service. The details should be read from that system's supported player integration rather than inferred from the filename. Offline bytes and offline authorization are separate resources An offline protected session can require retained media and a supported persistent license. Downloading the media alone establishes only the first resource. Persistent authorization also does not imply that every condition has disappeared: its own system-specific lifetime and playback/output requirements still apply. EME makes persistent-license sessions optional. See Also Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) and browser key sessions What determines playback compatibility? Common Media Application Format (CMAF) Offline playback and prepared local media Client playback capabilities References W3C Recommendation: Encrypted Media Extensions (2017) W3C Working Draft: Encrypted Media Extensions Android Media3: Supported formats and decoder paths Google Cast: Supported media

articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.title: Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) and browser key sessions | Emby Learn
articles/playback-streaming/players/prot.keywords: Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) and browser key sessions Encrypted Media Extensions provides browser APIs for selecting a supported key system and coordinating key sessions needed for encrypted media playback. Encrypted Media Extensions , or EME , is the browser API layer through which an application works with a supported media key system. It coordinates the protected-playback configuration and the key sessions required for encrypted media. EME is not itself one DRM product, a media-delivery protocol or a video codec. The application, browser and selected content decryption module have different responsibilities. Media loading and key acquisition take separate paths The media player obtains encoded media through its normal supported loading route, possibly using MSE . Protection information identifies what the key system needs to interpret. In parallel, the application manages a key-system exchange. A key session can produce a message for the application to send to an appropriate service. The response is returned to the session for system-specific interpretation. The diagram describes authorized playback. It does not depict an application obtaining unrestricted raw keys to use as ordinary decoder options. Configuration is negotiated before a usable key session requestMediaKeySystemAccess() asks about a named key system and candidate configurations. These include encoded-media capabilities and relevant session requirements. A configuration can require properties that the browser/device path cannot supply. Support for unprotected H.264 alone does not answer that negotiation question. The returned access object can create MediaKeys . The application associates those keys with its media element through setMediaKeys() . Key sessions then belong to that selected key-system context. Object or operation Responsibility MediaKeySystemAccess An accepted key-system configuration MediaKeys Key-system context associated with playback MediaKeySession One session's request/response and key-status lifecycle generateRequest() Begin the session's request from suitable initialization data message event Deliver a key-system message to the application update() Supply a response for the session to process These are roles in a lifecycle, not a complete portable license-server implementation. Message contents and server exchanges depend on the key system and service. The application transports the message EME does not choose a universal license endpoint or standardize every provider's account and entitlement workflow. The app receives a session message, communicates it through the supported service integration and passes the resulting response to update() . Network access, application authorization and the key system's interpretation each can fail at their own boundary. For example, successfully obtaining the media bytes can coexist with an incomplete license exchange. A client waiting for a usable key may therefore stop presenting while its media buffer already contains encrypted intervals. A useful observation identifies both media readiness and key readiness. Treating every wait as “the video download is slow” loses the separate key-session path. Key status and session lifetime are observations The session can expose key-status changes and an expiration value. A usable key, an expired key and an output restriction have different implications. The application can update controls and diagnostics in response to those changes. A successful HTTP response from a service is not by itself proof that the session accepted it or that all needed keys are usable. Likewise, completing one key session does not make an unsupported encoded representation decodable. Media capabilities and protection capabilities are cooperating prerequisites. Persistent sessions retain a different kind of state The temporary session type and the optional persistent-license type have different storage lifecycles. Persistent-license support can retain key-session state for later authorized playback. It does not download or retain the movie itself. An offline protected presentation still needs its corresponding local media resources and an application capable of using the persisted session. The 2017 EME Recommendation establishes the baseline model. The cited level-two document is a W3C Working Draft, so its additions should be distinguished from implemented browser behavior. See Also DRM-protected media and authorized playback paths Media Source Extensions (MSE) and scripted media delivery Browser media playback and its loading paths Browser codec detection and capability predictions Offline playback and prepared local media References W3C Recommendation: Encrypted Media Extensions (2017) W3C Working Draft: Encrypted Media Extensions WHATWG: HTML media elements and playback W3C Working Draft: Media Capabilities

articles/storage/data-protection/index.h.title: Overview: Data protection | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/index.h.keywords: Overview: Data protection Data protection combines integrity evidence, retained generations and recovery mechanisms with the failures they are intended to address. Redundancy can preserve service through defined device failures. Checksums identify byte differences, snapshots retain views, backups provide recoverable copies and a UPS supplies time for power-related completion. Each mechanism has a distinct boundary; this branch connects it to the recovery outcome needed by the server. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Redundancy and pooling Redundancy and pooling organize physical capacity and reconstruction information under a selected storage layout. File checksums A file checksum summarizes bytes for comparison with a reference, detecting a change without supplying the missing original content. File system snapshots A file-system snapshot preserves a point-in-time view within its storage system, often by retaining old blocks that later writes would otherwise replace. Backups and recovery Backup and recovery preserve media or application state as usable generations for a supported restoration. Uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) A UPS supplies temporary power during an interruption, allowing a supported shutdown sequence to complete before its available energy is exhausted. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References SQLite online backup API IEC 62040-3: UPS performance and test requirements

articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.title: Overview: Redundancy and pooling | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.keywords: Overview: Redundancy and pooling Redundancy and pooling organize physical capacity and reconstruction information under a selected storage layout. Pooling presents managed capacity, while mirroring or parity can add a particular failure tolerance. The layout determines which surviving information is required after a device loss. These pages explain that structure and its capacity implications before a large logical volume is assumed to contain independent recovery copies. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> RAID RAID combines drives in a layout that can provide particular failure tolerance, capacity and I/O behavior for a media server. Storage pooling Storage pooling presents capacity from several devices through logical storage, while allocation and redundancy remain separate choices. Parity protection Parity stores reconstruction information that can recover specified missing data, provided the remaining blocks and parity describe a consistent generation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux kernel: RAID arrays Microsoft Storage Spaces

articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.title: Parity protection and reconstruction | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.keywords: Parity protection and reconstruction Parity stores reconstruction information that can recover specified missing data, provided the remaining blocks and parity describe a consistent generation. Parity protection stores information derived from data so a specified missing part can be reconstructed. It saves capacity compared with keeping a full additional copy of every block, but the reconstruction relies on the remaining information being available and consistent. A single-parity example is easiest to see with exclusive OR, or XOR. Recovering one known missing block Use two four-bit data values: A = 1010 B = 1100 P = A XOR B = 0110 If B is missing: B = A XOR P = 1010 XOR 0110 = 1100 The surviving data and parity reproduce B exactly. If both A and B are missing, one parity value does not provide enough independent information to recover both. Real storage operates on larger blocks. Dual-parity layouts use two independent reconstruction relationships; simply storing the same XOR value twice would not supply the missing second equation. Updating data also updates parity Suppose A changes from 1010 to 0011 while B remains 1100 . The new parity is 1111 . A small update can calculate that new value from the old data, old parity and new data: New P = Old P XOR Old A XOR New A = 0110 XOR 1010 XOR 0011 = 1111 The storage system must coordinate data and parity writes. If interruption leaves new data with old parity, the stripe no longer represents one consistent generation. Journaling, protected caches or other implementation mechanisms can address this update problem. Their guarantees belong to the actual storage system. A wrong block is not a labelled missing block Reconstruction above assumes the system knows which block is absent. If a parity comparison instead reveals a disagreement, ordinary single parity does not necessarily identify which data or parity block is wrong. Checksums can provide independent content-integrity evidence. Some storage systems combine checksums with redundant copies or parity to locate and repair damage. Parity alone should not be credited with every such integrity capability. For an Emby library, parity can protect against the defined device-loss case while writes, rebuild work and integrity checks share I/O resources.
