The recovery question is whether enough correct, consistent information survives—not merely whether a device called a parity drive is present. See Also RAID: drive redundancy and failure boundaries File checksums and content verification References Linux kernel: RAID arrays Linux kernel: RAID parity cache and recovery

articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.title: Storage pooling and logical capacity | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.keywords: Storage pooling and logical capacity Storage pooling presents capacity from several devices through logical storage, while allocation and redundancy remain separate choices. A storage pool groups physical capacity so software can present logical storage without treating every drive as a separate library location. The pool may provide virtual disks, file-system datasets or another managed arrangement. Pooling answers where capacity is managed. The chosen layout answers how data are distributed and protected. One large visible volume does not prove that it can survive a drive failure. Physical space and advertised space An original example starts with 20 TB of usable physical pool capacity after the selected layout's overhead: Virtual disk A advertises 15 TB Virtual disk B advertises 15 TB Total advertised capacity: 30 TB Physical pool capacity: 20 TB With thin provisioning, the pool need not allocate every advertised byte immediately. Both virtual disks can appear spacious while their combined actual allocation approaches the shared physical limit. Quantity What it describes Physical pool capacity Space available in the underlying pool Logical capacity Space presented to a virtual disk or dataset Allocated space Physical capacity currently consumed Reservation Capacity held for a particular purpose under the implementation's rules An Emby recording can run out of allocatable pool space even when its logical volume's displayed limit is larger. Quotas, reservations and snapshots can further influence the available amount. Combining devices does not define a copy count Microsoft Storage Spaces separates a pool from the virtual disks and their resiliency configurations. OpenZFS separates pools, device groupings and datasets. These are examples of layered storage management, not interchangeable configuration formats. A simple or striped arrangement can aggregate capacity without redundant copies. A mirrored or parity arrangement gives up some raw capacity for a stated failure tolerance. Different-sized devices and expansion rules affect the resulting usable space. The relevant question for a media server is which physical failures affect the logical location it uses. Several logical volumes backed by the same pool can share one underlying failure domain. Expansion also has a layout Adding a device does not universally mean that every existing block is redistributed evenly or that every redundancy group expands in the same way. Some systems rebalance, some add a new grouping, and some require a particular supported expansion procedure. Keep the library's stable path separate from the pool's physical allocation. The storage system can change its device arrangement while presenting the same pathname, but the server still depends on the resulting capacity, access and recovery behavior. See Also RAID: drive redundancy and failure boundaries Parity protection and reconstruction File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata References Microsoft Storage Spaces OpenZFS storage concepts

articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.title: RAID: drive redundancy and failure boundaries | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/redunda.keywords: RAID: drive redundancy and failure boundaries RAID combines drives in a layout that can provide particular failure tolerance, capacity and I/O behavior for a media server. RAID organizes several drives into one storage arrangement. Depending on its layout, it can spread data, keep additional copies, or store reconstruction information. These choices affect usable capacity and which drive failures the array can survive. For an Emby library, redundancy can keep media accessible after a drive fails. It does not preserve every earlier version of the files or move a recovery copy outside the server. Capacity and failure tolerance belong to a layout The following examples use four equal 8-TB drives and ignore metadata, spare space and implementation overhead. Layout Illustrative usable capacity Drive-failure boundary RAID 0, striping 32 TB No drive redundancy RAID 1, two-drive mirror 8 TB for one pair Either member of that pair can fail RAID 5, four drives 24 TB One missing member can be reconstructed RAID 6, four drives 16 TB Two missing members can be reconstructed RAID 10, two mirrored pairs 16 TB At least one member must survive in each pair The RAID 1 row describes a pair rather than all four drives. RAID 10 can survive two failures when they occur in different pairs, but losing both members of one pair exceeds that arrangement's redundancy. “Two drives failed” is therefore incomplete evidence without their positions. A degraded array has less protection After a member fails, an array can continue using its remaining copies or parity. It is then degraded : the failure tolerance available before the failure has been partly or fully consumed. Reconstruction reads surviving storage and writes replacement data. That competes with playback, scans and recording. A successful rebuild restores the layout's redundancy; until then, another failure or unreadable required region can prevent recovery. A larger drive's nominal capacity does not by itself predict rebuild time. The layout, amount of data rebuilt, I/O rate, competing work and error handling all matter. Redundancy follows current changes An authorized deletion or unwanted overwrite changes the array's current logical contents. Mirroring faithfully preserves that current change on the other member. Ordinary RAID does not recognize it as an event that should be undone. Media backups retain recoverable generations and can occupy another failure domain. Snapshots can retain earlier versions within their own scope. RAID supplies a different property: continued service or reconstruction under the stated device failures. The implementation also matters. A controller array, Linux software RAID and a pooled file-system layout do not share every cache, integrity or recovery rule. Use the actual system's documented degraded and recovery states when interpreting an Emby storage outage. See Also Parity protection and reconstruction Storage pooling and logical capacity References Linux kernel: RAID arrays Microsoft Storage Spaces

articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.title: File checksums and content verification | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.keywords: File checksums and content verification A file checksum summarizes bytes for comparison with a reference, detecting a change without supplying the missing original content. A checksum is a value calculated from data. Comparing a file's current value with a recorded reference can reveal that the input bytes changed. This is useful after copying a media collection or checking a recovery copy. The checksum does not contain another complete film, so discovering a mismatch is different from being able to repair it. The exact input matters For a small, original UTF-8 example: Input bytes: 61 62 63 Text: abc SHA-256: ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223 b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad The two displayed digest lines form one 64-hex-character value. Adding a newline changes the input and produces another value. A filename or modification timestamp is not automatically part of a content hash. A whole-file comparison must use the same algorithm and the same byte range on both sides. Comparing a downloaded checksum for one edition with another remuxed file is not a test of whether their films look equivalent. A reference gives the result meaning Reference What a comparison can support Recorded before the transfer Whether the destination matches the earlier byte content Trusted publisher's value Whether the received bytes match that published artifact Newly calculated on both copies Whether the two current inputs agree under the algorithm Newly calculated only on the suspect file A baseline for later comparisons, not proof of its earlier correctness A cryptographic hash makes accidental equal-digest results extraordinarily unlikely for ordinary integrity checking. It does not make collisions mathematically impossible. A digest copied from an untrusted source also does not authenticate that source's intended content. Detection needs a recovery source If the live file and backup disagree, the hash says that the observed inputs differ. It does not independently tell you which version is intended. Retained generations, trusted manifests and application context help make that decision. Reading every byte also consumes storage and network work. A checksum pass across a large library can compete with playback and scans. That operation provides stronger byte-content evidence than size and timestamp comparisons, at the cost of actually reading the content. An intact checksum does not test the decoder, subtitles or library identification. A perfectly copied but unsupported media format remains unsupported. Integrity checking answers the byte-preservation question. See Also Parity protection and reconstruction References NIST FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard

articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.title: File-system snapshots and retained versions | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.keywords: File-system snapshots and retained versions A file-system snapshot preserves a point-in-time view within its storage system, often by retaining old blocks that later writes would otherwise replace. A file-system snapshot preserves a view of a filesystem or dataset at a particular point. In copy-on-write systems, later changes can use new blocks while the snapshot keeps references to the earlier ones. This can make a snapshot quick to create without immediately copying every movie into another complete directory tree. It also means its space consumption develops as the live data change. Old blocks remain reachable An original sequence begins with a 10-GB file. A snapshot refers to its current blocks. The live version then replaces three GB of distinct blocks. Original data blocks: 10 GB New replacement blocks: 3 GB Blocks needed by live view plus retained snapshot: 13 GB The model excludes metadata, compression, shared references and further snapshots. Its point is that changed old blocks stay allocated while the snapshot still needs them. Deleting the live filename may therefore release little or no physical space while snapshots retain its blocks. Removing one snapshot does not universally free everything it references if other views still reference the same blocks. A filesystem point is not every application's completed operation A snapshot can present a structurally consistent storage view without representing a clean application shutdown. A database may need its journal or WAL to recover. Several files updated separately may have been captured between related changes. Captured state Question still needed One dataset's snapshot Were all application files in that dataset? Filesystem-consistent point Can the application recover that state? Separate snapshots of several volumes Do they represent a coordinated point? Snapshot of database and journals Does the supported restore process accept that complete set? For Emby application data, use the documented backup method and its consistency requirements. Do not replace those requirements with the assumption that every filesystem snapshot equals an application-aware backup. Retained history still has a failure domain A snapshot on the same pool can help undo an unwanted change while that pool remains available. Failure of the pool, loss of the host or removal of all snapshots can remove that history. A copy or replication to another destination can extend protection, but its independence and retained generations need their own explanation. The snapshot is the preserved source view; the recovery copy is another storage relationship. For a media library, snapshots can provide convenient earlier filenames and versions. Their retention and space use should be understood together so preserving history does not unexpectedly exhaust capacity for new media or recordings. See Also Database transactions and atomic application changes References OpenZFS snapshot semantics OpenZFS storage concepts SQLite online backup API

articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.title: UPS power continuity and orderly shutdown | Emby Learn
articles/storage/data-protection/Storage.keywords: UPS power continuity and orderly shutdown A UPS supplies temporary power during an interruption, allowing a supported shutdown sequence to complete before its available energy is exhausted. An uninterruptible power supply provides power through an interruption, usually using stored battery energy. For a media server, that time can keep brief interruptions invisible or allow an orderly shutdown before power is lost. The UPS does not retain yesterday's version of a deleted film. Its role is power continuity and the opportunity to finish the required shutdown work. Capacity and runtime are different limits A UPS has power-capacity ratings, commonly stated in watts and volt-amperes, as well as runtime that depends on the attached load. Watts describe real power; VA describes apparent power. Equipment and UPS specifications determine the relationship and applicable limits. An original idealized energy example assumes 120 Wh of usable output energy and a constant 180-W load : Ideal runtime = 120 Wh ÷ 180 W = 0.6667 hours = 40 minutes The usable-energy assumption already excludes losses. Real battery behavior, age, temperature and changing load mean a product's measured runtime curve is more useful than deriving a guarantee from a nominal battery label. Quantity Relevant question Maximum W/VA ratings Can the UPS support the connected load? Runtime at that load How long can it support it during this condition? Shutdown interval Can the software and storage finish before the cutoff? Remaining reserve What margin remains if the estimate changes? A shutdown is a chain of dependencies If media live on a NAS, powering only the Emby host does not keep the NAS available. A router, switch or external enclosure may also be required for that storage path. The relevant powered equipment follows the operation you need to finish. In an original budget, 12 minutes of usable runtime minus a seven-minute shutdown sequence leaves five minutes. That margin is conditional on both estimates. Waiting until the last estimated minute makes delayed application or storage work harder to accommodate. Orderly completion still depends on software The host needs a supported way to observe the power event and initiate shutdown. Applications must finish or recover their writes, and the storage stack must honor its completion contracts. A battery remaining charged does not prove that dirty cached data reached durable storage. IEC 62040 provides UPS safety and performance specification scopes; the references are standard catalogues, not a claim that this server arrangement was electrically tested. For Emby, power continuity belongs alongside consistent application backups and the storage system's own recovery guarantees. See Also Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Server sleep, wake and availability References IEC 62040-3: UPS performance and test requirements IEC 62040-1: UPS safety requirements APC: UPS capacity and runtime

articles/storage/execution/containers/in.title: Overview: Container execution | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/in.keywords: Overview: Container execution Container execution connects packaged software with mapped storage, process isolation and shared resource controls. An image, a running container and a persistent volume have different lifetimes. Bind mounts define path relationships, while resource limits constrain work within the host environment. These topics explain how a replacement container can reach the intended Emby data without assuming that its image contains the previous server state. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Software containers A software container gives a process an isolated view of selected resources while using the kernel supplied by its execution environment. Docker images and containers A Docker image supplies a packaged filesystem and configuration, while a container adds a running lifecycle and a writable layer. Container bind mounts A container bind mount exposes a selected daemon-host path at a container path, with the source tree and process identity still determining access. Container volumes A container volume stores data outside one container's writable layer, with a managed identity and lifecycle that require deliberate reuse and backup. Container resource limits Container resource controls bound or prioritize a workload's CPU and memory use within a shared host rather than creating dedicated hardware. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Docker containers Docker images Docker bind mounts Docker volumes Docker container resource constraints

articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.title: Container bind mounts and host-path mappings | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.keywords: Container bind mounts and host-path mappings A container bind mount exposes a selected daemon-host path at a container path, with the source tree and process identity still determining access. A bind mount exposes a host file or directory at a chosen path inside a container. The two pathnames can be entirely different. An original media mapping is: Daemon-host source: /srv/media/Movies Container target: /media Container file: /media/Film.mkv Host file: /srv/media/Movies/Film.mkv Emby configured inside the container uses /media . It does not need the host's path text to be identical, but the mapping must point at the intended source. The source belongs to the daemon's host If a Docker client controls a remote daemon, the bind source is resolved on the daemon's machine. A directory on the client laptop is not automatically uploaded into that source path. Similarly, a desktop container environment may have a supported file-sharing path into its Linux execution environment. The surrounding host arrangement participates in access and performance. A source pathname can identify the wrong tree Source condition Possible result Intended mounted media tree is available The mapping exposes that tree Mount absent but underlying directory exists The mapping can expose the underlying directory Source path absent Behavior depends on the mount syntax/options Source present but unreadable to container identity Mount existence does not supply file read permission Docker's ordinary --mount bind syntax reports a missing source rather than silently creating it. The -v syntax can create a missing host source as a directory; documented options can change particular behavior. This is a syntax distinction, not a guarantee that the mounted data are the correct collection. A read-only bind mapping restricts writes through that view. It does not automatically make every other host or container view read-only. Mapping and permissions are separate The container process's actual IDs, any user-namespace mapping, underlying file permissions and other access rules determine what it can open. A correct mapping can still produce denied access. For an Emby scan, verify the intended tree and readable files from the container's environment. A wrong empty directory and a correct directory with denied access are different failures even when neither yields movies in the scan. See Also Mount points and the file system behind a path Linux user and group IDs in storage access Container volumes and managed persistent storage References Docker bind mounts

articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.title: Container CPU and memory limits | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.keywords: Container CPU and memory limits Container resource controls bound or prioritize a workload's CPU and memory use within a shared host rather than creating dedicated hardware. A container can have resource controls that constrain its processes. CPU controls affect where or how much work is scheduled; memory controls affect the amount charged to the container's resource scope. The host can still be shared. A limit does not manufacture dedicated physical processors or an independent supply of RAM. CPU quota measures aggregate time In a Linux-style bandwidth model, a quota is an amount of CPU time available during a period. Quota: 200,000 microseconds of CPU time Period: 100,000 microseconds of wall time Average allowance: 200,000 / 100,000 = 2 CPU equivalents Several threads can consume that allowance concurrently. On a host with four suitable execution resources, four fully busy threads could use the 200-ms aggregate budget in 50 ms, then wait for further budget under the declared scheduling model. The “two CPU equivalents” result does not imply that exactly two physical cores are exclusively assigned. The real schedule also depends on host contention and controller rules. Control What it expresses CPU affinity/set Where the workload is eligible to run CPU weight/shares Relative scheduling priority under contention CPU quota A bandwidth ceiling over the specified accounting interval Dedicated reservation, where supported A different allocation guarantee Weights are not a universal rate guarantee. An idle competitor and a busy competitor produce different opportunities to use the host. Memory is charged beyond one heap A container's accounting can include application memory, native allocations, kernel-related charges and file cache. The managed-runtime heap is only part of that total. Linux cgroup v2 distinguishes memory.high , which applies reclaim pressure and throttling behavior, from memory.max , a hard limit associated with allocation and out-of-memory handling. Docker's supported flags and the host implementation determine the resulting arrangement. Observation What remains to check Host has free RAM Container may still be near its own limit Managed heap is small Native work and charged cache can be larger Memory usage reaches a boundary Reclaim, stalls and allocation outcomes depend on the control Process exits unexpectedly Logs and resource events are needed to attribute an OOM cause An original 2,000-MB limit with 1,700 MB of active allocations and 500 MB of charged cache exceeds the limit by 200 MB. Reclaiming enough suitable cache can change the result; if active demand alone rises above the boundary, that route no longer supplies enough room. Limits shape server deadlines An Emby encoder that succeeds without a quota can lose real-time progress when available CPU time is capped. More encoder threads cannot bypass the aggregate ceiling. Concurrent scans and playback also share the same container budget when charged together. A limit useful for containing a background workload can therefore affect foreground response if both use that scope. Read the quota, accounting and pressure evidence alongside the media workload. A physical core count or host-wide graph alone cannot explain the resources available to the container. See Also CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads RAM, reclaim and memory pressure Thermal throttling and sustained server throughput References Docker container resource constraints Linux kernel: control group v2

articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.title: Software containers and shared-kernel isolation | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.keywords: Software containers and shared-kernel isolation A software container gives a process an isolated view of selected resources while using the kernel supplied by its execution environment. A software container runs an application with a controlled view of resources such as files, processes and networking. In a typical Linux container arrangement, isolation uses kernel mechanisms including namespaces, while control groups account for or limit resource use. The application still runs as operating-system processes. It does not automatically receive a separate operating-system kernel merely because its package is called a container. The process sees a constructed environment An Emby container can see source media at /media and application data at another mounted path. Those names can differ from the host's locations. A bind mount or volume defines how they are connected. Boundary What it can change Filesystem view Which paths and mounts are visible Process namespace Which processes are visible through that namespace Network namespace Interfaces, ports and routes available to the process User namespace Mapping between inside and outside IDs Resource controls CPU, memory or I/O accounting and limits These are configured properties, not proof that every container uses identical isolation settings. The kernel boundary differs from a VM A VM runs a guest operating system with a guest kernel. Containers on a Linux host usually use that host kernel. A desktop container environment can itself run Linux containers inside a VM; those containers use the kernel of that Linux execution environment. An image that contains Linux user-space files therefore does not carry an unrestricted new Linux kernel for each container. Native code must fit the actual operating-system and architecture arrangement. Media access is an explicit mapping Containerized Emby still needs readable media, writable persistent data and writable temporary output. A host file being visible to the administrator does not make it visible or readable in the container. Hardware acceleration also needs a supported device interface and required libraries or drivers in the relevant environment. Container packaging does not manufacture a missing codec engine. Resource limits govern available work within that shared system. They can constrain a container without reserving an equal set of physical devices solely for it. See Also Virtual machines and the guest server environment Docker images, running containers and writable layers Container bind mounts and host-path mappings Container CPU and memory limits References Docker containers Linux kernel: control group v2

articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.title: Docker images, running containers and writable layers | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.keywords: Docker images, running containers and writable layers A Docker image supplies a packaged filesystem and configuration, while a container adds a running lifecycle and a writable layer. A Docker image is a packaged starting point for containers. It contains filesystem layers and metadata such as the default command. A container adds a particular runtime configuration, writable layer and process lifecycle. Several containers can start from the same image while using different mounted data and settings. Restarting and replacing are different operations Operation Usual relationship to the writable layer Stop and restart the same container Its existing writable layer remains Remove that container Its writable layer is removed with it Create another container from the image A new writable layer begins Reuse an existing mounted volume The volume's data can remain across replacement Writing important application data only into the container's own layer can therefore seem persistent through ordinary restarts but disappear when the container is replaced. For Emby, the server's intended persistent-data path has to map to storage with the required lifecycle. Reusing the same image alone does not reuse the old container's stored state. A tag names a reference An image tag is a reference that can be updated to identify another image. A digest identifies particular image content under the digest mechanism. An original lifecycle model is: Tag "server:example" -> image digest D1 today Tag "server:example" -> image digest D2 later Existing container C1: still based on its selected D1 image New container C2: can start from the newly selected D2 image The labels are fictional. Updating or downloading the tagged image does not rewrite the software running in every existing container automatically. Software updates can also update stored data A replacement image can contain a new server or dependency version. When that software opens persistent data, it may perform a supported migration. Reverting the image is not automatically a valid reversal of that data migration. A reproducible recovery description therefore records both the software selection and the persistent-state generation. The backup scope answers the data part; image identity answers the packaged software part. See Also Software containers and shared-kernel isolation Container volumes and managed persistent storage Persistent application data across server recreation References Docker images Docker containers Docker volumes

articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.title: Container volumes and managed persistent storage | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/containers/Se.keywords: Container volumes and managed persistent storage A container volume stores data outside one container's writable layer, with a managed identity and lifecycle that require deliberate reuse and backup. A Docker volume is a managed storage resource that can be mounted into a container. Its contents live outside that container's writable layer. For Emby application data, that allows a replacement container to reuse persistent state—provided it mounts the intended volume at the application's actual data path. A volume has an identity and lifecycle Object What happens when its container is removed Container writable layer Removed with the container Named volume Can remain and be reused unless a separate applicable removal operation deletes it Anonymous volume Can remain under its generated identity; reuse requires finding or retaining that association Bind-mounted host tree Follows the host storage's lifecycle Persistence does not mean that every cleanup command preserves all volumes. Volume-removal and pruning operations have their own scopes. A new named volume with a similar label is also not the old volume's content. An original example is: Container C1: /config -> volume V1; state generation G1 Container C2: /config -> volume V1; can open G1 Container C3: /config -> new volume V2; does not thereby contain G1 The paths and labels are fictional rather than a universal Emby image configuration. Initial content can be copied When an empty volume is mounted over a container directory that contains files, Docker normally copies those existing files into the volume. A nonempty volume mounted there instead covers the image's directory contents. Options such as volume-nocopy affect initialization. That mechanism explains why changing an image's packaged defaults does not necessarily replace configuration already stored in an existing volume. Persistence is not consistency or backup Several containers can mount a volume, but simultaneous access must be supported by the applications using its files. Sharing one database directory between independent servers does not make those servers a coordinated database cluster. Back up volume content through supported access and the application's consistency method. Docker documents managed volume access rather than treating its private host-storage layout as a directory to edit arbitrarily. The volume preserves a data lifecycle. Application-data backup supplies another recoverable generation, and restoration verifies that it can be used with the intended software and paths. See Also Container bind mounts and host-path mappings Persistent application data across server recreation References Docker volumes

articles/storage/execution/index.html.title: Overview: Server execution environments | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/index.html.keywords: Overview: Server execution environments Server execution environments define the process, resource and dependency context in which media operations run. A service, virtual machine and container expose different views and lifecycles around the application. Processor architecture, memory and native dependencies affect what can execute within that view. The topics here connect those conditions to persistent state and to the resources the server actually uses. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Server processes and background services A server process runs application work, while a background service adds an unattended lifecycle with configured identity, startup and recovery behavior. Processors and memory Processor and memory properties shape software compatibility, parallel work and the resources available to a server workload. Virtual machines A virtual machine runs a guest operating system on virtualized hardware, so the server depends on both guest configuration and host resources. Container execution Container execution connects packaged software with mapped storage, process isolation and shared resource controls. Persistent application data Persistent application data outlives a replaced process or container only when the application's real data paths connect to storage with the required lifetime. Native libraries and runtime dependencies Native dependencies must match the process's architecture, operating-system ABI and runtime requirements, and some are loaded only when a feature is used. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References systemd service execution specification Microsoft Hyper-V architecture Docker volumes Microsoft .NET runtime identifiers

articles/storage/execution/processors/in.title: Overview: Processors and memory | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/processors/in.keywords: Overview: Processors and memory Processor and memory properties shape software compatibility, parallel work and the resources available to a server workload. Architecture determines a native-code compatibility layer; core concurrency describes a scheduling opportunity; memory pressure describes another resource cost. Their different roles connect software compatibility to the amount and cost of available work. These pages separate them before the demands of concurrent media work are assessed. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> x86-64 processor architecture x86-64 is a 64-bit processor architecture used by common server packages, but software also needs a matching operating system, ABI and instruction support. ARM64 processor architecture ARM64 commonly identifies software for Arm's AArch64 execution environment, with operating-system and native-library compatibility still required. CPU cores and concurrent workloads CPU concurrency distributes runnable work across available execution resources, with serial dependencies and shared limits preventing simple multiplication by thread count. RAM and memory pressure Memory pressure occurs when useful allocations compete with available memory, causing reclaim, swapping, stalls or allocation failure within the applicable scope. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Intel architecture software developer manuals Microsoft .NET runtime identifiers Intel architecture optimization manuals Linux kernel: pressure stall information

articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.title: ARM64 architecture and native software compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.keywords: ARM64 architecture and native software compatibility ARM64 commonly identifies software for Arm's AArch64 execution environment, with operating-system and native-library compatibility still required. ARM64 commonly names a 64-bit software target using Arm's AArch64 execution environment. It is different from 32-bit Arm software, often labelled ARM, armv7 or armhf in package ecosystems. A processor capable of AArch64 does not alone establish which operating-system environment is installed. A compatible server package must match that environment. Similar names can identify different targets Name What to establish ARM64 or AArch64 The intended 64-bit execution target AArch32 or a 32-bit Arm package A different execution and binary target Linux ARM64 Linux platform contracts plus Arm64 code Another ARM64 operating system Its own loading and ABI requirements A native x86-64 library cannot simply be loaded into an ARM64 process because both are “64-bit.” Translation or emulation, where available, is another supported environment with its own limitations. The complete dependency path has to match An Emby server can include managed code and also invoke native components. The native executable or library needs the correct architecture, operating-system ABI and supporting libraries. Hardware media access additionally depends on the platform's device and driver interfaces. This explains a partial-success case: the server's main interface starts, but a later media operation fails when it reaches a missing or incompatible native dependency. Initial startup did not exercise that entire path. An original identifier comparison is: linux-arm64 and linux-x64 share a Linux label. Their native instruction-set targets are different. Matching architecture does not remove other ABI/library requirements. Architecture is a compatibility property AArch64 systems range across very different core designs, power limits, memory arrangements and media engines. The architecture name does not specify transcoding capacity or guarantee a particular codec feature. For a supported Emby installation, establish the operating-system and package match first. Performance then follows the actual processor and workload rather than a general assumption that every ARM64 server is either faster or slower than every x86-64 server. See Also x86-64 architecture and compatible server software Native libraries and runtime dependencies CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads References Arm A-profile Architecture Reference Manual Microsoft .NET runtime identifiers

articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.title: CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.keywords: CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads CPU concurrency distributes runnable work across available execution resources, with serial dependencies and shared limits preventing simple multiplication by thread count. A media server can have several kinds of work active at once: requests, scans, metadata processing and software encoding. Operating-system threads let that work be scheduled concurrently, but a thread is not a reserved processor. Physical cores, logical processors and application threads describe different layers. Two threads can share one physical core Some processors expose multiple logical processors per physical core. Those logical processors share execution resources, so they do not behave like an equal number of independent full cores. Other processors use different core types with different capabilities. A process with twenty runnable threads on four available execution contexts still needs the scheduler to alternate or distribute that work. Threads waiting for storage are not demanding CPU continuously. Serial work limits parallel speedup Suppose a fictional job spends 20% of its original time in unavoidable serial work and 80% in ideally parallel work. With four equal cores: Ideal relative time = 0.20 + 0.80 / 4 = 0.40 Ideal speedup = 1 / 0.40 = 2.5 Even the ideal model does not give a fourfold improvement. With infinitely many cores, its serial fraction limits speedup to five. Real coordination, unequal cores and memory competition can reduce the result further. An encoder may have frame dependencies, stage dependencies or a finite amount of parallel work. Increasing its worker count cannot remove those relationships. Several real-time jobs share a budget For a simple model, four equal cores provide at most four core-seconds during one wall-clock second. If each fictional stream requires 1.5 core-seconds per second of presentation, three streams demand 4.5—before other server work. That does not prove a real stream uses that amount. It explains why individually successful jobs can miss deadlines when combined. Observation Possible implication One stream succeeds; several fall behind Aggregate demand or another shared resource exceeds supply Low total CPU use with one busy thread Serial work or a limited parallel stage Many threads but little progress Waiting, contention or quota can be involved Hardware encoding active CPU still handles other pipeline and server work A container quota can reduce the available aggregate time without changing the host's physical core count. Memory and storage bottlenecks can instead leave processors waiting. For Emby, relate CPU evidence to real-time transcoding and the actual concurrent workload. Processor utilization is an observation of scheduled work, not a complete explanation of where a media pipeline lost time. See Also Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines Container CPU and memory limits Thermal throttling and sustained server throughput References Intel architecture optimization manuals Linux kernel: control group v2

articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.title: RAM, reclaim and memory pressure | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.keywords: RAM, reclaim and memory pressure Memory pressure occurs when useful allocations compete with available memory, causing reclaim, swapping, stalls or allocation failure within the applicable scope. RAM holds active application data, temporary working memory and reusable caches. A server can appear to use most of its RAM without being under harmful pressure, because some of that memory can be reclaimed when needed. Pressure is the cost of satisfying demand under the available memory constraints. It can appear as reclaim work, swapping, stalled tasks or failed allocations—not just a large “used” number. Different allocations have different lifetimes Memory role What can happen under pressure File pages retained for reuse Clean pages can often be discarded and read again later Application objects still in use The application must retain or release them according to its lifecycle Dirty cached file data Writeback may be needed before reclamation Memory-backed temporary files Their pages count against relevant memory resources and may use swap Native codec or driver allocations Accounting and release depend on the component and platform A discarded clean artwork page can be fetched again. Reclaiming it still has a performance cost if it is immediately needed again. Repeatedly evicting and reloading useful data can make a workload slow despite little permanent growth. A working set can exceed its scope An original memory model has a 3,000-MB limit: Active application and native work: 2,500 MB Reusable clean cache: 800 MB Combined demand: 3,300 MB Required reduction to fit: 300 MB The arithmetic does not imply that the runtime can always free exactly 300 MB promptly. If enough clean cache can be reclaimed, the workload may continue with more misses. If the genuinely required active allocations exceed the limit, cache eviction alone cannot solve the shortage. Stalls describe the performance effect Linux pressure stall information reports time during which work was delayed by resource pressure. For memory, “some” and “full” pressure have different task-scope meanings; they are not percentages of bytes occupied. In a fictional 100-ms observation, 20 ms with at least one relevant task stalled gives a 20% “some” interval for that declared model. It says something about delay, while an occupied-memory counter says something about capacity. A server can also suffer from swapping without growing indefinitely. If frequently needed pages repeatedly move between RAM and slower storage, useful work spends time waiting for them. Containers have another memory boundary A container's memory accounting can include application allocations and charged file cache. Its own hard limit can be reached while the host still has free RAM. A host-wide memory graph therefore does not prove that the container has headroom. Failure can occur through different allocation and out-of-memory paths depending on the platform. A resource limit is not a promise that every process can use that entire amount independently. For Emby, consider the number of active encoders, scans and temporary-memory consumers together. Memory pressure explains the shared-workload delay when the evidence shows reclaim, stalls or allocation failure; it should not be inferred solely from a full-looking cache graph. See Also Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Temporary storage and RAM disks Container CPU and memory limits References Linux kernel: pressure stall information Linux kernel: control group v2

articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.title: x86-64 architecture and compatible server software | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/processors/Se.keywords: x86-64 architecture and compatible server software x86-64 is a 64-bit processor architecture used by common server packages, but software also needs a matching operating system, ABI and instruction support. x86-64 is the 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction-set family. Software labels such as x64 , x86-64 and AMD64 commonly identify this architecture. The AMD64 label does not mean that a package runs only on AMD-branded processors. Choosing an Emby server package requires more than seeing “64-bit” in a processor description. Compatibility has several layers Layer Example distinction Processor instruction set x86-64 versus ARM64 Operating system Windows versus Linux Binary format and ABI How the platform loads code and passes arguments Native library environment Required runtime libraries and their versions Optional instruction features Instructions beyond the baseline architecture A Linux x64 native library is not automatically loadable by a Windows x64 process. They share the processor architecture but differ in platform contracts. An original package model illustrates the naming: linux-x64: Linux environment, x86-64 architecture win-x64: Windows environment, x86-64 architecture linux-arm64: different processor architecture These are .NET runtime-identifier examples, not a list of every available Emby package or a guarantee that a particular package has no other requirements. A 64-bit label does not specify all hardware The architecture supports a 64-bit execution environment, but implementations have particular virtual-address and physical-address limits. It is not correct to infer that a machine can install or address the entire theoretical 64-bit range of RAM. Core counts, instruction extensions, memory bandwidth and hardware media engines also vary. Two x86-64 processors can provide very different sustained encoding performance. For Emby, use the supported package for the actual operating system and architecture, then assess the workload's required features. A compatible CPU can execute the server while a particular native library, driver or hardware-acceleration path still needs another supported component. See Also ARM64 architecture and native software compatibility Native libraries and runtime dependencies CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads References Intel architecture software developer manuals Microsoft .NET runtime identifiers

articles/storage/execution/Server-Native.title: Native libraries and runtime dependencies | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/Server-Native.keywords: Native libraries and runtime dependencies Native dependencies must match the process's architecture, operating-system ABI and runtime requirements, and some are loaded only when a feature is used. A server can combine managed application code with native executables or libraries. Media processing, database access and hardware interfaces can use native components. The native component has to fit the process and platform that load it. A file being present in a directory is not enough. A feature can exercise a later loading path Imagine a server that starts successfully and displays its library. A playback request then invokes a native media component whose architecture does not match the running process. Startup success is consistent with that later failure if startup did not load or execute the component. The same pattern can occur when only a particular codec or hardware interface needs an additional dependency. Requirement Example mismatch Instruction-set architecture ARM64 process and x86-64 library Process binary environment 32-bit component and 64-bit process without a supported bridge Operating-system ABI Linux binary used as a Windows native library Runtime/library environment Required native symbol or version unavailable Device interface User-space library exists but its driver/device path is unavailable A managed assembly and a native library therefore need different compatibility evidence. The server's language does not remove the native component's platform contract. The loader searches and resolves symbols The operating system and runtime apply loading rules: finding the component, opening its dependencies and resolving the expected functions. A “not found” error can refer to a dependency of the named file, rather than that named file itself. A symbol error can mean that a file was found but does not provide the expected API or ABI. A device-access error can occur later still, after the library loaded successfully. For .NET packages, runtime identifiers such as linux-x64 and linux-arm64 help select platform-specific assets. They do not promise that every native prerequisite or driver is bundled. Preserve the intended software combination Use the supported server package and documented dependency arrangement for the platform. Replacing a library with a similarly named file can change the ABI or supported behavior without satisfying the missing requirement. For Emby diagnostics, retain the server version, architecture, invoked feature and exact loading or device error. Those facts identify which compatibility layer failed more precisely than a general statement that “the server works except for transcoding.” See Also x86-64 architecture and compatible server software ARM64 architecture and native software compatibility Docker images, running containers and writable layers References Microsoft .NET runtime identifiers Microsoft .NET native library loading

articles/storage/execution/Server-Persis.title: Persistent application data across server recreation | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/Server-Persis.keywords: Persistent application data across server recreation Persistent application data outlives a replaced process or container only when the application's real data paths connect to storage with the required lifetime. Persistent application data is the stored state that the server must carry into its next execution: configuration, databases, user records and any other required durable files. The operating system, service manager or container can replace the process while those files remain. The persistence depends on where the application actually writes them. A configured mount must cover the real data path An original arrangement maps a volume to /config . If the application instead writes its database under /var/example/data in the container layer, that database does not acquire the volume's lifecycle merely because /config exists. Location used by the application Lifetime to establish Process memory Ends with the process Container writable layer Can survive a restart but ends when that container is removed Mounted volume or host directory Follows that storage resource's lifecycle Temporary memory-backed storage Does not provide ordinary reboot persistence Remote share Depends on the remote storage and accessible mount The path names above are illustrative. Emby's supported package or image defines its own paths and settings. A restart can hide a placement mistake Suppose a container restarts repeatedly and its user state survives. That observation shows the files outlived those process restarts. It does not prove they will outlive container removal. Recreating the container with another image exercises a different boundary. Verify that the replacement maps the existing persistent state, rather than a newly created empty volume. Server state can also refer to media paths, credentials and plugin resources outside its own directory. Persisting the directory does not keep all those external dependencies available. Some data can be regenerated Caches and generated indexes may have supported regeneration paths. User histories, manually configured settings and plugin-owned records can have different value and recovery requirements. Classify data by the application's documented role, rather than declaring every database a disposable index or every file below a directory named “cache” harmless. Application-data backups preserve another usable generation. Persistence keeps the current storage relationship across an ordinary lifecycle event; backup and restoration address loss or unwanted changes to that relationship. See Also Docker images, running containers and writable layers Container volumes and managed persistent storage Media files and server application data References Docker volumes Emby manual backups

articles/storage/execution/Server-Proces.title: Server processes and background services | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/Server-Proces.keywords: Server processes and background services A server process runs application work, while a background service adds an unattended lifecycle with configured identity, startup and recovery behavior. Emby Server does its work inside an operating-system process. A background-service arrangement lets that process start and run without a user keeping a desktop session open. The service manager supplies a lifecycle around the application: when to launch it, which identity to use, and what to do when it exits. Those choices affect availability as well as storage access. A running process has not passed every startup step State What it establishes Service launch requested The manager has attempted to start the application Process exists The operating system is running it Listener is available A connection can reach that listening endpoint Application is ready Required startup work has completed under its readiness rule Media operation succeeds The needed source, identity and processing path also work A server can accept connections while an optional source is unavailable, or fail startup because required application data cannot be opened. A process identifier alone does not distinguish those results. Service dependencies can coordinate startup ordering. They do not continuously guarantee that a NAS remains reachable after startup. A restart changes volatile state Restarting replaces the process's memory, open connections and running work. Persistent configuration and databases remain on their storage unless another operation changes them. Data or work Typical relationship to a process restart In-memory cached result Lost and later rebuilt Open playback or API connection Interrupted Persistent user state Loaded from stored data again Task in progress Completion or recovery depends on the application Service identity and environment Established for the new process A restart can pick up changed group membership or configuration. It does not repair an incorrect library path or turn a missing volume into the expected storage. Unattended operation depends on the execution context A desktop launch can inherit that user's environment and path view. A service uses its configured account and service environment. Containers and restricted namespaces can introduce further differences. For an Emby server expected to resume after a reboot, verify the lifecycle and the resources it needs: persistent application data, writable temporary output and readable media paths. Background-service storage access develops the identity and pathname checks separately. See Also Storage access from background services Persistent application data across server recreation Background task scheduling and shared resources References systemd service execution specification Microsoft Windows services

articles/storage/execution/Server-VM.htm.title: Virtual machines and the guest server environment | Emby Learn
articles/storage/execution/Server-VM.htm.keywords: Virtual machines and the guest server environment A virtual machine runs a guest operating system on virtualized hardware, so the server depends on both guest configuration and host resources. A virtual machine presents hardware to a guest operating system. Emby Server runs inside that guest, while the hypervisor and host supply its processor time, memory, storage and devices. This is a different boundary from an ordinary application process. The guest has its own operating-system environment and its own view of the hardware made available to it. The guest has paths and identities of its own Resource Guest's view Host relationship CPU Virtual processors Scheduled on available host execution resources Memory Assigned guest memory Backed by host memory under hypervisor policy Storage Virtual disks or exposed devices Files, devices or storage services managed below Network Virtual interface Connected through the host's configured virtual network GPU Device interface presented to guest Requires a supported virtualization or assignment arrangement A host directory is not automatically a guest library path. The guest needs a supported route to that storage, and its server identity must have access there. Eight virtual CPUs are not eight reserved cores A VM can advertise eight virtual processors while competing with other VMs for physical time. The host's scheduling, limits and reservations determine the result. A virtual-CPU count therefore describes the guest's available execution contexts rather than a universal physical allocation guarantee. In an original contention model, two VMs each request four core-seconds of work during a second, but the host has four equal cores. Their combined demand is eight core-seconds against four available. No scheduling policy can supply all that demand in that interval. Memory overcommit and storage contention can create other waits that a guest sees as slow operations. Measurements inside the guest may not reveal which competing host workload caused them. Hardware media access crosses the boundary A virtual display adapter does not automatically expose a physical GPU's video decoder or encoder. Device assignment or a supported virtual-GPU arrangement, guest drivers and application support all participate. A server can therefore start and stream directly while hardware transcoding is unavailable in the guest. Verify the actual device interfaces visible there rather than deriving codec support from the host's GPU name. VM snapshots have their own consistency scope. Capturing virtual disks does not universally equal an application-aware backup of a running Emby server. Application-data backups explain the stored-state requirement separately. See Also Software containers and shared-kernel isolation Persistent application data across server recreation References Microsoft Hyper-V architecture Intel architecture software developer manuals

articles/storage/file-systems/activity/i.title: Overview: File activity and notifications | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/activity/i.keywords: Overview: File activity and notifications File activity mechanisms report time, coordinate concurrent access and notify applications of observed changes. A timestamp, an open-handle conflict and a change event describe different evidence. None is a universal declaration that an import is complete. This branch explains what each mechanism reports so library scanning can relate observed activity to the current readable file state. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> File timestamps File timestamps record particular kinds of activity, with meanings and precision that depend on the operating system and file system. File locking File locks and open-handle sharing rules coordinate concurrent operations, while permissions and file completeness remain separate questions. File system change notifications File-system notifications report observed changes with platform-specific limits, so a trustworthy library inventory also needs reconciliation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Windows file times Linux man-pages: flock RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 .NET FileSystemWatcher contract and limitations

articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.title: File locking, share modes and concurrent access | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.keywords: File locking, share modes and concurrent access File locks and open-handle sharing rules coordinate concurrent operations, while permissions and file completeness remain separate questions. A media file can exist and be readable while another process is still writing it. Whether a reader can open it depends partly on the writer's open mode and any locking arrangement. This matters during imports, recordings and metadata updates. A failed open may reflect an incompatible existing handle, even when the server identity has permission to read the file. Permissions do not describe concurrent handles Permissions determine whether an identity may request an operation. A lock or sharing rule coordinates that operation with other activity. A process can pass the permission check and still fail because another process has established an incompatible state. On Windows, CreateFile includes both the access requested by a new handle and the access it permits other handles to share. Compatibility is checked in both directions against existing opens. A writer can allow readers to coexist, or omit read sharing and cause a later read open to fail with a sharing violation. On Linux, ordinary flock locks are advisory: cooperating processes request shared or exclusive locks. A local reader that ignores the advisory mechanism is not automatically prevented from reading simply because another process holds such a lock. Different lock APIs and remote file systems can have different interactions. An importer and a reader An original Windows-style scenario declares the relevant handle choices: Existing importer: requests WRITE; shares READ New player: requests READ; shares READ and WRITE Read open: compatible with these stated access/share choices Existing importer: requests WRITE; shares no access New player: requests READ; shares READ and WRITE Read open: incompatible The model omits delete access, other handles and detailed API flags. Its purpose is to show that permitting shared reads changes concurrency, not the content's completeness. If the first read succeeds, it may still encounter only the bytes written so far. A media container may lack final indexes or have fields awaiting completion. A recording that is still growing is not equivalent to a finished import. Several completion conditions Observation Meaning File can be opened Current access and sharing checks permit the open Writer closes its handle That handle has finished its activity File is renamed to its final name A naming operation has occurred Application reports a successful import The application's completion rule has been met Required data and metadata are synchronized The requested durability contract has completed A workflow can deliberately write under a temporary name and rename when ready. That offers a clearer publication point than asking whether the visible file has stopped growing for a short interval. The exact guarantees depend on the operation and storage. A rename within one file system and a transfer between volumes are not automatically the same operation. Network file access adds protocol behavior SMB implements open/share state and caching coordination. NFS versions and implementations have their own locking, state and recovery rules. Local API behavior can be translated into remote protocol operations, so a local advisory-lock explanation should not be assumed to describe every mounted share. For an Emby scan error, identify the failed operation and its result: permission denied, sharing violation, timeout and incomplete media parsing mean different things. The fact that a file later plays successfully can be consistent with an earlier scan encountering an in-progress or conflicting operation. See Also SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping File-system notifications and library reconciliation References Linux man-pages: flock Windows CreateFile access and sharing modes RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1

articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.title: File-system notifications and library reconciliation | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.keywords: File-system notifications and library reconciliation File-system notifications report observed changes with platform-specific limits, so a trustworthy library inventory also needs reconciliation. File-system notifications let software react when files or directories change without repeatedly scanning every entry. Emby's real-time monitoring uses available file-system support to notice additions and changes. A notification stream is not a complete transaction log. An event says that an observed kind of activity occurred; it does not by itself describe a finished media import or a trustworthy current inventory. One file can produce several events A copy may create a file, write many chunks, change metadata and rename the result. Depending on the notification API and workload, software may receive several events, combined events or repeated events for that work. An original sequence is: 00:00 create Film.part 00:01 write first range 00:02 write another range 00:03 close writer 00:04 rename Film.part to Film.mkv The first event occurs before the movie is complete. Even a close event has the meaning supplied by its API and producer; it does not universally certify a durable, valid media file. A scanner may need to reopen and analyze the result. An event queue has limits Events consume memory and require processing. If a producer outruns the consumer, a bounded queue can overflow. Linux inotify reports queue overflow; .NET FileSystemWatcher documents loss when its internal buffer is exceeded. An original four-slot queue model receives six separate events before any are consumed. At most four fit, so the remaining events cannot all be retained under that model. The overflow signal tells the consumer that completeness has been lost; it does not recreate the missing details. Increasing a buffer can help with a particular burst, but it does not turn a finite queue into an unlimited history. Notification scope, filters and processing work also matter. A remote change may bypass the watcher Linux inotify observes events generated through the local kernel's file-system activity. It does not generally catch changes made by other machines directly on a network file system. Another protocol or platform may supply server-side change notifications. SMB change notification, an NFS mount and a local ext4 watch do not all provide identical behavior. “The path is readable” is therefore insufficient evidence that every remote edit will produce the events a monitoring API expects. Emby's documentation limits real-time monitoring to supported file systems. A server restart after changing that setting is also part of its documented setup. Scheduled or explicit scans remain relevant when the notification path is incomplete. Reconciliation asks what exists now A reconciliation scan enumerates the current tree and compares it with the stored library view. That can recover an addition whose notification was lost or combine several events into one current file state. The observation still needs context. A successful scan of the intended accessible tree can support an inventory update. A failed enumeration, a disconnected share or an uncovered mount-point directory is different evidence. Observation Appropriate interpretation Several events for one path Recheck the current file; do not assume several independent movies Queue overflow The event history is incomplete No remote notification The watch mechanism may not observe that remote activity Successful enumeration of the intended tree Current inventory evidence Enumeration fails or reaches the wrong tree Incomplete or misleading inventory evidence The implementation may debounce changes, retry analysis or schedule reconciliation. Those are application choices, not guarantees inherent in receiving a file event. The useful model is a notification prompting observation, with scanning restoring current state when event completeness cannot be relied upon. See Also Incremental library scans Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state References .NET FileSystemWatcher contract and limitations Linux man-pages: inotify Emby library setup

articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.title: File timestamps and what each clock field means | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/activity/S.keywords: File timestamps and what each clock field means File timestamps record particular kinds of activity, with meanings and precision that depend on the operating system and file system. A file does not have one universal “date.” Its timestamps record different events. A copy tool can preserve some of them, a file system can record them at limited precision, and an application can choose which ones to compare. For Emby, those dates can contribute to library scanning or displayed file information. They do not replace the server's own playback history or identify every change to the content. Which event does the field describe? Field Usual meaning in the stated model What it does not establish Linux mtime Last content modification When the file first entered this library Linux ctime Last file-status change, including relevant metadata changes File creation time Birth/creation time, where supported Creation of this file object Original release date or the age of copied content Access time Access activity recorded under the platform's policy A complete record of who watched a film Linux ctime is particularly easy to misread. A permissions or ownership change can update status-change time without changing the film's bytes. Birth time is a separate field and is not available through every file system or API. A new copy can have an old modification time Suppose a transfer finishes today but preserves the source's modification time from last year. The destination is newly created, yet its modification timestamp remains old. An original comparison illustrates the consequence: Previous observation: length 1,000,000 bytes; mtime 2026-09-01T12:00:00Z Current observation: length 1,000,000 bytes; mtime 2026-09-01T12:00:00Z Those equal observations do not prove identical bytes. A tool could have preserved the time while replacing equal-length content. Detecting that replacement may require stronger evidence, such as a checksum, rather than only the two fields shown. Precision and clock conventions FAT's write timestamp has two-second resolution; its access field records a date. NTFS stores its timestamp values in UTC, while traditional FAT records local-time values. The field's storage precision and an application's displayed formatting are different issues. For an illustrative two-second bucket, changes at 12:00:00.4 and 12:00:01.2 can map to the same bucket. A comparison at that precision cannot distinguish their order. Copying through a format with lower precision can also lose detail that existed on the source. Do not interpret access-time updates as a playback counter: mount policies, delayed updates and operations unrelated to watching affect them. Incremental scanning uses file observations to decide what needs more work; those observations should retain the meaning and limits of their source fields. See Also Incremental library scans File-system notifications and library reconciliation File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata References Windows file times Linux man-pages: inode metadata and timestamps

articles/storage/file-systems/index.html.title: Overview: File systems and paths | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/index.html.keywords: Overview: File systems and paths File systems connect names and stored data through allocation, limits, access rules and activity mechanisms. A path identifies a file through a particular filesystem and its current view. Format limits, links and mounted trees influence that lookup, while timestamps, locks and notifications describe activity around the file. The branches here follow those relationships from stored capacity to a server's actual observation. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> File systems A file system turns storage space into named files and directories, with allocation, metadata and access rules defined by its format and implementation. File size limits A file-size limit restricts one file independently of the volume's total free space, which matters for long recordings and high-bitrate media. Path names and links Path names and links determine how a process resolves a visible location to a particular file or mounted tree. File activity and notifications File activity mechanisms report time, coordinate concurrent access and notify applications of observed changes. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux kernel: ext4 inodes Microsoft exFAT file-system specification

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/inde.title: Overview: Path names and links | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/inde.keywords: Overview: Path names and links Path names and links determine how a process resolves a visible location to a particular file or mounted tree. Two similar spellings can compare differently, and one unchanged pathname can expose a different tree after a mount changes. Symbolic and hard links add distinct naming relationships. These topics explain the identity behind the path the server opens, rather than only the text displayed in a file browser. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Case-sensitive paths Case-sensitive lookup distinguishes names such as Film.mkv and film.mkv, while case preservation merely retains their spelling. Unicode file names Unicode file names can contain visually identical text encoded as different character sequences, so normalization and filesystem comparison rules affect path matching. Mount points A mount point attaches a file system to a pathname, so the same visible path can expose different data when the mount state or namespace changes. Symbolic links A symbolic link stores a target pathname that is resolved when accessed, allowing indirection across directories or file systems. Hard links Hard links give one file multiple directory names on the same file system, so changes through either name affect the same content. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft: directory case sensitivity Unicode Standard Annex 15: normalization forms Linux man-pages: mount namespaces Linux man-pages: symbolic links Linux kernel: ext4 directory entries

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.title: Case-sensitive paths and preserved spelling | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.keywords: Case-sensitive paths and preserved spelling Case-sensitive lookup distinguishes names such as Film.mkv and film.mkv, while case preservation merely retains their spelling. A file system can preserve the spelling Film.mkv while allowing it to be opened as film.mkv . That is case-preserving but case-insensitive lookup. With case-sensitive lookup, those names can identify different files. The distinction affects media collections moved between systems and paths written into scripts, sidecar references or server configuration. Two names, two possible inventories Names present Sensitive lookup Insensitive lookup Only Film.mkv Exact spelling is needed for that name Differently cased spellings can resolve to it Film.mkv and film.mkv Both can be distinct entries They cannot normally coexist as two distinct names under the same insensitive naming rules Request FILM.mkv Can fail when no matching entry exists Can resolve to the existing case variant These are naming models. The application may also perform its own comparisons, and a network server can expose rules different from the client's local file system. A move can introduce a collision Imagine a source directory containing Poster.jpg and poster.jpg as two different images. A transfer to a case-insensitive destination cannot preserve both using only those original names. A tool may stop, replace one according to its policy, or generate another name. That is a naming collision, not evidence that one image was corrupt. Resolve the intended names and references before treating a transfer as complete. A sidecar reference that still uses the old spelling may become broken on a sensitive destination. Windows and Linux are useful defaults, not universal rules Many Linux file-system arrangements use case-sensitive names. Windows commonly uses insensitive lookup while preserving case. NTFS can support case-sensitive directories, including arrangements used with Windows Subsystem for Linux. The directory setting and application behavior therefore matter more than an absolute “Windows never distinguishes case” rule. For a network share, the remote server's naming policy participates. For a container, the mounted file system still has its own rules; starting Linux software does not automatically convert the underlying names. Use the server's actual path spelling when investigating an unavailable Emby source. If a path works only with one capitalization, that observation describes the current lookup behavior. It does not establish how a later copy, share or mounted directory will compare the same name. See Also Unicode file names and visually identical spellings Mount points and the file system behind a path References Microsoft: directory case sensitivity Windows file and path naming

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.title: Hard links: several names for one file | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.keywords: Hard links: several names for one file Hard links give one file multiple directory names on the same file system, so changes through either name affect the same content. A hard link gives a file another name on the same file system. Both directory entries refer to the same file object. There is no “original file” containing the data and a separate link containing its pathname. That is the key difference from a symbolic link , which stores a target path. Two names, one content An original example uses an arbitrary file identifier: /srv/archive/Film.mkv -> file object 740 /srv/library/Film.mkv -> file object 740 Link count: 2 Writing to the file through either name changes the content seen through the other. A hard link is therefore not an independent backup. Corruption or an unwanted overwrite of that shared object affects both paths. Removing one name reduces the link count but leaves the other name usable. Removing the final name makes the file unnamed; actual reclamation can also wait for remaining open references, according to platform behavior. The boundary is the file system Arrangement Same content object? Can ordinarily cross file systems?
