Hard link Yes No Symbolic link Resolves a target path Yes Independent full copy No Yes The same-file-system restriction follows from how file identifiers are scoped. A directory entry cannot simply refer to an unrelated inode number on another file system. Windows NTFS hard links likewise remain within the volume. Hard links normally concern files, not unrestricted directory graphs. Systems restrict directory hard links because arbitrary directory linking would complicate tree traversal and consistency. A library can encounter both names If both paths fall within an Emby library's scanned locations, the scanner can encounter the same content through two names. Whether the resulting entries are merged or presented separately depends on the library's matching and organization behavior, not merely on shared disk allocation. Storage accounting can also differ depending on whether a tool counts path lengths or unique file objects. Two five-GB names do not imply ten GB of distinct stored media in this example. When interpreting duplicates, establish whether the files are independent objects before drawing conclusions from their names or displayed sizes. See Also Symbolic links and target-path resolution File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata References Linux kernel: ext4 directory entries Linux kernel: ext4 inodes Windows hard links and junctions

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.title: Mount points and the file system behind a path | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.keywords: Mount points and the file system behind a path A mount point attaches a file system to a pathname, so the same visible path can expose different data when the mount state or namespace changes. A mount attaches a file system at a location in a directory tree. On a Linux server, /srv/media might expose a local disk or an NFS share. On Windows, storage can be reached through drive letters or supported mounted-volume paths. The text of the path is only part of its identity. Which file system is mounted there, and which namespace the process sees, determine the content behind it. A mounted directory covers what was underneath Suppose the local root file system already contains the directory /srv/media . Mounting another file system there makes lookups enter the mounted tree. The underlying local directory is covered, rather than merged with the new files. An original state example is: Mount active: /srv/media/Film.mkv -> file on the media volume Mount absent: /srv/media -> underlying local directory /srv/media/Film.mkv -> not found if that directory has no Film.mkv Files already stored in the covered directory are not deleted by mounting another tree over it. They can become visible again when that covering mount is absent. An absent mount can still leave a writable path A recording or import aimed at /srv/media might write into the underlying local directory if the expected mount is absent and that directory permits writes. The application can then fill the wrong volume. Similarly, an empty directory is not proof that the intended share is empty. It may be the uncovered directory. Compare mount or volume identity as well as path existence before interpreting the contents. This is particularly important for a library inventory. A successful enumeration of the wrong empty directory is a different observation from a successful enumeration of the intended media volume. The process has its own view Linux mount namespaces let processes see different mount arrangements. A container can have /media mapped from a host path such as /srv/media . A service can also have namespace restrictions. Seeing a mount in an administrator's shell does not prove that the server process sees the same one. The relevant check is whether the server's pathname resolves to the expected storage in its own execution environment. Ownership, directory traversal and remote credentials are later access checks; they do not correct a path that points at the wrong tree. Library paths should identify the intended storage In Emby, configure a library path that exists and remains meaningful in the server's environment. A viewer's desktop path is not automatically the server's path. If a volume reconnects under another drive letter or a container mapping changes, the old library path can refer to nothing or to something else. Unavailable network mounts explains the additional distinction between an absent mount and a mount that is still present but cannot complete file operations. See Also Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state Symbolic links and target-path resolution Storage access from background services References Linux man-pages: mount namespaces Linux man-pages: pathname resolution Emby library setup

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.title: Symbolic links and target-path resolution | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.keywords: Symbolic links and target-path resolution A symbolic link stores a target pathname that is resolved when accessed, allowing indirection across directories or file systems. A symbolic link is a directory entry whose content names another path. Accessing it normally continues pathname resolution at that target. Unlike a copy, the link does not store another complete set of the movie's bytes. A link can point across file-system boundaries, and it can exist even when its target is absent. A relative target begins beside the link Consider this original layout: Link location: /srv/library/Recent/Film.mkv Stored target: ../../archive/Film.mkv Resolved path: /srv/archive/Film.mkv The target starts from /srv/library/Recent , the link's containing directory. It does not start from the caller's current working directory. An absolute target instead starts from the root visible to the resolving process. Moving a relative link to another directory can change what it resolves to. Moving the target without updating the link can leave the old target name dangling. A visible link is not evidence of accessible content Link observation What the operation still needs The link entry exists A resolvable target The target exists elsewhere The target must exist in this process's namespace The link's directory can be listed Search/traversal rights along the target path The target name is correct Permission to open the target file On Linux, the ordinary permission bits on the symbolic link itself are not the regular-file access gate; the target and directory resolution checks matter. Link ownership and specialized protections can still affect particular operations. Windows also has symbolic links and other reparse-point mechanisms, including junctions. Those mechanisms have their own creation, target and platform rules; a junction is not merely another spelling for every kind of symbolic link. The link changes the tree a scanner encounters A linked directory can lead outside the apparent library root or back into a location already visited. Scanner behavior must account for supported link traversal, cycles and repeated paths. The existence of an operating-system link does not establish how a particular application's scan treats it. For Emby, verify that the supported library arrangement reaches the intended target under the server identity. The same link can work on the host and fail inside a container where its absolute target path is not mounted. Hard links avoid target-path indirection but have a different same-file-system boundary. See Also Hard links: several names for one file Mount points and the file system behind a path File ownership and permissions across a library path References Linux man-pages: symbolic links Linux man-pages: pathname resolution Windows hard links and junctions

articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.title: Unicode file names and visually identical spellings | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/paths/Stor.keywords: Unicode file names and visually identical spellings Unicode file names can contain visually identical text encoded as different character sequences, so normalization and filesystem comparison rules affect path matching. A title such as Café.mkv looks straightforward on screen. Its accented letter can be represented by one Unicode code point, or by a base letter followed by a combining accent. The text can look identical while the stored sequences differ. That matters when a path moves between tools or systems that compare, preserve or normalize names differently. One visible word, two sequences Composed: C a f é . m k v U+0043 U+0061 U+0066 U+00E9 ... Decomposed: C a f e ◌́ . m k v U+0043 U+0061 U+0066 U+0065 U+0301 ... Unicode normalization defines standard ways to transform canonically equivalent sequences. NFC commonly produces the composed form where a composition exists; NFD produces canonical decompositions. In this example, both names normalize to the same NFC string. Comparison Result for these two names Exact code-point sequence Different NFC-normalized sequence Equal Original appearance in a typical font Often indistinguishable Upper/lowercase comparison A separate rule from normalization Normalization is not a universal test for all visually similar text. A Latin letter and a similar-looking letter from another script need not be canonically equivalent. It also does not remove every restriction on reserved characters or pathname lengths. The file system chooses its own naming behavior Windows naming documentation describes Unicode storage for long names in its modern file systems. Linux ext4 directory entries store names as byte strings. Other file systems or network services may use particular normalization and comparison rules. It is therefore incorrect to assume that every file system converts all names to NFC, or that every Linux directory contains valid UTF-8 names. The application, transfer tool and destination can each influence the resulting representation. An Emby library may contain a correctly displayed title while an external script fails to open the visually matching path. The displayed media title can also come from metadata rather than from the filename, so it is not a reliable source for reconstructing that filename. Inspect the actual directory entry When an apparently matching name fails, compare the name enumerated from the directory with the requested name, including code points or encoded bytes where appropriate. Preserve the exact path during that investigation. Changing names can affect sidecars, playlists and existing path references. A name comparison should establish the difference first. Normalization explains this particular mismatch; it does not imply that every accented filename needs renaming. See Also Case-sensitive paths and preserved spelling File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata References Unicode Standard Annex 15: normalization forms Windows file and path naming Linux kernel: ext4 directory entries

articles/storage/file-systems/Storage-Fi.title: File size limits and large media files | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/Storage-Fi.keywords: File size limits and large media files A file-size limit restricts one file independently of the volume's total free space, which matters for long recordings and high-bitrate media. A volume can have plenty of free space and still reject a large movie. Free space is the amount available for allocation; a file-size limit is the largest single file the format and implementation can represent. FAT32 is the familiar example. Its file-length field is 32 bits, giving a maximum of 4,294,967,295 bytes , or 4 GiB minus one byte . A 5-GB file exceeds that boundary even on a nearly empty, much larger volume. Why the units matter One decimal GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes. One GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. A displayed value near “4 GB” can therefore conceal which side of FAT32's boundary the file actually occupies. Candidate file length Fits the FAT32 field? 4,000,000,000 bytes Yes 4,294,967,295 bytes Yes, exactly at the field limit 4,294,967,296 bytes No 5,000,000,000 bytes No Available space, application behavior and other limits still apply to entries marked “Yes.” Duration can turn an ordinary bitrate into a large file For a constant 20-Mbit/s payload, reaching the boundary takes approximately: 4,294,967,295 bytes × 8 ÷ 20,000,000 bits/s = 1,717.986918 seconds ≈ 28 minutes 38 seconds Container overhead consumes additional bytes. Variable bitrate changes accumulation over time. The example explains the order of magnitude; it is not a guaranteed recording duration. Splitting a recording into several files changes the organization and requires suitable application support. Renaming a file or changing its extension does not reduce its byte length. Other limits remain separate exFAT and commonly deployed modern file systems can support much larger files. Their actual supported limits depend on format fields, allocation parameters, operating-system implementation and sometimes application APIs. A theoretical field maximum is not a claim that a particular installed system can create a file of that size. A path-length error concerns the name used to reach a file. A quota concerns an account's or directory's allocation. A full disk concerns available capacity. These failures may all occur during a copy, but they call for different evidence. Check the source file's exact length and destination format before interpreting a failed large transfer. See Also File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata Bitrate References Microsoft FAT on-media specification: fatgen103.doc in the legacy document collection Microsoft exFAT file-system specification Windows file-system features and limits

articles/storage/file-systems/Storage-Fi.title: File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata | Emby Learn
articles/storage/file-systems/Storage-Fi.keywords: File systems: names, allocation and persistent metadata A file system turns storage space into named files and directories, with allocation, metadata and access rules defined by its format and implementation. A block device supplies addressable storage. A file system adds names, directories, file lengths and the rules for finding and updating data. It also records metadata such as timestamps and, where supported, ownership and permissions. An Emby library addresses files through paths. The file system and the operating system turn those paths into readable data. A network share adds another server and protocol to that process. A name is not the file's physical location A file can occupy several ranges of a device. Its directory entry does not need to contain every physical block address. For example, ext4 directory entries refer to inode numbers, and inodes hold file metadata and allocation information. This separation enables names to change without rewriting the movie's bytes. It also explains hard links , where several names refer to one file object. Logical length and allocated space A file's logical length describes the byte positions accessible through it. Allocated space describes storage consumed according to the file system's allocation rules. These can differ because of allocation units, sparse regions, compression or shared storage features. For a simple non-sparse file with a 4,096-byte allocation unit: Logical file length: 5,000 bytes Allocation units needed: ceiling(5,000 ÷ 4,096) = 2 Allocated data space: 2 × 4,096 = 8,192 bytes The model excludes metadata and format-specific optimizations. Sparse files can instead have a logical length larger than the data space currently allocated. A media file's displayed size is therefore not always the best measure of its physical storage cost. Features appear in ordinary library work Feature Why it matters Large-file support A long recording must fit as one file Naming rules Imported names must remain addressable Native access controls The server identity needs suitable rights Journaling Interrupted metadata updates can be recovered according to the format's rules Change notification support Real-time library monitoring depends on available mechanisms NTFS provides native Windows ACLs; exFAT does not provide equivalent per-file ACLs in its on-media format. A host can still apply mount-level or sharing access rules to exFAT storage. Those external rules do not become native ACL entries stored in each exFAT file. A journal is also not a backup of every previous movie version. It supports consistency or recovery of specified updates. Which data are covered depends on the file system and its operating mode. When moving a collection, consider the format, host driver and access method together. A format that accepts a large file on one computer can still present different naming, permission or notification behavior through another operating system or a NAS share. See Also File size limits and large media files Mount points and the file system behind a path File ownership and permissions across a library path References Linux kernel: ext4 inodes Linux kernel: ext4 directory entries Microsoft exFAT file-system specification Windows file-system features and limits

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/i.title: Overview: Storage hardware and connections | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/i.keywords: Overview: Storage hardware and connections Storage hardware and connections describe the medium, command interface and path supplying file data. An SSD names a medium, SATA or NVMe names an interface arrangement, and USB or network attachment adds another part of the path. HDD behavior contributes mechanical positioning and rotation. These pages keep those layers separate so a large interface-rate label does not stand in for the observed workload. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Hard disk drives A hard disk drive reads magnetic platters through moving heads, so positioning and rotation influence small and mixed workloads. Solid-state drives A solid-state drive accesses flash through a controller that manages physical pages, erased blocks, spare space and write endurance. SATA storage SATA connects storage devices through a negotiated serial interface whose link rate is separate from useful file throughput. NVMe storage NVMe defines storage commands and queues, commonly carried over PCIe for local SSDs, while slot wiring and workload determine usable performance. USB-attached storage USB-attached storage adds a negotiated host connection and enclosure bridge between the server and the physical drive. Network-attached storage (NAS) A NAS serves files over a network, so media access depends on its disks, sharing protocol, access policy and connection to the Emby server. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Shingled recording and data management (Seagate-hosted research paper) SATA-IO naming and interface specifications NVM Express NVM Command Set specifications NVM Express Base Specification USB 3.2 specification Microsoft SMB versions 2 and 3 protocol specification RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads A hard disk drive reads magnetic platters through moving heads, so positioning and rotation influence small and mixed workloads. A hard disk drive stores data on rotating magnetic platters. Its heads move to the required tracks, then wait for the relevant sectors to arrive underneath them. Once positioned, a drive can read a long run of adjacent data without repeating the full positioning operation for every byte. That makes HDDs well suited to storing large media collections and serving sustained reads. Their behavior changes when requests keep jumping between distant locations. What 7,200 RPM actually tells you At 7,200 revolutions per minute, one rotation takes about 8.33 milliseconds: Rotation period = 60 seconds ÷ 7,200 = 0.008333... seconds Ideal average rotational wait = half a rotation = 4.1667 ms The second result assumes requests arrive at uniformly distributed rotational positions. It excludes head movement, controller work, queued requests and data transfer. It is not a promise that an arbitrary read completes in 4.17 ms. RPM alone cannot rank complete drives. Track layout, recording density, firmware, workload and request size also affect results. Even one drive can have different sustained transfer rates across its recording surface. Several films can create repeated head movement Each player may read forward through its own film. The drive still has to alternate between their locations, as well as artwork requests, scans or background writes. Read-ahead and request scheduling can combine operations, but they do not make several distant files occupy one continuous run. When playback buffers already contain enough data, short positioning delays can be invisible. A library scan may expose the same delays as slower progress through many files. Storage latency describes that response-time aspect separately from bulk transfer speed. CMR and SMR affect the write workload Conventional magnetic recording leaves tracks that can be rewritten without the shingled dependency of overlapping tracks. Shingled magnetic recording increases density by overlapping tracks, which introduces additional data-management work when existing regions are updated. With drive-managed SMR , firmware preserves the ordinary block-device interface and handles that work internally. A fast initial write can consume a staging area; later writes may have to wait for rearrangement. Host-managed SMR exposes sequential-write constraints that require suitable host software. These are distinct arrangements. This distinction is especially relevant to repeated imports, recording, rebuilding or other sustained writes. It does not imply that every read from an SMR drive is slow. Evaluate the exact model and operation, rather than deriving suitability from capacity or RPM alone. An idle HDD may also spin down . The first access then includes a wake delay before normal positioning and transfer begin. See Also Sequential and random I/O in media workloads Disk spin-down, wake latency and idle workloads SATA storage and negotiated interface rates References Shingled recording and data management (Seagate-hosted research paper) SATA-IO naming and interface specifications

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: Network-attached storage: files served by another computer | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: Network-attached storage: files served by another computer A NAS serves files over a network, so media access depends on its disks, sharing protocol, access policy and connection to the Emby server. A network-attached storage system is a computer that supplies storage services to other computers. An Emby server can open media on the NAS through a file-sharing protocol such as SMB or NFS . The NAS reads its own disks and returns file data. The Emby server still performs its own library work and any transcoding. Merely placing a film on a NAS does not move the encoder onto that NAS. Where the work runs There are two common arrangements. Emby Server can run on a separate computer with the NAS as a media source, or it can run directly on a supported NAS platform. In the second arrangement, storage and server workloads share the NAS's processor, memory and other resources. In the first arrangement, a remote viewer's stream may involve both the NAS-to-server connection and the server-to-viewer connection. If those use the same constrained interface, their traffic can compete. A client that is explicitly configured and supported for direct file access is a different path again; an ordinary Emby HTTP stream does not require the viewer to mount the NAS share. The slowest active part of a read A simplified sustained-read model uses independent useful-rate limits: Disk service: 180 MB/s Network file delivery: 110 MB/s Client receive path: 150 MB/s Upper bound: min(180, 110, 150) = 110 MB/s The figures are teaching assumptions. Actual results include protocol operations, caching, queues and any shared resources. Small operations can be latency-limited even when their combined byte rate is tiny. For four 40-Mbit/s films, average source payload is 20 MB/s. That comparison suggests capacity in the model, but it does not establish real peak behavior, recording coexistence or fast scans. A scan can produce far more file opens and metadata operations than four long reads. A reachable NAS is not yet a readable library Successful check What remains unproven The NAS responds on the network The file-sharing service is available The share is visible The server process can authenticate The directory opens Each required file is readable The desktop can play a file The background service has the same identity and path Emby lists an existing item The source remains accessible now The file-sharing account is usually separate from an Emby viewer account. Share permissions and the NAS's underlying file permissions both influence operations. For NFS, identity mapping and export policy also matter. Stable names and mounted paths help the library continue to address the same content. During an outage, establish whether the share is truly empty, inaccessible, or absent from the current namespace before treating missing observations as file removals. Unavailable mounts develops those states. See Also SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state Network throughput and useful delivery rate References Microsoft SMB versions 2 and 3 protocol specification RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 Emby library setup

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: NVMe storage: commands, PCIe lanes and queues | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: NVMe storage: commands, PCIe lanes and queues NVMe defines storage commands and queues, commonly carried over PCIe for local SSDs, while slot wiring and workload determine usable performance. NVMe, short for Non-Volatile Memory Express, defines how host software submits storage commands and receives completions. Local NVMe SSDs commonly communicate over PCI Express. NVMe also has network transport specifications, so “NVMe” and “PCIe” are not interchangeable names for the entire standard. Its queue-based design allows multiple outstanding operations without using the older SATA command interface. That is useful for parallel storage workloads, but an application must actually issue enough work to use that concurrency. Three specifications on one product label Label Question it answers SSD What kind of storage medium is used? NVMe What command interface is used? PCIe generation and lane count What local transport capacity is available? M.2, U.2 or an add-in card What physical arrangement is used? M.2 does not guarantee NVMe. An M.2 slot can support particular protocols, lengths and keying arrangements, and an M.2 device can be SATA. Compatibility depends on the board and device specifications together. Lanes establish a transport boundary Consider PCIe 3.0 at 8 GT/s per lane with 128b/130b encoding. An original four-lane calculation gives: 8 × 10^9 transfers/s × 128/130 ÷ 8 × 4 lanes ≈ 3.938 × 10^9 bytes/s in one direction This is an encoding-adjusted transport ceiling. PCIe packets, NVMe commands and the device's operation reduce useful file throughput. It is not an SSD benchmark. A drive designed for four lanes may operate with fewer lanes or an older generation in a particular slot. Several devices can also share an upstream connection. The negotiated connection and topology matter more than the largest number printed on the box. Outstanding commands and response time With more than one command in flight, a device can work on operations in parallel or schedule them efficiently. A library scan, simultaneous file access and application-data activity may provide that work. One small read that must finish before the next starts still depends on its individual latency. Increasing queue depth can increase aggregate throughput while also increasing the time a request waits. For an interactive server, those are different outcomes. A high-depth benchmark does not predict how quickly the next poster or database lookup will appear. NVMe does not remove flash write management, storage caches or thermal behavior. It gives a capable storage device an efficient command and transport arrangement; the benefit still follows the actual work the server asks it to perform. See Also Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance SATA storage and negotiated interface rates Storage latency: waiting for individual operations References NVM Express Base Specification PCI-SIG specification library

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: SATA storage and negotiated interface rates | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: SATA storage and negotiated interface rates SATA connects storage devices through a negotiated serial interface whose link rate is separate from useful file throughput. SATA, or Serial ATA, is a storage interface used by both hard disks and SSDs. A controller sends commands over a serial connection to the drive. The drive's medium then has to perform the requested operation. The distinction matters when reading specifications: SATA 6Gb/s describes an interface capability. It does not mean an attached HDD supplies six gigabits of movie data each second. From the link rate to a useful ceiling For SATA's 8b/10b encoding, eight data bits occupy ten transmitted bits. The encoding-only calculation for a 6-Gbit/s link is: 6,000,000,000 bits/s × 8/10 ÷ 8 bits/byte = 600,000,000 bytes/s = 600 decimal MB/s Protocol traffic reduces the useful payload ceiling further. An individual drive's actual workload rate can be much lower again. A slow HDD read does not necessarily indicate that its SATA link negotiated incorrectly. SATA-IO uses the names SATA 1.5Gb/s, SATA 3Gb/s and SATA 6Gb/s for the interface rates. A controller, device and connection must support the negotiated mode. A capable drive on a slower controller does not bypass that controller. Interpreting an attached drive Observation What it establishes SATA 6Gb/s appears in the device specification The specified interface capability A lower negotiated link rate is reported The rate of this connection A large sequential copy reaches a given rate That transfer's observed workload result Small-file operations are slow A latency or workload problem that needs separate evidence A usual internal arrangement has a SATA data cable and a separate power connection. M.2 SATA devices use another physical arrangement while retaining SATA as the storage protocol. Conversely, an M.2 NVMe device uses NVMe over PCIe. Connector, protocol and medium answer different questions. For an Emby server, a healthy SATA connection is often sufficient for bulk media reads. The next useful question is whether the workload is limited by the link, the drive's positioning or write behavior, or competition from other requests. Sequential and random I/O helps distinguish those cases. See Also Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance USB-attached storage and the enclosure connection References SATA-IO naming and interface specifications Serial ATA Revision 3.3 specification

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance A solid-state drive accesses flash through a controller that manages physical pages, erased blocks, spare space and write endurance. A solid-state drive stores data in nonvolatile memory, commonly NAND flash. It has no rotating platter or head to reposition, which greatly changes the cost of scattered reads. Opening artwork, looking up small files and serving database operations can benefit even when a film's bulk read rate would fit comfortably within HDD performance. An SSD is still a storage system with a controller, firmware and finite resources. The absence of a seek motor does not make every operation instantaneous. Why writing is more complicated than reading Flash is organized into pages within larger erase blocks. Existing data cannot generally be overwritten in place like an ordinary logical sector suggests. The controller maps logical addresses to physical storage, writes new versions and eventually reclaims blocks containing obsolete data. This mapping lets applications use the drive as a normal block device. It also creates work beyond the bytes the application wrote: moving still-valid data during reclamation contributes to write amplification . Operation What changes for the SSD Scattered reads No mechanical positioning between addresses Sustained writes New pages must remain available and blocks must be reclaimed Deallocation/TRIM The host tells the drive which logical data need not be preserved Very little free capacity The controller may have less flexibility for reclamation A file deletion does not itself prove that every storage layer passed a deallocation request through to the physical device. Bridges, arrays and file-system support participate. The fast beginning of a copy Some drives use a faster writing area, often by operating part of their flash with fewer bits per cell. Writes can begin at that area's speed, then slow when it fills and data must be folded into denser storage. The size and behavior of such a cache depend on the model, free space and current workload. A short copy into an idle drive therefore does not establish its sustained write rate during a long recording or bulk import. Thermal limits can also influence long transfers. Endurance is a workload budget An endurance rating such as TBW describes an amount of host-written data under the manufacturer's stated warranty conditions. It is not a counter that predicts an exact failure instant. For a fictional 300 decimal TB rating and 100 decimal GB of host writes per day, the arithmetic is 300,000 ÷ 100 = 3,000 days. The real interpretation also needs the warranty's time limit and conditions. Reads of an existing movie collection contribute little to that host-write total; temporary output, recordings and application updates contribute writes. Finally, “SSD” describes the medium, while SATA and NVMe describe interfaces and command arrangements. A SATA SSD is still solid-state storage, and an M.2-shaped device does not identify its protocol by shape alone. See Also NVMe storage: commands, PCIe lanes and queues SATA storage and negotiated interface rates Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes References NVM Express NVM Command Set specifications NVM Express Base Specification

articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.title: USB-attached storage and the enclosure connection | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/hardware/S.keywords: USB-attached storage and the enclosure connection USB-attached storage adds a negotiated host connection and enclosure bridge between the server and the physical drive. An external USB drive is usually more than a disk with another plug. The path includes the host controller, port, cable, enclosure bridge and the drive inside. The bridge may translate USB storage commands to SATA or NVMe commands. That extra chain can work well for an Emby media library. It also supplies several places where bandwidth, power management or a connection fault can affect access. Shape does not specify the rate A USB-C connector describes a physical connector. It does not by itself establish the data rate, storage transport or power available to a particular enclosure. The USB 3.2 specification includes 5, 10 and 20 Gbit/s arrangements. The host, device and connection need compatible capabilities; a “USB 3” label alone can be ambiguous. These are signalling/interface rates, not sustained movie-file transfer measurements. Part of the chain Useful evidence Host and port Supported and negotiated USB rate Cable Data capability and connection integrity Hub or upstream controller Other devices sharing the path Enclosure Bridge protocol, drive support and firmware Physical drive Its own read/write behavior and health A fast enclosure does not make a rotating disk an SSD. A fast SSD inside an enclosure can instead make the USB connection or bridge the limiting component. Two drives may share one upstream path Ports that look separate can share a controller or hub connection. Concurrent copies, recordings and media reads can therefore compete before reaching the drives. For illustration, an idealized shared path that supplies 400 decimal MB/s of useful data cannot independently provide that full rate to each of two simultaneous transfers. If one uses 250 MB/s, at most 150 MB/s remains in that simplified capacity model. Real allocation and overhead are workload-dependent; the numbers are invented, not a USB product test. When the library path disappears Disconnecting the enclosure can remove a drive letter or mount . Reconnecting may restore a device without restoring the exact pathname the library uses. Enclosure sleep, insufficient power and physical disconnects can also have different evidence in operating-system logs. Verify the path and readable file from the server process's environment. A disk appearing in the desktop's file browser does not establish background-service access . A stable volume path and a consistent connection are as relevant to a library as peak transfer speed. See Also SATA storage and negotiated interface rates Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads Mount points and the file system behind a path References USB 3.2 specification SATA-IO naming and interface specifications

articles/storage/fundamentals/index.html.title: Overview: Media storage fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/index.html.keywords: Overview: Media storage fundamentals Media-storage fundamentals relate source reads, application work and temporary output to storage capacity and response time. An Emby workload can combine long media reads with small catalogue operations and continuing writes. Those operations stress storage in different ways. The hardware and performance branches establish that distinction, while temporary-storage topics connect space requirements to the lifetime of active work. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How media storage affects a server Media storage serves large playback reads, small library operations and writable server data, each with different demands. Storage hardware and connections Storage hardware and connections describe the medium, command interface and path supplying file data. Storage performance Storage performance depends on request pattern, queue and service delays, device state and reusable cached data. Temporary storage and RAM disks Temporary storage holds disposable work such as transcoding output, and a RAM-backed location trades disk activity for memory use and volatility. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby library setup Linux kernel: tmpfs

articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.title: Overview: Storage performance | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.keywords: Overview: Storage performance Storage performance depends on request pattern, queue and service delays, device state and reusable cached data. A long sequential copy exercises a different pattern from thousands of small file opens. Latency describes the response of an operation, while spin-down and caches change the state it encounters. This group explains those relationships before storage is described with one general speed figure. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Sequential and random I/O Sequential and random I/O describe the order and size of storage requests, which can affect media reads and library work very differently. Storage latency Storage latency is the response time of an operation, including waiting in queues as well as the device's own work. Disk spin-down Disk spin-down stops an idle drive's platters, saving some power while adding a wake interval to a later access. Storage caches Storage caches retain reusable data or accept writes before slower storage work completes, so cache hits and durable writes have different meanings. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Shingled recording and data management (Seagate-hosted research paper) NVM Express Base Specification Seagate Spinpoint M8 manual: standby command behavior SATA-IO naming and interface specifications Linux man-pages: fsync

articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.title: Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.keywords: Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Storage caches retain reusable data or accept writes before slower storage work completes, so cache hits and durable writes have different meanings. A storage cache holds data so an operation can avoid or defer slower work. The operating system can retain file pages in RAM. A NAS can cache data on the remote side. A drive can buffer commands and writes internally. Some SSDs also have a faster flash-writing area. These are separate caches with different lifetimes and guarantees. Calling a second read “the disk speed” can therefore describe memory reuse instead of a disk transfer. Cold reads and warm reads The first uncached read must obtain data from the lower storage layers. A later read can use retained pages if they remain valid and have not been evicted. An original model reads 100 MiB. Ninety MiB are hits taking 0.1 ms per one-MiB request; ten are misses taking 10 ms each. Serial request time is 90 × 0.1 + 10 × 10 = 109 ms. That result comes from the declared hit distribution, not a real benchmark. A library can have a responsive second visit because artwork or database pages are now warm. Other activity can reclaim those pages. RAM used for cache is often reclaimable, so a large cache figure does not alone mean the server has run out of usable memory. A buffered write has several states The application submits bytes. The operating system may copy them into memory and complete the buffered call. Background writeback sends modified pages to storage. A synchronization operation asks the storage stack to complete the durability work required by its contract. Bytes can be readable after step two while still vulnerable to loss on power failure. “Another process can read it” and “it will survive a crash” answer different questions. On Linux, fsync synchronizes file data and associated metadata as specified by the API. Making a newly created name durable can also require synchronization of its containing directory. Hardware and remote-server implementations must honor their part of the contract; a successful API call is not a substitute for understanding the configured storage arrangement. Why a copy starts fast and slows down If new writes arrive faster than lower storage can absorb them, cached dirty data accumulates. Once a limit is reached, the writer may have to wait. For a simplified 2,000-MB staging capacity, 300 MB/s incoming writes and 100 MB/s draining writes, the cache fills at 200 MB/s and reaches capacity in ten seconds. Thereafter it cannot sustain the initial incoming rate indefinitely. That model applies to a finite staging area. It is different from a reusable read cache: a read hit need not create later writeback. It is also different from an SSD's fast flash area, whose folding and reclamation behavior depends on that drive. Caches in a shared workload A large media read can compete with small frequently reused files for memory and storage service. Operating systems use policies to avoid retaining every streaming byte, but behavior depends on the workload and implementation. For Emby, compare the access that matters: cold startup, a warmed library, sustained recording or synchronized application writes. Record whether a result includes cache reuse. Otherwise two accurate measurements can appear to contradict one another simply because they exercised different states. See Also Storage latency: waiting for individual operations Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance Temporary storage and RAM disks References Linux man-pages: fsync NVM Express Base Specification

articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.title: Storage latency: waiting for individual operations | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.keywords: Storage latency: waiting for individual operations Storage latency is the response time of an operation, including waiting in queues as well as the device's own work. Storage latency answers “How long did this operation take?” Throughput answers “How much useful data arrived over an interval?” A system can score well on one and poorly on the other. For a media server, individual latency affects the start of a read, artwork retrieval, seeking and small application-data operations. Continuing playback can absorb some delays through buffering, but a buffer must contain enough data before it can hide a pause. The operation has a timeline A read may wait in an operating-system queue before the device services it. A remote file read adds network and server processing. A cached read may bypass physical storage entirely. An original request budget is: Client queue wait: 12.0 ms Device service: 8.0 ms Completion handling: 0.1 ms Observed response: 20.1 ms The eight-ms service component is not the whole response time. Conversely, a tool reporting a device-level measure may not include all delay observed by the application. State the measurement layer before comparing numbers. Averages can hide the operation that stalled Suppose 99 operations each finish in 1 ms and one takes 500 ms. The average is 5.99 ms. That average is mathematically correct, yet none of the individual operations took 5.99 ms. A distribution, maximum or suitable percentile helps reveal the slow tail. Percentile definitions and sample size matter: a small sample cannot precisely characterize a rare stall. A time series can also show whether delays occur together during a scan, import or wake event. For a queued workload, increasing the number of outstanding operations may improve total throughput while increasing how long each request waits. That tradeoff is particularly visible when background work shares a device with interactive reads. Why a small request can matter to a large film Before reading the main body of a film, software may need to open its path, inspect metadata and seek to a starting location. Slow dependent operations add together even if they transfer few bytes. A high sequential MB/s result measures a different part of the job. A write adds another question: was it accepted into a cache, or did the caller request synchronization to durable storage? Compare equivalent completion conditions. Storage caches explains why a rapid buffered completion and a durable write have different timelines. To interpret a playback stall, relate delayed source reads to the player's reserve. If source bytes arrived promptly, the next investigation belongs in conversion or delivery rather than in the disk's latency. See Also Sequential and random I/O in media workloads Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Buffering, ready media and playback reserve References NVM Express Base Specification Linux man-pages: fsync

articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.title: Sequential and random I/O in media workloads | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.keywords: Sequential and random I/O in media workloads Sequential and random I/O describe the order and size of storage requests, which can affect media reads and library work very differently. Sequential I/O accesses successive ranges. Random I/O accesses ranges that are scattered relative to the preceding requests. These descriptions apply to an observed request stream: a file can be large while the application accesses it randomly, and many small files can sometimes be serviced efficiently from cache. Playback often reads forward through a media file. Seeking moves to another range. Scanning and artwork access produce a mixture of directory, metadata and content operations. Same device, different cost per useful byte Consider two original uncached workloads. Assume a device transfers data at 150 decimal MB/s, and every scattered operation adds 8 ms of positioning or other service delay. There is one operation at a time. 4 KiB operation: transfer = 4,096 ÷ 150,000,000 seconds = 0.0273 ms total = 8 + 0.0273 = 8.0273 ms useful rate ≈ 0.510 MB/s 1 MiB operation with the same added delay: transfer = 1,048,576 ÷ 150,000,000 seconds = 6.9905 ms total = 8 + 6.9905 = 14.9905 ms useful rate ≈ 69.949 MB/s The device's assumed transfer rate did not change. Larger operations amortized the fixed delay over more bytes. Long adjacent runs can reduce repeated positioning further. These figures describe a deliberately simplified model, not a representative HDD or SSD benchmark. Why IOPS needs an operation size IOPS means input/output operations per second. Multiplying by the average bytes per operation gives a useful-data rate only for the workload being described. Operation rate Operation size Data rate 1,000 IOPS 4 KiB 4.096 decimal MB/s 1,000 IOPS 1 MiB 1,048.576 decimal MB/s The equal operation counts do not imply equal work. Read/write mix, queue depth, caching and whether operations are dependent also belong in a meaningful comparison. Individually sequential, collectively mixed Four players can each read sequentially while the device alternates among four files. On an HDD, this may require head movement. Read-ahead can gather larger ranges and the operating system can combine or reorder requests, so the physical device may see a different pattern from the application's calls. This is why a single large-file copy is incomplete evidence for an Emby server's mixed workload. If a film reads smoothly alone and slows during a scan, the relevant change may be the ordering and latency of requests, rather than a lack of average byte-rate capacity. See Also Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads Solid-state drives: flash access, writes and endurance Storage latency: waiting for individual operations Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References Shingled recording and data management (Seagate-hosted research paper) NVM Express Base Specification

articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.title: Disk spin-down, wake latency and idle workloads | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/performanc.keywords: Disk spin-down, wake latency and idle workloads Disk spin-down stops an idle drive's platters, saving some power while adding a wake interval to a later access. A rotating drive can enter a standby state after inactivity. Its platters stop, and a later request must wait for the drive to become ready before normal access resumes. This is different from a whole server sleeping: the operating system can remain awake while an individual disk is stopped. The result can be a noticeable pause on the first film after a quiet period, followed by normal playback once the disk is running. The first request includes wake time If a fictional drive takes 7 seconds to become ready and the subsequent access takes 15 ms, that first request cannot finish in 15 ms. Its simplified duration is 7.015 seconds. Later reads avoid the wake component until the drive enters standby again. Read-ahead and an existing player buffer can hide some delays during continuing playback. They cannot provide uncached source bytes before the device wakes. A library entry remaining visible also does not mean its disk is currently spinning. What counts as idle? An idle policy measures activity at a particular layer. An application can read a cached file without accessing the physical disk; a background task can access the disk without any viewer starting playback. Activity Possible effect on the drive's idle interval Artwork already held in memory May require no physical disk operation Library scan opening uncached paths Can create storage activity Monitoring or health software May wake a drive, depending on the command and implementation Recording to that drive Continuing writes prevent an idle period Access through an enclosure The bridge may have a separate power policy For an original ten-minute idle model, an actual disk access at 09:57 moves the earliest eligibility to 10:07. A cached read at 10:03 does not reset this model's disk-activity clock. Real firmware and operating systems define their own policies. A repeated pause has a different explanation If every short interaction is slow, examine whether the drive repeatedly enters standby, whether an enclosure disconnects, or whether a storage/network request is timing out. These produce different operating-system evidence. A wake delay should be associated with a transition from an idle state; it is not a general explanation for all slow disk operations. There is no universal best timeout. Frequent starts and stops, response expectations and the exact drive's documented power behavior influence the choice. For an Emby server, relate the quiet periods and background workload to the first-access behavior you actually observe. See Also Hard disk drives: rotation, positioning and media workloads Storage latency: waiting for individual operations Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References Seagate Spinpoint M8 manual: standby command behavior SATA-IO naming and interface specifications

articles/storage/fundamentals/Storage-Ov.title: How media storage affects an Emby server | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/Storage-Ov.keywords: How media storage affects an Emby server Media storage serves large playback reads, small library operations and writable server data, each with different demands. A movie is a large file, but an Emby server does more than read movies. Browsing a library can request many small artwork files. Scanning opens directories and examines media headers. Transcoding reads a source while producing temporary output. Recording adds a continuing write workload. The storage arrangement has to serve the combination that is active. This explains a familiar result: a disk that easily supplies one film may feel slow during a scan, even though the film's bitrate is far below the disk's advertised transfer rate. From a stream to storage demand A 40 Mbit/s source requires about 5 decimal MB/s of encoded data, because there are eight bits in a byte. Four such sources average 20 MB/s. This is payload arithmetic, not a measured drive requirement: variable bitrate, read-ahead, container access and competing work change the requests reaching storage. An original planning example makes the layers explicit: Four source reads: 4 × 40 Mbit/s ÷ 8 = 20 MB/s One recording: 24 Mbit/s ÷ 8 = 3 MB/s Combined payload: 23 MB/s The reads and recording may not use the same disk. Conversely, four streams of one already cached file may not cause four identical physical reads. Measure at the layer you are trying to understand. A path for each kind of data Data Typical access What must remain available Source media Large reads, seeks, occasional additions Files and their stable library paths Server application data Small reads and writes, database updates Persistent writable storage Transcoding output Continuing creation and consumption Enough writable temporary capacity Recording destination Sustained writes plus later reads Space and write access for the recording A media share can be read-only while the server's application-data and temporary locations remain writable. Playback permission for an Emby account is another decision: it does not give the operating-system process permission to open a file. Why a fast copy can coexist with a slow library A large copy measures a relatively orderly transfer. Opening thousands of separate files introduces directory lookups, metadata reads and many small requests. On a rotating drive, positioning between those requests can dominate the elapsed time. On network storage, request round trips and the remote server also participate. The sequential and random I/O distinction is therefore more useful than asking whether a drive is simply “fast.” Separating busy application data from bulk media can reduce competition, but the benefit depends on the actual workload. Moving a media file to another disk does not accelerate a CPU-limited transcode. For a playback problem, establish whether the server is waiting for source bytes, waiting for conversion, or waiting to deliver output. A rising storage queue and slow source reads tell a different story from a quickly read source and a fully occupied encoder. The storage evidence belongs alongside transcoding bottlenecks and network delivery evidence. See Also Sequential and random I/O in media workloads Storage latency: waiting for individual operations Read-only media access and separate writable data Transcode temporary files and generated output References Emby library setup Linux man-pages: fsync

articles/storage/fundamentals/Storage-Te.title: Temporary storage and RAM disks | Emby Learn
articles/storage/fundamentals/Storage-Te.keywords: Temporary storage and RAM disks Temporary storage holds disposable work such as transcoding output, and a RAM-backed location trades disk activity for memory use and volatility. “Temporary” describes data's role, not its physical medium. Temporary files can live on an SSD, HDD or memory-backed file system. They remain necessary while an active operation uses them, even when they are not intended to survive afterward. For Emby, transcoding output is a useful example. The server creates data for the player to consume. Source media and persistent application data have different lifetimes and should not be treated as disposable because the current playback is temporary. Space follows retained output If a session retains 120 seconds of 12-Mbit/s output, its encoded payload occupies about 180 decimal MB: 12,000,000 bits/s × 120 seconds ÷ 8 = 180,000,000 bytes Three equal sessions: 3 × 180 MB = 540 MB The example assumes this specific retention window. Actual formats, overhead, throttling, cleanup and seeking affect the amount retained. It is not a statement that Emby always keeps 120 seconds. Capacity also has to accommodate concurrent sessions and interrupted work that has not yet been removed. An output bitrate lower than the source bitrate can reduce temporary bytes without reducing the source's own read demand by the same factor. What a RAM-backed file system consumes Linux tmpfs stores file data in memory and can move eligible pages to swap when configured to do so. It is not necessarily a guarantee that every byte stays in physical RAM. A size limit caps growth; it does not preallocate that entire amount as occupied memory. Location Resource used Behavior after loss of volatile state Ordinary disk directory Disk capacity and I/O Files can remain until cleanup tmpfs Memory, and possibly swap Files do not provide persistent storage across reboot Fixed RAM-disk arrangement Reserved or allocated memory, depending on implementation Persistence requires a separate mechanism A RAM-backed output directory shares memory resources with the server, encoders and operating system. If it grows too far, swapping, reclaim or memory exhaustion can make a previously fast system slower. Container memory accounting can add another limit. Choosing the location around the operation A useful temporary location has sufficient capacity, predictable write access and a lifetime that covers active playback. Its speed matters when temporary I/O is a demonstrated bottleneck. Moving output into RAM does not remove the CPU or GPU work required to encode it. Keep persistent database and configuration files outside disposable storage. For existing installations, use the documented transcoding settings and the server's actual data paths to distinguish those roles; a directory's name alone does not establish that deleting its contents is harmless. See Also Transcode temporary files and generated output Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Read-only media access and separate writable data References Linux kernel: tmpfs Emby transcoding settings Linux man-pages: fsync

articles/storage/index.html.title: Overview: Storage and server platforms | Emby Learn
articles/storage/index.html.keywords: Overview: Storage and server platforms Server storage connects readable media, persistent application state and temporary work to the machine and identities performing those operations. An Emby server performs large media reads, small catalog operations and continuing temporary or recording writes. Those workloads can share a device while having different latency, capacity and persistence requirements. This area follows storage from hardware and file paths through shared access and recovery. Execution-environment topics explain the process, VM or container that sees those paths; workload topics explain databases, caches and background activity. A successful desktop file test, a visible mount and a usable server backup each establish different pieces of that environment. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Media storage fundamentals Media-storage fundamentals relate source reads, application work and temporary output to storage capacity and response time. File systems and paths File systems connect names and stored data through allocation, limits, access rules and activity mechanisms. Shared storage and permissions Shared-storage access combines a file-service path, accepted identity and the current availability of the remote tree. Data protection Data protection combines integrity evidence, retained generations and recovery mechanisms with the failures they are intended to address. Server execution environments Server execution environments define the process, resource and dependency context in which media operations run. Server data and workload Server data and workload topics describe the stored roles and background operations sharing the application's resources. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/storage/sharing/index.html.title: Overview: Shared storage and permissions | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/index.html.keywords: Overview: Shared storage and permissions Shared-storage access combines a file-service path, accepted identity and the current availability of the remote tree. A readable desktop share and a background server's view can differ in credentials, paths or permissions. A mount can also exist while its operations fail to complete. This area separates the network protocol, access decision and unavailable-source states involved in opening media remotely. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Network file access Network file access uses protocol-specific identities and operations behind shared or mounted paths. Access identities and permissions Storage permissions evaluate the process identity, pathname and operation under the applicable filesystem or sharing rules. Unavailable network mounts An unavailable mount can be absent, present but unreachable, or replaced by another visible tree, and those states provide different library evidence. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Linux man-pages: mount namespaces RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/ind.title: Overview: Access identities and permissions | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/ind.keywords: Overview: Access identities and permissions Storage permissions evaluate the process identity, pathname and operation under the applicable filesystem or sharing rules. Reading a film, listing its directory and saving a sidecar can require different rights. Ownership, ACLs and numeric IDs supply parts of that decision, while a service has its own running context. The topics here connect those rules to specific operations instead of treating desktop access as a complete server test. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Read-only media access Read-only media access lets a server consume source files while directing required application and temporary writes to other locations. File ownership and permissions File access depends on the process identity, rights along the directory path and the requested operation, rather than the file owner's name alone. Access control lists (ACLs) Access control lists assign rights to named identities, but masks, entry order and inheritance determine how visible grants become effective access. Linux user and group IDs Linux storage access uses process and file user/group IDs, so matching account names do not guarantee matching permissions across hosts or namespaces. Storage access from background services A background service opens storage through its own credentials and pathname environment, which can differ from an interactive desktop session. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Emby library setup Linux man-pages: process credentials Linux ACL specification and access checks RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 Windows services and redirected drives

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.title: Access control lists: entries, masks and inheritance | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.keywords: Access control lists: entries, masks and inheritance Access control lists assign rights to named identities, but masks, entry order and inheritance determine how visible grants become effective access. An access control list gives an object access rules for particular identities. It can express more than one owner, one owning group and an “everyone else” class. The phrase “has an ACL” does not identify one universal evaluation algorithm. Linux POSIX-style ACLs and Windows discretionary ACLs have different structures and rules. A network file server may map one arrangement into another. A visible Linux grant can be capped An original Linux access ACL is: user::rw- user:1100:rw- group::r-- mask::r-- other::--- The owner has read/write access. Named user 1100 also has a visible read/write entry, but the mask limits the effective permissions of named users and the applicable group entries. It does not cap the owner or other entry in this model. For a nonowner process with UID 1100, the calculation is: Named-user entry: rw- = binary 110 Mask: r-- = binary 100 Effective rights: 110 AND 100 = 100 = r-- Read request: allowed Write request: denied The visible rw- entry is therefore not proof of an effective write grant. Changing the mask can affect several entries, not just the named user whose result you are investigating. If a named-user entry matches, that branch is evaluated. A denial there does not simply fall through to the other class to find a more generous permission. Mode bits can show the mask With an extended POSIX ACL, the group-class bits displayed by a traditional mode listing correspond to the ACL mask. They do not necessarily describe only the owning group's entry. That is why a short ls listing may be insufficient to explain access. Inspect the full ACL, the requested operation and the relevant identity. ACL element Role Owner entry Owner's rights Named user entries Rights associated with particular UIDs Owning/named group entries Applicable group rights Mask Effective ceiling for the group class and named users Other entry Rights when the earlier applicable classes do not match Directory search and listing rights still matter before a file's ACL can be used. An effective read grant on a film does not bypass a blocked directory component. A new child can have fewer rights than its parent Use the preceding access ACL as a starting idea, but consider a directory with this separate default ACL: default:user::rwx default:user:1100:rwx default:group::r-x default:mask::rwx default:other::--- An importer creates an ordinary file and requests mode 0640. The new object's access ACL is derived from the default ACL, then constrained by the requested mode. The owner-class ceiling is read/write, the group-class ceiling is read, and the other-class ceiling is none. The inherited named-user entry may still visibly include broader permissions, but its effective access is constrained by the resulting mask. UID 1100 does not get write merely because the parent's default named-user entry contained write. If a later creation requests mode 0660 instead, its group-class ceiling includes write, so the resulting mask can permit the named user's write in this example. These are two different creation requests under the same default policy. New file's requested mode Group-class ceiling Named user 1100's effective read/write result 0640 Read Read, without write 0660 Read and write Read and write When a default ACL is present, this inheritance-and-requested-mode process determines the initial ACL; applying a separate simplistic “always subtract umask from the inherited ACL” rule does not describe the Linux contract. Without a default ACL, ordinary creation mode and umask supply the basic permissions. This explains why two import tools can create different access results in the same directory. Inspect the actual child ACL and the creator's requested mode rather than assuming that the parent dictates one identical outcome for every file. A Windows DACL is an ordered list A Windows DACL contains access-control entries for security identifiers. Entries can allow or deny rights. The access check evaluates the entries in order while tracking the requested rights; ordering is part of the meaning. Consider an original simplified ordered list: 1. DENY service-SID WRITE 2. ALLOW media-group READ, WRITE Process belongs to service-SID and media-group A read-only request can be satisfied by the group allow. A write request is denied by the earlier applicable deny. This example assumes the shown rights and identities; it does not model every Windows right or inheritance flag. It would be inaccurate to describe every possible DACL as an unordered union of allows followed by one universal denial rule. Windows tools normally maintain canonical ordering, and inherited entries have their own ordering and applicability. A null DACL and an empty DACL are also different: the former has no discretionary ACL restriction, while the latter grants no discretionary access. That distinction is useful when reading security descriptors; it is not a suggestion to remove a DACL to solve a storage error. Inheritance describes creation and propagation A Linux directory's default ACL supplies a starting ACL for newly created child objects, constrained by the requested creation mode. Its access ACL controls access to the directory itself. Editing a default ACL does not retroactively rewrite every existing child's access ACL. Windows inheritance uses entry flags and propagation behavior. A child can contain explicit and inherited entries, and protected inheritance changes the result. Copying or moving content can also affect how the destination obtains its security state, depending on the operation and tool. For an Emby library, compare the ACL on an old readable file with one newly imported file that fails. The parent policy, creation identity and actual child ACL can explain the difference. A grant visible on the parent is only part of that lifecycle; inspect the child's effective access under the running server identity. See Also File ownership and permissions across a library path Linux user and group IDs in storage access SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations References Linux ACL specification and access checks Microsoft DACLs and access-control entries Microsoft: how access checks work

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.title: Linux user and group IDs in storage access | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.keywords: Linux user and group IDs in storage access Linux storage access uses process and file user/group IDs, so matching account names do not guarantee matching permissions across hosts or namespaces. Linux identifies users and groups numerically. Account names provide readable labels, but a file's ownership and a process's credentials contain IDs. A media directory owned by a user named emby on one computer does not automatically belong to the server process named emby on another. The numbers and any mapping rules have to line up. One name can label different numbers An original example uses ordinary file-permission checks without extended ACLs or privilege overrides: Host A: emby -> UID 1100 Host B: emby -> UID 1200 File owner: UID 1200 Host A process with UID 1100 is not this file's owner. The reverse is also possible: two computers can display different names for the same numeric ID. That matters for simple numeric-ID network arrangements and for files moved without translating ownership. For local Linux file access, filesystem UID and GID are used with supplementary groups. These usually match the effective UID and GID. Specialized programs can change them, so the general rule concerns the process's actual credentials rather than the desktop's visible account name. Groups belong to the running process A process has a primary group and a set of supplementary groups. Those credentials are normally established when it is launched. Changing an account's group membership in the account database does not automatically rewrite the supplementary groups of every existing process. A newly launched shell can therefore have a group that a still-running server lacks. Observation What it describes Account database says “member of media” Membership available to a new credential setup Running process lists GID 2000 That process currently has the group File's group is GID 2000 Group associated with this file object A label displays “media” A local name for an ID, not proof of all three states In a fictional read test, a file owned by another UID with group 2000 and mode 0640 is readable through the basic group class when the process has GID 2000. Removing that GID from the process's current groups changes the result. The name printed for group 2000 does not change the calculation. A namespace can translate IDs A user namespace can map an ID inside a container to another ID outside it. An apparent UID zero inside the namespace is not automatically the host's privileged UID zero. Mount arrangements can also have ID mappings that affect ownership interpretation. For NFS, the authentication arrangement and server mapping determine the accepted identity. For SMB, session credentials can be mapped to a server-side user. A host id result cannot alone establish those remote decisions. When Emby can see a directory but cannot read newly added files, compare the running process's IDs and groups with the actual file ownership and permissions. This keeps the investigation specific to the file and credential state, rather than treating matching names as evidence of access. See Also File ownership and permissions across a library path Access control lists: entries, masks and inheritance NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping References Linux man-pages: process credentials Linux ACL specification and access checks RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.title: File ownership and permissions across a library path | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.keywords: File ownership and permissions across a library path File access depends on the process identity, rights along the directory path and the requested operation, rather than the file owner's name alone. A permission question needs three pieces of information: which process identity , which path , and which operation . “The file belongs to me” supplies only part of the answer. For Emby, the process identity is the account under which the server runs. It may be a background-service account rather than the desktop user currently looking at the files. The Emby account signed in on a television is a separate application identity. A file read begins with directories To open /srv/media/Movies/Film.mkv , a Unix-style process resolves the path through each directory. Search permission, represented by the directory's execute bit, allows traversal to a named entry. Directory read permission allows listing names. These are different rights. A process can be able to open a known file in a directory that it cannot list. A library scanner normally needs enumeration as well as access to the files it discovers. Right On an ordinary file On a directory Read Read file content List directory entries Write Modify file content Create or remove entries, subject to other checks Execute/search Execute as a program when applicable Traverse to entries by name The table describes basic Unix discretionary permissions. ACLs, security modules, read-only mounts, capabilities and other restrictions can alter the complete access result. Owner, group and other are selected classes Consider this original example without extended ACLs or privilege overrides: Process: UID 1100; groups {2000} Directories /srv, /srv/media, /srv/media/Movies: searchable File: owner UID 1200; group GID 2000; mode 0640 owner rw-; group r--; other --- Requested operation: read Selected class: group Result from these basic file-mode inputs: allowed The process is not the owner. Its group set includes the file's group, so the group read bit supplies access. It does not matter whether the two users have friendly names such as “emby” or “media”; the numbers drive this model. Now change the process UID to 1200 while retaining a file mode whose owner bits deny read and group bits allow it. The owner class applies. The check does not fail the owner test and then fall through to a more generous group or other class. That rule prevents a common misdiagnosis: adding the owner to another group does not make the basic mode check ignore restrictive owner bits. A blocked parent stops the path Return to the first example and remove search permission from /srv/media for the relevant identity. The file's group read bit remains present, yet the process cannot reach the file through this path. Increasing the final file's permissions would not fix the blocked parent. Inspect the component that actually failed. A container mapping or symbolic-link target can introduce a different path whose parents also need traversal rights. For a scan, directory listing is another requirement. Successfully opening one precisely named file does not prove that enumerating its containing folder works. Deletion acts on a directory entry Changing file bytes and removing a filename are different operations. In ordinary Unix directory semantics, deletion depends on write and search rights on the containing directory, with additional checks such as the sticky bit where applicable. A file whose contents are read-only can therefore still have its name removed by an identity with the relevant directory rights. Conversely, file write permission alone does not grant permission to remove that name from an unwritable directory. This is why “the file is read-only” is incomplete evidence for a no-deletion policy. Hard links make the distinction especially visible: removing one permitted name does not necessarily remove the shared object's other names. Listing, reading and saving can split into three outcomes Suppose the service has read and search access to a media directory, and read access to its film. The scan can enumerate the name and open the film. Now the server attempts to save a newly downloaded subtitle beside it. That save creates a new directory entry.
