It needs the relevant directory write permission as well as traversal. Read access to the film does not grant that operation. If the subtitle already exists, updating its bytes instead involves that file's own access rights. A tool that saves by creating a temporary file and renaming it can also require rights for the directory operations. “Save a subtitle” can therefore represent more than one operating-system request. Intended work Basic Unix checks emphasized in this example Discover the film by listing Directory read and search Read the known film Path traversal and file read Create a new sidecar Parent directory write and search Modify an existing sidecar in place Path traversal and sidecar write Publish by rename Applicable source/destination directory rights and other rename checks This is a deliberately limited discretionary-permission model, not a complete platform access check. It makes the failure location concrete: successful playback and a failed sidecar save are consistent with a directory that allows reads but denies creation. Shared storage adds more decisions For SMB, the accepted session identity and share policy participate before underlying file access. For NFS, the credential arrangement, export policy and identity mapping participate. A remote username displayed in a client interface is not proof of the final server-side identity. Windows uses its own access rights and ordered DACL evaluation rather than the Unix owner/group/other algorithm. Translate the intended operation into the platform's real access model instead of trying to apply a Linux mode number to every system. When diagnosing an Emby storage failure, identify the service identity, the resolved location and the failed operation first. Then inspect the relevant directory, file, share or mount rule. This creates a specific explanation for “permission denied” and avoids broadening access to unrelated files merely because the initial error was vague. See Also Access control lists: entries, masks and inheritance Linux user and group IDs in storage access Read-only media access and separate writable data Storage access from background services References Linux man-pages: process credentials Linux man-pages: pathname resolution Linux ACL specification and access checks Microsoft: how access checks work

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.title: Read-only media access and separate writable data | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.keywords: Read-only media access and separate writable data Read-only media access lets a server consume source files while directing required application and temporary writes to other locations. Emby Server can read a source film without needing permission to overwrite that film. A media library can therefore use a read-only storage arrangement while the server's application-data and temporary locations remain writable. This is a useful separation of data roles. It also makes the affected operations easier to understand: reading an existing movie and creating a new subtitle file are different storage requests. Which workflow needs a write? Workflow Source media access Separate writable data Read and stream an existing film Read required Server application data remains writable Transcode that film Read source Write temporary output Store downloaded sidecars beside media Read relevant media; write sidecar location Depends on the chosen save location Record into the media directory Write destination Recording and server state also update Delete a media file Applicable deletion rights A viewer's delete permission is another check A library configured to save artwork or metadata beside source media needs suitable writes for those files. If that location is read-only, those saves can fail even though playback succeeds. This is a consequence of the operation's destination, not an inconsistency in read-only access. Mount, share and file restrictions A mount can be read-only. A share can restrict writes. File-system permissions or ACLs can grant only the relevant access. These mechanisms have different scopes. For example, a read-only mount seen by a container can restrict that container's view while the host has another writable view. File permissions apply according to identity and the underlying file system. A Windows file's read-only attribute is not a complete substitute for an access-control design governing creation and deletion of names in its directory. The effective result comes from the entire path and operation. Directory traversal must still work, and listing a folder does not establish that its files are readable. Viewer permissions are another boundary An Emby viewer allowed to play a film does not acquire the server process's operating-system rights. Likewise, a viewer denied media deletion does not make the source mount read-only for every process. Keep those checks distinct when diagnosing a failure. A permitted playback request can fail because the server cannot read the source. A prohibited delete request should remain prohibited even when the service identity technically has write access. The server also needs persistent writable application storage for its configuration, database and other state. Making every location read-only does not create an ordinary read-only media server; it prevents required server work. Separate the media source from temporary output and persistent application data according to their actual roles. See Also File ownership and permissions across a library path Storage access from background services Library access permissions and the user’s media scope Transcode temporary files and generated output References Emby library setup Windows CreateFile access and sharing modes Linux man-pages: pathname resolution

articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.title: Storage access from background services | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/permissions/Sto.keywords: Storage access from background services A background service opens storage through its own credentials and pathname environment, which can differ from an interactive desktop session. “I can open the file in Explorer” proves that the interactive process can open it. Emby Server running as a service performs its own open under another process context. That context includes identity, group membership, network authentication, mounted paths and sometimes service-specific file-system restrictions. The desktop test can be completely accurate while the service still fails. Compare the two access attempts Property Interactive desktop Background service Identity Logged-in user Configured service identity Windows drive mappings This logon session's mappings A separate logon context Linux groups Current shell credentials Server process's current credentials Mounted tree Desktop or shell view Service namespace and mappings Network connection Credentials available to that context Credentials available to the service A service configured with the same Windows account name still receives its own logon session. It does not inherit every redirected drive letter created in that account's desktop session. A UNC path names the share without that drive-letter dependency. The service still needs appropriate remote credentials and rights. Replacing a letter with a UNC name fixes one possible naming failure, not every access failure. Linux service restrictions can change the view A Linux service manager can select the service's user, groups and execution environment. It can also establish restricted mount arrangements or make selected paths read-only or inaccessible. A root-owned host directory being visible in an administrator's shell therefore does not tell you whether /media inside a service or container maps to it. The service's pathname and namespace must reach the expected tree before file permissions can be interpreted. Likewise, adding an account to a group does not automatically update credentials of the existing server process. A supported restart can establish new process credentials, but it will not fix an incorrectly mapped path or a remote share denying the resulting identity. Startup timing can create a different failure A server may start before its network storage is ready. If the path exists as an uncovered mount-point directory, the process can see the wrong contents. If a remote mount remains present but is unreachable, operations can wait or time out. Making the service start later can address an ordering problem. It does not establish continuous availability after startup. The distinction between startup dependency and ongoing mount health matters for a server intended to run unattended. An original comparison captures the observations without using real accounts: Desktop: M:\Film.mkv -> mapped share; read succeeds Service: M:\Film.mkv -> mapping absent; path lookup fails Service: \\nas.example.test\Media\Film.mkv -> destination named; authentication and read checks still required Identify the failed operation For a concrete storage error, establish the server process's identity, the path as that process sees it, and the operation that fails. Enumeration, reading a film and creating a sidecar may have different outcomes. Testing only as an administrator can hide the relevant restriction. The useful evidence is the result under the running service's intended context. Operating-system and server logs can then distinguish path-not-found, denied access, incompatible handles and remote timeouts, each of which has a different mechanism. See Also UNC paths and network-share names Mount points and the file system behind a path Linux user and group IDs in storage access Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state References Windows services and redirected drives systemd service execution specification (upstream source) Linux man-pages: process credentials

articles/storage/sharing/protocols/index.title: Overview: Network file access | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/protocols/index.keywords: Overview: Network file access Network file access uses protocol-specific identities and operations behind shared or mounted paths. SMB and NFS provide different ways to reach a remote file tree. A UNC path identifies a network destination under its naming convention; it does not supply the credential needed to use it. These pages explain the path and session relationships that sit beneath a server's ordinary file open. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> SMB file shares SMB serves network file operations through authenticated sessions and named shares, with access and caching rules distinct from Emby playback delivery. NFS file shares NFS exposes a remote file tree through a client mount, with protocol state and identity mapping affecting access and recovery. UNC paths A UNC path identifies a Windows network server, share and remaining pathname without depending on a mapped drive letter. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Microsoft SMB versions 2 and 3 protocol specification RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 Windows file and path naming

articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.title: NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.keywords: NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping NFS exposes a remote file tree through a client mount, with protocol state and identity mapping affecting access and recovery. NFS, the Network File System protocol, lets a client use files provided by another server. On a Linux Emby host, an exported NAS tree might be mounted at /srv/media . The application opens an apparently local pathname while the NFS client performs operations on the remote server. That appearance is convenient, but it does not remove the network, remote server or access mapping from the read. A local path reaches a remote file The mount defines how the remote tree appears in the client's namespace. NFS uses protocol-level file handles and operations; the local path is not simply sent as a Windows UNC string for every action. NFS versions have different arrangements. NFSv4 integrates stateful open and locking behavior, and version 4.1 specifies sessions and recovery mechanisms. Older NFS versions use other protocol structures. Evidence from one version should retain that scope. Usernames are not a universal cross-machine identity With RPC AUTH_SYS , a client supplies a numeric user ID, group ID and supplementary-group information in its authentication data. Those values are not cryptographic proof that an untrusted client is entitled to claim them. The security arrangement and trusted-client boundary matter. NFSv4 also represents owner and group attributes through protocol names such as name@domain . Mapping those names to local identities is another step. Stronger arrangements can use RPCSEC_GSS, including Kerberos-based mechanisms, instead of treating a numeric assertion as sufficient identity evidence. An original AUTH_SYS-style example illustrates a mapping problem: Client label "emby": UID 1100 Remote file owner: UID 1200 Client and server both display a user named "emby" Numeric owner identities in this example: different Matching displayed usernames do not make those numeric IDs equal. Conversely, different names on two machines can represent the same number in a simple numeric-ID arrangement. Export policy and file permissions both participate Layer Example question Export policy Is this client allowed to use this export in the requested mode? Authentication arrangement Which credential or asserted identity is accepted? Identity mapping Which local server identity does it become? File access Can that identity traverse directories and read the file? An export can be read-only. A server can also map a client's privileged identity to an anonymous one, commonly called root squashing in Unix NFS administration. This is an export policy, not a rule that every protocol operation from every UID zero must have one universal result. Running a client application as root therefore does not establish that the remote file server grants it privileged file access. Check the accepted and mapped identity instead. A present mount can still wait for the server The mount entry can remain visible while the remote server is unreachable. File operations can retry or fail according to the client implementation and mount policy. A directory appearing in the mount table is not proof that enumeration completes. That distinction matters for Emby scans and playback. A timed-out remote operation is not an observed empty export. After recovery, establish that the intended mounted tree is readable under the server process's identity, then reconcile the library's current state. Unavailable mounts separates these failure states in more detail. See Also Linux user and group IDs in storage access Mount points and the file system behind a path Network-attached storage: files served by another computer References RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 RFC 5531: RPC authentication including AUTH_SYS

articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.title: SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.keywords: SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations SMB serves network file operations through authenticated sessions and named shares, with access and caching rules distinct from Emby playback delivery. SMB is a protocol for accessing files and other shared resources on another computer. A Windows path such as \\nas.example.test\Media\Film.mkv commonly reaches an SMB share. If Emby Server uses that path as a media source, it acts as a file-sharing client. The NAS or file server performs the remote file operations. Emby then supplies playback through its own connection to the viewer. Connection, session, share, file The client and server negotiate a supported SMB dialect. The client establishes an authenticated session, connects to a named share and opens a file with requested access and sharing behavior. These stages explain why one successful test does not establish all later operations. Reaching the server is not authentication. Authentication is not permission to connect to every share. Listing a share is not permission to modify every file. The same connection can support multiple resources and operations. It is not necessary to establish a completely new transport connection for every file read. Which identity is allowed to do what? Operation Relevant access question Connect to Media Does the session identity have share access? Enumerate a directory Can that identity list the required directory? Open a film Can it read the file and satisfy open/share compatibility? Save a sidecar Can it create or update that file? Remove media Is the required delete operation permitted? On a Windows file server, share permissions and underlying file-system access checks both participate. A NAS can have its own mapping and policy. An account allowed to read the share is not thereby granted every underlying write. The SMB identity used by a background service may differ from the desktop login. A UNC path removes dependence on a particular drive-letter mapping, but it does not provide credentials. Signing, encryption and caching are different features SMB signing protects message integrity and authenticity under the negotiated security arrangement. Encryption protects the contents of applicable SMB traffic. Support, negotiation and policy determine what a particular connection uses; an SMB version label alone is not proof that a transfer is encrypted. Modern SMB versions also coordinate caching and reconnect behavior through protocol mechanisms. Those can improve performance and recovery, but they do not guarantee that every interruption is invisible. The negotiated features, server configuration and operation state matter. These protections apply to the file-sharing leg. HTTPS between an Emby app and Emby Server protects another connection. Enabling HTTPS for playback does not cryptographically extend it backward to the NAS share. A share is a source, not the viewer's library identity An ordinary viewer signs in to Emby and requests permitted media. Emby Server reads the source under its storage identity. The viewer need not receive the NAS credential just because that source uses SMB. Some supported direct-file-access arrangements use paths visible to the client, as documented in Emby's optional network-path setup. That changes which computer opens the shared file. Establish the actual playback path before diagnosing which account, protocol or connection failed. See Also UNC paths and network-share names Storage access from background services Access control lists: entries, masks and inheritance Network-attached storage: files served by another computer References Microsoft SMB versions 2 and 3 protocol specification Windows services and redirected drives Emby library setup

articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.title: UNC paths and network-share names | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/protocols/Stora.keywords: UNC paths and network-share names A UNC path identifies a Windows network server, share and remaining pathname without depending on a mapped drive letter. A Universal Naming Convention path identifies a network resource directly. For a media file, the familiar form is: \\nas.example.test\Media\Movies\Film.mkv Component Meaning nas.example.test The named server Media The shared resource on that server Movies\Film.mkv The remaining path within the share The share name is not necessarily the NAS's physical directory name. A share called Media can expose storage whose server-side location has a completely different path. Why a mapped drive can work only on the desktop A desktop user might map M: to \\nas.example.test\Media . The letter is an alias established in that user's logon context. A background service runs in a separate context and may not have that mapping, even when it uses the same account name in another logon session. Microsoft therefore documents UNC names for service access to remote resources rather than relying on another session's redirected drive letters. Using the UNC path solves the naming dependency. The service still needs a reachable server and appropriate authentication and access rights. “I changed M: to a UNC name” does not establish that those later checks succeeded. A path is not a credential or a web URL The UNC string identifies the destination; it does not grant access. It also does not identify an Emby HTTP playback endpoint. An app receiving media from Emby Server generally uses that server's playback connection, while the server separately opens its media source. On Linux, the same share may be mounted and presented through a path such as /srv/media/Movies/Film.mkv . That is the path the Linux server process uses. Copying a Windows UNC string into every application's path field is not a universal cross-platform substitute for configuring a supported file-access arrangement. See Also SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations Storage access from background services Case-sensitive paths and preserved spelling References Windows file and path naming Windows services and redirected drives Emby library setup

articles/storage/sharing/Storage-Unavail.title: Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state | Emby Learn
articles/storage/sharing/Storage-Unavail.keywords: Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state An unavailable mount can be absent, present but unreachable, or replaced by another visible tree, and those states provide different library evidence. An Emby item can remain visible in the library while its media source is unavailable. The catalog records what the server previously discovered; playback needs the source to be accessible now. “Unavailable mount” covers several different situations. The distinction matters because an inaccessible tree should not be interpreted as a successful observation that its files have disappeared. Three states that can look like missing media State What the server can encounter What it establishes Mount absent No path, or an uncovered local directory The expected attachment is missing Mount present, server unreachable A visible mount entry with blocking or failing I/O Attachment metadata exists; remote access is not completing Another tree exposed at the same path Valid enumeration of different contents The pathname exists, but storage identity changed A Linux mount point can expose its underlying directory after the intended mount is absent. That directory may be empty or contain files written during an earlier outage. A successful listing there can be misleading if the application intended to scan the NAS tree. A Windows share or mapped drive can fail through name resolution, connectivity, logon-context changes or credentials. Different failures can produce similar symptoms in the library interface. Presence is not responsiveness A mount table records an attachment arrangement. It does not continuously certify that the remote server is answering file operations. On NFS, client retries and timeout behavior depend on mount policy and implementation. SMB reconnection and handle recovery depend on negotiated features and state. An outage can therefore surface as a long wait, an explicit error or a later reconnect, rather than one uniform “directory not found” response. Existing open files can also behave differently from new opens. A process holding a handle may have a relationship with the previously opened object that a fresh pathname lookup does not reproduce. Inventory needs a successful observation of the intended tree An original scan model starts with two catalog entries: Known inventory: {Film-A.mkv, Film-B.mkv} Scan 1: enumeration times out observed inventory is unknown, not {} Scan 2: intended share restored; enumeration succeeds observed inventory is {Film-A.mkv, Film-C.mkv} The second scan supplies evidence that A remains, C is newly observed and B is absent from that successfully enumerated tree. The first supplies no equivalent missing-file evidence. Applications have their own retry and removal policies. This model explains what the observations mean; it does not claim that every Emby version performs a particular removal action on every outage. Recovery has more than one checkpoint First establish that the correct share or volume is attached at the server's configured path. Then establish that directory operations and a known file read succeed under the service identity. Finally, use the relevant library scan to reconcile current content. If a mount was restored but a watcher lost its subscription or never received remote change events, recovery of the storage alone may not trigger every pending library update. A fresh inventory observation provides stronger evidence than waiting for an event that may not arrive. A recording destination deserves the same identity check. If the expected mount was absent, a recording may have been created in an underlying local directory and become covered when the remote tree returned. The recorded file has not necessarily vanished; it may now be hidden behind the mount. The practical distinction is between a file observed to be absent on the correct readable storage and a file that could not be observed . Keeping those states separate makes playback errors and scan results much easier to interpret. See Also Mount points and the file system behind a path SMB file shares: sessions, shares and file operations NFS file shares and server-side identity mapping Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References Linux man-pages: mount namespaces RFC 8881: NFS version 4.1 .NET FileSystemWatcher contract and limitations Emby library setup

articles/storage/workload/databases/inde.title: Overview: Databases | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/databases/inde.keywords: Overview: Databases Server databases organize persistent records through transaction, logging and locking mechanisms. A catalogue record has to remain coherent as readers and writers perform work. Transactions supply completion boundaries, WAL changes where committed state can be represented, and locking coordinates conflicting operations. These pages connect the library's stored information to those mechanisms and their recovery implications. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Library databases A library database organizes indexed media records and relationships for queries, while source files and user-specific state retain separate roles. Database transactions A database transaction groups related changes under atomicity and isolation rules, while commit durability and external effects require their own guarantees. Database write-ahead logging Write-ahead logging records committed database changes in a log before checkpointing them into the main file, supporting reader snapshots with particular concurrency rules. Database locking Database locking coordinates conflicting operations, and a busy result can require waiting, ending a snapshot or restarting a transaction according to its cause. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References SQLite database-file format SQLite transaction control SQLite write-ahead logging SQLite isolation and concurrency

articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.title: Database locking and competing operations | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.keywords: Database locking and competing operations Database locking coordinates conflicting operations, and a busy result can require waiting, ending a snapshot or restarting a transaction according to its cause. A database lock coordinates operations whose concurrent execution would violate its storage or transaction rules. A waiting operation is not necessarily corrupt or unauthorized; it may be competing with another legitimate operation. The useful diagnosis identifies what is held, what the new operation requests and whether waiting can change that relationship. A second writer can wait for the first SQLite serializes writes, including in WAL mode. An original scheduling example is: Writer A holds the required write state until 110 ms. Writer B requests it at 40 ms. B's deadline is 140 ms. If A releases at 110 ms and no other conflict appears: B can proceed after 70 ms of waiting, before its deadline. A busy timeout bounds how long the caller waits under the applicable API behavior. It does not reserve the resource or guarantee that the owner finishes in time. Long transactions hold their relevant state longer. Work that could occur before beginning a transaction or after committing it need not always occupy that same critical interval. A stale read snapshot is a different conflict Suppose connection R begins a WAL read transaction at state S1. Another connection commits S2. R then tries to turn its old read into a write. SQLite can reject that upgrade with a snapshot-busy result. Simply waiting for more time does not make R's S1 snapshot become S2. The application needs to end the old transaction and re-evaluate its intended work against an appropriate current state. This matters for a “read, calculate, update” operation. Retrying only the final write can apply a calculation based on information that is no longer current. Conflict What can resolve it Another writer temporarily holds the resource Release and a supported wait/retry Caller has an obsolete read snapshot for an upgrade End that transaction and start a suitable new attempt Database path is unwritable Correct the storage access problem Required storage is unavailable Restore that resource, rather than increasing a lock timeout Long-lived reader limits checkpoint progress End the relevant reader when the application can do so Locking mode affects readers too Rollback-journal and WAL arrangements have different reader/writer coordination. WAL readers can continue from their snapshots while another connection writes, but there is still one writer and there can still be busy conditions. Database-level coordination is also different from an arbitrary file lock acquired by another program. Opening the database files outside the database engine does not participate correctly in every engine lock protocol. For an Emby workload, overlapping scans, user-state updates and other database activity can be relevant context for a busy operation. The exact error and transaction state determine the retry boundary. An isolated toy example verifies writer contention and stale-snapshot recovery without using a real server database. See Also Database transactions and atomic application changes Database write-ahead logging, readers and checkpoints File locking, share modes and concurrent access Background task scheduling and shared resources References SQLite isolation and concurrency SQLite locking and rollback journaling SQLite transaction control

articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.title: Library databases, identities and indexes | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.keywords: Library databases, identities and indexes A library database organizes indexed media records and relationships for queries, while source files and user-specific state retain separate roles. A library database stores records that help a media server find and organize its collection. Queries can select films, sort titles and connect records without reopening every media file for each request. The database is a catalog of application information. It is not another copy of each film's encoded content. A query uses stored relationships An original logical record might include: Item identity: item-A Media location: /media/Film.mkv Display title: The Example Film Collection: Movies The example describes roles rather than Emby's internal tables. Its public API exposes documented item fields; those fields are an API projection, not a specification of the database's on-disk schema. Indexes can let a query find relevant records without visiting every row. They also occupy space and need updating when relevant data change. Work Database consequence Browse a sorted library Reads records and suitable indexes Add discovered media Creates records and updates relationships Change indexed metadata Updates records and relevant indexes Record user activity Updates the supported user-state relationships Rebuild an index Performs work without creating another media file Scanning observes sources; browsing queries the catalog A scan enumerates accessible media and performs the required analysis. Browsing generally uses the information already stored from those observations. That separation explains why a title can remain visible during a storage outage. A catalog entry establishes that the server has a record; opening its source requires current storage access. It also explains why a newly copied file may not appear until the relevant observation and catalog update complete. Rebuilding is not a universal restoration A scan can recreate information obtainable from source files and providers. It does not inherently recover every user-specific or manually configured relationship from a lost database. Database files can also need companion journals and a supported version relationship. Transactions , write-ahead logging and application backups describe those consistency and recovery roles. For Emby, use supported library and recovery operations instead of deriving an editing procedure from an illustrative table or API field name. See Also Database transactions and atomic application changes Database write-ahead logging, readers and checkpoints Media item identity Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation References SQLite database-file format Emby browsing the library

articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.title: Database transactions and atomic application changes | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.keywords: Database transactions and atomic application changes A database transaction groups related changes under atomicity and isolation rules, while commit durability and external effects require their own guarantees. A database transaction gives related changes a shared completion boundary. If an application needs to update two records together, it can arrange that other connections do not observe a half-completed result under the database's supported isolation rules. Atomicity, isolation and durability describe different parts of that promise. A transaction is most useful when the application knows which changes need to belong together. A complete change has more than one field Consider a demonstration table holding a playback-like position in seconds and a count. This is a purpose-built SQLite example with a constraint that prevents negative values. CREATE TABLE demo_state ( item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, position INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (position >= 0), plays INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (plays >= 0) ); INSERT INTO demo_state VALUES ('film-A', 0, 0); BEGIN; UPDATE demo_state SET plays = plays + 1 WHERE item = 'film-A'; UPDATE demo_state SET position = 120 WHERE item = 'film-A'; COMMIT; After the successful commit, the row contains position 120 and count one. The application intentionally chose one boundary for both updates. Two separate automatically committed statements would instead create two completion points. The same idea applies to more complex server state, but the actual schema, constraints and units belong to the application. Emby's public playback positions use documented units that should not be inferred from this table. A failed statement needs deliberate error handling Now begin another transaction, increase the count and then attempt a negative position: BEGIN UPDATE count: plays becomes 2 inside this transaction UPDATE position to -1: constraint failure Caller chooses ROLLBACK Committed row remains: position 120, plays 1 The constraint prevents the invalid statement from completing. It does not mean that every SQLite error automatically reverses every earlier statement in the active transaction. For common constraint behavior, the failed statement is rolled back while prior work in that transaction can remain pending. The caller's explicit rollback gives this example its all-abandoned result. An application that catches the error and carelessly commits the remaining work could publish the increased count without the intended position change. The database cannot infer the application's original grouping intention after the application chooses a different completion action. Isolation governs what another reader sees Other connections do not ordinarily see those uncommitted changes under SQLite's normal isolation arrangements. After a commit, a new observation can see the completed state. A reader already holding a WAL snapshot can continue seeing its older point until that read transaction ends. That is a coherent snapshot, not necessarily the newest committed value. The transaction's own connection can observe its pending changes. “I read back the new value” from that connection therefore does not prove that other clients can see it or that it is durable. A commit can fail to complete A commit request can encounter a busy or failing condition. In SQLite, a busy commit can leave the transaction active so the caller may retry the commit when the relevant condition changes. Other failures have their documented effects. This is why a complete operation includes checking the commit result. Issuing COMMIT is not identical to receiving a successful completion. Retrying also needs the right boundary. If the transaction is still active, blindly repeating all updates can duplicate a count increment. If the earlier transaction is known to have rolled back, the caller can start a fresh attempt according to the operation's policy. The example verifier checks successful commit and explicit rollback against isolated demonstration data. It does not operate on a real server database. Durable state depends on the storage contract A database coordinates its journal or WAL and the synchronization calls appropriate to its configuration. Durability after a power failure depends on those settings and on the storage stack honoring them. A completed transaction does not promise survival under every possible weakened synchronization policy. Likewise, writing the main database file is not the only way a transaction can become part of the current logical state: committed WAL records can participate. For backups, capture a consistent supported data set rather than copying an arbitrary file between these stages. A database rollback does not undo the outside world If an application sends a notification or changes a lamp between two SQL updates, database rollback cannot unsend that message or restore the lamp automatically. Those effects occur in another system. A reliable design records an intended external action under a durable database boundary and then processes it with its own retry and identity rules. That separates “state committed” from “effect delivered” without pretending one database transaction controls every service. For an Emby integration or plugin, the lesson is to identify the real completion boundary and inspect its result. A coherent database operation, a visible API response and a completed external action can be related while remaining distinct observations. See Also Database write-ahead logging, readers and checkpoints Database locking and competing operations References SQLite transaction control SQLite atomic commit SQLite isolation and concurrency

articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.title: Database write-ahead logging, readers and checkpoints | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/databases/Serv.keywords: Database write-ahead logging, readers and checkpoints Write-ahead logging records committed database changes in a log before checkpointing them into the main file, supporting reader snapshots with particular concurrency rules. Write-ahead logging, or WAL, lets a database record changes in a log before incorporating them into its main data file. In SQLite's WAL mode, committed changes can therefore be part of the current logical database even while the main file still contains an earlier version of those pages. That is the starting point for understanding concurrent readers, checkpoints and backups. The main file's last-write time is not a complete report of the current database state. A commit adds a new visible generation An original logical example uses two generations: Main file contains: S1 Writer appends changed pages and commits: S2 in WAL New reader's current database: S2 Main file alone still contains: S1 for the uncheckpointed changes The WAL includes the information needed to identify completed transactions. A reader does not simply treat every byte at the end of a log as a valid committed change. SQLite's actual log uses database pages and transaction markers rather than the symbolic S1/S2 names above. Readers have an end mark When a WAL read transaction starts, it establishes the committed point it is allowed to see. Later writes can extend the log while that reader continues to see its earlier snapshot. Moment Original reader R1 Writer New reader R2 R1 begins at S1 Sees S1 No new commit yet Not started Writer commits S2 Still sees S1 S2 complete Not started R2 begins Still sees S1 S2 remains current Sees S2 R1 ends and begins again Can observe the newer point — Its own snapshot remains defined A reader may obtain the relevant page from the main file or from an applicable WAL record. Its end mark determines which version is eligible. This is how reading and writing can coexist without exposing a partly written transaction. It is not a promise that every reader always sees the newest committed state immediately. Checkpointing moves the storage representation A checkpoint transfers eligible committed page versions from the WAL into the main file. That changes where the state is represented; it is different from the original application commit. An older active reader can prevent checkpoint progress beyond the point it still needs. A long-lived read transaction can therefore keep WAL history needed even while later writers continue making progress. The log file's physical size also does not map directly to “this many uncommitted changes.” Reuse, checkpoint progress and retained allocations influence it. Deleting or truncating a companion file outside the database's supported lifecycle is not an ordinary cache cleanup operation. There is still one writer SQLite WAL allows readers and a writer to overlap, but it does not supply unrestricted simultaneous independent writers. The implementation serializes writes to one WAL. A second write operation can encounter a busy condition. Recovery, exclusive access and connection cleanup can also produce busy results. WAL improves a particular concurrency arrangement; it does not abolish all locks or waiting. SQLite's ordinary shared-memory WAL coordination also requires participants on the same host. Placing a live WAL database on a network file system does not become a supported multi-host database merely because both machines can read its files. Crash recovery needs the completed state A crash can leave the main file and WAL together representing the last recoverable committed point. The database's recovery rules distinguish valid completed records from incomplete work. An application response, a transaction commit result and durability after power loss still have different meanings. Synchronization configuration and the lower storage stack influence durability. The WAL file is part of the protocol that coordinates those writes, not a universal replacement for storage guarantees. A backup must capture a consistent database Copying only the main file while committed changes remain in WAL can omit those changes. Copying the main file and WAL at unrelated moments can also fail to establish one consistent capture. A supported database-aware backup API or the application's documented stopped-server procedure coordinates the relevant state. SQLite's online backup API supplies an engine-managed mechanism; Emby's manual backup documentation requires the server process to be stopped. A useful recovery record identifies the supported capture method and required files rather than advising users to delete a “large temporary WAL.” The file may contain state needed for the latest generation or for active readers. The accompanying isolated reader/writer example checks old-reader and new-reader observations, competing writer behavior and checkpoint recovery. It demonstrates SQLite mechanics on new toy data; it does not attest the journal configuration or engine version of an installed Emby server. See Also Database transactions and atomic application changes Database locking and competing operations References SQLite write-ahead logging SQLite online backup API SQLite atomic commit

Media files, catalogue state and caches serve different purposes. Database operations, scheduled work and logs then add activity around playback, while thermal or sleep behavior can change the available execution state. articles/storage/workload/logging/index..title: Overview: Logging | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/logging/index..keywords: Overview: Logging Logging controls determine which diagnostic events are recorded and how long their storage remains available. A level filter selects detail; rotation and retention bound the surviving history. The two mechanisms therefore affect different parts of an investigation's evidence. These pages explain why a missing event needs context about both the configured logging and the interval still retained. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Logging levels Logging levels select which diagnostic events are recorded, so the available evidence depends on the enabled detail and the component producing it.
