articles/storage/workload/logging/Server.title: Logging levels and diagnostic detail | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/logging/Server.keywords: Logging levels and diagnostic detail Logging levels select which diagnostic events are recorded, so the available evidence depends on the enabled detail and the component producing it. A logging level classifies a diagnostic event by its purpose or severity. A configured filter determines which of those events the logging system records. Detailed messages can help explain a particular operation, while concise operational messages make longer periods easier to inspect. These are different views of the same workload rather than different proof standards. A level selects evidence The common .NET level names illustrate the roles: Level Typical purpose Trace Very fine-grained activity Debug Details useful for diagnosing behavior Information Ordinary operational events Warning An unexpected condition that may still permit progress Error Failure of an operation or component Critical Severe failure affecting continued operation The application decides which events belong at each level. A warning in one component is not automatically equivalent to a warning in another. An original filter model accepts Information and more severe messages. Debug and Trace events are omitted from that model's output. Their absence says nothing about whether the corresponding activity occurred. An error line needs operation context A background lookup can fail while playback succeeds. A failed playback attempt can be followed by a successful retry. Reading only the word “error” loses the operation and time relationship. Useful context includes the request or task, timestamp, component, input being processed and subsequent result. A transcode log describes another layer from a general server log; it can explain command and media-processing details that the general log does not contain. Emby's log-file documentation identifies the supported way to locate its logs. Its current controls and component behavior determine the recorded detail. More detail also creates more volume Verbose activity can increase write work and make relevant events harder to find among repeated messages. Record the interval and enabled detail when interpreting a diagnostic capture. Logs may include sensitive request context, paths or identifiers. The useful evidence is the relevant operation with secret values handled appropriately; a credential is not made safe to distribute because it appeared in a diagnostic line. Rotation and retention determine how long those events remain available. A missing historical event can reflect filtering or retention rather than proof that the server never performed the operation. See Also Log rotation, retention and bounded evidence Reading a transcoding log References Emby log files Microsoft logging levels

articles/storage/workload/logging/Server.title: Log rotation, retention and bounded evidence | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/logging/Server.keywords: Log rotation, retention and bounded evidence Log rotation changes the active log or retained segments so diagnostic storage remains bounded, with size and retention controlling available history. Log rotation limits a continuing stream of diagnostic data by starting or selecting another active segment and retaining earlier segments under a policy. Rotation determines file boundaries. Retention determines which old segments remain. Neither alone guarantees a fixed number of days of evidence. A size budget has a rate In an original model, the active log can reach 50 MB and the system retains five completed 50-MB segments. The maximum uncompressed file budget is about 300 MB: one active segment plus five retained ones. (1 active + 5 retained) × 50 MB = 300 MB At 1 MB/minute: about 300 minutes of uniformly produced data At 10 MB/minute: about 30 minutes Real segments can be smaller, compressed or constrained by other limits. A sudden diagnostic burst can shorten the retained time window dramatically. Policy What it bounds Maximum segment size How much one segment can accumulate Retained segment count Number of older segments kept Maximum age Age eligibility under that policy Total storage budget Aggregate retained volume Changing a name does not necessarily change an open handle One rotation mechanism renames the current file and asks the writer to reopen a new one. A process with an existing handle can continue writing to the previously opened object until it follows the required reopen lifecycle. Other mechanisms copy and truncate or use a managed logging service. These have different timing and consistency behavior. A filename becoming “old” is not universal proof that the writer has stopped using it. Emby's supported logging lifecycle defines how its own files are created and retained. The systemd journal is another example of a managed system with documented storage and retention controls, rather than the same file-rotation configuration. Preserve the relevant interval When investigating a failed operation, establish the event time and which retained segments cover it. A current log can contain only the later successful operation, while the initial failure was in an older segment. The absence of that older file changes the available evidence. It does not reverse the earlier event. Logging levels determine what was recorded within the surviving interval. See Also Logging levels and diagnostic detail File size limits and large media files References Emby log files systemd journal retention specification

articles/storage/workload/power/index.ht.title: Overview: Power and thermal behavior | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/power/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Power and thermal behavior Power and thermal behavior change the execution rate or availability of a server under particular operating states. A warm component can enter a protective performance state, while system sleep suspends ordinary work until recovery. Those are different explanations for delayed or unavailable media operations. The two pages identify the state and observations needed before a slow interval is attributed to the processor or storage. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Thermal throttling Thermal throttling reduces available execution performance to respect temperature limits, so sustained media work can behave differently from a cold start. Server sleep and wake behavior System sleep suspends ordinary server execution, and recovery after wake must restore the process's network and storage environment before service is fully available. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References Intel architecture software developer manuals Linux kernel: system sleep states

articles/storage/workload/power/Server-S.title: Server sleep, wake and availability | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/power/Server-S.keywords: Server sleep, wake and availability System sleep suspends ordinary server execution, and recovery after wake must restore the process's network and storage environment before service is fully available. When a server enters a system sleep state, ordinary application execution is suspended according to that state's rules. Emby cannot continue its normal playback, API handling or background tasks as if the system were fully active. This is different from one disk spinning down , where the operating system can remain awake and only that device needs to resume. Which part stops? Condition What changes Individual drive standby First access to that drive can need a wake interval System suspend Ordinary server work stops until resume Hibernation System state is stored for later restoration under the platform's rules Shutdown A new startup is needed Platform-specific low-power idle Capabilities depend on the platform's documented state The names and implementations differ between operating systems. A modern low-power state should not be assumed to behave identically to every traditional suspend state. Wake capability has a path Wake-on-network behavior depends on hardware, firmware, operating-system policy and which sleep state is in use. The network also has to deliver the applicable wake signal to the machine. A server that can wake from a local test does not thereby have an internet-reachable wake mechanism. Discovery, routing and any forwarding arrangement have their own scopes. After wake, an existing process may resume, but its earlier connections can be invalid. Address changes, disconnected shares and device reinitialization can affect the operation it performs next. Availability returns in stages An original resume sequence is: System resumes Network interface becomes usable Expected media share becomes readable Server operation succeeds under its service identity Those observations need not happen at the same instant. A configured library path can exist before the intended remote tree is actually accessible. A task scheduled during suspension also did not execute its normal work at that time. Any catch-up behavior belongs to the scheduler and task policy. For an Emby host, establish the availability expected during quiet periods and after resume. A visible process or responding host is only part of the evidence that the required media operation can now complete. See Also Disk spin-down, wake latency and idle workloads Background task scheduling and shared resources Emby server discovery and advertised endpoints Unavailable network mounts and trustworthy library state References Linux kernel: system sleep states Microsoft system sleeping states

articles/storage/workload/power/Server-T.title: Thermal throttling and sustained server throughput | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/power/Server-T.keywords: Thermal throttling and sustained server throughput Thermal throttling reduces available execution performance to respect temperature limits, so sustained media work can behave differently from a cold start. Thermal throttling is protective behavior that reduces work rate when a component approaches its temperature constraints. A processor or storage device can change performance while remaining operational. For Emby, a software transcode can begin comfortably ahead of presentation and later fall behind after sustained load. That pattern needs evidence about the limiting component rather than just a comparison with its advertised maximum frequency. A cold start is one operating condition An original encoding model begins at 45 frames/s and settles at 24 frames/s after warming. Its source needs 30 frames/s for real-time presentation. Cold measured interval: 45 / 30 = 1.5 times real time Warm measured interval: 24 / 30 = 0.8 times real time These rates illustrate a result, not a prediction from a particular clock speed or processor model. A buffer can temporarily conceal a deficit, but continuing below the presentation requirement consumes that reserve. Frequency can fall for several reasons Evidence Interpretation to investigate Temperature reaches the component's stated boundary with thermal indicators Thermal protection is relevant A power/current limit is active below that thermal boundary Power management can be the limit Processor waits for storage or another stage Low useful progress need not be throttling Only one thread is busy Parallelism or serial work can limit the job A container's CPU bandwidth is exhausted Scheduling limits can cap progress A low frequency alone does not identify which condition applies. CPU, GPU and storage can each have their own thermal and power behavior. Sustained results need the full interval Record the actual operation, its duration and throughput alongside supported temperature and limit indicators. A short benchmark that finishes before the thermal state settles answers a different question from an hour-long encoding job. Cooling, ambient conditions and concurrent workload affect the operating state. The article's illustration does not specify a universal safe temperature or hardware remedy; the component's documented constraints provide that context. For an Emby pipeline, determine whether the limiting work belongs to CPU encoding, a GPU stage, storage or another resource. Protective throttling is a mechanism for a demonstrated decline, not a generic explanation for every playback pause. See Also CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads Real-time transcoding and playback deadlines NVMe storage: commands, PCIe lanes and queues References Intel architecture software developer manuals Intel: thermal and power throttling

articles/storage/workload/Server-Caches..title: Server caches, reuse and invalidation | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/Server-Caches..keywords: Server caches, reuse and invalidation Server caches retain reusable application results, with keys and invalidation determining whether those results remain suitable for a later request. A server cache keeps a result that may be reused instead of recalculated or fetched again. It can hold artwork, a query result, analyzed media information or another expensive derived value. This is an application-level decision. The operating system's page cache is a separate mechanism that reuses stored bytes below the application. A cache key defines which requests are equivalent Suppose a fictional cache stores a library listing under the key Movies . Two users have different library permissions. Reusing one user's listing for the other would be wrong if the key omitted the relevant user and policy context. A better key must represent the inputs that determine the result. The exact design can use identity, query parameters, data generation and other applicable state. Reuse condition Why it matters Same relevant query A differently sorted or filtered request needs another result Same applicable user/policy context Access and user state can change the content Same underlying data generation A new item can invalidate an old list Acceptable age A result may be intentionally allowed to be somewhat stale A high hit rate is useful only when the reused result is suitable. Invalidation connects a change to stored results An original generation model is: Library generation G1 -> cached result for G1 New item committed -> library generation G2 Request for current G2 -> old G1 result is not a current-generation hit An application can invalidate entries on changes, give them a lifetime, check a version or combine these methods. A restart often clears in-memory caches, but it does not prescribe how every on-disk cache is rebuilt. A cache miss also does not automatically mean failure. It can trigger the ordinary computation or storage lookup that produces the result. Regenerable data have a documented role Generated thumbnails can have a supported rebuild path. User history and settings are persistent state with a different recovery role. A directory's name or a file's small size is insufficient to classify it. For Emby, warm and cold operation can have different response times because of reusable application results as well as storage caches . Distinguish those layers before interpreting an improvement after browsing the same title twice. See Also Storage caches: reusable reads and deferred writes Library databases, identities and indexes RAM, reclaim and memory pressure References Emby browsing the library Docker volumes

articles/storage/workload/Server-Data-Ro.title: Media files and server application data | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/Server-Data-Ro.keywords: Media files and server application data Source media and server application data have different contents and recovery lifecycles, even when they occupy the same physical device. A film file contains encoded media. Emby application data describes how the server organizes and serves that collection, alongside settings and user state. The two can occupy the same disk, but they have different jobs. Moving the films does not automatically move the server's organization, and restoring the server configuration does not recreate missing film bytes. One title has several kinds of state Stored information Example role Source film Encoded video, audio and embedded media information Local sidecars Subtitles, artwork or metadata stored beside media Catalog record Server item identity and indexed information User-specific state Resume position, played status or favorites Server configuration Library paths and behavior settings Plugin state Data maintained by a particular extension Some media containers have rich embedded metadata, but that does not make them a complete copy of every server user's state. A user's favorite selection belongs to the server/application relationship rather than to the movie's video stream. A migration can recover one role and miss another An original migration copies all source films to a new host. The new server can scan those files and create a catalog. That does not establish that it recovered the previous users' resume positions or the same item identities. Conversely, restored application data can still refer to the old host's paths. The catalog may be present while playback fails because the source is inaccessible. A complete migration must reconcile those relationships through the supported workflow, including the server's actual execution identity and paths. Regeneration has a scope Generated thumbnails or some caches can have documented rebuild paths. User history and manually configured relationships have different recovery value. Treating every application-data file as disposable because a scan can rediscover films loses that distinction. Media backups protect the content files. Application-data backups protect the supported set of server state. A restoration is successful when the recovered roles connect into the service you intended to recover. See Also What is a media library? Library databases, identities and indexes Persistent application data across server recreation References Emby server backup and restore Emby manual backups

articles/storage/workload/Server-Tasks.h.title: Background task scheduling and shared resources | Emby Learn
articles/storage/workload/Server-Tasks.h.keywords: Background task scheduling and shared resources Background task scheduling chooses triggers and execution opportunities, while actual completion depends on resource availability, overlap and application policy. A scheduled task has a reason to run and an operation to perform. The trigger might be a time, an interval, a startup condition or an explicit request. The trigger is not the start time, and the start time is not the successful completion time. Emby's scheduled-task interface provides documented controls and results for background work. Overlap changes the workload An original schedule places three jobs on one server: 02:00–02:20 library scan 02:10–02:35 thumbnail work 02:15–02:45 integrity read All three overlap from 02:15 to 02:20: five minutes Each job can complete acceptably alone while their overlap creates storage queues, CPU competition or database waits. Changing the nominal trigger does not establish the actual load if a previous run is still active. Scheduler observation Additional question Trigger fired Was the job started or queued? Job started Which resources are now in use? Job ended Did it succeed, fail or stop early? Next interval arrived Is overlap allowed or a previous run still active? A lower priority can change competition without turning an expensive operation into free work. Downtime creates missed opportunities If a server is asleep or stopped at a scheduled time, the task cannot perform its ordinary work then. A scheduler might run missed work after startup, skip it or apply another policy. That behavior belongs to the particular task and application. Do not infer a successful scan from a schedule entry alone. Check the last completion and the task's actual result. Timing should reflect the resources used A media scan can exercise many small directory and metadata operations. Thumbnail generation can read media and use an encoder. A full integrity pass reads every relevant byte. Their effects need not resemble one another even if all are called background tasks. For Emby, use observed duration and resource demand to understand the schedule. A task intended for a quiet period can extend into active playback when its source becomes slower or its scope grows. Database locking and memory pressure provide mechanisms for that shared-workload delay. See Also Library scanning and catalogue reconciliation CPU cores, threads and concurrent workloads Database locking and competing operations References Emby scheduled tasks Linux kernel: pressure stall information

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/index.title: Overview: Subtitle processing in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/index.keywords: Overview: Subtitle processing in Emby Subtitle processing in Emby connects track compatibility with direct delivery, rendering and optional video composition. The subtitle can remain a separate representation for the app to render, or it can become part of the video picture through an overlay operation. The available path depends on the subtitle, player and processing support. Delivery and compatibility topics establish that decision. Filter and pipeline topics then explain how composition is performed and how it connects to decoding and encoding. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle delivery in Emby Emby's subtitle delivery route connects the selected source track to an app-supported representation or a rendered video output. Subtitle rendering compatibility in Emby Subtitle compatibility in Emby includes source recognition, delivery, presentation features and resources at the selected app/server rendering stage. Subtitle overlay filters Subtitle overlay filters render or composite timed content onto video pictures through supported software or device interfaces. Subtitle overlay pipelines Subtitle overlay pipelines connect decoding, subtitle composition and output encoding through a particular sequence of stages. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Overview: GPU subtitle overlay | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Overview: GPU subtitle overlay GPU subtitle overlay uses supported interfaces to render or composite subtitle content with device-resident pictures. OpenCL, CUDA and Vulkan paths have to agree with the picture representation entering and leaving the operation. Rendering the subtitle and compositing its image are also meaningful stages to identify. The pages below explain the GPU routes in that dataflow context, including the handoffs to other processing work. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> OpenCL subtitle overlay OpenCL subtitle composition operates on compatible device image planes, after subtitle content has been rendered into an accepted image representation. CUDA subtitle overlay CUDA subtitle composition blends accepted device video/image formats and remains distinct from text rendering, codec engines and the selected Emby graph. Vulkan subtitle overlay Vulkan overlay uses synchronized device images and a compute shader; subtitle rasterization, format matching and colour interpretation remain separate requirements. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: CUDA subtitle overlay | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: CUDA subtitle overlay CUDA subtitle composition blends accepted device video/image formats and remains distinct from text rendering, codec engines and the selected Emby graph. CUDA can execute a subtitle-image blend on NVIDIA device data. That composition step is distinct from rendering the text and from the dedicated video decode/encode stages. The inputs must satisfy the specific filter's format contract . A generic claim that a GPU supports CUDA is not enough to establish that a chosen subtitle canvas can be composed with the selected video surface. The examined filter has a limited format set In Emby FFmpeg 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 , the overlay_cuda format-matching code accepts these pairs: Main software format underlying the CUDA frames Accepted overlay format NV12 NV12 YUV420P YUV420P or YUVA420P The overlay format list includes YUVA420P's alpha plane, but the matching code does not pair it with an NV12 main input. It also does not make an arbitrary RGBA, 10-bit P010 or another surface acceptable. This is a source-verified table for that dated filter, not a current support table for all Emby CUDA routes. The layer needs conversion without losing its meaning A text renderer can produce coverage and colour on CPU memory. A route preparing CUDA input must select a compatible representation, preserve alpha where supported, upload/map it appropriately and retain its timing. Dropping alpha can change transparent background into an opaque rectangle. Choosing another format can also change range, colour or chroma sampling. Those are conversion decisions before the kernel does the blend. Kernel and codec work occupy different stages CUDA kernels operate on device memory. A hardware encoder consumes picture surfaces through its applicable codec interface. A session can use one stage without placing every preceding task on that same engine. The kernel needs correctly synchronized inputs and produces an output whose completion the next stage observes. Image pitch and per-plane dimensions matter alongside the visible width/height. For Emby, the hardware overview , actual binary capabilities and selected graph describe the available combination. The reference source proves the table's interface; it does not prove that a session used it. See Also Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline Subtitle overlay filtering Software subtitle overlay References Emby FFmpeg source archive: 2023_06_25-u1 NVIDIA CUDA programming guide FFmpeg filter documentation

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: OpenCL subtitle overlay | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: OpenCL subtitle overlay OpenCL subtitle composition operates on compatible device image planes, after subtitle content has been rendered into an accepted image representation. OpenCL can execute image composition on device-accessible data. For subtitles, the text or graphics must first become a compatible image layer with the correct time, placement and coverage. The OpenCL blend kernel does not itself parse an ASS script, choose a font or recover a caption service. Those are preceding responsibilities. A concrete source reference The pinned Emby FFmpeg 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 contains the video filter overlay_opencl . Its source reads main/overlay hardware-frame contexts and selects kernels for no-alpha, internal-alpha or separate-alpha cases. That verifies a composition design in this dated source. It does not say which filter graph every current Emby build selects or whether a particular compiled binary enabled it. A subtitle-to-video stage can bridge from subtitle media into this video-overlay input model. The representation and resource cost of that bridge are part of the route. Plane interpretation must agree A multi-plane video format has distinct luma/chroma image grids. The source's separate-alpha handling includes the relevant chroma subsampling adjustments. For an ideal 3840 × 2160 NV12 picture, the luma plane has that sample grid and its interleaved chroma plane has 1920 × 1080 two-component locations . Position and alpha calculations must respect which plane is being processed. A packed RGBA layer has another representation. It cannot become compatible merely because both inputs are called “GPU images”. Context and synchronization complete the job The image objects must be usable in the OpenCL context/queue executing the kernel. Compatible device sharing or a supported mapping path can avoid some copying; otherwise transfers are needed. Video decode completion, subtitle image readiness and composition completion establish dependencies. The encoder must consume the completed output rather than an image whose writes are still in progress. A CPU-rendered layer can therefore coexist with GPU composition. If the main video remains in a compatible device route, uploading the subtitle layer can avoid downloading every main picture. For an Emby investigation, identify the bundled version, selected graph, underlying formats and device contexts. OpenCL availability describes a technology boundary; the actual route describes the work it performed. See Also Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline Software subtitle overlay Subtitle overlay filtering References Emby FFmpeg source archive: 2023_06_25-u1 Khronos OpenCL specification libass: Subtitle rendering library FFmpeg filter documentation

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Vulkan subtitle overlay | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Vulkan subtitle overlay Vulkan overlay uses synchronized device images and a compute shader; subtitle rasterization, format matching and colour interpretation remain separate requirements. Vulkan represents image processing through device resources and explicitly submitted work. For subtitle composition, a compute shader can read the video and a prepared subtitle image, then write a combined picture. The text has already been rendered by the time it reaches this boundary. Fonts, script shaping and cue interpretation are jobs upstream of the image shader. Two compatible images enter the examined filter The overlay_vulkan filter in Emby FFmpeg 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 accepts two Vulkan video inputs. At initialization, its source rejects main and overlay frames whose underlying software pixel formats differ. “Both are Vulkan frames” therefore does not establish that they form an accepted pair. A CPU-generated RGBA subtitle layer is not automatically compatible with a differently represented video surface. Preparing it requires an accepted format and suitable device images. That conversion must preserve transparent regions and the intended colour values. The filter derives overlay offsets and sizes separately for luma and subsampled chroma planes. A position expressed in full-resolution picture coordinates cannot simply be copied unchanged into every plane. Transparent edges need the right shader branch The source contains both a replacement shader and an alpha shader. In the replacement branch, samples inside the overlay rectangle replace the corresponding video samples. Outside it, the main image is retained. The alpha branch calculates a weighted combination, corresponding to S × a + V × (1 − a) for subtitle sample S, main sample V and coverage a. It sets the resulting alpha to one for the opaque output. The source chooses the branch from the configured input format's alpha flag. This is arithmetic on the supplied sample representation. It does not, by itself, prove a linear-light blend or perform an HDR-to-SDR tone map. Range, transfer function and colour conversion must be established elsewhere in the graph. Completion is part of the interface The examined code creates image views, changes image layouts for shader reading/writing, records a compute dispatch and submits it with dependencies on the input and output frames. Those steps allow the shader to read completed input data and let subsequent processing observe the output. Being on the same device does not remove this ordering requirement. This dated source explains one implementation. The Vulkan API's availability, enabled filters in the actual binary and the selected session graph determine whether an Emby route can use it. See hardware subtitle pipelines for how that device stage fits into the complete picture route. See Also Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline Subtitle overlay filtering OpenCL subtitle overlay References Emby FFmpeg source archive: 2023_06_25-u1 Khronos Vulkan specification FFmpeg filter documentation

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Overview: Subtitle overlay filters | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Overview: Subtitle overlay filters Subtitle overlay filters render or composite timed content onto video pictures through supported software or device interfaces. Burn-in describes the visible result; a filter describes an operation used to produce it. Software, GPU and legacy filter topics explain different execution routes for that operation. Their picture formats and interfaces matter when connecting an overlay to the rest of an Emby conversion pipeline. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle burn-in Subtitle burn-in composites caption pixels into decoded video pictures before encoding an output whose subtitles are no longer separately removable. Subtitle overlay filtering Subtitle overlay filtering synchronizes a current subtitle layer with video and blends its colour/coverage into the applicable picture geometry. Software subtitle overlay Software subtitle overlay renders/decodes and blends subtitle content into CPU-accessible video frames, with any hardware transfers determined by the surrounding route. GPU subtitle overlay GPU subtitle overlay uses supported interfaces to render or composite subtitle content with device-resident pictures. Legacy subtitle overlay filters Legacy ass and subtitles video filters obtain a script through their own resource path and render it into CPU video frames; native subtitle-stream filters expose a different graph boundary. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Subtitle burn-in | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Subtitle burn-in Subtitle burn-in composites caption pixels into decoded video pictures before encoding an output whose subtitles are no longer separately removable. Subtitle burn-in makes the subtitle's rendered pixels part of an output video. The pipeline decodes the relevant pictures, composes the subtitle presentation over them, and encodes the resulting pictures. The original subtitle can remain selectable in the library. The burned-in output version no longer has a separate switch that removes those pixels. One caption affects several pictures Take a cue active from 2.25 to 3.25 seconds and video picture times n/24. Under the half-open interval model, pictures 54 through77 carry the caption: 24 pictures . The caption image can be rendered or cached efficiently if it is static. Composition still has to include it in each applicable output picture. An animated caption can additionally change during that interval. At the end, the subtitle must disappear from subsequent pictures. Reusing the last nonempty overlay without respecting its lifetime can leave text stuck on screen. Burn-in adds a video processing route Stage Work Decode Recover video pictures in a usable format/context Subtitle rendering/decoding Produce current glyphs or graphics with required resources Composition Combine subtitle pixels with each relevant picture Encode Produce compatible output video Delivery Supply that video and its remaining media components A text decoder does not do all those steps. Neither does a hardware encoder eliminate the other stages. For an Emby session, the selected route and requested presentation determine whether burn-in is used. Playback-method documentation is the source for product behavior; this page explains the work introduced by that choice. Rendering and composition are distinct A font lookup or shaping failure occurs before blending. A palette/alpha error affects the image supplied for composition. A coordinate transform can put otherwise correct lettering outside the retained picture. Fixing the encoder setting does not resolve those subtitle-input relationships. Compare the current rendered layer, placement and timing before the final encode. Colour treatment also matters for HDR/SDR. The subtitle's intended display colour must be interpreted in the selected working/output model. Overlay placement relative to tone mapping can affect its appearance; the pipeline needs a deliberate ordering. Hardware can accelerate parts of the work Hardware decoding, GPU composition and hardware encoding describe different stages. A CPU-rendered subtitle image can be uploaded and composed with device-resident video. Another route can download full pictures for CPU composition and upload them again. Pipeline fundamentals develops those memory and timing relationships. Burn-in describes the resulting permanent picture content, rather than one fixed hardware backend. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Subtitle overlay filtering | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Subtitle overlay filtering Subtitle overlay filtering synchronizes a current subtitle layer with video and blends its colour/coverage into the applicable picture geometry. Overlay filtering combines the current subtitle presentation with a video picture. Its inputs must agree on time, geometry, format and the meaning of colour/alpha. That task is different from recognizing speech, selecting a subtitle track or shaping its text. An overlay can receive correct pixels and still produce the wrong result if it interprets their coverage or placement incorrectly. Alpha controls coverage For straight-alpha colours expressed in one declared working domain, a simple opaque-video blend is: output = alpha × subtitle + (1 − alpha) × video Take subtitle colour (1,0.9,0.1) , video colour (0.1,0.2,0.3) and alpha 0.25 : Component Calculation Output R 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 0.1 0.325 G 0.25 × 0.9 + 0.75 × 0.2 0.375 B 0.25 × 0.1 + 0.75 × 0.3 0.250 This is a numerical blend model. It does not assert that every filter automatically converts its inputs into linear light or applies the same HDR colour policy. At alpha 0 the video remains; at alpha 1 the subtitle covers it. Antialiased edges use intermediate coverage values. Straight and premultiplied colour need different handling In premultiplied form, the subtitle colour has already been multiplied by alpha. The equivalent blend adds that premultiplied colour to (1−alpha) times the video. Multiplying it by alpha again darkens the subtitle edge. Treating unmultiplied colour as premultiplied can make another incorrect edge. A byte format called RGBA does not by itself establish which convention its values use. The selected format also matters for subsampled YUV. Luma and chroma planes have different grids, and alpha/position calculations need the relevant plane relationship. A luma-coordinate displacement is not automatically the same numeric displacement on a half-resolution chroma plane. Synchronize the layer with picture presentation The subtitle event's lifetime is evaluated against picture PTS. Its packet arrival or decode time can be earlier. A clear/empty presentation at the appropriate time is as meaningful as a nonempty layer. End-of-stream and repeated-frame policies must preserve the intended disappearance, rather than repeat the previous caption indefinitely. The geometry includes source script/display planes and any crop/scale. Rendering establishes how that placement reaches the composition surface. Native subtitle input and video-overlay input differ In the pinned Emby FFmpeg 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 , overlaytextsubs accepts a main video input and a subtitle input, while overlaygraphicsubs handles graphical subtitle composition. The former invokes libass rendering before blending. A generic overlay or hardware overlay filter instead works with video/image frames. A subtitle-to-video conversion can bridge that boundary. Those are verified source interfaces of this dated build. A session's actual filter graph and compiled capabilities identify which form was used. The SDK processing-step descriptions express semantic roles, not a one-to-one guarantee of filter names. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Legacy subtitle overlay filters | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Legacy subtitle overlay filters Legacy ass and subtitles video filters obtain a script through their own resource path and render it into CPU video frames; native subtitle-stream filters expose a different graph boundary. The familiar FFmpeg subtitles and ass filters are video filters that render a script over incoming picture frames. Their script-reading path is part of the filter's own initialization. “Legacy” here distinguishes that interface from Emby's later native subtitle-stream filtering design; it does not mean the established filters are unusable. Who owns the subtitle input? Interface in the examined Emby source Inputs visible to the filter graph Subtitle acquisition ass Video frames The filter reads an ASS script subtitles Video frames The filter opens a resource, selects/decodes subtitle content and prepares a libass track overlaytextsubs Video frames and native subtitle frames A subtitle branch supplies decoded text events overlaygraphicsubs Video frames and native subtitle frames A subtitle branch supplies decoded graphics The first two still combine timed text with video. The difference is where selection, decoding and resource ownership enter the graph. For example, selecting one subtitle track from a media file and passing its events down a native branch keeps that selection in the ordinary demux/decode path. A filter that opens a resource independently needs its own correct resource and stream selection. A script includes more than dialogue strings The renderer needs a valid script header, style definitions, event timings and fonts. In the examined subtitles path, the filter can also recover font attachments from the opened media resource. An external script can instead rely on available font-provider resources. A font directory or attachment is useful only if the requested face resolves at the active renderer. The font attachment article explains the difference between carrying a font file and actually selecting its face. The renderer evaluates the script at the video frame's presentation time and blends its generated images into that frame. It is therefore a CPU video-processing boundary in this implementation, even if video decoding and encoding elsewhere use hardware. Script time must meet picture time Suppose a script cue is at 12.5–15.0 seconds in the original programme. If a video branch rebases a trimmed excerpt to zero, the script and video no longer share the same time origin unless the route also establishes the corresponding mapping. Reading the right words from the right file does not repair that clock relationship. Seeking also requires a valid presentation state at the destination. A native subtitle branch and a separately initialized script can obtain that state by different mechanisms. Their output should be assessed using cue intervals, presentation time and recovered state, rather than assuming that every resource is reread identically. These interfaces are verified in the public 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 source archive. Classic pipelines show the script-owning route; subtitle filtering pipelines develop the separate native branch. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Software subtitle overlay | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Software subtitle overlay Software subtitle overlay renders/decodes and blends subtitle content into CPU-accessible video frames, with any hardware transfers determined by the surrounding route. Software overlay performs subtitle rendering/decoding or picture composition through CPU-accessible data. These can be separate operations: libass can shape/render text, then a blend stage combines its coverage with decoded video. A pipeline using a hardware video decoder and encoder can still have software composition between them. The accelerator labels do not describe every intermediate stage. The native and legacy CPU forms The pinned Emby FFmpeg archive contains overlaytextsubs and overlaygraphicsubs , which consume subtitle media directly for composition. Its older subtitles / ass filters represent another software design that renders a script associated with the filter. Both can produce subtitle pixels in video. Their input acquisition and lifetime handling are different, so the filter name helps identify the work rather than simply a quality level. Full pictures and small caption layers have different sizes For a tightly packed 3840 × 2160 , 8-bit NV12 picture: bytes = width × height × 1.5 = 3840 × 2160 × 1.5 = 12,441,600 At 24 pictures per second, one traversal of those logical picture bytes is 298,598,400 bytes/s . A download and upload pair is 597,196,800 bytes/s , before padding, protocol and additional processing. A small 800 × 80 RGBA subtitle image is 256,000 bytes . A full-frame RGBA canvas at 3840 × 2160 is 33,177,600 bytes . The cropped object's size and the converter's actual output canvas are not interchangeable. These are payload calculations, not measured bus traffic or a hardware-performance promise. Caching reduces some work, not every picture operation A static cue need not be reshaped from scratch for every video picture. Its image or glyph data can be reused where the implementation permits. The blend still modifies applicable picture content. An animation can also require updated subtitle pixels, and fonts/effects can affect the renderer's cost. If CPU overlay is the bottleneck, reducing glyph complexity and reducing full-frame memory work address different causes. The useful evidence is the active graph and its measured stage behavior. For Emby, hardware-acceleration documentation explains supported platform contexts. The source and actual session details establish whether pictures stayed on hardware surfaces or crossed a CPU composition boundary. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Overview: Subtitle overlay pipelines | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Overview: Subtitle overlay pipelines Subtitle overlay pipelines connect decoding, subtitle composition and output encoding through a particular sequence of stages. A working overlay needs compatible connections between the stages, not just a filter that can run in isolation. Picture location, transfers and synchronization influence that sequence. The fundamental, classic, filtering and hardware pipeline pages show how the arrangement changes while keeping the intended subtitle presentation recognizable. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle overlay pipeline fundamentals A subtitle overlay pipeline joins two timed branches: decoded video and interpreted captions. Correct output depends on representation, geometry, alpha, colour, resources and memory boundaries. Classic subtitle overlay pipeline The classic subtitle route lets a video filter own script reading and libass rendering, then composes into CPU pictures before output encoding. Subtitle filtering pipeline Native subtitle filtering keeps decoded text or graphics in a separate timed branch, exposing transformations before direct composition or conversion into an image/video layer. Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline A hardware subtitle pipeline separates codec engines, CPU text preparation, device composition and memory transfers; accepted formats and timed image updates determine the usable route. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Classic subtitle overlay pipeline | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Classic subtitle overlay pipeline The classic subtitle route lets a video filter own script reading and libass rendering, then composes into CPU pictures before output encoding. A classic script-based route inserts a subtitle-rendering video filter into the picture chain. The filter opens the subtitle resource, prepares a renderer and draws the script onto incoming pictures. “Classic” is a teaching label for this architecture. It is not an Emby setting name or a promise that a particular session selects it. Initialization builds a presentation In the examined Emby FFmpeg source, ass reads an ASS script, while subtitles can open a media resource and decode its chosen subtitle content into a libass track. The latter also has an attachment-recovery path for applicable fonts. Initialization gives the renderer event data, styles and font-provider resources. It does not mean all cues are drawn once as static bitmaps. When a picture is processed, the filter supplies its presentation time to libass and receives the images appropriate to that instant. That per-picture evaluation matters for motion, fades and karaoke within an event. A single cue can have the same words for several seconds while its presentation changes from frame to frame. The filter blends those images into CPU picture samples. The output of that boundary is ordinary video with visible caption pixels. A trimmed excerpt has two possible clocks Suppose the original programme contains a cue at 612.5–615.0 seconds . A delivered excerpt starts at original programme time 600 seconds . Clock carried by the picture branch Correct cue interval in that clock Original programme time retained 612.5–615.0 s Excerpt rebased to zero 12.5–15.0 s Rebasing the pictures while retaining an unadjusted script would make the cue wait until 612.5 seconds of the excerpt. Subtracting 600 from both start and end establishes the second mapping; subtracting it twice would be equally wrong. This is a timeline model, not a command recipe. Containers, demuxing, seeking and filter setup determine which origin a real route uses. The renderer must receive a coherent relationship between picture time and script time. Placement follows the chosen rendering plane ASS can describe an authored script plane, anchor positions and margins. The filter must relate that plane to the current video geometry and any original-size information it uses. For a 1920 × 1080 source reduced to 1280 × 720, a simple proportional mapping has scale 2/3. An anchor at (960, 900) maps to (640, 600). Crop, aspect-ratio treatment and text-layout rules can require more than this proportional model. Rendering into the full-size picture and then scaling also resamples the caption edges. Rendering at the target resolution allows a fresh rasterization, but still needs correct script geometry and fonts. The chosen graph order therefore affects appearance even when the text and cue interval remain identical. The CPU boundary determines transfers Hardware decoding can produce device frames. If those pictures pass through this CPU subtitle filter, the route needs an appropriate transition to CPU memory. A later hardware encoder may require them to return to device memory. This transition is distinct from rendering a small subtitle image on the CPU and uploading only that image to a device compositor. The software overlay article quantifies the frame-sized payloads, while hardware pipelines examine the alternative boundary. The script-owning design keeps its presentation resource inside the video filter. The native subtitle filtering route exposes that resource as a separate decoded branch, making subtitle transformations visible before the compositor. These implementation observations refer to 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 . Filter presence in a source archive does not identify which route a current installation selected. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Subtitle filtering pipeline | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Subtitle filtering pipeline Native subtitle filtering keeps decoded text or graphics in a separate timed branch, exposing transformations before direct composition or conversion into an image/video layer. A subtitle filtering pipeline keeps decoded subtitle content as a branch in the processing graph . The branch can transform text, style or graphical geometry before joining the picture branch. This exposes intermediate representations. A filter can accept subtitle frames rather than pretending that all captions have already become video pictures. “Filtering pipeline” here describes that graph architecture, not a fixed Emby menu option. A native event carries timing and presentation The public Emby FFmpeg 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 source extends subtitle handling with a native subtitle media type. The filter pads identify subtitle inputs and outputs separately from video. For text, the branch can carry ASS event content and track configuration. For graphics, it can carry areas with palette/image data and placement. The frame's subtitle timing identifies when the event belongs to the presentation. A subtitle-to-subtitle transformation can preserve that event interval while changing its content. A conversion to video instead produces picture samples on a video timeline. Both routes may display the same static sentence, but their clocks and capabilities are not interchangeable. What the examined filters do Filter/interface in the dated source Transformation boundary Consequence stripstyles ASS subtitle → ASS subtitle Reduces selected formatting; configurable keep flags can retain some classes of overrides textmod family Text subtitle → text subtitle Changes text content according to the selected operation subscale Graphic subtitle → graphic subtitle Resizes graphical areas and updates presentation geometry text2graphicsub Text subtitle → graphic subtitle Evaluates a rendered image at the event midpoint textsub2video Text subtitle → video Renders the text at generated video-frame times overlaytextsubs Video + text subtitles → video Renders and composes text at picture time overlaygraphicsubs Video + graphic subtitles → video Blends supplied graphical presentation into pictures This table is an interface map for the examined implementation. It is not a list of features guaranteed to be compiled into every current Emby tool. Style reduction changes an authored layout Removing an ASS position or movement override can turn an authored sign into a default-position caption. Removing font or size instructions can change line breaks, even when all characters survive. The examined stripstyles filter has keep flags for classes of overrides, including position/movement and other presentation commands. Its name alone therefore does not specify exactly what remains in a configured graph. The meaningful description is which classes that invocation retains. A content transformation has a different responsibility. Modifying words can change line width, reading load and the meaning of a caption. Preserving timestamps does not guarantee that the new content fits the old layout or duration. Graphical scaling cannot recover those semantics. It resizes an already rendered appearance. A stretched glyph remains the same drawn object; it has not been reflowed or reshaped as text. A midpoint image freezes internal animation Take a 12.5–15.0-second event whose anchor moves from x = 160 to x = 480 in its first second. Its midpoint is 13.75 seconds. The examined text2graphicsub converter calls libass at that midpoint. The generated graphical subtitle therefore shows the completed position, x = 480. Holding that graphical event over its interval presents a static result, even though the original text event was animated. By contrast, textsub2video and overlaytextsubs evaluate the presentation at picture times. At 13.0 seconds, the same authored movement places the anchor at x = 320. The pipeline fundamentals plot shows both results. Choosing the conversion boundary determines whether the internal time behavior is represented. A static subtitle can be suitable for a midpoint image; movement, fades and karaoke require examination of the specific converter's evaluation model. The final join accepts a particular representation A native text branch can join overlaytextsubs directly, leaving text evaluation at the CPU compositor. A branch intended for a video-image overlay needs an appropriate conversion and frame timing first. A device compositor additionally needs compatible device images. The graph cannot connect a native subtitle frame to an arbitrary video-input filter solely because both eventually produce visible words. Media type, image format, canvas geometry and timestamps form the interface contract. Emby's SDK step types include categories for style stripping, text modification, scaling, text-to-video conversion and overlay. Those labels help describe intent. They do not provide a one-to-one mapping from every model value to a filter name or prove the selected implementation's preservation of animation. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Subtitle overlay pipeline fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Subtitle overlay pipeline fundamentals A subtitle overlay pipeline joins two timed branches: decoded video and interpreted captions. Correct output depends on representation, geometry, alpha, colour, resources and memory boundaries. An overlay pipeline produces picture frames that already contain the subtitle presentation. It joins a video branch with a subtitle branch before the output is encoded. The branches have different jobs and often advance at different rates: pictures arrive regularly, while subtitle events can be sparse and stateful. The important question is what crosses each boundary. A sentence with timestamps, a decoded graphical object, a transparent video canvas and a GPU image are different kinds of input, even when they ultimately show the same words. Recover, interpret, render, compose The video branch reconstructs picture samples from the selected stream. Scaling, cropping or colour conversion may then change the surface on which the captions will appear. The subtitle branch recovers the selected track or caption service. A decoder can produce text events and associated style/configuration, or graphical objects with position, palette and transparency. A broadcast caption decoder may first have to interpret commands that modify a display state. Rendering turns that presentation into image samples. For styled text it can include character decoding, shaping, font selection, line layout, outlines, movement and timed highlighting. A graphical subtitle already has much of its appearance, but may still need palette expansion, placement and scaling. Composition combines those samples with the corresponding video picture. It uses the layer's transparency and geometry; it does not recover missing characters or infer the intended meaning of the dialogue. The combined pictures are then encoded for delivery. This is why burn-in changes video output, even when every audio packet is retained. Six agreements at the join Contract What must agree A recognizable failure Time Picture PTS, cue intervals and any internal effect times share a usable mapping Right caption on the wrong scene Geometry Script/object plane, output dimensions, crop origin and placement Caption shifted, stretched or clipped Appearance/resources Styles, fonts, glyphs, palettes and language/script requirements Wrong face, missing glyph or reduced layout Transparency Alpha location and straight/premultiplied interpretation Opaque rectangle or dark text edges Colour Sample format, range and applicable colour processing Wrong white level or colour tint Memory/execution CPU/device representation, accepted formats and completion order Unsupported input or a stalled/failed processing stage These contracts interact. A subtitle layer can have correct text and timing but wrong colour because it was composed on the wrong side of a conversion. Matching visible dimensions can conceal a different crop origin or aspect interpretation. An event interval is not its whole time model An ASS sign might be active from 12.5 to 15.0 seconds and move horizontally from x = 160 to x = 480 during its first second. At programme time 13.0, the movement has advanced half a second, so the anchor is x = 320. At 13.5 it reaches x = 480. A renderer evaluated for each picture can show those intermediate positions. A converter that evaluates only one instant and holds that image for the entire event cannot. The examined Emby source provides both kinds of boundary. textsub2video in vf_overlaytextsubs.c renders the text at the generated video frame's time. The native text2graphicsub converter in sf_text2graphicsub.c calls libass at the event midpoint . For this 2.5-second event, that instant is 13.75 seconds, after the one-second movement has finished. The static conversion can represent a stationary caption effectively. For this animated sign, preserving start, end and final position still does not preserve the moving presentation. This is a property of the dated 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 implementation, not a claim that every current Emby text conversion behaves this way. Picture operations also affect captions If composition precedes a downscale, the subtitle pixels are resampled with the picture. Fine outlines and character edges can change. If text is rendered after scaling, it can be rasterized for the target dimensions, but its script plane and placement still need a correct mapping. Cropping is similar. Composing an object in a region that will subsequently be removed loses those pixels. Rendering after the crop allows placement in the retained output, provided the graph accounts for the new origin and geometry. Tone mapping adds a colour-order issue. A layer composed into an HDR picture can pass through the later HDR-to-SDR mapping with that picture. A layer added to the mapped SDR picture needs values suitable for the SDR output. The two orders do not automatically produce the same caption white or coloured lettering. There is no universal instruction to put every subtitle operation last. The graph must preserve the intended placement and colour while satisfying the available filter interfaces. Rendering geometry and tone mapping explain the corresponding picture properties. Read a pipeline by its boundaries Consider a caption with readable letters but a solid box covering the scene. Character decoding and font rendering have probably succeeded enough to produce those letters. The next useful observations concern the layer's alpha, pixel format and compositor interpretation. Retiming the cue does not address that presentation. For a moving sign frozen at its final location, compare how the text became an image: per-frame evaluation and a held snapshot have different semantics. For a correctly shaped caption that shifts after a crop, inspect the geometry mapping rather than replacing the text file. These observations connect a visible result to the stage that produced it. In Emby, SDK pipeline step types and subtitle pipeline information can describe stages. The names are semantic categories; the actual session details, tool version and resulting pictures establish which graph ran. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.title: Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/overl.keywords: Hardware subtitle overlay pipeline A hardware subtitle pipeline separates codec engines, CPU text preparation, device composition and memory transfers; accepted formats and timed image updates determine the usable route. “Hardware transcoding” can describe only some stages in a subtitle pipeline. Video decoding, text rendering, image composition and video encoding need separate descriptions. A device video decoder may reconstruct pictures while the CPU resolves fonts and rasterizes text. A device compositor can then blend the prepared layer into those pictures. Another route downloads each picture for CPU composition and uploads the result before hardware encoding. Move the picture or move the layer The first route moves the full picture across the CPU/device boundary: Device decode → picture download → CPU composition → picture upload → device encode. The second can keep the picture in device memory: Device decode → device composition → device encode , with a separate CPU subtitle render → layer preparation/upload branch. The second route still has CPU work. It can reduce frame-sized transfers without making font selection, shaping or every subtitle conversion a GPU task. Device mapping or shared memory can change how a boundary is implemented. The diagrams show logical residency transitions; they do not assert a physical bus copy for every mapping on every system. Payload sizes expose the difference For tightly packed, 8-bit 4:2:0 NV12 at 3840 × 2160 , the ideal picture payload is: 3840 × 2160 × 1.5 = 12,441,600 bytes. At 24 pictures per second, moving that amount once per picture is 298,598,400 bytes/s . A download and upload of the same ideal payload total 597,196,800 bytes/s , before pitch padding, synchronization, extra copies or bus overhead. Prepared object Ideal payload 3840 × 2160 NV12 video picture 12,441,600 bytes 3840 × 2160 P010 video picture in 16-bit storage 24,883,200 bytes 3840 × 2160 RGBA subtitle canvas, 4 bytes/pixel 33,177,600 bytes 800 × 80 RGBA subtitle object, 4 bytes/pixel 256,000 bytes A small visible sentence does not prove that only 256,000 bytes are uploaded. The renderer/converter may produce a full-size transparent canvas. Uploading that RGBA canvas at 24 updates/s would be 796,262,400 bytes/s in this ideal calculation, greater than the one-way NV12 picture payload. A cropped-object route needs a supported image size and position model. A full-canvas route has different costs. These are payload calculations, not measured throughput, and compression rates do not reduce the size of decoded picture samples. Accepted device formats govern the join The device compositor must accept both representations. The examined CUDA overlay pairs NV12 with NV12, or YUV420P with YUV420P/YUVA420P. The examined Vulkan overlay requires matching underlying software formats. OpenCL operates through its own image and alpha-plane handling. That is why a CPU renderer's RGBA layer cannot be assumed to join any hardware-decoded surface unchanged. The route needs suitable conversion, transparency and colour treatment, then a valid device context. Moving between APIs on the same physical GPU is another interface boundary. A CUDA, Vulkan or OpenCL object is not interchangeable merely because it names that device. Supported interoperation, mapping or transfers must establish a usable representation and completion order. The individual CUDA , Vulkan and OpenCL pages describe the dated source interfaces in more detail. Sparse cues and changing layers have different costs A stationary caption can retain one rasterized appearance for many video pictures if the graph supports reuse. Composition still occurs for each output picture while the cue is active, but text shaping and an upload need not necessarily repeat for every picture. A moving anchor, fade or karaoke highlight changes the layer over time. The renderer or another stage must evaluate that changing presentation at the required picture times. Holding one image for the full event changes the result. The subtitle branch must also handle clear intervals, seeks and new events. Repeating a previous layer after its end can leave a stale caption on the screen. A useful route description therefore includes image-update policy and timing alongside device residency. Throughput and latency answer different questions Consider an invented three-stage model taking 8 ms to decode, 12 ms to prepare/compose and 7 ms to encode each picture. If those stages serialize, the per-picture work totals 27 ms. With independent stage resources, adequate buffering and no other limits, steady-state throughput is instead bounded by the slowest stage: one picture every 12 ms. An individual picture still passes through all three stages. Pipelining improves throughput without removing its end-to-end work or queueing. Real stages can contend for memory or the same device resources. Extra transfer waits can also dominate. Increasing encoder speed alone cannot resolve a bottleneck in text preparation, composition or transfer. The actual Emby app/server/tool combination and selected graph establish the available route. The public 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 source and SDK pipeline information explain designs and stage descriptions; these payload and timing models are not hardware performance measurements. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/Subti.title: Subtitle rendering compatibility in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/Subti.keywords: Subtitle rendering compatibility in Emby Subtitle compatibility in Emby includes source recognition, delivery, presentation features and resources at the selected app/server rendering stage. Subtitle compatibility is more specific than a file extension. A route can recognize ASS, recover its text correctly and still fail to reproduce the intended animated sign because it lacks a presentation feature or font resource. The meaningful comparison is the selected app and delivered representation , including what that representation needs to present. A compatibility ladder Boundary Requirement Source recognition Identify the selected subtitle track/service and its coding Recovery Obtain payloads, timing and configuration Delivery Supply an accepted representation and usable resources Rendering Interpret the text/graphics, styles, geometry and timed effects Composition Place the correct result over the correct picture at the right instant Recognizing a codec answers the first question. A readable sentence answers part of rendering, but not every layout or timing requirement. A sign exposes the difference Consider an ASS translation with a named font, top-left anchor, a one-second movement and a clipping window. A plain text conversion can preserve its words and whole-event interval without representing that geometry. A player drawing the resulting simple cue has not “lost the video”. It received a narrower subtitle presentation. The useful evidence is which features the conversion retained. Font attachments add another boundary. A renderer can support the style syntax but use fallback if the requested face never reached its font provider. The actual Emby route is version and platform dependent Transcoding behavior , selected subtitle format and app capabilities explain why one route presents text separately while another requests upstream rendering. The public Emby FFmpeg archive examined here is specifically 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 . It contains native subtitle filters and text/graphics converters. Their source demonstrates processing designs; it does not identify the binary or enabled features of every current installation. The current SDK subtitle pipeline field provides a way for its model to describe processing. A complete investigation still uses the actual session/tool details and output. Compare one requirement at a time Keep the selected resource and media edition fixed when comparing routes. Test readable characters, appearance/resources, dynamic effects, cue timing and seeking as separate observations. The result can then distinguish wrong selection, missing resources, a reduced conversion and a renderer behavior. Changing a codec, a font and a timing offset together makes those boundaries harder to assess. articles/subtitles/emby-processing/Subti.title: Subtitle delivery in Emby | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/emby-processing/Subti.keywords: Subtitle delivery in Emby Emby's subtitle delivery route connects the selected source track to an app-supported representation or a rendered video output. An Emby session selects an audio/video source and a subtitle resource. The subtitle can be external, a container track or a recovered caption service. The next question is how the selected app can receive and present that content . A subtitle's source location does not determine the final delivery route. An embedded text track can be extracted for separate delivery; an external styled script can instead be rendered upstream when that route requires it. Three different outputs Route What reaches the app Supported separate presentation Subtitle data the app can render with the media Subtitle conversion/extraction Another accepted subtitle representation retaining the selected content Server composition and video encoding Video pictures containing the subtitle pixels These outputs have different consequences for switching tracks, preserving styles and changing appearance. Permanent pixels belong to that output video version, even if the original subtitle remains a separate track in the library. The video decision and subtitle decision are related, not identical Emby's playback documentation describes Direct Play, Direct Stream and transcoding. Compatible video can remain unchanged while a subtitle is extracted or converted separately. A server burn-in route instead needs decoded pictures for composition and a suitable encoded output. A small subtitle file can therefore introduce substantial video work even when its text itself is quick to read. The public SDK processing-step descriptions distinguish operations such as subtitle overlay, text-to-video conversion and style stripping. Those semantic steps are evidence of what kinds of work the model can describe, not proof that every session performs them. Configuration and resources reach the consumer Text can need global styles and fonts; graphics can need palette/object state and display geometry. Cue times must map to the media programme timeline. For app rendering, usable resources belong at the app's subtitle consumer. For server rendering, they belong where the server draws/composes the presentation. A resource preserved somewhere in the original container is not automatically available at every downstream boundary. The selected app/platform, source representation, requested appearance and server/tool build determine the actual route. Compare its output with the selected resource's content, timing and visual requirements rather than treating “subtitles enabled” as one universal operation. articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/index..title: Overview: Bitmap subtitle formats | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/index..keywords: Overview: Bitmap subtitle formats Bitmap subtitles carry timed graphic elements that a renderer composites with the picture. A bitmap subtitle arrives as image data rather than ordinary character strings. Its palette, placement and timing still need interpretation before composition. DVD, Blu-ray and DVB topics explain the particular representations, providing context for delivery, scaling and the separate task of turning an image into recognized text. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Bitmap subtitles Bitmap subtitles describe timed image graphics, palettes and placement rather than storing the visible words as character text. DVD subtitles (DVDSub and VobSub) DVD subtitle subpictures are compressed indexed graphics, while VobSub packages related subtitle data into external SUB and IDX files. Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) PGS assembles timed Blu-ray presentation graphics from palette, object, window and composition segments. DVB subtitles (DVBSub) DVBSub carries broadcast subtitle services using timed page, region, object and colour-table segments in a transport stream. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ETSI EN 300 743 V1.6.1: DVB subtitling

articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.title: Bitmap subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.keywords: Bitmap subtitles Bitmap subtitles describe timed image graphics, palettes and placement rather than storing the visible words as character text. A bitmap subtitle supplies an image of the lettering rather than the characters from which a font renderer would draw it. The data also describes timing and placement, and commonly uses compressed pixel codes plus a palette. This preserves much of the author's visual result: glyph shape, outline and spacing are already part of the graphics. It gives the player a different job from drawing a text subtitle. Pixel codes select colour and transparency An indexed subtitle image can store small integer codes for each pixel. A palette maps those codes to colours and alpha values. The decoder reconstructs the image and the compositor places its visible pixels over the video. The figure is an original four-entry teaching image, not a packet from a disc or broadcast format. In a real format, palette syntax, run-length coding, transparency and update rules belong to that format. A transparent background does not paint a black rectangular panel over the scene. An opaque outline can remain visible around white lettering, while partly transparent edge pixels can blend it with the underlying picture. For a simplified linear-light blend, the result is: output = alpha × subtitle colour + (1 − alpha) × video colour White (1,1,1) at alpha 0.5 over video colour (0.1,0.2,0.3) gives (0.55,0.60,0.65) . Fully transparent pixels leave the video unchanged. This illustrates compositing; it does not specify every renderer's colour pipeline. The image occupies a subtitle plane The format can describe a logical display size and position a cropped object within it. An image only 800 pixels wide can belong to a 1920-pixel-wide subtitle plane. Suppose an object of 800 × 80 sits at (560,900) in a 1920 × 1080 plane. Mapping that plane uniformly to 1280 × 720 gives a factor of 2/3: Quantity Scaled result Object size Approximately 533.33 × 53.33 Position Approximately (373.33,600) Output plane 1280 × 720 The compositor ultimately rasterizes onto integer output pixels, so its sampling and rounding policy matters. Scaling just the object while leaving its position in the old coordinate system would create a different layout. Changing the output size rescales an existing image. It does not automatically select a new font or reflow the lettering into a new line length. Selectable graphics and permanent pixels A bitmap track remains separate data until composition. A player supporting the format can draw it over the movie and allow the viewer to disable it. If a server renders the subtitle into newly encoded video, its appearance becomes part of that video's pixels. This is why “bitmap” and “burned in” are different descriptions. The first identifies the subtitle source representation; the second identifies what happened in an output route. To create text from bitmap letters, a tool needs OCR or manual transcription. Copying the bitmap into another container is an extraction or packaging operation, not recognition. OCR must also recover punctuation, speaker cues and ordering; preserving an image is not evidence that those characters were recovered correctly. In an Emby comparison, the delivered representation identifies whether the app draws a separate image or receives video with the subtitle already incorporated. The separate-image route keeps image placement and composition at the app; the incorporated route has completed them upstream. articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.title: DVB subtitles (DVBSub) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.keywords: DVB subtitles (DVBSub) DVBSub carries broadcast subtitle services using timed page, region, object and colour-table segments in a transport stream. DVB subtitles, often called DVBSub , are a broadcast subtitling system defined by ETSI EN 300 743 . Their common graphical mode assembles subtitles from indexed-pixel objects, regions and a timed page composition. The system can support character-code objects under local agreements as well. It should therefore be described as a graphics-oriented subtitle system with defined additional modes, rather than as proof that every possible DVB subtitle contains only bitmap runs. Transport identity and subtitle-service identity DVB subtitle data travels in PES packets within an MPEG transport stream. The PES timing supplies presentation timestamps.
