Transport packets use a PID to identify the carrying stream. A single such stream can carry more than one subtitle service. Signaling identifies the intended language/type and the composition page ID , with an ancillary page ID when applicable. The PID alone can therefore be insufficient to choose the desired caption service. An Emby recording retaining the broadcast transport can preserve those relationships. When a tool extracts or repackages a subtitle track, it must keep the service configuration needed to interpret its data. A page is built from regions and objects The roles form a hierarchy: Role Purpose Page composition Selects regions, their positions and page state Region composition Defines region dimensions, depth, colour-table identity and placed objects Object data Supplies graphical content or the applicable alternative coding Colour lookup table, CLUT Resolves indexed values to colour/transparency Display definition Establishes display geometry where provided Objects can be updated without replacing the whole page. Regions can move or become visible through a page update. The stored data is therefore a sequence of state changes, not necessarily a collection of independent screenshots. Adding the two levels of position Suppose a region begins at (100,500) on a 720 × 576 display plane. An object begins at (20,15) within that region. Its plane position is: x = 100 + 20 = 120 y = 500 + 15 = 515 For a 500 × 40 object, its extent reaches x = 620 and y = 555, within this illustrative plane. The region must also be large enough to contain the object. Confusing the region-relative position with the page-relative position would put the graphic in another location. The CLUT and pixel-depth interpretation complete the picture. A valid object run decoded with the wrong colour-table state is not the intended subtitle. Tuning and seeking require an acquisition state An update in the middle of a service may assume that earlier objects or regions are already known. A live receiver tuning into that stream needs an acquisition point containing the information required for the next page. A recording seek has a comparable need to reconstruct state. The page composition also supplies a timeout in seconds. If the page is not replaced or redefined, it eventually ceases to be valid and should be erased. This prevents a stale caption from remaining indefinitely after a lost update. A timeout is a recovery bound, not a universal substitute for exact authored cue endings. Later display updates provide the normal intended progression. See Also Bitmap subtitles Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS Streams and Tracks References ETSI EN 300 743 V1.6.1: DVB subtitling Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings ETSI EN 300 468 V1.19.1: DVB service information and subtitling descriptor

articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.title: DVD subtitles: DVDSub and VobSub | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.keywords: DVD subtitles: DVDSub and VobSub DVD subtitle subpictures are compressed indexed graphics, while VobSub packages related subtitle data into external SUB and IDX files. DVD-Video subtitles use subpictures : compressed indexed graphics with controls for placement, colour, transparency and display timing. Media tools commonly call the decoded subtitle format DVDSub . VobSub is closely related external-file packaging. A typical pair uses a binary .sub for subtitle data and a text .idx for indexing and presentation information. Form Where its information lives DVD subtitle in disc content Subpicture data plus the disc's associated stream and palette information External VobSub Binary SUB data with its IDX companion VobSub track inside Matroska Timed payloads plus the track's VobSub configuration These are related representations of subpicture content, not three interchangeable filenames. The subpicture carries pixel codes and controls The compressed picture uses run-length-coded pixel values. In a conventional DVD subpicture, four pixel-code values select colours through a mapping into the DVD palette, with separately controlled transparency. The decoded lettering therefore depends on both the pixel runs and the control/palette information. A correct outline can appear in the wrong colour if the palette is missing or misinterpreted. Treating the pixel codes themselves as grayscale values would also produce the wrong image. The controls establish the displayed area and its changes over time. The binary payload is not a string containing the sentence's letters. Rendering it is decoding graphics; getting an editable sentence from it requires recognition. The IDX provides the way into the SUB An index entry can look like: timestamp: 00:00:12:500, filepos: 0000000200 The timestamp identifies a presentation position. The hexadecimal filepos identifies a location in the binary SUB data: 0x200 = 512 bytes from its start. This is an illustrative entry, not a complete pair or proof that a subtitle packet exists at that offset. The IDX can also provide palette, display size and language-stream information. Sending the binary SUB alone can deprive a consumer of the information needed to find or interpret the chosen stream. When muxed into Matroska, those roles are reorganized. Relevant configuration goes into the track's codec-private information; the container carries the timed payloads. The pair is not simply attached as two unrelated documents. Emby's external-subtitle naming documentation covers identification of a SUB/IDX pair. The format question is what data the selected decoder receives after that identification. The subtitle's display plane can be resized DVD subpictures are associated with a standard-definition display plane and its presentation geometry. A stored 720-pixel-wide plane does not by itself establish its displayed aspect ratio. The relevant disc and output geometry must be respected. A high-definition output can scale the decoded bitmap. That does not recover a higher-resolution font outline or rewrite the layout as newly shaped text. Preserving the original visual content and improving its sampling on a larger output are different tasks. See Also Bitmap subtitles MicroDVD subtitles DVD-Video File Structure References FFmpeg n8.1: DVD subtitle decoder implementation Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings Library of Congress: VobSub subtitle files

articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.title: Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/bitmap/Subtit.keywords: Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) PGS assembles timed Blu-ray presentation graphics from palette, object, window and composition segments. PGS, the Presentation Graphics Stream , is the bitmap subtitle representation associated with Blu-ray presentation graphics. An inspection tool can identify it as hdmv_pgs_subtitle ; an extracted stream commonly uses a .sup file. Its displayed image is assembled from several kinds of segment. Reading each segment as if it were an independent subtitle sentence misses that assembly. Objects, palettes and the composition Segment role Information supplied Palette Colour and transparency entries Object Dimensions and run-length-coded pixel data Window Areas used for presentation Presentation composition Which objects to use and where to put them End of display set Completes the set of data for that presentation An object refers to palette indices rather than carrying arbitrary full-colour values for every pixel. Composition refers to object identities and positions. A decoder keeps relevant objects and palettes available according to the stream's state rules. The diagram shows logical dependencies, not a requirement that every display set transmits a fresh copy of every component. A palette or image object can be reused or updated. That reduces delivery work while making decoder state important. A cropped object such as an 800 × 80 line can be positioned on a larger display plane. The object dimensions and the plane dimensions answer different questions. A display set can show or clear graphics Consider a simplified presentation sequence: Presentation time Composition result 12.5 s Show object 7 using the selected palette at its indicated position 15.0 s Clear the active subtitle composition 16.2 s Show the next subtitle object The display-set terminator marks the completion of its data. It is not automatically an instruction to remove the caption at that same instant. Clearing belongs to a later presentation state, such as a composition containing no displayed objects. A consumer or container mapping may derive an interval from the next update or an explicit duration. That produces a conventional cue view for inspection, but the original graphics data still has a stateful composition model. Seeking directly to a small update can fail if the referenced palette or object was established earlier and has not been reconstructed. Acquisition points and the required preceding data let the decoder rebuild an appropriate state before presentation. Forced graphics can be identified within a composition PGS composition objects can carry a forced-display indication. That is distinct from a container's flag on the whole subtitle track. A stream can contain ordinary dialogue plus selected forced objects, or a separately authored track can contain only the necessary selected passages. Discarding those distinctions while converting or packaging the track can change selection behavior. The label shown in an app's track menu does not by itself reveal the object flags present in the source. The source graphics and the rendering route An Emby client that can receive and draw a suitable PGS presentation can keep it separate from the video. Another route can render the graphics upstream and incorporate them into an encoded output. The resulting video then includes those pixels, even if the source was a selectable PGS track. Changing PGS to another bitmap packaging can preserve image content. Producing SRT additionally needs OCR or transcription. See Also Bitmap subtitles Subtitle cues Blu-ray File Structure Matroska: MKV and MKA References Blu-ray Disc License Office: BD-ROM format specifications FFmpeg n8.1: PGS decoder implementation Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: ARIB STD-B24 captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: ARIB STD-B24 captions ARIB STD-B24 captions combine coded characters, display controls and resources such as DRCS glyphs under their applicable broadcast profile. ARIB STD-B24 defines data coding and transmission functions used in digital broadcasting, including captions. The caption presentation combines coded characters, display controls and the resources needed to draw them . The applicable profile matters. Japanese character coding, other supported language/profile arrangements and UCS-based interpretations should not be collapsed into one assumption that every payload is ordinary UTF-8 text. Characters and controls have distinct roles Information Role Character coding and selected character sets Identify the text or symbol being represented Caption display controls Establish placement, size, writing direction and presentation changes Additional-symbol mapping Resolve supported symbols outside a simple basic-character assumption DRCS resource Supply a dynamically defined character's visual shape Programme timing/service information Establish when and which caption presentation applies A valid coded symbol can need a mapping or resource before it becomes a useful Unicode character or visible glyph. Treating all bytes as printable text discards that structure. DRCS can carry the shape of a character DRCS , Dynamically Redefinable Character Sets, lets the presentation use defined glyph resources. A decoder can draw the supplied shape without pretending that the bytes were an already known Unicode letter. A converter may map a recognized DRCS symbol to an appropriate Unicode alternative when such a mapping is available. Otherwise, a plain-text export needs a deliberate representation or review. Dropping the symbol silently changes the content. The public libaribcaption implementation documents additional-symbol and DRCS support, font fallback and several rendering backends. That demonstrates a concrete decoder/renderer design; it does not establish which implementation every player uses. Preserving words and preserving presentation are different A character export can retain readable text while flattening placement, size, ruby-related layout or other applicable controls. Rendering the original caption model retains another set of properties. Language/service selection remains necessary too. Finding a caption group does not determine which of its available language information the viewer intended to read. For an Emby source using ARIB captions, identify the actual recovered representation and the selected route's support. A converted text track and a rendered caption image can both be useful outputs while retaining different aspects of the broadcast presentation. See Also Closed-caption services Unicode in subtitles Subtitle font fallback In-band captions References ARIB STD-B24: Data coding and transmission for digital broadcasting libaribcaption: ARIB decoder and renderer Matroska subtitle mappings

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: CEA-608 / CTA-608 captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: CEA-608 / CTA-608 captions CTA-608 describes legacy line-21 caption data with channel selection, character/control codes and a cell-based presentation model that can also be carried digitally. CTA-608, also encountered as CEA-608 or EIA-608, defines the line-21 data model associated with legacy NTSC captions. Its caption character and control data can also be carried in a digital video system. The display model is cell-based, with 15 rows and 32 columns . Characters, cursor placement, style controls and display commands establish the visible presentation. It is not an SRT list transported one sentence at a time. Caption channels and byte interpretation The two field relationships provide caption channels: Field association Caption channels Field 1 CC1 and CC2 Field 2 CC3 and CC4 Channel context comes from the caption coding, not simply from counting the first four video tracks. The broader line-21 system also carries other services; not every recognized data pair is visible caption wording. A transmitted caption byte contains seven data bits and an odd-parity bit. For an illustrative character pair, ASCII H and i have data values 0x48 and 0x69 . Their parity-bearing values can be 0xC8 and 0xE9 , each with an odd number of one bits. The decoder interprets the relevant code sets and controls. Removing parity and treating every byte as ordinary Unicode text would confuse character, control and service information. Pop-on uses two presentation memories In pop-on mode, a caption is prepared in nondisplayed memory while another presentation remains visible. An end-of-caption operation changes which prepared memory is displayed. Imagine these conceptual operations, not a complete encoded packet: The visible memory contains the previous caption. Nondisplayed memory receives “The platform is empty.” At programme time 12.5 seconds, the prepared caption becomes displayed. At 15 seconds, a display-clearing operation removes it. The new sentence's visible interval is 12.5–15 seconds . Its characters can have been transmitted earlier so that the whole caption is ready when it appears. This is why an extractor must interpret display commands rather than use each data arrival as the beginning of the final text cue. Repeated control transmissions and decoder state also matter when processing the byte sequence. Other modes update the display differently Mode Presentation behavior Pop-on Prepare off screen, then reveal the completed caption Paint-on Add content to displayed memory as it arrives Roll-up Update a limited group of displayed rows and roll older rows upward For an invented two-row roll-up display containing lines A and B, adding C leaves B and C visible. It does not present A, B and C forever as three independent overlapping cues. Converting a roll-up display to conventional timed text requires a decision about which changed presentation constitutes the next cue. A character-by-character transcript and a readable sentence-level caption are different extraction products. 608 data can remain 608 inside digital carriage A digital caption transport can carry compatibility data preserving the 608 model as well as native 708 service data. Its presence in a digital packet does not rewrite the caption commands into 708 window commands. For an Emby recording, identify the caption channel/service actually recovered. A source's “closed captions” indication cannot establish whether it contains 608 compatibility data, native 708 content or another presentation system. See Also Closed-caption services CEA-708 / CTA-708 captions Scenarist Closed Captions (SCC) In-band captions References CTA: Line 21 Data Services, CTA-608 ATSC A/53 Part 4: Video and caption data carriage Emby FFmpeg source archive: 2023_06_25-u1

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: CEA-708 / CTA-708 captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: CEA-708 / CTA-708 captions CTA-708 describes digital caption services with window, pen, text and visibility commands, alongside separate 608 compatibility carriage. CTA-708, also known as CEA-708 , defines a digital closed-caption model built from numbered services and presentation commands. A service can control several caption windows with their own placement, visibility and text properties. Its digital transport can also carry 608 compatibility bytes. Those remain a separate coding model rather than becoming native 708 captions merely because both are in the same delivery. A packet is not a displayed window The transport organizes data into digital caption packets and service blocks. A service block identifies the service receiving its commands. The native service numbering supports services up to 63 , while each service can define up to eight caption windows . Those are capacity/model descriptions, not a promise that every consumer implements every possible service or feature. Identity What it identifies Carrying video stream Where the caption payload travels Digital caption packet/service block The coded transport grouping and selected service Window within that service A particular area of caption presentation Pen/text state How subsequently written characters are presented Selecting service 1 does not mean selecting window 1. A service can update several windows as part of one caption presentation. Windows have state and visibility Take an invented service with a lower window for dialogue and an upper window for a speaker/location annotation. Operation Result Define both windows Their geometry/properties become known Write dialogue into the lower window Its text state changes Display the lower window The dialogue becomes visible Hide the upper window Its stored content can remain while invisible Clear a window Its text contents change; this is not the same operation as hiding it Window commands can establish position, rows/columns and other presentation parameters. Pen commands establish text properties such as size, style or colour. A decoder reconstructs the state specified by the stream and its supported presentation model. The visible result can therefore change without a new complete sentence arriving. A window can be revealed, hidden or moved while retaining its text. The viewer's display policy also has a role The standard includes presentation attributes associated with caption appearance. The available viewer controls and their interaction with authored attributes belong to the receiving implementation and its applicable rules. That is distinct from choosing a service language or accessibility content role. A font-size preference does not select another translation. For Emby, compare the selected recovered service and the delivered presentation representation. A conversion to plain text can retain the wording and times while flattening window placement or richer pen/window effects. Recover the presentation at the requested time A seek can land after window-definition and text-writing commands but before a later visibility update. The decoder needs sufficient preceding state or a suitable acquisition/reset sequence. Extracting a cue list requires interpreting those commands and identifying the visible intervals. Capturing only the final character strings loses the operations that establish when and where those strings are shown. See Also CEA-608 / CTA-608 captions Closed-caption services Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) Subtitle rendering References CTA: Digital Television Closed Captioning, CTA-708 ATSC A/343:2025-07: Captions and subtitles CCExtractor: DTVCC decoder source ATSC A/53 Part 4: Video and caption data carriage

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: Scenarist Closed Captions (SCC) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: Scenarist Closed Captions (SCC) SCC stores timecoded hexadecimal 608 caption words whose decoder commands determine the actual visible caption presentation. SCC, Scenarist Closed Captions , stores 608 caption data as timecoded hexadecimal words. It is a file packaging convention for the caption byte/control model, rather than a plain-text subtitle sentence format. An original small record can look like: Scenarist_SCC V1.0 00:00:12:00 9420 9420 c8e9 942f 942f The words carry caption bytes. They are not character strings to display as “9420” or “c8e9”. Decode the words through the 608 model In this illustrative sequence, 9420 represents a parity-bearing Resume Caption Loading control pair, c8e9 carries H and i, and 942f is an End Of Caption control pair. Repeated control pairs are part of the relevant 608 transmission/decoder handling; they should not produce repeated visible words. A reader needs the caption command state and applicable channel context. The example is a small control sequence, not a complete professionally authored caption programme. Arrival time and visible time can differ Pop-on captions can be loaded into nondisplayed memory before a command reveals them. The timecode associated with a data record is therefore not automatically a complete visible interval for its final sentence. A text extractor interprets the command sequence, derives display changes and constructs resulting cues. It must also schedule the words according to the applicable SCC timecode/transmission convention. That is different from an SRT block whose first line directly states a cue's start/end timestamps. Frame labels require their convention At a rate of 30000/1001 frames per second , ten nominal minutes of non-drop-frame 30-based labels represent 18,000 frame intervals : 18,000 / (30,000 / 1,001) = 600.6 seconds For the corresponding drop-frame counting convention, two labels are skipped at each applicable minute except each tenth minute. At ten minutes the skipped count is 2 × 9 = 18 , leaving 17,982 intervals , about 599.9994 seconds . Drop-frame skips labels, not picture frames. The colon/semicolon convention and the reader's timecode model must be handled appropriately; merely parsing four numeric fields cannot establish the correct elapsed time. Reader versions can implement different details The pinned Emby FFmpeg source 5.1-emby_2023_06_25_u1 accepts colon or semicolon at the final separator in its SCC demuxer, then calculates millisecond positions using a 33 ms frame term without a separate drop-frame-label adjustment in that code path. That is an observed implementation detail of that dated parser, not the definition of SCC timing and not evidence of the parser in every current Emby installation. For an Emby extraction comparison, identify the bundled tool version and compare recovered display times against known scenes. The valid-looking header and hexadecimal words establish the file's structure; command interpretation and timecode conversion establish its resulting caption presentation. See Also CEA-608 / CTA-608 captions Frame-based subtitle timing Subtitle timestamps Subtitle extraction References CCExtractor: Scenarist caption output CTA: Line 21 Data Services, CTA-608 Emby FFmpeg source archive: 2023_06_25-u1

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: Closed-caption services | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: Closed-caption services A closed-caption service is a selectable timed content stream whose commands, characters and presentation state must be recovered from its carrying media. A closed-caption service supplies one selectable caption presentation. Its identity is separate from the video track carrying it and from the appearance controls used by the viewer. A video source can contain multiple services, such as a primary caption language and another translation. Selecting the correct video track does not necessarily select the desired caption service inside it. Service labels belong to a particular system System Example selection identity CTA-608 compatibility captions CC1 through CC4 CTA-708 digital captions Numbered digital caption services Teletext subtitles A signaled page and language ARIB captions The applicable caption language/service information Those identities are not interchangeable track indices. A player's “English captions” menu entry can describe a recovered service rather than a separately multiplexed SRT track. The caption contents can include dialogue and meaningful sound/speaker information. Language and accessibility role still need to match what the viewer wants to read. Commands produce a presentation state A caption stream can transmit characters, placement and controls that modify a display. One transmission is not necessarily one independent sentence with a complete start/end pair. Consider an invented sequence: Programme time Caption operation Visible result 12.0 s Prepare a line in nondisplayed memory Previous display remains 12.5 s Make the prepared presentation visible New caption appears 15.0 s Clear the display Caption disappears An extractor can derive a 12.5–15-second cue from that state. Treating the first character's arrival at 12.0 as the cue's appearance would place it early. A recording seek similarly needs the required state or an acquisition point. Starting in the middle of commands that refer to earlier content can produce an incomplete display. Selection, recovery and drawing are separate boundaries For an Emby recording, investigate which service was present, which was selected, and how its data was delivered to the app. Correct video decoding alone does not establish that the caption commands were recovered. A conversion can retain a supported service, extract it into timed text, or incorporate its rendered appearance into video. Those outputs preserve different selection and styling properties. Caption extraction and in-band carriage explain those boundaries. The service itself identifies the content whose presentation is being reconstructed. See Also CEA-608 / CTA-608 captions CEA-708 / CTA-708 captions In-band captions Subtitle track selection References CTA: Line 21 Data Services, CTA-608 CTA: Digital Television Closed Captioning, CTA-708 ATSC A/53 Part 4: Video and caption data carriage ATSC A/343:2025-07: Captions and subtitles W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.title: Teletext subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/Cap.keywords: Teletext subtitles Teletext subtitles select a caption page whose character/control data, row updates and broadcast signaling establish the timed display. Teletext can carry subtitle pages as part of a broadcast data service. The consumer selects the signaled subtitle page and reconstructs its character/control presentation. The familiar page number, such as 888 , identifies a page in that system. It is not a subtitle cue number, a timestamp or a promise that every broadcaster uses the same page for the same language. A page has identity and character-cell layout The basic Teletext page model uses character positions; its normal row spans 40 columns . Page/header information and applicable subtitle signaling identify the intended service. Characters are interpreted through the applicable character sets and presentation state. Controls can affect colour, size, concealment and other behavior. A raw row is consequently not just an arbitrary UTF-8 sentence. An extractor needs to distinguish printable content from those controls and convert the character repertoire appropriately. A national-character option or enhancement changes interpretation without changing the page's apparent language label. Pages are updated, not streamed as SRT blocks Consider an invented sequence of subtitle-page states: Programme position Selected-page result 12.5 s A row displays “The platform is empty.” 14.0 s Another row adds “[train approaching]” 15.0 s The relevant page content is cleared/replaced Repeated transmission can refresh an unchanged page. Counting every repeated packet as a new caption would create duplicates. Discarding a changed row because its page number repeats would lose content. A text conversion therefore resolves the selected page and its updates, then derives suitable visible intervals and line ordering. Teletext and graphical DVB subtitles are different A MPEG transport stream can carry Teletext data or a graphical DVB subtitle service under their applicable signaling. The shared broadcast container does not give both the same page/region/object model. A Teletext decoder commonly interprets character/control data. DVB graphical subtitles normally assemble palette-coded objects and regions. Their extraction and rendering stages are related tasks with different input structures. For an Emby recording, check the selected page/service, language signaling and actual decoded output. Correct reception of the video stream does not establish that the intended Teletext page was recovered. See Also Closed-caption services DVB subtitles (DVBSub) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS Subtitle character encoding References ETSI EN 300 706 V1.2.1: Enhanced Teletext Matroska subtitle mappings CCExtractor: Closed-caption extraction

articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/ind.title: Overview: Broadcast captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/broadcast/ind.keywords: Overview: Broadcast captions Broadcast captions use defined services and signaling to carry timed text and related presentation information. A caption service belongs to the broadcast signal's organization, with its own selection and rendering rules. The standards below cover different service arrangements and character or presentation capabilities. SCC adds a stored interchange representation to that picture, so a caption service and a subtitle sidecar are not assumed to be the same object. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Closed-caption services A closed-caption service is a selectable timed content stream whose commands, characters and presentation state must be recovered from its carrying media. CEA-608 / CTA-608 CTA-608 describes legacy line-21 caption data with channel selection, character/control codes and a cell-based presentation model that can also be carried digitally. CEA-708 / CTA-708 CTA-708 describes digital caption services with window, pen, text and visibility commands, alongside separate 608 compatibility carriage. Teletext subtitles Teletext subtitles select a caption page whose character/control data, row updates and broadcast signaling establish the timed display. ARIB STD-B24 captions ARIB STD-B24 captions combine coded characters, display controls and resources such as DRCS glyphs under their applicable broadcast profile. Scenarist Closed Captions (SCC) SCC stores timecoded hexadecimal 608 caption words whose decoder commands determine the actual visible caption presentation. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles ETSI EN 300 706 V1.2.1: Enhanced Teletext

articles/subtitles/formats/index.html.title: Overview: Subtitle formats | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/index.html.keywords: Overview: Subtitle formats Subtitle formats define the timed content, graphics or service information available for presentation. Some formats carry text and styling instructions; others carry ready-made images or caption-service data. That distinction changes the work a renderer performs. The format branches below establish the representation first, before storage, delivery and player support determine how it reaches the viewer. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle formats explained A subtitle format defines how timing, text or image content, and presentation information are encoded separately from their storage or delivery. Text subtitle formats Text subtitle formats combine cue timing with character content and format-specific presentation rules. IMSC timed text IMSC defines constrained TTML profiles for interoperable internet-media subtitles and captions, with version-specific text and image capabilities. Bitmap subtitle formats Bitmap subtitles carry timed graphic elements that a renderer composites with the picture. Broadcast captions Broadcast captions use defined services and signaling to carry timed text and related presentation information. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/formats/Subtitle-Form.title: Subtitle formats explained | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/Subtitle-Form.keywords: Subtitle formats explained A subtitle format defines how timing, text or image content, and presentation information are encoded separately from their storage or delivery. A subtitle format describes how a timed sequence is encoded: its text or image content, timing, and any presentation instructions. Its filename extension, its container, and the renderer used for playback describe other parts of the route. SRT inside an MKV is still text subtitle content. PGS inside the same MKV is still graphics. Matroska packages the tracks; it does not turn one representation into the other. Layer What it describes Subtitle representation Characters, styles, graphics, and format-specific events File or container packaging Where track descriptions and timed payloads are stored Delivery How that data reaches the player Rendering and composition How the content becomes visible over the picture The format families Text subtitles retain characters that a renderer draws. Individual formats have separate explanations: SubRip / SRT : numbered text cues with start and end times. WebVTT : web timed text with cue settings and defined markup. SSA : an earlier script format with reusable subtitle styles. ASS : styled script events with positioning and timed visual instructions. TTML : XML timed text with a structured timing and layout model. MP4 timed text / tx3g : timed text samples within a container track. SAMI : HTML-like synchronized caption blocks. MicroDVD : text tied to numbered video frames. IMSC constrains TTML features for particular delivery profiles. It is a profile relationship, not a filename-only classification. Bitmap subtitles supply pre-rendered graphics: DVDSub / VobSub : DVD subpictures and their external-file packaging. PGS : Blu-ray presentation graphics assembled into timed display sets. DVBSub : broadcast subtitle services built from pages, regions and objects. Broadcast caption systems also have service and command models that do not fit a simple “one sentence per file block” description. Their service identifiers and carriage must be understood alongside their character data. Format changes have a purpose and a cost Converting a simple text cue between two formats can retain its wording and timing. Converting an extensively positioned ASS sign into plain text can retain the words while discarding their placement and animation. Turning a bitmap into text additionally requires recognizing the letters, usually through OCR or manual transcription. Rendering any of those representations into video preserves the displayed result in that particular output picture. It removes the separate subtitle choice from that version. For Emby, a supported media container and a selected subtitle renderer are separate compatibility questions. The underlying playback route determines whether the track is delivered separately, converted into another subtitle representation, or incorporated into the video. A container extension alone cannot decide which work the selected subtitle requires. See Also Text-based subtitles Bitmap subtitles IMSC timed text Streams and Tracks References Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 ETSI EN 300 743 V1.6.1: DVB subtitling

articles/subtitles/formats/Subtitle-IMSC.title: IMSC timed text | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/Subtitle-IMSC.keywords: IMSC timed text IMSC defines constrained TTML profiles for interoperable internet-media subtitles and captions, with version-specific text and image capabilities. IMSC constrains the broad TTML language into profiles intended for internet-media subtitle and caption delivery. The profile establishes an agreed set of timing, styling and presentation rules that an author and a consumer can implement together. It is not simply another name for every TTML file. A document can be valid XML and use TTML elements while still using features outside the selected IMSC profile. The version belongs in the description Reference Profiles specified IMSC 1.2, W3C Recommendation from 2020 Text-only and image-only profiles IMSC Text Profile 1.3, W3C Recommendation of 21 May 2026 Text profile; the earlier image profile is not specified in this version The IMSC 1.3 recommendation points applications needing the image-only profile to IMSC 1.2. “IMSC supports images” and “IMSC is text-only” can therefore each be incomplete statements when the version and profile are omitted. A text profile preserves characters that a renderer draws. The older image profile supplies image resources for presentation. Packaging both in an XML-based system does not make an image's pictured letters editable character text. The profile is a contract about features The profile constrains such things as applicable time bases, layout, styling and permitted extensions. Profile signaling identifies the intended content contract. A consumer still needs to implement that contract, obtain supporting resources and map the presentation to its video display. This is more specific than checking the filename extension. It is also more specific than an XML parser confirming that tags are balanced. For example, a caption can request a named font, a region and a styled span. Conformance defines the applicable rules, but the available font face and its metrics still affect the drawn text. A pipeline must either provide suitable resources and support the presentation or make a deliberate conversion to another model. Rendering capacity is another part of delivery IMSC's hypothetical render model provides a defined way to assess a document's rendering complexity. It is a model for constrained content processing, not a promise that every actual player draws any conforming document at the same speed. A small file can still contain many active elements or expensive presentation changes. Network file size and the work needed at a cue boundary are different quantities. For an Emby stream arriving from a system that uses IMSC, identify the actual version/profile and the delivered subtitle representation. A conversion to WebVTT or another client format needs to resolve the source's timing and decide which layout/styling information can survive. See Also Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) Text-based subtitles Bitmap subtitles References W3C IMSC Text Profile 1.3: Recommendation, May 2026 W3C IMSC 1.2: Text and image profiles W3C IMSC Hypothetical Render Model W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2

articles/subtitles/formats/text/index.ht.title: Overview: Text subtitle formats | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Text subtitle formats Text subtitle formats combine cue timing with character content and format-specific presentation rules. Text-based subtitles can carry anything from simple lines to detailed placement and styling. The common formats below define different cue structures and rendering expectations. A correct text extraction can therefore preserve the words while leaving another question about how the player interprets their appearance. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Text-based subtitles Text-based subtitles store characters and timed presentation instructions that a renderer turns into visible glyphs. SubRip (SRT) SRT stores numbered text cues with millisecond start and end timestamps separated into plain-text blocks. WebVTT WebVTT defines UTF-8 timed text cues, presentation settings, and cue markup for web-oriented text tracks. SubStation Alpha (SSA) SSA is a styled subtitle script format whose v4 sections describe reusable styles and timed dialogue events. Advanced SubStation Alpha (ASS) ASS stores styled subtitle events with a script coordinate system, reusable styles, and local or timed override instructions. Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) TTML uses XML to describe timed text, styles, regions, and the timing relationships of nested content. MP4 timed text (tx3g) tx3g identifies a 3GPP timed-text sample entry whose container timing and text modifiers describe a subtitle track. SAMI SAMI stores HTML-like synchronized caption blocks and can associate different language classes with the same media timing. MicroDVD subtitles MicroDVD stores text cues using numbered frame boundaries, so their elapsed times depend on the associated frame rate. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 3629: UTF-8 W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 libass: ASS file format guide W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 3GPP TS 26.245 Release 18: Timed text format

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) ASS stores styled subtitle events with a script coordinate system, reusable styles, and local or timed override instructions. An ASS subtitle can be a simple dialogue line near the bottom of the picture, or a translated sign positioned over a sign in the scene. Advanced SubStation Alpha stores the timing, text and instructions for that presentation in one script. The format's power comes from two levels of styling: a named style shared by many events, and override tags within an event. An event can change position, colour or other properties while it is active. The subtitle therefore describes more than a string to place in the player's usual caption box. A minimal script with a positioned event [Script Info] ScriptType: v4.00+ PlayResX: 1280 PlayResY: 720 ScaledBorderAndShadow: yes WrapStyle: 0 [V4+ Styles] Format: Name, Fontname, Fontsize, PrimaryColour, SecondaryColour, OutlineColour, BackColour, Bold, Italic, Underline, StrikeOut, ScaleX, ScaleY, Spacing, Angle, BorderStyle, Outline, Shadow, Alignment, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Encoding Style: Default,Arial,36,&H00FFFFFF,&H000000FF,&H00000000,&H80000000,0,0,0,0,100,100,0,0,1,2,0,2,20,20,30,1 [Events] Format: Layer, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Effect, Text Dialogue: 0,0:00:12.50,0:00:15.00,Default,,0,0,0,,{\an7\pos(160,90)}LAST TRAIN\NAT MIDNIGHT The original example supplies one style and one event. Its event is active from 12.5 to 15 seconds. It chooses Default , then overrides its alignment and position. \N in the rendered text is a forced line break; it is not a new timed event. The Fontname requests a font family. The file does not become self-contained merely because it names Arial. The selected rendering environment still needs an appropriate face. ASS colour notation also differs from ordinary web RGB notation. Style colours use alpha plus blue, green and red byte order. Alpha 00 is opaque and FF is fully transparent. The example's white primary colour is opaque, while the background/shadow colour includes transparency. Script coordinates establish the anchor PlayResX and PlayResY define the script's logical resolution. In this example it is 1280 × 720 . The \pos(160,90) override places the alignment anchor at x = 160, y = 90 within that coordinate system. With \an7 , the anchor is at the line's top left . With \an2 , it would be at the bottom centre . The same position numbers can therefore put the visible lettering in a different place when alignment changes. For an ideal same-aspect mapping to 1920 × 1080 , the scale is 1.5 in each direction: x = 160 × 1.5 = 240 y = 90 × 1.5 = 135 This diagram explains the coordinate relationship, not the output of a particular ASS renderer. Cropping, letterboxing, sample aspect ratio and render-surface choices can add another transform. The logical script dimensions should not be casually replaced with the new output dimensions while keeping all position values unchanged. The style's margins determine default placement when an explicit position does not take over. Scaling border/shadow and other renderer conventions also affects appearance. Those details are why a precise sign layout needs more than matching a font-size number. One event can change during its lifetime An override such as: {\an7\move(160,90,480,90,0,1000)}LAST TRAIN moves the anchor from (160,90) to (480,90), beginning at the event's start and completing 1,000 ms later . The motion times are relative to the event. They are not new absolute movie timestamps. In the ideal linear motion, halfway through that interval the anchor is at (320,90) . Once the motion has completed, it remains at the final position for the event's remaining active time. Other instructions can change properties over time, fade text, use drawing shapes or time karaoke syllables. A renderer evaluates the event at the current playback instant. It cannot recreate an animated sign by drawing one immutable caption image for the entire interval. A seek into the middle of the event likewise needs the presentation at the sought time, including the relevant animation state. Fonts affect the geometry The selected face supplies glyph shapes, advance widths and baseline metrics. A fallback with wider letters can change where a line wraps or how it fits a sign, even when \pos and the event text are unchanged. For an invented 300-unit-wide sign area, advances totalling 280 units fit, while a 320-unit total does not. A different font does not merely change decoration; it changes the layout calculation. Matroska can carry font attachments alongside ASS. In an Emby app-rendered route, usable resources must reach that renderer. In a server-rendered route, the server needs them where the text is drawn. The file's attachment list and the chosen font face are related evidence rather than interchangeable labels. Converting the script means choosing what to retain A plain SRT conversion can preserve this example's wording and cue interval. It has no equivalent for the complete positioned, moving presentation described above. A web or native text renderer may support another subset. Keeping ASS with a compatible renderer retains the script model. Incorporating its rendered result into video retains the appearance of that output version. These produce different deliverables: one keeps the timed instructions and a selectable subtitle; the other stores the resulting pixels in the video. See Also SubStation Alpha subtitles (SSA) Text-based subtitles Subtitle cues Matroska Attachments References libass: ASS file format guide Aegisub: ASS override tags Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: MicroDVD subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: MicroDVD subtitles MicroDVD stores text cues using numbered frame boundaries, so their elapsed times depend on the associated frame rate. MicroDVD is a text subtitle format using numbered frame positions, often with the extension .sub . Despite the name, it is different from DVD bitmap subpictures and the binary .sub file in a VobSub pair. A cue can look like this: {300}{375}The platform is empty.|The last train has left. The braces contain the starting and ending frame numbers. The vertical bar separates displayed text lines. The same numbers give different times Using zero-origin frame boundaries and the indicated constant rate: Rate used for the numbers Start at frame 300 End at frame 375 Interval 25 fps 12.000 s 15.000 s 3.000 s 24 fps 12.500 s 15.625 s 3.125 s The conversion is time = frame number / frame rate . A wrong rate changes every cue's interpretation by a factor; a single fixed offset cannot correct the whole file. MicroDVD files can supply an initial frame-rate declaration, for example: {1}{1}25.000 That is interpreted as a rate declaration by supporting readers rather than as a caption saying “25.000”. Files without usable rate information need the matching video's timing context or an explicitly supplied rate. Different reader fallback choices can explain different playback results; a default chosen by one tool is not evidence of the author's intended rate. The suffix is only a starting clue A readable file containing {number}{number} records is text. A VobSub .sub contains binary subpicture data and normally accompanies an .idx . Their matching suffix does not make them interchangeable. For an Emby collection containing a frame-based legacy subtitle, a time-based conversion should use the rate associated with the subtitle's original edition. Merely reading the output video's advertised rate can be wrong if its timing was changed during a prior conversion. Frame-based timing develops that relationship. See Also Frame-based subtitle timing Subtitle timing drift DVD subtitles: DVDSub and VobSub Video Frame Rate References FFmpeg 8.1: MicroDVD text decoder FFmpeg n8.1: MicroDVD demuxer and frame-rate handling

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: SAMI captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords:
SAMI captions SAMI stores HTML-like synchronized caption blocks and can associate different language classes with the same media timing. SAMI, Synchronized Accessible Media Interchange , is Microsoft's HTML-like caption format, commonly stored in .smi or .sami files. A synchronized block can contain caption paragraphs for more than one language. Here is an original body excerpt, assuming that the header defines language classes ENCC and FRCC :

The platform is empty.

Le quai est vide.

 

  The first synchronization block starts at 12,500 milliseconds . The second starts at 15,000 milliseconds and clears the captions with a non-breaking-space entity. The result is a 2.5-second displayed interval for the chosen language. Synchronization blocks update the caption state SAMI does not use the SRT pattern of one explicit start/end pair on every paragraph. A synchronization point supplies the next caption content. A later synchronization block can replace or clear it. That is why dropping the empty-looking second block changes the meaning: the sentence may remain visible into the following scene. A converter must derive intervals from the update sequence and retain the effect of clearing events. SAMI feature Information SYNC Start Synchronization time in milliseconds Paragraph class Language association through a declared class Header style definitions Language names and supported presentation properties Clearing paragraph Ends the visible content for that language Languages share timing without sharing words The header can associate a class with a language name and code. The class itself is an identifier, not a universal language-code syntax. A reader uses the declaration to identify the language stream. Converting a multilingual SAMI file into a single-language SRT requires selecting the intended class and resolving its sequence of updates. Concatenating all paragraphs would combine translations into one caption. For an Emby library with older caption files, a conversion to a currently accepted external text format can preserve the chosen language and resolved intervals. SAMI's HTML-like syntax does not imply that a modern web player can treat the file as WebVTT or as an arbitrary HTML document. Microsoft's documentation separates parsing the SAMI source from the application's work of displaying the captions. See Also Text-based subtitles Subtitle cues SubRip subtitles (SRT) References Microsoft: Understanding SAMI 1.0 Microsoft: SAMI media source and language streams

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: SubRip subtitles (SRT) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: SubRip subtitles (SRT) SRT stores numbered text cues with millisecond start and end timestamps separated into plain-text blocks. An SRT file is easy to inspect because its main structure is plain text. Each block identifies a subtitle cue, gives its interval, and contains the text to display. 1 00:00:12,500 --> 00:00:15,000 The last train leaves at midnight. 2 00:00:16,200 --> 00:00:18,000 Then we still have time. The first cue begins at 12.5 seconds and lasts 2.5 seconds . The second begins at 16.2 seconds and lasts 1.8 seconds. The 1.2 seconds between them contains no cue in this example. The block's fields Field Meaning 1 or 2 Cue sequence number, not a video frame number 00:00:12,500 Hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds --> Separates start and end timestamps Following text lines The visible wording and explicit line breaks Blank line Separates this block from the next Changing the number from 2 to 3 does not move the cue in time. Changing its timestamps does. A cue can contain several text lines; those lines still belong to one interval. SRT is a widely implemented convention rather than a format with one comprehensive normative standard for every extension. Basic italic, bold or other markup is interpreted by many players, but the supported subset and its appearance vary. A simple portable cue should not rely on elaborate positioning instructions that the reader may ignore. The file needs the right character decoding The timing punctuation can parse correctly while accented or non-Latin text is garbled. SRT files encountered in existing libraries can use UTF-8 or legacy encodings; the extension alone does not declare which bytes were written. A recognizable wrong-decoding pattern such as Ã© where é was intended points to character interpretation. An empty square in otherwise correct text can instead point to missing font coverage. These are different stages of text rendering . An external SRT also does not inherently identify its language, the corresponding movie edition, or whether it contains only selected foreign dialogue. File naming and library metadata provide those associations. Emby's naming documentation explains the external-file conventions. Inside Matroska, the container carries time Matroska's S_TEXT/UTF8 mapping stores the UTF-8 cue text as a subtitle payload. Container timing and duration describe when it appears. The standalone SRT counter and timestamp line are therefore not simply copied into every packet as visible content. Extracting that track to a standalone SRT reconstructs text blocks and timestamp lines from the track. Its cue numbering or millisecond rounding can differ while the intended presentation remains equivalent at the output format's precision. See Also Subtitle cues Subtitle timestamps WebVTT subtitles References Library of Congress: SubRip subtitle format Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings RFC 3629: UTF-8

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: SubStation Alpha subtitles (SSA) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: SubStation Alpha subtitles (SSA) SSA is a styled subtitle script format whose v4 sections describe reusable styles and timed dialogue events. SubStation Alpha, or SSA , is a text subtitle script format with reusable styles and timed events. It can describe font choice, colours, margins and alignment in addition to the words. The commonly encountered SSA v4 script has three main sections: Section Contents [Script Info] Script identification and rendering-related information [V4 Styles] Named styles with font and presentation fields [Events] Timed dialogue and comment records A dialogue event selects a style by name. Changing that style can alter all events using it without rewriting their text. An SSA event is a structured record Format: Marked, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Effect, Text Dialogue: Marked=0,0:00:12.50,0:00:15.00,Default,,0,0,0,,The platform is empty. This is an event-section excerpt, not a complete script. It assumes a Default style exists. The final field is text and can contain commas; the preceding commas separate defined fields. The start and end use hundredths of a second here. The Marked field comes from the SSA record model. It is not a declaration that the event is forced, is a translation, or must always be displayed. SSA v4 and ASS v4+ are related formats SSA uses ScriptType: v4.00 and [V4 Styles] . ASS uses v4.00+ and [V4+ Styles] . Their style records differ; ASS also uses Layer where the SSA dialogue record has Marked . The legacy SSA alignment values are not the same overall numbering scheme as ASS's keypad-style alignment. Renaming a file from .ssa to .ass leaves those declarations and records unchanged. A proper conversion interprets them and writes the target model. For an Emby collection containing older styled subtitles, the useful identification is the script's declared format and the renderer handling it. A route using a compatible renderer can retain its styles; a conversion to plain text keeps a more limited description. Matroska's SSA mapping retains script/style information as track configuration and stores timed event payloads separately. Associated font attachments are another resource. Preserving the dialogue words alone does not preserve the named styles or provide the requested font. See Also Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) Text-based subtitles Matroska Attachments References libass: ASS file format guide Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings Aegisub: ASS override tags

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: Text-based subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: Text-based subtitles Text-based subtitles store characters and timed presentation instructions that a renderer turns into visible glyphs. Text-based subtitles store characters , rather than a finished image of the lettering. Timing and presentation instructions tell a renderer when and how to draw those characters. This makes the words editable without repainting an image. It also leaves part of the displayed result to the renderer: decoding the characters, selecting fonts, shaping the script, laying out the lines, and producing pixels. Bytes, characters and glyphs are different In UTF-8, the word café occupies five bytes: 63 61 66 C3 A9 . It has four Unicode characters in this composed spelling. Reading the last two bytes as the wrong legacy encoding can produce cafÃ© instead. That failure occurs before typography. Installing another font does not repair characters that were decoded incorrectly. Conversely, correctly decoded characters can still display as missing-glyph boxes when the selected font lacks their shapes. A glyph is a drawn shape selected for the script and context. The correspondence need not be one character to one glyph: combining marks, ligatures and connected scripts can change the mapping. This is why a byte count is not a useful measure of the rendered line width. Layout depends on actual font metrics Consider an invented subtitle box with 300 pixels of available width . One font produces a line whose glyph advances total 280 pixels . A fallback totals 320 . The first fits; the second needs another layout decision, such as wrapping. The words and cue times have not changed. The difference is the font's metrics. For precisely positioned text, a changed width can also move the line relative to an alignment anchor. Formats vary in how much presentation they specify. A simple SRT can leave most choices to the app. ASS or TTML can carry more detailed styling and placement. Font attachments provide supporting resources, but the renderer consuming the subtitle must actually receive and use them. Preserving the text is one level of conversion If a cue reads “Meet me outside” from 10 to 12 seconds, a simple conversion can preserve those words and that interval. A source may additionally place the words on a sign, draw an outline and move them during the cue. A format unable to represent those instructions preserves less of the intended presentation. For an Emby route that converts subtitles for the selected client, compare wording, times and presentation separately. An intact sentence can look different after conversion without implying that the video itself changed. The final visible text is still a rasterized image, even though its source is character data. The advantage is that the player can rerender those characters at an appropriate output size and, where the format and app permit, apply the viewer's text preferences. See Also SubRip subtitles (SRT) Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) WebVTT subtitles Matroska Attachments References RFC 3629: UTF-8 W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 libass: ASS file format guide W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords:
Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) TTML uses XML to describe timed text, styles, regions, and the timing relationships of nested content. TTML is an XML language for timed text and its presentation . A document can describe the words, their active intervals, named styles, layout regions and relationships between nested timed elements. That structure makes TTML useful when a caption delivery system needs an explicit layout and timing model. It also means that finding a text element and reading its immediate timestamps is not always enough to determine the final caption. One simple timed paragraph

The last train leaves at midnight.

 The tt root identifies the TTML vocabulary through its XML namespace. In this simple document, the paragraph begins at 12.5 seconds and ends at 15. The XML language attribute declares English; it does not prove whether the wording is a translation or includes sound descriptions. The namespace identifier is part of the syntax. A TTML document is not an ordinary HTML page whose elements can be styled or executed as arbitrary browser content. Styles and regions have separate jobs A style supplies properties such as colour, font size and alignment. A region describes a presentation area. Content can refer to both, and inherited or directly specified properties determine the resolved result. Here is a complete small document with one region and one style:

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: MP4 timed text (tx3g) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: MP4 timed text (tx3g) tx3g identifies a 3GPP timed-text sample entry whose container timing and text modifiers describe a subtitle track. tx3g is the sample-entry identifier for the 3GPP timed-text format commonly encountered in MP4 and 3GP subtitle tracks. Inspection tools can also label the decoded codec mov_text . This is not a standalone SRT file hidden inside MP4. The track has container timing and a sample description, while its timed samples contain text and optional presentation modifiers. Component Responsibility tx3g sample entry Default text box, style, font-table references and presentation flags Container sample timeline When each sample starts and how long it is presented Text sample A byte-length field, encoded text and any modifier boxes Renderer Decode and lay out the sample using its defaults and modifiers Bytes and characters are counted differently A text sample starts with a 16-bit text-length field. That length counts the text bytes , not all modifier bytes and not the number of visible glyphs. For the UTF-8 spelling café , the text occupies five bytes although it has four composed Unicode characters. Its two-byte length field plus text therefore occupy seven bytes before optional modifier boxes. The 3GPP format supports UTF-8 and signaled UTF-16 text. Styling ranges use their defined character positions. A byte index into a UTF-8 string cannot be casually used as the position of a displayed character. Modifiers can describe styled spans, highlighting, links or other supported behavior. The receiving player chooses the implementation of those defined features; the identifier tx3g alone does not mean that the track has only plain unstyled sentences. Empty samples can represent the gaps Take a track on a 1,000-unit-per-second time scale : Sample start Duration Text 0 12,500 Empty 12,500 2,500 The last train leaves at midnight. 15,000 1,200 Empty 16,200 1,800 Then we still have time. The empty sample starting at 15 seconds prevents the first sentence from remaining on screen until the next sentence. The timing comes from the container's sample schedule. Any edit-list mapping or other applicable track timing also needs to be applied. A simple text extraction reconstructs cues from that schedule. It must account for empty text and sample duration rather than copying every packet into a visible subtitle line. For an Emby MP4, container recognition and subtitle rendering are separate capabilities. A route can retain the track, convert its decoded text for the app, or render its presentation upstream. Its styled ranges and other modifiers determine which presentation details a simpler text conversion can retain. See Also Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) Subtitle timestamps MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Time Bases References 3GPP TS 26.245 Release 18: Timed text format RFC 4396: 3GPP timed text sample structure

articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.title: WebVTT subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/formats/text/Subtitle.keywords: WebVTT subtitles WebVTT defines UTF-8 timed text cues, presentation settings, and cue markup for web-oriented text tracks. WebVTT is the Web Video Text Tracks format. It gives web-oriented text tracks a defined syntax for UTF-8 cues, settings and markup. The W3C reference used here is the 20 May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft . A small file can look like this: WEBVTT station-announcement 00:00:12.500 --> 00:00:15.000 line:85% position:50% align:center size:80% <v Announcer>The last train leaves at midnight. The cue occupies 12.5 through 15 seconds. station-announcement is its identifier, not a time or a required numeric counter. The voice annotation names the speaker for the cue's markup; it is not automatically part of the displayed sentence. The settings describe a cue box Setting in the example Intent line:85% A percentage-based line position in the rendering area position:50% The cue's percentage position align:center Centre alignment of its text size:80% A cue-box size relative to the relevant dimension These settings participate in WebVTT's positioning model. They are not pixels on the original encoded movie and do not guarantee one identical physical location across every player size, writing direction and supported rendering path. WebVTT also has defined text markup for functions such as emphasis, classes, ruby and voice annotations. Its CSS cue styling is restricted to the specified model. Arbitrary HTML, script or a page's general stylesheet is not a replacement for that model. Parsing has specific rules A WebVTT file begins with WEBVTT , is encoded as UTF-8, and uses a decimal point for the timestamp fraction. The blank line after the header and those separating cue blocks are part of its structure. The cue starts must be in nondecreasing order in a conforming file, and each cue's end must be later than its start. End times need not be in the same order. Two subtitle cues can overlap. Renaming an SRT file to .vtt does not add the header, change the fraction punctuation, or interpret its presentation extensions. A proper conversion parses the source and writes the target format. More than one cue can be active Take cue A from 12 to 15 seconds and cue B from 14 to 16 . Between 14 and 15, both are active. A player might use them for two speakers or for dialogue and another annotation. Rendering then needs to handle their boxes and avoid inappropriate collisions. The original example above has one box. A more complex layout can use multiple cue settings or regions; an app converting the stream into a simpler subtitle representation might not retain those choices. WebVTT can also carry other text-track uses, such as chapters or timed metadata. That does not make every WebVTT payload a caption for display. The file and its delivery remain separate An Emby route can supply text a web player can render separately, including through a suitable subtitle conversion. Another route may use a native renderer. The selected app's behavior determines how much of WebVTT's presentation model it uses. The WebVTT format describes the text track. Fetching it as a whole resource, delivering it in streaming segments, or storing its payload in a container adds timing and packaging rules outside the simple file shown here. Those rules must preserve the cue's place on the media timeline. See Also SubRip subtitles (SRT) Subtitle cues Subtitle timestamps Text-based subtitles References W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings

articles/subtitles/index.html.title: Overview: Subtitles and captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/index.html.keywords: Overview: Subtitles and captions Subtitles and captions combine timed content, language and presentation rules with a delivery path supported by the player. A subtitle can be present in a file yet never become visible in the expected way. Selection, timing, delivery and rendering each have a role: the right track must be chosen, its cues must match the programme, and the chosen playback path must be able to display them. The format and storage branches describe what is being carried. Sources and accessibility explain which track suits the viewer; timing and text presentation explain how it appears. The Emby processing branch connects those properties to direct subtitle delivery and the cases where text or graphics become part of the video image. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Understanding subtitles and captions Subtitles and captions present timed language and sound information as selectable tracks or as part of the video picture. Subtitle formats Subtitle formats define the timed content, graphics or service information available for presentation. Subtitle storage and delivery Subtitle storage and delivery connect a timed representation to the player through files, container tracks or stream signaling. Subtitle sources Subtitle sources and matching methods connect available timed content to the edition and language the viewer needs. Track selection and accessibility Subtitle selection combines track metadata, language preferences and accessibility needs with the available playback choices. Timing and synchronization Subtitle timing places cues on the media timeline and distinguishes offsets, drift and edition-specific mismatches. Text rendering and styling Subtitle rendering turns timed content and presentation instructions into visible text or graphics. Subtitle processing in Emby Subtitle processing in Emby connects track compatibility with direct delivery, rendering and optional video composition. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.title: Overview: Character encoding and scripts | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.keywords: Overview: Character encoding and scripts Character encoding and script handling connect stored subtitle bytes to the characters and reading order intended by the text. A wrong byte interpretation can produce the wrong characters before a font is involved. Unicode representation then supplies character identities, while right-to-left handling influences their presentation order. These pages locate those stages so an encoding error is investigated differently from a missing glyph or a layout problem. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle character encoding Character encoding specifies how subtitle bytes become characters, and incorrect decoding can produce mojibake before font rendering begins. Unicode in subtitles Unicode represents subtitle characters, while code units, grapheme clusters, normalization and glyph shaping describe different text-processing boundaries. Right-to-left subtitles Right-to-left subtitle rendering resolves logical text order, bidirectional runs and script shaping separately from caption alignment. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.title: Subtitle character encoding | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.keywords: Subtitle character encoding Character encoding specifies how subtitle bytes become characters, and incorrect decoding can produce mojibake before font rendering begins. Character encoding defines the relationship between stored bytes and text characters . An incorrectly decoded subtitle can show Ã© where é was intended even when its timestamps and basic punctuation remain readable. That is a text-decoding problem. Font selection happens later and cannot reinterpret the original bytes once the decoder has produced the wrong characters. The same word can use different bytes For the composed spelling café : Encoding Bytes in hexadecimal UTF-8 63 61 66 C3 A9 Windows-1252 63 61 66 E9 In UTF-8, C3 A9 together encode U+00E9. In Windows-1252, E9 represents that character directly. If the UTF-8 bytes are decoded as Windows-1252, C3 and A9 become two different characters, producing the familiar cafÃ© . If the single E9 byte is decoded as though it begins a complete UTF-8 character, that incomplete/invalid sequence needs an error policy. ASCII digits and timing separators have the same familiar byte values in these two encodings. The timing header can therefore look correct while the dialogue is wrong. A label or signature supplies evidence Some formats prescribe an encoding: WebVTT is UTF-8. XML can describe its encoding under XML's rules. Existing SRT collections can contain legacy encodings, so the extension alone is insufficient evidence. A byte-order mark can identify a Unicode encoding signature: Leading bytes Common signature EF BB BF UTF-8 BOM FF FE UTF-16 little-endian BOM FE FF UTF-16 big-endian BOM A UTF-8 BOM is not required for all UTF-8 text. Absence of a BOM does not make a file a legacy code page. The format's rules and any valid metadata determine which interpretation should be used. A signature is also not visible caption content. Leaving U+FEFF where the applicable parser treats it as a signature and displaying it as a letter are different actions. Replacement can lose information A decoder can reject invalid data or insert a replacement character, U+FFFD . If the resulting replacement text is saved over the source, the original byte sequence may no longer be available to reconstruct the intended wording. The replacement character is not a font's missing-glyph box. One comes from the text decoding/error policy; the other comes from a renderer unable to draw a character that is already known. For an Emby subtitle investigation, inspect the resource actually delivered and the interpretation used at the decoding stage. A file on disk can be correct while a conversion reads it with another encoding; a client cannot recover the original byte meaning from already corrupted text alone. Conversion preserves characters through a new encoding A correct Windows-1252-to-UTF-8 conversion first decodes E9 as U+00E9, then encodes U+00E9 as C3 A9. It changes the stored bytes while preserving the character. Saving an already misdecoded Ã© string as UTF-8 encodes those wrong characters faithfully. It is not the same operation. The encoding conversion should therefore begin with a verified source interpretation. The resulting character sequence, not a successful “save as UTF-8” message, establishes whether the wording survived. See Also Unicode in subtitles Text-based subtitles SubRip subtitles (SRT) Subtitle OCR References RFC 3629: UTF-8 WHATWG Encoding Standard W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.title: Right-to-left subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.keywords: Right-to-left subtitles Right-to-left subtitle rendering resolves logical text order, bidirectional runs and script shaping separately from caption alignment. Right-to-left subtitles need text processing that understands logical order, bidirectional display and the script's shaping rules . Arabic and Hebrew captions can also include left-to-right elements such as numbers, Latin names and file identifiers. Reversing every character in a subtitle file is not a rendering solution. It changes the content and also reverses the embedded left-to-right runs. Store the logical sequence Take the Hebrew phrase חדר 120 , meaning “room 120”. Its stored code-point sequence contains the Hebrew word, a space, and the digits 1, 2, 0. The Hebrew word is displayed in its right-to-left reading direction. The number is displayed as 120 , retaining the left-to-right order of its digits. Reversing the whole sequence would turn that number into 021 . The diagram uses a basic mixed-direction example. Complex punctuation, embedding and line breaks require the algorithm's full context. Paragraph direction supplies a base context The Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm resolves direction from character classes, paragraph context and applicable formatting controls. A strong Hebrew or Arabic character and a strong Latin character provide different directional evidence. Neutral punctuation and spaces are resolved in context. Parentheses or punctuation near a Latin identifier can therefore appear differently depending on the surrounding paragraph/run structure. A renderer can receive a base direction from its presentation model or determine it according to the applicable rules. The format's specification matters; an app should not invent a byte-reversal rule because a line begins with digits. Direction also interacts with line wrapping. The logical sequence is shaped and arranged for the line under the appropriate bidi model. Moving already visually reversed text through another bidi renderer can reorder it a second time. Alignment positions the box; direction orders the text A right-aligned caption box is placed against its right boundary. That setting does not establish that every character inside it must be reordered right-to-left. Likewise, a centred RTL line can remain correctly shaped and ordered. The line's alignment anchor and its paragraph/run directions are independent properties.
