This distinction is especially useful for an Emby comparison where the caption sits in the expected location but numerals, punctuation or a Latin name are wrong. Changing the bottom-edge position does not repair the text's directional processing. Isolates contain a run's directional influence Unicode supplies directional isolates: Control Code point Purpose LRI U+2066 Starts a left-to-right isolate RLI U+2067 Starts a right-to-left isolate FSI U+2068 Starts an isolate whose direction is determined from its contents PDI U+2069 Ends the isolate An authoring system can use an appropriate isolate around an embedded identifier so its direction is resolved without unexpectedly influencing adjacent text. These are formatting controls, not visible letters. Removing all nonprinting characters without understanding their roles can change the display. Adding controls indiscriminately can also change the intended structure. The correct operation follows the input text and the receiving format's permitted directional model. Arabic shaping is an additional stage The bidi algorithm determines ordering and directional context. Shaping selects and positions the glyphs appropriate to the script and font. Arabic letters can use contextual connected forms; combining marks need their positions relative to base glyphs. A suitable font and shaper are needed after character decoding succeeds. A line can have correct logical order and still display disconnected forms if its rendering stage does not perform the required shaping. Font fallback can affect that stage. A font containing individual code-point shapes is not by itself proof that a complete shaping/layout path is operating correctly. Recognition should recover logical text OCR begins with visible graphics. Its output needs the intended logical reading order for text conversion. Simply sorting every detected glyph by increasing x-coordinate is inappropriate for an RTL line and its mixed-direction runs. Compare an OCR result's content and order before applying another bidi renderer. A numeral changing from 120 to 021 identifies a content/order problem rather than a harmless difference in how the caption box was positioned. See Also Unicode in subtitles Subtitle character encoding Subtitle font fallback Subtitle OCR References Unicode UAX 9: Bidirectional Algorithm HarfBuzz: Shaping concepts W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.title: Unicode in subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/encoding-sc.keywords: Unicode in subtitles Unicode represents subtitle characters, while code units, grapheme clusters, normalization and glyph shaping describe different text-processing boundaries. Unicode identifies the characters used in subtitle text. It allows one resource to represent many scripts and symbols, but “character count” still needs a definition. A byte, a code point, a UTF-16 code unit, a user-perceived character and a drawn glyph can have different counts. Those differences matter when software wraps a caption, highlights text, truncates a line or positions an OCR result. One accented letter has two common representations The visible letter é can be represented as: Representation Code points UTF-8 bytes Composed U+00E9 C3 A9 Decomposed U+0065 followed by U+0301 65 CC 81 The second sequence contains an ordinary e and a combining acute accent. A capable renderer positions the mark with the base letter. It is one extended grapheme cluster under the applicable segmentation rules even though it contains two code points. Deleting just the final code point from the decomposed sequence removes the accent. Deleting the grapheme cluster removes the perceived letter. Splitting it carelessly between display lines separates information that belongs together. A longer sequence makes the counts visible Consider the family emoji 👩‍👩‍👧‍👦 , made from four person characters joined by three zero-width joiners. Text example Unicode code points UTF-16 code units UTF-8 bytes Extended grapheme clusters Composed é 1 1 2 1 Decomposed e + acute 2 2 3 1 Family emoji sequence 7 11 25 1 Each person code point in this sequence uses two UTF-16 code units or four UTF-8 bytes. Each joiner uses one UTF-16 unit or three UTF-8 bytes. The totals are therefore 4 × 2 + 3 = 11 and 4 × 4 + 3 × 3 = 25 . A renderer with appropriate emoji/font support can present the family as a combined symbol. Another renderer can present constituent symbols. The segmentation boundary and the exact glyph appearance are distinct responsibilities. An index measured in UTF-16 code units is consequently not the same index as one measured in Unicode code points. Passing it into an API expecting another unit can select the wrong range or split a surrogate pair. Use boundaries suited to the operation Grapheme segmentation identifies useful boundaries for user-perceived text units. Word segmentation and line-breaking rules answer different questions. A line does not have to break after every grapheme, and a grapheme count does not determine its width. For subtitle highlighting, a format can define its own character-range or timing units. The producer and consumer need to agree on those units. A karaoke instruction timing one syllable is not automatically an instruction timing one byte, one code point or one glyph. Font shaping can create ligatures or contextual glyphs after the character sequence is known. A font's glyph IDs are meaningful in that selected font; they are not Unicode character identifiers. These distinctions are useful when an Emby conversion preserves most wording but produces a broken accent, an incomplete symbol or a highlight on the wrong part of a line. Inspect the unit and boundary used at the transformation, rather than assuming a font change will repair every text operation. Normalization addresses equivalent sequences Unicode normalization can transform canonically equivalent sequences. NFC composes where applicable; NFD decomposes into canonical components. The two accented-letter forms above become the same sequence when normalized to NFC. Normalization does not translate text, reverse writing direction, choose fonts or repair an incorrect byte decoding. Applying it to cafÃ© does not discover that the author intended café . Compatibility normalization forms, NFKC and NFKD, can additionally collapse distinctions such as some presentation or width variants. That broader transformation can change text choices a caption author intended to retain. A subtitle parser can also have exact string-matching rules for identifiers or style names. Normalizing visible wording and arbitrarily rewriting every identifier are different operations. Preserve the format's required matching semantics. See Also Subtitle character encoding Right-to-left subtitles Subtitle font fallback Karaoke subtitle timing References RFC 3629: UTF-8 Unicode UAX 29: Text segmentation Unicode UAX 15: Normalization forms HarfBuzz: Shaping concepts W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.title: Overview: Fonts and typesetting | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.keywords: Overview: Fonts and typesetting Fonts and typesetting translate subtitle characters and styling instructions into positioned, shaped visual text. A selected font contributes glyph appearance and coverage. Fallback or attached fonts affect which resource is used; ASS typesetting and karaoke timing add placement, transforms and timed presentation behavior. The result depends on the renderer applying those instructions with the available font resources. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle font fallback Subtitle font fallback selects usable faces when a requested font or required glyph is unavailable, which can change both shape and layout metrics. Subtitle font attachments Subtitle font attachments bundle font resources with media so a supporting renderer can use the intended faces for styled text. ASS typesetting ASS typesetting coordinates font layout, anchors, layers, transforms, clipping and event timing to integrate subtitle text with a scene. Karaoke subtitle timing Karaoke subtitle timing controls changes within a displayed line, using syllable durations and highlight behavior relative to its event interval. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.title: ASS typesetting | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.keywords: ASS typesetting ASS typesetting coordinates font layout, anchors, layers, transforms, clipping and event timing to integrate subtitle text with a scene. ASS typesetting uses styled events to place translations and other subtitle text where the scene calls for them. A translated shop sign can need a particular shape, position, rotation, outline and lifetime instead of the player's usual bottom caption box. The task is to construct one coherent presentation from font metrics, geometry and time . Merely enlarging the subtitle or choosing a decorative face does not describe those relationships. The sign starts with shaped text The selected font and shaping produce glyphs, positions and advances. The advance width establishes how the line fits around an alignment anchor; the ink bounds describe the visible glyph outlines, including overhangs. An outline or shadow can extend beyond the unadorned lettering. A typesetter therefore needs to account for the visible result when fitting text to a sign, rather than comparing only the sum of advances with the available width. Fallback can alter that geometry. A replacement face with wider glyphs can wrap the text or protrude beyond the sign even when the event retains its original position commands. For a readable translation, preserving meaning, avoiding a collision with other captions and keeping the line on screen for the relevant scene are also part of the typeset result. Anchor and rotation origin have separate roles This original override excerpt assumes a declared ASS style and 1280 × 720 script plane: {\an5\pos(640,360)\org(640,360)\frz30}EXIT 10 The middle-centre alignment, \an5 , makes (640,360) the line's positioning anchor. The explicit \org sets the same point as its rotation origin. Positive \frz30 rotates the presentation 30 degrees counterclockwise in the screen plane. A different rotation origin would move the anchor itself around that other point as rotation is applied. It is not simply another spelling of the line's initial position. The coordinates are script units. The renderer's mapping into the output surface then affects how they reach actual video pixels. A rotation can enlarge the required rectangle Take an invented 200 × 80 unrotated layout rectangle centred at (640,360). Its corners are (540,320), (740,320), (740,400) and (540,400). With screen y increasing downward, a counterclockwise rotation by angle θ around this origin transforms relative offsets dx, dy as: x' = 640 + dx cos(θ) + dy sin(θ) y' = 360 − dx sin(θ) + dy cos(θ) At 30 degrees, the rotated rectangle's axis-aligned extent becomes: width = 200 cos(30°) + 80 sin(30°) ≈ 213.205 height = 200 sin(30°) + 80 cos(30°) ≈ 169.282 Its vertical extent is more than twice the original 80 units. A fixed box that fitted the original line does not automatically fit the rotated one. This is a geometry model, not a measured bounding box for “EXIT 10” or an actual libass capture. It makes the transformation's space requirement visible. A clip is a window on the script plane Adding this rectangular clip: \clip(540,320,740,400) retains the portion inside that fixed script-plane rectangle. It does not enlarge to the new 213.205 × 169.282 rotated extent simply because the text rotated. The clip and the text transform are different elements of the presentation. Their interaction can intentionally reveal text through a window or can accidentally cut off a rotated translation. The rectangular coordinates use the format's integer script-coordinate model and eventual raster boundaries. A diagram's ideal floating-point corners do not imply subpixel precision for every clipping operation. Vector clipping and drawing modes can describe more complex shapes. Their supported animation and scaling rules differ from a rectangular clip, so a typeset conversion must interpret the actual commands rather than reduce every shape to its bounding box. Layers coordinate simultaneous events A sign translation and a normal dialogue line can be active at the same time. ASS layers establish relative drawing order. Ordering does not in itself resolve a collision: the typesetter still needs suitable locations or a deliberate overlap. An outline can keep light lettering readable on a changing background, while a shadow has another spatial effect. Treating them as the same single “border” property changes the presentation. A plain text conversion can keep “EXIT 10” and its cue interval but omit the sign's transform, clip, layers and font choices. Keeping the event model with a compatible renderer or storing the rendered result into video preserves different properties. The geometry has a lifetime in the scene Position, motion and transforms belong to an event's active interval. A sign leaving the camera view can require the translation to leave with it. A cut can end the event even though the last line would otherwise remain readable. Timed override parameters can use units different from event timestamps. A one-second motion window is relative to the event, while its start/end identify positions on the programme. Karaoke timing introduces another internal timing model. For an Emby comparison of a typeset subtitle, inspect the delivered event model, the resources used and the stage doing the rendering. Matching the sentence and whole-event times establishes only part of the result; the geometry and its evolution determine whether the translated sign stays integrated with the scene. See Also Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) Subtitle font fallback Subtitle font attachments Karaoke subtitle timing Subtitle rendering References Aegisub: ASS override tags libass: ASS file format guide HarfBuzz: Shaping concepts

articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.title: Subtitle font attachments | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.keywords: Subtitle font attachments Subtitle font attachments bundle font resources with media so a supporting renderer can use the intended faces for styled text. A styled subtitle can request a font that is not installed on the playback device. A font attachment bundles the resource with the media, giving a supporting consumer access to the intended face. In Matroska, attachments are supporting files with identifying metadata and bytes. They are not timed subtitle tracks and do not have cue intervals. Carrying the resource is the first boundary The stages are distinct: The media source contains the font attachment. The selected processing route recovers or forwards the resource. The renderer's font provider makes the face available. The style's family/face request resolves to that face. Shaping and layout use its glyphs and metrics. A track list containing ASS and an attachment list containing a font do not prove that every downstream client used it. The attachment's filename and MIME type identify a carried file. Registered types such as font/ttf and font/otf describe font formats. The internal family/style names determine font matching; they need not equal the attachment's filename. A container change can affect the two lists separately Output from an invented source Subtitle result Resource result Remux retaining ASS and fonts Styled event model retained Intended faces remain carried Remux retaining ASS but omitting attachments Same timed events and family requests Fallback may be needed Extract standalone ASS only Global styles and events retained Fonts need separate delivery Convert to simple SRT Words and basic intervals can remain The original face request may no longer be represented A font can also survive in an output container but become unused when the subtitle style that requested it was removed. Keeping bytes and maintaining their reference relationship are different requirements. Matroska attachments explains the generic container mechanism. For subtitles, the practical result is whether the active renderer obtains the requested face. Locate the consumer When an Emby app renders text, its route needs usable subtitle data and font resources at the app's renderer. When the server renders text into video, the server's font provider needs them before composition. Those are different resource destinations. An extraction or delivery path can preserve the source media perfectly and still fail to provide a font to the particular consumer drawing the sign. See Also Matroska Attachments Subtitle font fallback Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) Subtitle extraction References Matroska: Attachments and font resources RFC 9559: Matroska container format RFC 8081: Font media types libass: ASS file format guide

articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.title: Subtitle font fallback | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.keywords: Subtitle font fallback Subtitle font fallback selects usable faces when a requested font or required glyph is unavailable, which can change both shape and layout metrics. Font fallback supplies a usable font face when the requested face or a needed glyph is unavailable. It lets a subtitle remain visible, but the replacement can change letter shapes, widths, baselines and line breaks. Two different failures can trigger it: Situation Typical matching question Requested family is unavailable Which available family/style is an acceptable substitute? Family exists but lacks characters in a run Which face covers those characters and suits their script? A renderer can therefore use fallback for part of a line rather than replace the entire caption. The filename is not the selected family Subtitle styles request font family and properties such as weight or italic style. The font's internal names and available faces supply that identity. A file named MovieFont-Regular.ttf need not contain a family named “MovieFont-Regular”. Matching can consider family, style, character coverage, language and other properties. Fontconfig documents one such matching system; other platforms and renderers use their own font providers and policies. Inspect the selected face rather than assume that the first vaguely matching filename must be the font being used. A fixed anchor can produce different visible bounds Imagine a line centred at x = 800 . With face A, its advance width is 240 units . With fallback face B, it is 300 . Face Advance width Left bound in this simplified model Right bound A 240 800 − 120 = 680 920 B 300 800 − 150 = 650 950 The anchor did not move. The wider line extends farther in both directions. In a 280-unit-wide layout area, face A fits and face B does not, which can trigger wrapping or another layout decision. These are invented advance-width values, not measurements of named fonts. Actual ink bounds can also differ from advance bounds, and shaping determines the advances used by a real line. Coverage and shaping work together A font can contain a base letter while a needed combining mark comes from another face. Coordinated shaping and placement must keep the mark related to the base. A substitution that changes metrics or separates a shaping run can alter the result. Arabic and other contextual scripts also need appropriate shaping. Individual code-point coverage is useful, but not the complete test of connected forms or mark positioning. A missing-glyph box is different from mojibake. The box can mean a known character lacked a drawable glyph. Mojibake can mean wrong characters were produced before the font provider was asked. Resources belong to the active renderer For an Emby comparison, identify where text is drawn and which face that renderer actually selected. A font attached to the source file must be made available at that consumer; a font installed on a separate machine does not automatically enter its matching process. Retaining the intended face can improve repeatability of a typeset sign. Fallback remains useful for missing resources and coverage, while its metric differences explain why an unchanged style and position can still look different. See Also Subtitle font attachments Unicode in subtitles Right-to-left subtitles ASS typesetting References Fontconfig: Font matching and configuration HarfBuzz: Shaping concepts libass: ASS file format guide W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2

articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.title: Karaoke subtitle timing | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/fonts-types.keywords: Karaoke subtitle timing Karaoke subtitle timing controls changes within a displayed line, using syllable durations and highlight behavior relative to its event interval. Karaoke timing changes the appearance of parts of a subtitle line while the line remains displayed. The timing usually corresponds to syllables or other authored units of speech/music. The word “karaoke” does not imply that a subtitle engine discovered the syllables automatically. The resource contains authored timing instructions, and the renderer evaluates them within the event. ASS durations accumulate within the event Consider an original ASS event starting at 12.5 seconds and ending at 15 seconds . Its text excerpt is: {\k30}Meet {\k40}me {\kf80}outside. The \k family uses centiseconds : 100 units = one second. The tags in this example specify 0.3 , 0.4 and 0.8 seconds . Without an explicit alternative start instruction, each tagged unit begins after the preceding units' durations: Unit Relative interval Programme interval Meet 0.0–0.3 s 12.5–12.8 s me 0.3–0.7 s 12.8–13.2 s outside. 0.7–1.5 s 13.2–14.0 s The total authored highlight sequence is 1.5 seconds . The whole event lasts 2.5 , leaving another second after those highlights have completed. This is an invented timing example, not an analysis of a recording. Step and sweep have different visual behavior Tag Behavior in the documented ASS model \k A unit changes from secondary to primary fill when its highlight interval starts \kf or \K Fill sweeps from secondary to primary from left to right over the unit's duration \ko Step-like fill behavior, with the pre-highlight outline treated differently For the final word's 0.8-second sweep, programme time 13.6 is 0.4 seconds after its start at 13.2. In the ideal linear sweep, it is 50% through that word's sweep. That percentage refers to the progression across the rendered unit. It is not a claim that half its Unicode code points have independent highlight times. Shaping and glyph widths determine the visual surface being swept. The tag names are case-sensitive: uppercase \K and lowercase \k describe different behavior. Cue timing and internal timing are separate quantities ASS event timestamps commonly use hundredths of a second. Karaoke durations use centiseconds too, but describe relative lengths. Motion and several other override arguments use milliseconds. Similar-looking numbers can therefore have different roles or units. Moving the whole event by a constant +0.8-second offset moves the highlights with it; their relative durations need not change. A rate transformation is different. Extending only the event's end leaves the original internal highlights running at their original relative pace. A 1.1× time expansion Suppose the entire presentation is retimed by new time = 1.1 × old time . The event becomes 13.75–16.5 seconds , and its internal durations should become: Original tag duration Expanded duration New unit interval 30 cs 33 cs 13.75–14.08 s 40 cs 44 cs 14.08–14.52 s 80 cs 88 cs 14.52–15.40 s The completed highlight sequence now lasts 1.65 seconds , followed by 1.1 seconds of the event's remaining display time. Keeping 30/40/80 would finish the highlight sequence at 15.25 seconds , rather than 15.40. The outer event would have the new lifetime while its internal presentation had the old rate. A real conversion also needs a rounding policy when scaled durations are not whole centiseconds. Its cumulative result should be compared with the intended anchors rather than rounding each unit without inspecting the total. The renderer needs the instructions, not just the sentence WebVTT has its own timed-text and past/future cue mechanisms; that is another presentation model rather than a literal interpretation of ASS tags. Converting the example to simple SRT can retain “Meet me outside.” and the overall interval without retaining the authored highlight sequence. For an Emby route using styled karaoke subtitles, the consumer must receive the supported event instructions and resources. A plain-text caption of the same words does not establish that the internal timing survived. See Also Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) Subtitle timing drift Subtitle format conversion Unicode in subtitles References Aegisub: ASS override tags libass: ASS file format guide W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/rendering/index.html.title: Overview: Text rendering and styling | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/index.html.keywords: Overview: Text rendering and styling Subtitle rendering turns timed content and presentation instructions into visible text or graphics. The renderer decides where and how the selected cue appears. For text, character interpretation and font shaping are part of that work; graphics have their own composition path. This area focuses on visible presentation so a valid cue can be distinguished from a correctly rendered one. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle rendering Subtitle rendering evaluates timed content, shapes or decodes its visual elements, and composes them in the applicable output geometry. Character encoding and scripts Character encoding and script handling connect stored subtitle bytes to the characters and reading order intended by the text. Fonts and typesetting Fonts and typesetting translate subtitle characters and styling instructions into positioned, shaped visual text. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/rendering/Subtitle-Re.title: Subtitle rendering | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/rendering/Subtitle-Re.keywords: Subtitle rendering Subtitle rendering evaluates timed content, shapes or decodes its visual elements, and composes them in the applicable output geometry. A subtitle renderer produces the presentation appropriate to the current media time . It determines which events are active, resolves their appearance and placement, and supplies visible pixels for composition with video. For text, that includes font selection and shaping. For bitmap subtitles, it includes decoding image/palette state. Styled text can add motion, clipping and changes within an event. Drawing the same initial caption image throughout the whole cue is insufficient for such an event. Evaluate the event at programme time Suppose an ASS event starts at 12.5 seconds and moves for its first second. At programme time 13.0 , the event is 0.5 seconds into its motion. A seek directly to 13.0 should produce that current state, rather than start the movement over. Faster playback also traverses the programme-time animation faster in wall-clock time. An implementation that drives it from a fresh wall-clock timer after each seek would produce another presentation. The renderer needs applicable global styles, resources and decoder state as well as the local event text. Geometry describes the drawing surface The source subtitle can use a script/display plane, while the player shows video in a differently sized viewport. Scaling, sample aspect ratio, letterboxing and cropping establish the relationship between those planes. Take a 1920 × 1080 picture cropped by 140 rows at the top and bottom. The retained picture is 1920 × 800 , corresponding to original y coordinates 140 through 939 . A subtitle anchor at original y = 960 lies outside that retained area. Merely subtracting the crop's top offset gives y = 820 , which is also outside the new 800-row surface. The pipeline must decide whether the intended presentation includes the original lower area, is clipped with the picture, or is deliberately repositioned on the new viewport. Those choices are not equivalent transforms. Operation Consequence in this example Compose on the full original plane, then crop A caption confined to the removed lower area is cropped away Crop first, retain original coordinates unchanged The coordinate system no longer matches the surface Crop first, apply a defined mapping/repositioning The renderer can produce a selected new layout This is a geometry illustration, not a claim about a particular Emby crop policy. Shape and rasterize at the required size Shaping determines glyph selection and positions for the chosen font and script. Layout determines line breaks and alignment. Rasterization then samples those outlines into the output pixels, with outline, shadow, fill and transparency as applicable. Rendering text at the final output size can retain useful glyph detail. Enlarging an already rasterized small caption instead scales existing pixels. A bitmap subtitle begins with already drawn lettering, so it follows that latter kind of image-resampling problem. An outline and partly transparent edge also have to be composited in the intended colour/transparency model. The caption's apparent weight can change when sampling or compositing changes, even if its font-size number stays the same. User preferences and authored styling have different scope A simple dialogue track can delegate much appearance to the app. A typeset sign can prescribe font, placement and effects for a scene. Which user overrides are applied depends on the format, renderer and chosen policy. Emby's appearance preferences describe its controls for text size, colour, background, shadow and position. Those controls are not a promise that every bitmap or authored effect is reconstructed as editable text. Composition can take place at the app, preserving a separately selectable subtitle. If the server composes it into encoded video, the client receives those completed subtitle pixels as part of that video version. The relevant rendering surface and resources belong to the stage doing that work. See Also Text-based subtitles Bitmap subtitles ASS typesetting Subtitle font fallback References HarfBuzz: Shaping concepts Aegisub: ASS override tags W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/selection/index.html.title: Overview: Track selection and accessibility | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/selection/index.html.keywords: Overview: Track selection and accessibility Subtitle selection combines track metadata, language preferences and accessibility needs with the available playback choices. A default flag, a preferred language and a forced passage describe different reasons to show subtitles. SDH content serves another accessibility purpose. These topics explain how to identify the kind of track the viewer wants before interpreting the server or app's final selection. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle track selection Subtitle track selection chooses a content track or caption service using language, role, user policy and any explicit or remembered choice. Subtitle language preferences Subtitle language preferences guide selection through language identifiers, script/region distinctions and the subtitle content role required for viewing. Forced subtitles Forced subtitle metadata identifies selected content intended to be shown in a viewing context and is distinct from permanent subtitle pixels. Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) SDH subtitles include dialogue and relevant speaker, music and sound information for viewers who cannot rely on the soundtrack. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-Fo.title: Forced subtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-Fo.keywords: Forced subtitles Forced subtitle metadata identifies selected content intended to be shown in a viewing context and is distinct from permanent subtitle pixels. A movie can contain a short passage in another language, a written sign or another piece of information needed by its intended viewers. A forced subtitle presentation identifies the selected text needed in that viewing context, even when the viewer does not normally enable a full subtitle track. “Forced” describes selection intent or signaling. It does not mean that the words have been permanently encoded into the video picture. The required passages can be stored in two ways Representation Where the selection is expressed A separate sparse track The track contains only the intended passages and can carry a forced designation A fuller track with marked events/objects Individual parts identify forced content through the applicable format Permanent on-screen translation The text is already in the video pixels; no forced-track choice removes it PGS can mark composition objects for forced display. A container can mark a track. Those operate at different levels: an unflagged full track can still contain selected forced objects, while a separately authored track can contain only the required passages. The viewing context matters Consider an English-language film with three foreign lines. Its English forced presentation can translate those three lines for an English-speaking audience. A Spanish full subtitle track can translate the complete film. Selecting the Spanish full track is not the same content decision as selecting the English sparse track. The audio language, viewer language and subtitle policy determine the intended choice. A forced label does not inspect the words to confirm that the resource contains only three passages. If a full-dialogue file is labeled as forced, a forced-only policy can end up displaying the whole film's dialogue. Identification and presentation are separate Emby's naming rules allow external resources to be identified as forced. Its subtitle preferences include a forced-only mode. The metadata identifies the intended role; the selected format and route still determine how those passages are rendered. A route incorporating selected text into video produces permanent pixels in that output version. It can begin with a forced track, a full track or another subtitle source. The forcing designation and that processing result remain separate properties. See Also Subtitle track selection Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) Embedded subtitle tracks Default Track Flags References RFC 9559: Matroska container format FFmpeg n8.1: PGS decoder RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-La.title: Subtitle language preferences | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-La.keywords: Subtitle language preferences Subtitle language preferences guide selection through language identifiers, script/region distinctions and the subtitle content role required for viewing. A subtitle language preference tells a player which language the viewer wants to read. It does not determine whether that track contains all dialogue, accessibility captions or just selected passages. The player needs language identity and the intended content role. Language identifiers can be more specific than a name BCP 47 language tags can express language, script and region. For example: Tag Meaning en English en-GB English with a United Kingdom regional distinction zh-Hans Chinese using Simplified script zh-Hant Chinese using Traditional script Script and region are different subtags. A regional label can be associated with a customary script in a library convention, but it is not identical to an explicit script declaration. Containers and naming systems can use other representations, including ISO 639 codes or supported language names. A matching system needs to interpret those schemes rather than compare arbitrary display strings. Emby's external naming documentation describes supported language identification in filenames. The format's cue text remains a separate property from that label. Language matching does not resolve the role Suppose a viewer prefers English and sees these candidates: Candidate Language match Remaining question English dialogue Yes Is dialogue-only content sufficient? English SDH Yes Are sound/speaker descriptions desired? English forced passages Yes Should only the required selected passages appear? Spanish full dialogue No Is another language being explicitly selected? A hearing-impaired preference may distinguish the first two. A forced-only mode can distinguish a sparse required-passage track from a full translation. The selected audio language can also be relevant to a policy that decides when translation is needed. A track title is a useful clue, but incorrect metadata can make the choice disagree with the actual text. Inspecting its contents establishes what the resource supplies. The current viewing choice can override a general preference A viewer can explicitly choose another language for one film. A player can remember that selection. Changing a preferred language and choosing a specific track are different operations with different scope. Emby's preference documentation is the appropriate source for its selection controls. For a surprising result, compare the active choice, remembered selection, language identifiers and role metadata before assuming that the language decoder is broken. See Also Subtitle track selection Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) Forced subtitles Track Language Metadata References RFC 5646: Language tags RFC 9559: Matroska container format RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-SD.title: Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-SD.keywords: Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) SDH subtitles include dialogue and relevant speaker, music and sound information for viewers who cannot rely on the soundtrack. SDH means subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing . The content normally includes dialogue plus sound information needed to understand the scene without relying on the soundtrack. A line such as “I'll be there” can be insufficient when the speaker is off screen or when an approaching sound changes the scene's meaning. Dialogue-only wording Useful additional caption information in an invented scene I'll be there. MAYA: I'll be there. when the speaker is otherwise unclear No spoken line [train approaching] No spoken line [music stops abruptly] when that change matters Did you hear that? A description of the relevant sound prompting the question The goal is meaningful scene information, not indiscriminately labeling every sound. A speaker label can be unnecessary when the picture makes the identity obvious; its value depends on the scene. SDH describes content, not storage An SDH presentation can use SRT, WebVTT, ASS, a bitmap format or a caption service. It can be external, embedded or streamed. A file extension does not determine whether the track contains sound descriptions. Likewise, a track can be in the same language as the dialogue or provide an accessible translation. Language and accessibility role are independent dimensions of selection. A conversion to a simpler text format should preserve speaker and sound information if that is the selected content's purpose. Discarding bracketed descriptions as “non-dialogue” changes what the viewer receives. Layout and timing make the information usable The captions still need to coincide with the relevant speech or sound, remain readable and fit the presentation. Several sounds or speakers can compete for limited caption space. An app's text-size or background preference can improve legibility where the representation permits it. It cannot add a missing sound description to a dialogue-only track. A bitmap's lettering is already drawn; resizing that image is different from reflowing editable text. For Emby, subtitle preferences provide a hearing-impaired selection mode, while external naming identifies SDH resources. The actual track contents establish whether those descriptions are present. Audio description serves another information need An audio-description track narrates relevant visual information for a listener who cannot rely on the picture. SDH supplies relevant audio information in visible captions for a viewer who cannot rely on the sound. A media item can provide both. They are separate content choices rather than alternate names for the same accessibility track. See Also Understanding subtitles and captions Subtitle track selection Subtitle language preferences Audio-Description Tracks References W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-Se.title: Subtitle track selection | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/selection/Subtitle-Se.keywords: Subtitle track selection Subtitle track selection chooses a content track or caption service using language, role, user policy and any explicit or remembered choice. Track selection chooses which subtitle content to present. The same movie can have multiple tracks in one language because they serve different viewing needs. Track in an invented movie Contents English dialogue Spoken dialogue English SDH Dialogue plus useful sound/speaker information English selected passages A small set of necessary foreign-language passages Spanish A translation for Spanish readers Choosing the first “English” entry is therefore not equivalent to choosing the desired role. Metadata gives hints; policy makes a choice Language, title, default/forced flags and accessibility descriptions help distinguish candidates. A container's default flag expresses a preference in its selection model. It is not a command that overrides every user's choice in every app. A user can explicitly select a track, prefer captions for a particular language, request only necessary forced passages, or disable subtitles. A player can also remember a previous selection. The applicable policy determines which of those observations takes priority. Emby's subtitle preferences expose language, subtitle mode and remembered-selection controls. The documentation lists modes including default, smart, forced-only and hearing-impaired. Their presence should not be replaced with an invented universal algorithm for every platform and version. Track identity survives better than its list position A remux can reorder or remove tracks. “Subtitle 2” may consequently identify different content before and after the change. Match language, title, role and codec when comparing the intended choice. An external subtitle and an embedded one can also share a language. Their sources and editions may differ. A remembered selection or explicit override can explain why a viewer gets another resource despite an apparently suitable default. For in-band captions, service identity is another layer. A selected service within video is not necessarily represented by the same numbering as a standalone subtitle track. Rendering follows the selected content Once the track is selected, the route has to deliver and present its representation. An ASS translation and a PGS caption track can impose different work even when both are English. A suitable selection can thus change the playback route. It should not be silently substituted with another content role merely to make the codec simpler. If a conversion is used, it should preserve the intended selected content. An Emby playback comparison is clearest when it records the chosen resource's language/role and actual source, followed by the delivered format. That separates a wrong content choice from a correct choice whose rendering failed. See Also Subtitle language preferences Forced subtitles Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) Default Track Flags References RFC 9559: Matroska container format RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming RFC 5646: Language tags W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles

articles/subtitles/sources/index.html.title: Overview: Subtitle sources | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/index.html.keywords: Overview: Subtitle sources Subtitle sources and matching methods connect available timed content to the edition and language the viewer needs. The programme title is only the beginning of a match. Editing, release timing and language can determine whether an otherwise plausible subtitle fits the actual media. Provider, release-matching, speech-recognition and translation topics describe different ways of obtaining content and the information needed to assess that fit. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Finding subtitle sources Subtitle sources provide caption content through existing media, external releases, providers or authored recognition/translation, with distinct matching and provenance questions. OpenSubtitles OpenSubtitles provides searchable subtitle candidates and file downloads, with separate release-matching, authentication and quota relationships. Subtitle release matching Subtitle release matching compares identity, cut, timing and optional file fingerprints to choose a candidate suited to the actual media edition. Automatic speech recognition for captions ASR estimates spoken text from audio, after which alignment, caption segmentation and content review produce a useful timed-caption resource. Subtitle translation Subtitle translation expresses caption meaning in another language while preserving context, role and a readable timed presentation. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-ASR..title: Automatic speech recognition for captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-ASR..keywords: Automatic speech recognition for captions ASR estimates spoken text from audio, after which alignment, caption segmentation and content review produce a useful timed-caption resource. Automatic speech recognition, or ASR , estimates spoken words from audio. Producing a caption resource additionally requires timing, segmentation into readable cues, and review of the information the viewer needs. Recognition, alignment and caption authoring can be combined in a tool, but they answer different questions: Stage Question Speech recognition Which words were spoken? Alignment/timing Where do those words belong in the audio? Caption segmentation Which words form a displayed cue and interval? Caption editing Which speaker/sound information and corrections are needed? A transcript without timestamps is not yet a timed subtitle. Word timestamps alone are not automatically a readable cue layout. Audio windows provide context A model or processing pipeline can analyze windows with overlap. That gives neighboring windows shared context around a boundary. Take an invented 180-second clip, using 30-second windows and a 25-second hop . Window starts are 0,25,50,75,100,125 and 150 seconds. There are seven windows , each 30 seconds in this example. The processing sees 210 seconds of window content even though the source is 180 seconds. Six adjacent overlaps of five seconds account for the extra 30 seconds. Repeated audio does not mean the final subtitle should repeat the boundary words. The output needs an appropriate merge/alignment strategy. A chosen input sample rate also belongs to the model's requirements. At an illustrative 16 kHz, the 180-second mono clip contains 2,880,000 sample frames . Resampling to a model's expected rate should preserve programme time; changing a rate label without converting the signal would alter duration and pitch. Recognition errors can be easy to miss Suppose the intended sentence is: Please meet me at the station. and the estimated transcript is: Please meet me at station. With whitespace tokenization, the reference has six words . One deleted word gives a word error rate of 1/6 ≈ 16.7% for this defined example. A wrong name or negation can be more consequential than a small average rate suggests. Fluency does not establish that the text matches the audio. The example is not a benchmark of any named model. Music, overlapping speech, accents, unfamiliar names and poor recordings can affect the observation. The appropriate review compares against the audio rather than against a second sentence guessed from the same output. Edited text can need renewed alignment Correcting a word changes the transcript. Existing word timings may need adjustment to the corrected sequence before cues are rebuilt. Cue boundaries should reflect the relevant speech and reading presentation. Arbitrarily putting every recognized word into its own cue can produce a flickering, awkward result. Conversely, a whole-minute transcript in one caption leaves little useful synchronization. A rate or origin change later in the media route also needs to preserve the caption's programme timeline. Accessible captions can require more than speech A dialogue recognizer does not inherently provide useful speaker identity, an off-screen sound description or the significance of music stopping. SDH explains that content role. For Emby, a reviewed generated resource can be supplied as an external supported subtitle with appropriate identification. This is an authored-file workflow, not a declaration that every Emby build includes a particular recognizer or model. See Also Finding subtitle sources Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) Subtitle cues Subtitle translation References wav2vec 2.0: Self-supervised speech recognition W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2

articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Open.title: OpenSubtitles | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Open.keywords: OpenSubtitles OpenSubtitles provides searchable subtitle candidates and file downloads, with separate release-matching, authentication and quota relationships. OpenSubtitles provides subtitle searches and downloads. A search produces candidate records; retrieving the selected subtitle produces a file that a player can read. The service's record identifiers, downloaded file identifiers and the movie's own identity are different things. A candidate appearing in a result list is not evidence that its bytes have already reached the media library. From search evidence to a file The provider's public integration code shows a REST workflow for OpenSubtitles.com alongside distinctions from older service interfaces. API/application identification and any authenticated user session have separate roles. A download can return a temporary resource link. The client then retrieves those bytes and saves the result with its intended media association. Stage Observation Search Candidate matches the supplied identity/language criteria Candidate selection A particular release/role/file is chosen Download authorization The service permits the requested retrieval File retrieval Subtitle bytes arrive Library association and playback The resource is identified and presented for the item Failure at a later stage does not imply that the search found no match. A title match and a file match have different scope OpenSubtitles' published OSHash reference describes a fingerprint built from file size and sample data near the beginning/end. The API uses it as a movie-file matching clue. A hash-associated candidate can be more specific than a title-only result. It is still useful to inspect language, content role and known cue positions. A file fingerprint is not a quality score for translation or sound descriptions. A re-encoded movie can retain the same scene timing while acquiring another byte fingerprint. A same-title extended cut can differ in both content and timing. Release matching separates those cases. Service limits and authentication are operational boundaries Search, download, rate limits and account entitlements can have different rules. A valid user credential does not automatically remove every limit, and a quota error does not make the subtitle format invalid. Those policies can change. The current service/account response and official documentation are the relevant evidence; this article does not hardcode a daily limit or price. Emby's Open Subtitles documentation describes its plugin setup and account association. Learn's concern is the relationship between a found candidate and a successfully available subtitle. Installation and configuration remain in that Support workflow. See Also Subtitle release matching Finding subtitle sources References OpenSubtitles.com: Subtitle service OpenSubtitles: API documentation OpenSubtitles: Official VLSub.com integration source OpenSubtitles: OSHash algorithm reference

articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Rele.title: Subtitle release matching | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Rele.keywords: Subtitle release matching Subtitle release matching compares identity, cut, timing and optional file fingerprints to choose a candidate suited to the actual media edition. A subtitle must match the release being played , not merely the title listed in the library. Different cuts, opening material, recaps, frame playback speeds and episode combinations can change the content timeline. Language is another independent requirement. A perfectly synchronized track in an unsuitable script or role can still be the wrong viewing choice. Combine evidence rather than one label Clue What it helps establish Title/year or series/episode identity The intended work Edition and release description A proposed cut/source relationship Duration and recognizable scene positions Timing correspondence File fingerprint match Association with a particular byte-based release identity Language, forced/SDH and content metadata The intended reading content Several verified cue positions Actual synchronization across the programme A filename's release-group text is an identification clue, not proof. So is a duration: two different edits can have nearly equal total lengths. Compare distinct scenes. A repeated generic sentence is a poor anchor because it can match the wrong moment. OSHash is a sampled file fingerprint The published OpenSubtitles algorithm adds the file size and little-endian 64-bit words from the first and last 64 KiB of a file, keeping the result modulo 2⁶⁴ . The reference specifies the applicable file-size requirements and exact block handling. It is not a full-file cryptographic digest. Its matching role should be described accordingly. For a small arithmetic illustration—not a complete OSHash calculation—take a size term of 200,000 , one word of 2⁶⁴ − 16 , and another word of 48 : (200000 + (2^64 − 16) + 48) mod 2^64 = 200032 = hexadecimal 0000000000030d60 The example shows unsigned wrap/sum behavior. A real fingerprint uses all the required sampled words; replacing it with this three-term sum would not implement the algorithm. File identity and timing identity differ A remux or transcode can change the file's bytes while retaining the same programme timing. A new fingerprint therefore does not automatically require retiming a subtitle. Conversely, an extra 60-second scene can change all later cue positions while earlier ones remain aligned. Edition mismatch explains that piecewise timing relationship; a global duration stretch can damage the earlier section. For an Emby candidate comparison, keep the actual media edition, language/role and sampled cue evidence together. Provider match metadata can prioritize the search, while checking the resulting presentation closes the match to the movie being watched. See Also Subtitle edition mismatches Subtitle timing drift OpenSubtitles Subtitle language preferences References OpenSubtitles: OSHash algorithm reference OpenSubtitles: Official VLSub.com integration source Matroska subtitle mappings

articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Sour.title: Finding subtitle sources | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Sour.keywords: Finding subtitle sources Subtitle sources provide caption content through existing media, external releases, providers or authored recognition/translation, with distinct matching and provenance questions. A usable subtitle begins with the right content for the programme and viewer . Its format and delivery matter afterward. A file can be valid SRT and still be the wrong edit, language, translation or accessibility role. Source What needs checking Existing media track or caption service Intended track/service, timing, styles and resources External release file Edition, language, role and integrity Subtitle provider Candidate identity, release match and successful download Human-authored transcript/translation Content accuracy, timing and presentation Speech recognition output Recognized wording, alignment and caption authoring Automated translation Meaning/context, retained timing and readable layout Those sources can produce similar filenames while having different provenance. Match the programme before changing timing Title/year or episode identity is an initial search key. It does not establish an exact cut. Release details, duration and a provider's supported file fingerprint can strengthen the match. Compare recognizable lines near the beginning, middle and end. A fixed difference suggests an offset; progressive change or a scene-boundary step suggests other relationships. Release matching considers those candidate clues without replacing the timing analysis. A subtitle already inside the matching media can provide useful timing evidence, but selecting another language or role still changes the content. An extracted dialogue track does not become SDH because it was found locally. Retain the content's role and provenance A sparse forced-passage track and a complete dialogue translation can both be English. A transcript with speaker/sound descriptions serves another need from plain spoken-word text. Provider metadata, filenames and authored records can describe those distinctions. The actual wording establishes whether they are present. Keeping the source description helps explain why two candidates differ. For Emby, manual and automatic downloads cover the configured provider workflows; external naming covers identification. These instructions are separate from judging which candidate fits the edition being played. Generated content needs its own review Speech recognition estimates spoken words from audio. Translation expresses meaning in another language. Neither inherently reconstructs a full accessible caption presentation, and both can need content and timing work. Extraction from a caption service instead interprets coded content already present in the source. OCR recognizes pictured letters. Choosing the appropriate operation avoids asking a simple extraction tool to recover information its input never contained.
