articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Tran.title: Subtitle translation | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/sources/Subtitle-Tran.keywords: Subtitle translation Subtitle translation expresses caption meaning in another language while preserving context, role and a readable timed presentation. Subtitle translation expresses the source content in another language. It must preserve the meaning of the scene and provide a useful timed reading presentation , rather than merely replace words independently. Dialogue can be split across several cues. A pronoun, an incomplete phrase or an ambiguous word can need context from the neighboring cues and the picture. Cue boundaries are not sentence boundaries Consider an invented English line mentioning “the bank”. The scene can make that a river bank or a financial institution. A translation system using only those two words has less evidence than a translator considering the surrounding dialogue and scene. A sentence split into two captions has the same problem. Translating each fragment independently can select incompatible wording, repeat material or lose the intended reference. Retain enough surrounding context, then decide how the translated sentence should be distributed into cues. That distribution need not preserve every original line break. The translated length can change A cue with unchanged start/end retains its available reading interval. A longer translated sentence can require different wrapping, condensation or timing decisions. For an invented cue lasting 2.5 seconds , a 40-character translation has 16 characters per second under that simple counting convention. A 70-character version has 28 . These are descriptive example rates, not universal readability limits or a substitute for considering script, audience and scene. Property Translation question Meaning Are negation, names, numbers and intent preserved? Cue interval Does the text appear with the relevant scene/speech? Length and breaks Can the intended audience read the presentation? Language/script Does the output identify and encode the intended text? Content role Are sound/speaker descriptions retained where required? Changing the target language label does not change the bytes or prove that the translated wording is correct. Accessibility content also needs translation A selected SDH track can contain dialogue, speaker labels and meaningful sound descriptions. Removing the descriptions because they are not spoken changes the resource's purpose. Likewise, a forced-passage resource should remain the intended subset unless a fuller track is deliberately authored. Translation and content selection are independent decisions. Names and quoted text can also retain another script inside the target language. Bidirectional rendering , Unicode and suitable fonts remain part of the presentation. For Emby, the translated file needs a truthful language/role association and matching edition timing. The automatic/manual download or authoring route supplies a resource; reviewing its content and presentation establishes the translation the viewer actually receives. See Also Finding subtitle sources Automatic speech recognition for captions Right-to-left subtitles Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) Subtitle cues References W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.title: Overview: Extraction and conversion | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.keywords: Overview: Extraction and conversion Subtitle extraction, conversion and OCR perform different changes to the location or representation of timed content. Extraction obtains a subtitle representation from its surrounding source. Conversion changes its format, while OCR recognizes characters from graphical subtitles. Naming the operation precisely helps establish which timing, styling or textual information is being preserved and which part needs checking in the result. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle extraction Subtitle extraction recovers a selected subtitle track or service into another representation while preserving the timing and configuration needed to interpret it. Subtitle format conversion Subtitle format conversion translates timing, content and presentation from one subtitle model into another with explicit choices about what the target can represent. Subtitle OCR Subtitle OCR recognizes character text from subtitle graphics and combines it with recovered timing and reviewed reading order. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.title: Subtitle format conversion | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.keywords: Subtitle format conversion Subtitle format conversion translates timing, content and presentation from one subtitle model into another with explicit choices about what the target can represent. Subtitle conversion interprets one format's model and writes another. A good conversion identifies the required content, timing and presentation , then determines which of those the target can represent. Changing an extension does not perform that interpretation. Nor does preserving the sentence establish that its full visual behavior survived. Conversion Work and possible information change Simple text to another simple text format Re-express cue syntax and timing; preserve supported markup Styled text to plain text Retain words/intervals while reducing presentation instructions Text to bitmap Shape and render with selected fonts and geometry Bitmap to another bitmap representation Repackage/recode graphics, palette, placement and updates Bitmap to character text Recognize/transcribe words, then author the target timing and layout A moving sign and a plain-text cue Imagine an ASS event from 12.5 to 15 seconds with this override, using a previously declared style and script plane: {\an7\move(160,90,480,90,0,1000)}LAST TRAIN The anchor moves during the event's first second. A simple SRT output can retain: 1 00:00:12,500 --> 00:00:15,000 LAST TRAIN The words and interval match. The target does not contain an equivalent moving anchor, script plane or complete style. It normally presents the words using its own supported caption layout. This can be an appropriate result when readable dialogue is the goal. It is a different result when the intended translation must remain attached to a moving sign. Precision and origin can change the time description A target with millisecond times and a source with centisecond times use different representations. Converting to finer timestamp precision does not recover timing detail that the source never supplied. Moving from a container or segmented stream into a standalone file also requires resolving the original time base and origin. A cue local to one segment must be placed on the final programme timeline rather than copied to movie time zero. Compare resolved times before examining tiny text-format rounding differences. A several-second shift usually has another cause. Internal timing is not just the event boundary A styled event can have motion, fades or karaoke durations inside its active interval. If a rate correction changes a programme's time scale, those internal instructions may need the same transformation. Extending an event's end while leaving a one-second movement unchanged creates a longer event containing the original-speed movement. That differs from slowing the whole presentation proportionally. A target unable to express internal timing needs another preservation choice, such as simpler static text or rendered images. It should not claim to preserve an animation merely because its first and last cue times were copied. The target renderer needs its resources Retaining a font-family name does not bundle the font face. Retaining a graphics object's palette indices does not recreate an omitted palette. Resource handling and track conversion need to agree on what reaches the consumer. For an Emby route converting subtitles for a selected app, assess the delivered track's wording, resolved intervals and intended appearance separately. A conversion preserving a readable sentence can be useful while still producing a different typeset result. See Also Subtitle extraction Subtitle OCR Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitles (ASS) Karaoke subtitle timing Subtitle timestamps References Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 libass: ASS file format guide Aegisub: ASS override tags

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.title: Subtitle extraction | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.keywords: Subtitle extraction Subtitle extraction recovers a selected subtitle track or service into another representation while preserving the timing and configuration needed to interpret it. Subtitle extraction takes a selected subtitle track or service out of its current packaging. It can produce a standalone subtitle file or feed another processing stage. The first decision is which component to extract . Two tracks can share a language while containing different dialogue, sound descriptions or selected foreign passages. A numeric track index alone is not a durable identity if another file's tracks were reordered. Reconstructing a standalone text cue Suppose an embedded Matroska UTF-8 subtitle block has this information: Container information Value Presentation position 12,500 units Duration 2,500 units Time scale in this example 1,000 units per second Payload The platform is empty. A standalone SRT representation reconstructs the interval: 1 00:00:12,500 --> 00:00:15,000 The platform is empty. The cue number is created for the output file. Its start and end come from the recovered presentation time and duration. Global track offsets or applicable edit mappings must be included before writing the final programme positions. The output file bytes differ from the container block, but the timed sentence can remain equivalent. Container timing and standalone timestamp text are different ways to describe the same interval. Global configuration must come with the packets Extracted representation Context needed for a useful result ASS script Global script/style section and event fields VobSub pair Binary subpictures plus indexing/palette/display configuration PGS stream Graphics segments and their applicable timed state In-band caption service Selected service and its recovered presentation commands Text relying on a named face Font resources available at the eventual renderer Dumping isolated packet bytes can omit the information that made them meaningful. A small graphics update can refer to an object or palette transmitted earlier. An ASS event can refer to a style defined in track configuration. Font attachments are supporting resources, not ordinary timed subtitle packets. They may need their own selection when preparing a reusable styled subtitle. Extraction and recognition recover different things Extracting PGS retains graphics. Getting SRT words from those graphics requires OCR or transcription. Extracting ASS can retain styled events; writing only its visible wording into SRT is a conversion with a narrower presentation model. Likewise, rendering subtitles into video is not extraction. The result stores their appearance in the new picture sequence rather than a separate subtitle resource. For an Emby library, an external subtitle produced from an embedded track should be checked against the same selected content and movie timeline. Compare a few known cues, their language/role and any styling resources. See Also Embedded subtitle tracks Subtitle format conversion Subtitle OCR Matroska Attachments References FFmpeg: Streamcopy, conversion and stream selection Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings RFC 9559: Matroska container format

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.title: Subtitle OCR | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/extr.keywords: Subtitle OCR Subtitle OCR recognizes character text from subtitle graphics and combines it with recovered timing and reviewed reading order. OCR, optical character recognition , turns pictured letters into character text. For subtitle graphics, it normally follows decoding the image and its palette. The recognition result is then combined with the recovered subtitle intervals. It does not extract a hidden text sentence from PGS or DVDSub. It estimates characters from the visible shapes. Prepare the actual lettering for recognition A subtitle decoder first reconstructs the image from pixel runs, palette and transparency. A useful OCR input then needs the appropriate region, readable contrast and suitable treatment of its outline/background. White lettering on a transparent background illustrates the problem. Blending it onto a white page can remove the contrast needed to recognize the fill. Choosing a suitable background, retaining a useful outline or transforming the image can yield a more legible input. Tesseract's quality documentation discusses alpha handling, scaling, noise, borders, skew and page-segmentation assumptions. An OCR engine expecting a full scanned page can interpret a small subtitle line differently from one configured for that kind of region. The selected language/model affects character possibilities. A Latin-only assumption is a poor starting point for an Arabic, Hebrew or CJK caption. Mixed scripts and numerals require particular attention. The image's timing comes from the subtitle stream If a decoded presentation is active from 12.5 to 15 seconds , those times are available independently of whether OCR reads its words correctly. Recognition does not need to invent a new speech-alignment time for every image. The difficult cases are updates: an image can change while part of the line remains, or another line can be added. Treating each update as a completely new sentence can create duplicates. Conversely, collapsing two similar images can lose a word that actually changed. A converter must resolve the source's display state and intervals, then decide how to represent them as text cues. A small error can change the meaning Take this invented reference and recognition output: Reference: Room 101 OCR: Room IOI The output looks like the same short label, but three characters have changed from digits to letters. It is not reliable navigation text. Using a character edit-distance comparison that includes the space, the reference has 8 characters . Three substitutions give a 37.5% character error rate : CER = (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference characters = 3 / 8 = 0.375 With whitespace-separated words, the reference has two words . One substituted word gives a 50% word error rate . These are measures for this defined example, not an OCR-engine benchmark. Longer dialogue can have a low average error score while still containing a wrong name, negation or number. A recognition confidence value is another engine-specific observation; it is not automatically a calibrated probability that the displayed sentence is correct. Review content and order before saving it Useful review targets include names, addresses, digits, punctuation, accented letters, speaker labels and sound descriptions. Compare against the decoded image, not just the neighboring text generated by the same recognizer. Multi-line reading order matters. Bidirectional text also needs logical character order rather than a string assembled by reversing visually located glyphs. The new text should use an intentional character encoding . Saving correctly recognized text through an unsuitable legacy encoding can lose characters after recognition succeeded. For Emby, OCR can make a bitmap subtitle available as an editable text representation for an appropriate route. The new file still needs its matched edition, retained intervals and content review. See Also Bitmap subtitles Subtitle extraction Subtitle character encoding Right-to-left subtitles Subtitle format conversion References Tesseract: Improving recognition quality Tesseract: Output formats and language selection Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings Unicode UAX 9: Bidirectional Algorithm

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/inde.title: Overview: Subtitle storage and delivery | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/inde.keywords: Overview: Subtitle storage and delivery Subtitle storage and delivery connect a timed representation to the player through files, container tracks or stream signaling. A subtitle's format and its location answer different questions. The same kind of text may be stored separately, embedded in a container or delivered through a streaming arrangement. This area follows that path and the extraction or conversion operations used when a different representation is needed. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle transports Subtitle transport determines where subtitle data travels and how its identification, timing and resources reach the renderer. Subtitle locations Subtitle locations describe whether timed content is carried separately, within a media container or in-band with another stream. Subtitle support in media containers Container subtitle support requires a defined codec mapping and preserved timing/configuration, while player support determines whether that representation can be presented. Streaming subtitle transports Streaming subtitle transports relate timed text to segmented HLS or MPEG-DASH presentations. Extraction and conversion Subtitle extraction, conversion and OCR perform different changes to the location or representation of timed content. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.title: Overview: Subtitle locations | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.keywords: Overview: Subtitle locations Subtitle locations describe whether timed content is carried separately, within a media container or in-band with another stream. An external file has its own path and matching relationship. An embedded track belongs to the container, while in-band captions use another relationship with the media signal. The distinction matters when Emby discovers, selects or extracts a subtitle and when the receiving player needs to obtain it. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> External subtitle files An external subtitle file is a separate subtitle resource associated with a media item through naming or other library metadata. Embedded subtitle tracks An embedded subtitle track is a separately described timed component inside a media container rather than permanent text in the video pixels. In-band captions In-band captions are caption data carried within another media elementary stream and must be extracted and interpreted separately from its visible pictures. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.title: Embedded subtitle tracks | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.keywords: Embedded subtitle tracks An embedded subtitle track is a separately described timed component inside a media container rather than permanent text in the video pixels. An embedded subtitle track is stored within a media container alongside video, audio and other tracks. It remains a separate timed component . A subtitle switch can therefore enable or disable it when the player supports that representation. Text already incorporated into video pixels is another case. It has no separately selectable subtitle track to remove. A container can describe several choices Track in an invented file Representation Role Video 1 Encoded pictures Main movie Subtitle 1 SRT-style UTF-8 text English dialogue Subtitle 2 PGS graphics English captions with sound descriptions Both subtitle tracks can share the video's programme timeline. Their language and title describe selection choices; their codecs describe how the chosen data is decoded and rendered. Merely storing an unused subtitle track does not mean it must be rendered. For an Emby comparison, inspect the selected subtitle, rather than treating every track in the file as an active processing requirement. Timing and configuration are container relationships The container describes track identity and applicable timestamps or durations. Codec-specific configuration can supply global styles, display geometry or other interpretation data. For Matroska's SRT mapping, the timed block contains UTF-8 cue text while container time and duration provide its interval. The standalone SRT counter and timestamp line do not need to appear as literal text inside that block. ASS can carry global script/styles as configuration. A graphics stream can use prior palette/object state. A raw packet dump without that context is not necessarily a complete independently playable subtitle. A track is not a font attachment A font resource can be stored separately from the timed track as a supporting container attachment. Retaining video, audio and ASS while dropping its intended fonts can preserve all timed track entries and still change the appearance. Track indices can also change during remuxing. Removing an earlier track can make “track 2” refer to another component. Language, title, codec and stable identifiers help compare the intended track across files. A supported remux can omit or retain a subtitle without reconstructing the video pictures. Rendering that subtitle into a new video is a different operation: it changes the pictures and introduces the video encoding work needed for the output. See Also Streams and Tracks Subtitle support in media containers Subtitle extraction Subtitle font attachments References RFC 9559: Matroska container format Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings MPEG: Timed text in ISO base media files, ISO/IEC 14496-30

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.title: External subtitle files | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.keywords: External subtitle files An external subtitle file is a separate subtitle resource associated with a media item through naming or other library metadata. An external subtitle lives beside or separately from the movie rather than inside its media container. A player or library associates that resource with the item, then reads and presents the chosen subtitle. That separation is useful when a translation is added or corrected: the video and audio file can stay intact while the subtitle resource changes. Association supplies information the format may omit Information Possible source Which movie or episode this file accompanies Filename association or a library record Language Naming, subtitle metadata or library metadata Content role, such as SDH or selected foreign dialogue Naming/flags and the actual contents Cue wording and intervals The subtitle file's own data Display styles or images The subtitle representation and its resources A simple SRT carries cue text and times, but does not inherently identify the exact movie edition. A language label is also not evidence that its sentences match the cut being played. Emby's naming documentation specifies the association and language/role conventions for external subtitles. Those are identification rules; they do not rewrite the cue times or inspect whether a translation is accurate. The timeline still belongs to the matching programme Suppose a sidecar's first line begins at 12.5 seconds. The player interprets it on the applicable movie timeline. Selecting the file does not automatically discover a missing opening logo and add an offset. A different release can have the same title and language but an extra scene. The resulting edition mismatch can require different corrections in different sections, even though the library found the file successfully. Replacing a sidecar likewise does not imply that every active viewing session has already loaded the replacement. Resource discovery and the bytes currently being consumed are distinct observations. Some external presentations use companion resources VobSub commonly uses a binary SUB plus an IDX carrying indexing/configuration. Styled text can depend on fonts. “External” does not mean “one self-contained text document.” When those resources are needed, they must be available to the consumer that interprets the presentation. Providing an index but not its binary data, or a named font without a usable face, leaves a different missing boundary. An Emby route can deliver the selected sidecar in an accepted representation or render it upstream when required. The external location makes the file separately manageable; format and client capabilities determine how it becomes visible. See Also Embedded subtitle tracks Subtitle edition mismatches SubRip subtitles (SRT) References Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.title: In-band captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/loca.keywords: In-band captions In-band captions are caption data carried within another media elementary stream and must be extracted and interpreted separately from its visible pictures. In-band captions travel inside another elementary stream , commonly video. A media inspector can therefore find caption services within a video track even when the container lists no separate subtitle track. The caption data is still separate information from the picture's visible pixels. A consumer extracts its commands/characters and renders the resulting caption presentation. The carrying layer matters ATSC's MPEG-2 video provisions define caption carriage in video user data. Other specified video paths use supplemental enhancement information, or SEI , to carry registered caption data. The applicable video and carriage standard defines the packet structure. That is different from a separately multiplexed subtitle elementary stream, such as a DVB subtitle service in a transport stream. Both are within the delivered media, but only the former is in-band within the other elementary stream . The term “embedded” is sometimes used loosely for either situation. Naming the precise carrying layer avoids that ambiguity. Service selection happens after discovering caption data A video stream can contain more than one caption service. The consumer must identify the intended service, recover its timed data and interpret its presentation model. Observation What it establishes Video stream contains caption data A caption payload exists in that carrying stream Caption service is selected A particular content service was chosen Caption commands are decoded The service's presentation state was reconstructed Captions are visible The state was successfully drawn/composed at the required time One observation does not substitute for the next. Successfully decoding the video picture, for example, does not prove that caption commands were extracted. Re-encoding pictures does not automatically preserve the payload A video decoder can output frames without exposing caption information to the subsequent encoder. An encoder rebuilding video from those frames cannot recover hidden caption data simply by looking at the picture. A conversion can preserve/reinsert a supported caption payload, extract it into another timed representation, or render it into the video. These are deliberate routes with different resulting properties. For an Emby recording or streamed source, investigate the caption service and the actual delivered output. A source with captions and a converted output without them can both have correct-looking video. The comparison needs to include the data carried with the video, rather than only its visible frames. HLS also distinguishes separate subtitle renditions from identified closed-caption services carried in media. A caption service declaration is not a URL to an external WebVTT file. See Also Embedded subtitle tracks Understanding subtitles and captions Subtitles in HLS Packet Timestamps References ATSC A/53 Part 4: MPEG-2 video and caption user data DASH-IF IOP Part 9 v5.0.0: Subtitles and captions RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.title: Overview: Streaming subtitle transports | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.keywords: Overview: Streaming subtitle transports Streaming subtitle transports relate timed text to segmented HLS or MPEG-DASH presentations. A subtitle stream must remain aligned with the presentation's media timeline as segments are selected and delivered. HLS and MPEG-DASH provide their own signaling and transport conventions for that job. Their pages connect cue timing and track selection to the streaming representation received by the player. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitles in HLS HLS can deliver separately selected WebVTT subtitle renditions whose cue times must be mapped to the shared media timeline. Timed text in MPEG-DASH MPEG-DASH describes selectable timed-text representations and maps their sample timelines into periods on the presentation timeline. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming DASH-IF IOP Part 9 v5.0.0: Subtitles and captions

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.title: Timed text in MPEG-DASH | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.keywords: Timed text in MPEG-DASH MPEG-DASH describes selectable timed-text representations and maps their sample timelines into periods on the presentation timeline. MPEG-DASH can describe timed text alongside its video and audio representations. A text Adaptation Set identifies the content role and language, while its representations and segment descriptions tell the client what to retrieve and interpret. The subtitle's representation can use TTML/IMSC or WebVTT carriage. The exact codec/profile declaration matters: “an MP4 segment” identifies the container family, not the timed-text model inside it. A text adaptation set describes a choice This original XML excerpt illustrates one text representation within a period. It omits the surrounding MPD and video/audio sets: <Period start="PT600S"> <AdaptationSet lang="en" mimeType="application/mp4" codecs="stpp.ttml.im1t"> <Role schemeIdUri="urn:mpeg:dash:role:2011" value="subtitle"/> <Representation id="english" bandwidth="4000"> <SegmentTemplate timescale="1000" presentationTimeOffset="1000000" initialization="text-init.mp4" media="text-$Time$.m4s"> <SegmentTimeline> <S t="1000000" d="6000" r="1"/> </SegmentTimeline> </SegmentTemplate> </Representation> </AdaptationSet> </Period> The codec identifier describes an IMSC text carriage profile, not every possible TTML feature. The example's language is English and its role is subtitle content. The segment description uses a 1,000-unit-per-second time scale and two six-second intervals. DASH-IF's published profiles distinguish stpp -based XML timed text from wvtt WebVTT samples. Caption accessibility roles can supply additional selection information. A client still needs to implement the declared representation. A sample timeline is mapped to the period A stored sample time can be far from zero even when the period begins at a convenient programme position. presentationTimeOffset , or PTO, establishes which sample-timeline point corresponds to the period start. Using sample time q and timescale f: presentation time = period start + (q − PTO) / f In the example, a sample position of 1,002,500 maps to: 600 + (1,002,500 − 1,000,000) / 1,000 = 600 + 2.5 = 602.5 seconds Sample position Position within period Presentation position 1,000,000 0 s 600 s 1,002,500 2.5 s 602.5 s 1,006,000 6 s 606 s PTO is measured in the representation's units, not directly in seconds. Subtracting it after dividing only the sample position, or adding it instead of subtracting, produces a different origin. Segment numbers and URI values identify retrieved resources. They do not replace the sample timestamps within those resources. A text document can contain its own cue timing The calculation above describes the sample timeline mapping . An XML timed-text sample can contain a document with its own begin/end expressions, nested timing and profile rules. Its internal cue intervals must be interpreted using the applicable carriage/profile relationship. That is why extracting XML and treating every begin as an absolute whole-movie timestamp can fail. TTML timing resolves the document's internal relationships; the delivery model places the resulting presentation in its period. A sample's interval can also bound what the client presents. A cue described outside the applicable period or sample context is not automatically an instruction to continue indefinitely into later periods. Period boundaries are presentation boundaries A presentation can move into another period with a different origin relationship or representation. A caption active around that transition needs appropriate representation in the retained intervals. The client must distinguish retained common content from a fresh timeline. Carrying an old PTO forward blindly can move otherwise valid subtitle data into another scene. A live stream adds availability timing : when a segment can be requested is not the same quantity as when its subtitle is shown. Wall-clock availability, sample timestamps and the player's selected presentation delay describe different relationships. For an Emby route consuming or producing a DASH presentation, inspect the actual subtitle representation and its period mapping. A source file's correct standalone cue times do not establish that the segmented delivery preserved the same programme origin. See Also Subtitles in HLS IMSC timed text Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) Subtitle timestamps References DASH-IF IOP Part 9 v5.0.0: Subtitles and captions DASH-IF: Restricted timing model MPEG: Timed text in ISO base media files, ISO/IEC 14496-30 W3C IMSC Text Profile 1.3

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.title: Subtitles in HLS | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/stre.keywords: Subtitles in HLS HLS can deliver separately selected WebVTT subtitle renditions whose cue times must be mapped to the shared media timeline. HLS can deliver subtitles separately from video and audio. In the WebVTT route, the presentation's main playlist identifies subtitle renditions, and each chosen rendition has its own media playlist and subtitle segments. This keeps selection separate from video pixels. A viewer can choose a language while continuing to use a compatible video rendition. The playlist connects the choices Here is an illustrative main-playlist excerpt, not a complete playable presentation: #EXT-X-MEDIA:TYPE=SUBTITLES,GROUP-ID="subs",NAME="English",LANGUAGE="en",AUTOSELECT=YES,DEFAULT=YES,URI="english.m3u8" #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2400000,SUBTITLES="subs" video.m3u8 The SUBTITLES attribute links the video variant to the group named subs . The URI on the media entry points to that subtitle rendition's playlist. NAME is a displayed identifier; LANGUAGE describes its language. They are not its cue text. Those attributes help a client select a rendition. They do not remove its need to read the subtitle format or synchronize the cues. Map the cue clock to the media clock RFC 8216 defines an X-TIMESTAMP-MAP header for WebVTT synchronization. It relates a WebVTT local time to an MPEG-2/PES timestamp on a 90,000-tick-per-second scale. Take this original WebVTT segment example: WEBVTT X-TIMESTAMP-MAP=LOCAL:00:00:00.000,MPEGTS:900000 00:00:02.500 --> 00:00:05.000 The platform is empty. The mapping makes local zero correspond to 900,000/90,000 = 10 seconds on the media clock. The cue therefore corresponds to media time 12.5 through 15 seconds . mapped time = MPEGTS / 90000 + (cue time − LOCAL) start = 900000 / 90000 + (2.5 − 0) = 12.5 s end = 900000 / 90000 + (5.0 − 0) = 15.0 s The shared media timeline can itself have an origin relative to a player's programme time. The map is a relationship between clocks, not necessarily a claim that the movie began at timestamp zero. RFC 8216 recommends providing this map in the WebVTT header. Without it, its specified fallback maps WebVTT zero to MPEG timestamp zero. An application that assumes a different origin can produce a constant timing error even when every cue timestamp parses correctly. A cue can span a segment boundary Suppose a cue is active from programme time 5.5 to 7 seconds , while two subtitle segments cover 0–6 and 6–12 . The cue is relevant to both segment intervals. RFC 8216 requires a WebVTT segment to include the cues needed during its interval with their complete display times , even when part of a cue extends outside that segment. It should not become two independently authored sentences whose times were arbitrarily clipped to 6 seconds. Correct assembly and presentation avoid a gap, duplicate display or reset at the boundary. A segment with no active cues is a legitimate interval without subtitles. It is different from a missing segment that should have supplied a caption. Long-running streams can cross timestamp wrap The MPEG/PES timestamp count is 33 bits. Its raw value wraps after 2³³ ticks , about 26.5 hours on the 90 kHz scale. Cue clocks and other timeline values do not necessarily wrap at the same point. For a teaching example, the local-zero mapping is one second before wrap, at 2³³ − 90,000 . A cue two seconds later belongs at the unwrapped count 2³³ + 90,000 , although its raw 33-bit value is 90,000 . Subtracting raw values without the appropriate cycle relationship would turn a nearby later cue into an apparently remote earlier one. A client needs wrap-aware synchronization and the applicable discontinuity/timeline context. Separate subtitles and in-band caption services HLS uses TYPE=SUBTITLES for a separately described subtitle rendition. A TYPE=CLOSED-CAPTIONS entry instead identifies a service carried in media, such as a supported caption channel or digital service. It does not supply a separate WebVTT playlist URI. For an Emby route using HLS, identify the actual subtitle delivery selected by that route. Compatible video can be retained while text is delivered separately or converted into an accepted representation. Another route may incorporate subtitles into video, in which case the separate language playlist is no longer the mechanism producing the visible lettering. See Also WebVTT subtitles In-band captions Subtitle timestamps Subtitle track selection References RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming W3C WebVTT, May 2026 Candidate Recommendation Draft Apple: HLS authoring specification

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/Subt.title: Subtitle support in media containers | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/Subt.keywords: Subtitle support in media containers Container subtitle support requires a defined codec mapping and preserved timing/configuration, while player support determines whether that representation can be presented. A container needs a defined way to identify a subtitle codec, store its payloads, and describe their timing and configuration. A player then needs to interpret that mapping and present the recovered subtitle. Those are two compatibility boundaries . A valid subtitle track can be inside a valid media file without every player supporting it. Examples of defined mappings Container/framework Subtitle representation or identifier Interpretation Matroska S_TEXT/UTF8 SRT-style text, with container cue timing Matroska S_TEXT/ASS ASS event payloads and global script/style configuration Matroska S_HDMV/PGS Presentation-graphics segments ISO base media / MP4 tx3g 3GPP timed text ISO base media / MP4 wvtt WebVTT sample carriage ISO base media / MP4 stpp family XML timed-text carriage with applicable profile identification MPEG transport stream DVB subtitle service Timed subtitle segments plus service signaling This is a set of mapping examples, not a product support matrix. Container brands, profile requirements and the intended receiving system can impose additional restrictions. Changing a filename extension does not construct these structures. Copying arbitrary SRT bytes into an MP4 track also does not make them a conforming tx3g , wvtt or stpp sample. The same sentence can be packaged differently A standalone SRT gives “The platform is empty” its start and end in a text timestamp line. Matroska can store the wording in a UTF-8 subtitle block, with the block timestamp/duration representing the interval. Those literal bytes differ while the timed sentence can remain equivalent. A muxer writes the target mapping; an extractor can reconstruct the standalone cue. For ASS or graphics, global styles, palette/object state and supporting resources also matter. Moving only the visible text or only selected binary packets can discard interpretation information. Playback support has another scope An Emby route considers the selected app's container, codec and subtitle requirements. A container readable by the app can still contain a subtitle that needs conversion or upstream rendering. Conversely, compatible video can remain unchanged while a separate subtitle conversion supplies an accepted format. A remux to another container preserves a subtitle only if the output has a suitable mapping and the necessary configuration is retained. It does not turn a PGS image into character text. It also does not make a reader implement a format it previously could not render. See Also Subtitle formats explained Embedded subtitle tracks Matroska: MKV and MKA MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS References Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings MPEG: Timed text in ISO base media files, ISO/IEC 14496-30 DASH-IF IOP Part 9 v5.0.0: Subtitles and captions RFC 9559: Matroska container format

articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/Subt.title: Subtitle transports | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/storage-delivery/Subt.keywords: Subtitle transports Subtitle transport determines where subtitle data travels and how its identification, timing and resources reach the renderer. The same subtitle sentence can arrive in a file next to a movie, in a track within the movie, or in a separate streaming rendition. Transport describes that carriage. The subtitle format describes the data being carried. Changing the carriage can leave the wording and appearance intact. It can also require a format conversion, a new timeline mapping or a different renderer. Those are separate operations rather than consequences of the word “streaming” alone. The routes carry different relationships Route Where the subtitle information is found External file A separate resource associated with the media Embedded track A separately described timed component in a container In-band captions Caption data within another elementary stream, commonly video Streaming rendition A selected resource/track described by a streaming manifest None of those descriptions says whether the visible content is character text or graphics. Nor does “embedded” mean that subtitle pixels have been permanently painted into the video. The renderer needs more than a payload A sentence without its start and end times is no longer the same timed presentation. A palette-indexed picture without its palette cannot be interpreted correctly. An ASS event can depend on global styles and font resources. The delivered representation therefore needs its applicable configuration, identity and time mapping. For an embedded track, the container can supply times while the payload supplies text. For streaming text, a segment-local clock may need mapping to the shared programme clock. A transport conversion must preserve the meaning of those relationships even when their storage changes. Copying the literal standalone timestamp line into a container payload is not equivalent to setting that container's presentation timestamp. Carriage and video processing are separate decisions An Emby app may receive compatible video alongside separately delivered subtitles. A subtitle conversion can change the text delivery without changing the encoded video. If the selected route instead needs subtitle pixels incorporated into the pictures, rendering and video encoding enter the path. Direct Play, Direct Stream and transcoding describe the media-delivery choices. The selected track and its renderer explain the subtitle work within that route. See Also External subtitle files Embedded subtitle tracks In-band captions Subtitles in HLS Timed text in MPEG-DASH References Matroska: Subtitle codec mappings RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming DASH-IF IOP Part 9 v5.0.0: Subtitles and captions ATSC A/53 Part 4: MPEG-2 video and caption user data

articles/subtitles/Subtitle-Fundamentals.title: Understanding subtitles and captions | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/Subtitle-Fundamentals.keywords: Understanding subtitles and captions Subtitles and captions present timed language and sound information as selectable tracks or as part of the video picture. A movie's spoken dialogue, a translation of that dialogue, and a caption such as [door slams] communicate different things. Subtitles and captions put that information on the programme's timeline so a viewer can read it when it matters. In common usage, subtitles often means dialogue or translation. Captions often includes the speech and meaningful sound information needed by a viewer who cannot hear the soundtrack: speaker identity, music, and sound effects. Terminology varies between countries and delivery systems, so the contents of a track are more informative than its label alone. Three independent questions about the words on screen Question Examples What information is included? Translated dialogue; original-language dialogue; speech plus meaningful sound cues How is it represented? Characters and styling instructions; pre-rendered images How does it reach the picture? A separate selectable track; permanently incorporated into the video A text subtitle is not automatically a translation, and an image subtitle is not automatically permanent. A disc's bitmap subtitle track can be switched on or off because its images remain separate from the movie pictures. “Closed” normally describes captions available as a separate presentation the viewer can enable. “Open” captions are presented as part of the picture and cannot be removed with a subtitle switch. The caption's wording and the mechanism for presenting it are different properties. A track supplies content; a cue supplies an interval A subtitle track is a separately described sequence. It can have a language, title and selection flags. A cue is one timed item within that sequence: for example, a sentence intended to appear from 12.5 to 15 seconds. The player combines the chosen track with the chosen audio and video. An English movie can have an English caption track and a Spanish translation track without duplicating its picture. Choosing another track changes which sequence is presented. The stored cue also needs presentation. For text, a renderer selects glyphs, lays out the line and draws it. For images, it decodes and positions the supplied graphics. Either result can be composed over video by the app, or incorporated into encoded video upstream when that route requires it. What a viewer can infer from the selection Suppose a film lists these three entries: Track description Intended content English Dialogue in English English SDH Dialogue plus useful speaker and sound descriptions Spanish, forced Selected passages needed for the intended viewing context Those descriptions help select content. They do not identify the subtitle format or guarantee the exact selection policy of every player. A track labeled “forced” might contain only particular passages; another representation can flag selected events within a fuller track. A permanent on-screen translation is a separate situation. For Emby, subtitle preferences describe the user's selection policy, while subtitle naming explains identification of external files. This Learn section explains the data and processing behind that selection. A correctly identified language can still refer to a different edit of the movie, and a correctly timed track can require a renderer capable of its format. See Also Subtitle formats explained Subtitle cues Streams and Tracks References W3C WAI: Captions and subtitles W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 Matroska: Subtitle storage and codec mappings

articles/subtitles/timing/index.html.title: Overview: Timing and synchronization | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/index.html.keywords: Overview: Timing and synchronization Subtitle timing places cues on the media timeline and distinguishes offsets, drift and edition-specific mismatches. If every cue is late by the same amount, the timing problem differs from one that grows as the programme continues. Frame-based timing introduces another relationship, and a differently edited edition may resist a single correction altogether. This branch gives those symptoms distinct names and connects them to the cue and timestamp representation. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Subtitle cues A subtitle cue is a timed presentation item whose active interval and content determine what a renderer presents at a media instant. Subtitle timestamps Subtitle timestamps express presentation positions whose meaning depends on their syntax, unit, time base and timeline origin. Subtitle time offsets A subtitle time offset moves all applicable cue boundaries by the same amount without changing the cue durations or spacing. Subtitle timing drift Subtitle timing drift is a growing synchronization difference caused by a time-scale mismatch or another changing relationship between subtitles and the programme. Frame-based subtitle timing Frame-based subtitle timing maps numbered frames to presentation time using the correct rate, frame origin and boundary convention. Subtitle edition mismatches Subtitle edition mismatches arise when subtitles and video refer to different scene sequences, requiring more than one global time adjustment. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Cues..title: Subtitle cues | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Cues..keywords: Subtitle cues A subtitle cue is a timed presentation item whose active interval and content determine what a renderer presents at a media instant. A cue is one timed subtitle or caption presentation item. It has an active interval and content to present during that interval. The content can be a sentence, a multi-line caption, styled text, or a view reconstructed from graphics. A cue is not necessarily one word, one video frame or one packet. Its interval describes presentation time; file and transport structures describe how the information is delivered. Two cues can overlap Consider these text cues: Cue Interval Content A 12.5–15.0 s The last train leaves at midnight. B 14.0–16.0 s [station bell] For a simple half-open interval model, a cue is active when start ≤ current time < end : Current time Active cues 12.0 s None 13.0 s A 14.5 s A and B 15.0 s B 16.0 s None The overlap is one second . A renderer needs to present both applicable items, with layout rules determining whether they appear in separate positions, stack, or interact. A format such as WebVTT allows overlapping subtitle cues. A tool that assumes each cue must end when the next starts can unintentionally shorten A. A cue's end belongs to that cue, not automatically to the next cue's start. The interval includes all its text lines A two-line caption stored in one cue has one active interval unless the format supplies additional internal timing. The explicit line break describes layout, not a second cue. The interval's duration is end minus start. A 12.5–15-second cue lasts 2.5 seconds . A number or identifier such as 42 identifies a cue record; it does not supply that duration. Endpoint conventions belong to the format or processing model. The half-open model above makes adjacent intervals unambiguous at a shared boundary. Frame-based authoring can instead describe a last displayed frame and need an explicit conversion to time boundaries. Presentation can change inside one cue An ASS event can move or fade during its interval. A karaoke caption can progressively highlight syllables. Timed spans in another text model can make parts of a line active at different moments. At 14 seconds, drawing the event's initial appearance again would be wrong if it has already moved or changed colour. Rendering depends on both the active interval and the event's internal state at the current time. Graphics formats also transmit objects, palettes and composition updates. A conventional cue list can be derived from their presentation changes, but every palette segment is not independently a new sentence to display. Seeking asks for the active state at the destination If playback jumps directly to 14.5 seconds in the example, the correct active set is A and B. The player does not need to visibly replay every preceding cue to get there. It does need the data and state required to construct the current presentation. A simple text cue can be found through its interval. A graphics update may refer to a palette or object established earlier. A nested TTML element may inherit timing and style. The information required after a seek is therefore format-dependent. For an Emby subtitle that disappears after seeking but works from the beginning, inspect the selected track and whether the route can reconstruct the active presentation. That is a different behavior from a correctly displayed cue appearing at a constant wrong time. See Also Subtitle timestamps WebVTT subtitles Blu-ray subtitles (PGS) Timed Text Markup Language (TTML) References WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 FFmpeg n8.1: PGS decoder implementation

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Drift.title: Subtitle timing drift | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Drift.keywords: Subtitle timing drift Subtitle timing drift is a growing synchronization difference caused by a time-scale mismatch or another changing relationship between subtitles and the programme. A subtitle can match the opening and then slowly move away from the speech. That pattern is drift : the required correction changes with programme position. Moving every cue by one constant amount can fix one point while leaving the rest wrong. The first useful evidence is several matched moments—not just the displayed duration of the whole file. Choose recognizable dialogue in the subtitle and the corresponding speech in the actual movie. Measure matching events, not arbitrary nearby lines Let s be the stored subtitle time and v the corresponding intended movie time. The correction required at that event is v − s . A positive value means the stored cue is early and must move later. Here is an invented set of observations: Event Stored subtitle time s Intended movie time v Required correction Opening line 60.0 s 61.5 s +1.5 s Later line 1,860.0 s 1,879.5 s +19.5 s Test line 3,600.0 s 3,636.9 s +36.9 s The correction grows. It cannot be explained by one +1.5-second offset. Matching the wrong repeated sentence or measuring a different speaker's adjacent line corrupts the anchors. The calculation is only as useful as those correspondences. Solve a scale and an offset For a sequence that differs by one constant rate and one origin shift, use: v = a × s + b The two first anchors give: a = (v2 − v1) / (s2 − s1) = (1879.5 − 61.5) / (1860 − 60) = 1818 / 1800 = 1.01 b = v1 − a × s1 = 61.5 − 1.01 × 60 = 0.9 seconds The corrected time is 1.01 × s + 0.9 . The required adjustment is therefore 0.01 × s + 0.9 . For a cue from 600 to 602.5 seconds : Boundary Corrected result Start 1.01 × 600 + 0.9 = 606.9 s End 1.01 × 602.5 + 0.9 = 609.425 s Duration 2.525 s The duration grows by the same factor of 1.01. Adding only the calculated start correction to both boundaries would preserve the old duration, producing a different transformation. This is a timing-model example, not a claim that every drift needs a 1% adjustment. The third anchor tests the model The equation predicts the test line at 3,636.9 seconds , matching the third observation. Additional observations near the middle and across scene changes should also fit within the expected authoring and rounding differences. For each event, calculate a residual : residual = observed movie time − predicted movie time Small scattered residuals can reflect authoring judgments or finite timestamp precision. A sudden persistent jump suggests an edit difference. A changing slope suggests more than one rate relationship. No single affine model can explain every such sequence. Using widely separated reliable anchors makes the rate estimate less sensitive to a small timing error on one line. If two anchors are just ten seconds apart, a 0.2-second uncertainty strongly affects the slope; over 1,800 seconds, its influence is much smaller. More anchors can support a fitted model and expose outliers. A frame-rate mismatch has a predictable factor Suppose subtitles were timed to a programme running at 24 fps , and the same source frames are played at 25 fps without changing their count. For frame number n: stored time s = n / 24 movie time v = n / 25 therefore v = (24/25) × s = 0.96 × s A source event at s = 600 seconds now belongs at 576 seconds . At s = 3,600 it belongs at 3,456 seconds . The required corrections are −24 and −144 seconds . That exact ratio follows from the specified frame playback change. It should not be applied merely because one file reports 24 and another reports 25: a frame-rate conversion can preserve duration by adding or repeating frames. Frame-based timing explains that distinction. Likewise, 24 and 24000/1001 fps differ by a much smaller factor that still accumulates over a long programme. Treat the fractional rate exactly rather than as the rounded decimal label when doing the calculation. Drift or a different movie edit? If a subtitle matches until an extra scene or a different opening logo, the error can change in a step. Stretching the whole track to make its final line match will then disturb lines that were already right. For Emby, compare the selected subtitle against the actual edition being played. A constant rate/origin correction works when the content relationship is constant. A different sequence of scenes needs a piecewise edit map , replacement subtitles for that edition, or manual retiming of the affected material. See Also Subtitle time offsets Frame-based subtitle timing Subtitle edition mismatches Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 FFmpeg n8.1: MicroDVD demuxer and frame-rate handling WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Editi.title: Subtitle edition mismatches | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Editi.keywords: Subtitle edition mismatches Subtitle edition mismatches arise when subtitles and video refer to different scene sequences, requiring more than one global time adjustment. A subtitle can be in the correct language, belong to the correct film, and match perfectly for twenty minutes before suddenly becoming wrong. Different editions can add a scene, remove a recap, change an opening, reorder material or combine episodes differently. The relationship is then about which content occurs where , not merely about a subtitle clock running at the wrong rate. Two editions with one extra scene Take an invented 60-minute programme, edition A. Edition B contains the same material but inserts a 60-second scene at A's 20-minute boundary . For cues tied to matching content: Time in A's subtitle Matching time in B Correction 10 min: 600 s 600 s 0 30 min: 1,800 s 1,860 s +60 s 50 min: 3,000 s 3,060 s +60 s The first section needs no shift. The later section needs +60 seconds. This is a step , unlike the steadily increasing correction from a constant rate mismatch. The inserted scene also contains material for which A's subtitle has no lines. A time transform cannot invent that missing translation or caption content. Matching the complete duration is not enough A is 3,600 seconds; B is 3,660. Stretching all A times by 3660/3600 = 61/60 makes the endpoint durations match. But a cue at 600 seconds would move to 610 , although its matching speech in B is still at 600. A cue at 2,400 would move to 2,440 , while its intended position after the insertion is 2,460 . The total duration fits and the intermediate content does not. Matching an opening and final anchor similarly cannot establish that every intervening scene has the same timing relationship. A piecewise map describes matching sections For this simple example, using s as A's cue time: matching material before 1200 s: v = s matching material from 1200 s onward: v = s + 60 Each unchanged section has its own origin relationship. A deletion gives a later negative shift; several edits produce several boundaries. Reordered scenes need correspondence by content rather than one monotonically increasing shift formula. A cue spanning the insertion boundary requires review. Moving only its start leaves the old end in the wrong place. Moving both by one section's offset can make it cover the inserted scene. Splitting the cue, retiming the text or finding the correctly authored edition can be appropriate, depending on what the words describe. For graphics or animated subtitles, presentation state around that boundary also needs to remain coherent. An object or animation established in removed material may not have a meaningful state at the next retained scene. Identify the content before retiming it For an Emby library, confirm the actual version being played and the actual subtitle selected. Release labels, theatrical versus extended editions, opening/recap lengths and distinctive scene transitions provide useful matching evidence. Sample several recognizable lines before and after suspected boundaries. A sudden stable jump supports an edit-origin change; a smooth slope supports a rate relationship. A track can contain both. When the scene sequence differs substantially, subtitles authored for the actual edition provide the missing content and timing together. A piecewise map can retime shared material, but it cannot recover dialogue that its source edition never contained. See Also Subtitle timing drift Subtitle time offsets Streams and Tracks References W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues RFC 9559: Matroska container format

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Frame.title: Frame-based subtitle timing | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Frame.keywords: Frame-based subtitle timing Frame-based subtitle timing maps numbered frames to presentation time using the correct rate, frame origin and boundary convention. Frame-based subtitle timing identifies positions using frame numbers . Converting those positions to seconds requires the rate associated with that numbering and its origin. For a zero-origin, constant-rate sequence, frame 0 begins at time zero and frame n begins at n / f seconds , where f is frames per second. Start and end conventions affect one frame At 25 fps, frames 300 through 374 occupy time 12.000 through 15.000 seconds . The ending boundary is frame 375. If an authoring tool instead gives 374 as the last displayed frame , that inclusive index needs one additional frame interval to become an exclusive time endpoint. Confusing the two conventions changes duration by 40 ms at 25 fps. A format or tool's definition determines which interpretation applies. The article's calculations use zero-origin frame boundaries. They do not redefine every frame-based file's end convention. Exact fractional rates matter 24000/1001 is approximately 23.976 fps; it is not exactly the rounded decimal 23.976. For 24,000 frame intervals: Interpreted rate Elapsed time 24 fps 1,000 s 24000/1001 fps 1,001 s After 86,400 intervals, the difference between these two interpretations is 3.6 seconds . A small per-frame difference becomes visible drift across a movie. Use the declared rational rate where available. A rounded value in a display or filename can be an informal label, not the value to use in a long-duration calculation. A frame-based timecode label is also a notation with its own counting rules. Drop-frame timecode skips designated labels to keep clock correspondence; the label convention does not itself remove picture frames from playback. More output frames do not always mean faster playback There are two distinct operations: Playing the same 24 source frames in 1 second at 24 fps, then in 0.96 seconds at 25 fps, changes the programme's speed. Converting one second of 24 fps material into 25 output frames while preserving that second changes frame sampling and leaves programme duration intact. Only the first produces the 24/25 subtitle-time factor for matching source frame positions. In the second, time-based cues can remain on the same elapsed timeline even though output frame indices have changed. For an Emby file that was converted earlier, identify whether its programme timing changed. The current average frame-rate field alone does not establish the relationship to the subtitle's original frame numbers. Variable-rate pictures need their timestamps With variable frame rate, frame intervals are not all equal. Dividing an index by an average rate gives an approximation rather than the actual presentation position. The useful map is the frame's presentation timestamp on the programme timeline. A frame-based subtitle conversion tied to that sequence needs those actual positions or an appropriate reference time map. See Also MicroDVD subtitles Subtitle timing drift Video Frame Rate Variable Frame Rate Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References FFmpeg n8.1: MicroDVD demuxer and frame-rate handling W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Offse.title: Subtitle time offsets | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Offse.keywords: Subtitle time offsets A subtitle time offset moves all applicable cue boundaries by the same amount without changing the cue durations or spacing. A time offset shifts a subtitle sequence earlier or later by a constant amount . It is the appropriate kind of correction when the same subtitle track is consistently displaced relative to its matching programme. Suppose a line begins at 12.5 seconds , but the corresponding speech begins at 13.3 . The subtitle is early by 0.8 seconds . It needs to move later. Define the sign through the result Here, a positive offset means delay the subtitle : new start = old start + offset new end = old end + offset A cue from 12.5 to 15.0 seconds with +0.8 becomes 13.3 to 15.8 . Property Before After +0.8 s Start 12.5 s 13.3 s End 15.0 s 15.8 s Duration 2.5 s 2.5 s Gap to any equally shifted following cue Unchanged Unchanged If the subtitle is late, it needs a negative correction under this convention. Interfaces can describe the control as subtitle delay, audio-relative adjustment or another sign convention. Confirm which action moves the displayed line in the intended direction instead of assuming the plus sign has one universal UI meaning. A fixed shift preserves the sequence's time scale The distance between any two cue boundaries remains the same. The slope of the timeline is unchanged. An offset therefore cannot correct a sequence that is synchronized near the opening and progressively farther out later. Test the same recognizable speech at several positions. If +0.8 works near the opening, middle and end, a constant displacement is a plausible model. If later passages need +3 or +8 seconds instead, examine timing drift or edition differences . Cues can cross the playable boundary Consider a cue from 0.4 to 1.4 seconds moved earlier by 0.8 . Its mathematical interval becomes −0.4 to 0.6 seconds . A playback timeline beginning at zero can present only the portion from 0 to 0.6. A file format that does not permit negative standalone timestamps needs a deliberate clipping or omission policy when saving the result. Clamping both times without checking the interval can create an empty cue if the entire event has moved before zero. There is no reason to wrap a negative result around to an enormous positive time as if it were a time-of-day clock. A playback control and a file edit have different scope An app can apply a viewing offset without rewriting the subtitle file. An editor can instead save shifted cue times into a new file. Applying both adds their effects: a saved +0.8 correction and another playback +0.8 produce +1.6 seconds . For an Emby comparison, identify whether the selected track has edited timestamps and whether the app has a session offset. A setting that belongs to one viewing route need not describe a changed file on the server. See Also Subtitle timing drift Subtitle edition mismatches Subtitle timestamps References W3C WebVTT: Candidate Recommendation Draft, May 2026 W3C Timed Text Markup Language 2 WHATWG HTML: Text track timing and active cues

articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Times.title: Subtitle timestamps | Emby Learn
articles/subtitles/timing/Subtitle-Times.keywords: Subtitle timestamps Subtitle timestamps express presentation positions whose meaning depends on their syntax, unit, time base and timeline origin. A subtitle timestamp means when to present content on an applicable timeline . Its digits alone are not enough: the syntax establishes units, and the surrounding format or delivery establishes the time base and origin. A cue can be correctly parsed and still land in the wrong scene if the wrong origin is applied. The last field can mean different things Representation Interpretation SRT 00:00:12,500 12 seconds plus 500 milliseconds WebVTT 00:00:12.500 The same 12.5 seconds ASS 0:00:12.50 12 seconds plus 50 hundredths, also 12.5 seconds TTML offset 12.5s A 12.5-second offset in its applicable timing context TTML frame offset 300f 300 frames, interpreted using the declared rate Container timestamp 1125000 at 90,000 ticks/s 12.5 seconds before any additional origin mapping The fraction's number of decimal digits matters. .050 seconds is 50 ms ; .50 seconds is 500 ms . Neither should be read as “fifty frames” simply because a field follows a separator. A clock expression with a frame field uses its format's frame-rate rules. Copying the textual punctuation into another format is not sufficient conversion. A time base turns integers into duration On a 90,000-tick-per-second scale: 1,125,000 ticks / 90,000 ticks per second = 12.5 seconds 225,000 ticks / 90,000 ticks per second = 2.5 seconds The first can be a cue's start; the second can be its duration. Raw numbers from a 1,000-unit-per-second track are much smaller for the same times. The time base establishes that numerical interpretation. The relevant presentation timestamp is also distinct from a packet's arrival time or a decode-order timestamp. Preparing an image ahead of its display time should not make the subtitle appear ahead of the scene. Local time needs a timeline origin Suppose a delivered subtitle item starts at 2 seconds on a local timeline whose origin is programme time 600 seconds . Its programme position is: programme time = local time + mapped origin = 2 + 600 = 602 seconds Displaying it at movie time 2 seconds would be an origin error, not a failure to parse its decimal fraction. Container track timing, edit mappings or a segmented delivery convention can supply that relationship. Nested TTML timing can similarly change the reference of a child's time expression. A reader must apply the applicable mapping rather than guessing that every timestamp is measured from the start of the complete movie. For an Emby extraction or conversion comparison, convert the original and resulting times to a common programme timeline. That makes it possible to distinguish rounding, an offset, a rate change and an origin mismatch without interpreting different raw tick values as different scenes. Numerical precision and actual synchronization SRT records milliseconds; ASS event timestamps commonly record hundredths. Rounding a source time to the nearest hundredth can change it by up to 5 ms . That quantization is a different scale of problem from a subtitle arriving several seconds before speech. Likewise, a file with three fraction digits is not guaranteed to be authored accurately to a millisecond. Its representation can express a precision greater than the timing decision actually used. articles/video/codecs/index.html.title: Overview: Video codecs | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/index.html.keywords: Overview: Video codecs Video codecs define coded-picture formats whose properties and implementation support influence playback compatibility. A player must understand the picture coding inside a track before it can reconstruct the video. Codec families reflect different standards and workflows, from delivery-oriented formats to editing and preservation formats. For an Emby session, the selected codec, stream constraints and available decoder together determine the usable path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How video codecs affect playback compatibility Video codec compatibility depends on the encoded stream and the decoder available to a particular playback app. MPEG and ITU-T video codecs MPEG and ITU-T video codec families define widely used generations of standardized picture coding. VPx and AV1 VP8, VP9 and AV1 are distinct video coding formats with different tools and decoder requirements. VC-1 VC-1 is the video coding format standardized in SMPTE ST 421 with Simple, Main, and Advanced profiles. Production and preservation codecs Production and preservation codecs serve workflows where editing access, reconstruction quality or long-term fidelity influence coding choices. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->
