articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.264 / AVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.264 / AVC Video H.264, also called AVC, defines a video coding format used for compressed moving pictures. H.264 , AVC , and MPEG-4 Part 10 name the same video coding standard. It defines the instructions a decoder follows to reconstruct compressed pictures, rather than a particular encoder's recipe for choosing those instructions. A film in an MP4 file, a camera clip in another container, and a television stream can all carry AVC. Their packaging supplies the coded track to the same kind of reconstruction process. An Emby session can show AVC at both input and output when the server has decoded and encoded a new AVC representation. The reconstruction steps below explain what differs from copying the encoded track. The coded data comes in units AVC's Network Abstraction Layer units , or NAL units, organize the bitstream. Some carry coded picture regions called slices. Others supply configuration or additional information. A coded picture can contain several slice units. The media packet or container sample that carries them is a packaging boundary; the AVC units describe the coding boundary. Before reconstructing a slice, the decoder needs the applicable sequence parameter set (SPS) and picture parameter set (PPS) . These describe such things as the coded grid, permitted sample format, picture-order behavior, and relevant coding options. A slice identifies the parameters and coding decisions it uses. This is why extracting one piece of picture data without its configuration does not necessarily provide a complete decoder input. Divide the picture into reconstruction work AVC's basic macroblock footprint covers 16 × 16 brightness positions . The picture is divided into those regions, with further partitions for prediction and transforms. For a progressive 1920 × 1080 presentation, the coded macroblock grid is 120 columns by 68 rows: 8,160 macroblocks , representing a 1920 × 1088 grid before display cropping. The crop describes the visible picture boundary; the coding grid determines this part of the decoder's work. Different regions can use different prediction choices. An edge, a flat area, and a moving object need not receive the same description. Construct a predictor An intra-coded region predicts from available reconstructed samples in the same picture. For example, values along an upper boundary can be extended in a chosen direction to form a candidate block. An inter-coded region identifies a decoded reference picture and motion information telling the decoder where to sample it. Fractional positions use the interpolation rules specified by AVC. A region can combine permitted reference information according to its coding type and mode. The encoder searches for a useful predictor. The decoder instead follows the predictor encoded in the syntax. Its task is deterministic reconstruction from the supplied information. Reconstruct the correction The source region usually differs from its predictor. The encoder represents that difference as a residual and can transform it into coefficients describing patterns within blocks. The decoder entropy-decodes those coefficients, reconstructs their scale from the quantization parameters, and applies the specified inverse transform. It then adds the resulting correction to the predictor. AVC uses integer transform operations for common 4×4 residual blocks; selected profiles permit additional tools such as an 8×8 transform. Quantization can discard precision, so the decoded correction need not equal the original source difference. The compression walkthrough demonstrates that approximation numerically. The entropy-coding mode is another syntax choice. CAVLC and CABAC use different coding procedures, so the decoder needs the selected mode even when both ultimately reconstruct the same kind of sample array. Filter and retain the reconstructed picture AVC can apply its in-loop deblocking filter to reduce selected discontinuities between coded regions. “In-loop” matters: the appropriately filtered reconstruction can become a reference for later pictures. The encoder reconstructs the same result locally when preparing those later predictions. Otherwise it would predict from samples the decoder does not have. The decoded-picture buffer retains references and pictures waiting for their display times. An anchor can be decoded before a B-picture that will appear earlier on screen. Picture-order information and presentation timing restore the intended viewing sequence after the dependency work. AVC profiles, x264, and container labels Profiles restrict this tool/sample set. Baseline, Main, High, and High 10 are different permitted AVC representations. Levels constrain picture size, throughput, buffering, and other resources. Label Place in the process H.264 / AVC The bitstream and reconstruction standard x264 One encoder implementation choosing valid AVC instructions High / High 10 Profile constraints on tools and sample formats A container's AVC track identifier The wrapper's description of its coded video An x264-made track can be decoded by another conforming AVC implementation. The encoder's search effort and quality settings change which valid representation it creates, while the decoder follows that representation. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles H.265 / HEVC Video Video Encoder Presets References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.265 / HEVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.265 / HEVC Video H.265, also called HEVC, defines a video coding format with tools intended to improve compression efficiency. H.265 , or High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) , represents pictures with a flexible block structure and prediction/correction tools designed to use data efficiently. A common place to encounter it is a UHD film or recording, where there are many picture positions to describe. The way a picture is divided helps explain that efficiency. Start with a coding tree A stream can organize the picture in 64 × 64 coding-tree blocks . An encoder does not have to give every part of such a region the same small-block description. It can subdivide where detail or movement makes a smaller region useful. Imagine a 64 × 64 region with mostly smooth background and a detailed lower-right corner. One illustrative tree splits it into four 32 × 32 regions, then splits only the lower-right one into four 16 × 16 regions: 64 × 64 ├─ 32 × 32, retained ├─ 32 × 32, retained ├─ 32 × 32, retained └─ 32 × 32 ├─ 16 × 16 ├─ 16 × 16 ├─ 16 × 16 └─ 16 × 16 There are seven leaf coding blocks. Their areas still total the original region: 3 × 32² + 4 × 16² = 4,096 = 64². This is a possible partition illustration, not the mandatory layout of every HEVC picture. The stream's coding parameters and rules determine its allowed tree choices. The larger flat regions can use fewer region descriptions, while the detailed corner gets more local choices. Subdivision therefore follows the information the encoder is trying to represent rather than a single grid size chosen for every scene. Prediction and transform divisions have different jobs A coding block's prediction describes what reconstructed scene information can be reused. Intra modes use same-picture boundaries, including directional or smoothly varying predictions. Inter modes use decoded reference pictures and motion information. The transform division describes how the remaining correction is represented. A coding region and its residual transform blocks are related but do not have to be one identical subdivision. The decoder follows the supplied tree and modes to form predictions and reconstruct corrections. Quantization selects the precision of those corrections. Extra partition choices can help an encoder describe a region effectively, while the rate-control settings decide how much data it is allowed to spend. A good tree choice does not remove the need to encode changed or unpredictable content. Grain, newly revealed scenery, and complicated movement still require information. Finish the reconstruction inside the coding loop HEVC includes in-loop deblocking and sample-adaptive offset (SAO) tools. Deblocking addresses selected discontinuities around coded block boundaries. SAO can apply signaled corrections to categories of reconstructed samples, such as brightness bands or local edge relationships. These operations help form the reconstruction that later prediction references. The decoder must apply the applicable signaled behavior, and the encoder's reconstruction loop must make corresponding reference samples available for its next decisions. The decoded picture then participates in reference storage and presentation ordering, much as the dependency principles described in the reference-picture and GOP articles. Identify the sample representation Common HEVC profile Sample depth Sampling Main 8-bit 4:2:0 Main 10 8-bit or 10-bit 4:2:0 These are selected profiles. Additional HEVC profiles define other permitted sample/tool sets. Main 10 is common for HDR delivery, but its name describes sample precision and coding permissions. The transfer/color information establishes how those values represent SDR or HDR light. HDR10 combines the relevant HDR interpretation and metadata in common HEVC delivery workflows. x265 is one encoder that chooses an HEVC representation. A hardware encoder is another implementation of that job. Their effort and rate-control decisions can produce different pictures and sizes within the standard. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Video Codec Profiles HDR10 How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-2 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-2 Video MPEG-2 Video, standardized as ITU-T H.262 and ISO/IEC 13818-2, is a compressed video format found in older disc and broadcast media. An older television recording or disc-derived film often carries MPEG-2 Video , standardized as ITU-T H.262 and ISO/IEC 13818-2. Its compressed track describes how to build pictures; a transport or program stream supplies the packaging around that track. To understand the format, follow one of its coded pictures. Sequence headers, macroblocks, and DCT corrections Sequence information establishes the picture grid and relevant timing/format parameters. Picture information identifies the coding type and applicable reconstruction choices. In common 8-bit 4:2:0 material, a macroblock covers a 16 × 16 brightness region . Its brightness corrections are represented in four 8 × 8 blocks , with corresponding color-difference blocks. The encoder uses a discrete cosine transform (DCT) to represent correction patterns as coefficients. Quantization reduces their precision. The decoder reconstructs those coefficients, applies the inverse transform, and adds the correction to the picture's predictor. The block representation explains familiar low-bitrate artifacts: lost fine patterns or disagreeing coded regions can reveal softened texture and block-shaped boundaries. Picture dependencies and decoding order An I-picture reconstructs its picture content without a temporal sample reference. A P-picture can predict from an available anchor and encode what changed. A B-picture can use the permitted prediction from surrounding anchors, which have to be decoded first. For a visible sequence I0, B1, B2, P3 , the decoder can reconstruct I0 and P3 before B1 and B2. It then shows them in their original viewing order. MPEG-2's I/P anchor structure differs from modern structures that can use B-pictures as references. The GOP explanation gives the general dependency trace; the specific codec's rules determine the legal graph. An entry at a GOP boundary also needs appropriate access handling if picture dependencies extend across it. Interpret a broadcast picture's time MPEG-2 can represent progressive and interlaced material. A reported 25 fps recording can mean 25 field pairs containing 50 native field times/s , rather than 25 complete progressive camera moments. Its picture and sequence signaling guide field presentation. Film transfers can instead use repeated-field timing to place a progressive source on a television cadence. The reconstruction task is then cadence recovery , while native interlaced movement calls for deinterlacing if the output is progressive. These differences matter when creating a new playback version: preserving a film's picture sequence and preserving a sport recording's field movement are different jobs. Identify the surrounding names Name Place in the recording MPEG-2 Video / H.262 Picture compression MPEG Transport Stream Packetized carriage of the video and other streams MPEG Program Stream Another systems packaging form MPEG Audio Separate soundtrack coding A TS file can carry video codecs other than MPEG-2, and a MPEG-2 picture track can be carried in other supported packaging. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References ITU-T H.262: MPEG-2 Video

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid MPEG-4 Part 2 is the visual coding standard associated with Xvid and classic MPEG-4-based DivX video. Label on an older video What it identifies MPEG-4 Part 2 / MPEG-4 Visual The video coding standard Xvid An implementation of MPEG-4 Visual, commonly Advanced Simple Profile Classic MPEG-4-based DivX A branded implementation of this coding family AVI A possible container carrying the coded track H.264 / AVC / MPEG-4 Part 10 A different video standard These distinctions make a legacy AVI collection easier to interpret. “MPEG-4” names a standards family; Part 2 identifies this visual format. The DivX brand also covers other formats, including AVC in DivX Plus. Picture coding in the common rectangular form Common Simple/Advanced Simple video represents rectangular pictures with block-based prediction and corrections. Independently coded pictures establish scene content, while inter-predicted pictures reuse reconstructed references. The residual correction is transformed into block coefficients and quantized before coding. The decoder reverses the coded operations and adds the correction to the selected predictor. A newer encoder library does not change the decoder's job into a different standard: it chooses another permitted representation of the same format. The profile determines which tool set is available. Advanced Simple Profile (ASP) adds useful choices beyond the simpler form, including B-picture coding and enhanced motion tools. Two motion options with concrete meanings Quarter-pixel motion compensation allows finer reference positioning. An integer displacement selects an existing sample location; a quarter-position displacement requires the codec's interpolation to form a predictor between grid points. This can better follow movement that falls between whole positions. Global motion compensation (GMC) can describe a shared transformation across a larger portion of a scene. A camera pan or related movement can make many block displacements follow one common relationship, instead of describing every region solely as an unrelated local shift. Those modes change the encoded instructions. The Xvid project documents ASP support for them, but a particular file can use a narrower selection. A decoder must implement the modes actually present. XVID and DX50 identify the coded track FourCC labels such as XVID and DX50 help identify a container's track and its intended format association. They do not contain the prediction and transform operations themselves. A classic MPEG-4 Visual track moved into another supported wrapper still contains MPEG-4 Visual instructions. Turning it into AVC requires source decoding and a new encoding process; changing “Part 2” to “Part 10” in a label does not perform those operations. For an Emby library migration, inspect the actual codec, profile and coding features before deciding whether the work is repackaging or video conversion. The name table establishes the family, and the tool descriptions establish what its decoder needs to do. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Containers and Codecs Codec Identifiers and FourCC How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References ISO/IEC 14496-2: MPEG-4 Visual Xvid: MPEG-4 video codec implementation DivX: DivX Plus and H.264 at a glance

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.266 / VVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.266 / VVC Video H.266, also called VVC, is a video coding standard that requires its own compatible decoder and playback integration. H.266 , also called Versatile Video Coding (VVC) , extends block-based picture coding with additional ways to divide, predict, and reconstruct regions. Its aim is to give encoders useful choices for different scenes and delivery uses. The “versatile” part becomes concrete when looking at a region's shape. Fit the coding regions to the picture A VVC picture can use a 128 × 128 coding-tree footprint and subdivide it into smaller coding regions. Alongside a four-way square split, its multi-type tree can use binary and ternary splits. For an illustrative 64 × 64 region: Split Resulting regions Quad Four 32 × 32 squares Vertical binary Two 32 × 64 rectangles Vertical ternary 16 × 64, 32 × 64, and 16 × 64 rectangles The ternary regions cover the same area: 16 × 64 + 32 × 64 + 16 × 64 = 4,096 = 64². The middle region can receive one coding description while narrower regions around it use others. A tall moving subject, a sharp vertical boundary, and broad flat surroundings can benefit from different region shapes. These are coding possibilities, not a compulsory layout. The stream's tree-size, depth, and split restrictions determine which choice is permitted at a particular point. The decoder reads the selected structure and reconstructs its leaves. Describe more than a uniform shift A basic motion vector translates a reference region by one displacement. Real camera movement can also rotate or zoom a region, making the displacement vary across it. VVC includes motion tools that can describe such varying relationships, including affine prediction. Rather than assuming every point in a region moves identically, a motion model can determine related displacements at different locations. Other prediction choices and coded residuals still provide the information needed to reconstruct the target. The benefit is a potentially better predictor for that region. A better predictor leaves less correction to describe. A poor model still needs larger corrections or another coding choice. The encoder explores; the decoder follows More region shapes and prediction tools give an encoder a larger set of candidates to evaluate. Its search must balance reconstructed-picture error against the bits needed for tree decisions, motion information, and corrections. The decoder does not repeat that entire search. It follows the signaled candidates, but it must implement their syntax, interpolation, transforms, filtering, and reference rules. This is why a HEVC decoder cannot simply treat VVC as another HEVC profile. Compression efficiency comes from the selected representation and settings. To measure a particular saving, compare encodes of the same source under an appropriate picture-quality evaluation; the standard's name does not supply a fixed percentage. Put the format into a playback path For direct playback, a receiving app needs a usable VVC decoder and compatible extraction/presentation of that stream. For conversion into another codec, the server needs the VVC input decoder first: VVC source → VVC reconstruction → processing → target encoder → target playback decoder. The target encoder cannot bypass the source reconstruction. The source's profile, workload, and packaging determine that input job, while the output format determines the client's job. For a VVC file in an Emby library, inspect the actual server and app implementations at those boundaries. The format explanation describes the work that needs to exist; it does not declare a particular Emby version or device to implement it. See Also H.265 / HEVC Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.266: Versatile video coding

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Overview: Production and preservation codecs | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Overview: Production and preservation codecs Production and preservation codecs serve workflows where editing access, reconstruction quality or long-term fidelity influence coding choices. A format chosen for editing may prioritize efficient picture access over the smallest delivery file. A preservation workflow can place another emphasis on exact reconstruction. The codecs in this group span those purposes; their individual pages distinguish picture access, compression and reconstruction properties. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Motion JPEG Motion JPEG stores video as independently JPEG-compressed pictures or fields, with packaging details that vary by implementation. DV video DV video is an intra-frame compressed video format commonly encountered in digital tape transfers. Apple ProRes Apple ProRes is a family of intra-frame video codecs used for production and editing, with separate variants for different quality and sample requirements. Avid DNxHD Avid DNxHD identifies the established HD production-codec workflows within the VC-3 video coding family. Avid DNxHR Avid DNxHR identifies resolution-independent production workflows in the VC-3 video coding family. FFV1 FFV1 is a lossless video coding format whose decoded sample values match the samples supplied to its encoder. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding SMPTE ST 314: DV-based audio, data, and video at 25 and 50 Mb/s SMPTE RDD 36: Apple ProRes bitstream syntax and decoding process SMPTE ST 2019-1: VC-3 picture compression and data stream format (2016) RFC 9043: FFV1 video coding format versions 0, 1, and 3

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHD Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHD Video Avid DNxHD identifies the established HD production-codec workflows within the VC-3 video coding family. A legacy DNxHD name often includes a number such as 115, 120, or 145. Read it with the recording's picture format and frame rate. Those are nominal rate-oriented mode names, rather than a quality score that can be transferred unchanged to any raster. DNxHD is the established HD production use of the VC-3 coding family. Its independently coded pictures support editing and exchange without a long temporal prediction chain. A picture rate changes the data rate Avid's published HD bandwidth table gives a 1920 ×1080 SQ example with 602,112 coded bytes per frame . Using that fixed frame size: Picture rate Calculation Video rate 24000/1001 fps 602,112 ×24000/1001 ×8 Approximately 115.490 Mb/s 25 fps 602,112 ×25 ×8 120.4224 Mb/s 30000/1001 fps 602,112 ×30000/1001 ×8 Approximately 144.363 Mb/s Calculated from this published frame-size example, not a rule that every historical file carrying a115/120/145 label has exactly that payload. The per-picture representation is unchanged in the calculation. More pictures per second require more data each second. This explains why legacy nominal rates need the frame-rate context. For 25 fps, the byte rate is 15,052,800 bytes/s , or 15.0528 decimal MB/s, approximately 14.36 MiB/s. Avid's current naming table explicitly uses the binary MiB/s convention. Data units matter when comparing that number with a network or storage description. The coded mode is more than its rate name A decoder needs the applicable picture dimensions, sampling/precision and coding-mode information. VC-3 picture coding transforms and quantizes within-picture regions, then codes their coefficient information. Its mode identifiers and frame structure select the reconstruction behavior. The result is a lossy production picture with convenient independent access. Its quality depends on the source and chosen coding representation, while its nominal rate helps plan storage and transfer. A metadata inspector's broad codec name is only one field in that description. For example, FFmpeg groups DNxHD and DNxHR profiles within its dnxhd implementation. Inspecting the profile and raster distinguishes the actual representation even if that implementation family name is shared. Legacy DNxHD and the unified Avid DNx name Avid's newer naming scheme uses Avid DNx , removing the HD, HR and GX suffixes. It retains familiar quality-level names and adds broader capabilities and customizable rates. An older DNxHD file still contains its original mode. The current name does not rewrite its bits. The related DNxHR label identifies resolution-independent production workflows, while the newer unified codec should be read with its applicable specification and implementation. When using a legacy production copy as a source for an Emby viewing encode, keep its complete raster/rate/profile description attached to the file. That records the actual reconstruction input, while the delivery copy can have its own codec and data allocation. See Also Avid DNxHR Video Apple ProRes Video Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Generation Loss References SMPTE ST 2019-1: VC-3 picture compression and data stream format (2016) Avid: DNx naming scheme and data rates Avid: DNx SDK and specification overview Avid: DNxHR and HD coded-frame bandwidth table

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHR Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHR Video Avid DNxHR identifies resolution-independent production workflows in the VC-3 video coding family. A production needs to edit pictures larger or differently shaped than traditional fixed HD modes. DNxHR supplies resolution-independent production workflows in the VC-3 family, retaining independently coded pictures while extending the useful raster choices. That does not give one fixed data rate to the letters “HR.” The chosen picture size, quality representation and picture rate determine how much data the source supplies. Data rate from a published UHD frame size Avid's published legacy UHD table gives 3,641,344 coded bytes per frame for its 3840 ×2160 HQ/HQX example. At 25 fps: 3,641,344 ×25 =91,033,600 bytes/s. At 50 fps: 3,641,344 ×50 =182,067,200 bytes/s. Declared example Decimal byte rate Binary byte rate UHD example at 25 fps 91.0336 MB/s Approximately 86.8164 MiB/s Same coded frame size at 50 fps 182.0672 MB/s Approximately 173.6328 MiB/s The 25 fps case is 728.2688 Mb/s when expressed in decimal bits per second. This is a calculated production-data example from the published frame size, excluding additional wrapper/audio traffic. It is not the rate of every DNxHR file. Avid's current data-rate table uses MiB/s explicitly. Multiplying the published byte count first makes the unit conversion transparent and helps compare it with other storage or delivery numbers. Select a production representation Familiar level Role suggested by its name LB Low-bandwidth production/proxy representation SQ Standard quality HQ High quality HQX High quality extended 444 Higher-fidelity color representation A smaller proxy can make an editing session easier to handle, while finishing can return to the retained higher-quality source. Independent pictures provide direct frame access in both roles; quantization and coding choices determine the picture information retained. The sample-format permissions belong to the actual codec generation and mode. The names alone should not be used to impose historical 8-/10-bit restrictions on newer Avid DNx output. The newer name is Avid DNx Avid now uses Avid DNx without the HD, HR orGX suffixes, with its updated quality-level and capability scheme. Its newer implementation offers broader precision/alpha options and adjustable rates within the defined levels. The old DNxHR label remains useful for existing files, older exports and the historical specification. Record the actual raster, rate, profile and sample format when distinguishing those sources. A conversion for Emby viewing begins by reconstructing that production source. A delivery codec can exploit temporal relationships between its pictures and choose a much smaller viewing-data budget. The independently coded source remains the finishing input, while that output is a separate presentation designed for delivery. articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: DV Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: DV Video DV video is an intra-frame compressed video format commonly encountered in digital tape transfers. When a digital tape transfer copies DV data , it can preserve the tape's existing compressed representation. The computer is receiving the encoded video, audio, and associated recording data rather than necessarily making a new picture encode. That distinction explains both the value of a copied transfer and its familiar large file rate. What DV25 counts Common consumer SD DV has roughly 25 Mb/s of coded video . A complete DV data stream includes more than the video payload. Common consumer system Stored picture grid Frame rate 525/60 720 × 480 30000/1001, approximately 29.97 fps 625/50 720 × 576 25 fps Selected SD forms, not every professional or HD member of the DV family. The system's 525/625 line designation includes lines beyond the active stored picture. Its complete DV frame is organized in Digital Interface (DIF) blocks , which provide the transferable structure. Count a complete frame A DIF block has 80 bytes . A sequence contains 150 blocks , allocated as: Section Blocks in one sequence Header 1 Subcode 2 Video auxiliary 3 Audio 9 Video 135 The total is 150 . The 25-Mb/s structure has ten such sequences per 525/60 frame or twelve per 625/50 frame: 525/60: 80 × 150 × 10 = 120,000 bytes/frame . 625/50: 80 × 150 × 12 = 144,000 bytes/frame . For the 25 fps form, that is 144,000 × 25 = 3,600,000 bytes/s , or 28.8 Mb/s , for the complete stream. One hour is 12.96 decimal GB before an additional file wrapper's overhead. The apparent disagreement with “DV25” is thus a difference in what is being counted. The complete representation carries audio and structural/auxiliary data alongside its coded picture information. Reconstruct the independently coded picture DV picture compression works within a frame rather than relying on a long picture-to-picture prediction chain. This gives editing software direct access to individual recorded pictures once their data is located. The ordinary picture coding is lossy. Copying the DV bytes avoids another video-encoding generation; it preserves the camera's encoded result rather than changing that result into an uncompressed original. An export that decodes DV and then makes H.264 is a new representation. The two jobs can be useful for different purposes: retaining the transferred source and creating a delivery copy. Present the source picture correctly The reconstructed raster also needs its display interpretation. Standard-definition DV often uses nonsquare pixel presentation, and the same stored dimensions can describe different intended aspect ratios. Aspect information supplies that geometry. Native interlaced recordings contain two field capture times in each frame. For progressive presentation, field order and the chosen reconstruction cadence determine how their motion is retained. This is the information a playback or conversion stage needs from the transferred recording. A correctly copied DV source preserves that data for an Emby playback version whose picture shape and field motion can then be interpreted deliberately. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Video Field Order Deinterlacing References SMPTE ST 314: DV-based audio, data, and video at 25 and 50 Mb/s IEC 61834-2: Consumer DV standard-definition recording format

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: FFV1 Lossless Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: FFV1 Lossless Video FFV1 is a lossless video coding format whose decoded sample values match the samples supplied to its encoder. FFV1 preserves the sample values supplied to its encoder. Its compression comes from prediction and compact coding of exact corrections, rather than rounding away the parts that require more bits. The equality is between codec input and reconstructed output in the same sample representation. Calculate the specified predictor For an ordinary 8-bit sample example, let: l , the reconstructed left neighbor, be 40. t , the reconstructed upper neighbor, be 42. tl , the upper-left neighbor, be 41. FFV1's median predictor is: median(l, t, l + t − tl). Here the three candidates are 40,42,41 , so the median is 41 . If the actual sample is 44, the encoded residual is 44 −41 =3 . Decode that exact residual and add it to the same predictor: 41 +3 =44 . The local difference estimate can adapt to edges. With left 40, top 70 and upper-left 30, the extrapolated candidate is 80. The median of 40, 70 and 80 is 70, so the predictor stays within the range supplied by the two immediate neighbors. The values demonstrate the specified ordinary-sample rule. The RFC defines separate handling for certain 16-bit coding cases and for slice borders. Use context to code the residual Nearby sample differences describe whether a region is smooth, changing gradually, or crossing an edge. FFV1 uses such context information to select coding behavior for residuals. A smooth area can contain many predictable small corrections. The coder can describe those common events compactly. Grain or noise leaves less predictable residual data and may require more bits. Either way, the correction is retained exactly. A different compression result does not select a different decoded picture quality. The lossless coding example illustrates this principle with a small reversible prefix rule. FFV1's actual range/Golomb coding and context rules are defined in its specification rather than by that toy code. Slices and coding state Version 3 organizes a frame into slices with relevant headers, sample content and footer information. Dividing the picture provides independent regional work and a useful boundary for error checking. The decoder also needs configuration and entropy-coder state. An FFV1 keyframe initializes the applicable coding states. In this format, “no temporal sample prediction” should not be confused with “any packet can be decoded without its coding configuration or state.” RFC 9043 defines versions 0, 1 and 3, including how version 3 configuration is carried by supporting containers such as Matroska. That supplies the information needed to interpret each coded frame's samples. Verify reconstruction and integrity separately Check Question it answers Compare decoded samples with the encoder input Did this round trip preserve the same values? Validate the configuration CRC Is the stored configuration consistent with its checksum? Validate enabled version 3 slice CRCs Are the coded slice bytes consistent with their checksums? A CRC detects corruption; it does not contain the missing sample information needed to repair an arbitrary damaged slice. If a source was resized before FFV1 encoding, the exact round trip preserves the resized array. Place the sample comparison at the encoder's actual input to verify that intended preservation boundary. This makes an FFV1 master useful as a stable source for future viewing conversions: its decoder restores the retained samples, and each derivative begins from that defined input rather than from an earlier lossy delivery copy. See Also Lossless Video Compression Video Generation Loss Lossy and Lossless Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References RFC 9043: FFV1 video coding format versions 0, 1, and 3

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Motion JPEG Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Motion JPEG Video Motion JPEG stores video as independently JPEG-compressed pictures or fields, with packaging details that vary by implementation. Motion JPEG (MJPEG) builds moving video from independently JPEG-compressed pictures. The usual frame-based form does not use another picture's samples to predict the next one. The diagram shows a frame-based form. Some implementations code the two interlaced fields separately. An independent picture can still be highly compressed Common MJPEG uses JPEG's lossy DCT-based picture coding. Within a picture, blocks are transformed into coefficients representing spatial patterns. Quantization approximates those coefficients, and entropy coding describes their values compactly. The decoder reconstructs each picture from its JPEG coding information. The neighboring video pictures do not supply its temporal predictor. Its JPEG tables and the applicable sample/container description still have to be available. This combines compressed picture storage with straightforward frame access. Once the reader locates picture C and supplies its coding information, it does not first need to reconstruct A and B as scene references. The independence also determines what gets repeated. A wall unchanged between A, B, and C is described within each new JPEG picture again. An inter-predicted codec can instead reuse an earlier reconstructed wall and describe mainly its changes. Assign pictures to the timeline The surrounding video format supplies the sequence and timing. At 25 fps, each picture spans 40 ms. Let three independently encoded pictures have these illustrative sizes: Picture Duration JPEG payload A 40 ms 40,000 bytes B 40 ms 30,000 bytes C 40 ms 50,000 bytes Their total is 120,000 bytes across 0.120 second: 120,000 × 8 ÷ 0.120 = 8,000,000 bit/s , or 8 Mb/s . Constructed sizes, excluding container and audio overhead; no encoder benchmark or recommended setting is implied. C can contain more difficult texture than B and need a larger JPEG even though both have the same dimensions and duration. Independence does not require identical frame sizes. A frame can contain two coded fields Some MJPEG representations encode interlaced fields separately and carry their JPEG bitstreams together in one video frame. The decoder must recover both field images and interpret their order and times correctly. QuickTime's documented Motion-JPEG A and B forms differ in marker and header conventions, including where required compression tables and field information are supplied. Other containers can use other conventions. The JPEG image standard therefore supplies the underlying picture coding, while the particular MJPEG representation supplies its video organization. Those two pieces determine how to locate, decode, and schedule the images in an older camera clip or capture. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Compression Artifacts Apple ProRes Video References ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding Apple: QuickTime video sample data and Motion-JPEG variants

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Apple ProRes Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Apple ProRes Video Apple ProRes is a family of intra-frame video codecs used for production and editing, with separate variants for different quality and sample requirements. An editor needs to jump to arbitrary frames, make cuts, combine layers, and render repeatedly. A streaming copy instead aims to deliver an acceptable finished picture with an economical data rate. Apple ProRes is designed around the production job, which explains why a ProRes export can be much larger than its playback derivative. Access one picture without a long prediction chain Conventional ProRes video encodes each picture independently. The decoder does not need earlier picture samples to predict a selected frame. It reconstructs that frame's block-coded data using the stream and frame information. This is useful for scrubbing and distributing complete pictures among processing tasks. Its within-picture transforms and quantization still compress the data; “independent” describes temporal dependence, rather than uncompressed storage. Keeping more picture information through a production workflow leaves later rendering and delivery encoders a useful source. A smaller proxy can serve the editing job when responsiveness or storage is more important, with finishing performed from the retained higher-quality media. Selected 422 variants and their data budgets Apple gives these approximate target rates for 1920 × 1080 at 29.97 fps : Variant Approximate target video rate Two-hour picture-only estimate ProRes 422 Proxy 45 Mb/s 40.5 GB ProRes 422 LT 102 Mb/s 91.8 GB ProRes 422 147 Mb/s 132.3 GB ProRes 422 HQ 220 Mb/s 198 GB The size estimate uses rate × 7,200 seconds ÷ 8 . It assumes the listed target is the exact average for that example and excludes audio and container overhead. Actual ProRes rate varies with source characteristics, raster, rate, and encoding choices; the table is not a measurement of every export. The profile names select different coding-quality/data-rate priorities within the 422 family. They do not mean that a Proxy converted into HQ acquires source detail that the Proxy discarded. Color and alpha are separately represented The 422 variants support 10-bit source picture workflows with 4:2:2 sampling. ProRes 4444 and 4444 XQ provide higher-fidelity color representation and optional alpha, the transparency information used when compositing layers. Conventional 422/4444 color-picture coding is lossy . The 4444 variants can encode their alpha losslessly, up to the supported alpha precision. A graphic's transparency can therefore be preserved exactly while its color picture uses another reconstruction guarantee. This separation matters when inspecting a production asset: sample depth, color sampling, and alpha presence describe different parts of its usefulness in a composite. RAW follows another input path ProRes RAW and RAW HQ represent a separate sensor-data workflow. Their input is intended for RAW processing rather than the conventional already formed video picture described by the 422/4444 coding family. A file using a logarithmic camera transfer is not automatically RAW. Its codec variant and its color/transfer description identify different stages of representation. Retain the source for finishing A ProRes production copy can supply an Emby viewing version after the relevant decoder and processing stages reconstruct it. That viewing version can use temporal prediction and another rate allocation suited to delivery, while the production source remains available for later work. The useful choice is the role of each copy: proxy for efficient editing, retained production media for finishing, and delivery encode for viewing. The format and variant make those roles explicit. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Avid DNxHR Video Video Generation Loss How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References SMPTE RDD 36: Apple ProRes bitstream syntax and decoding process Apple: ProRes white paper Apple: About ProRes

articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.title: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.keywords: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video codec compatibility depends on the encoded stream and the decoder available to a particular playback app. Consider a playback target with this illustrative usable video capability: H.264 High, 8-bit 4:2:0. Up to a suitable 1080p30 workload and its supported level/buffer limits. MP4 packaging accepted by the selected player. Compatible audio, no subtitle rendering requirement, and adequate delivery bandwidth. This is a declared example, not an Emby device support table . It lets us follow why three similar-looking files take different paths. Source Video decision Packaging decision H.264 High, 8-bit 1080p24, in MP4 Matches the declared video target Matches The same encoded video, in an unsupported wrapper Video still matches Repackage if a compatible mapping is available H.264 High 10, 10-bit 1080p24, in MP4 Sample/profile requirement differs Already acceptable The first source can be delivered without video conversion. The second may only need the video packets placed into compatible packaging. The third needs a new video representation even though “H.264,” “1080p,” and “MP4” all appear in both descriptions. Container, decoder, resource, and presentation failures The container reader first needs to identify and extract the track correctly. It supplies the codec configuration and coded data to a decoder. Repackaging changes this outer representation while preserving video coding when the new mapping supports it. The decoder then needs the stream's actual tools and sample format . A 10-bit High 10 stream asks for different processing from an 8-bit High stream. A profile conversion requires reconstructing the source and encoding pictures using the target's permitted format and tools. Next come resource requirements . The same codec and profile at a higher rate or larger raster can exceed the target's throughput or decoded-buffer limits. The level calculations show how those demands are assessed. Finally, the player must present the decoded pictures with their timing, aspect, and color information. A successful decode is a necessary stage, while display processing gives the samples their intended presentation. A hardware capability has to be usable by the app A chip's media engine, the operating-system API that exposes it, and the playback framework selected by the app are separate components. The app needs a working route through them for the requested format. A software decoder can provide another route. Its required picture processing still has to finish quickly enough for playback. Whether a given source uses hardware, software, or another conversion therefore depends on the active implementation, rather than simply on the codec's name. Put the server decoder into a conversion path Video transcoding contains two decoder boundaries: Source file → server input decoder → processing and output encoder → client decoder → display. For the High 10 example, the server must first understand the source's 10-bit AVC. It can then construct the required 8-bit target representation and encode it for the client. The client only decodes that new stream. The source and delivered video may both be labeled H.264 because their codec family is the same. The profile, precision, bitrate, or other properties changed. Conversely, a server that can encode a target codec still needs an input decoder for the source before it can perform that conversion. In an Emby session, compare the selected source track with the delivered stream and the reported conversion reason. If the video already matches but audio, subtitles, or a delivery limit needs work, those requirements can choose another route. The case analysis locates the operation instead of treating every change as a missing codec. See Also Containers and Codecs Video Codec Profiles Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.title: VC-1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.keywords: VC-1 Video VC-1 is the video coding format standardized in SMPTE ST 421 with Simple, Main, and Advanced profiles. VC-1 is the video coding format standardized in SMPTE ST 421. It is associated with the Windows Media video ecosystem and older movie collections. The useful source description includes its Simple, Main, or Advanced profile , rather than only the broader Windows Media name. The standard reconstructs 8-bit 4:2:0 picture samples. Its coding tools determine how the compressed track turns into those samples. Reconstruct an inter-coded region The decoder selects the available reference information and applies the coded motion description to form a predictor. A correction block describes how the target region differs from that predictor. VC-1 can use different transform shapes for inter-coded corrections: Transform shape Region it represents 8 × 8 A square correction block 8 × 4 A horizontally extended sub-block 4 × 8 A vertically extended sub-block 4 × 4 A smaller square sub-block Transform signaling and sub-block patterns tell the decoder which structure to apply. Different shapes can describe a localized correction more effectively than one fixed square basis for every region. The coded coefficients are inverse-quantized and inverse-transformed. The decoder adds the resulting samples to the predictor. Applicable overlap-smoothing and loop-filter operations complete the specified reconstruction behavior. As in other predictive codecs, the encoder chooses a representation, while the decoder follows its syntax. Quantization controls reconstruction precision; selecting a transform shape is a way to represent the correction, rather than a new display resolution. Interpret the picture's scan structure Advanced profile includes interlaced picture coding. The picture structure tells decoding and motion handling how its line sets relate. For a native interlaced scene, alternating rows come from successive field times. Frame-shaped and field-shaped coding decisions have to preserve that relationship. A final progressive presentation then needs the appropriate field reconstruction . For a film transfer, repeated or related field presentation can instead reflect a progressive source cadence. The picture's format and timing information help identify that case, with inverse telecine providing the corresponding recovery process. This makes interlaced VC-1 more than a progressive picture with an “i” label: its decoder needs the relevant prediction and picture-structure operations. Keep reconstruction and display interpretation together ST 421 specifies coded reconstruction, while a complete player also interprets sample aspect, color, and timing information for presentation. Reconstructed samples with the wrong display shape are still being interpreted incorrectly. In an Emby library inspection, record the actual VC-1 profile and scan structure along with its raster and rate. That identifies the reconstruction job before a playback route either presents the decoded source or supplies it to another encoder. The format's standard reference is SMPTE ST 421:2013, VC-1 Compressed Video Bitstream Format and Decoding Process . It supplies the profile-specific syntax and reconstruction rules behind those observations. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References SMPTE ST 421: VC-1 bitstream format and decoding process

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/index.html.title: Overview: VPx and AV1 | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/index.html.keywords: Overview: VPx and AV1 VP8, VP9 and AV1 are distinct video coding formats with different tools and decoder requirements. A web-oriented format label does not identify one universal decoder. VP8, VP9 and AV1 use their own coded-picture definitions, and support depends on the particular player or processing path. The pages here explain each format separately so container choice and codec capability can be compared without merging the two. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> VP8 VP8 is an 8-bit 4:2:0 video coding format associated with WebM and real-time web media. VP9 VP9 is a video coding format whose profiles distinguish supported bit depths and color sampling. AV1 AV1 is a video coding format defined by the Alliance for Open Media with profiles, levels, and optional film-grain signaling. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References RFC 6386: VP8 data format and decoding guide WebM Project: VP9 bitstream and decoding specification (draft) AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: AV1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: AV1 Video AV1 is a video coding format defined by the Alliance for Open Media with profiles, levels, and optional film-grain signaling. AV1 is the video coding format defined by the Alliance for Open Media. Its bitstream contains instructions for reconstructing picture samples, maintaining reference state, and preparing visible output. One useful AV1 distinction is that the picture retained for later prediction and the picture prepared for display can pass through different operations. OBUs, frame headers, and superblock partitions AV1 organizes coded data into Open Bitstream Units (OBUs) . Sequence information establishes the applicable profile, sample format, and other stream parameters. Frame information describes the picture's reconstruction choices, reference updates, and output behavior. Tile data supplies the coded regional information. A decoder needs the relevant headers as well as the block payloads. The picture isn't described by an isolated list of pixel values. Its block organization can start with 64 × 64 or 128 × 128 superblocks . Regions are partitioned further to fit the picture structure. The chosen partitions define where prediction and correction decisions apply. Construct the scene and its correction Intra modes use reconstructed information within the picture. Inter modes use retained decoded pictures with motion information, including permitted compound predictions from multiple views. A compound predictor can combine corresponding estimates of a region. Masks or weights can give different contributions where the coding mode permits them. The aim is to leave a correction that can be described efficiently. Transform and quantization operations represent that remaining correction. The decoder recovers coefficients, constructs the correction, and adds it to the predictor. Quantization settings control the approximation in ordinary lossy AV1, while the partition and prediction choices control how effectively the input is represented. Filter the reconstructed picture inside the coding loop AV1 includes several reconstruction-filtering stages. Deblocking addresses selected block-boundary behavior. CDEF , the Constrained Directional Enhancement Filter, identifies a local direction and constrains its filtering so the operation can address artifacts while respecting that structure. Loop restoration supplies additional signaled processing of reconstructed regions. The result used for reference updates is the applicable loop-restored picture. Later prediction needs these samples, so the encoder must locally reconstruct corresponding reference state. This separates coding-loop work from optional presentation processing. A filter used outside the reference loop can change what is shown without changing the samples later blocks predict from. Add grain to output when it is signaled Some AV1 streams describe film grain with parameters rather than coding every original grain sample as picture texture. An encoder can represent a cleaner scene and supply information for synthesizing grain in output processing. Those parameters describe such things as how grain strength varies with brightness, how nearby grain samples relate, and the generation seed. The decoder uses the specified process to produce the intended grain-like appearance. Grain is applied to output samples; the loop-restored reference picture remains the predictor state. Keeping the newly synthesized pattern outside that reference avoids making future scene prediction depend on that particular display grain realization. The film-grain explanation follows the preservation and modeling tradeoff. The metadata describes an appearance model, rather than an exact archive of every grain sample captured in the source. Decoded pictures and visible pictures AV1 can decode a hidden reference picture and later show a retained picture through its output instructions. A coded unit count therefore need not equal the number of new visible camera moments. The container's timeline and the format's picture/output instructions cooperate to schedule the visible result. In an Emby conversion, the chosen decoded output needs to include the applicable grain and presentation interpretation for the result being encoded or displayed. Reference details for the format Detail Meaning Main profile, sequence profile 0 8-bit or 10-bit, 4:2:0 or monochrome sample permissions Other profiles Additional permitted sample formats Level and tier Workload and coded-rate constraints libaom, SVT-AV1, hardware encoder Implementations choosing an AV1 representation Grain parameters An optional output-synthesis description An encoder's search and rate-control decisions determine which valid representation is produced. A decoder follows its AV1 syntax and reconstruction rules; it does not need to be the implementation that created the stream. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility VP9 Video Film Grain in Compressed Video Video Codec Levels and Tiers References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP8 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP8 Video VP8 is an 8-bit 4:2:0 video coding format associated with WebM and real-time web media. A web recording can contain a changing foreground over a mostly stable background. If every new picture used only the immediately preceding one, the best view of an uncovered background region might have disappeared behind the foreground. VP8 provides three logical reference roles so its predictor can use more than that immediately preceding view. Reference role Purpose in reconstruction Last A retained recent reconstructed picture Golden A picture retained separately for later reuse Altref An alternate retained picture available for prediction These are decoder reference roles, not three independently selectable video tracks. Retain a useful view Suppose a decoded picture shows the whole wall. The encoder can preserve it in a golden reference while later displayed pictures show a person crossing in front of it. When a wall region becomes visible again, a predictor can use the retained wall samples instead of the recently obscured region. The bitstream tells the decoder which available reference to select for each relevant block and which motion information locates its samples. A coded residual supplies the changes needed for the current picture. VP8 divides picture work into 16 × 16 macroblocks with smaller block operations. Its common reconstructed sample representation is 8-bit 4:2:0 . Integer reconstruction rules, transforms, quantization, and filtering define the result that later prediction will reuse. Refresh the reference state A decoded frame can replace the last, golden, or alternate reference according to the stream's update instructions. A picture retained as golden need not be replaced just because another picture has been shown. A keyframe establishes independently reconstructed content and refreshes the relevant reference state. Initially several logical roles can refer to the same newly reconstructed picture. Their later updates create the differing views used for prediction. This makes reference updating part of decoding. A picture is not simply forgotten after display; the next blocks may still need its samples. Decode a frame without showing it VP8 has a show_frame flag. A coded frame can reconstruct useful reference content while not becoming a displayed picture at that point. The decoder still performs its work and can retain the result. Later visible frames can predict from that state. Counting coded frames and counting displayed pictures therefore answer different questions. An output timeline is supplied by the surrounding media system. WebM is a common wrapper for VP8, carrying timestamps and other tracks. The coded reference operations and the container's scheduling cooperate to produce the recording. RFC 6386 documents the format and decoding process as an informational publication. It also says the supplied reference decoder takes precedence over conflicting narrative. This is the appropriate specification context when following the technical details. See Also VP9 Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Inter-Frame Video Prediction Containers and Codecs References RFC 6386: VP8 data format and decoding guide

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP9 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP9 Video VP9 is a video coding format whose profiles distinguish supported bit depths and color sampling. VP9 organizes video reconstruction around flexible picture regions and retained reference pictures. It is often found in web-origin media and is commonly carried by WebM. Build the picture in regions The coded picture is organized into 64 × 64 superblocks , with smaller blocks selected for local content. A broad predictable area can use a larger region while a changing edge can be split more finely. The decoder constructs the selected intra or inter predictor, decodes the transformed correction, and applies the specified reconstruction and loop filtering. Prediction divisions and transform choices let different parts of a picture use different descriptions. Tiles organize groups of coded blocks and provide processing boundaries useful for parallel decoding. The picture header and the required references supply state beyond an individual block's local bytes. Choose from retained views A VP9 decoder maintains eight reference slots . The frame header selects at most three of those reference pictures for its prediction choices. Blocks then choose the applicable reference or permitted compound pair. This separates two decisions: Decision Scope Which decoded pictures are retained? Reference-slot state across frames Which references are available for this frame? Frame-header selection Which available reference prediction is used? Block-level coding choice A frame can refresh selected slots with its reconstructed picture. A useful older view can remain in another slot while newer views are decoded. For compound prediction , the decoder forms predictions from two references and combines them. If they describe the scene from useful neighboring views, their combination can leave a smaller residual than either alone. The coded residual still defines the necessary correction. VP9 also permits reference pictures of different dimensions under its scaling and format constraints. Prediction can include the specified reference rescaling rather than assuming every stored view has the current picture's grid. Reconstruction and display are separate instructions A coded frame can be hidden : decoded and retained without being shown as the next visible picture. The format can also instruct the decoder to show an existing retained picture rather than send a complete new reconstruction. These choices explain why coded-frame count and visible-picture count can differ. They are part of the representation, not evidence that a camera necessarily recorded an additional moment. The container timeline schedules visible output, while the VP9 header and block syntax rebuild the reference state and picture content needed for it. Identify the sample format precisely VP9 profile Sample depth Color sampling 0 8-bit 4:2:0 1 8-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 2 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:0 3 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 The depth and sampling determine the sample arrays those operations reconstruct. Color and transfer information then establish their display interpretation, including an appropriate HDR path for HDR content. A decoder target is consequently described by the actual profile, sample format and resource limits, rather than just “VP9.” In an Emby conversion, those source arrays are reconstructed before processing creates the output representation. The WebM Project labels its linked bitstream/decoding description a draft . Its published profile definition and implementation provide the accompanying reference context; the draft's status should remain explicit when using its detailed coding rules. See Also VP8 Video AV1 Video Video Codec Profiles What HDR Video Adds to SDR References WebM Project: VP9 bitstream and decoding specification (draft) WebM Project: VP9 coding profiles

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/index.title: Overview: Color and pixel formats | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/index.keywords: Overview: Color and pixel formats Color representation describes how picture components, sample precision and memory layouts carry a video signal. A decoded frame needs an interpretation as well as a pixel count. RGB or YCbCr components, chroma sampling, range and bit depth shape that interpretation; a memory layout determines how software and devices exchange the samples. This branch connects those properties to common color errors and to the formats used within a media pipeline. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How video color is represented Video color is represented by component samples together with information that gives those samples their spatial and colorimetric meaning. RGB video RGB video represents picture positions using red, green, and blue component values interpreted through specified primaries, range, and transfer characteristics. YCbCr video YCbCr represents video using luma and two color-difference components that can be coded and sampled separately. Chroma subsampling Chroma subsampling reduces the spatial density of color-difference samples while retaining a denser luma grid. Chroma sample location Chroma sample location specifies the position of color-difference samples relative to the luma grid so reconstruction can align color with the picture. Precision and banding Sample precision, banding and dithering explain how smooth color or luminance changes become discrete signal values. Limited and full range Video range defines the numerical scaling and offsets that connect stored component codes to their intended signal values. Pixel layouts Pixel layouts define how picture components are arranged in memory and exchanged between processing stages. Video color tags and signaling Color signaling describes how a playback or conversion stage should interpret the component values of a video picture. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.title: Overview: Pixel layouts | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.keywords: Overview: Pixel layouts Pixel layouts define how picture components are arranged in memory and exchanged between processing stages. Two buffers can describe the same picture while storing its samples differently. Plane arrangement, component packing and precision affect how a decoder, filter or hardware interface accesses that data. NV12 and P010 are concrete layouts in this branch, following the general page on pixel formats and memory organization. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Pixel formats and memory layout A pixel format defines how decoded picture components are represented and arranged for access by a processing stage. NV12 NV12 stores 8-bit 4:2:0 video using a luma plane followed by interleaved Cb and Cr samples. P010 P010 stores 10-bit 4:2:0 video in 16-bit words, with a luma plane and an interleaved Cb/Cr plane. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.title: NV12 Pixel Format | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.keywords: NV12 Pixel Format NV12 stores 8-bit 4:2:0 video using a luma plane followed by interleaved Cb and Cr samples. NV12 is an 8-bit 4:2:0 semiplanar sample layout. One plane stores Y; another stores alternating Cb and Cr bytes. APIs commonly call those chroma components U and V, so the second plane is often called the UV plane. For a linear, tightly packed 4 × 2 example, all active bytes can be listed: Byte offsets Content 0–3 Y00, Y01, Y02, Y03 4–7 Y10, Y11, Y12, Y13 8–11 Cb0, Cr0, Cb1, Cr1 There are eight luma samples and two samples of each chroma component. That gives twelve active bytes. The chroma row has half as many sample pairs as a luma row has positions, but each pair occupies two bytes, so their active row byte widths match. Why NV12 appears during processing The Y plane is straightforward to access for luma operations, and the two chroma components needed together are adjacent. This layout is used by video-processing and hardware-decoding interfaces; Microsoft documents it for accelerated 4:2:0 video rendering. An Emby conversion can therefore use an NV12 working surface even when its source file is described by an H.264 codec name and an MKV container. These labels describe different layers of the session. NV12 specifies sample precision, grouping, and order. The frame still needs range, matrix, transfer, and primaries to establish color meaning. Swapping Cb/Cr order produces the related NV21 organization; increasing component precision to the P010 convention changes storage word size and bit placement. A processing boundary must match the concrete format it receives. Finding a chroma pair For even picture dimensions, the chroma array has W/2 columns of pairs and H/2 rows. In a simple contiguous linear allocation with pitch P, height H, and no extra allocated rows, its base follows the Y plane at base + P × H . The pair indexed for luma column x and row y is located at: chroma base + floor(y/2) × P + 2 × floor(x/2). Cb is at that address and Cr at the next byte. In the tightly packed 4 × 2 frame above, luma position (3, 1) is at Y offset 7 . Its indexed chroma pair begins at 8 + 0 × 4 + 2 × 1 = 10 , with Cb at 10 and Cr at 11. Color reconstruction still uses the intended sample location and interpolation. The addressing calculation identifies a stored pair; it does not turn that pair into a directly measured full-resolution color at every nearby luma position. Pitch belongs to the allocation In this 4 × 2 allocation, pitch is 8 rather than 4. The Y rows start at offsets 0 and 8, and the UV row at 16. Its total illustrated storage is 24 bytes. The sample counts are unchanged. Use the surface's reported plane locations and strides when accessing it. A tightly packed 1.5 × W × H byte calculation counts active samples; it is not a universal allocation-size rule. Related API formats can also provide noncontiguous planes or explicitly tiled storage. See Also Pixel Formats and Memory Layout P010 Pixel Format Chroma Subsampling Video Color Tags and Signaling References Microsoft: NV12 layout and 8-bit video formats Linux V4L2: NV12 and related planar formats Microsoft: DXGI format definitions

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.title: P010 Pixel Format | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.keywords: P010 Pixel Format P010 stores 10-bit 4:2:0 video in 16-bit words, with a luma plane and an interleaved Cb/Cr plane. P010 gives every 10-bit component sample a 16-bit storage word . The ten meaningful bits occupy bits 15 through 6, with the low six bits zero in the defined representation. In the little-endian P010 layout described here, the low byte is stored first. For the illustrated sample 940 , shifting the sample left by six positions gives 940 × 64 = 60,160 = 0xEB00 . Its two bytes, in increasing address order, are 0x00, 0xEB . A processing format for ten-bit values P010 and a fully planar 10-bit format can represent equivalent component values while organizing and aligning their bits differently. A conversion between them moves and places the values correctly. It does not need to reduce their ten-bit precision. In an Emby processing description, P010 can identify a working surface used after decoding or between filters and an encoder. It describes the sample layout at that boundary. The color description establishes whether those samples represent SDR, PQ, HLG, or another intended interpretation. Those properties together determine the next stage's reading and processing of the picture. Sample numbers and stored words 10-bit sample value Stored 16-bit word Bytes, low address first 64 4,096 = 0x1000 00 10 512 32,768 = 0x8000 00 80 513 32,832 = 0x8040 40 80 940 60,160 = 0xEB00 00 EB These codes include common limited-range black, neutral chroma, and nominal white values. The example 513 also shows that increasing the sample by one increases its stored word by 64, not one. Reading a P010 word as an ordinary unshifted 10-bit sample consequently produces the wrong value. A CPU reader of this defined representation obtains the code by shifting the word right by six. The value's range interpretation is a subsequent calculation. Two planes, wider elements P010 retains the semiplanar organization familiar from NV12 : all Y samples in one plane and interleaved Cb/Cr samples in another. For an even W × H picture, each chroma component has W/2 × H/2 samples. A 4 × 2 picture has eight Y words and four chroma words, or 24 active bytes . With a tight 8-byte pitch, Y rows start at offsets 0 and 8; the interleaved chroma row starts at 16. Its Cb0, Cr0, Cb1, Cr1 words start at byte offsets 16, 18, 20, and 22. The active byte width of a Y row is 2W. A chroma row holds W/2 pairs, each four bytes, so its active width is also 2W. Padding or extra allocated rows can enlarge a real surface; the API's supplied strides and offsets describe that allocation.
