articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.title: Pixel Formats and Memory Layout | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/pixel.keywords: Pixel Formats and Memory Layout A pixel format defines how decoded picture components are represented and arranged for access by a processing stage. A video decoder's output has to be usable by the next stage. That stage needs to find the components for a picture position, determine their precision, and move from one row to another. Pixel format describes the sample representation and organization that makes this possible. The compressed movie file has a codec and container. The decoded frame has component arrays or a hardware surface. Pixel format concerns this latter representation; its memory footprint is different from the compressed file's size. One picture can have several byte arrangements Consider an 8-bit 4:2:0 frame with even dimensions. Its luma samples form a full-size grid. Each color-difference component has half as many columns and rows. The same samples can be laid out in different ways: Arrangement Memory regions What lies beside what? Fully planar YCbCr, such as yuv420p Y, then separate Cb and Cr planes in a simple contiguous allocation Neighboring samples of the same component Semiplanar NV12 Y plane and a Cb/Cr plane Chroma appears as alternating Cb, Cr values Packed RGB24 after a component conversion A region with three component bytes per picture position R, G, B for one position, then R, G, B for the next The first two rows can organize identical YCbCr values. The third row also changes the component representation, requiring the YCbCr-to-RGB calculation . A processing stage should distinguish a rearrangement of existing values from a conversion that calculates new values. “Plane” means a region or array used for a component or component group. It need not be a separate allocation, and the generic name does not guarantee that every implementation places all planes consecutively in one block. A twelve-byte frame, first without padding Use a tiny 4 × 2 picture so every active sample can be counted: Y: four columns × two rows = eight samples. Cb: two columns × one row = two samples. Cr: two columns × one row = two samples. At one byte per sample, that is twelve bytes. In a tightly packed planar Y–Cb–Cr allocation, offsets 0–7 hold Y, offsets 8–9 Cb, and 10–11 Cr. In a tightly packed NV12 allocation, offsets 0–7 still hold Y, while offsets 8–11 contain Cb0, Cr0, Cb1, Cr1 . Reading the NV12 chroma bytes as if they were two separate planes pairs the wrong values together. The resulting colors can be badly wrong even though the total byte count is correct. The layout's component order matters just as much for RGB. A physically stored B, G, R sequence interpreted as R, G, B swaps red and blue. The exact format definition supplies that order; a broad label such as “32-bit RGB” is insufficient to determine every byte's role and alpha convention. Row pitch explains the extra bytes Stride , or row pitch , is the byte distance from the start of one row to the start of the next. It can exceed the active row width because an allocator aligns rows or reserves padding. This deliberately small linear example has an 8-byte pitch. It is one possible allocation, not a required pitch for all four-column surfaces. With that pitch, the two Y rows occupy sixteen bytes. A chroma row occupies another eight bytes: four active component bytes and four padding bytes. The allocation illustrated holds 24 bytes , although the active samples still need only twelve. For a linear plane whose base pointer is B, a byte-sized sample at column x, row y is found at: address = B + y × pitch + x. For a two-byte sample, the horizontal term becomes 2x. For interleaved components, each stored element's size and component offset also enter the calculation. The NV12 and P010 examples work through those specific conventions. Using active width as if it were pitch makes the second row start too early whenever padding is present. A reader then treats padding or the tail of the previous row as picture data. The defect can repeat across the frame as shifted or corrupted rows. Some image APIs can expose negative strides for bottom-up storage. Others impose positive strides for a specific video format. The API-provided base, plane offsets, dimensions, and strides establish the accessible rows; a generic width calculation cannot replace them. Precision is not always the storage width The 4 × 2 frame contains twelve component samples regardless of whether they use 8-bit or 10-bit coding precision. NV12 holds each in one byte. P010 holds each in a two-byte word, with its ten meaningful bits in specified positions. An unpadded P010 version consequently needs 24 bytes for its active sample words. The extra storage does not add picture positions. It provides a wider word for each component sample. Names such as yuv420p10le and p010le therefore encode useful differences: both can describe 10-bit 4:2:0 values, while their plane grouping and significant-bit positions differ. A stage receiving one cannot simply rename it as the other. The values must be read and stored according to their respective layouts. Frame size and the cost of repeated access For a linear unpadded 1920 × 1080 NV12 frame, the active storage is: 1,920 × 1,080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes , about 2.97 MiB . The corresponding P010 sample words occupy 6,220,800 bytes , about 5.93 MiB . Real allocations can add row padding, extra allocated height, or device-specific organization. Now imagine a processing pass that reads every active NV12 byte and writes a same-sized output at 60 frames per second. Its simple sample-traffic budget is: 3,110,400 × 2 × 60 = 373,248,000 bytes per second. The equivalent P010 read/write budget is twice that. Several distinct passes can repeatedly touch this data. Combining operations, reusing surfaces, or keeping suitable data on a device can reduce transfers between stages. These totals are arithmetic for the stated hypothetical pass, not measurements of a GPU bus or an Emby session. Cache reuse, tiling, fused operations, and which memory is accessed change actual traffic. They explain why moving decoded pictures can become substantial work even when the compressed movie arrives at a modest network bitrate. Hardware surfaces have access rules A hardware frame may be described by a device surface rather than a CPU pointer to a simple row-major array. Its storage can be tiled, device-local, or otherwise accessible only through the relevant API. A transfer or mapping operation makes an appropriate representation available to a stage that cannot operate on that surface directly. Hardware format and software sample format can both appear in a processing description: the first identifies the device-backed frame, while the latter describes the sample representation associated with it. Reading a reported device format as if it named an ordinary byte array omits the surface's access contract. In an Emby conversion, compatibility between decoder output, filters, and encoder input determines where rearrangement, precision conversion, or memory transfer is needed. A pixel-format change in a log is useful evidence about that boundary. The format names, dimensions, and device context together explain the operation it requires. See Also NV12 Pixel Format P010 Pixel Format RGB Video Chroma Subsampling Video Bit Depth References FFmpeg 8.1: Pixel-format definitions FFmpeg 8.1: AVFrame planes, line sizes, and color properties Microsoft: Uncompressed video buffers and stride Linux V4L2: Planar, semiplanar, contiguous, and tiled layouts

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.title: Overview: Precision and banding | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.keywords: Overview: Precision and banding Sample precision, banding and dithering explain how smooth color or luminance changes become discrete signal values. A smooth gradient has to be represented by a finite set of sample values. When those steps become visible, the picture can show bands. Bit depth describes the available precision, while dithering changes the pattern and visibility of quantization differences. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Video bit depth Video bit depth determines how many distinct coded values are available for each component sample. Color banding Color banding occurs when a smooth change in picture values is represented by visible plateaus and transitions. Dithering Video dithering varies quantization decisions across positions or time so rounding error is less likely to form coherent visible bands. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.title: Video Bit Depth | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.keywords: Video Bit Depth Video bit depth determines how many distinct coded values are available for each component sample. An 8-bit component sample can select one of 256 unsigned values. A 10-bit sample can select one of 1,024 . Bit depth changes how finely a component's value can be represented; it does not change how many picture positions are present. Precision per component Possible unsigned codes Code interval 8 bits 2⁸ = 256 0–255 10 bits 2¹⁰ = 1,024 0–1,023 12 bits 2¹² = 4,096 0–4,095 “10-bit video” usually describes the precision of each coded component sample. It does not mean ten bits for all three components combined. With chroma subsampling , a frame also contains different numbers of luma and chroma samples. Smaller steps across the same signal interval For a normalized full-range component, the endpoints 0 and 1 span 255 intervals at 8 bits or 1,023 intervals at 10 bits. Adjacent reconstructed values are therefore separated by 1/255 or 1/1,023 respectively. A magnified interval of encoded signal values. The axes are normalized signal coordinates, not physical light or nits. At input value 0.43 , nearest rounding gives: 8-bit: round(0.43 × 255) = 110; reconstructed value 110/255 ≈ 0.431373 . 10-bit: round(0.43 × 1,023) = 440; reconstructed value 440/1,023 ≈ 0.430108 . The errors for that point are approximately +0.001373 and +0.000108. Their ratio varies with the selected point. The general bound is more useful: away from clipping, nearest rounding is within half a step, about 0.001961 at 8 bits or 0.000489 at 10 bits in this example. The finer grid lets a gentle gradient cross more intermediate values before reaching its endpoint. Whether those steps become visible also depends on the transfer relationship, the image, subsequent processing, and viewing conditions. Color banding develops that visual consequence. Nominal range uses a subset of the codes Limited-range video assigns black and nominal white inside the available unsigned interval. For a common luma coding, 8-bit black and white are 16 and 235; the equivalent 10-bit codes are 64 and 940. The nominal luma interval consequently has 220 integer code points at 8 bits and 877 at 10 bits, including both endpoints. The spacing is governed by 219 and 876 intervals. Chroma uses its own scaling and neutral offset. Bit depth and range jointly determine those numerical conventions. At a fixed transfer relationship, finer encoded steps usually give finer light steps too, but those light steps need not be uniform. For example, PQ assigns a nonlinear light meaning to its signal coordinates. Ten bits describe precision; PQ supplies the light interpretation. Precision through a conversion For an Emby playback route, the source precision helps establish the decoder's required profile, while the working format describes the processing surface. The encoder's output precision is another explicit choice. Those stages identify where intermediate values can be retained or rounded. Higher-precision working values are useful even when the source is 8-bit. Scaling, color conversion, and tone mapping can calculate intermediate values between its original codes. Keeping those results at higher precision postpones a new rounding decision until the output needs a particular representation. Simply promoting unchanged 8-bit samples does something narrower. In a compatible limited-range conversion, code 110 can become code 440 at 10 bits: (110 − 16)/219 = (440 − 64)/876 . The numerical signal meaning is preserved, but the original intermediate gradations have not been discovered. Reducing precision makes the opposite decision. Multiple higher-precision results must share fewer output codes. Dithering can distribute those rounding choices to reduce coherent visible steps. Coding precision and storage width A 10-bit sample may occupy a 16-bit word in a decoded processing buffer. P010 , for example, stores ten meaningful bits in a wider word. That storage convention makes samples convenient to access; it does not give the coded picture sixteen bits of original precision. See Also Color Banding Video Dithering Limited and Full Video Range P010 Pixel Format Chroma Subsampling References ITU-R BT.709: 8-bit and 10-bit component coding ITU-R BT.2100: 10-bit and 12-bit HDR representations ITU-T H.265: Component bit depth and coded video profiles

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.title: Color Banding | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.keywords: Color Banding Color banding occurs when a smooth change in picture values is represented by visible plateaus and transitions. A sky fades gradually from one shade to another, but the video shows broad ribbons with visible boundaries. Those ribbons are color banding : neighboring regions share the same or very similar reconstructed values, separated by abrupt changes that were not apparent in the intended smooth gradient. The middle strip deliberately uses only 16 levels to make the plateaus easy to see. This is an original arithmetic illustration, not a claim about the precision of a particular video. How a gentle ramp becomes a plateau Imagine a high-precision signal that increases gradually from 100.1 to 100.4 when expressed in the destination's code units. Nearest rounding sends every one of those values to code 100. Their small differences disappear. As the signal reaches 100.5, rounding can switch to 101. If the original gradient crossed that threshold over a large, otherwise uniform area, a narrow numerical step now outlines a broad region. The absence of texture helps the eye notice it. The process can repeat across a sky, an animated background, or a wall under soft lighting. Higher bit depth provides smaller destination steps. Dithering changes how neighboring positions choose between steps, breaking up the common boundary. More than one stage can create the steps Stage How the gradient can change Useful comparison Source preparation or prior encoding Fine variations have already been rounded or discarded Inspect a decoded original frame Lossy video encoding Coarse reconstruction of transform corrections can flatten subtle variation Compare the encoder input with its decoded output Tone, color, or precision conversion A smooth calculated result is rounded into fewer usable values Compare values before and after the conversion Final rendering or display processing The delivered picture is reduced or processed further Compare the same output through another rendering path The coded sample depth establishes an available value grid. It does not require an encoder to preserve every subtle difference on that grid. A 10-bit stream can still contain flat regions produced by an earlier low-precision stage or by its compression decisions. This distinction helps interpret an Emby session that looks smooth during original playback but develops bands during conversion. The comparison should use the same passage and a similar presentation size. A higher output bitrate can help when the encoder is discarding gradient detail; a precision-conversion problem needs attention to the relevant output grid and rounding. The shape of the defect is useful evidence Bands tend to track contours of similar tone or color. Compression blocks tend to reveal the boundaries of a coding structure; ringing tends to appear beside an edge. A picture can contain several of these together, but locating the smooth region and its contour-shaped steps makes the banding question more specific. Pause on the same source frame and inspect it without repeatedly saving it through lossy image formats. A screenshot also represents the screenshot path's precision and color conversion, so it is evidence about that captured result. Comparing the decoded samples themselves can distinguish stored plateaus from a rendering effect. What an already banded source can yield Once many distinct inputs have collapsed to one code, a later stage cannot know their exact former values. A debanding operation can estimate a smooth surface from nearby samples; it changes the image according to that estimate. It can also soften genuine low-contrast texture if the two are difficult to distinguish. The clearest improvements happen before the unwanted collapse: preserve suitable working precision, control the encoder's reconstruction loss, and make the final precision reduction deliberately. This treats the point where the plateaus arise, rather than expecting a larger output file to recreate variation that is already gone. See Also Video Bit Depth Video Dithering Video Compression Artifacts How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References ITU-R BT.709: Component quantization ITU-T H.265: Quantization and reconstructed sample coding FFmpeg: Debanding filter implementation options

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.title: Video Dithering | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/preci.keywords: Video Dithering Video dithering varies quantization decisions across positions or time so rounding error is less likely to form coherent visible bands. Suppose an output representation has only integer codes, but a calculated picture region needs 2.25 . Rounding every position to 2 creates a uniform region whose stored average is 2. A pattern containing twelve positions at 2 and four at 3 has an average of: (12 × 2 + 4 × 3) / 16 = 2.25. Each position still uses a valid output code. The area contains a finer distribution of rounding choices instead of all positions making the same choice. Dithering uses that idea to reduce the coherent error that can turn gentle gradients into visible bands. The two lower strips both have only 16 permitted gray levels. Dithering changes where those levels occur. View the original image at full size to see the fine pattern. A threshold example you can calculate An ordered dither assigns different thresholds to positions in a small repeating grid. For the 16-position example, choose thresholds (k + 0.5)/16 for k = 0 through 15, arranged across the grid. Compare the fractional part 0.25 with each threshold. Exactly four thresholds are below 0.25. At those positions, choose the upper code 3; at the other twelve, choose the lower code 2. The desired sample average follows directly from the number of upper choices. The figure uses a four-by-four threshold arrangement and a deliberately coarse output grid. A slowly increasing input changes the proportion of upper choices within a neighborhood, giving it more gradual average changes than the uniform rounded plateaus. These are averages of encoded component values. The corresponding average display light also depends on the transfer relationship and reconstruction. The illustration demonstrates the quantizer's decision, rather than promising an exact light average for every video transfer function. Different ways to distribute error Approach How it makes the decisions Character of the result Ordered thresholds Uses a spatial threshold arrangement Repeatable fine pattern; the arrangement determines its texture Randomized dither Perturbs thresholds or values using a noise process Noise-like variation whose spatial and temporal design matters Error diffusion Carries a quantization error into later decisions Local choices compensate for earlier errors Each approach replaces a large correlated error pattern with another distribution of error. That distribution matters: a visible repeating texture or distracting temporal shimmer can be less desirable than the bands being reduced. Dither design concerns where the error's energy appears as well as how much error is present. FFmpeg's scaler and zscale offer documented dither choices, with different available methods. Their names describe implementation options; the arithmetic grid above is an independent illustration, not a reproduction of an Emby preset or a claim about a particular filter's default. The rounding boundary is the useful place Dithering is most useful when a stage still has intermediate values to decide between output codes. For example, a tone-mapping operation can calculate a high-precision gradient and then dither its conversion to an 8-bit output. If the input is already a flat plateau, simply adding variation does not reveal its lost original gradient. Debanding and precision preservation address different parts of that problem. Likewise, promoting a dithered 8-bit output to 10 bits preserves its existing pattern rather than recovering earlier sample values. In an Emby conversion, the relevant question is where precision is reduced relative to filtering and encoding. A lossy encoder can suppress the fine variations, or spend some of its budget preserving them. An effective result depends on the combined processing and encoding path. Inspect a decoded output gradient at its intended viewing size: the purpose is a smoother-looking transition with an acceptable texture, not a larger count of distinct codes for its own sake. See Also Video Bit Depth Color Banding Audio Quantization Noise References FFmpeg: Scaler dithering algorithms FFmpeg: zscale precision conversion and dither choices

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: Chroma Sample Location | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: Chroma Sample Location Chroma sample location specifies the position of color-difference samples relative to the luma grid so reconstruction can align color with the picture. Two pictures can both be 4:2:0 and still place their chroma samples differently. The subsampling ratio gives the spacing of the smaller color grids. Chroma sample location , or chroma siting , gives their position relative to the luma grid. The distinction is similar to knowing the spacing between fence posts without knowing where the first post stands. Reconstructing color needs both spacing and starting position. Gray dots are luma sample positions; orange dots are Cb/Cr pairs. Each example has the same number of samples. Coordinates use one luma spacing as the unit. Half a sample changes the interpolation Place the top-left luma sample at coordinate (0, 0). In the progressive examples pictured above, the first chroma pair is at: Location Horizontal coordinate Vertical coordinate Left 0 0.5 Center 0.5 0.5 Top-left 0 0 The next pair is two luma spacings away horizontally, and the next chroma row two spacings away vertically. The word “left” describes alignment with a luma column; it does not put every chroma sample at the left edge of the image. Suppose a horizontal chroma signal has values 0 at x = 0 and 0.4 at x = 2 , with no change vertically. Linear interpolation at luma position x = 1 gives 0.2 : that position is halfway between the samples. Now interpret those same stored values as centered samples at x = 0.5 and x = 2.5. Position x = 1 is only one quarter of the way between them, so the interpolated result is 0.1 . The array values and dimensions are unchanged; its assumed coordinates have changed the color reconstructed at a picture position. This simple interpolation is an illustration. More elaborate reconstruction filters still need the correct phase of the sample grid. Why a color edge can move Luma and chroma contribute together to reconstructed RGB. A siting mismatch moves the color transition relative to the luma transition. A colored outline beside a fine contrasting edge, or a small horizontal color displacement after conversion, can be the visible result. Uniform patches provide little evidence: moving a constant chroma field leaves its values the same. A test image with fine colored edges is more informative because it exposes the alignment between color structure and luma structure. This differs from subsampling loss . A lower-density grid cannot preserve all fine color detail, even when correctly located. Siting establishes where its surviving information belongs. An Emby conversion may pass through decoded surfaces and filters before encoding a new stream. If a color edge shifts only on that route, comparing the source, processing, and output chroma interpretations helps locate the change. Color signaling puts the sample-location field beside the other frame properties used in that comparison. Signaling and resampling have different jobs A codec can describe chroma location in its bitstream, and a decoder can carry that interpretation with its output frame. H.264 includes sample-location signaling with top-field and bottom-field distinctions. Interlaced material needs the appropriate field interpretation; the progressive coordinate table above is not a substitute for that geometry. Changing a location label tells the next stage where to interpret existing samples. Converting an image from one location to another requires resampling the chroma at new coordinates. That operation creates different sample values around edges while preserving the intended alignment of the picture. See Also Chroma Subsampling YCbCr Video Video Color Tags and Signaling References ITU-T H.264: Chroma geometry and VUI sample-location signaling FFmpeg 8.1: Chroma-location definitions FFmpeg: Input and output chroma-location conversion in zscale

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: Chroma Subsampling | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: Chroma Subsampling Chroma subsampling reduces the spatial density of color-difference samples while retaining a denser luma grid. Fine lettering can reveal a difference that a photograph hides. A narrow edge drawn mainly by a luma change can remain sharp in a 4:2:0 video. A similarly narrow edge distinguished mainly by color may spread or lose its original shape. The video has retained more spatial samples for luma than for color differences. Chroma subsampling makes that trade: it reduces the Cb and Cr sampling grids of YCbCr video . The luma grid retains its stated picture dimensions. A 1920 × 1080 4:2:0 frame still has 1920 × 1080 luma positions. In an Emby media report, the sampling format and sample precision describe different aspects of the decoder's input. Interpreting them alongside codec profile explains the actual picture format being delivered to the playback stack. Orange marks represent Cb/Cr pairs. The diagram illustrates sampling density; chroma siting specifies their exact positions. What the ratios mean for a frame For the common rectangular formats below, the middle number describes horizontal chroma density relative to luma. In 4:2:0, chroma is reduced vertically as well. The zero does not mean that a color component is missing or that the second row is monochrome. Sampling Y dimensions Dimensions of each of Cb and Cr Component samples in a 4 × 2 patch 4:4:4 W × H W × H 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 4:2:2 W × H W/2 × H 8 + 4 + 4 = 16 4:2:0 W × H W/2 × H/2 8 + 2 + 2 = 12 This table assumes even dimensions and progressive rectangular sample grids. Field-based video also needs its field geometry taken into account when color is reconstructed. At a fixed sample precision, 4:2:0 contains half as many component samples as 4:4:4. For an unpadded 8-bit 1920 × 1080 decoded frame, that is 3,110,400 bytes rather than 6,220,800 bytes . These are sample-buffer totals. A compressed file's bitrate also depends on its coding decisions and content. Reduction needs a filter, not just missing columns Imagine a row of color-difference values that alternates between +0.4 and −0.4. Keeping only every other value could retain all the +0.4 values, or all the −0.4 values, depending on the starting position. The reduced signal would suggest a uniform color bias that was never present in the row's average. A suitable reduction first filters the signal to control detail that the coarser grid cannot represent, then samples the filtered result. In a simple two-position averaging illustration, each +0.4/−0.4 pair becomes zero. That preserves the pair's neutral average while discarding its fine alternation. Actual filters have their own response and sample-location conventions. The illustration exposes the underlying choice: some high-frequency color structure must be removed before a lower-density grid can represent the result reliably. Filtering controls which structure is kept and how an edge changes. Reconstruction supplies color at the missing positions A display ultimately needs a color for every output position. Its renderer estimates the required Cb and Cr values from the available chroma samples and combines them with luma. Interpolation can create smooth transitions between measured positions, but it cannot identify which of several possible fine source patterns originally produced the same reduced samples. This is why converting a decoded 4:2:0 picture to a 4:4:4 working buffer increases the number of stored chroma values without recovering the camera's discarded fine color detail. That fuller buffer can still be useful for subsequent processing and compositing. For example, rendering new subtitle text after color reconstruction can give the text sharper color edges than text already embedded in a 4:2:0 source. If the combined picture is then encoded as 4:2:0, its new colored edges enter the chroma-reduction stage too. The placement of the overlay in the processing path therefore matters. Precision and spatial density solve different problems A 10-bit 4:2:0 picture offers finer component-value steps than an 8-bit 4:2:0 picture, with the same chroma-grid dimensions. An 8-bit 4:4:4 picture retains a denser chroma grid, with the same number of available values per component as other 8-bit formats. These choices affect different features: value precision is particularly relevant to smooth gradients, while chroma density is relevant to fine color structure. The sample-count table and the bit-depth grid measure those two dimensions separately. See Also YCbCr Video Chroma Sample Location Video Bit Depth NV12 Pixel Format References ITU-T H.264: Chroma formats and sample arrays Microsoft: Chroma sampling and video formats ITU-R BT.709: Component sampling for HDTV

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: Limited and Full Video Range | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: Limited and Full Video Range Video range defines the numerical scaling and offsets that connect stored component codes to their intended signal values. If a movie's blacks become gray and its whites look subdued, a range mismatch is one possible cause. The sample codes may have arrived intact, but the renderer has used the wrong black point and scale when interpreting them. In a common 8-bit limited-range luma representation, code 16 represents black and 235 nominal white. Full-range 8-bit luma instead uses 0 and 255 . Both conventions can describe the intended black-to-white interval. The mapping between that interval and its stored numbers is different. Inspection tools may abbreviate these conventions as tv and pc respectively. Those labels describe component coding; the intended interpretation still applies on either kind of display. Range interpretation can appear at the source decoder, a server conversion stage, an Emby app's renderer, and the final output path. For a result that changes between original playback and converted playback, compare the source and delivered stream's range fields and the actual sample transformation. Two mappings, calculated from the same signal Let E be a normalized luma signal from 0 to 1. In these 8-bit examples, form a stored code by nearest rounding: Limited: code = round(16 + 219 E) Full: code = round(255 E) Intended signal E Limited-range luma code Full-range luma code 0: reference black 16 0 0.25 71 64 0.5 126 128 0.75 180 191 1: nominal white 235 255 The two columns depict approximately the same signal levels through different numerical scales. Their integer rounding errors differ because their available code grids differ. The reverse calculation removes the corresponding offset and scale. Limited-range code 71 represents (71 − 16)/219 ≈ 0.25114 . Full-range code 64 represents 64/255 ≈ 0.25098 . Both are close to the intended quarter-scale signal. Why the wrong interpretation changes contrast Take limited-range black 16 and interpret it as full range. The signal becomes 16/255 ≈ 0.06275 , above black. Nominal white 235 becomes 235/255 ≈ 0.92157 , below white. The original black-to-white span is squeezed into the middle of the expected full-range interval. These percentages describe the encoded signal coordinate , not emitted light. The display's transfer relationship determines what light follows from each coordinate. The numerical mismatch nevertheless explains the raised black and compressed contrast. In the opposite direction, interpret full-range code 12 as limited range: (12 − 16)/219 ≈ −0.01826. The result lies below reference black. Full-range code 245 similarly becomes (245 − 16)/219 ≈ 1.04566 , above nominal white. If the subsequent presentation clips to the nominal interval, multiple dark or bright input codes collapse to the same endpoint. Detail is lost at those ends rather than merely shifted. Chroma has a neutral offset of its own Luma and RGB components describe nominal values from 0 to 1. YCbCr chroma describes signed color differences around zero, so its digital mapping also needs a neutral point. Common limited-range coding Luma black–white Chroma nominal interval Neutral chroma 8-bit 16–235 16–240 128 10-bit 64–940 64–960 512 For 8-bit limited chroma, the scale is 224 and the offset 128. Reusing the luma scale 219 or treating the chroma byte as an unsigned RGB intensity changes color reconstruction. Full-range chroma has its own defined mapping too; a generic 0–255 luma formula is not the complete three-component conversion. The codes beyond nominal luma black and white provide working margins in the relevant video systems. Filtering can produce excursions into those margins. A nominal range description and a specific clipping policy are separate decisions. A tag correction or an image conversion? A range tag describes how to interpret existing codes. Changing a tag does not rescale them. If our correctly coded limited-range black is 16, changing only its label to full range makes it the raised signal value calculated above. A real limited-to-full conversion instead maps each luma code through its source interpretation and into the destination scale: destination = round(255 × (source − 16)/219) Within the nominal interval, source 16 becomes 0, 235 becomes 255, and 71 becomes approximately 64. Chroma is converted using the appropriate chroma mapping. The output description must then agree with the converted samples. If a file contains full-range samples mislabeled as limited, correcting that incorrect label can restore the intended interpretation without changing its samples. Establishing what the samples actually represent is the step that distinguishes these two cases. articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: How Video Color Is Represented | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: How Video Color Is Represented Video color is represented by component samples together with information that gives those samples their spatial and colorimetric meaning. A decoder can recover every sample in a video frame correctly and still produce the wrong colors if the next stage gives those numbers the wrong meaning. A sample value is a coordinate in a representation. The playback path needs to know what that coordinate describes before it can turn it into display light. Consider three values at one picture position: 102, 93, 186 . As an 8-bit RGB triplet, they describe one mixture of red, green, and blue. As limited-range BT.709 YCbCr, they describe a luma value and two color differences, which reconstruct approximately to encoded RGB (0.80, 0.30, 0.10) . The bytes alone do not choose between these interpretations. These are relationships that a renderer must account for. A hardware or software implementation can combine several operations into one stage. The description that travels with a picture Several independent properties complete the representation. Each answers a different question. Property Question it answers Example Component representation What do the numbers describe? RGB components or YCbCr luma and color differences Sampling geometry Where are those samples in the picture? 4:2:0 chroma , with a specified sample location Precision and range Which numbers are available, and how are they scaled? 10-bit precision with limited-range coding Color interpretation Which primaries and light relationship are intended? BT.709 SDR, or BT.2020 primaries with PQ Storage layout Where does a processing stage find each component? Planar storage, NV12, or P010 The distinction becomes useful when two reports appear to disagree. A source can contain 10-bit 4:2:0 coded video while its decoded frame is held in P010, whose samples occupy 16-bit words. These descriptions refer to coding precision and memory storage respectively. They can both be correct. Likewise, BT.2020 does not specify a byte layout. 4:2:0 does not specify whether the picture is HDR. A renderer combines the relevant fields rather than treating one label as a complete color description. From a movie frame to a screen In a common YCbCr playback path, the decoder reconstructs a full-resolution luma plane and smaller chroma planes. Color reconstruction accounts for the chroma positions and obtains the component values needed at display positions. The range interpretation removes the numerical offsets and scales; the matrix relates luma and color differences to encoded RGB. The resulting RGB values still have a transfer-function meaning. They are not automatically proportional to emitted light. The player and display use the intended transfer relationship and primaries, and may adapt the picture to the display's color gamut or brightness capability. HDR-to-SDR tone mapping is one example where that adaptation becomes an explicit image operation. This explains why two failures can look different. A range mismatch can raise blacks across the whole picture. A matrix mismatch can move the colors of objects while leaving neutral grays much less affected. A transfer mismatch changes the relationship between signal values and brightness. Each symptom points to a different part of the representation. What survives a change of playback route? When an Emby app plays the original video, its playback stack interprets the source's samples and signaling. When the server converts the video, both the processed samples and their output description must agree. A correct conversion can change precision, component representation, range, or brightness encoding; the resulting tags should describe that new picture. The useful comparison is therefore a pair of complete descriptions: source and delivered output. Color signaling identifies the fields to examine, while ffprobe inspection shows where they appear in a report. Reading those fields together makes a green cast, washed-out black, or unexpected HDR result a question about specific interpretation steps. See Also RGB Video YCbCr Video Chroma Subsampling Video Color Tags and Signaling Color Gamut Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV image parameters ITU-R BT.2100: HDR television image parameters ITU-T H.264: Video coding and color signaling

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: Video Color Tags and Signaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: Video Color Tags and Signaling Color signaling describes how a playback or conversion stage should interpret the component values of a video picture. What should a renderer do with 102, 93, 186 ? Those three stored sample codes do not provide a complete color instruction. Their range and matrix establish how to reconstruct the encoded components, while primaries and transfer characteristics establish their color and light meaning. Color signaling carries those instructions alongside coded or decoded pictures. An inspector's “color space” line is often only one field of that description. A report with several independent fields Here is an illustrative ffprobe-style description of an 8-bit SDR video stream: pix_fmt=yuv420p color_range=tv color_space=bt709 color_transfer=bt709 color_primaries=bt709 chroma_location=left Field What this example describes pix_fmt The sample format reported for the stream: planar 8-bit 4:2:0 color_range Limited-range component coding; tv is this tool's label color_space The BT.709 matrix interpretation for YCbCr color_transfer BT.709 transfer characteristics color_primaries BT.709 RGB primaries chroma_location The left chroma-location convention The three bt709 entries answer different questions. One matrix label cannot stand in for all three properties. Likewise, a 10-bit pixel format does not itself select PQ or make a picture HDR. ffprobe can request just these stream fields: ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=pix_fmt,color_range,color_space,color_transfer,color_primaries,chroma_location -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 "movie.mkv" This inspects the source description. It is not a measurement of every intermediate hardware surface or the app's final display output. Those stages can use other formats and carry their own interpreted frame properties. Metadata must describe the samples it accompanies In the YCbCr worked example , limited-range BT.709 codes (102, 93, 186) reconstruct approximately to encoded RGB (0.80045, 0.30075, 0.10276). If a stage applies another matrix, its recovered color changes even though the coded bytes are intact. That gives two different correction cases: Correct samples, wrong description. Repairing the description allows the intended calculation to be applied to existing samples. Samples genuinely converted to another representation. The output needs that new representation's description. Restoring old labels would tell the next stage to interpret the converted numbers incorrectly. For example, a proper limited-to-full conversion changes nominal luma black from code 16 to 0 at 8 bits. Only relabeling the original 16 as full range instead raises its interpreted black. A parameter-marking operation and a numerical conversion serve different purposes. FFmpeg's setparams is an example of frame-property marking; its documentation distinguishes this from changing the samples. Where the instructions can appear Codec bitstreams can carry color description in video usability information. Containers can also carry color information through their own mappings. A decoder resolves the available description into properties attached to the decoded frame; filters can preserve or change those properties along with their output. If a field is unspecified, a processing stage may use a standard-defined inference or a context-based assumption. A report of unknown therefore means that the inspected description has not supplied a definite value there. It should prompt examination of the stream's format and provenance, rather than an automatic choice based only on its pixel dimensions. If descriptions disagree, the useful evidence includes where each value was found: container metadata, coded-stream signaling, or a decoder's interpreted output. Different playback stacks may handle an incomplete or conflicting description differently. Inspecting only the merged summary can hide that disagreement. Comparing original and converted playback For an Emby picture that changes color during conversion, start with the source and delivered video's complete field sets. Record the actual conversion that occurred too: a change in pixel layout is not necessarily a change in primaries, and a tone-mapped HDR picture needs an output description consistent with its SDR result. Several symptoms suggest focused comparisons. Raised black points make range especially relevant. Changed colored objects with stable neutrals suggest checking the matrix . Misaligned color edges suggest chroma location . Unexpected brightness behavior calls for checking transfer interpretation and any HDR conversion. These comparisons turn “the colors look wrong” into a question about the samples, the operation that changed them, and the description used to display the result.
