articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: RGB Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: RGB Video RGB video represents picture positions using red, green, and blue component values interpreted through specified primaries, range, and transfer characteristics. (204, 77, 26) is a possible 8-bit full-range RGB value at one position in a frame. The first number controls the red component, the second green, and the third blue. With an ordinary sRGB interpretation, that combination appears orange. The preview uses ordinary sRGB. A video RGB triplet needs its own primaries and transfer information to define the intended color. The three channels are not three overlaid photographs with independent subjects. They are three coordinates for each picture position. Increasing the green coordinate changes that position's mixture, just as changing one ingredient changes the combined result. Component values and color meaning For an unsigned 8-bit full-range representation, each component has values from 0 through 255. There are therefore 256³ = 16,777,216 possible triplets before considering alpha. Some familiar encoded triplets are: RGB triplet Interpretation within the chosen RGB space (0, 0, 0) Reference black (255, 255, 255) Reference white (255, 0, 0) The red primary at its nominal maximum (255, 255, 0) Red and green together, producing yellow (128, 128, 128) A neutral encoded gray The primaries specify which red, green, and blue these coordinates refer to. The transfer relationship specifies how encoded values relate to light. A triplet halfway up its code range is consequently an encoded midpoint, rather than a statement that the display emits half its reference-white light. Video range adds another numerical convention: studio-range RGB can use offset black and white codes. RGB describes the components; full range is a separate property. When arithmetic needs linear light An operation that mixes light should work with values proportional to light. This matters when a renderer blends an overlay or averages samples while resizing a picture. In an Emby playback path, a client or server stage can need that calculation when combining a subtitle image with the video. The component values and their transfer meaning establish what is being blended. Take a deliberately simple transfer model, light = encoded value² . Averaging encoded black 0 and encoded white 1 gives 0.5, which represents light 0.25 under that model. Averaging the actual light values gives 0.5, requiring an encoded result of √0.5, approximately 0.707 . The model is an arithmetic illustration, not the sRGB or BT.709 transfer formula. It shows why “RGB processing” needs a further question: encoded RGB or linear-light RGB? The same three component names can appear at both stages, with different numerical meanings. RGB in a video processing path A video stored as YCbCr can be reconstructed into RGB for composition and display. An RGB screenshot taken at that point describes the renderer's output representation; it does not establish that the compressed movie was stored as RGB. The channels can also have several memory layouts . RGB24 commonly stores three adjacent bytes per position; a planar RGB format stores each component in its own region. A four-component format may add alpha for coverage or transparency, which is interpreted during compositing. See Also YCbCr Video Pixel Formats and Memory Layout Color Gamut Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References ITU-R BT.709: RGB primaries, transfer, and coding Linux V4L2: RGB formats Microsoft: RGB and YUV video representations

articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.title: YCbCr Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-pixel-formats/Video.keywords: YCbCr Video YCbCr represents video using luma and two color-difference components that can be coded and sampled separately. A decoded movie frame often consists of a large plane called Y and two smaller planes called Cb and Cr . Y describes luma. Cb and Cr describe color differences. Together, they provide the information needed to reconstruct the picture's RGB components. Separating these quantities allows a format to keep fine luma structure while storing color differences at a lower spatial density. That is the basis for chroma subsampling . The component representation and the sampling reduction are separate choices: YCbCr can also carry all three components at full resolution. Luma is a mixture of encoded components The prime mark in Y′ or R′G′B′ means that the values have already undergone the relevant nonlinear encoding. In a BT.709 example, normalized encoded RGB components produce: Y′ = 0.2126 R′ + 0.7152 G′ + 0.0722 B′ The green coordinate has the greatest weight, while blue has the smallest. These weights define this particular matrix. Applying a different standard's weights constructs a different luma coordinate from the same RGB triplet. Y′ is often described casually as brightness. More precisely, it is luma calculated from encoded components . Physical luminance is a light quantity; it is not obtained by treating every Y′ code as a direct measurement in nits. The transfer interpretation remains part of the relationship to light. If all three encoded RGB components are equal, their weighted sum equals that common value, because the coefficients sum to one. This is why a neutral gray has a useful simple representation in YCbCr. The two differences that complete the description For the same BT.709 representation: Cb = (B′ − Y′) / 1.8556 Cr = (R′ − Y′) / 1.5748 These equations take the blue-minus-luma and red-minus-luma differences and scale them. In the normalized representation used here, both differences lie in the nominal interval −0.5 to +0.5 for in-range RGB inputs. Cb is not the blue channel itself. A positive Cb says that B′ exceeds the mixture represented by Y′. Similarly, Cr expresses R′ relative to that mixture. For neutral gray, both differences are zero, even when the gray is bright. There is no separately stored green-minus-luma plane in this representation. Once Y′, R′, and B′ are known, the luma equation supplies the missing green coordinate. Three independent numbers still describe the position; the coordinate system has changed. An orange sample, calculated in both directions Start with an original normalized encoded RGB triplet: R′ = 0.8, G′ = 0.3, B′ = 0.1. Its luma is: Y′ = 0.17008 + 0.21456 + 0.00722 = 0.39186. The color differences become: Cb = (0.1 − 0.39186) / 1.8556 ≈ −0.157286. Cr = (0.8 − 0.39186) / 1.5748 ≈ +0.259169. Notice that neither difference resembles an unsigned blue or red intensity. They are signed differences around the neutral point. To recover RGB before quantization, rearrange the same equations: R′ = Y′ + 1.5748 Cr = 0.8 B′ = Y′ + 1.8556 Cb = 0.1 G′ = (Y′ − 0.2126 R′ − 0.0722 B′) / 0.7152 = 0.3 The forward and inverse calculations return the original triplet. The matrix itself is a change of coordinates. Precision reduction, subsampling, or subsequent lossy coding can introduce losses, which should be distinguished from this unrounded conversion. Turning signed differences into unsigned codes A common 8-bit limited-range coding scales luma by 219 and offsets it by 16. Chroma uses scale 224 and neutral offset 128. Round the resulting values to the nearest integer: Component Unrounded code calculation Stored code Y 16 + 219 × 0.39186 = 101.81734 102 Cb 128 + 224 × (−0.157286) ≈ 92.7679 93 Cr 128 + 224 × 0.259169 ≈ 186.0539 186 The negative Cb is now stored as a positive byte below neutral 128. A reader recovers the signed coordinate by removing that offset, then dividing by the chroma scale. For these rounded bytes: Y′ = (102 − 16) / 219 ≈ 0.392694 Cb = (93 − 128) / 224 = −0.15625 Cr = (186 − 128) / 224 ≈ 0.258929 Using the inverse matrix gives approximately (0.80045, 0.30075, 0.10276) . The small difference from the original comes from rounding the three coded coordinates. Increasing coding precision makes those coordinate steps finer. This is a single-position example with full chroma information. With 4:2:0, a reconstruction stage also estimates the chroma needed at that position from the smaller, correctly located chroma grids. Where this enters playback A source file's color signaling tells the playback stack which interpretation is intended. An Emby client rendering original video uses that source interpretation; a conversion must interpret the input correctly before producing and describing the output. For a color error that appears only after conversion, comparing the source and output matrix and range fields is therefore useful. Changing a label is appropriate when the samples were merely mislabeled. If the samples have actually been transformed using the wrong matrix, producing correct colors requires correcting the sample calculation as well. Why the matrix name matters BT.601, BT.709, and BT.2020 do not all use the same matrix. Suppose our unrounded BT.709 Y′, Cb, and Cr are instead reconstructed using the BT.601 inverse coefficients. The result is approximately (0.7552, 0.2609, 0.1132) , rather than (0.8, 0.3, 0.1). Every sample can have reached the decoder intact; the visible color still moves because the inverse calculation disagrees with the forward one. Neutral grays are a poor test for this particular mistake: their chroma differences are zero, so several matrices reconstruct them similarly. Colored objects expose the disagreement more clearly. The term YUV frequently appears in APIs and pixel-format names for this family of video representations. In digital file and frame descriptions, the actual components are commonly Y′CbCr. The API's documented equations, range, and component order establish the intended representation. BT.2020 also distinguishes constant-luminance and non-constant-luminance representations. A matrix identifier should be interpreted as its specified representation, rather than shortened to a generic assumption that every YCbCr conversion uses the equations above. See Also RGB Video Chroma Subsampling Limited and Full Video Range Video Color Tags and Signaling ITU-R BT.709 References ITU-R BT.709: Luma, color-difference equations, and digital coding ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition component video ITU-R BT.2020: UHD component representations ITU-T H.264: Component coding and matrix signaling

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.title: Color Gamut | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.keywords: Color Gamut Color gamut describes the range of colors a system can represent or a display can reproduce. The points at the corners of an RGB gamut identify its red, green, and blue primaries. Mixing their light produces the colors between them. A wider gamut gives a system coordinates for more saturated colors, such as greens or reds that lie beyond a smaller gamut's boundary. Primary coordinates in CIE 1931 xy. The colored lines identify the standards; they do not reproduce the extreme colors. Luminance is omitted, and distances on this diagram are not perceptually uniform. RGB mixtures inside the gamut triangle A point inside a triangle can be formed from nonnegative mixtures of that triangle's primaries. On an edge, one primary contributes nothing; at a corner, only that primary contributes. The white point is the mixture that the system treats as its neutral reference. The same physical color generally has different RGB values in different spaces. The values describe amounts of particular primaries. For example, a green made from a mixture in BT.709 can be represented within BT.2020 by another mixture of its wider primaries. Keeping the numbers unchanged while changing the primaries would ask for a different color. This distinction explains a useful question about a film: does it use very saturated colors, or can its signal merely represent them? A BT.2020-encoded scene of a gray wall and a face need not use the outer part of the BT.2020 gamut. The encoding defines the available coordinates, while the picture determines which coordinates are occupied. Three gamuts can appear in one playback session Consider a movie graded with colors that fit within P3, stored using BT.2020 signal primaries, and played on a television with its own measured gamut. The grading range, encoding space, and display capability describe different stages. The player first interprets the encoded values in their declared space. It then needs a color-management path to produce those colors on the display. Colors within the display's capabilities can be reproduced using suitable mixtures of its primaries. A color outside those capabilities needs gamut mapping : a choice of an achievable replacement that maintains useful relationships with neighboring colors. An Emby Direct Play session preserves the delivered encoded video, but the player and screen still perform this interpretation. A larger native display gamut is beneficial when the output path also reproduces smaller encoded gamuts correctly. Stretching a conventional BT.709 image to the screen's outermost primaries would change the intended colors. What to keep separate when reading specifications Property Question it answers Encoding gamut Which color coordinates can the signal describe? Measured display gamut Which chromaticities can this screen reproduce under the test conditions? Bit depth How finely can values be represented? Color volume Which colors are available at different light levels? A gamut boundary describes the reach of the primaries. Smooth gradients also need adequate precision and processing; bright saturated colors need an adequate color volume . When comparing two systems, keep those questions separate so that a large triangle is interpreted as a color-range property, rather than a complete picture-quality score. See Also Color Volume ITU-R BT.2020 P3 Color Gamuts References ITU-R BT.2407: Color gamut conversion ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.title: Color Volume | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.keywords: Color Volume Color volume describes which colors can be reproduced across a range of light levels. A red light and a white reflection can ask very different things of a screen. The reflection can use all three RGB components. A saturated red uses mostly the red component, so it can run out of available output well before the screen reaches its maximum white brightness. Color volume describes colors together with their light levels. It extends the two-dimensional idea of color gamut into the brightness dimension: which colors can be reproduced near black, at middle levels, and near the brightest output? Why the volume is not a straight stack of gamut triangles Imagine an ideal additive RGB display using BT.709 primaries, with linear component values limited to zero through one and 100-nit white. Its neutral white is R = G = B = 1. In this example, luminance is: Y = 100 × (0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B) nits The coefficient sum is one. Setting all components to one produces 100 nits, but setting just one component to one gives different results: Linear RGB setting Color Calculated luminance 1, 0, 0 Red primary 21.26 nits 0, 1, 0 Green primary 71.52 nits 0, 0, 1 Blue primary 7.22 nits 1, 1, 0 Red plus green 92.78 nits 1, 1, 1 White 100 nits An idealized calculation with fixed primaries and component limits. It is not a measurement of a television. To make that pure red brighter while retaining the same chromaticity would require increasing its red component beyond one. The display has already reached the limit. Adding green and blue can raise luminance, but moves the color toward a less saturated mixture. This is the brightness/saturation tradeoff the word “volume” helps describe. Near the top of this ideal volume, fewer saturated colors remain available. At the very highest white level, all components are already at their maxima. Real displays add other limits: their primaries and channel behavior vary, their black floor affects dark colors, and power or thermal control can change output during a bright scene. Brightness and saturation in an orange flame Consider an HDR picture containing a bright orange flame. Its encoded RGB values describe both its color and light level. The display may have sufficient reach toward orange at a moderate luminance but insufficient output to reproduce that particular orange at the requested high luminance. A conversion can reduce the flame's brightness, reduce its saturation, or combine adjustments. Keeping only the brightness target and clipping individual color components can shift hue. Keeping only the hue and saturation target can require a larger luminance reduction. A useful mapping balances the relationships that make the flame look convincing alongside the rest of the scene. This is why tone mapping and gamut mapping interact. Their jobs can be integrated into one color-volume mapping. Treating the output as a brightness ceiling plus an independent fixed triangle misses part of the problem. Reference volume and display measurement conditions A color-volume percentage needs a reference volume and a specified measurement method. Different coordinate systems weight color differences differently; a percentage relative to one reference cannot be compared directly with an unrelated percentage. Test conditions also matter. A brief small white patch, a large bright area, and a sustained colored patch can produce different output limits on the same screen. Measurements across luminance and color give more information than one peak-white number. Near black, useful separation between dark colors matters even when the high-brightness result is impressive. Mastering-display metadata records properties of the mastering reference. During Emby playback, the receiving screen can have a different volume. The renderer adapts the produced image to the output; retaining the original source allows that adaptation to be chosen again for another display. See Also Color Gamut Why Tone Mapping Is Needed ITU-R BT.2100 References SMPTE study group report: HDR ecosystem ITU-T H.274: Supplemental enhancement information ITU-R BT.709: Primary coordinates and luminance weights

articles/video/color-standards/index.htm.title: Overview: Color standards and transfer functions | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/index.htm.keywords: Overview: Color standards and transfer functions Color standards and transfer functions define how encoded values relate to color and light. A numeric sample becomes a meaningful color only within a defined interpretation. Primaries and white point establish part of that interpretation; transfer functions establish relationships between signal values and light. Gamut and color-volume topics describe the resulting bounds, while the standards pages identify the conventions used to communicate them. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Color gamut Color gamut describes the range of colors a system can represent or a display can reproduce. Color volume Color volume describes which colors can be reproduced across a range of light levels. Color standards Video color standards specify signal conventions that help devices interpret and exchange a picture consistently. Transfer functions Transfer functions describe relationships between encoded signal values and light at different stages of image creation and display. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2020 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2020 ITU-R BT.2020 defines UHD television parameters and a wide set of color primaries. BT.2020 defines a set of wide-gamut RGB primaries for UHD television. Their coordinates identify the colors from which mixtures are formed: Primary CIE 1931 x CIE 1931 y Red 0.708 0.292 Green 0.170 0.797 Blue 0.131 0.046 Reference white, D65 0.3127 0.3290 Coordinates show the encoding gamut. The diagram omits luminance; its line colors identify the triangles. An encoding space can be larger than the colors in the movie Suppose a film is graded with colors that fit in P3 , then represented with BT.2020 coordinates for delivery. The converter finds BT.2020 RGB mixtures for those existing colors. The film does not acquire more saturated objects simply because the available coordinate space grew. This is similar to choosing a larger map for a journey: the map has room for more places, while the route still visits its actual locations. In video, the important operation is converting coordinates correctly. Reusing P3 numbers and merely changing the primary label would describe different colors. The standard also defines UHD image sizes of 3840 × 2160 and 7680 × 4320 and 10- or 12-bit signal precision. The color-primary label in a media report identifies only the primary-coordinate part of that system. A renderer still needs the rest of the signal description. Transfer, matrix, range, and precision fields Transfer characteristics: BT.2020 includes a conventional nonlinear transfer characteristic. HDR television systems in BT.2100 reuse these primaries with PQ or HLG. Consequently, the transfer field tells a player which light interpretation applies. Matrix coefficients: The standard defines constant-luminance and non-constant-luminance component representations. A report of BT.2020 non-constant describes the nonlinear RGB-to-luma/chroma arrangement; it is not another set of primaries. Reconstructing RGB needs the corresponding matrix interpretation. Range and precision: These establish how code values carry the signal. Ten bits give the number of levels; numerical range establishes the code positions for nominal black and white. Neither replaces the transfer characteristic. For an Emby source with BT.2020 primaries and PQ, the playback path needs the PQ interpretation, then appropriate rendering for the output display. A BT.2020 SDR signal follows a different light relationship. Comparing the fields together lets two apparently similar 4K files be distinguished before choosing color or tone-mapping processing. See Also ITU-R BT.2100 P3 Color Gamuts Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2100 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2100 ITU-R BT.2100 specifies HDR television image parameters for PQ and HLG systems. BT.2100 is the HDR television system specification that joins image geometry, wide color, signal precision, and HDR transfer relationships. A file usually exposes those pieces in separate fields rather than carrying a single “BT.2100” badge. System part Defined relationship Primaries The wide-gamut coordinates also used by BT.2020 HDR transfer systems PQ and HLG Image sizes 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160, 7680 × 4320 Scanning Progressive Precision 10 or 12 bits per component The current recommendation is BT.2100-3, approved in February 2025. Its transfer-system definitions connect scene light, the encoded signal, reference display light, and viewing conditions. Recognize the system in a media report An HDR recording can identify BT.2020 primaries, a PQ transfer characteristic, and a compatible component matrix. Those fields provide the instructions for interpreting the decoded pictures. A different recording can use the same primaries with HLG, changing the light relationship while retaining the color coordinates. The decoder first reconstructs samples from the compressed video. HDR-aware presentation then interprets those samples and prepares the picture for the output. Being able to decode HEVC, for example, answers a coding question; handling the resulting HDR signal answers a rendering question. Emby playback needs both parts of the selected path to work. Can 1080p be HDR? Yes. HD geometry is part of the BT.2100 system. A 1920 × 1080 HDR picture has fewer spatial samples than UHD, while its brightness and color interpretation can still require HDR-aware presentation. Reducing the grid to a smaller delivery size changes spatial detail. It does not automatically replace the transfer function. An SDR destination needs an actual HDR-to-SDR conversion , including the appropriate brightness and color operations, rather than a resolution change alone. Where do HDR formats fit? Formats such as HDR10 combine defined signal characteristics with delivery conventions and metadata. BT.2100 supplies the underlying television image parameters; the format describes how a particular presentation is carried and identified. Reading an HDR label becomes more useful when those layers are kept visible: compressed coding, television signal interpretation, format metadata, and the intended display output. See Also ITU-R BT.2020 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.601 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.601 ITU-R BT.601 defines digital component-video encoding for standard-definition television. An archived SD recording is enlarged to 1080p, and its colored objects change slightly even though neutral gray still looks sensible. One possibility is a disagreement about the luma/color-difference matrix: an image represented using BT.601 values is being reconstructed as if those values used BT.709. BT.601, or Rec. 601, defines digital component-video encoding for standard-definition television. Its matrix remains relevant after a picture is resized, because enlarging the sample grid does not automatically change what the samples mean. BT.601 color after upscaling Start with nonlinear RGB components R′, G′, and B′. The familiar BT.601 luma weighting is: Y′ = 0.299R′ + 0.587G′ + 0.114B′ Two color-difference components describe the color around that luma value. A playback stage uses the matching inverse relationship to recover RGB. The weights operate on nonlinear signal components; this luma is different from a direct measurement of emitted light. For a neutral signal with R′ = G′ = B′, any weighting whose coefficients sum to one gives the same luma value, and the color differences are neutral. That explains why a matrix mismatch can leave a gray patch plausible. Colored patches exercise the different weights and reveal the disagreement. Resizing the luma/chroma grids can retain the BT.601 interpretation. Alternatively, a processing path can reconstruct color and perform an appropriate conversion to a destination representation, such as BT.709. The delivered values and their signaling must then describe that destination. These are actual processing choices, rather than consequences of the output resolution alone. When comparing an Emby Direct Play and transcoded session , inspect the source and delivered matrix information. An SD-to-HD conversion can change more than geometry, so comparing only the resolution leaves the color conversion unexplained. Useful reference details Detail BT.601 role Standard 4:2:2 family Full horizontal luma sampling with half-rate color-difference sampling Luma sampling rate 13.5 MHz for the standard 525-line and 625-line 4:2:2 systems Corresponding chroma sampling rate 6.75 MHz for each color-difference component Nominal 8-bit luma black/white Code values 16 and 235 Familiar nonlinear luma weights 0.299 red, 0.587 green, 0.114 blue The numerical range must also be interpreted correctly. Nominal black at 16 and white at 235 are not the same code positions as full-range black and white. A range mismatch affects contrast, while a matrix mismatch mainly changes the reconstructed colors. BT.601-era material can have differing primary and transfer descriptions depending on its television system and history. Read those fields individually when available. The matrix answers how component signals relate; it does not replace the rest of the source's color description. See Also ITU-R BT.709 Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.601-7: Digital television studio encoding ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.709 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.709 ITU-R BT.709 defines HDTV image and signal parameters, including the familiar SDR color primaries. A media inspector can show “BT.709” in several fields. Each occurrence answers a different question about the same signal: Field Meaning of BT.709 there Color primaries The red, green, blue, and D65 reference-white coordinates Transfer characteristics The source's nonlinear light-to-signal relationship Matrix coefficients The conversion between nonlinear RGB and luma/color-difference signals BT.709 , or Rec. 709, specifies HDTV image and signal parameters. It is the familiar color system for conventional SDR HD video, but those parameters continue to matter when the same signal is carried at another resolution. Why one field cannot stand in for the others The primaries define what RGB mixtures mean. The transfer characteristic defines how the signal represents light. The matrix describes how nonlinear RGB becomes Y′CbCr. A processing stage can change one of these representations while retaining another, so a reader needs the complete description. The nonlinear luma weights are 0.2126R′ + 0.7152G′ + 0.0722B′ . Green contributes most strongly to luma under this relationship. These weights differ from BT.601 , which explains why using the wrong matrix can shift colored objects. Neutral RGB values produce neutral color differences in both systems, so a gray-only test can miss the error. The source OETF and the display response have different roles. BT.1886 supplies a reference SDR display EOTF, including the effect of display black and white. A BT.709 transfer tag identifies the source characteristic; it does not instruct a reader to treat the picture as linear light. Put an SDR signal on a wide-gamut screen Suppose a television's native primaries reach farther toward saturated red and green than BT.709. The intended BT.709 colors still need to be reproduced as BT.709 colors. The output path can mix the display's primaries to obtain those colors inside its larger gamut. Driving the screen's most saturated red for a BT.709 red value would stretch the source gamut, changing the produced image. Correct color management lets the larger panel serve both smaller and wider gamuts. This is relevant to Emby playback even when the server delivers the original file unchanged: the app and display must agree on signal interpretation. A 4K file can carry SDR BT.709 video, and an HD file can carry HDR. Resolution identifies the grid; the color fields identify its interpretation. For an HDR-to-SDR conversion , the brightness and color processing must actually produce suitable SDR values, then describe those values using coherent output signaling. When recording a playback comparison, keep the source's primaries, transfer, matrix, and range alongside the delivered stream's fields. That makes an apparent “BT.709 mismatch” a specific question about the part of the representation that changed. See Also ITU-R BT.601 ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: Overview: Color standards | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: Overview: Color standards Video color standards specify signal conventions that help devices interpret and exchange a picture consistently. BT.601, BT.709, BT.2020 and BT.2100 belong to different video contexts, while P3 identifies related color-gamut conventions. Their names should not be reduced to interchangeable “color-space” labels. The pages here separate the properties each convention defines and the signaling used to carry that interpretation through playback. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> ITU-R BT.601 ITU-R BT.601 defines digital component-video encoding for standard-definition television. ITU-R BT.709 ITU-R BT.709 defines HDTV image and signal parameters, including the familiar SDR color primaries. ITU-R BT.2020 ITU-R BT.2020 defines UHD television parameters and a wide set of color primaries. ITU-R BT.2100 ITU-R BT.2100 specifies HDR television image parameters for PQ and HLG systems. P3 color gamuts P3 names a family of color spaces that share wide-gamut primaries but can differ in white point and transfer function. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-R BT.601-7: Digital television studio encoding ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters W3C CSS Color 4: Display P3

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: P3 Color Gamuts | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: P3 Color Gamuts P3 names a family of color spaces that share wide-gamut primaries but can differ in white point and transfer function. The name P3 turns up on cinema standards, photographs, mastering reports, and television specifications. Resolve the context before treating those uses as the same color encoding: Name or use Primaries White/transfer information Cinema DCI-P3 P3 Cinema white point and 2.6 display gamma P3-D65 P3 D65 white; specify the transfer characteristic separately Display P3 P3 D65 white with the sRGB transfer curve “P3 coverage” on a screen A measured capability relative to P3 Depends on the stated measurement method All three named spaces use the same primary coordinates: red (0.680, 0.320), green (0.265, 0.690), and blue (0.150, 0.060) in CIE 1931 xy. P3 reaches farther than BT.709 toward saturated red and green. The coordinates determine the gamut; the white and transfer choices complete the interpretation. Two uses that are easy to confuse An image in Display P3. Its RGB values use P3 primaries, D65 white, and the defined nonlinear transfer curve. A color-managed image viewer can convert those values to the destination screen while preserving their intended colors. Display P3 provides a wider gamut than sRGB without, by itself, defining a PQ HDR presentation. A movie graded within P3 and delivered using BT.2020. The movie can fit within the grading display's P3 capabilities while its encoded video uses BT.2020 coordinate values. The conversion expresses the same intended colors as mixtures of different primaries. The player's input interpretation follows the delivered video fields. In the second case, choosing a P3 input mode merely because the film was graded on a P3-capable display would assign the wrong meaning to the delivered numbers. The mastering range and encoding space have separate places in the production chain. Use a coverage claim for the question it answers A percentage of P3 describes a screen's measured reach relative to a reference gamut under particular conditions. Different area or volume methods can give different numbers, so compare measurements that state the same reference and method. For an Emby video, record the signal's primaries and transfer characteristic independently of the display's P3 coverage. The signal tells the renderer what colors were requested; measured capability tells it what can be reproduced. For bright colored highlights, color volume extends that second question across light levels. See Also Color Gamut ITU-R BT.2020 Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References SMPTE EG 432-1: Color processing for digital cinema ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3 W3C CSS Color 4: Display P3 ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Overview: Transfer functions | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Overview: Transfer functions Transfer functions describe relationships between encoded signal values and light at different stages of image creation and display. Camera encoding, display output and the overall picture transform describe different relationships. OETF, EOTF and OOTF identify those stages, while gamma, BT.1886 and PQ describe particular conventions within that vocabulary. Understanding the stage makes brightness signaling and HDR interpretation much easier to discuss precisely. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Electro-optical transfer function (EOTF) An EOTF maps an encoded picture signal to the light a display should produce. Opto-electronic transfer function (OETF) An OETF maps scene light into the nonlinear signal used to represent a captured image. Opto-optical transfer function (OOTF) An OOTF describes the overall relationship between scene light and the light reproduced by a display. Video gamma Video gamma describes power-law relationships used to encode or display image brightness. ITU-R BT.1886 ITU-R BT.1886 defines a reference SDR display response using a 2.4 exponent and the display black and white levels. Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 PQ is an HDR transfer function that assigns encoded signal values to absolute light levels up to 10,000 nits. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: ITU-R BT.1886 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: ITU-R BT.1886 ITU-R BT.1886 defines a reference SDR display response using a 2.4 exponent and the display black and white levels. A reference SDR display response needs more than a gamma number: its black floor and white level determine the light available at the endpoints. BT.1886 defines an EOTF for HDTV reference displays using those measured endpoint luminances and an exponent of 2.4. Calculated reference responses. The shadow panel shows the effect of the black floor; these are selected display parameters, not measurements of a television. Calculate the response from its endpoints Let Lw be white luminance, Lb black luminance, and V the normalized signal. With gamma = 2.4: a = (Lw^(1/gamma) − Lb^(1/gamma))^gamma b = Lb^(1/gamma) / (Lw^(1/gamma) − Lb^(1/gamma)) L = a × max(V + b, 0)^gamma The coefficients make V = 0 reach the specified black and V = 1 reach the specified white. If black is zero, b becomes zero and a becomes Lw, leaving the familiar pure power response L = Lw × V^2.4. For 100-nit white, compare zero black with 0.1-nit black: Signal V Light at zero black Light at 0.1-nit black 0 0 nits 0.1 nit 0.1 0.398 nit 1.064 nits 0.5 18.946 nits 21.605 nits 1 100 nits 100 nits The second response reaches the higher black floor and redistributes the lower tones to meet the same white. It is not obtained simply by adding 0.1 nit to every output of the zero-black curve. Use the shadow panel to interpret a dark scene A dark jacket can contain several distinct low-level folds. Their encoded values have a display-light relationship; the black floor and response determine how much separation is produced. Room reflections and the viewer's adaptation can further affect whether that separation is visible. BT.1886 gives a reference response for this part of the system. It is distinct from the BT.709 source transfer characteristic , so a conventional BT.709 file is not retagged BT.1886 to describe reference display behavior. In a playback comparison, use the same SDR source and inspect the app's output and screen mode. A difference in shadow appearance can arise after decoding. Keeping the response's endpoints and middle-tone behavior visible makes the investigation more precise than comparing a single “gamma” label. See Also ITU-R BT.709 Video Gamma Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) An EOTF maps an encoded picture signal to the light a display should produce. What light should a screen produce for a signal value of 0.5? An electro-optical transfer function , or EOTF, supplies the relationship needed to answer. The signal is electrical or numerical; the result is light. For an ideal SDR display with zero black, 100-nit white, and a 2.4 power response, use L = 100 × V^2.4 . V is the normalized signal and L is neutral-gray luminance: Signal V Calculated light 0.25 3.6 nits 0.50 18.9 nits 0.75 50.1 nits 1.00 100 nits Halfway through the signal range therefore produces about 19% of white's light in this example. Equal signal steps do not create equal light steps. These are the zero-black conditions of BT.1886 ; another EOTF gives another relationship. Apply the function to the right input The stored video code first needs the correct numerical-range interpretation. Nominal black and white may occupy only part of the available integer range. Interpreting those endpoints produces a normalized signal; the EOTF then supplies its light meaning. The order is significant. If nominal black is mistakenly normalized to a positive signal, the EOTF produces light for a sample that was meant to be black. If a nonlinear sample is treated as already linear, later arithmetic also begins from the wrong light value. A color-processing path applies the relevant component relationships and transfer interpretation to obtain a suitable working representation. A neutral-gray calculation keeps the example above simple; colored pictures additionally need their primaries and component matrix interpreted correctly. Reconstruct light, then choose what the output can show PQ gives HDR samples an absolute reference-light interpretation. Recovering that interpretation can reveal a 1,000-nit highlight, but a destination with a smaller usable range still needs a mapping decision. The EOTF identifies the requested light. Tone mapping adapts it. After a light-domain operation, the output needs an encoding appropriate to its own display relationship. In the ideal SDR example, a desired 50-nit gray requires V = (50/100)^(1/2.4), approximately 0.749. Writing 0.5 instead would request 18.9 nits. That inverse operation explains why light values and final video signal values cannot be interchanged. An Emby Direct Play session identifies how the server delivers the file. The app and display still render the samples using their output path. Comparing displayed brightness therefore requires the source interpretation and the destination response alongside the delivery mode. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) ITU-R BT.1886 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) An OETF maps scene light into the nonlinear signal used to represent a captured image. A camera measures light, but the video signal usually represents it nonlinearly. An opto-electronic transfer function , or OETF, supplies that light-to-signal relationship. The BT.709 reference below assigns more signal space to low scene-light levels than a straight linear encoding would. Normalized scene light becomes a normalized video signal. Neither axis is a raw sensor code or an absolute number of nits. Encoding and recovering a scene-light value For normalized scene-light E, the BT.709 curve uses 4.5E below 0.018 and 1.099E^0.45 − 0.099 at or above that point. The lower straight segment avoids the behavior of a bare power near zero. The full function is more precise than calling it simply “gamma 0.45.” At E = 0.18, the signal is approximately 0.409 . The encoded value has increased numerically, but that does not mean the camera recorded more light. It is another representation of the same input. To return from the upper segment's signal value V to scene light, use E = ((V + 0.099) / 1.099)^(1/0.45) . That inverse is what a light-domain processing stage needs when its input uses this encoding. An averaging example shows why the distinction is useful Suppose an operation is intended to average two light contributions: black at E = 0 and white at E = 1. Their light average is E = 0.5. Applying the OETF gives a signal of approximately 0.706 . Averaging their encoded values instead gives V = 0.5, because black and white encode to zero and one. Inverting that signal gives scene light of only about 0.260 . The two computations therefore describe different results: Operation Resulting scene-light value Average light, then encode 0.500 Average encoded signals, then interpret About 0.260 The nonlinear relationship is the cause. This matters for operations whose purpose is to combine light contributions, such as a physically motivated blend. Other processing can deliberately choose a perceptual working space; its intended effect determines the right arithmetic. Capture encoding and display appearance are separate stages An OETF is not automatically the exact inverse of the eventual display EOTF . The full imaging system also chooses an appropriate relationship between scene light and reproduced light for the viewing environment. The OOTF describes that overall relationship. For camera footage stored in an Emby library, preserve the actual transfer description through editing and export. A conventional camera signal, a camera-specific log representation, and HDR can use different light relationships even if they share a codec. Correctly converting footage requires interpreting the source, performing the intended rendering, and encoding the destination—not merely assigning it a familiar transfer label. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) ITU-R BT.709 References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) An OOTF describes the overall relationship between scene light and the light reproduced by a display. A camera points at a scene, and a screen later produces light for the viewer. The opto-optical transfer function , or OOTF, describes the relationship between those two kinds of light across the complete imaging system. The OOTF spans scene light to reproduced light. A real chain can include exposure, grading, tone mapping, and viewing adjustments in addition to the illustrated transfer stages. Compose the functions rather than cancel their names The OETF describes light becoming a signal. The EOTF describes a signal becoming light. Combining those operations determines the overall scene-to-display relationship. Use a deliberately simple model. Suppose capture encodes relative scene light E as E^0.5, and display produces relative light V^2.4 from the encoded signal V. For E = 0.25: Capture gives V = 0.25^0.5 = 0.5 . Display gives L = 0.5^2.4, approximately 0.189 . The combined relationship is L = E^1.2, since 0.5 × 2.4 = 1.2. The result is not the original relative light 0.25. The system's overall rendering has changed the relationship. This is a constructed demonstration of function composition; specified video functions can include linear segments, offsets, and luminance-dependent operations, so their complete equations must be combined. Why a useful reproduction can change scene contrast Looking at a screen in a room differs from standing in front of the photographed scene. The screen has a limited light range, the image occupies part of the field of view, and the viewer adapts to a particular surround. Reproducing the scene's light numerically, without accounting for those conditions, need not produce the intended appearance. An imaging system can therefore include an overall rendering that adjusts contrast for its reference viewing environment. Camera encoding and display behavior are parts of that design. An exponent greater than one in the simplified overall model darkens middle relative levels while leaving zero and one unchanged. This is an appearance relationship, not an instruction to use one fixed extra filter on every produced movie. A colorist may already have established the intended display image during grading. Locate the rendering in the source you have A scene-referred representation retains a relationship to captured scene light. A display-referred representation describes an intended produced image. The same named operations cannot be added indiscriminately to both: applying a scene-to-display rendering twice can alter a picture that was already rendered. For HLG , the system relationship includes adaptation to display and viewing conditions. PQ provides an absolute reference-display interpretation. These systems place parts of the rendering relationship differently. Emby normally begins with already authored media. The playback path needs to know which interpretation it receives and adapt that produced picture to the output. The diagram is useful for locating an operation: did it occur in capture, in production, in the app's presentation, or in the display? That location determines whether the required overall rendering is being completed or applied again. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 PQ is an HDR transfer function that assigns encoded signal values to absolute light levels up to 10,000 nits. A PQ signal assigns picture samples an absolute reference-display light meaning. A normalized signal of 0.5 requests approximately 92.2 nits for neutral gray; it does not request half of an arbitrary television's brightest output. Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) is standardized in SMPTE ST 2084. Its nonlinear function distributes precision across a reference-light range extending to 10,000 nits, taking human visual sensitivity into account. ST 2084 neutral-gray reference EOTF. The logarithmic panel reveals shadows; zero cannot be plotted on its logarithmic luminance axis. 100 nits represented by a 10-bit PQ code A 100-nit neutral gray has a normalized PQ signal of approximately 0.508078 . That value is a signal coordinate, not a luminance percentage. Encoding into a numerical format comes next. For an illustrative 10-bit narrow-range neutral-gray component, nominal black is code 64 and the top nominal signal is code 940. There are 876 intervals between those endpoints. Rounding 64 + 876 × 0.508078 gives code 509 . On interpretation, (509 − 64) / 876 gives approximately 0.507991. Applying PQ recovers about 99.913 nits . The slight difference from 100 is the finite-precision rounding in this example. That chain connects three representations: Representation Example Intended neutral-gray light 100 nits Normalized nonlinear PQ signal About 0.508078 Stored 10-bit narrow-range component 509 A player needs the correct range before applying PQ. Treating the integer 509 as a full-range value would produce a different normalized signal and therefore another light request. For colored video, component and primary interpretation also participate in recovering the intended picture. Unequal signal spacing across the light range Light level Normalized PQ signal, rounded 1 nit 0.150 100 nits 0.508 1,000 nits 0.752 10,000 nits 1.000 The large light changes in the table occupy uneven signal intervals. This lets a finite set of signal values serve a much wider luminance range than a simple linear allocation would. Bit depth then determines how finely those signal intervals are divided. The 10,000-nit endpoint defines the reference range of the function. An actual movie uses its own distribution of light levels; its brightest encoded content can be far below that endpoint. Content-light metadata and measured picture statistics describe aspects of that content. The equation, for reproducing the values For normalized signal V, use p = V^(1/m2), then: L = 10,000 × [max(p − c1, 0) / (c2 − c3p)]^(1/m1) The exact constants are m1 = 2610/16384, m2 = 2523/32, c1 = 3424/4096, c2 = 2413/128, and c3 = 2392/128. L is luminance in nits for neutral gray at the reference white chromaticity. The inverse function finds the PQ signal for a desired light level. Adapt the interpreted picture to the destination Suppose a highlight requests 1,000 nits and the output's usable peak is 400. PQ identifies the request; it cannot expand the screen's light capability. A subsequent tone-mapping decision fits that highlight alongside the rest of the picture. A capable renderer can retain PQ's intended light relationship over a supported range and adapt the regions beyond the display's useful output. An SDR conversion instead prepares values with an SDR transfer meaning after brightness and color processing. For Emby playback, these operations can happen in a server conversion or in local presentation. The Windows app documentation describes presentation-stage tone mapping. The source transfer, actual content range, and destination are each inputs to understanding the delivered appearance. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Video Gamma | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Video Gamma Video gamma describes power-law relationships used to encode or display image brightness. Both curves below reach the same black and white. Their difference is in the tones between those endpoints: Zero-black display models with white normalized to one. The dotted diagonal is a linear reference. Gamma is the exponent in a power relationship. For a display model written as L = V^gamma, a higher exponent gives less light at intermediate normalized signal values. At V = 0.5, gamma 2.2 gives about 0.218 of white , while gamma 2.4 gives about 0.189 . With a hypothetical 100-nit white, that is 21.8 versus 18.9 nits. The darker middle tone does not require a change in peak white. State the direction of the relationship Use of a gamma number What the exponent acts on Capture or encoding shorthand Light values becoming a nonlinear signal Display response Signal values becoming light Image adjustment An existing image representation changed by another power For values between zero and one, a power below one raises the number; a power above one lowers it. That mathematical direction is why “increase gamma” can mean different visual changes in controls that apply different conventions. Real transfer functions can use more than a power. The BT.709 OETF has a straight segment near black; BT.1886 includes display black and white; PQ uses a different nonlinear function. When comparing an Emby picture across playback paths, keep the output and display modes consistent. Then distinguish a deliberate tone adjustment from the transfer relationship the signal expects. The graph gives a concrete check: a pure power adjustment chiefly redistributes intermediate tones, while a range error can move the black and white endpoints too. See Also ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/compression/index.html.title: Overview: Video compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/index.html.keywords: Overview: Video compression Video compression represents pictures efficiently through coding choices, prediction and constraints on the resulting stream. Compressed video carries instructions for reconstructing pictures, not necessarily a complete independent image for every moment. The relationships among predicted pictures influence seeking and error recovery, while profiles and levels describe constraints on the stream. Lossy and lossless topics establish what is preserved before those structural choices are examined. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How video compression works Video compression represents picture information with fewer bits by exploiting patterns and, in lossy modes, accepting approximation. Lossy video compression Lossy video compression reduces data by allowing the reconstructed pictures to differ from the encoder input. Lossless video compression Lossless video compression reproduces the picture samples supplied to the encoder exactly. Picture prediction and random access Picture prediction creates dependencies that determine how video can start decoding at a requested point. Codec profiles A video codec profile constrains the coding tools and sample formats a stream may use. Codec levels and tiers Codec levels and tiers describe resource limits that a compatible decoder must satisfy. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.title: Lossless Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.keywords: Lossless Video Compression Lossless video compression reproduces the picture samples supplied to the encoder exactly. The samples 40, 42, 43, 43 can be stored in four 8-bit words, requiring 32 payload bits. They can also be stored as a starting sample plus differences: 40; +2, +1, 0. Nothing has been rounded. Knowing the starting value, the decoder can reverse every addition and recover all four samples exactly. A complete small coding rule Give common differences short prefix codes: Difference Code 0 0 +1 10 +2 110 Anything else 111 , followed by a signed 9-bit difference No complete prefix is the start of another. The decoder can distinguish the short codes and knows to read nine more bits after the escape prefix. Nine signed bits cover differences between arbitrary 8-bit sample values. For the four-sample example, store: starting sample 40 +2 +1 0 00101000 110 10 0 The payload is 8 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 14 bits , instead of 32. Real byte storage can add padding, and a real format must communicate length and coding rules. This is an original toy codec, not FFV1's entropy coding. Decode it: Read the first eight bits: 40. Read 110 : add 2, giving 42. Read 10 : add 1, giving 43. Read 0 : add zero, giving 43. The values and their order are identical. That is lossless sample compression . A good predictor saves space without taking a risk A predictor tries to make differences small and statistically common. In the toy rule, zero needs only one bit. An unpredictable sequence uses the escape code more often and can become larger. The decoder still recovers the exact values because every difference is retained. A poor prediction hurts compression efficiency, not correctness. Real lossless codecs use more capable predictors and coding methods to exploit picture structure. FFV1 is a specified video format built for this kind of exact reconstruction. Some delivery codecs also have lossless modes, with their own format and decoder requirements. Place the guarantee around the encoder Imagine decoding an existing lossy film, resizing it, then losslessly encoding the result. The lossless decoder recovers the resized samples exactly. It does not recover the earlier camera samples, because the losses and resize happened before that codec received its input. This identifies a practical verification boundary: compare the samples immediately supplied to the lossless encoder with the samples restored by its decoder, in the same sample format and order. A file checksum answers a different question. Repackaging or changing tags can change file bytes while leaving decoded video identical. Conversely, an intact file can faithfully preserve an input that already contained damage. For an Emby preservation master, the exact sample representation can be retained separately from a smaller delivery version. The master supplies the stable input for future derivatives; the playback copy supplies the representation appropriate for its viewing route. See Also Lossy Video Compression How Video Compression Works Intra-Frame Video Compression References RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.title: Lossy Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.keywords: Lossy Video Compression Lossy video compression reduces data by allowing the reconstructed pictures to differ from the encoder input. Lossy video coding saves data by allowing a reconstructed picture to differ from the encoder's input. The useful question is which information was approximated, and what did that change in the picture? Which corrections survive quantization? Suppose a predictor supplies values 100, 100, 100 for three positions. The actual input is 117, 97, 139 , so the differences needed to reproduce it are 17, −3, 39 . Now use a deliberately simple quantizer that rounds those corrections to the nearest multiple of eight: Position Input Predictor Exact correction Rounded correction Decoded result 1 117 100 17 16 116 2 97 100 −3 0 100 3 139 100 39 40 140 The decoder adds the rounded correction to the predictor. Its errors relative to the input are −1, +3, +1 . Original scalar example. It omits transform coding and uses arbitrary sample values to isolate quantization; it is not the exact quantizer of a named video codec. The compressed representation says “zero correction” for position 2. That could have arisen from −3, +2, or zero. Several different inputs map to the same coded result, so the decoder has no information with which to choose the original one. This many-to-one mapping is the irreversible step. Why approximation can reduce data Small corrections often occur where a predictor already describes the picture well. Rounding more of them to zero leaves fewer significant values to transmit. Coarser quantization can also reduce the precision required to describe the remaining values. In block-transform codecs, quantization operates on coefficients representing patterns across a region, rather than directly on the simple scalar corrections above. Removing or coarsening a coefficient changes the corresponding pattern when the block is reconstructed. A fine texture can weaken, or an edge can gain a faint oscillating outline. The complete compression walkthrough connects prediction, transform, quantization, and reconstruction. Lossy behavior comes from the permitted approximation, rather than from the fact that prediction was used. Allocate the compromise within a scene A stationary wall may have predictable regions and small corrections. Grainy foliage in motion can have more changing information. Preserving the latter at the same fidelity needs a different allocation of bits. An encoder makes decisions about predictors, block divisions, and quantization strength. With a constrained bitrate, difficult regions compete for that budget. With a quality target, the encoder can let size grow as the source becomes harder. The visible consequences follow the information affected. Simplified texture looks smoother; disagreeing neighboring regions can reveal block boundaries; coarse gradients can lose distinct levels. Some differences remain invisible at the intended display size, while others affect details the viewer notices quickly. Identify the stage being compared For a library file that is played directly, the decoder reconstructs the representation already stored. During video transcoding, Emby Server reconstructs that source and supplies its decoded pictures to another encoder. The second encoder's input already contains the first encode's changes. Giving the second stage more bits can preserve that input more closely; it cannot reverse the first stage's many-to-one decisions. Generation loss follows what happens when such stages are repeated. A useful comparison keeps the same source pictures, timing, and presentation and examines the converted reconstruction against them. That reveals the additional change caused by this encode, which is the quantity its quality settings can control. See Also How Video Compression Works Lossless Video Compression Intra-Frame Video Compression References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Overview: Picture prediction and random access | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Overview: Picture prediction and random access Picture prediction creates dependencies that determine how video can start decoding at a requested point. Seeking to a picture and beginning to decode there are different operations. A predicted picture may need earlier reference information, so a useful access point has to satisfy the codec's dependency rules. Intra coding, keyframes, groups of pictures and reference frames explain how that starting point is built. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Intra-frame compression Intra-frame compression represents a picture using information from within that picture rather than other pictures. Inter-frame prediction Inter-frame prediction reconstructs a picture using previously decoded reference pictures and coded corrections. Keyframes and random access A video random-access point lets decoding begin without reconstructing the whole preceding stream. Groups of pictures (GOPs) A group of pictures describes a sequence of coded pictures and their prediction relationships around access points. Reference frames Reference frames are decoded pictures retained so that other pictures can use them for prediction. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Inter-Frame Video Prediction | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Inter-Frame Video Prediction Inter-frame prediction reconstructs a picture using previously decoded reference pictures and coded corrections. A new video picture often contains much of the scene already visible in another one. Inter-frame prediction describes a useful part of that decoded scene, then sends the information needed to correct it into the new picture. The decoder is not asked to identify the object or guess its true movement. The encoded stream tells it which reference to use, where to sample it, and which correction to apply. Conceptual motion prediction plus residual reconstruction, not a measured codec result. Find a useful reference region Suppose a reconstructed reference row is: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. The current four-sample region needs values 31, 39, 53, 60 . The reference region starting two positions to the right of the current block's coordinate is 30, 40, 50, 60 , already a close match. The encoder can select that reference and transmit an offset corresponding to +2 reference-sample positions in this declared convention. A motion vector locates the predictor. Its sign describes that coordinate relationship, rather than directly declaring a person's real-world velocity. A camera pan, object movement, or a repetitive texture can all make a shifted region useful. The encoder searches among permitted predictors and balances their fit against the cost of describing them. Add the residual The required difference between the current input and predictor is: Position Input Predictor Residual 1 31 30 +1 2 39 40 −1 3 53 50 +3 4 60 60 0 These are the residual values. A real codec can transform and quantize them before entropy coding. In a lossless representation they can be retained exactly. In a lossy representation the reconstructed corrections can differ. For a toy quantizer rounding these corrections to multiples of four, none of the values are half-step ties: +1, −1, +3, 0 → 0, 0, +4, 0. Add those decoded corrections to the predictor and the result is 30, 40, 54, 60 . Its errors relative to the input are −1, +1, +1, 0 . The sample arithmetic isolates prediction and approximation. It omits the named codecs' transform, quantization, and filtering details. A well-matched predictor leaves a small correction. A region containing a new object, an uncovered background, or different lighting can need larger corrections. The encoder can select another reference or use intra prediction for that region instead. Reconstruct the same reference on both sides Now imagine using this reconstructed picture to predict the next one. The decoder has 30, 40, 54, 60 , not the encoder's original 31, 39, 53, 60 . The encoder must build the next predictor from the reconstructed picture too. It therefore contains a local reconstruction loop that follows the decoder's operations. If it predicted from the original input instead, its transmitted residual would assume values the decoder does not have, causing a mismatch that could propagate into later pictures. This is why decoded reference pictures are part of the coding process. They are not merely pictures the player happened to retain for display. The vector can point between samples Movement need not be an exact number of sample positions. A codec can specify fractional-position prediction, using defined interpolation rules to construct reference values between the stored grid points. For example, a requested reference position halfway between two samples needs a calculated predictor rather than an integer array lookup. Each codec specifies its filters and rounding so compatible decoders construct the expected values. The residual then corrects this calculated predictor just as it corrects an integer-position one. This interpolation forms a predictor for a coded picture. It does not add new video presentation times. Combine available references A predictor can also combine information from two decoded references. For a scalar illustration, reference predictions of 40 and 44 average to 42. A residual of +1 reconstructs 43. A full picture can have different reference choices and coding modes in different regions. The picture's “P” or “B” description does not mean every sample uses one identical operation. One reference may be earlier and another later in display order . A decoder can process the later-displayed anchor first, retain it, then decode pictures scheduled before it on screen. The coded order satisfies the dependencies; presentation timestamps and the picture order then restore the viewing sequence. GOP structure and reference storage follow those relationships in more detail. When seeking into an Emby film, reconstruction starts from a suitable access point and rebuilds the needed reference state before the requested picture can be shown. Motion interpolation performs a different job: it estimates an extra picture at a time never supplied by the original coded sequence. Inter-frame coding instead has a represented target picture and transmitted corrections that define its reconstructed result.
