articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Intra-Frame Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Intra-Frame Video Compression Intra-frame compression represents a picture using information from within that picture rather than other pictures. A picture can be compressed efficiently even when no earlier picture is available. Intra-frame compression finds useful structure within that picture: similar neighboring samples, continuing edges, and patterns that can be represented compactly. Predict a block from its boundary In a common block-based codec, some regions have already been reconstructed while the next block is still being decoded. Suppose the samples immediately above a four-column block are: 10, 20, 30, 40. A simple vertical predictor extends those values downward: 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 If the input block's first row is 12, 21, 30, 38 , its correction from that prediction is +2, +1, 0, −2 . The encoder can describe the predictor choice and those relatively small corrections. The decoder constructs the same prediction from its available upper boundary, adds the decoded corrections, and obtains the reconstructed block. Original numerical illustration of a directional predictor. It does not specify every mode or coding step of a particular codec. A horizontal predictor could instead extend samples from the left boundary. Other modes continue diagonal structures or form a flatter estimate. The encoder chooses a suitable description; the decoder follows the transmitted choice rather than searching for the original camera image. Why reconstructed neighbors matter The encoder's original boundary samples can differ from the decoded boundary after lossy coding. To keep prediction consistent, the encoder builds its predictor from the reconstruction the decoder will have. Both sides then start from the same known samples. Any approximation occurs in the coded correction and related reconstruction operations, rather than through a hidden disagreement about the boundary. This creates dependencies within the picture. Intra coding removes sample prediction from other pictures, but it does not imply that every block is decoded in arbitrary order or that a raw block is independently meaningful. Not every intra-frame codec uses this exact predictor style. Motion JPEG, for example, emphasizes independent JPEG picture coding. The general property is that picture samples are represented without temporal prediction from another picture. Work with independent pictures An all-intra video avoids chains that require reconstructing earlier picture samples before a chosen picture. An editor can seek to a picture, read its coded representation, and decode it using the stream's configuration and same-picture rules. That is useful for scrubbing, cutting, and assigning complete frames to processing jobs. The source's own picture content is available without a long temporal reconstruction chain. The cost is that a nearly unchanged wall has to be described within each new picture again. Temporal prediction can reuse an earlier decoded wall and transmit mainly its changes. Intra-only formats allocate the coding budget differently. An intra-coded picture inside an otherwise inter-predicted stream still needs the surrounding access rules interpreted. It can reconstruct its own samples independently, while reordered or following pictures may use references from before it. Random access therefore considers more than the picture's intra coding alone. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Video Keyframes and Random Access How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Reference Frames | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Reference Frames Reference frames are decoded pictures retained so that other pictures can use them for prediction. A decoder reconstructs pictures into memory. Some are kept because another picture will use their samples for prediction; these are reference pictures . Others are kept because their display time has not yet arrived. One picture can have both roles. The decoded picture buffer tracks these uses so a surface is not released while either job still needs it. A displayed picture can remain a reference Consider a GOP where I0 is displayed first and P3 later predicts from it. Displaying I0 does not make its samples dispensable: P3's reconstruction still needs them. After decoding P3, the decoder can retain both I0 and P3 for B1 and B2, which use the anchors around them. Once every required dependent has been decoded and the stream no longer retains I0 as a reference, that reference role can end. A picture's lifetime is therefore set by the actual dependency instructions, not simply by whether the user has already seen it. A reference can also wait for display P3 may be decoded before B1 and B2 because they need it. Its samples already exist, but showing it immediately would put the film out of order. Picture state Why memory remains occupied Already displayed, still a reference Future decoding needs its samples Decoded ahead of display Its presentation time has not arrived Both reference and pending output Both requirements apply to one picture Neither role remains The surface can become available for reuse These roles can overlap, so adding a reported reference count to a reported reorder count does not automatically give the number of distinct stored pictures. Some reference pictures remain useful for longer stretches, such as an older view of a background temporarily covered by a foreground object. Codecs provide explicit rules for retaining and releasing the available references. Count the samples in a surface For an even-sized, tightly packed 8-bit 4:2:0 example, the main plane has width × height samples. Each of the two color-difference planes has half the width and half the height: W × H + 2 × (W/2 × H/2) = 1.5 × W × H samples. With one byte per sample: Grid One picture's sample payload Four pictures' payload 1920 × 1080 3,110,400 bytes, 3.1104 MB 12.4416 MB 3840 × 2160 12,441,600 bytes, 12.4416 MB 49.7664 MB The bytes are decoded sample payloads , not compressed packet sizes. A low-bitrate UHD stream still reconstructs a UHD surface. If the same sampling grid uses 16-bit containers for its samples, one FHD picture requires 6,220,800 payload bytes and four require 24,883,200 bytes . A 10-bit sample can occupy such a 16-bit container, so valid precision and allocated storage width are different quantities. Actual decoder allocations can add row alignment, a larger coded raster, additional working surfaces, and an output queue. The calculation isolates the visible-grid payload rather than estimating every implementation's total memory. Connect lifetime to decoder capacity More retained pictures need more surface storage. Larger pictures increase each surface's footprint. Codec level constraints describe relevant buffer resources along with picture size and throughput. In Emby playback, this helps explain why recognizing the codec is only one part of source decoding. The active decoder must hold the pictures required by that bitstream's dependencies and presentation order. When inspecting a reference count, establish whether it is a declared maximum, an encoder setting, or observed use. Individual blocks can choose among a smaller set at a particular moment. The dependency graph determines which decoded surfaces must actually stay alive. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) A group of pictures describes a sequence of coded pictures and their prediction relationships around access points. A group of pictures (GOP) is easiest to understand by following which decoded pictures other pictures use. The visible sequence below contains seven pictures: I0, B1, B2, P3, B4, B5, P6. In this example, I0 is intra-coded; P3 uses I0; P6 uses P3. B1 and B2 use I0 and P3, while B4 and B5 use P3 and P6. Declared dependency example. Its B-pictures are not references. Other legal structures use different dependencies and orders. Decode the anchors before the pictures that need them The decoder can begin with I0 . It creates that picture's samples and retains them as a reference. Next it decodes P3 , using I0 and P3's coded corrections. P3 appears later on screen, but it must exist before B1 or B2 can use its samples. The decoder now has both anchors and can reconstruct B1 and B2 . It can then present the initial sequence in viewing order: I0, B1, B2, P3. The next anchor is P6 . Decode it from P3, then use P3 and P6 to reconstruct B4 and B5. The remaining viewing order is B4, B5, P6. One valid coded order is therefore: I0, P3, B1, B2, P6, B4, B5. Decoding follows dependencies. Display follows the picture timeline. The decoder needs picture storage to bridge those two orders. What the letters tell you Letter in this example How its samples are predicted I Within the picture, without another picture as a sample reference P From an available reference picture, with coded corrections B From the permitted reference choices, including the two anchors used here The letters describe coding possibilities and picture/slice types, not a universal lifecycle. A modern B-picture can itself become a reference. A picture can also mix prediction choices across its regions. For example, a hierarchical structure might decode a B-picture between two distant anchors, then use that intermediate picture to predict other B-pictures. The dependency graph becomes deeper even if the visible I/P/B sequence looks similar. “B” therefore does not mean that the decoder can always discard it immediately. References can outlive their display time I0 can already have been shown when P3 and the early B-pictures use it. It remains in memory because prediction still needs it. P3 may first be held because it was decoded ahead of display. After it has been displayed, it still remains a reference for P6, B4, and B5. Being displayed and being safe to release are separate events. In this declared graph, I0 can cease being a reference after its last dependent picture is reconstructed. P3 lasts longer. These decisions affect the decoded picture buffer , while output reordering decides when each finished picture is shown. GOP length in pictures and seconds An encoder's maximum keyframe interval is often expressed as a picture count. At 24 fps, 48 pictures span two seconds . At 24000/1001 fps they span 2.002 seconds ; at 60 fps they span 0.8 seconds . The same picture count therefore gives different time spacing in different sources. Scene-change decisions can also create an entry earlier than the configured maximum. More frequent independently usable pictures provide closer starting places for seeking or joining playback. Longer prediction runs can reuse more scene information before a reset. Their benefit depends on how well the scene remains predictable; a cut replaces much of that useful relationship. Closed and open boundaries A closed GOP can reconstruct its pictures without sample references from an earlier group. The illustrated seven-picture graph is closed because all its references are inside the group beginning at I0. An open GOP allows dependencies across a nominal boundary. As a conceptual example, leading pictures displayed before a new intra anchor can use both that anchor and an older one from the preceding group. The new anchor is independent, but those leading pictures are not. A random start needs the codec's rules for those relationships: which pictures can be reconstructed, which must be skipped, and where valid presentation begins. Starting continuously with the previous group already decoded is a different situation from starting with an empty reference buffer. This is why access-point type matters alongside a GOP length. A run of “48 frames” does not by itself describe the boundary dependencies. In an Emby seek or transcode start, the decoder reconstructs the required graph before it can deliver the requested pictures. Understanding that graph explains why picture order, access spacing, and reference storage work together. See Also Video Keyframes and Random Access Inter-Frame Video Prediction Video Reference Frames References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Keyframes and Random Access | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Keyframes and Random Access A video random-access point lets decoding begin without reconstructing the whole preceding stream. You seek to 11.3 seconds in a film, but the picture you want is predicted from earlier decoded pictures. Jumping directly to its compressed bytes would leave the decoder without those references. A random-access point , commonly marked as a keyframe , provides a place from which the required state can be rebuilt. Seeking to 11.3 seconds from a 10-second entry point Assume a constant 24 fps stream with clean entry points every two seconds. For this example, the player selects the first picture at or after the requested time. 11.3 × 24 = 271.2 , so that picture is frame 272 , at 11.3333 seconds . The preceding entry point is frame 240 , at 10 seconds . Stage Work performed Locate an entry Find the coded access point at 10 seconds Configure decoding Supply the codec's required stream parameters Rebuild pictures Decode from frame 240 toward the target Begin requested presentation Show the selected picture at its assigned time For a deliberately simple I/P-only chain where each picture depends on its predecessor, frames 240 through 272 require 33 picture decodes , including both endpoints. The earlier output pictures are not necessarily shown; they supply reference state and are discarded from the requested presentation. The selection policy and dependency chain are declared examples. Reordered structures can need additional anchors or different preroll handling. The container index helps locate byte positions associated with access points. The codec determines whether the decoder can actually begin there. Both pieces are needed for a useful seek. Supply the configuration An independently reconstructable picture still needs its codec configuration. The decoder must know dimensions, sample format, and the applicable coding parameters. These can be supplied by the container or repeated in the stream, depending on its format. For H.264, sequence and picture parameter sets are part of that configuration. A bare picture payload without the needed parameters is not a complete decoding starting package. An I-picture answers a narrower question An intra-coded picture reconstructs its own samples without temporal prediction from another picture. That says nothing by itself about dependencies of following or reordered pictures. Consider a group that starts with an ordinary I-picture but also contains leading B-pictures using an older reference. Starting with an empty decoder at the I-picture cannot reconstruct those leading pictures just because the I-picture itself is independent. H.264 IDR pictures establish a reference reset: subsequent prediction cannot rely on pictures preceding that reset. HEVC defines IDR and additional access types, including CRA , with specific handling for leading pictures when playback begins at the access point. These rules determine which pictures can validly be presented after a random start. Access spacing changes the work More frequent clean entries can reduce how far the decoder needs to work forward after a seek. In the example, starting at 10 seconds is much closer to the target than starting at the beginning of the film. Encoders also spend data establishing new independently usable pictures. Access-point spacing is therefore a tradeoff between prediction efficiency and convenient starts, with scene changes sometimes creating additional entries. In Emby, the same source reconstruction can precede transcoded output after seeking. Its delay can include storage reads, decoder work, and output initialization; the reference chain explains the part due to picture dependencies. Changing an index flag does not rewrite those dependencies. If a byte location is incorrectly marked as an entry, uninterrupted playback can work because the decoder already has state, while seeking there fails. The useful repair is a correct access description or a newly encoded entry structure, rather than an unsupported “keyframe” label. See Also Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Intra-Frame Video Compression Inter-Frame Video Prediction References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.title: Video Codec Levels and Tiers | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.keywords: Video Codec Levels and Tiers Codec levels and tiers describe resource limits that a compatible decoder must satisfy. A codec level defines a resource envelope for a bitstream: how large its coded pictures can be, how quickly they must be processed, how much picture state can be retained, and how much coded data must be buffered. A profile selects the kinds of operations. Level limits describe the scale at which those operations are required. Some codecs also define tiers , particularly for bitrate and coded-buffer limits. Work through a 1080p AVC stream H.264 counts several level resources in 16 × 16 macroblocks . For a progressive picture presented as 1920 × 1080, round each coded grid dimension up to a macroblock boundary: Width: 1920/16 = 120 macroblocks . Height: ceil(1080/16) = 68 macroblocks . Picture size: 120 × 68 = 8,160 macroblocks . The coded macroblock grid is 1920 × 1088 . A signaled crop can remove the extra eight rows from presentation. The decoder's coded-picture work still follows the larger macroblock grid. For H.264 Level 4.1, selected limits are: Resource Level 4.1 limit Macroblocks in a coded frame, MaxFS 8,192 Macroblocks processed per second, MaxMBPS 245,760 Decoded-picture-buffer macroblocks, MaxDpbMbs 32,768 These are selected standard constraints, not the whole conformance test. Picture size and throughput give different answers The example's 8,160 macroblocks fit the per-picture limit of 8,192. At 30 fps , processing demand is: 8,160 × 30 = 244,800 macroblocks/s , below 245,760. At 60 fps , demand is: 8,160 × 60 = 489,600 macroblocks/s , above that limit. The dimensions are identical, but the second stream requires a larger throughput envelope. A label assigning “1080p” to one universal level would hide this difference. Other level constraints still need checking, including bitrate, coded buffering, motion limits, and profile-dependent factors. Passing the two calculations above explains one part of the requirement rather than certifying an arbitrary file. The reference-buffer calculation At this coded picture size, the selected DPB limit gives: floor(32,768 ÷ 8,160) = 4 picture slots. References and pictures awaiting output have to satisfy the decoded-buffer rules. A stream requesting more state cannot be made compliant by reducing only its bitrate. Conversely, a small compressed file can still require the full decoded picture surfaces. The reference-buffer article explains those surfaces' lifetimes and sample-memory footprints. A standard's logical DPB constraint and an implementation's total allocated memory are related but distinct measurements. HEVC Main 10, Level 5.1, and Main tier HEVC defines Main and High tiers. Where High tier is defined, it permits higher bitrate and coded-buffer limits within the relevant level. It does not select a different camera resolution or automatically improve the picture. In the description “HEVC Main 10, Level 5.1, Main tier” : Main 10 is the profile's sample/tool permission. 5.1 is the level's resource envelope. Main tier selects the corresponding bitrate/buffer limits. The word “Main” serves two different names in this family. The entire codec-specific description supplies the meaning; H.264 Level 4.1 and HEVC Level 4.1 do not share one interchangeable resource table. Change the demand, or correct an excessive declaration If a source really exceeds a target's throughput, producing a suitable representation can require a lower picture rate, smaller raster, different reference structure, or other encoding changes. Editing its level flag does not reduce the coded work. A file can also be declared at a higher level than its actual demand needs. Correcting such a declaration requires checking the complete applicable constraints, including peak and buffer behavior, rather than looking only at the visible resolution. For an Emby decoder target, these calculations turn a broad resolution claim into questions about the actual stream: its coded grid, picture rate, retained state, profile, tier, and delivery demand. See Also Video Codec Profiles Video Reference Frames Video Resolution Video Frame Rate References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers Android decoder video capabilities

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.title: Video Codec Profiles | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.keywords: Video Codec Profiles A video codec profile constrains the coding tools and sample formats a stream may use. A decoder needs to understand every coding operation a stream can ask it to perform. A profile selects a permitted set of those operations and sample formats within a codec. This is useful both for designing a decoder and for creating a file for a known playback target. The encoder can restrict its choices to the target's tool set, rather than asking the decoder to handle every feature in the complete standard. Selected sample-format permissions Profile Sample depth Sampling covered by this row H.264 Baseline 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 Main 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 High 8-bit 4:2:0; monochrome also permitted H.264 High 10 Up to 10-bit 4:2:0; monochrome also permitted HEVC Main 8-bit 4:2:0 HEVC Main 10 8-bit or 10-bit 4:2:0 These rows describe selected format permissions, rather than a complete profile specification. They show why a decoder for an ordinary 8-bit stream may need additional sample-processing capability for a 10-bit stream. The tools can differ even at the same depth H.264 Baseline, Main, and High can all represent 8-bit 4:2:0 pictures, yet their bitstreams can use different operations. Entropy coding: CABAC encodes syntax through context-adaptive binary arithmetic coding. Its decoder follows a probability state and arithmetic decoding process. H.264 Main and High permit it; Baseline uses the permitted non-CABAC coding route. Identical final pixel depth does not make those compressed syntax representations interchangeable. Picture prediction: Main and High permit B-slices. The associated reference choices and possible reordering require the relevant prediction and buffering behavior. Baseline's restrictions exclude that B-slice tool set. Block transforms: High adds permission for an 8×8 transform tool, while Main's transform set is narrower. The decoder must apply the transform described by the stream to reconstruct its corrections. The profile label identifies these restrictions as a package. More tools give an encoder different options for representing the source, but the label itself does not select its quantization strength or measure the finished picture. Make a stream conform to another profile Suppose a target requires H.264 Baseline, while the source uses High with CABAC and 8×8 transforms. Changing the word “High” in metadata leaves the CABAC-coded syntax and transformed blocks in place. The decoder would still encounter operations excluded from the claimed profile. Creating the target requires decoding the source and encoding its pictures using the target's actual permitted tools. The encoder restricts entropy coding, prediction, transforms, and any other relevant choices together. A High 10 source converted to an 8-bit target also needs a change of sample representation. That happens in the processing/encoding path, rather than being accomplished by relabeling a 10-bit payload. A Main 10 HEVC stream can contain SDR or HDR. HDR interpretation comes from the appropriate transfer/color signaling and content; the profile's depth permission describes the sample/tool set. Pair the profile with its resource limits “HEVC Main 10, Level 5.1, Main tier” describes three aspects: a permitted tool/sample set, a workload level, and a bitrate/buffering tier. The level and tier need to accompany the profile when establishing a decoder target. For an Emby playback route, identifying the source profile and the app's usable decoder makes a profile-related conversion understandable. The target encode supplies a representation that conforms to the chosen tool set; it does not improve the source merely by giving it a different profile name. See Also Video Codec Levels and Tiers How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers x264 source: Profile restrictions

articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.title: How Video Compression Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.keywords: How Video Compression Works Video compression represents picture information with fewer bits by exploiting patterns and, in lossy modes, accepting approximation. A camera following a person across a plain wall records much of the same scene again and again. Storing every picture as a fresh list of sample values would spend a large amount of data describing that repetition. Video compression finds a cheaper description from which a decoder can reconstruct the pictures: where to get a useful prediction, how to correct it, and which small differences to retain. That description is what Emby stores and delivers as a compressed video stream. The player reconstructs full pictures for display. To understand the savings—and why quality, encoding speed, and seeking behave as they do—it helps to follow one region through this process. How much data is being replaced? For a 1920 × 1080 picture stored as 8-bit 4:2:0 video, four picture locations use four luma samples and two chroma samples. Luma carries the brightness-related signal; the two chroma components carry color differences. The lower chroma sampling density gives an average of 1.5 bytes per picture location. Ignoring padding and headers: One picture occupies 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes . At 24 pictures per second, that is 74,649,600 bytes per second , about 74.65 MB/s or 597 Mb/s . One minute would occupy about 4.48 GB in decimal units. A hypothetical compressed video stream averaging 6 Mb/s would use about 45 MB for that minute, before audio and container overhead. The raw-to-compressed ratio in this example is roughly 100:1. That calculation describes the data reduction, not a guarantee of what any particular source will look like at 6 Mb/s. The raw baseline already has a defined sample format. Comparing it with full-resolution RGB or with samples of a different bit depth would give a different ratio. Compression operates on the picture representation supplied to the encoder; scaling, reducing bit depth, and changing chroma sampling are additional ways a workflow can change that input. Find a prediction worth describing The encoder divides a picture into regions and looks for useful ways to predict their samples. Region sizes and available prediction tools depend on the codec. A large region can describe a smooth wall efficiently. Around a moving hand or a detailed edge, smaller regions may provide better matches. There is a cost to that flexibility. Dividing a region means describing the divisions and their individual choices. The smallest possible regions do not automatically make the smallest file. The encoder has to weigh improved predictions against the extra instructions. Predict from the same picture With intra-frame prediction , a region can be predicted from neighboring samples that have already been reconstructed. If nearby samples have similar values, extending those values into the new region can be a good starting point. A directional prediction can continue an edge across the region. Both encoder and decoder know those reconstructed neighbors and the selected prediction rule. The encoder sends the choice of rule and a correction, rather than a completely independent value for every sample. “Intra” therefore does not mean “uncompressed.” Even a picture that has no dependencies on other pictures can exploit a great deal of repetition within itself. A broad, evenly lit wall is much easier to describe this way than a field of unrelated random values. Predict from other pictures With inter-frame prediction , the encoder can obtain samples from reconstructed reference pictures. When the person moves to the right, a region at the person's new position may resemble a region farther left in a reference picture. A motion vector tells the decoder where to obtain the selected prediction. The decoder does not need to recognize a person or understand the motion of an arm. It follows sample-location instructions. The encoder does the search; the decoder uses the result. Depending on the codec, predictions can use several reference pictures, interpolated sample positions, or combinations of predictions. Motion prediction is especially useful when a camera pans across a scene. Many sample positions change, but large areas still resemble shifted versions of an earlier picture. Conversely, a small newly revealed strip behind a moving object may have no useful match. The encoder can choose another prediction or code that region using intra prediction. The prediction is often imperfect: illumination changes, an edge moves by a fraction of a sample, or a surface deforms. The remaining difference is the residual . A useful prediction makes that correction easier to describe. Encoding the prediction error Take four illustrative luma samples. The prediction is close to the source: Stage Four sample values Prediction 100, 102, 104, 106 Source 102, 101, 108, 107 Residual: source minus prediction 2, −1, 4, 1 If the decoder receives that exact residual, adding it to the prediction recovers the source exactly. This subtraction is reversible. Lossy compression enters when the encoder chooses to describe an approximation of the correction. Change the representation before rounding A transform expresses a region as a mixture of patterns. One pattern might represent a constant offset; others describe variations across the region. The resulting numbers are coefficients : how much of each pattern is present. A constant residual of 2, 2, 2, 2 illustrates the attraction. Instead of treating the four equal corrections as unrelated numbers, a suitable transform represents their common component and leaves the variation components at zero. Real picture regions often contain smooth areas and gradual changes that concentrate much of their information in relatively few coefficients. For a transparent numerical example, use a small reversible add-and-subtract transform. This is a teaching example, not the transform prescribed by H.264 or H.265. Given residual samples a, b, c, and d, calculate: c0 = (a + b + c + d) / 2 c1 = (a + b − c − d) / 2 c2 = (a − b + c − d) / 2 c3 = (a − b − c + d) / 2 For 2, −1, 4, 1, the coefficients are 3, −2, 3, 0 . For the constant residual 2, 2, 2, 2, they would be 4, 0, 0, 0 : all the correction is in the common component. The transform has not thrown away information. Applying the corresponding inverse to the unrounded coefficients recovers the original residual. It has put the information into a form that is often cheaper to approximate and code. Quantize the coefficients Quantization reduces the number of coefficient values that need distinct representations. For this example, round to the nearest multiple of two, with halfway cases rounded away from zero: Coefficient values Before rounding 3, −2, 3, 0 After rounding 4, −2, 4, 0 Levels, expressed in units of the step size 2, −1, 2, 0 A decoder given the levels and step size reconstructs 4, −2, 4, 0. It cannot determine whether an original coefficient of 3 or 4 led to the reconstructed value 4. Those distinctions have been merged. Larger quantization steps merge more distinctions and often make more coefficients zero. That can reduce the number of bits substantially, while changing the reconstructed picture more. Actual codecs define their own scaling and quantization rules, and encoders can adjust choices across a picture. The simple step of two here is not a codec QP setting. Code the remaining symbols compactly The bitstream must describe more than coefficients. It also contains prediction choices, region divisions, reference information, motion data, and other syntax. Entropy coding represents those symbols using their statistical patterns. For example, a long region of zero coefficients does not need a separate full-sized integer for every zero. Contexts in which one outcome is very likely can also be represented more economically than contexts with many equally likely outcomes. The exact method depends on the codec. This stage preserves the symbols it is given. It does not decide that a coefficient should become zero; quantization and the encoder's coding decisions have already established what will be represented. A decoded coefficient sequence can be an exact copy of the coded sequence even while the resulting picture differs from the original. Reconstruct the picture the player will get Applying the inverse toy transform to the rounded coefficients produces a residual of 3, −1, 5, 1 . Adding that correction to the same prediction gives: Four sample values Original source 102, 101, 108, 107 Decoded reconstruction 103, 101, 109, 107 Reconstruction minus source 1, 0, 1, 0 Two sample values changed by one. The decoder has done its job correctly: this is the picture specified by the compressed description. It has no access to the discarded distinctions needed to restore the two original values. The example also shows why a compression error need not look like a single missing pixel. Changing a transform coefficient changes a pattern spread over several samples. In real pictures, stronger approximation can soften texture, alter an edge, or produce visible patterns around it. Compression artifacts are the visible consequences of those decisions. The encoder keeps a local reconstruction so later predictions use pictures that the decoder can also obtain. The codec defines the actual transforms, syntax, and reconstruction rules. Why the encoder needs its own reconstruction For later pictures, the encoder must predict using the samples the decoder will have. After the example above, a reference region contains 103, 101, 109, 107, even though the original source contained 102, 101, 108, 107. Suppose the next source picture has a sample value of 104 at the corresponding position. Predicting from the reconstructed value 103 leaves a correction of 1. The decoder can make that same prediction and obtain 104. Predicting instead from the pristine source value 102 would leave a correction of 2; adding it to the decoder's reference value 103 would produce 105. That disagreement is why the encoder reconstructs its chosen approximation and uses the result for future references. Both sides must operate from matching information. A lossy reference does not inevitably make all following pictures worse: later corrections can account for differences, provided the encoder uses the correct reconstructed reference. Reconstruction can also include codec-defined processing such as in-loop filtering. In block-based coding, this processing can reduce some discontinuities or adjust reconstructed samples. When those filtered pictures serve as references, the encoder must account for the same processing. A filter used only for display has a different role because it does not redefine the samples used for subsequent predictions. Lossless video compression retains the information needed to recover the input samples exactly. It can still exploit prediction and statistical coding. It does not have to use this lossy transform-and-rounding path; FFV1, for example, codes sample differences without discarding them. Lossless applies to the samples supplied to that encoder. Any earlier scaling or color conversion remains part of how those samples were produced. Picture dependencies explain decoding order and seeking A reference picture must be reconstructed before a picture that uses it. The order in which pictures are decoded can therefore differ from the order in which they appear on screen. Consider a simplified sequence displayed as A, B, C. Suppose C is predicted from A, and B is predicted using both A and C. The decoder needs this order: Decode A. Decode C using A. Decode B using the two available references. Present A, B, C at their intended times. The player holds the necessary pictures and uses their timing information to restore presentation order. “A later picture” in a prediction description can mean later in display order; it is already available when the dependent picture is decoded. The same dependencies matter when seeking. Jumping directly into a dependent picture may omit references needed to reconstruct it. A player typically starts at a suitable random-access point , then decodes the necessary path to the requested time. Merely having a picture coded without inter prediction does not, for every codec structure, guarantee that all subsequent dependencies have been reset. More frequent independent access points can make entry into the stream easier, but give the encoder fewer opportunities to reuse earlier pictures. This is one reason a seek-friendly or low-latency stream can have different compression characteristics from a stream designed mainly for efficient sequential playback. The encoder chooses between competing descriptions For one region, an encoder may have several plausible descriptions: one large prediction, several smaller predictions, a different reference picture, or an intra prediction. Each produces a different residual and requires a different amount of syntax. A prediction with the smallest raw residual is not necessarily the best final choice. It might require many extra motion instructions. Conversely, accepting a slightly less accurate prediction can be worthwhile if its coded description is much smaller. Rate-distortion optimization expresses this tradeoff. “Rate” is the number of bits needed; “distortion” is a measure of the reconstructed picture's difference from the source. As a constructed example, consider two complete coding choices: Choice Bits for this region Distortion in illustrative units A 120 10 B 70 14 If the cost is distortion + 0.05 × bits, A costs 16 and B costs 17.5, so A wins. If bits are more expensive and the multiplier is 0.2, A costs 34 and B costs 28, so B wins. Nothing about the source changed; the available tradeoff changed. Real encoders use more involved calculations, and a simple sample-error score does not capture every aspect of perceived quality. The example explains why a coding decision can change when a bitrate budget changes. The x265 analysis options expose controls for how thoroughly such alternatives are evaluated. Scene complexity affects those alternatives. A static wall offers predictable samples and often small corrections. Film grain and sensor noise contain variations that are harder to predict. Leaves moving independently, splashing water, or newly revealed detail can require many corrections. Preserving that information costs bits; smoothing it makes the picture cheaper to describe. Rate control manages these choices over time. A quality-oriented encode can allow difficult sections to use more data. A constrained stream has to fit its delivery budget, potentially using stronger approximation in a difficult scene. A full movie's average bitrate hides those local differences. Resolution and frame rate describe the output grid and timing, while the coding decisions determine how faithfully that grid represents the source. Encoding effort and playback effort are different The decoder follows a selected description. The encoder may have tried many descriptions before choosing it. That search is why increasing encoder effort can improve compression without requiring the player to repeat the search. The x265 presets provide a concrete example: slower presets evaluate more possibilities, while faster presets take more shortcuts. Comparing encoders fairly means considering the resulting quality, bitrate, and time together. Identical codec names or nominal quality settings do not establish identical decisions. Playback still has work to do: entropy decoding, reference management, prediction, reconstruction, and any required filters. A device must support the particular codec features and sample format, and perform those operations fast enough for the picture rate. A compact stream can consequently be harder for a device to decode than a larger stream in a simpler supported format. For Emby, these distinctions separate three common paths. During Direct Play, the app decodes the stored compressed video. When the server copies that video into a different container, the compressed picture description remains intact. During a video transcode , the server decodes the source, performs any required processing, and creates a new compressed description for the destination. The new encoder sees the reconstructed source, including any texture or edge changes already present in it. More output bits can preserve that input better; they cannot identify discarded original detail. That is why keeping the original library file gives future playback and conversion paths the best available starting point. articles/video/encoding-quality/index.ht.title: Overview: Encoding and picture quality | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/index.ht.keywords: Overview: Encoding and picture quality Encoding quality depends on rate allocation, encoder effort and the picture changes introduced by compression. The codec defines a format, but an encoder still chooses how to spend bits and computation on a particular sequence. Rate-control and preset choices influence that work. Artifact and metric topics then provide different ways to examine the result, including the effects of grain and repeated encoding. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Rate control Rate control allocates encoded data under quality, bitrate or buffering objectives. Encoder presets Video encoder presets choose a bundle of coding decisions that trades encoding effort against compression efficiency. Quality changes and artifacts Compression artifacts, generation loss and grain describe different changes to the appearance of encoded pictures. Quality metrics Video quality metrics compare pictures through numerical models that measure particular kinds of difference. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Overview: Quality changes and artifacts | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Overview: Quality changes and artifacts Compression artifacts, generation loss and grain describe different changes to the appearance of encoded pictures. A soft edge, a block pattern and changing film grain do not all have the same origin. Compression can alter detail within one encode, and further lossy generations can compound those changes. These topics help describe the visible result before blaming resolution, scaling or the display. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Generation loss Generation loss is the additional change introduced when already compressed video is decoded and encoded again with lossy settings. Compression artifacts Video compression artifacts are visible changes introduced when coding compromises cannot preserve the source's intended appearance. Film grain Film grain is fine varying picture texture that can be preserved, simplified, or modeled during video encoding. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Compression Artifacts | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Compression Artifacts Video compression artifacts are visible changes introduced when coding compromises cannot preserve the source's intended appearance. A moving fabric texture becomes smooth, an edge gains faint ripples, or a dark sky breaks into steps. Compression artifacts are the visible effects of reconstruction decisions that failed to retain an important part of the source's appearance. Different appearances come from different relationships inside the picture. Boundaries between coded regions Block-based coding gives neighboring regions their own predictions and corrections. If quantization simplifies them differently, their reconstructed edge values may disagree. A smooth surface can then acquire a rectangular boundary that was not in the source. In-loop deblocking can address selected discontinuities, but the reconstructed representation still reflects how the regions were coded. The visible block size need not equal one fixed macroblock size: partitioning, motion, filtering and error propagation can produce larger or less regular patches. Patterns around a sharp edge A sharp transition needs a combination of spatial patterns to represent it. Transform coding describes those patterns with coefficients. Coarsening or dropping coefficients changes their balance when the block is reconstructed. The edge can soften or gain small alternating ripples around it, often called ringing. Similar appearances can also arise from scaling or sharpening filters, so compare where the ripple first appears in the processing path. This is more informative than treating every halo as proof that a particular codec was selected. Why a smooth gradient becomes banded Use a simple scalar quantizer that rounds to multiples of four: Source values 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 Rounded values 100 100 104 104 104 104 108 108 The source advances one unit at a time. The reconstructed array repeats a few levels and jumps between them. Spread such repeated values over a visible gradient and the smooth transition can appear as bands. Original rounding example with half-step ties upward. Real video transforms and sample processing introduce their own region and precision behavior. Limited source precision or a later display conversion can also create stepped gradients. The calculation demonstrates the loss of distinct levels; locating the responsible stage determines which operation can change it. Texture can change in time Fine detail and grain need many changing correction values. A constrained encoder can simplify them, making a region smoother. When the allocation or prediction changes in later pictures, the amount of retained texture can change too. A surface may then shimmer, pulse, or briefly become sharper at certain picture boundaries. A still frame does not reveal that temporal inconsistency. Observation Relationship worth inspecting Rectangular surface changes Region reconstruction and boundaries Edge ripples Transform approximation and later filters Soft detail Retained high-frequency patterns Pulsing texture Picture-to-picture allocation or prediction Stepped shading Available sample/reconstruction levels Find the first changed representation For an Emby conversion, compare the selected source with the delivered result at the same picture time and presentation scale. If the source already contains the defect, the output is working from that reconstruction. If it appears only in the new stream, examine that encode and any preceding processing. Then view the passage in motion. Grain consistency, flickering outlines and movement-specific breakup can be missed by paused comparisons. A controlled second encode with more available precision or data can test whether the new coding compromise caused the change. A filter can instead conceal it by removing or modifying detail; that is another picture operation, not recovery of the original coefficients. The comparison identifies the actual transformation to improve, while generation lineage identifies which earlier source information is still available. articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Film Grain in Compressed Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Film Grain in Compressed Video Film grain is fine varying picture texture that can be preserved, simplified, or modeled during video encoding. A still wall can be difficult to compress when its scanned film texture changes in every picture. The wall is stable, but the grain is additional varying information the encoder has to represent. Film grain can be part of the intended appearance of a film scan or a deliberately added effect. Its strength, scale and behavior belong to that presentation. A static scene can have a changing residual Take a simplified underlying scene sample of 100: Picture Grain contribution Observed sample A −3 97 B +4 104 Predict B from A without any movement and the residual is 104 −97 =7 . The scene's underlying value did not change; the grain contribution did. Across many samples, that varying texture weakens the usefulness of directly reusing the previous picture. Finer grain can leave many changing coefficients rather than a small predictable scene correction. Original scalar illustration, not a film-grain generator or measured codec result. Direct coding spends data on the visible pattern An encoder can represent the grain as part of the picture samples. Its predictions, transforms and quantization then handle both the underlying scene and the texture. At a tight budget, some grain detail can become smoother or form coarser patches. If the coding decisions change sharply between regions or pictures, the retained texture can also appear uneven: one area has stronger grain, then another frame suppresses it. This can make a film seem to pulse or “breathe,” even when its overall resolution and average bitrate remain unchanged. A grain tuning can prioritize consistency x265's documented tune grain emphasizes avoiding artifacts caused by uneven grain distribution. It restricts selected QP-varying behaviors and biases decisions toward more high-frequency content. Its specialized rate control also tries to limit quantizer fluctuations. That is a specific allocation priority. It is not a promise to reproduce every original grain sample or simply a universal instruction to keep all noise. A whole-scene review should therefore assess whether the texture remains coherent in motion, alongside the resulting data requirement. Model the appearance instead AV1 can encode a cleaner picture and signal parameters for adding modeled grain during output processing. Parameter role What it contributes to the generated appearance Strength versus brightness Grain can behave differently in dark and light areas Relationships between nearby samples Gives the texture structure rather than independent noise alone Generation seed Specifies the generator's repeatable pattern behavior The decoder applies the specified synthesis to the output. The reconstructed scene retained for future prediction is separate from that added grain realization. This can reduce the need to transmit every grain sample in the coded picture while retaining a designed grain-like appearance. It preserves an appearance model, rather than the exact source texture array. Evaluate texture rather than a single paused speck Compare passages at the intended scale and in motion. Look at grain strength, clumping, continuity across regions and stability around picture changes. A paused enlargement can emphasize isolated samples without showing temporal pumping. Pixel-error metrics can also react to a different grain pattern even if its intended texture is similar. A synthesized realization and the original scan need not match sample for sample. Decide whether the comparison aims at exact sample preservation or the intended viewing appearance. For an Emby viewing version, that distinction explains whether a grain change came from simplification, filtering, inconsistent direct coding, or a different modeled texture. Those are different operations on the film's appearance. See Also AV1 Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts Video Generation Loss References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification x265: Presets and tunings

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Generation Loss | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Generation Loss Generation loss is the additional change introduced when already compressed video is decoded and encoded again with lossy settings. If two viewing copies are made separately from the same retained source, each begins with that source's picture information. If a third copy is made from one of the viewing copies, it begins with an already altered reconstruction. That difference is the useful way to understand generation loss . The diagram shows conversion lineage, not measured visible damage. Separate new encodes from a chain Let M be a retained master. Make A for one playback target and B for another: M →A and M →B . B does not inherit A's encoding errors because A was not its input. Ordinary Emby playback conversions that each read the retained library source have this branching relationship. Repeated viewing does not itself turn the previous delivery stream into the next source. A chain instead looks like M →A →C . A user might create it by converting a small copy and later using that copy for another export. Each stage's encoder receives the samples reconstructed at the preceding stage. How successive sample errors combine For pictures in the same sample representation, let A's error relative to M be A −M , and C's new error relative to A be C −A . Then: C −M =(A −M) +(C −A). Take a scalar example: M is 17, A is 16, and C is 18. The first stage changes the value by −1, the second by +2, and the final error relative to M is +1. This does not mean every encode adds the same visible damage, or that each sample's absolute error must increase. Errors can reinforce or partly cancel at a position. The equation identifies the inputs whose differences are being combined. Original scalar illustration; it is not a prediction of a named codec's multigeneration quality. Why lost distinctions cannot be recovered from size Suppose a first quantizer rounds both 17 and 19 to 16. The stored result no longer identifies which of those two inputs occurred. A later process might produce 18, but it cannot know which original input to recover from the shared 16. More output bits can describe that input reconstruction more accurately; they do not supply the discarded distinction. In a picture, such distinctions can correspond to texture, grain or subtle gradients. A delivery copy can therefore be an adequate viewing source while being a reduced input for later production. Locate the operation that creates a generation Operation Video sample/coding effect Copy the file Existing coded video is retained Repackage the same video packets Existing picture coding is retained Convert audio while copying video No new video encode Decode and encode video with lossy settings A new video reconstruction is created Losslessly encode the decoded samples That stage retains its input exactly Display metadata or timestamps can also change presentation without a new video encode. Cropping/resizing/filtering followed by encoding changes the input array as well as its later coding. Identify those operations before interpreting a difference between copies. A useful source strategy follows from the lineage: keep the best retained input and make needed derivatives from it. When editing requires an intermediate, a suitable lossless or production representation can serve the next stage, while its guarantee remains tied to the samples it actually received. articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Overview: Quality metrics | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Overview: Quality metrics Video quality metrics compare pictures through numerical models that measure particular kinds of difference. A quality score is the output of a defined comparison, not a direct measurement of every viewer's preference. PSNR, SSIM and VMAF examine different relationships between a reference and a processed picture. Their pages explain what a score represents so the metric can be used alongside visible evidence. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> VMAF VMAF predicts perceived video quality by comparing a decoded test video with a reference under a selected model and viewing context. PSNR PSNR expresses decoded sample error relative to a declared peak value using a logarithmic decibel scale. SSIM SSIM compares local luminance, contrast, and structure between decoded pictures and a reference. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video PSNR expresses decoded sample error relative to a declared peak value using a logarithmic decibel scale. Start with four 8-bit grayscale sample values in a reference picture and the corresponding four values in a test picture: Position Reference Test Difference Squared difference 1 50 52 +2 4 2 100 98 −2 4 3 150 153 +3 9 4 200 196 −4 16 The squared differences total 33 . Dividing by four gives the mean squared error, MSE =8.25 . Its square root is the RMS error , approximately 2.8723 sample units . Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) expresses this error relative to a declared peak using a logarithmic scale. Convert the sample error to decibels For this example, choose peak =255 , the maximum code value of an 8-bit sample: PSNR = 10 × log10(peak² /MSE) So: 10 × log10(255² /8.25) = 38.9663 dB , approximately 38.97 dB. The peak is the declared sample-format convention, not the brightest observed reference value, which happened to be 200. Selecting a different peak changes the score even if every error remains the same. Original paired-sample calculation for one plane. It is not a measured video encode. Why doubling RMS error lowers PSNR by 6 dB Calculated curve for one plane, peak 255, and positive RMS error; no encoder benchmark or perceptual threshold is implied. RMS error in this convention PSNR 1 48.13 dB 2 42.11 dB 4 36.09 dB 8 30.07 dB Doubling RMS error multiplies MSE by four. Its PSNR change is 10 × log10(4) ≈6.02 dB downward . With zero sample error, the mathematical value is infinite. That establishes exact equality of the compared sample arrays. Their file bytes, metadata and earlier source history are separate observations. The statistic records energy, not location One four-sample error pattern could be +2,+2,+2,+2 : a uniform offset. Another could be +4,0,0,0 : a localized error. Both have MSE 4 and the same PSNR. Their distribution differs. In an image, a change on a sharp outline can be noticed differently from error spread across a smooth region. PSNR averages squared magnitudes and does not describe that placement or local structural relationship. SSIM develops a different comparison using local picture statistics. Aggregate the quantity you intend Suppose two equally sized frames have MSE values 1 and 100 , using peak 255. Pool their squared errors first: mean MSE =(1 +100)/2 =50.5. The resulting PSNR is 31.10 dB . Average their separately calculated frame PSNR values instead: (48.13 +28.13)/2 =38.13 dB . These are different calculations because the logarithm is nonlinear. The score's aggregation rule therefore belongs with its reported number. FFmpeg's PSNR filter documents accumulation/averaging of MSE before calculating its aggregate. Prepare corresponding pictures A valid conversion comparison needs corresponding content at corresponding times, with a declared geometry, sample format and peak convention. A shifted crop, a one-picture offset or an unintended range conversion can measure those changes rather than the encoder's reconstruction error. For an Emby derivative, compare the actual delivered reconstruction with the selected retained source after the intended common preparation. Record the compared span and plane handling as well as the aggregate. The calculation then tells you which sample error the reported decibels represent. See Also Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video VMAF Video Quality Metric Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Generation Loss References FFmpeg: PSNR filter Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli: Image quality assessment from error visibility to structural similarity

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video SSIM compares local luminance, contrast, and structure between decoded pictures and a reference. Take a small reference patch with values 40,40,60,60 . It contains a step from a darker region to a lighter one. Now compare two reconstructions: Patch Values Mean squared error from reference A: brightness shifted 50,50,70,70 100 B: step flattened 50,50,50,50 100 Both have the same squared sample error. A retains the step and its contrast, while B removes it. Structural Similarity (SSIM) compares local statistical relationships that distinguish those results. Separate mean, contrast and structure The original SSIM approach uses three relationships: Local mean: the average sample value. This is its luminance comparison; in this grayscale example it refers to code values, not physical display luminance. Local contrast: the spread around that mean, described by variance or standard deviation. The step patch has variation; the flat patch has none. Local structure: how corresponding deviations vary together, described by covariance. When both pictures put their below-mean and above-mean values in the same places, that correspondence is positive. For the reference, the mean is 50 . Its deviations are −10,−10,+10,+10 . Using sample variance with denominator N−1: (100 +100 +100 +100)/3 =133.333… Patch A has mean 60 and the same deviations. Patch B has mean 50 but all its deviations are zero. Calculate the combined comparison For this illustration, use the original combined form: SSIM =((2µxµy +C1)/(µx² +µy² +C1)) ×((2σxy +C2)/(σx² +σy² +C2)) Here µ denotes the local mean, σx² and σy² are variances, and σxy is covariance. Choose an 8-bit peak convention L = 255, with K1 =0.01 and K2 =0.03: C1 =(K1L)² =6.5025 , and C2 =(K2L)² =58.5225 . The constants stabilize comparisons when a mean or variation is small; two identical flat patches should not require dividing zero by zero. Test patch Mean Variance Covariance with reference Calculated SSIM A 60 133.333… 133.333… 0.983624… B 50 0 0 0.305034… A's contrast/structure factor is 1, with a smaller change in its mean factor. B's mean matches, but its variance and covariance describe the missing step. Original four-value arithmetic using uniform local statistics and N−1 variance/covariance. It demonstrates the formula, not the output of a particular video tool's 2D windowing implementation. Reverse the step A third patch, 60,60,40,40 , has the same mean and variance as the reference, but its deviations are opposite at every position. Its covariance is −133.333… . With the declared constants, its SSIM is approximately −0.640071 . Negative covariance can therefore produce a negative index. SSIM is not universally a 0–1 percentage of retained picture quality. Identical local content gives 1 in this original formulation. That identity case and the reversed-pattern example describe what the mathematical comparison is measuring. Move from a patch to a video A real implementation calculates local windows across each picture and combines their results. Window size and weighting, color/plane handling, scale preparation and frame aggregation all affect the number. The author's suggested image scaling is one concrete example. Netflix's VMAF FAQ documents that its included SSIM applies empirical downsampling that differs from FFmpeg's SSIM filter. Equal input filenames do not make those preprocessing choices identical. For a conversion comparison, align the picture content and times and declare the measurement geometry. Then examine local or per-frame results where detail changed, rather than relying only on a whole-film aggregate.
