articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: VMAF Video Quality Metric | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: VMAF Video Quality Metric VMAF predicts perceived video quality by comparing a decoded test video with a reference under a selected model and viewing context. Suppose you are making smaller playback versions of the same retained movie source. Looking at every frame of every candidate is impractical, but file size alone says little about which version preserved the picture better. VMAF supplies one way to measure that comparison. VMAF, Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion, is a full-reference video-quality metric. It receives decoded pictures from a reference and a test sequence, extracts comparison features, and uses a trained model to predict quality in a defined viewing context. What goes into the score The comparison begins with corresponding pictures, not with file extensions or compressed byte sizes. Features capture aspects of the relationship between the reference and test content, such as retained detail and motion-related behavior. A model combines the features using relationships learned from subjective-quality data. The published v0.6.1 model, for example, lists an ADM detail feature, a motion feature, and VIF features at four spatial scales. These give the model several measurements of the picture relationship rather than one overall sample-error value. The selected model defines which measurements it consumes. Training supplies examples for which comparison features and viewer assessments are both available. The fitting process learns a mapping from the feature combinations to those assessments. Evaluation then measures a new reference/test pair and applies the fitted mapping. The training happened before this evaluation; choosing a VMAF model does not train a new model on the movie being tested. That last stage is why the result differs from a direct error formula such as PSNR . VMAF's number is the output of a particular learned model. It is intended to be useful for perceptual comparison; it is not a count of retained bits, pixels, or original information. A score of 95 therefore needs context. Which model produced it? How were the inputs prepared? Is it a mean for a whole film, or the score of one scene? Prepare the comparison before interpreting it Corresponding input pictures must represent the same content at the intended comparison geometry. A frame offset can compare two different moments. A crop difference can compare different regions. A range or color conversion applied on only one side can become part of the measured difference. When comparing a lower-resolution playback version with a larger reference, scaling is an explicit part of the evaluation. Use a consistent preparation that represents the intended viewing situation. A different scaler can change what the metric sees. This is especially relevant to HDR-to-SDR material. A straightforward comparison of incompatible signal representations does not isolate compression quality. Establish which picture representation is being compared and whether the selected model is suitable for it. For repeatable results, keep a small record with each test: The reference source and the tested encode. Model/version and tool settings. Sample format, geometry, scaling, and timing preparation. How per-frame results were aggregated. Viewing distance and model-specific score scales Artifacts that are visible close to a large screen may be much less visible from farther away. Models calibrated for different viewing conditions can therefore assign different values to the same reconstruction. Netflix's familiar v0 models and the v1 models released in June 2026 have documented viewing assumptions. Common models use a 0–100 scale; the v1 4K model for viewing at three screen heights uses 0–110. These are model conventions, not a universal percentage scale. A score from one model should not be treated as the same quantity as an equal-looking score from another. Even within one model, changing clipping settings or input preparation can change the interpretation of the result. Look past the whole-film average Consider a hypothetical constant-frame-rate, one-minute test: fifty seconds score 95, and ten seconds score 50. The arithmetic mean is 87.5. That single number cannot tell you whether the lower-scoring section is an inconsequential transition or the scene the viewer most cares about. Per-frame and per-scene results help locate the weakness. A low-tail summary can be useful alongside the mean, and a targeted viewing check can show what happened: smeared grain, unstable texture, blurred fine detail, or another visible change. Enhancement processing can complicate the measurement. Sharpening may change measured features while introducing a look that a viewer dislikes. Grain handling can also affect a reference comparison even where a synthetic-grain presentation is intentional. The metric and a viewing check answer related questions, rather than replacing one another. For an Emby library conversion, use VMAF to narrow the candidate encodes and identify passages worth inspecting. After choosing a satisfactory picture reconstruction, test the intended playback path separately for decoding and delivery performance. That preserves a clear meaning for the score: how the tested pictures compare under the stated model and preparation. See Also Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts References Netflix: published v0.6.1 model inputs Netflix: available comparison features Netflix: VMAF project Netflix: VMAF documentation Netflix: VMAF v0 models and viewing conditions Netflix: VMAF v1 model selection, viewing assumptions, and score ranges Netflix: VMAF frequently asked questions

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Overview: Rate control | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Overview: Rate control Rate control allocates encoded data under quality, bitrate or buffering objectives. Some encodes aim at a data budget; others let the rate vary to maintain a selected quality objective. Buffer constraints add a timing boundary that an average bitrate alone does not describe. This branch explains the objectives and controls behind those choices, including multi-pass analysis and quantization. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Video bitrate Video bitrate is the data budget for the encoded picture stream and can be a target, a limit, or a measured result. Constant bitrate encoding Constant bitrate encoding controls video output toward a specified rate over the encoder's buffering model. Variable bitrate encoding Variable bitrate encoding allows the coded video rate to change as the content and encoding constraints require. Constant quality encoding Constant quality encoding targets an encoder-defined quality level while allowing bitrate and output size to vary. Constant rate factor (CRF) Constant rate factor is an encoder-specific quality control that produces variable bitrate without targeting an exact output size. Quantization parameter (QP) A quantization parameter selects quantization strength in a video coding process and is not a universal picture-quality score. Two-pass encoding Two-pass video encoding analyzes a source before a final encode so the encoder can allocate an overall bitrate budget across it. VBV buffering VBV constrains encoded video using a modeled buffer capacity and input rate rather than a whole-file average alone. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Bitrate Video bitrate is the data budget for the encoded picture stream and can be a target, a limit, or a measured result. Average video rate Bytes for one second of pictures Video-only size over two hours 4 Mb/s 0.5 MB 3.6 GB 8 Mb/s 1 MB 7.2 GB 16 Mb/s 2 MB 14.4 GB Decimal units. Two hours is 7,200 seconds; the calculation excludes soundtracks and packaging. Video bitrate counts coded picture data against media duration. It is the video's data budget or measured rate, rather than the whole file's rate when that file also contains audio and other tracks. Divide one second among its pictures At 8 Mb/s, one media second contains 1,000,000 video bytes on average. At 24 fps, the average allocation is 1,000,000/24 =41,666.67 bytes per picture . At 60 fps it is 16,666.67 bytes . The same per-second budget is spread among more pictures. Actual pictures need not have those average sizes. Consider a deliberately constructed 24-picture interval: Pictures Bytes per picture Combined bytes One independently coded picture 195,000 195,000 23 predicted pictures 35,000 805,000 Total 1,000,000 The interval still has 8 Mb/s of coded video. The large picture establishes content that the following pictures can reuse. Their sample count is not smaller; their encoded descriptions are. This example explains why a source can contain substantial frame-size variation at a stated average bitrate. Decide what the encoder is trying to hold A target average rate tells rate control to allocate data around an overall budget. It may use more in difficult sections and less elsewhere. A rate/buffer limit constrains local coded demand. Its meaning includes the relevant time and buffering model, not only a maximum number printed beside a file. A quality-based encode lets the resulting average rate emerge from its source and target. The measured bitrate is then an outcome rather than an exact amount selected in advance. CBR , VBR , and CRF develop these policies separately. Connect the budget to the source An encoder can reuse a wall across neighboring pictures with small corrections. Grain, fine texture and changing scenery require more information. Adding more frames also creates additional prediction opportunities, so a simple bits-per-picture division does not by itself determine visible quality. Presets change how thoroughly the encoder searches for a representation; quantization changes what approximation it accepts. The rate budget constrains their result. In an Emby session, compare the source video's measured rate with the delivered video's rate . Video conversion can create a different allocation while the original library file keeps its own rate. A file-wide bitrate can also include unused soundtracks, so keep the measurement's counted streams and duration explicit. See Also Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets References FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Constant bitrate encoding controls video output toward a specified rate over the encoder's buffering model. A channel supplying 4 Mb/s can deliver four million bits in one second. Constant bitrate (CBR) encoding controls the video around a selected rate and its buffering requirements so that delivery can be planned predictably. Pictures still require different amounts of data. A keyframe may establish an entire scene; a predicted picture may mainly describe what changed. Supply a large picture over time Suppose one coded picture contains one megabit . At 4 Mb/s, supplying it takes: 1,000,000 ÷4,000,000 =0.25 second. A 30 fps presentation interval is only 33.33 ms. The complete picture therefore cannot be expected to arrive from an empty buffer solely during its own display interval. Its data must have been supplied ahead of its decoding deadline. Smaller surrounding pictures leave more opportunity to build that buffered supply. The model limits both data rate and how much data can be retained. VBV follows the occupancy calculation in detail. The blue series uses equal one-second totals as a simple illustration. Actual CBR control need not make every one-second bucket or individual frame identical. Both plotted allocations contain 32 megabits over eight seconds. Rate control changes the picture description The encoder estimates how many bits a candidate picture description will need. As the available budget tightens, it can increase quantization strength or choose a less expensive coding representation. After encoding, the actual number of produced bits updates its rate-control state. If a difficult scene needs more data than the permitted model allows, that feedback must affect the representation. Fine texture can be simplified or reconstructed less precisely. Easy scenes can meet the same delivery requirements with smaller corrections. This is why CBR places predictability in the data path while allowing picture fidelity to change with the source. It does not assign an equal-quality amount of data to every scene. Strict output can include filler An easy section may not need all the channel's allowed data to reach the intended coding result. Some implementations offer filler or padding to keep strict coded output at the required rate. NVIDIA's NVENC API explicitly documents filler/padding controls for that purpose. Their presence is an implementation and mode choice, rather than a requirement that all encoders calling a mode “CBR” produce identical bytes every instant. Filler occupies data capacity without adding new photographed picture information. Counting it as part of encoded traffic and evaluating picture payload alone are different measurements. Coded rate and transfer speed are separate observations An Emby player can fetch data faster than it consumes it, then pause requests while buffered video plays. Its network graph can show bursts even when the video was encoded under CBR constraints. To interpret the result, use the coded stream's data across media time, its rate-control settings and relevant buffer model. Network arrival across wall-clock time describes how that representation was transported. The buffer bridges those two schedules. See Also Video Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Constant Quality Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Quality Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Quality Video Encoding Constant quality encoding targets an encoder-defined quality level while allowing bitrate and output size to vary. When preparing a library viewing copy, one possible objective is to preserve an acceptable appearance and let the resulting size follow the source. Constant quality encoding starts with that kind of quality policy instead of requiring the video to spend exactly a chosen amount of data. The policy belongs to the encoder. It guides reconstruction choices; it is not a measurement stamped onto every finished scene. A quality target makes bitrate the result The encoder analyzes picture structure and predicts how difficult regions will be to represent. It chooses prediction, partition and quantization decisions that serve its quality objective. A largely static region may need only a short correction. Changing fine texture can need many significant coefficients. The same quality policy can therefore produce a small description of one region and a larger description of another. After coding those choices, the number of produced bits is the result. Across a film, varying source difficulty makes bitrate fluctuate and determines the final size. This reverses an average-budget control priority: Objective Held as the main target Allowed to respond to content Average bitrate Overall data budget Reconstruction compromise and local allocation Quality-led encoding Encoder-defined quality policy Overall size and local bitrate Fixed quantizer mode Selected quantizer policy Bits and scene-dependent visible error The last row is related, but not identical to the middle one. Holding one quantizer does not ensure equal perceptual quality across different scenes. Preserve the parts that matter to later pictures A reference region can influence more than its own displayed picture. If later predictions reuse it repeatedly, improving that reconstruction can benefit many dependent pictures. An encoder can incorporate that importance into its quantization decisions. Regional adaptation can also distribute precision differently between smooth areas, detail, and motion according to the chosen model. These operations explain why the same quality setting does not require a single unchanging QP. CRF , hardware target-quality controls, and CQP have different mechanisms and scales. The model need not be an external score such as VMAF. Its internal coding estimates and perceptual priorities guide the encode; a later quality measurement evaluates the resulting pictures using another defined method. A delivery cap adds a competing requirement Suppose the quality-led choices for a difficult section would require more coded data than its permitted rate and buffer deadline. The encoder cannot both transmit that full representation and satisfy the restrictive deadline. It must change the picture description: coarser quantization, another prediction/partition choice, or other permitted rate-control behavior. The desired quality becomes a goal constrained by delivery. VBV provides the buffer model behind that decision. The source and chosen cap determine when this tradeoff occurs. Without the cap, the encode can use more data for that section; with it, the output has another obligation besides the quality policy. Evaluate the policy on the actual source A useful evaluation includes material that exercises the policy differently: static detail, grain, rapid movement and smooth gradients. Compare candidate settings using the same source and encoder configuration, looking at the reconstruction as well as its data demand. For an Emby viewing copy, this establishes both the picture you want to retain and the stream the playback route must supply. Size is then an observed outcome of those decisions, rather than a quality value selected independently of the source. See Also Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Variable Bitrate Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Constant rate factor is an encoder-specific quality control that produces variable bitrate without targeting an exact output size. At one constant rate factor (CRF) setting, a video can produce different bitrates and different picture quantizers from scene to scene. The constant is an encoder model's selected rate-factor control, rather than the number of bytes allocated to each second. x264 and x265 use CRF as quality-led variable rate control. Within a fixed setup, lowering the selected value generally moves toward finer reconstruction and more data; raising it moves toward stronger approximation. For exact sample preservation, use the encoder's documented lossless mode. x265 documents an explicit mode for that purpose; CRF 0 is not a universal lossless convention. This separates quality-led approximation from a different reconstruction guarantee. Separate the control from the quantizer it produces QP selects quantization strength. CRF guides the decisions that produce those quantizers. The controller analyzes the source and applies its quality/importance model. It can choose a different baseline or regional QP as content and picture role change while retaining the same user CRF. Observation at one CRF Reason it can change Frame QP Picture role and rate-control analysis Regional QP Adaptive precision/importance decisions Bits per frame Source information and selected representation Whole-file average The accumulated demands of that source The CRF number therefore does not mean “all frames used QP 23” or “every second received the same rate.” Those would be different control policies. Picture complexity and reference roles in quantizer selection An encoder's analysis estimates how well the pictures can be predicted and how much correction their structure leaves. More complicated content can have more significant information to represent. In x265's implementation, a fixed rate factor participates in the conversion from modeled terms into quantizer scale. Additional picture and regional analysis changes the resulting allocation. The full code has separate branches for its enabled analysis tools, rather than one equation directly mapping CRF to visible error. Picture role is important. An independently coded anchor establishes information needed by later pictures. A region reused by many future predictions can be worth reconstructing more carefully than a region that disappears immediately. Adaptive decisions can distribute precision accordingly. The encoder then chooses partitions, predictors and coded corrections at those quantizers. The actual produced bits update its coding estimates. Size emerges from this process instead of being an exact budget requested for the film. What a rate cap changes A CRF encode can also have a maximum rate and buffer constraint . The model's preferred representation must then fit local delivery deadlines. If a demanding section needs more data than the cap allows, the controller changes its reconstruction choices to satisfy the constraint. Its output can depart from the unconstrained quality policy there. The cap is therefore part of the encoding setup, not an invisible accessory to the CRF value. The same CRF with two different caps can create different results in the scene that binds those caps. Evaluate the value with the encoder fixed Choose representative passages that include the important source characteristics: grain or clean animation, motion, fine static detail and smooth shading. Make candidate encodes that differ in the CRF value while keeping the codec implementation, version, preset, sample format and other constraints stable. Then compare the decoded pictures and their observed rate/size. A setting is useful when the reconstruction serves the intended viewing context and its data demand serves the intended delivery. The source's easy passages and difficult ones need to be assessed together. CRF 20 in x264, CRF 20 in x265, and a CRF-like AV1 control belong to different models. Their shared number is not an equal-quality specification. Record the implementation and settings with the result so the comparison can be repeated. See Also Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Video Encoder Presets References x265: Quality and rate-control options FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) A quantization parameter selects quantization strength in a video coding process and is not a universal picture-quality score. A coded correction value of 21 can be reconstructed as 20 with one quantizer and 24 with a coarser one. The choice changes both the value recovered and the amount of detail the encoder needs to describe. A quantization parameter (QP) selects quantizer strength through the particular codec's rules. Original scalar model: output =step ×floor(input/step +0.5), with arbitrary steps 4 and 8. It isolates rounding, not the exact quantization equation of a named codec. Rounding to coarser reconstruction levels Input correction Round to multiples of 4 Error Round to multiples of 8 Error 3 4 +1 0 −3 9 8 −1 8 −1 21 20 −1 24 +3 27 28 +1 24 −3 The coarser step has fewer reconstruction levels. Several precise input values share one output, leaving less precision to encode. The error can also change direction, depending on where the input falls between levels. In a transform codec, those quantized values describe patterns across a block. Changing a coefficient changes its contribution to the reconstructed correction, rather than necessarily changing only one visible pixel. A codec maps QP onto its scale For ordinary 8-bit AVC luma coding, QP ranges from 0 to 51. With the same relevant scaling, an increase of six doubles the quantization step. Using QP 20's scale as 1 for a declared relative comparison: QP Relative scale 20 1 26 2 32 4 These are relative factors at six-step separations, not a declaration that QP 20 has an absolute step of one sample unit. The transform/scaling context supplies the absolute meaning. Different codecs and greater sample depths use their own indices and conventions. AVC's higher-depth internal quantizer index includes a depth offset, for example. A reported QP needs that context before being compared to another encode. A mode decides how the parameters are assigned Constant QP is an encoder's quantizer-control policy. It can define a base value and different picture-type settings or offsets. x265 documents its selected base for P-slices and related I/B values. CRF uses an adaptive rate-factor model that can produce varying picture and region quantizers. Bitrate control can also change QP to fit a data/buffer budget. These modes operate at different levels of the decision. A fixed base quantizer does not impose equal frame bytes: one picture can contain far more information to code at that precision than another. Interpret a reported average Imagine two equally weighted regions using QP 20 and QP 32. Their arithmetic mean QP is 26 . In the relative AVC scale above, their scales are 1 and 4, whose mean is 2.5 . A uniform QP 26 region instead uses relative scale 2. The equal mean QP has hidden a different distribution. This is a numerical illustration with equal weights and unchanged scaling, not a reconstruction-quality prediction. A log can also average over picture types, region sizes or other weights. Its number summarizes those assignments, while the actual bitstream reconstructs each region with its applicable quantizer. See Also Lossy Video Compression Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Compression Artifacts References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Two-Pass Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Two-Pass Video Encoding Two-pass video encoding analyzes a source before a final encode so the encoder can allocate an overall bitrate budget across it. Suppose an offline conversion must fit 40 seconds of video into an average 4 Mb/s . Its video budget is: 40 ×4 =160 megabits , or 20 decimal MB. The encoder can spend that budget differently in different scenes. Two-pass encoding first analyzes the source so its final allocation can use knowledge of the complete sequence. The final pass reads the original source again; statistics guide its choices. Analyze before making the final allocation A first pass evaluates picture difficulty and coding relationships. Its statistics can describe prediction costs, picture types, bits produced or estimated, and information useful for allocating precision later. Suppose four ten-second scenes receive illustrative difficulty weights 1,1,4,2 . A deliberately simple planner assigns budget proportional to these weights: Scene Declared weight Allocated data Rate across ten seconds A 1 20 Mb 2 Mb/s B 1 20 Mb 2 Mb/s C 4 80 Mb 8 Mb/s D 2 40 Mb 4 Mb/s Total 8 160 Mb 4 Mb/s overall This is an original proportional-planning example, not x265's rate-control formula or a measured encode. Real allocation models and local buffer constraints are more involved. Knowing that C is difficult lets the planner reserve more data for it while keeping the whole budget. A controller making decisions with only a short lookahead has less information about the complete video's later demands. Encode the source with the plan The second pass decodes or reads the same source pictures , uses the statistics to guide its quantizers and other choices, then produces the final bitstream. Actual coded sizes can differ from an estimate, so rate control updates its decisions as the encode proceeds. A local rate/buffer limit can also prevent spending the planned 80 megabits evenly or freely in C. The complete-file objective and the local deadline constraints both need to be satisfied. The first pass's compressed pictures are not ordinarily the second pass's source. Its useful output is the statistics. That is why analyzing and then encoding do not automatically create two successive lossy generations. Keep the statistics attached to their source The analysis describes a particular picture sequence. Changing its trims, picture order, scale, filtering or other relevant processing before the final pass can make those statistics describe the wrong input. The two passes therefore need consistent source and processing context. If a first pass uses faster analysis settings, those are deliberately chosen as part of the encoder's documented process, while the source relationship remains intact. Audio and packaging also occupy space if the objective is a complete-file size. The 160-megabit example is a video-only budget; reserve those other contributions separately when planning a full output. Hardware multipass has a smaller scope An encoder such as NVENC can analyze a frame in an internal pass, then use the result when encoding that frame. Its analysis can improve the distribution within the picture. That is not a first scan of the entire 40-second clip followed by a second reading. Both are called “passes,” but the amount of future source information available differs. Whole-source two-pass preparation suits an offline library derivative whose final budget matters. An immediate Emby playback transcode needs to begin output without waiting for a whole-film analysis. Its controller instead works with the information available at that stage of delivery. See Also Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets Video Bitrate References x265: Quality and rate-control options NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Variable bitrate encoding allows the coded video rate to change as the content and encoding constraints require. The variable-rate allocation in this figure uses 2, 3, 6, 7, 2, 3, 5 and 4 Mb/s across eight one-second intervals. Original allocation example, not encoder measurements. Each column represents one media second. The total is 32 megabits , giving an average of 32/8 =4 Mb/s . An equal 4 Mb/s allocation also contains 32 megabits. The two have the same total data, distributed differently through time. Variable bitrate (VBR) permits that changing allocation. Simple content can use less data and difficult content more, under the encoder's selected overall or local constraints. Supply the plotted sequence Use a simplified delivery model: the connection supplies 4 megabits per second continuously, and the video consumes each plotted interval's amount evenly within that second. Begin with 2 megabits already buffered. Interval Video demand Supplied Buffer at interval end 1 2 Mb 4 Mb 4 Mb 2 3 Mb 4 Mb 5 Mb 3 6 Mb 4 Mb 3 Mb 4 7 Mb 4 Mb 0 Mb 5 2 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb 6 3 Mb 4 Mb 3 Mb 7 5 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb 8 4 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb The quiet first two intervals build supply for the demanding third and fourth. With an empty initial buffer, the same accounting would fall 2 megabits below zero by the end of interval 4. Matching the average rate would not be enough to start this simplified sequence without advance data. The assumptions deliberately isolate the arithmetic. Real frame removals, request timing, overhead and network interruptions require their own scheduling; this is not a decoder-buffer conformance test. A seek beginning near interval 4 also starts with a different buffer state. Earlier quiet content cannot supply a surplus unless it was actually fetched for that playback start. Two objectives can produce variable output An average-budget encode tries to fit the complete video into an overall amount of data. It can transfer allocation from easier sections to harder ones. Two-pass analysis provides additional knowledge of where those sections occur. A quality-led encode allows the size to follow the source at a chosen quality policy. The final average can be different for two films, or for a clean and grainy version of the same scene. CRF is one implementation of that kind of control. Both produce variable rates, but they are solving different optimization problems. “VBR” by itself does not identify which objective was used. Add a local limit deliberately A whole-film data budget says little about a short burst's deadline. A maximum-rate/buffer constraint adds local delivery requirements. The encoder may need to accept a less detailed picture when a difficult section reaches those limits. In an Emby session, original delivery retains the source's local variation; a video transcode creates another allocation with its own constraints. The plotted calculation shows which parts of that rate description explain total size, and which explain the supply needed during playback. See Also Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Two-Pass Video Encoding Bitrate Variation References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) VBV constrains encoded video using a modeled buffer capacity and input rate rather than a whole-file average alone. A film can average 4 Mb/s and still contain a short section that needs data faster than a decoder can accept it. Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) constraints address that problem by asking whether the encoded pictures can pass through a defined rate-and-buffer model. The model has three essential ingredients: how data arrives, how much coded data can be stored, and when each picture removes its required data. An average for the whole film leaves the last two questions unanswered. Rate, capacity, and occupancy Suppose a simplified model accepts data at 4 Mb/s , has a capacity of 8 megabits , and starts with 4 megabits already available . The input rate describes how quickly the buffer can refill. Capacity is its maximum stored amount. Occupancy is how much it contains at a particular moment. A large picture can use data accumulated during easier pictures. It can require more than one frame interval's worth of arriving data without exceeding the model, provided that enough has arrived before its removal time. A picture fails the model if it needs bits that are not available when it must be decoded. The opposite limit matters too: arrivals and removals must follow rules that keep stored data within the permitted capacity. Codec models specify these details more precisely than this simplified illustration. A sustained burst exhausts the reserve The following calculation groups picture removals into one-second intervals to make the arithmetic visible. Real bitstream conformance checks operate at the codec's specified removal times. Interval Starting occupancy Data arrives Pictures use Ending occupancy 1 4 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb 2 2 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 0 Mb 3, same demand continues 0 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb short The first two demanding intervals succeed because the buffer had a reserve. Continuing the burst exhausts it. An easier interval using 2 Mb could rebuild the reserve by 2 Mb under the same arrival rate. The film might still average 4 Mb/s overall. That would not repair the shortage in interval 3: data from a later easy scene cannot travel backward in time. Buffer capacity divided by arrival rate gives a useful scale. Here, 8 Mb / 4 Mb/s is two seconds. It is a description of the model's capacity relative to the rate, not an automatic two-second player startup setting. What the encoder changes An encoder enforcing VBV has to fit its choices to the available budget at each point. During a difficult scene it may increase quantization, simplifying the residual information and reducing the number of coded bits. The result can be a local loss of texture or visible artifacts even when a quality setting stays unchanged. In x265, vbv-maxrate supplies the rate constraint and vbv-bufsize supplies the capacity. Their documented units differ: kilobits per second for the former, kilobits for the latter. Initial fullness is another setting because starting with a larger reserve changes what an early burst can use. Combining CRF with these constraints lets the encoder pursue its quality target while the model permits it. When the two conflict, the delivery constraint can take priority. A smaller buffer or lower rate leaves less room to accommodate a difficult sequence at that quality. VBV is also not a synonym for CBR . A variable-rate encode can obey a bounded-buffer model. The buffer is exactly what allows some variation in picture sizes and short-term demand. Coding buffer versus playback buffer The coding model describes a constrained decoder's coded-data supply. An app's downloaded-data buffer deals with the actual network: requests, bandwidth variation, latency, and stalls. They are related in use but are different quantities. A player can accumulate data before starting, yet still have a decoder with limits on coded-picture size, timing, or buffering. Conversely, a conforming bitstream can stall over a connection that delivers less data than it needs. For an Emby transcode whose picture becomes softer during a busy scene, bitrate and buffering constraints provide a possible causal explanation: the encoder had to reduce that scene's data demand. For a stream whose picture is fine but playback pauses, examine delivery as well. The two observations lead to different parts of the playback path.
