articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.title: What HDR Video Adds to SDR | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.keywords: What HDR Video Adds to SDR HDR video gives filmmakers more room to separate bright highlights, ordinary scene content, and dark detail. Picture a dim room with a face beside a window and a reflection on glass. In the finished image, the face should remain readable, the window should feel brighter, and the reflection can be brighter still. HDR gives the filmmaker more room to separate those light levels in one picture. A conventional SDR rendition has a smaller reference range. Its production or conversion must fit bright areas closer together, choose which differences to compress, and establish a coherent image within that range. HDR can retain more of the separation, so a reflection stands out without requiring the whole room to become bright. What changes in the picture? Part of the scene Use of the additional range Face and ordinary surfaces Can remain at a deliberately chosen comfortable level Bright window Can stay distinct from the interior Small reflection Can stand out above nearby bright surfaces Dark folds and corners Can retain useful low-level distinctions in an appropriate presentation The creative choice comes first. A night scene can remain dark, a gray day can remain muted, and a deliberately flat shot can remain low in contrast. The extra range is available room for the image, rather than an instruction to fill every shot from black to the highest supported light level. Dynamic range has its own place beside resolution and color Resolution determines how many samples describe the scene. Bit depth determines the possible numerical precision of the signal. Gamut determines its color-coordinate reach. HDR's light relationship can improve alongside those properties, but each answers a different question. For example, a 4K SDR video can contain fine spatial detail while still using an SDR light representation. A 1080p HDR picture can use a wider light range with fewer spatial samples. A ten-bit file provides more levels than an eight-bit file, while its transfer characteristic determines whether those levels describe SDR, PQ, HLG, or another representation. BT.2100 specifies HDR television image parameters. PQ and HLG establish different HDR light relationships. Delivery formats add their particular packaging and metadata conventions. Rendering HDR on displays with different ranges The source describes a produced image. A receiving display has a usable light range and color volume of its own, and the room affects the appearance. When source requests exceed the destination, tone mapping fits the picture while deciding where to retain contrast. An Emby server can deliver HDR unchanged for a compatible playback path or produce a converted rendition for the destination. Local presentation can also adapt an unchanged source to the screen. The playback method identifies server delivery, while the app's output and display mode identify the later presentation. To compare HDR results, keep the same source release and scene, then inspect ordinary objects, dark detail, and bright texture together. That evaluates how the image uses its range, rather than judging only the largest brightness number. See Also Why Tone Mapping Is Needed Luminance and Nits HDR10 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function BBC R&D: HDR television frequently asked questions

articles/video/hdr/index.html.title: Overview: High dynamic range (HDR) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/index.html.keywords: Overview: High dynamic range (HDR) HDR video represents a wider range of light and color under defined capture, mastering and presentation conventions. HDR connects what a camera records, how a programme is mastered and what the display can present. Luminance supplies the light-level vocabulary; metadata and format definitions carry additional interpretation through that path. This area establishes those relationships before tone mapping addresses a mismatch between source and output. It also keeps capture and mastering choices distinct from the capabilities of the screen showing the finished programme. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> What HDR video adds to SDR HDR video gives filmmakers more room to separate bright highlights, ordinary scene content, and dark detail. Luminance and nits A nit is one candela per square metre, a unit used to describe the luminance of displayed images. HDR capture in cameras HDR capture preserves a wide range of scene light so the final grade can retain both highlights and darker detail. HDR mastering in the studio HDR mastering establishes the finished image on a reference display and prepares it for distribution. HDR metadata and light levels HDR metadata describes mastering conditions or content light levels that can inform presentation and adaptation. HDR formats HDR formats define how an HDR signal and its associated interpretation are carried to a compatible playback path. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 SMPTE ST 2086 describes the color primaries, white point, and luminance range configured for the mastering display. A source report might contain this mastering-display record: Field Illustrative value Primaries P3 coordinates Reference white D65 Minimum luminance 0.005 nit Maximum luminance 1,000 nits SMPTE ST 2086 describes the configured color volume of the display on which the finished image was judged. Read the record as mastering context, not as a measurement of each frame. Interpret the two apparent mismatches The video uses BT.2020 primaries. That can coexist with P3 mastering primaries. The image was graded within one display's capabilities and expressed for delivery using a larger coordinate space. The two records name different stages. Correct coordinate conversion preserves the intended colors. MaxCLL is below 1,000 nits. The mastering display could support a highlight brighter than any used in the actual sequence. Content-light metadata describes that sequence under its definition, while ST 2086 records the configured display range. The numbers need not be equal. The minimum field likewise describes the mastering reference's lower luminance limit. It does not imply that every dark pixel reaches that level, or predict the black floor of the television currently showing the movie. Use the record during adaptation A renderer can use the reference volume as one input when deciding how to fit the produced image to a different output. The metadata supplies primary coordinates, white point, and luminance endpoints. It does not specify a complete transfer function or a sequence of shot-specific creative trims. During an Emby comparison, keep this source record beside the actual delivered signal and display target. A display with another volume can use tone mapping and color adaptation. The record explains the source reference; the playback path determines how that reference is used. See Also HDR Metadata MaxCLL and MaxFALL HDR Mastering in the Studio References SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: MaxCLL and MaxFALL | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: MaxCLL and MaxFALL MaxCLL and MaxFALL summarize the highest content light level and highest frame-average light level reported for a video. One small highlight and one broadly bright frame can determine different content-light fields. MaxCLL is the reported maximum content-light bound; MaxFALL is the reported maximum frame-average bound. Both use cd/m², commonly called nits. Calculate the two summaries from three simple frames Use neutral-gray pictures so component-light and luminance values coincide. The constructed sequence contains: Frame Picture contents Highest level Frame average A 1% at 1,000 nits; 99% at 10 nits 1,000 19.9 B 50% at 300 nits; 50% at 20 nits 300 160 C Entire frame at 50 nits 50 50 Frame A's average is 0.01 × 1,000 + 0.99 × 10 = 19.9. Frame B's average is 0.5 × 300 + 0.5 × 20 = 160. Using the measured maxima as the declared bounds gives MaxCLL 1,000 and MaxFALL 160 . A determines the content peak; B determines the largest frame average. No averaging across the three frames is needed to obtain MaxFALL. This explains the distinction physically. A tiny reflection can be intense while most of its frame remains dark. A broadly illuminated scene can have a lower peak while placing a larger average-light demand on the display. What the measurement definition adds for colored pictures The standardized content-light messages describe bounds for linear-light RGB component intensities. A strong colored component can consequently give a value different from true CIE luminance calculated with color-dependent weights. Production measurement methods must be interpreted with their component definitions and picture-area treatment. The neutral-gray table above deliberately avoids that distinction. For a real program, keep the measuring tool and its definition identified when comparing reported values. The field records a declared bound; it is not a live measurement made by the television during playback. Unspecified bounds and the mastering display In the standardized messages, zero indicates that the corresponding upper bound is not supplied. It does not describe a movie whose light levels are all zero. A media report can also omit fields or carry values that were not correctly measured. Mastering maximum identifies the grading display's configured range. It can exceed the program's content peak, so a 1,000-nit mastering record and a lower MaxCLL can be consistent. A tone mapper may use reported content bounds, mastering context, measured picture statistics, or a combination. When an Emby conversion changes across different source editions, recording these fields beside the exact release helps identify whether the mapper began with different source assumptions. See Also HDR Metadata Luminance and Nits Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 References Dolby: Calculating MaxFALL and MaxCLL SMPTE: HDR Imaging Ecosystem report ITU-T H.274: Content light level information

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: HDR Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: HDR Metadata HDR metadata describes the signal, mastering conditions, or content characteristics used to interpret and adapt an HDR picture. A media report can show BT.2020 primaries, PQ transfer, a 1,000-nit mastering maximum, content-light fields, and dynamic-metadata information. Those fields describe different parts of the picture's journey. Read them by role before treating them as one HDR quality score. Role Typical information What a renderer learns Signal interpretation Primaries, transfer, matrix, range What the decoded numbers mean Mastering context Display primaries, white point, luminance limits The reference volume used for judgment Content bounds MaxCLL, MaxFALL Reported light-level bounds of the produced sequence Adaptive instructions or statistics Format-specific dynamic metadata Information applicable to a shot or frame Signal interpretation is often called color signaling rather than HDR metadata in the narrower sense. It is essential because a valid compressed stream can reconstruct samples whose meaning still depends on those descriptions. Color interpretation, mastering context, and content bounds Suppose a source has BT.2020 primaries and PQ, a mastering maximum of 1,000 nits, and a reported MaxCLL of 600 nits. The first pair specifies color and light coordinates. The mastering number describes a display configuration. The content number supplies a bound for the picture under its measurement definition. A compatible app can interpret the source, read whichever metadata its rendering path supports, and adapt the produced picture to its output. A display with a different range does not have to imitate the mastering monitor's hardware; it needs an appropriate reproduction of the authored image. Some metadata is carried in codec supplemental messages; other signal descriptions can also appear in container structures. The container reader and video decoder make the needed information available to later processing. Correct packaging and interpretation are both parts of preserving it. Static and dynamic describe when information applies Static information applies to the relevant sequence or program. A mastering-display description can remain constant while the movie cuts between a dim room and a bright outdoor scene. Dynamic metadata can vary with a shot or frame. It can describe that image's brightness distribution or carry adjustments intended for a mapping target. A converter can therefore choose different parameters for scenes with different demands, while managing transitions over time. The format defines what those parameters mean. A dynamic block is not a hidden higher-resolution picture, and dynamic metadata from one format cannot simply be assigned to a different one. It needs the corresponding processing that interprets its values. The individual subjects— mastering metadata , content-light bounds , and Dolby Vision RPU —explain their particular roles. When the pixels change, their descriptions need review During Emby video transcoding , a new picture stream is created. Several possible operations have different metadata consequences: Copying the encoded video into another container can preserve its picture values, while requiring correct carriage of their descriptions. Resizing retains or changes the relevant color representation according to the processing path; spatial size alone does not select a new transfer function. HDR-to-SDR conversion changes brightness, color, and transfer representation. The output descriptions must identify that converted SDR picture. Cutting or reordering a sequence changes which pictures correspond to timed dynamic information. The metadata must still match the delivered sequence. Blindly copying a source field after processing can leave a plausible number attached to the wrong output. Conversely, dropping essential color signaling can make the destination assign another interpretation to otherwise valid samples. For a playback investigation, compare the stored source record with the stream actually delivered to the app and the output mode used for presentation. That locates the change: source information, carriage, picture conversion, or final rendering. See Also Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 MaxCLL and MaxFALL Dolby Vision RPU Metadata References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata SMPTE ST 2094-40: Dynamic metadata, Application 4 Dolby Vision: Metadata levels ITU-T H.274: Supplemental messages for coded video

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: Overview: HDR metadata and light levels HDR metadata describes mastering conditions or content light levels that can inform presentation and adaptation. A mastering display description and a report about the programme's brightest content describe different things. This group separates those signals, including ST 2086, MaxCLL and MaxFALL. Their meaning provides context for a renderer's decisions rather than one universal instruction for the screen's brightness. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> HDR metadata HDR metadata describes the signal, mastering conditions, or content characteristics used to interpret and adapt an HDR picture. Mastering display metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 SMPTE ST 2086 describes the color primaries, white point, and luminance range configured for the mastering display. MaxCLL and MaxFALL MaxCLL and MaxFALL summarize the highest content light level and highest frame-average light level reported for a video. <!-- learn-index:children:end --> References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata Dolby: Calculating MaxFALL and MaxCLL

articles/video/index.html.title: Overview: Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/index.html.keywords: Overview: Video Digital video combines picture content, timing, compression and color information that must survive the path to a display. A picture can be sharp but stretched, correctly sized but juddery, or smoothly played with the wrong brightness. Those symptoms involve different properties of video. Resolution and geometry describe the picture's shape; timing describes its motion; coding and color describe how the stored signal becomes visible. The topics below connect those properties to the work a player or Emby Server performs. HDR and tone mapping explain brightness and color adaptation, while scaling and spatial video address how pictures are reconstructed or arranged for presentation. Each branch supplies the vocabulary needed to investigate that part of the image. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How digital video represents moving pictures Digital video describes a sequence of pictures and the timing needed to display them as motion. Picture geometry Picture geometry relates stored dimensions and orientation to the shape of the image shown on screen. Frame timing and interlacing Frame timing and interlacing determine how picture samples become motion on a playback timeline. Video compression Video compression represents pictures efficiently through coding choices, prediction and constraints on the resulting stream. Video codecs Video codecs define coded-picture formats whose properties and implementation support influence playback compatibility. Encoding and picture quality Encoding quality depends on rate allocation, encoder effort and the picture changes introduced by compression. Color and pixel formats Color representation describes how picture components, sample precision and memory layouts carry a video signal. Color standards and transfer functions Color standards and transfer functions define how encoded values relate to color and light. High dynamic range (HDR) HDR video represents a wider range of light and color under defined capture, mastering and presentation conventions. Tone mapping Tone mapping adapts a source's brightness representation to the useful range and characteristics of an output. Scaling and image processing Video scaling and image processing reconstruct samples and alter picture detail for the intended presentation. Stereoscopic and spatial video Stereoscopic and spatial video carry related views that must be reconstructed and presented in the intended viewing arrangement. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Overview: Image cleanup | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Overview: Image cleanup Image-cleanup filters alter bands, noise or edge contrast through distinct processing goals. Debanding addresses visible steps in gradients, denoising addresses unwanted variation, and sharpening changes perceived edge contrast. Each operation responds to a different feature of the image. Identifying that feature first makes the filter's effect easier to judge and keeps several superficially similar “improvements” from being confused. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Debanding Debanding estimates smoother picture values where a gradient has collapsed into visible steps, while attempting to preserve genuine structure. Video denoising Video denoising estimates picture content from noisy observations using spatial or temporal evidence while deciding which variations to preserve. Video sharpening Video sharpening increases selected local picture contrast, often by adding a correction derived from a blurred version of the image. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Video Debanding | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Video Debanding Debanding estimates smoother picture values where a gradient has collapsed into visible steps, while attempting to preserve genuine structure. Original model: a 16-level background ramp, a dark line, and a patch of fine low-contrast texture. The smoothing footprint contains 25 horizontal samples. The gate uses a maximum component deviation below 0.15. This is a teaching example, not a capture from a named filter. Debanding estimates a smoother surface in regions where quantization or prior processing has produced visible steps. Its difficult decision is which variation belongs to an unwanted band boundary and which belongs to the picture's real structure. For an Emby source that already shows bands in its decoded frames, this is a different task from simply assigning a higher output bitrate. The operation needs to calculate new sample values. Color banding explains where the original plateaus can arise. An estimate from neighboring values Suppose a boundary joins a plateau at 0.4 to a plateau at 0.466667. A local mean crossing that boundary can create intermediate values. As the footprint moves across the edge, its mixture of the two plateaus changes gradually. For example, a window with fifteen samples at 0.4 and ten at 0.466667 gives approximately: (15 × 0.4 + 10 × 0.466667)/25 = 0.426667. That value was absent from either plateau. It is an estimate based on nearby information, representing one possible smoother transition. Several different original gradients could have produced the same quantized plateaus, so the operation's neighborhood and assumptions determine the constructed result. The middle image applies a horizontal local mean everywhere. It softens the bands, but also spreads the narrow dark line and changes the fine checker-like texture. The same averaging cannot know which of those changes the viewer wanted. A variation test limits where smoothing is used The third image uses the same mean only when every sample in its neighborhood is sufficiently close to the center value. In the model, the maximum difference must be below 0.15. Otherwise the original center value is retained. The dark line differs by about 0.3 from its background, so the test rejects smoothing there. A single background quantization step is about 1/15, or 0.066667, and can pass the test. The fine texture's small deviations can also pass it and be smoothed. This exposes the central tradeoff through an actual decision rule. A lower threshold preserves more variation but may leave bands. A higher threshold admits stronger smoothing and can include genuine texture. A larger neighborhood spans broader structures and reaches farther across edges. Practical debanders can compare selected neighboring positions, estimate local gradients, or use other edge-sensitive decisions. FFmpeg documents neighborhood distance, thresholds, and component handling for its debanding filters; libplacebo documents its renderer's controls. The illustrated gate is a deliberately simple independent model of that decision. Precision after the estimate The smoother estimate can contain values between the source's original codes. If it is immediately rounded back to the same coarse grid with the same correlated decisions, visible steps can return. Suitable working precision keeps the estimate available until the required output conversion. Dithering can distribute that later rounding across positions. Debanding estimates a surface; dithering controls the representation of a calculated surface on a finite value grid. They act at different parts of the process. The PNG shows the model through a finer ordinary 8-bit preview grid than its deliberately 16-level source ramp. Its smooth appearance does not claim that every real eight-bit video acquires additional original precision through filtering. A comparison needs both a gradient and detail Feature to inspect Question it answers A broad, smooth sky or wall Are the step contours less apparent? Fine low-contrast surface texture What genuine variation has been changed? A narrow contrasting line Has the decision preserved its shape? The same passage during motion Does the estimate remain stable from frame to frame? A renderer's debanding changes the displayed picture. A server-side filtered conversion also needs to encode the altered frames, and that encoding can change their newly estimated variations. Comparing the delivered frames and the final presentation keeps those effects identifiable. In the figure, the dark line survives the gated estimate while some fine texture is altered. Those two observations together describe the model's result more accurately than examining the smooth gradient alone. See Also Color Banding Video Dithering Video Bit Depth Video Denoising References FFmpeg: Debanding by neighborhood comparison FFmpeg: Gradient correction and dithering libplacebo: Debanding controls

articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Video Denoising | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Video Denoising Video denoising estimates picture content from noisy observations using spatial or temporal evidence while deciding which variations to preserve. A dim recording can show moving speckles across an otherwise plain wall. Each frame contains an observation of the wall mixed with variation from the capture and processing path. Denoising estimates the underlying picture from those observations and decides which variation to suppress. The distinction between variation and error is essential. Fine surface texture, motion, and deliberately retained film grain are also variation. An effective estimate needs evidence that distinguishes the content being preserved from the noise being reduced. Original synthetic examples. The stationary frames have independent zero-mean noise with standard deviation 0.06. The moving clean edge shifts eight source samples per frame. The figure illustrates two different averaging circumstances, not an Emby filter preset. What does averaging actually improve? Model an observed sample as value = signal + noise . If several observations contain the same signal and independent zero-mean noise, their average has the same expected signal. Their positive and negative errors partly cancel. For N equally weighted observations, noise variance becomes σ²/N , and standard deviation becomes σ/√N . With σ = 0.06 and N = 5, the expected standard deviation of the mean is approximately 0.02683 . The numerical data behind the stationary figure has observed RMS errors of approximately 0.05963 for the first noisy frame and 0.02675 for the five-frame mean, before display rounding. Those values are close to the model's expectations. The diagonal edge remains in the same place in every frame, so averaging can reduce the noise without changing the noiseless edge's position. A smaller example uses four observations of an unchanged signal near 100: 98, 103, 99, 104 . Their mean is 101 . Cancellation has reduced this example's variation, but a finite set of observations need not land exactly on the unknown signal value. More evidence improves the estimate under the model's assumptions; it does not make the particular mean automatically exact. Spatial evidence: which neighbors describe the same surface? A spatial estimate uses information within a frame. On a flat wall, nearby positions may have similar underlying values, making a local average useful. At a boundary, nearby samples may instead describe different surfaces. Take a dark region near value 40 and a bright region near 180. Averaging an equal number from each gives 110, which belongs to neither side. Applying that mixture across an edge spreads its transition. Broad averaging can also remove texture whose variation is real content. An edge-sensitive estimate can reduce contributions from positions that differ substantially from the target, or compare more of their surrounding structure before treating them as related. The similarity decision becomes as important as the average itself. A faint texture can still resemble small noise variations, which is why the chosen strength changes the character of the result. Spatial filtering supplies nearby evidence without needing other frames. Its neighborhood and similarity policy determine both the amount of noise reduction and which fine features survive. Temporal evidence: what happened to this point between frames? Temporal filtering draws evidence from different instants. The stationary example works well because the same coordinate depicts the same edge position in all five frames. During motion, that assumption changes. Imagine a fixed coordinate that receives values 40, 40, 180, 180 as an edge passes it. Their mean is 110. This is a mixture of different scene states, not merely a cleaner observation of one state. The third panel averages a moving edge without alignment. Several shifted transitions form a spread-out staircase. In real video, similar mixing can create trails behind motion, smear moving texture, or cause detail to appear and disappear as temporal history is admitted or rejected. Motion-aware processing can find source positions in other frames corresponding to the same scene feature. If a feature moved two positions right, the current coordinate and the earlier coordinate displaced two positions left can refer to that same feature. Comparing and aligning those observations gives a more appropriate basis for combination. Newly revealed regions, occlusion, scene cuts, and uncertain motion leave less reliable history. A temporal filter needs to limit, reject, or reset that history where its assumptions no longer hold. Otherwise evidence from the old picture can influence a new one. Which parts of the noise persist? The σ/√N result depends on independence and zero mean. A fixed pattern repeated in every frame does not cancel like independent fluctuations. If every observation of signal 100 carries the same +5 offset, their mean remains 105. Compression errors can also have structure and correlations. Blocking or ringing follows the coding and reconstruction process rather than the stationary independent-noise model. A filter designed for speckled variation and an operation designed for a particular structured artifact can make different decisions. Luma and chroma may have different noise characteristics. Processing them separately can reduce color speckling while preserving more luma detail, or make another chosen balance. The plane precisions, ranges, and sampling grids establish the numerical scale in which any threshold acts. Grain and fine detail need an editorial decision Film grain can be part of a work's intended presentation. Surface detail such as hair, fabric, or foliage also has fine irregular structure. Aggressive filtering may produce a smoother, less costly picture to encode while changing its intended texture. That makes preservation a content decision, not simply a maximum-noise-reduction target. A useful comparison examines a flat area, fine texture, a moving object, and a transition between scenes. Each supplies evidence about a different filtering assumption. For an Emby collection, this distinction is relevant when preparing a cleaned-up conversion of an old recording. The output should be evaluated as a version of that recording, including the texture and motion the viewer wants to retain. Why the encoded result can change again Frame-to-frame variation is less predictable than an unchanged flat surface. Reducing that variation can change the work needed by a video encoder and how it spends its data budget. At a selected bitrate, this can give other structure more room; at another rate-control mode, the encoder's resulting size can change. The result depends on the encoder, its settings, and the material. Encoding a denoised intermediate can further alter the remaining texture. Inspecting only the intermediate misses that final reconstruction. See Also Video Debanding Video Sharpening How Video Compression Works Video Compression Artifacts References FFmpeg: Spatial and temporal denoising with hqdn3d FFmpeg: Similarity-based denoising with nlmeans Dabov and colleagues: BM3D publications and author-provided examples

articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Video Sharpening | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Video Sharpening Video sharpening increases selected local picture contrast, often by adding a correction derived from a blurred version of the image. A narrow edge can appear more distinct when a processor increases the contrast immediately around it. Sharpening makes that local change. One common construction, unsharp masking , derives a correction from the difference between the original picture and a blurred copy. If I is the original value, B its blurred version, and a the amount: sharpened = I + a(I − B). The name comes from using the unsharp, or blurred, copy as a mask. Subtracting it isolates variations that the blur suppressed; adding a scaled version of that difference reinforces them. Original one-dimensional example. The blur weights are (1/4, 1/2, 1/4), amount is 0.5, and values are shown before clipping. Lines connect the discrete sample positions for readability. The correction at a black-to-white edge Take a source whose integer positions below zero are 0 and whose positions zero and above are 1. Blur each position using one quarter of the previous sample, one half of itself, and one quarter of the next. The last black position has blurred value 0.25 . Its difference I − B is −0.25. With amount 0.5, its sharpened value is: 0 + 0.5 × (0 − 0.25) = −0.125. The first white position has blurred value 0.75 and difference +0.25. Its sharpened value becomes: 1 + 0.5 × (1 − 0.75) = 1.125. Flat regions remain unchanged because their blurred values equal their originals. The operation has increased contrast near the transition, producing dark and bright overshoot around it. An appropriate output constraint can clip or limit those values, changing the final edge shape. This construction explains the appearance of a halo. It is a spatially organized correction beside an edge, rather than a uniform contrast change applied to the entire picture. Amount and neighborhood affect different features Amount scales the correction. Doubling it doubles the difference being added in this linear model. A blur neighborhood's width selects the spatial variations used to form that difference. A small neighborhood tends to emphasize narrower features. A broad blurred copy differs from the original over a wider region, so its correction can create broader outlines around objects. The mathematical blur and its radius matter as much as the amount label. Some implementations use thresholds or other constraints to avoid amplifying very small differences. Others process luma, chroma, or alpha separately. FFmpeg's unsharp documentation describes component-specific amounts and neighborhood sizes. The diagram's three-sample blur is a deliberately small worked example. Existing fine variation is reinforced too The difference I − B contains high-frequency texture and noise as well as useful edge structure. Increasing that difference can make grain more prominent, outline compression defects, or exaggerate a previously created ringing pattern. If a weak fluctuation survives in the original but is largely removed from B, its correction is close to a times that fluctuation. Adding it back increases the original variation. This is why denoising and sharpening are distinct decisions about the picture's texture, and why their order can affect a combined operation. Sharpening also depends on the grid where it runs. A neighborhood measured in source samples covers a different displayed extent after a resize. Applying the same nominal radius before and after scaling can therefore emphasize different visible feature sizes. In an Emby comparison, a server conversion and the app's presentation may each change local contrast. Inspecting the delivered frame before its display enlargement helps determine which stage supplied the visible outline. Measuring the intended change Evaluate a narrow genuine edge, fine texture, a gradient, and motion in the decoded final output. A stronger outline can increase the apparent separation of a feature while also changing neighboring values; a still frame alone can understate amplified temporal grain. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Overview: Scaling and image processing Video scaling and image processing reconstruct samples and alter picture detail for the intended presentation. Changing picture dimensions requires a rule for estimating samples. Chroma upsampling applies a related reconstruction question to color components, while cleanup operations address noise, bands or edge appearance. This branch connects the chosen filter to the detail and artifacts visible in the result. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How video scaling works Video scaling constructs a new picture grid by mapping output positions into the source and filtering the samples that contribute to each result. Chroma upsampling Chroma upsampling reconstructs color-difference values at the positions required by a fuller picture or output grid. Scaling kernels Scaling kernels define how neighboring source samples contribute to a reconstructed output sample. Scaling ringing Scaling ringing is overshoot and oscillation around picture transitions caused by the reconstruction filter's response. Spatial aliasing Spatial aliasing occurs when a sample grid represents fine picture variation as a different, often coarser pattern. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Overview: Scaling kernels | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Overview: Scaling kernels Scaling kernels define how neighboring source samples contribute to a reconstructed output sample. Nearest-neighbor, linear and higher-order filters assign different weights and neighborhoods to the reconstruction. Those choices influence sharpness, smoothing, ringing and aliasing. The individual kernel pages show the weighting and its visible consequences, making them useful comparisons for an actual scaling task. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Nearest-neighbor scaling Nearest-neighbor scaling assigns each output position the value of the closest source sample. Bilinear scaling Bilinear scaling interpolates an output value from the four neighboring source positions using linear weights on each axis. Bicubic scaling Bicubic scaling uses cubic weight functions along two axes to reconstruct output values from a wider source neighborhood. Lanczos scaling Lanczos scaling reconstructs samples with a finite windowed-sinc kernel whose radius controls the contributing neighborhood. EWA Lanczos (Jinc) EWA Lanczos uses a radial Jinc-based reconstruction footprint to combine source samples around an output position. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Bicubic Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Bicubic Video Scaling Bicubic scaling uses cubic weight functions along two axes to reconstruct output values from a wider source neighborhood. “Bicubic” describes a family of reconstruction methods. Its cubic weights can be chosen to interpolate through original samples, smooth them, or trade sharpness against overshoot. The parameters make those choices concrete. In a common separable implementation, four nearby samples contribute along each axis. A direct two-dimensional evaluation therefore combines a four-by-four neighborhood. Reusable horizontal and vertical passes can perform that calculation without evaluating sixteen independent weights from scratch for every output. The curves use the classical B,C polynomial form below. They describe weight functions, not output brightness. Output contributions are normalized for each sampling position. Two parameters change the shape One widely used cubic family has parameters B and C . B changes smoothing through the sample positions, while C shapes the outer contributions and edge behavior. Three illustrative choices are: Choice B C Raw central value K(0) in the classical form Catmull-Rom 0 0.5 1 Mitchell-Netravali 1/3 1/3 8/9 Cubic B-spline 1 0 2/3 Catmull-Rom's weights at the other integer source positions are zero, so it passes through an isolated original sample at its own coordinate. The other two choices distribute some contribution among neighboring samples even there. For an isolated unit sample surrounded by zeros, their reconstructed value at that source coordinate is respectively 1, 8/9, or 2/3 under the normalized classical weighting. This explains a visible difference between interpolation and smoothing. The B-spline-shaped curve is broad and positive. The Catmull-Rom and Mitchell curves include negative outer portions that can reinforce a transition while permitting overshoot . An Emby conversion or app renderer encountering the label bicubic needs the actual stage's implementation and parameters to reproduce its appearance. A family name alone does not select one of these three curves. Four contributions at a half-sample position Place the output at x = 0.5, between source indices 0 and 1. For Catmull-Rom, the participating indices −1, 0, 1, and 2 receive weights: Source index Example value Weight Contribution −1 0.1 −0.0625 −0.00625 0 0.3 0.5625 0.16875 1 0.8 0.5625 0.45 2 0.9 −0.0625 −0.05625 The weights total 1 and the contributions total 0.55625 . Linear interpolation of only the central pair would give 0.55. Bicubic reconstruction responds to the neighboring context as well as the pair surrounding the requested coordinate. With the Mitchell parameters, the same four weights are approximately −0.034722, 0.534722, 0.534722, −0.034722 , giving 0.553472 for these values. The difference is small for this particular smooth sequence. At an isolated feature or abrupt edge, the shapes' different central and outer contributions become more apparent. Apply a corresponding four-weight calculation on the vertical axis to obtain the two-dimensional bicubic result. The normalized product weights retain a constant field because their total is one. The mathematical reference For r equal to the absolute distance in source-sample spacings, the classical B,C function is: 0 <= r < 1: K(r) = [(12-9B-6C)r^3 + (-18+12B+6C)r^2 + (6-2B)] / 6 1 <= r < 2: K(r) = [(-B-6C)r^3 + (6B+30C)r^2 + (-12B-48C)r + (8B+24C)] / 6 r >= 2: K(r) = 0 The pieces meet continuously, with an outer support radius of two. At a fractional position, distance to each neighboring source index selects its raw weight. Dividing by the total raw weight handles the applicable finite sample set and normalization convention. The pinned libplacebo implementation scales its raw cubic function to a central value of one. That differs from the raw vertical scale plotted for B greater than zero, but multiplying all weights by the same factor cancels when their sum is used for normalization. The resulting normalized contributions in the worked examples agree. Radius, reduction, and boundaries The four-position example concerns reconstruction without a downscaling enlargement of the footprint. A reduction can require a wider source-space footprint to suppress detail beyond the output grid's sampling capacity. The scaling process explains that scale adaptation. At a picture border, some nominal neighbors lie outside the available array. Edge extension establishes their values before or during filtering. Around a high-contrast interior edge, negative weights can instead produce values beyond the local minimum or maximum. Those are different circumstances: one concerns access to the finite picture, the other the cubic function's response to the picture values. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Bilinear Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Bilinear Video Scaling Bilinear scaling interpolates an output value from the four neighboring source positions using linear weights on each axis. Source corner Value Top-left, (0, 0) 0.1 Top-right, (1, 0) 0.3 Bottom-left, (0, 1) 0.7 Bottom-right, (1, 1) 0.9 What value belongs one quarter of the way right and three quarters of the way down inside this cell? Bilinear interpolation answers by applying a linear mixture along both axes. First interpolate across each row: top = 0.75 × 0.1 + 0.25 × 0.3 = 0.15 bottom = 0.75 × 0.7 + 0.25 × 0.9 = 0.75 Then interpolate vertically: output = 0.25 × 0.15 + 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.6. The result is a smooth mixture of the surrounding values, with the closer bottom-left corner receiving the largest contribution. The four weights behind the calculation For horizontal fraction t and vertical fraction u, the four weights are (1−t)(1−u), t(1−u), (1−t)u, tu . At t = 0.25 and u = 0.75: Corner Weight Contribution Top-left 0.1875 0.01875 Top-right 0.0625 0.01875 Bottom-left 0.5625 0.39375 Bottom-right 0.1875 0.16875 The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The interpolated result therefore lies within the range of those four component values. This conventional interpolation does not create the overshoot associated with negative reconstruction weights. The one-dimensional weight function is a triangle: K(d) = max(0, 1−|d|) . Multiplying one triangle along x by another along y gives the bilinear footprint. At a source center, its value is recovered; midway between centers, contributions are shared. Smooth transitions and a spread-out narrow line In the synthetic enlargement, neighboring dark and bright source values produce intermediate gray values. The diagonal's hard pixel blocks become gradual transitions. A one-sample bright line also spreads into neighboring reconstructed positions and can have a lower peak between source centers. This is the practical character of the triangular weights: they replace abrupt sample selection with local blending. A video renderer can use that inexpensive interpolation for enlargement or chroma reconstruction. For an Emby comparison involving small text or thin lines, inspecting the same feature at the same presentation size shows how those mixtures change its apparent width and contrast. Reduction also needs its footprint adapted The four-corner calculation describes reconstruction at a position in the source grid. For a large reduction, one output position represents a much larger source area. Simply selecting four nearby corners can omit fine structures elsewhere in that area. A bilinear-based downscaler can widen its triangular filtering footprint with the reduction ratio. Its input neighborhood then covers more source samples than the basic interpolation example. The scaling walkthrough distinguishes this scale adaptation from the weight function's triangular shape. The sample values' interpretation matters too: bilinear interpolation in encoded RGB and interpolation in linear light give different mixtures. The distance weights define the spatial contribution; the processing stage determines what numerical quantity those weights are averaging. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: EWA Lanczos (Jinc) Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: EWA Lanczos (Jinc) Video Scaling EWA Lanczos uses a radial Jinc-based reconstruction footprint to combine source samples around an output position. The maps use a shared color legend. The radial example is the unsharpened libplacebo v7.360.1 EWA Lanczos construction, before phase-dependent normalization. The separable example uses Lanczos radius three on each axis. A separable filter builds its two-dimensional footprint by multiplying horizontal and vertical weights. EWA Lanczos , often called Jinc scaling , instead assigns a weight from radial distance around the requested output position. The different spatial footprint changes which neighboring directions receive the same contribution. Equal radius, equal radial weight Place the output position at the origin. Compare the continuous weight function at two offsets, A = (1, 0) and B = (1/√2, 1/√2) . Both are exactly one source spacing from the origin. This geometric comparison evaluates the function's shape, rather than choosing two simultaneous samples from one integer lattice. For a radial filter, their weights are equal because both use r = 1. For separable Lanczos3, their weights are K(1)K(0) and K(1/√2)². The first is zero because sinc(1) is zero; the second is approximately 0.106498 . In the radial construction pictured above, both positions instead have raw weight approximately 0.151279 . Thus, moving a feature's orientation can expose a different directional response even when the distances involved look similar. The maps make the cause visible. Separable multiplication creates axis-related zero lines and a rectangular support. Radial weighting produces circular bands and a circular support for this isotropic case. The Jinc function supplies a two-dimensional shape The normalized Jinc convention used here is: J(r) = 2 J₁(πr)/(πr), with J(0) = 1. J₁ is the first-order Bessel function. Its oscillation gives Jinc a positive central region followed by alternating lobes, playing a role in radial reconstruction analogous to sinc in one dimension. The first zero is at r ≈ 1.219669891 , rather than the integer zero at one for the normalized sinc convention. Jinc's function and its support geometry together therefore change the weights; a radial version is not obtained by merely replacing x with a distance in the ordinary Lanczos sinc formula. For the pinned unsharpened example, define R = 3.238315484 and Z = 1.219669891 . The raw windowed function is: W(r) = J(r) × J(Zr/R), for r < R; otherwise W(r) = 0. The first factor has three lobes inside that support, ending at its third zero. The second stretches Jinc's positive first lobe into a window that reaches zero at R. Their product is what the radial map depicts. The output is formed by evaluating those weights at contributing source positions, multiplying by their values, and dividing by the weight sum. A flat field then remains flat even as the fractional output coordinate changes the discrete set of distances and contributions. Where the ellipse in EWA comes from EWA expands to elliptical weighted average . In the broader resampling framework, an output footprint mapped into source coordinates can be elliptical, for example when its scale differs along two directions. The distance measure can then describe an ellipse rather than a circle. A simple axis-aligned elliptical coordinate uses r² = (dx/a)² + (dy/b)² . Different a and b describe the two axes; a rotated footprint adds the appropriate coordinate rotation. Samples at the same elliptical radius receive the same kernel weight. The figure uses a circular, radial case to isolate the Jinc construction. Video-rendering libraries also use EWA as a name for their polar reconstruction filters. The kernel, footprint mapping, and normalization establish the concrete operation. General EWA filtering and a particular named Jinc preset are related parts of that description. A different computation neighborhood For a fractional midpoint at (0.5, 0.5), the illustrated radius includes 32 integer-grid source positions . At an exactly aligned origin it includes 37 . The count changes with phase because a disk intersects a square sample lattice differently as its center moves. A direct separable radius-three calculation at a fractional position uses a six-by-six set, while its product structure permits reusable horizontal and vertical passes. The radial weights generally cannot be factored into those same independent passes. This affects implementation work and reuse, not just the number of points inside the footprint. Real GPU implementations can use lookup tables, texture sampling, cutoffs, and other optimizations. The counts here describe the stated mathematical support, not measured texture-fetch counts or playback speed. Negative lobes and parameter variants The blue regions of the maps are negative contributions. They can make an edge overshoot its neighboring range, just as signed separable reconstruction can. An anti-ringing stage changes the permissible result or contribution mixture, so its effect belongs alongside the chosen kernel. Named sharpened Jinc variants can alter parameters or anti-ringing behavior. The plotted weights specifically use the stated unsharpened construction. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Lanczos Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Lanczos Video Scaling Lanczos scaling reconstructs samples with a finite windowed-sinc kernel whose radius controls the contributing neighborhood. An idealized reconstruction of a regularly sampled, suitably band-limited signal uses a sinc function whose oscillating contributions extend indefinitely. A practical scaler needs a finite neighborhood. Lanczos makes that neighborhood finite by multiplying sinc by another stretched sinc window and cutting the result off at a selected radius. The resulting shape has a positive center and smaller alternating lobes. Those lobes help shape the reconstruction response, and their negative weights also explain why a strong edge can acquire ringing . Both functions have central value one. The horizontal axis is distance in source-sample spacings; the vertical axis is a raw weight before normalization at an output position. Sinc multiplied by a finite window Define sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx) , with the limiting value sinc(0) = 1. For radius a: K(x) = sinc(x) × sinc(x/a), when |x| < a; otherwise K(x) = 0. The first factor supplies the reconstruction shape. The second smoothly suppresses its outer contributions toward the selected support boundary. Radius two and radius three therefore differ in both how many neighbors can contribute and the weights inside that neighborhood. At nonzero integer distances within the radius, the first sinc factor is zero. At an exactly aligned source position, the other integer-indexed neighbors consequently contribute zero and the central sample is recovered in this idealized calculation. Fractional output positions make the other lobes participate. That is where the finite-radius choice becomes especially visible. Six weights for a midpoint At x = 0.5 with a = 3, source indices −2 through 3 form the contributing set. Evaluating the kernel and normalizing its raw sum gives: Index Distance Normalized weight −2 2.5 +0.024457 −1 1.5 −0.135870 0 0.5 +0.611413 1 0.5 +0.611413 2 1.5 −0.135870 3 2.5 +0.024457 The values are rounded here; their unrounded sum is one. A uniform source row of 0.4 therefore remains 0.4. An abrupt transition responds to the same signed contributions differently: the combination can be above a nearby bright value or below a nearby dark value. Normalizing is useful because truncating and windowing the infinite sinc reconstruction does not guarantee a raw sum of exactly one for every fractional phase. The weighted average uses the actual phase's sum to preserve a constant signal. Applying the function to a two-dimensional picture A conventional separable Lanczos scaler uses one such function horizontally and one vertically. A source position's direct contribution is the product K(dx) × K(dy) . The support is rectangular, and the filter can be implemented through reusable one-dimensional passes. EWA Lanczos uses a different, radial Jinc-based construction. Its similar name reflects a windowed-reconstruction idea; the spatial weight function is different. Its footprint page shows the distinction visually. For an Emby resize comparison, the radius and processing stage are useful context. A server conversion and the app's final presentation can each apply their own reconstruction. Examining the delivered frame separately from its display enlargement distinguishes those contributions to a fine line or edge. A reduction changes the source-space support At half width, each destination sample represents a larger input span. A properly scale-adapted radius-three filter can cover six source spacings on each side of the requested position, rather than using the enlargement footprint unchanged. This broadens the low-pass action before the coarser grid is sampled. A finite-window choice still has a frequency response rather than a perfect brick-wall cutoff, so a useful visual comparison contains both repeating fine texture and isolated edges. The texture exposes alias control ; the edge exposes the signed lobes already visible in the plotted function. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Nearest-Neighbor Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Nearest-Neighbor Video Scaling Nearest-neighbor scaling assigns each output position the value of the closest source sample. The source has only two scalar values. Nearest-neighbor retains those values and enlarges their regions; bilinear calculates intermediate values. All panels are displayed at the same inspection size. Nearest-neighbor scaling maps an output position into the source grid, selects the nearest sample, and copies its value. It makes no weighted mixture of neighboring values. That can be exactly the desired behavior for an image whose individual pixels are part of its design, such as pixel art or a diagnostic sample pattern. In an Emby app displaying such source material, the renderer's enlargement determines whether those sharp pixel regions remain distinct or become blended. Which sample is closest? For a source row (0.1, 0.5, 0.9) at positions 0, 1, and 2, a mapped output coordinate x = 0.4 selects position 0 and value 0.1 . Coordinate x = 0.6 selects position 1 and value 0.5 . Crossing the boundary at x = 0.5 changes the choice abruptly. An implementation specifies how to break an exact-distance tie and handle positions outside the source. With the illustrative rule floor(x + 0.5), a tie selects the higher index. Edge clamping restricts that index to the available array. In two dimensions, the same coordinate selection applies to rows and columns. The operation's small neighborhood makes it inexpensive, and the output uses source values directly. Why noninteger enlargement changes the block widths At a regular integer enlargement, source regions can occupy equal numbers of output columns and rows. At a noninteger factor, some must receive more output positions than others. For the center-aligned three-to-five mapping developed in the scaling walkthrough , the source coordinates are −0.2, 0.4, 1.0, 1.6, and 2.2. Nearest selection with clamped edges produces 0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.9 . The first and last source values each occupy two output positions; the middle occupies one. As an image moves or the mapping phase changes, those unequal assignments can change. A thin diagonal can acquire a different staircase shape, and a narrow line can vary in width. The blocks arise from coordinate selection rather than a change in the source's component values. A reduction can omit an entire feature If the destination is smaller, nearest-neighbor still selects one source position per result. A thin feature lying between the selected positions may contribute nothing. The alternating row 0, 1, 0, 1, ... makes this explicit: selecting every second sample can produce only zeros. Shifting the selection by one source position produces only ones. A downscaler designed to represent the average area instead filters the fine alternation before placing the new samples. That aliasing question is a consequence of the one-sample selection itself. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Spline Video Scaling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Spline Video Scaling Spline scaling reconstructs picture values with piecewise polynomial weight functions whose support and shape depend on the specified spline family. Illustrated function Support radius in source spacings Typical fractional-position samples per axis Direct two-dimensional neighborhood Spline16 2 4 4 × 4 Spline36 3 6 6 × 6 Spline64 4 8 8 × 8 These named reconstruction functions use piecewise polynomials. Their suffixes identify the conventional two-dimensional neighborhood sizes; they are not video bit depths. The figure uses their definitions from libplacebo v7.360.1. All three have central weight one and zeros at the other integer positions inside their support. Their curves differ between those positions. Increasing support adds further positive and negative contributions, so a wider spline changes the reconstruction rather than simply adding more copies of the same average. The generic label spline can also refer to other polynomial reconstruction choices. For example, a cubic B-spline shape is one member of the bicubic family , and FFmpeg documents its own natural bicubic spline scaler. A specific function name and implementation identify the coefficients needed for reproduction. Half-sample coefficients Spline16 makes a compact worked example. At output coordinate x = 0.5, indices −1, 0, 1, and 2 receive weights −0.075, 0.575, 0.575, −0.075 . For source values 0.1, 0.3, 0.8, 0.9 , the result is: −0.075 × 0.1 + 0.575 × 0.3 + 0.575 × 0.8 − 0.075 × 0.9 = 0.5575. The weights sum to one. The neighboring context shifts the result slightly from the central-pair linear average of 0.55. Around an abrupt step, the negative terms can instead create ringing . At the same phase, the wider functions have more terms: Function Normalized coefficients, from the lowest contributing index upward Spline16 −0.075000, 0.575000, 0.575000, −0.075000 Spline36 0.019737, −0.118421, 0.598684, 0.598684, −0.118421, 0.019737 Spline64 −0.005282, 0.031690, −0.126761, 0.600352, 0.600352, −0.126761, 0.031690, −0.005282 Rounded entries are shown for reading; the calculations use the full coefficients. For a flat source, each set preserves its value. For textured material, the sequence of signs and distances determines which variations are reinforced or suppressed. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Chroma Upsampling | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Chroma Upsampling Chroma upsampling reconstructs color-difference values at the positions required by a fuller picture or output grid. A 1920 × 1080 4:2:0 frame has full-size luma but only 960 × 540 samples of each color-difference component. To display a color at each final picture position, the renderer needs to reconstruct the chroma values required there. Chroma upsampling performs that reconstruction. It happens even when the displayed picture dimensions match the source luma dimensions: the chroma grids themselves still need a fuller representation. A conversion preparing RGB or 4:4:4 working values can make the same operation explicit. Four stored values, seven required positions Take a horizontal Cb signal stored at luma coordinates 0, 2, 4, 6 , with values −0.25, −0.25, +0.25, +0.25 . Assume it is constant vertically, with luma Y′ = 0.5 and Cr = 0, so the horizontal chroma decision can be isolated. The color previews use the BT.709 YCbCr matrix and ordinary RGB display in this PNG. The example illustrates component reconstruction, not a calibrated measurement of display light. At the stored positions, both illustrated methods retain the original values. Between them, their choices differ: Luma position Nearest sample choice Linear reconstruction x = 1, between two −0.25 samples −0.25 −0.25 x = 3, halfway across the color transition +0.25 with the stated upper-index tie rule 0 x = 5, between two +0.25 samples +0.25 +0.25 Linear reconstruction at x = 3 gives 0.5 × (−0.25) + 0.5 × (+0.25) = 0 . This produces a neutral chroma value at the transition, while nearest selection changes directly from one endpoint to the other. Using the example's matrix, the blue coordinate is B′ = Y′ + 1.8556 Cb . It is approximately 0.0361 for Cb = −0.25, 0.5 at the interpolated midpoint, and 0.9639 for Cb = +0.25. The green coordinate changes too, because it must preserve the specified luma relation. Reconstruction supplies a complete RGB mixture at that intermediate position. Correct coordinates come before filter choice The example placed its chroma at specified luma coordinates. A centered grid would put its samples half a luma spacing farther right. The same array values would then be interpolated with a different fraction at each luma position. Chroma sample location describes that phase. A stronger or wider filter cannot repair a coordinate interpretation that systematically places the color transition in the wrong location. In a two-dimensional 4:2:0 picture, both horizontal and vertical reconstruction matter. Interlaced sources also require the correct field geometry; combining chroma from different motion instants as if it were one progressive grid can change moving edges. Those geometry decisions establish which samples a reconstruction stage should combine. The working grid and the displayed grid A renderer can first build full-resolution chroma aligned with luma, then convert to RGB and resize the resulting picture. Another implementation can map the final output coordinates directly into each source plane, combining chroma upsampling and picture scaling in one processing stage. Both approaches need the same essential information: source plane dimensions, sample locations, output geometry, and suitable reconstruction weights. A separate luma and chroma filter choice is possible because each plane has different source spacing. In an Emby playback comparison, that helps distinguish a general soft picture from color-specific edge behavior. Fine white text against black tests luma structure strongly. Fine color transitions at similar luma make the chroma reconstruction more visible. The same material can look different if the app and a server-converted route reconstruct its planes differently. A denser representation for subsequent processing The reconstructed grid gives an overlay or color operation component values at the positions it needs. New subtitle artwork can then contribute sharp color structure at those positions. If the finished picture is later encoded as 4:2:0, the combined chroma enters a new reduction stage. That sequence explains why the input chroma density, the working density, and the encoded output density can all differ. Upsampling estimates the values between surviving source samples; compositing adds new information; the final encoder determines how densely their combined color structure is represented. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: How Video Scaling Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: How Video Scaling Works Video scaling constructs a new picture grid by mapping output positions into the source and filtering the samples that contribute to each result. A 1920 × 1080 movie shown across a 1280 × 720 picture area needs a new set of samples. A player cannot obtain that grid by changing the resolution label. It must calculate which source information contributes to each of the 1280 × 720 output positions. Video scaling is that calculation. It occurs during display, during a saved conversion, or inside a server's video processing path. An Emby session can contain more than one such operation: the server may create a smaller encoded picture, and the app may then fit that picture to its display area. The important decisions are the output grid, the source coordinates it maps to, and the filter used to construct its samples. Those decisions explain both a good resize and familiar defects such as a softened line, a bright halo, or false patterns in fine texture. A new position between old samples Take a single row with three scalar values: 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 . Place their centers at coordinates 0, 1, and 2. We want five output samples spanning the same picture extent. This is a scalar-signal example with linear interpolation and clamped edges. It establishes the coordinate and weighting calculation; color and light interpretation are considered below. One common center-aligned mapping is: source x = (output j + 0.5) × source width/output width − 0.5. The half terms refer to sample centers rather than frame borders. For widths 3 and 5, output indices 0 through 4 map to −0.2, 0.4, 1.0, 1.6, 2.2 . An interior output at x = 0.4 lies 40% of the way between source samples 0 and 1. With linear interpolation, its value is: 0.6 × 0.1 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.26. At x = 1.6, the corresponding calculation is 0.4 × 0.5 + 0.6 × 0.9 = 0.74 . At x = 1, the original middle sample is recovered. The remaining positions require an edge policy because their coordinates extend beyond the first and last sample centers. For this example, clamping means treating values beyond the sample array as repetitions of the nearest edge sample. The completed row is 0.1, 0.26, 0.5, 0.74, 0.9 . Other coordinate conventions or edge policies can produce different results, so an implementation's complete mapping matters. A filter assigns the contributions Linear interpolation uses the two adjacent samples in a row. A wider reconstruction filter can also use samples farther away. Its kernel is a function that assigns a weight according to distance from the desired output coordinate. For a scalar row, write the calculation as: output(x) = Σ weight(j, x) × source(j). The weights normally sum to one. If every participating source sample equals 0.4, the result is then 0.4 × Σ weight = 0.4 , preserving a constant field. Normalization becomes particularly useful when the chosen phase or a finite window changes the raw weight sum. Some kernels use only positive contributions. Others include negative contributions to shape their frequency response. That can retain a stronger transition at an edge, while also allowing the reconstructed value to go outside the neighboring sample range. Ringing works through that effect numerically. The individual kernel pages explain their mechanisms: nearest-neighbor selects a sample; bilinear interpolates neighboring samples; bicubic , Lanczos , EWA Lanczos , and spline use wider or differently shaped contributions. Extending the calculation to a picture A separable filter applies a one-dimensional weighting along each axis. It can first construct horizontally filtered rows, then filter those intermediate results vertically. The product of the horizontal and vertical weights describes the contribution from each source position in the neighborhood. A radial or polar filter instead assigns weights from two-dimensional distance. Its footprint need not factor into those two independent passes. The EWA example shows why an axis-aligned neighbor and a diagonal neighbor at the same radius can receive equal radial weights but different separable weights. The source also has multiple component grids. In 4:2:0 video , luma is full size while each chroma component has half the width and height. A stage needs to map each grid correctly, including chroma sample location . It may combine chroma reconstruction with picture resizing rather than making two separate full-size intermediate pictures. That distinction explains why “the scaler” can process luma and chroma differently. The planes have different source dimensions and may have different reconstruction settings, even when they contribute to the same final RGB picture. Shrinking requires a wider view of the source Upscaling asks for more output positions across the same image. Downscaling also asks the result to represent a larger source area with each output sample. Fine changes that fit between the source's samples may be too fine for the new grid. Consider a row alternating between 0 and 1 at every source position. Keep only every second sample and the output becomes all zero or all one, depending on phase. The original row had a balanced average, but the reduced result can acquire a uniform dark or bright bias. For that particular two-to-one reduction, averaging each pair gives 0.5 at every output position. It removes the alternation that the coarser grid cannot reliably represent. A general downscaler uses a suitable low-pass footprint before or as part of sampling the output, controlling more complicated high-frequency structure too. For a reduction factor s below one, a scale-adapted kernel can widen its source-space support by 1/s . At half width, a radius-three footprint can extend six source spacings rather than three. More source samples contribute to each destination value, reflecting the greater area represented there. This is the reason that applying an upscaling-style neighborhood unchanged while discarding most positions can produce spatial aliasing . It is also why a label such as bilinear or Lanczos needs its downscaling behavior considered along with the kernel formula. Footprint adaptation, implementation limits, and the reduction ratio affect the result. Which values are being averaged? Encoded RGB values and linear-light RGB values do not have the same arithmetic meaning. A renderer averaging encoded coordinates performs a different operation from one that first recovers light-proportional values and averages those. With a deliberately simple transfer model light = encoded value² , averaging encoded black 0 and white 1 gives code 0.5, which represents light 0.25. Averaging their light gives 0.5, requiring code √0.5 ≈ 0.707 . The model is an illustration, not the BT.709 or sRGB transfer formula. This difference matters near contrasting edges and small bright features. It belongs to the processing stage's color policy as well as its distance weights. RGB video explains the component interpretation, and color signaling identifies the fields that establish it. Calculations may also need more precision than the final stored output. An interpolated value can fall between integer source or destination codes. Keeping sufficient working precision postpones the final rounding; dithering can distribute that output rounding where appropriate. Geometry, filtering, and encoding are separate choices Resizing dimensions should agree with the intended display shape. A 1440 × 1080 anamorphic source with pixel aspect ratio 4:3 can be resampled to 1920 × 1080 square pixels. That is a change in sample grid and pixel aspect information describing the same 16:9 composition. Cropping removes part of the image extent. Padding adds border area. Scaling resamples the selected extent. These can be combined to fit a target rectangle, but changing the dimensions without deciding which extent and aspect to preserve can distort the composition. For a compressed output file, the newly calculated frame then needs encoding. That introduces another set of decisions about precision, chroma sampling, and the preservation of subtle detail. A soft result can originate in the resize, the encode, or a later display resize. The output dimensions identify a grid, not all the operations used to produce it. Accounting for a complete playback route Suppose a source is 3840 × 2160, the server creates 1920 × 1080 video, and the app presents it at 1280 × 720. The server's first reduction and the renderer's second reduction each make filtering and sampling choices. The final result need not equal a single direct 3840-to-1280 operation. For an Emby comparison, record the source dimensions and pixel aspect, the delivered stream's dimensions and sample format, and the app's actual picture area. A kernel name from one conversion stage describes that stage. It does not identify the display's later filtering. Then inspect the feature that prompted the comparison. A fine repeating texture tests the reduction's alias control; an isolated edge exposes overshoot; colored text exposes chroma reconstruction; a gradient exposes precision and output rounding. Those observations connect a visible difference to the particular calculation that made it. articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Scaling Ringing | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Scaling Ringing Scaling ringing is overshoot and oscillation around picture transitions caused by the reconstruction filter's response. Integer source positions below zero contain 0; positions zero and above contain 1. The curves use normalized weights with no anti-ringing or output clipping. Catmull-Rom uses B = 0, C = 0.5; Lanczos has radius three. A reconstructed edge can have a dark dip before its transition and a bright overshoot after it. In a picture, that response can appear as narrow dark and light outlines. Scaling ringing is the filter's oscillating response around the transition. The source need not contain those outlines. Its samples in this example contain only zero and one. The signed reconstruction weights create the intermediate overshoot. Negative contributions create a value below black At x = −1.5, Catmull-Rom combines source indices −3, −2, −1, and 0 with weights −0.0625, 0.5625, 0.5625, −0.0625 . The first three source values are zero, while index 0 is one: output = 0 + 0 + 0 − 0.0625 × 1 = −0.0625. At x = 0.5, three contributing positions are on the white side and one on the black side. Their combination gives 1.0625 , above the neighboring maximum of one. Those values follow directly from a useful general distinction. Positive weights summing to one produce a mixture within the source neighborhood's range. Signed weights summing to one preserve a flat field, but a transition can make the positive and negative contributions cancel differently. The result can lie outside that range. The bicubic coefficient example develops these weights; the Lanczos function shows another signed-lobe construction. Their plots describe the cause of their different edge responses. Clipping and anti-ringing change the response Clipping the example to [0, 1] makes both the negative dip and the excess above one hit an endpoint. It changes the displayed response but does not change the kernel that produced it. In another signal interval, overshoot can remain inside the available output codes and still appear as a visible outline around the local transition. Anti-ringing processing can constrain a reconstruction relative to neighboring values or mix it with a more limited result. Its neighborhood, strength, and implementation establish what is constrained. Restricting the range can also alter thin bright features or the shape of an edge. The relevant comparison is therefore the final response of kernel plus its constraints . The raw function alone explains a potential overshoot; the complete reconstruction determines how much survives. Which stage produced the outline? An Emby session can show an outline already present in the encoded source, introduced during a server resize, or introduced when the app fits the delivered frame to its display area. Compression artifacts and sharpening can produce related edge patterns through other operations. Comparison What it isolates Decoded source versus decoded converted output Changes introduced before output encoding or by that encoding Same decoded output at different presentation sizes Changes introduced by the presentation path Flat edge versus fine repeating texture Edge overshoot versus an aliasing pattern A narrow outline tied to an edge is useful evidence about edge response. A broad wave pattern in repeating detail instead suggests examining spatial aliasing .
