articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.title: Spatial Aliasing in Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/scaling-image-processing/.keywords: Spatial Aliasing in Video Spatial aliasing occurs when a sample grid represents fine picture variation as a different, often coarser pattern. A fine fence, striped shirt, or tiled roof can acquire a broad wave pattern when a video is reduced. The resulting waves are not merely a blur of the original texture. The coarser sample grid has represented its fine variation as a different pattern: spatial aliasing . An Emby app resizing a frame to its viewport and a server producing a smaller encoded frame both encounter this sampling problem. It can also arise earlier, during camera sampling or previous conversions. Locating the grid reduction helps locate the cause of the visible pattern. Two signals with the same retained samples Consider the normalized scalar signal: high(x) = 0.5 + 0.4 cos(2π × 0.4x). It has 0.4 cycles per original sample spacing. Its variation can be represented on the original unit-spaced grid, whose Nyquist limit is 0.5 cycles per spacing. Now retain only samples at x = 2m , where m is an integer. The new grid has half the spatial sampling rate. Its Nyquist limit, expressed in original coordinates, is 0.25 cycles per original spacing . Our 0.4-cycle variation is above that limit. The black dots are samples retained at every second original position. Both curves pass through those dots. This isolates sampling ambiguity rather than simulating a particular scaler. A second signal is: low(x) = 0.5 + 0.4 cos(2π × 0.1x). At the retained positions, both produce the same values: m Source position 2m high(2m) and low(2m) 0 0 0.9 1 2 0.623607 2 4 0.176393 3 6 0.176393 4 8 0.623607 5 10 0.9 For high, the phase per output index is 0.8 cycles. On an integer-indexed grid, that cosine is equivalent to a −0.2-cycle cosine; cosine's even symmetry makes it the +0.2-cycle pattern. Low produces exactly +0.2 cycles per output index too. The output samples therefore support an apparent period of five output spacings , even though the original fine signal varied at a different frequency. A reconstruction stage given only those samples cannot choose uniquely between the two candidate sources. Filtering before the grid becomes coarser A downscaler suppresses variation that the destination cannot represent before placing the coarser samples. A wider low-pass footprint uses more of the source area associated with each destination value. The alternating row 0, 1, 0, 1, ... provides a compact special case. Taking every second point gives a uniform 0 or 1 depending on phase. Averaging each corresponding pair gives 0.5, removing that alternation before reducing the sample count. General textures need more than that particular pair-average example. A finite filter has a frequency response with a transition region rather than an ideal sharp cutoff. The reduction ratio, footprint width, and permitted work determine how much unwanted high-frequency structure reaches the output. Interpolating more smoothly after the coarse samples have acquired the five-spacing pattern cannot determine that the original was the high curve. The ambiguity was created at sampling. It needs to be controlled at that boundary. Why the pattern changes during motion Fine structure can move by a fraction of a source spacing from frame to frame. That changes which parts of it land on the output sampling positions. An aliased texture can consequently shimmer, change apparent orientation, or produce crawling patterns during a pan. The temporal change comes from repeated spatial decisions at different phases. A frozen frame shows one phase; the sequence makes the instability more obvious. Comparing a fence throughout a slow pan can therefore reveal aliasing that a single screenshot understates. Two-dimensional sampling extends the same ambiguity to lines and grids in different directions. Their interference with the picture's sampling lattice can form moiré. Chroma has a separate, often coarser lattice, so chroma reduction can introduce color-specific aliasing even when luma structure is retained. Aliasing, ringing, and missing detail Loss of very fine detail after a reduction can be the intended low-pass result. Aliasing instead creates a misleading surviving pattern. Ringing is an oscillating edge response and can be present without a repeating source texture. These distinctions help interpret what a comparison is testing. For the plotted example, a suitable reduction must control the 0.4-cycle variation relative to the new 0.25-cycle limit. Retaining it unfiltered makes the 0.1-cycle candidate indistinguishable at the output samples, producing the apparent five-sample period calculated above. articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.title: Overview: Frame packing layouts | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.keywords: Overview: Frame packing layouts Frame-packing layouts arrange left and right views so a receiving system can separate and present them. Side-by-side and top-and-bottom layouts place views within a combined picture, while frame-packed presentation uses another defined arrangement. A receiving system needs to know the layout to assign the views correctly. The pages below illustrate those structures and the resolution or presentation consequences of each. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Side-by-side 3D Side-by-side 3D places the two eye views in adjacent horizontal regions of one video frame. Top-and-bottom 3D Top-and-bottom 3D stores the two eye views in vertically stacked regions of a conventional video frame. Frame-packed 3D HDMI frame packing transports two full stereoscopic views within a defined paired video timing. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.title: Frame-Packed 3D Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.keywords: Frame-Packed 3D Video HDMI frame packing transports two full stereoscopic views within a defined paired video timing. A 3D movie can be stored using MVC and sent to a television using HDMI frame packing . The first describes compressed view data; the second describes how reconstructed views travel over the display connection. The two labels identify different stages of one playback route. The phrase frame packing also has a broad use for placing two views into one image, including side-by-side and top-and-bottom arrangements. This article develops the specific HDMI frame-packing structure commonly meant by a frame-packed 3D output . Two full views and a timing interval In the nominal 1080p24 example, each eye receives a 1920 × 1080 view. The defined packed active region includes one full view, an intervening 45-row active-space interval, and the other full view: 1080 + 45 + 1080 = 2205 rows. The pictured order is left then right. The diagram concerns the display-link structure, with the interval drawn to scale relative to the two view rectangles. The link's full timing also includes blanking outside the pictured active region. For the nominal example, the total is 2750 sample periods per line and 2250 rows , at a pixel clock of 148.5 MHz . The paired-picture rate is consequently: 148,500,000 / (2750 × 2250) = 24 pairs per second. Each eye gets 24 distinct scene pictures per second. The two full views increase the transported information for each scene instant; they do not make the movie's motion 48 frames per second per eye. The fractional-rate counterpart uses its corresponding timing. Linux's display-mode helper makes the timing relationship visible: for the frame-packing flag, it doubles the pixel clock and total vertical timing, while adding the original vertical total to the active height. A 1080-line picture with an original 1125-row total therefore becomes 1080 + 1125 = 2205 active-region rows and a 2250-row total. The player has to construct the output The source decoder first makes the two required views available. They can originate from MVC , MV-HEVC , or a packed source that has been unpacked. The output stage then places the reconstructed views into the required timing and supplies the 3D signaling expected by the link and display. An Emby investigation should therefore identify both the source representation and the app's output path. Showing a compatible base view from an MVC source establishes one reconstruction result. Transporting the complete stereo pair requires the additional view and an output method capable of presenting it. The connection chain matters too. The source, intervening receiver or other device, and display need to handle the selected 3D timing and signaling. The file's extension cannot establish those link capabilities. A tall coded picture is a separate representation A full top-and-bottom file with two 1920 × 1080 regions can use a 1920 × 2160 coded raster. Its views meet at row 1080 with no intervening 45-row space in that simple arrangement. The pictured HDMI active region has height 2205. Its second view begins after the first view and the 45-row interval, at row 1125 . Those different boundaries matter to any operation extracting the two views. Encoding a tall combined picture as ordinary video causes its decoder to reconstruct that picture grid. A display-link stage still needs to supply the applicable timing and stereo signaling. Top-and-bottom unpacking and the construction of an HDMI output describe the respective operations. Reading the names in a playback trace Description Stage it identifies MVC Multiview H.264 coding of source views MV-HEVC Multiview HEVC coding of source views Side-by-side or top-and-bottom Spatial placement of views in a picture HDMI frame packing Paired display-link timing and 3D signaling See Also How Stereoscopic Video Works Top-and-Bottom 3D Video Multiview Video Coding (MVC) MV-HEVC and Spatial Video References HDMI Licensing Administrator: HDMI 1.4b and 3D formats Linux v6.17: Frame-packing display-timing adjustment Linux v6.17: Standard HDMI/CTA timing tables FFmpeg: Stereo picture arrangements

articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.title: Side-by-Side 3D Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.keywords: Side-by-Side 3D Video Side-by-side 3D places the two eye views in adjacent horizontal regions of one video frame. Left-first example: a 1920 × 1080 packed frame holds two 960 × 1080 regions. The pictured output expands one region into a 1920 × 1080 grid. Diagram panels use different inspection scales. Side-by-side , or SBS , stores the two views next to each other inside a conventional frame. An ordinary decoder can recover that combined raster. Stereoscopic presentation then extracts its left and right regions and assigns them to the intended eyes. This explains an Emby playback result that shows two narrow pictures beside each other: the packed image has been decoded, while the view-unpacking and stereoscopic presentation have not been applied on that route. Half width and full width For a target view shape of 1920 × 1080 square pixels: Layout Combined coded frame Stored region for each eye Half SBS 1920 × 1080 960 × 1080 Full SBS 3840 × 1080 1920 × 1080 Half SBS retains the usual overall frame dimensions by giving each view half the horizontal sample count. Its region is 8:9 as a raw square-pixel rectangle; presenting that region as the intended 16:9 view expands the width by two. The reconstruction uses video scaling or an equivalent display mapping to produce the required output positions. The scene's intended shape is restored, while its horizontal detail still originates from the 960 stored columns. Full SBS instead supplies 1920 stored columns for each eye. The combined luma counts are 2,073,600 for half SBS and 4,147,200 for full SBS in these examples. Compressed size also depends on coding and content; those numbers describe the picture grids. Extracting the correct columns For a packed frame of even width W and height H, the first region uses columns 0 through W/2−1 . The second uses W/2 through W−1 . Each covers all H rows. For the 1920-wide example, the regions are 0–959 and 960–1919. Extracting the first region gives a 960 × 1080 image. Correct shape reconstruction is a further operation; copying that crop to a square-pixel output without the intended mapping produces a narrow picture. Left-first storage associates the first region with the left eye. Right-first storage reverses that association. Swapping the eye assignments changes the stereo disparity sign, even though the same two regions remain present. The Matroska registry distinguishes left-first SBS with StereoMode 1 and right-first SBS with 11 . Its specification also separates the combined raw pixel dimensions from the display dimensions of one view: a full SBS track can have PixelWidth 3840 and per-view DisplayWidth 1920. Those fields describe compatible parts of one representation. Preserving or converting the arrangement A compatible stream copy can retain the encoded packed picture. Repackaging also needs the relevant stereo interpretation retained in the destination's description. Emby's 3D naming documentation covers the library identifiers for half and full SBS; the file's region order and view geometry still establish what the renderer should do. A converter can unpack both views, process them, and encode another stereo arrangement. It can also select one region to make a 2D version. For half SBS, that selected view needs its intended display shape handled as part of the conversion. If a half-SBS combined frame is reduced to 1280 × 720 while preserving its layout, its two regions become 640 × 720 . Their intended 16:9 presentation can expand each to 1280 × 720. Accounting for both the combined width and the per-view width makes the retained horizontal sample count clear. articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.title: Top-and-Bottom 3D Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/fram.keywords: Top-and-Bottom 3D Video Top-and-bottom 3D stores the two eye views in vertically stacked regions of a conventional video frame. Layout for intended 1920 × 1080 views Combined coded frame Stored region for each eye Half top-and-bottom 1920 × 1080 1920 × 540 Full top-and-bottom 1920 × 2160 1920 × 1080 Top-and-bottom , also called above-below or over-under , places the two eye pictures in stacked regions. The top region and the bottom region represent separate views of the same instant. The half-height form keeps a conventional overall frame size. Each view has the full horizontal sample count and half the vertical count. Its raw square-pixel shape is 32:9; restoring the intended 16:9 shape requires doubling its displayed height. Left-eye-on-top example. The 1920 × 540 crop is reconstructed into a 1920 × 1080 output grid. Diagram panels use different inspection scales. Rows, view order, and display shape For an even height H, the top region occupies rows 0 through H/2−1 ; the bottom occupies H/2 through H−1 . Both use the full frame width. For H = 1080, this means rows 0–539 and 540–1079. A crop operation identifies the region, while scaling or an equivalent display mapping supplies the additional output positions needed for its intended height. The reduced vertical sampling affects horizontal edges and fine vertical variation. A 1920 × 540 region and a 960 × 1080 half-SBS region contain the same 1,036,800 luma positions , allocated differently across the two directions. This is a spatial sampling distinction, rather than a difference in how many eye views are supplied. Eye order is explicit information. In Matroska, StereoMode 3 means left eye first in the top region; 2 means right eye first. The name top-and-bottom alone does not establish that assignment. What an ordinary playback path shows A conventional decoder recovers the combined raster. If the app presents it as one 2D image, both views appear stacked and vertically compressed in the half-height form. For an Emby session, the 3D identification information describes the stored layout. The app/output path needs to use that information to separate the regions, restore their geometry, and send each to the correct eye. A frame copied unchanged through a server route can therefore retain both views as pixels while the final presentation still shows the combined rectangle. The separator belongs to the specified layout These simple top-and-bottom examples split the coded image directly at half its height. HDMI frame packing uses an output timing structure with full views and an intervening active-space interval. Its familiar 1080p24 arrangement contains 1080 + 45 + 1080 rows, so cutting it at the halfway row is a different extraction from the one above. For a top-and-bottom file being converted to another layout, preserve both view regions and their same-instant pairing. For a 2D conversion, select the desired region and restore its view shape. The row ranges and per-view dimensions provide the concrete input geometry for either operation. articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/inde.title: Overview: Stereoscopic and spatial video | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/inde.keywords: Overview: Stereoscopic and spatial video Stereoscopic and spatial video carry related views that must be reconstructed and presented in the intended viewing arrangement. Depth-oriented video needs more than one ordinary flat picture. The stored views and their arrangement determine what a compatible decoder and display have to produce. This area connects that viewing model to frame packing, multiview coding and spatial-video representations. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> How stereoscopic video works Stereoscopic video presents related views to the left and right eyes so their differences supply a binocular depth cue. Frame packing layouts Frame-packing layouts arrange left and right views so a receiving system can separate and present them. Multiview Video Coding (MVC) MVC extends H.264/AVC to encode related camera views with temporal and inter-view prediction while retaining an AVC-compatible base view. MV-HEVC and spatial video MV-HEVC represents related views in HEVC layers, while a spatial video profile adds the geometry and presentation information needed to interpret a stereo pair. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.title: Multiview Video Coding (MVC) | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.keywords: Multiview Video Coding (MVC) MVC extends H.264/AVC to encode related camera views with temporal and inter-view prediction while retaining an AVC-compatible base view. The left and right pictures of a stereo pair often contain much of the same scene. Encoding them entirely independently repeats some of that information. Multiview Video Coding , or MVC , extends H.264/AVC so a view can use reconstructed information from another view as a prediction reference. The representation retains an AVC-compatible base view . An additional view can use both its own temporal references and permitted references from other views. For a stereo movie, those two reconstructed viewpoints supply the eye pair; MVC's general multiview tools also cover representations with more than two views. MVC is used by Blu-ray 3D. Its role is to reconstruct the views from compressed data. HDMI frame packing describes a possible subsequent display output, after the views have been recovered. Prediction across time and across viewpoints Ordinary H.264 prediction can use previously reconstructed reference pictures to predict a new block. A temporal prediction describes how scene content changes across instants. Inter-view prediction instead uses another camera's reconstructed picture. Corresponding scene regions appear at different image positions because of camera geometry, so locating the prediction can include a displacement between the viewpoints. The encoder still needs to describe changes that the reference cannot predict. A and B identify views in this chosen reference structure. The blue arrows use a reconstructed base-view picture for the additional view at the corresponding instant. Actual references and picture types are described by the bitstream. Using a reference does not replace the additional view with a duplicate of the base. It provides a starting estimate, which the decoder corrects to produce the additional viewpoint. Reconstructing one small predicted block Take a toy decoded base-view sample row: 10, 20, 50, 80, 90, 100. Suppose the signaled correspondence selects the four-position prediction 20, 50, 80, 90 for a block in the additional view. After the codec's residual reconstruction, let its decoded corrections be 0, −5, +2, +5 . Position Prediction Decoded correction Reconstructed additional-view value 0 20 0 20 1 50 −5 45 2 80 +2 82 3 90 +5 95 The new block becomes 20, 45, 82, 95 . Both the selected reference and the correction matter. The correction alone is not a complete eye picture, and the base block alone is not the intended other viewpoint. This arithmetic isolates decoded sample reconstruction. The compressed syntax can describe prediction modes, reference choices, displacement, transforms, and quantized corrections; it does not simply store the four raw numbers in the table. At occlusions, one camera sees regions hidden from another. Those regions need information beyond the corresponding base samples. The encoder can select other permitted predictions or supply the necessary coded correction. This is why similar views create a compression opportunity without making one viewpoint fully determined by the other. Why an ordinary AVC path can show a 2D movie The base-view portion is designed for compatible single-view AVC decoding. A suitable non-MVC decoder can reconstruct that view without performing the additional multiview reconstruction. Its output can therefore look like a normal 2D movie rather than a side-by-side frame. An MVC-aware decoder recovers the requested view set while honoring its dependencies. If the additional view references the base, extracting its coded data does not make it independently decodable. The relevant base reference content and configuration remain part of the required reconstruction. Base-view compatibility is also distinct from which eye is intended for that view. The stream's view description and stereo association establish eye identity. A default 2D presentation of the base and a correctly assigned stereo pair are different outputs from related source data. For an Emby session, 3D identification describes the source category in the library. The practical playback trace then asks which view data reached the decoder, which views were reconstructed, and how the app presented them. A clear single image, a decoded two-view pair, and a correctly signaled 3D output each establish a different stage of that trace. Seeking needs the relevant reference history A seek to a presentation time may require earlier reference pictures in one or both view timelines. The decoder has to establish the state needed by the requested pictures, including applicable references between views. The GOP and reference discussion explains why presentation order alone does not describe that state. MVC adds view relationships to the temporal dependency problem. A random-access point and the source's signaled dependencies determine where a complete requested pair can be reconstructed reliably. A conversion makes an explicit view choice Once both views are reconstructed, a converter can encode side-by-side or top-and-bottom output. It chooses the per-view resolution, frame arrangement, eye order, and output coding. A half-width packed output has a different sample allocation from the full-resolution views used as its input. A 2D conversion instead selects a single reconstructed view and encodes or otherwise delivers that version. Repackaging the MVC-coded material can preserve its coding dependencies, but it does not turn it into an ordinary independent two-track movie without changing the representation. articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.title: MV-HEVC and Spatial Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.keywords: MV-HEVC and Spatial Video MV-HEVC represents related views in HEVC layers, while a spatial video profile adds the geometry and presentation information needed to interpret a stereo pair. An inspection report can show one HEVC video track, 1920 × 1080 , while a supporting reader reconstructs two 1920 × 1080 eye pictures from each presentation sample. The source is not necessarily a side-by-side rectangle: Multiview HEVC , or MV-HEVC , can place the related views in codec layers within the same track. The codec reconstructs those viewpoints. A spatial-video description also supplies information about capture geometry and presentation. Reading a complete file therefore involves its layers, eye association, timing, and applicable movie-profile metadata. From layer data to a pair of pictures MV-HEVC uses the multilayer and multiview tools of HEVC . A compatible base view can be coded using ordinary HEVC tools. The additional view uses multiview coding, including permitted prediction from another reconstructed view. Apple's published HEVC Stereo Video Interoperability Profile v0.9 beta describes a focused two-view carriage in one MPEG-4 or QuickTime video track. Its base view is Main or Main10, and the corresponding additional view uses Multiview Main or Multiview Main10. Both have matching sample dimensions and precision in that profile. The profile's sample entry uses hvc1 , with hvcC supplying the primary decoder configuration and lhvC the additional-layer configuration. Each media sample contains the two view components for the same presentation instant. The track's 1920 × 1080 description in our example applies to a view; it does not mean the two pictures have been reduced to 960-pixel-wide halves. The arrow denotes a prediction dependency on the reconstructed base. The numerical IDs are a permitted illustrative mapping, not a claim that every file uses them. The base view can be the right eye The base layer has layer ID 0. That coding role is independent of whether its picture belongs to the left or right eye. The published interoperability profile allows either eye to be primary. In the illustration, the stream describes: Coding role Layer ID View ID Eye assignment Base 0 7 Right Additional 1 4 Left The Video Parameter Set establishes the connection from layers to view identities; stereo reference-display information identifies which view is for each eye. The reader follows that connection. Replacing it with the assumption “layer zero means left” would swap this example's presentation. Apple's conversion sample chooses the simpler IDs 0 and 1 with left first. Its layer-ID list, view-ID list, and left/right association list are separate configuration properties even when their chosen numbers happen to match. Requesting and returning the required views A decoder interface may require the caller to request the multiview layer set. A path that requests or exposes only the compatible base can produce a normal single-view image; a stereo path needs both requested views and their dependencies. Apple's multiview-reading workflow returns related image buffers with tags identifying their layer and stereo-eye roles. The application can then route the left-tagged picture to the left eye and the right-tagged picture to the right. Array position or the smallest numeric ID should not substitute for that role. The two buffers share the intended presentation time. Their decode work can depend on reference state and other reconstructed views, but they belong to one stereo instant. Pairing buffers from different instants would introduce the motion-related disparity error described in the stereoscopic walkthrough . Two full decoded pictures also imply two picture buffers at that instant. For an unpadded 10-bit 4:2:0 representation stored as P010 , two 1920 × 1080 views contain 2 × 6,220,800 = 12,441,600 active sample bytes . Alignment, hardware layout, and reference history can add storage. This arithmetic describes decoded samples, not the compressed file size. Geometry metadata completes the spatial description Apple's Movie Profiles v0.9 beta , published in June 2025, distinguishes stereo 3D delivery from its Spatial Video Profile. The latter adds a specific geometry and presentation description to the MV-HEVC stereo track. Property Meaning for the representation Camera baseline Separation between the camera optical centers Horizontal field of view Angular extent represented by the captured image Disparity adjustment An alignment adjustment for the stereoscopic presentation Projection Mapping from image coordinates to the intended viewing geometry Optional hero-eye preference A preferred view for an applicable single-view presentation In that published profile, the Video Extended Usage description contains eye, camera, and presentation information, and the sample entry carries horizontal field-of-view information. The linked specification identifies the required boxes and constraints for that version. Baseline and field of view describe different aspects of capture. The former affects the viewpoints' separation; the latter affects how image position relates to angle. Disparity adjustment changes presentation alignment. The capture and display calculations show why those roles should not be combined into a single generic “depth” value. A hero-eye preference likewise describes presentation. It does not change the codec's dependency structure or turn an additional predicted layer into an independently coded base. Converting a packed source For a full side-by-side source of 3840 × 1080, splitting its columns supplies two 1920 × 1080 pictures. A converter assigns their eye roles, encodes the MV-HEVC view layers, and writes the matching track description. That changes both the spatial arrangement and the coding of the pictures. A half-SBS source instead supplies two 960 × 1080 regions whose intended view shape needs to be restored or described correctly. Expanding them into a 1920-column grid creates reconstructed samples; the new codec still starts from the detail retained in those narrower source regions. Spatial capture metadata should describe the source's real geometry. Writing an arbitrary baseline or field-of-view value does not establish that the original pictures were captured using those values. A conversion with known camera information can preserve or transform that description consistently with its image operations. The movie profile and the output route The linked Apple profiles describe particular interoperability targets. MV-HEVC as a codec representation is broader than one movie profile, and its use does not by itself specify SDR, HDR, or an immersive projection. Dolby Vision Profile 20 adds its own color and metadata requirements to supported forms of multiview delivery. For an Emby investigation, record the actual source layers and eye description, what the selected playback or conversion path delivered, and which views the app reconstructed. Then examine the final presentation's stereo and spatial interpretation. A remux preserving coded views and a conversion selecting the base eye can create different outcomes from the same source. articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.title: How Stereoscopic Video Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/stereoscopic-spatial/Vide.keywords: How Stereoscopic Video Works Stereoscopic video presents related views to the left and right eyes so their differences supply a binocular depth cue. Hold a finger in front of a distant object and alternate which eye is open. The finger changes its apparent position against the background because the eyes observe the scene from different locations. Stereoscopic video supplies a related pair of views and delivers each to the corresponding eye, using that difference as a depth cue. The useful unit is a stereo pair at one scene instant . Its left and right images are related, but not identical. A file needs a way to represent both; a decoder or reconstruction stage needs to recover them; a presentation path needs to keep their identity and timing intact. These jobs explain why an Emby library can contain several kinds of 3D files with very different playback requirements. A packed ordinary frame and a multiview-coded stream can represent similar stereo content through different arrangements. The position difference carries information When the camera pair is calibrated and its views are rectified, corresponding features lie along matching image rows. Their horizontal coordinate difference is called disparity . Rectification is the geometric preparation that makes those comparisons meaningful; the original two camera images need not already have that simple alignment. For an ideal pair of parallel pinhole cameras, let f be focal length in image pixels, B the camera separation, and Z the feature's distance. With the appropriate common coordinate convention: disparity d = fB/Z. Take f = 1000 pixels and B = 0.064 metres: Feature distance Z Horizontal disparity d 0.5 m 128 pixels 1 m 64 pixels 2 m 32 pixels 4 m 16 pixels The inverse relationship is the important result: a nearer feature changes its relative position more strongly between the two views. Both focal length and camera baseline also affect the disparity. Arbitrary images from unrelated viewpoints cannot be interpreted using these numbers without establishing their geometry. The markers use the stated ideal camera model and a 1920-pixel view width. The figure shows the two images as ordinary illustrations; it is not a stereoscopic display test. Capture disparity and displayed depth The recorded pixel difference does not by itself specify a physical distance in front of a television. Presentation also involves the size of the displayed images, their alignment, and the viewer's position. Imagine the separate idealized display geometry of two eyes 0.064 m apart and a screen 2 m away. A feature shown at the same screen coordinate in both images has zero display disparity and corresponds to the screen plane in this simple ray model. Now show the left-eye feature 0.02 m to the right of the central screen position and the right-eye feature 0.02 m to its left. The eyes' sight lines meet before reaching the screen. With display disparity δ defined as left position minus right position, their intersection distance is: apparent distance = eye separation × screen distance / (eye separation + δ). For δ = +0.04 m, the result is 0.064 × 2 / 0.104 ≈ 1.231 m . Reverse the offsets and δ becomes −0.04 m; the intersection is approximately 5.333 m , beyond the screen. These are geometric illustrations, not a prediction of every viewer's perception or a capture-calibration recipe. Swapping the two eye images changes the sign of their disparity and can reverse this depth cue. Perspective, occlusion, and other cues may still suggest the original scene, so the result can be inconsistent even though each individual image is sharp. The two views must describe the same instant If an object moves between frames, a left image from time t and a right image from time t+1 contain motion as well as the intended camera difference. Combining them can turn that motion into a false disparity. In the capture model above, a feature at 2 m has disparity 32 pixels. Suppose its right-eye image moves eight pixels right in the next frame. Pairing that later right image with the original left image gives an apparent disparity of 24 rather than 32. Interpreting it through the same model would suggest 64/24 ≈ 2.667 m instead of 2 m. The storage may use one packed frame, two view components, or another arrangement, but the pairing still needs the correct presentation time. Decode order can differ from presentation order, especially when coded pictures depend on references. A view's position in a packet list is not a substitute for its time and identity. Representations preserve the pair in different ways Each representation has its own article: Side-by-side puts the two views in neighboring frame regions. Top-and-bottom stacks them in frame regions. MVC uses H.264 multiview coding, including predictions between views. MV-HEVC uses HEVC layers for the views and can carry additional spatial presentation information. The spatially packed forms can be decoded as one conventional picture grid. Their reconstruction stage extracts the regions and applies the intended view geometry. Multiview coding instead needs the codec's view reconstruction and dependencies understood before the separate pictures are available. A view identifier describes a camera view; a layer identifier locates coded data in some representations. Neither should be casually equated with a left/right eye label. The association between the recovered view and the intended eye completes that description. Presentation keeps the eye channels separate A headset can route images to separate eye displays. Other systems use polarization or synchronized shutter glasses to separate the views from a shared screen. The mechanisms differ, while their task remains the same: each eye receives the picture intended for it at the appropriate instant. An active-shutter display can alternate eye presentation. That refresh sequence should not be confused with the number of distinct scene instants in the movie. A 24-pair-per-second source provides 24 new pictures per second for each eye, although it contains 48 eye images in total per second. HDMI frame packing is one output arrangement for transporting a pair to a display. The compressed movie codec and the selected display timing remain separate parts of the route. What a change of playback route needs to preserve For an Emby comparison, start with the selected representation and delivered output. If a server preserves a packed frame, both regions can survive as picture content, but the app still needs their layout and eye interpretation. If a conversion produces just one decoded view, the result has become a monoscopic version. If it retains two views while changing their dimensions, their intended shape and relative positioning need to survive that transformation. Emby's 3D identification documentation covers the library's format labels and naming conventions. Identification records the representation being used. The remaining questions concern reading its data, reconstructing the pair, and presenting it through the selected app and output path. A stereo pair samples the scene from two viewpoints. A large new head position would require information for a different viewpoint, including regions that may be hidden in both original images. Binocular depth in the supplied pair and the ability to freely navigate a fully represented scene are different capabilities. articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Gamut Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Gamut Mapping Gamut mapping adapts colors that fall outside the range the target color space or display can reproduce. A neon green can be correctly described in BT.2020 coordinates and still lie outside the colors a BT.709 destination can produce. Gamut mapping chooses a reproducible replacement while managing the relationships among color, brightness, and neighboring detail. Primary-coordinate plot, with luminance omitted. The line colors identify the gamuts rather than displaying their extreme primaries. First convert coordinates without discarding the desired color RGB values specify mixtures of particular primaries. A color conversion finds another set of coordinates for the same requested color. If the requested color lies outside the target triangle, some new coordinates can be negative: the target would need to subtract one of its primary lights to reproduce it exactly. Take the full BT.2020 green primary, with linear RGB 0, 1, 0 and D65 white. Converting to linear BT.709 coordinates using the published primaries gives approximately: Target component Converted value Red −0.588 Green 1.133 Blue −0.101 The coordinate transform is mathematically describing the requested color. The negative components and over-range green show why the target cannot directly reproduce it within zero-to-one component limits. A floating-point intermediate can retain those values until a mapping decision is made. See what independent clipping does Clipping each target component to zero through one changes the triplet to 0, 1, 0 , the BT.709 green primary. That is an achievable color, but it has another chromaticity from the original BT.2020 green. Its location has moved to the smaller triangle's corner. The same operation can merge distinctions. A BT.2020 green at linear level 0.9 converts to approximately −0.529, 1.020, −0.091. Clipping again gives 0, 1, 0. Source levels 0.9 and one have now reached the same target triplet. This example combines gamut reach with a component-output ceiling. It shows why merely transforming coordinates and clipping them can remove both color and light differences. The transformation identifies the problem; the mapping chooses how to resolve it. Compress color relationships deliberately A mapping can reduce chroma toward a neutral color, alter lightness, or use a combined color-volume strategy. In a perceptual hue/chroma representation, a method can try to keep the hue direction while reducing chroma until the target contains the color. Its chosen representation affects how that path behaves. Soft compression can start near the boundary, bringing extreme colors inward more gradually. It can preserve distinctions that hard clipping merged, but may also modify colors near the boundary that already fit. Broad desaturation moves every color inward, including ordinary colors that did not require much adjustment. Decision Image relationship affected Reduce chroma Saturation and separation among vivid colors Change lightness The object's brightness relative to its surroundings Clip components Component proportions and potentially hue/detail Preserve interior colors Limits how much of the image participates in compression A smaller target cannot retain every source color and every difference unchanged. The useful strategy preserves the relationships that matter to the produced scene, rather than just satisfying component bounds at the end. Combine the decision with brightness fitting In HDR-to-SDR conversion, the destination commonly has both a smaller light range and a smaller gamut. Brightness adaptation can change how a saturated color fits within the output color volume . A very bright colored light may need joint brightness/chroma treatment. A neutral-gray curve isolates brightness and cannot show that behavior. Inspect a red stage light, flame, or shop sign alongside gray surfaces when comparing an Emby rendition. Keep the source and output primaries, transfer, matrix, and range correctly interpreted so that a signaling mismatch is not mistaken for a deliberate gamut mapping. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough places the color decision within the complete conversion. The negative-component example explains why an otherwise correct coordinate transform still needs that decision before producing the target's final values. articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Overview: Color and luminance handling | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Overview: Color and luminance handling Color and luminance handling connect brightness adaptation with gamut limits, highlight shape and changing scene content. A brightness adjustment can affect the appearance of color as well as light. Peak detection and highlight roll-off influence the luminance treatment; gamut mapping addresses colors outside the destination's range. Scene adaptation connects those choices to content that changes over time, giving the curve an appropriate context. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Gamut mapping Gamut mapping adapts colors that fall outside the range the target color space or display can reproduce. Peak-luminance detection Peak-luminance detection estimates the brightness range present in decoded pictures so tone mapping can respond to the content. Highlight roll-off Highlight roll-off gradually reduces the separation between bright input levels so they fit below the output limit. Scene-adaptive tone mapping Scene-adaptive tone mapping changes its mapping over time according to the brightness characteristics of the current scene. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping Highlight roll-off gradually reduces the separation between bright input levels so they fit below the output limit. Follow two bright folds in a white shirt. Clipping can give both the same maximum output. A highlight roll-off instead lets the brighter fold receive a little more output, while progressively reducing the room given to further source increases. Qualitative sketch with illustrative axis spacing. It is not a measured display response or the plot of a specified implementation. The relevant property is slope . A smaller slope maps neighboring source levels closer together. A completely flat segment maps them to the same value. A shoulder can therefore retain ordering and some texture while compressing the light differences that made the texture strong in the source. Place the transition while there is room above it The transition is often called a knee. Starting earlier changes more ordinary levels but leaves a larger output interval for the highest values. Starting later preserves more of the lower range while squeezing highlights into less remaining room. For one numerical example, the smooth mapping in the curve overview takes inputs 4 and 8 to 0.9 and one. It retains a distinction, but only 0.1 of the output separates a four-unit source difference. Keeping different numbers is one part of retaining visibly useful texture. The whole response matters in an Emby comparison: inspect the folds alongside faces and nearby ordinary surfaces, so an improved highlight is judged together with any changed lower tones. Saturated colored highlights also need color fitting . Roll-off describes the brightness response's shoulder; it does not specify the complete color conversion. articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping Peak-luminance detection estimates the brightness range present in decoded pictures so tone mapping can respond to the content. A mapper needs a source-range estimate. Peak detection obtains one by examining the decoded picture, rather than using only a mastering record or a configured assumption. Define the statistic before taking its maximum Stored video values need their range, transfer, and color interpretation. Taking a raw integer maximum does not by itself give a light level. A detector analyzes a defined quantity, such as a light-domain component statistic or a perceptual representation, then supplies it in the units its mapper expects. For a neutral PQ-gray example, recovered light levels can be expressed in nits. Colored pictures need the statistic's component/luminance definition too: a maximum RGB component and weighted luminance are different quantities. Test a frame with a few extreme samples Suppose 10,000 neutral-gray samples consist of 9,990 at 100 nits and ten at 1,000 nits: Estimate Result in this constructed frame Absolute maximum 1,000 nits 99.9th percentile, nearest-rank method 100 nits Average 100.9 nits The maximum sees the ten intense samples. The percentile selects the 9,990th sorted sample, at 100. The average is (9,990 × 100 + 10 × 1,000)/10,000 = 100.9. These statistics describe the same frame differently. Using the absolute maximum can reserve mapping range for a tiny sparkle. Discounting a small upper tail can give the rest of the scene more room but may compress or clip those rare highlights more strongly. The selected policy establishes that tradeoff. A practical detector can use sampled pixels or a histogram rather than sorting every value. Bin precision, selected picture area, and the treatment of exceptional values then affect the estimate. The example demonstrates percentile reasoning, not a particular library's binning or default setting. Keep source information in its proper role Input to a mapping Role Mastering-display maximum Context about the grading reference MaxCLL A reported sequence-level content bound Dynamic scene statistics Prepared information for the current content interval Runtime detected peak The detector's estimate from analyzed pictures Destination peak The output range to fit These values can be combined or selected according to the implementation. Missing metadata can make picture analysis especially useful, while a detector still needs an appropriate interpretation of the source. Finally, the estimate should be managed across time. A single flash can otherwise change a global curve for an unchanged face. Scene-adaptive mapping develops that stability problem. For an Emby comparison, record the source information and actual processing path, then watch a dim scene with isolated lights as well as a broadly bright one. Those scenes exercise the estimator's real decision. See Also Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References FFmpeg 8.1: mastering-display and content-light metadata libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection parameters

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping Scene-adaptive tone mapping changes its mapping over time according to the brightness characteristics of the current scene. A tiny flash enters the window beside an otherwise stationary face. The source face stays at the same values, but the picture's detected peak rises. If a global mapper immediately changes its curve for that peak, the face can change brightness too. Scene adaptation needs to react to content without making that reaction distractingly visible. Conceptual responsibilities, not a description of one Emby implementation. Watch a simple smoothing model respond Let the estimated peak begin at 200 nits. In an illustrative model, update it as new estimate = 0.75 × previous estimate + 0.25 × new measurement . A single measured jump to 1,000 followed by a return to 200 produces: Frame event Measured value Smoothed estimate Initial stable scene 200 200 Flash 1,000 400 Next ordinary frame 200 350 Following ordinary frame 200 312.5 The model reduces the abrupt peak change, but its memory also leaves a smaller change after the flash. If those estimates control a global curve, they can still move the face's output over several frames. This arithmetic isolates temporal lag. Actual detectors can smooth other representations, use different time constants, and discount exceptional samples through percentiles . The model is not a product setting or a claim that a library uses these coefficients. A cut and a flash need different responses Now replace the flash with a real cut to a bright scene. A slowly smoothed estimate can keep applying the previous scene's assumptions for too long. Scene-change handling can reset or accelerate adaptation when the measured change warrants it. The tension is between stability inside a continuing scene and responsiveness to another scene. Brightness statistics are useful evidence but cannot always identify an edit unambiguously: camera motion, exposure changes, and flashes can also move them. Implementations choose detection and response policies for that ambiguity. Prepared dynamic metadata supplies another source of changing information. It can describe a shot from production; runtime analysis instead estimates from the pictures received. Both still need coherent timing and appropriate transitions. Keep temporal adaptation separate from spatial adaptation A curve can change over time while remaining the same across one entire frame. Local processing varies by region within a frame and is another choice. Calling a mapper adaptive does not specify which dimension varies. During an Emby test, let the picture move. Examine a stationary face when a bright object enters, then the first frames after a cut. Identify the processing location so the observed change can be attributed to the source, app, converter, or display. The temporal example explains why one attractive paused frame cannot establish stable adaptation. See Also Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection and scene-change handling FFmpeg 8.1: OpenCL tone-mapping kernels

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Overview: General-purpose curves | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Overview: General-purpose curves General-purpose tone-mapping curves offer different mathematical shapes for preserving contrast and compressing brightness. Hable, Reinhard, Mobius and the other curves below make different choices about the shape of the brightness transform. Linear, gamma and clipping behavior also provide useful points of comparison. Their diagrams show how source values are preserved, compressed or clipped across the output range. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Hable Hable is a filmic tone mapping curve that compresses bright highlights while also shaping shadows and midtones. Reinhard Reinhard is a tone mapping curve that compresses increasingly bright values into a limited output range. Mobius (Möbius) Mobius is a tone mapping curve that preserves lower signal values and smoothly compresses values above a chosen transition point. Spline Spline tone mapping joins polynomial curve segments around an adaptable pivot to fit the source brightness range to the output. Linear Linear tone mapping scales a source range into an output range, with the result depending on the space in which that scaling is performed. Gamma Gamma tone mapping uses a power function to redistribute brightness, with implementation-specific handling near black. Clip Clipping leaves in-range values alone and replaces every value above the output ceiling with that ceiling. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable Hable is a filmic tone mapping curve that compresses bright highlights while also shaping shadows and midtones. Hable's filmic curve shapes the darker and middle region as well as rolling bright values toward white. The lower-range panel makes that whole-image behavior visible: FFmpeg 8.1 scalar Hable mapping, source peak 8 and output white 1, neutral gray in relative linear light. Dashed gray is clipping. Hable changes more than the brightest pixels Input Output in this plotted example 0.18 About 0.0731 0.3 About 0.1183 1 About 0.3315 4 About 0.7769 8 1 Lower values do not pass through unchanged. The curve allocates its output range across the whole input, so an ordinary object can become darker while bright regions retain gradations. The shoulder supplies less additional output as the input rises, compressing highlight separation. John Hable developed the original response for Uncharted 2 and explains its filmic construction in the referenced articles. A toe shapes the transition out of black, the middle controls much of the apparent brightness, and the shoulder approaches the upper range gradually. Reproduce the stated implementation For FFmpeg's fixed coefficients, the unnormalized function is: H(x) = [x(0.15x + 0.05) + 0.004] / [x(0.15x + 0.50) + 0.06] − 0.02/0.30 With source peak P, the plotted mapping is T(x) = H(x) / H(P) . This normalization makes the assumed source peak land at output white. It also affects other points: at x = 1, P = 8 produces about 0.3315, while P = 4 produces about 0.4266. The peak assumption is thus part of the image transformation, not merely a label on its brightest point. If an Emby route uses this mapping, comparing the source peak and surrounding conversion explains why two runs can differ with the same curve name. The HDR-to-SDR example shows where brightness mapping sits between source interpretation and output encoding. Use the lower panel here to inspect the ordinary objects whose brightness that mapping changes. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius Mobius is a tone mapping curve that preserves lower signal values and smoothly compresses values above a chosen transition point. Mobius leaves a lower interval unchanged, then joins it to a curved upper section. The knee is where the mapping begins reducing the extra output assigned to brighter inputs. FFmpeg 8.1 scalar mapping, knee 0.3, source peak 8, output white 1, neutral gray in relative linear light. Dashed gray shows clipping. What changes when the knee moves? Input Knee 0.3 Knee 0.6 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.6 About 0.516 0.6 1 About 0.667 About 0.806 4 About 0.937 About 0.976 8 1 1 The plot shows the first column's mapping. Raising the knee keeps more inputs on the unchanged line, but leaves less output range above that point. For example, the knee-0.6 version places input 4 at about 0.976, leaving only 0.024 before the peak. The knee-0.3 version leaves about 0.063 there. These numbers make the tradeoff visible: more preservation in the lower region means stronger compression of the remaining highlight interval. The knee uses the input working units; 0.3 is not 30% of a source peak of eight. The join is constrained, not an arbitrary corner The upper part uses a rational Möbius relationship, a scaled ratio of two linear functions. Its coefficients are chosen so it meets three conditions: output equals input at the knee, the slope there is one, and the source peak maps to output white. Matching both value and slope makes the transition continuous without a sharp first-derivative corner. Above it, the curve gradually becomes shallower. The unchanged portion and the compressed portion therefore form one coherent response. In an HDR-to-SDR path , surrounding color and output operations also act on the picture. An Emby comparison can use this plot to separate the curve's lower-interval behavior from those other stages: inspect an ordinary object below the knee and bright texture above it under the same conversion conditions. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard References FFmpeg: tonemap filter FFmpeg 8.1: tonemap implementation libplacebo: tone mapping options

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard Reinhard is a tone mapping curve that compresses increasingly bright values into a limited output range. Start with the simple relationship T(x) = x/(1+x) for an already scaled linear-light input. At small x, the denominator is near one. As x grows, the denominator grows too, making further input increases contribute less output. Input x Basic output Output after normalization to peak 8 0.1 0.0909 0.1023 1 0.5000 0.5625 4 0.8000 0.9000 8 0.8889 1.0000 The basic function approaches one gradually. At a finite source peak of eight, its endpoint is eight-ninths. Multiplying by nine-eighths makes that known peak reach one and also raises the other mapped values. FFmpeg 8.1, public parameter 0.5, source peak 8, output white 1, relative linear light for neutral gray. Dashed gray shows clipping. Highlight compression and lower-tone brightness Inputs 4 and 8 are four units apart, but the normalized outputs differ by only 0.1. The values remain ordered and distinct; much less output contrast separates them. An input of one moves to 0.5625, showing that this mapping also changes ordinary levels. Uniform division by eight would put the same input of one at 0.125. The nonlinear relationship spends more of the output on the lower region and compresses the top more strongly. That is the actual compromise visible in the plot. Distinguish the curve from the complete photographic operator Reinhard and coauthors' original photographic tone-reproduction work also includes exposure scaling and a spatially varying method. A global function called Reinhard in a video filter represents one part of that family, with its own parameter and peak convention. FFmpeg's stated parameter corresponds to the normalized function in the table. In general its scalar form is x/(x+k) × (P+k)/P, with k derived from the public parameter. Changing k or P changes the mapping even before surrounding color operations. When comparing an Emby conversion, identify the actual curve implementation and normalization, then inspect both ordinary objects and highlight texture. The arithmetic here explains their relative placement rather than assuming the historical photographic method and a video option produce identical pictures. Clipping puts a hard ceiling on a value. Below the ceiling it keeps the value unchanged; above it, every input becomes the same maximum. FFmpeg 8.1 clip mapping with scale parameter 1. Both axes use relative linear light for neutral gray; output white is 1. The flat section is the important part. Three parts of a bright cloud with inputs of 2, 4, and 8 all become 1. The cloud's positions remain, but the brightness differences that made its texture visible disappear. Input Output 0.2 0.2 1 1 2 1 8 1 A highlight roll-off bends toward the limit gradually, leaving output space for some of those differences. It starts changing the values before they reach the ceiling. Clipping preserves the in-range part exactly and spends none of that range on brighter values. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Gamma Gamma tone mapping uses a power function to redistribute brightness, with implementation-specific handling near black. A power mapping can give lower values more output room than uniform scaling. In the plotted FFmpeg example, most of the curve uses T(x) = (x/8)^(1/1.8) , fitting a source peak of eight into output white one. FFmpeg 8.1 scalar CPU function, relative linear light for neutral gray. Its very dark region uses the implementation's linear extension. Input Mapped output Uniform division by eight 1 About 0.315 0.125 4 About 0.680 0.500 8 1 1 The endpoint fits in both cases. The power function assigns more output to the lower and middle inputs, changing the contrast distribution. The straight segment near black A bare power with exponent below one becomes very steep near zero. FFmpeg replaces the part below input 0.05 with a straight extension that meets the power value there: T(x) = x × (0.05/8)^(1/1.8) / 0.05 for x up to 0.05. Input 0.01 therefore produces about 0.01193, and 0.05 produces about 0.05963. The plotted function includes that treatment; using the power expression down to zero would describe a different shadow response. Resolve the parameter's meaning before reproducing a result libplacebo's mapper also uses the name gamma, but preserves an unchanged lower interval and chooses a power above its knee. Its knee parameter has a different role from FFmpeg's gamma parameter. Neither is simply the display gamma . This function remaps a brightness range. Display gamma participates in a signal-to-light response. During an Emby comparison, locating that operation within the playback path keeps the mapping arithmetic separate from output interpretation. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Linear Linear tone mapping scales a source range into an output range, with the result depending on the space in which that scaling is performed. Divide each linear-light input by the peak ratio, and the source range fits proportionally. For a ratio of eight, T(x) = x/8 : Input Output 0.8 0.1 1 0.125 4 0.5 8 1 The output preserves the ratios of these light values. It also darkens every lower value by the same factor, which can spend too little brightness on ordinary objects when the source has only a small very bright highlight. Peak ratio 8:1. Green scales linear light; blue follows libplacebo's PQ-space stretch with output white 203 nits. Both axes show relative linear light; gain is one and black is zero. Why the blue proportional mapping bends PQ coordinates are nonlinear with respect to light. The blue operation proportionally changes those coordinates, then the figure converts its result back to linear light. The operation is linear in its selected representation, while its plotted light relationship is curved. This distinction occurs in software: FFmpeg's CPU linear mapper operates on linear-light samples; libplacebo distinguishes its PQ-space linear option from linearlight. The selected space is part of the method, not a minor naming detail. A useful Emby comparison therefore starts with the implementation, source range, target, and working space. For the green example, input 4 and input 8 stay distinct at 0.5 and one. Clipping would merge both at one. That retained separation is what proportional fitting buys, and the lower-value arithmetic shows what it costs. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Spline Spline tone mapping joins polynomial curve segments around an adaptable pivot to fit the source brightness range to the output. A spline lets the mapper shape two parts of a brightness relationship around a selected pivot. In the plotted libplacebo implementation, a quadratic lower segment and a cubic upper segment meet with the same value and slope. libplacebo 7.360.1 defaults, zero black, 1,000-nit input peak, 100-nit output peak, and no scene-average value. The function operates in PQ coordinates; the axes show light levels. What is fixed and what can move? The source and target endpoints set the range to fit. The pivot sets an input/output pair inside that range. A contrast control adjusts the slope at the pivot, while the polynomial coefficients make both segments meet their remaining constraints. Changing the pivot's output moves that part of the scene to another brightness. Changing its input moves where the two pieces meet. Changing the slope alters nearby contrast. These are different controls over the shape, even when its endpoints remain unchanged. Input light Output in the displayed example 10 nits About 5.98 nits 100 nits About 36.16 nits 500 nits About 76.78 nits 1,000 nits 100 nits The function distributes much of the available output below the highest input. A 500-nit difference from 500 to 1,000 nits becomes about 23.22 nits. Those values belong to the stated default selection, not to every spline. With scene average absent, a defined fallback selection still produces a curve, as in the figure. Scene adaptation provides and stabilizes changing information; the spline provides a form that responds to it. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 The BT.2390 EETF uses a smooth highlight roll-off to adapt an HDR signal to a display with a smaller luminance range. The BT.2390 electrical–electrical transfer function, or EETF, adapts a signal to another display range. Its highlight section joins a lower segment to a smooth roll-off in PQ coordinates. libplacebo 7.360.1, zero source and target black. Offset 0.5 follows the report's knee convention; offset 1.0 is this library's default. The calculation uses PQ, while the axes show light levels. Compare points rather than only endpoints Input light Knee offset 0.5 Knee offset 1.0 10 nits About 10.00 nits About 9.84 nits 100 nits About 69.45 nits About 53.73 nits 500 nits About 98.95 nits About 94.37 nits 1,000 nits 100 nits 100 nits Both peaks fit. The earlier transition for offset 1.0 changes more of the range, including the 100-nit point. A comparison of peak white would miss that difference. How the roll-off is joined The mapper expresses the destination ceiling relative to the source range in PQ. The knee convention chooses where a lower unchanged segment ends. A Hermite-polynomial segment connects that point to the destination ceiling with controlled endpoint behavior. That gives the upper region a gradual reduction in slope. Neighboring bright inputs remain distinct, but their output spacing becomes smaller. The curve's joining constraints avoid an abrupt break in its value relationship. The full adaptation also accounts for black-level differences. Setting black to zero on both sides in this figure isolates the highlight behavior. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A BT.2446 Method A defines a conversion between HDR and SDR that includes a shaped brightness mapping and associated color processing. BT.2446 Method A is an HDR/SDR conversion method. A renderer option called BT.2446A can use its brightness function within a larger conversion pipeline; the complete report also defines associated color processing. Power, logarithmic, and piecewise coordinates The plotted library function normalizes source light to the source range and applies a power representation. It then compresses that coordinate through a logarithmic relationship whose scale depends on the peak. A piecewise function treats three coordinate regions differently: a scaled lower segment, a quadratic middle segment, and a linear upper segment. Finally, the calculation converts back through the destination relationship to obtain output light. The changing slope is what distributes contrast across the range. libplacebo 7.360.1 brightness function, zero black at both ends. The plot isolates this scalar stage of Method A. Source light Output light in this example 10 nits About 3.13 nits 100 nits About 22.66 nits 500 nits About 73.15 nits 1,000 nits 100 nits The peak fits, while the hundred-nit region uses less than a quarter of the target peak. The function has chosen a particular contrast distribution; it is not simply source light divided by ten. For example, 500 nits would become 50 under that proportional scaling, rather than 73.15 here. Work one 100-nit point through those coordinates For the stated 1,000-nit source and 100-nit target, define h = 1 + 32 × (1,000/10,000)^(1/2.4), about 13.260, and s = 1 + 32 × (100/10,000)^(1/2.4), about 5.697. These peak-dependent factors set the two logarithmic ranges. Normalize the source point and take the power: (100/1,000)^(1/2.4) ≈ 0.3831. Form q = ln[1 + (h−1) × 0.3831] / ln(h), about 0.6732. This q is in the lower piecewise region, q ≤ 0.7399. Apply 1.077q, giving about 0.7250. Return through the target logarithmic relationship: V = (s^(1.077q) − 1)/(s − 1), about 0.5387. The zero-black target response gives 100 × V^2.4 ≈ 22.66 nits . The upper regions use a quadratic and then another linear expression instead of the lower 1.077q rule. The branch is selected in the intermediate coordinate, so its breakpoints are not direct input-nit thresholds. Put the function back into the complete conversion For a neutral gray, brightness can be followed with a scalar. For colored objects, changing light also changes color appearance, and the target can have another gamut or volume. Method A's color operations address that relationship; a renderer using only the named brightness stage combines it with its own surrounding color path. Output transfer encoding is another required job. The mapped light value is a processing result, not automatically a final YCbCr code. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough explains that handoff. In an Emby comparison, locate whether the complete method or a scalar stage is being used, then retain the same source and target assumptions. That identifies why two results with the same Method A name can use different color processing around the brightness curve. The middle point can change the whole curve Use a constructed zero-black example with source peak 1,000 nits and target peak 100. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-40 in libplacebo libplacebo's ST 2094-40 mapper can use a metadata-defined Bézier curve and adapts it to the output display range. The ST 2094-40 mapper in libplacebo can use a content-supplied knee and Bézier curve anchors. It then adapts that prepared relationship to the actual output range. When those anchors are absent, the implementation constructs a fallback curve. How an anchor changes the curved section A knee specifies the transition into the upper mapping, with input and output coordinates. The section above it is normalized between that transition and its endpoint. Bézier controls shape how the output travels between those ends. For a simple mathematical illustration, a quadratic section with endpoint controls zero and one and middle control a is: B(t) = 2a × t(1−t) + t² At t = 0.5, a = 0.25 gives output 0.375, while a = 0.75 gives 0.625. Both sections still start at zero and end at one. Moving a control changes the middle shape rather than changing those endpoints. The controls shape the curve; they are not ordinary measured image samples that the curve must pass through. Actual metadata defines its knee, anchor set, and target under the standard's conventions. The mapper accounts for a destination whose peak differs from that prepared target. It can also use source brightness information when a content-provided curve is unavailable. The fallback curve without HDR10+ anchors libplacebo 7.360.1 fallback, defaults, 1,000-nit source, 100-nit target, zero black, no scene average or curve-anchor metadata. The displayed fallback maps 100 nits to approximately 48.42 nits and 500 to approximately 98.68 . This shows one generated relationship under those inputs. A real metadata-defined relationship can select another shape. Which inputs reach the mapper? articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.title: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.keywords: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls A tone-mapping curve determines how input brightness levels are distributed across the available output range. Choose an input on the horizontal axis, trace upward to a curve, then trace across to the vertical axis. The point answers: what output brightness does this mapping assign to that input? Calculated examples in relative linear light. Clipping is min(x,1), straight scaling is x/8, and the smooth curve is (9/8) × x/(1+x). These are illustrative relationships, not Emby presets. Curve slope and brightness separation On the clipping curve, inputs 2 and 4 both map to 1. Their separation has gone. On the scaling curve, they become 0.25 and 0.5. On the smooth curve, they become 0.75 and 0.9. Inputs 2 and 4 Output difference Clipping 0 Scaling 0.25 Smooth example 0.15 The difference is part of the available output contrast. A flatter segment gives less separation to neighboring inputs; a steep segment gives more. Smooth compression can retain distinct highlight values while reducing their spacing substantially. Now check a lower input, x = 1. Scaling produces 0.125; the smooth curve produces 0.5625. A curve that makes the peak fit can consequently place an ordinary object very differently. The highest endpoint alone does not describe the picture. Look across the shape The lower part controls separation near black. The middle affects a large amount of scene content. A shoulder gradually reduces the extra output assigned to very bright inputs. A knee marks a transition in behavior; its numerical meaning depends on the curve's working representation. The axes are therefore essential. A function that is straight in PQ coordinates can bend when plotted against linear light. Physical-nit axes, normalized-light axes, and signal-coordinate axes show different relationships. State the source peak, target, and parameters before comparing two plots. Use curve names to find a specific relationship The individual pages show Hable , Reinhard , Mobius , and other curves. Each page identifies the plotted implementation and its assumptions. The curve is one part of a conversion. Input interpretation, color handling, adaptation over time, and output encoding affect the final picture too. In an Emby comparison, hold those conditions steady while examining how ordinary objects and bright texture move along the selected relationship. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: Overview: GPU execution | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: Overview: GPU execution GPU tone mapping uses a supported compute or rendering interface to transform picture data within a media pipeline. OpenCL, CUDA and Vulkan provide different routes to GPU processing. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: CUDA Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: CUDA Tone Mapping CUDA tone mapping executes a tone-mapping implementation on an NVIDIA GPU using CUDA parallel computation. NVIDIA video processing can involve three separate engines or execution roles. Follow a possible decoded-picture route: Stage Work NVDEC Reconstruct compressed video into decoded surfaces CUDA program Perform programmable picture calculations, such as tone mapping NVENC Encode the prepared pictures into another video stream The decoder and encoder are hardware video engines. CUDA supplies programmable parallel computation. A tone mapper's kernel defines the brightness and color calculations; those decisions do not come from choosing the NVIDIA brand for decoding or encoding. Keep a decoded surface accessible to the next stage NVIDIA's NVDEC API supports decoding to video memory and making the resulting surfaces available for CUDA processing. The application can use those decoded samples as the input to its kernel, then hand the processed result onward through a supported route. This is a memory and synchronization relationship. The filter must understand the surface's format and layout, wait until decoding has produced it, and ensure its output is ready for the next consumer. Shared access avoids a needless trip through system memory when the complete path supports it. Now insert a software-only operation between the stages. The application may need to download a representation to system memory, process it there, then upload the result again. The tone kernel can still be fast while those transfers add cost. CPU mapping gives raw-frame storage arithmetic that explains the scale of such traffic. What video-engine and compute activity indicate An Emby session can use an accelerated encoder while another stage handles tone mapping. Video-encode activity then describes NVENC's job, not the location of every preceding calculation. Different monitoring views can aggregate or separate video and compute activity. To understand the session, identify its decoder, filter, frame transfers, and encoder. The hardware overview supplies the product's platform context; the actual application implementation chooses which supported operations use CUDA. The kernel's chosen curve, input peak, color interpretation, and output target determine the prepared picture. Comparing these inputs alongside the memory route explains both the image result and the execution cost without treating one activity percentage as a description of the entire conversion.
