articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: OpenCL Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: OpenCL Tone Mapping OpenCL tone mapping runs a software-defined tone-mapping operation through the OpenCL parallel-computing interface. An OpenCL filter is selected, but processing fails before a picture is delivered. Locating that failure requires three distinct pieces: the application's filter, the runtime's selected device, and the frame representation passed between stages. Piece Responsibility Application/filter Supplies the mapping program and accepted formats OpenCL platform/runtime Discovers devices and compiles or loads programs Device/context/queue Executes the work and provides accessible frame resources OpenCL can target supported CPUs or GPUs. The interface name alone does not identify which device was selected or which curve the application implements. Device contexts, kernels, and frame access The application chooses a platform and device, creates the relevant context, and obtains a command queue for submitted work. It supplies a kernel program: a function executed across many work items so regions of a picture can be processed in parallel. Decoded pictures must be made accessible in the filter's expected hardware-frame arrangement. The filter then supplies its color descriptions, range and mapping parameters, launches the program, and makes the result available to the next stage after the required synchronization. FFmpeg 8.1's OpenCL tone mapper provides a concrete implementation. It checks supported source transfer and component information, prepares the corresponding color/transfer operations, and uses the selected mapping function in its OpenCL program. Its accepted hardware formats constrain that filter's path rather than defining all OpenCL devices' possible formats. Resolve two different failure cases No usable OpenCL device appears. Check the runtime and device access in the application's environment. A hardware video decoder can work while a separate compute runtime is absent. A container also needs the applicable runtime and device resources, not only a device visible to the host. A device is selected but the frame format cannot reach the filter. Inspect the preceding decoder's frame format, the required mapping or upload, and any supported sharing between APIs. Successful device discovery does not supply the missing representation or interoperability operation. In Emby logs, those stage failures differ from an inability to decode the source codec. Hardware-acceleration documentation describes the surrounding platform options; the bundled implementation and session specify the actual filter route. Once the path works, frame transfers and synchronization remain part of its cost. Keeping accessible frames across decoding, filtering, and encoding can avoid unnecessary copies. A faster kernel alone may leave the surrounding traffic or another stage as the limiting operation. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: Vulkan Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: Vulkan Tone Mapping Vulkan tone mapping uses GPU shader processing through Vulkan to adapt a picture to the output brightness range. A renderer can use Vulkan to submit shader work on a GPU. The shader supplies the picture calculations; Vulkan provides the device, resources, command submission, and synchronization used to execute them. GPU images and shader synchronization A decoded picture becomes accessible as the required GPU image or buffer. A rendering library can assemble operations such as source interpretation, color conversion, tone mapping, scaling, and output preparation into shader processing. The application submits the work and manages when resources can be read or written. A following presentation or encoding operation must wait for the prepared result. These relationships matter when frames are shared with another API or transferred from a decoder using a different memory arrangement. libplacebo is a rendering-library example with a Vulkan backend. Its image-processing controls sit above Vulkan's lower-level interface. The source/target descriptions, selected curve, and adaptation inputs determine the brightness relationship that its programs perform. Use the result in either of two contexts Consumer of the processed picture Purpose Display presentation Prepare the image for an output surface and screen Video encoder Produce another compressed rendition from processed frames FFmpeg's libplacebo filter demonstrates the second use. GPU rendering calculations can be part of a conversion pipeline even when their immediate result is not being drawn to a window. Vulkan Video decoding is another capability. Running a tone-mapping shader does not imply that the source was decoded using Vulkan Video; an application can support another decoder and the needed upload or resource sharing. The representation and synchronization at that boundary decide whether the pieces can connect efficiently. Locate a Vulkan message in the Emby path A renderer's Vulkan-related message describes that renderer's execution route. A separate server transcode can use another filter and API. Start with the playback-path diagram , then identify the application and stage producing the message. Two routes using Vulkan can choose different image-processing programs, target descriptions, or library versions. Holding those inputs steady is what makes an image comparison meaningful; following the resource handoffs is what makes an execution comparison meaningful. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/in.title: Overview: Tone-mapping execution | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/in.keywords: Overview: Tone-mapping execution Tone-mapping execution locates brightness adaptation within the client or server pipeline and its available processing resources. The same adaptation goal can be carried out at different points in playback. A client can render for its own display, while a server conversion can produce a representation for the receiving app. CPU and GPU topics then explain the execution resources and data movement at the chosen point in that path. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Where tone mapping happens in an Emby playback session Tone mapping can occur during server transcoding or later in the player and display path, depending on the playback session. CPU tone mapping CPU tone mapping performs the picture conversion on the general-purpose processor rather than running the mapping on a GPU. GPU execution GPU tone mapping uses a supported compute or rendering interface to transform picture data within a media pipeline. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: CPU Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: CPU Tone Mapping CPU tone mapping performs the picture conversion on the general-purpose processor rather than running the mapping on a GPU. A CPU tone mapper processes reconstructed pictures in system memory. Its work follows the picture grid and processing representation, even if the source's compressed file is small. Count the picture work before the compressed bytes Grid and rate Picture positions per second 1920 × 1080 at 24 fps 49,766,400 3840 × 2160 at 24 fps 199,065,600 3840 × 2160 at 60 fps 497,664,000 These are input sizes, not measured CPU throughput. Each position can require component conversion, transfer-function calculations, curve evaluation, and output preparation. The chosen implementation determines how those operations are combined or accelerated with vector instructions and threads. Float RGB storage and memory traffic FFmpeg's CPU tonemap filter operates on floating-point RGB in linear light. A suitable surrounding path interprets the incoming HDR signal, supplies that working representation, runs the mapping, and prepares the final output format. For a 3840 × 2160 picture with three 32-bit float components, the logical sample storage is: 3840 × 2160 × 3 × 4 = 99,532,800 bytes , about 99.53 MB per picture before padding. At 24 fps, one full read and one full write of that representation account for approximately 4.78 GB/s of logical traffic . Additional passes can require more; cache reuse and implementation choices change the physical traffic. This is a storage calculation, not a benchmark or a required network bitrate. The example explains why an operation's cost includes memory access as well as the scalar curve formula. A decoded working picture can be much larger than the compressed data used to deliver it. Keep the other CPU jobs visible An Emby transcode can also decode, rescale, render subtitles, convert audio, and encode. A high total CPU reading covers those jobs together. To locate a bottleneck, inspect the actual stages and whether their completed-picture rate keeps up with the source. A hardware encoder at the end does not move all earlier filtering to the GPU. Conversely, software decoding can feed GPU presentation; the Windows FAQ describes that combination. A transfer between system and device memory may be needed at that boundary. When frames already occupy system memory and the required software path is supported, CPU mapping avoids introducing an additional device-transfer stage solely for the curve. When a supported GPU path can keep frames accessible across several operations, its residency changes the traffic picture. The playback-path article locates those choices within the session. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session Tone mapping can occur during server transcoding or later in the player and display path, depending on the playback session. Two sessions can show the same HDR library file yet perform brightness adaptation in different places. Follow the delivered video before attributing the displayed result to a server setting. Conceptual routes. A particular app's supported signal and processing path determines which route it can use. Session A: the server prepares SDR The server decodes the HDR picture, interprets its light and color representation, and performs HDR-to-SDR conversion . It encodes the resulting picture with matching SDR descriptions. The app receives that SDR rendition and presents it through an SDR output path. The mapping has occurred before delivery. The library source remains HDR, while the delivered video describes the processed SDR image. Source metadata and final stream metadata consequently answer different questions. Session B: unchanged HDR reaches a local renderer With Direct Play , the server supplies the original file. Direct Stream can change packaging or other tracks while retaining the coded video. A supported app then decodes and interprets the delivered picture. If its presentation adapts HDR to the selected output, the pixel change occurs after delivery. The Windows app FAQ describes GPU-shader tone mapping during presentation, including a path with software decoding. Decoding location and mapping location can therefore differ. Session C: the display fits an HDR signal An HDR signal reaches an HDR display whose useful range is smaller than the source request. The display can perform HDR-to-HDR adaptation . Its HDR indicator identifies the signal mode, while its internal mapping determines the reproduced light. Other device or operating-system stages can participate in the output chain. The relevant evidence is the actual signal and processing at each boundary rather than the library's HDR badge alone. Record a comparison by boundary Boundary Useful observation File to server Exact source release, HDR format and color fields Server to app Video copied or re-encoded; delivered HDR/SDR representation App to output Decoder, renderer, selected presentation mode Output to screen Received signal mode and display processing Video transcoding can be required for reasons other than tone mapping, so it should be inspected for the actual picture processing. Likewise, copied video locates any later pixel adaptation downstream. This boundary record makes two Emby sessions comparable: it identifies which stage could have changed the image and which conversion inputs belonged to that stage. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: Overview: Fundamentals | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: Overview: Fundamentals Tone-mapping fundamentals explain why source and display ranges differ and what HDR adaptation aims to preserve. Begin with the source's light range and the output's useful range. An HDR-to-SDR conversion has a different target from adapting one HDR representation to another HDR display. These pages establish the purpose of the transformation before individual curves and processing choices are compared. <!-- learn-index:children:start --> Why tone mapping is needed Tone mapping adapts a picture's brightness range to what the output display can reproduce. How HDR-to-SDR tone mapping works HDR-to-SDR tone mapping compresses the picture's brightness range within a conversion that also handles color and signal encoding. HDR-to-HDR tone mapping HDR-to-HDR tone mapping adapts HDR pictures to a different HDR brightness range while keeping the output in HDR. <!-- learn-index:children:end -->

articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping HDR-to-HDR tone mapping adapts HDR pictures to a different HDR brightness range while keeping the output in HDR. A source contains 2,000-nit highlights, while the intended HDR output has a usable peak of 600 nits. The source and destination are both HDR, but their available light ranges differ. HDR-to-HDR tone mapping fits that image to the smaller range while keeping an HDR output representation. Establish the actual source and destination For PQ material, the transfer function supplies absolute reference-light requests. A source's mastering maximum describes the grading display, while content bounds and picture analysis describe what the produced sequence uses. These are different inputs to selecting the range that needs fitting. The destination is also a rendering target. Its useful peak depends on the relevant area and duration, and its black floor and color volume constrain the reproduced picture. A supported HDR signal format does not define all those physical limits. The worked example below chooses zero black, a source peak of 2,000, and a target peak of 600. It is a constructed brightness relationship that makes the decisions visible. Preserve a lower interval and fit the highlights Let L be source light in nits. Leave values through 200 unchanged. Above 200, define d = L − 200 and use: T(L) = 200 + d / (1 + 7d/3,600) At the transition, d is zero and the output is 200. The initial upper slope is one, matching the lower unchanged segment. As d grows, the denominator grows and the response flattens. At L = 2,000, d = 1,800, the denominator is 4.5 and output is 200 + 400 = 600 nits . Original neutral-gray example for the stated ranges. It is not a measured Emby preset or the specified BT.2390 function. Source light Smooth-knee output Uniform scaling by 0.3 100 nits 100 nits 30 nits 200 nits 200 nits 60 nits 500 nits About 389.47 nits 150 nits 1,000 nits About 513.04 nits 300 nits 2,000 nits 600 nits 600 nits All source values in the declared range fit. Compared with uniform scaling, the constructed function devotes more light to the lower region. Compared with clipping, it retains differences above the destination ceiling instead of merging them. Those differences are compressed: a 1,000-nit separation between the last two source rows becomes about 86.96 nits. The lower interval is preserved because it was a deliberate constraint; another mapper can choose a different transition and redistribute ordinary tones too. Prepare an HDR output with the new light meaning Interpreting the input, applying the mapping, and encoding the result are separate operations. In the example, a 2,000-nit PQ neutral has a normalized input signal of about 0.827. After mapping to 600 nits, the corresponding PQ output signal is about 0.696. Both numbers use PQ, but they describe different light requests. Keeping the original sample and only changing a peak metadata field would not perform the calculated brightness adaptation. A renderer can make the change in its presentation pipeline; a newly encoded HDR rendition needs values and signaling consistent with the prepared output. Colored pictures add another operation. Scaling brightness can preserve linear component ratios within one color system, while the destination volume may require further saturation or hue handling. A small bright saturated light can exceed a colored-output limit even when neutral white fits. Gamut mapping explains that fitting problem. Black-level adaptation has its own effect near the bottom. The zero-black diagram intentionally isolates highlight fitting. A screen with a higher useful black floor needs a response that accounts for lower-level separation, as discussed in the BT.2390 report. Locate the adaptation in the playback session With an Emby Direct Play session, the original coded video can reach the app, while the app or display still maps it to the selected output. A server transcode can instead prepare another rendition before delivery. The playback-path diagram separates those locations. Two HDR screens can therefore produce different pictures from the same delivered file. To assess the actual fitting, inspect ordinary objects, dark separation, and bright texture in the same moving scene. The curve's source range, target, and temporal inputs explain the differences more precisely than the common HDR signal badge. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works HDR-to-SDR tone mapping compresses the picture's brightness range within a conversion that also handles color and signal encoding. Imagine a scene with a person beside a window: the face has ordinary indoor brightness, the outdoor sky is much brighter, and a reflection on glass is brighter still. An HDR picture can keep those regions distinct across a large range of light. An SDR conversion has less brightness range available, yet still needs to show a convincing face, a bright window, and some structure in the reflection. Tone mapping decides how to redistribute that brightness. The complete HDR-to-SDR conversion also has to interpret the original signal, fit its colors into the output color system, and produce correctly encoded SDR samples. Each part affects the result. A well-chosen highlight curve cannot repair incorrectly interpreted input values. For Emby playback, this conversion can happen in a server transcode or during presentation by a playback renderer. Both paths need to solve the same underlying problem, even though their implementations and output targets can differ. These are the jobs in the conversion. An implementation can combine operations or perform parts in different working spaces. Decoding gives samples; their meaning still matters A video decoder reconstructs numerical picture samples from the compressed stream. The converter then needs to know what those numbers represent. Many video sources store luma and color-difference components rather than directly storing red, green, and blue. Their matrix coefficients describe the relationship to color components. Signal range describes how stored code values represent nominal black, white, and color differences. Color primaries establish the meaning of the RGB color coordinates. Transfer characteristics relate nonlinear signal values to light. Those properties work together. If limited-range values are interpreted as full-range values, nominal black and white are assigned the wrong positions. The picture can have raised blacks or altered contrast before tone mapping starts. If the wrong matrix is used, reconstructing the color components can introduce a different error. Changing the tone curve would then adjust an already misinterpreted picture. Bit depth has a separate role. Ten bits provide more possible sample values than eight bits. They do not identify which color system or transfer function those values use. A ten-bit source can be SDR. For a PQ source, the signal has an absolute reference-display light meaning. A normalized PQ value of 0.5 corresponds to approximately 92.2 nits for neutral gray. It does not mean half of a television's peak brightness or half of PQ's 10,000-nit reference range. The nonlinear transfer function is what establishes that relationship. Before applying a curve defined in linear light, the converter must obtain linear-light values. For a neutral PQ gray, applying the PQ electro-optical transfer function gives its reference luminance. In a common linear-RGB processing path, the converter first restores nonlinear RGB from the luma/chroma samples using the appropriate range and matrix. It then applies the PQ transfer interpretation to those components to obtain linear RGB. Encoded luma and linear-light luminance are different quantities, so applying the PQ equation to luma alone would not perform this full color reconstruction. A method designed for a perceptual working space performs a different set of transformations. The conversion of HLG also needs to account for its system relationship to the intended display. Assigning PQ's absolute-light interpretation to HLG samples would skip that relationship. The important question at this stage is which representation the particular mapping expects. For example, FFmpeg's CPU tone-mapping filter expects linear-light input. Decide which brightness range to fit There are two ends to the decision: the useful brightness range in the source and the intended brightness behavior of the destination. A source can provide several kinds of information: Mastering-display metadata describes the display used during mastering, including its luminance capabilities. That is information about the mastering environment. Content-light metadata can summarize properties such as the maximum content light level. That is a description of the content under the metadata's measurement definition. Measured picture statistics come from inspecting the actual decoded pictures. A renderer can use them to adapt its mapping to the material being shown. A mastering display capable of 1,000 nits does not require every picture to contain a 1,000-nit highlight. Similarly, a whole-program maximum describes the brightest relevant content, not the brightness of each scene. These distinctions matter because reserving output range for a peak that is absent from the current scene can change how much brightness is available to its ordinary objects. The mapper may use a fixed source assumption, trustworthy metadata, peak detection , or a combination. If its assumed peak is too low, brighter source values can reach a part of the mapping that was never intended to preserve their distinctions. If the assumed peak is unnecessarily high, more compression may be applied than the scene needs. The destination also needs a defined target. A conventional SDR reference-display example can use 100 nits for white and a specified display transfer function. An actual television may show SDR white more brightly, particularly in a bright room. The largest brightness number on its product sheet does not, by itself, establish the intended SDR rendering. Reference white, black level, and viewing conditions influence the relationship between the converted picture and its appearance. The converter can prepare a conventional SDR signal for later display adjustment, or a renderer can adapt directly to a particular output. Those are different targets for the mapping. For the worked example below, choose an 800-nit source peak and a 100-nit SDR output peak . Use 100 nits as one unit on both sides solely to make the arithmetic easy: input values run from zero to eight, and output values from zero to one. This normalization does not assign a 100-nit reference white to all HDR material. Work through what the brightness curve does Three simple mappings show the tradeoff clearly. Let x be the input light level in the relative units just defined. Straight scaling uses x / 8. It fits the entire range, with the same scaling factor everywhere. An 800-nit highlight becomes 100 nits, but a 100-nit object becomes only 12.5 nits. If most of the scene sits well below its brightest highlight, the picture can become unnecessarily dark. Clipping uses the smaller of x and one. Inputs up to 100 nits retain their light levels in this example; every higher input becomes 100 nits. A 200-nit cloud and an 800-nit reflection then have the same output value. Their original brightness separation has disappeared. A smooth nonlinear mapping can devote more output range to ordinary brightness levels and compress the highlights more strongly. For an easily calculated example, use: T(x) = (9/8) × x / (1 + x) This function maps zero to zero and eight to one. For an input of one, its result is (9/8) × 1/2 = 0.5625. With the chosen output reference, that means 56.25 nits. Illustrative neutral-gray mappings. For this example, multiply either axis by 100 to express its light level in nits. The green curve is T(x) above; these are calculated relationships, not measured Emby presets. Source light level Straight scaling Clipping Smooth mapping T(x) 20 nits 2.5 nits 20 nits 18.75 nits 80 nits 10 nits 80 nits 50 nits 100 nits 12.5 nits 100 nits 56.25 nits 200 nits 25 nits 100 nits 75 nits 400 nits 50 nits 100 nits 90 nits 800 nits 100 nits 100 nits 100 nits All three make the 800-nit peak fit. They produce very different pictures everywhere else. The smooth example keeps substantially more brightness in the 80-nit region than straight scaling does, while retaining some separation among the highlights that clipping merges. That separation is still compressed. Under the smooth curve, a 600-nit region becomes about 96.43 nits, while an 800-nit region becomes 100. A source difference of 200 nits has become about 3.57 nits. The converter has preserved an ordering and a distinction, but has greatly reduced their spacing. Curve slope explains the contrast redistribution The slope of the curve describes how a small change in input light affects the output. A flat segment gives no separation to neighboring inputs. A shallow segment gives little separation; a steeper segment gives more. The green curve gradually becomes shallower toward its top. This is a highlight roll-off : extra source brightness has progressively less effect on output brightness. Fine texture in a very bright region can consequently become difficult to see even while its values remain mathematically distinct. A practical mapper has to choose how much separation to retain in shadows, middle brightness levels, and highlights. Preserving more of one region's brightness differences spends part of the finite output range. A curve's midpoint and any transition into highlight compression matter as much as its endpoint. The example's 100-nit object becomes 56.25 nits. That makes the effect on ordinary objects explicit: mapping is not confined to the few pixels above the SDR ceiling. Other curves can preserve a selected lower interval more closely or place the transition differently. The curve overview links to individual shapes and their behavior. Keep brightness changes from distorting the colors A neutral-gray example has equal RGB components, so a scalar curve is easy to interpret. Color introduces another choice: which quantity drives that curve, and how is the resulting brightness change applied to the components? Consider a linear RGB color with components 2, 1, 0.5 in one fixed set of primaries. Applying the example curve independently to each component gives 0.75, 0.5625, 0.375 . The original red-to-green ratio was 2; it is now about 1.33. The component proportions have changed, so the operation changes the color's chromaticity as well as its brightness. An alternative is to derive a single brightness-related quantity, calculate a scale factor, and apply that same factor to all three components. If the maximum component 2 drives the example curve, it maps to 0.75. The factor is 0.75 / 2 = 0.375 , producing 0.75, 0.375, 0.1875 . The original component ratio of 4:2:1 is retained. This calculation illustrates why a tone mapper needs a color strategy. A luminance-driven method can use a different driving quantity from a maximum-component method. Preserving linear RGB proportions retains chromaticity in that fixed color system, while perceived saturation can still change with brightness and viewing conditions. There is also the question of which colors the destination can represent. HDR material commonly uses a wider color gamut than a BT.709 SDR destination. Conversion between their primaries changes the RGB coordinates needed to describe a color. For a color outside the destination gamut, those coordinates can include a negative component or a component beyond the output range. Scaling the brightness alone does not necessarily bring that color into gamut. Independently clipping offending components changes their proportions and can cause hue shifts or merge distinct colors. Gamut mapping instead provides a strategy for fitting the color—for example, reducing its distance from a neutral color while trying to preserve hue. Brightness and saturation limits interact through the destination's color volume . A strongly saturated color cannot necessarily reach the same luminance as neutral white. A conversion may therefore adjust both brightness and chroma to obtain a useful result. The different methods in ITU-R BT.2446 show why HDR-to-SDR conversion includes color processing alongside tone mapping. A movie also needs stable decisions over time A fixed mapping produces the same output for the same input throughout the program. That consistency can be useful, but a single curve chosen for the brightest scene may use the available range less effectively in a much dimmer scene. Scene-adaptive tone mapping changes parameters based on the content. It can make better use of the output range, but the parameter changes themselves become visible if they are too abrupt. Imagine a stationary face beside a window. A tiny flash in the window raises the measured peak for one picture. If that peak immediately changes the mapping for the whole picture, the face can darken for that instant, although its source values did not change. When the flash ends, it brightens again. The viewer sees pumping caused by the adaptation. A method can moderate that response by considering the distribution of bright samples, smoothing parameter changes over time, or distinguishing a scene cut from a brief highlight. Those choices balance responsiveness against stability. Looking at one still frame will not reveal whether the conversion maintains a consistent appearance through movement, flashes, and cuts. Turn the mapped light back into an SDR signal After brightness and color processing, the converter has to produce samples whose encoding matches the intended SDR interpretation. Linear-light values cannot simply be written into a nonlinear video signal without the appropriate transfer operation. Continue the neutral-gray example. An original 100-nit PQ gray has a normalized PQ signal of about 0.508 . Interpreting PQ recovers 100 nits, which is x = 1 in the chosen working units. Applying T(x) produces y = 0.5625, meaning 56.25 nits in the chosen SDR display model. For an ideal SDR reference display with zero black, 100-nit white, and the BT.1886 exponent of 2.4, the nonlinear signal needed to obtain that light is: signal = 0.5625^(1/2.4) ≈ 0.787 The sequence is therefore: Representation Value for this neutral gray Normalized input PQ signal About 0.508 Interpreted HDR light 100 nits Linear mapping input x 1 Linear mapping output T(x) 0.5625 Intended output light 56.25 nits Normalized SDR signal for the stated ideal display About 0.787 The input and output signal numbers differ because they have different transfer meanings. Writing 0.5625 directly as that nonlinear SDR signal would produce only about 25.14 nits under the same display model. The tone-mapping calculation could be correct while the displayed brightness was wrong because the output encoding step was skipped. The real output process also accounts for black level and the selected conversion method. BT.2446 describes several methods; their processing spaces and transfer operations differ. The calculation above isolates one display-referred example so that the distinction between light values and signal values is visible. For a conventional video output, the converter prepares the required luma/chroma representation, numerical range, bit depth, and matching color signaling. Retagging original HDR samples as SDR performs none of the brightness or color calculations. Correct labels describe the converted values; they do not create those values. Precision matters during this work. Intermediate calculations can retain more precision than the final video format. When values are reduced to the output bit depth, rounding can make smooth gradients form visible steps. Dithering can make those steps less conspicuous by distributing rounding error. It helps represent the converted gradient; it cannot restore highlight differences that the mapping has already merged. Relate the conversion to the playback path During an Emby video transcode , the server decodes the HDR source, processes the pictures for the selected output, and encodes the resulting stream. Tone mapping is a picture-processing operation within that path. It changes the delivered rendition while the library file remains available as the source. During local presentation, a playback renderer can perform adaptation as it prepares pictures for the screen. The Windows app documentation describes tone mapping at this stage. Direct Play therefore identifies the server's delivery behavior; it does not, on its own, describe every color or brightness operation performed by the app, operating system, and display. To investigate an unexpected result, first establish where conversion happens and what output is intended. Then use the appearance to narrow the stage worth examining: Raised black or incorrect contrast throughout the picture: check input and output range interpretation, transfer characteristics, and display mode before adjusting highlight compression. Ordinary objects look sensible but bright texture disappears: examine the assumed source peak and highlight mapping. Check several frames to distinguish strong compression from time-dependent adaptation. Brightness looks plausible but vivid colors shift: examine primary conversion, gamut handling, and chroma processing. A stationary object brightens and darkens when another area flashes: examine how the mapping adapts over time. These observations connect a visible change to the operations that can cause it. Comparing the same scene along known playback paths—using both moving pictures and representative stills—makes that investigation much more informative than judging the brightest highlight alone. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: Why Tone Mapping Is Needed | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: Why Tone Mapping Is Needed Tone mapping adapts a picture's brightness range to what the output display can reproduce. An HDR source asks for a 1,000-nit reflection beside a 100-nit surface. A destination with a 100-nit output peak has room for the surface, but cannot reproduce the reflection at its requested absolute light level. Tone mapping chooses how both parts fit into the available picture. There are two simple solutions with visibly different costs: Choice in this example Surface Reflection Result Clip at 100 nits 100 100 Brightness separation is lost Divide all light by ten 10 100 The whole lower range is darkened A nonlinear mapping can give ordinary levels more room while compressing highlights more strongly. It redistributes contrast according to the source and destination instead of making only an all-or-nothing cutoff decision. Why this is an image operation Changing resolution alters the spatial sample grid. Changing bitrate alters how the encoder describes the picture. Neither operation, on its own, changes the light interpretation enough to solve this range mismatch. A transfer-function label describes the meaning of the samples. Relabeling HDR as SDR would ask the player to apply another meaning to the existing values. Correct conversion first interprets the source, adapts its brightness and colors, then prepares suitable output values and signaling. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough follows those steps. Curves show the brightness relationship; gamut and color-volume handling also matter for a bright colored object. Place the mapping in the playback path Emby Server can process pictures during a video transcode. A renderer can also adapt them locally; the Windows app documentation describes presentation-stage tone mapping. Direct Play identifies delivery from the server, while later app and display processing still determines the light produced. Mapping can also be needed between two HDR ranges, not only from HDR to SDR. A source peak above an HDR display's usable output presents the same fitting problem, even when the destination remains HDR. The useful comparison is the relationship among objects in the same scene: ordinary surfaces, dark detail, and bright texture. A good peak fit is one part of that relationship. The mapping's available range and its chosen distribution explain the rest.
